<meta>This page contains a formal dedicatory letter written by Giovanni Francesco Pico della Mirandola (the nephew of the famous philosopher) to Ludovico Sforza, the Duke of Milan. It serves as an introduction to the collected works listed on the previous page, establishing the scholarly and moral significance of his uncle’s life and writings.</meta>

<margin>Catalog 187</margin>

## Giovanni Francesco Pico della Mirandola to Ludovico Maria Sforza Visconti, the Anglian <note>original: "Anglo"; a title used by the Visconti and Sforza families to claim descent from the mythological hero Anglus, or referring to their lordship of Angera.</note>, Duke of Milan. Greetings.

Most illustrious prince, among those who have recorded the lives of famous men in writing for the reading of posterity, some have done so to ensure that the names of those to whom they were bound by blood or indebted for their education would not fade away through the consumption of age, but would be completely rescued from the injury of oblivion. This was the kind of devotion that Pliny the Younger showed to his uncle Pliny, and Porphyry to his teacher Plotinus. Others, however, achieved this same goal even more auspiciously: namely, they consulted not so much the eternal memory of the dead as the improvement of the lives of the survivors. Therefore, we find that Jerome recorded the life of Hilarion, Athanasius that of Anthony, Severus that of Martin, and Paulinus that of Ambrose—their tireless studies, their most disciplined characters, and their most noble works—on the written page. From these records, the glory of God spread throughout the world, and men are still stirred to live well and blessedly by both their teaching and their example.

Enticed by these examples, I thought I would be doing something worthwhile if I followed the life of Giovanni Pico with my pen. I did this partly to fulfill a debt of service to him as my uncle and teacher, by whose spiritual benefits I have been enriched and overwhelmed, and partly to propose a man to be admired by both our own and future ages. By his example, mortals can be instructed in frugality and warned of impending death, but also abundantly enriched by learning. For among the widely lettered (not to mention the ancients), he obtained the first place beyond all risk of dispute. This is perhaps an enviable claim, but it is undoubtedly true. To those who examined him "inside and out" <note>original: "intus & in cute"; a classical idiom from the poet Persius meaning to know someone's true character thoroughly.</note>, as the saying goes, it will not seem absurd that he mastered both human and divine languages and philosophy, and drank deeply of all the disciplines used by mortals—indeed, he even rescued some from darkness and invented others—even before he had completed his eleventh three-year period <note>original: "undena triteride"; a poetic way of saying 33 years. Giovanni Pico died young, at the age of 31.</note>.

The fullest proof of this will be found in those commentaries, never sufficiently celebrated for their merits, which are now coming out in public: the *Heptaplus* <note>A mystical explanation of the seven days of Creation.</note>, the *Apology* <note>Pico's defense against charges of heresy.</note>, the treatise *On Being and the One*, and several other small works. All of these are so brilliant by their own nature and recommended by the judgments of so many wise men, that anyone who either condemns them, approves them poorly, or fails to extol them with the highest praise, immediately delivers a sentence against himself, revealing either his ignorance of literature or a malicious mind. Many may envy him because he is admired by all, imitated by very few, and can be criticized by none.

His remaining writings will be published in the following order: most importantly, the *Confutations of the Astrological Pestilence* <note>His massive work attacking the pseudo-science of judicial astrology.</note>. These were composed with much labor and have been expected and demanded with many sighs by men of well-ordered minds. They have been reduced by us into a single volume from a manuscript that was both messy and torn into many parts, and they will soon be released so that, as quickly as possible, they may illuminate dim eyes infected by the destructive vapor of superstitions with their life-giving splendor. 

If, while resting from the business of ruling the kingdom, you occasionally taste these books, you will beyond all controversy become certain of this: that the dogmas of the astrologers are the purest nonsense <note>original: "meracissimas nugas"</note> and like the dreams of madmen, and that their deceptions are exposed by these monuments of writing. Once these have been read and understood, the professors of that vanity—who, imitating the frogs of our land, have croaked for a long time—will fall silent in the manner of the Macedonians <note>A classical reference to sudden silence or defeat.</note>, unless they fall into open insanity. I remember testifying to this to you in part while we were discussing this matter.

In the meantime, you will receive these things with a willing mind, for I judged they should be dedicated to no one more than you. I wish for you to recognize that my loyalty and devotion toward you—which you saw and tested while I earned your wages—has not only not been consigned to oblivion, but perseveres and increases daily. I also thought I would be doing something not ungrateful to you, since such is the dignity of these books that the greatest kings have always considered it an honor and a glory to have them inscribed to them. 

It remains for me, with the love I have for you, to exhort you to perform the duties of two-fold justice and to invite you to constantly remember (which is always the duty of a most prudent prince) that it is a burden rather than an honor that you reign. Thus, seeing the obstacles that beset both a man and a prince on all sides, you may overcome them with the most moderate passions and earn eternal happiness for yourself.

Farewell, most distinguished Prince.
From Mirandola, on the Kalends of March, 1496.

<a><note>This "a" marks the first signature of the printed gathering in the original book.</note></a>

# THE LIFE OF GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA, A MAN MOST ACCOMPLISHED IN EVERY GENRE OF DISCIPLINE, PUBLISHED BY GIANFRANCESCO, SON OF THE ILLUSTRIOUS PRINCE GALEOTTO PICO

**A**s I begin to write the life of Giovanni Pico, my paternal uncle, I consider it essential to first state to my readers—lest they suspect that I, as his brother’s son or his pupil, might say anything out of favor or in the manner of a flatterer—that nothing here is granted to friendship, nothing to family, and no false praise is offered in return for the benefits I received, which were indeed very great. For my narrative is as far removed from adulation as the necessity of flattering was absent. I have taken great care that those reading should not think I have either lied or been excessive in my praises. Had I committed to writing everything I had conceived of him, there might perhaps have been a danger that his own exalted virtues, or those who champion them, could accuse me of being stingy. This can be seen from this very argument: many of the most learned men of our age—and indeed from the very best among them—have, through their most diligent writings, not only provided the richest testimony to the things we are about to say, but also, both while he enjoyed this light <note>i.e., while he was alive</note> and after he exchanged it for a better one <note>i.e., after his death</note>, they surpassed me in their public praises of his character and learning. I have ordered some of these praises to be appended at the end of this book, following his own commentary, so that a firmer trust might be granted by witnesses who are not of his own kin.

<margin>
Paternal lineage
</margin>
Setting aside his paternal lineage—although it is recorded that it took its origins from Constantine Caesar through his great-grandson Pico, from whom the surname of the entire family is said to have been derived—we shall take our beginning from the time of his birth. This is because he perhaps brought no less honor to the family than he received, and because I thought it best to reveal the personal gifts of his mind and the rest of the sequence of his life and death, which I have gathered either with my own ears or eyes, or received from the most reliable witnesses. I have decided that the pedigree and the famous deeds of his ancestors should be set aside. He was born in the year 1463 from the birth of the Virgin <note>original: "Anno a partu uirginis tertio & sexagesimo supra milesimum & quadringētesimū"</note>, while the pious Pius II <note>Pope Pius II, reigned 1458–1464</note> was the Supreme Pontiff presiding over the Church, and Frederick III <note>Holy Roman Emperor, reigned 1452–1493</note> was moderating the reins of the Roman Empire.

<margin>
Mother Julia
Gianfrancesco the father
Galeotto
Antonio Maria, brothers
Sisters
Alberto Pio
</margin>
His mother Julia, from the noble Boiardo family, bore him as her last child to his father, Gianfrancesco. For she had already given birth to Galeotto the eldest (from whom I was born), Antonio Maria, and two sisters. One of these sisters, whose husband was Leonello, gave birth to Alberto Pio, one of the princes of Carpi; she is now the consort of Prince Rodolfo Gonzaga. The other sister, after the death of Pino Ordelaffi, the prince of Forlì to whom she had long ago been married, entered into a second marriage with the Count of Monteagone.

<margin>
The prodigy
</margin>
A prodigy of no small significance appeared before his birth. For a circular flame was seen to stand over the chamber of the mother while she was in labor, and soon it vanished—perhaps suggesting to us that he who would be brought forth among mortals at that same hour would be most similar in the perfection of his intellect to a circular figure <note>In Renaissance philosophy, the circle was considered the most perfect and complete geometric shape, often symbolizing the divine or the intellect.</note>...

<meta>This page continues the biography of Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, moving from the author's introductory justifications to the early life, physical description, and initial education of the subject. It follows the narrative of Pico's predestined greatness.</meta>

...the whole globe, the excellence of his name was to be celebrated everywhere. His mind, like fire, would always seek heavenly things; his fiery eloquence, in harmony with his burning mind, would one day celebrate our God—who is a consuming fire <note>original: "ignis comburens," a biblical reference to Deuteronomy 4:24 and Hebrews 12:29</note>—with all its strength, though it would soon be hidden from the sight of men, just as fire vanishes. Indeed, we read that at the births of the most learned and holy men, unusual signs have sometimes preceded or followed them, as if by divine will setting their infant cradles apart from the common crowd and 
<margin>Ambrose</margin>
marking them as born for the greatest deeds. Thus (to omit others), a swarm of bees hovered over the mouth of the great <term>Ambrose<gloss>Saint Ambrose (c. 340–397), Bishop of Milan and a Doctor of the Church</gloss></term>; they entered his mouth and then flew out, soaring high and hiding themselves among the 
<margin>Paulinus</margin>
clouds, escaping the sight of his father and the others present. <term>Paulinus<gloss>Paulinus of Nola, a biographer of Ambrose</gloss></term>, a writer who placed great value on this omen, argued that it indicated the honeycombs of his future writings: 
<margin>Form and physical appearance, etc.</margin>
which would announce heavenly gifts and raise the minds of men from the earth to heaven. Giovanni was of distinguished and noble form: tall and stately of stature, with soft skin, and a generally beautiful face. His complexion was fair, interspersed with a becoming blush; his eyes were blue-grey <note>original: "caesiis," often used for light-colored or "owl-like" eyes</note> and alert, his hair blond and natural, and his teeth were white and even. 
<margin>Progress in the study of humanities at a tender age</margin>
Under his mother’s direction, he was brought to masters and disciplines; he cultivated the study of humanities with such a burning spirit that, in a short time, he was—not without merit—placed among the foremost poets and orators of that age. He was truly very fast in learning, 
<margin>A swift wit</margin>
endowed with such a ready wit that he could recite poems once heard from a reader—whether in the direct or reverse order—to the great admiration of everyone. He possessed a most tenacious memory, which is often the opposite for others; for it is frequently the case by nature that those with quick wits do not have strong memories, while those who learn with labor become more tenacious retainers of what they have grasped. When he was fourteen 
<margin>He studied Canon Law as a boy.</margin>
years old, at his mother’s command (for she vehemently desired him to be initiated into sacred orders), he moved to <term>Bologna<gloss>The University of Bologna was the preeminent center for legal studies in the Middle Ages and Renaissance</gloss></term> to learn <term>Canon Law<gloss>original: "ius pontificium," the legal system of the Catholic Church</gloss></term>. After he had tasted this for two years, seeing that it relied on mere traditions, he turned elsewhere. This was not, however, without some good fruit; for even as a boy (and a very tender one at that), he compiled a certain <term>Epitome<gloss>A summary or condensed version of a larger work</gloss></term> or <term>Breviary<gloss>A concise summary of key legal or religious texts</gloss></term> from the letters of the Supreme Pontiffs—which are called <term>Decretals<gloss>Papal decrees that formed the basis of church law</gloss></term>. In this work, he concluded the opinions of all those sanctions and councils as briefly as possible; it was no small work, even for accomplished professors. But as an eager explorer of the secrets of nature, leaving these well-trodden paths, he dedicated himself entirely to the intellectual speculation of philosophy—both human and divine. For the sake of attaining this knowledge, he traveled through the literary gymnasiums <note>The "gymnasia" here refer to universities or centers of higher learning</note> not only of Italy but also of the <term>Gauls<gloss>France</gloss></term>, seeking out the famous teachers of that time in the manner of <term>Plato<gloss>The Greek philosopher</gloss></term> and <term>Apollonius<gloss>Apollonius of Tyana, a Neo-Pythagorean philosopher known for his extensive travels in search of wisdom</gloss></term>. He devoted such tireless effort to those studies that he was both a master theologian and a master philosopher while still "beardless" <note>meaning he was still a very young man</note>, and was regarded as such. He had already spent seven years among those studies when, desirous of human praise and glory—for he was not yet warmed by divine love, as will become clear—he moved to Rome, and there he showed...

<meta>This page follows the description of Pico's youth and physical appearance, moving into his arrival in Rome and his ambitious attempt to host a grand philosophical debate, which triggered significant ecclesiastical opposition.</meta>

<sig>a ii</sig>

...was desiring to test how much envy awaited him from his first bloom <note>original: "a summis floribus," likely referring to the height of his youth and early success</note> in the future. 
<margin>Nine hundred conclusions proposed at Rome to be disputed</margin>
He proposed nine hundred questions on dialectics, mathematics, and natural and divine matters. These were drawn not only from the stores of the Latins and excerpted from the archives of the Greeks, but even unearthed from the mysteries of the Hebrews, and tracked down from the secrets of the <term>Chaldeans<gloss>Often used in this period to refer to ancient Mesopotamian or Babylonian wisdom and astrology</gloss></term> and the Arabs. Likewise, he included many things concerning the ancient and obscure philosophy of Pythagoras, <term>Trismegistus<gloss>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure associated with the Hermetic writings on philosophy and magic</gloss></term>, and Orpheus. He also included much concerning the <term>Cabala<gloss>Kabbalah; a Jewish mystical and speculative tradition that Pico believed could prove the divinity of Christ</gloss></term>—that is, the secret reception of Hebrew doctrines—
<margin>Origen, Hilary</margin>
of which <term>Origen<gloss>An early Christian scholar and theologian (c. 185–254)</gloss></term> and <term>Hilary<gloss>Saint Hilary of Poitiers (c. 310–367), a prominent Latin theologian</gloss></term> among our own writers especially make mention. He wove into those questions many things regarding <term>natural magic<gloss>The study of the occult powers of herbs, stones, and stars, which Pico argued was a legitimate science distinct from "demonic" magic</gloss></term>, which he taught was separated by no small distance from that which is impious and wicked. This he proved most elegantly by the testimony of many. Nor were there lacking seventy-two new physical and metaphysical dogmas, his own inventions and meditations, which were adapted to elucidate any questions of philosophy. To these he annexed a new system of philosophizing through numbers. He posted all of these together in public places so they might be more easily circulated, promising that he would pay the expenses of those who had traveled to Rome from remote lands for the sake of the debate. 

But because of the rivalry of detractors (which always seeks the heights, like fire), he could never manage to have a day for the debate appointed. For this reason, he remained in Rome for a year, during which time those "vituperators" <note>original: "uitiligatores," a term for carping or malicious critics</note> did not dare to attack him openly or in a free examination. Instead, they tried to insult him through tricks and "burrows" <note>original: "cuniculis," a metaphor for undermining someone via secret tunnels or mines</note> and to undermine him with hidden weapons, driven by a pestilential envy. (Indeed, very many people have judged that they were primarily moved to such malice for this reason: that many who had long applied themselves to literary business—perhaps out of ambition or greed—thought it would be a mark against them if that young man, with the ancestral wealth he had gathered and his vast learning, like a fertile field luxuriating in the first city of the world, did not fear to test his learning and intellect regarding natural and divine matters, and many things which for several centuries had not been accessible to our people). 

When they realized they could do nothing against his learning with honest means, they brought into the open the torments of calumny. They cried out that thirteen of the nine hundred questions were suspect regarding the true faith. To these critics, some joined themselves who—perhaps with more piety than learning, and under the pretext of religious zeal—attacked those questions as being unusual to their ears. Nevertheless, not a few celebrated doctors of theology had previously approved those same questions as pious and pure, and had signed their names to them. 
<margin>Bonfrancesco of Reggio, Bishop</margin>
Among that group was numbered <term>Bonfrancesco of Reggio<gloss>Bonfrancesco Arlotti (d. 1508), Bishop of Reggio Emilia and a diplomat</gloss></term>, the Bishop of Reggio: a man of all-encompassing learning, keenest judgment, and famous for the gravity of his character, who at that time was acting as legate in Rome to the Supreme Pontiff on behalf of the Duke of Ferrara. However, those "babblers" <note>original: "Blaterones"</note> attempted nothing against him, since they happened to know his reputation could not be shaken by them...

<summary>This page describes Pico della Mirandola's 1486 arrival in Rome to debate his 900 Theses, his incorporation of diverse sources like the Kabbalah and Natural Magic, and the subsequent theological controversy where 13 of his points were labeled suspect by envious critics.</summary>

--- Page 8 ---
<meta>Continuing the narrative of Pico della Mirandola's 900 Conclusions and the ensuing theological controversy. This page discusses his defensive "Apology" and the shifting papal responses from Innocent VIII to Alexander VI.</meta>

<margin>The Apology</margin>
...they should have respected him, since he had submitted whatever he treated to the correction of Mother Church and the Pope. But he, not enduring these damages to his reputation, published the *Apology*. It is certainly a varied and elegant work, filled with the knowledge of many things worth knowing, and composed in only twenty nights of labor. Through this edition, it was made clearer than day that it was not so much that the conclusions could not receive Catholic interpretations, but rather that those who had previously barked at them were to be convicted of insolence and ignorance. He committed the book itself, and whatever he might write in the future, to the judgment of Mother Church and her most holy leader, in the manner of a most Christian man. For he was most convinced that this ought to be done, either explicitly or implicitly, as if he were putting forward that saying of <term>Augustine<gloss>Saint Augustine of Hippo (354–430 AD), one of the most influential theologians in Western Christianity</gloss></term>: **"I can err, but I cannot be a heretic,"** <note>original Latin: "Errare poſſum hereticus eſſe nõ poſſum"</note> since the one is a human trait, while the other belongs to a perverse and obstinate 
<margin>Pope Innocent VIII</margin>
will. But when Pope Innocent VIII learned, through the publication of the *Apology*, that those conclusions—which had previously been plagued by slanders—had been interpreted in a Catholic sense and cleared of any mark of crime; and yet, because some to whom the examination of the conclusions had been entrusted reported that snares could be set for the faithful if some of those questions (which lay there raw and unexplained in the manner of things to be debated) wandered about everywhere, he forbade the reading of the little book in which they were contained. 
<margin>Alexander VI</margin>
All of these things are clearly seen through the decree (which they call a <term>brief<gloss>A formal letter or diplomatic document issued by the Pope</gloss></term>) of Pope Alexander VI, under whom we now live. This decree we have decided to hand over to the printers to be inscribed along with the *Apology* itself. Indeed, at the very end <note>original: "calce," literally "at the heel"</note> of the *Apology*, he had already done with his own arguments what the Pope later did with his authority. 
<margin>Note</margin>
For he had beseeched friends and enemies, the learned and the unlearned, to read the *Apology* but to leave the little book of unexplained conclusions unread, since many things were contained in it which he had undertaken to be disputed not everywhere in the streets, but in a secret meeting among a few learned men. Having planned a scholastic exercise in the manner of the <term>academies<gloss>Refers to the ancient Platonic Academy or the university traditions of philosophical debate</gloss></term>, he professed that he had proposed many doctrines of the ancient 
<margin>Alexander, Averroes</margin>
philosophers—specifically of <term>Alexander<gloss>Alexander of Aphrodisias (c. 200 AD), a celebrated commentator on Aristotle</gloss></term> and <term>Averroes<gloss>Ibn Rushd (1126–1198), an influential Al-Andalusian philosopher known for his commentaries on Aristotle</gloss></term>, and many others—which he had always asserted, both publicly and privately, to deviate no less from the paths of true and right philosophy than from the paths of faith. And speaking in this way about that little book of nine hundred conclusions, he concluded his apologetic work: "Therefore, let those who hate me not read them because they are mine; let those who love me not read them because from those things which are mine, they might think many things which are not ours." <note>Pico is distinguishing between his own personal beliefs and the opinions of other philosophers he was merely presenting for the sake of debate.</note> 
<margin>The goodness of God</margin>
Furthermore, he judged (as he reported to me) that by the immense goodness of God, which draws good even from evil, it had come to pass that the slander falsely inflicted by the malevolent corrected true errors. To him, wandering in the darkness (so that he might behold how much he had strayed from the path of truth), it was as if a most brilliant...

<summary>Pico defends his controversial 900 theses by writing the "Apology" in just twenty days, arguing that he is a faithful son of the Church despite the suspicions of his critics. He clarifies that many of the proposed points were for academic debate rather than personal belief, a position eventually recognized by Pope Alexander VI.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the biography of Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, shifting from his intellectual defenses to his personal spiritual transformation, his rejection of secular poetry, and the composition of his theological masterpiece, the Heptaplus.</meta>

<sig>a iii</sig>
<meta>catchword: læ.</meta>

the first light of dawn began to shine: for previously he had been both eager for glory and kindled by a vain love, and had been moved by feminine enticements. Indeed, very many women—on account of his beauty, the grace of his body and face, to which were added his ample learning, riches, and nobility of birth—burned with love for him. Not shrinking from their devotion, he had for a little while set aside the way of life and drifted into delights. But, awakened by that rivalry <note>The Latin 'simultate' can refer to a specific conflict or a general awakening from his previous state.</note>, he checked his soul which was dissolving in luxury

<margin>The conversion of his soul to God</margin>
and turned it toward Christ. And he exchanged feminine flatteries for the joys of the heavenly homeland; and neglecting the breeze of petty glory which he had once sought, he began to seek with his whole mind the glory of God and the utility of the Church, and so to compose his character that thereafter he could be approved even by the judgment of an enemy. And when he learned that a glorious reputation concerning him was immediately flying through both neighboring and remote shores, many of the philosophers—who were considered the most learned—flocked to him as if to a **"marketplace of the good arts"** (as <term>Cicero<gloss>Marcus Tullius Cicero (106–43 BC), the Roman statesman and orator whose works were the foundation of Renaissance humanist education.</gloss></term> says), either for the sake of

<margin>Cicero</margin>
engaging in literary contests, or those in whom there was a more upright mental purpose: for the sake of hearing and holding the health-giving dogmas of right living. These were expected all the more because they flowed from a man who was most learned and equally most noble, who had once followed the devious paths of voluptuous softness. For those things seem to have the most weight in instilling a discipline of character into the minds of listeners which are both good by their own nature and are set forth by a teacher who has turned to the paths of justice from the distorted and crooked path of lusts. He had toyed with loves in <term>elegiac verse<gloss>A classical poetic meter traditionally associated with themes of love and lamentation.</gloss></term>, which, having been composed in five

<margin>The burning of the love poems</margin>
books, he delivered to the fires for the sake of religion. He likewise composed many things in <term>Italian verses<gloss>original Latin: "rhythmis hetru scis" - literally "Etruscan rhythms," a common humanist way to refer to the Tuscan/Italian vernacular.</gloss></term>, which a similar fire consumed for a similar reason. Then, having embraced Sacred Scripture with the most burning zeal—immediately in the temple of God, as if they were the first fruits of his labor—being then in his twenty-eighth

<margin>The study of sacred letters</margin>
year, he offered the *<term>Heptaplus<gloss>Pico's 1489 work, 'Heptaplus: de Septiformi Sex Dierum Geneseos Enarratione,' which provides a sevenfold mystical interpretation of the creation story in Genesis.</gloss></term>* concerning the works of the six days of <term>Genesis<gloss>The first book of the Bible, detailing the creation of the world.</gloss></term> and the day of rest. Indeed, it is a work both perfect in genius and elaborated with industry, most full of both the sublime dogmas of the philosophers and the deepest mysteries of our Christian theology. It is connected by a sevenfold various narration, and with a sevenfold number of chapters joined to each sevenfold exposition, it most greatly fits the name of the book. 
      However, because of the things unearthed from the bosom of nature and the difficult explanations of divine questions, and because of the most hidden meanings of the Prophet <note>Refers to Moses, traditionally considered the author of the Pentateuch/Genesis.</note> and the elegance of the speech, it does not offer itself everywhere to those who are unrefined in philosophy and eloquence. Rather, the use of that precious and rare furniture is prepared for few; which he himself noticing, made a not ungraceful mention of this matter at the end of the same preface.

<margin>What he announced about sacred letters; the epistles of Paul.</margin>
As soon as he first tasted the sacred letters, he exulted joyfully, having found not only true wisdom but also true eloquence. And to omit many of the praises of the New Testament brought forward by him, [he preferred] the epistles of <term>Paul<gloss>Saint Paul the Apostle, whose New Testament letters Pico studied with great intensity later in his life.</gloss></term> [above those] of orators...

<meta>This page continues the biography of Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, moving from his moral conversion to his intellectual defense of the Bible’s eloquence and his major philosophical projects, specifically the reconciliation of Plato and Aristotle.</meta>

...he used to say that eloquence excelled in the writings of all. He specifically cited the late-night labors of <term>Cicero<gloss>Marcus Tullius Cicero (106–43 BC), the Roman orator whom the Renaissance saw as the gold standard for Latin style.</gloss></term> himself and of <term>Demosthenes<gloss>The greatest of the ancient Greek orators (384–322 BC).</gloss></term>, the primary craftsman of speaking (as he called him). He did not cite them because they were **"singed with curling irons"** <note>A metaphor for overly artificial or superficial rhetorical style.</note>, or covered with **"scraped-up dyes"** and crowded with **"tight curls,"** but rather because they possessed a **true, solid, fragrant, and flavorful eloquence**, supported by genuine thoughts and true art. They were, to put it briefly, not intentionally stuffed with the **"wealth of the Egyptians."** <note>A common theological metaphor ("spoils of the Egyptians") referring to the use of pagan philosophy and secular learning to serve Christian truth.</note> Furthermore, 

<margin>The eloquence of the Old Law</margin>
he preached that the words of the Old Law were full of the most consummate knowledge and wisdom. Even if others, such as <margin>Augustine</margin> **Augustine** in his book *On Christian Doctrine*, have shown this clearly—and <margin>Septimius</margin> **Septimius Tertullian**, <margin>Eusebius</margin> **Eusebius Pamphili**, and <margin>Cassiodorus</margin> **Cassiodorus** affirm it—arguing that the grammarians, rhetoricians, orators, and all the ancient philosophers drank the streams of their own eloquence and teaching from the fountains of the Divine Scriptures, he himself pursued this with countless other reasons. It is worth the effort to see a part of these in the introductions to his very famous <term>Heptaplus<gloss>Pico’s 1489 work, a sevenfold commentary on the first chapters of Genesis explaining the creation of the world.</gloss></term> and in the preface to the second exposition itself. Amidst so many ongoing studies of the Divine Law, in the second year after the publication of the *Heptaplus*, he finished 

<margin>The little book On Being and the One</margin>
a small work titled *On Being and the One*, divided into ten chapters. It is brief in body but great in its power, filled everywhere with the deepest doctrines of the philosophers and theological insights. In it, he shows that **"Being"** is not superior to **"the One,"** but that they correspond to one another and are of equal scope. He reviewed the controversy held on this matter by the followers of <term>Plato<gloss>The Greek philosopher (c. 427–347 BC) whose followers often argued that "The One" was superior to "Being."</gloss></term> and <term>Aristotle<gloss>The Greek philosopher (384–322 BC) whose followers generally identified "Being" and "the One."</gloss></term>, asserting that those members of the Academy who argued the contrary did not understand Plato's true dogma. He was prepared to demonstrate that there was a complete harmony of thought between Aristotle and Plato regarding "the One" and "Being," just as with other matters, even if their words differed. <margin>Note</margin> In the final chapter of the work, he turned the entire discussion toward the instruction of life and the reform of morals, with no less ingenuity than piety. 

<margin>Antonio of Faenza</margin>
Against this work, **Antonio of Faenza**, otherwise an excellent philosopher, brought forward several objections in four letters. Pico himself replied to three of them; regarding the fourth, he made no mention of it that I know of—either because it was not faithfully delivered, or because he thought it could be answered based on what he had already written, or for some other reason which must be believed to be just. After he departed this life, I myself undertook the task of responding, so that no opportunity would be given to the malevolent to bark falsehoods or to the unlearned to believe something sinister. I took particular care to show that he had already largely answered from his own previous statements. 

We also saw 
<margin>Some Platonic things</margin>
certain Platonic works composed by him in the **vernacular tongue** <note>Meaning Italian, rather than the scholarly Latin used for his main treatises.</note>. In these, many things are found that serve to unravel the theology of the ancients, and many hidden things are discovered that reveal the insights of the wise through riddles and puzzles. Perhaps, when I have more leisure, I will attempt to translate these into **Latin**, lest the pre-eminent teaching of such a man on these matters—which are quite accessible to anyone—be carried before the eyes of the common people. <note>The author, likely Pico’s nephew Gianfrancesco, expresses the elitist humanist view that deep philosophical truths should be kept in Latin to prevent them from being misunderstood or trivialized by the uneducated public.</note>

<meta>This page continues the biography of Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, shifting from his general views on eloquence to a specific catalog of his scholarly works and his grand project to defend Christianity against "seven enemies" using his linguistic and philosophical expertise.</meta>

a iiii

So much for the completed works of late-night study <note>original: "lucubrationibus," referring to scholarly work done by lamplight</note> that he had published before his death, which served as messengers and forerunners of the distinguished works he had conceived and was in the process of producing. 

<margin>The Old Testament interpreted</margin>
For he was already illuminating the **Old Testament** with the torches of interpretation, and he was girt to perform that same service for the **New Testament**. In these works, he did not merely set forth the literal meanings of the text, but in those places which were capable of bearing other meanings specific to the divine oracles, he built upon them further. He compared the differing readings of our Latin manuscripts with the **Greek and Hebrew originals**. 

But this thought was most deeply planted in his mind, and it sat deeper than all the other projects he had conceived for the genre of commentary: that he would not simply bring in the dogmas of others—which were already available, read, and known—but would instead set forth his own discoveries and meditations. He did this so that he might satisfy hungry souls seeking truth to the best of his ability with his own resources, not those of others. 

After this, being highly skilled in the **Hebrew language**, 
<margin>A booklet on the truth of Jerome's translation</margin>
he published a booklet on the truth of **Jerome's** <note>Saint Jerome (c. 347–420 AD), the translator of the Latin Vulgate Bible.</note> translation against the slanders of the Hebrews. He also wrote a defense for the **Seventy Translators** <term>Septuagint<gloss>The ancient Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible, traditionally attributed to seventy-two Jewish scholars.</gloss></term> regarding the Psalms against those same critics. 

<margin>A booklet on the true calculation of times</margin>
Likewise, he wrote a booklet on the **true calculation of times** <note>A work on chronology, a major concern for Renaissance scholars trying to synchronize biblical and secular history.</note>. Finally, he had applied his mind to defeating the **seven enemies of the Church**. 

For whoever obeys neither Christ nor His Church is, by consequence, His enemy. These are:
1. The **impious**, who receives no dogma of belief.
2. The **idolater**, who serves false idols and worships demons under these images.
3. The **Jew**, who observes the **Mosaical law** according to the rite of the most lost people.
4. The **follower of the abominable Muhammad**, enslaved to his detestable decrees.
5. The **nominal Christian**, who lives the life only in name, perverting the teachings of the Gospel with a mind that is not sincere in works or spirit.
6. The **heretic**, who does not consent to the Catholic Church and kicks back with an obstinate heart, receiving the Gospels with a faith that is not pure, but adulterated and profaned by various superstitions.
7. The **hypocrite**, who, although he receives the faith with a solid, bright, and constant mind, opposes it by his works.

He had summoned these seven—who are like leaders under whom the rest are contained like common soldiers—to a conflict, intending to fight them with their own weapons. 

Against the **impious philosophers**, who are pressed by the yoke of no religion and addicted to no deity, worshipping only natural reasons, he fought using those same reasons. He battled most strongly against the **Hebrews** using the authorities of the Old Testament and the specific teachings of the Jewish schools. He engaged with the **Muslims** by relying on the **Quran**. 

He had already prostrated the worshippers of idols with many wounds and great force, specifically those entangled in vain superstitions who worship **divinatory astrology**. He sharply censured them with both true philosophy and the specific arguments of the astrologers themselves. In **twelve books**—and indeed most perfect ones—out of the thirteen destined for this purpose, he had pursued their delusions. Finally, he turned his attention to **hydromancy** <note>divination by water</note>, **geomancy** <note>divination by earth/land patterns</note>, **pyromancy** <note>divination by fire</note>, **haruspicy** <note>divination by inspecting entrails</note>, and other vanities of that kind...

<keywords>Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, Jerome, Vulgate, Septuagint, Hebrew, Quran, Astrology, Divination, Seven Enemies of the Church, Chronology</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the biography of Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, focusing on his intellectual assault against the "superstitions" of his age, specifically judicial astrology and heresy, as well as his moral critique of nominal Christians.</meta>

...had rejected each of these superstitions one by one. But he directed his battle-line specifically against those astrologers who claim to prophesy. He leveled his battering ram against them with all his might, because other superstitions seek support for their errors in the futile and worthless dogmas of astrology. Whether they are weighing the moments of a birth chart <note>original: "geneſeos," referring to a natal horoscope</note> or selecting favorable hours, or reconciling the "aspects"—the hexagons or triangles <note>In astrology, "sextile" and "trine" aspects are specific geometric angles between planets believed to be harmonious.</note> which they call "benign"—and other such nonsense, even the madman **Orestes** <note>A figure from Greek mythology often used by Roman poets like Persius as a symbol of utter insanity.</note> would not agree with them. 

Nor was he content with merely overturning the foundations of all astrology. He also wished to demonstrate to the astrologers of our time—who are mostly ignorant of the **Greek language**—that this "astrology," the vainest of all professions, had been rendered even vainer (if such a thing is possible) by perverted translations. 

<margin>Ptolemy’s Centiloquium translated from Greek into Latin</margin>
Even while he was writing against them, as if he were doing something else entirely, he translated the "Fruits" of **Ptolemy** (commonly called the *Centiloquium* <term>Centiloquium<gloss>A collection of 100 astrological aphorisms traditionally, though likely falsely, attributed to the astronomer Claudius Ptolemy.</gloss></term>) from the Greek into the Latin tongue. He graced it with a most elegant commentary, in which he demonstrated that the common translation contained more errors than words. Yet, the lazy followers of that art had always guarded that old version among their secrets like a precious treasure. 

Regarding those who hold erroneous views on the faith of Christ and do not obey the authority of Mother Church—whom we more commonly call **heretics**—he attacked them with a remarkable rebuke, using both new instruments and reasons. Nearly ninety heresies were publicly known; however, by searching through everything, he discovered two hundred. He intended not only to eliminate and drive these out one by one, but also to teach how they had drawn or "forked" their errors from a failure to rightly understand **philosophy**.

Finally, he launched a vehement invective against those **Christians** whose faith is seen without works. He diligently investigated how it could be that men believe there is a fire situated in the very center of the earth—where the bodies of the damned and other souls will suffer unthinkable punishments of both mind and body forever—and that they believe in the immense joys of the vision of God with which souls joined to bodies are blessed, yet they are not obedient to the dictates of the Church which compel them to believe. Instead, they run wild everywhere, sinking into vices and the accumulation of riches. They fear nothing less than that punishment, and desire nothing less than the **Kingdom of God**.

<margin>Note</margin>
He also attempted to apply appropriate help according to the nature of the diseases: specifically, to burn away foul and naturally impure diseases with sharp and bitter medicines; but for those wounds infected with less malice and corruption, which desired to form a scar, he sought to soothe them with gentle and calming treatments. For those who had regained their health but feared a relapse, he prepared the most wholesome potions and celebrated antidotes. 

He had begun many other works by which it was hoped that the study of **philosophy** would flourish again throughout the world, once errors had been eliminated and "barbarism" <note>In Humanist rhetoric, "barbarism" referred to the unpolished and complex Latin used by medieval Scholastic philosophers.</note> exploded. Among these, the most important was the:

<margin>The Harmony of Plato and Aristotle</margin>
**Harmony of Plato and Aristotle**, which he had already begun...

<meta>This page continues the biography of Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, likely written by his nephew Gianfrancesco Pico. <sig>a v</sig>

...which he would have completed, if life had remained his companion for just a few more years. For he had nourished philosophy from its very cradle <note>original: "ab incunabulis," a metaphor for the earliest stages of development</note> with milk, and had brought it forth into our times as a mature adult. Thus, there would have been nothing more to be desired by a philosopher of our age: neither in Greek, nor Latin, nor in barbarian <note>In the Renaissance, "barbarian" often referred to non-Classical authors, such as medieval Scholastics or Arabic thinkers like Avicenna.</note> books. He would have summoned the "watery" **Thales**, the "fiery" **Heraclitus**, and **Democritus** surrounded by his atoms. **Orpheus**, 
<margin>Marsilio <note>Referring to Marsilio Ficino, the leader of the Platonic Academy in Florence.</note></margin>
likewise, and **Pythagoras**, and other ancients would have gathered in the Academy by his effort and favor. 
Finally, the princes of philosophy—namely **Plato**, though he is often hidden behind the veils of fables 
<margin>Ficino</margin>
and mathematical wrappings, and **Aristotle**, though walled in by his theories of motion—would have joined right hands to seal a vow of future friendship. Between **Averroes** and **Avicenna** too, and between **Thomas Aquinas** and **Duns Scotus**—who had long been in conflict—he would have obtained, if not a total peace, then at least a truce in many matters. For in many of their controversies, if someone were to scrutinize the differing words more attentively and weigh them more exactly 
<margin>apologia</margin>
—searching more scrupulously beneath the skin <note>A metaphor for looking past the surface level of the text.</note>, leaving the surface behind, and penetrating with the mind into the deepest hiding places and profound inner chambers—he would find, without ambiguity, a union of meanings beneath those inseparable and clashing words. The crowd of modern thinkers would have been both honored and corrected, partly according to their merits and partly for their faults. 

<margin>Pico</margin>
Therefore, dedicated entirely to God, he defended the Church with what weapons he could. He drew out the Truth which lay hidden (as they say) in **Democritus’s well** <note>A classical proverb: Truth lies at the bottom of a well, meaning it is difficult to find.</note>, and he thoroughly cut down and uprooted the unassailable weeds of ignorance—the pernicious herbs springing up—which stifle the minds of many. 

<margin>Heptaplus <note>Pico's famous "sevenfold" commentary on the creation story in Genesis.</note></margin>
But death, arriving suddenly, rendered the labor of so many vigils and the birth of his refined nighttime studies almost empty. This was the primary reason why he left behind many commentaries that were, for the most part, 
<margin>Pico</margin>
rough-hewn, unpolished, and imperfect. This was because he wrote only for himself, and not for us. For just as he possessed a swift mind for composing, so he had a fast hand for writing. And although he used to draw the most beautiful letterforms, it happened that through the habit of excessive speed in composing, he himself was scarcely able to read what he had scribbled. He was accustomed to writing here and there, 
<margin>The Highest</margin>
sometimes obliterating old notes when new ones occurred to him. For this reason, I found certain things that were obsolete or struck out, others written only in snatches or bits and pieces; in short, everything was so confused and disordered that they might be thought of as "forests" or "medleys" <note>original: "syluae / aut farragines," referring to raw, unorganized collections of notes.</note>. 

From the sevenfold book which he had titled against the enemies of the Church, that part which especially attacks the soothsaying astrologers and casters of birth-charts was brought "from the anvil to the file" <note>A Latin idiom meaning the work was brought from a rough state to a polished, finished form.</note>, as the saying goes. We have drawn this out—not without great labor nor mediocre care—from a manuscript that was blotted and nearly torn to pieces. In this work, he demonstrates himself to be the supreme philosopher, the supreme theologian, the supreme orator, and the fiercest defender of Christ’s Church, endowed with the incomparable genius that is perceived in all his commentaries. I have also found in my possession certain very small pieces, not yet smoothed on the lathe...

<meta>This page continues the catalog of Giovanni Pico della Mirandola's literary and philosophical remains, shifting from his grand project of reconciling philosophers to his smaller, unfinished works on theology, his musical talent, his extensive correspondence, and a detailed analysis of his unique rhetorical style.</meta>

<margin>
Music highly cultivated
</margin>
...an interpretation only of the Lord's Prayer <note>original: "dominicæ orationis"</note>. There were also about fifty rules for living well—certainly far too brief and unexplained—which he would have undoubtedly expanded into many chapters had he lived. He also composed two prayers to God: one in Italian rhymes <note>original: "rhithmis hetruscis," literally "Etruscan rhythms," referring to the Tuscan or Italian vernacular</note>, the other in elegiac meter, with which he could soothe his mind by singing to the lyre when exhausted by weightier studies. In his first years of youth, he had so cultivated every kind of musical art that the melodies he devised and the harmonies he noted with their proper chords were considered famous. We have also looked through many things in his desk, though they were disorganized; from these, however, I believe something useful could be compiled, especially his exposition of the Psalms. 

<margin>
Multiform letters
</margin>
But there also emerged about fifty letters published at various times: some personal, some doctrinal, and some exhortatory, together with the oration <note>This refers to the famous *Oration on the Dignity of Man*, intended to introduce his 900 theses in Rome.</note> he was to have delivered in Rome if the debate had taken place. This work does not only reflect the most perceptive genius and most abundant learning of a young man not yet twenty-four years old (as all his writings do), but it also offers us the richest testimony of his most fertile eloquence. 

<margin>
Proven character of speaking
</margin>
He always used a style that was truly admirable: not borrowed, but natural, and even multifaceted according to the variety of subjects. Even if it "exhausted the entire perfume-chest of Isocrates" <note>original: "Isocratis myrothecion," a classical metaphor for a highly polished and ornate rhetorical style</note> as they say, it nevertheless preserved the ornaments of purity and the decorum of majesty. 

<margin>
Genres of speaking: Copious and Brief
</margin>
For those celebrated genres of speaking—of which Gellius lists three and Macrobius four—can be gathered from his commentaries without great effort. There one finds the **copious** style, in which **Cicero** is said to rule, and the **brief** style, which is ascribed to **Sallust**. 

<margin>
Dry, florid, and rich
</margin>
The **dry** style given to **Fronto**, and the **rich and florid** style in which they say **Pliny** and **Symmachus** delighted. Yet perhaps **Brutus** would not have called this abundance "weak," nor **Sallust** called it "immoderate." An orator with right judgment will easily detect that Fronto's dryness has been moistened, Sallust's brevity elongated, and the flowers and richness of Pliny carried into a wider field. To these, add **Livy's** "milky fountain," perhaps without his "Patavinity" <note>original: "patauinitate," a term used by ancient critics to describe a certain regional dialect or local flavor in Livy's writing</note> (as the critic said), with many little flowers of **Apuleius** added. However, he did not exercise himself here in philosophy borrowed from the Greeks, nor in "Attic Nights" <note>Referring to the *Noctes Atticae* of Aulus Gellius, a collection of miscellaneous notes on grammar, history, and philosophy.</note>, nor in the "fictional Saturnalia" <note>Referring to the *Saturnalia* of Macrobius, a work of literary criticism and antiquarian lore.</note> fabricated to praise Virgil's *Aeneid*, nor in Roman history, nor in mere natural history devoid of the highest and most difficult speculations. Instead, he toiled in that admirable fabric of the world, in attacking the enemies of the most holy Catholic Church, and was worn out in eliminating the astrologers. He labored in examining theological questions and in the harmony of **Aristotle** and **Plato**. He applied himself to explaining sacred scripture and devoted his energy to advising and exhorting his friends. Indeed, he was so far from affecting this eloquence we are discussing that he rather condemned those who, searching too scrupulously for "painted charms" <note>original: "pigmentata lenocinia," referring to artificial rhetorical embellishments or "meretricious" style</note>, applied all the strength of their talent to investigating the origins of words. All these things...

<meta>This page continues the description of Giovanni Pico della Mirandola’s intellectual habits, moving from his rhetorical style to his immense reading speed, his mastery of both ancient Church Fathers and medieval Scholastic theologians, and his particular respect for Thomas Aquinas despite his own youthful provocations.</meta>

...[this turned] many more readily toward admiration of him, because he had long and most diligently engaged with the writings of those who did not profess Latin literature filled with the flowers of eloquence. Let the excessive lovers of antiquity bear this with an even mind; for though these things are stated more concisely and briefly, they are perhaps more true, as men more learned than I—Hermolao Barbaro, Battista the Carmelite <note>original: "Baptista Carmelita," referring to the poet and theologian Battista Spagnoli of Mantua</note>, Marsilio Ficino, Matteo Bosso, and many other most learned and eloquent men—have recorded. 

<margin>
Speed of reading
</margin>
He read through and took excerpts from vast libraries of both Latin and Greek works with incredible speed. He never passed over any commentaries without reading them, if the opportunity was given. He had attained such a high level of knowledge regarding the ancient Doctors of the Church that it is difficult to believe, even for someone who had spent their whole life solely in studying them. Regarding the modern <note>original: "neotericis," referring to the medieval Scholastic thinkers who were "modern" compared to the ancient Church Fathers.</note> theologians who used the style commonly called "the Parisian way" <note>The Scholastic method associated with the University of Paris.</note>, such judgment resided in him that if someone unexpectedly asked for the explanation of an abstruse and poorly clarified question from any one of them, he would open it up with such fertility of genius and unlock it with such skill that you would say he had all the sayings of that doctor before his eyes and ready for use. He recognized all their "families" <note>The different schools of thought, such as Thomism, Scotism, etc.</note> in the same way, had thoroughly examined all their papers, and you should not believe he was so devoted to one of them (as is the custom among our people) that he despised the others. 

For he was so instructed from childhood and so inclined that he sought the truth in them; and with equal honor, until the truth shone forth, he venerated it once found, stripped of private affection. What he thought of each of those who are generally considered more famous can be seen in the preface to his *Apology*, where he reported the properties and particular praises of the "barbarian" <note>The humanists often called Scholastic philosophers "barbarians" because they did not use Classical Latin style.</note>, Greek, and Latin philosophers. 

<margin>
Thomas Aquinas
</margin>
Indeed, whenever mention was made during conversation about those philosophers or theologians who wrote by debating in the French manner, he used to praise Thomas Aquinas above all others, as one who relied on a more solid foundation of truth than the rest. He also calls him "the splendor of our theology" in the *Heptaplus* <note>Pico's work on the sevenfold hidden meanings of the Book of Genesis.</note>. I often asked him about this, and he gave me the same answer. Nor should certain things to be debated in his *Apology* persuade anyone to the contrary, even though they openly contradict Thomas's opinions; for he was then a very young man, eager for glory, and in that most celebrated city [Rome], in the manner of Gorgias of Leontini <note>A Greek Sophist famous for claiming he could debate any subject from any side.</note>, he was hunting for fame by defending any side of an argument. 

<margin>
Gorgias of Leontini
</margin>
Add to this that out of ten thousand <note>original: "decem millibus." While the text says ten thousand, Pico’s famous "900 Theses" are likely what is meant here, using "ten thousand" as a rhetorical figure for a vast number.</note> propositions, he disagreed with or opposed only three or four; that does not prove [he rejected Thomas]. Furthermore, he was most skilled in debating, and while his mind was fervent, he devoted frequent and most intense effort to literary contests. 

<margin>
Sharpness of Scotus
</margin>
In raising objections, one could easily detect the sharpness and vigilance of [Duns] Scotus, the acrimony of Francis <note>Likely Francis of Meyronnes, a noted Scotist theologian.</note>, and the abundance and multitude of Aureolus <note>Referring to Peter Aureolus, a Franciscan philosopher and theologian.</note>. 

<margin>
Aureolus
</margin>
Nor were those "knots" <note>Technical logical or theological difficulties known as "insolubles."</note> lacking, complicated by many twists, supported not so much by tickling subtleties as by weightiness in responding...

<meta>This page continues the biography of Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, shifting from his reading habits to his participation in academic debates and his disdain for the "vain" logic of certain medieval schools.</meta>

<sig>A ii</sig>

<margin>
Ercole d'Este
</margin>
In him, the strength and power of **Thomas** <note>Thomas Aquinas (c. 1225–1274), the preeminent Scholastic theologian.</note> and the vast breadth of **Albert** <note>Albert the Great (c. 1200–1280), a polymath and teacher of Aquinas.</note> could be seen. Truly, he had long ago sent away any messenger of interest in these academic conflicts <note>Referring to public disputations or debates.</note>; he grew more loathsome of that duty day by day and avoided it to such an extent that even when **Ercole d'Este, Duke of Ferrara**, through intermediaries and in person, most earnestly requested it—while the general synod of the Preaching Friars <note>The Dominican Order.</note> was being held at Ferrara—he long resisted complying. Yet, yielding finally to many requests from that Prince, for whom he had no small affection, he complied. From this, it was debated whether he appeared more skillful or more eloquent, more learned or more kind. From the mouth of the disputant, such an alacrity of spirit was always evident that he seemed to be arguing over something pleasant and peaceful rather than something sharp and difficult. Therefore, those who hung on his every word were moved to a wonderful love for him. 

<margin>
An Adage
</margin>
But he had a frequent saying: that such a display was the duty of a <term>dialectician</term> <note>A specialist in logic and formal debate, often seen by Renaissance humanists as prioritizing technique over truth.</note>, not a philosopher. He likewise said those disputations were beneficial which were conducted with a calm mind to search for and inquire after the truth in private places, without witnesses; but those that took place in public to show off learning or to catch the popular favor and the applause of rulers were most harmful. He thought it almost impossible for the desire for honor—which drives those wandering, "front-line" disputants—not to be joined by an inseparable bond to a desire for the shame and confusion of the opponent, a lethal wound to the soul and a deadly poison to charity. 

Nothing was hidden from him regarding the 
<margin>
Sophist traps
</margin>
<margin>
Swinesheadian trifles
</margin>
traps and quibbles of the sophists and the <term>Swinesheadian trifles</term> <note>original: "suiseticas quisquilias," referring to Richard Swineshead, a 14th-century English logician known as "The Calculator." Pico and his contemporaries often viewed these complex logical exercises as pedantic.</note> which are called **calculations**. These are mathematical commentaries applied to more subtle—I might even say more peevish—natural inquiries. Even though he was learned in them and had read such writings which perhaps Italy does not fully know (for no path of literature could be found so trackless or inaccessible that he had not thoroughly explored it), he nevertheless seemed to hate and detest them. In my judgment, he noticed that their common use served only to build the reputation of fools and weaken the memory during rebuttal, but for finding the truth—to which he thought tireless effort should be devoted—they contributed nothing, or very little. 

But lest I pursue too much and detain the reader, I will summarize briefly. One person might shine in eloquence but be disgraced by ignorance of the secrets of nature; another knows foreign languages but has not mastered the universal decrees of the philosophers; another reads the inventions of the ancients but has not fashioned any new doctrines. Knowledge was sought by others only for the sake of men and human glory, not for the benefit of the Christian republic or for divine and human things. He, however, had embraced all these things with such equal zeal that they seemed to have flowed into him in troops and heaps. Nor was he like many who, excelling in no single thing, merely participate in all...

<meta>This page continues the biography of Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, written by his nephew Gianfrancesco Pico. But he had progressed so much in all the sciences that if you had considered any one of them in him, you would have judged that he had chosen that one as his own and peculiar field; these things were also the more wonderful because he attained them by himself, through the force of his intellect and love of truth, as if without a teacher. We might say of him what **Epicurus** used to say of himself: <note>original: "Se sibi ipsi fuisse magistrum"</note> "That he was his own master." I have found that five causes converged to produce such wonderful results in so small a space of time:

<margin>
Five causes of such wonderful results
</margin>
An incredible intellect, a most tenacious memory, and ample resources, with which he was assisted in purchasing books in our own language (Latin), as well as Greek and foreign languages. 

<margin>
Seven thousand gold coins spent in gathering books
</margin>
Indeed, I recall from memory that he spent seven thousand gold coins—up to that very day—in acquiring volumes of every kind of literature for himself. Lastly, there was his constant and indefatigable study, and his contempt for earthly things. If, therefore, that ancient age of the Spartans had produced him, or if we believe **Aristotle**, he would have been called a "divine man." 

But now, I think, the virtues of his intellect should be left aside, and the noble parts of his soul regarding his actions should be followed, and his most exacting character should be brought to light, so that his soul, inflamed toward God, might become known; so that his riches distributed to the needy might be praised; and so that those who are finally devoted to the divine law might be prepared, most abundantly, to give thanks to the author of all good. 

Therefore, three years before he died, so that he could live in deep peace, setting aside the cares of ruling and secure in wherever the scepters might fall, he handed over to me—I know not whether by gift or sale—all the patrimony he possessed in **Mirandola** and **Concordia**; that is, a third part of them. This act was later confirmed with imperial generosity by **Maximilian Augustus** <note>Maximilian I (1459–1519), Holy Roman Emperor.</note>, who is our king and, so to speak, immediate lord (for in all the centuries since Mirandola and Concordia were built, we have recognized no other lord except those who successively sit upon the Royal or Imperial throne of the Romans). 

<margin>
Distribution to the poor
</margin>
Whatever money he received from this transaction, he partly bestowed upon the poor and partly spent on buying lands from which he and his household might be supported. Specifically, he had purchased for himself estates in the territory of **Ferrara** for many thousands of gold coins. Likewise, he distributed many silver vessels and precious pieces of furniture for the use of the poor. 

<margin>
A moderate table
</margin>
He was content with a moderate table, though it retained something of his former elegance in terms of the dishes and the silver vessels used. Every day at the designated hours, he poured out prayers to God. He always gave money to any poor people he encountered; not content with that, he entrusted **Girolamo Benivieni** <note>A Florentine poet and close friend of Pico, known for his religious devotion.</note>, a learned Florentine citizen whom he loved greatly for his great charity and integrity of character, to always assist the needy with his own funds. He also provided dowries for young women to be married, telling Benivieni to report to him immediately so he could reimburse the spent money as soon as possible. Indeed, he had delegated that duty to him so that he might more easily...

<margin>Jerome</margin>

His own body beaten with whips
</margin>
But he, especially in those days which represent the torture and death of **Christ** for the sake of our salvation, would beat his own flesh in memory of that supreme benefit and for the expiation of sins; and quite often with my own eyes (let all things return to the glory of God) I saw the whip. 

<margin>
A cheerful countenance
</margin>
He was always of a cheerful and calm countenance, and of such a mild nature that he testified, even in the hearing of many, that he had never been disturbed by anger. 

<margin>
A mild nature
</margin>
I recall him saying to me during a conversation that he believed he could not be moved to anger by any event (even if things turned out for the worst) unless certain chests were lost, in which his late-night labors and vigils were stored <note>These "chests" or *scrinia* contained his precious unpublished manuscripts, the result of years of intense study.</note>.

<margin>
Steadfastness of mind
</margin>
But when he considered that he labored for God the Best and Greatest and for His church, and that he had dedicated all his works, studies, and actions to the same, and that this could not happen except by His command or permission, he trusted he would not be saddened. O happy mind! which could now be depressed by no adversities, nor (as will become clear) exalted by any conveniences. 

<margin>
Knowledge of five languages
</margin>
Certainly, his expertise in universal philosophy did not make him prideful, nor did his knowledge of the Hebrew, Chaldean <note>In this period, "Chaldean" usually referred to Aramaic or Syriac.</note>, and Arabic languages, in addition to Latin and Greek. Neither ample riches nor nobility of birth had inflated him; the beauty and elegance of his body did not, nor could the great license for sinning recall him to that soft and spacious road of the many. What then could be so admirable that it might subvert his mind? What, I ask, could be above him? He who (to use the words of **Seneca**) <note>original: "Senecæ"</note> was "above fortune." 

<margin>Seneca</margin>
For he looked upon fortune, whether swollen with favorable winds or humble with adverse blasts, in such a way that his mind might be joined by a spiritual glue to **Christ** and the citizens of the heavenly fatherland. This is clearly perceived by this proof: while he saw the offices and dignities of the church being bid for and auctioned off by many of our time (alas, the sorrow!) and sought, demanded, sighed for, and purchased most strenuously, he himself rejected those offered by two kings through messengers. 

<margin>
Dignities offered by two kings and rejected
</margin>
Most grave witnesses are present, and I myself am a witness: responding that he did not wish to be initiated into the sacred orders, he turned them down. Another person indeed, when he had promised that he would give him secular dignities and large revenues if he would come to his king, saw that not a corner was left into which Pico could hide himself; having reached the end of all his excuses, Pico gave him such an answer so that the man would understand he did not seek dignities or riches, but rather had neglected them so that he might be free for God and his studies. 

<margin>
Wealth neglected for the sake of God and studies
</margin>

<meta>This page continues the biography of Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, shifting from his physical self-discipline to his rejection of ecclesiastical honors and his ultimate preference for divine love over intellectual achievement. ...it seemed to many it would happen) that he should embrace these honors. Regarding this, **Pandulphus** <note>Pandolfo Collenuccio, a scholar and associate of Pico.</note> was somewhat hesitant and weary, for he was not unaware that Pico would prefer anything rather than being entangled in honors of this kind. Pico himself, with the greatness of soul that he possessed, immediately ordered that this prophetic saying be sent in reply by letter:

> "My thoughts are not your thoughts" <note>original: "Non sunt cogitationes meæ: cogitationes uestræ." A quotation from Isaiah 55:8.</note>. Perhaps considering the goods of the Church—of which the greatest part is owed by hereditary right to the poor—he thought it not right to maintain magnificent displays.

<margin>Ambrose / Augustine / Martin / Celestine</margin>
Likewise, he kept before his eyes the examples of the holiest men—namely **Ambrose**, **Augustine**, **Martin**, and others—who fled from the offered dignity of the episcopate [the office of bishop] and for a long time refused that duty before they undertook it. Furthermore, he had read that the most holy **Celestine** <note>Pope Celestine V, famous for his "Great Refusal" or abdication from the papacy in 1294.</note> had abdicated not only from the cardinalate itself, but even from the supreme power of the high pontificate, shaking that burden from his shoulders for the sake of the whole Christian republic. Truly, it is a burden for which a maximum reward is prepared for those who undergo it; it was his firm persuasion that such honors should only be embraced by those who are unwilling, and only for the sake of obeying and being of service. To a philosopher, it was no matter of praise to have accumulated riches or to have sought honors, but rather to have refused them; and by refusing shadowy glory, to attain the true glory which always follows virtue like an inseparable companion and attendant.

<margin>Despiser of human glory</margin>
He held human glory as almost nothing. He often said that fame would be of some use to the living, but of no use at all to the dead. We recognize that he valued his own learning only insofar as it served the utility of the Church and the elimination and rejection of opposing errors. Indeed, we perceived that he had reached such a goal of perfection that he cared little if his commentaries were published under his own name, provided that the very work performed under the name of **Pico** <term>Pici</term> <note>Giovanni Pico della Mirandola.</note> brought benefit to men. 

<margin>Note</margin>
He was very little moved by other books except the **Old and New Testament**; and he had decided to consume the rest of his life always poring over them, unless public utility spurred him on, when he saw so many and such great things which he had conceived and labored over were not only demanded by everyone everywhere, but even required prematurely.

<margin>The true education of a Christian mind</margin>
He valued even the smallest, tiny affection toward God from a devout person—even a commoner or a little old woman—more than all his own knowledge of human and divine things. He very often advised his friends during conversation to notice how much mortal things struggle and falter, how fleeting and fluid is the life we live, and how firm and stable is what we shall be in the future—whether we are thrust down to the underworld or raised up to the heavens. He urged them to turn and incite their minds to love God, a work that outweighed any knowledge we could have in this life.

<margin>What he judged concerning loving and knowing God in this life</margin>
This he also carried out most brilliantly in that very book **On Being and the One** <term>De ente et uno</term> <note>One of Pico's most famous philosophical works, written to reconcile the systems of Plato and Aristotle.</note>, when, turning to **Angelo Poliziano** <term>Angelum Politianum</term> <note>A renowned humanist poet and scholar who was Pico’s close friend.</note>, to whom he dedicated the book, he uttered these words in the discussion itself:

> "But see, my Angelo, what madness holds us: while we are in the body, we can love God more than we can know Him..."

<meta>This page continues the biography of Giovanni Pico della Mirandola. The previous page discussed his rejection of high Church offices. The "Franciscus" mentioned in the margin is Gianfrancesco Pico della Mirandola, Giovanni's nephew and the author of this biography.</meta>

...in the body, we are capable of more than we can either express or know; by loving, we profit ourselves more, labor less, and obey Him <note>God</note> more. Yet, we still prefer to never find what we seek through knowledge, rather than to possess through love that which, without love, would be sought in vain. This was also his divine <margin>A saying that **Gianfrancesco** <note>Gianfrancesco Pico della Mirandola, Giovanni’s nephew and the biographer writing this text.</note> frequently had on his lips.</margin> sentiment.

Furthermore, generosity alone exceeded moderation in him; he was so far from applying any care to earthly things that he was even stained by the blemish of negligence. We have learned that he was <margin>Excessive generosity</margin> frequently warned by his friends not to utterly despise his riches. They asserted that it brought shame upon him—whether the rumor was true or false—that he had provided his stewards with the opportunity for theft. Nevertheless, that mind, which was always intent on contemplating and examining the designs of all nature, could not easily lower itself to weigh these lowest and most abject matters.

I remember when I was staying with him in **Ferrara** <note>A major center of the Italian Renaissance where Pico spent significant time.</note>, a caterer presented him with a small ledger, seeking approval of expenses. Seeing this, I stood there marveled, and asked him if he had finally applied his mind to that which he had neglected in times past. My friend replied that people had not only begged him but demanded that he undertake this duty; he had done so merely to comply with their customs, but he possessed just as little actual care for it as he had before. 

Furthermore, when his primary steward <term>dispensator</term> <note>A high-level servant or official responsible for managing a household's finances.</note> interrupted him to request that he order a settlement of accounts <term>dispunctionem</term> for the money he had handled over many years—so that the steward might set his own mind at ease—and had brought the books before him for that purpose, we heard Pico give him this response: 

"I know that I could have been cheated by you very often, and still could be. Therefore, there is no need for a clearing of these expenses. If I owe you, I shall pay the coins as soon as possible; if you owe me, either pay the debt now if you can, or in the future if the means are not currently available."

<margin>Benevolence toward friends</margin> Truly, he always treated his friends with great indulgence, using encouraging words to lead them toward living well. I knew a man who, relying on Pico's learning and reputation, spoke with him; when the conversation turned to morals, he was so moved by only two of Pico's words that he abandoned the path of vice and reformed his character.

<margin>Two very healthy remedies against vices</margin> The words were of this kind: "If we kept the death of Christ, suffered for love of us, before our eyes, and likewise guarded against vices by repeatedly thinking of our own [death], we would be safe."

He exhibited an admirable modesty and courtesy toward those whom he felt should be bound to him, not because of their power or fortune, but because of their devotion and learning. He was accustomed to love those whom he saw were diligent and fit, however slightly they might excel in letters or at least in the study of the liberal arts. For likeness <margin>Likeness is the cause of love</margin> is the cause of love. As **Philostratus** <note>A Greek sophist of the Roman imperial period.</note> reports, **Apollonius** <note>Apollonius of Tyana, a first-century philosopher and teacher.</note> said there is a certain affinity in the way knowledge perfects a man as a human being; but to achieve goodness is to rise above others who are merely upright...

It also records his "two remedies" for a moral life: contemplating the death of Christ and one's own mortality.</summary>

...that they should be loved is not doubted. However, nothing was more intolerable to him than (to use the words of **Horace** <note>original: "uerbis horatii".
