He had also set aside worldly military service and the bond of marriage; and when asked in jest which burden would seem lighter to bear if he were forced by necessity and given the choice: after hesitating a little, nodding, and smiling slightly, he replied: marriage—in which there was not as much servitude and danger attached as there was in military service. For he loved freedom <margin>Freedom of the soul</margin> beyond measure, which both his nature was so inclined toward and his studies in philosophy suggested to him. 

I believe that for this reason he was mostly a wanderer, and never chose a fixed home for himself, although he stayed often in **Florence** and sometimes in **Ferrara**. He was not much given to the <margin>External worship</margin> external worship of <term>latria</term> <note>latria: A technical theological term for the supreme worship offered to God alone.</note>. I am not speaking of that which the Church commands to be observed (for we saw him keep that before his eyes), but I mention those ceremonies which some pursue and promote while neglecting the true <margin>True interior worship of God</margin> worship of God, who is to be worshipped in spirit and truth. Instead, he pursued God with the most fervent worship of love in his internal affections. Sometimes that eagerness of mind almost withered and fell away; then, gathering strength with a greater effort, I remember him burning for God in God. As when we were walking together in a certain orchard in **Ferrara** <margin>Fervor of love for God</margin>, talking about the love of Christ along the long paths, he broke out into words of this kind: 

"Let me tell you this in secret: once I have finished and completed certain of my nightly labors <note>His scholarly writings and books.</note>, I will bestow what riches I have left upon the poor, and, armed with the crucifix, with bare feet, I will travel the world through castles and cities preaching Christ."

<meta>This page continues the biography of Giovanni Pico della Mirandola by his nephew, Gianfrancesco. Having previously discussed Pico’s time in Florence and his preference for intellectual freedom over worldly status, the narrative now turns to the final days of his life and his pious death in 1494.</meta>

<margin>In which year of his life he died</margin>
In the year 1494 of our redemption: while he was completing his thirty-second year of age and staying in **Florence**, he was seized by a most treacherous fever. It spread so violently through his humors <note>The "four humors" (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile) were believed in medieval medicine to govern health; an imbalance caused disease.</note> and vital organs that it defied every kind of medicine applied to it, and within thirteen days it forced him to fully satisfy the debt of nature <note>A common euphemism for dying.</note>. But concerning how he conducted himself during his illness—although I was far from him at that time—I shall not cease to recount what I have received from the most solemn witnesses who were present.

<margin>How he conducted himself in his illness.</margin>
For instance, after he had received the sacrament of the **Eucharist**, the image of the crucified Christ was offered to him, so that from it he might take full draughts of love in memory of that ineffable passion suffered for the sake of our salvation; and before he breathed his last, he might receive a most powerful defense against all adversities and a most mighty bulwark against wicked demons.

<margin>The praiseworthy end of a Christian man is told</margin>
An elder <note>Likely a priest or monk, possibly Girolamo Savonarola or one of his associates.</note> soon questioned him as to whether he firmly believed that this was the true image of the true God and true man: who, insofar as he is God, was begotten before time and eternity by God the Father himself,

<margin>The image of God</margin>
to whom he was born equal in all things; and who, by the **Holy Spirit** (who is also God, proceeding eternally from him and the Father, which three are one), was conceived in the womb of **Mary**, ever virgin. This same God, in time, suffered hunger, thirst, labors, heat, and sleepless nights; and finally, to wash away our filth contracted from the seed of **Adam**, and to unseal the great gate of heaven, he embraced the human race with the greatest charity and shed his most precious blood, both voluntarily and most willingly, upon the altar of the cross. 

<margin>Alberto Pio</margin>
When these and other such things usually recounted in such moments were reviewed, Pico replied not only that he believed them, but that he was certain of them. He said the same to **Alberto Pio** <note>Pico's nephew (1475–1531), the Prince of Carpi and a noted scholar.</note>, the son of his sister whom we mentioned at the beginning of this life, a young man conspicuous for his talent, his study of the liberal arts, and his character. 

<margin>Alexander of Aphrodisias, Themistius, Averroes</margin>
By the same reasoning that **Alexander of Aphrodisias** and **Themistius** <note>Ancient commentators on Aristotle.</note> declared in the prefaces of their books on physics <note>original: "auscultatoriorum librorū," referring to Aristotle's *Physics* (Physica Auscultatio).</note> that fortitude against the fear of death is drawn from the contemplation of nature—a sentiment which **Averroes** <note>The 12th-century Islamic philosopher known as "The Commentator" on Aristotle.</note> later adopted—Pico spoke to Alberto, attempting to make the borders of death more peaceable. He said the mind is not calmed by that reasoning alone, nor is the fear of death laid aside by it; but rather, it is calmed chiefly by this: that an end was now being put to his offenses against his God. For he judged that a longer span of life would only contain more frequent offenses against God. 

Furthermore, he revealed to several from the college of preachers <note>The Dominicans.</note>, who were most trustworthy witnesses, and to the aforementioned **Alberto** himself, a vision he had shortly before. 

<margin>The Queen of Heaven visited the sick man at night</margin>
He told them that the **Queen of Heaven** <note>The Virgin Mary.</note> had come to him at night, fragrant with a wonderful scent, and had refreshed all his limbs that had been bruised and broken by that fever; she promised that he would not be yielded up entirely to death. While he was ill, he was found lying in his bed with a cheerful and peaceful face. And amidst the stings of death which he endured, as if he saw the heavens opened to him, he spoke to the heavenly citizens; and to all those greeting him and promising their help (as is the custom), he replied with the most charming words.

...welcomed and kissed with [gentle] speech. We have further been informed that he requested forgiveness from all his servants, should he have happened to be troublesome to any of them. In a will made the previous year, he had provided that food and clothing should be given to some for as long as they lived, and money to others according to their merits. <margin>His death caused distress to all ranks of men.</margin>
How much distress his death caused to the lowest and highest ranks of all is witnessed by the princes of Italy, the cities, and the peoples. Witness to this is the kings whom we cited above. Witness again is the kindness and grace of **Charles, King of the Gauls** <note>Charles VIII of France, who invaded Italy in 1494.</note>, which should not be passed over in silence. When it was announced to the King—who was then arriving in **Florence** to head toward **Rome** to conquer the Kingdom of Naples—that Pico was suffering from a grave illness, he immediately sent two of his own physicians to visit and help him, who were also serving as his ambassadors. He gave them letters, which we have both seen and read, written in his own hand, full of both humanity and those promises which the most benevolent mind of a magnanimous king and the distinguished virtues of the sick man required. Indeed, Pico was at that time very well known to him by fame and joined to him by a certain familiarity; for he had been honorably received by the King in Gaul while visiting **Paris**. Truly, He who made him an object of admiration to the whole world and for many ages while he lived, likewise

<margin>Praise of Friar Girolamo Savonarola. Apuleius.</margin>
decreed that his death be celebrated as no less famous and extraordinary. Therefore, I think I should relate here those things which I heard with my own ears while I was in **Florence**—where I had traveled upon hearing of his illness, though I did not arrive in time. In the sacred building called **Santa Reparata** <note>The ancient name for the Cathedral of Florence (the Duomo), which was still commonly used even after the new structure was dedicated to Santa Maria del Fiore.</note>, I heard **Girolamo Savonarola** of Ferrara—of the Order of Preachers <note>The Dominicans.</note>, a man most learned in theology, most distinguished, and most famous for his holiness—delivering sacred sermons to the Florentine people. But

<margin>The words of Brother Girolamo.</margin>
first, it is my intention to warn those ignorant of sacred letters using the words of **Apuleius** <note>A 2nd-century Roman philosopher and author; Savonarola uses a classical reference to bridge the gap between secular learning and divine revelation.</note>: let them not, with "thick ears" and an obstinate heart, think those things are lies which seem new to the hearing, or strange to the sight, or certainly difficult beyond the reach of thought. If they explore these things a little more deeply, they will find them not only evident to the understanding but even very easy in the doing.

He, therefore, declaiming from the pulpit, suggested to all who were present the things I am about to say: "A secret must be revealed to you, O **Florence**, which is as true as that Gospel of **John** so frequent among you. I would have remained silent, certainly, but I am compelled to speak; and He who can command me has ordered that I make these things public. Furthermore, I think there is no one among you who did not know **Giovanni Pico della Mirandola**. He was heaped with great benefits and great graces from God. He was endowed with multifaceted learning; perhaps no mortal ever possessed such a celebrated genius. I would have judged his death a great loss to the Church if a longer span of life had been granted to him, for he would have excelled all who have died in the last eight hundred years by the monuments of writing he would have left behind. He used to converse with me in private, revealing secrets from which I knew that he was summoned by God to the religious life through internal voices; and so, obeying these inspirations...

...who, desiring [this], had intended to obey more than once. I say this, however, not as a certainty, but as my own conjecture and presumption. Because of this, I threatened him for two years with a scourge <note>A "scourge" (flagellum) here refers to a divine punishment or trial predicted by Savonarola.</note> if he should negligently carry out the work God had proposed for him to complete. I did not ask for *this* [death] by which he was struck; I had not thought of this. <margin>Almsgiving</margin> 

Truly, the most kind Judge bore Himself most mercifully toward him. And on account of the alms bestowed upon the poor with a large and most generous hand, and the prayers most urgently poured out to God, it was brought about that his soul neither exults yet in the "bosom of the Father" <note>A biblical expression for heaven or a state of peace after death.</note> above the heavens, nor is it assigned to the lower regions to be tortured with eternal torments. 

<margin>State of the soul</margin> 

But, delivered to the fire of purgatory for a time, he pays the temporary penalties. I would most willingly say this in this part, so that those who knew him—and especially those who were enriched by his favors—might help him with their suffrages <note>Intercessory prayers or good works intended to help a soul in Purgatory.</note>.

The man of God [Savonarola] asserted these things and many others with a clear voice, adding that it was not hidden from him that for lies of this kind, if any were mixed in, the heralds of God's word are made worthy of eternal punishment. He also added that for several days these things had been known to him in general. But because of the words which the sick man [Pico] had affirmed the Virgin <note>Refers to the Virgin Mary, who Pico claimed had appeared to him promising he would not die.</note> had said to him, Savonarola had stood wavering and feared for a long time that the man had been mocked by the works of demons, since by his death the Virgin's promise would be frustrated. 

<margin>Double death</margin> 

Yet it became known to him that the deceased had been deceived by an "ambiguity of death." While she had spoken of the second and eternal death <note>The "Second Death" in Christian theology refers to damnation in Hell.</note>, he had believed she meant the first and temporary death [physical death]. If anyone should say that this man [Savonarola] lied through hypocrisy, or was deluded by phantasms, or circumvented by the tricks of demons: unless he is either of bad faith or disturbed in mind, he must confess that God has, in many ways, revealed to the living—and is still able to reveal—the happiness or misery of those who have died. 

<margin>Praise of the teaching and uprightness of Brother Jerome [Savonarola]</margin> 

And in that same span of time, He makes those to whom these things are made public certain that they are not mocked by visions or specters, but that the things they perceive with either mind or eyes are true. Truly, that a man of such learning and authority, of such uprightness and prudence—whose brief theorems on Aristotle's philosophy, public admonitions, most noble interpretations of holy eloquence, and predictions of future events (which almost all of <term>Italy</term> <note>original: "Italia"; here referring to the Italian peninsula and its various states during the Renaissance.</note> knows have come true precisely), and most holy way of life have long since established the greatest trust—should have pronounced these things as true and to be held unshaken before so many thousands of people in the principal church of such a celebrated city, no one but a malevolent person will deny. Add to this that while he was inquiring not a little into that matter...

<meta>This page continues the account of Giovanni Pico della Mirandola’s death and the supernatural testimonies regarding his soul’s fate in Purgatory. It follows Savonarola’s public declaration that Pico had been punished for delaying his entry into monastic life.</meta>

...I heard that one who had been present at the sermon went to the preacher <note>Girolamo Savonarola (1452–1498), the Dominican friar and reformist leader in Florence.</note> and reported to him—in order to give more weight to what he had already made public—that the deceased had appeared to him surrounded by fire, confessing that he was still paying the penalty for his ingratitude. 

Moreover, a certain nun, famous for many prophecies, who had predicted many future things to Pico himself while he was alive (all of which came to pass exactly), produced this one prediction among others two years before he departed from this life: that at the "time of the lilies," by the work and encouragement of Brother Jerome <note>original: "Hieronymi" — Girolamo Savonarola.</note> (whom we have mentioned), he would dedicate himself to the college of the Friars Preachers <note term="Friars Preachers">The Dominican Order, known for their focus on preaching and scholarship.</note>. At the same time, she predicted that a certain Florentine family (whom they call the Pazzi <note>original: "pactiam"</note>), then living in exile, would return to their homeland. Many to whom this report had reached wondered about this "nomenclature of the lilies," thinking she was speaking of the springtime when lilies bloom. 

But it was discovered that this "Lily" was actually the King of France <note>Charles VIII (1470–1498), whose royal emblem was the fleur-de-lis (the lily).</note>, who entered Florence with a great retinue while making a journey through Tuscany to claim the Kingdom of Naples by force of arms. He arrived on the day before Pico would have professed his religious vows (as he had intended before he died) and four days after that exiled family returned to their home city.

However, before I make an end, I think it not useless to say a few more things at the conclusion <note>original: "in calce" — literally "at the heel."</note> of this work. For I seem to see hounds barking at these revelations as if at the shadow of the moon. A little morsel must be thrown to them (since they are perhaps not content with the previous ones) lest they beat the air with vain barking. I see them shaken with mad laughter; I see sport being made by those who consider themselves "know-it-alls" <note term="sciolos">Those who possess superficial knowledge but claim great expertise.</note>, who will perhaps contend that souls ought not be tortured by fire for an unfulfilled religious vow, and that in our time, men inspired by the divine spirit who enjoy conversations with Christ are not to be found. 

But if they considered that sins worthy not of death but of pardon <note>The author is distinguishing between "mortal" sins (punishable by death/Hell) and "venial" sins (purgable by fire).</note> are to be punished by the fire of purgatory, they would not wonder that the just must also pay penalties. Likewise, they cannot be ignorant—as Truth itself <note>A common title for Jesus Christ in theological texts.</note> testifies—that the servant who knows the master's will and does not fulfill it will be beaten many times. Thus, for this man who knew God's will and delayed in fulfilling it, it is not revealed as an ecstasy, but as a suffering of punishment, even if he were immune from every other fault. 

On the other hand, I cannot wonder enough at the crude and insipid cunning of those who, while they believe that Christ died for men, do not believe that he can easily speak to those same men. They argue vehemently that mortal men cannot become participants in the speech of the Virgin Mother, the angels, or the blessed spirits. Surely they ought to notice that all inferior things are governed by superior things, as witnessed by Dionysius the Areopagite <note>A Christian theologian and philosopher of the 5th–6th century, whose works on "Celestial Hierarchy" were foundational to medieval angelology.</note> in his book *On the Celestial Hierarchy*. Spirits of an inferior grade and nature, to whom the care of men is entrusted, are illuminated by superior minds, which in turn draw divine mysteries either from the highest ranks or from God himself. Thus, men inspired by the divine spirit receive these same revelations to be revealed to the multitude of men when it is expedient. This is the sacrosanct law of divinity, as we are taught by the same Dionysius in his book *On the Celestial Hierarchy*: that through the first things, the following things are raised up toward the most august light. Those who deny this are undoubtedly ignorant of the divine scriptures...

There, in ineffable **divinity** <note>original: "diuinitate"</note>, he shall enjoy without end that which will also bring us help day by day.

# THE SEVEN-FOLD EXPOSITION OF GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA ON THE SIX DAYS OF GENESIS, ADDRESSED TO LORENZO DE' MEDICI.

-> PREFACE <-

<margin>m</margin>
**E**MULATION OF YOUR STUDIES, **Lorenzo de' Medici**, has moved me to review the secret volumes of **Moses** <note>The first five books of the Bible, traditionally attributed to Moses.</note>: for last winter, I noticed that in whatever leisure you were granted from the affairs of the state, you applied yourself nowhere more greatly or more willingly than to that reading. Then, a private reason also invited me to the same task: because for another work of mine—begun long ago under your auspices, but growing in your name—I have attempted to defend the Davidic hymns <note>The Psalms.</note> (translated by the **Seventy** <note>The Septuagint (LXX), the influential Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible.</note> and continually sung in the Church) not only from all suspicion and slander, but also to illuminate them with the torches of interpretation. For that work, no treatment is found more useful, none more fruitful, and none more consistent—or to speak more truly, more necessary—than a study of these books of Moses.

<margin>That the mysteries of all nature are in the Genesis of Moses.</margin>
It happened, moreover, during these days, that I was diligent in the study of the fabric of the world and those celebrated works of the six days. Great reasons present themselves for us to believe that the secrets of all nature are contained within them.

<margin>Moses was the most learned by the testimony of all.</margin>
For, to omit the fact that our prophet, full of God and at the dictation of the heavenly spirit, received these things from the mistress of all truth, have not the testimonies of our own people, of his own people, and finally of the gentiles, proclaimed him to be most skilled in human wisdom and in all doctrines and literature?

<margin>The legitimate book of Solomon which is called Wisdom</margin>
There exists among the Hebrews a book by that most wise **Solomon**, titled *Wisdom*—not the one currently in circulation which is the work of **Philo** <note>Philo of Alexandria, a Jewish philosopher; Pico is distinguishing between the canonical Book of Wisdom and a different tradition.</note>, but another composed in the more secret language of Jerusalem—in which that man, an interpreter of the nature of things as is believed, confesses that he received all such discipline from the inner recesses of the **Mosaic law**.

<margin>Why Moses appears unrefined and popular</margin>
Likewise, as far as our own authors are concerned, **Luke** <note>Referring to Acts 7:22, "Moses was educated in all the wisdom of the Egyptians."</note> and Philo are most weighty authorities that he was most learned in the universal doctrine of the Egyptians. Moreover, all those Greeks who were considered more divine—**Pythagoras, Plato, Empedocles, and Democritus**—employed Egyptian teachers. That saying of **Numenius** the philosopher is well known: that Plato is nothing other than an **Attic Moses** <note>original: "atticum Mosem" — meaning an Athenian version of Moses.</note>.

<margin>The custom of the ancients in writing divine things</margin>
<margin>Mysteries</margin>
<margin>Gymnosophists</margin>
<margin>Egyptians</margin>
<margin>Pythagoras</margin>
<margin>Golden Verses</margin>
<margin>Philolaus</margin>
<margin>Lysis</margin>
<margin>Hipparchus</margin>
But even **Hermippus** the Pythagorean attests that Pythagoras transferred many things from the Mosaic law into his own philosophy. But if, meanwhile, Moses appears in his books to be unrefined and popular <note>Written for the common people rather than scholars.</note> rather than a philosopher, a theologian, or a master of some great wisdom, let us recall that it was a celebrated custom of the ancient sages to write of divine things in such a way that they either did not write clearly at all, or they wrote dissemblingly. Hence they were called "mysteries," for they were not mysteries if they were not hidden. This was observed by the **Indians**, by the **Ethiopians** (who are called **Gymnosophists** <note>Ancient Indian philosophers known for their asceticism and nudity.</note> from their nakedness), and by the Egyptians. This is also what those **Sphinxes** placed before the temples signified. Taught by them, Pythagoras became a master of silence, nor did he himself commit anything to writing except for a very few things which he commended to his daughter **Damo** as he was dying. For the **Golden Verses** <note>A collection of moral exhortations.</note> which are circulated are not by Pythagoras, as is commonly persuaded even among the more learned, but by Phi... <note>Pico is likely about to name Philolaus.</note>

<summary>In this preface to the Heptaplus, Pico della Mirandola addresses Lorenzo de' Medici, explaining that the Book of Genesis contains hidden natural and divine secrets. He argues that Moses was the source of wisdom for ancient Greek philosophers like Plato and Pythagoras, but wrote in a "veiled" style to protect these sacred mysteries from the uninitiated.</summary>
<keywords>Heptaplus, Lorenzo de' Medici, Moses, Genesis, secret wisdom, Egyptian doctrine, Pythagoras, Plato, mysteries, Hermeticism, Septuagint</keywords>

--- Page 28 ---
<meta>This page continues Pico’s defense of the "Heptaplus," his seven-fold interpretation of the creation story in Genesis. Having addressed Lorenzo de' Medici in the previous page, he now argues that divine truth is naturally hidden behind allegories, citing both Greek philosophers and Christian tradition to justify his search for "secret" meanings in the text of Moses.</meta>

<margin>
Lysis, Hipparchus, Ammonius, Origen, Plotinus, Herennius, Porphyry; the writing style of Plato; Jesus Christ; the Gospel
</margin>
...of the people. Thereafter, the Pythagoreans most religiously guarded that law <note>The "law" refers to the Pythagorean tradition of keeping philosophical secrets from the uninitiated.</note>. **Lysis** complained that it had been violated by **Hipparchus**. Finally, **Porphyry** is the authority that the disciples of **Ammonius**—namely **Origen**, **Plotinus**, and **Herennius**—were bound by an oath regarding this practice. Our **Plato** also concealed his dogmas within the wrappings of enigmas, the veil of fables, mathematical images, and under the obscure signs of retreating meanings. He himself said in his letters that no one would openly understand his true opinion on divine matters from what he had written, and he proved this to those who were less believing. Therefore, if for this reason we think the reading of **Moses** is common or trite because its outward surface contains nothing extraordinary, we would by the same example condemn all the ancient philosophers for crudeness and ignorance—the very men we venerate as the masters of all wisdom. Indeed, we see this same practice observed in the Church. **Jesus Christ**, the image of God’s substance, did not write the Gospel; rather, he preached it. Moreover, he preached to the crowds in parables, but separately to a few disciples, to whom it was given to know the mysteries of the kingdom of heaven, openly and without figures. Yet he did not reveal everything even to those few, because they were not capable of everything and there were many things they could not bear until the coming Spirit taught them all truth. If those few chosen disciples out of so many thousands could not bear many things, how could the entire Israelite crowd—the sausage-makers, cooks, butchers, shepherds, and male and female servants, to all of whom the Law was given to be read—have been able to bear the burden of all Mosaic, or rather divine, wisdom?

<margin>Why Moses’s face was veiled</margin>
Moses indeed stood upon the height of the mountain—that very mountain where the Lord also often spoke to his disciples—and, illuminated by the light of the divine sun, his whole face shone in a wonderful manner. But because the people, with their blinking and night-owl eyes, could not bear the light, he spoke his words to them with a veiled face. Let us return to our own teachers.

<margin>Matthew was the first to write a Gospel. John</margin>
**Matthew** was the first to write a Gospel; and as the prophet says, "hiding the words of God in his heart so that he might not sin," <note>A reference to Psalm 119:11.</note> he followed the history of those things which pertained only to the humanity of **Christ**, so that the memory of his deeds would not be lost to oblivion. For this reason, in the mystical vision of **Ezekiel**, we understand him through the figure of the **man** <note>In traditional Christian iconography, the four Evangelists are linked to the four creatures in Ezekiel's vision: the Man (Matthew), the Lion (Mark), the Ox (Luke), and the Eagle (John).</note>. **John**, who more than all others revealed the secrets of divinity, did so only after the three Gospels had already been published and many years had passed since the Lord’s cross. He was compelled to speak the things he had long kept silent in order to abolish the heresy of the **Ebionites** <note>An early Jewish Christian sect that viewed Jesus as a human prophet rather than divine.</note>, who maintained that Christ was a man but not also God. He spoke regarding the eternal generation of the Son, but did so to a few and obscurely. He began: *In the beginning was the Word.*

<margin>Ebionites, Paul, Dionysius</margin>
**Paul** denied "solid food" to the Corinthians because they still lived by the laws of the flesh and not by the spirit; he spoke "wisdom among the perfect." The disciple of Paul, **Dionysius the Areopagite** <note>A 1st-century convert of St. Paul, though the writings attributed to him (the Pseudo-Dionysian Corpus) are now dated to the late 5th century. He was a major authority on mystical theology.</note>, writes that it was a holy and established custom in the churches that the more secret dogmas should not be communicated through letters, but only by voice to those who had been properly initiated. I have pursued these points at length because there are many who, drawing their argument from the "rough bark" of the literal words, despise and scorn the Book of Moses as something commonplace and trivial. To them, nothing is less credible than that it possesses something more divine in its inner depths than what it promises on its face.

<margin>Among all the books of Moses, this one is the chief</margin>
If that has been sufficiently refuted, it is now easy to believe that he treated nature and the craftsmanship of the entire world. That is, if in any part of his work—as if in some field—treasures of all true philosophy have been buried by him. This was done primarily in this part, where he treated most loftily the emanation of all things from God, the degree, the number, and the order of the parts of the world...

<summary>Pico argues that Moses, like the great Greek philosophers and the authors of the Gospels, hid profound "divine secrets" beneath a simple literal surface to protect them from the uninitiated. He justifies his esoteric interpretation of Genesis by comparing Moses's veiled face to the parables of Jesus and the mystical silence of the early Church.</summary>
<keywords>Pico della Mirandola, Heptaplus, esoteric wisdom, allegorical interpretation, Pythagoras, Plato, Moses, Gospels, Ebionites, Dionysius the Areopagite, Neoplatonism</keywords>

--- Page 29 ---
<meta>This page continues Pico della Mirandola’s introduction to the Heptaplus. He has just explained that divine mysteries are intentionally hidden. Now, he addresses the daunting task of writing a new commentary on the Creation (Genesis) despite the immense library of existing scholarship by Christian, Greek, and Jewish authors.</meta>

<sig>A ii</sig>

...philosophizes. For this reason, there was a decree of the ancient Hebrews—which <margin>Jerome</margin> **Jerome** also mentions—that no one should touch upon this story of the creation of the world until they had reached a mature age. I will perhaps seem, therefore, to have done something worthwhile if I have lingered longer, with more exact care and more labor (as far as my own weakness allowed), to investigate the meaning of the reading of **Moses** with great study. <margin>Why he dared to write after so many interpreters.</margin> When I saw that many Latin and Greek authors had worked on this explanation—and besides them, almost innumerable ancient and modern Chaldean <note>Refers to Aramaic translations and paraphrases of the Bible known as Targums.</note> and Hebrew interpreters—I did not even dare to think of writing or commenting on anything new regarding this matter. However, I remembered that it was cautioned in the <term>Mosaic Law</term><note>Refers to the practice of "gleaning" from Leviticus 19:9-10, where farmers were commanded not to harvest the very edges of their fields so the poor could gather the leftovers.</note> that no one should reap their field entirely and completely, but should leave an untouched portion of it for the poor and the needy, so they might take <term>sheaves</term><note>original: "mergites"</note> and handfuls from there to satisfy their hunger. When this came to mind, I began to survey the vast fields of the Prophet <note>Moses is frequently referred to by Pico as "the Prophet."</note> with searching eyes, to see whether the most learned interpreters—who were no less cultivators of the Law than its interpreters—had, according to the edict of the Law, left some part untouched for us, who are as it were the weaker ones, to reap. From there, I too might pluck a few ears of grain to be placed on the altars of the Church as the firstfruits of the harvest, so that I might not be excluded from the privileges of the temple as if I were not a true Israelite or one who <term>contributes nothing</term> <note>original: "asymbolus"; a Greek term for a guest who does not pay his share of a meal.</note>. The matter succeeded according to my wish; not because I can achieve anything that they could not, but because they, following the precept of the Law, chose not to block the way for the industry of those who came after. Furthermore, such is the vastness and fertility of that field that no number of harvesters could ever be enough for it. Even though nearly infinite and most capable minds have exercised themselves in it with all their strength, we can still say that phrase from the Gospel: <note>original: "Messis multa operarii pauci"</note> *The harvest is plentiful, but the laborers are few.* Therefore, those things which the most holy men <margin>Latin interpreters</margin> **Ambrose** and **Augustine**, and likewise **Strabo**, **Bede**, and **Remigius**, and among the younger ones **Giles** and **Albert**, have written on this book; and likewise among the <margin>Greek interpreters</margin> Greeks, what **Philo**, **Origen**, **Basil**, **Theodoret**, **Apollinaris**, **Didymus**, **Diodore**, **Severus**, **Eusebius**, **Josephus**, **Gennadius**, and **Chrysostom** have written—all these will be left entirely untouched by us. <margin>He will bring nothing from those things which others have already brought</margin> For it would be both reckless and superfluous for a weak man to exert himself in that part of the field where the most robust minds have already worked long ago. Likewise, regarding those things which <margin>Chaldean interpreters</margin> **Jonathan**, **Onkelos**, or the ancient **Simeon** <note>Likely referring to Simeon bar Yochai, traditionally the author of the Zohar.</note> handed down in Aramaic, or those which the <margin>Hebrew interpreters</margin> Hebrews—either the ancients like **Eleazar**, **Abba**, **John**, **Nehunia**, **Isaac**, and **Joseph**, or the younger ones like **Gersonides** <note>Levi ben Gershom.</note>, **Saadia**, the two **Abrahams**, the two **Moseses** <note>Likely referring to Maimonides and Nahmanides.</note>, **Solomon** <note>Solomon ben Isaac, known as Rashi.</note>, and **Menahem**—have composed, we shall make no mention for the present. <margin>Seven new expositions</margin> Instead, we shall bring forth, beyond all these, seven other expositions of our own, discovered and meditated upon. In these, we shall first take care to overcome, if we can, <margin>Three difficulties in the explanation of this book</margin> three difficulties with which there seems to have been a great and difficult struggle for all those who undertook to explain this book. <margin>First</margin> The first is to prevent anything said by Moses from appearing either insufficiently supported or lacking in learning and wisdom. Some have freed themselves from this problem by the following reasoning: they claim he did not speak of everything, nor did he bring forth grand and sublime things, because he was speaking to a <term>rough people</term><note>A common medieval trope suggesting that the ancient Israelites were intellectually unready for high philosophy, necessitating a simpler literal text.</note> who were not sufficiently capable of understanding everything. We can believe that the unlearned audience was satisfied if he drew a veil over the light of knowledge—which the wise would look into—surrounding it with "thick words" as if with a <term>horn-lantern</term><note>original: "cornea testa"; a lantern made of translucent horn which softened the glare of the candle inside.</note>, so that weaker eyes would not be dazzled. Thus, he brought light to benefit healthy eyes, yet he brought it enclosed and veiled so as not to harm those with weak vision. Nor...

<summary>Pico explains that he is offering seven new interpretations of Genesis, not to compete with the vast tradition of Christian and Jewish scholars, but to harvest the "gleanings" they left behind. He identifies the first major challenge of the text: reconciling its seemingly simple language with the profound divine wisdom it contains.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the preface of the Heptaplus. Pico has been discussing his hesitation to write a new commentary on the creation of the world (Genesis) given the many existing works. He now shifts to describing the three specific challenges he faced in this project and dedicating the work to his patron, Lorenzo de' Medici.</meta>

<margin>The second difficulty</margin> For indeed, he <note>Referring to Moses, whom Pico calls "the Prophet."</note> either ought to, could, or wished to help the learned less than the unlearned. The second difficulty is that the tenor of the interpretation must be consistent with itself, fitting in its parts, and as if drawn with a single stroke, so that the entire sequence is referred back to that same primary sense from which it first proceeded. Nor, if we perhaps introduce him speaking of <term>Ideas</term><note>Pico uses "Ideas" in the Platonic sense—the eternal, perfect archetypes of things that exist in the divine mind.</note> here, should we want him to deal with the elements in the next clause, or with man in the one after that. This would be an arbitrary and violent kind of exposition. Yet, to avoid this in the narration of this book has seemed to many—not to say difficult—assuredly laborious to everyone.

<margin>How difficult the undertaking is</margin> So great is the perplexity, so great the ambiguity, and so great the variety of the entire reading. See how much labor it is, and how far from easy it is to achieve what we have conceived in our mind (may we attain it!): that we might explain this whole creation of the world not by one sense alone, but by a sevenfold sense, always beginning a new work from the start in a continuous and unmixed order of exposition.

<margin>The third difficulty</margin> While using nothing from the works of previous interpreters. The third difficulty lies in this: that we do not make the Prophet—or rather the Divine Spirit through the Prophet—assert anything foreign, prodigious, or alien to the nature of things as they are now seen, or to the truth found by the best philosophers and accepted by our own thinkers. But why we have brought forward seven expositions, for what reason they were undertaken, what our plan is, <margin>The reason for undertaking the commentary</margin> and what necessity drove us to them, and what is entirely new in what we strive to bring forth, we shall make clear in the following chapter. In that chapter, painting the **Idea** of one who would write most perfectly on this matter—that is, on the creation of the world—in imitation of nature itself, we shall then try to prove in what follows that our Prophet has fallen short of that archetype in no respect. <margin>Moses is the ideal of writing correctly about nature</margin> Rather, he has attained it in every detail, so that nothing else should be proposed as such an **Idea** than the man himself; and we can all more easily admire his greatness than estimate it according to his worth. 

These works of ours, whatever they may be—the fruits of our youth—are owed to you, **Lorenzo** <note>Lorenzo de' Medici (1449–1492), known as "the Magnificent," the ruler of Florence and Pico's patron.</note>, most illustrious man; both because they are mine, and I have long ago dedicated and vowed myself to you, and because you yourself prepared for us that leisure of the **Fiesolan retreat** <note>The Villa Medici at Fiesole, where Pico and his circle of humanist friends often met to study.</note> in which they were born. <margin>Angelo Poliziano</margin> This retreat is also seasoned by the frequent intervention, or rather the constant presence, of your friend **Angelo Poliziano** <note>A famous Italian humanist, poet, and close friend of both Lorenzo and Pico.</note>, whose delightful and fertile genius, which previously produced various flowers of literature, now, as I judge, promises the solid and mature fruit of philosophy. 

Furthermore, it is customary that when something festive or joyful happens to those we love or revere, we should not only congratulate them with words but also favor their happiness, so to speak, with some gift, and make our heart's joy known to them. <margin>Giovanni de' Medici, cardinal</margin> Opportunely, therefore, this late-night study of ours comes to you at the time when your son **Giovanni** <note>Giovanni de' Medici, who would later become Pope Leo X.</note> has been appointed to the highest college of Christian orders by the Supreme Pontiff **Innocent VIII** <margin>Innocent VIII</margin> at an age like no one before him; both his own character, which promises all good things for itself, and your merits and authority rightly and deservedly demand this for him. It remains for us to hope that he shows himself worthy of this dignity. This he will do if he follows his father, who is both the author of his dignity and the exemplar of his life—that is, of prudence and all virtue. **Farewell.**

<meta>This page continues the "Other Preface" of the Heptaplus. In the previous section, Pico discussed the difficulties of interpreting the creation story in Genesis. Here, he begins to lay the cosmological foundation for his sevenfold interpretation by describing the three-tiered structure of the universe.</meta>

<sig>A iii</sig>

### ANOTHER PREFACE TO THE ENTIRE WORK.

<margin>
The three levels and differences of the worlds

The angelic world

The celestial

The sublunary

Why the sky is called "shamayim" by the Hebrews

In the tabernacle of Moses, the three worlds were prefigured

Latin, Greek, and Hebrew interpreters

What the tearing of the veil at Christ's death signifies
</margin>

**ANTIQUITY** depicts three worlds: The highest of all is the ultra-mundane, which theologians call the angelic and philosophers call the intellectual. Plato says in the *Phaedrus* that no one has yet sung of it worthily enough. Next to this is the celestial; the last of all is the sublunary, this one which we inhabit. This is the world of shadows; that one, however, is of light; the sky <note>The celestial world</note> is tempered from both light and shadows. This world is marked by waters because of its flowing and unstable substance; that one by fire because of the brilliance of its light and the height of its place. The sky, being of a middle nature, is therefore called *shamayim* <note>original: "sciamiam"</note> by the Hebrews, as if from *esh* <note>original: "es," meaning fire</note> and *mayim* <note>original: "maim," meaning water</note>—that is, composed of the fire and water we mentioned. Here there is an alternation of life and death; there, perpetual life and stable activity; in the sky, there is stability of life but an alternation of activities and locations <note>Referring to the constant, circular motion of the planets and stars.</note>. This world is made of the decaying substance of bodies; that one of the nature of the divine mind; the sky is made of body, but incorruptible, and of mind, but bound to a body. The third is moved by the second; the second is ruled by the first; and there are many other differences between them which I do not intend to recount here, where we are merely skimming the surface rather than flooding the reader with detail.

I should not omit that these three worlds were most evidently prefigured by Moses in the construction of that admirable tabernacle of his. For he divided the tabernacle into three parts, which could not more expressively represent the three worlds we have mentioned. For the first part, protected by no roof or shade, was exposed and vulnerable to rains, snow, sun, heat, and cold; it is a clear image of our world—the sublunary world. Not only clean and unclean, sacred and profane men inhabit it, but animals of every kind; and in it, because of the sacrifices and perpetual offerings, there was a constant alternation of life and death. The other two parts were both covered and free on all sides from every outside harm, just as both worlds—the celestial and the super-celestial—are capable of neither injury nor insult. Both were likewise honored with the name of holiness, yet in such a way that the one which was more secret was called the "Holy of Holies," while the other was adorned only with the title "Holy." Similarly, although both the celestial and angelic worlds are holy—since above the moon, after the fall of Lucifer, neither stain nor sin exists or can exist—the angelic world is held to be far holier and more divine than the celestial. 

But why do we pursue these more remote similarities? For if the last part of the tabernacle was common to men and beasts, the second part—which shone entirely with the brilliance of gold—was illuminated by a candelabra distinguished by seven lamps, which, as all Latin, Greek, and Hebrew interpreters say, signify the seven planets. In the third part, the most sacred of all, were the winged <term>cherubim</term><note>The highest rank of angels, often associated with divine wisdom and guarding the presence of God.</note>. Do these not place our three worlds before our eyes? This one which both beasts and men inhabit, the celestial in which the planets flash, and the super-celestial dwelling of the angels. We are also reminded here of a higher Gospel mystery. For since the way to the super-celestial world and the company of angels has been opened to us through the cross and blood of Christ, therefore, when he died, the veil of the temple was torn—the veil by which the Holy of Holies (which we said signifies the angelic world) was closed off from the other parts. This was a sign that the way is now open for man to the kingdom of God, to God himself.

<summary>Pico explains the Neoplatonic division of the universe into the sublunary, celestial, and angelic worlds, arguing that Moses represented this structure through the three sections of the Tabernacle. He concludes by interpreting the tearing of the Temple veil as the opening of the angelic realm to humanity through Christ.</summary>
<keywords>cosmology, three worlds, sublunary, celestial, angelic, Moses, Tabernacle, shamayim, Holy of Holies, cherubim, Christ’s sacrifice</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Pico della Mirandola's "Other Preface" to the Heptaplus. Having established the three worlds (angelic, celestial, and sublunary), he now explains the Neoplatonic principle of "all things in all things," which allows for the allegorical interpretation of Scripture.</meta>

...who flies above the cherubim, the entrance to which has been closed from the beginning by the laws of justice because of the sin of our first parent. This is enough concerning the three worlds. In these, we must first and foremost observe—as our entire project depends on this—that **these three worlds are actually one world**. This is true not only because they are all traced back to one principle and the same end, or because they are bound together by appropriate proportions, a certain harmonic kinship of nature, and an orderly series of steps; it is also because whatever exists in all the worlds together is also contained in each individual one. There is not one among them in which everything found in the others does not also exist. This, I believe, was the opinion of **Anaxagoras** <note>An ancient Greek philosopher who famously taught that "everything is in everything."</note>, if we assume his view was correctly understood and subsequently explained by the **Pythagoreans** and **Platonists**. 

<margin>That every world is in every other world</margin>
<margin>Three reasons why the world is one</margin>
<margin>Anaxagoras</margin>
<margin>Pythagoreans</margin>
<margin>Platonists</margin>
<margin>How the worlds are within one another</margin>

Truly, those things which are in the lower world are also in the higher ones, but in a better state; likewise, those things in the higher worlds are also seen in the lowest, but in a degenerate condition and with a "bastardized" nature, so to speak. Among us, heat is an elemental quality; in the heavens, it is a heating power; in the angelic minds, it is the Idea of heat. Let me speak more clearly: among us, there is **fire**, which is an element. The **Sun** is fire in the heavens. In the ultra-mundane region, there is the **seraphic fire** of the intellect. But see how they differ: the elemental fire burns; the celestial fire gives life; the super-celestial fire loves. 

<margin>An example of the proposed truth</margin>

There is **water** among us; there is water in the heavens, whose mover and mistress is the moon (the vestibule of the heavens); and there are waters above the heavens—the **cherubic minds**. But see the disparity of condition in the same nature: elemental moisture overwhelms the heat of life; celestial moisture nourishes it; super-celestial moisture understands it.

<margin>The ten spheres of the intellectual world</margin>

In the first world, **God**, the primary Unity, presides over nine orders of angels (as if they were spheres) and, being unmoved himself, he moves them all toward himself. 

<margin>The ten spheres of the celestial world</margin>

In the middle world—the celestial—the **Empyrean heaven** <note>The highest, most outer part of the physical universe in medieval cosmology, thought to be the abode of God.</note> likewise presides as a leader over nine celestial spheres. While each of these revolves with unceasing motion, that heaven remains unmoved, imitating God. 

<margin>The ten spheres of the elementary world</margin>

In the elementary world, beneath **prime matter** <note>original: "materia prima," the formless "stuff" from which all physical things are made.</note> which is its foundation, there are also nine spheres of corruptible forms: 

<margin>Body</margin>
<margin>Nature</margin>
<margin>Soul</margin>
<margin>Each of these is divided into three</margin>

1.  Three spheres of bodies lacking life: the elements, the mixtures, and those things in between which are mixed but imperfect (such as the impressions formed in the upper air).
2.  Three spheres of the **vegetable nature**, which is first divided into three types: herbs, shrubs, and trees.
3.  Three spheres of the **sensual soul**: that which is imperfect (as in **zoophytes** <note>original: "zoophytum"; organisms like coral or sponges that were thought to be half-animal, half-plant.</note>), that which is perfect but remains within the limits of irrational imagination, and that which is the highest in brutes, being even capable of human instruction. This last is a middle point between man and beast, just as the zoophyte is a middle point between beast and plant.

But enough of these things, perhaps more than was necessary. We should only add that the mutual containment of these worlds is indicated in the Holy Scriptures. For it is written in the Psalms: "Who created the heavens in understanding" <note>Psalm 136:5. Pico reads "intellectu" as referring to the Intellectual/Angelic world.</note>, and we read that the angels of God are "spirits" and his ministers a "flame of burning fire."

<margin>Evidence from the Holy Scriptures</margin>
<margin>Only the most learned men can correctly write or interpret allegories</margin>

Because of this, celestial names are often given to divine things, and even earthly names: at one moment they are figured as stars, at another as wheels, or animals, or elements. Conversely, celestial names are often given to earthly things. For since all these worlds are bound by the chains of concord, they grant each other their names just as they do their natures, through a mutual generosity. 

From this principle—if perhaps someone has not yet noticed it—the entire discipline of the **allegorical sense** flowed. Nor could the ancient fathers have decently represented one thing by another through different figures, except by having learned the hidden alliances and affinities of all nature. Otherwise, there would be no reason why they should represent this thing by this image rather than another.

<summary>Pico explains that the three worlds (Angelic, Celestial, and Elemental) are unified because every entity in one has a corresponding version in the others. This cosmic "correspondence" is the philosophical foundation that allows the Bible to use physical metaphors to describe divine realities.</summary>
<keywords>correspondence, allegory, macrocosm, microcosm, spheres, zoophyte, Seraphim, Cherubim, Anaxagoras, Neoplatonism</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the "Other Preface" to Pico della Mirandola's Heptaplus. After describing the three cosmic worlds (angelic, celestial, and sublunary) and the principle that "all is in all," Pico now introduces a fourth world—Man—and explains how these four worlds provide the foundation for his multi-layered interpretation of the Book of Genesis.</meta>

...to represent them, unless they were taught the secret—so to speak—friendships and affinities of all nature. Otherwise, there would be no reason why they would have represented this thing by this image rather than another, or vice versa. But being experts in all things and driven by that spirit which not only knows all these things but created them, they most aptly depicted the natures of one world through those things they knew corresponded to them in the other worlds. Therefore, the same knowledge is required (unless the same spirit is also present) for those who wish to correctly interpret their figures and allegorical meanings. 

Besides the three we have described, there is
<margin>The fourth world</margin>
another fourth world in which all those things found in the others are also discovered. This
<margin>Man as every creature</margin>
is man himself, who, for this reason—as Catholic doctors say—is designated in the Gospel by the term "every creature." For while the Gospel must be preached to men, and not to brutes and angels, the command to preach to "every creature" is nonetheless demanded by Christ. 
<margin>How man is the lesser world</margin>
It is a common saying in the schools that man is a **lesser world** <term>microcosm</term>, in whom is seen a body mixed from the elements, a celestial spirit, the vegetative soul of plants, the senses of brutes, reason, the angelic mind, and the likeness of God. 

<margin>That Moses treated all these worlds</margin>
If we establish these four worlds, it is credible that Moses, who was going to speak sufficiently about the world, discussed all of these. And since a writer will depict nature if he is skilled in nature—such as we believe this man of ours was, if ever any was—it is credible that his teaching about them was arranged no differently than the Almighty God, the Craftsman, arranged them in themselves. Thus, this scripture of Moses is a truly expressed image of the world, just as we read he was commanded on the mountain where he learned these things to "make everything according to the pattern" <note>This refers to Exodus 25:40, where God instructs Moses to build the Tabernacle according to the heavenly pattern shown to him.</note> he had seen on the mountain. 

<margin>This Scripture is an image of nature</margin>
First, therefore, what is greatest of all: just as we showed that the things in all worlds are contained in each individual one,
<margin>No part of the work in which all worlds are not treated simultaneously</margin>
Moses, as an emulator of nature, ought never to treat any one of those worlds without simultaneously and equally treating all of them under the same words and context. From this, a **fourfold exposition** of the entire Mosaic reading immediately arises, so that in the first place, we narrate whatever is written there concerning the angelic and invisible world, making no mention of the others. Second, likewise, we narrate everything concerning the celestial world; then concerning this sublunary and corruptible world; fourth, concerning the nature of man. 
<margin>The root of the fourfold exposition</margin>

For if the intelligible world <note>The "intelligible world" refers to the realm of ideas and angelic intellects.</note>, for example, is never discussed without the Scripture reminding us of the other worlds (just as that world contains all subsequent natures within itself), we certainly can—indeed, we must—interpret every part regarding all of them. Again, just as 
<margin>The root of the fifth exposition</margin>
the natures are mutually contained within one another in a promiscuous way, yet have obtained distinct proper seats and certain peculiar laws, so too, if the quadruple nature is discussed in the same series of letters in each part of the present work, it must be believed that the first nature is treated more particularly in the first part, and so on in the same order through the rest. From this arises the necessity of a **fifth exposition**. 

<margin>The root of the sixth exposition</margin>
Furthermore, by the same reasoning that these things are distinct, because there is no multitude that is not one, they are bound together by a certain **discordant concord** <term>concordia discors; the harmony of opposites</term> and are bound fast by multiform chains of connections. Since it is likely that Moses deals with this throughout the whole work, he calls us to the interpretation of the text even if we are unwilling. In this, we shall show there are fifteen modes by which we can understand one thing as related or joined to another. 
<margin>The root of the seventh exposition</margin>
And since there are no more, the prophet has expressed them all so sufficiently and clearly that **Aristotle** <note>The Greek philosopher often cited as the ultimate authority on natural science in Pico's time.</note> never wrote anything more clearly about the nature of things. Finally, just as the Sabbath—that is, rest—follows the six days of Genesis...

<summary>Pico identifies man as the "fourth world" or microcosm and argues that Moses's writing in Genesis mirrors the interconnected structure of the entire universe. This provides the basis for a multi-layered interpretation—including the "fourfold" and "fifth" expositions—where every word of Scripture describes all worlds simultaneously.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the "Other Preface" of Pico della Mirandola's Heptaplus. After establishing that the four worlds (angelic, celestial, sublunary, and the human microcosm) are interconnected, Pico now explains his plan for a "sabbatic" (seventh) exposition that reveals Christ and the Church hidden within Moses's account of creation.</meta>

It is fitting that we also—after the preceding orders of things distributed by God have been arranged, and their union, difference, covenants, and relationships have been explained—should now touch upon some things in this seventh and (if I may say so) **sabbatic** <note>original: "sabbataria"; Pico refers to the seventh and final section of his book, mirroring the Sabbath or seventh day of rest</note> exposition. This section concerns the happiness of creatures and the return to God, which falls to man through the Mosaic and Christian laws after he was distanced from God by the sin of our first parent. We shall report those things which Moses most clearly hid in the present scripture, so that it may become plain that a most express prophecy is read here concerning the coming of Christ, the progress of the Church, and the calling of the Gentiles. Thus, this book—if any other is such—is truly a **book sealed with seven seals** <note>A reference to the Book of Revelation 5:1, implying the text contains hidden divine secrets</note>, full of every doctrine and all mysteries.

However, we will not imitate those who, when they occasionally set out to explain this creation of the world, gathered here whatever had been disputed among philosophers and theologians concerning God, angels, matter, heaven, and all of nature. In this,
<margin>Isaac the Persian / Samuel Ophinides</margin>
Isaac the Persian and Samuel Ophinides <note>original: "Isaac Persa / Samuel ophinides"; these refer to medieval Jewish commentators, likely Isaac of Fez and Samuel ibn Tibbon</note> especially erred. Instead, we shall strive to the best of our ability to declare only what the Mosaic letter intends, and what the context of the words either indicates or signifies. Nor, if we show that the **firmament** <term>the sphere of the fixed stars</term> signifies, for instance, the eighth sphere, will we immediately begin a dispute about how it carries the other spheres, how many signs or images it is distinguished by, or whether it rotates with a simple motion, or rather two, or more truly three. Or, if in some passage we say the human soul is indicated, we will not digress to clarify everything written about the soul; rather, we will note only those things about each subject briefly and in passing which the author seems to make express mention of.

<margin>These things are written for the learned, not those ignorant of philosophy</margin>
I said "briefly and in passing" because the intention of this work is not that those who have not learned these things elsewhere should learn them here for the first time. Rather, it is so that they may recognize the truths they already know in the words of the Prophet; and that, understanding how the things they have read at length in the volumes of theologians and philosophers are here both contained and hidden in few words, they may hear the law-giver speaking with a "revealed face." 

But if anyone, perhaps moved by a spirit of "holy rusticity" <note>original: "sanctæ rusticitatis"; a common term in the Renaissance for pious simplicity or "holy ignorance" that prefers faith over complex philosophy</note>, does not approve of these more deeply sought mysteries, but instead desires a simpler explanation of the sacred context more suited to himself,
<margin>Paul</margin>
I will bid him first to remember Paul's instruction: that neither he who eats should despise him who does not eat, nor he who does not eat judge him who eats.
<margin>Augustine</margin>
Then I will address him not with my own words, but with those of Augustine from his own exposition on Genesis, in this manner: "If you can grasp these things, do so; if you cannot yet, leave them to those more capable. Indeed, you may make progress as the Scripture does not fail your weakness, walking more slowly with you with a motherly gait." 
<margin>The power of Scripture</margin>
For Scripture speaks in such a way as to mock the proud with its height, terrify the attentive with its depth, feed the great with truth, and nurture the small with affability. But let us return to ourselves and, beginning from this corruptible world that we inhabit, let us provide as much as we are able what we have promised. Otherwise, even in great things, it is enough to have willed them; and, 
<margin>Pomerius</margin>
as Pomerius <note>original: "Pomerius"; Julianus Pomerius, a 5th-century Christian writer</note> says, a great effort in great matters is itself progress.

->The Mosaic words to be explained.<-

## FIRST EXPOSITION ON THE ELEMENTARY WORLD.
### Chapter One of the First Book.

<margin>
On the principles of <term>corruptible things</term> <note>In Renaissance philosophy, "corruptible things" refers to anything in the physical world made of the four elements that can decay, die, or change.</note>
Matter
Privation
Dimensions of matter
Efficient cause
End
</margin>

**NATURAL** Philosophers, when they discuss the nature of corruptible things, generally establish their principles as follows: that there is a crude <term>matter</term> <note>original: "materia"</note> devoid of forms, which is indeed suitable for receiving all forms but by its own nature is deprived of them all. For this reason, besides matter, they also make <term>privation</term> <note>The state of being "without" a specific form or quality.</note> a principle of natural things. <term>Averroes</term> <note>A 12th-century Islamic philosopher from Spain whose commentaries on Aristotle were foundational to Western thought.</note> added that matter is extended in a triple dimension—in length, width, and height—to ensure that corporeal things are not said to be made from an incorporeal subject. Then, they assert a transforming cause which they call the **efficient** cause. By its power, the matter being worked upon—which exists as "potentiality"—becomes "actuality" at some point, just as soft and indefinite wax is transformed into various figures by the movement and touch of a hand according to the will of the one shaping it. However, since nature does nothing at random but rather for the sake of attaining some good, the **final** cause immediately introduces itself. The immediate end (goal) of the acting cause is the **form**, which it draws out from the "bosom of matter." It acts and turns the matter with this purpose: to lead it toward the perfect state of form. Thus, <term>form</term> is established by <term>Aristotle</term> <note>The Greek philosopher whose "Physics" defined the four causes: material, formal, efficient, and final.</note> as the third principle.

<margin>
Form
Dispositions of Matter
</margin>

This form, however, cannot be drawn out from the heart of matter unless the matter is first affected and prepared by appropriate qualities. The entire labor of the craftsman and the entire duration of the action are consumed by these qualities, while the species itself shines forth in an indivisible moment, as if it were the reward of the labor. The <term>Peripatetics</term> <note>Followers of Aristotle, named for his habit of walking while teaching.</note> call the craftsman a cause rather than a principle.

<margin>
Natural causes are the instruments of the divine
</margin>

The divine <term>Platonists</term>, however, always mindful of sacred things, wish for us to be reminded that even if natural acting causes appear to us to be the only things that act upon, form, and transform bodies, they are nevertheless not the *primary* causes of what is made. Instead, they are the **instruments** of the divine art, which they obey and serve. It is just as when a builder's hands, even if they themselves assemble, arrange, and transform all the material of a house—the wood, stones, and mortar—and nothing else seems to be responsible for the making of the house except them; yet we know that those hands are an organ obeying and serving the **art** which resides in the mind of the architect. That art, having conceived of the house as a whole, arranges it piece by piece and unfolds it within the unfeeling material. From this, it follows that the Platonists add two more causes: the **organic** and the **exemplary**.

<margin>
Organic Cause
Exemplary Cause
Agreement of Platonists and Peripatetics
Exposition of the words of Moses
</margin>

The Peripatetics do not deny this; indeed, they confirm it, for among them that saying is common: *Every work of nature is a work of intelligence.* These are the things generally said about corruptible things. Moses so encompassed all of these in his account of the first day that the most esteemed philosophers have said nothing about them more certain or more fitting.

They called the material heaven and earth by these names, as Varro writes, not to mention the Greeks. Indeed, Varro’s reasoning stands firm. For matter is the most <term>despised</term> <note>original: "despicatissima." In this context, it means the lowest in the hierarchy of being, having no shape of its own.</note> of all natures, just as the earth is the most lowly of all elements. They correspond in exactly the same proportion: as the Peripatetics prove, the heaven is the "agent" to the "matter" of the earth. Moreover, this "earth"—that is, matter—is "empty and void," as Jerome translated it, or "invisible and uncomposed," as the <term>Septuagint</term> <note>The influential Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible.</note> has it. All these descriptions suit crude and unformed matter; since it lacks all forms, it is deservedly called "empty and void," and is entirely uncomposed and invisible.

However, the Hebrew words **Tohu** <note>original: "tou"</note> and **Bohu** <note>original: "bou"</note> which are read in this passage are explained differently by many Hebrews. They interpret *Tohu* as a "brute thing," stunned and astonished. This is referred by them to the dark and deformed face of matter for this reason: when we fix our attention on knowing it, it leaves us astonished. Because of this, Aristotle said matter is known "by proportion," and Plato said it is known by a "bastard reason" <note>original: "notha ratione." Plato used this term in the *Timaeus* to describe how we perceive prime matter, which is neither purely sensible nor purely intellectual.</note>. Many explain *Bohu*, however, by the force of the word, as the "inchoation" or the "first rudiment" of a form. Indeed, if we translate word for word, *Bohu* is as if we said "in it is," or "through it something is."

If we follow this, we will understand that beyond the "potentiality" of the subject, there is an "incipient form" within it. This was believed not only by **Albertus Magnus** <note>A 13th-century Dominican friar and philosopher who reconciled Greek science with Christian faith.</note> and many Peripatetics, but also by the ancient Hebrews, as we clearly gather from the records of the most ancient **Simeon** <note>Likely referring to Rabbi Simeon bar Yochai, to whom the authorship of the Zohar was traditionally attributed.</note>. But in what way this "beginning" is to be understood, he declares by adding:
> *And darkness was over the face of the abyss.*
He calls the "abyss" the earth—that is, matter—extended in a triple dimension into the deepest depths. Over this is "darkness"—that is, <term>privation</term> <note>The absence of a form that should naturally be present.</note>. Among the Peripatetics, this is a famous principle, and no name suits it better than "darkness."

<margin>
The arrangements of matter.
The power of the divine agent’s tool.
The agent does not touch matter except through mediating qualities.
</margin>
However, "privation" differs from "negation," as the great Albertus most firmly maintains; it is this very "beginning of form" of which we speak, a matter on which that same philosopher discoursed copiously and subtly. Furthermore, if the earth lies beneath the waters and, being irrigated, then conceives and finally gives birth—would not the "waters" in this passage signify the "accidental qualities" and "affections" of matter? By their flow and tractable nature, they carry the appearance of waters. When matter is "moistened" by these, so to speak, it conceives the form, which it brings forth into the light at the final moment of time. Over these waters, the "Spirit of the Lord"—that is, the power of the Lord’s **efficient cause**, His tool and instrument—is rightly said to be moved. Nor is it said to be moved over the "earth" <note>matter</note> because the "agent" does not touch or permeate the subject except through those mediating qualities.

<margin>
Light arises.
Light is made by God’s command.
One day is made from evening and morning.
One composite made from matter and form.
Light is good.
Epilogue.
</margin>
While it [the Spirit] turns and drives these qualities, **Light** arises—that is, the beauty and appearance of the form, the expeller and putter-to-flight of the "darkness" (which we called privation). And this happens by the voice of God so commanding, because natural causes do nothing that the order of the **Divine Art** has not first prescribed. Then, "one day" is made from evening and morning: when, from the nature of "potentiality" and "actuality," a "third substance"—which we call a **composite**—has leaped forth. The reason is now clear, according to this sense, why he said "one day" and not "the first day." And deservedly he saw the light, because it was **good**; since the nature of "form" is nothing other than a thin image and shadowy likeness of the **First Good**. Thus far, we have spoken in general about **corruptible substance**, such as everything below the moon. There, we have seen both "heaven" and "earth"—that is, the nature that transforms and that which is transformed—and the "earth" itself, which is matter, empty of every kind of substance and void of every form.

<margin>Why darkness was over the face of the abyss.</margin>
...accidental: and over it, extended into abysses in three dimensions, sat the darkness of <term>privation</term> <note>In Aristotelian philosophy, "privation" is the absence of a form that a thing should naturally have, like darkness being the absence of light.</note>; not indeed internal to it (for privation is not the essence of matter, as Aristotle proves), but occupying its outermost face. We have likewise seen the Spirit of the Lord—that is, the force of the <term>agent cause</term> <note>The "agent" is the active force that brings about change or creation.</note>—borne over the waters, which are the fluid dispositions of matter present as if to the earth. This Spirit is not the principal cause, but the "Spirit of the Lord"—that is, the instrument of the divine art, just as our vital spirit is the instrument of the mind. And immediately, as the Spirit handled those waters and pervaded the subject at the command of God the Artisan, light arose: that is, the beauty and splendor of form.

### Chapter Three.

<margin>What we understand by "waters" on the second day.</margin>
Since we descend from common and general things to specific ones in the correct order, as Aristotle proves, Moses intended to do the same. After he spoke of those things which are common to all elementary things, he divided the entire elemental substance into three parts on the second day. First, however, it must be understood that all material forms are designated here by him under the name of "waters," than which nothing could be more fitting. For in this sphere of things that can be generated and corrupted, matter stands like the bed of a sea, where there is a perpetual and unceasing ebb and flow of waves—the coming and going of forms. "One generation passes away," as

<margin>Solomon</margin>
<margin>The Platonists, imitators of the Hebrews</margin>
<margin>Alexander</margin>
Solomon says, "and another generation comes; but the earth stands forever." <note>original: "Generatio præterit & generatio aduenit; terra autem ſtat in æternum." Quoting Ecclesiastes 1:4.</note> For among the Platonists—who are always imitators of Hebrew teaching—these forms are called "generations" rather than "forms," because it is truer to say they are "becoming" than "being." For this reason, just as he used the name "waters" above to call the qualities and accidental forms of matter, so here he uses the same name for the material substances themselves. This was to advise us—not indeed that he believed what Alexander <note>Likely Alexander of Aphrodisias, an influential commentator on Aristotle who had specific views on the nature of form.</note> did, that qualities themselves are the substantial forms of elements—but of what the Platonists strongly confirm: that every species in matter should be referred more to the condition of an <term>accident</term> <note>A property that is not essential to a thing's nature, like color or size.</note> than to that of true substance. That title of substance is legitimately claimed by those things which stand by themselves, leaning on themselves, and which are what they are by true reason, unmixed with foreign things and not at all adulterated. 

<margin>Heraclitus</margin>
<margin>The Poets</margin>
Heraclitus <note>A pre-Socratic Greek philosopher known for the idea that "all things flow."</note> called the substance of sensible things "the sea." And among the poets, who veil philosophy in the wings of fables: when, after the <term>Saturnian unity</term> <note>Refers to the primordial state of the world (associated with Saturn/Cronus) before it was divided or "fragmented" into the physical world.</note>—that is, the union of the intelligible world infolding all things within itself—they divided the sensible world into three parts, they assigned the celestial region to Jove, the subterranean to Pluto, and this middle region to Neptune—that is, the part extending from the moon to the earth, which we are discussing now. They called Neptune the lord of the sea because among the Platonists he is understood as that power which presides over generations <note>Pico is connecting the Roman god of the sea (Neptune) with the concept of "becoming" or physical generation, which he compares to the "waters" of Genesis.</note>.

<margin>The threefold division of sublunary bodies.</margin>
<margin>The pure element</margin>
<margin>The imperfect mixture</margin>
<margin>The perfect mixture</margin>
But let us return to Moses dividing the waters from the waters by means of the firmament. For there is a threefold division of <term>sublunary</term> <note>Under the moon; the physical world where change and decay happen.</note> bodies. Some are above the middle region of the air: namely, the highest part of that same element and the purest fire, the whole of which is designated by the name of "ether." There, the elements are pure, unmixed, and legitimate. Others are below the middle of the air itself, which are where we are, where there is no pure element (for a pure element is not sensible), but everything consists of mixtures from the dreggy and thicker part of the worldly body. The intervening region of air is what is here called the "firmament"; hence birds are said to be "under the firmament"...

<summary>Pico explains that Moses uses "waters" as a metaphor for the physical world's constant state of flux and "becoming." He correlates this with the Greek philosophical concepts of Heraclitus and the Platonists, and begins to describe the physical layers of the atmosphere.</summary>
