<meta>This page continues the "First Exposition" of Pico della Mirandola's Heptaplus. Having established that "waters" represent the fluid nature of matter, Pico now explains the second and third days of creation, focusing on the "firmament" as a boundary and the emergence of life from the "gathering" of material mixtures.</meta>

the birds of the sky are introduced by him as flying from it: that is the region in which those <term>lofty impressions</term> <note>Latin: "sublimes impressiones." In Renaissance science, this referred to atmospheric phenomena like meteors, rain, and lightning.</note> appear: rains, snows, lightning, thunder, comets, and others of that kind. See, moreover, how correctly this <term>firmament</term> <note>From the Latin "firmamentum," meaning a support or expanse. Pico identifies this with the middle region of the air.</note> distinguishes and separates the higher elements from the lower, as if "waters from waters," not only by position but by the property of their nature. Above it, the elements are pure; below it, they depart from elemental simplicity through a perfect mixture. There, they become mixed, but in an imperfect and intermediate way, so that it may be most truly called a middle ground between the nature of mixtures and the nature of pure elements.

### Chapter Four

<margin>The waters are gathered into one place and let the dry land appear</margin>
But let us see what further Moses philosophizes. He says, "Let the waters which are under the heaven be gathered into one place, and let the dry land appear." "The dry land" is matter, as we have already established, and matter does not appear or become visible unless it is clothed in the beauty of forms. But it does not even appear when clothed in the form of a pure element; for, as we have said and as the philosophers prove, a simple element can neither be seen nor touched, nor can it fall under any sense at all. If, therefore, the earth which was once invisible is to come into view, it is necessary for the waters under the heaven—that is, under the middle region of the air—to be gathered into one place. This means they flow together into a common "dregs" of mixture, yet are prescribed by certain laws as if by shores, to coalesce into a single form of mixture. This happens to the "lower waters," as we have shown, but not to the "higher" ones, where there is either no mixture at all or an imperfect one. <margin>The earth brings forth plants</margin> But if the <term>vegetative soul</term> <note>The "anima vegetalis" was considered the lowest level of the soul, responsible for growth, nutrition, and reproduction in plants.</note> immediately follows the form of the mixture: what else would we expect from our philosopher than that, after that gathering of waters, he would immediately bring forth the earth fertile with herbs, shrubs, and trees?

### Chapter Five.

Although from here it might seem that we should proceed in order to the animals, whose soul is most closely joined to the vegetative soul, nevertheless—since one goes from animals to man, in whom all discussion of the corruptible world ends—Moses therefore interposed some things about those things which are made in the firmament, and by which the firmament itself is adorned, just as the earth is adorned by those things produced in it: metals, plants, and living creatures. These are those "impressions" which occur on high, that is, in the middle region of the air. This region above he called both "heaven" and "firmament"; but here he calls it the "firmament of heaven," so that we may know it is not that which is truly heaven, but that which is placed under heaven. For this reason <term>Ennius</term> <note>Quintus Ennius (c. 239–169 BCE) was an early Roman poet often cited by later philosophers.</note> in his *Achilles* called this part the "under-layer," because it is placed most closely under the heaven. <margin>Ennius</margin> It is better known than can be proved with many words that these secondary impressions are called "stars," "constellations," and "heavenly bodies" by the philosophers; nor should it seem a bit harsh to anyone that we explain here what is said about the constellations. Since the entire diversity of these things is referred back to two primary causes, heat and cold, we shall appropriately refer those things which are hot by cause to the Sun, and those which are cold to the Moon. Nor do these things claim this name of Sun, Moon, and the rest of the stars for themselves only because they are the same in the lower heaven as those others are in their own (though more divine) heaven, or because they show themselves to men with a similar face, shining and sparkling alike; but rather because some of them follow one star in heaven and others follow another as their prince and leader. Whence they are also signs of those things which the stars, by which they were stirred up, are accustomed to portend to the lower realms. An argument for this is that they follow the motion of the stars, by whose force and influence they consist of matter fashioned from the earth—that is, from a vaporous exhalation.

### Chapter Six:

<margin>The Pythagoreans</margin> What follows regarding the production of animals and of man is now manifest. For after plants, those things were brought forth which are mixed <note>In this context, "mixed" refers to bodies composed of the four elements (earth, air, fire, water) in varying proportions.</note> and which possess both sensation and movement—although the Pythagoreans attribute a <term>dull sense</term> <note>original: "stupidum sensum." The Pythagoreans believed plants had a passive form of awareness or life-force, though they lacked active perception.</note> to plants as well. This is a point we shall discuss in that *Harmony* <note>Pico refers here to his planned, but never completed, work *The Harmony of Plato and Aristotle*, where he intended to reconcile the two greatest traditions of ancient philosophy.</note> which we are laboring on with the help of a longer study. But as for these living beings which participate in motion and sense beyond all controversy: here, both by Moses and in the *Timaeus* <note>Plato’s famous dialogue on the origin of the universe, which Renaissance thinkers often compared to the Book of Genesis.</note>, the <margin>Timaeus</margin> winged things, those living in the waters, and the terrestrial creatures are distinguished. The highest and prince of them all is man; at him the nature of the corruptible world stops its advance and, having finished its progress, sounds the retreat.

### Chapter Seven:

<margin>Christ our happiness</margin> Just as man is the absolute consummation of all lower things, so Christ is the absolute consummation of all men. For if, as the philosophers say, all perfection is derived from that which is most perfect in each <term>genus</term> to all others of the same order as if from a fountain, no one can doubt that the perfection of all goodness is derived from the man Christ into all men. To him alone, surely, was the Spirit given without measure, so that from his fullness we might all receive. See how undoubtedly this prerogative is owed to him, both as God and man; a privilege which belongs to him by a peculiar and legitimate right even in his nature as man.

# SECOND EXPOSITION ON THE CELESTIAL WORLD.

## PROLOGUE.

Let us press on from the elements to the heavens: from corruptible bodies to those that are incorruptible. <margin>Three reasons why Moses wrote figuratively.</margin> Our goal is to make it clear to everyone that the very same words used to show us the nature of the elements also contain the highest dogmas concerning the celestial things, as grasped by the prophet Moses. When we reflect on this in our minds, there is another reason ready at hand, beyond those we mentioned in the earlier prologues. Consider, for example, why Moses, when about to speak of the <term>efficient cause</term> and <term>matter</term>, did not call the former "efficient" and the latter "matter" in express words, but instead called them "heaven and earth." Similarly, he called the arrangements of matter "waters" rather than "qualities," as the philosophers do; and he called form "light" rather than "form." He likewise named comets, lightning, and other such phenomena as "stars" and "luminaries" rather than by their proper technical names, and so on with the rest. In our introductions, we noted that the ancients had a custom of writing about great physical and divine matters in a hidden and figurative way. We also noted the ignorance of the original audience, who could not bear the splendor of Mosaic teaching; it was necessary to speak to them with a "veiled face," lest those who were meant to be illuminated be blinded by too much light. Now we have the occasion for a third reason: namely, that if he had used the terms "matter," "form," "qualities," and "efficient cause," those terms could indeed serve for <margin>The wonderful craftsmanship of Moses</margin> treatises on this corruptible world, but not for the other worlds. Therefore, it is a brilliant and wonderful artifice of Moses—truly a divine rather than human industry—to use such terms and to arrange his discourse in such a way that the same words, the same context, and the same sequence of the whole scripture appropriately <margin>The most perfect kind of writing</margin> suit the figuring of the secrets of all worlds and of all nature. This is why the book of Moses surpasses all the learning, eloquence, and genius of the nations. <margin>Mosaic scripture emulating angelic intelligence</margin> This is the new and hitherto untouched thing which we have attempted to bring forth: namely, that we might prove to our people by the fact itself that this was done by Moses. This is the idea, this is the exemplar of the most perfect writer: not only because this kind of writing, as we demonstrated above, portrays and emulates nature; for just as between...

<summary>Pico concludes his first exposition by identifying Man as the peak of the physical world and Christ as the peak of humanity, then begins the second exposition by arguing that Moses used deliberately multi-layered language to describe both elemental and celestial realities simultaneously.</summary>
<keywords>Pythagoreans, Timaeus, Christology, Moses, Celestial World, allegory, matter and form, efficient cause, sacred philology</keywords>

<meta>This page marks the beginning of the "Second Exposition," where Pico shifts his focus from the elemental world (Earth) to the celestial world (the Heavens). Having previously discussed the creation of man as the bridge between worlds, he now begins to interpret the Mosaic account of Genesis as a description of the planetary and super-celestial spheres.</meta>

<sig>B ii</sig>
<meta>Manicule in upper right margin pointing to the first line.</meta>

<margin>Dionysius</margin>
<margin>Saint Thomas</margin>
According to the authority of Dionysius <note>Dionysius the Areopagite, a Christian theologian and philosopher of the late 5th century, famous for his writings on the celestial hierarchy.</note> and Saint Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the influential Dominican friar and Scholastic philosopher.</note>, among the angelic minds, that one is supreme which comprehends the splendor of our theology with the fewest notions and forms; those minds which are lower require various and manifold forms. So it is among the scriptures: that one is the highest and holds the peak of all perfection which embraces all things deeply and appropriately in the fewest possible words, as if they were one. But why do we delay the prophet <note>Referring to Moses, the traditional author of Genesis.</note> as he comes forth with his face revealed, to speak to us of heavenly mysteries? Nevertheless, before we hear him speak—so that we may be more capable of receiving his words—it will be useful to say a few things beforehand regarding the tenth heaven.

### Chapter One.

<margin>The Empyrean Heaven</margin>
<margin>Strabo</margin>
<margin>Bede</margin>
<margin>Abraham the astrologer</margin>
<margin>Isaac the philosopher</margin>
<margin>Ezekiel on the Empyrean heaven</margin>
<margin>Zechariah</margin>
Above the nine spheres of the heavens—that is, the seven planets, the eighth sphere which is called the "unwandering" <note>The sphere of the fixed stars, which do not move independently like the planets.</note>, and the ninth sphere which is detected by reason rather than by the senses <note>The *Primum Mobile*, or the "First Moved" sphere, which provides motion to all lower spheres.</note> and is believed to be the first among moving bodies—there is a tenth heaven, fixed, remaining, and quiet, which participates in no motion. This is not only believed by our own writers, especially the more recent Strabo <note>Walafrid Strabo (c. 808–849), a Carolingian scholar.</note> and Bede <note>The Venerable Bede (c. 672–735), an English monk and polymath.</note>, but also by many of the Hebrews, and additionally by certain philosophers and mathematicians. It is enough to cite two of these: Abraham the Spaniard <note>Abraham Ibn Ezra (c. 1089–1167), a celebrated Jewish astronomer and biblical commentator.</note>, a most great astrologer, and Isaac the philosopher <note>Likely Isaac Israeli (c. 832–932), a Jewish physician and Neoplatonist.</note>, both of whom attest to this. Indeed, this Isaac understands the tenth sphere to be designated by Ezekiel through the <term>Sapphire</term> <note>original: "Zaphirum." A reference to Ezekiel 1:26.</note> in the likeness of a throne: so that the color of the sapphire signifies the brightness of light, and the likeness of the throne signifies its immobility. He likewise understands the ten spheres to be figured by Zechariah through the golden lampstand distinguished by seven lamps, and a bowl <note>original: "lampadem." Here meaning the reservoir or "bowl" of the lampstand.</note> above its head, and then two olive trees above the bowl. For since the seven lamps indicate the seven planets, and the bowl indicates the eighth circle glowing with so many lights, he wishes the ninth and tenth spheres to be indicated by the two olive trees. This is because oil flows from the olives to the bowl and the lamps to nourish the light. Therefore, by a similarity of reason with the heavens we see, light emanates from and is preserved by those supreme ones (for he who gives light also preserves it). Justly, then, are the latter compared to olives, and the former to the lamps and the bowl. But if two primary sources of the same water cannot be established, it is necessary that one of those two supreme spheres be the principle of all light.

<margin>The source and unity of light</margin>
<margin>Three degrees of participated light</margin>
<margin>Unity</margin>
<margin>Coelementary number</margin>
<margin>Theology of the Phoenicians</margin>
<margin>Julian</margin>
If this source is to be referred to one of them, it must be to the first—that is, the tenth—so that it is itself the <term>Unity</term> <note>In Neoplatonic thought, the "Unity" or "Monad" is the indivisible source from which all multiplicity arises.</note> of lights. Then, the ninth sphere receives light next, in the total essence of its substance. From there, it arrives thirdly at the Sun by full participation; and from the Sun, in the fourth and thus final degree, it is divided among all the stars. Therefore, above the nine heavens let us place the tenth, which theologians call the <term>Empyrean</term> <note>From the Greek "empyros," meaning "in fire"; the highest heaven of pure light and fire.</note>. Some have doubted whether its nature is corporeal or rather incorporeal. For perhaps it befits "Unity"—just as the analogy of nature responds to the <term>coelementary number</term> <note>The number ten, or "decad," which in Pythagorean thought completes the set of primary numbers.</note>—not to be of the same kind. But whatever is decided about this question, let it remain unshaken that the treasures of light are there, and from there whatever light is held and seen in physical bodies is derived, as if from a first source, into the rest. For it does not stand in the way even if someone wishes to believe, more stubbornly than truly, that it is not of a truly corporeal nature; since in the theology of the Phoenicians (as Julian the Caesar <note>The Emperor Julian "the Apostate" (331–363), in his *Hymn to King Helios*.</note> writes in his *Oration on the Sun*) corporeal light emanates from an incorporeal nature. Therefore, this heaven presides over the nine heavens succeeding it in a continuous series, like a leader to an army or like <term>Form</term> to <term>Matter</term>, and bearing the type of the <term>Monad</term> <note>The mathematical/mystical One.</note>, it completes the number ten.

### Chapter Two.

<summary>Pico introduces the concept of the Tenth Heaven or Empyrean, arguing for its existence as the immobile source of all light based on Christian, Jewish, and Pagan authorities. He explains the hierarchy of light as it descends from this tenth sphere through the lower heavens to the Sun and stars.</summary>
<keywords>Empyrean, Tenth Heaven, celestial spheres, hierarchy of light, Dionysius the Areopagite, Thomas Aquinas, Ezekiel, Zechariah, Monad, Julian the Apostate</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Pico della Mirandola's "Second Exposition" of Genesis. Having established the existence of the Empyrean or tenth heaven on the previous page, he now turns to the specific words of Moses to explain how the celestial hierarchy—from the highest angelic realms down to the planetary spheres—is encoded in the opening verses of scripture.</meta>

<margin>
Explanation of the words of the prophet:
Heaven
Earth
</margin>

Let us come to Moses who, about to speak of all things, has deigned to honor this one <note>The Empyrean heaven.</note> with the name "Heaven" as the first and principal thing. In the same way, although we may call the nine <term>angelic choirs</term> <note>The traditional hierarchy of angels, such as Seraphim, Cherubim, etc.</note> "gods" because they participate in divinity—whence comes that phrase "God of gods"—nevertheless, when we say "God" absolutely, we do not mean any one of them, but we understand the indivisible Trinity presiding over them. Similarly, the Empyrean heaven presides over the nine spheres subject to it. However, he called the eight remaining spheres "Earth," and not without cause, but because the extremes of this number claim the name of "earth" for themselves. These are the moon and the <term>stellar heaven</term> <note>The sphere of the fixed stars, the eighth sphere.</note>; we are compelled to call both of them "earth" by both the authority of the ancients and by reason besides.

<margin>
Eighth sphere
Academics
Moon
Aristotle
Pythagoreans
In what way the elements are in heaven
Lucan
</margin>

For regarding the eighth sphere, it is very common in the <term>Academy</term> <note>The school of Platonic philosophers.</note> to give it the name of "earth." Likewise, Aristotle said the moon was similar to earth, clearly imitating the Pythagoreans <note>Followers of the philosopher Pythagoras, who believed the universe was ordered by numbers and harmony.</note> who call it both a "celestial earth" and a "terrestrial heaven." But see what reason leads us to both: for if we seek the <term>elements</term> <note>The four building blocks of matter: earth, water, air, and fire.</note> in heaven, we establish the moon as "earth," the lowest and least noble of all the stars, just as the earth is among all the elements, being very similar to it in opacity of substance and in its spots. Then we call Mercury "water," a changeable and transformable star, and therefore called the "arbitrator of waves" in the poet Lucan. Venus is "air," life-giving with a tempered heat; the Sun is "fire" for the most obvious reason. Then, in reverse order: Mars is "fire"; Jupiter is "air," related to Venus by nature; Saturn is "water," being an old man of cursed coldness. It remains that we call the eighth sphere—the "unwandering" one—"earth," as the very order of the calculation demands. Rightly, therefore, he called this whole space "earth," which is enclosed by two "earths" on either side, and above which nothing is visible to us.

<margin>
Empty and void
Darkness
Abyss
Ninth sphere
Waters
</margin>

Then he adds: *and the earth was empty and void*—empty, that is, of light, which had not yet been propagated to it from the first heaven, and empty of the other virtues of which light is the vehicle. Nor do we say this of ourselves, but the author himself declares of what thing he speaks regarding this emptiness, adding: *and darkness was upon the face of the abyss*. He rightly calls such a great height, so many spheres, and a wonderful depth an "abyss." But lest we believe there is nothing in the middle between the eighth sphere and the Empyrean seats—as many have believed, following only the evidence of the senses—he warned us of an intervening sphere. Because he represented this as "waters," it has been called the <term>crystalline heaven</term> <note>A transparent sphere traditionally placed between the fixed stars and the Empyrean.</note> by more recent writers.

<margin>
Ephrem
Spirit of the Lord
</margin>

Over this sphere was moved—or as the Hebrew truth has it, and the Syrian <term>Ephrem</term> <note>Saint Ephrem the Syrian (c. 306–373), a prominent Christian theologian and hymnodist.</note> translated—the Spirit of the Lord "incubated" or "brooded" over this; that is, the spiritual Olympus <note>A poetic term for the highest heaven.</note>, adhering most closely as the seat of the spirits of the Lord, cherished it with its life-giving light.

<margin>
Why the ninth heaven is invisible
</margin>

And it was rightly done so that this sphere, being so close to the source of light, might drink in the light with its whole body and its whole mass; it is invisible to us because it is not bounded by a more solid thickness. Therefore, the Empyrean, brooding over it first, bestowed its light upon it, which soon—at God’s command—was derived into the remaining spheres (which we say are designated by "earth" and the "abyss") once the darkness was shaken off.

<margin>
One day
Epilogue
</margin>

*And there was evening and morning, one day*; because through the reception of light and celestial influence, the lower parts of heaven are allied with the first parts. In summary, therefore, on the first day, the eminence of the first heaven over the others, the derivation of light from it to them, and many properties of the ninth sphere and the others are indicated through the nicknames of "water" and "earth."

### Chapter Three.

<margin>
Firmament between the waters
</margin>

Now indeed, announcing more particularly the moved spheres, he teaches that the "unwandering" sphere—which we call the <term>firmament</term>—is in the middle between two waters. The reason for this saying is manifest from what we have said; for both the ninth sphere and the planet Saturn, as we have declared, claim the name of "waters" for themselves...

<summary>Pico explains that Moses uses "Heaven" for the Empyrean and "Earth" for the lower planetary spheres, mapping the four elements onto the planets and identifying the biblical "waters" as the invisible ninth crystalline heaven. This interpretation aligns the Genesis creation account with classical cosmology and the views of Aristotle, the Platonists, and Saint Ephrem.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Pico della Mirandola's "Second Exposition" of Genesis. Having previously identified the Empyrean as the highest "Heaven," Pico now moves to interpret the creation of the "Firmament" and the gathering of the "Waters," explaining how Moses encoded the entire planetary system within these verses.</meta>

<sig>B iii</sig>

...claim. Therefore, the firmament was placed by God in the midst of the waters, and the waters which are under the heaven were gathered into one place, and it was done so that the dry land—that is, the earth—might appear, and all this was provided for the salvation of living things. Let us see what these words of Moses mean.

<margin>The waters under the heaven gathered into one place</margin>
The waters that are under the heaven are the seven stars <note>The "seven stars" refers to the seven classical planets: Saturn, Jupiter, Mars, the Sun, Venus, Mercury, and the Moon.</note> which are under the firmament, which he called "heaven." The first of these is Saturn. These waters are gathered into one place for this reason: because the entire power of the planets is collected in the one Sun, which all philosophers and all mathematicians <note>In the Renaissance, "mathematicians" often referred to astronomers and astrologers who calculated celestial movements.</note> confirm with one voice. This gathering of the waters is called "the sea"—not absurdly, for this will be that great **Ocean** who is called the father of gods and men by those <note>Refers to Homer and the ancient Greek poets.</note> who deemed the planets worthy of the names of gods.

<margin>Ocean</margin>
<margin>The Earth appears</margin>
As for the **earth**, what else shall we call it but the **moon**, so named by **Aristotle** and the **Pythagoreans**? When the moon is entirely overwhelmed by the waves of the aforementioned "sea" <note>This likely refers to the moon being "combust" or obscured by the sun's power, or its placement within the influence of the higher planets.</note>, it is neither useful to us nor visible. But then it becomes suitable for the use of animals and ourselves when, receding from that sea, it comes more and more into view.

<margin>And the principal power of the moon according to the Chaldeans</margin>
Then it is fertile, then fruitful, especially regarding those things which belong to a vegetative nature, whose gifts are growth, nutrition, and generation. For in this earth lies the principal power of the moon, as the <term>Chaldeans</term> <note>Ancient Babylonian astronomers and mystics whose secret wisdom Pico often synthesized with Christian theology.</note> have said.

<margin>Why no mention is made of four planets</margin>
This is most aptly demonstrated here by Moses: as soon as the moon appears, he makes it the parent of herbs, fruits, and trees. See how he has indicated to us the nature of the moon and the sun in very few words and figuratively. But why is he silent about the others, since in our prefaces we promised to treat all of them sufficiently and learnedly? Why, when he has made mention of the tenth, ninth, and eighth spheres, as well as of **Saturn**, the **sun**, and the **moon**, is there not even a word about the four that remain—**Venus**, **Mercury**, **Jupiter**, and **Mars**?

<margin>First solution</margin>
<margin>Refutation</margin>
You might perhaps say it was done because an unrefined people only knew the sun and the moon. But I have removed this refuge from myself, nor can I turn there without blushing, I who have testified above that nothing was omitted by Moses that would lead to a perfect understanding of all the worlds.

<margin>Second solution</margin>
Another might say that by dealing with the sun and moon, he dealt with the rest: because these hold the kingdom of heaven, and while the power of the others is particular, these two stars prevail with a universal influence.

<margin>Refutation</margin>
<margin>Third solution</margin>
<margin>Dogma of the ancient Hebrews concerning the stars</margin>
But this does not satisfy us either; for by the same reasoning, he should have omitted Saturn, of whom we have shown mention was made. I believe a deeper mystery of the ancient Hebrew discipline lies hidden: among its dogmas concerning heaven, the chief one is that **Jupiter** and **Mars** are enclosed by the **sun**, while **Venus** and **Mercury** are enclosed by the **moon**. Nor is the reason for this opinion obscure if we examine the natures of these stars, even if they themselves offer no reason for their dogma.

<margin>Affinity of the sun with Jupiter and Mars</margin>
Jupiter is hot, Mars is hot, and the sun is hot. But the heat of Mars is sharp and violent, while that of Jupiter is beneficial. In the sun, we see that sharp and violent quality of Mars and the beneficial property of Jupiter—that is, a certain nature mixed from these and tempered in the middle, so to speak. Jupiter is fortunate, Mars is unfortunate; the sun is partly good and partly evil—good in its radiation, evil in its conjunction <note>In astrology, a planet "in conjunction" with the sun is often "combust" or weakened by the sun's intensity, though the sun's light itself is life-giving.</note>. Aries is the house of Mars; Cancer is the <term>exaltation</term> <note>A specific sign of the zodiac where a planet's influence is thought to be most powerful.</note> of Jupiter. The sun, having attained its highest point in Cancer and its dignity in Aries, shows a manifest kinship with both stars.

<margin>Affinity of the moon with Venus and Mercury</margin>
Let us come to the moon, which clearly participates in the waters of Mercury; and how much affinity it has with Venus is indicated primarily by this: that it is so <term>exalted</term> in Taurus—the domicile of Venus—that it is judged nowhere more happy or beneficial.

<margin>Epilogue</margin>
Concerning the **Empyrean** heaven, therefore, the ninth sphere, the firmament, the star of Saturn, and the sun and moon (which embrace the rest, reminding us by this very silence of this embrace), he has spoken sufficiently thus far.

# Chapter Four.

<summary>Pico explains that Moses omits four planets (Jupiter, Mars, Venus, Mercury) because they are inherently contained within the natures of the Sun and Moon. He uses astrological affinities, such as planetary houses and exaltations, to justify this hidden "Hebrew mystery."</summary>

<meta>This page continues Pico della Mirandola's "Second Exposition" of Genesis. Having previously interpreted the "sea" as the gathering of planetary powers in the Sun and the "earth" as the Moon, Pico now moves to the functions of the celestial bodies (motion and illumination) and begins to explain the creation of "living creatures" and "man" as allegories for the higher celestial spheres and the rational soul.</meta>

<margin>
Timaeus
<note>Timaeus is the title of Plato's famous dialogue concerning the creation of the universe, which Pico frequently harmonizes with the Book of Genesis.</note>
Motion
Illumination
</margin>
It remained that, after speaking of the nature of the stars, he should discuss their works and their office, declaring for what use they were founded and to what duty they were delegated by God. Know, however, that he is still dealing with the heaven as a luminous body; nothing has yet been said by the prophet <note>Pico refers to Moses as "the prophet."</note> regarding its intellect or its moving power. This is the same order that **Timaeus** follows: first fashioning the body, and then applying a soul to the completed body. Two operations of the celestial bodies are manifest to the universe: **motion** and **illumination**. Motion is established as twofold: one of the whole world, by which the heaven and the ether are revolved in a perfect circuit through the whole space of the universe in twenty-four hours; the other is the specific motion of the stars, which is manifold and various, among which the principal is the motion of the sun, which circles all the signs of the Zodiac in the space of twelve months. The former creates the day, whence it is called the "diurnal" motion; the latter, however, creates the year. The motions of the remaining stars are completed through various intervals of time. Rightly and briefly, therefore, **Moses** reminded us of all these things when he said the stars were placed in the firmament for "days, years, and seasons." He added "for signs," which, because it is sufficiently explained by other interpreters, I shall pass over. He further expressly indicated the remaining operation of the stars, which is **illumination**, when he said those things were established so that they might "shine in the heaven and illuminate the earth." Although the opinions of the ancients differ as to how celestial things influence lower things, the words of **Moses** fit each one aptly. For if they influence nothing other than light—which **Aristotle** seems to have intended, if we interpret his words religiously and not according to our own whim—nothing more consistent with the Mosaic sayings could be imagined. If, besides light, they also influence heat, and nothing else—as **Averroes** the Arab <note>Averroes (Ibn Rushd) was a 12th-century Islamic philosopher known for his commentaries on Aristotle.</note> and **Abraham** the Jew <note>Likely referring to Abraham Ibn Ezra, a noted 12th-century Jewish scholar and astrologer.</note> maintain—it was enough to have spoken of light, from which these same authors admit heat proceeds. Likewise, if many other and manifold virtues are sent down from the heavens—as seemed true to **Avicenna** <note>Avicenna (Ibn Sina) was a Persian polymath and one of the most significant physicians and philosophers of the Islamic Golden Age.</note> and the **Babylonians**—mention was not made of light alone by chance: for as **Avicenna** himself writes, it is light alone that carries all other virtues from the heaven to us. Into these ministries, therefore, the bodies of the moon, the sun, and the stars are distributed.

How celestial things influence lower things

## Chapter Five.

<margin>Signs of the eighth and ninth spheres.</margin>
It remained for him to make mention both of the signs that are visible in the Zodiac and of those which, though invisible to us, are yet far more effective in the **crystalline heaven** <note>In medieval cosmology, the Crystalline Heaven was a sphere located above the firmament of fixed stars.</note>. For nothing has been said of these until now. This, therefore, is what is meant by the "living creatures" which both the waters and the earth bring forth: namely, those waters which are above the heavens and the earth which is the firmament itself, as was proven above. For the signs seen in those two spheres are in the form of animals, such as those noted among us by the **Egyptians** and **Indians**; they were able to discern these more easily and correctly than our people, aided by the very flatness of the ground and the serenity of the sky. Otherwise, the fleeting production of animals that are here on earth pertains no more to these two elements, earth and water, than to the others—namely, fire and air. And since he gave the name "water" to the crystalline sphere, he appropriately called the animals there "fishes"; conversely, those in the firmament (which he calls "earth"), he called "cattle and beasts."

<margin>
Concerning the moving power of the heavens

Thus far concerning the corporeal nature of the heavens. Now, being about to declare them endowed with a rational soul, he mentions **Man** allegorically—not indeed that man who is fleeting and earthy and whom we see, but the one by whom (as **Plotinus** <note>Plotinus was the founder of Neoplatonism; Pico is referencing his idea of the "Higher Man" or the soul.</note> says) the visible man is governed. That is the rational soul itself, which **Timaeus** also constitutes from the same elements and in the same mixing bowl as the soul of the heaven...

<summary>Pico explains the celestial functions of motion and illumination, harmonizing Genesis with philosophers like Aristotle and Avicenna. He then interprets the "living creatures" of the creation story as the constellations of the higher celestial spheres and begins an allegorical treatment of "Man" as the rational soul.</summary>
<keywords>celestial motion, illumination, Zodiac, crystalline heaven, rational soul, Aristotle, Averroes, Avicenna, Plotinus, Timaeus, cosmology</keywords>

--- Page 45 ---
<meta>This page continues Pico della Mirandola’s "Second Exposition" of Genesis. Following the discussion of the physical stars and their motions, he now transitions to the "soul" of the heavens—the angelic or intellectual movers—and how the biblical creation of "man" refers to these celestial intelligences.</meta>

<margin>Sacred Scripture</margin>
What is said of the human soul is fittingly transferred also to the soul of the heaven. Sacred Scripture supports our exposition: in its pages, the entire angelic and rational nature is often designated by the term "man." This is most frequent in the prophets when speaking of good angels; and even of the evil demon—who differs in nature not at all from them—it is written in the Gospel: "An enemy man has done this" <note>original: "inimicus homo haec fecit"; a quote from the Parable of the Weeds in Matthew 13:28.</note>. Therefore, God added to the celestial machinery a living and rational substance, a participant in intellect, and thus made in His own image and likeness.

<margin>Celestial things obey their movers</margin>
He willed this substance to preside over those "living creatures" we spoke of shortly before—namely, all the starry signs and planets. These are turned by its nod and obey its word so perfectly that there is no delay and no rebellion. This does not happen in the same way with the brute bodies of the elements. Nor will you easily find any other topic upon which the Peripatetics <note>The followers of Aristotle, who argued that the celestial spheres move without friction or resistance.</note> labor more than to prove that the celestial body does not resist its mover at all, just as our own bodies resist us. For this reason, they experience neither boredom, difficulty, nor fatigue from perpetual motion as we do. This is the "dominion over the living creatures" that Moses touched upon regarding the celestial man.

<margin>In what way the celestial man is male and female</margin>
Likewise, it is not without mystery that He created that man "male and female." For it is the prerogative of celestial souls that they perform both duties at once: both contemplating and ruling bodies. Neither duty cries out against the other, nor can one be an impediment to the other. This was used extensively by the ancients; we observe in the Orphic hymns <note>Ancient Greek poems attributed to the mythical Orpheus, highly valued by Renaissance Neoplatonists.</note> that these two powers in the same substance—one which contemplates and the other which presides over the body—are designated by the names "male" and "female." These things concerning the celestial world, the divine body, the number of orbs, their nature, properties, and office, and finally, concerning its moving force, its rational substance, and its character, are handed down by the prophet.

### Chapter Seven.

<margin>To what extent the heaven is to be honored by us; Plato</margin>
This is a noble creature, to be looked up to and celebrated by us. But even if we follow the Platonic sentiment (to say nothing of the theologians), we have not forgotten that our own souls were tempered by God the Maker in the same mixing bowl <note>A reference to the *krater* in Plato's *Timaeus*, where the Creator mixes the soul of the world and human souls from the same ingredients.</note> and from the same elements as the celestial souls. Let us see to it, then, that we do not wish to be the servants of those whose brothers nature willed us to be. Nor should we measure our condition by this weak body. For "man" is not (as it is written in the *Alcibiades* <note>A Socratic dialogue attributed to Plato which argues that "man is nothing other than his soul."</note>) this fragile and earthly thing we see, but he is soul; he is intellect, which exceeds the entire circuit of the heaven and the entire course of time.

We must be careful, therefore, lest we do what many do—giving more to the heaven and attributing more to it than is necessary—and so resist the will of the Maker and the order of the universe. At the same time, we might displease the heaven itself (to which God’s counsels and the order of the world are most dear) while we strive to please it.

<margin>Chaldeans, Jeremiah, Moses; That the heaven cannot be the author of man; Christ, the one good</margin>

Jeremiah proclaims this: "Do not fear," he says, "the signs of heaven which the nations fear" <note>original: "Ne timeatis... signa caeli"; Jeremiah 10:2.</note>. Our prophet <note>Moses</note> commands this elsewhere, warning man that, looking up at the sun, moon, and stars, he should not worship those things which God created for the service of all nations. Even if one does not take this to mean that those bodies serve us as if they were ignoble or dead things, let us nevertheless understand that the author or mistress of our nature cannot be a substance of which even one part is found to be viler than any part in us that is considered ignoble. For in a finished work, nothing can or should be more perfect than what is found in the maker. Let us therefore fear, love, and venerate Him from whom everything comes. In whom, as Paul says, all things were created, whether visible or i[nvisible]...

# THIRD EXPOSITION: ON THE ANGELIC AND INVISIBLE WORLD.
## PREFACE TO THE THIRD BOOK.

<margin>Dionysius</margin>
Thus far, according to the strength of our intellect, we have discussed the celestial world while revealing the mysteries of Moses. But now, "who will give me wings like a dove—wings silvered over and gleaming with the paleness of gold? And I will fly into the super-celestial region where there is true rest, true peace, true tranquility" <note>A paraphrase of Psalm 55:6 and Psalm 68:13.</note>: a peace, certainly, which this visible and corporeal world cannot give. Reveal my eyes, O spirits beyond the world <note>i.e., the Angels</note>, and I shall contemplate the miracles of your city, which God has set aside for those who fear Him; which "no eye has seen, nor ear heard, nor has it entered the heart of man" <note>1 Corinthians 2:9.</note>. Since many things concerning this angelic and invisible nature have been handed down both by the ancient Hebrews <margin>Ancient dogmas of the Hebrews</margin> and likewise by Dionysius <note>Dionysius the Areopagite, a 5th-century Christian theologian whose "Celestial Hierarchy" was a primary source for angelology.</note>, it was my intention to explain the words of Moses according to the doctrine of both traditions. But because the things said by the Hebrews—since they are unfamiliar among the Latins—could not easily be understood by our people unless we started "from the twin egg" <note>original: "a gemino quod aiunt ovo"; a Latin idiom meaning to start from the very beginning, referring to the myth of Leda and the swan.</note> as they say, and related many—indeed, almost all—the dogmas of the ancient discipline of the Hebrew nation, I have decided to delay this until I have written more extensively elsewhere on these matters and made their opinions known to our countrymen. In that work, I will examine how much they agree with Egyptian monuments <note>Refers to the ancient Egyptian wisdom and the Hermetic tradition.</note>, how much with Platonic philosophy, and how much with Catholic truth. Wherever they harmonize with us, we shall command the Hebrews to stand by the ancient traditions of their fathers; wherever they differ, we—instructed by Catholic legions—shall make an assault upon them. Finally, whatever we find that is foreign to the Gospel truth, we shall refute as best we can; whatever is holy and true <margin>Dionysius, Paul, Hierotheus</margin>, we shall transfer from the Synagogue (as from an unjust possessor) to ourselves, the legitimate Israelites. Meanwhile, following in the footsteps of Dionysius—or rather of Paul and Hierotheus <note>According to tradition, Hierotheus was the teacher of Dionysius, who was in turn converted by the Apostle Paul.</note>, whom he followed—we will attempt to bring light into the shadows of the Law, which the Spirit of God, the author of the Law, placed as His hiding place because of our weakness.

### Chapter One:

<margin>Unity</margin>
Whatever exists after unity is "number," and it is perfected and completed by unity. Unity alone is entirely simple and perfect of itself; it does not depart from itself, but clings to itself in indivisible simplicity and solitude, for it is sufficient unto itself, needing nothing, and full of its own riches. <margin>Number</margin> Since number is by its nature a multitude, it becomes "simple" only by the benefit of unity, insofar as it is capable of simplicity. Yet, the further each number is from unity, the more it falls into a greater multitude, and the more dissimilarity, parts, and composition there are within it. There is no number so close to unity that it is not still a multitude, having only an "adventitious" unity—that is, being one not by nature, but by composition. <margin>An ascent from mathematics to divine things</margin> Let us transfer these things to divine matters in the Pythagorean manner. God alone, from whom all things come and who is from no one, is the simplest and most indivisible essence. Whatever He has, He has from Himself: by the same thing that He *is*, He also knows, He wills, He is good, and He is just. Nor is the thing...

we can understand in some way what He is beyond the fact that He is <term>Being itself</term> <note>original: "ipsum esse"; in scholastic philosophy, God is not just a being among others, but the very act of Existence itself.</note> which He is. Other things are not that—that is, Being itself—but they exist by that. Therefore, an angel is not <term>Unity itself</term>; otherwise, an angel would be God, or there would be many gods, which cannot even be conceived. For what will be "one" if Unity itself is not one? It remains that an angel is a <term>number</term> <note>Pico follows the Platonic idea that created things are "numbers" because they are composed of parts (multiplicity), unlike God who is simple Unity.</note>. But every number is imperfect insofar as it is a multitude, yet perfect insofar as it is one. Therefore, let us ascribe whatever is imperfect in an angel to the angelic multitude (which it has from being a number, that is, a creature) and whatever is perfect to the approaching unity (which it has from being joined to God). We find a twofold imperfection in an angel: one, because he is not Being itself but only an <term>essence</term> <note>original: "essentia"; the "what-ness" of a thing, which in creatures is distinct from their "is-ness."</note> to which being happens by participation so that he may exist; the other, because he is not <term>Intellection itself</term> <note>The act of understanding.</note>, but it comes to him so that he may understand—even though he is by his nature an intellect capable of understanding. However, the second depends on the first: since he does not exist of himself, he certainly does not understand of himself either, since nothing can act where it does not exist. Both of these, therefore, happen to the angel because he is a multitude. It remains that his release and completion must come from the Unity approaching from above. But God is Unity, from whom being, life, and all perfection are derived toward the angel. Moreover, just as the imperfection is twofold—as if it were a twofold multitude—so let us understand a twofold approach of Unity so that both may be perfected. The first is that by which there is a raw essence, devoid of forms, life, and being. This is the **earth without form and void** <note>Genesis 1:2.</note> which God also created, lest you perhaps believe, as some have believed, that only the *forming* of essence belongs to the Craftsman, and not also its *creation*. Together with the earth He created **heaven**, that is, the act of that essence and the participated unity in the multitude, which is Being itself. Thus, the creation of heaven and earth is, as it were, the same, as a shared embrace of two natures coming together by a similar bond toward the same end. Not out of harmony with the ancients, we call Being itself—the participation in divinity—"heaven," since **Xenophanes** called the <term>archetypal world</term> <note>The world of perfect ideas in the mind of God.</note> a "sphere," and the **Saracens** <note>original: "Saraceni"; referring to Medieval Islamic philosophers such as Avicenna or Averroes.</note>—and indeed our own people too—call God a "circle."

<margin>The Spirit of the Lord</margin>
The angel, through what we have already said, has perfectly attained his nature and intellectual property. Nevertheless, he does not yet have that from which he may fulfill his gifts of understanding—namely, of contemplating—unless he is first clothed by God with intelligible forms. Therefore, there is still **darkness over the face of the deep**. The **Deep** <note>original: "Abyssus"; the abyss.</note> is the intellectual property that penetrates and searches out all deep things. Upon this there is darkness, until it is illuminated by the rays of spiritual notions through which all things are seen and gazed upon. However, it is written **over the face of the deep**, not **over the deep**, because the place of darkness and light is the same. But the light—that is, the intelligible forms—occupies the "face," that is, the outermost parts of the angelic intellect, because they are qualities happening to it and do not belong to its essence itself. What medium intervenes before the darkness is driven out and the light arises? He immediately adds, saying: **and the spirit of the Lord was moved over the waters.** What would the Spirit of the Lord be rather than the Spirit of Love? For we do not call the spirit of knowledge the "Spirit of the Lord" so properly, since knowledge sometimes leads away from God, but Love always leads to God. Unless this Spirit is moved over that deep, light will not be made. For just as the eye will not be filled with light unless it is turned toward the sun, so the angel is not filled with spiritual light unless he is turned toward God. But this motion of turning is not, nor can it be, anything else in the angelic nature than the motion of love. Therefore, the Spirit of the Lord was...

### Chapter Three.

We have seen the nature of the angel created by God, and that same nature turned toward God by the spirit of love; then illuminated by him and perfected by the light of intelligible reasons. Let us now see by what order the angelic hosts are distinguished among themselves.
<margin>
The firmament in the midst of the waters
</margin>
We read that a <term>firmament</term> was placed in the midst of the waters, where three angelic hierarchies are indicated to us (for we always call them by these customary names). Of these, the first and the last are designated by the waters: the former by the super-celestial waters; the latter by those beneath the heaven; the middle one, dividing them, is called the firmament. If we weigh the nature and offices of these three hierarchies, all these things could not harmonize more with the doctrine of <term>Dionysius</term> <note>Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, a 5th-century author whose "The Celestial Hierarchy" defined the nine ranks of angels.</note>.
<margin>
Super-celestial waters
Firmament
</margin>
Since the highest hierarchy, as he writes, is devoted to contemplation alone, it is rightly symbolized by the waters that are set above the heavens—that is, above all action concerning worldly things, whether celestial or earthly—and they praise God incessantly with a perennial sound. But since the middle order is assigned to celestial duties, it certainly could not be more appropriately signified than by the firmament, that is, by the heaven.
<margin>
Sub-celestial waters
</margin>
The last hierarchy, even if by nature it is above every body and above the heaven, nevertheless cares for those things that are below the heaven. Since it is divided into <term>Principalities</term>, <term>Archangels</term>, and <term>Angels</term>, the entire operation of all these is only concerning those things that are sublunary: of the Principalities, concerning republics, kings, and princes (as we learn from Daniel); of the Archangels, concerning mysteries and sacred ceremonies. The Angels attend to private matters, and individuals are assigned to individual men <note>Pico refers here to the concept of Guardian Angels.</note>. Rightly, therefore, is this sub-celestial host symbolized by the sub-celestial waters. For it presides over things that are fluid and transitory, and it is subject to that order which is occupied with celestial things.

### Chapter Four.

<margin>
The gathering of the sub-celestial waters to one place

What it means for the waters beneath the heaven to be "gathered into one place" would perhaps be doubtful, unless Paul declared this to us. For this reason they are sent to us, appearing in various forms, places, and times, now while we rest and now even while we are awake. For different angels preside over different physical things and other human concerns. On this point, **Augustine** also constantly asserted that there is no visible thing among us which does not have an angelic power presiding over it, and that all bodies are ruled by a rational spirit of life; a point which **Gregory** later confirmed. **Origen**, similarly, in his commentaries on the Book of Numbers, says that the world has need of angels to preside over the beasts, the births of animals, the growth of shrubs and plantations, and the increase of all other things. **Damascene** <note>John of Damascus, an 8th-century theologian.</note>, being of this same opinion, believed that the angel who sinned <note>Lucifer or the fallen angels.</note> was from among those of the lowest rank, who preside over the terrestrial order. But just as all these things beneath man are directed toward man, so too does the entire care of the angels regarding these things serve as an assistant and handmaid to human effort and study; they care for human affairs and, by helping our weakness, they ensure—at least as much as we allow—that we live a pious and happy life.

<margin>The earth spoken of in the Gospel</margin>

For this reason, Moses immediately added what that "gathering of waters" intended: so that the earth might bring forth fruit, herbs, plants, and trees. But what is this "earth" other than the one of which it is written in the Gospel <note>The Parable of the Sower in Matthew 13.</note>, where one part brings forth fruit a hundredfold, another sixtyfold, and another thirtyfold?

<margin>Paul</margin>

It is surely the "earth" of our soul, of which **Paul** spoke these words: *The earth that drinks in the rain often falling on it, if it produces a crop useful to those for whom it is farmed, receives a blessing from God; but that which produces thorns and thistles is worthless and near to being cursed, and its end is to be burned.* <note>Hebrews 6:7-8.</note>

Let us therefore take care that our own "earth" yields fruit in its proper time: let it produce "purgative herbs," which are the virtues; let it produce knowledge and wisdom, like the greater shrubs; let it produce absolute and perfect virtue, like the cedars of Lebanon. Thus its end may be a blessing and not a burning. And let us hear the Father saying: *Behold, the scent of my son is like the scent of a full field which God has blessed.* <note>Genesis 27:27.</note>

<margin>Basil</margin>

## Chapter Seven

Finally, he mentions man—not because man is an angel, but because he is the boundary and the end of the angelic world. Just as when Moses treated corruptible nature, he brought man forward not as a part of that nature, but as its principle and head. Thus it happens that the study of man belongs to three worlds: to the one that is his own, and to both extremes—namely, the incorporeal and the elementary. He is positioned in the middle of these so that he is established as the end of the one and the beginning of the other. But I see a trap prepared for our interpretation, since it is added that man is "to rule over the fish of the sea, the birds of the air, and the beasts." For if those animals signify the angelic nature to us, how will it be true that it is written that man rules over them?

May He be present with us and crush the snare, He who also crushed Satan under our feet—Jesus Christ, the firstborn of all creation <note>original: "primogenitus omnis creaturæ"; a title for Christ from Colossians 1:15</note>. He truly crushes the snare and loosens and breaks every knot. For not only in Him—in whom the whole fullness of divinity dwelt bodily <note>Colossians 2:9</note>—was human nature so highly exalted that the man Christ, insofar as He is man (if we believe Dionysius <note>Dionysius the Areopagite, whose "Ecclesiastical Hierarchy" argues that Christ, even in His humanity, remains the source of illumination for the angels</note>), teaches, illuminates, and perfects the angels; but He was also made "so much better than the angels as He has inherited a more excellent name than they," as Paul says <note>Hebrews 1:4</note>. Furthermore, all of us to whom power was given to become "children of God"—through the grace of which Christ is the giver—can be raised above the dignity of angels.

# FOURTH EXPOSITION ON THE HUMAN WORLD, THAT IS, ON THE NATURE OF MAN.

## Preface to the Fourth Book.

<margin>
The Delphic inscription
Plato
Triple punishment for ignorance of self:
Above oneself
From oneself
Behind oneself
</margin>
**A**fter we have sufficiently shown through the Prophet <note>Referring to Moses, the presumed author of Genesis</note> how he treated all parts of the world and all nature—celestial, angelic, and corruptible—it remains for us (if we are mindful of our promise) to interpret the entire reading once again regarding man. We shall prove this by the facts themselves: that there is no discourse in this entire work <note>Genesis</note> which does not embrace hidden meanings and the highest truths regarding the nature of man, just as it dealt with the three worlds discussed above <note>Pico's cosmology consists of the Elemental, Celestial, and Angelic worlds; Man is the fourth</note>. Nor shall we have performed a less worthwhile task if we are diligent in explaining this fourth exposition than we were in the previous ones. For how useful and necessary the knowledge of oneself is for man (to pass over the Delphic inscription <note>The famous command "Know Thyself" (Gnothi seauton) inscribed on the Temple of Apollo at Delphi</note>) was so demonstrated by Plato in the first *Alcibiades* that he left nothing for those coming after him to attempt to bring as something new on this matter. Indeed, the zeal of that man is wicked and rash who, while still ignorant and unaware of whether he is even capable of knowing anything at all, nevertheless boldly seeks knowledge of things that are so far away from him.

Let us return, therefore, to ourselves, and see (as the prophet says) "what great things God has done for our soul" <note>Psalm 66:16</note>. Lest, if perhaps the soul is less diligent in recognizing herself, she might hear the Father saying in the Song of Songs: "If you do not know yourself, O most beautiful of women, go out and depart after the tracks of your flocks" <note>Song of Songs 1:7. Pico interprets "self-ignorance" as a fall from grace</note>. You see what punishment awaits us for our ignorance! First, one must depart: namely, from the Father, a departure followed by disinheritance—and what could be unhappier? Second, one must "go out": truly, out of ourselves. For the mind is not with itself if it does not see itself. But he who goes out of himself is torn apart—and what could be more bitter? Third, one must walk "after the tracks of our flocks," that is, after the tracks of the <term>brutes</term> <note>Technical term for non-rational animals, emphasizing the lower, sensory nature</note> that are within us (about which we shall say enough in the exposition)—and what could be more wretched? What is more despicable and more contemptible than to become the attendants of beasts, over whom nature had appointed us as leaders? Therefore, walking not after the brutes but after the tracks of Moses, let us enter into ourselves; let us enter the inner chambers of the soul, with the prophet himself unlocking the entrance for us, so that in ourselves we may happily recognize all the worlds, as well as the Father and our homeland.

### Chapter One.

<summary>Pico introduces the fourth part of his commentary, shifting focus to man as a microcosm who can surpass even the angels through self-knowledge and grace. He warns that failing to "know thyself" leads to a loss of divine inheritance and a descent into animalistic behavior.</summary>

<margin>
The rational soul
Aristotle
The Platonists
Plotinus
</margin>

Before we proceed more accurately with the exposition according to the words and order of the prophet <note>Moses, whom Pico traditionally regards as the author of Genesis</note>, it is necessary to say a few things beforehand regarding the nature of man and to briefly explain some terms, so that the understanding of the entire meaning may then be clearer. Man consists of a body and a rational soul. The rational soul is called "heaven." For Aristotle calls heaven an "animal" moved by itself; and our soul (as the Platonists prove) is a substance moving itself. Heaven is a circle, and the soul likewise is a circle; indeed, as Plotinus writes, heaven is a circle for the reason that its soul is a circle. Heaven is moved in an orbit; the rational soul, transferring itself from causes to effects, and again returning from effects back to causes, revolves in the circular orb of reasoning.

<margin>
Body
Spirit
</margin>

And if these things had to be explained individually to those who have not read them elsewhere, we would no longer be interpreters of Moses, but of Aristotle and Plato. The body is called "earth," because it is an earthy and heavy substance. Therefore, because it was made from the soil (as Moses writes), it gave man his name <note>A reference to the Hebrew name "Adam," which is related to "adamah," meaning ground or earth</note>. But between the earthly body and the celestial substance of the soul, there was need for a middle bond which would couple together such distant natures. Assigned to this task is that thin and spiritual <term>little body (spiritus) — In Renaissance medicine, "spirit" was not a ghost, but a refined, vaporous substance that acted as the bridge between the immaterial soul and the physical flesh</term> which both physicians and philosophers call "spirit."

<margin>Aristotle</margin>

Aristotle writes that this spirit is of a more divine nature than the elements and corresponds in proportion to heaven; here it is called "light," a name which could not better agree with the opinion of philosophers and physicians, whose common consensus is that it is a most lucid substance and rejoices in, is nourished by, and is refreshed by nothing more than light.

<margin>Avicenna</margin>

Additionally, just as all the power of the heavens (as Avicenna <note>A famous Persian polymath and physician whose medical texts were standard in European universities</note> writes) is transferred to the earth by the vehicle of light, so all the power of the soul (which we called "heaven")—all the power of life, namely movement and sense—is conveyed and poured through the intervening lucid spirit into this earthly body (which we called "earth"). Let us now descend to the words of the prophet. In his work, we first see the creation of "heaven and earth"—that is, the extremes of our substance: the rational power and the earthly body. These are finally united when "light" (that is, the lucid spirit) arrives, so that from "evening and morning"—that is, from the nocturnal nature of the body and the morning nature of the soul—one man is made. And since (as we have shown) all vital and sensory power descends to our "earth" through this "light," it is rightly said that before the birth of light, the earth was "empty and void." For the earth could not share in the benefits of life and movement from its "heaven" except through that messenger light. Therefore, he immediately added the cause of this emptiness: because "darkness was still over it," since the light had not yet arisen.

## Chapter Two.

But it still remains to be asked what this means: *and the spirit of the Lord moved over the waters* <note>original: "spiritus domini ferebatur sup aq̄s"</note>. Here, an indistinct and universal teaching is handed down concerning the waters, which is further distinguished in what follows, when he teaches at other times that there are waters "above the heaven" and others "below the heaven." If we desire the true sense of all these things, let us consult nature itself, which our prophet (as we have often said) portrays and represents with exact precision. We have seen mention made of the threefold part of human substance: namely, the rational, this mortal body, and the middle spirit.

<margin>The sensory soul</margin>

Two parts remain. For between the rational part by which we are men and all that is bodily in us—whether it be thick or thin and spiritual—there is a middle sensory part which we share with the beasts. And since we have no less in common with angels than with beasts...

For if reason is called "heaven" (as we have proved), it is now manifest that there are within us "waters above the heavens" and likewise "waters below the heavens." The name "waters" applies to both parts—the intellectual and the sensual—for different reasons: to the former because it is most accessible to the rays of divine illumination; to the latter because it pants for and delights in fleeting and flowing things. The Scripture sufficiently warns us of this diversity when it places the latter "under the heaven," where all things are flowing and fleeting, and the former "above the heaven," where there is the administration of pure and perpetual intelligence. Therefore, when we read that on the first day "the spirit of the Lord brooded over the waters," <note>Genesis 1:2</note> and that the waters were divided in two, we certainly should not take this to refer to the waters under the heaven; for it is not the spirit of the Lord, but rather the heaven itself that is carried over these. It remains, then, that this was said of those waters which are above the heaven.

<margin>Unparticipated divine intellect</margin>
<margin>The Greeks</margin>
<margin>The Arabs</margin>
<margin>The Hebrews</margin>
<margin>Al-Farabi</margin>
<margin>Moses the Egyptian</margin>
From this, a most important doctrine concerning the soul is reported to us. For the intellect that is in us is illuminated by a greater and even divine intellect, whether it be God (as some wish) or a mind closest and akin to man (as almost all the Greeks, the Arabs, and many of the Hebrews believe). This substance is what the Jewish philosophers and Al-Farabi, <note>Pico calls him "Abunafar Alpharabius," a famous 10th-century Islamic philosopher.</note> in the book he wrote *On Principles*, called "the spirit of the Lord" in express words. It was not done without cause that [Moses] mentioned this thing—that is, the spirit moving over the waters—before he had established man from the bond of light between the soul and the body. It was done so that we might not happen to believe that this spirit is not present to our intellect unless it were coupled to a body. This is what Moses the Egyptian <note>Maimonides, the preeminent Jewish philosopher.</note> and Abubacher the Arab, <note>Ibn Bajja, an Andalusian philosopher.</note> and certain others, falsely believed.

## Chapter Three.

<margin>Abubacher the Arab</margin>
<margin>The collection of waters into one place</margin>
<margin>Aristotle</margin>
<margin>Plato</margin>
It remains for us to explain what it means when he says that "the waters which are under the heaven"—that is, the sensual powers which are under the rational part—are "gathered into one place." <note>Genesis 1:9</note> This is most manifest to those not entirely unrefined in philosophy. For all the sensitive powers are gathered into that sense which we call "common sense" from the thing itself; <term>Common sense (sensus communis)</term> <note>In medieval psychology, this was a specific internal faculty that combined the data from the five external senses into a single perception.</note> and this, if we follow Aristotle, is in the heart, just as rivers flow together into the sea. We might not absurdly say that from that sea, the five senses of the body—which we see as hearing, sight, taste, touch, and smell—enter the continent of the body like five diffused Mediterranean seas; this was a view appropriate to Plato's *Theaetetus*. And since from the perfection of these sensitive powers (which we understand from this collection toward their source) there comes to the body—which we call "earth"—both life, health, and nourishment, he rightly introduces the "green and flowering earth" immediately after that gathering of the waters. For the senses were provided by nature to all mortals for the procurement of life and the health of the body: so that through them they might recognize what is harmful and what is healthy, and once recognized, they might reject the former and desire the latter through the appetite annexed to the senses; and finally, through the joined power of motion, they might flee evils and pursue useful things. The eye sees food; the nostrils smell it; the feet approach; the hands take it; the palate tastes it. We say all these things so that we may recognize that the "abundant happiness" of the earth (which has long signified the body to us) is aptly joined to the "stabilizing of the waters" (that is, the sensitive powers).

## Chapter Four.

But since the rational nature is distinguished by many powers and potencies, we have spoken above of its bare substance. Now we shall speak of its ornament and, so to speak, its royal furniture...

<margin>Platonists</margin>
...must be said. This is what is written: that the moon, sun, and stars were placed in the firmament. Indeed, the younger philosophers <note>Pico likely refers to the Neoplatonists here, who refined earlier Platonic thought.</note> might perhaps interpret the sun as the *intellect in act* and the moon as the *intellect in potentiality*. But since we have a great controversy with them on this matter, let us meanwhile explain it this way: that part of the soul which turns toward the "waters above" and toward the spirit of the Lord should be called the **Sun**, because it shines completely. That part which looks toward the "waters below"—that is, the sensual powers—and from which it contracts some stain of infection, should have the name of the **Moon**. The Greek Platonists, according to the dogmas of their teaching, would call the Sun, understood in this way, <term>Dianoia</term> <note>original: Διανοιαν; discursive reason or thinking</note> and the Moon <term>Doxa</term> <note>original: Δοξαν; opinion or belief</note>.

Since, however, while we are pilgrims away from our fatherland <note>A common metaphor for the soul's exile from heaven into the physical world.</note> and live in the night and darkness of this present life, we use that part most which is turned toward the senses—from which we form more opinions than we have certain knowledge. But when the day of the future life dawns, having turned away from the senses and toward divine things, we shall understand with that other, higher part. Thus, it is rightly said that this Sun of ours rules the day, and the Moon rules the night. Likewise, because when we have cast off this dying garment <note>the physical body</note>, we shall behold with the single light of the Sun that which, in this most wretched night of the body, we try rather to see through many forces and powers than actually see. Therefore, the day shines with a single Sun; the night, on the contrary, gathers and unites many stars to the Moon—as if she were less powerful—as auxiliaries: namely, the power of *composing* and *dividing*, of *reasoning*, likewise of *defining*, and the rest.

### Chapter five.

Thus far concerning the cognitive powers of the soul. Now he <note>Moses, as the author of Genesis.</note> moves on to those whose work is to desire—namely, the seats of anger and lust (that is, concupiscence). He designates these by **beasts** and the **irrational kind of living things**, because we have them in common with the beasts; and what is more unfortunate, they often drive us toward a brutal life. 

<margin>
Chaldeans
Plato
Pythagoreans
Theocritus
Circe
</margin>

Hence that saying of the Chaldeans: *Beasts of the earth inhabit your vessel.* <note>Pico is quoting the "Chaldean Oracles," a text he believed contained ancient wisdom compatible with the Bible.</note> And in Plato’s *Republic*, we learn that we have various kinds of brutes within our own home; so it is not difficult to believe the Pythagorean paradox (if understood correctly) that wicked men migrate into brutes. For the brutes are within us and in our very vitals, so that we do not have to travel far to migrate into them. From this come the fables of Circe, and that saying of Theocritus: those whom the goddesses—namely, Virtue and Wisdom—have looked upon cannot be weakened by Circe’s cups <note>Circe was the sorceress who turned Odysseus's men into swine; Pico uses this to show how wisdom protects the soul from losing its human nature to animal passions.</note>. 

But let us see what distinction among these brutes the Mosaic reading suggests to us. Some are produced by the waters which are under the heaven; others by the earth. The "waters," as we have said, signify the sensual part which is "under the heaven," because it is subject to reason and serves it most closely. The "earth" is this very earthly and fragile body by which we are surrounded. Let us consider, therefore, whether among the passions by which we are moved, some pertain more to the body and others to the "inner sense," which the philosophers call <term>phantasia</term> <note>the faculty of imagination or mental imagery.</note>.

Those passions which drive us either toward food or toward sex seem to me to look toward the body. For these were given to us by God, partly for the protection of the body which we nourish, and partly for the procreation of children, in whom we might survive when we ourselves pass away. 

<margin>Paul</margin>
We abuse these same passions when we are lured more than is proper by the bait of pleasure, through gluttony and through lust, *making provision for the flesh*—as Paul says—*in its desires*. <note>Romans 13:14</note> In his words, it should be noted that he did not say "do not make provision for the flesh," but "do not do so in its desires." This is because they must be used for necessity, not for pleasure—much less should our happiness be placed in them. Therefore, let us understand these passions as "beasts of burden" and "wild animals," which are called the offspring of the earth rather than of the waters. This is because they are both satisfied and excited through the members of this thick body, and were provided for us by God for its well-being...
