...they existed: though to them they become a means of destruction, for they waste away in drunkenness and are dissolved in lust. But to the "waters"—that is, the sense of the imagination—let us refer those affections which can be called the offspring of our thought rather than of our flesh, for they are more spiritual. Of this kind are those which call us toward honors, toward anger, toward vengeance, and to other similar affections related to these. These are necessary and useful for those who use them in moderation. For one must get angry, but within measure; and vengeance is often a work of justice; and each person must protect their own dignity; nor are honors to be refused when they are obtained through honorable means. I say this for this reason: lest, because God created these "brute" things (which indicate our sensual desires) and blessed them after they were created, we might believe them to be evil by their own nature. We must not believe, along with the **Manicheans**, <margin>Manicheans</margin> <note>The Manicheans were a religious group who believed the physical world and its desires were created by an evil principle; Pico argues here that the desires themselves are naturally good and only become evil through human excess.</note> that they were established by an evil beginning rather than by a good God. All those things are therefore good and necessary for man; but we, exceeding the limit and turning toward ambition, rage, hot-headedness, and pride, make those things evil by our own fault, which that best Creator had instituted as best.

## Chapter Six

Observe, however, how perfectly what follows agrees with what we have said: that man was made by God in His own image so that he might rule over the fish, the birds, and the beasts which both the water and the earth had produced. And indeed we were already discussing man above, but now for the first time we understand the "image of God" in him, from which comes his dominion and command over the brute creatures. For man was so established by nature that reason should rule over the senses, and that by its law every fury and appetite of both anger and lust should be restrained. But once the image of God was blotted out through the stain of sin, we wretches and unhappy ones began to serve our own "beasts"; and like the **Chaldean king**, <margin>The Chaldean king</margin> <note>A reference to Nebuchadnezzar II, the King of Babylon (Chaldea), who, according to the Book of Daniel, was punished by God with madness and lived like a wild animal in the fields.</note> we live among them, groveling on the ground, greedy for earthly things, having forgotten our fatherland, forgotten our Father, and forgotten the kingdom and the privilege of ancient dignity given to us. Truly, "man, when he was in honor, did not understand: but was compared to the foolish beasts of burden and became like them" <note>A quote from Psalm 49:20.</note>.

## Chapter Seven

<margin>Jesus Christ, the last Adam</margin>
But just as we all exist in the first Adam, who obeyed Satan more than God—and as his children according to the flesh, we are deformed and degenerate from humans into brutes; so in the **last Adam**, Jesus Christ, <note>A theological title for Jesus from the letters of St. Paul, contrasting the first man who brought sin with the new man who brings life.</note> who fulfilled the will of the Father and overcame spiritual wickedness with His own blood—as His children according to the spirit, we are reformed through grace and reborn from man into the adoption of the sons of God; if only, as in Him, so in us the prince of darkness and of this world finds nothing <note>A reference to the Gospel of John 14:30.</note>.

# FIFTH EXPOSITION: CONCERNING ALL THE WORLDS SEPARATELY IN THEIR FOLLOWING ORDER

## Preface to the Fifth Book

<margin>which so</margin>
Just as Moses, as we have shown, discussed all the worlds simultaneously—the intellectual, the celestial, the elementary, and the human—in the individual parts of his text, imitating nature (or rather God, the craftsman of nature), who has embraced all things within each individual world; so following the example of that same nature, which distributes proper seats, proper rights, and peculiar laws to each one, our **Prophet** <note>Pico consistently refers to Moses as the "Prophet."</note> also arranged his scripture with a wonderful and perfect mastery of divine art. He did this so that, although he discusses all things everywhere, he does so with the same appearance and under the same veil of words.

# Chapter One

<margin>
Angels consist of act and potency.
Averroes the Arab.
</margin>
Now, as we are about to speak concerning the **angelic nature**—which is pure intellect—let us first conceive in the mind that minds are like eyes. For what the eye is among bodily things, the mind itself is in the spiritual genus. Even if the eye possesses some light within the mixture of its innermost substance, it nevertheless requires external light to perform the function of vision, in which it observes the colors and differences of things. Moreover, it is not the case that the eye is not "sight" by its own nature, even if it does not see except by the benefit of light. For even the ears—not to mention inanimate things—and all the other parts of the body are illuminated by light, yet they do not see. Therefore, that which has obtained the nature of seeing and is "sight" through the very principle of its essence is that which can see once light has been received. 

Let us consider these same things in intellects: Intellects are the eyes; intelligible truth is the light. And since the intellect itself is intelligible, it has some light within it by which it can see itself, but it cannot see other things as well. Rather, it requires the "forms" and "ideas" of things; by using these as certain rays of invisible light, the intelligible truth is undoubtedly discerned. Nor should it be said—as we declared through the example of the eye—that they are not intelligent by nature, or that they obtained their intellectual property by accident in a condition equal to our own minds. From this [misunderstanding] flows the opinion of those who judge the title of "intellect" to be unworthy of God. For if we take the intellect to be like an eye which sees not from itself but by the participation of light—since God is light (for truth is light) and vision is the action by which the eye touches the light—God does not need this operation, as He is the light itself. He is as much further removed from the ignorance of all things than the angels are, as the nature of light is further from darkness than the eye is. 

But let us return to the angels. The eye—that is, the intellectual substance—is not entirely simple; otherwise, it would not allow for the composition of the light coming into it. Hence the common proverb that **angels consist of <term>act and potency</term>**, <note>"Act and potency" (actus et potentia) are Aristotelian terms. "Potency" is the potential to receive something or become something; "Act" is the fulfillment or reality of that thing. Pico argues that only God is "Pure Act," while angels, though high, still have a "potential" side that must be filled by God’s light.</note> although it is an anxious dispute as to what that "act" is and what that "potency" is, and what the rationale of their composition may be. Likewise, there is the question of what <term>Averroes</term> <note>original: "Auerrois arabs"; Averroes was a 12th-century Islamic philosopher whose commentaries on Aristotle were essential to Renaissance philosophy.</note> the Arab intended when he said that both intellects—the one which is in "act" and the one which is in "potency"—exist in all intellects beneath God. But for our purposes in this passage, the common opinion suffices, however it may be understood. 

<term>Moses</term> reveals all these things to us on the first day. For he divides the substance of the angel into "heaven" and "earth"—that is, the nature of **act** and the nature of **potency**. Just as the same thing has different properties, so too does it have different names. Therefore, this same "act"—insofar as it is a virtue granting sight to the eye and is taken as the consummation of the "potency"—is called **heaven**, because it stands in the same relationship to potency as the heaven does to the earth. Again, insofar as it lacks light and cannot perform its own function of intelligence by itself, it is represented by the **waters**: a body capable of light, yet by its own nature shining very little. There is also another reason for the likeness, because this "act" of "potency"...

<summary>Pico begins his first exposition of Genesis, interpreting the "first day" of creation as the creation of the angelic world. He uses the analogy of the eye and light to explain how angels, as pure intellects, are composed of "act and potency" and require divine light to perceive truth.</summary>

...calls it earth, just as water is closest to the earth. But now let us proceed to the words of the prophet. "God created heaven and earth": that is, the nature of **act** and the nature of **potency**, from which he fashions the angel. And the "earth"—that is, potency—is "empty and void": empty of act and void of light, which it does not receive except through the mediation of the waters. And because opposites occur around the same thing, and it pertains to the same subject to host both light and darkness, he added: "and darkness was upon the face of the abyss." <margin>What the abyss is</margin> Nor did he say "upon the earth." For the abyss is nothing other (unless we misuse the word) than the depth of the waters. <margin>James the Apostle</margin> Over these waters "the spirit of the Lord was moved": a spirit that is indeed called the "Father of Lights" <note>original: "pater luminum"; see James 1:17.</note> by the apostle James; from him, the light of <term>intelligible forms</term><note>In Neo-Platonic thought, these are the "blueprints" or pure ideas in the mind of God that give shape to reality.</note> soon arises over them—that is, over the angelic minds. <margin>Saracens</margin> This perhaps the **Saracens** <note>In the Renaissance, "Saracens" usually referred to Muslim philosophers like Averroes or Avicenna, whom Pico studied extensively.</note> also understood when they said that the angels were led by God from darkness to light and filled with eternal joy. For pleasure follows intelligence; no pleasure is greater, none truer, and none more permanent than this.

### Chapter Two

Closest to this world is the celestial world. Its first property is that it is the interval between both worlds: namely, the **intelligible** world of which we have just spoken, and this **sensible** world which we inhabit. Nor can we more clearly indicate the essence of any "middle nature" than by expressing the extremes by which it is enclosed, since a middle nature is tempered by its extremes. He therefore reveals to us the greatest knowledge concerning the condition of heaven when he says that heaven is placed as a medium "between the waters and the waters"—that is, between the angelic and the corruptible substances—not so much by reason of its physical location as by the nature of its essence. Moreover, we have already said that by "waters" are understood the "forms," which are present closest to potency (as if to the earth) and bring essence to perfection. Just as the "earth" of the angels is one thing and the "earth" of the elements another—because the potency in each is different—so too the nature of the "waters" (that is, the forms) is different in each. Between these, heaven is truly the middle; it has received from the one side [the angelic] divine life, and from the other [the elemental] embodiment; from there incorruptible substance, from here visible substance; from there the firmness of essence, from here change of place; from there whatever is self-same, simple, and uniform, and from here whatever is varied, mixed, and dissimilar—all disposed by the providence of the Craftsman.

### Chapter Three

After this, he briefly reminds us of the integrity, positioning, and order of the elements through the "gathering of the waters into one place" and the laws prescribed for the sea, so that it might not overwhelm the earth. For there is nothing that better indicates that laws have been implanted in the elements by an intelligent cause—by which they are both governed and held in their places, beyond the mere inclination of a bodily and brute nature—than these "barriers of the waters." By these the ocean is restrained, whose force would otherwise carry it over the entire circuit of the earth (just as the whole of fire lies upon the whole of the air), yet as if warned by the rod of a schoolmaster, it pulls back its foot and does not advance further than our safety and the life of all living creatures requires. This cannot be attributed to the necessity of matter (which would rather incline all elements equally toward a spherical shape), nor to a "fortuitous collision of atoms" as <margin>Epicurus</margin> **Epicurus** dreams, nor to a "seminal force of nature," as <margin>Strato</margin> **Strato** <note>Strato of Lampsacus was a Greek philosopher who argued that the world was governed by natural forces rather than divine providence.</note> says, which is ignorant of any purpose; rather, it must be referred to the final cause alone, to which...

<summary>Pico explains that the "waters" of Genesis represent metaphysical forms and that God's laws, rather than random chance or material necessity, maintain the balance between the elements and the various levels of existence.</summary>

After he dealt with the celestial and elementary spheres, and thus with the entire integrity of the corporeal universe, it remained to speak of the inhabitants and "citizens" (so to speak) of this worldly city. First, he speaks of the celestial beings, as if of the senate and officials of the city; then of the terrestrial beings, as if of the commoners and the people. Therefore, he first mentions the heavenly bodies, which "God placed in the firmament so that they might be for signs and seasons, and that they might shine in the sky and illuminate the earth." I speak of the sun, the moon, and the stars. Here, the loftiest questions would have to be examined, each of which would require a full volume: in what way these stars are in the firmament—whether as its more noble parts (as the <term>Peripatetics</term><note>The followers of Aristotle, known for walking while they taught.</note> believe) or as living creatures in their own spheres, like fish in water or cattle on land (as Eusebius of Emesa and Diodorus maintain). This place would also demand a confrontation with the <term>astrologers</term><note>original: "genethliacos," those who predict the future based on birth charts.</note> who confirm their science of divining by the stars and foreknowing future events from the fact that Moses said the stars were "placed by God as signs." This science is not only sharply censured by our own writers—such as **Basil**, who rightly called it a "most laborious vanity," and by **Apollinarius**, **Cyril**, and **Diodorus**—but even the good Peripatetics reject it, and **Aristotle** despised it. What is more, **Theodoret** testifies that it was repudiated by **Pythagoras**, **Plato**, and all the **Stoics**. Here also, some might perhaps think we should inquire into the nature of the stars, their motion, their dominion, the spots on the moon, and the whole of stellar science. But if we were to descend to these matters, as beautiful and worthy of knowledge as they are, we might perhaps hear that line of **Horace**: "But now was not the place for these things." <note>A quote from Horace's *Ars Poetica*, used to signal a digression that isn't fitting for the current moment.</note> Therefore, we postpone these things to the work we have destined for this purpose: where we have undertaken to examine and treat the whole of philosophy to the best of our ability, reconciling **Aristotle** with **Plato**.

...where he said: *Let the waters bring forth the creeping thing of a living soul.* <note>Genesis 1:20; original: "pducant aquæ reptile animæ uiuentis."</note> He added afterwards: *God created every living soul.* <note>Genesis 1:21.</note> In this place, one should not merely observe that the waters bring forth at God's command, and then God Himself also brings forth. There are **creeping things**, which have an imperfect imagination and are midway, as it were, between brutes and plants. There are **beasts of burden**: although they lack reason, they are nonetheless capable of human instruction in some way, and thus they seem to participate in something of reason, having obtained a middle condition between brutes and men.

## Chapter Six.

Thus far we have dealt with the three worlds: the supercelestial, the celestial, and the sublunary. Now we must treat of 
->**Man**<-
concerning whom it is written: *Let us make man in our image.* <note>Genesis 1:26.</note> He is not so much a fourth world, as if some new creature, but rather the **embrace and bond** of the three worlds we have already described. It is a custom often used by the kings and princes of the earth that if they happen to build a magnificent and noble city, once the city is completed, they place their own image in its center to be seen and gazed upon by everyone. We see that God, the Prince of all, has done no differently; having constructed the entire machine of the world, He placed Man, formed after His own image and likeness, in its center as the last of all things. But it is a difficult 

<margin>Melito</margin>
question why this privilege of having the image of God belongs to man. For if we reject the exploded insanity of **Melito**—who depicted God with a human form—and return to the nature of the reason and the mind (which, like God, is intelligent, invisible, and likewise incorporeal), we shall certainly 

<margin>In what part man is said to be like God</margin>
prove from that that man is like God, especially in that part where the **image of the Trinity** is represented in the soul. Yet we must acknowledge that these same qualities are greater in the angels than in us; being more powerful and mixed with less of a contrary nature, they possess more likeness and kinship with the divine nature. Therefore, we seek something peculiar in man: from which a dignity proper to him and an image of the divine substance might be found that is shared with no other creature. 

<margin>Greek interpreters</margin>
What else can this be but that the substance of man (as some **Greek interpreters** also hint) actually embraces in itself the substances of all natures and the fullness of the entire universe? I say "actually" because even though an angel or any intelligent creature contains all things in itself in a certain way (insofar as it knows all things, being full of the forms and reasons of all things), yet just as 

->**God**<- 
is the center not only because He understands all things, but because He unites and gathers in Himself the entire perfection of the true substances of things; so also **Man** (though differently, as we shall show, otherwise he would not be the image of God but God Himself) claims for himself and unites all the natures of the whole world into the integrity of his own substance. We can say this of no other creature, whether angelic, celestial, or sensible.

This, moreover, is the difference between God and man: that God contains all things in Himself as the source of all, while man contains all things in himself as the center <note>original: "medium"</note> of all. Because of this, it happens that in God all things are of a better quality than they are in themselves; whereas in man, lower things are of a nobler condition, while higher things degenerate. Fire, water, air, and earth exist in the purest property of their own nature within this thick and earthly body of man which we see. Besides these, there is another more divine, spiritual body <note>often referred to as the "astral body" in Renaissance philosophy</note> (as **Aristotle** says) than the elements, which corresponds in proportion to the heavens. There is, furthermore, in man the life of plants, performing for him all the same functions as for them: nourishing, growing, and generating. There is the sense of <term>brutes</term> <note>irrational animals</note>, both internal and external. There is a soul <note>original: "animus"</note> excelling in celestial reason. There is a participation in the angelic mind. There is a truly divine possession of all these natures flowing together at once into one; so that one might gladly cry out that saying of **Mercury** <note>referring to Hermes Trismegistus</note>: ->**Man is a great miracle, O Asclepius.**<- The human condition can boast specifically of this name, whereby it has also come to pass that no created substance disdains to serve him. The earth and elements are at hand and serve him; the heavens battle for him; the angelic minds provide for his safety and well-being—if what **Paul** writes is true: that they are all <note>Hebrews 1:14</note> *ministering spirits, sent to minister for them who shall receive the inheritance of salvation.* Nor should it seem a wonder to anyone that he is loved by all things, in whom all things recognize something of themselves—indeed, their very selves and all that they possess.

## Chapter Seven.

<margin>
Man is the bond and knot of earthly and heavenly things
</margin>
Earthly things are enslaved to man; heavenly things favor man; because he is the **bond and knot** of both heavenly and earthly things. Nor can both of these fail to have peace with him—provided that he himself has peace within himself—who sanctions the peace and treaties of these things within his own person. But let us take care, I pray, that we do not fail to understand ourselves while established in such great dignity. Let us always keep this before our mind’s eye as a certain, tested, and indubitable truth: just as all things favor us when we keep the law that was given to us, so too, if through sin and the transgression of the law we wander from the path, we shall find all things to be adverse, hostile, and enemy-like. For it is reasonable that, just as we do injury not only to ourselves but to the universe—which we encompass within ourselves—and even to the author of the world, the almighty God, we should also experience all things in the world, and God first of all, as the most powerful avengers and the gravest punishers of the injury received. From this, let us estimate what punishments and what tortures await those who transgress the divine law. These are they:
<margin>

For they are guilty of violating the universe and of offending the divine majesty, whose image they have defiled with the foulest stain of iniquity. This is perhaps why, among the prophets, when any command or prohibition from God is proclaimed, heaven and earth are summoned as witnesses: namely, because the transgression of that command also violates them, and since they have received a common insult, they too will receive the wicked to be punished while they serve God. Nor was it right, since all of nature was endangered by man’s loss, that its ruin should be either neglected or repaired by any other than the one through whom all of nature had been established.

### SIXTH EXPOSITION: ON THE KINSHIP OF THE WORLDS WITH ONE ANOTHER AND OF ALL THINGS.

#### Preface to the Sixth Book.

<margin>
Vestige of the Trinity
</margin>
**G**OD is unity, yet so distinguished by a trinity that He does not depart from the simplicity of unity. There is a manifold vestige <note>A "trace" or "footprint" of the divine in the created world</note> of the divine Trinity in the creature. We shall bring forward here only this one, which so far as I know has been brought forward by no one else: that whatever unity we see in creatures, we find distributed by a <margin>Triple unity in things</margin> threefold logic. First, there is that unity in things by which each thing is one with itself and remains consistent and coherent. Second, there is that by which one creature is united to another, and by which finally all parts of the world are one world. The third and most principal of all is that by which the whole universe with its Maker is one, like an army with its leader. This threefold union is present in every single thing through its one simple unity derived from that One which is both the first One and Trinity, simultaneously One: I mean from the Father, the Son, and the Holy <margin>Father / Son / Spirit</margin> Spirit. For the power of the Father, producing all things, bestows His unity upon all; and the wisdom of the Son, rightly disposing all things, unites and couples all things to each other; and the love of the Spirit, turning all things back to God, <margin>Root of all ordered charity</margin> joins the whole work to the Maker with the bond of charity. Just as God is more intimate to us—and thus more "one" with us—than we are to ourselves, so conversely each thing is more closely joined to itself than to other parts of the world. Thus, having been taught the order of universal charity, if we wish to follow the divine law inscribed on the tablets of nature, we will love God Himself first—above us and above all; in the second place, ourselves; and in the third, our neighbor. Our Prophet <note>Pico refers to Moses, the presumed author of Genesis</note>, however, said enough regarding that unity by which each thing is one with itself when he examined the nature of all things individually. Regarding that unity by which we are united to God, it will be discussed in the next treatise, where we shall dispute concerning the height of happiness. What remains is that unity by which the diverse parts are coupled to each other by a mutual covenant, of which we must now treat.

He argues that man, as the "bond" of the universe, required the Incarnation of Christ to restore the balance of all nature.</summary>

<meta>This page transitions from the general discussion of Man as the cosmic bond to a systematic analysis of the "Heptaplus" (the sevenfold account of creation). Pico begins his first and second chapters of this section to explain how different parts of the universe are joined together, using Moses's account in Genesis as a guide for understanding both natural philosophy and spiritual union.</meta>

## Chapter One.

Therefore, after we have seen the distinct natures of things and arranged them—so to speak—in their separate stations, we should not believe that the whole universe becomes a single unit only because individual things are contained by other individuals according to the condition of their own nature (as we have shown above). The prophet <note>referring to Moses as the author of Genesis</note> also wished to indicate in the context of his writing what and how many modes there were by which the natures of things are coupled together. He does this not only to call us toward this scholarly <term>curiosam</term> <note>literally "careful" or "diligent," here meaning a deep intellectual inquiry</note> understanding, but through this, to instruct and demonstrate by what way and reason we are able to be coupled to those things that are better for us. 

However, as I was thinking—before I approached the explanation of the words—about how many modes there are or could be conceived by which any things might obtain either an affinity or a coupling with each other, and as I ran through all the dogmas of the philosophers (in which I have toiled since childhood), no more than fifteen kinds occurred to me. Then, approaching Moses, I saw them indicated by him so clearly and so appropriately that I believe no one could ever be better instructed concerning them anywhere else.

## Chapter Two.

<margin>
The essence of the thing to which it belongs.
The property of the essence.
Form: to the Subject.
The transmuting: to the transmuted.
Art: to the matter.
Heaven: Earth.
Earth: emptiness.
Abyss: Darkness.
Spirit of God: waters.
Light: bodies.
</margin>

Immediately, then, on the first day, he embraces five modes—I know not whether more briefly or more clearly—by which something can be joined to another. For that which is joined to another is either its **essence**, or it is a **property** of that essence, or it exists within it as a **form** in a subject, or it touches it either as a **transmuting agent** <note>an "efficient cause" that changes something else</note> to that which is transmuted, or as **art** to the matter subjected to it. 

Similarly, we read of five pairs compared and connected by Moses: heaven and earth; earth and emptiness; the abyss and darkness; the spirit of God and the waters; light and bodies. 

First, the "earth, empty and void" <note>original: "terra inanis et uacua"</note> designates for us the first mode of connection, because "earth"—that is, matter—is by its own nature empty unless it is filled from elsewhere by forms. 

The "darkness over the face of the abyss" indicates the second mode. For the abyss, by its own nature, is neither luminous nor dark; yet darkness follows its nature unless the approaching light puts it to flight. In the same way, the darkness of privation <note>the philosophical state of lacking a quality</note> follows the formlessness and emptiness of matter until the arriving "species" <note>original: "species," here meaning the formal types or shapes of things</note> expel them. 

The third mode is shown by the "light" that arose upon the "bodies." For light is in them like a **form in a subject**. 

The fourth is "heaven and earth," because heaven does not dwell in the earth like a form or an accident <note>a non-essential quality, like being "tall" or "green"</note> dwells in the thing it completes; rather, it is joined to it as an efficient and transmuting cause to the body that is being changed. 

The example of the last mode is the "spirit of the Lord" which is "carried over the waters." For the Artificer—the wisdom of the Lord and the spiritual nature, which is entirely separated from the commerce of the body—is understood to be joined to bodies in no other way than **art**, which is in the mind of the architect, is joined to cement, wood, and stones. 

But consider again this logic of consequence: that the earth, being empty of itself, possesses its own domestic darkness; then it is joined most closely to light through "light," to heaven through "heaven," and through heaven to spiritual substance. 

But let us see how these things behave within us. The "earth" is the earthly body, empty of life and void of sense; over it are "darkness"—death, numbness, lack of efficacy, and immobility in sensation. "Light" is life, which enlivens, excites, drives, moves, and [gives] sense...

### Chapter Three.

Let us examine what Moses intends in the following passages; we will see ten other modes suggested by him, through which we may understand a mutual alliance between things. For besides those we have mentioned, there are these others, which we shall enumerate: for either something is a part of another, or an effect. Likewise, if it is a part, it is either an indivisible part of its whole—in the same way that the sun, moon, and stars are in the firmament—or it is separable, like the portions of water from the integrity of their own element, toward which they have flowed together. 

If it is an effect, it either sprouts from an intrinsic <term>seminal reason</term> <note>Latin: *seminaria ratione*; a Stoic and Neoplatonic concept of formative forces or "blueprints" within nature</note>, just as plants sprout from the earth, yet remain fixed to their parent and connected by natural cords and bonds; or it consists of and is fused from its own principles, like a compound made from the elements. In this way, the bodies of animals are made from water and earth; or it has an external cause, which can be divided threefold into the efficient, the exemplar, and the end <note>These represent three of the "four causes" of classical philosophy: the 'efficient' is the agent that acts; the 'exemplar' is the pattern or model; the 'end' is the purpose or goal</note>. We have examples of these three from Moses: while God creates and effects man; He creates him after His own image as if after an exemplar; and the beasts are subject to man and are made for man’s sake as if for an end.

### Chapter Four.

We have spoken of the part and the effect, and by the same reasoning, of the whole and the cause. For these relations correspond to each other. But we have not yet completed all the types of kinship. For regarding the cause, there remains this species of affinity: in which a secondary cause obeys and is joined to the primary one; 

<margin>The primary cause has a greater influence than the productive cause.</margin>

just as when God produces, the waters produce. And these indeed produce first, because they are the proximate cause, but not otherwise than by God's command, because the primary cause flows in more than the <term>productive cause</term> <note>Latin: *fecunda*; referring to secondary or instrumental causes in nature that produce effects under the influence of God</note>. Similarly, a secondary end is appended and annexed to the principal one; which he [Moses] wisely signifies by saying the stars were placed so that they might shine in the heavens and illuminate the earth. 

For the well-being of lower things is not the primary end of the celestial bodies. Rather, they intend this first: that they might shine for themselves; then finally, that they might also illuminate us. 

<margin>Homer</margin>

Therefore, also in Homer, we read that both the dawn and the sun rise and bring light first to the immortals, and then to mortals <note>original: *immortalibus primum tum & mortalibus*</note>. 

Besides all these, man is also kindred to man, and lion to lion; and yet a lion is neither a part nor an effect of another lion, if it was not begotten by it. The prophet signifies this when he gathers and unites the fish together, the birds together, and the beasts of the earth together. 

There is one last reason for affinity: that of a middle nature to the extremes. For man agrees with man and animal with animal because they share the same essence, whether specific or general. But the "middle" thing is not of the same essence as the extremes, but is tempered in some way from them; thus it differs from both while communicating with both. This was indicated to us by Moses when he places the firmament as a middle between the waters, dividing the super-celestial waters from the waters beneath the heavens; there he sufficiently reveals the nature of the "middle," just as we have abundantly declared in the preface of the first book and the second chapter of the fifth.

<summary>Pico identifies and explains ten modes of cosmic connection found in Genesis, including part-whole relationships, causal links, and the role of "middle" natures. He argues that all natural things are bound together through these specific philosophical affinities, ranging from stars in the firmament to the shared nature of species.</summary>

We are also reminded from this what we must do: that we may be united to better natures, in which the whole force and summit of our happiness is placed. For the first day also teaches us that light first arose once night was driven from the waters, when the spirit of the Lord hovered over them. From this is signified that saying of James: *Every best gift is from above, from the Father of lights.* <note>James 1:17</note> Lest I mention only our own authors, Iamblichus <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher (c. 245–325 AD) who emphasized the role of ritual and theurgy in reaching the divine</note> confirms it así: that human nature should not wish to promise itself anything even mediocre from its own power, unless it is aided by a greater—that is, divine—will. If this is true, and approved not only by our own theologians but also by the philosophers, then surely all our zeal should be in this: that having turned toward higher things—which happens through sacred religion, through <term>mysteries</term> <note>Latin: *mysteria*; here referring to sacred rites or hidden spiritual truths</note>, through vows, through hymns, prayers, and supplications—we seek strength for our weakness from that source. 

Hence the Platonic and Pythagorean discussions, having begun from sacred prayers, end in the same. Regarding these, Porphyry, Theodorus, and all the Academics <note>Followers of the skeptical or Platonic traditions of the Academy in Athens</note> confirm with one voice that nothing is more useful, indeed more necessary, for man. We read that the <term>Brahmins</term> <note>original: *bragmanes*; the priestly caste of India</note> of the Indians and the Magi of the Persians never attempted anything without first offering a prayer. I bring these testimonies of the nations for this reason: so that those who have been persuaded by an evil demon to believe the pagans rather than the Church might at least learn from those they trust that it is neither a laughing matter, nor useless, nor unworthy of a philosopher to take up work—and indeed great and constant work—in sacred prayers, in mysteries, in vows, and in hymns to be sung continually to God. 

If this practice helps and suits any kind of person most, it is especially useful and fitting for those who have devoted themselves to the study of letters and the leisure of contemplation. For them, nothing is more necessary than that they repeatedly turn the eyes of their mind toward divine things, purify themselves through integrity of life, and be more abundantly illuminated by the light requested from above through the rod <note>Latin: *ferulam*; likely a metaphor for prayer as a staff or a conductor of divine influence</note> of prayer; and, always reminded of their own weakness, say with the Apostle: *Our sufficiency is from God.* <note>2 Corinthians 3:5</note>

# Chapter Six.

<margin>A deeper mystery</margin>

Let us examine again what the arrangement of the water and the earth teaches us. Let us learn from the earth that we will not produce the fruit we are pregnant with unless we restrain the onset of the flowing and falling matter that invades us, and drive away and expel from our seats the whirlpools and torrents of pleasures that rush into us like waters. Let us learn from the waters that they were not considered fit for procreating fish until they were gathered into the single integrity of their whole element. 

For neither we, if we are torn apart and distracted toward different things—if we are not carried as a whole with all our gathered strength toward one intention—will be able to produce any offspring worthy of divinity in the light. A deeper mystery is also contained here: just as it is the happiness of drops of water to approach the ocean where there is a fullness of waters, so too is our happiness: that the portion of intellectual light within us be joined to the first... <note>The text ends mid-sentence, likely continuing on the next page regarding the union of the human intellect with the Divine.</note>

### Chapter Seven.

<margin>That men cannot be joined to God except through Christ, God and man</margin>
<margin>John</margin>
<margin>Paul Christ</margin>
But that greatest thing of all which the doctrine of the <term>firmament</term> <note>Latin: *firmamentum*; in the Genesis account, this is the "expanse" or sky created to separate the waters above from the waters below</note> signifies to us: where we see that the lower waters cannot be enriched by any benefit of the upper waters unless the heaven intervenes, which is placed as a medium between them. So let us set before our mind that the coupling of extremes cannot happen except through that nature which, being the medium of the extremes, has embraced both within itself. Therefore, it conveniently unites those extremes among themselves, because in itself it first united them through the property of its own nature. We are reminded here of that great <term>sacrament</term> <note>Latin: *sacramenti*; here used in the sense of a "sacred mystery" or "divine plan"</note> which is *foolishness to the Gentiles and a stumbling block to the Hebrews, but to us is the power and wisdom of God* <note>original: "gentibus stultitia hebreis scandalum nobis dei uirtus & sapientia"; a reference to 1 Corinthians 1:23-24</note>: that man cannot be joined to God except through Him who, when He joined man to God in Himself, having been made a true <term>mediator</term> <note>Latin: *mediator*; an intermediary who bridges the gap between the human and the divine</note>, is able to so annex men to God that, just as in Him the Son of God put on man, so through Him men might become sons of God. If what we say is true—that extremes are not coupled to each other except through a medium, and that that is truly called a medium which has already united the extremes in itself—surely if that ineffable <term>dispensation</term> <note>Latin: *dispensatio*; the divine arrangement or administration of the world, specifically the Incarnation</note> happens in Christ alone (so that the Word became flesh), then Christ alone is also He through whom flesh can ascend to the Word. Nor is there (as John rightly wrote) *any other name under heaven in which men must be saved.* <note>Pico attributes this quote to John, though it is famously found in Acts 4:12 as spoken by Peter</note> Let those who say they believe with Christ carefully observe this, yet believe that a common religion—either their own or the one in which each was born—is sufficient for attaining happiness. Let them believe not me, nor these reasons, but John, Paul, and Christ himself, who said: *I am the way.* <note>John 14:6</note> *I am the door; and he who does not enter through me is a thief and a robber.* <note>John 10:1-9</note>

# SEVENTH EXPOSITION ON HAPPINESS, WHICH IS ETERNAL LIFE.

## Preface to the Seventh Book.

<margin>Double happiness</margin>
If we have completed the order and nature of the levels of the whole world in the sixth exposition, as if in six days, it remains that in this seventh treatise, as if on the <term>Sabbath</term> <note>Hebrew: *Shabbat*; the day of rest. Pico uses this as a metaphor for the soul's final rest in God</note> of our commentary, we treat of the Sabbath of the world and the rest of the creatures whose nature we established in the previous parts—that is, we treat of their happiness. Or (to speak more correctly), let us hear Moses treating of these things as a true prophet of all future things. Happiness, however (as theologians preach), is of two kinds: one which we can attain through nature, and another through grace. They call the former "natural" and the latter "supernatural." Regarding the first—that is, the natural—enough has been said by Moses, since once the nature of things is known, we also know their natural happiness. It remains, therefore, that he should teach concerning the second, showing himself as a prophet rather than a teacher; for when Moses wrote, grace was not yet present, but it was destined to be.

<meta>This page continues the seventh book of Pico della Mirandola's Heptaplus. The previous page discussed the necessity of Christ as a mediator between the human and the divine. But since I seem to see certain know-it-alls—or should I rather call them scoundrels and idlers?—who call themselves philosophers when they are anything but: they immediately mock both grace and supernatural happiness as if these were empty names and old wives' tales. I wanted to engage in a very brief disputation with them on this matter as a preface to the seventh book. This subject is both useful to everyone on its own and very necessary for the work

<margin>How true and stable is the opinion of theologians regarding supernatural happiness</margin>
we have undertaken, wherein we shall clearly prove that the opinion of theologians stands firm, supported by the deepest roots of philosophy. I define **happiness** in this way: the return of each thing to its own <term>principle</term> <note>Latin: *principium*; meaning the source, origin, or first cause from which a thing derives its existence</note>. For happiness is the **highest good**; the highest good is that which all things desire; and that which all things desire is that very thing

<margin>Alexander and the Greek interpreters</margin>
which is the principle of all, as <term>Alexander of Aphrodisias</term> <note>A celebrated 2nd-century commentator on Aristotle</note> testifies in his commentaries on the "First Philosophy" <note>An older name for Aristotle's *Metaphysics*</note> and the Greek interpreters in their works on Aristotle's *Ethics*. Therefore, the end of all things is the same as the principle of all things: the one God, almighty and blessed, the best of all things that can either exist or be thought. Hence, those two primary names

<margin>Pythagoreans: Two names of God</margin>
given to Him among the **Pythagoreans**: *the One* and *the Good*. He is named **the One** because He is the principle of all, just as unity is the principle of all number; but He is named **the Good** because He is the end of all things, the rest of all, and absolute happiness. We can now see,

<margin>The root of the double happiness</margin>
if we are a little more diligent, the reason for a **double happiness**. For happiness is the possession and attainment of this first good. Created things can attain this good in two ways: either in themselves or in Him. For in Himself, this good is exalted above all, dwelling in the abysses of His own divinity; yet it is also found diffused through all things, being found in everyone—here more perfectly, there more imperfectly, according to the condition of the things by

<margin>Poets: What natural happiness is</margin>
which it is shared. Whence (as the poets write): *Jupiter is whatever you see* <note>original: "Iuppiter eſt quodcūq; uides"; a quote from the Roman poet Lucan</note> and *all things are full of Jove* <note>original: "Iouis omnia plena ſunt"; a common classical trope found in Virgil and Aratus, suggesting the divine presence permeates the universe</note>. Therefore, since every nature has God within itself in some way (because it possesses as much of God as it possesses goodness, and all things God made are good), it follows that when a nature possesses its own form, perfected in all its parts, it has attained itself and thus attains God within itself. And if the attainment of God is happiness—as we have proven—it is in some way happy in itself. This is **natural happiness**, which different things have obtained as greater or lesser according to the diversity of their natures. Fire is a thing lacking a soul,

<margin>In what way fire participates in God</margin>
yet it participates in God in many ways. For first, it *is*, and everything that *is* participates in God, who is Being itself. Likewise, insofar as fire is a certain species and an act, it is like God, who is the first species and the first act. And while fire produces fire, it imitates divine fecundity; while it contains itself within the boundaries of its own sphere, it imitates justice; while it serves us, it imitates beneficence, according to the small measure of its own nature. While fire does these things, having attained its own perfection, it is happy as far as it is capable of happiness. Plants are happier, which additionally have life; animals are happier still, having also been granted cognition. As they find more

<margin>Man is in the best condition of all mortals</margin>
perfection, so they find more divinity within themselves. **Man** is in the best condition of all mortals; just as he excels others in nature, so he excels them in natural happiness, being endowed with intelligence and freedom of choice—chief gifts and most conducive to happiness. Supreme among creatures is the **angelic mind**, both in the nobility of its substance and the attainment of its end, of which it is most a participant because it is both joined and closest to Him. But...

The imperfection of natural happiness; The philosophers' opinion on happiness

<meta>This page continues Pico della Mirandola's discussion of the two types of happiness from the Seventh Book of the Heptaplus. Having previously defined natural happiness as the fulfillment of a creature's innate potential, he now moves to supernatural happiness, which requires a direct, divine intervention—the "influx of grace."</meta>

<margin>
Who are capable of supernatural happiness and in what way
</margin>
They <note>Referring to humans and angels</note> can indeed be lifted up, but they cannot ascend by themselves. **This is why Lucifer sinned, saying: "I will ascend into heaven."** <note>A reference to Isaiah 14:13, traditionally interpreted as the pride of the fallen angel seeking to reach the divine level by his own power.</note> Man cannot go toward this happiness on his own; he must be drawn. Thus, Christ—who is happiness itself—said of himself: **"No one comes to me unless my Father draws him."** <note>John 6:44.</note> Animals and things below man can neither go to it nor be drawn to it. Therefore, only man and the angels were made for this happiness, which is the true happiness. A vapor can rise on high, but only if it is attracted by a sunbeam; yet a stone or any heavy, solid substance can neither admit the sunbeam into itself nor be lifted by it into the heights. This "beam," this divine power, we call the influx of **grace**, <term>grace</term> <note>Latin: *gratia*; here used in the technical theological sense of a gift from God that elevates human nature beyond its natural limits.</note> because it makes both man and angel pleasing to God. 

<margin>
An example of both kinds of happiness in physical bodies
</margin>
The philosophers have a clear example of this doctrine in physical bodies. For of bodies, some are moved in a straight line, while others are moved in a circle. **Linear motion,** <term>linear motion</term> <note>Latin: *motus rectus*; in Aristotelian physics, the "straight" movement of the four elements—earth, water, air, fire—to their "natural place."</note> by which the elements are carried to their proper places, represents that happiness through which things are stabilized in the perfection of their own nature. **Circular motion,** <term>circular motion</term> <note>Latin: *motus circularis*; the movement of the celestial spheres, returning to their point of origin.</note> through which a body revolves back to the same point from which it departed, is the most expressive image of true happiness, through which the creature returns to the same beginning from which it had proceeded. 

But see how everything corresponds on both sides. Only immortal and incorruptible bodies move in a circle. Only an immortal and eternal substance returns to God. The elements do not need any force to complete their movements other than the impulse of weight or lightness implanted in them from their birth; in the same way, individual things are carried toward <term>natural happiness</term> by their own impulse and power. But the heavenly bodies, even if they are fit for circular motion, do not suffice for themselves to complete this movement; rather, they require a divine mover to turn and revolve them. Finally, those bodies are so suited for perpetual revolution that they do not *create* it, but rather *receive* it. 

It happens no differently to us and the angels. We are such by nature that we cannot turn and reflect ourselves back [to God], but we can be turned by the moving power of grace and reflected back into God. Hence the saying: **"Those who are led by the Spirit of God are the sons of God."** <note>Romans 8:14.</note> He said "those who are led," not "those who lead." We differ from the heavens in this: they move by natural necessity, while we move according to our freedom. For the Moving Spirit constantly knocks at your soul. If you turn a deaf ear, <note>OCR "ob audias" is likely a misreading of *obsurdeas* (if you should be deaf).</note> you are left to your own sluggishness and your own wretched and unhappy weakness. If you admit it, immediately full of God, you are carried back through the circle of religion to the Father and the Lord; in Him, you will possess life forever—the very same life you were even before you were made. 

<margin>
The summary of true happiness
</margin>
This is true happiness: that we may be one spirit with God; that we may possess God with God, not within ourselves, knowing Him just as we are known. <note>1 Corinthians 13:12.</note> For He knew us not through us, but through Himself; so also shall we know Him through Himself and not through ourselves. This is the whole reward; this is eternal life; this is wisdom which the wise of this world did not know: that we may be brought back from all the imperfection of multiplicity into unity through an indissoluble bond with Him who is the One Himself. 

<margin>

</margin>
For this happiness, Christ prayed to the Father in this way: 

<margin>
Paul; The fall of the demon
</margin>
**"Father, make it so that just as I and You are one, so also they may be one with us."** <note>John 17:21.</note> Paul hoped for this, saying: "I shall know, not in part, but just as He is"; and since he hoped for this, did he not rightly say: **"Who shall separate me from the love of Christ?"** <note>Romans 8:35.</note> and desire to be dissolved so that he might become one with Christ. From this [happiness] the demon <note>Lucifer/Satan.</note> fell, because he...

<meta>This page continues Pico della Mirandola's discussion from the Seventh Book of the Heptaplus. He is currently contrasting the fall of Lucifer, who tried to "ascend" to divine happiness by his own power, with the necessity of being "drawn" or "carried" by God's grace to reach supernatural bliss.</meta>

He <note>Referring to Lucifer</note> wished to ascend to that happiness, but did not wish to be carried to it; and therefore he lost that which he would have possessed had he remained <note>original: "permansisset"; meaning remaining in his proper state of dependence on God</note>.
<margin>The fate of infants who die</margin>
From this root it is known what the fate is of infants who die before they have been initiated <note>In this context, "initiation" refers to the sacrament of Baptism.</note>. Clearly, they remain within themselves: neither stripped of their own natural goods, nor enriched by divine ones. For us adults, we must fall into one side or the other: either the greatest misery or the greatest happiness. Since one who is not yet initiated, and who is the cause of not receiving the **Mover** <term>Mover</term> <note>original: "motorem"; in Aristotelian physics, the "unmoved mover" (God) provides the motion for all things. Pico uses this to describe God's grace acting on the soul.</note>, not only makes himself exempt from grace but also corrupts his own nature. For it belongs to the integrity of nature to seek the spirit it has recognized and not refuse it; and without doubt, a nature cannot be upright if it either rejects or despises the hope of a greater good set before it. Therefore, after Christ has been recognized, if any do not "clothe themselves in Christ," they are deprived not only of that first happiness <note>Supernatural happiness</note> but also the second—that is, their natural right—because to refuse grace belongs only to a corrupt and weakened nature. 

Just as we, living under the Gospel, receive Christ—the power and wisdom of God—into ourselves because we love and hold fast to Him as He has already been given to the human race, so also the Fathers under the Old Law <note>The patriarchs and prophets of the Old Testament.</note> received Him, since they both believed in His future coming without doubt and hoped for it eagerly and desired it ardently. But just as they received Him not as present but as future, so too they did not experience the fruit of the indwelling Spirit as present until after He arrived. When, after the unspeakable sacrifice was completed on the altar of the Cross, Christ descended to them <note>A reference to the "Harrowing of Hell," where Christ was believed to have descended to Limbo to liberate the souls of the righteous.</note>, they were turned by Him, as if by a **Mover**, in a whirlwind moment toward liberty, and were raised to the level of the highest happiness. 

Religion promotes, directs, and impels us toward this happiness, just as we use **philosophy** as a guide toward natural happiness. Because if nature is the foundation of grace, then certainly philosophy is the beginning of religion; nor is there a philosophy that distances a person from religion.
<margin>Philosophy is the beginning of religion, and it does not distance man from religion</margin>
Rightly, therefore, we also—following Moses—after we have philosophized for six days about nature, shall speak on the seventh day about supernatural happiness, devoting ourselves to divine things.

### Chapter One:

<margin>Angelic and human nature is capable of supreme happiness</margin>
As we have shown, a twofold nature is capable of this supreme happiness: the angelic and the human. The former is called **"heaven,"** the latter **"earth,"** because angels inhabit heaven and we inhabit the earth. And there is no more to say about "heaven," because he <note>Moses, as the presumed author of Genesis</note> is going to write the law not for angels, but for humans. Therefore, descending to men, he says: **"The earth was empty and void, and darkness was over the face of the abyss."** <note>Genesis 1:2.</note> God does not create emptiness; He does not create darkness. But the earth (he says) *was* empty and there *was* darkness. He does not say these things were "created," but that they "were." Why this was said will become clear as soon as we recognize what this emptiness and these shadows are. Human nature, which is called "earth" when compared to the angels, was from the very beginning—because it sinned immediately—**empty and void** of original justice, and its "face"—that is, its reason—was covered by the darkness of sin. Nor did God make these things, but rather the malice of man, who willingly deprived himself of those goods with which God had enriched him. 

Thus the state of corrupted nature is described by the prophet; and how it was then restored by God through Abraham, through Moses, through the prophets, and finally through the Only-Begotten...

<meta>This page continues Pico della Mirandola’s allegorical interpretation of the creation story in Genesis. ...how through her Son, nature was restored to her former dignity and prepared for the highest happiness, as will be demonstrated in what follows. Truly, even at the time when the waters were veiled in darkness—infected, that is, with the primitive filth of the original stain—the Spirit of the Lord was nonetheless hovering over them. <note>original: "spiritus tamen domini fovebat eas"; an allusion to Genesis 1:2. Pico interprets the "waters" as human nature and the "darkness" as the state of original sin.</note> 

This must be understood in two ways: first, that men were being ruled by the light of the divine countenance which is marked upon us—that is, by the light of **natural intelligence**; <term>natural intelligence</term> <note>original: "lumine naturalis intelligentiæ"; the innate human capacity for reason, which Pico believes remains even after the Fall.</note> and second, that the human race was not abandoned by the care of divine providence, but the Spirit of the Lord was hovering over the waters.

<margin>The Apostle</margin> That Spirit which (as the Apostle says) intercedes for us with inexpressible groanings <note>original: "intercedit pro nobis gemitibus inenarrabilibus"; a reference to the writings of St. Paul in Romans 8:26.</note> was even then constantly considering by what means he might purge those waters of the poisons with which the ancient serpent had infected them. And behold, he immediately commands light to arise, and light was made: namely, that most wise **Abraham**, the first founder of the true religion. 

<margin>Abraham</margin> He was the first who would fulfill the law of nature and meditate upon the divine law. He was the first who would persuade men to worship the one God over and against idols and the pagan nations. He was the first who attempted to dispel the darkness of error and to declare war on the evil demons who are called the "princes of darkness"; for this reason, he is rightly called "Light." Because all the disciples of the Lord did the same, they were all called by the Lord "the light of the world." This is the first light that shone upon the world, and it distinguished between the religion of the demons and the religion of the true God, just as light is distinguished from darkness.

## Chapter two.

<margin>The Mosaic Law</margin> The Law followed him, which is rightly called by the name "the firmament." <note>In the Genesis creation story, the "firmament" is the sky that separates the waters above from the waters below. Pico uses this as a metaphor for the Law of Moses.</note> Right at its beginning, it announces to us this very thing we are now treating—the works of God’s hands (as David sang: *and the firmament proclaims the work of his hands*). <note>original: "et opera manuum eius annuntiat firmamentum"; a citation of Psalm 19:1.</note> Therefore, the Law was given through an angel to Moses and confirmed by the word of God. Even more than the previous light, it distinguished the Israelites from the Gentiles—that is, it separated the godly from the ungodly, just as the super-celestial waters are separated from the waters beneath the heaven. 

<margin>Jeremiah</margin> Furthermore, the Jews are called "super-celestial waters" because they alone (as Jeremiah says) do not fear the signs of the heavens, which the Gentiles fear. <note>original: "signa cæli non timent"; a reference to Jeremiah 10:2, where the prophet tells the Israelites not to be dismayed by celestial omens like the pagans are.</note> They alone recognize, worship, and venerate not the stars or the heaven, but the Author and Lord of the stars and heaven. The Gentiles, by contrast, are "waters under the heaven" because they adore and worship the demons who inhabit the murky air (the region just above the waters), and they make the visible heaven, the stars, and the planets into their gods and masters.

## Chapter three.

It would have come to pass that, unless some greater power and mercy of God had intervened, the waters under the heaven—that is, those serving idols—would have invaded and occupied the whole earth. Thus the infection of the entire world from the first stain, and the empire and right of Satan the avenger, demanded justice against us, who were guilty of the ancient offense and subject to the punishment of such slavery. But the always beneficent and saving providence of God willed that one part of the earth—though small, as far as the laws of justice allowed—should be free from the injury of the waters. This is Judea, called the **Promised Land**, because it was promised by God to Abraham and his posterity.

Therefore, that part of the earth claimed from the yoke of the waters was a work of God’s providence, so that if the rest of the earth—overwhelmed by the waves of spiritual wickedness—was to be useless and deserted, and unfit for the fruits of true religion, at least this part would remain. <margin>Messiah</margin>

And behold, now is the **fullness of time**. For if the number four is the fullness of numbers, <note>In Pythagorean and Neoplatonic thought, which Pico favored, the number four (the tetraktys) was considered the "perfect" number because 1+2+3+4 equals 10, the basis of the decimal system.</note> will not the fourth day also be the fullness of days? See, therefore, what the fourth day brings to us. The heaven established on the second day—that is, the Law—was without sun, moon, or stars; it was indeed capable of future light, but it was still dark and not yet illuminated by any distinguished light. Then arrives the fourth day, on which the sun, the lord of the firmament—that is, **Christ**, the Lord of the Law—and the lunar **Church**, Christ's partner and bride, and the apostolic teachers (who would instruct many in righteousness) were to shine out in the firmament like stars into everlasting eternities, calling the world to eternal life. 

The sun does not dissolve the firmament, but perfects it; and Christ did not come to dissolve the Law, but to perfect it. Most pious **Abraham**, the light of the first day, saw the fourth day—which is the day of Christ—and he rejoiced. <note>original: "uidit diem quartam & gauisus est"; an allusion to John 8:56.</note> He saw the ray of his own light—that is, of true religion—which he had brought to the world through the **Sun of Justice**, through the true light illuminating all men, to be spread most widely throughout the whole world. We shall then conclude most evidently, by the calculation of time, that the Christ is not to come in the future, but that Jesus of Nazareth, the son of the Virgin, was the Messiah promised to the Hebrews.

<margin>Jewish Dogma</margin>
It is among the decrees of the ancient Hebrew discipline that the six days of Genesis designate six thousand years of the world in this way: that what is called the "work of the first day" is a prophecy of those things which were to happen in the first millennium of the world; likewise, the works of the second day are of those things in the second; and so on, always preserving the same order of succession in both.

<margin>Moses of Gerona</margin>
To this opinion even Moses of Gerona <note>Also known as Nahmanides (1194–1270), a leading medieval Jewish scholar and mystic.</note> bears witness, a theologian of the highest fame among the Hebrews.

<margin>Saint Jerome</margin>
Saint Jerome also mentions this in his exposition of that Psalm which is inscribed to Moses; <note>Jerome refers to Psalm 90 (the 89th in the Vulgate), "A Prayer of Moses."</note> and this opinion seems to rest chiefly on that foundation:

<margin>A day of God is a thousand years</margin>
that "a thousand years" (as the prophet says) "are as one day" before God. <note>A reference to Psalm 90:4 and 2 Peter 3:8, used here to justify the "Day-Age" theory of history.</note> Therefore, if this doctrine is true, the fourth day is a prophecy of those things which were to occur in the fourth millennium of the world. Come now, let us show that according to the annals of the Hebrews and by the calculation of years which they themselves approve, Jesus appeared in the fourth millennium of the world.

<margin>At what time Jesus appeared according to the Hebrew annals</margin>
They calculate from Adam to the flood one thousand five hundred and fifty-six years; from the flood to Abraham, two hundred and ninety-two years; and thus from Adam to Abraham, one thousand eight hundred and forty-eight years are collected. From the birth of Isaac to the ruin of the second Temple (which was after the death of Christ), they count approximately—for I am not cutting to the quick <note>i.e., not being overly pedantic about every single year</note>—one thousand six hundred and sixty years. For they calculate from Isaac to the exit from Egypt four hundred and thirty years; from the exit to the Temple which Solomon built, almost the same number. From Solomon to the desolation of the Temple by the Babylonians, four hundred and ten years; and from the restoration of the Temple under Ezra to this sudden captivity, four hundred and twenty years. Therefore, if you collect all these together, you will calculate from the beginning of the world to Christ, according to the mind of the Hebrews themselves, three thousand five hundred and eight years. Thus, Christ arrived in the very middle of the fourth millennium; and within that same millennium—as if within the boundaries of the fourth day—the light of the moon (that is, the Church) shone upon the whole world. Likewise, the innumerable multitude of martyrs, apostles, and doctors—all of whom grew famous within five hundred years after the death of Christ—illuminated the obscurity of the "firmament" (that is, the Old Law) and the shadows of our night. But the Hebrews will say: "Suppose Jesus did arrive during these times. You still do not have proof that he was the Christ unless you show it was believed by our people that the Christ was *destined* to come during those times." The matter stands well; they ask for what is fair, and we can easily provide what they rightfully demand.

<margin>Oracles of Elijah</margin>
For there are manifest and commonly known oracles of Elijah circulating among them which, without any figure of speech or veil, say outright that the Messiah would come in the fourth millennium of the world.

The sons—or rather, the disciples—of Elijah said: **The world is six thousand years. Two thousand are void; two thousand are the Law; two thousand are the days of the Messiah.** And because of our sins, which are many, those years of the Messiah's time that have already passed, have passed. So say they. Come now, with these very words set before everyone's eyes, since I cannot bring forward anything fabricated or arbitrary, let us discuss and examine the words of this oracle, and we shall immediately achieve our purpose. **The world, it says, is six thousand years.** We might interpret this to mean that after a circuit of six thousand years, the consummation of the world will occur like a future Sabbath—which many of our own writers have also believed. Or if (as is more true) no one knows that day, let us take it in this sense: that no prophecy is contained in the Law concerning any time further than this. But this does not pertain to the question at hand.

<margin>Hebrew interpreters</margin>
Let us see what follows. Two thousand years of emptiness, two thousand of the Law, then the Messiah. By "emptiness" <note>original: "inane," translating the Hebrew *tohu*.</note> they mean (as all Hebrew interpreters say) the time before any law was given by God to men. But I see the mocking Jew saying: if there are two thousand years before the Law and two thousand of the Law, then the Messiah should come not on the "fourth day"—that is, while the fourth <term>millennium</term> <note>A period of one thousand years.</note> is passing—but rather on the fifth day, because it would be after the fourth millennium has ended. But the response is easy, as truth itself courageously supplies it. For when it is said by Elijah "two thousand of emptiness" and "two thousand of the Law," it is by no means to be understood as if the world would be without law for a full span of two thousand years, and similarly that the Law would remain for exactly two thousand years. Rather, it means that the time of the law of nature will reach into the second millennium, and the time of the Law will reach as far as the fourth. But even before the second is finished, there is the Law; and before the fourth slips away, there will be the Messiah.

<margin>Elijah / Talmudists</margin>
I do not invent nor dream up this exposition for myself; rather, Elijah himself teaches it to me, and the <term>Talmudists</term> <note>Scholars of the Talmud, the primary text of Jewish civil and ceremonial law.</note> teach it themselves. This will soon be manifest to you, O Jewish viper (unless you stop up your ears). Elijah says: two thousand of emptiness and two thousand of the Law. Let us see in what sense what he said about the emptiness was true; from that, let us learn the method of explaining what he said about the Law.

<margin>How the beginning of the Law should be received</margin>
We must take the beginning of the Law either from Moses or from Abraham. It cannot be taken from Moses, because then the state of emptiness would have lasted for more than two thousand three hundred years, or thereabouts. For roughly that many years passed from Adam to Moses. Therefore, the beginning of the Law must be taken from Abraham, to whom the covenant of circumcision was given—the root and foundation of the entire ancient Law. But from Adam to Abraham, if they consult their own histories, they find that a full space of two thousand years had not passed, but only one thousand eight hundred and forty-eight years had flowed by. Thus it happened that the fullness of the Law succeeded the emptiness not *after* the second millennium, but *within* its boundaries. Therefore, by the same reasoning, the evangelical fullness <note>The arrival of Christ and the Gospel.</note> ought to succeed the emptiness of the Law not after the fourth millennium, but while the fourth was still passing. Even if the **Talmudists** <term>Thalmutistae: scholars and compilers of the Talmud, the central text of Jewish civil law and tradition.</term> persist in their stubborn denial, let them hear their own authorities who most strongly confirm our opinion. For they themselves confess that even at the time they were writing, the time predicted by Elijah for the coming of the Messiah had already passed; and they attribute this delay to their own sins.

Now, if the words of Elijah were to be understood as meaning that Christ was to come *after* the fourth millennium—rather than *within* the boundaries of that very fourth millennium—the Talmudists would not have said, nor could they have said, that the time promised by the prophets for the Messiah had passed. This is because at the time when the Talmudic doctrine we have cited was written, four thousand years had not yet passed since the beginning of the world.

The Jerusalem Talmud;
The Babylonian Talmud

Moreover, as they themselves hand down, the Jerusalem Talmud was written in the three hundredth year after the death of Christ, while the Babylonian Talmud was written one hundred years after the Jerusalem one. Therefore, both were composed within the limits of the fourth millennium; and yet, they both confess and complain that the time spoken of by Elijah for the coming of Christ had already passed.

Where will they hide themselves here, or what lurking-places will they seek, so that they might utterly flee from and fail to see this sun of ours, which shines through the whole universe even against their will? The Talmudists confess (even if they do not believe the ancient prophets) that the times predicted by the prophets for the coming of Christ have passed. They confess it was believed by the prophets that he would come during those very times in which we maintain Jesus arrived. 

Nor are their own doctors entirely untruthful when they say that the Messiah did not come because of their sins. For indeed, he did not "come" to those who did not recognize him. Nor is he the Messiah—that is, the redeemer, the avenger of the worst captivity, the benevolent king, and the granter of the promise of the **heavenly Jerusalem** <note>original: "supernæ Hierusalem"</note>—except to those who have confessed him as the Messiah. 

But if, when he came to his own, his own did not receive him, those who were once "his own" are no longer his. Instead, those who come from the east and from the west <note>original: "ab ortu & ab occasu"</note> shall recline in the **bosom of Abraham** <note>A traditional expression for the peace of the righteous in the afterlife.</note>; but the "children of the love" <note>Referring to the Israelites as the formerly chosen people.</note> are cast out into the outer darkness. Thus, their troublesome question is resolved: whether the Messiah would bring salvation to the Hebrews, whereas Christ brought them ruin and destruction. 

For they are not truly "Hebrews" who not only fail to follow or worship the King and Lord promised to the Hebrews from the line of David, but who also—treating him like a thief, a sacrilegious man, and a profane person—affixed him to a cross with every kind of injury and insult. If they were the children of Abraham, they would persist in the teachings of Abraham; and they would also joyfully welcome him as he arrived, for Abraham foresaw this day—namely, the **fourth day** <note>The fourth millennium of world history.</note>—and rejoiced. 

The Messiah brought peace to men, but not to all. For it was not said by the angels simply, "and on earth peace to men," but there was added: "**to men of good will.**" Certainly, the same sun that illuminates healthy eyes blinds and darkens those that are sick and weak. And it happens by right reason that what is healthy for the good is harmful to the evil; and he who blesses his friends, being powerful and not ungrateful, likewise strikes his enemies with lightning and scatters them. 

If things had gone poorly for the Jews after accepting Christ, he would not have been the Christ. But if things went poorly for them because they crucified him, then he certainly was the Christ. For even when he was nailed to the cross by his victors, appearing at that moment most defeated, he triumphed over them with such slaughter and calamity. 

Why then, you blind ones, do you wait for the sun? The sun is here and it shines, but it shines in the darkness, and your darkness does not comprehend it. The **fourth day** has passed, on which the sun rose—He who does not abolish the law, but...

For he **placed his tabernacle in the sun** <note>original: "in sole posuit tabernaculum suum"; a reference to Psalm 19:4, traditionally interpreted by Christians as a prophecy of the Incarnation.</note>, and he came from the tribe of Judah, whose sign is the lion, a solar animal.
