If He is the "true light" who illuminates every mind, He has a most clear likeness in this sun, which is the symbolic light illuminating every body. 

But why do we seek other evidence? Let us ask the sun itself: which, at the time of Christ’s suffering, failed <note>The darkening of the sun during the Crucifixion.</note> while the moon was in opposition, clearly showing us the agreement of its own nature with His. Thus, with the best of reasons—not to mention a higher cause—we have called that day which the astronomers <term>mathematici: in this context, those who calculated the calendar and studied the stars.</term> call "the day of the sun" [Sunday] also "the Lord’s day," and have dedicated it entirely to His worship. <margin>The day of the sun is the Lord's day</margin> Even by this, we show that there is no reason why we should any longer worship the corporeal sun as the king and lord of heaven (as the Gentiles once did), now that the invisible Sun—co-eternal and co-equal with the Father, through whom both heaven and earth were made—has illuminated those sitting in the shadow of death.

## Chapter Five

<margin>The Gentiles are figured by the waters; the Israelites by the earth.</margin>
But now let us examine whether the works that follow the Fourth Day correspond to those things known to have happened after the coming of Christ. Only then can we finally accept our exposition as true and stable: when we recognize that all things everywhere testify to it and harmonize with it. Let us see what happens after the Fourth Day. The waters produce fish and birds; the earth produces cattle and beasts of burden. Let us recall to mind what we said earlier was signified by the "waters" (which, located under the heavens, were gathered into one place) and by the "earth" (which was made dry and visible by the receding of those floods). We said that the **Gentiles** are figured by the waters and the **Israelites** by the earth, which we proved through many testimonies of the prophets and through logical similarities. 

We saw, moreover, that before the rising of the sun, the sterile waters produced nothing that was good. The earth, however, was indeed fertile, but only with meager fruit—namely, vegetables and herbs. But after the sun appears, even the waters—with a greater fecundity than the earth—bring forth two kinds of living creatures: birds and fish. The earth, no longer content with trees and shrubs, produces both great cattle and beasts of burden. <margin>Simeon</margin> Do you not see, even if I remain silent, the fulfillment of the word of the good **Simeon**: <margin>Before the advent of Christ, there was no sign of life or fruit of true religion among the Gentiles. Do we not have before our eyes—even if we interpret it in no other way—both the calling of the Gentiles and the transformation of the earthly Jerusalem and the shadowy synagogue into the true Church and the eternal and heavenly city of God? Before the rising of the sun, the waters produce nothing. The earth produces something, but it is thin and meager. For before the coming of Christ, there was no sign of life and no fruit of true religion among the Gentiles. Among the Israelites, there was indeed some hope of life, and they knew the way of light in part...

For (to deal with the first point), it is not enough to say what some have said: that herbs and plants were brought out of the earth before the making of the sun so that they would not seem to have been created by its power. For by the same reasoning, much more should the fish and birds and all the adornment of the elements have been made before the sun, lest they be believed to have been made by its power. Moses would therefore have left behind a suspicion: even if the light of the sun were not needed to produce plants (as being less perfect things), it was nonetheless needed to produce animals, which are more perfect. 

For it follows that if more perfect things had come to light without its help, then those which are less perfect could also be made without it. However, the reasoning does not work in reverse: just because those things which are more lowly were made without it—namely plants, the most humble kind of living things—it does not follow that every kind of animal nature could have been produced without its work intervening. 

Therefore, the author's intention is more truly investigated from what we have said. Similarly, if someone were to speak of the living things related to the waters—those that live in the waters—he would see that one kind rather than two should have been referred to them, while two should have been referred to the earth; for the home of birds is the earth rather than the water. And beyond all controversy, if we consider the nature of the animal, a bird is either a terrestrial or an aerial animal; it is in no way aquatic.

### Chapter Six.

<margin>
Why on the second day it was not said "that it was good."
</margin>
From this also comes the clear resolution of a question that has long tormented the interpreters of this book: Why, on the second day, was it not said, "And God saw that it was good"? For if we say what is usually said—that it was done because the work of the waters was not completed on that day, but on the third, when the waters under the heaven flowed together into one place—it will seem hardly a full satisfaction. For the specific work of the second day is not the arrangement of the waters, but the arrangement of the **firmament** <term>firmamentum: the vault of the sky believed to separate the waters above from the waters below</term>, which was fixed in the middle place between the waters. On that day there was both the making of the firmament (when God said, "let there be a firmament") and the distinction of the waters (when He said, "and let it divide the waters from the waters"), which was quite complete. However, the collection of waters which is called the "sea," the revealing of the dry land, and the production of plants belong to an entirely different work; thus they were finished on another day, that is, the third, to which they belonged. Therefore, a reason must be sought from a higher mystery. The firmament (as we showed above) figures the **Law**. And the firmament was as unformed as it was simply imperfect until it was furnished with the sun, moon, and stars. In the same way, the Law was not indeed bad (as the **Manichaeans** <note>Followers of Manichaeism, a dualistic religion that viewed the material world as evil and often rejected the Old Testament.</note> say), but it was not "simply good"—that is...

## Chapter seven.

<margin>What the power of baptism works</margin>
Since, however, the supreme benefit of the Word made flesh was this: that through the sacrament of baptism—by which the power of Christ is poured into us—we are reborn as children of God, born not of blood but of God; finally, Moses indicates this to us when, after the sun has risen and been shown to the world, and after the fertility of the waters and the earth, he makes man in the image of God—not an earthly man, but a heavenly one. For once the Gentiles and Jews were converted to Christ, this alone remained: that through the most holy washing, conforming themselves to the cross of the Lord, they might be reformed to the image of God. For if baptism makes us children of God, and the Son is the image of the Father, is it not the power of the entire Trinity working in baptism that says, **"Let us make man in our image"**? If, therefore, we are in the image of God, we are also children. If we are children, we are also heirs: heirs of God and co-heirs with Christ. But who are the children?
<margin>Paul</margin>
It was written by **Paul** <note>Specifically referring to Romans 8:15 and Galatians 4:6 regarding the adoption of sons.</note> that we cry out "Abba, Father" in the Holy Spirit. Those, therefore, who live by the Spirit are the children of God; these are the brothers of Christ; these are destined for the eternal inheritance, which reward of both faith and a well-lived life they shall happily possess in the **heavenly Jerusalem** <note>The spiritual city of God, representing eternal life.</note>.

A paradoxical dogma of the true Hebrews

We shall not do this before we have touched upon a certain dogma, which is truly a **paradox** <term>paradoxon: a statement that sounds absurd or contradictory but may reveal a deeper truth</term> of the ancient Jewish discipline. It is the firm opinion of all the ancients, which they confirm with one voice as beyond doubt: that the complete knowledge of all arts and all wisdom, both divine and human, is included in the five books of the Mosaic law; yet it is concealed and hidden in the very letters with which the words of the law are woven, in the manner we shall now declare. 

Let us take, for example, the first small section of the book of Genesis, namely from the beginning up to the place where it is written: *And God saw the light, that it was good.* That entire scripture is composed of one hundred and three elements <note>By "elements," Pico refers to the individual Hebrew letters that make up the text.</note>; which, being arranged in the way they are there, constitute the words we read, presenting nothing but the common and trivial. This order of letters surely forms the **bark** <note>original: "corticem," a common metaphor for the literal or surface meaning of Scripture</note> of the text, while the marrow of hidden mysteries lies concealed within. 

But they say that if we take those same elements, broken apart and resolved into words, and if we rightly join them together according to the rules they themselves pass down—forming whatever words can be made from them—it will come to pass that marvelous and most secret dogmas about many things will shine forth to us, provided we are capable of receiving that locked-away wisdom. And if this were done in the whole law, then finally, from this rightly established position and connection of elements, all the doctrine and secrets of all the liberal arts could be brought to light. 

I said, however, *if we are capable of receiving that locked-away wisdom.* For it can happen that while we are treating, dissolving, and composing some words, a manifold series of speech may be produced therefrom, which may teach great things and signify great things; but unless someone has obtained the doctrine of what those things signify from elsewhere, they cannot help but look down upon them as useless and accidental, not understanding them. For we cannot learn dogmas and doctrines there for the first time; we can only recognize them. 

As for me, I neither prove these things by asserting them nor do I attest to them, because I have neither made a trial of them, nor do I trust that I am able to do so. Yet I neither deny nor despise them—partly because this opinion has great authors, and

This entire sentence results from the breaking down and reassembling of that first word <note>The word is "Bereshit" (In the beginning), the very first word of the Bible.</note>. Other matters are a little more obscure: namely, what is meant by the **head**, the **fire**, and the **foundation of the great man**; what that **covenant** is, and for what reason it is called **good**. For it is not immediately ready for everyone to see explained here the entire system of the four worlds <term>four worlds: in Kabbalah, these are levels of existence—Atziluth (Emanation), Beriah (Creation), Yetzirah (Formation), and Asiyah (Action)</term> of which we are treating, as well as their kinship and happiness, about which we shall ultimately dispute. 

First, therefore, it must be noted that the world is called a **Great Man** by Moses. For if man is a **small world** <term>microcosmus: the idea that a human being reflects the entire universe in miniature</term>, then surely the world is a **great man** <term>macrocosmus: the universe viewed as a large-scale human organism</term>. Taking this opportunity, he most aptly represents the three worlds—the **intellectual**, the **celestial**, and the **corruptible** <note>The "corruptible" world refers to the Earthly realm where things decay and change.</note>—through the three parts of a man. In this figure, he shows not only that all worlds are contained within man, but he also briefly declares which part of man corresponds to which world. 

Let us imagine, therefore, three parts in man: the highest is the **head**; then that which extends from the neck to the <margin>Which part in man corresponds to which world: Knowledge, Motion, Generation</margin> navel; and the third, which extends from the navel to the feet. These are distinct and separated in the human form by a certain variety. But it is wonderful how beautifully and precisely, by the most exact reasoning, they correspond in proportion to the three parts of the world. In the head is the **brain**, the source of **knowledge**. In the chest is the **heart**, the source of **life, motion, and heat**. In the final part are the **generative organs**, the principle of **reproduction**. 

In the same way, in the world, the highest part (which is the **angelic** or **intellectual world**) is the source of **knowledge**, because that nature was made for understanding. The middle part (which is the **heaven**) is the principle of **life, motion, and heat**, in which the **Sun** rules just as the heart does in the chest. Below the **Moon** is that which is known to all as the realm of **generation**...

The second, however, he called **fire** <note>Latin: *ignem*; Pico relates this to the Hebrew *Esh*, signifying the celestial or middle realm</note>: both because by this name the heavens are judged by many, and because in us this portion is the source of heat. This covenant is "good" for this reason: because it is so directed and ordered toward God—who is Goodness itself—that just as the whole world is one within itself, so also may it ultimately be one with its Author. Let us also imitate this most holy covenant of the world: so that through mutual charity we may be one with each other, and at the same time, through true love for God, we may all happily become one with Him.

## GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA [SENDS] GREETINGS TO LORENZO DE' MEDICI.

<margin>a</margin> <note>The letter 'a' is a guide for a rubricator—an artist who would later paint a large, decorative capital letter 'A' over it.</note>
**I** have dedicated my Defense <note>original: "Apologiam"; Pico is referring to this specific text, written to justify his 900 philosophical and theological theses which had been criticized by a papal commission.</note> to you, Lorenzo de' Medici, not because I consider it (God is my witness) a work worthy of so great a man, but because it is owed to you by that same right by which I have long understood that I owe everything of mine to you. For be most certain of this: whatever I am or am to be, it is yours, Lorenzo, and shall always remain so in the future. I say less than I wish, and these words are altogether too cold to sufficiently express what I feel—that is, with what love, with what faith, and with what respect I follow you, and have followed you for many years now. I am moved both by the many kindnesses bestowed upon me, which clearly testify to your most loving spirit, and by your own virtues—not so much those of fortune as those of the soul—those rare and indeed unique qualities of yours which your own modesty does not allow me to recount at present. I return to the *Defense*: I ask that you receive it with a cheerful countenance; it is a small gift, to be sure, but a significant testimony of my faith and respect toward you for all time. If it should happen that you touch upon it amidst the great affairs with which you are always most busy, remember not so much this work itself—which was rushed rather than polished—but that the subject of the work had to be taken up by me because of the judgment of others, not my own. I have not dedicated it to you so that you might recognize in me some excellence of talent or learning that I do not possess, but so that I might know—for I shall say it again—that whatever I am, I am most devoted to your magnificence.

## THE DEFENSE OF GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA, COUNT OF CONCORDIA.

<margin>c</margin> <note>A guide letter for the rubricator to add a decorative 'C'.</note>
<margin>Innocent VIII, Supreme Pontiff.</margin>
**W**hen I had recently come to Rome to kiss the feet of the Supreme Pontiff, Innocent VIII—whose name is most deservedly earned from the innocence of his life—according to the custom of God. So that I might not depart from my practice of always commenting upon and treating something of a literary nature, and to do something to the best of my ability worthy of the city of Rome, pleasing to a Christian prince, and useful to myself and to scholars, I proposed nine hundred questions <note>These are Pico's famous "900 Conclusions," intended to synthesize all known philosophy and theology.</note> concerning divine and natural matters. To these I was to respond in a public assembly of most learned men. They had scarcely been made public when, among some who might at least approve of my zeal for the noble arts even if not my talent or learning, a manifold crowd of detractors arose. And although one could see the disdain, the upturned noses, the censures, and all the various judgments of each person—as always happens when we attempt something new and not trivial—nevertheless, there were about five principal points which these whisperers, one after another, condemned in me. For some carped at philosophy and literature altogether, even doing so that they might appear to be know-it-alls <term>scioli (smatterers); a derogatory term for people who have superficial knowledge but pretend to be experts</term>. Sometimes they added that Adam was cast out of paradise because, through the knowledge of good and evil, he wished to make himself equal to the gods. They claimed that those who wish to know more than is proper should be banished from the court of Christ by a similar example. Others disapproved not so much of philosophy as of this very kind of disputing and this method of publicly debating about literature, claiming it was done rather for show...

<meta>This page continues the introductory epistle of Giovanni Pico della Mirandola's "Apologia." ...barking that it was an ostentation of genius and learning rather than for the sake of acquiring knowledge. 
<margin>Age of the author.</margin> Some called me bold and rash. I, who at this age—being not yet twenty-four years old—did not 
hesitate to propose a disputation in a most celebrated city, before a most ample assembly of very learned 
men, concerning the highest points of philosophy, the sublime mysteries of Christian theology, and unknown disciplines. 
Many accused me—not so much because it was in Rome, or that I was a youth, but because I was going to dispute 
such a number, that is, nine hundred questions—calumniating that it was done superfluously, ambitiously, and beyond my strength. 
Among those who profess wisdom <note>original: "sapientiam"</note>—that is, the study of theology—there were some who, perhaps 
not content with lighter insults, proclaimed me no longer bold, nor rash, nor boastful, but a magician, 
but impious, but a new leader of heresy <note>original: "heresiarcham"</note> in the Church of Christ. I was (God be my 
witness) in doubt for a long time whether I should clear away these objections or if they should rather be passed over 
in silence. Two things especially moved me to keep silent. First, that I, abhorring both contention and 
brawls, have always loved peace of mind and the tranquility of a most placid life, which my studies have 
afforded me; nor did I hate any task of writing more than that which is based on dispute and 
bitter altercation in any form—for I have never judged it the part of a good man nor a 
philosopher to return an injury or insult any more than to inflict one. The second reason was this: 
I was content with the judgment of the Supreme Pontiff <note>Innocent VIII</note>, whose memory I must always deservedly celebrate, and of 
many from the most holy Apostolic Senate <note>The College of Cardinals</note>, whose kindness and most benevolent 
spirit toward me I can or should never forget. I seemed able easily to ignore both the 
hatred and the insults of wicked men; and indeed, regarding other matters, I was of the opinion that I 
should consider them unworthy of a response. But regarding the one crime of heresy charged against me: if I did this, 
I feared that what I did not clear away I would seem to acknowledge. 
<margin>Rufinus</margin> Moreover, Rufinus <note>A 4th-century monk and theologian</note> writes most wisely that it is indeed glorious to bear injuries patiently 
following Christ’s example. But he who bears or ignores a single mark of 
<margin>Jerome</margin> heresy is not a Christian. And our Jerome <note>St. Jerome, the translator of the Vulgate Bible</note>, with the greatest possible effort of mind, 
exclaims in a most clear voice: *I do not want anyone to be patient under the suspicion of heresy.* 
Therefore, Jerome does not want me to be silent; and by his authority, he draws and impels me—even against my 
will and as a man of leisure—to write. Therefore, if there are some who perhaps wish me to keep silent, let 
them know that their controversy is not with me, but with Jerome, who does not want me to be silent. 
Who can fail to hear Jerome without a sense of shame? Therefore, at his persuasion, or rather his compulsion, 
I have undertaken to write even a brief defense <note>original: "apologiam"</note>—not to tear down or accuse anyone, 
but to rightfully excuse myself from the greatest crime of impiety which is unjustly charged against me. 
I ask my detractors to endure this with the same spirit in which I have always endured their 
unfair offense. Let them endure it, I say, so that I—who am a Christian born of Christian parents, 
who bear the banner of Christ Jesus on my forehead, who would even willingly die for the 
<margin>Paul</margin> faith of Christ—might exclaim as if with Paul, while they listen with an even mind: 
"I am no magician, no Jew, no Ishmaelite <note>original: "ysmaelita"; in this period, a term often used for Muslims or non-believers</note>, no heretic. 
But I worship Jesus, and I carry the cross of Jesus in my body, through whom the world is crucified 
to me, and I to the world." Finally, since I [do not claim] for myself titles of holiness or wisdom 
or excellent titles of that kind...

<meta>This page continues Pico della Mirandola's defense of his character and his right to engage in intellectual debate. ...arrogate to myself nor derogate from them. I only ask that they do not take away this one thing from me—for the protection of which I would even willingly shed my blood—so that I may be able to call myself a Christian. But if they grant this, I do not write these things to those from whom I have already obtained what our entire defense <note>original: "apologia"</note> strives for. I write to others: those who believe or suspect that I am, or once was, a heretic. Although my main purpose is to show that it is not I, but those who slander me as a heretic, who deviate from the orthodox and catholic path, nonetheless, since I must write, I will also say something about the things first objected against me. I do this so that my detractors cannot exploit my silence as if it were a guilty conscience.

Now, the primary fault that many found with me was my very act of "philosophizing." I will say nothing to them in this place, because it is my plan to defend the cause of philosophy separately in a specific work. Besides, if it is a shameful thing to devote oneself to letters and to cultivate the fine arts and disciplines, I would rather acknowledge this fault than beg for forgiveness. To those who even detest this manner of debating and this practice of publicly discussing God, nature, and morals, I will not say much. For this crime—if it is a crime—is common to me and to great men, indeed to the most esteemed philosophers not only of our age but of almost all ages. To them, nothing was more certain for achieving the knowledge of truth they sought than to be most frequent in the exercise of debating.

<margin>Through gymnastics, the powers of the body become stronger.</margin>
For just as the body’s strength grows firmer through gymnastics, so in this "literary arena" <note>original: "litteraria palestra"</note>, the mind’s powers emerge far stronger and more vigorous. Nor would I believe that the Poets meant anything else by the famous "Arms of Pallas" <note>referring to Pallas Athena, the Greek goddess of wisdom and strategic warfare</note>, or the Hebrews when they say that iron is the symbol of the wise, except to show us how necessary these most honorable contests are for attaining the citadel of wisdom.

<margin>Chaldeans</margin>
It is perhaps for this reason that the Chaldeans <note>an ancient people often associated with the origins of astrology</note>, in the horoscope <note>original: "Genesi"</note> of one who is to be a philosopher, require that Mars look upon Mercury in a trine aspect <note>original: "triquetro aspectu"; an astrological position where two planets are 120 degrees apart, historically considered a harmonious and powerful alignment</note>. It is as if they imply that if you remove these encounters and these "wars," all philosophy would become drowsy and sluggish. But regarding these matters, as I have said, I prefer to defend myself with the authorities and judgments of great men rather than with mere arguments. It seems a greater task to satisfy those who say that I am unequal in age, talent, and learning to such a great undertaking <note>original: "prouincie," literally "province" or sphere of duty</note>, and that, following Horace, I have not consulted my shoulders to see what they can bear and what they refuse.

<margin>Horace</margin>
Truly, here the manner of my defense is difficult; for if I say I am equal to the task, I will seem immodest and full of myself; if I confess I am unequal, I will seem to bear the mark of one who is reckless and ill-advised. I have fallen into a grave predicament, since I cannot promise of myself what I cannot do without fault, nor can I fail to provide it without fault.

<margin>Job</margin>
And indeed, I could cite that passage from Job—that the spirit is in everyone—and perhaps hear with Timothy:

<margin>Timothy</margin>
*Let no one despise your youth.* <note>A reference to 1 Timothy 4:12</note> But from my own conscience, I will more truly say this: there is nothing in me that is great or unique. I do not deny that I am perhaps studious and a lover of the fine arts; however, I neither claim nor arrogate to myself the title of "learned" <note>original: "docti"</note>.

<margin>Hermolaus</margin>
For as my dear Hermolaus <note>Hermolaus Barbarus (1454–1493), a prominent Italian humanist and close friend of Pico</note>—the delight of the Roman tongue and the splendor and glory of our age—once wrote: "He cannot but be unlearned who believes himself to be learned." Therefore, that I have placed such a great burden on my shoulders was not because I was unaware of my own weakness, but because I knew...

<meta>This page continues Pico della Mirandola's defense of his intellectual project. Having established his identity as a Christian, he now defends the specific method of his work: a public disputation on nine hundred diverse philosophical and theological theses. He addresses critics who find the sheer number of topics to be arrogant or excessive, arguing that a true philosopher must be "eclectic"—not bound to one single school of thought but familiar with all of them.</meta>

...I knew that this kind of battle—namely, literary ones—is unique because in them there is profit in being defeated. Thus it happens that even the weakest person not only can but rightfully should not avoid but even seek them out. For indeed, he who yields receives a benefit from the victor, not an injury, because through the victor he returns home more enriched—that is, more learned—and better prepared for future battles. Inspired by this hope, I, a weak soldier, have not feared at all to decide upon so serious a battle with the strongest and most vigorous of all. However, whether this was done rashly or not, one could judge more rightly by the outcome of the battle than by my age. 

It remains for me to respond to those who are offended by the vast number of proposed topics, as if this burden sat upon their shoulders, and not rather that I alone had to exhaust this labor, however great it may be. <margin>Cicero</margin> It is surely unseemly and overly irritable to wish to set a limit on another's industry, and, as Cicero says, to desire moderation in a matter that is better the larger it is. In such grand undertakings, it was entirely necessary for me either to succumb or to satisfy the requirements. If I were to satisfy them, I do not see why what is praiseworthy to perform in ten questions should be considered blameworthy to have performed in nine hundred. If I were to succumb, they would have had cause to accuse me if they hate me; if they love me, cause to excuse me. Since in so grave and so great a matter, for a young man with slender talent and small learning to have failed was more worthy of pardon <margin>Gorgias of Leontini</margin> than of accusation; indeed, as the poet <note>The poet is Propertius</note> says, "if strength fails, the daring will certainly be praised," and "in great things, it is enough to have willed." 

But if in our age many, imitating Gorgias of Leontini <note>A Greek Sophist famous for claiming he could speak on any subject</note>, have been accustomed to propose disputes—not without praise—not only concerning nine hundred questions but even concerning all questions of all arts, why should I not be allowed, at least without blame, to dispute concerning many topics indeed, but nonetheless certain and determined ones? "But," they say, "this is superfluous and ambitious." I contend, however, that this was done by me not only not superfluously, but necessarily—which they themselves must clearly admit, even if unwillingly, if they consider my method of philosophizing. <margin>Thomas, Scotus</margin> For those who have devoted themselves to any one of the families of philosophers—namely, to Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas</note> or to Scotus <note>Duns Scotus</note>, who are now most often in people's hands—may indeed, by supporting their chosen master, put their learning to the test in the discussion of even a few questions. 

But I have so trained myself that, sworn to no man's words <note>original: "in nullius uerba iuratus"—a quote from Horace signifying intellectual independence</note>, I might pour myself through all the masters of philosophy, examine all records, and become acquainted with all schools. Therefore, since I had to speak concerning all of them, lest if I had defended a private dogma and neglected the rest, I might seem bound to that one. Even if only a few things were proposed about each, there could not fail to be a great many when they were brought forward about all of them together. Nor should anyone condemn me for being "carried as a guest wherever the storm takes me." For it has always been observed by all the ancients that, in unrolling every kind of writing, they passed over no commentaries they could read. <margin>Aristotle, Plato</margin> This was done most especially by Aristotle, who for that reason was called by Plato "the reader" <note>original Greek: "anagnōstēs"</note>. And surely it is the mark of a narrow mind to have confined oneself within a single Porch or Academy <note>The "Porch" refers to the Stoics; the "Academy" to the Platonists</note>. Nor can one rightly select a philosophy of his own from all the others, who has not first become familiarly acquainted with them all. Add to this that in each family there is something...

<meta>This page continues Pico della Mirandola's defense of his nine hundred theses. Having previously listed the merits of various Scholastic, Arabic, and Greek thinkers, he now moves into his own original contributions and his project of "syncretism"—the reconciliation of seemingly opposing philosophical systems.</meta>

<margin>The harmony of Plato and Aristotle: Simplicius, Augustine, John the Grammarian</margin>
Just as a good husband hates sterility in his wife, certainly the divine mind, long folded and associated with the soul, will hate a barren soul all the more because a far nobler offspring is desired from it. Therefore, I was not content with common doctrines, but have proposed for discussion many things from the ancient theology of Hermes Trismegistus <note>a legendary Hellenistic figure associated with a body of esoteric wisdom</note>, many from the teachings of the Chaldeans and of Pythagoras, and many from the more secret mysteries of the Hebrews. We have also proposed many things discovered and meditated upon by us concerning natural and divine matters. We have proposed, first of all, the harmony of Plato and Aristotle, believed in by many before this but sufficiently proven by no one. Among the Latins, Boethius <note>a 6th-century philosopher who aimed to reconcile the two</note> promised to do this, but he is not found to have ever done what he always wished to do. Among the Greeks, Simplicius <note>a Neoplatonist commentator</note> professed the same; would that he had fulfilled it as well as he promised! Augustine also writes in the *Academics* that there were several who attempted to prove the same through their very subtle discussions: namely, that the philosophy of Plato and Aristotle is one and the same. Likewise, John the Grammarian <note>John Philoponus, a 6th-century Christian philosopher</note>, though he says that Plato differs from Aristotle only in the eyes of those who do not understand Plato's words, nevertheless left the proof of this to posterity.

<margin>Note: New dogmas devised</margin>
Moreover, we have added several points in which we assert that the opinions of Scotus and Thomas <note>Duns Scotus and Thomas Aquinas</note>, and several in which those of Averroes and Avicenna <note>the two most influential Islamic philosophers in the West</note>, which are thought to be discordant, are in harmony. In the second place, we have set forth what we ourselves have thought out in both Aristotelian and Platonic philosophy, as well as seventy-two new physical and metaphysical dogmas. If anyone holds these, he will be able—unless I am mistaken—to resolve any proposed question concerning natural and divine things by a method far different from that which is taught in the schools and cultivated by the doctors of this age.

<margin>Note.</margin>
Nor should anyone wonder so much that I, in my first years, in a tender age at which it was hardly permitted (as some boast) to read the commentaries of others, should wish to bring forth a new philosophy, rather than simply praising that philosophy if it is defended or damning it if it is rejected. Finally, since these discoveries are ours and our own, those who are to judge my writings should count their merits or demerits rather than the years of the author.

<margin>A new method of philosophizing through numbers: Plato, Aristotle, Abunafar, Avenzoar, Plato</margin>
There is, moreover, besides that one, another new method of philosophizing through numbers which we have introduced. It is indeed ancient, observed by the earliest theologians—especially by Pythagoras, by Aglaophemus, by Philolaus, by Plato, and the earlier Platonists. But in this time, like other noble things, it has grown so obsolete through the neglect of those who followed that hardly any traces of it are found. Plato writes in the *Epinomis* that among all the liberal arts and contemplative sciences, the chief and most divine is the science of numbering. Seeking also why man is the wisest animal, he answers: "because he knows how to count." Aristotle also mentions this opinion in his *Problems*. Abunafar <note>Al-Farabi</note> writes that it was a saying of Avenzoar the Babylonian <note>likely a reference to Ibn Zuhr, though Pico often conflates names from the Arabic tradition</note> that he knew all things who knew how to count. These things can in no way be true if by the art of numbering they understood that art in which merchants are now most skilled. Plato also testifies to this, warning us with a raised voice not to think that this divine arithmetic is the arithmetic of merchants. This arithmetic which is so extolled, since I seem to have explored it after many sleepless nights...

<summary>Pico outlines his project to harmonize the philosophies of Plato and Aristotle, as well as the divergent views of Scholastic and Islamic thinkers. He also introduces his "new" method of philosophizing through Pythagorean numerology, distinguishing it from common commerce-based arithmetic.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Pico della Mirandola's defense of his nine hundred theses. In making a trial of this matter, I have publicly promised to answer, by the use of numbers, seventy-four questions which are considered primary among physical and divine matters. We have also proposed magical theorems, in which we indicate that magic is twofold. One of these <margin>Twofold magic</margin> consists entirely of the work and authority of demons; a thing, by heaven <note>original: "medius fidius"</note>, to be cursed and monstrous. The other, when well explored, is nothing else than the absolute fulfillment of natural philosophy. 

When the Greeks mention both of these, they do not deem the former worthy of the name of magic, calling it <note>original: "γοητείαν"</note> sorcery; the latter they call by its own peculiar name, <note>original: "μαγείαν"</note> magic, as if it were a perfect and supreme science. Indeed, as Porphyry <note>a 3rd-century Neoplatonist philosopher</note> says, in the Persian language "magus" means the same as an "interpreter and worshiper of divine things" among us. 

Moreover, there is a great—indeed, a maximum—disparity and dissimilarity between these arts. Not only does the Christian religion condemn and curse the former, but so do all laws and every well-ordered republic. All wise men and all nations devoted to the study of heavenly and divine things approve and embrace the latter. The former is the most fraudulent of arts; the latter is a deeper and holier philosophy. The former is vain and empty; the latter is firm, faithful, and solid. Whoever practiced the former always hid it, because it would result in the ignominy and reproach of its author. From the latter, the highest clarity and glory of letters has been sought since antiquity and almost always thereafter. No philosopher or man eager to learn the good arts was ever a student of the former; yet, to learn the latter, Pythagoras, Empedocles, Democritus, and Plato <margin>The words of Pliny, Book 30. Xamolxis. Abbaris the Hyperborean. Zoroaster. Plato. Charondas. Damigeron. Apollonius. Dardanus. Homer. Eudoxus. Hermippus. Al-Kindi the Arab. Roger Bacon. William of Paris. Antonio the Chronicler. As the former is supported by no rational arguments, so it is supported by no reliable authors. The latter, honored by what we might call the most illustrious parents, has two primary authors: Xamolxis <note>a legendary social and religious reformer of the Getae</note>, whom Abbaris the Hyperborean imitated, and Zoroaster—not the one perhaps commonly thought of, but that son of Oromasius. If we ask Plato what each of their magics entails, he will answer in the *Alcibiades* that the magic of Zoroaster is nothing other than the science of divine things, in which the kings of the Persians educated their sons, so that they might be taught to rule their own republic according to the model of the commonwealth of the universe. He will answer in the *Charmides* that the magic of Xamolxis is the "medicine of the soul," through which temperance is achieved in the soul, just as health is acquired for the body through medicine. 

Later, Charondas, Damigeron, Apollonius, Hostanes, and Dardanus followed in their footsteps. Homer also persisted in this, and we shall one day prove in our *Poetic Theology* that he concealed this science, as he did all other wisdoms, under the wanderings of his Ulysses. Eudoxus and Hermippus also followed it, as did almost all who have searched into the Pythagorean and Platonic mysteries. Among the more recent scholars who have caught the scent of it, I find three: the Arab Al-Kindi, Roger Bacon <note>a 13th-century English friar and pioneer of the scientific method</note>, and William of Paris <note>William of Auvergne, a bishop and philosopher</note>. In our own time, I have also seen Antonio the Chronicler <note>likely Antonio Cornazzano</note>, who, although occupied with the conduct and management of great affairs, nevertheless possesses such sublimity and elegance of genius that he has touched upon this science most beautifully, just as he has all other liberal arts. Plotinus <note>the founder of Neoplatonism</note> also mentions it, where he demonstrates that the magus is a servant of nature and not an artifice; he approves and asserts this magic, while the other...

This latter one, full of the highest mysteries, embraces the most profound contemplation of the most secret things and at last the knowledge of all nature. <margin>Esdras, Hilary, Origen.</margin>
Not only the famous doctors of the Hebrews write this, but from among our own, Esdras <note>the biblical scribe Ezra</note>, Hilary <note>Saint Hilary of Poitiers</note>, and Origen <note>a prominent early Christian theologian</note>. They write that Moses received on the mountain from God not only the Law, which he left to posterity written in five books, but also a more secret and true explanation of the Law. It was commanded to him by God that he should indeed make the Law public to the people, but the interpretation of the Law he should neither commit to writing nor make public; instead, he himself should reveal it only to Joshua <note>original: "iesunauæ"</note>, and then he in turn to the other succeeding chief priests, with a great religious silence. And rightly so. For it was enough for the common people to recognize through simple history now the power of God, now His wrath against the wicked, His mercy toward the good, and His justice toward all, and through divine and salutary precepts to be instructed toward living well and happily and in the worship of true religion. But the more secret mysteries, hidden under the bark <note>a metaphor for the literal meaning or outer covering</note> of the Law and the rough cover of words...

<meta>This page continues Pico della Mirandola’s argument for the necessity of a secret, oral tradition within religion. <meta>This page transitions from Pico della Mirandola's defense of his sources—the Kabbalah and ancient philosophy—to a direct legal and theological defense of his "900 Theses." Having argued for the harmony of all wisdom, he now addresses his accusers and begins his point-by-point rebuttal of the specific charges of heresy, starting with the nature of Christ's descent into Hell.</meta>

I could have gathered the headings of this debate into a much larger volume. If I had wished to divide them into their individual parts and carve them up, as others are accustomed to doing, their number would surely have grown to an infinite count. To say nothing of other matters, who does not know that one single dogma out of the nine hundred <note>original: "nongentis." This refers to Pico's famous 900 Theses, which he offered to debate in Rome</note>—specifically, the one concerning the reconciliation of the philosophies of Plato and Aristotle—could have been expanded by me into six hundred headings, if not more? I could have done this without any suspicion of trying to inflate the numbers, simply by enumerating bit by bit all the points on which others think those two philosophers disagree, but I believe they agree.

But why do I linger on these things any longer, and why do I not instead come to the very reason this entire work was undertaken? My goal is to prove, as clearly as light and beyond all controversy, that not only am I not impious, but that those men are impious and heretical who do not blush to say that I am—or ever was—a heretic. I shall do this not with insults and abuse, but by bringing the facts and arguments themselves into the open: what I said, what I wrote, and what I felt. Thereafter, other learned and distinguished men in our own and foreign Universities <term>Academies</term> <note>Referring to the great centers of learning like Paris or Bologna</note> will examine these things, and the Holy See will judge, as will Innocent VIII who sits upon it. 

<margin>Holy See. Innocent.</margin>

To neglect or violate his judgment is a sin and an outrage. He is the supreme judge on earth, representing Him who is the judge of the living and the dead. He is the storehouse and secret chamber of truth, acting in the stead of Him who is Truth itself, and who, having been made flesh, dwelt among us to announce the truth to us. But let us now descend to the examination of those questions which these masters have condemned as heretical. As I begin this, my manner of speaking must change. 

<margin>A witty proverb.</margin>

For I am now to speak with barbarians <note>A jab at the Scholastic theologians, whom Humanists like Pico accused of using "barbaric," unpolished Latin</note>, and as the witty proverb goes: "stutterers understand only stutterers."

-> ## FIRST QUESTION: CONCERNING THE DESCENT OF CHRIST INTO HELL. <-

<margin>p</margin>
**T**HE first conclusion among those proposed by me in my disputation—and which these men have condemned—was this: *Christ did not truly and in terms of real presence descend into hell, as Thomas <note>St. Thomas Aquinas, the influential medieval theologian</note> and the common path hold, but only in terms of his effect.*

<margin>How the conclusion is to be clarified.</margin>

Regarding this conclusion, I first wish to declare my meaning: what my mind and opinion are concerning the manner of Christ’s descent, which it was my intention to explain in the proposed conclusion. I will show that this view is not only Catholic and believed and approved by many Catholic doctors, but also far more probable than its opposite. Secondly, I will explain how the proposition itself—based on the property of speech and the force of the words—should by no means be judged by learned men as heretical or even "tasting of heresy" <note>A formal theological category for ideas that seem close to heresy without being explicitly condemned</note>. Thirdly, I will explain that they themselves err in the faith if they persist in the opinion that I cannot defend my conclusion from heresy, even in the sense that the force of the words allows. Fourthly and finally, I will show, with an abundance of evidence, that they cannot excuse themselves from the fact that their condemnation was made without proper consideration. 

But before I set forth the manner in which I hold that Christ descended into hell, I wish to premise this: although we are bound to believe explicitly and in particular that Christ descended into hell as an article of faith handed down and promulgated to us by Philip <note>Traditional belief held that each of the twelve Apostles contributed one clause to the Apostles' Creed; the descent into hell was attributed to Philip</note>, such that even my own protestation or one similar to it would not save a man who...

<meta>Pico has just concluded his introduction, asserting his right to be judged by the Holy See and learned universities rather than by his immediate detractors. He now moves into the specific theological defense of his theses, starting with the controversial article on Christ’s descent into Hell.</meta>

...would hold the opposite of this article. However, it does not seem that every member of the faithful is bound to believe explicitly and in detail the specific manner of that descent. But it seems sufficient for a Christian to believe that Christ descended to the underworld <note>original: "ad inferos," referring to the place of the dead</note> not according to his body, nor according to both body and soul, but according to his soul alone. One should believe that this descent according to the soul happened in a manner that was possible, fitting, expedient, and appropriate. This is because the specific manner of that descent is not explicitly stated, nor does it seem to be proven by Holy Scripture, nor by any determination of the universal Church, nor by special revelation from God, or the faithful account of the Apostles. 

<margin>Scotus
Francis of Mayronis</margin>
Indeed, what is more, Scotus <note>John Duns Scotus (c. 1266–1308), a highly influential Franciscan philosopher and theologian</note>—who was no amateur in the sacred letters—says that it is not held from Holy Scripture that Christ descended to the underworld, as Francis of Mayronis <note>A prominent follower of Scotus</note> reports in the fourth book of his *Sentences* <term>Sentences</term> <note>The "Libri Quattuor Sententiarum" by Peter Lombard, the standard textbook for medieval theology students</note>. How much less, then, can we say that a certain and defined manner of Christ’s descent is found in Scripture? Hence there has even been a certain doctor—whose condemnation on this point I have never read—to whom it seemed probable and defensible alongside the truth of the article that Christ’s soul was not present in Hell in a local, physical sense. And all the authorities that Francis in his fourth book and other theologians in their third book bring forward might seem to someone to be explained as a descent "by effect" rather than by "real presence." This remains true even if one follows the same method of interpreting Scripture used by the very doctors who hold the opposite view. 

For we read in Ecclesiasticus 24 <note>specifically verse 45 in the Vulgate Bible</note>: *I will penetrate all the lower parts of the earth.* Explaining this in the third part of his *Summa*, Thomas <note>St. Thomas Aquinas</note> says it is to be understood as being "by effect." 

<margin>Francis</margin>
Therefore, by similar reasoning, someone might perhaps say that the authorities stating he penetrated into Limbo or the Bosom of Abraham <note>A place of rest for the souls of the righteous who died before the coming of Christ</note> could be explained in the same way. For "to penetrate" is the same as to enter deeply and within, which is even more 

<margin>Thomas</margin>
than simply "to descend." Therefore, if he is said not only to have entered but even to have deeply penetrated the lower parts of the earth—not because he was really present there, but because he was there only by effect—then it could also be said that he was in the Bosom of Abraham and entered the Bosom of Abraham only by effect and not by real presence. 

Now, I do not say these things because I ever believed that Christ, while existing elsewhere in person, was said to be in Hell only because he performed some action there—just as a king, while remaining in his palace, is said to be in another part of the province where he effectively works something through the authority of his power and command. For that was never my opinion, as will soon be clear in the declaration of my views. 

<margin>Augustine.
Note.</margin>
On the contrary, I firmly hold and have held, and have always said both publicly and privately, that if Christ's soul was anywhere during those three days <note>The time between the Crucifixion and the Resurrection</note>, it was in Hell, and it was truly present there. <meta>Pico is continuing his defense regarding Christ's descent into Hell. On the previous page, he argued that the exact manner of this descent is not defined by Scripture. Now, he delves into the metaphysical debate over how a "separated substance" (a spirit or soul without a physical body) can be said to exist in a physical location.</meta>

...is granted that being located or moved locally does not apply [to a spirit] except by reason of its operation <note>The "operation" refers to the actions or effects a spirit produces in the physical world</note>. Therefore, I say that to have descended into the underworld, or to have been in the underworld locally, seems not to have applied to Christ except by reason of his operation. This means that although the soul of Christ was truly present in the underworld, his substance itself was not the cause of that presence, but only his operation was. In order that these words may be more fully understood,

<margin>Twofold opinion of those who posit that separated substances are in a place through a passing operation.</margin>

it should be noted that there is a twofold opinion among those who posit that separated substances are not in a place except through a "passing" <note>original: "transeuntem," referring to an action that exerts influence on an external object</note> operation. For some say that by reason of its own substance, a place is in no way owed to an incorporeal substance. Just as a substance itself is never truly "white" or "black," they argue—not irrationally—that it is not in a place and is nowhere, just as it is also 

<margin>First [opinion]</margin>

truly said to be neither hot nor cold. As for the authorities of Scripture which seem to give angels a location—as when they say angels are in heaven, or are sent to this place or that—these must be understood as follows: it is not that the angels are actually "here" or "there" (since they are not properly in a place), but that they act here or there, or begin to act where they were not acting before. These people rely heavily on the words of Gregory of Nyssa <note>A 4th-century Greek theologian and bishop</note>, who says that while we 

<margin>Gregory of Nyssa</margin>

ought to say a spirit "acts" here, we incorrectly say it "is" here. This opinion holds that the substance of an angel or a separated soul can never be said to be present to this or that place except in a "negative" sense—that is, it is simply not distant. But if it is ever said to be or have been somewhere, it is the same as if it were said to act or to have acted somewhere. They add that this way of speaking is borrowed from physical things. Because we see that physical things cannot act unless they are present (at least according to common opinion), we conclude that the same is true for incorporeal things: that where they act, and where the effect of their operation is found, there also their substance is locally present.

They conclude, finally, that it is a lack of mental sophistication and a failure of imagination to be unable to understand that something can be a real being and yet not be in a physical place. They argue it is a frivolous argument to say that "being" presupposes "acting." While that statement is true in the sense that a non-entity cannot act (for an agent must be in a state of actuality), it is not true in the sense that acting in a place requires "being" in a place. This is because the actor might be of such a nature that neither local presence nor distance is relevant to it, any more than whiteness or blackness would be. Those who think this way would say that the soul of Christ, when separated from his body, was—according to its substance—neither in the underworld nor outside the underworld, but was truly nowhere. However, he is said to have been in the underworld because he acted in the underworld; and he is said to have been principally in that part of the underworld where he principally acted.

<margin>Second opinion, which the author held</margin>

Although many doctors hold this opinion regarding the manner of being essentially in a place, I do not hold it, nor did I follow it in my conclusion. Instead, I held the one I will immediately subjoin.

There is another opinion which says that a separated substance, such as an angel or a soul not united to a body, is indeed truly in a place. It is "definitively" present locally, just as a 

<margin>Difference between this opinion and the opinion of the Scotists</margin>

physical body is "commensurately" <term>commensurately</term> <note>meaning a physical body occupies a volume of space exactly equal to its own dimensions</note> present locally. In this, this view agrees with the common path of Scotus <note>John Duns Scotus, a famous medieval philosopher</note> and all the Scotists. But they differ in this: the Scotists say that the limitation of the spirit's essence and the internal determination of its substance is the reason for its being in a place. 

This opinion, which I followed in my conclusion, says that while a physical substance is "commensurately" in a place, the reason for its being in that place is not its "substanceness," but its quantity <note>its physical size or extension</note>, which is external and...

<meta>Pico continues his defense of his thesis regarding Christ's descent into Hell. Having previously argued that spirits do not occupy space the way physical bodies do, he is now listing the esteemed theologians and philosophical arguments that support his view that a soul is "in a place" only through its actions or effects.</meta>

...external to the nature of its substance. Thus, even though an incorporeal substance <note>A spirit, like an angel or a soul, that has no physical body</note> is truly and "definitively" <note>original: "definitive," a technical term meaning to be present within a boundary without occupying space like a liquid fills a jar</note> in a place and locally present, the reason for its being in that place is not its substance itself, but its operation passing out from it to the exterior.

<margin>Declaration of the opinion</margin>

I judge that this opinion should be understood in this way, and once so understood, I judge it not only to be non-heretical, but even more probable than its opposite. And the point is this: even if the finitude or limitation of a **separated nature** <note>A soul or spirit existing apart from a physical body</note> is the reason why it is not everywhere—or the reason why, if it is in one place, it is not simultaneously in another in its entirety—this is not so much the reason for the separated substance's existence simply within the place itself. Rather, it is its effect or operation—taking "operation" to mean every relationship to a body or place that exists by way of active or passive action—that is distinct from the mere fact of being present in a location. I understand this as a matter of fact, without denying that there might be some other possible way a separated soul descends or is located (as I state in the following conclusion), though such a way remains unknown to us.

Following this opinion in my conclusion, I say that Christ was in the underworld solely through his effect, because he was not there except according to his soul. According to this opinion, it must be said that just as it does not belong to a physical substance to be somewhere "commensurately" <note>original: "commensurative," meaning to occupy a space equal to its own size</note> except through its physical bulk, so it did not belong to that soul [of Christ] to be in the underworld (where it is believed to have been) except through effect and operation. 

But just as the reason for the presence of the souls of the **Holy Fathers** <note>The righteous people of the Old Testament who died before Christ's redemption</note> was their relationship to that place—acting by way of a "passing operation," such as their detention and binding to that place until the gate was opened by the Redeemer and they were led out—so too the reason for the presence of Christ's soul was the operation which he performed there. I will show below that this was my meaning and that the words of my conclusion intended this. There, I will declare that the conclusion itself—even according to the literal force <note>original: "virtute sermonis," the strict logical meaning of the words</note> and power of the language—is not to be judged heretical.

<margin>Note.</margin>

Which of the two opinions regarding the manner of existence of separated substances in a place is truer—that of the <term>Scotists</term> <note>Followers of the philosopher John Duns Scotus</note> or that of those whom I have followed—I do not determine here. I say only this: my opinion has been believed and held as most true by so many great masters and Catholic doctors, most celebrated for both their learning and holiness, that those who dare to judge the opinion of such proven doctors as heretical or "tasting of heresy" should be judged far more reckless than I am for preferring the authority of those ancient theologians over the rulings of more recent ones.

To the first, a manifold response is evident according to the aforementioned doctors. For there are some who, wishing to save the authority of the Article while keeping this position, say that the meaning of the Article is this: the opinion stating that a separated substance is not in a place except through an operation that is an **external local motion** or a real alteration is an error. This is because its power is of no less **abstraction** <note>The state of being separate from physical matter</note> than its substance. Therefore, it follows that one must either concede that the "reason" for its being in a place will be something that acts as a **secondary act** <note>original: "actus secundi," a technical term for an operation or function that follows the primary existence of a thing</note> passing into a body (whatever that may be, and it is what the position I follow maintains), or there will be a manifest contradiction in the Articles. Regarding the third point, I say that that argument proceeds from a lack of full understanding of our position. For the position regarding the **operation** 
<margin>Operation is understood in two ways</margin>
by which an incorporeal thing is said to be located does not understand only that operation which is an external local motion or a real alteration, as we also touched upon somewhat in the response to the first point in the exposition of the **Parisian Article**. Instead, it takes "operation" broadly for every motion, influence, or relation signified by the manner of an operation passing into a body and exiting from an angel, or vice versa. And that this is the understanding of the position is clear from the words 
<margin>Saint Thomas</margin>
of **Thomas** in the first book of the *Sentences*, distinction thirty-seven, question one, article one, where he seems to follow this opinion, saying:

These are the word-for-word remarks of Thomas. From these words, the response to the argument is clear: because although angels may not have an operation toward the **empyrean heaven** <note>The highest, most spiritual level of heaven in medieval cosmology</note> that is a local motion or a real alteration, they nevertheless have something that functions by way of a "passing operation," such as **presidency** <note>The state of governing or being present as a protective or guiding force</note> or something similar.

Regarding the fourth point, upon which that **Master General** <note>Likely referring to the head of a religious order or a lead inquisitor who opposed Pico</note> relied so heavily: if anything needs to be said, it could be made clear enough from the words of Henry alleged above in the solution to the second point. <margin>Henry, Saint Thomas</margin>

Some say that an angel is not in a place **circumscriptively** <note>Occupying space by filling it and being bounded by it, like water in a glass</note> but **definitively** <note>Being limited to a certain area without physically "filling" it</note>, because it is determined to some place such that it is in this place and not in another, since its essence is finite. For they say that because it is created, it must be understood to be determined to some place. 
<margin>The "End" is understood in two ways</margin>
But this is a very **crude proof**, for it proceeds from an equivocation of the word **"end"** <note>original: "finis"; can mean a physical boundary or a conceptual limit/goal</note>. For when the essence of an angel is called "finite" (ended), "end" is taken as the end of essence and power—just as a **definition** is called a "term" or boundary—and not as an end of **dimension**. A place, however, is called "finite" according to the three dimensions of quantity. An "end" according to these two different meanings has no commensuration or proportion. Hence, it is not necessary that what is finite in essence be limited by the boundaries of a place. These are the literal words of Thomas.

From which it follows that, if Thomas is not lying, that Master is **crude** who called his own crude proof a "demonstration." Regarding the other argument concerning a **point**, I say that it is even cruder than the first. For a point is a thing in the category of **quantity**, having a location by its very nature. An **incorporeal thing**, however, is entirely abstracted from location, and it is a truly great crudeness to imagine a similarity between the indivisibility of an incorporeal thing and the indivisibility of a point...

For **Metaphysics**, as is clear according to everyone, deals with abstractions far beyond **Arithmetic**, which is one of the mathematical sciences. of an angel, let him at least consider the abstraction of unity. Let him hear what should be said about this according to **Henry** <note>Henry of Ghent (c. 1217–1293), a prominent theologian at the University of Paris</note>. For in the place cited above, speaking on this matter, he says:

> Those, therefore, who cannot understand an angel according to the nature of its substance as a **unity** without the concept of a **point**, are those of whom the **Commentator** <note>Averroes (1126–1198), the famous Islamic philosopher whose commentaries on Aristotle were standard in medieval universities</note> speaks regarding the second book of *Metaphysics*: those in whom the **imaginative power** dominates over the **cognitive power**. Whatever they think of, they imagine as a magnitude or as having a position in a magnitude, like a point. Hence, such people are **melancholic** <note>In the medieval theory of the four humors, "melancholics" were thought to be prone to deep study but also trapped by their physical senses and imagination</note> and they become the best mathematicians, but they are inept at **natural philosophy**.

...which is in a place is enclosed and contained by the place in which it is; and an <term>intelligence</term> <note>In this context, a "spiritual being" like an angel or a soul</note> by its own nature is not in a place, nor in any variation of a place. These are the literal words of **Albert** <note>Albert the Great (c. 1200–1280), a teacher of Thomas Aquinas</note>. He does not approve of that common distinction of "being in a place <term>definitively</term> and not <term>circumscriptively</term>," <note>A technical distinction: "circumscriptive" means filling a space point-by-point (like water in a cup), while "definitive" means being present in a region without being confined to specific points (like a soul in a body)</note> even though some masters thought it a complete crime to deny this distinction in any way.

Now finally it remains for me to show how the words of my conclusion are to be understood, and to declare that according to the <term>literal meaning of the words</term> <note>original: "virtute sermonis"</note> the conclusion is itself Catholic. The conclusion says:

->**Christ did not truly and**<-
<margin>Explanation of the words of the conclusion according to the literal meaning</margin>
->**in terms of real presence—as Thomas and the common way posit—descend into hell, but only as to the effect.**<-

Here it must be noted that the word "and," where it says "and in terms of real presence," is held **conjunctively**. And the word "as," when it says "as **Thomas** posits," is held **specifically** and **determinatively**, as I will soon declare. From this it is clear that the aforementioned conclusion is a single "negative conjunctive proposition" <note>A logical statement that denies two things happening at once</note>. Its sense is: "It is not the case that Christ truly **and** in terms of real presence, *in the specific manner that Thomas posits*, descended to hell."

And that conjunction is equivalent to an affirmative **disjunctive** <note>An "either/or" statement</note> of contradictory parts, namely: "Either Christ did not descend truly to hell, **OR** he did not descend to hell according to that specific real presence," etc. From this it follows that if someone tries to infer from my conclusion that "Christ did not truly descend to hell," they are arguing from the whole "either/or" statement to just one of its parts. Such an argument fails the rules of logic <note>original: "peccat secundum consequens," referring to the fallacy of the consequent</note>.

Indeed, in a similar case, this proposition is true: "Socrates is a man." But this one is false: "Socrates is a man **and** God is not God." To argue from this that "therefore Socrates is not a man" is truly childish. In the same way, to argue from my negative conjunction—"Christ did not descend truly **and** in the way Thomas posits"—to the claim "therefore Christ did not truly descend," is childish and characteristic of a man who is completely ignorant of logic and philosophy, let alone theology.

I do not only intend for this proposition in my conclusion to be true: "Christ did not truly descend to hell," nor even this: "Christ (or the soul of Christ) was not present in hell through a real and true presence of his substance." Rather, I only intend that he was not there through a real presence **in the manner that Thomas and the common way posit**. Therefore, I said that the word "as" is used specifically to define "real presence." It is not a valid argument to say: "He was not there really present in the way that specific Doctor says, therefore he was not there really present at all."

Now, the "**common way**"—that is, the way of **Scotus**, **Bonaventure**,
<margin>Scotus, St. Bonaventure, Nominalists, St. Thomas, the common way</margin>
and all the **Scotists** and almost all the **Nominalists**—holds that he was present there in such a way that his very substance was the reason for his presence and his being located. Because **Thomas** also seems to me to follow this opinion in this matter, I said "as Thomas and the common way posit."

I call the "common way" of theologians that which is commonly held now in **Paris**, where the study of theology especially flourishes. There, almost everyone proceeds in this matter of the presence of the soul in a place along with the Scotists and Nominalists. And for this reason alone—namely, out of reverence for the **University of Paris**—
<margin>University of Paris</margin>

This part stands in opposition to that. If, therefore (as was proven in the upper part), only the presence of the soul by its <term>substance</term> <note>The essential "stuff" of the soul</note> is denied—not as to the "what," but as to the "by which" (that is, it is not denied that the substance was present, but it is denied that the substance was the *reason* for that presence)—then also in this last part, which posits the affirmative specifically in opposition to that, "being in hell through the effect" is to be understood not as to the thing located, but as to the <term>reason for being located</term> <note>original: "rationem locandi"</note>. <margin>Objection</margin>

<margin>Solution</margin>
However, they would not have this doubt if they had considered my conclusions well. For I am of the opinion that **Thomas**, on this matter regarding the mode of being in a place for separate things <note>Separate things: entities existing without physical bodies, such as angels or human souls.</note>, felt differently at different times and did not follow the same opinion everywhere. 

<margin>Different opinions of Thomas regarding this question</margin>
Wherefore, although in the First Book of the *Sentences* he seems to hold that way which I follow in my conclusion, nonetheless elsewhere—such as in the Fourth Book of the *Sentences* and especially in the Third Part of the *Summa* <note>The *Summa Theologiae*, Aquinas’s mature masterpiece.</note> where he treats this descent and by which his opinion ought to be judged rather than by his earlier writings—he seems to side with the opinion of the **Scotists**.

<margin>Scotists</margin>
Namely, that [Christ] was there by essence <note>By his very being or substance.</note>, such that his essence was for him the <term>reason for being in a place</term> <note>original: "ratio locabilitatis"; the metaphysical ground that allows a spirit to be assigned to a specific location.</note> and not just his effect or operation. For **Thomas** says there that the soul of Christ was present through its "effect" in other parts of hell, but "by essence" in Limbo <note>Limbo of the Fathers: where the souls of the Old Testament righteous waited for Christ.</note>, etc. From this statement, I argue as follows: 

Wherever something is present by that which is its "reason for being in a place," there it is present by its substance and real presence. Therefore, if "effect" was the reason for the soul of Christ being in a place, wherever he was present by effect, he would have been there by the real presence of his substance. But according to **Thomas**, in some places Christ was present by effect where he was *not* present by real presence. Therefore, according to **Thomas**, effect was not his "reason for being in a place." 

This moved me to the probable belief that **Thomas**, in this article, walks with the **Scotists**. But whatever **Thomas’s** opinion may be, it is irrelevant to the point, because to err regarding the opinion of **Thomas** is not to err in the faith. 

<margin>Disagreement among Thomists</margin>
Furthermore, there is often a multiplicity of opinions among **Thomists** <note>Followers of Thomas Aquinas.</note> concerning what his actual opinion was. It suffices that this much is clearly apparent: when I proposed the conclusion, I believed this to be the opinion of **Thomas**, and I am not now twisting the proposition to a meaning foreign to the one I held then.

<margin>Note.</margin>
That I believed this from the beginning, and that this was my judgment regarding **Thomas’s** opinion when I proposed the conclusions, is most clearly evident from the fact that I proposed this specific conclusion: that concerning the "mode of being in a place" for angels, **Thomas** and **Scotus** do not differ. It is well known, however, that **Scotus** expressly says that even if all "operation" were excluded, a place is still owed to an incorporeal substance. Therefore, it was necessary for me to believe that **Thomas** was of this same opinion. 

And therefore, although I firmly held that Christ was truly and presentially in hell—and in this I agreed with **Thomas** and with all Catholics—nevertheless, because I thought **Thomas** believed his substance itself was the "reason for being in a place" and not his operation, I said in my conclusion: "not in the way **Thomas** and the common path posits."

Likewise, in the Second Book of the *Sentences*, he follows the opinion of the **Commentator** regarding the "matter of the heavens," which he then rejects in the second book of *On the Heavens* and in the *Summa*. <margin>He argues against his opponents</margin>
And so that I may show briefly, by way of a recapitalization of my argument, that those who believe my proposition cannot be defended from heresy are in error, I argue thus: A person positing a conclusion that is in itself heretical can be accused of heresy insofar as heresy exists in the intellect. But one who posits my aforementioned conclusion cannot be accused of heresy by the fact of its position; therefore, the aforementioned conclusion is not heretical in itself. They accept the major premise as granted; I prove the minor premise thus: Whenever someone posits everything from which proposition *A* necessarily follows, they cannot be accused of heresy even if they posit proposition *A*. But one who posits everything from which the position of my conclusion follows—in the manner in which it was posited by me—cannot be accused of heresy; therefore, even the one who posits the proposition itself as I have posited it cannot be accused. I prove the minor premise thus: the contradictory of this statement—"the reason for being in a place (that is, 'here' or 'there' in the manner declared above) for separate substances is **operation**, not the limitation of nature"—is not a matter of faith; and the contradictory of this statement—"it is not permitted to argue from the whole conjunctive to one of its parts"—is not a matter of faith; and the contradictory of this statement—"if someone, having put forward an assertion, whether negative or affirmative, adds the authority of some doctor with a proposition like the word **as** <note>original: "ly ut"; the word 'as' or 'like'. Pico is arguing about whether he was comparing his view to Thomas's view or defining it by Thomas's view.</note>, it can be held just as well determinatively as relatively"—because it can just as well be equivalent to the phrase "in the manner in which" as to the word "similarly"—which likewise is not a matter of faith; and the contradictory of this statement—"through the common path in theological matters, we can suitably understand the way that is commonly held in that university..."

<meta>Pico continues his defense against the charges of heresy, specifically regarding his proposition about Christ's descent into hell.
