...that the university in which you say the study of theology is more vigorous <note>original: "tempore sic dicetis magis uiget studium theologie." Pico is arguing that specific academic reputations are not matters of religious dogma.</note> is not a matter of faith. And the contradictory of this statement—that the study of theology is more vigorous at this time in the **University of Paris** than elsewhere—is not a matter of faith. And the contradictory of this statement—that in the **University of Paris** it is now commonly held that the "limitation of nature" is the reason for the "locatability" of a separate substance <note>term: separate substance (substantia separata). In medieval philosophy, this refers to an immaterial being, such as an angel or a human soul, that exists independently of a physical body.</note>—is not a matter of faith. And the contradictory of this statement—that **Scotus** and the greater part of the **Nominalists** <note>A school of thought that argued universal categories (like "humanity") do not exist in reality, only as names or concepts.</note> hold the aforementioned opinion, and **Thomas** <note>Thomas Aquinas</note> seems to hold it in the third part of the *Summa* where he treats the descent of Christ—is not a matter of faith.

Then it follows: if the contradictories of these statements are not matters of faith, it follows that to propose, believe, and dispute these statements is not in itself heretical or against the faith; nor can one who proposes, holds, and disputes them—whether disjunctively or conjunctively—be accused of heresy. But the position of my conclusion follows from these statements when placed together and conjunctively, exactly as it stands. Therefore, one who proposes my conclusion precisely as it stands cannot be accused of heresy.

The proofs of all the aforementioned points are found in what was written above. For regarding the first statement, it is clear that it is not only not heretical, but more reasonable than its opposite, and is believed and approved by many Catholic doctors. And in the second statement, all dialecticians <note>logicians</note> and all theologians who have ever known dialectic agree. The same is true for all the others; even if someone might doubt whether they are true or false, no one is so unrefined, so devoid of all learning, so ignorant of the faith and of those things which pertain to the faith, that they would say those things cannot be believed without heresy, and thus that their contradictories are matters of faith. 

Then, however, let it be argued further: whoever believes that this conclusion regarding **Christ**, etc., cannot have a Catholic sense according to the force of the words and according to proper and not distorted usage, believes that the contradictory of one or some of the seven aforementioned statements is a matter of faith. But those who hold something to be a matter of faith which is *not* a matter of faith have a wrong understanding of the faith, because it is against the word of the Lord in **Deuteronomy 4**: <note>original: "nō addetis ad uerbum quod ego loquor uobis neq̄ minuetis ab eo."</note> *You shall not add to the word which I speak to you, nor shall you take away from it.* Therefore, those who have a wrong understanding of my conclusion (as stated above) have a wrong understanding of the faith.

<margin>Exclamation</margin>
Look, O **Supreme Pontiff**! <note>The Pope.</note> Look, O most august senators of the apostolic order! <note>The Cardinals of the Roman Curia.</note> Look, O all of **Rome**, indeed **Italy**, indeed the **Church of Christians**, so that they may be convicted in this first proposition! This was the one in which they most heavily struck me with lightning <note>figuratively: excommunication or severe condemnation</note>, and in which many seemed to have some handle for excusing themselves for their condemnation of me, rather than just for accusing me. Regarding the other conclusions, it will be clearer than light that they could not have had even the slightest occasion for condemning them as heresy. And now, concerning this first one where they were strongest, it has been seen what sort of thing it is, and whether it was rightly or wrongly condemned by them—especially now that the sense which I intended through it has been explained to them, and applied to the words of the conclusion without any abuse or distortion of terms or speech.

<margin>He defends the conclusion lastly by the authority of Durandus, out of an abundance of evidence</margin>
And although this should be sufficient for the defense of my conclusion, yet for a fuller discussion of this matter, I say that even by interpreting the conclusion in the way they themselves interpreted it—namely, that Christ was in hell only "effectively" and not "presentially" <note>This refers to the debate over whether Christ's soul was physically present in hell or only present through its power/effect.</note>—it might still seem to some that it was perhaps presumptuously determined by them that the conclusion was simply heretical.

<margin>Durandus, the words of Durandus</margin>
Since it is the case that **Durandus** <note>Durandus of Saint-Pourçain (c. 1275–1334), a prominent Dominican theologian known for his independent mind.</note>, a greatest theologian of the **Order of Preachers**, who perhaps exceeds these masters in learning no less than I am exceeded by them, held that opinion to be probable and well-defensible alongside the truth of the Article <note>A specific "Article of Faith" or dogma.</note>. For thus he writes in the third book of the *Sentences*: "To the third..."

<meta>This page continues the theological investigation into the nature of Christ's descent into hell, a topic Pico della Mirandola was defending in the previous section. Thus the argument proceeds, and it seems that Christ according to his soul did not descend into
hell <note>original: "infernum"</note> because the same finite thing cannot be in different places at once, but the soul of Christ, since
it was a finite creature, was in paradise immediately after death with the soul of the thief.
To whom it was said in Luke 23: "Today you will be with me in paradise"; therefore, at least then, he could
not have been in hell. Furthermore, those things which Christ did and suffered in his assumed nature were
ordered toward human salvation. But for this salvation, it would not have been beneficial for Christ to descend
to the underworld because, through the passion <note>term: Passion (passio). The suffering and death of Jesus on the cross.</note> which he endured in this world, he freed us from
all guilt and punishment; therefore, it seems that Christ did not descend to the underworld. On the contrary is
what is said in the Creed <note>original: "simbolo". Referring to the Apostles' Creed.</note>: "He descended into hell." And the Apostle says in Ephesians 4: "Now that
he ascended, what is it but that he also descended into the lower parts of the earth?" The Gloss <note>A standard medieval biblical commentary.</note> says: "to the underworld."
I respond that since it is an article of faith that Christ descended into hell, and this cannot be understood by reason of
his divinity (according to which he is everywhere) nor by reason of his body (according to which he was in the
tomb), it remains that it be understood by reason of the soul of his human nature. Assuming this, two things
must be seen: the first is by what manner the soul of Christ descended into hell.
The second is to which hell <note>scholastic theologians distinguished between different "regions" of the underworld, such as the hell of the damned, Purgatory, and Limbo.</note> he descended. Regarding the first, it must be known
that since a separate soul <note>term: separate soul (anima separata). A soul existing apart from its physical body after death.</note> is not a body nor a power in a body, it cannot be said that the soul
of Christ descended to the underworld by that kind of motion or descent by which bodies are moved.

simply said to descend to hell. Because they are simply
assigned so that, having resumed their bodies, they may be in hell, for which reason they are said to be there where they are

From the Latin for "edge" or "border"; a place for those who died in friendship with God but could not enter heaven until Christ opened the way.</note> or to have descended to Limbo

assigned to have been the cause of blessedness in others. For it is fitting that a being in potential
be reduced to act by that which is already in act. The other effect, according to some, was...

<meta>This page continues the theological investigation into how Christ's soul could be in two places at once—Hell and Paradise—following his death on the cross. It utilizes scholastic logic (influenced by Thomas Aquinas) to argue that Christ’s "descent" was not a physical relocation, but an extension of his power and influence.</meta>

<sig>CC</sig>

The soul of Christ <note>original: "anima xpi"</note> conducted itself directly in the manner of an agent, namely, to illuminate the souls of the Fathers who were in Limbo <note>term: Limbo of the Fathers (limbus patrum). A region of the underworld where the souls of the righteous who died before Christ were said to wait for his arrival.</note> and regarding the mysteries that fall under revelation. <margin>Dionysius</margin> For according to Dionysius <note>Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, a highly influential 5th-century mystical theologian.</note> in the seventh chapter of *The Celestial Hierarchy*, Christ, according to the soul, has the task of teaching the angels; and by reason of this twofold effect, the soul of Christ can be said to have descended into hell. This is confirmed, moreover, by a threefold reason. 

<margin>First reason</margin> The first is because to move or to descend belongs to a separated soul <note>original: "animae separatae". A soul that has been separated from the body by death.</note> not in the manner of physical movement, but in the manner by which movement belongs to a spiritual substance. But for other spiritual substances—such as God and an angel—it does not belong to them to move from place to place by a movement that occurs within them as subjects, but by the effect they have on other things. Therefore, in a similar way, it belongs to a separated soul and specifically belonged to the soul of Christ. 

<margin>Second reason</margin> The second reason is this: Christ is said to have descended into hell so that he might illuminate the souls of the holy Fathers to see God. However, in the very same instant that Christ died, the holy Fathers saw God. But in that same instant, the soul of Christ could not have been in hell by means of physical movement. Therefore, he did not descend there by a movement within himself, but by the effect which he had upon others. 

<margin>Third</margin> Furthermore, just as the soul of Christ is said to have been in hell during that three-day period <note>original: "triduo". The period between Good Friday and Easter Sunday.</note> with the souls of the holy Fathers, so in that same period or part of it, he is said to have been in paradise with the soul of the thief. To whom it was said in Luke 23: "Today you will be with me in paradise." But this cannot be understood in terms of a physical location reached through movement. Since, according to those who hold that spirits are in a place definitively <note>term: Definitive presence (diffinitive). A scholastic term meaning a spirit is "present" wherever it exerts its power, rather than occupying a physical volume.</note>, a spirit cannot move from place to place [physically], nor can the same spirit be in several places at once or move simultaneously with multiple movements toward different places. Therefore, it must be understood according to the effect produced. 

<margin>Paradise is spoken of in two ways</margin> For if someone should say that "paradise" is defined in two ways: One way as a physical place, namely the Empyrean Heaven <note>term: Empyrean Heaven. The highest point of heaven, believed to be the dwelling place of God.</note>, and in this sense the soul of Christ was not in paradise except after the Ascension. The other way it is called paradise is the vision of the divine essence, and in this way the soul of Christ was in paradise from the instant of conception, and the soul of the thief on the very day of the Passion <note>The suffering and death of Jesus.</note>. In this way, it is not contradictory for the soul of Christ to have been simultaneously in paradise—that is, that he saw God—and to have been locally in hell. 

If this is said, I say it is not valid, because just as paradise is defined in two ways, so is hell. <margin>Hell is spoken of in two ways</margin> In one way, hell is called the place corresponding to the area beneath the earth. In the other way, it is the lack of the divine vision. Therefore, just as the soul of the thief is not said to have been with the soul of Christ in paradise except because, by the merit of Christ’s Passion, the soul of the thief saw God, so the soul of Christ is not said to have been with the souls of the chosen Fathers in hell except because their souls—which lacked the divine vision and were thus said to be in hell—were purged of this lack by the merit of this Passion. Therefore, both must be understood equally in terms of the effect, not in terms of place or local movement occurring within the soul itself as a subject. 

Although this may be a probable explanation and seems sufficient to preserve the article of faith and the words of Scripture, nevertheless, because divine power is not fully grasped by human reason, one must not stubbornly assert that the soul of Christ could not have descended to hell by some other way unknown to us. 

To the first argument, it must be said that the same finite thing cannot be simultaneously in multiple places definitively or circumscriptively <note>term: Circumscriptive presence (circumscriptive). Occupation of space where the object's boundaries match the space's boundaries, like a body in a room.</note>, nor is it claimed that the soul of Christ was simultaneously in paradise and in hell in that manner. However, according to the effect, nothing prohibits the same finite thing from being said to be in multiple places when the effects are compatible and are simultaneously subject to the power of the same agent. Thus, the soul of Christ is said to have been in paradise and in hell at the same time, because by his merit, the soul of the thief saw [God]...

<summary>This page argues that Christ's descent into hell should be understood as a "spiritual effect" rather than a physical relocation. It explains how Christ could simultaneously be in Paradise and Hell by exercising his divine power to grant the vision of God to both the thief on the cross and the Old Testament patriarchs.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion on Durandus of Saint-Pourçain’s controversial view that Christ’s descent into hell was not a physical movement of his soul, but rather a "descent by effect"—meaning the power of his sacrifice reached the souls in hell without his soul physically changing location.</meta>

...God, which is to be in paradise; and the souls of the Fathers <note>The "Fathers" refers to the righteous people of the Old Testament, such as Abraham and David, who died before Christ.</note> who lacked the divine vision—and for this reason were said to be in hell—were liberated from this lack and consequently from hell. Indeed, according to one and the same effect—namely, according to the liberation of the Fathers—the soul of Christ <note>original: "anima christi"</note> could be said to be simultaneously in paradise and in hell, considering the starting point and the end point of that effect. For by reason of the lack of the divine vision, from which they were liberated through the passion of Christ, it could be said that the soul of Christ had been in hell. Truly, by reason of the divine vision to which they were admitted, he could be said to be in paradise. To the second point, it must be said that by the very fact that through the passion of Christ we are liberated from fault and punishment, Christ is said to have descended into hell, because by the merit of his passion some have attained release from the punishments of hell. For that descent is not regarded according to local motion <note>term: local motion (motus localis). Physical movement from one geographic place to another.</note> existing in the soul, but according to the effect which he had in those to be saved. These are the words of Durandus exactly <note>original: "ad verbum"</note>.

Since he is never found to have retracted such an opinion, if it is simply heretical and consequently against what has already been determined by the Church, it follows that Durandus died a heretic.

<meta>This page continues the investigation into the theological status of Durandus’s opinions, specifically addressing whether a theologian can be considered a heretic for contradicting the writings of the Church Fathers (the "Saints") when those writings are not part of the official biblical canon.</meta>

CC ii

<margin>On the authority of the doctors, namely Augustine, Jerome, Gregory, and others</margin>
...it will also be clearly proven by me. For although the writings of the holy doctors <note>term: Doctors of the Church (doctores). A title given to saints recognized as having made significant contributions to theology through their research or writing.</note>, which are placed outside the canon of the Bible, are to be handed down and read and looked upon with due reverence, their sayings are nevertheless not of such firm and immovable authority that one is not permitted to contradict them or doubt them, unless they are clearly and expressly proven otherwise by Holy Scripture, or if it has been firmly determined by the authorizing Church itself that those writings contain firm and indubitable truth. Therefore, a heretical opinion cannot be clearly convicted solely through the sayings of the saints outside the biblical canon; for where there is no infallible truth, there is neither certain nor indubitable faith.

<margin>Reason.</margin>
Since certain faith rests on infallible truth—indeed, regarding such matters, there is neither infallible assent nor firm adherence. For where there is no certain truth and indubitable faith, <margin>Augustine</margin> assent is not always given without doubt and fear of the false. For as Augustine says in his letter to Jerome and in book 11 *Against Faustus* and book 16 against the same Faustus: if Scripture does not contain infallible truth and is found to be false in any part of itself, there remains no certain faith in it by which it may be firmly believed; and because of the falsity found in one part, the whole is held suspect, and thus faith would falter. As Augustine says in *On Christian Doctrine*, chapter 7: "Faith totters if the authority of the Holy Scriptures wavers."

<margin>First proof that there is no infallible truth in the sayings of the saints outside the canon of the Bible</margin>
As for the fact that there is no infallible truth in the sayings of the saints outside the canon of the Bible, as far as the present matter is concerned, three proofs occur to me. The first is because the doctors themselves doubt their own sayings, wondering whether they have erred in them or not. Thus Augustine says in the first book of *On the Trinity*, chapter 1:

> I will not be slow to seek if I hesitate anywhere, nor will I be ashamed to correct myself if I err. And in chapter 2: Therefore, whoever reads this, where he hesitates along with me, let him seek; where he recognizes his own error, let him return to me; where he recognizes mine, let him call me back. From this comes Augustine's book of *Retractions*, in which he condemns and retracts many things from his earlier sayings.

Wherefore also in the second book of *On the Trinity*: "I would rather be rebuked by anyone than be praised by someone who is either in error or a flatterer. For the praiser and the one in error confirm the error; the flatterer, however, entices one into error. Let the righteous man correct me in mercy and rebuke me; but let the oil of the sinner not fatten my head." <margin>Guido the Carmelite</margin> And as Guido the Carmelite <note>Guido Terreni (c. 1270–1342), a Carmelite theologian and Bishop of Mallorca known for his work on heresy.</note> says in his *Book on Heresies*: although Augustine speaks humbly in these sayings, <margin>Augustine</margin> he nonetheless speaks truthfully. Hence he himself says to Vincent: "I cannot nor should I deny that just as in the greats themselves, so in my many little works there are many things that can be criticized by a just judgment and without rashness." And in the book *On True Religion* he says: "Whatever error is found in my books, this is to be attributed to me alone; but whatever is true or well-explained, let that be attributed to the one Rewarder and Giver of all things, God." Therefore, the sayings of Augustine, that distinguished and divine doctor, may not always contain indubitable truth in all things. Since he himself doubts whether he has erred or not, and what has been said of Augustine is to be understood similarly regarding the other doctors.

<margin>Second proof</margin>
The second proof is taken from the discord that exists among the authors themselves. For discord among writers is a testimony of falsity. Since it is necessary that at least one of those disagreeing <margin>Augustine.</margin> says what is false, because necessarily one side of a contradiction is false. Therefore, Augustine in book 16 of *The City of God* proves the truth of Holy Scripture from the mutual concord of its writers, in which all agree and no one disagrees with another, which testifies to the indubitable and infallible truth of the Holy Scriptures. For to the true and to truth, as the Philosopher <note>The Philosopher (philosophus) is the standard medieval title for Aristotle.</note> says in the first book of the *Ethics*...

<meta>This page continues the argument that while the Church Fathers are to be respected, they are not infallible and often contradict one another, unlike the canonical Scriptures. This supports the author's broader point that disagreeing with a Saint is not necessarily heresy.</meta>

<margin>Disagreement in the sayings of the saints outside the biblical canon</margin>
Disagreement exists in their works, though all things in the Bible harmonize, which does not happen in other writings. For how great the discord is in the sayings of the saints outside the canonical scriptures, no one is ignorant unless they have not read their books.

<margin>Augustine, On the works of the six days</margin>
Augustine disagrees with the other holy <term>doctors</term><note>term: Doctors. Highly influential theologians and saints whose writings are officially recognized by the Church as having great authority.</note> concerning the understanding of the <note>original: "operum sex dierum"</note> works of the six days of creation. This is because the others posit that God made those works of the six days according to a chronological succession of days. Augustine disagrees with them, as he posits that all things were made at once, according to the scripture: "He who lives forever created all things at once" <note>Ecclesiasticus (Sirach) 18:1</note>. Therefore, moved by this, Augustine numbers those six days not according to a succession of time, but according to the distinction of the angels' knowledge of things in their own nature and in the <note>term: Word (Verbo). Referring to the Logos or the Second Person of the Trinity through whom all things were made.</note> Word. And yet, neither these nor those are called heretics, even though it is certain that one of these opinions is false and, consequently, their sayings do not lean upon infallible truth.

<margin>Jerome and Augustine</margin>
Similarly, Jerome and Augustine disagree. For Augustine,
<margin>On the author of the Psalms</margin>
makes David the author of all the Psalms, which Jerome denies.

<margin>On the rebuke of Peter</margin>
Similarly, they disagree regarding the rebuke of Peter by Paul <note>The "Incident at Antioch" described in Galatians 2:11–14</note>, whether it was regarding a mortal or a venial sin on Peter's part.

<margin>On the cessation of legal ceremonies</margin>
They also disagree on the cessation of the legal ceremonies <note>The Old Testament laws and rituals</note>, such that by contradicting each other, one necessarily speaks a falsehood, and yet neither of them is considered a heretic because of this.

<margin>Bede and Augustine with Jerome on the priesthood of Samuel</margin>
Similarly, Bede, in his commentary on the first book of Kings, says that Samuel was a true priest, which Augustine expressly denies in the book *On Questions of the New and Old Testament*, saying Samuel was not a priest since he was not of the sons of Aaron. And Jerome, in the first book *Against Jovinian*, says that it must be recognized at the same time that Samuel was a Levite, not a priest nor a high priest. Therefore, he is not named among the priests, but among those who call upon the name of the Lord. Therefore, the sayings of these men do not lean upon infallible truth since they contradict themselves, of which one part is necessarily false,
<margin>Aristotle</margin>
as is clear through the Philosopher in the fourth book of the *Metaphysics* <note>Referring to Aristotle's principle of non-contradiction.</note>.

<margin>Augustine varying on the priesthood of Samuel and his resurrection</margin>
Indeed, Augustine himself seems to oppose himself in this opinion. For in the book *On Questions of the New and Old Testament*, question 46, he says (as we have mentioned) that Samuel was not a priest; and yet, in book 12 *Against Faustus*, chapter 35, he says the priesthood was changed into Samuel when Eli was rejected, and the kingdom was changed into David when Saul was rejected. Here, Augustine clearly says the priesthood was transferred to Samuel, so that Samuel was truly a priest just as David was truly a king. Concerning the same Samuel, as to whether he was truly raised from the dead, Augustine seems to disagree with himself. For in *Questions of the New and Old Testament*, question 27, he holds that Samuel was not truly raised by the <term>pythoness</term><note>term: Pythoness (Phitonissam). A term for the medium or "Witch of Endor" who summoned the spirit of Samuel for King Saul in 1 Samuel 28.</note>, but a demon appeared to Saul in the likeness of Samuel. However, in the book *On the Care to be Taken for the Dead*, he posits that the soul of Samuel, truly summoned from the dead by a demon through magic arts, spoke to Saul.

<margin>Jerome varying on Salem</margin>
Jerome also, in that question of whether Salem was Jerusalem, seems contrary to himself in a certain letter of his, the title of which I do not remember.

<margin>On the 70 interpreters</margin>
He also holds an opinion contrary to Augustine regarding the <note>term: 70 interpreters (LXX). The Septuagint, the Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible.</note> seventy interpreters.

<margin>Gregory and Dionysius on the orders of angels</margin>
Likewise, Gregory and Dionysius disagree about the orders of angels; and Jerome alone opposes the others regarding the promotion of a <term>bigamus</term> <note>term: Bigamus. In this context, a man who had been married twice (e.g., a widower who remarried). Jerome argued that if the first marriage was before baptism, it shouldn't count against him becoming a priest.</note> to the priesthood. For he himself holds and writes in his letter to Oceanus that a twice-married man can be promoted if he married before baptism and after baptism, provided that after baptism he did not know more than one wife. The others contradict him, saying that a twice-married man, whether before baptism or after baptism, cannot be promoted, and in this, the latter are judged to have spoken better,
<margin>Augustine, Ambrose</margin>
as Augustine writes in *The Good of Marriage* and Ambrose in *On Duties*. Likewise, Jerome, writing to Marcella regarding five questions, says the saints who are found at the end of the world will not die but will be taken up alive; Augustine, however, in the book *The City of God*, says all will then die as...

<margin>Jerome and Augustine on the Book of Wisdom</margin>

Augustine, however, in the third book of his *Retractions*, shows that he once held it was published by Jesus, son of Sirach, which he retracts there; and although he does not express by whom it was published, nevertheless, in his book *On Christian Doctrine*, he numbers it among the sacred books. 

<margin>Jerome and Augustine</margin>

Augustine, however, in his literal commentary on Genesis, explains "from the beginning" to mean the third day. Likewise, Augustine, in his book *On the Harmony of the Evangelists*, asserts that the entirety of Peter’s denial took place in the courtyard of Annas, and that the things said there after Jesus was sent to Caiaphas were said as a recap.

But not all these things come to mind for one in such a great hurry; for I could not work on this with more exact diligence because I wanted to immediately meet the disease of unjust infamy <note>The author likely refers to accusations of heresy or lack of respect for tradition leveled against him.</note> that was coming upon me. I will, however, add that which now occurs to me from Jerome’s letter to Augustine, speaking thus: "Do not wonder if in your books, and especially in your expositions of the Scriptures, which are most obscure, some things seem to deviate from the straight line. And I say this not because I judge anything in your works to be reprehensible now—for I have never devoted study to reading them, nor is there a supply of these copies among us, except for the books of your *Soliloquies* and certain commentaries on the Psalms—which, if I wished to discuss them, I would show (I will not say from myself, who am nothing, but from the interpretations of the ancient Greeks) that they differ from the truth." Thus says Jerome. Therefore, just as they disagreed among themselves, so too can we dissent from them in many things, while preserving the faith and truth of Scripture and the determination of the Holy Church. 

The third proof is taken from the special prerogative of the Holy Scripture and the decrees of the universal Church,

...most firmly believe they erred in writing; or, if I encounter anything in those letters that seems contrary to the truth, I will not hesitate to think that either the manuscript is faulty, or the translator did not follow the sense <note>original: "non assecutum esse," literally "did not reach" or "did not grasp" the meaning</note>, or that I understood it very little. <meta>This page continues the author's defense of his theological method. Having established that even the Church Fathers can err, he now addresses a specific objection: that his own propositions might be interpreted as heretical, just as the works of the medieval theologian Durandus were sometimes judged.</meta>

<margin>Objection</margin>
It is presumptuous of **Durandus** <note>Durandus of Saint-Pourçain (c. 1275–1334) was a Dominican theologian known as the "Resolute Doctor" for his independent and often controversial views that frequently clashed with the official positions of his Order.</note> to call [the proposition] simply heretical. If it is found to be so, however, Durandus must bear this mark patiently. But someone will say: "Suppose the sense you have declared for that proposition is indeed Catholic. Even if the force of the words allows for that meaning, couldn't your proposition also produce that sense used by Durandus—which you yourself detest? Therefore, you have erred by putting forward a conclusion that could cause a scandal in the minds of the faithful."

<margin>First Response</margin>
To this I say, first, that the reasoning for things proposed for debate is one thing, and the reasoning for things handed down in writing for instruction is another. For when something is proposed for debate, the proposition is presented in a brief, concise, and unexplained way, involving many difficulties of both words and meanings in itself, which are to be untangled in the heat of the debate <note>original: "in ipso disputandi congressu," literally "in the meeting of the dispute."</note>. Otherwise, if everything were explained there, no room would be left for the debate itself. Therefore, a person putting forward an ambiguous, obscure, or equivate proposition for debate is excused, because he will distinguish and declare its meaning during the argument. However, those who commit something to writing for the purpose of teaching do by writing what is done here by debating. For that reason, everything in writing ought to be clear, lucid, and settled.

<margin>Second [Response]</margin>
Second, let these most severe censors consider that it is not only difficult, but almost impossible, to so weigh and examine the words of every proposition one puts forward so that no ambiguity of meaning can exist, and no erroneous opinion can be drawn from it. I certainly do not wish to claim for my own propositions a perfection that many **Evangelical and Apostolic** <note>This refers to the writings of the four Gospels and the letters of the Apostles in the New Testament.</note> propositions do not have. For many are found among them which have multiple understandings and can be turned toward an erroneous sense—indeed, some even seem to sound like heresy at first glance.

<margin>From where heresies sprouted</margin>
<margin>Heresy of **Arius**</margin>
<margin>Heresy of **Helvidius**</margin>
<margin>Heresy of **Marcion** and the **Manicheans**</margin>
<margin>Heresy of **Basilides**</margin>
<margin>Heresy of **Eunomius**</margin>
All heresies have sprouted from this: namely, when people did not look into the depth of the meaning as much as they attended to what the "bark" of the Gospel words sounded like <note>The author uses the metaphor "cortex verborum" (the bark or skin of the words) to describe a superficial, literal reading that misses the "pith" or true spiritual intent.</note>. From this, **Arius** hearing *The Father is greater than I* <note>original: "pater maior me est," from John 14:28</note>, believed the Father was greater than the Son and said the Son was a created being. From this, **Helvidius**, hearing that *Joseph did not know Mary until she brought forth her firstborn son* <note>original: "non cognouit Mariam donec peperit primogenitum suum," from Matthew 1:25</note>, attended more to the grammatical force of that word *until* than to the truth of the Gospel sense regarding the perpetual virginity of Mary, and so he doubted it. From this, **Marcion**, reading that passage of Paul, *But the law entered in that sin might abound* <note>original: "Lex autem subintrauit ut abundaret delictum," from Romans 5:20</note>, believed the Law of Moses was evil and from an evil principle, as did **Manichaeus**. And **Basilides**, reading the verse *I was once living without the law* <note>original: "ego aliquando sine lege uiuebam," from Romans 7:9</note>, believed that the soul of Paul had once lived in another body <note>A reference to the doctrine of metempsychosis or reincarnation.</note>. From this, **Eunomius**, hearing Christ responding to the Jews who accused him of calling himself the Son of God, that it was written *I have said, "You are gods and all sons of the Most High"* <note>original: "ego dixi dii estis & filii excelsi oēs," from Psalm 82:6 and John 10:34</note>, attended to the thing said and the response itself rather than the intention and purpose of the one responding; he believed Christ is called the "Son of God" in the same way that any holy person is called a son of God.

<margin>The error of many</margin>
Similarly, this proposition—*concerning that day, not even the Son knows* <note>original: "illam diem neque filius nouit," from Mark 13:32. This was a major point of debate regarding Christ's divine omniscience.</note>—was the occasion for many to believe that the Father understands more than the Son believes. If we interpret it according to the common sense the words make, it seems to suggest that; yet the truth of the hidden meaning is otherwise. I could bring forward infinite similar propositions from the <term>canon of scriptures</term> <note>term: canon of scriptures. The official list of books recognized as the inspired Word of God.</note>.

<margin>**Hilary**</margin>
<margin>Gloss</margin>
And therefore **Hilary** <note>Saint Hilary of Poitiers (c. 310–367), a champion of orthodoxy against Arianism.</note> said well: "The understanding of things said must be taken from the reasons for speaking, because the matter is not subject to the speech, but the speech is subject to the matter." <note>original: "non sermoni res sed rei est sermo subiectus." This is a famous rule of interpretation: words must be understood in light of the subject they describe, not the other way around.</note> And the **Gloss** <note>The "Glossa Ordinaria," the standard medieval commentary on the Bible.</note> on that text...

<meta>This page continues the author's defense of his theological method. Having argued that ambiguous statements must be judged by the speaker's intent rather than a literalistic reading, he now marshals the authority of the Church Fathers—Gregory, Jerome, and Augustine—as well as the medieval philosopher William of Ockham to support his position that he should not be labeled a heretic for debatable propositions.</meta>

<margin>Gregory</margin>
He says that we should not always understand things as the words seem to sound at first glance, especially where they are ambiguous, but we should return to the **intention of the speaker** <note>original: "intentionem loquentis"</note>. And **Gregory** <note>Pope Gregory the Great (c. 540–604), a foundational theologian for the medieval church.</note> says that frequently, while the literal property of the words is attended to, the sense of truth is lost. And Gregory, in the 26th book of his *Moralia*: "One ought not to consider the words, but the will and the intention, because the intention should not serve the words, but the words the intention."

<margin>Jerome</margin>
And **Jerome** <note>St. Jerome (c. 347–420), best known for translating the Bible into Latin (the Vulgate).</note>, in his commentary on the Epistle to the Galatians, testifies that the Gospel is not found in the words of the Scriptures, but in the sense; not on the surface, but in the **marrow** <note>original: "medulla," a common metaphor for the deep, spiritual meaning hidden beneath the literal text.</note>; not in the leaves of language, but in the root of reason.

<margin>Ockham</margin>
Therefore **Ockham** <note>William of Ockham (c. 1287–1347), a controversial English friar and philosopher famous for "Ockham's Razor."</note> in his *Dialogue* proves false this common proposition: "Words are to be received not from the opinions of individuals, but from common usage"—especially in the second part. For he says that in ambiguous and manifold words, one must not return to common understanding, but rather to the intention of the speakers. And so, while there is ambiguity in the teaching of someone speaking or writing, one must similarly return to the speaker’s intention so that he may explain himself and express the true sense which the force of the words permits. Nor should he be rejected unless it can be proven that such a sense would be contrary to his other sayings or irrelevant to his purpose. And so even in simple speech, the same **doctor** <note>Referring here to a "Doctor of the Church" or a recognized academic authority.</note> says that one must return to the intention of the speaker, and one should stand by his interpretation unless it is established, or probably or violently presumed, that he used such an ambiguous way of speaking to deceive or for some other evil end.

<margin>Epilogue</margin>
From all of these points, I conclude that I did not err—I, who with a protestation [of intent] proposed an arguably complex proposition to be declared during a debate. Such a proposition could not produce any sense that some non-reprobated doctor—or one not yet declared as such by the Church—has not held. Rather, those have erred who judged a proposition to be simply **heretical** <note>Holding a belief contrary to established Church dogma.</note>, even though it had a **Catholic sense** <note>In this context, "Catholic" means "orthodox" or "universally accepted Christian truth."</note> which the force of the words permits, and which had already been declared as its Catholic sense to them by the person proposing it.

Even if they had done so before my sense was declared—though they might have erred more excusably—nonetheless, if they are truly learned, they could have recognized by themselves that the proposition had a double sense. Noting this, they should not have simply condemned it, but rather should have interpreted it in a good sense.

<margin>Augustine</margin>
For **Augustine** <note>Augustine of Hippo (354–430), whose writings formed the backbone of Western Christian theology.</note>, in his book *On the Harmony of the Evangelists*, explaining that passage of Matthew, "Do not judge, and you will not be judged," says: "In this place, I think nothing else is commanded except that we should interpret those deeds in the best way when it is doubtful with what spirit they were done." For regarding neutral deeds, which can be done with a good or bad spirit, it is rash to judge, especially to condemn. Therefore, what Augustine says concerning things that are done, let us understand as being said equally concerning things that are spoken. And so, applying Augustine’s sentiment to speculative matters, let us conclude that in these sayings which can have a good and bad sense, it is rash to judge, and especially to condemn.

<summary>The author defends himself against charges of heresy by citing Gregory the Great, Jerome, Ockham, and Augustine to argue that the speaker's intention—not just the literal words—must be the basis for judgment. He concludes that his critics were rash to condemn his debate propositions without considering his clarified, orthodox meaning.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the author's defense of his theological propositions. Following his argument that a speaker's intention should take precedence over a literalistic reading of their words, he now moves to his "Second Question," which deals with the controversial topic of whether a finite sin deserves an infinite punishment—a point for which his critics have labeled him a heretic.</meta>

# SECOND QUESTION CONCERNING THE PUNISHMENT FOR MORTAL SIN.

> This is the second conclusion that those men <note>The "men" refers to the author's inquisitors or academic rivals who condemned his work.</note> have condemned: for a **mortal sin** <note>In Catholic theology, a "mortal" sin is a grave offense that destroys the relationship with God, as opposed to a "venial" or lesser sin.</note> of finite duration, an infinite punishment in terms of time is not owed, but only a finite one.

And because, when I set down this conclusion in my booklet, I prefaced it with these words: "Unless the sayings of the **Saints** <note>The "Saints" here refers to the "Church Fathers," authoritative early Christian theologians like Augustine or Gregory the Great.</note> seemed in their manifest speech to say the opposite, I would firmly assert the following conclusions. However, I do assert that they are **probable** and can be reasonably defended." The first of these is this: A mortal sin is in itself a finite evil. The second is this: For a mortal sin of finite duration, etc. A certain **Master** <note>A "Master" (magister) was a formal academic title for a professor of theology.</note> held a dispute with me regarding this conclusion. "What other testimony do we seek," he asked, "that your conclusion is heretical, since you yourself clearly say it is against the sayings of the Saints? For the consequence holds: it is against the sayings of the Saints, therefore it is heretical." I then showed him—as I will also show below—how my conclusion in no way contradicted the opinions of the Saints, and how those words were to be understood. But even if it were the case that the conclusion was against the sayings of the Saints, how much his "consequence" would be worth—and how unworthy it would be of a theologian who boasts of himself as he does—can be clear to anyone from what was said above regarding the first conclusion. I know what I might say here about that Master; for he is the one who has so many times sent letters home about me, promising, as it were, a trophy and a triumph. But I wish to conduct my case as I promised at the beginning: with reasons, not with insults. I come now to the conclusion. And because these Masters have judged both the conclusion itself and the responses I gave them when they questioned me on it to be false, erroneous, and heretical, I wish first to declare that the conclusion itself is **Catholic** <note>In this context, "Catholic" means "orthodox" or in alignment with universal Church teaching.</note> and in harmony with the sayings of almost all the **Doctors** <note>The "Doctors" were the established medieval university authorities, such as Thomas Aquinas or Duns Scotus.</note>. I say it is "mine" in this sense: if you take it in a sense other than the one I intend for it, it is no longer the conclusion that I proposed.

<margin>What he intends to do regarding the declaration and in what order</margin>
<margin>A manifold proposition</margin>
For a manifold proposition <note>A proposition that can be interpreted in multiple ways.</note> is actually many propositions. Therefore, I wish to declare that my responses themselves are of such a nature, explaining both the conclusion and the responses in a way that the force of the words always allows for my meanings—that is, those meanings which I intend through them. For the declaration of this conclusion, five things must be noted.

<margin>First point to be noted regarding sin</margin>
<margin>Turning toward</margin>
<margin>Turning away</margin>
First, it must be noted that in sin two things can be considered: a **turning toward** <note>original: "conuersio," referring to the sinner's attachment to a created, worldly thing instead of God.</note> a created good, and a **turning away from** <note>original: "auersio," the rejection of God's grace.</note> the unchanging and uncreated good. In the first way, sin is a **finite evil**, even according to all the Doctors. In the second way, sin is an **infinite evil** according to the common path <note>original: "communem uiam," the standard or most widely accepted theological opinion of the time.</note>. And because the turning toward a created good—which the sinner misuses by sinning—is part of the intrinsic nature of the sin itself, it is therefore said that sin is **intrinsically** a finite evil. However, the turning away from the uncreated good makes it **extrinsically** infinite, because it is called an infinite evil only insofar as it is a turning away from an **infinite good** <note>i.e., God. The author argues sin isn't infinite in "size," but only by virtue of who is being rejected.</note>. Therefore, it only remains that it is an extrinsically and objectively infinite evil.

<margin>Second point to be noted</margin>
<margin>The time of the way and of the end</margin>
Secondly, note that by "time" we can understand only the **time of the way** <note>original: "tempus uie," a technical term for a person's lifespan on earth, during which they are a "wayfarer" (viator).</note>; in this sense, it is certain that neither sin nor anything else pertaining to a human being can be infinite in terms of time, since the "time of the way" for any wayfarer is not only finite in duration, but even brief. In another way, we can understand by "time" both the time of the way and of the **end** <note>original: "termini," referring to the state of the soul after death (heaven, hell, or purgatory).</note> and...

<summary>The author begins a formal defense of his proposition that mortal sin does not deserve infinite punishment in duration. He argues that sin is only "infinite" in an extrinsic sense because it involves turning away from an infinite God, while the act itself remains a finite, human deed.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the author's technical defense of his second theological conclusion. He is refining his definitions of "mortal sin" and "what is owed" to prove that his previous statements, though controversial, align with the established logic of Church scholars.</meta>

...is understood in this way in the conclusion, and thus it is clear that something can endure in a person for an infinite time.

<margin>
**Third Point.**
Mortal sin is understood as:
An Act.
Guilt.
</margin>

Thirdly, note that **mortal sin** <note>A grave sin that "kills" the life of grace in the soul.</note> can be understood in two ways. In one way, it is a prohibited act or the failure to perform an act commanded by God. In the other way, it is the **guilt** <term>reatus: the state of being liable or "on the hook" for punishment after an act is over</term> left behind from that prohibited act or failure. Indeed, in many places in Holy Scripture, this guilt is called "sin," and by such a "sin" someone is named a "sinner" even when the act of sinning (in the first sense) has ceased or passed away.

From this third note, it is clear that it must reasonably be said that, although for one who is damned for a mortal sin, the sin itself might eventually end in terms of its "internal being"—that is, the actual deed which is called sin in the first sense—it does not, however, end in terms of the **guilt**. Rather, if the guilt were to end in that way, eternal punishment would not be owed to him; and so a sin to which infinite punishment is owed is "infinite" in terms of time specifically regarding its guilt.

<margin>
**Fourth Point.**
"To be owed" is understood in two ways.
</margin>

Fourthly, it must be noted that "to be owed" <note>original: "deberi"</note> is understood in two ways, or there are two ways to understand how a punishment is "owed" to a sin. 

In the first way, something is said to be owed to someone because it will actually be rendered to them at some point. In this sense, it is said reasonably and according to Catholic teaching that for a sin of finite duration—in terms of both its deed and its guilt—an infinite punishment in time is *not* owed. It is in this way that my present conclusion is understood: that for a sin of finite time, such punishment is not owed, etc. For every sin to which punishment is "owed" in this way (meaning punishment will eventually be delivered), that sin is infinite in the aforementioned way. No one is ever damned unless the sin for which they are damned is "infinite" in that sense regarding time.

However, the conclusion has another Catholic sense, namely: that eternal punishment is never "owed" (rendered) to someone unless he himself is finally **impenitent** <note>refusing to repent or seek forgiveness before death</note> and endlessly neglects to repent for that sin which he committed or failed to do in life. Thus, for a temporal sin, an infinite punishment is "owed" only if the sinner does not return to righteousness. 

For just as **repentance** <note>original: "penitētia"</note> ends a sin regarding its rejection by God—according to the verse: *at whatever hour the sinner shall groan [in repentance], etc.*—so too does **impenitence** regarding a sin perpetuate it in guilt and rejection toward infinite punishment. Thus, in this first sense, infinite punishment is never "owed" to someone unless they possess a sin that is infinite in time.

<margin>
The **vengeance** which God seeks from a sinner.
</margin>

Indeed, the **vengeance** <note>original: "Vindicta"</note> which God seeks from a sinner is simply that the sinner should return voluntarily to his duty of obedience, grieving for his contempt; otherwise, he will be tormented as long as he chooses to remain in that state.

<margin>
Note.
</margin>

In the second way, "to be owed" can be understood as that which someone is worthy of through **merit or demerit** <note>the theological "points" earned for good or bad actions</note>, and which would be rendered to them if they were to die in that state. In this sense, an infinite punishment *is* "owed" for a mortal sin of finite duration, because whoever sins mortally for even one hour is worthy of infinite punishment. That punishment would be rendered to him if he were to die in that state, even assuming he had no other sin that was infinite in time.

<margin>
The common use of this distinction of "being owed."
</margin>

This distinction regarding the word "owed" is in frequent use among **theologians**. Therefore, according to this wording, the **Doctors** <note>the authoritative teachers of the Church</note> say that for one who is **foreknown** <term>prescito: those whom God knows will ultimately reject him and be lost</term>, eternal life is not "owed" even while he is performing a meritorious act in a state of grace—if we use the first definition of "owed"—because it will never actually be given to him. Similarly, it is said that for one who is **predestined** <term>predestinato: those whom God knows will ultimately be saved</term>, eternal punishment is not "owed" even while he is in a state of mortal sin, because it will never be rendered to him, since that sin will eventually end and he will die in grace rather than in sin.

<margin>
**Epilogue.**
</margin>

From the points stated above, it is clear that my conclusion itself has a Catholic meaning, even according to the usual way of speaking among Catholic Doctors. It should not have been condemned as heretical, false, and erroneous, since its opposite is actually the false position.

<summary>The author clarifies that "mortal sin" refers both to the act and the lasting guilt, and that "owed" punishment can mean either what a person deserves or what they will actually receive. He argues his views on finite sin and eternal punishment are consistent with standard theological distinctions between the "foreknown" and the "predestined."</summary>

...and erroneous. Furthermore, it was the height of ignorance to believe that from my aforementioned conclusion I intended to deny the eternal punishment of the damned. 

<margin>

</margin>

On the contrary, from my conclusion one finds an investigation into the cause for which the damned are punished eternally. This cause, I said, is the perpetuation of **guilt** <term>reatus: the state of being legally or spiritually liable for punishment even after the act of sinning has ended</term> in the soul of the sinner through their final impenitence and the perpetual failure to lament their sin. This opinion not only appears not to be heretical, but it is so Catholic that no one—if they are a Catholic and trained in the Holy Scriptures—can rightly and reasonably deny it. 

<margin>
He explains that the conclusion is not heretical based on the force of its terms.
</margin>

That the proposition conveys this sense by the very force of its terms is clear. For the proposition says: **"Infinite punishment in terms of time is not owed to a mortal sin of finite duration."** <note>original: "Peccato mortali finiti temporis non debetur poena infinita secundum tempus"</note> In this proposition, I take "to be owed" <note>original: "deberi"</note> to mean that which will at some point be paid in full, a usage that was already shown above to be very common among the Doctors of the Church. And I take "sin" to mean the offense and the guilt. This usage is not only not improper or abusive, but is frequent in the Holy Scriptures. Indeed, after the **Master of the Sentences** <note>Peter Lombard (c. 1096–1160), whose "Sentences" was the standard textbook of medieval theology.</note> inquires in his second book whether, after the act of sinning has passed, the sin remains in the one who sinned until he repents, he responds thus: "It must not be ignored that sins exist in someone in two ways: in the **act** and in the **guilt**." 

<margin>
Master of the Sentences
</margin>

<margin>
Durandus
</margin>

**Durandus** <note>Durandus of Saint-Pourçain (c. 1275–1334), a prominent philosopher and theologian.</note> also says in the same place that a sin is understood to be finished in two ways: 

<margin>
Sin is finished in two ways
</margin>

1.  In one way, by the cessation of the act alone. 
2.  In the other way, by the dismissal of the sin (forgiveness). 

That **guilt** is also sometimes expressly called "sin," **Thomas** <note>Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the most influential medieval theologian.</note> says in the same place, stating: "Guilt, acting as a bridge between the fault and the punishment, draws its name from both extremes." 

<margin>
Thomas
</margin>

But is "sin" not also taken for "guilt" in that passage: "It is therefore a holy and wholesome thought to pray for the dead, that they may be loosed from sins" <note>A reference to 2 Maccabees 12:46.</note>? For those dead for whom we must pray to be loosed from sins are not in a state of "sin" if we take sin to mean the mortal fault itself—nor are they loosed from such a sin after death—but rather they are loosed from sin taken as the punishment or the **debt of punishment**. In this same way, "sin" is also understood in the passage: "Redeem your sins with alms" <note>A reference to Daniel 4:27 (or 4:24 in some versions).</note>, and so it is in many other passages of Scripture. 

If, therefore, both the sense of the proposition is Catholic and the usage of the terms in the proposition is Catholic and highly approved, why was there any reason to condemn this conclusion of mine as heretical?

That I intended these Catholic meanings and nothing discordant with the faith is clear from what I added in the response when I said that it remains consistent with the truth of the conclusion that **anyone dying in mortal sin will be punished forever.**

<meta>This page continues the author's defense of his theological conclusion regarding eternal punishment. He argues that the damned are punished forever not just for a single past act, but because they remain in a state of sin and "omission of repentance" for all eternity.</meta>

<margin>Note</margin>
...for infinite omissions of repenting and for infinite other evil acts, whether total or partial, in which the damned person persists. For just as the damned person continually wills evil, he thus continually sins and incurs demerit—not indeed a new and different essential punishment (at least not one that is distinct from the fault itself), but rather he is punished more manifoldly for those same evil acts in which he continues. Because this seems to be against the common way of speaking used by the Saints <note>In this context, "Saints" refers to the authoritative Church Fathers like Augustine or Jerome</note>, though not against the underlying reality or their intended meaning, I stated both in writing and by word of mouth that I do not strictly assert this opinion—that is, I do not use that specific way of speaking—out of reverence for the Saints. However, I did say that it could be defended as probable. 

Finally, beyond the things already mentioned, I added that anyone dying in **mortal sin** <term>peccatum mortale: a grave sin that destroys the relationship with God and leads to eternal damnation if not repented</term>, by the very **guilt** <term>reatus: the state of being legally or spiritually liable for punishment</term> of that sin, is punished eternally. This is because by dying in that state of guilt, the person is placed in such a state that they are necessitated to sin eternally—at least through the sin of the perpetual omission of repenting and of disposing themselves toward grace. 

These aforementioned responses of mine were said by those masters <note>Referring to the university faculty or inquisitors accusing him</note> to be unsatisfactory to their arguments and inquiries. Indeed, they claimed I added error upon error through such a response; for this reason, they declared my responses and declarations to be false, erroneous, and heretical. But who could fail to see that they themselves add error to error in this reprehensible condemnation of theirs, and not I—unless it be one who hates Catholic truths along with them or does not understand them?

<margin>Recapitulation</margin>
Briefly recapitulating, what I intend in this conclusion is this: it is indeed true that a mortal sin of finite duration is worthy of **eternal punishment** <note>original: "pena eterna"</note>, and such punishment is owed to it, and will indeed be paid as eternal punishment if the sin was not forgiven before death. 

However, if a mortal sin is finite in terms of time—not only regarding the intrinsic positive act prohibited by God or the omission of an act commanded by God, but also regarding its imputation, non-acceptance, guilt, and the stain—this is what is often called "sin" in many places of Scripture and in the common usage of the Doctors <note>Academic theologians</note>. It is of the nature of a sin to be punished eternally. If the said imputation or stain does not remain, eternal punishment would never be owed to the sin, nor would it ever be paid. 

Regarding such a sin, I say, which is finite in all the aforementioned ways—which "finishing" occurs through **repentance** <note>original: "penitencia"</note>, at least regarding an actual mortal sin—I say that eternal punishment is not owed to it (understanding "owed" to mean it will eventually be rendered or paid). Rather, to whomsoever eternal punishment is rendered for mortal sin, they were in that sin without end in the manner stated above.

<margin>Gregory</margin>
<margin>Thomas</margin>
And this is what **Gregory** <note>Pope Gregory the Great (c. 540–604 AD)</note> intends to say: that the sinner is punished with eternal punishment because he "sinned in his eternal" <note>original: "peccauit i suo eterno." This refers to Gregory's argument that the damned would have sinned forever if they had lived forever on earth</note>—that is, without end. And so we say that every person who is damned dies in the sin for which he is damned. 

**Thomas** <note>Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the influential Scholastic philosopher</note> agrees in the fourth book of the *Sentences* <note>The "Sentences" of Peter Lombard, on which Aquinas wrote a famous commentary</note>, saying that the punishment of the damned lasts forever because the **fault** lasts forever. Therefore, I say that in everyone who is damned there is one sin of infinite time, speaking of both the time of the journey <note>Life on earth</note> and the time of the end <note>The afterlife</note>: namely, the omission of repenting, which in the damned never has an end. 

And so it is clear that the infinity of the duration of this sin in the person who is damned—an infinity, I say, regarding the guilt of imputation, the stain, and the impenitence or omission of repenting—is the cause why eternal punishment is owed and will eventually be paid to him. And this is sufficient regarding this conclusion.

# THIRD QUESTION CONCERNING THE ADORATION OF THE CROSS AND IMAGES

The **third conclusion** which they condemned was this:
> Neither the cross of Christ nor any image is to be adored with the adoration of *latria* <term>latria: the supreme worship and heart-felt devotion due to God alone, as opposed to honor given to saints or objects</term>, even in the manner that Thomas [Aquinas] posits.

<margin>
Thomas
Durandus
Henry of Ghent
John of Guarra
Robert Holcot
Peter of Aquila
</margin>
Not only do I believe this conclusion, which was condemned by those masters, to be Catholic, but I believe it to be truer than its opposite, which is this: "The cross of Christ and images are to be adored with *latria* in the manner that Thomas posits." For the opinion of Thomas in this matter seems less reasonable to me than the opinion of Durandus, Henry of Ghent, John of Guarra, Robert Holcot, Peter of Aquila, and many others whom I follow in this conclusion. To make this manifest, I will first set forth the opinion of Thomas, which I do not hold, and then the opinion of the doctors whom I follow. From these it will be clear that the determination of those masters regarding my conclusion is not only neither correct nor just, but it also presupposes the total opposite of what I intend in my conclusion.

<margin>Opinion of Saint Thomas</margin>
Thomas says, therefore, that because (as the Philosopher <note>Aristotle</note> says in the book *On Memory and Reminiscence*) the movement of the soul toward an image is twofold: one toward the image itself according as it is a certain thing, and the other way toward the image as it is the image of another. Between these two movements there is a difference, because the first movement—by which something moves toward the image insofar as it is a certain thing—is distinct from the movement toward the thing of which it is an image. However, the second movement toward the image, insofar as it is an image, is one and the same as the movement toward the thing itself. Therefore, he concludes that although adoration is not due to the image of Christ as it is a certain thing in itself, nevertheless, as it is an image, the same reverence is due to it that is due to Christ himself, which is the adoration of *latria*. This is Thomas’s manner [of reasoning], which rightly seems strange and dangerous to other doctors. For the image itself, even as an image, is distinct from the thing imaged; it is referred to the thing imaged as to something distinct from itself. Wherefore, if as such it terminates <note>i.e., acts as the final destination of</note> the adoration of *latria*, it seems to follow that something other than God will be adored with *latria*, which is absurd.

<margin>Against the response of Capreolus</margin>
Nor can it be said, as Capreolus <note>Jean Capreolus, a major defender of Aquinas’s theology</note> says when wishing to save Thomas’s statement, that the image itself is not adored separately, but that the image and the thing imaged are one single "total object" of adoration. For either one part of this total object is the image itself (which is a created relative being) or it is not. If it is not, then it should not be said that from those two a single "total object" is made; for from such a statement it follows that each of them is a partial object, even if one of them is more principal. If this is so, it follows that some created thing of the "genus of relation" would, at least partially, terminate the adoration of *latria*. To say this certainly seems poorly Catholic <note>original: "male catholicum," implying a view that borders on heresy or is doctrinally unsound</note>, especially since this cannot be said of a created thing; indeed, even the Persons in the Godhead, by reason of their relative properties, are not the formal term of adoration <note>The author argues that we worship the Divine Essence, and even the distinct Persons of the Trinity are not worshipped as mere "relations" in the way Thomas's theory might suggest for images</note>.

<margin>Against the foundation of the opinion</margin>
Moreover, Thomas’s foundation seems poorly effective. For when the Philosopher says that the movement of the soul toward the image and the thing imaged is the same, he does not mean it in the sense that the soul declares the image (as an image) to be the same as the exemplar <note>the original person being depicted</note>, and thus whatever is due to the one is also due to the other. Rather, the Philosopher only intends this...

<summary>The author disputes Thomas Aquinas’s view that images of Christ should receive 'latria' (divine worship) by arguing that an image is always distinct from what it represents. He aligns himself with other medieval theologians like Durandus and Holcot, asserting that giving divine worship to a created object—even as a surrogate for God—is logically and theologically dangerous.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the author's critique of Thomas Aquinas's position on the adoration of the Cross. On the previous page, the author began explaining Thomas's view that the movement of the soul toward an image is the same as the movement toward the object it represents. Here, the author challenges that logic and presents the alternative views of several prominent medieval theologians.</meta>

...because the movement of memory, by which the soul is moved through memory toward the image insofar as it is an image, also terminates at the object imaged. It also has another true sense: if I have a definitive concept of one relative term, I also understand the other. But that every movement of the soul, and especially of the will, should be the same toward the image and the object imaged—this the Philosopher <note>Aristotle</note> in no way intends. This is clear from a similar case according to the way of speaking which **Thomas** himself uses. For he often says that the movement of the will is the same by which the will is carried toward the end and toward the means, when it wills them for the sake of the end. And yet it is certain, even according to him, that this movement, as it reaches the end, is "fruition" <term>fruitio: the joyful enjoyment of an ultimate end for its own sake</term>, but as it reaches the means, it is "use" and not fruition.

<margin>Opinion of other doctors</margin>
Therefore, it seems to other doctors that it should in no way be said that we adore the image of Christ, even as an image, with the adoration of *latria* <term>latria: supreme worship and heart-felt devotion due to God alone</term>. 

<margin>Opinion of Durandus</margin>
For as such, it is a created thing not united to the divinity; and what is more, as such, it is a relational entity. Therefore, **Durandus** <note>Durandus of Saint-Pourçain, a 14th-century Dominican known for his independent thinking</note> says that this proposition—"the cross of Christ is adored with *latria*"—is false in its proper sense, though it has an improper but true sense. It is this: Christ, as remembered through the cross or as present in the cross (just as the object imaged is present in its image), is adored with the same adoration as if He were present in Himself. And according to this sense, I also concede this proposition: "The cross is adored with the adoration of *latria*." 

<margin>Opinion of Robert Holcot, Henry, John of Guarra, and Peter of Aquila</margin>
This, then, is what **Durandus** says: that it is adored "rememoratively" <note>acting as a trigger for memory</note>. **Robert Holcot** intends the same meaning when he says that it is a more proper way of speaking to say "we adore before the cross" than "we adore the cross." Finally, **Henry** <note>Henry of Ghent</note> and **John of Guarra** intend the same opinion when they say it is adored *by accident* <term>per accidens: an indirect or secondary relationship, rather than something belonging to its essential nature</term>, and **Peter of Aquila** says the same. 

<margin>What Henry and John of Guarra add</margin>
But what **Henry** and **John of Guarra** add—who speak more fully on this matter—is this: they say that to the image, "by accident" or through memory, is owed that honor which is owed *of itself* to the thing imaged and remembered. However, it is certain that there is nothing to which *latria* is owed of itself except God, three and one, and Christ on account of the unity of His divine person; but a literal image of God cannot exist. 

It remains that if there is any image to which *latria* is owed by accident and through memory, it would be the image of Christ. But because such an image primarily represents Christ's humanity to us, and secondarily His divinity, it seems that primarily "by accident" such honor is owed to it as is given "of itself" to Christ's humanity. But Christ's humanity, taken of itself, is only adored with *hyperdulia* <term>hyperdulia: a level of honor higher than that given to saints but lower than that given to God</term>; therefore, to such an image, primarily and by accident, only the adoration of *hyperdulia* will be owed. Secondarily, however, by accident, the adoration of *latria* will also be owed in the manner stated, because the image itself also secondarily represents and brings to memory the divinity of Christ Himself. 

<margin>Opinion of Francis de Mayronis and the Scotists</margin>
And in this, **Francis de Mayronis** and all the **Scotists** <note>followers of Duns Scotus</note> agree with **Henry**, as they say that *latria* is not owed to Christ's humanity. 

<margin>The opinion of Thomas is somewhat dangerous in this matter</margin>
**Thomas**, however, because he seems to hold the opposite regarding the adoration of Christ's humanity, would perhaps also disagree with **Henry** in this case. Indeed, the opinion of **Thomas**, as **Francis** says in the third [book of *Sentences*], is somewhat dangerous, and in this matter of adoration, his way does not seem very safe to me. For he went so far as to say in the third book of the *Sentences* that some adoration was owed even to the physical cross of Christ on which He hung, even as an inanimate thing. And yet we know, according to all theology, that what cannot be a subject capable of receiving holiness or virtue cannot be the term...
