<meta>This page continues the author's argument against Thomas Aquinas's view that the cross should be worshiped with the same honor as Christ. On the previous page, the author cited Durandus to argue that images are merely reminders, not the target of worship itself.</meta>

<sig>DD ii</sig>

<margin>Jean Capreolus</margin>
...less of any adoration. And that **Jean Capreolus** <note>Jean Capreolus (c. 1380–1444) was known as the "Prince of Thomists" for his fierce defense of Thomas Aquinas's theology.</note>, the defender of **Thomas**, himself even confesses that this statement of **Thomas** cannot be defended; nor does he have any other way of saving **Thomas**'s reputation except by saying that **Thomas** himself seems later to have felt differently in his *Summa* <note>The *Summa Theologiae*, Aquinas's most famous work.</note>.

<margin>Recapitulation of the meaning of the conclusion</margin>
From these things, therefore, it can be clear what my "Catholic conclusion" is—and it is more reasonable than the opposite view and more in harmony with the common way of the theologians. Briefly recapitulating its meaning, I say that this proposition—"the cross of Christ is adored"—can have two meanings. One is the **proper** sense: namely, that the cross of Christ—whether as a physical thing, or as an image, or as a partial or total object—is adored as the *terminus* <term>terminus: the final point or goal of an action</term> of adoration. This is the sense that **Thomas** intends, and which I deny. The other is the **improper** sense of said proposition, which is: "the cross of Christ is adored," meaning Christ is adored in it as in a reminder of Him, just as if He were present in Himself. And this sense I grant, and I pray with the Church, saying:

> Hail, O Cross, our only hope. <note>original: "O crux ave spes unica", a line from the famous 6th-century hymn *Vexilla Regis* used in Passiontide.</note>
> And let us adore your cross, O Lord. <note>original: "Et crucem tuam adoremus domine", a chant from the Good Friday liturgy.</note>

<margin>Many things are deduced</margin>
<margin>First</margin>
From what has been said, many things can now be clear. First, it is clear what I meant when I said elsewhere that, following the opinion of **Henry** <note>Henry of Ghent, a 13th-century philosopher-theologian.</note> and **Jean de Guarra**, *hyperdulia* <term>hyperdulia: a level of religious veneration higher than that given to ordinary saints (dulia) but lower than the worship due to God alone (latria)</term> is owed to the image of the Crucified. This was to be understood, namely, by reason of that which is primarily brought to our memory, which is the humanity of Christ. I spoke briefly here because I was referring to those authors whom I considered well-known to these masters, as if they were veterans who had already read and re-read them ten times over.

<margin>Second</margin>
Second, it is clear that they falsely claimed I deny every mode of the adoration of *latria* <term>latria: supreme worship and heart-felt devotion due to God alone</term>, since I expressly say in my conclusion that I deny **Thomas**'s mode. Even if I had not said this, but the proposition stood simply as "neither the cross nor any image is to be adored with latria," still, by the force of the wording, that proposition would not deny every mode of the adoration of *latria*. For it is clear according to sound logic that the negation or distribution of a "multiple term" <note>An "equivocal" term, or a word with several distinct meanings.</note> does not negate or distribute it for every single thing it might signify. Otherwise, the proposition "every dog is a star" would have to be simply granted or simply denied. Just as it does not say collectively that "every celestial dog" <note>Referring to the star Sirius, the "Dog Star."</note> and "every sea dog" <note>A shark or seal.</note> and "every barking dog" is a star (though it might be said of each individually), so in this negative—"the cross is not adored with the adoration of latria"—where the word "adored" is used with two meanings (adoration as a final goal versus adoration as a reminder), every mode of adoration is not denied collectively, though it is denied for each separately.

<margin>Third</margin>
Third, it is clear that this proposition could also be stated absolutely and without distinction: "The cross is not to be adored with the adoration of *latria*," because in its **proper** sense it is true, or at least more probable than its opposite. The proper sense is to be followed according to the strictness of speech more than the improper sense, in which the statement would be false. For just as an "analogical term" <term>analogical term: a word used in related but different ways, such as "healthy" referring to both a person and their diet</term> when used by itself stands for its most common or famous meaning, so a statement having both a proper and improper sense, if spoken without specification, is to be understood according to the proper sense rather than the improper. And therefore, as I said, I could have put it forward without distinction, intending to clarify the sense in which I understood it during the course of the debate.

<margin>Note</margin>
From this I infer that although in a proposition with multiple meanings it might perhaps be better to do as I did in this one—namely, to define the sense in which it is used rather than posing it without distinction—nevertheless, there is a greater fault in condemning a proposition that is true in its proper sense, indistinctly and simply, just because of the falsity of its improper sense, than there is in posing that proposition without distinction.

Truly, however it may be regarding my conclusion, they cannot excuse their own condemnation from error. First, let them tell me where it appears to them that I deny every mode of **divine worship** toward the cross according to the way of the Catholic doctors? Likewise, they could not have gathered from my response that I deny every mode of **divine worship** according to the way of the Catholic doctors.

<margin>**John of Guarra**, teacher of **Scotus**; **Henry of Ghent**</margin>

This necessarily follows from their words; for since I told them that I follow **Henry** and **John**, and they then say that I do not follow Catholic doctors, who would not infer from this that those whom I said I followed are not Catholic doctors? But who could bear this? Who could endure with an even mind that **Henry** and **John**—such distinguished and excellent doctors of the Church, lights of the faith, and bulwarks of defense—should be rejected as non-Catholics and consequently as heretics and infidels? I cannot help but be angry at times; but nevertheless, I will restrain myself.

Let us look, however, to the second error. They say that the conclusion is **scandalous** and **offensive to pious ears** and against the custom of the universal Church. Oh, most damned judgment! Let them see how they cannot escape the snares.

For either my conclusion denies nothing except the method of **Thomas** in the manner explained above—and then it is clear that my conclusion is not against the custom of the Church, as has been most extensively declared—or, as they themselves wish, it denies every mode of adoration and denies that

Therefore, he who judges a conclusion that denies this as "scandalous" and not "simply heretical" must himself be called a simple heretic.

<sig>DD iii</sig>

# FOURTH QUESTION: WHETHER AN IRRATIONAL NATURE CAN BE ASSUMED AS A SUBJECT BY GOD.

**T**he fourth conclusion condemned by those men is this: **I do not assent** to the common opinion of theologians who say that God can assume any nature as a subject <term>suppositare: to take a nature into a personal union, making it part of a divine "suppositum" or person, as happened in the Incarnation</term>, but I grant this only concerning a rational nature.

By this conclusion, I do not intend to deny that God *could* assume any nature as a subject. Rather, I only intend to deny a particular and explicit assent to this assertion: "God can assume any nature as a subject." There is a great difference between these two intentions. Even if this were among the things possible according to the **absolute power of God**, nevertheless, a proposition which—by the strict force of the words <note>original: "de uirtute sermonis"</note>—merely denies a positive, explicit assent to that specific statement in detail, does not detract from the omnipotence of God. Nor, by the strict force of its words, does it savor of any heresy. The reason is that not every member of the faithful is bound to assent explicitly and in detail to all things possible according to God's absolute omnipotence, nor to profess these things explicitly. It is sufficient to believe some such things in a general and implicit way, and to stubbornly disbelieve nothing.

Therefore, not without purpose <note>original: "non sine misterio," literally "not without mystery," implying a deliberate scholarly caution</note>, I did not frame my conclusion in these terms: "God *cannot* assume any nature as a subject," but rather in these: "**I do not assent** to the opinion saying that God can assume any nature as a subject." From this conclusion, by the strict force of the words, it cannot be inferred that God is unable to do this. Nor can it be said that I asserted such a thing in the conclusion—neither in the first part, which is negative, nor in the second, from which it only follows that a granting act is held specifically and in detail regarding a rational nature.

I therefore deny that there is in me a particular and explicit assent to this assertion: "God can assume any nature as a subject." And I can reasonably deny it, both because—even if the opposite were true—it can remain unknown to us in detail, and it seems I am not obliged to believe it explicitly. Furthermore, it is not easy to disprove or refute that assertion: "God cannot [do this]..." <margin>**Henry of Ghent** etc.</margin> as if it were detracting from God's omnipotence. This is strongly confirmed by the authority of the Solemn Doctor, **Henry of Ghent**, who, after he had once held the opposite opinion—namely, that any nature <margin>Words of **Henry**</margin> could be assumed—later leaned toward the view that only a rational nature can be assumed. For **Henry** writes thus: "Regarding the possibility of the nature to be assumed, there is no doubt whether <margin>The first position which **Henry** recites</margin> God can take to Himself any assumable nature. Therefore, the whole difficulty of this question turns on the possibility of the nature being assumed, and there are two solemn positions on this matter."

For the more common and solemn position says (to which I once used to assent somewhat): "Any nature subsisting in creatures can be assumed." <margin>Against this position it is argued: God has being in creatures in two ways.</margin> These people hold that a nature can be elevated even if its corresponding power is not elevatable, which does not seem to me to be something that can be reasonably posited. To understand this, it must be noted that God has "being" in creatures in two ways: one way naturally and in a manner agreeable to nature; the other way voluntarily and in a manner exceeding the limits of nature. In the first way, He has being through "illapse" <note>An "illapse" refers to the divine presence or "flowing into" all created things to sustain them in existence.</note> in every nature and creature. In the second way...

And although through <term>indwelling: the way God's presence "flows into" and sustains all created things</term> God is intimate to every creature—and more intimate to it than the creature is to itself, or than a form is to its matter—nevertheless, through interpenetration, He is most intimate of all to the assumed nature. He is more intimate there than He is within any nature by indwelling alone. For through the intimacy of interpenetration with the assumed nature, the "Assuming One" <note>the Divine Word or Son</note> is united ineffably and incomprehensibly to the nature being assumed. In this union, it is necessary for the assumed nature to lose its own proper existence of <term>subsistence: the independent, individual "personhood" of a thing</term>, if it had such a thing before the assumption. Or, if it never had it, it must enter into the existence of the subsistence of the nature into which it is assumed, so that there is the same <term>suppositum: the underlying person or subject that "owns" the natures; in Christ, this is the Divine Person</term> subsisting in a twofold nature. 

For each of those natures in their union retains its own proper existence of essence. However, through indwelling, God is made intimate to every creature naturally and in a manner fitting to that nature for two purposes: namely, for the "first act" of nature, which is the stabilizing of its being so that it persists; and for the "second act" of nature, which is the producing of its operation so that it exists in action. For without that indwelling, a creature cannot persist in being, nor can it draw out its own proper operation. This is because, through indwelling, God preserves the creature in being and, by cooperating, provides it with every action or operation. This is as **Gregory** says in the sixteenth book of his *Moralia*, commenting on that passage of **Job 23**: "He is alone." Are there not also angels and men, heaven and earth? Indeed. But it is one thing to be, namely, *absolutely*, and another to be *principally*. For these things exist, but they do not exist *principally*, because they do not subsist in themselves since the time they were created. For all things were surely made from nothing, and their essence would tend back toward nothing unless the hand of the Ruler of the realm held it fast. 

Behold the first of these sayings; and what follows concerns the second: "And at the same time, they would be able neither to subsist nor to move by themselves. They subsist only insofar as they have received that they ought to be; they move only insofar as they are arranged by a hidden instinct." The earth dries up, the sea is shaken, the air becomes fire, the sky grows dark, men are emboldened, and the angelic powers are moved. Are these things not driven by their own instincts, or rather, are they not moved by divine impulses?

For without the said interpenetration, the nature could not be elevated into the being of the divine subsistence, nor could it perceive the distinction of operations—namely, by seeing and loving the divine essence in a manner fitting for a creature. <meta>This page continues the scholastic debate on whether God can assume any nature or only an intellectual one. The author uses Aristotle and John of Damascus to prove that for a nature to be united with God, it must possess an intellectual capacity.</meta>

...those two things. But no creaturely nature is capable, nor can it be capable, of the <term>divine indwelling: the way God's presence flows into a soul</term> to receive within itself—in a manner suited to its nature—the first operation of God mentioned previously, unless it is also capable of receiving the second operation within itself. This is because no creature can exist through its substance if it is not also granted some operation through its power. For, according to 
<margin>The Philosopher <note>Aristotle</note></margin>
the Philosopher at the end of the fourth book of *Meteorology*, all things are defined by their operations and exist for the sake of those operations; they exist only as long as they are able to perform their own proper operations. When they cease to be able to perform their proper operations, they simultaneously cease to be. For as 
<margin>Damascene <note>John of Damascus</note></margin>
Damascene says in chapter 17 of the same work: An intellect that is foolish and deprived of cognition will never truly exist. For if it is inoperable and immovable, it is entirely non-existent. By this, he clearly suggests that if the substance of the intellect could not be elevated <note>to a higher spiritual state</note> because of its intellectual nature, it would not be <term>assumable: capable of being taken up by God into a union of persons</term>, nor would the man himself be. This is because he would not truly be a man, as [Damascene] states earlier in the same passage: Since the human is by definition a rational, intellectual being, how then could God have become a man if he had assumed a lifeless body or a soul that was <term>anoin</term> <note>original Greek: ἄνουν, meaning "without mind" or "witless"</note>, that is, without an intellect? For that is not what a man is. 

Therefore, in the same way, no nature of a creature is capable, or could be capable, of the <term>circumincession: the mutual interpenetration of the divine and human natures</term> of God to receive the aforementioned first operation of God within itself beyond the limits of nature, unless it is also capable of the second operation. However, a nature is not capable of this second operation except through the powers of the intellect and the
<margin>Augustine</margin>
will. Therefore, and so on. For this reason, although the argument of Augustine touched upon in the first reasoning does not hold strictly as a matter of logical <term>form: the structural validity of a syllogism</term>, it nevertheless does not fail in any specific <term>matter: the actual content or subject being discussed</term> such that this conclusion follows: if this nature (say, of a man) is capable of being elevated according to its essence, it must necessarily also be capable of being elevated according to its power. And if it cannot be elevated according to its power, then it cannot be according to its essence either. This is similar to the following logic: if the soul of a strong man is immortal, then the soul of every man is immortal; and if the soul of every man is not immortal, then neither is the soul of the strong man. This is because the same principle of immortality or mortality exists in all of them. Therefore, such an argument holds well by reason of its subject matter, just as if it held by the logical form of the argument—which in truth it does hold by virtue of its form when considering the common principle that applies to a specific nature, such as the immortality of the soul. For that principle is the same in every soul. 

Let us therefore look at the possibility and impossibility of this <term>assumption: the act of God taking on a nature</term>. On God's part, as we have said, there is no doubt. But because it is unknown to us on the part of the nature capable of receiving God, the understanding of the truth in this question is difficult for us. 
<margin>Another position cited by Henry <note>Henry of Ghent</note></margin>
For this reason, there is another position here besides the one mentioned, though it is less common. However, because it is more applicable to the mind—even if it does not seem as true because it is unfamiliar—it is perhaps truer: namely, that no nature is capable of being assumed by God in the said manner through circumincession unless it is an intellectual nature. This view pleases me more. 

Holding this opinion for the present, I say in response to the first opposing argument regarding the incorporeal nature of the rational soul or an angel: in man, the nature of the body is included insofar as it is ordered toward the soul, like a thing to be perfected is ordered toward its perfection. In the body, the soul performs its intellectual operation more effectively (once every accidental hindrance is removed) than when it is separated from it. Thus, the whole <term>composite: the human being as a single unit of body and soul</term> of body and soul, with its intellectual capacity, is the thing capable of receiving God. The body is included through the mediation of the substance of the soul and in relation to that substance of the soul, as the soul itself is the intellectual power. Thus, in no way can something be capable of receiving God if it does not possess an intellectual power. And this includes under "intellectual power" everything in which the nature of the <term>image: the "Imago Dei" or image of God in man</term> principally consists, existing within the substance of the soul.

<meta>This page continues the argument that only an intellectual nature (like the human soul) can be "assumed" or taken up into union with God. It focuses on the "image of God" as the necessary prerequisite for this union, citing John of Damascus and Henry of Ghent to refute the idea that God could assume a purely physical or non-rational nature.</meta>

...so that nothing is capable of being assumed except by reason of the **image of God** which is within it. This happens either through <term>circumincession: the mutual indwelling or "interpenetration" of the divine and human natures</term>, or according to substance and power simultaneously (as in Christ alone), or according to power alone. In all these cases, the image of God is, as it were, imprinted back onto its prototype, just as a coin 

<margin>Damascene <note>John of Damascus, an 8th-century theologian and Doctor of the Church.</note></margin>
is formed by the die from which its own image was impressed upon it. Hence Damascene says in the aforementioned chapter that, according to the "image," God is in the willing creature; the willing Word was made human. The "image of God" exists according to the intellect. What else is "according to the image" if not the intellect? Therefore, leaving behind what was inferior, He assumed what was better. This is as if to say: this could never have been possible except by reason of the order which [the nature] has toward the intellect. 

He speaks here against those who claimed that a human body was assumed in Christ without a rational soul. He includes the very substance of the soul under the term "intellect," and showing its force and power even in the <term>assumption: the act of God taking on a created nature, specifically in the Incarnation</term>, he adds: "For the intellect is in the middle, between God and the flesh." The inhabitant of this intellect is the image of God. Therefore, intellect is "mixed" with intellect, and the intellect mediates between the purity of God and the thickness of the flesh. 

By this "mixture," I mean the union through the circumincession of the divine intellect with the human intellect. Since the human intellect exists according to three powers—**memory, intelligence, and will**—it is united to the soul and, through a certain circumincession, is united to the Trinity of persons in the unity of the divine nature. Thus, the direct and proximate cause or reason why something may be assumed by God is the "reason of the image of God," which exists only in intellectual substance. Because of this, only an intellectual substance is susceptible to union. 

According to this, in the glorious assumption, through the circumincession by which the divine nature enters into the assumed nature, the Image—which is the assumed intellectual nature—is intimately united to that which is in the divine nature. It is just as if a piece of wax, in which the figure of a seal is impressed, were reapplied to the seal itself in the same way it was first impressed—by entering into all its corners. This could not happen to something where the figure had not been previously impressed, but where there was only some likeness, such as the <term>vestige: a "footprint" or faint trace of God's handiwork</term> of God found in every non-intellectual creature. 

Thus, no non-intellectual nature can be assumed except through the mediation of an intellectual one in the manner described. To the second point—that an assumption into God is possible because the "reason for being" and subsistence exists in the assumed nature—I say it is true that this is a "co-cause." Without it, nothing could be assumed by God, just as one creature cannot be assumed by another. But this is not the *whole* cause. Although it is a cause on the part of the one assuming (God), it is not the cause on the part of the thing to be assumed. In that thing, the entire cause of "assumability" is that it is an image. Through this alone is it "circumincessible" by God and capable of being elevated to the aforementioned union in the divine essence in the unity of the Person. 

Furthermore, there is no final purpose for which God would assume any nature other than an intellectual one. This is because "assumption" exists ultimately for the promotion and perfection of that nature in its elevation—a state which only an intellectual nature can possess. These are the words of Henry <note>Henry of Ghent, a prominent 13th-century philosopher and theologian.</note> almost word for word.

<meta>This page continues the discussion of Henry of Ghent’s Christological views. The previous page established that only an intellectual nature, being made in the "image of God," is fit to be united with the Divine Word. Here, the author defends Henry against charges of heresy by explaining how Henry answers his critics regarding God’s omnipotence and the status of Christ’s body while it lay in the tomb.</meta>

<margin>
Robert of Colletorto
Bernard of Gannat
Two arguments against Henry
</margin>
Neither Robert of Colletorto <note>A 13th-century Dominican theologian.</note> nor Bernard of Gannat <note>A contemporary of Henry of Ghent at the University of Paris.</note>—both of whom I have seen reciting the opinion of Henry—ever judged that opinion to savor of heresy or to be a heresy itself. Lest they themselves appear to have acted irrationally, I wish to briefly set down the way in which Henry seems to defend his position. There are, however, two chief arguments against Henry. The **first argument** stands in this: that in God is every principle of <term>substantiating: the act of giving a nature its own underlying reality or substance</term>, because He is the fullness of all being. Therefore, it seems that He should be able to substantiate and <term>supposit: to act as the personal "subject" or "foundation" for a nature, as the Divine Word does for Christ's humanity</term> any nature whatsoever. The **second argument** is that during the <term>triduum: the three-day period between Christ's death on the cross and His resurrection</term>, God "supposited" the body that was in the tomb, even though it was not then rational <note>because the soul had departed</note>. And just as He supposited it for three days, He could have supposited it for as long a time as He willed. These are the two chief foundations of the opposing opinion, and Henry himself, as was seen in the recitation of his opinion, brings these very points against himself. To the first argument, as we have seen:

<margin>Solution to the first</margin>
he responds that it is true that the fullness of all being is in God, and the principle of substantiating and "suppositing" is found most fully in Him. But this is not the *total* cause of the <term>assumability: the capacity of a created nature to be taken up into union with a divine Person</term> of any nature; rather, it is a "co-cause." For unless the one assuming were such, He could not assume. But beyond this, something is required in the thing being assumed so that it *can* be assumed; and this is the **character of the image**, and finally a supernatural aptitude for being raised up to the <term>beatific operation: the act of seeing and enjoying God in heaven</term>. Since this is found in intellectual nature alone, it seems fitting that only such a nature is "assumable." For it seems reasonable that a nature which cannot be raised up to the "second act" <note>the activity of knowing God</note> cannot be raised up to the "first act" <note>the state of being personally united to God</note>. From this response, Henry seems to want to preserve the idea that nothing is taken away from divine omnipotence. For while they posit that all power is in God, and conclude from this that He *can* so supposit a nature, Henry also attributes all this to God. He does not deny that, because of what is required on the part of the one assuming, God could most fully assume any nature. Rather, he says that an irrational nature itself is not "assumable"—not because of a defect in divine omnipotence, but rather because of the excellence of the divine nature and the deformed deficiency of irrational nature.

<margin>
The solution to the second is manifold.
First.
</margin>
To the second argument, it seems multiple things can be said. First is the response of Henry, who says that He assumed the nature of that body insofar as it was ordered toward an intellectual soul; by reason of this ordering, even the body itself can be called "intellectual" in a ministerial and preparatory sense. And to respond more completely, it must be said that when it is said that "nothing but an intellectual nature can be assumed by God," it is understood that nothing else can be assumed in such a way that it is the *primary* thing assumed, or the whole and adequate object of assumption. The body in the three days of death, however, was not assumed in that way, as is clear; it was assumed only as a part of the rational nature which was the total and primary object of the assumption.

<margin>Second</margin>
Furthermore, perhaps someone might say that this body was not properly said to be "supposited" during those three days, because it is not a nature capable of being "supposited" by its own foundation. Whence it could consequently be said, not improbably, that to "terminate the dependence" of the nature of this body is not the same as to "supposit" it. Otherwise, everything that terminates the dependence or leaning of a part would "supposit" it, which is not said. And thus, although the Word during those three days terminated this dependence of the body (which the whole humanity would have terminated), and by virtue of this the body in those three days communicated to Christ its own <term>idiom: a property or characteristic belonging to a nature</term>—namely, "lying in the tomb"—the Word did not, however, properly "supposit" the body in the same way He would "supposit" a whole human nature. The most evident sign of this is that the nature of that body did not communicate that "idiom" to Christ in a <term>concrete: a grammatical and metaphysical way where the property is predicated of the person (e.g., "This Man is in the tomb")</term> sense during the three days, in the way that the human nature had communicated it to Him before, and still communicates it to Him now, such that one says "the Man" <note>referring to Christ the person</note> possesses it.

<summary>This page addresses objections to Henry of Ghent’s view that only intellectual beings can be assumed by God, explaining that God's power is not limited, but rather irrational natures lack the "aptitude" for such union. It also clarifies that Christ's body in the tomb was only united to the Word as a part of his human nature, not as a standalone object of the Incarnation.</summary>

And thus the response to the aforementioned objections against the opinion of Henry is clear. Regarding other irrational natures, he seems to say that the Word could not assume them through <term>circumincession: the mutual indwelling or interpenetration of natures</term> or <term>supposit: to act as the underlying person or subject for a nature</term>, especially when considering the <term>final cause: the ultimate purpose or goal of an action</term>. For he himself says:

> "Nor can there be any purpose for the assumption of any nature other than an intellectual one. For assumption is only for the sake of the promotion <note>that is, the spiritual elevation or salvation</note> of the assumed nature, which only an intellectual nature is capable of receiving."

Hence <margin>Augustine</margin> says in his commentary on John: "The Word willed to be born from man so that you might be born securely from God." <note>original: "verbum voluit nasci ex homine ut tu securus nascereris ex deo"</note> From this it seems that God would be born from any other nature—which cannot be born from God through grace—in vain. From these points, it can be clear that it is not irrational for me to lack an explicit act of contradicting this opinion in particular. 

And because these masters also especially insisted that such conclusions should at least not be disputed because of the <term>scandal: an action or statement that leads others into spiritual confusion or sin</term> it might cause, I wish to say this regarding that conclusion: even if the opposite view is "truer" and more in line with the common path, nevertheless, if it were publicly disputed, it would be far more scandalous to the common people and offensive to "pious ears." 

For what unrefined and simple person would not be offended if he heard someone saying it is possible that these propositions are true: "**God is a donkey**" or "**God is a piece of wood**"? Or what of those propositions which many following the aforementioned opinion <note>the opinion that God can assume any nature</note> concede: "**God can be damned to hell**," "**God could be tortured by the devil in hell**," or "**The devil can be God**"? 

Although among many learned men—speaking of God’s <term>absolute power: the theoretical total power of God to do anything that does not involve a logical contradiction</term>—these [statements] cause no scandal, nevertheless the common and simple folk would certainly be much more offended than if they heard that a donkey *cannot* be united to the divine nature in a unity of "supposit" <note>meaning God cannot become a donkey</note> in the way declared in my conclusion. Yet these fathers have said that my conclusion, by the "force of the words" <note>Latin: "ex vi sermonis"; meaning the literal phrasing</note>, derogates from divine omnipotence and therefore "savors of heresy" <note>a formal theological term for a statement that, while not explicitly heretical, strongly suggests a heretical error</note>. I do not know what logic, or indeed what theology, they are relying on. 

For let me ask: does he who says he does not "assent" to a certain proposition say, by the rigor of the words, the opposite of that conclusion to which he does not assent? Let them say whether this consequence holds: "I do not assent (or I do not hold an act of assent) to this conclusion: 'The Pope is sitting'; therefore, I believe the conclusion: 'The Pope is not sitting'." Would the first part not be true of a sleeping person? A person who has no mental act at all could not be said to believe the false consequence. 

Furthermore, if the present conclusion [of Henry's] derogated from divine omnipotence according to true theology, it would not merely "savor of heresy" but should be judged as outright heretical. Indeed, even a sleeping Catholic or a small child who lacks the use of reason and does not hold an "assent" to the proposition "God can supposit any created nature" would then be a heretic—or at least would be erring in the faith—which no one would say. 

From these things it is clear that their condemnation of these points is not correct. For this was formally their determination, considering the response of the proponent and the motives and reasons of Henry, upon whose opinion he leans when stating the conclusion: 

> "It has seemed to us that the aforementioned conclusion, by the force of the words, derogates from divine omnipotence and through this savors of heresy."

For they were first deceived because, when I said that I followed Henry in this, they did not understand that by the pronoun "this" I was denoting the very conclusion that was being asked to be explained. Therefore, "in this"—that is, in the conclusion itself, namely in *not assenting* to this: "God can [supposit] any nature etc."—I said I followed Henry. I did not mean by "this" the opinion which says: "God *cannot* supposit any nature." But they perhaps believed there was no difference between the one statement and the other; although, if they are learned theologians, they ought to know...

## QUESTION FIVE: CONCERNING NATURAL MAGIC AND THE KABBALAH OF THE HEBREWS.

<margin>q</margin>
The fourth conclusion condemned by these men was this: **There is no science that makes us more certain of the divinity of Christ than magic and Kabbalah.** 
In clarifying this conclusion, I said that among the sciences—which are "sciences" in such a way that they do not rely on revelation, neither in their method of proceeding, nor in their principles, nor in their conclusions—there is none that makes us more certain (in the way that sciences discovered by human means can) than that <term>magic</term> about which the conclusions are placed there, which is a part of <term>natural science</term>, and that part of <term>Kabbalah</term> which is a science and is not revealed theology. These masters said that my clarification was not relevant to the meaning of the words of the aforementioned conclusion, and that the aforementioned conclusion, <term>by the force of the words</term>, was false, erroneous, and heretical. In this condemnation of theirs, let us see how many things are to be condemned, taking them one by one. <margin>First</margin> First, let them tell me how my clarification could be more relevant to the meaning of the words of my conclusion. For what else is in that clarification but an explicit declaration of the force of each individual term placed in the conclusion? For there, first, it is explained what I understand by "science" when I say "no science," and what I mean by "to make certain," what by "magic," and what by "Kabbalah." Nor do I see what further remains to be clarified. <margin>Second</margin> Second, I want to show that by the force of the words, it is not only not false and heretical, but rather its opposite is false and, according to them, totally heretical. For the said conclusion is a negative one, which is explained disjunctively through three categorical statements thus: "No science that is not revealed, etc., other than magic and Kabbalah, makes us certain of the divinity of Christ; OR magic and Kabbalah do not make us certain, etc.; OR magic and Kabbalah make us more certain of the divinity of Christ than any other non-revealed science." This disjunctive statement is true and Catholic, because it has at least one true part. And thus it is already clear that by the force of the words, it is not false. But that its opposite, according to them, is heretical is clear: for the opposite of "No science not revealed, etc., makes us more certain" is this: "Some science not revealed makes us more...

For first, the assignment of names <note>original: "impositio nominum"</note> is not done by us now; rather, we use names and their meanings according to the custom of the ancients. <margin>Magus is a Persian name</margin>
It is easy to understand the name *Magus*. For this word *magus* is neither Latin nor Greek, but Persian. In the Persian language, it signifies the same thing that "wise man" <note>original: "sapiens"</note> signifies among us. Indeed, those who are considered wise men among
<margin>Pythagoras</margin>
the Persians are the same as those called "philosophers" among the Greeks—who were so named by Pythagoras, whereas they were previously

called "wise men." For among almost all diverse nations, their wise men were called by different names: such as Druids among the Gauls; prophets among the Hebrews, or the **Sanhedrin** <note>The supreme council or court in ancient Israel.</note>, or **Pharisees**, or **Kabbalists**; among the Indians, **Gymnosophists** <note>literally "naked philosophers," a group of ancient Indian philosophers known for their asceticism.</note>; among the Egyptians,
<margin>Gymnosophists</margin>

<margin>Priests, Philosophers, Magi</margin>

If, therefore, magic is the same as wisdom, they rightly wished to call this practical branch of natural science—which presupposes an exact and absolute knowledge of all natural things, like the peak and summit of all philosophy—by the peculiar and appropriated name of **Magic** (that is, wisdom), just as we call Rome "the City," Virgil "the Poet," or Aristotle "the Philosopher." Those *magi* were not necromancers or in league with demons, who came to adore the enemy of demons—indeed, their Lord, who would soon triumph over them. But they were truly wise men, learned in the science of celestial and earthly things, who worshiped and venerated the very Wisdom of the Father made visible in a human body. Jerome <note>Saint Jerome, c. 342–420 AD, best known for translating the Bible into Latin.</note> makes this distinction very clearly understood
<margin>Jerome, Apollonius of Tyana</margin>

Therefore, since this term "magic" is equivocal—referring to both the superstitious and the natural kind—a general rule applied to it will not apply to every possible meaning. Instead, from the statements that "all magic is prohibited," it will be understood only that all species of *superstitious* magic are meant, which are all grouped under one name and one definition. For it is clear that they possess such activity according to all philosophers, both in acting and in the manner of acting and receiving. ...material realities. Yet the **Pythagoreans** <note>Followers of the Greek philosopher Pythagoras, who believed that numbers were the fundamental building blocks of reality.</note> would say—whose philosophy I call "more secret philosophy" in my 24th conclusion because it is less known and less in use than mathematics—that just as mathematical things are more **formal** <note>Relating to the "form" or essence of a thing rather than its physical matter.</note> than physical things, so too they are more actual. And just as they depend less on matter in their being, so too they depend less in their operation.

<margin>Pythagoreans</margin>
And so, what I said about their greater power—although the disagreement between the Pythagoreans and the **Peripatetics** <note>Followers of Aristotle’s philosophy, who generally prioritized physical observation over mathematical abstraction.</note> is indifferent to the faith—nevertheless I did not say it as true in itself and absolutely, but as a consequence of the "secret philosophy" of the Pythagoreans, to be understood in the manner aforesaid. 

Their opinion is also that among all mathematical things, numbers are more actual as they are more formal. And among odd numbers, they favor the **number three** <note>original: "ternarium"</note>, because it is the first odd number, and the first in every genus is the most perfect in that genus. Among even numbers, they favor the **number ten** <note>original: "denarium"</note>, which is "every number," as is clear. For from ten onward, we count further only by repeating the sequence. And this is what I intended by what I said about the numbers three and ten in **natural magic** <note>A branch of science in the Renaissance that sought to understand the hidden powers within nature, distinct from "black magic" or sorcery.</note>. 

Moreover, the **Catholic doctors** <note>The authoritative theologians and scholars of the Church.</note> also attribute efficiency and power—for both good and evil—to numbers. Hence **Hilary** <note>Hilary of Poitiers (c. 310–367), a prominent early Christian theologian.</note>, in his commentary on the Psalms, inquiring into the reason why the order of the Psalms is not according to history—but often a Psalm that was composed earlier is placed later in the order—says this:

<margin>Hilary</margin>
"It must not be ignored that among the Hebrews, the number of the Psalms is indistinct and they were written down without any note of order. For they are not pre-noted as first, second, third, fiftieth, or hundredth there; but they are mixed together into one without any prescription of order. For **Ezra** <note>original: "Hesdras"; the biblical scribe credited with reviving the Jewish law after the exile.</note>, as ancient traditions report, collected and brought them into one volume, unarranged and dispersed according to the diversity of authors and times."

<margin>Ezra</margin>
"But the **seventy elders** <note>The legendary group of Jewish scholars who translated the Hebrew Bible into Greek (the Septuagint).</note>—remaining in the synagogue for the custody of the law and doctrine according to the tradition of Moses—after the care of translating the whole law from Hebrew into the Greek language was entrusted to them by King **Antiochus** <note>Traditionally, this was Ptolemy II Philadelphus; Pico’s text mentions Antiochus, possibly following a specific source or variant tradition.</note>, understanding the powers of the Psalms through spiritual and heavenly knowledge, restored them to number and order. They assigned each individual number according to its own efficiency and resolution, matching the order to the power of the specific Psalms." These are Hilary's words verbatim.

<margin>Jerome</margin>
From these things it is most clearly evident that number gives power and efficiency. **Jerome** <note>St. Jerome (c. 347–420), best known for his Latin translation of the Bible.</note> also, writing against Jovinian, says that the **number twenty** is ill-fated <note>original: "infaustum"</note>, as it was the number in which Jacob served, and Joseph was sold, and which Esau loved when receiving certain gifts. In the same place, he praises the **number ten**, saying that he had spoken of its praises quite often. And in the same book, chapter 8, he says that the reason why it was not said on the second day of creation, "and God saw that it was good" [Genesis 1:8], is because the **number two** <note>original: "binarius"</note> is evil. 

<margin>Basil</margin>
Furthermore, he takes an argument from the number two against those who marry twice; and for this reason, he says that all **unclean animals** entered Noah's ark in pairs of two, while those that are clean entered in groups of seven.

<margin>Nazianzen</margin>
<margin>Ambrose</margin>
<margin>Origen</margin>
<margin>Augustine</margin>
You will find similar things a hundred times in **Basil**, **Nazianzen**, **Ambrose**, **Origen**, **Augustine**, and others. Indeed, **Rabanus** <note>Rabanus Maurus (c. 780–856), a major scholar of the Carolingian era.</note>, a distinguished doctor of the Church, composed a special book on the virtues of numbers. You will find that ecclesiastical doctors always observe the properties of these numbers everywhere—and sometimes almost to the point of curiosity, if it may be so called. 

<margin>Rabanus</margin>
<margin>Note on numbers.</margin>
For instance, they refer the two Testaments, the two cherubim, the two precepts of charity, the two primary dignities, and the two primary peoples to the **number two**. Now, moreover, the mystery of the **number three**...

He argues that numbers possess inherent "efficiency" and "power" that can be used to understand spiritual and natural truths.</summary>

...substantial divinity during the three days in the tomb; in the three theological virtues <note>Faith, Hope, and Charity.</note>; in the three times of **nature**, **law**, and **grace**; and in the three states of perfection which are contemplated. Now, not without mystery, but also because of the hidden property of the number itself, they wish it to be that **Moses** fasted for forty days, **Elijah** for forty, and **Christ** for forty; and that Christ ascended forty days after the Resurrection; and that he was among the dead for forty hours; and that after forty days **Nineveh** <note>The ancient city mentioned in the Book of Jonah.</note>, which is a type and figure of this world, was to be overturned; and that the Lord caused it to rain upon the earth for the same number of days and nights. They also say it contains a great sacrament <note>In this context, a "sacrament" refers to a sacred mystery or hidden meaning.</note> that the remission of sins occurs in the **number fifty**. In this same number, the **Holy Spirit** descended. <margin>Hilary, Origen</margin> 
which **Hilary** and **Origen** <note>Two influential early Christian scholars; Hilary of Poitiers and Origen of Alexandria.</note> especially note. Among them, the Holy Spirit is also signified by **fire**, 
<margin>Note</margin> 
in which form and in which number of days he descended upon the Apostles. And among them, the Holy Spirit is the third person or property in divine matters, proceeding from the first and the second; which second is called **Wisdom** and proceeds from the first, and differs from both only by the nature of its "procession" <note>A theological term describing how the persons of the Trinity originate from one another.</note>. Just as, for instance, that which proceeds differs from those from whom it proceeds, even though it is the same with them in substance and essence. These things are expressly said by the Cabalists, whose words—brought forward by me against the Jews—these masters used to detest as suspicious regarding the faith. They also call this same third property **"Repentance,"** which agrees with what was just said: that the same number is attributed to the Holy Spirit as to the sacrament of repentance. 
<margin>What the sin against the Holy Spirit properly is</margin> 
From this we can also gather that the **sin against the Holy Spirit** is properly the sin of impenitence <note>The refusal to repent.</note>, which is not forgiven in this age nor in the future. But of these things elsewhere. They also observe some secret property of the **number twelve** in the twelve tribes of Israel, the twelve Apostles, and the twelve stones of the heavenly Jerusalem. They also believe it was neither without cause nor by chance that the **number ten** coincided with the commandments of the law and the ten strings of the psaltery; and among the 
<margin>Singers of the Psalms</margin>

A traditional Jewish commentary on the Book of Psalms.</note>, there are ten singers of the psalms: **Adam**, **Abraham**, **Melchizedek**, **Moses**, **Asaph**, **David**, **Solomon**, and the **three sons of Korah**, although they are listed differently by our scholars. Corresponding to these are ten organs—that is, ten instruments or ten modes of music in which they are sung, named as follows among the Hebrews:

*Nezach, Neginoth, Mizmor, Shir, Tephila, Beracha, Hallel, Hodaiah, Ashre, Hallelujah.* <note>Pico lists Hebrew musical and liturgical terms: Victory, Stringed Instruments, Psalm, Song, Prayer, Blessing, Laud, Thanksgiving, Beatitude, and Praise God.</note>

I have observed that these should be distinguished such that **Odes** are sung by the first; the second is the same as an **instrument**; **Psalms** by the third; **Canticles** by the fourth; **Prayers** by the fifth; **Blessings** by the sixth; **Laudations** by the seventh; **Thanksgivings** by the eighth; the **felicity** of someone by the ninth; and by the last, only the **praises of God**. You may also add *Maskil* <note>original: "meſchil." A Hebrew term for a contemplative or instructive poem.</note>, by which **contemplations** are sung, and *Hallelujah* will be like the *Ein Sof* <note>original: "eiſoph." The Infinite or "Without End" in Kabbalah, representing God before manifestation.</note>, not being placed in the number with the others. They also add the ten days during which the Spirit descended after the ascension of Christ, and the ten curtains in the Temple, and innumerable and infinite similar things. They always say that **nothing happens by chance**, but God disposed all things through his wisdom, just as in weight and measure, so too in **number** <note>A reference to the Book of Wisdom 11:20: "Thou hast ordered all things in measure, and number, and weight."</note>. I shall remain silent on how many and how great things they observe in the **number nine**, such that—beyond the hierarchies of angels and the nine degrees of beatitudes according to Matthew—they do not believe even the length of the cubits of **Og, King of Bashan** <note>A giant mentioned in Deuteronomy 3:11 whose bed was nine cubits long.</note>, who is a type of the devil, to be accidental and without mystery; observing also that the Lord [died] at the **ninth hour**...

...of the Hebrews, but also of our own doctors—as I shall show below—that besides the Law which God gave to **Moses** on the mountain, and which he left written and contained in five books, there was also revealed to the same **Moses** by God himself a true exposition of the Law, with a manifestation of all the mysteries and secrets which were contained under the "bark" <note>A common metaphor in medieval philosophy where the "bark" or "husk" is the literal meaning and the "pith" or "fruit" is the spiritual meaning.</note> and rough face of the words of the Law. And those books are called the books of **Kabbalah**, in which books many—indeed, almost all—things are found to be in harmony with our faith. <meta>This page continues the argument that Moses received a secret, oral tradition (Kabbalah) alongside the written Law. Having explained the definition of "Kabbalah" as "reception," the text now provides historical and patristic evidence—citing Saint Hilary of Poitiers and the book of Ezra—to prove that this oral tradition was restricted to a small circle of elders before being written down during the Babylonian Exile to prevent its loss.</meta>

<margin>Hilary</margin>
...already received from God. That it was to be communicated only to the seventy elders is clearly testified by **Hilary** <note>Saint Hilary of Poitiers (c. 310–367 AD), a prominent Bishop and Doctor of the Church known for his works on the Trinity and Psalms.</note>, who in his exposition of the second Psalm, *Why do the nations rage?* <note>original: "Quare fremuerunt gentes"</note> etc., writes as follows: "It had already been instituted by **Moses** that there should be seventy teachers in every synagogue. For although **Moses** had preserved the words of the Old Testament in writing, he had nonetheless separately communicated certain more secret mysteries from the hidden depths of the Law to the seventy elders, who would thereafter remain as teachers. The Lord also mentions this doctrine in the Gospels, saying: *The scribes and Pharisees sit on the seat of Moses. Therefore, do all things whatsoever they tell you to do and observe; but do not do according to their works.* <note>Matthew 23:2–3.</note> Truly, their doctrine remained for posterity." These are the words of **Hilary** verbatim. Behold how **Hilary** expressly testifies that besides the written Law, there was a certain other more secret doctrine which **Moses** communicated to those seventy wise men. Furthermore, that this more secret and truer exposition of the mysteries of the Law was not made public to everyone everywhere, but was revealed specifically by God to **Moses**, and by him only to the other seventy wise men, is also testified by **Origen** <note>An early Christian scholar and theologian (c. 184–253 AD).</note> in the place previously cited, speaking thus of **Moses**, the prophets, and others like them: "These things are to be understood as being spoken to those to whom the oracles of God were entrusted." He adds: "And if there was anyone among them who was a wise and understanding listener and a wonderful counselor." Thus says **Origen**. By these

<margin>Sanhedrin</margin>
"wonderful counselors," however, are understood those whom the Hebrews call the **Sanhedrin** <term>Sanhedrin</term> <note>The supreme council and tribunal of the Jews, traditionally composed of 71 members.</note>—that is, those seventy elders whom **Moses** chose by the command of the Lord, whose place the **Cardinals** in our Church seem to me to hold. And in imitation of the number of those seventy elders, as we shall now declare, the mysteries of the **Kabbalah** were reduced into seventy principal books in the time of **Ezra**. For until the time of **Ezra**, nothing of this doctrine was written down, but as I said, it was handed down only through successive reception; hence it took the name "Kabbalistic." However, after they were restored from the Babylonian captivity through **Cyrus**, and the Temple was restored under **Zerubbabel**, then **Ezra**, who was the leader of the Synagogue, after he repaired the written Law of **Moses** and corrected the Old Testament, wished also that these secret oracles of God, which had not been written until that time, should be put into writing. This was because, due to the captivity of the nation, they could not maintain that order of handing down that doctrine by hand-to-hand transmission; and it was rightly to be feared that, because of their dispersion, if the teachings were not found in writing, they might eventually perish. Therefore, **Ezra** decreed that they should be written down, employing scribes specifically for this purpose. And because there were seventy elders or counselors among whom this doctrine resided, he commanded that all those secrets be redacted into seventy principal volumes, which nonetheless were even then not to be communicated except to the wise. And this is what is read in **Ezra** <note>Pico is quoting from the apocryphal book 2 Esdras (also known as 4 Ezra) 14:45–47, which was often included in the Latin Vulgate Bible.</note> in these words: "When the forty days were ended, the Most High spoke, saying: The first things you wrote, set out in public so the worthy and unworthy may read them; but the last seventy books you shall preserve to hand over to the wise of your people. For in these is the vein of understanding, the fountain of wisdom, and the river of knowledge. And so I did." These are the words of **Ezra** verbatim. Moreover, a broad and extensive mention of that council in which these books were written is found among the Hebrews

<margin>Seder Olam</margin>
in the book called the **Seder Olam** <term>Seder Olam</term> <note>Hebrew for "Order of the World," a 2nd-century chronological work detailing Jewish history from the Creation.</note>—that is, the "Book of Ages"—where it is recorded who sat in the council, and finally the acts and order of the entire council. From all of which it can be sufficiently clear that it is not a fiction of my own making that **Moses** received a true exposition of the Law from God besides the written Law, and that it was thereafter passed down through succession from **Moses** to the seventy elders, and from them...

<meta>This page continues the author’s defense of "Christian Kabbalah," moving from the historical origin of these secret books in the time of Ezra to a systematic comparison of Jewish and Christian hermeneutics (interpretive methods). The author argues that because the Kabbalah represents the highest "anagogical" level of meaning, it proves Christian doctrines more effectively than the literal sense of the Hebrew Bible.</meta>

...revealed to his other successors. From this it took its name, so that they called it **Cabalistic**, and in the time of **Ezra** it was redacted into several books, which are called the books of the **Kabbalah**. These books, <margin>Note</margin> which I acquired for myself at great expense—for the Jews are not willing to share them with us Latins—I have read through diligently. Finding there many things—indeed, almost everything—in agreement with our faith, it seemed to me that Christians could have a means by which to pierce the Jews with their own weapons, since the authority of the Kabbalists, whom they hold in great honor and reverence, cannot be denied by them.

<margin>Note</margin> Furthermore, it should be known that this exposition of the Bible is proportioned to the mode of interpreting the Bible which among us is called <term>anagogical</term> <note>The "anagogical" sense is the highest level of medieval interpretation, focusing on how a text points toward heavenly or eternal realities.</note>. For just as among <margin>The fourfold mode of interpreting the Bible among the Hebrews is just as it is among us.</margin> us there is a fourfold mode of interpreting the Bible—the literal, the mystical or allegorical, the tropological, and the anagogical—so it is also among the Hebrews. The literal mode among them is called <margin>Pesat.</margin> **Peshat** <note>original: "Pesat"; the "plain" or direct meaning of the text.</note>, which mode is held among them by **Rabbi Solomon** <note>original: "Rabi Salamon"; referring to Rashi (1040–1105), the most influential Jewish commentator.</note>, **Kimhi** <note>original: "Chemoy"; likely David Kimhi (Radak), a grammarian and exegete.</note>, and those like them. This sense is also the most sublime and divine among them all, leading us upward from earthly things to the celestial, from the sensible to the intelligible, from the temporal to the eternal, from the lowest to the supreme, from the human to the divine, and from the corporeal to the spiritual. And it is from here that the <margin>Example</margin> most powerful arguments are held against the Jews. For the discord that exists between them and us—as is most clearly evident from the epistles of **Paul**—depends chiefly on this: that they follow the "killing letter," while we follow the "vivifying spirit" <note>A reference to 2 Corinthians 3:6: "For the letter kills, but the Spirit gives life."</note>. But if they were willing, along with the **Kabbalists**, to understand those things anagogically by interpreting the Scripture as referring to the celestial **Jerusalem**, to spiritual captivity, and to the celestial land of the living, they would necessarily recognize and confess that he was the true **Messiah** through whom almost the whole world was liberated from the hand of the demon, whom it was serving through idolatry. That this was the principal effect of the coming of **Christ** is the firm opinion of the **Kabbalists** themselves.

<meta>This page continues the author's defense of the Kabbalah, specifically clarifying the different types of Kabbalah and distinguishing the "true" tradition from superstitious or magical practices that have usurped the name.</meta>

Catholics, following the testimony of **Jerome** <note>Saint Jerome (c. 347–420 AD), the translator of the Vulgate Bible, who was noted for his study of Hebrew traditions.</note>, grant so much to this tradition and approve of it so thoroughly that even our own doctors confess and believe it was revealed by God to **Moses**, and from **Moses** through a line of succession to other wise men. This is that which, because of its mode of delivery, is called **Kabbalah** <term>Kabbalah: from the Hebrew 'qabbalah', meaning 'tradition' or 'that which is received'.</term>, which I often see designated by our own authors by saying "as the ancient tradition says."

<margin>The first and true Kabbalah</margin>
This is the first and true **Kabbalah**, of which I believe I was the first among the Latins to have made explicit mention. It is the one I use in my conclusions, which I put forward expressly against the Hebrews for the confirmation of our faith; I do not know how these masters could have held me suspect in the faith. However, because this mode of delivery through succession, which is called "Kabbalistic," seems to suit every secret and mystical matter, the Hebrews have usurped the term so that they call every science held among them as secret and hidden "Kabbalah." Thus, any knowledge obtained from elsewhere through a hidden path is said to be held "through the way of Kabbalah."

<margin>The Hebrews honored two sciences with the name of Kabbalah</margin>
In general, however, they have honored two sciences with this name. One is called the **art of combining** <note>original: "ars combinandi"</note>, which is a certain method of proceeding in the sciences; it is something similar to what is called among our people the **Art of Raymond** <note>Referring to Raymond Lull (c. 1232–1315), a philosopher who developed a logical system for combining concepts to discover universal truths.</note>, although they perhaps proceed in a different manner. <margin>Art of Raymond</margin> The other concerns the virtues of superior things which are above the moon, and it is the supreme part of **natural magic**. Both of these are also called **Kabbalah** among the Hebrews for the reason already stated, and we have also occasionally made mention of both of these in our conclusions.

For that "art of combining" is what I call in my conclusions the **alphabetical revolution**. And that which concerns the virtues of superior things—which in one way can be understood as a part of **natural magic**, and in another way as a thing distinct from it—is that which I speak of in the present conclusion, saying that it aids us in the knowledge of the divinity of **Christ** in the manner already declared. And although the name of **Kabbalah** does not suit these two sciences by its primary and proper application, it could nevertheless be applied to them metaphorically. Indeed, just as of old the **Magi** <note>Originally referring to Persian priest-sages, but later misused to mean sorcerers.</note> were only said to be wise men, but then **necromancers** and diabolical men, falsely claiming the name of "wise man" for themselves, called themselves "Magi."

So also some among the Hebrews, promising divine things through false and vain superstitions—indeed, in reality differing almost nothing from **necromancers**—said that they possessed secret names of God and virtues by which they could bind demons and perform miracles; and they claimed that **Christ** performed miracles by no other way. These men falsely claimed the name of **Kabbalists** for themselves, saying that their art was that true **Kabbalah** which God revealed to **Moses**. In the same way, **necromancers** also say they received their incantations and brutish acts from **Solomon**, **Adam**, **Enoch**, and the like.

However, this falsely named **Kabbalah** I have not only not approved in my conclusions or followed, but I have expressly rejected it, putting forward a special conclusion directly against that which says the miracles of **Christ** could not have been performed by the way of **Kabbalah**. Let these things suffice for the present conclusion, which would require a special book if we wished to declare exactly what **natural magic** is and what **Kabbalah** is. Here it is enough to have shown that nothing is contained in them which is repugnant to the Catholic and orthodox faith.

<meta>This page continues the author's defense of his "900 Theses," moving from the discussion of Kabbalah to a specific theological dispute regarding the Eucharist. He is responding to accusations of heresy by distinguishing between what is "possible" by God's power and what the Church actually teaches as fact.</meta>

# SIXTH QUESTION ON THE SACRAMENT OF THE EUCHARIST.

**IF ONE HOLDS** the common path regarding the possibility of "assumption" <note>original: "suppositionis". In scholastic theology, this refers to a divine person (a "suppositum") taking up or "assuming" a nature, as the Word assumed human nature.</note> with respect to any creature, I say that without the conversion of the substance of bread into the body of Christ, or the annihilation of the "bread-ness" <term>bread-ness: a technical term (paneitas) referring to the essential nature or substance of bread.</term>, it is possible that the body of Christ be on the altar according to the truth of the sacrament. This is said regarding what is **possible**, not how things **actually are**. By this conclusion, I do not intend to say that the bread is not converted into the body of Christ, or that the body of Christ is not actually in the sacrament instituted by Christ, or that the actual truth of that sacrament is the presence of Christ's body alongside bread that has been assumed or "supposited" by the Word <note>The "Word" (Verbum) refers to the second person of the Trinity.</note>. For I expressly reject those claims regarding actual existence at the end of the conclusion, where I said "that it is said regarding what is possible, not how it is." I want the term "possible" to refer not only to the preceding statement about the assumption of bread by Christ, but to the truth of the sacrament of the Eucharist and even to the sacrament itself—indeed, even to the presence of the body of Christ together with the assumed bread. Thus, perhaps it would not be necessary that, by virtue of this assumption of bread by the incarnate Word, it would be the same body of Christ that He already took from the Virgin along with the bread. Nevertheless, it is possible that He would be on the altar together with the bread if the bread were assumed by Christ.

I am speaking, therefore, in the present conclusion about a **possible** sacrament, its **possible** truth, and the **possible** presence of Christ’s body together with this "assumable" bread. Therefore, I am surprised that the present conclusion has been condemned as erroneous on the grounds that the aforementioned things are false regarding the sacrament of the Eucharist as it is already instituted, which they claim I am talking about; for I explicitly profess in the conclusion to be speaking about a **possible** sacrament and its **possible** truth. They should therefore consider the words of the conclusion more carefully before they condemn a conclusion that so expressly refutes the sense which they are condemning. Indeed, they should consider that their own determination can hardly be defended from error, because if the conclusion intended to uphold the truth of the sacrament according to the institution of Christ which the Church holds (as they say), then it would be not only erroneous but simply heretical. But if the sense of the conclusion is the one explained by me, it is not only not erroneous in faith, but rather it is erroneous to say the opposite. For there are many things which, regarding how things **actually are**, are heretical, but their opposite regarding what is **possible** would be heretical. For example, to say that the Father was incarnate as a matter of fact <note>The Father was not incarnate; only the Son (the Word) was. To say otherwise is the heresy of Patripassianism.</note> is heretical; but to say the Father **could** have been incarnated is not only not heretical, but to say the opposite would be heretical <note>To deny that God the Father *could* become human if He willed it would be to limit God's omnipotence.</note>. Let these things suffice for the declaration and defense of the conclusion.

<margin>Question</margin>
But for the sake of scholastic exercise, leaving aside my conclusion, let us see whether it is true that the body of Christ can be preserved on the altar by a method other than the conversion of bread into it—namely, through the "sustentation" of the nature of bread in the divine Person <note>original: "supposito"</note> together with the assumed humanity, so that there would be one Person in three natures: namely, divinity, humanity, and bread-ness. And by reason of the Person, each nature in the concrete would be predicated of the others, and there would be a **communication of idioms** <term>communication of idioms: a theological principle where the properties of the different natures of Christ (divine and human) can be attributed to His one Person (e.g., saying "God died on the cross").</term> so that God is bread and man, and vice versa. Thus, Christ-as-man would be on the altar just as Christ-as-bread is on the altar, and so on. This would be "sacramentally" or by virtue of the sacrament, if the power for this had been given.

<summary>Giovanni Pico della Mirandola defends his thesis on the Eucharist, arguing that while the Church teaches transubstantiation, it is theoretically possible by God's power for Christ's person to "assume" the nature of bread (impanation) alongside his human and divine natures.</summary>

...divinely by the sacramental word. Nor should we concern ourselves with whether this word—"This is my body" <note>original: "hoc est corpus meum"</note>—would be sufficient for this by the aforementioned power, or if something else would be required. 

<margin>First argument for the affirmative side. Damascene.</margin>And first, it is argued for the affirmative side that this position should be held because Damascene <note>St. John Damascene (c. 675–749), a prominent Syrian monk and Church Father.</note> seems to hold this as a fact—namely, that this sacrament exists through "assumption" <note>In this context, "assumption" refers to the Divine Word taking up the nature of the bread, similar to how the Word took up human nature in the Incarnation.</note>. For he speaks thus: "And now, being asked how bread becomes the body of Christ, and wine and water become the blood of Christ, I say to you: the Holy Spirit will come upon them and performs that which is beyond reason and intellect." <note>original: "spiritus sanctus superueniet"</note> "But bread and wine are assumed"—and so forth in the same place. And further in the same chapter, speaking of this sacrament of the altar: "Isaiah saw a coal; <note>A reference to the vision in Isaiah 6:6-7 where a seraph touches the prophet's lips with a burning coal.</note> but a coal is not simple wood, but wood united with fire. <margin>Dionysius</margin>Moreover, Dionysius <note>Dionysius the Areopagite, a Christian Neoplatonist whose writings on the "Ecclesiastical Hierarchy" were highly influential in the Middle Ages.</note>, in the third chapter of *The Ecclesiastical Hierarchy*, calls this sacrament an "assumption." Therefore, what these Doctors seem to say regarding how things *actually are* can much more easily be held as a *possibility*. 

<margin>Second argument.</margin>Secondly, it is argued because, according to Augustine in his letter to Volusianus: "In miraculous things, the whole reason for the deed is the power of the Doer." <note>original: "in rebus mirabilibus tota ratio facti sit potentia facientis"</note> To confine this miraculous sacrament to a specific mode of defense which is not expressly found in the canon of Scripture or the determination of the Church is to confine divine power to the capacity of our intellect. This is dangerous and contrary to Augustine, who says in the same place: "If a reason is sought, it will not be a wonder; if an example is provided, it will not be singular." <note>original: "Si ratio queritur non erit mirabile si exemplū ponitur non erit singulare"</note> Let us grant that God can do something that we admit we cannot investigate. 

<margin>Third argument</margin>Thirdly, it is argued that a position whose opposite is not clearly held from the sayings of the Saints can much more easily be held as a possibility. But the opposite of this—namely, that "bread-ness" <term>bread-ness: the technical term "paneitas," referring to the essential substance or "what-ness" of bread.</term> remains substantiated by a divine Person <note>original: "supposito"</note> on the altar—is not clearly found in the sayings of the Saints; therefore, etc. 

<margin>Gregory</margin>This is proven because Gregory <note>Pope Gregory the Great (c. 540–604).</note>, in his Easter homily, says: "The appearance and likeness of those things are the names of the things that were before," namely, of bread and wine. Those who hold the opinion that they *were* bread and wine before, but are now not those things alone because the body of Christ lies hidden there, explain the phrase "that they were before" in this way. 

<margin>Ambrose</margin>Likewise, there is the saying of Ambrose <note>St. Ambrose (c. 340–397), Bishop of Milan.</note> that the power of God, which creates creatures from nothing, here changes the creatures. Other sayings that state that bread and wine do not remain after the consecration but are converted will be explained thus: that the bread which *was* bread does not remain, even though the same "bread-ness" exists, and this is because of the different "suppositum" <note>The "suppositum" is the underlying subject or person. The author argues that the "bread-ness" remains, but it is now "owned" by the Divine Word rather than existing as a piece of ordinary bread.</note>. For this term "bread" signifies a subject in the nature of bread-ness, and this does not remain. However, there is a great difference between saying that bread-ness remains "hypostasized" <note>meaning: "made into a person" or "sustained by a person."</note> in a divine subject and saying that bread-ness remains in its own subject. This is because, in this second way, there would be no communication of properties <term>communication of properties: a theological principle (communicatio idiomatum) where the attributes of two different natures—human and divine—are shared by one person.</term>, which does occur in the first way. However, I believe these authorities are entirely against those who posit this as a fact, but they do not rule it out as a possibility. 

<margin>Fourth argument. Berengarius</margin>Fourthly, it is argued as follows: This opinion is approved as a fact in the confession of Berengarius <note>Berengarius of Tours (c. 1000–1088) was famous for his Eucharistic controversies; he was forced to sign a confession of faith at the Roman Council of 1059.</note>, which was approved by Pope Nicholas at Rome in the presence of 114 bishops; therefore, it can much more easily be held as a possibility. The premise is deduced thus: because Berengarius confesses that after the consecration not only...
