...let there be two subjects <term>supposita; the underlying "person" or "subject" that makes a thing what it is</term>—one of Christ and one of bread. This view posits that both are to be adored with a single act of worship, and that whatever is under the sacrament is adored because of the unity of the subject.

<margin>The second subject.</margin> Secondly, it is argued that there is no way it can be maintained that the body of Christ can be on the altar through that method. For when it is asked whether the body of Christ can be on the altar, etc., this is not understood as the "body" that Christ *is* in a general sense <note>original: "accipitur pro genere" — meaning "body" as a general category of physical substance.</note>, but rather it is understood as the "body" which is a *part* of him and is not spoken of as the whole man directly. Such a body, which is a part, does not share its properties <term>ydioma; the unique characteristics or "idioms" of a nature</term> with the nature it is joined to, nor with the subject, nor vice versa. 

For although God is man and vice versa, God is not the "head" of Christ, nor is the "head" of Christ God. And although Christ as man is everywhere by reason of his divine person, the "head" of Christ the man is not everywhere, because the individual parts of the assumed human nature do not share their specific properties with the divine person, nor are they defined as that person, or vice versa. Therefore, even if "bread-ness" <term>paneitas; the essential nature of bread</term> were assumed by the Word <note>The "Word" refers to the Second Person of the Trinity, Jesus Christ.</note> along with "body-ness," it would still not be said that the body of Christ *is* bread, or that the body of Christ is on the altar simply because bread is on the altar. It might be said and verified that the bread is the "body" that Christ *is* only if "body" is used as a general category of physical substance. 

That "body" is not used in any other way in this question or in the sacrament is apparent: first, because "body" as a general category (which is spoken of directly regarding Christ) is not called the "body of Christ," just as the "animal" or "man" that Christ is, is not called "the man of Christ" or "the animal of Christ." Second, the form of words in which this sacrament was instituted is this: **"This is my body."** <note>Latin: "Hoc est corpus meum."</note> It is certain that the truth of those words is not maintained if "body" is meant as a general category. For the "animal" <note>In medieval logic, "animal" simply means a living, sensing creature.</note> that is spoken of as being me is not "my animal" [something I own], but the "animal" that I actually am. Third, if the consecration had happened during the three days of Christ’s death <term>triduo mortis; the period between Good Friday and Easter Sunday</term>, there would have been on the altar not "body" as a general category, but "body" as a part only. For a "body" in the general sense is a living body, which he was not at that time. Therefore, the "body of Christ" as it is asked here and as it is treated in the sacrament is "body" as a structural part only, which is not defined as bread, or God, or man. Nor does it share the properties of those other natures. Therefore, it would not be true to say that the body of Christ was on the altar in the aforementioned way by reason of the bread or the subject.

<margin>Third.</margin> Furthermore, even if we granted that by reason of this "sustenance" <term>substentificatio; the act of the Divine Word supporting or "holding" the existence of the bread</term> within one subject the bread was the body, it still would not follow that wherever the bread is on the altar, there is the body of Christ. Instead, the bread on the altar would be the body of Christ that is in heaven. This is just as during the three days of death, the soul and body were both sustained by the divine person, yet the soul was not for this reason in the tomb with the body, nor was the body in hell with the soul.

<margin>Fourth.</margin> Furthermore, if this "sustenance" existed, it would have to end at the same point where we say the "conversion" <note>The traditional Catholic view of Transubstantiation, where bread changes into the body.</note> of the bread ends—which is the body of Christ. But the sustenance of a foreign nature [like bread] cannot end at the body of Christ. According to the common way of thinking, this is a property only of an uncreated subject. Therefore, the sustenance of "bread-ness" cannot occur in a subject of another nature in this sacrament. 

<margin>Fifth.</margin> Likewise, it is argued that according to the predicted mode of sustaining "bread-ness" in the Word along with the body of Christ (which was assumed long ago), the body does not *begin* to be on the altar; rather, something else *begins* to be the body of Christ anew. If it does not begin to be there when it was not there before, it follows that it will not be on the altar. 

<margin>Sixth.</margin> Likewise, it is argued that although the Person of the Word could assume "bread-ness" (which it would create in the act of assuming, just as we hold regarding Christ’s humanity), nevertheless it does not...

<margin>First response to the ninth [objection].</margin>
Regarding the claim that Christ does not abandon what he has once assumed: this is said on the presupposition that he is only bound to have assumed human nature—just as, in fact, he only assumed that nature. However, it remains possible that he could assume another nature and then set it aside.

<margin>Second [response].</margin>

He might set it aside because of the corruption of the assumed nature—just as he laid aside his humanity during the three days <note>original: "in triduo"; the period between Christ's death and resurrection when his soul and body were separated, though both remained united to the Divine Person</note>.

<margin>Another question.</margin>
<margin>Argument for the affirmative side.</margin>
But let us inquire further through debate whether it can be maintained that the body, which is a part of Christ's being, is truly present on the altar without the conversion of the bread into it. It seems possible, because just as color is sustained in a substance as its subject through the mediation of another "accident"—for instance, a surface—not because the surface is the subject of the color (since one accident is not the subject of another, as the Philosopher <note>Aristotle</note> says that a quality does not have its own quality), but because color only exists in a subject in relation to the surface. In this same way, bread-ness can be sustained in the Word through the mediation of the body. This is not because the body is the immediate sustainer and giver of existence to the assumed bread-ness while the Word is secondary, but because the bread-ness is only given existence in the subject <term>supposito; the person or underlying reality</term> of the Word in relation to Christ’s body as a part. God can establish this order between assumable natures even if they do not have that order in their own nature, just as he can take away from certain things the natural order they have between each other—such as between heat and the act of heating in the furnace of the Chaldeans <note>A reference to the story in Daniel 3, where the fire of the furnace retained its heat but lost its power to burn the three youths</note> and in many other cases. Therefore, just as color—because it exists in a substance in relation to a surface—is spoken of in relation to the surface in a concrete way as an accidental quality (saying "the surface is colored"), so bread-ness, which is a substance, would be spoken of in relation to the body of Christ in a concrete way as a substantial quality. One could say, "the Son of God is bread" and vice-versa. Just as "humanity" is spoken of regarding the subject as a statement of what it is, by saying "the Son of God is man" and vice-versa; and just as God is man and vice-versa, they consequently share their properties <term>idiomata; the "communication of idioms," where attributes of the human and divine natures are both predicated of the one person of Christ</term> so that where God is, there the man is. And just as it is with the surface and the white color, so it is with the bread and the body.

<margin>Ancient theologians.</margin>
For if bread is on the altar, the body of Christ is on the altar. Perhaps it should be said differently: that assumed natures have the character of an "accident" <term>accidentis; a property that exists in a subject but is not essential to its being</term>, as the ancient theologians <note>Likely referring to early Scholastics like Peter Lombard</note> used to say, insofar as they come to a subject that already exists in actuality and do not constitute that subject themselves, but rather are themselves constituted in being through it. Therefore, just as among accidents one is found to be the subject of another—though not the ultimate subject—as we say the power of the soul is the subject of virtues and habits insofar as it is sustained by the soul; and similarly the surface is said to be the subject of color in a certain way; so, although one assumed nature cannot through itself and primarily sustain another nature, nevertheless, insofar as it is united to the Word and sustained in it, it can sustain another in itself. It could have a mode as if it were a subject in respect to that other nature, and that second nature would then have a mode like an accident in respect to the first, solely in that one is sustained in the other as it is united to the Word and sustained by it. <meta>This page continues the scholastic inquiry into "impanation"—the theory that Christ could assume the nature of bread. The previous page discussed whether this would break the Eucharistic fast and how the Word might set aside an assumed nature if that nature were to corrupt.</meta>

...the Word does not give subsistence to an assumed nature except by reason of its own infinite being. To this being, it draws the nature united and associated with it. To whichever nature it communicates its infinite being, it also communicates the power to give subsistence to another nature united to itself. So too a substance, insofar as it draws an accident to its own being—because an accident is not a "being" except insofar as it is "of a being" <note>This follows the Aristotelian principle that accidents (like color or shape) only exist because they belong to a substance (like a body).</note>—it gives to that accident the power to support another accident coming upon it (just as act comes to potentiality) within itself and within its own being. 

Therefore, the Body, taken as a part united to and supported by the Word in its own being (which is the being of the Word communicated to it), can give subsistence within itself to the "assumable" nature of bread, which has the mode of an accident. For it is presupposed that just as God gives to accidents the mode of a substance <note>A reference to Transubstantiation, where the "accidents" (appearance) of bread exist without their original substance.</note>, so He can give to "bread-ness" <term>paneitas; the essential nature or "what-it-is-to-be" bread</term> the mode of an accident by supporting it in something else which will relate to it as a subject. Nor does it matter for this purpose whether the subject is a "perfect species" <term>species perfecta; a complete, independent living thing</term> or not. For sometimes the subject of an accident is an "imperfect species," such as a head or a hand.

Just as God produces some creatures immediately and some through the mediation of others, and just as He terminates some creatures in Himself as their final end by means of others, so also can the Word terminate in Himself—as the sustaining subject <term>suppositum; the underlying individual person or "thing" that possesses a nature</term>—one creature through the mediation of another. And just as the creatures through which God produces things are called "producers," and the creatures through which He terminates things as an end are called "ends" or "sub-ends," so the creature through which the Word gives subsistence to another will be said to "give subsistence." 

Therefore, by reason of such subsistence in the body of Christ as a "quasi-subject" and immediate support, it will be said in the concrete that "the bread is the body" and vice-versa, just as "the Son of God is man" and vice-versa. And they will share their properties <term>communicatio idiomatum; the theological rule where the properties of the human and divine natures are both attributed to the one person of Christ</term> in the way mentioned above, like a "surface" and a "colored thing." For "bread" stands for that which gives subsistence to bread-ness, just as "white" stands for that which gives subsistence to whiteness. For as the Philosopher <margin>Aristotle.</margin> <note>Aristotle, *Topics*, Book I.</note> says, "white" is a body having such a color; and Damascene <margin>Damascene</margin> <note>John of Damascus, *De Fide Orthoxa*, Book III, Chapter 11.</note> says that "God" is He who has a divine nature, and "man" is he who has a human nature, and so on for the rest. And just as it makes no difference to something being "white" whether that in which the whiteness is supported is a perfect species or not, so it makes no difference to something being called "bread" whether that which is the "bread-ness"—acting as the immediate subject in which the bread-ness is given subsistence—is a perfect or imperfect species, or a nature or a part of a nature.

<margin>Against.</margin> On the contrary: an assumed nature (or a part of an assumed nature) does not have the character of a "subsisting subject" <term>suppositum</term>. Nor does it have the being of "subsistence" in itself. For although the being of the Word is communicated to it, nevertheless, insofar as it belongs to that nature, it is not the being of "subsistence" but of "existence in another." Therefore, the assumed nature, as it is united, cannot support another nature in itself, nor draw it to the "subsisting subject," since it does not itself have the character of a subject.

<margin>Response.</margin> But if this argument holds, would it not also conclude that a surface cannot support color within itself? Since the "being" of subsistence with respect to the substance—as communicated to the accident—is merely "existence in another," the surface could not be the subject of color because the surface itself is an accident. Must we not say that the being of the Word, as it belongs to the assumed humanity in relation to the Word, is "existence in another," but as it belongs to that same humanity in relation to the bread-ness, it is "subsistence"? However, as it belongs to the *last* assumed nature [the bread], it is "existence in another" simply, just as might be said of the surface.

But against the aforementioned points, it is argued again: a nature is united immediately to the subject... <margin>Against again.</margin>

<margin>Response.</margin>
It is therefore not possible that "bread-ness" <term>paneitas; the essential nature or "what-it-is-to-be" bread</term> be united to the Person of the Word <note>original: "supposito uerbi"</note> through another nature as a middle ground, since nothing can fall as a medium between a nature and its person. But perhaps a nature is united immediately to its own proper person; however, regarding an external person—in respect to which that nature has a certain mode of an accident—this is not necessary. Rather, one nature can be united to a person by means of another in the manner aforesaid. 

<margin>Against.</margin>
**Against this:** if the analogy of a surface holds, it would follow that just as a surface separated from a substance is the subject of color and is "colored," so too if the Body of Christ were separated from the Person of the Word, it could exist as the subject of "bread-ness" and would still be called "bread," which is absurd. 

<margin>Response. Hilary.</margin>

<meta>This page continues the scholastic inquiry into the nature of Christ's presence in the Eucharist, specifically comparing the theory of "impanation" (where Christ assumes the nature of bread) against the traditional doctrine of "transubstantiation" (where bread is converted into Christ's body).</meta>

...that the bread which, as Berengar <note>Berengar of Tours (c. 999–1088), a theologian who famously questioned the material change of the bread and wine, sparking centuries of debate on the Real Presence.</note> says, is ground by the teeth of the faithful, becomes the true body of Christ. It is better to adhere to this way [of assumption] than to the way of conversion, through which these things are not maintained without a multiplication of miracles. <margin>Fourth.</margin> Fourth, because Paul says in the first [letter] to the Corinthians, chapter 10: 

> The bread which we break, is it not the participation in the body of the Lord? 

<margin>Fifth.</margin> Fifth, because Christ is sacramentally there where He is directly by the power of the sacrament. But Christ is more directly made present on the altar through assumption than through conversion, because the form of this sacrament—which effects [what it signifies] by the act of signifying—more directly effects that which it more properly signifies. And this is the union through assumption, by which the properties <term>idiomata; the specific characteristics of a nature</term> are shared so that "this" is "that," which the formal words sound: **this is my body**. However, a union of conversion is not like this, because that bread is not Christ, nor vice versa; rather, the bread "becomes" Christ or is "converted" into Christ. <margin>Sixth.</margin> Sixth, because that way of conversion is intricate and holds many difficulties, whereas this way is clear and efficient. For we already believe in "assumption" through another article [of faith, the Incarnation]. Furthermore, whatever things are the same in their subject <term>supposito; the underlying individual person or "thing" that possesses a nature</term> when they are limited, wherever one is, the other is there too—just as wherever the musicianship of Socrates <note>original: "sortis" (a common logical abbreviation for Socrates). The author argues that if two qualities belong to the same person, they occupy the same space.</note> is, there too is his whiteness. I say "limited" because if one were limited and the other unlimited, then where the limited thing was, the unlimited would be, but not necessarily vice versa. But if the bread were assumed, the human body of Christ and the substance of the bread would be one in the subject, and both would be limited. Therefore, since the assumed bread would be on the altar, the body of Christ would consequently be there. 

Likewise, the medium is closer than the extreme. But if Christ were to assume bread or "bread-ness" <term>paneitatem; the essential nature of being bread</term>, He would do this by means of His own corporeity, because a less worthy thing to be assumed is taken up by means of a more worthy thing, according to the fitness of the assumption. Therefore, since the person <term>suppositum</term> of Christ who assumes would be on the altar with the assumed bread, much more so would the body of Christ be there, which would be the "middle ground" of the assumption. <margin>Lastly.</margin> Lastly, it seems that the authorities of the Saints <note>The "Saints" refers to the Church Fathers and established theological authorities.</note> regarding "conversion" can nonetheless be preserved while holding to "assumption." Since "to be" <term>esse; actual existence</term> differs from "essence" <term>essentia; what a thing is</term>, one can be assumed while the other is not. Hence, the Word is not "incarnate" <note>original: "incarnatum"; made flesh</note> in the same way He is "impanated" <note>original: "inpaneatum"; made bread</note>, because in that [human] assumption, the essence was anticipated before it had its own being. Thus, it never had a being other than the divine being communicated to it, which is why there was an assumption without any conversion of the assumed into the assumer or vice versa. Whence the Church says: 

> Not by conversion of the Godhead into flesh—nor, it follows, vice versa—but by assumption of the humanity into God. <note>A reference to the Athanasian Creed (*Quicunque Vult*), used here as an analogy for how the bread might be taken up into Christ without disappearing.</note>

Pre-existing bread has both "being" and "essence," and the assumption into the humanity of the person <term>suppositi</term> consumes its [the bread's] own self-subsistence—not through annihilation, but this mystery is perfected through the assumption of the substantial essence. And thus all authorities speaking of "transubstantiation" and "conversion" can be referred to the "being" <term>esse</term> and not to the "essence." And the authorities saying that after the consecration the bread does not remain, but *was*—this is true regarding its "being," because it remains only regarding its "essence." From which it seems that the body of Christ can just as truly be sacramentally on the altar through the assumption of bread-ness as is now commonly held through conversion. Indeed, a good distinction between these three terms—assumption, conversion, and annihilation—cannot be understood except by presupposing <margin>Assumption.</margin> the way of this opinion, by saying that that thing is assumed which [existed] before...

<meta>This page continues the scholastic debate regarding the presence of Christ in the Eucharist, specifically critiquing the theory that Christ "assumes" the nature of bread (impanation) by defining the terms "annihilation" and "conversion."</meta>

<margin>Annihilation.</margin> To be held as a subject for a new existence of a <term>supposit; an individual, self-subsisting subject or person</term>, those things are assumed. That which simply ceases to be is **annihilated**, such that its reproduction would be a new creation; it is entirely irrelevant to this definition whether something else succeeds it or nothing succeeds it, because that is entirely external to the thing which ceases to be. <margin>Conversion.</margin> On the other hand, that which is **converted** remains according to its essence, but having lost its own "being of a subject," it passes into the being of another subject and truly becomes that subject. This is the true nature of conversion, in which two things are understood: <margin>The nature of conversion.</margin> namely, that the thing remains in its essence (by which it differs from the annihilated) and it becomes something else by reason of its subject (by which it differs from that which is not converted). Furthermore, while it becomes something else, it sets aside the nature of its own subject (by which it differs from that which is "assumed"). However, if one holds the common way of explaining conversion, the bread is not "converted" but is rather "annihilated." Those who wish to maintain that it is a conversion and not an annihilation seem to satisfy the problem with words rather than with the reality of the matter. Whence many who follow that path have conceded that it is, in fact, an annihilation, etc.

<margin>An argument is made for the opposite (the true side).</margin> On the other hand, an argument is made for the true side: that the opinion claiming the sacrament of the Eucharist is actually brought about through the **assumption of bread-ness** <note>original: "paneitatis"; the essential nature of being bread</note> is unfitting and irrational. <margin>Durandus's first argument.</margin> First, **Durandus** <note>Durandus of Saint-Pourçain (c. 1275–1334), a Dominican theologian known as the "Resolute Doctor" for his independent and often controversial views on transubstantiation.</note> argues thus: it is ridiculous that every day one nature—or rather many—should be assumed by the divine subject and then every day be set aside. This is what would happen if the substance of the bread in this sacrament were newly assumed, because there would be as many "assumptions" as there are consecrations, and as many "depositions" (settings aside) as there are consummations of the sacrament. <margin>Response.</margin> But perhaps this "ridiculousness" does not, by itself, prove the falsehood of the underlying premise. 

<margin>Second [argument].</margin> Second, it is argued that it seems impossible for such an assumption to occur by means of any created thing, as the aforementioned opinion claims. For that medium must act either as the <term>efficient cause; the agent that brings something about</term> of such an assumption or as the factor that completes it. But nothing created can relate to the "assumption" in either of these ways. The <term>minor premise; the second step in a logical argument</term> is proven: that no created thing can be the efficient cause of such an assumption is clear, because such an assumption happens when a thing loses its own natural mode of being and takes on a foreign one. It does not seem that anyone can do this except the **Author of Nature**, who alone instituted the natures of things; thus, He alone seems able to change them. <margin>Response.</margin> This argument by Durandus perhaps shows that a created thing cannot be the *principal* efficient cause. By the same logic, it seems that nothing created can "complete" such an assumption, because one cannot attribute to any nature that which is above nature and the whole course of nature. This [supernatural act] is to provide "subsistence" to another nature that is born to subsist in itself. And perhaps this erroneous opinion mentioned above would believe it could avoid this through the points already stated. For a falsehood is not always easily convicted of its own falsity through evident reasons; the light of our intellect is so weak, being the lowest among intellectual natures.

<margin>Third [argument].</margin> Furthermore, Durandus argues as follows: whatever one thinks of the possibility of such an assumption, it is nonetheless entirely unfitting for it to occur by means of a **body** as a **part**. <margin>Body.</margin> For a "body," when taken as a part of human nature (positing that there is only one form <note>The "soul" as the single substantial form of the human being.</note> in a human), cannot name the matter alone. Rather, it must necessarily name the composite of matter <margin>As a part. As a whole.</margin> and the form that gives "corporeal being." It is necessary that the term "human body" refers to the whole reality and not just a part, even though according to logic it can name a part because the soul gives all...

<summary>This page defines the theological difference between annihilation (ceasing to exist) and conversion (changing into another subject), specifically critiquing the idea of "impanation." Durandus of Saint-Pourçain provides arguments against the bread being "assumed" by Christ, calling it irrational and philosophically impossible for created things to effect such a change.</summary>

...perfections which lower forms provide. And therefore, if one considers the composite of matter and form—which is the soul insofar as it gives only bodily existence—and compares it to the same composite insofar as it possesses through the soul not only bodily existence but also sensation, life, and reason, then the "body" in the first sense is taken as a **part**, and in the second sense as a **whole**. But since this difference is only a conceptual one <note>original: "differentia rationis"; a distinction made by the mind rather than a physical division in reality</note>, it is not relevant to the proposal of those who claim a real **assumption** of the bread occurs by means of the "body" as a part. For a conceptual difference contributes nothing to the difference of a real assumption.

<margin>Response to the Fourth</margin>
Whatever the case may be regarding the effectiveness of that argument against those who posit only one form <note>The "unicity of forms" was a major medieval debate about whether a human has one soul or multiple forms for bodily existence, sensation, etc.</note>, it is clear that it does not hold weight against those who do not maintain a single form.

Item, he <note>Durandus</note> argues as follows: This position fails because it posits that through such an "assumption," the body of Christ taken from the Virgin is in this sacrament through the **communication of properties** <term>communication of properties; (Latin: communicatio idiomatum) a theological principle where the attributes of Christ's human and divine natures can be spoken of as belonging to the same single Person</term>, because one is predicated of the other. For by the same reasoning that the body of Christ would be in the sacrament of the altar through the assumption of the bread, by that same reasoning the blood would be in this sacrament through the assumption of the substance of the wine. But this is not true, as will be proven, therefore, etc. The premise is proven: because if the blood of Christ were in this sacrament by the assumption of the substance of the wine, just as it is posited of the body of Christ by the assumption of the substance of the bread, then it would be necessary that just as the bread is assumed by means of the body (which pertains to the unity of the <term>supposit; the individual person or self-subsisting subject</term> who assumes), so the wine would be assumed by means of the blood pertaining to the unity of the supposit who assumes. Now, it is established that the blood of Christ does not pertain to the identity of the person of Christ, since blood is not yet under a human form, but is a fluid <note>original: "humor"</note> on the way toward conversion so that it may come under the human form; therefore, it cannot be assumed by the person of Christ by means of the blood—unless perhaps it were said that in every consecration of this sacrament there was an assumption of the blood of Christ immediately, and through that blood, an assumption of the wine. And thus, every day there would be an assumption of a new nature—namely, blood—without any relationship to the nature of the assumed bread (which others deny), and through this, there would be an assumption of the wine.

<margin>Response</margin>
But in this matter, many would perhaps not only reject the reasoning of Durandus, but would also rebuke him no less than the aforementioned opinion—specifically regarding the non-assumption and non-hypostatic union <note>The union of divine and human natures in one person.</note> of the blood of Christ shed on the cross and presented in the sacrament to the person of the Son. For it seems that according to this view, that blood would not have been a sufficient price for the redemption of the human race, since it would not have been hypostatically united to the divinity.

<margin>St. Thomas</margin>
Whence Saint Thomas, in his *Sixth Quodlibet, question 6*, says: "The blood of Christ shed in the Passion sanctified the human race, according to the end of the letter to the Hebrews: *'Jesus, that he might sanctify the people through his own blood, suffered outside the gate.'* <note>Hebrews 13:12</note> Furthermore, the humanity of Christ possessed its soul-saving power from the power of the Word united to it."

<margin>Damascene</margin>
As **Damascene** <note>John of Damascus, an 8th-century theologian.</note> says in his third book: "Whence it is manifest that the blood shed in the Passion, which was the greatest cause of salvation, was united to the divinity, and therefore it was necessary that in the resurrection it be joined to the other parts of humanity," etc. This is his view.

<meta>This page continues the logical and linguistic critique of the "impanation" theory (the idea that Christ assumes the nature of bread). It uses the words of institution from the Gospel of Luke to argue that the body present in the Eucharist is identical in nature to Christ's human body, not a new hybrid "bread-nature."</meta>

...the words of Luke 22: *This is my body which will be given for you,* etc. And *this is the cup in my blood which will be poured out for you.* <note>original: "Hoc est corpus meum quod pro uobis tradetur... Et hic calix i meo sanguine qui pro uobis effundetur"</note> Therefore, it is that same identical body which was later given to the apostles in the sacrament to be eaten. But the body that was given to be crucified was not of the nature of bread, but was a body belonging to the nature of humanity. Therefore, the body given to the apostles in the sacrament of the altar was truly of the nature of humanity. By the same reasoning, in our sacrament, the body of Christ is present as belonging to his humanity; it is not there solely through a <term>communication of properties</term> <note>original: "communicationem ydiomatum"; the theological doctrine that properties of Christ’s two natures—divine and human—can be attributed to his one Person</note> resulting from an "assumption" of <term>bread-nature</term> <note>original: "paneitatis"; the essential "bread-ness" of the bread</note>.

<margin>Removal of an objection</margin>
Now, someone might say that the relative pronoun refers to the same thing according to the <term>person</term> <note>original: "suppositum"; the individual subject or person (in this case, the Person of Christ) in whom the natures exist</note>, but not the same thing according to the nature. Thus, one could truly say—while pointing at the assumed bread—"this is my body which will be given for you," because it is the same **person** who possesses both the assumed bread-nature and the bodiliness that was later sacrificed. In this view, the same **person** was first pointed out (as bread) and then later sacrificed (as a body), even though he acted according to different natures. However, this argument does not hold. Because when it is said, "This is my body," the word "body" cannot be used there to mean the **person** possessing a body, but rather refers to the nature being possessed. This is shown by the possessive pronoun "my," which is added when one says "my body"—meaning "this is the thing I have." But perhaps this argument would carry more weight with grammarians than with theologians.

<margin>Response: Another argument of Durandus</margin>
Furthermore, he <note>Durandus of Saint-Pourçain</note> argues as follows: the aforementioned "assumption" is not sufficient for the body of Christ to be on the altar either in reality or according to the **communication of properties**. It is not there in reality because the assumption of two natures by one **person** is not enough to make one nature present wherever the other nature is. For if the Person of the Son had, from the beginning, assumed the humanity of Peter in Rome and the humanity of Paul in Judea, it would not mean that wherever Peter was, Paul would also be, and vice versa—except in regard to the **person** who is predicated of both and of whom both are predicated concretely. Similarly, even granted that the Person of the Son assumed both humanity and bread-nature, it does not follow that where the nature of bread is, the nature of humanity must also be. 

Nor, by reason of the **person**, could it be said that where the bread is, there is the body of Christ due to the **communication of properties**. This is because, according to that opinion, the name of the **person** does not receive the predication of the assumed bread, nor of the body’s parts. For according to those thinkers, it is not true to say that the "Son of God is bread" or that he "is the body" (which is a part). Therefore, by reason of a common **person**, one cannot be predicated of the other so as to say one *is* the other, or one is *where* the other is. 

The case is not like an Ethiopian's tooth and its whiteness. There, the tooth is called "white" and the white thing is called "the tooth," and where one is, the other is. This is because they are one in their subject, and consequently are not distinct in subject or location. This cannot be said of the human body and the assumed bread-nature. Whatever one makes of this argument, it remains true that while it does not follow by necessity, it follows as a possibility, etc.

<margin>Response: The first argument of Peter of Palude</margin>
Peter of <term>Palude</term> <note>Peter of La Palud (c. 1275–1342), a prominent Dominican theologian</note> argues in this way: Christ would either assume the substance of bread with its <term>accidents</term> <note>original: "accidentibus"; the sensible properties like color, taste, and smell that are not the essence of the thing</note> or without them. Not without them, because that is impossible; a thing that cannot be made or sustained on its own by any power—such as a relationship or something of that sort—cannot be assumed on its own. A physical **substance** cannot exist without <term>quantity</term> <note>original: "quantitate"; the physical extension or size of a thing</note>, because quantity (or shape) is its own boundary and proper attribute—though many would deny this. However, if he assumed the substance *with* the accidents, then he would not be in the altar sacramentally, but locally, through the quantity of the assumed substance.

It features technical arguments from Durandus and Peter of La Palud regarding how substances, their properties (accidents), and their locations relate to one another.</summary>

It specifically addresses arguments from the Thomists (followers of Thomas Aquinas), a thinker named Peter (likely Peter Ailly), and the Church Father John of Damascus.</meta>

And perhaps this concludes that it is not present sacramentally in the way the Thomists <note>followers of the theology of St. Thomas Aquinas</note> describe <margin>Response.</margin> by means of conversion. They say that Christ is not present there through his own physical dimensions <note>original: "quantitatem"</note>, but through the dimensions of the bread. Enough has been said about this above regarding the body as a part and the body as a genus. <margin>Third point.</margin> Third, he argues that just as the assumed human body of Christ was not permitted to decay or rot—neither in its substance nor its dimensions—so too the bread should not be permitted to decay if it were assumed into his person. <margin>Response.</margin> Perhaps, however, this comparison does not necessarily hold true. <margin>Response to the opposing arguments.</margin> Regarding the arguments for the opposite side, in response to the authority of <term>John of Damascus</term> <note>an 8th-century monk and theologian influential in both East and West</note>, it is said that just as it is clear that the water of baptism is not assumed into the unity of the divine <term>subject</term> <note>original: "suppositum"; the individual substance of the Person of the Word</note>, nor is the grace of the Holy Spirit united to it <margin>To the first point.</margin> so as to create a single subject, likewise the bread and wine are not assumed into the divine subject, nor is divinity joined to them in a unity of person. Instead, just as the water is used there as the **permanent matter** of the sacrament, so the bread and wine are used as **transient matter**. This is because the matter of the sacrament is converted into the body of Christ and, consequently, is said in some way to be united to the divinity—not through "assumption" while the nature of bread or wine remains, but through <term>transubstantiation</term> <note>the change of the whole substance of bread into the substance of the Body of Christ</note> into the humanity previously assumed. This is clear from what follows, where it is said: *Just as naturally, through the eating of bread and the drinking of wine and water, they are transformed into the body and blood of the one eating and drinking, and do not become a different body than before, so also the bread, wine, and water of the offering are supernaturally changed through the coming of the Holy Spirit into the body and blood of the Lord, and therefore they are not two things, but one and the same.* From these words, it appears that it is not the intention of Damascus that the substance of the bread and wine remain and are assumed by the divine subject, but rather that they pass into the body and blood of Christ and are thus united to the divinity. <margin>Objection.</margin> But those people persist, asking how something that is "annihilated" <gloss>that is, it truly ceases to be in itself</gloss> can be united. They insist on the comparison of the **burning coal**, in which it is said that just as a coal is not simple wood but is wood united to fire, so the bread of communion is not simple bread but is united to the divinity. <margin>Solution.</margin> And the response is that the coal and the fire are not the same single subject; however, when the wood is consumed, it passes into something else. In the same way, the bread of communion is not one single subject with the divinity, but through its ending, it passes into the body of Christ which is united...

<meta>This page continues the theological debate between "impanation" (the idea that Christ assumes the substance of bread) and "transubstantiation" (the orthodox doctrine that the bread's substance is converted into Christ's body). The author is defending the traditional view while addressing difficult metaphors used by earlier Church Fathers like John of Damascus.</meta>

<margin>Against.</margin> ...to the divinity. But on the contrary, if that were true, then the bread of communion would be compared to fire into which a coal has passed through its own destruction <note>original: "per sui corruptionem"</note>, and not to the charcoal itself, in which the nature of the fire is found alongside the preservation of the nature of the wood. Seek the response, and perhaps it is this: that the similarity does not hold in every respect, and perhaps it would have been better if <term>Damascus</term> <note>John of Damascus (c. 675–749), a Syrian monk and influential Church Father</note> had not used that comparison. 

<margin>Response.</margin> And when the same Damascus says that God joined the divinity to the bread, it must be said that this is not through "assumption" <note>the theological act of a divine person taking on a nature, as in the Incarnation</note>, even if it is similar to the way food is joined to the one who eats it because it is converted into him. 

<margin>Solution to the objection.</margin> However, let the similarity that can apply there be taken between this conversion and that one. <margin>St. Thomas.</margin> **St. Thomas** <note>Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the preeminent Dominican theologian</note> says in the fourth book [of the *Sentences*], distinction 11, question 1, that the word of Damascus is to be understood regarding the <term>species</term> <note>original: "species"; the outward appearances of the bread, such as taste, color, and smell, which remain after the substance has changed</note> to which the body of Christ—united to the divinity—is joined in an ineffable <note>too great or sacred to be expressed in words</note> manner. These are his words. And since this manner is ineffable, one ought not to seek further regarding it. Moreover, in the third part of the *Summa* [Theologiae], question 75, he says God joined his divinity (that is, his divine power) to the bread and wine, not so that they remain in this sacrament, but so that they might make from them his body and blood. 

<margin>To the authority of the Apostle.</margin> Regarding the authority of the Apostle <note>St. Paul, specifically in 1 Corinthians 10:16: "The bread that we break, is it not a participation in the body of Christ?"</note>, it is said that this speech is figurative, both on the part of the subject and the predicate. For "bread," as the subject, stands for the sensible sacrament—namely, the appearances of the bread. But "the body of Christ" is also taken figuratively. 

<margin>The Gloss.</margin> Therefore, according to the **Gloss** <note>the *Glossa Ordinaria*, the standard medieval commentary on the Bible</note>, by that phrase it is not meant to be understood that the substance of the bread or the appearance of the bread is truly and really Christ or the body of Christ; nor that the body of Christ is predicated directly <note>original: "in recto"</note> of the substance of the bread or the appearance of the bread. Rather, the sense is: "the bread which we break in the sacrament" (that is, the participation in the bread broken on the altar) "is the participation in the divine body" (that is, it makes us one with Christ). 

Let those masters who were condemning my views remember that if the words of Damascus and Paul in this matter were taken as they seem to sound at first glance and superficially, they could create a sense of faith that is erroneous to many. 

<margin>First solution to the other point.</margin> When it is said that fewer difficulties follow from this position regarding "assumption," it must be said that in matters of faith, one should not always choose that which presents the fewest difficulties, but that which is more in harmony with apostolic traditions and church dogma, even if more difficulties occur. For it is necessary to "take the intellect captive" <note>a reference to 2 Corinthians 10:5</note> in service to the faith and to commit oneself in obedient humility to the traditions of the Fathers—as even <margin>Plato.</margin> **Plato** says well and most religiously in the *Timaeus*. 

<margin>Second.</margin> Likewise, someone might say that although that theory of "assumption" would better preserve the appearance to the senses, the theory of "conversion" <note>transubstantiation</note> better preserves the appearance to the intellect—that is, the words of the Gospel, which it is better to preserve because they cannot lie, whereas the senses can be deceived. 

<margin>Again it is argued for the opposing side.</margin> But it is argued further for the opposite side: If this does not happen through "assumption"—in such a way that it would be included in the article of the Incarnation (for the belief would be the same)—then there ought to have been a special article of faith concerning this "conversion," which nevertheless is not in the <term>Creed</term> <note>original: "symbolo"; the formal statements of Christian belief like the Apostles' Creed</note>. 

<margin>First.</margin> <margin>Response.</margin> <margin>Peter of la Palu.</margin> Some, such as **Peter of la Palu** <note>Petrus de Palude (c. 1275–1342), a French Dominican theologian</note>, say that the article concerning the Eucharist is perhaps specifically under that phrase, "the communion of saints," etc. <margin>St. Thomas.</margin> **St. Thomas** says in the *Secunda Secundae* [of the *Summa*] that in the sacrament of the Eucharist two things can be considered. One is that it is a sacrament, and this follows the same logic as other effects of sanctifying grace. The other is that the body of Christ is contained there miraculously, and thus it is included under the article on [God's] omnipotence, just like all other miracles which are attributed to omnipotence.

In the third book of the *Sentences* <note>The *Sentences* by Peter Lombard was the standard theology textbook of the Middle Ages</note>, however, he says that faith concerning the body of Christ, all the sacraments, the "keys" of the Church, and all such things is included in the article of faith which concerns the effect of grace, which is: "the holy Catholic Church," etc. <margin>On the confession of Berengarius.</margin> Regarding the confession of Berengarius <note>Berengarius of Tours (d. 1088) was forced to recant his views denying the physical presence of Christ in the bread; his confession became a benchmark for orthodox teaching</note>, it must be said, as the <margin>Gloss.</margin> Gloss <note>The *Glossa Ordinaria*, a standard collection of biblical and legal commentaries</note> says there: that unless you understand Berengarius’s words healthily, you will fall into a greater error than he himself held. <margin>Peter de la Palu.</margin> Therefore, **Peter de la Palu** <note>Petrus de Palude (c. 1275–1342), a prominent Dominican theologian and Archbishop</note> says that when it is said "the body of Christ is broken," it must be explained as meaning: it remains under the <term>species</term> <note>original: "species"; the outward appearances of the bread (taste, color, smell) which remain after the substance has changed</note> which are broken, so long as it remains in any part whatsoever. <margin>Note.</margin> Furthermore, Peter adds these words: "Thus I say that God *could* have assumed the bread and wine just as he *could* have converted them, and he could have instituted words at whose pronunciation 'assumption' <note>the idea that Christ's divinity took on the bread like he took on human flesh</note> would follow, just as now, at the pronunciation of these words, 'conversion' <note>transubstantiation, where the bread's substance is replaced entirely</note> follows. Nevertheless, he did not give this power to these specific words; nor could the sense of the moderns be saved if 'assumption' occurred and not 'conversion.'" These are his words. These words are most effective for the truth of my conclusion, which is entirely about what is *possible*, not about how things actually are, etc. <margin>To the other point.</margin> To the point that: whenever there are two things identical in their underlying reality <note>original: "idem supposito"</note> but limited, wherever one is, the other is as well. <margin>To the last point.</margin> It is said that this reasoning holds only for those things which are in a place by accident. It is otherwise for those things which are in a place by their own nature. However, when it is said that these phrases—namely, "the bread is the body of Christ" and "the body of Christ is the bread"—cannot be verified unless the bread remains, it must be said that it should be explained as: "where the bread was, there the body of Christ now is." And let this suffice for the dispute on this question, from all of which I hold those things which are in harmony with the declaration of my conclusion explained above. Those things which are dissonant, I judge should be rejected and condemned.

### QUESTION SEVEN: ON THE SALVATION OF ORIGEN.

-> It is more reasonable to believe that Origen is saved than to believe that he is damned. <-

Those masters <note>The "masters" are the author's academic and ecclesiastical opponents</note> have said that this conclusion is rash, reprehensible, "tasting of heresy," and against the determination of the universal Church. I, however, to speak of them more modestly, wish to show that their judgment is not correct, and that this conclusion is not against the determination of the Church. What is more: even if everything they assert against me were true, it still cannot be said that this conclusion is heretical or "tastes of heresy." For a fuller declaration of this matter, there will be seven articles. <margin>Seven articles on how to proceed in the declaration of the conclusion.</margin> In the first, it will be seen whether Origen ever wrote or believed any heretical opinion regarding matters of faith. In the second, granted that he wrote them, whether he wrote dogmatically and with personal attachment <note>original: "adhesive"</note>, or merely in an investigative manner. In the third, granted he wrote them with attachment, whether by writing such things he sinned mortally and could be called a heretic. In the fourth, granted that he wrote and held such things and erred in writing them, whether he ever repented for such things. In the fifth, granted that neither his repentance nor his lack of repentance is certain, whether it is more reasonable to believe him damned or saved. <margin>For the first article.</margin> In the sixth, what is to be judged from the text of the decrees regarding what the Church has determined about Origen. In the seventh, how much the determination of the Church binds our belief in this matter. <margin>Rufinus, Jerome, Augustine.</margin> Regarding the matter of the first article, there was a bitter contention between **Rufinus** and **Jerome** <note>Rufinus of Aquileia and St. Jerome were 4th-century scholars whose friendship ended in a famous feud over whether Origen's works were orthodox</note>; regarding whom, as **Augustine** says (who witnessed the conflict...

Rufinus <note>Tyrannius Rufinus (c. 345–411), a monk and translator who was a close friend of Jerome before their bitter falling out over Origen’s legacy</note> believes that the heretical dogmas found in Origen's books were falsely inserted by heretics who corrupted his books, and that they do not represent Origen's own mind. <margin>On the controversy between Jerome and Rufinus regarding the first article.</margin>
But let us see what probability each opinion holds, and it will perhaps appear that—saving the faith and full satisfaction of all those things which we are bound to believe of necessity for salvation—it can still be freely and probably believed that those principal heresies for which Origen’s <note>Origen of Alexandria (c. 184–253) was one of the most influential early Christian theologians, though some of his views on the pre-existence of souls and universal salvation were later condemned</note> sin and consequent damnation are proven were not from Origen’s mind, but were falsely imposed upon him by treacherous heretics corrupting his books.

<margin>Pamphilus the martyr.</margin>
On this side, there is first the authority of Pamphilus the martyr <note>Pamphilus of Caesarea (d. 309), a scholar and martyr who was a devoted student of Origen’s works</note>, whose book is said to be in defense of Origen, in which that most glorious martyr—using Origen’s own words from his books recited there—shows that he [Origen] thought catholically <note>i.e., held orthodox Christian views</note> in those matters for which he is accused of being a heretic. 

<margin>Jerome</margin>
Jerome, however, denying that this book belongs to Pamphilus, speaks thus in his responsive apology to Oceanus and Pammachius:

> If you say that his books were violated by his enemies so that he might be defamed, why should I not be allowed to say that a volume was composed under the name of Pamphilus by his friends and followers, which would claim him from infamy by the testimony of a martyr?

From these words, it seems it can be sufficiently noted that Jerome treats both as probable, suggesting that just as Rufinus cannot be convinced <note>convinced here means "conclusively proven wrong"</note> that those books were not corrupted, so too he [Rufinus] cannot prove that that book belongs to Pamphilus. And below, Jerome adds that the very name of an "apology" <note>An *apologia* in this context is a formal defense or justification of one's positions</note> shows an excuse. For nothing is defended unless it is under accusation. But perhaps someone might say: "Therefore, since Jerome himself labels this very treatise in which he writes these things with the title of an *Apology*—in which he defends himself, saying he followed Origen's teaching but not his dogma—he likewise shows himself to be guilty of a crime, since nothing is defended unless it is under accusation." And thus no one could be justly excused if an excuse always presupposes a just accusation. 

But let us see now by what conjectures Jerome is moved to believe the book does not belong to Pamphilus. 

<margin>Jerome</margin>
The first thing that moves Jerome is that the same things are read in the first book of the six which Eusebius wrote on behalf of Origen. The second is that Eusebius himself, writing the *Life of Pamphilus*, said that he [Pamphilus] wrote no work of his own. For Jerome speaks thus in the first book against Rufinus, [addressed] to Pammachius and Marcella:

<margin>Eusebius of Caesarea, Bishop.</margin>
Eusebius, the Bishop of Caesarea, once the standard-bearer of the Arian faction <note>Arianism was a major early Christian heresy that claimed Jesus was a created being, not co-eternal with God the Father</note>, wrote six books for Origen—a very extensive and elaborate work—and by many testimonies he proved that Origen was a "Catholic" according to him (that is, an "Arian" according to us). You translate the first of these books under the name of the martyr [Pamphilus], and further on: "If this book belongs to Pamphilus, which of the six books will be the first of Eusebius's?" and further on: "Likewise Eusebius, the lover, herald, and companion of Pamphilus, wrote three most elegant books containing the *Life of Pamphilus*, in the third of which he speaks thus of Pamphilus: 'And he indeed wrote absolutely no work of his own, except perhaps letters which he sent to friends.' To such an extent had the defender of Origen and praiser of Pamphilus lowered himself in humility, saying that Pamphilus composed absolutely nothing, not even any speech of his own. And he said these things after Pamphilus had already been crowned with martyrdom, so that you might have no refuge after the books published by Eusebius..."

What then will the letters of Bishop Theophilus <note>Theophilus of Alexandria (d. 412), a powerful patriarch who initially supported Origen but later became a fierce opponent</note> and Pope Anastasius <note>Pope Anastasius I (reigned 399–401), who condemned Origenism after being urged by Jerome’s supporters</note> do, which pursue him as a heretic throughout the whole world? <margin>Rufinus.</margin>
Rufinus, however, proving that the book belongs to Pamphilus the martyr and serves as a defense of Origen, writes in his second book of invective against Jerome. After saying that it can easily be said of any work that it does not belong to the author to whom it is attributed, he then says: “But let us suppose that this little book is not by a martyr, but by any single person from the Church. Did whoever that writer was use his own words, such that it should seem necessary to yield to the merits of the author? No, he sets down examples from the volumes of Origen himself. And what he thinks about each individual point, he shows not in the words of his defender, but in the words of the one who is accused. And therefore, the question of authorship is superfluous where the defense is such that it needs no advocate.” Thus says Rufinus. 

To those things which Jerome says, someone might perhaps respond for Rufinus in this way: first, when he says Eusebius wrote six books in which he proves Origen was an Arian <note>Arianism: the heresy which denied the full divinity of Christ, claiming he was a created being</note>, and that the first of these was translated by Rufinus under the name of Pamphilus—how can it stand that Pamphilus’s book is the first of Eusebius, when entirely diverse and conflicting things are intended in those books? For Eusebius, according to you, O Jerome, is proven to try in his books to show that Origen was an Arian. But in the book of Pamphilus, nothing else is done but to prove that Origen was *not* an Arian. Rather, it argues that whatever things confirming the heresy of Arius are found in his books were inserted by the Arians themselves—such as Eusebius was, and many others. Therefore, this book must be entirely different from that one [of Eusebius], which argues an entirely different, indeed contrary, cause. Nor is it enough if someone says that the parts regarding the Arian heresy were changed from Eusebius’s book. For even regarding what pertains to other heresies, Jerome cannot say that Eusebius showed in those books that Origen’s works were corrupted. Because Jerome himself says in his second book against Rufinus that, except for what pertains to the Son and the Holy Spirit, in other dogmas Eusebius and Didymus most openly concede to Origen's sect.

<meta>This page continues the examination of the conflict between Jerome and Rufinus regarding the authorship of the 'Apology for Origen.' The previous page established Jerome's accusation that Rufinus forged or misattributed the work to Pamphilus the Martyr, whereas Rufinus claimed it was a genuine defense of Origen written by the saint.</meta>

Therefore, it cannot easily be understood how the same things read in the book of Pamphilus could also be read in the first book of Eusebius <note>Eusebius of Caesarea (c. 260–339), a historian who was a disciple of Pamphilus and an admirer of Origen</note>, unless they were perhaps some common points regarding Origen that do not pertain to the specific point of the conclusion being discussed. Nor does it seem as marvelous as Jerome wonders that Pamphilus and Eusebius wrote similar things, since, as Jerome himself says, they were close companions <note>original: "contubernales" — literally "tent-mates," implying they lived and studied together in the same community</note>. Eusebius could have either repeated in his own books things he had read in Pamphilus’s writings, or, as happens daily, discovered and thought them out for himself by a similar movement of the mind. 

And these things regarding the first book of Eusebius. However, as for Jerome’s claim that Eusebius writes in his *Life of Pamphilus* <note>A lost biography Eusebius wrote about his mentor</note> that out of humility Pamphilus wrote no work of his own except for letters; and he adds that Eusebius, the defender of Origen and praiser of Pamphilus, says this. 

<margin>First.</margin>
<margin>Second.</margin>
Perhaps Rufinus would respond that this does not do much against his case. **First**, because that little treatise of Pamphilus leans more toward the brevity of a letter than toward the magnitude of a proper book. **Second**, because that brief defense <term>apologia|a formal written defense of one's opinions or conduct</term> for Origen cannot perhaps be rightly called a "work of his own," since Pamphilus lays down no dogmas there; indeed, no question is treated there in a universal sense, but it deals briefly only with a particular man, namely Origen. Whether Origen's books were corrupted or not, to write about that is not to "compose" a work of one's own; nor is it a way for one to elevate oneself who, out of humility, avoids the name of a formal teacher or author. 

<margin>Third.</margin>
**Third**, it is possible that this book did not even come to the notice of Eusebius, both on account of the smallness of the book and on account of the humility which he [Eusebius] ascribes to the author, who wrote nothing "great" and was more inclined to hide even those slight and tiny things he did write rather than display them. 

<margin>Fourth.</margin>
**Fourth**, Rufinus will say it is even possible that Eusebius—as a defender of the Arian treachery <note>Arianism: a major early Christian heresy that claimed Jesus was a created being, not co-eternal with God the Father</note>—wished not only to hide the book of the martyr [Pamphilus], which deprived his own sect of Origen's testimony, but also to act through this indirect testimony of his so that posterity would believe it was not written by Pamphilus. Therefore, what Jerome says (as if to corroborate his own reasoning)—that the "defender of Origen" [Eusebius] says Pamphilus wrote nothing, and so on—is rather against Jerome than for him. Because, since Eusebius defended Origen not as a Catholic but as an Arian, he could rightly be suspected in this matter, as I have said.

But why is it necessary to labor over these things, or how can Jerome prove at all from Eusebius’s testimony that the *Apology for Origen* is not by Pamphilus, when Eusebius himself, in the sixth book of his *Ecclesiastical History*, says that the apology for Origen was written by the holy martyr Pamphilus? 

Moreover, when Jerome adds: "What will the letters of Bishop Theophilus do? What of Pope Anastasius?" and so on, Rufinus would perhaps say that the book of Pamphilus does not fight against their primary intention. For their purpose was to extirpate from the world those most wicked heresies and poisonous dogmas, whosever they might be; because this pertained to the faith, to the confirmation of religion, and the stability of the Church. But these most religious pontiffs would have cared little whether those views belonged to Origen (as was believed by many) or did not. Indeed, it would perhaps have been desirable and most acceptable to them if it could have been proven by certain and valid arguments that those heretical opinions were not believed by Origen; because this would be done for the sake of the faith, not against the faith—against heretics, and not for heretics...

It suggests that Church leaders like Pope Anastasius were more concerned with defeating heresy than with the specific reputation of Origen himself.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the logical defense of Rufinus against Jerome’s accusations regarding the authorship of the 'Apology for Origen.' The previous page discussed whether Pamphilus or Eusebius wrote the work, noting that the two were close companions with similar ideas.</meta>

They relied not a little on the testimony of such a great man, who was so highly praised by Catholics, and they defended their error by his authority. Therefore, Pamphilus’s book would fight against those [heretical] letters if the heresies they were accused of were actually excused within it. This is not the case, however, if the book's entire effort is directed toward ensuring that the supporters of those letters are deprived of such a good patron <note>Rufinus argues that by proving Pamphilus wrote the defense, he takes a "saintly shield" away from the heretics by defining what the saint actually believed.</note>; for if they follow those letters, they follow them only to maintain credit for their opinion of the heresiarch <term>heresiarcha|a leader or founder of a heretical sect, here referring to Origen</term>.

As for those things Jerome brings forward in the second book, one might respond as follows. **First**, when he says that he himself once believed and wrote that this was Pamphilus’s book, before he read in Eusebius’s work that Pamphilus wrote nothing, and so forth. From this statement of his, Rufinus would perhaps argue against him:

"If, O Jerome, you once both believed and wrote that the book of Pamphilus you read was indeed by Pamphilus, tell me, I pray: did you recognize in what you were reading any lies, heresies, or support for heresies? Or did you find rather truth, or things resembling truth, that in no way harmed the Catholic faith? If the contents were false and heretical, how could you be led to believe the author of the book was a Catholic martyr? For no one could suspect anything sinister in a martyr's testimony and words without committing a disgrace. 

But if the contents were Catholic and worthy of a Christian martyr, why do you now condemn them and call them fabricated, and spread to introduce heresies? Briefly, why do you now judge as unworthy of a martyr what you then judged worthy of a martyr? For the contents are the same, whether you read them now or then—if we set aside the author's title and consider the actual arguments made there in defense of Origen on their own merit. If they are bad, why did you then judge them to belong to a holy martyr? If they are good, why are they not accepted as good even now, regardless of who wrote them? 

Furthermore, how can you say, O Jerome, that I distributed the book to introduce heresies? For in that book, as was said above, nothing else is attempted but to prevent heretics from being able to strengthen themselves by Origen’s testimony—which serves to uproot heresy, not to spread it. 

Besides, this book is found not only in Latin but in Greek. I, Rufinus, made the Latin version by translating it from the Greek. Who published the Greek if not Pamphilus? Certainly not I, Rufinus—for according to you, who accuse me of ignorance of Greek letters, I could not have written a book so Greek and so eloquent as to equal the style of Eusebius." 

If another author is proposed, Jerome responds that it belongs to Didymus <note>Didymus the Blind (c. 313–398), a famous theologian in Alexandria who taught Jerome but later fell under suspicion for his Origenist views.</note> or someone else. Rufinus will insist: 

"Whoever that other person is, I, Rufinus, will no longer be held guilty of this crime, but that other person. And if it is Didymus, then according to you, your own teacher Didymus is a liar and a deceiver. You, O Jerome, have called him a 'seeing prophet' and 'the eye of the bride' in your commentary on the *Song of Songs* <note>original: "cantico canticorum"</note> and an 'apostolic man' in your books. I say, he himself is the liar who, by publishing the Greek, falsely attributed it to Pamphilus—not I, who, having found the Greek under Pamphilus’s name, communicated it to the Latins by translating it under that same author’s name. Nor should it be a wonder to you that I believed Didymus in this matter, since you yourself believed him in the explanation of the Scriptures."

As for Jerome's claim that it is one way in Latin and another in Greek, Rufinus would say: "Why do you not produce the passages, O Jerome, that were poorly translated? Is it so that I cannot clear myself of blame? You act just as you did when Augustine <note>St. Augustine of Hippo (354–430), the famous Bishop of Hippo.</note> wrote to you that someone was condemned regarding your translation from the Hebrew, yet he did not specify the exact passages."

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the debate between Jerome and Rufinus. You say this was done so that you could not defend yourself and prove the truth of your interpretation. Therefore, let me also be permitted to suspect the same of you, O Jerome, just as Rufinus was permitted to say of Augustine. These things are said regarding the disagreement between Jerome and Rufinus over the book of Pamphilus <note>Pamphilus of Caesarea (d. 309 AD) was a martyr and scholar who wrote an "Apology for Origen." Secondly, regarding the possibility brought forward that Origen's books are corrupted: this is based on the fact that we see this has similarly happened to many other books of the Catholic doctors <note>The term "Doctor" here refers to the great authoritative teachers of the early Church.</note>.
<margin>Clement, a disciple of the Apostles.</margin>

These are the Pseudo-Clementine Recognitions, an early Christian philosophical romance.</note>. In these, although the doctrine is set forth from the person of Peter as if truly apostolic, in some parts the dogma of Eunomius <note>Eunomius of Cyzicus (d. 393 AD) was a leader of an extreme Arian sect that argued Jesus was a created being, not equal to God the Father.</note>
<margin>The error of Eunomius.</margin>
is inserted, so that one would believe no one other than Eunomius himself was disputing, saying that the Son of God was created from nothing. Likewise, in the writings of Clement, a priest of the Alexandrian church and a Catholic man,
<margin>Clement, priest of the Alexandrian church</margin>
it is found written that the Son of God was created. And in the four books of Dionysius, Bishop of the city of Alexandria, where he disputes against Sabellius <note>Sabellius taught that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit were merely different "modes" of one person, rather than three distinct persons.</note>, there is a confirmation of the Arian dogma.
<margin>Dionysius, Bishop of Alexandria.</margin>
And why is it necessary to bring forward apostolic men <term>apostolicos viros|early Christian leaders who were believed to have been taught directly by the Apostles</term>, when we know that the Gospels themselves and the words of the Apostles themselves have often been depraved by heretics? This can be clear to anyone, especially from the book of Tertullian
<margin>Tertullian against Marcion.</margin>
against Marcion <note>Marcion was a 2nd-century figure who rejected the Old Testament and edited the Gospel of Luke to fit his theology; Tertullian wrote a famous polemic against him.</note>. Therefore, since this happened to their books, why could it not also have happened to Origen’s books? And in an entirely similar case, why is a completely similar excuse not accepted? This excuse seems even more acceptable regarding Origen’s books because he himself, while still living, complained about this in his letters (as will appear below): namely, that his books were being corrupted and depraved by heretics. 

But if Jerome considers this "impossible," asserting that if we allow this, then whatever is found in anyone's books could be claimed to be corrupted by others, and that it is difficult for all copies to be spoiled—I do not know how he himself will be able to respond to the Eunomians who prove their dogma by the testimony of Clement, the disciple of the Apostles, in whose works it is found expressly written that the Son of God was created. For if he resorts to this—that the books of Clement were corrupted by those heretics—they will argue with Jerome’s own words that this is impossible, saying the same thing: namely, that "whatever is found in the books of everyone could be said to be corrupted by others," and "it is impossible for all copies to be corrupted." 

Therefore, perhaps one must take care lest, while we wish to make Origen entirely a heretic, we make the Apostles and the disciples of the Apostles heretics as well. For since heresies no less detestable and execrable—and dogmas no less impious—are found in their books than in the books of Origen, I do not see why they should not either be accused in the same way or excused in the same way. Jerome, however, responds to the corruption of the books of Clement and others with these words: "And how," you will ask, "are there some faulty things in their books? If I respond that I do not know the causes of the faults, I will not immediately judge them as heretics. For it is possible that they either simply erred, or wrote with another meaning, or their writings were gradually corrupted by unskilled copyists, or they spoke some things innocently and with less caution, which could not avoid the slander of perverse men." To this response of Jerome, Rufinus would perhaps respond in this way: that not because of those things...

<meta>This page continues the argument defending Origen by citing precedents where the works of other orthodox Church Fathers were allegedly corrupted by heretics or clumsy scribes.
