...in books, some things are flawed even if you do not know the causes of the flaws, yet you do not immediately wish to judge those authors as heretics. Why, after seeing some flawed things in a book of Origen—given that elsewhere you have seen Origen himself contradicting <note>original: "contradicentem," referring to Origen's own writings that align with orthodox views, which the author argues should outweigh the "flawed" passages.</note> these points—do you immediately judge Origen a heretic? What is the reason for such a difference in treatment, especially since you yourself knew there was such sublimity of genius in Origen, such zeal for the faith, and such great study of the Scriptures, and you have even written and preached this? It would be more meritous to suspect that the fault lay in the manuscripts, from whatever source they came, rather than in his own mind. Furthermore, just as it was possible, according to you, that those others either simply erred or wrote with a different meaning, or spoke innocently and without enough caution; why could it not similarly have happened that Origen either simply erred or wrote with a different meaning?

<margin>Didymus.</margin>
...as Didymus <note>Didymus the Blind (c. 313–398 AD), a famous Alexandrian theologian and teacher who was a staunch defender of Origen's legacy.</note> contends—or that he spoke innocently and less cautiously about certain things that cannot escape the perverse slander of men? And just as you say their writings could have been corrupted by unskilled scribes, why could Origen's writings not have been similarly corrupted, either by unskilled scribes or by treacherous heretics?

<margin>Hilary. The Synod of Ariminum.</margin>
Rufinus also reports that a book by Hilary the Confessor <note>Saint Hilary of Poitiers (c. 310–367 AD), known as the "Hammer of the Arians."</note> was falsified by heretics after the Synod of Ariminum <note>A major church council held in 359 AD where the Arian faction—who believed the Son was not equal to the Father—briefly held sway.</note>. For this reason, when a question was raised against him in a council of bishops, he ordered a book to be brought from his house; without his knowledge, a heretical version was being kept in his own chests. He says that when it was produced and judged heretical by everyone, the author of the book, Hilary, left the council excommunicated. Jerome says this is false and a story made up to slander Hilary, though he offers no other evidence. But whether it was true or not cannot be well known, nor does it matter much for the defense of Origen. This much is true: Rufinus, about to recount this regarding Hilary, prefaces it with these words: "And lest anything be lacking to open belief, I will retrace things that are still within our memory, so that the truth of the testimony may be hidden from no one." Therefore, it was either true, or it was a great impudence on Rufinus's part to weave an open lie and a new fable about an event so recent in memory. But whether it be true or false, it does not seem to have been invented or recited to slander Hilary, because he slanders those who had corrupted Hilary's book rather than Hilary himself, whom he testifies was innocent of heresy, unjustly excommunicated, and craftily deceived.

<margin>Tertullian. Cyprian.</margin>
After this, Rufinus relates that a book by Tertullian <note>A prolific early Christian author (c. 155–220 AD) from Carthage.</note> titled *On the Trinity* was being read under the name of Cyprian the Martyr <note>St. Cyprian (d. 258 AD), the highly respected Bishop of Carthage.</note> in Constantinople by heretics of the Macedonian party <note>A sect also known as the Pneumatomachians, who denied the full divinity of the Holy Spirit.</note>. Jerome says it is not a book by Tertullian, nor is it called Cyprian's, but rather Novatian's <note>Novatian (c. 200–258 AD) was a Roman priest. His works were often misattributed to others because he was eventually declared a schismatic.</note>. Neither of them offers anything else on their own behalf, except that Jerome says the eloquence of the author demonstrates the specific character of the style. Yet, in many cases, it is often possible to detect a similar face and tone of style.

<margin>Damasus, Bishop of the city of Rome.</margin>
But these points do nothing for Origen. However, Rufinus himself shows that the same thing happened to Jerome as happened to the books of Origen. For he relates that when ecclesiastical letters to be dictated were handed to Jerome by Damasus, bishop of the city of Rome <note>Pope Damasus I (r. 366–384 AD), whom Jerome served as secretary and advisor.</note>, the Apollinarists <note>Followers of Apollinaris of Laodicea, who were accused of teaching that Christ did not have a human soul or mind.</note> took a book of Athanasius where the phrase "the Lordly man" <note>original: "dominicus homo." A controversial theological term used to describe the human nature of Christ; heretics often manipulated such phrases to support their views.</note> was written. They corrupted it so that,

<margin>Note.</margin>
they wrote again in the book what they had erased, specifically so that it would be thought not to have been falsified by them, but added by Jerome. And notice that Jerome, responding to Rufinus on this part, says, "My own little story is being thrown back at me," yet [he admits] it was nevertheless true...

...he denies it. But at the end he says this: "It is possible, Rufinus, that even if you heard the truth from me, someone else who is ignorant of this matter might say it was composed and fabricated by you." The third point 
<margin>Note the words of Origen.</margin>
making it likely that Origen’s books were corrupted is that he himself complained of this while he was still alive. For some people wrote a false letter under the name of Paul to disturb the Thessalonians, as if the day of the Lord were imminent, and to seduce them. Because of this letter, therefore, in the second letter which he wrote to the Thessalonians, he said these things: 'Now we beseech you, brothers, by the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ and our gathering together to him, that you be not soon shaken in mind, nor troubled, neither by spirit, nor by word, nor by letter as though sent by us, as if the day of the Lord were at hand. For a certain leader of a heresy, after our debate had been held in the presence of many people, took the transcriptions from those who had copied the volume and added what he wanted, and took away what he wanted, and changed what seemed good to him. And he carries it about as if in our name, mocking us and showing off those things which he himself wrote. Because of this, the brothers who are in Palestine, being indignant, sent a man to me in Athens to receive from me the original, authentic copies—which had not even been re-read or reviewed by me before. But they lay there so neglected that they could scarcely be found. Nevertheless—and I speak with God as my witness—when I met that very man who had corrupted the book and asked why he had done this, he replied to me as if making amends: 'Because I wanted to better adorn the debate and to purify it.' These things are read word-for-word in Origen’s letter. If, while he was still living, heretics did not hesitate to corrupt his books, how much more must we believe that these books suffered the same after his death? He also complains of a certain other heretic in Ephesus who brought together many false things as if they were Origen's own; and there exists also in another of his letters a complaint about the falsity of his books. The fourth point which gives the greatest credibility to this matter is that those heretical views are not Origen’s, but were inserted by heretics, because Origen is found elsewhere to determine those same points in a pious and Catholic <note>In this context, "Catholic" refers to the universal, orthodox teachings of the early Church as opposed to heretical sects.</note> manner. From which it follows that if those heretical views were Origen’s, he would be contradicting himself. Moreover, one can see very many places where he writes in a Catholic manner regarding these points in the 
<margin>The Apology of Pamphilus.</margin>
*Apology of Pamphilus* <note>Pamphilus of Caesarea (d. 309 AD) was a martyr who wrote a famous defense of Origen's orthodoxy.</note>. And by this, it also seems that a certain saying of Jerome against Rufinus is answered. For when Rufinus said this same thing—namely, that Origen determined these matters piously and Catholically elsewhere—Jerome said this against him: "Where is that confidence with which, with puffed-out cheeks, you so frequently proclaim..."

<meta>This page continues the defense of Origen's orthodoxy, specifically addressing charges regarding his views on the Trinity and the nature of hell. The previous page discussed how Origen himself complained of his writings being tampered with by enemies.</meta>

...you claimed that you corrected what you had read in other books of Origen within the books of <term>Periarchon</term> <note>original: "periarchon," the Latin title for Origen’s "On First Principles," a foundational but controversial work of systematic theology.</note>. You did not provide someone else's ideas, but restored his own thoughts to his own books. From such a vast forest of books, you cannot even produce a single branch or a sprout. For Rufinus might perhaps reply that he ought not to bring forth "sprouts" from that forest from which Pamphilus <note>Pamphilus of Caesarea (d. 309 AD) was a martyr and a devoted defender of Origen who wrote an "Apology for Origen" while in prison.</note> had already brought forth many whole, intact trees. For Pamphilus recites those passages most abundantly; and with that already established, Rufinus acts on this in his own booklet which he adds to Pamphilus's book, in order to show why it is that contradictory statements are found in Origen's books—attributing that cause to falsification by heretics.

The fifth point, which does much to assert that those heresies are not truly Origen’s mind, is that from the testimony of many to whom we are rightly bound to give faith, we find that Origen held the <term>Catholic</term> <note>In this context, "Catholic" refers to the universal, orthodox teachings of the early Church rather than the modern denomination.</note> view on the principal opinions in which he is said to have erred.

<margin>Two principal heresies attributed to Origen.</margin>
For there are two principal heresies which are charged against Origen. The first concerns the Trinity: that he thought wrongly—namely, about the Son, and even worse about the Holy Spirit. The second is about the salvation of the devil: namely, that his punishment and the torment of hell would not be eternal, but that he would eventually be liberated from it. From this second point, many other views ascribed to him seem to depend: such as that, for the sake of the salvation of these demons, Christ would have to be crucified again in a higher element; and that all things are to be restored into one; and that the devil can repent; and that the punishment of the damned is not eternal.

<margin>Defense for the first heresy charged against him. Didymus, Athanasius, Methodius. Note.</margin>
Regarding these two heresies, however, there appear to be evident arguments that they were not Origen’s true intent. For concerning the Trinity, not only does Didymus—the teacher in whom Jerome so greatly glories—say that Origen held orthodox views (and proved this in his own published commentaries on the <term>Periarchon</term>), but even Athanasius <note>St. Athanasius (c. 296–373 AD), the champion of the Council of Nicaea and the chief opponent of Arianism.</note>, the defender of the Council of Nicaea, in his own books against the <term>Arians</term> <note>Followers of Arius who believed that Jesus was a created being, not co-eternal with God the Father.</note>, called this man a witness of his own faith with a clear voice. We also read that Methodius repented of having condemned Origen, and says that he was finally found to believe nothing wrongly concerning the Holy Trinity. Furthermore, we have Origen’s own words about the Trinity, which differ in nothing from the orthodox faith. For regarding that passage of Paul to the Romans, "and the Spirit helps our infirmity," <note>Romans 8:26</note> he expressly holds that the Holy Spirit is not a creature. And regarding the passage, "He who did not spare even his own Son, but delivered him up for us all, how has he not also with him given us all things," <note>Romans 8:32</note> Origen,

<margin>The words of Origen.</margin>
explaining this, says: "For there is nothing, either of visible or invisible creation, which can be made equal to the Son. For in no way can a creature be compared to its Creator. And if the Creator himself was given to us, how will every creature not be given to us with him?" And below, on that passage of Paul, "who is God over all, blessed forever," <note>Romans 9:5</note> Origen says: "That Christ is one thing according to the flesh, and another according to the spirit, he [Paul] has already designated in the earlier parts of this very epistle where he says, 'Who was made from the seed of David according to the flesh, who was destined to be the Son of God in power according to the Spirit of sanctification.' And how he is the Son of God according to the spirit and the son of David according to the flesh, we have explained more fully there to the best of our ability. Therefore, him whom he there called the Son of God according to the spirit, here—as the doctrine proceeds in order for those progressing as listeners—he pronounces that he is the very God who is over all things. And I wonder how some, reading what the same Apostle said in other places, 'One God the Father from whom are all things, and one Lord...'"

<meta>This page continues the defense of Origen's orthodoxy, specifically addressing charges regarding his views on the Trinity and the nature of hell. The previous page discussed how Origen himself complained of his writings being tampered with by enemies.</meta>

Jesus Christ, through whom all things [were made], they deny that the Son of God must be confessed as God, lest they appear to confess and speak of two gods; and what will they do with this passage of the Apostle in which Christ, through whom all things are, is clearly described as being **God over all things**? But they do not notice that those who feel this way [do so] because, just as he said the Lord Jesus Christ is "one Lord" in such a way that God the Father is not thereby denied the title of "Lord," so also he said God the Father is "one God" in such a way that the Son is not believed to be anything but God. For the Scripture is true which says: *Know that the Lord himself is God.* <note>original: "Scitote q̃ dominus ipse est deus" — Psalm 100:3</note> However, both are one God because there is no other beginning of divinity for the Son than the Father; rather, as Wisdom says, the Son is a "most pure emanation" of that one paternal fountain. <note>original: "purissima est manatio" — an allusion to the Book of Wisdom 7:25.</note> Therefore, Christ is God over all things—all those things, without doubt, which we mentioned a little earlier: above principalities, and powers, and virtues, and every name that is named, not only in this age but also in the one to come. <note>Referencing Ephesians 1:21.</note> But he who is over all things has no one above himself. For he is not *after* the Father, but *from* the Father. This same thing must also be understood concerning the Holy Spirit of God where it is said: *The Spirit of the Lord has filled the whole world*, and that which contains all things has knowledge of the voice. <note>original: "Spiritus domini repleuit orbem terrarum" — Wisdom 1:7.</note> If, therefore, the Son of God is said to be over all things, and the Holy Spirit is remembered to contain all things, 
<margin>Note.</margin>
and God the Father is he from whom are all things—then the nature of the Trinity and the one **substance** <note>original: "sbã" (substantia). In theology, substance refers to the essential nature or "stuff" of God that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit share.</note> which is over all things is evidently shown. These are the words of Origen, verbatim. And elsewhere, upon that passage of Paul, *But how shall they preach unless they are sent?* <note>Romans 10:15</note> he says the following: "For there are some who indeed announce and preach concerning the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, but not sincerely or completely, as is the case with all heretics who announce the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit but do not announce them well or faithfully. For they either wrongly separate the Son from the Father, so that they say the Father is of one nature and the Son of another; or they wrongly confuse them, so that they make God a composite of three, or a matter of three names only. But those who announce good things well will give to the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit each their own properties, while confessing that there is no diversity in substance or nature." These are Origen's words. 

What could be more <term>Catholic</term> <note>In this context, "Catholic" refers to the universal, orthodox teachings of the early Church rather than the modern denomination.</note> or more clearly expressed than these words? It is necessary, therefore, that if anything is found written otherwise in the books of Origen, it is not Origen’s own, but belongs to the heretics who, through the corruption of his books, wanted to have Origen as a patron of their own error. 
<margin>
A defense regarding the second heresy charged against him. Origen himself denies it and asserts the contrary.
</margin>
Regarding the second heresy, however, there exists such evident testimony that, in my judgment, it can hardly be denied. For in his own letter, even according to the translation of **Jerome** <note>St. Jerome (c. 347–420 AD), a contemporary of Rufinus who became a fierce critic of Origen.</note>—who explicitly mentions that letter—Origen denies that the devil can ever be saved. He says that no one, unless they have lost their mind, could say such a thing. Furthermore, there exists a dialogue between Origen and Candidus, a follower of the <term>Valentinian</term> <note>Followers of Valentinus, a 2nd-century Gnostic teacher whose views were considered heretical by the early Church.</note> dogma. This Candidus was attributing this same error to Origen, and Origen refutes it and denies that he believes this. 
<margin>
A dialogue of Origen.

And upon that passage of Paul, *Have they stumbled so as to fall?* <note>Romans 11:11</note> Origen speaks thus: regarding this fall (of which Christ said, "I saw Satan fall like lightning from heaven" <note>Luke 10:18</note>), he denies that Israel has "fallen" [in the same way]. ...[concerning the] Father is falsely attributed to him. This is clear from what he himself says regarding that passage of Paul: *O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God.* <note>original: "O altitudo diuiciarum sapientiæ & scientiæ dei" — Romans 11:33.</note> For he says that he called this "depth of God" inscrutable to every creature; however, he could not say these things regarding the Son and the Holy Spirit. For the Son says to the Father in the Gospel: *Father, all mine are yours and yours are mine.* <note>original: "Pater omnia mea tua sũt & tua mea" — John 17:10.</note> And regarding the Holy Spirit, Paul himself pronounces, saying: *No man knows the things of a man except the spirit of man which is in him; even so, the things of God no one knows except the Spirit of God.* <note>original: "Nemo scit hominum quæ sũt hominis nisi spiritus hominis qui in ipso est. ita & quæ in deo sunt nemo cognouit nisi spiritus dei" — 1 Corinthians 2:11.</note> Therefore, when Paul says, "Who has known the mind of the Lord?" <note>Romans 11:34.</note> Origen argues that he speaks of creatures, but he excepted the nature of the Trinity.

It seems that one <term>heresy</term> <note>heresy: a belief or opinion contrary to orthodox religious doctrine.</note> remains attributed to Origen: namely, in his opinions concerning the soul—that they were created from eternity and fell from heaven into bodies. 
<margin>Defense against the charge of <term>heresy</term> regarding the creation of souls.</margin>
Indeed, Origen himself writes in his commentaries on the epistle of Paul to Titus that he can determine nothing from ecclesiastical <term>dogma</term> <note>dogma: a principle or set of principles laid down by an authority as incontrovertibly true.</note> except that all souls are of the same species, that they possess free will, that they are rational, that they are immortal, that they are created by God, and that they will have punishments for evil and rewards for good. He says he affirms only these things concerning the soul because evident testimonies are found concerning them in the Scriptures. 

However, in other questions regarding the soul, he says he states what seems more probable to him, and that he proceeds by way of inquiry rather than by definitive judgment, because nothing has been determined regarding them in ecclesiastical dogma. Moreover, all agree that what Origen thought was more likely—that souls were created before bodies and lived in the heavens—is a point of shared opinion. 
<margin>Rufinus</margin>
And Rufinus, in his apology to Anastasius, bishop of the city of Rome, after he recounted three opinions regarding the soul, says this at the end: "But as for me, having read these individual views, I say with God as my witness that up to the present I hold nothing certain or defined regarding this question, but I leave it to God to know what is true; and if he himself should deign to reveal it to anyone, I nevertheless do not deny that I have read these individual views, and I confess I am still ignorant—except for this, which the Church clearly teaches: that God is the founder of both souls and bodies." 

<margin>Pamphilus's book.</margin>
In the book of Pamphilus <note>Pamphilus of Caesarea (d. 309 AD) was a scholar and martyr who wrote an "Apology for Origen."</note> it is also not denied that Origen adhered to that opinion, but it is written thus in his defense: "But now, since there is diversity among churchmen and some feel one way and others another about the soul, and all have diverse views, why should he be accused here more than the others?" Then, after these words, the opinions concerning the soul that existed then are recited, among which is the one now held by <term>Catholics</term> <note>catholicis: here referring to the "universal" or "orthodox" Christian consensus of the time.</note>. And when it is shown that manifest proofs from the Holy Scriptures cannot be applied to them, and that great difficulties happen even to the authors of those views, it is concluded thus at the end: "What we wish to show from all of this is that, just as those who believe any one of these opinions we have set forth above to be true are not called heretics by right reason—because nothing certain or manifest seems to have been said about them in the divine Scriptures, nor is it thought to be contained in ecclesiastical preaching—so also it is not just to blame this man for discussing what seemed more likely to him."

<margin>First proposition</margin>
I, however, infer two propositions from all the things said above. The first is that if Origen thought <term>orthodoxy</term> <note>catholice: literally "catholically," meaning in line with the universal church's teachings.</note> regarding both the Trinity and the salvation of demons—as is seen to be proven by great testimonies—we cannot conclude his damnation on account of an erroneous opinion on the soul. This is because Origen was not bound to believe everything explicitly concerning the soul in his time that we are now bound to believe, for these things were neither held as manifest in Scripture nor [defined] by the Church as...

<margin>Augustine lived 200 years after Origen and was also doubtful in his opinion concerning the creation of the soul.</margin>
...[nothing] had been determined then. Indeed, not only in the time of Origen, but even in the time of Augustine—who lived 200 years after Origen—there had still not yet been anything determined by the Catholics, that is, by the universal Church, regarding the soul. For Augustine himself was doubtful in his opinion concerning the soul, as is clear from his letter to Jerome: namely, whether individual souls are created for individual people <note>original: "an singulis singulae creentur"</note> as the orthodox tradition now holds. Because of this opinion, it seemed to Augustine that it would follow that God was unjust, or whether they were propagated from that one soul which was made in Adam by God—the rest thereafter, just as body comes from body, so souls were propagated from soul. Do not believe that Augustine doubted this matter only in his youth; for even in the first book of his *Retractations* <note>The *Retractations* was a work written near the end of Augustine's life where he reviewed and corrected his earlier writings.</note>, which was among his final works, he doubts this question. For he writes thus in the first book: "Without controversy, therefore, some original region of happiness for the soul is God, who did not indeed beget it from himself, but created it from no other thing, just as he created the body from the earth. For as pertains to its origin, by which it is in the body—whether it be from that one soul which was first created when man was made into a living soul, or whether they are similarly made as individuals for individuals—I did not know then, nor do I know yet." These are Augustine’s words verbatim. From this, it is clearly evident that on account of the aforementioned erroneous opinion concerning the soul, Origen can in no way be called a <term>heretic</term>.

<margin>The second proposition: Saint Thomas.</margin>
The second proposition I state is this: that if it is true what <term>Thomas</term> <note>Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the influential Dominican friar and philosopher.</note> says in his *Quodlibets* <note>Disputations on "any topic" proposed by an audience.</note>, as will appear more broadly in the seventh article of the defense of Origen, and if good theology says that we are not bound by the necessity of salvation to believe not only the doctors of the Church like Jerome, Augustine, and the like, but not even the Church itself except in those things which pertain to the <term>substance of the faith</term> <note>The core, non-negotiable doctrines of Christianity.</note>; and if we add that it pertains nothing to the substance of the faith whether Origen was the author of those <term>heresies</term> or someone else—provided we confess that those heresies are indeed heresies (that is, impious <term>dogmas</term>)—it seems to follow that a faithful and true Christian man is not bound by the necessity of salvation in this question to believe Jerome (even if the Church inclines more toward him) rather than Athanasius, Didymus, Methodius, or Rufinus. The faith of the latter [Rufinus] is said to have been proven even in the time of the persecution of heretics in the holy Alexandrian Church by imprisonment and exile; indeed, one might believe the words of Origen himself. This is especially true because in many other matters which pertain even more to the substance of the faith, we do not approve of Jerome.

<margin>Jerome against Ambrose. Basil the Great.</margin>
Just as in the matter of ceremonial laws, it is likewise pious not to believe Jerome where he calls Ambrose’s commentaries on Luke "trifles" <note>original: "nugas"</note> and calls Ambrose himself now a "crow" and now a "jackdaw." <note>original: "nunc coruum nũc corniculã appellat." Jerome was notoriously critical and often used bird metaphors to accuse others of stealing Greek ideas or chattering nonsense.</note> And where, in condemning Ambrose's book on the Holy Spirit, Jerome says that he had seen good things from the Greeks but not good things in the Latin; and where he taxes <term>Basil the Great</term> <note>Bishop of Caesarea and a leading theologian of the Trinity.</note> with pride; and where in the letters of Augustine he says he has read certain heretical things—so perhaps also in this case. One might prefer to believe that those things which demonstrate Origen to be a Catholic are genuine and that the things which prove him a heretic are forged and corrupted, rather than adhering entirely to Jerome. This is neither impious nor does it appear ruinous to the faith; rather, it seems to strengthen the faith to offer patronage to Origen and to take away testimony from the heretics, according to what is written in the book of <term>Pamphilus</term> <note>Pamphilus of Caesarea (d. 309), an early defender of Origen who wrote an "Apology for Origen."</note> in these words: "They ought to have considered what great material for laughter they provide to the heretics, when they now see those whom they thought were the assertors and defenders of Christian dogma being confuted and refuted by their own people, and they rejoice as if in a civil war at an attack on someone whom they themselves could not hostilely overcome." There were also among the approved doctors...

<margin>The words of Haymo in testimony for Origen.</margin>

<margin>For the second article. Augustine.</margin>
Regarding the second article, it seems more reasonable that Origen should be excused because, if he wrote anything that is not accepted by Catholics, he proceeded in those writings neither **dogmatically** <term>dogmatically: presented as an unchangeable truth of the faith</term> nor **assertively**, but always **doubtfully** and **inquiringly**. Therefore, just as there may be many things in Augustine’s books on Genesis which are not accepted, they are nevertheless excused by us because, as he himself says in the book of *Retractations* <note>Augustine’s *Retractations* was a late-life work where he reviewed his earlier writings to correct errors.</note>, "more things in that book were sought than were found." So too, many things in the books of Origen may be worthy of rejection and condemnation, but because he spoke not by determining them but by inquiring, he is not on that account to be called a heretic. For **heresy** is properly called a dogma asserted against the express truth of Scripture or the determination of the church.

<margin>Heresy properly defined. Note. The words of Origen.</margin>
That Origen always spoke in this manner is clear from many places. For even after a dispute concerning the soul, he says: "Let these things, according to our opinion, not be dogmas but only inquiries and proposals, lest these matters should seem entirely unexamined." And elsewhere, speaking of the resurrection, he says: "If these things are not contrary to the faith," etc. And further down: "A threefold suspicion is therefore suggested to us concerning the end, from which the reader may inquire which is true and better." He then subjoins three opinions regarding the resurrection. And in the preface to his books on Genesis, he says: "If something profound occurs that must be said, it should indeed be spoken, but yet not affirmatively." And further down: "Regarding great things which are above us, we are not ignorant of our own ignorance." And in the second book on the *Epistle to the Romans*: "Let these things be said by us on the condition that if anyone says something better and more reasonable, those words should be held rather than ours." And in book four: "These things have been brought forth as far as we were able in places so arduous and difficult. If someone, perhaps, considers the intent of our study, they may embrace it; but if they wish to note the weakness of our perception, we ask for pardon, and we gladly yield to him who is able to discuss or explain these things better." And elsewhere: "Let him who reads prove which of these things better agrees with the apostolic sense, and let him hold that." And in the fifth book: "These things, in the meantime, were able to occur to us in the present place. But if anyone perceives anything better, let it not be a burden to disregard these and look to those." And that he may be read more widely, in the book *Periarchon* <note>original: "Periarchon," the Latinized title of Origen's most famous work, *On First Principles*.</note>, we shall see him proceed in this order: first he places those things which seemed to him to be expressly determined in the Scriptures, and in those he differed in nothing from the church. Other things he says are doubtful to him and he wishes to inquire about them, asserting of all of them that only that truth is to be received which in no way opposes apostolic and ecclesiastical dogmas.

<margin>The book *Periarchon*. For the third article.</margin>

<meta>This page continues the defense of Origen, building on the argument that his exploratory writing style was not dogmatic. It transitions into a legal and theological argument about the nature of heresy, specifically distinguishing between intellectual error and willful persistence.</meta>

...against Scripture and the Church. That person neither sins mortally nor should be properly called a heretic.
<margin>Corollary</margin> From this proposition, it follows as a corollary that it is possible for holding a certain opinion to be a mortal sin at one time, which would not be so at another time. This is because one can believe something without persistence <term>persistence: translated from the Latin "pertinacia," meaning a stubborn, willful refusal to submit to Church authority even after being corrected</term> at one time, which they would not believe without persistence at another—for instance, after a formal determination by the Church or a clarification of Holy Scripture. Concerning the opposite of what is believed, the opinion of all the doctors testifies that it is not precisely an error of the intellect that makes a man a heretic; rather, there must be malice and perversity in the will. Therefore, <margin>Augustine.</margin> Augustine used to say: "I can err, but I cannot be a heretic." <note>original: "errare possum hereticus esse non possum." This famous sentiment highlights that heresy requires the "will" to defy the church, not just a mistake in thinking.</note> This is confirmed <margin>Confirmation</margin> by the determination of the universal Church, which has canonized many who nevertheless persevered until death in erroneous opinions regarding the faith—opinions later condemned by the Church as heretical—and it is nowhere read that these opinions were ever retracted by them. Such were Papias, <margin>Papias, bishop of Hierapolis.</margin> bishop of Hierapolis; Victorinus of Pettau; Irenaeus of Lyon; the Blessed Cyprian; and many others <margin>Victorinus of Pettau.</margin> whom we know to have erred in the faith and whose opinions were condemned as heretical. Yet, they are held <margin>Irenaeus of Lyon.</margin> in the canon of the saints. From this, it follows that we must necessarily say either that they—even if they died in those <margin>Blessed Cyprian.</margin> erroneous opinions concerning the faith—did not die in mortal sin, or that the Church erred in their canonization. If anyone were to say—as indeed one of those who were attacking me said—responding that perhaps they did not err who are rightly canonized, then it is no longer I, but they themselves who hold views contrary to the determination of the universal Church.

<margin>Note.</margin> From this proposition, I infer the following regarding the case of Origen: even granted that Origen had many and numerous erroneous opinions in the faith, if there was no stain of malice in his will, this cannot in any way be an argument that his soul is damned. To argue thus: either a great error regarding any matters of faith in a person's intellect does not hinder their salvation as long as there is no stain in the will; or the smallest error regarding any matter at all does hinder it; or some errors hinder it and others do not. If even a great error does not hinder it, then even if Origen erred in many things and in the most important matters, provided his will was well-disposed and in no way stained, nothing hindered his salvation. And so, for those who wish to prove his damnation, it is not enough for them to show his errors and his perseverance in them. Rather, they must show his perseverance was combined with persistence, or negligence, or some other malice of the will. If the smallest error is enough to condemn, then the error regarding the rebaptizing of heretics <note>St. Cyprian famously disagreed with the Pope on whether people baptized by heretics needed to be rebaptized when joining the mainstream Church.</note> should have hindered the salvation of **Cyprian**; and the heresy of those <margin>Chiliast heretics.</margin> called Chiliasts <term>Chiliasts: from the Greek word for "thousand," these were early Christians who believed Christ would return to establish a physical kingdom on Earth for 1,000 years before the final judgment.</term> should have hindered the salvation of **Papias**, who was the author of that heresy and died with it. And if so, then they were wrongly canonized by the Church. If some errors hinder salvation and some do not, those who say so must state which errors hinder and which do not. And where is such a distinction ever found made by the Church? For example, to say that having an error in things pertaining to such-and-half an article—even if it is precisely a weakness and defect of the intellect and there is no perversity, negligence, persistence, or any other malice in the will—is a mortal sin; but having an error in things pertaining to another matter is not a mortal sin unless there is a defect in the will. If such a distinction is found <margin>Objection.</margin> neither from the Church nor from the doctors, and it does not seem possible to make it reasonably, then the claim of certain people appears to be invalid when they say there is one rule for **Cyprian** and **Papias** and their like, and another rule...

<meta>This page continues the legal and theological defense of the Church Father Origen. It specifically addresses the objection that Origen's errors were so fundamental that they must constitute mortal sin or heresy. The text relies heavily on the distinction between the "intellect" (making a mistake) and the "will" (stubbornly choosing to defy God), citing Jerome and Augustine to support Origen's potential salvation.</meta>

### HH iii

Concerning Origen: because Origen erred in principal matters <note>Fundamental doctrines of the faith.</note>. For however great an error may be, if it is only an error in the intellect and there is no malice in the will, it does not seem that such a person who errs in this way sins mortally. Therefore, since we do not read that there was such malice in the will of Origen—even granted that he erred in the principal mysteries of the faith with a most grave error, and was deservedly condemned by the Church—it cannot be proven that he himself is damned in his own person and in his soul. 

But if someone should say that there are many levels of propositions to be believed beyond this level—namely, those determined by the Church—and that even if there is no persistence <term>persistence: from the Latin "pertinacia," the willful and stubborn refusal to accept Church correction</term>, it is nonetheless a sign of persistence to assert things whose opposites one is bound to hold with explicit faith. And further, that an error is not only mortally culpable because of persistence, but sometimes it is blamed because of negligence in seeking the truth—which negligence is not "persistence" at least properly speaking—it seems that it can be reasonably answered as follows:

<margin>First response to the objection</margin>
First, Origen cannot be blamed for negligence in seeking the truth in this matter because, as **Jerome** <note>original: "Hieronymus"</note> rightly says, he labored in the scrutiny of the scriptures day and night. 

<margin>Second</margin>
Second, Origen erred in nothing that he was then bound to believe with explicit faith in such a way that one asserting the opposite—not dogmatically, but as it seemed more probable to him—could be called a heretic. And I clearly prove this from a certain saying of **Jerome** himself alleged above. For where **Jerome** says that even if some "vicious" things are found in the writings of **Clement** <note>Likely referring to Clement of Rome, a disciple of the Apostles.</note>, the disciple of the Apostles, and others like him, he would not immediately judge them to be heretics for that reason. 

He adds a fourfold cause: 
1. First, that the books could have been corrupted. 
2. Second, that they might have written in another sense. 
3. Third, that they simply erred. 
4. Fourth, that they spoke less cautiously. 

In these words, we ought to notice that even if the book of **Clement** (in which he says the Son of God is a creature <note>This refers to the Arian controversy, where the Son was viewed as a created being rather than co-eternal with the Father.</note>) is not corrupted, and even if the author intended no other sense, **Clement** is still not to be judged a heretic immediately, because he could have "simply erred." What, therefore, is it to "simply err" except to err from a defect of the intellect and an erroneous judgment of reason, and not from malice or perversity of the will? 

If one can simply err in that heresy where "the Son is made a creature"—which is the greatest charge against Origen—it is because there had not yet stood a determination of the Church on the matter, or a more certain verification through a greater clarification of the Scriptures. Only after such clarification would it be impossible to err simply. And if **Clement** was not then bound, under penalty of mortal sin, to believe that with explicit faith, what can we say of Origen being obligated to believe explicitly concerning those things in which he is said to have erred?

<margin>Note.</margin>
It must be noted, however, <margin>Augustine.</margin> that because heresy can exist both in words spoken badly and inordinately (as **Augustine** says) and in the underlying meaning, <margin>Jerome</margin> **Jerome** therefore gives a way of excusing one who has erred in both together, or in each separately, from a defect of the intellect alone and not the will. He says such a person either "spoke less cautiously" (if the heresy appears in the words) or "simply erred" (if the heretical sense is brought forth from a simple and upright will, but by a weak and erring intellect). Those words of **Jerome** are to be well noted and weighed, because in them a useful and healthy doctrine concerning heretical persistence is rightly founded.

<margin>For the fourth article.</margin>
For the fourth article, some who say that Origen repented allege the *Lament of Origen* <note>original: "planctu Origenis." A controversial work where Origen supposedly laments his temporary lapse into pagan sacrifice during persecution.</note>; <margin>An apocryphal book.</margin> but that book is considered apocryphal, as is held in the decrees (distinction 15). 

However, I allege the testimony of **Jerome** himself, <margin>Jerome</margin> which cannot be held as apocryphal, which expressly testifies that Origen repented of his errors. I do not bring this forward because it is reasonably necessary for believing in Origen's salvation...

...as will be clear in the following article. But because these masters never cease to cry out, I will show you that Origen erred; you show me that he repented. You will never show this, nor will you ever find it written that Origen repented of those things which he wrote. <margin>A humorous note</margin>
For when I, in order to defend Origen against the charge of stubbornness <term>stubbornness: "pertinacia," the willful refusal to correct an error after the Church has pointed it out</term>, said to someone who was insisting strongly that Origen was condemned by the Church for his stubbornness and damned in his soul, I told him that it is held in the Greek histories that Origen's dogmas were condemned many years after his death. ### Epilogue.
But let us now return to our purpose. In conclusion, we must either concede with Rufinus and others whom we cited above in the first article that Origen never sinned; or, if we contend with Jerome that he did sin, let us know that we must also concede with him that Origen repented of his sin in a personal book given to the Bishop of Rome. For my part, after I carefully weighed and examined those things said of Origen by Eusebius, Rufinus, and Jerome, I conjecture that Origen—laboring long in the scrutiny of the scriptures—was uncertain about many difficult and fundamental questions of theology, since it did not seem to him that he could assert anything with certainty and without doubt based on the testimony of the scriptures. Because of this, regarding many mysteries of the faith, he perhaps said much by way of inquiry and dispute in the earlier years of his life which the Catholic faith would not receive. Therefore, Origen—who, as he himself says, "was not ignorant of his own ignorance" and clearly recognized that he had not yet attained the truth of those questions—never wanted the things he preached in the churches to be recorded by <term>notariis: shorthand writers or stenographers who transcribed live speeches</term> for public release before his sixtieth year, as Eusebius reports.

Eusebius says that Ambrose seemed most worthy to have this duty bestowed upon him, and to have whatever was secret and hidden in the sacred letters revealed to him. ...to Ambrose, he dictated certain things in earlier years before he had discovered anything of the certain truth. However, Ambrose brought those things, which had been issued in secret, out into the public. Later, when the **Catholic truth** <note>The "universal" or orthodox doctrine of the Church.</note> was fully grasped by Origen—who was by then sixty years old—he began to write both boldly and publicly in an orthodox manner. He was deeply grieved that those things he had written for Ambrose's private use had already been published by him. For his own exoneration, as is gathered from the words of Jerome and Eusebius, he wrote to **Fabian, Bishop of Rome** <note>Pope Fabian, reigned 236–250 AD.</note>, setting forth the sequence of the whole matter and bearing witness to his orthodox faith. He explained, namely, that the writings found under his name from earlier times were not written to be published, as he himself was doubtful whether they were "Catholic" or not. But it was Ambrose who published them; for this is what Jerome himself says:

<margin>Jerome</margin>
Origen, in the letter he wrote to Fabian, Bishop of the city of Rome, expresses repentance for having written such things, and he blames his rashness on Ambrose, who brought into the public what had been issued in secret. **Eusebius** <note>Eusebius of Caesarea (c. 260–339 AD), the first great historian of the Church.</note>, moreover, in recounting what Origen wrote after his sixtieth year—after counting the book *Against Celsus*, twenty-five books of commentaries on Matthew, and twenty on the Prophets—adds: "He wrote also to Fabian, Bishop of the city of Rome, and to many other leaders of the churches concerning his own orthodox faith." So says Eusebius. Let it be true, then, that Origen was doubtful about many mysteries of the faith before his sixtieth year. And let it be true that he shared many things in writing with Ambrose in secret, which he then held not as firm beliefs but as inquiring opinions, and which are now not to be accepted by the **Catholics** <note>Here meaning "orthodox Christians."</note>. Thus Jerome speaks truly when he says that even the non-orthodox things found in many of Origen's books are indeed Origen's, because they were truly dictated by him—though not as things to be believed, but as things sought after rather than found. Consequently, these things should not be blamefully attributed to Origen, who later discovered the Catholic truth; in these works, many things were also devised by heretics, according to **Rufinus** <note>Tyrannius Rufinus (c. 345–410), who translated Origen and argued that his texts had been tampered with by heretics.</note>. We can even accept this as true based on Origen's own complaints while he was alive. Therefore, let it be true according to Eusebius in his *Ecclesiastical History* (approved as true by Jerome), that Origen should not be held responsible for any works as his own—that is, those in which he says something definitively and with adherence—except those he wrote after his sixtieth year. And let it also be true, according to Jerome, that he repented of the earlier writings rashly published by Ambrose, and consequently that he died an orthodox Christian. Thus, not only according to Rufinus, Pamphilus, and Eusebius, but even according to Jerome, it is more reasonable to believe that he is saved than to believe that he is damned.

<meta>This page continues a theological defense of the 3rd-century scholar Origen. The previous page discussed Origen’s own letters of repentance; this page addresses the theological uncertainty of "final impenitence" and uses historical precedents—like the biblical figures of Solomon and Moses—to argue that we cannot know for certain if someone is in hell.</meta>

### Concerning final impenitence

I do not firmly deny that one might believe Origen is in hell; however, I must show you evidence of his repentance. You, on the other hand, who assert that he is certainly damned, must provide proof of his final impenitence <note>The state of dying without repenting for one's sins.</note>. <margin>Henry of Affia</margin> On this point, the statement of Henry of Affia <note>original: "Henricus de affia"; likely referring to the 14th-century theologian Henry of Langenstein, also known as Henry of Hesse.</note> carries great weight. In his commentary on the third chapter of the Book of Genesis, he uses these exact words:

"If the argument used by some were effective—namely, those who try to prove that someone is damned (as they do with Solomon) simply because Scripture records his sin but makes no mention of his righteousness or repentance—then the first man <note>Adam</note> would be proven damned by his sin, just as the first angel <note>Lucifer</note> was." 

So says Henry. For nowhere in Scripture is mention made of the repentance of Adam, only of his sin. Similarly, in the eighth chapter of the Book of Judges, we read of the sin of Gideon <note>Gideon was a biblical judge who, late in life, created a golden ephod that led the Israelites into idolatry.</note> but not of his repentance; and yet, the Doctors <note>The established authorities and teachers of the Church.</note> rightly believe in his salvation. You can also see that through this same argument, certain people were deceived into erroneously claiming that Moses was damned, because his sin at the **waters of contradiction** <note>original: "in aquis contradictionis"; referring to the incident at Meribah (Numbers 20) where Moses disobeyed God by striking a rock, which prevented him from entering the Promised Land.</note> was recorded, while nothing was explicitly said of his repentance. And yet God said to Joshua: "Moses my servant is dead" <note>Joshua 1:2; the author implies that God calling him "my servant" after his death confirms his salvation.</note>.

<margin>Second corollary proposition</margin>
The second corollary proposition is this: **no one can be certain that anyone is damned to hell** unless they have received this through a special revelation from God, or from those to whom it is believed God has revealed it. The truth of this is evident from the previous propositions, because no one can be certain about final repentance or impenitence except the one who knows the secrets of the heart and the one to whom He chose to reveal them. Since no one is as certain of another's state as they are of their own—for "no one knows the things of a man except the spirit of the man which is in him," as is said in the second chapter of 1 Corinthians—and since a man cannot even be certain of himself, "whether he be worthy of love or hatred," as is said in the ninth chapter of Ecclesiastes, how much less can he be certain about another without a special revelation?

From this principal proposition and its corollaries, I infer for the purpose of my conclusion that even if we grant that Origen sinned mortally by erring in his teachings, since we are uncertain of his final impenitence or repentance, to assert that he is damned is an altogether rash judgment and must be rejected. Since we can be certain neither of his salvation nor of his damnation, it is nonetheless pious and highly reasonable to believe—as I have argued—that God saved a man of such great and profound knowledge. 

<margin>Jerome's words</margin>
Concerning him, Jerome writes in the preface to the *Song of Songs*: "While in other matters he surpassed everyone else, in this he surpassed even himself." In his case, that saying is fulfilled: *The king has brought me into his chamber.* <note>Song of Solomon 1:4. Jerome is using this biblical imagery to praise Origen’s mystical insights.</note> 

And elsewhere, Jerome, wishing to imitate Origen in some respects, calls him the man <margin>Origen Adamantius</margin> "whom no one but the unlearned would deny is the teacher of the churches after the Apostles." And elsewhere: "Origen toiled with such labor over the Scriptures that he rightly earned the name **Adamantius**." <note>original: "Adamantius"; a nickname meaning "man of steel" or "unconquerable," referring to Origen's legendary stamina for work.</note>

And after certain other remarks, he adds: "Who could ever read as much as he himself wrote? And what reward did he receive for this toil? He was condemned by Bishop Demetrius, with the exception of the priests of Palestine, Arabia, Phoenicia, and Achaia. The city of Rome itself concurred, convening a council against him—not because of some novelty of doctrine, nor because of heresy (as rabid dogs now falsely pretend), but because they could not bear the glory of his eloquence and knowledge. Why I have written these things and why I have dictated them by the flickering light of a poor lamp, in a hasty but perhaps incautious style, you may understand if you consider the Epicureans and the followers of Aristippus." <note>Aristippus and Epicurus were ancient Greek philosophers associated with pleasure and ease; Jerome is contrasting his own hard intellectual labor with those who live for comfort and criticize others' work.</note> 

These are Jerome's words, verbatim. I ask you to consider each of these words...

<meta>This page continues the theological defense of Origen, specifically addressing his reputation and the merit of his suffering. O ingenious reader, attend diligently and understand through these things for yourself what I do not express. In the preface to the *Hebrew Questions*, while speaking of the same Origen, Jerome <note>Saint Jerome (c. 347–420 AD), the translator of the Vulgate Bible, who had a complex relationship with Origen’s works, both praising his scholarship and later attacking his theology.</note> says this: "This one thing I say: I would wish to have his knowledge of the Scriptures even along with the envy <note>The ill-will or unpopularity.</note> directed at his name." He disregards the images and shadows of ghosts whose nature is said to terrify children and chatter in dark corners. I pass over what Jerome proclaims about him: that he trampled upon avarice; that he castrated himself <note>A famous, though debated, biographical detail where Origen was said to have literally followed Matthew 19:12.</note> out of zeal for God, though not according to knowledge; and that he toiled day and night in the explanation of the Scriptures, through which those who bring them to light shall have eternal life, as the wise man says. And as is written in the letter to Vigilantius, he explained the obscurities of the prophets and revealed the greatest mysteries of both the New and the Old Testament.

<margin>Note.</margin>
I pass over the fact that he was not only the son of a martyr, but he himself was barely short of the merit of martyrdom. For Eusebius <note>Eusebius of Caesarea (c. 260–339 AD), the "Father of Church History" and Origen's primary biographer.</note> says that even as a young boy, he burned with such a great passion for seizing martyrdom that he would willfully thrust himself into dangers.

<margin>The Decian persecution.</margin>
And later, during the time of the Decian persecution <note>The persecution of Christians under Emperor Decius, roughly 250–251 AD.</note>, he endured new crosses, new kinds of punishments, and torments unheard of in any age. Eusebius says that he was harassed by a thousand deaths so that the one single death he longed for might not reach him, for the persecutor worked with the greatest effort to ensure that neither death was granted nor punishment ceased. See how little he fell short of the praise of martyrdom, which so many of his disciples attained with him as their leader and encourager. I say again, he certainly fell little short of the praise of martyrdom; indeed, he earned a merit almost equal to it.

<margin>Augustine.</margin>
For Augustine also says in his book *On the Good of Marriage*: "The merit of martyrdom is not unequal between John, who did not suffer, and Peter, who did suffer." <note>referring to John the Evangelist (who died of old age) and Peter (who was crucified).</note> Note these words of Augustine well. Hence, just as John, though he did not pass by the sword, was nevertheless ready to undergo martyrdom when he was cast into a vat of boiling oil, so also Origen, though he did not undergo death by martyrdom, was nevertheless ready—indeed, most greedy—to undergo it. And as Eusebius says, he suffered so many torments that he underwent a thousand deaths for the sake of one. And this is what Bernard <note>Saint Bernard of Clairvaux (1090–1153 AD).</note> says

<margin>Bernard.
The triple martyrdom.</margin>
in his sermon on the holy martyrs: that there is a triple martyrdom. A martyrdom of the will only; a martyrdom of the deed only; and a martyrdom of both deed and will. John the Evangelist suffered the martyrdom of the will only, to whom it was said, along with his brother: "You shall drink of my cup" <note>Matthew 20:23; original: "M. xx. calicē meū bibetis".</note>.

<margin>Cyprian.</margin>
Whence Cyprian <note>Saint Cyprian of Carthage (c. 210–258 AD), a bishop and martyr.</note> says: "Among the servants of God, where martyrdom is contemplated and the mind is conceived as devoted to the good, it is crowned by God as judge. For it is one thing for martyrdom to be lacking for the soul, and another for the soul to be lacking for martyrdom." If, therefore, Origen’s soul was never lacking for martyrdom, and he underwent a thousand deaths for one, how can we not believe him to be crowned by God as judge—unless the martyr Cyprian is lying? And if he were damned, who, I ask, damned him to the death of Gehenna <note>The place of punishment; hell.</note>? Was it Jesus Christ, for whom he wished to die so many times?

<margin>Augustine.</margin>
Rather, just as Augustine says of Cyprian himself, that the blood of martyrdom washed away every stain of heresy in him, so also we piously believe regarding Origen: that the blood of martyrdom—poured out by him not so much outwardly upon the earth as inwardly within his celestial soul, burning with zeal for God and charity—washed away every stain of heresy. We say with David <note>The author is adapting the language of Psalm 1 here.</note>: Blessed is Origen, who, even if he sometimes "walked in the counsel of the erring," nevertheless did not "stand in the way of sinners" through impenitence, and never "sat in the seat of pestilence" through obstinacy, but "his will was in the law of the Lord, and in His law he meditated day and night." Blessed is Origen, whose "iniquities are forgiven" through baptism, and "whose sins are covered" through repentance, and to whom "the Lord did not impute sin" on account of his martyrdom. Finally, such and so great...

<meta>This page continues the defense of Origen, shifting from his character and the testimony of Jerome to a legal and theological argument regarding his eternal salvation. The author argues that even if Origen erred, he likely repented before death, and that Church law condemns his errors without passing judgment on the fate of his soul.</meta>

Even if this man [Origen], due to a defect of intellect and not from any malice of will, sometimes erred in the mysteries of faith, let us believe that he was not forsaken by the Lord in his final moments. Rather, through a visitation of His most clement mercy, he was illuminated regarding the secrets of faith in which he may have erred, and was called back from an erroneous path to the way of salvation. This is what I meant in my brief response when I said elsewhere: since he is not found to have been pertinacious <note>original: "pertinax"; in theological law, "pertinacity" refers to the stubborn, willful refusal to correct one's views after being shown they are wrong. Without it, one is not a formal heretic.</note> in error, it is plausible to believe that God saved him. That is, by visiting him with the aforementioned visitation, God placed him in a state worthy of salvation through His clemency and, by illuminating him regarding the secrets of faith in which he erred, called him to a salvific repentance for those things. 

Whether this actually happened or not, no one can know with certainty unless it was revealed to them from above. But to believe it happened this way rather than otherwise seems more consistent and thus more reasonable to one considering the acts and life of Origen. For it is reasonable that in doubtful matters, one should always adhere to the more favorable side. And let these things be said so they may have weight even if Origen's repentance were not established—though we have most clearly shown it to be established above in the preceding sections by the testimony of the most blessed Jerome <note>Saint Jerome (c. 347–420 AD), though often a critic of Origen's ideas, provided the historical basis for Origen's stature in the early Church.</note>.

<margin>For the sixth article.</margin>
Regarding the sixth article <note>This refers to one of the thirteen debated propositions or "articles" for which Giovanni Pico della Mirandola was investigated by the Church in 1487; the sixth article specifically claimed it was more reasonable to believe Origen was saved than damned.</note>, I say it does not seem believable that the Church ever determined Origen's soul to be damned to hell. I prove the truth of this proposition with two reasons.

<margin>First reason.</margin>
The first reason is this: regarding a person whose state cannot be determined with certainty except by rash judgment, one should not believe a determination has been made by the Church. But regarding the question of whether Origen is saved or damned, neither side can be determined except rashly, at least without a special revelation from God. Therefore, since no such revelation is established, it should not be believed that the Church has made a determination on this matter. The major premise <note>original: "maior"; the first part of a logical syllogism.</note> is well-known, and to believe the opposite would be insulting to the Church—namely, to think she could judge something inconsiderately and rashly. The minor premise <note>original: "minor"; the second part of a logical syllogism.</note> is evident from the articles discussed above.

<margin>Confirmation</margin>
This is confirmed because the Church could not be certain of Origen's damnation except through a special revelation made about him. But no mention is ever found of such a revelation having been made; therefore, etc.

<margin>Second reason.</margin>
The second reason is this: if there is anything that might persuade one that the Church determined Origen's damnation, it is certain texts of the decrees <note>The author refers to Canon Law, specifically the *Decretum Gratiani*, the standard textbook of Church law in the Middle Ages.</note> which seem to sound that way to those interpreting them in a crude manner. However, when they are rightly examined, they act against those people rather than in their favor. The texts they bring forward are mostly these: First, in Distinction 15, the chapter "The Holy Roman Church," as written by Pope Gelasius <note>Pope Gelasius I (reigned 492–496 AD); his decree was often cited to list which books were "apocryphal" or forbidden.</note>: "Likewise, we accept for reading certain small works of Origen which the blessed Jerome does not reject. But all the rest, along with their author, we say are to be refused." Also, in the 24th Case, question 3, the chapter "Sane": "Likewise, if anyone looks back to the times of Theophilus <note>Bishop of Alexandria (d. 412 AD), a fierce opponent of Origenism.</note> of holy memory or earlier, they will find Origen anathematized <note>Anathematized: formally denounced and excommunicated, often posthumously.</note> after his death, which your Holiness also does." And Julius, the most religious man of ancient Rome, and the gloss <note>A "gloss" is a standard legal commentary written in the margins of the law books.</note> there says: "Since he was damned, wouldn't his writings also be excluded?" On heretics, the chapter "Fraternitatis," where it is written:

<margin>The Council of Ephesus.</margin>
"Since Celestius and Pelagius <note>Heretics whose views on human nature were condemned by the Church.</note> were damned in the Council of Ephesus, how could their chapters be received, since their authors are damned?" From these authorities, some believe the damnation of Origen's soul to hell is proven. I, however, say that nothing more is contained in the premises except that the Church damns both the opinions and doctrines attributed to Origen as heretical, and damns and detests him as one teaching such doctrine, intending nothing at all regarding the damnation or salvation of his soul. And that this is true is clear for many reasons. First...

<margin>First.</margin>
<margin>Gelasius.</margin>
... because it does not belong to the Church to damn the souls of men or to save them. For that pertains only to Him who is the judge of the living and the dead. Therefore, it is ridiculous if one reads in the decrees: "We condemn Origen" <note>original: "Damnamus Origenem"</note> and interprets it to mean "we condemn his soul with the damnation of hell." This is also clearly evident from the way of speaking used by Pope Gelasius <note>Pope Gelasius I (died 496 AD) issued a famous decree, the *Decretum Gelasianum*, which listed books that were approved or rejected by the Church.</note> himself, who says: "his remaining minor works along with their author we say are to be rejected" <note>original: "reliqua opuscula eius cum auctore suo dicimus renuenda"</note>. For this word "to reject" <note>original: "renuere"</note> can in no way carry the meaning that these people intend. Rather, the Pope intends nothing other than this: namely, that his works are not accepted as authoritative <note>original: "autentica"</note> in the Church, nor is he himself received as an approved doctor whose sayings are to be believed in the Church. Even if the Pope had not only said "we reject" but even "we condemn," it would be no help to their argument. For we are also accustomed to speak this way: "In this matter, Scotus <note>John Duns Scotus (c. 1266–1308), a major High Medieval philosopher and theologian.</note> condemns Thomas <note>St. Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274). The author is pointing out that academic or doctrinal disagreement uses the word "condemn" without implying the other person is in hell.</note>" or "Herveus <note>Herveus Natalis (c. 1260–1323), a Dominican who famously critiqued the work of Duns Scotus.</note> condemns Scotus." In such common and proper modes of speaking, we must always understand "condemnation" to refer to the doctrine and not the soul.

<margin>Second, he argues against them.</margin>
Secondly, I argue against them from the gloss <note>A "gloss" is a marginal or interlinear commentary on a legal or biblical text, which often carried its own legal authority.</note> which they themselves cite, which says: "If the man himself is condemned, are not his writings also?" I ask these people: how is the <term>term</term> <note>original: "ly"; a medieval Latin technical term used to point to a specific word or concept being analyzed.</note> "condemned" understood in that premise? If it is understood as "not approved in his doctrine" and "not accepted as a teacher of dogma," then I have proven my point. However, if it is understood as "damned in his soul to the damnation of hell," then the conclusion is completely invalid. For it is possible for many doctors whose writings are Catholic—and are read daily as Catholic—to be in hell. For it is possible for someone to err in no part of the faith and to feel correctly about all the articles of faith, yet nonetheless be in some other mortal sin and die in it. The damnation of the soul is entirely irrelevant to the condemnation of doctrine; the former is based on the malice of the will, while the latter is based on a defect of the intellect. Therefore, this argument is invalid: "This man is in paradise, therefore his sayings are

<margin>Papias, Irenaeus, Victorinus, Cyprian. A confirmation.</margin>
Catholic." For Papias <note>Papias of Hierapolis (c. 60–130 AD), an early Church Father whose writings on the millennium were later rejected.</note> is in paradise, as are Irenaeus, Victorinus, Cyprian, and many others whose words in many matters (which they are never read to have revoked) are rejected as heretical. I confirm this from the saying to which the gloss refers concerning heretics in the <term>Decretals of Gregory IX</term> <note>original: "extra . c . fraternitatis"; a reference to the "Extra" or "Decretales" of Pope Gregory IX, specifically the chapter titled "Fraternitatis."</note>, where it is said: "If Celestius and Pelagius <note>Two figures associated with the Pelagian heresy, which emphasized human free will over divine grace and was condemned at the Council of Ephesus in 431 AD.</note> were condemned in the Synod of Ephesus, how can those chapters be received whose authors are condemned?"

Now, it is certain that in that synod, Celestius and Pelagius were not condemned in themselves—that is, in their souls—but in their doctrine. This is true partly because, as stated above, the Church is not accustomed to, nor is it able to, damn men in that way. It is also because we must understand a sentence to refer to the matter that was originally questioned and disputed. In that synod, as is clear from the acts of the council, the question was not whether the souls of Celestius and Pelagius were in paradise or in hell, but whether their sayings and dogmas were Catholic or not. Therefore, we must understand the sentence as referring to the truth of their dogmas and to the approval or rejection of the authors specifically as teachers of those dogmas.

<margin>Third.</margin>
Thirdly, it is foolish to say that the Church has determined Origen's soul to be damned. For while the Church is accustomed to canonize certain people, it is not similarly accustomed to "damn"—that is, to decree by a formal sentence—that specific people are in hell. The reason why it is accustomed to do the former and not the latter is that to decree that someone is saved, we must be certain that he...

<meta>This page continues the author’s defense of Origen’s soul, moving from a discussion of the Church's legal language to the theological limits of the Church's judgment. ...passed into grace. Although we can have indications of this, they are not certain. We cannot judge from what he did in life, because those actions are not sufficient, given that as long as a person is "on the way" <note>original: *in uia*; a theological term for a person still living and thus capable of moral change or repentance</note>, there is always a place for earning merit or demerit, and for changing from one purpose to another. But we have signs after death, such as miracles or something similar. However, it is not easy to find any such sign by which we might prove the damnation of someone after their death. Indeed, without a doubt, no other sign can be had unless there is a special revelation concerning the matter. If such a thing were to happen or had happened, the Church—just as it testifies to miracles when it canonizes someone and to the other things that moved it toward canonization—would also, if it were damning someone, make mention of a special revelation made concerning this, lest it should seem to have decreed such a thing rashly or ill-advisedly.

Yet the Church never reports such a thing regarding Origen. Therefore, we ought to understand that Origen was condemned by the Church in the manner that appears from what is narrated and testified about him. But nothing else is narrated about him except that he erred in the mysteries of the faith. From this error, the absolute damnation of Origen himself does not follow, but only the condemnation of his writings and his doctrine, as is clear from what has been said before. And thus we ought to judge him condemned by the Church, and not otherwise. Furthermore, we know that he was not obstinate <note>original: *pertinacem*; in canon law, for an error to be heresy, the person must be "pertinacious" or stubbornly persistent in their error after being corrected</note> against the determination of the Church in those opinions, because the councils in which those opinions were condemned took place long after Origen's death, as is clear from Greek and Latin histories. And we can in no way know whether he was unrepentant regarding them; rather, we have proved above from Jerome that either he did not write those things or, if he did write them, he repented.

<margin>
For the seventh 
article. 
St. Thomas:
</margin>
Regarding the seventh article, I state this proposition: that according to the teaching of Saint Thomas <note>St. Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the preeminent philosopher and theologian of the Catholic Church.</note>, no faithful person is bound by the necessity of faith to believe that someone is in hell whom the Church has judged and sentenced to be in hell. The truth of this proposition is derived as follows: because as much faith is to be applied to the Church in the condemnation of someone as is to be applied in the canonization of saints. But Thomas says in the last article of his *Quodlibetal Questions* IX <note>original: *quolibeti noni*; these were records of public "any-question-goes" academic debates held at the University of Paris.</note> that we are not bound by the necessity of faith to believe that saints canonized by the Church are in glory, but only by "pious belief" <note>original: *pietate fidei*; a belief that is considered devout and proper to hold, but is not a dogma required for salvation</note>. Therefore, we are also not necessarily bound to believe that those condemned by the Church are in hell, but it is only to be believed piously. Now, Thomas's foundation is this: that we are only bound by the necessity of salvation to believe those things in the Church which pertain to the substance of the faith. In those matters, the Spirit who comes teaches her all truth. Whether the soul of this or that person is in hell or in paradise pertains nothing to the substance of the faith. However, because the honor we show to saints is a certain profession of faith by which we believe in the glory of the saints, even though we are not bound to this by the necessity of salvation, it is nevertheless to be believed piously.

From this proposition, I infer for the purpose of my conclusion that even if the Church had determined Origen to be damned, we would still not be bound by the necessity of the Catholic faith to agree that it is so. From this, it is clear that even if what they bring against me were true—namely, that the Church had determined the opposite of my conclusion—it would still have been poorly judged by them that my conclusion "savored of heresy" <note>original: *heresim faperet*; a technical term for a proposition that sounds like heresy or leads toward it, even if not explicitly defined as such.</note>. Let these masters see, therefore, that it has not yet been correctly determined by them against my conclusion, even if the things they bring against me were true...

### QUESTION EIGHT: CONCERNING THE FREEDOM OF BELIEVING.

Just as no one thinks a certain way precisely because they *want* to think that way, so no one believes something to be true precisely because they *want* to so believe.

From this conclusion, I infer this corollary: It is not within the free power of a human being to believe an article of faith is true when it pleases them, or to believe it is not true when it pleases them. These masters <note>The "masters" refers to the commission of theologians appointed by Pope Innocent VIII to examine Pico della Mirandola's 900 theses.</note> judged that this proposition with its corollary was erroneous and "savored of heresy."
