<meta>This page continues the defense of the eighth conclusion regarding whether the act of belief is within the free power of the will. The author is responding to the "masters" (the papal commission) who condemned his view that belief is not a simple matter of choice.</meta>

II ii

...must be done because of what I said: "it is not in our power," etc. I do not present it as a statement on its own and a separate conclusion, but I present it as a <term>corollary</term><note>A corollary is a proposition that follows naturally from one already proved.</note> from the preceding one. If it does not please them to accept the meaning of the present corollary from its principal conclusion to which it is annexed and linked, let them pay attention to the fact that there are two ways something is said to be in "freedom" or in the "free power of the will."

<margin>
Two ways something is said to be in freedom or in the free power of the will.
</margin>

In one way: because once an <term>apprehension</term><note>In medieval philosophy, "apprehension" refers to the simple act of the mind grasping a concept or a statement without yet judging it true or false.</note> is placed in the intellect, and with no other act of the intellect required, it falls within the imperative power of the will to perform that act. In this way, it is denied in this conclusion that the act of believing is in the free power of man. Nor is it necessary for every act of a commandment—whether it be meritorious or demeritorious—to be in the power of man in such a way. For the "apprehension of terms" <note>original: "apprehensio terminorum"; this means simply understanding what the words of a religious article mean.</note> of an article of faith is not sufficient for believing; but beyond that, persuasion or some probable reason is required, as was cited from Augustine.

<margin>
First.
Second.
</margin>

In another way, something is said to be in the free power of the will because, once all other things required for that act are present, the will is able to bring it into being or not. In this case, the will is not necessitated <note>Meaning the will is not forced or compelled by logic alone.</note> to that act, even when all other conditions are met. In this specific way, the act of believing an article is in the free power of the will. This is the intended meaning of the corollary proposition. From what has been said, anyone who possesses understanding can recognize that those masters did not do well to say absolutely that the statement was erroneous and "savored of heresy."

That the opinion of those doctors whom I follow is probable and reasonable—namely, those who say that to cause the <term>assent</term><note>Assent is the mental agreement that a proposition is true.</note> of faith, the mere apprehension of terms combined with the sheer command of the will is not sufficient—can be clearly seen not only by the authority of Augustine (who affirms this in many places, as I have said), but also by most effective reasons.

<margin>
Augustine.
First argument.
</margin>

First, it is argued as follows: It is not in the free power of a human being to hold an <term>opinion</term><note>In this context, "opinion" is a technical term for a mental leaning toward one side of a doubt, but with the fear that the other side might be true.</note> that something is this way or that way just because they want to. Therefore, it is not in the free power of a human being to "believe" it is this way or that way just because they want to. The logic follows: if a thing does not belong to the greater case, it certainly does not belong to the lesser. It is a "lesser" thing to adhere to something with fear of the opposite (opinion) than it is to adhere to it without fear (belief). This premise is stated by Aristotle in the second book of *On the Soul* <note>original: "de anima", text 153</note>, and it is clear through experience.

<margin>
Aristotle.
</margin>

For everyone experiences in themselves that when a doubtful proposition is offered, if it is purely a matter of doubt, one is not inclined toward either side by an act of assent until some new "appearance" of truth arrives—either through a logical syllogism, or through intuitive knowledge, or through the testimony of many, or through the authority of a speaker, or something similar.

<margin>
Second.
</margin>

Second, it is argued thus: It is not in the free power of a human being to make something "appear" true to their own intellect, or to make it "appear" not true. Therefore, it is not in the power of a human being to believe it is true or not true in this or that way. The consequence holds because it is a contradiction for someone to believe something and assent to it if it does not "appear" true to them. The assumption is proven because for this or that to "appear" a certain way to the intellect means that the thing is represented to the intellect in a certain way. This cannot depend on a command of the will because this representation precedes the act of the will.

<margin>
Confirmed.
</margin>

This is confirmed because the fact that something appears a certain way to the intellect is due to the fact that the object being represented is a certain way, and the evidence (or whatever makes it credible or incredible) is a certain way, and the intellect itself is a certain way. But making the object be a certain way, or making the intellect be a certain way, is not within the choice of the will.

<meta>This page continues the logical defense of the claim that belief is not a simple choice of the will. ...therefore, for a thing to appear in this or that way to the intellect is not under the command of the will.

<margin>Thirdly.</margin>
**Thirdly**, it is argued as follows: Whenever there is a power that is purely neutral and indifferent toward two opposite "second acts," it cannot perform one of them unless it is first determined by something that is a "first act," or which stands in the place of a first act regarding the other of those second acts. But it is the case that the intellect is a power purely neutral and indifferent to the <term>specification</term><note>In medieval philosophy, "specification" refers to the specific content or "what" of a thought, whereas "exercise" refers to the "doing" of the thought. The author argues that while you can choose *to think* (exercise), you cannot choose *what* seems true to you (specification).</note> of any of its second acts. Therefore, it cannot be determined toward any such specification unless something else arrives which is either a first act or stands in the place of a first act regarding such a determination. Then, under this reasoning, I take up this consequence: a mere act of the will cannot stand as a first act regarding the specification of the acts of the intellect. Therefore, by the command of the will alone, the intellect cannot be determined toward such a specification. The consequence is noted from the previously assumed reasoning, and the <term>antecedent</term><note>The "antecedent" is the first part of a logical "if-then" statement.</note> is clear from the common opinion of all the doctors agreeing on this: that although the act of the intellect depends on the will regarding its **exercise** (the choice to engage the mind), it does not, however, depend on it regarding its **specification**.

**Having** pre-accepted these points, I argue as follows for the proposition: The act of assenting and the act of dissenting are acts having opposite specific natures. Therefore, the intellect cannot be determined to assent or not to assent by the command of the will. Therefore, the fact that someone believes an article of faith to be true through the intellect, or does not believe it, is not precisely because they *will* or *do not will* to believe, but results from something else determining the intellect, which is otherwise neutral toward the specification of such an act.

<margin>Fourthly.</margin>
**Fourthly**, it is argued as follows: a person is not determined to believe something precisely by an act of the will if, when asked why they believed it, they cannot assign a precise act of the will as the reason. But it is the case that if someone is asked why they believe in the Christian faith rather than the faith of the <term>Mohammedans</term><note>original: "maumethensium"; a historical term used by medieval Europeans to refer to Muslims.</note>, they will not assign a precise act of the will. Therefore, they are not inclined toward believing by a precise act of the will. That a mere act of the will is not assigned is clear from experience and from the sayings of our theologians, by whom those eight reasons are commonly cited.

<margin>Why we should believe the Gospel: eight reasons assigned by our theologians.</margin>
**Why we ought to believe the Gospel.** 1. Prophetic proclamation. 2. The harmony of the scriptures. 3. The authority of the writers. 4. The rationality of the contents. 5. The irrationality of individual errors. 6. The stability of the church. 7. The clarity of miracles. <note>The text mentions eight reasons but lists seven here; the eighth often referred to in this tradition is the "efficacy of the doctrine" or is continued on the following page.</note>

**Fifthly**, it is argued as follows: Whenever any two people are determined to believe opposite things, and each of them is determined precisely because they *will* to be so determined—entirely indifferent to any judgment or persuasion of reason—it cannot be said that one is moved to believe more reasonably than the other. But given two people, where one wills to believe "A" is true and the other does not will to believe it, one can say that this person wills more reasonably and the other more unreasonably. Therefore, they are not determined to will in this or that way simply because they precisely so will it.

<margin>Albertus.</margin>
The <term>major premise</term><note>The first part of a formal logical argument (syllogism).</note> of this reasoning is well-known because, as <term>Albert the Great</term><note>original: "Albertus"; a famous 13th-century philosopher and teacher of Thomas Aquinas.</note> says in the third book of *On the Soul*: when the will acts precisely because it wills to act, it is likened to a tyrant whose actions do not require a reason, because his acting is not according to reason but according to his whim. The <term>minor premise</term> is manifest, because we say daily that the Mohammedans or Jews act irrationally in this matter—that they do not believe—and that we act reasonably...

**Robert Holcot**, a most subtle doctor of the Order of Preachers <note>Robert Holcot (c. 1290–1349) was an English Dominican friar and influential philosopher known for his "subtle" logic.</note>, in his first book on the *Sentences* <note>The "Sentences" refers to Peter Lombard’s *Sentences*, the standard theological textbook of the Middle Ages; scholars wrote "commentaries" on it to establish their own views.</note>. This is because an act is not meritorious because it is free, but because it is conformable to some law promising a reward for that same act to the one performing it or to another; and consequently, he says the act of believing is not meritorious because it is free, but because it is conformable to the divine law which promises such a reward—namely, eternal life—to every believer. Moreover, God could change this law and decree that whoever tomorrow falls upon a <term>cornerstone</term><note>A reference to the "stumbling block" or "cornerstone" mentioned in the Bible (e.g., Psalm 118, Isaiah 28).</note> by accident should be saved, and then that fall would be meritorious of eternal life. <margin>In the Innocents there was no use of free will.</margin>

Nor does God act irrationally in doing so, because His will is a sufficient reason for all those things He decrees or ordains. Hence Holcot concludes that if we take "to believe" to mean adhering with firm assent to things whose truth is not evident to us except from the testimony of others—according to the way **Augustine**

<margin>The opinion of certain theologians which Peter of Palude recounts.</margin>

For there is one path of the theologians, as **Peter of Palude** <note>original: "Petrus de palude," a prominent 14th-century Dominican theologian</note> reports in the fourth book, distinction 12, question 3. They say that just as a quality remains here naturally because its immediate subject remains—which is **quantity**—even though its "remote" subject (the substance) is removed, and thus the quality does not exist on its own but adheres to something; so too, quantity lacks its remote subject (the essence of the substance) but has its own proper and proximate subject. This subject is the <term>being</term><note>original: "esse," referring to the actual act of existence as distinct from "what" a thing is</note> of the substance, through which it exists in the substance. They argue this because it is possible for that *being* to remain while the essence does not. 

Indeed, they say it is necessary for it to remain, considering the way "being" is defined here. They claim it is clear that this is possible because, although essence is prior to *being*—which would suggest that the essence could more easily be separated from the *being* than the other way around—yet considering it from another side, essence is related to *being* as <term>potency</term> is to <term>act</term>, or as <term>matter</term> is to <term>form</term>. Since the "act" depends less on "potency" than the other way around, it seems more feasible for *being* to exist without essence. Furthermore, in the **Incarnation** <note>The moment God became human in Jesus</note> of the Word, God made the essence of humanity exist without its own *being* (as many doctors say). Therefore, He can much more easily make the *being* of the bread exist here without its essence; just as in that case the essence was assumed and remains while the *being* does not, so here the essence can be converted and not remain, while the *being* remains.

Secondly, they show that this is not only possible but necessary, because nothing created can be converted into the uncreated. However, one created thing can be converted into another when they share in matter and genus; otherwise it is not possible—for example, an accident is not converted into a substance, nor into an accident of another category, according to common opinion. But the essence of the bread shares in matter and genus with the essence of Christ's body; hence one can be converted into the other—even by nature, if the body were mortal. But the *being* of the bread does not share in matter or genus with the substantial *being* of Christ's body, since that *being* is uncreated and divine. Therefore, it is impossible for the *being* of the bread to be converted, and it is necessary for it to remain.

<margin>The author's opinion.</margin>

I am of the opinion that it is not necessary for it to remain. This is because even if it cannot be converted, it can nonetheless be annihilated, or it can be corrupted by receding into the **potency of matter**. Thus, just as the humanity could be assumed without its own *being* remaining, so the essence can be converted without the *being* being converted, instead being reduced back into the potency of the essence—though, to tell the truth, these "reductions" are easier to say than they are to understand. Likewise, although the *being* of the bread cannot be converted into uncreated *being*, it can nonetheless be converted into a created essence, because things that share in matter are mutually...

The author ultimately disagrees, arguing that the bread's existence could simply be annihilated or reduced to potentiality rather than being forced to remain.</summary>

### QUESTION TEN: ON THE WORDS OF CONSECRATION.

**THOSE WORDS** *this is my body*: which are spoken in the consecration, are held **materially** and not **significantly**. <note>In medieval logic, to use a word "materially" means you are quoting it or referring to the word itself, rather than using it "significantly" to make a direct statement about reality in that moment.</note>

These masters have said that this conclusion is scandalous and against the common opinion of the holy doctors, and that the opinion of the **Glossator** <note>A standard commentator on canon law or scripture</note> is not held in this matter. But I say that *their* determination is scandalous and against the opinion of many doctors, and that the opinion of the Glossator ought to be upheld over theirs. That this is the case will be clearly evident once the meaning of the conclusion is understood.

Therefore, it must first be noted that I do not intend for these words to have been taken "materially" when they were 
<margin>Note.</margin>
uttered by Christ, but only when they are uttered by a priest of the Gospel when he is consecrating. And for that reason, I said in the conclusion: "the words which are spoken in the consecration," that is, those which are now uttered by those performing the consecration.

For it is certain that the priest, in consecrating, recites the aforementioned words of Christ, so that the prayer uttered by such a priest **supposits for** <note>A logical term meaning "stands in for" or "represents"</note> the prayer uttered by Christ, which was taken **significantly**. And such an opinion is not only not erroneous or scandalous, but rather the opinion opposite to the sense mentioned above seems to be contrary to the form of consecration in which the priest speaks those words **recitatively** <note>As a recital or quotation</note>. For the priest, in consecrating, recites that Christ said to the apostles: *Take and eat*, and so forth. Yet the priest who is consecrating neither speaks to the apostles nor says "take" etc. to them, except by way of recital. For he alone receives the sacrament, nor does he say "take and eat" to those standing by. 

Similarly, when he says *this is my body*, that which is recited by the priest is that prayer, *this is my body*, taken **materially** to stand for a similar prayer composed of similar words uttered **significantly** by Christ. This is also evident through those words which are spoken before or after the consecration of the blood: namely, *which for you and for many shall be shed*, and so forth. For these would be false if they were taken significantly [as a direct statement by the priest], because the blood of Christ...

## QUESTION XI. CONCERNING THE MIRACLES OF CHRIST.

<margin>m</margin>
**T**HE MIRACLES of Christ are the most certain argument of his divinity, not by reason of the thing performed, but by reason of the **manner of performing** it. 

In declaring this conclusion, I have said that there is a firm consensus among theologians that those miracles which Christ performed could be performed by a mere human being through the power of God. For Christ says in John 14: "Amen, I say to you, he who believes in me, the works that I do, he shall do also, and greater than these shall he do" <note>John 14:12</note>. Therefore, it is also unanimously concluded by those same theologians that the basis upon which we can conclude Christ was God is not the deed itself, but the manner of doing it. For he acted in the same way as those who act by their **own power** and not by a power received from elsewhere—which is the property of God alone, namely, to act independently and not by another’s power. This manner of acting cannot be communicated to a creature. Because, therefore, Christ did many such things not by praying or by asking, but by commanding and ordering as one having authority, it is clear that he worked as one who is himself God, and not merely as a man existing in the power of God. 

After seeing my declaration, they <note>the author's critics</note> said that this conclusion can be drawn toward a "bad sense" <note>A "bad sense" implies a heretical or dangerous interpretation</note>, because it is contained among **magical** matters, even granted that my declaration is true. Regarding their judgment on this, I marvel so much that I could not marvel more. First, let them tell me whether my words—to anyone interpreting them rightly and according to the upright and accustomed way of speaking—can have any other sense than the one I have stated. For what could be clearer than these words? What more expressive? "The miracles of Christ are the most certain argument of his divinity, not by reason of the thing performed, but by reason of the manner of performing." Second, let them tell me if this is the sentence of a righteous judge: "This conclusion, although it is true and catholic, is nevertheless to be condemned because it *can* be drawn toward a bad sense." If so, then the following must also be condemned: 

1. "Christ cast out demons," because the Jews drew this to a bad sense, saying that he cast out those demons by **Beelzebub** <note>The prince of demons</note>, the prince of demons. 
2. And this must be condemned: "The Father is greater than I," because **Arius** <term>Arius</term><note>A 4th-century priest whose teachings (Arianism) claimed that Jesus was a created being, not equal to God the Father</note> conceived from this an inequality of the Son to the Father.

If, indeed, from the present conclusion it is inferred that God is "improperly" said to understand—for the comparative degree implies the positive—let the resulting consequence be accepted only in this sense: God is not called "intellect" according to the proper or specialized meaning of the word "understand," etc., but according to the common, less proper way, as was clear from Dionysius's way of speaking.

# QUESTION 13. ON THE HIDDEN INTELLIGENCE OF THE SOUL.

**The soul understands nothing actually and distinctly except itself.**

<margin>Augustine</margin>
In clarifying this, I said that I meant the **"hidden understanding"** <note>original: "intelligere abdito"</note> which **Augustine** mentioned in his book *On the Trinity* and **Henry** in his *Quodlibets*.

<margin>Henry</margin>
These masters said that my conclusion was not according to the understanding of the doctors I brought forward in my response. I do not know how they can say this if they have actually seen those doctors' works. And because this matter of "hidden understanding" is sub[tle]...

<meta>This page continues Pico della Mirandola's defense (the "Apologia") regarding his 900 theses. He defends himself against charges of heresy by explaining his specific terminology and his rushed writing process.</meta>

...subtle and profound, I do not wish to explain it further here. Since those critics do not condemn the conclusion in any other way, I wish only to say two things: First, that I do not intend to universally deny that the soul, in any state whatsoever, has some distinct knowledge of things other than itself. For I concede that the soul of Christ understands other things actually and distinctly; and similarly, the souls of the blessed <note>Referring to those in heaven experiencing the "Beatific Vision."</note> do so through revelations or **infused species** <term>mental representations or concepts placed directly in the mind by God, rather than gathered from the senses</term>. 

Second, I say that I am speaking about that **hidden understanding** which exists without a **phantasm** <term>a mental image or "picture" in the mind derived from sensory experience</term> or the assistance of the senses or the imagination—and I am not even speaking of just any such understanding, but of a direct and permanent **hidden understanding**. Concerning this, I proposed the conclusion nearest to this one, stating: *The soul always understands itself, and by understanding itself, it in some way understands all beings.* And so, in all my conclusions, there is always a certain **hidden concatenation** <note>a chain of linked ideas</note> which they perhaps do not notice. 

But returning to the point, I say that the soul, through such direct and permanent **hidden understanding**, understands nothing actually and distinctly except itself. From this, it is clear that the present conclusion, understood in this way, should not have been condemned as erroneous without distinction, even if in some other sense it were not true. For in that case, many propositions of both the philosophers and the theologians—and even of Holy Scripture—would be condemned. 

<margin>Habakkuk. Matthew.</margin>
For example, this from Habakkuk 1:13: *Your eyes are too pure to behold evil, and you cannot look on iniquity.* And similarly, this from Matthew 25:12 regarding the foolish virgins: *I do not know you.* For although the vision of God or His knowledge is unique and most simple, these stated propositions seem to universally deny such vision or knowledge even to God in respect to evil, because of the negative used with the verb "to see" or "to know." However, they are explained by the Doctors <note>Authoritative theologians of the Church.</note> specifically as referring to God's **approving vision** or knowledge; the negation in them is not taken to deny every mode of God’s vision or knowledge. 

<margin>Psalms.</margin>
For that saying of the Psalmist is also true: *My sins are not hidden from You.* <note>Psalm 69:5</note> If, therefore, many such statements are distinguished by the commentators and Doctors and drawn toward a true sense rather than being condemned, I do not know what this statement of mine has done to deserve being so simply condemned—especially after it had been explained and clarified to the "condemners" in the manner previously described. 

Let these things be dictated by me for now in a hurried style; I shall write at another time with more leisure and care so that more things, and perhaps better things, may be said. This work itself, such as it is, was **worked out by lamplight** <note>original: "elucubratum"</note> over twenty nights. In publishing it, I had to hope for speed more than diligence. For it was necessary for my friends to have something to throw like a **scrap of food to Cerberus** <note>The three-headed guard dog of the underworld in Greek myth; here used to describe his critics.</note> to stop the barking of my enemies, and thus immediately meet the disease of unjust infamy that was coming upon me. 

<margin>Note:</margin>
Whatever I have written and shall write in the future is always said with this preface: that only that which the **Supreme Pontiff** <note>The Pope.</note> and all those whose judgment he approves shall decree as settled and holy, shall be held as settled and holy by me. And would that he had already decreed something concerning these opinions of ours that have been called into doubt, according to his wisdom and authority! It would not have been for me to undertake this work, as it would be rash to defend what he had condemned, and superfluous to defend what he had approved. 

Therefore, while we cannot yet use the judgment of so great a judge, we have written these things so that there may be no grounds for malicious detractors to speak ill of the questions I proposed for dispute, or for the unlearned and simple to be suspicious. For it can happen that when someone less learned encounters them, reading this proposition: *Christ did not truly and [insofar as...]*

<meta>This page continues Pico della Mirandola's "Apologia," a defense of his 900 theses. Having previously discussed the soul's self-knowledge, he now addresses the potential for readers to misinterpret his theological and philosophical propositions, specifically those regarding Christ's descent into hell, the eternity of punishment, and the salvation of Origen.</meta>

...to a real presence, as the common way of thinking holds, He descended into hell. Immediately, one might be untruly offended by that wording. Such a person might believe the sense of the proposition is that the article of faith concerning the **descent of Christ** <note>original: "descensu christi" — the "Harrowing of Hell," the belief that Christ descended to the realm of the dead between his death and resurrection</note> is not true. Likewise, when he reads that "infinite punishment is not owed to a mortal sin of finite duration," he might suspect me of the heresy that the punishment of hell is not eternal. And when he understands that I hold a favorable opinion regarding the **salvation of Origen** <note>Origen (c. 185–253 AD) was a hugely influential early Christian theologian whose views on the eventual salvation of all souls (apocatastasis) were later condemned as heretical</note>, he might suspect that I love the credited dogmas of Origen more than his life, character, teaching, and repentance. It is the same with many other propositions which perhaps might appear at first glance to have a certain **holy simplicity** <note>original: "sanctam rusticitatem" — a phrase often used by St. Jerome to describe unpolished or unlearned piety</note>—that is, they might offend pious but unlearned ears. For that reason, just as we have written these things so they may be read in such a way that no one thinks ill of us or of the orthodox dogma of our holy religion, I would not wish these "raw" and unexplained propositions to be read by our people unless they have first encountered this defense. For from those original theses, many might conjecture things that are as foreign to the Catholic faith as they are to my own mind—especially those who are duller or unlearned and unaccustomed to the more remote branches of study.

<margin>Note.</margin>
Therefore, I pray, beseech, and adjure friends and enemies, the pious and the impious, the learned and the unlearned, by the heart of Jesus Christ our Lord, by the wonderful mystery of His descent into hell, by the eternal fire of the damned which is not extinguished (due especially to heretics and the enemies of the most holy Roman Church), by the sacrament of the true and **mystical body and blood** <note>the Eucharist</note>, by the omnipotence of God, and by the reverence owed to the images of His Son and his co-heirs: let them read what we are now writing without malice or envy. Let them not read the earlier parts—that is, the propositions themselves—unexplained and unclarified. For we proposed them to be debated among the learned; we did not publish them to be read everywhere by everyone. For even there, many of the impious dogmas of the ancient philosophers—**Averroes**, **Alexander**, <margin>Averroes. Alexander.</margin> and many others—are found <note>**Averroes** (Ibn Rushd) was a medieval Muslim philosopher, and **Alexander** of Aphrodisiensis was a Greek commentator on Aristotle; both held views on the soul and intellect that were controversial in Christian theology</note>. Although we have always professed, asserted, and preached publicly and privately that these are no less foreign to true and right philosophy than they are to the faith, we nevertheless took them up to be disputed in a secret gathering among a few learned men, according to the custom of the **Academies** <note>referring to the Platonic Academy style of debating all sides of an issue for the sake of intellectual exercise</note>, for the sake of scholastic exercise. Whoever reads the booklet of propositions to be disputed—as the title itself warns—can see that I distinguish what is said from my own opinion and what is said from the opinions of others. I do not propose those items as my own or as true opinions, but as beliefs held by those authors. Thus, one might suspect that even if they are called the dogmas and inventions of others, they still seem to me to be true and probable. Therefore, let those who hate me not read them because they are mine; and let those who love me not read them because they might think many things from them are my own which are not truly ours.

## THE CONCLUSIONS WHICH I DEFEND IN THIS WORK AS CATHO-
## lic are written below.

### ->The first conclusion.<-

The soul of Christ descended into hell by a true and real descent, and thus Christ, according to the true and real presence of His soul, was in hell during the three days.
**Corollary.** I do not approve of the opinion of **Durandus** <note>Durandus of Saint-Pourçain (c. 1275–1334), a theologian who argued that Christ's "descent" was not a local movement of his soul, but only a "descent" in terms of his power or effects</note> regarding the descent of Christ into hell.

<meta>This page continues Pico della Mirandola's systematic defense of his disputed theses. Following the previous page’s introduction regarding the potential for his work to be misunderstood by those with "pious but unlearned ears," Pico here lists a series of formal conclusions. These clarify his positions on the nature of Christ’s descent into hell, the linguistics of theological debate, the nature of mortal sin, and the veneration of the Cross, aiming to prove that his statements align with Catholic orthodoxy despite their complex phrasing.</meta>

## Second conclusion.
Even if it were so, the nature of the true and real descent and the true and real location of Christ’s soul in **hell** <note>original: "inferno" — referring to the "Harrowing of Hell," the period between Christ's death and resurrection when he descended to the realm of the dead</note> was not based on essence or substance—as is held by the common way of the **Scotists** <note>Followers of John Duns Scotus (c. 1266–1308), a major Medieval philosopher and theologian</note> and the **Nominalists** <note>A school of thought, exemplified by William of Ockham, that denied the real existence of universal concepts</note>, which is commonly held at **Paris** <note>referring to the University of Paris, the premier theological center of the time</note>, and which **Saint Thomas** <note>Saint Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the Dominican theologian and author of the *Summa Theologiae*</note> seems to follow in the third part of his *Summa*—but rather only by effect or operation.

## Third conclusion.
The meaning explained through the conclusions written above is the meaning I intended by this proposition: Christ did not descend to hell truly and according to a **real presence** <note>The idea that Christ’s soul was physically or substantially present in the underworld</note>, as Thomas and the common way posit, but only in terms of his effect.

## Fourth conclusion.
The question of whether the aforementioned proposition allows for that meaning by the strictness of logic or the force of the words themselves is not a question of faith.

## Fifth conclusion.
Anyone believing that the proposition, by the power of language, allows for that meaning does not err in faith.

## Sixth conclusion.
Whoever believes something is a matter of faith which is not actually a matter of faith does not think rightly regarding the faith.

## Seventh conclusion.
One who puts forward a proposition that has a double meaning—if he has asserted it and continues to assert it in a **Catholic sense** <note>In a way that aligns with the universal and orthodox teachings of the Church</note>—is not required to revoke the proposition, but only to clarify it.

## Eighth conclusion.
Given the aforementioned case and the multiplicity of possible meanings, we ought to judge a proposition based on the meaning intended by the person proposing it, rather than according to the sense the words might seem to suggest.

## Ninth conclusion.
**Mortal sin** <note>In Catholic theology, a grave sin that destroys the state of grace in the soul and leads to damnation if not repented</note> is, by its lack of merit, worthy of eternal punishment.

## Tenth conclusion.
Anyone who dies in a state of mortal sin, even if they die with only one such sin, will be punished for eternity.

## Eleventh conclusion.
Unless the **guilt of mortal sin** <note>original: "reatus peccati mortalis" — the state of being liable for punishment due to sin, which Scholastic theologians distinguished from the act of the sin itself</note> were to persevere eternally in the soul of the sinner, the punishment of the sinner would not persevere for eternity.

## Twelfth conclusion.
Just as the term "mortal sin" is sometimes understood as the act of sinning—either by **omission** <note>failing to do what is required</note> or **commission** <note>performing a forbidden act</note>—so too is it frequently and properly understood by Catholic doctors as the guilt or liability for that sin.

## 13th conclusion.
When we say that a punishment or a reward is "owed" to someone, we can understand this in two ways: either that the person is worthy of such punishment or reward (due to a lack of merit or the presence of merit), or that such punishment or reward is actually being paid out to them.

## 14th conclusion.
The distinction of the word "owed" set forth in the preceding conclusion is not erroneous in matters of faith.

## 15th conclusion.
The **Cross of Christ** and sacred images are to be adored in the manner in which the Church adores them.

<summary>Pico presents fifteen theological conclusions clarifying that his views on Christ’s descent into hell and the nature of mortal sin are matters of technical definition rather than heresy. He emphasizes that the intent of the author should dictate the interpretation of a text when multiple meanings are possible.</summary>
<keywords>Pico della Mirandola, Christology, Harrowing of Hell, Scholasticism, Thomas Aquinas, mortal sin, guilt vs act, religious images, hermeneutics, orthodoxy</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the sequence of Pico della Mirandola’s "Conclusions," which were part of his 900 theses proposed for public debate in Rome in 1486. Having previously discussed Christ’s descent into hell, Pico now shifts his focus to the veneration of sacred objects, the limits of the Incarnation, the distinction between demonic and natural magic, and the relationship between human science and divine revelation.</meta>

<lang>Latin</lang>
<sig>KK ii</sig>

### xvi. conclusion.
The manner of adoring images and the cross proposed by **Peter of Aquila**, **Henry of Ghent**, **John Guarra**, **Durandus**, **Robert Holcot**, and generally all the **Scotists** <note>Followers of John Duns Scotus, a major Franciscan philosopher and theologian known for his complex "Subtle" reasoning</note> is more probable than the manner proposed by **Thomas** <note>Saint Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the influential Dominican theologian whose views often contrasted with the Scotists</note>.

### xvii. conclusion.
It does not follow that because someone denies that images should be adored in the way **Thomas** posits, they consequently deny they should be adored in the way the **Church** posits.

### xviii. conclusion.
Since the fullness of all being exists within God, God is able—insofar as it depends on Him—to **hypostatize** <note>original: "hipostatizare" — a technical term meaning to give a nature its own personal or substantial existence, similar to how the Divine and Human natures are united in the person of Jesus</note> every nature.

### xix. conclusion.
Regarding this question—whether a nature without reason <note>original: "nature irrationali"</note>, due to its own natural defect, is incapable of being **assumed** <note>taken up into a personal union with God</note> into the divine nature in a unity of person (as **Henry** believed), or whether it is not incapable (as the **common way** holds)—a Catholic may be so uncertain that he does not have to take a positive step to contradict Henry’s opinion.

### xx. conclusion.
A proposition that denies assent to a certain statement does not, by the literal force of the words <note>original: "de uirtute sermonis"</note>, imply a positive assent to the opposite statement.

### xxi. conclusion.
All magic which is commonly called **necromancy** <note>The practice of communicating with the dead or spirits, often associated with "black magic"</note>—and indeed any art or science whatsoever, if such things can even be called arts or sciences, that involves a pact or communion with **demons** in any way, whether explicit or implicit, whether as a primary goal or a side effect, whether beforehand, during, or after, or in any way at all—is a forbidden and superstitious thing, and is deservedly condemned by the Church.

### xxii. conclusion.
That science which is deservedly called the practical part of **natural philosophy**, and which **William of Paris**, **Bacon**, and all Greek authors call **natural magic** <note>In the Renaissance, this was considered a form of "high science" or physics that sought to understand the hidden powers of nature without using demons</note>, contains nothing in itself that is contrary to the Catholic and Orthodox faith.

### xxiii. conclusion.
There is no science—extending the name "science" to both revealed and non-revealed knowledge—which makes us certain of the **divinity of Christ** other than the doctrine of the Gospel and the science of Christian theology.

### xxiv. conclusion.
Among the sciences that are not revealed, but are discovered and acquired by human effort in all their parts, there is none that helps us more in recognizing the divinity of Christ than that through which we know what can be done by the power of **natural agents**, both below the moon and in the heavens. This allows us to understand from the works of Christ that He was truly the Lord and **Author of nature**, for He performed those works by His own power, which exceed the limits of all natural power, both celestial and earthly.

### xxv. conclusion.
A faithful person is not obliged to always use the term **"science"** <note>original: "scientia"</note> in his speech in such a way that it is common to both revealed and non-revealed sciences.

<summary>Pico distinguishes between forbidden demonic magic and "natural magic" (science), while arguing that natural philosophy helps prove Christ's divinity by defining the limits of what is naturally possible. He also defends the Scotist view of image veneration over that of Thomas Aquinas.</summary>

### xxvi. conclusion.
Among the many parts of **Kabbalistic science**, one specifically concerns the powers of the celestial bodies. <note>Kabbalah is a tradition of Jewish mysticism; Pico was one of the first Christian scholars to attempt to blend it with Christian theology and Neoplatonic philosophy.</note>

### xxvii. conclusion.
The heresies attributed to **Origen** are impious and detestable, and were deservedly condemned by the **Church**. <note>Origen of Alexandria (c. 184–253 AD) was a titan of early Christian thought, but several of his theories—such as the pre-existence of souls—were later declared heretical.</note>

### xxviii. conclusion.
Since it is likely that either **Origen** never actually believed those opinions, but they were falsely attributed to him by heretics (as **Rufinus**, **Pamphilus**, **Methodius**, **Didymus**, and **Haymo** <note>A group of early Christian writers and defenders of Origen</note> maintain), or that if he did believe them at one time, he eventually repented of them in the end (as **Jerome** maintains), it is reasonable to believe well regarding the salvation of his soul; we are not bound by the necessity of salvation to believe the opposite.

### xxviiii. conclusion.
The act of believing is a free act.

### xxx. conclusion.
The act of believing is not within a person's power in such a way that, when a purely and entirely doubtful proposition is presented, the intellect can adhere to one side rather than the other through the mere and sole command of the will. <note>Pico is arguing that you cannot simply "force" yourself to believe something if your reason finds it doubtful; belief requires intellectual conviction, not just willpower.</note>

### xxxi. conclusion.
One who believes this proposition—that it is not within the free power of the will to believe an article of faith is true when they please and false when they please (allowing for the explicit sense established by the preceding conclusion)—does not err in faith.

### xxxii. conclusion.
The **accidents** <note>original: "accidentia" — in philosophy, these are the external qualities of a thing (like color, taste, or smell) that do not belong to its essential nature</note> in the **Sacrament of the Altar** <note>The Eucharist or Holy Communion</note> exist in no subject. <note>Traditional Catholic doctrine held that in the Eucharist, the "breadness" vanishes, but the appearance of bread remains without being "attached" to any physical bread-substance.</note>

### xxxiii. conclusion.
It is possible, by the absolute power of God, for the **existence** of bread to remain without its **essence**, and for the **accidents** of the bread to be grounded in that existence; this assumes a real distinction between essence and existence.

### xxxiiii. conclusion.
One who believes this proposition—that someone who says an accident cannot exist unless it exists within something else could still hold to the sacrament of the **Eucharist** while also holding that the substance of bread does not remain (as can be verified by what was said in the previous conclusion)—does not err in faith.

### xxxv. conclusion.
<term>Paneitas</term> <note>Literally "Bread-ness"—the essential quality that makes bread "bread."</note> does not remain in the sacrament of the Eucharist as something **sustained** <note>original: "suppositata" — a technical term for a nature being given personhood or substantial grounding</note> by Christ, God-man; rather, through conversion, it passes into the essence of the body of Christ.

### xxxvi. conclusion.
If we hold with the **common way** <note>The prevailing theological consensus of the medieval universities</note> that God can sustain any nature, it is possible for Christ to assume "bread-ness" into the unity of the divine person; and it is possible that through such sustaining, Christ is present on the altar where the bread is. Thus, without the conversion or annihilation of the "bread-ness," Christ could be on the altar according to a possible truth of the sacrament of the Eucharist—not indeed the one instituted by Christ, but one possible to be instituted.

### xxxvii. conclusion.
One who believes this proposition, namely: if the **common way** concerning the possibility of being sustained by God is held regarding any creature, I say that without the conversion of the substan... <note>The text ends mid-sentence.</note>

[...the substance] of bread into the body of Christ, or by the annihilation of bread-ness <note>original: "paneitatis." ### xxxviii. conclusion.

These words **this is my body** <note>original: "hoc ẽ corpus meũ"</note> and so forth: when they were spoken by Christ, they were held significatively <note>To speak "significatively" means the words were intended to effect the change they described at that moment.</note>, not materially.

### xxxix. conclusion.

These same words, when they are uttered by an evangelical priest for consecration, are held materially—that is, recitatively <note>That is, the priest is "reciting" or quoting Christ’s original words rather than originating the command himself.</note>—not significatively.

### xl. conclusion.

The miracles of Christ, as far as the actual thing done is concerned, are an argument that they were performed by divine power.

### xli. conclusion.

The miracles of Christ, as far as the manner of performing them is concerned, are an argument that Christ himself, in performing them, possessed divine power from himself and not from elsewhere.

### xlii. conclusion.

God, in the most perfect mode of cognition, knows both himself and all things other than himself.

### xliii. conclusion.

In God there is every perfection, simply.

### xliiiI. conclusion.

If we use this term "intellectual" according to the manner of Dionysius <note>Referring to Dionysius the Areopagite, a theologian who argued that God is "beyond" all human descriptions. In this view, calling God "intellectual" is a metaphor because God’s mind is infinitely beyond an angel’s or human's.</note>, as it signifies a knowledge appropriate to the angelic nature—just as "rational" signifies a knowledge appropriate to human nature—then we say improperly that God is "intellectual" or that He "understands."

### xlv. conclusion.

The soul, through that hidden act of understanding which is direct and permanent, without the aid of the senses or the imagination <note>original: "fantaſie"</note>, understands only itself actually and distinctly.

### xlvi. conclusion.

The soul, through its multiple and various other acts, understands various and multiple things other than itself.

<meta>This document is a formal Brief from Pope Alexander VI to Giovanni Pico della Mirandola. It follows the previous page's listing of Pico's controversial "900 Conclusions" by addressing the legal and ecclesiastical status of Pico's work and his reputation. The Pope is reviewing the actions taken by his predecessor, Innocent VIII, regarding the investigation into Pico's potential heresy.</meta>

# Brief of Alexander VI, Supreme Pontiff, to Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, Count of Concordia.
## To our beloved son, the noble man Giovanni Pico, Count of Mirandola.
### POPE ALEXANDER VI.

BELOVED Son, health and apostolic blessing. We provide, as much as we are able with God's help, for the peace and reputation of all Catholics, especially those whom nobility of birth, the discipline of letters, and integrity of life and orthodox faith commend. Some time ago, when you first brought yourself to our predecessor of blessed memory, Pope Innocent VIII, and the Roman Curia, you posted nine hundred conclusions in theology and other faculties for public debate—as is the custom—under the permission of the said predecessor. You offered to maintain these conclusions under the correction of the Apostolic See <note>The "Apostolic See" refers to the authority of the Pope and the central administration of the Catholic Church in Rome.</note>. However, the said predecessor had heard from some individuals that among those conclusions were several contrary to our faith and religion, being erroneous, scandalous, and ill-sounding, and suspected of unsound doctrine. 

Desiring then to provide for the integrity of the faith, lest the minds of the faithful—especially the simple-minded who are accustomed to flock to such public debates—be corrupted, he commissioned and commanded several venerable brothers (then his, now our bishops) and other professors of Sacred Theology and of both Canon and Civil law <note>original: "utriusq; iuris." Refers to "Both Laws"—the legal training required for high church officials.</note> named by him in a letter in the form of a Brief. He ordered them to examine the contents of the said conclusions to see whether any of them, by the force of their words, were dissonant from the Catholic faith, or tasted of heresy <note>original: "heresī saperet̄." A common legal phrase in the Inquisition meaning a proposition "smells" or "savors" of heresy without being an explicit denial of dogma.</note>, or were doubtful and ambiguous and could be pulled toward an erroneous sense. They were to report back to the predecessor himself, as is contained more fully in the said Brief, so that once a faithful report was received, he might provide the appropriate remedy. 

These bishops and professors indeed reported back to the same predecessor that certain conclusions seemed to them suspected and, as they claimed, "tasting of heresy." Nevertheless, you had published those conclusions solely for the sake of scholarly debate and to be disputed under the correction of the Apostolic See; you finally professed that you would hold them only as they were judged by our same predecessor, promising by oath your assent to whatever declaration the predecessor himself should happen to make concerning this matter. 

Afterward, however, our predecessor received word that you had published another book, an *Apology* <note>original: "apologeticū." Pico's famous defense, the *Apologia*, written in 1487 to explain his positions.</note>, in which you interpreted and declared those same conclusions in a better and Catholic sense, explaining the understanding of the sincere faith regarding them. That same predecessor, lest the aforementioned propositions corrupt the hearts of the faithful in any way, forbade the reading of the booklet of the said nine hundred conclusions. However, he declared that you had incurred no mark of ill-repute, as is contained more extensively in the same letters, the tenor of which we wish to be considered as expressed here. 

But later, after some people suggested to the same predecessor that you had contravened your aforementioned oath under the pretext of the said *Apology*, he commanded that you be summoned to the Curia while you were living in France. Having received his commands reverently, you took up the journey to return to the Roman Curia. When you had arrived in Italy, you stayed in the region of Florence with the approval of the predecessor himself. 

In the meantime, the aforementioned matters having been brought to our notice and the truth of the entire business having been investigated by us, it was found—especially through the reports of our venerable brother Jorge, Bishop of Albano and Lisbon <note>Cardinal Jorge da Costa, a powerful Portuguese prelate.</note>, and our beloved sons Giovanni Battista Orsini, priest of the title of Saints John and Paul, and Francesco of Saint Eustachius, deacon, Cardinals of the Holy Roman Church. To these men we specifically commissioned that, having called upon our beloved son Paolo of Genoa <note>Paolo Moneglia da Genova, a Dominican who was the Master of the Sacred Palace and an influential theologian.</note>, a professor of theology and of the Order of Saint Dominic and Master of the Sacred Apostolic Palace, they should inform themselves accurately and report to us. It was found that nothing else had been done, proceeded, or attempted against you afterward, other than what was in that same *Apology*, which you had written to relieve your mind before all people from any mark of suspicion regarding the orthodox faith.

# GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA ON BEING AND THE ONE TO ANGELO POLIZIANO.

## PREFACE.

<margin>n</margin>
**Y**OU WERE TELLING ME in recent days of the discussion Lorenzo de' Medici <note>Lorenzo "the Magnificent" de' Medici (1449–1492), the ruler of Florence and a great patron of the arts and philosophy.</note> had with you concerning <term>being and the one<note>These are "transcendentals" in medieval philosophy—concepts that apply to everything that exists. A major debate was whether "to exist" (being) and "to be a single thing" (the one) were exactly the same thing.</note></term>. While you were publicly lecturing this year on Aristotle’s *Ethics*, he disputed with you by leaning on the arguments of the Platonists. He is a man of such effective and multifaceted genius that he seems suited for all things; in him, I especially admire that, although he is always most occupied with the affairs of the Republic, he is always either speaking or meditating on something literary. And because those who believe Aristotle disagrees with Plato also disagree with me—as I make the philosophy of both concordant—you asked how Aristotle might be defended in this matter and how he might agree with his teacher, Plato. I said then what came to mind, confirming what you had replied to Lorenzo during the dispute rather than bringing forward anything new. But this was not enough for you; you demand that, although I intend to write more extensively on these matters in the work <margin>The Concord of Aristotle and Plato.</margin> *The Concord of Plato and Aristotle* <note>original: "Platonis Aristotelisque concordia". This was Pico's ambitious, unfinished project to prove that all great philosophies eventually lead to the same truth.</note> which I am still "bringing to birth," I should nevertheless summarize for you in a brief commentary those things I spoke to you about in person regarding this question. <margin>Domenico Benivieni.</margin> Since Domenico Benivieni <note>A Florentine theologian and close friend of Pico and Savonarola.</note> happened to be present—a man most dear to us both for his learning and integrity—how could I deny you anything, especially in a literary matter, to a companion I might almost call inseparable? Let me be permitted by you, the defender of more polished language, to use certain words perhaps not yet granted the rights of <term>Latinity<note>original: "latio iure". Pico is apologizing for using "Scholastic" or technical medieval Latin words that wouldn't be found in ancient Roman literature.</note></term>. Yet the novelty of the subject matter and a certain necessity expressed them; do not seek the charms of an elegant style. <margin>Manilius.</margin> For as Manilius <note>original: "Mallius". Pico refers to Marcus Manilius, a 1st-century Roman poet and astrologer.</note> says: *The subject itself refuses to be adorned, content to be taught.* These, then, if I remember correctly, were the matters we were discussing.

### Chapter one in which he relates the arguments of the Platonists, by which they wish to establish that the "One" is superior to "Being."

<margin>a</margin>
<margin>What Aristotle thinks.</margin>
**A**RISTOTLE says in many places that these things correspond to one another and are of equal scope: namely, the <term>One<note>In this context, "The One" often refers to God or the ultimate, simplest source of all reality.</note></term> and <term>Being<note>That which exists.</note></term>; likewise the True and the Good; but more on these later. <margin>What the Platonists think to the contrary.</margin> The Academy <note>The followers of Plato.</note> resists this, for they prefer that the One be prior to Being. When they say "prior," they want it to be understood as both simpler and more common. <margin>First argument of the Platonists against Aristotle.</margin> For this reason, they say that God (who is of the highest simplicity) is indeed "the One," but is not "Being." <margin>Second argument.</margin> Likewise, they argue that the first matter of all things—that which is raw and formless—is included within the boundaries of the One. <margin>Third argument.</margin> Yet this matter, they claim, is outside the limits of Being. Then they bring forward the point that the same thing is not opposed to the One as is opposed to Being. For nothing is opposed to Being, but "Multitude" is opposed to the One. Therefore, by the same law by which opposites are judged, these two—Being and the One—are thought not to be interchangeable nor to correspond to one another.

<meta>This page continues the introduction to Pico della Mirandola's treatise "On Being and the One." After establishing the premise—a defense of Aristotle’s agreement with Plato—Pico now begins his specific critique of the Neoplatonic interpretation of Plato's dialogue, the *Parmenides*.</meta>

### Chapter two, in which he asks where Plato spoke concerning being and the one; he shows that Plato’s words favor the opinion stating that the one and being are equal rather than those who wish the one to be superior to being.

<margin>What is to be thought of Plato’s *Parmenides*.</margin>
These are the reasons upon which they rely. Before we dissolve them, it would not be irrelevant to bring into the open what is found expressed by Plato on this question. I find Plato disputing about <term>being and the one</term> <note>The central concepts of this work: 'being' refers to existence, while 'the one' refers to unity or singularity. Pico's rivals argued 'the one' was a higher category than 'being.'</note> in two places: in the *Parmenides* and the *Sophist*. The Academics <note>Pico is referring to the Neoplatonists of his era, particularly Marsilio Ficino, who believed Plato's philosophy was a form of mystical theology.</note> contend that in both places, the one is placed by Plato above being. But regarding the *Parmenides*, I will say first that nothing is asserted in that entire dialogue; and even if it were asserted most strongly, nothing can be found clearly enough to allow us to ascribe a dogma of this kind to Plato. Certainly, the book is not to be counted among the dogmatic works, since it is entirely nothing other than a kind of <term>dialectical exercise</term> <note>A logical training session or debate practice intended to sharpen the mind, rather than a statement of core doctrine.</note>. Our own opinion is so far from being contradicted by the words of the dialogue itself that no interpretations exist that are more arbitrary and forced than those brought forward by those who wished to interpret Plato’s *Parmenides* in another sense. But let us omit all interpreters. Let us look at the sequence of the dialogue itself: how it begins, where it tends, what it promises, and what it executes.

Furthermore, it proceeds in this way. When they were moving from the dispute over whether all things are one or whether the things that exist are many, Socrates had turned to the <term>Ideas</term> <note>Plato’s famous Theory of Forms: the perfect, eternal archetypes of all things in the world.</note> and asked many things of Parmenides about them. Parmenides responds that he is pleased by that impulse and the inclination of the mind toward defining the highest things. "However," he says, "collect yourself and exercise yourself more diligently while you are young in that faculty which seems useless to many—called by them 'nonsense' or 'chatter'—otherwise truth will flee from you." It is confessed by everyone, and the following parts manifest it, that by these words he signifies <term>dialectics</term> <note>The art of logical investigation through dialogue and contradiction.</note>. 
<margin>The utility of logic.</margin>
After this, when Socrates asks Parmenides, "What is the mode of this exercise, Parmenides?" he responds first that it is the one he had heard from Zeno <note>Zeno of Elea, a philosopher famous for his logical paradoxes.</note>. Then, teaching more particularly about this matter, he advises that he should look around with sharp skill, not only at what follows if a certain thing *is*, but also what follows if it *is not*. Then he should see what follows for that thing which we posit to be or not to be, both in respect to itself and in respect to other things; and likewise how other things regard themselves and that thing. When he had said more to this effect, Socrates said: "You bring a difficult work, and I do not entirely understand you. But why do you not posit something yourself and treat it in that way which you approve, so that my understanding of this matter might become clearer?" Parmenides responds that this is laborious for him as an old man. Finally, Zeno says that this must be done by Parmenides since it is in a small gathering; otherwise, he says, it would be less fitting for such things to be treated in a crowd of many by an old man, since everyone should know that this kind of treatment and "wandering" is necessary for attaining the truth. These words of Zeno give full credit to what we have said. For that which Parmenides is about to treat is of such a kind—if we believe Zeno—that it is not to be treated openly in a large assembly by an old man. But if, as those others wish, he were dealing with divine orders and the first principle of all things, what treatment would be more suitable for an old man or less to be ashamed of? But it is beyond all controversy, unless we wish to deceive ourselves: that business which Parmenides was about to engage in was a dialectical matter, and nothing other than what Socrates had requested. That, however, is a task for a youth rather than...

<summary>Pico argues that Plato’s dialogue *Parmenides* is a logical exercise (dialectics) rather than a theological revelation, countering the Neoplatonist view that it places "the One" above "Being." He emphasizes that Parmenides himself describes his method as a necessary training for the young to reach the truth.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Pico's critique of the Neoplatonic reading of Plato’s Parmenides. He has just argued that the dialogue is a logical exercise rather than a statement of fixed doctrine. Now, he addresses the specific arguments regarding the "One" being superior to "Being."</meta>

Zeno had judged it an office of old age <note>original: "senilis officii". This refers to the character Zeno in Plato's dialogue, who suggests that such difficult logical debates are a task for the mature mind.</note>. If we do not believe even these testimonies, let us run through the dialogue itself. And we will see that nowhere is anything affirmed; but everywhere it is only asked: if this is so, what follows? Likewise, if it is not so? The Academics, however, seized the occasion for their opinion concerning <term>being and the one</term> from this point: because in the first position Plato exercises himself with this problem to see, if all things are one, what might follow. And he responds that it will be that the "one" which we suppose to exist would be <term>indivisible</term> <note>original: "impartibile"; incapable of being divided into parts.</note>, infinite, and nowhere. Since he enumerates many things of that kind, he brings this among others: namely, that it will be that this "one" is not being.

Pay attention, however: even if this were not a dialectical exercise but a dogma being handed down concerning being and the one, how much these things differ: to assert, namely, that the one is above being, and to assert that it will be that *if* all things are one, that one is not being. And enough concerning Parmenides.

Truly indeed, in the *Sophist* he speaks rather toward this opinion: that the one and being are equal, rather than the one being superior to being.
<margin>
What he says in the *Sophist* concerning being and the one
</margin>
For I do not find where he explains the former <note>The idea that the One is superior.</note>. He signifies the latter <note>The idea that they are equal.</note> in many ways, as through these words: "For considering it thus, you confess it is necessary that he who says something says one thing, and soon, he who does not say something must say not even one thing: that is, to say nothing." These are his words. Therefore, with him, "not one" and "nothing" are equal—indeed, they are the same—and likewise "one" and "something" are equal. After this, he likewise proves it cannot be said that "non-being" is one. And thus he concludes: "Being does not happen to non-being; therefore, the one does not happen to non-being." But he speaks of the "one" which he said above was equal to that which is "something." He seems, therefore, to take it as granted that the one is being. But so be it: let us grant that Plato affirmed this—which he certainly never affirmed. Come, let us examine in what sense it could truly be said, first laying the foundations of the Aristotelian opinion itself in this manner.

### Chapter three, in which he declares in what way "being" is understood by Aristotle when he makes it equal to the one and encompassing all things.

<margin>
Being can be understood in a twofold way.
He proves the word is rightly understood in the way Aristotle understood it.
The first testimony.
According to Simplicius, defending Parmenides.
Solution to the first reason of the Platonists.
</margin>
**T**his word, "being," about which it is debated whether it is equal to the one, can be understood in two ways. The first is that when we say "being," we understand everything that is outside of nothingness. This is the way Aristotle used it when he made being equal to the one. Nor did he use the word without reason: for as it is truly said, we ought to feel as the few, but speak as the many <note>A famous philosophical maxim suggesting that while scholars have private, complex thoughts, they must use common language to communicate.</note>. For we feel and think for ourselves; we speak for others, that is, for the multitude, and therefore we speak so that we may be understood. The common people, and anyone from the crowd, understand "being" such that everything to which existence is not lacking—and which cannot truly be called nothing—is called "being." 

But we find that even those held to be most wise among those who hold the opposite view used the word in this way. For Parmenides the Pythagorean, when he said that "the one is that which is," meant God. If we believe <term>Simplicius</term> <note>A 6th-century commentator on Aristotle who tried to harmonize different Greek philosophies.</note> and many others who wish to defend Parmenides against those who misrepresent him. As if he had said all things are one! For with one voice they respond that it was never believed by Parmenides that there is no division, multitude, or plurality in things—which he himself openly confesses elsewhere in his poems. But when he said "the one is that which is," he judged that that to which the name of "being" truly belongs, and which truly is, is only the one; and this one is God. Therefore, if we believe Parmenides and his defenders (including even the Platonists), the one cannot be above being unless it is above God; and Parmenides is so far from denying that God is being, that he grants the true name of being to God alone.

<summary>Pico argues that Plato's dialogues, specifically the Sophist and Parmenides, actually support the equality of "Being" and "the One." He begins Chapter 3 by defining Being as everything that is not "nothing," aligning Aristotle's definitions with the common usage of language and the theology of Parmenides.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Pico della Mirandola's "On Being and the One" (De Ente et Uno). In the previous section, he argued against the Neoplatonists who used Plato’s Parmenides to claim that the "One" is superior to "Being." Here, he addresses arguments from Dionysius the Areopagite and begins a linguistic analysis of "being" vs. "to be."</meta>

<margin>Dionysius.</margin>
<margin>Fourth argument.</margin>
And so the solution to the first argument of the Platonists occurs to us in passing. But even Dionysius the Areopagite <note>A Christian theologian and philosopher of the late 5th to early 6th century, often cited by medieval and Renaissance thinkers to bridge Platonic philosophy and Christian theology.</note>—whom those who dispute against us claim as a supporter of their own opinion—will not deny that it is truly said by God to Moses: **I am who I am**. This we read in Greek as "I am being" <note>original: "ego eimi ho on" (εγω ειμι ο ων). This is the Septuagint translation of the divine name in Exodus 3:14.</note>. Indeed, since they themselves say that "nothing" or "non-being" is opposed to "being" just as the "multitude" is opposed to the "one," they must necessarily concede that whatever is not "being" is "nothing" or "non-being." Just as that which is not "one" is many or a "multitude." Therefore, if they preserve the same law of speech, they must confess either that God is nothing—a thought their very ears would dread—or that He is being.

<margin>Fifth argument.</margin>
<margin>He proves that when understood this way, being is necessarily equal to the one, even according to Plato.</margin>
In this way, when "being" is understood as that first axiom and universal discourse, we establish that about any thing it must necessarily be said that it either is or is not; and about nothing can both be said or thought at the same time. Since, therefore, outside of all things there is nothing except nothing itself, if "being" accepted in this way excludes only nothing from itself, it must undoubtedly encompass all things. Therefore, the "one" cannot encompass more things than "being" does, unless it encompasses nothing itself—which Plato denies in the *Sophist* <note>One of Plato’s dialogues dealing with the definition of a philosopher, a statesman, and a sophist, which involves a deep dive into the nature of being and non-being.</note>. When he says that "non-being" or "nothing" cannot be called "one" without it encompassing fewer things (as they wish); therefore, being and the one are equal.

### Chapter four, in which he declares in what way something can be said to be superior to being.

<margin>Concrete and abstract names</margin>
<margin>The difference between them.</margin>
We have explained one of these ways in which we said "being" can be understood; by those who use it in this way, they most truly affirm that nothing is more common than being. It remains for us to explain the other way, according to which it will be clear that something can nevertheless be truly said to be placed above the excellence of being. Some names are <term>concrete</term> <note>Words that refer to a thing having a quality, like "shining."</note>, others <term>abstract</term> <note>Words that refer to the quality itself, like "light."</note>. Concrete names are: "hot," "shining," "white," "man." Abstract names are: "heat," "light," "whiteness," "humanity." This is the power and the difference between them: that what is called "abstract" denotes that which is such of itself, not from another. A "concrete" name, conversely, signifies that which is such not of itself, but by the benefit of another. Thus, a "shining" thing shines by "light." A "white" thing is white by "whiteness." And a "man" is a man by "humanity." Since, however, nothing participates in itself—nor can the same condition be in the same thing both of itself and by the participation of another—it follows that what is called abstract cannot be named from the concrete. Therefore, it is not properly said that "whiteness is white" or "blackness is black." Indeed, he would be ridiculous who would say such things—not because whiteness is black or heat is cold, but because the former is so far from blackness and the latter is so far from coldness that whatever things are white are white by that whiteness, and whatever things are hot are hot by participation in this [heat].

<margin>That some things are denied to be in something in two ways.</margin>
We deny that certain things belong to a certain thing either because it does not have them—as when we say the black is not white—or because it has it in a more excellent way and a more perfect reason than we signify it having by such a statement. As when we deny that "whiteness" is white: not because it is black, but because it is not only "not black" because it is "white" (which is the same as saying it has whiteness), but because it is whiteness itself. 

<margin>How God is said not to be being but above being.</margin>
Let us come to our subject: "being" <note>original: "ens"</note> has the form of a concrete noun. For "being" and "that which is" mean the same thing. Its abstract form is seen in this word: "to be" <note>original: "esse"</note>. So that "being" is said to be that which participates in "to be" itself. Just as "shining" is said to be that which participates in light, and "seeing" is that in which "to see" itself is present. If we look at this exact significance of "being," we will deny that that "to be" is a "being"—not only because it is not, and because it is nothing, but because it is from God so that it is "to be" itself, which is from itself and of itself, and by whose participation all things are. Just as we would not only deny that to be "hot" which is devoid of heat, but also that which is heat itself. Such indeed... 

<summary>Pico argues that God is "Being" (Ens) according to Scripture, but then uses a linguistic distinction between concrete nouns (Being) and abstract nouns (To Be) to explain how God can also be said to be "above Being." He concludes that God is "To Be" (Esse) itself, the source in which all other beings participate.</summary>
