<meta>This page continues Pico della Mirandola's defense of the harmony between Plato and Aristotle. Having previously established that "Being" and "the One" are co-extensive, he now addresses the Neoplatonic argument that God is "above Being" and explains how both philosophical schools actually agree on this point.</meta>

<sig>LL iii</sig>

It is God who is the fullness of all being: He alone exists of Himself, and from Him alone—without any intermediary standing in between—all things have proceeded into existence. For this reason, we shall truly say that God is not "being," but is "super-being" <note>The term "super-being" (super ens) refers to the idea that God's existence is so vastly different from created things that the word "being" cannot be applied to Him in the same way.</note>, and that there is something higher than being, which is God Himself. Since the name "the One" is given to Him, it follows from this that we must confess "the One" to be above "being." 

<margin>Why God is called "the One."</margin>
However, we call God "the One" not so much to state *what* He is, but rather *how* He is all the things that He is, and how other things come from Him. For Dionysius <note>Dionysius the Areopagite, a late-antique theologian who attempted to reconcile Christian doctrine with Neoplatonism.</note> says that God is called "the One" because He is uniquely all things. Again, He is called "the One" 

<margin>How could it be said by Plato that "the One" is superior to "being" if he also said this?</margin>
because He is the principle of all things that exist, just as unity is the principle of all numbers. For this reason, if (as the Platonists <note>The "Academici" or followers of Plato's Academy.</note> wish) Plato affirms in the first part of the *Parmenides* <note>A notoriously difficult dialogue by Plato exploring the nature of unity and existence.</note> that "the One" is superior to "being," that "One" will be none other than God. Even the Platonists admit this by common consent, asserting that Plato is there treating the first principle of all things. 

But someone might say that on this point, at least, Aristotle will be at odds with Plato, because Aristotle never accepts "being" in such a way that it is subordinate to "the One" or that it does not include God, as Plato does. Those who say this have not read Aristotle. 

<margin>It is also accepted by Aristotle, when he is teaching, that God is not called "being" but "super-being."</margin>
For he also does this, and far more clearly than Plato. In the sixth book of his *First Philosophy* <note>Now known as Aristotle's *Metaphysics*.</note>, he says that being is divided into "being in itself" and "being by accident." Since "being in itself" is divided into the ten categories <note>Aristotle's classification of everything that exists into ten types, such as substance, quantity, and quality.</note>, there is no doubt among good interpreters that God is not contained under this "being." For He is neither "being by accident," nor is He contained under any of the ten categories into which "being in itself" is divided. 

Likewise, there is that division common among the Peripatetics <note>The followers of Aristotle's school.</note> in which "being" is said to be divided into "substance" and "accident." When we speak this way, we understand "being" in such a way that God is above being, and is not contained under it, just as Thomas <note>St. Thomas Aquinas, the 13th-century theologian who harmonized Aristotelian philosophy with Christianity.</note> teaches in the first book of his commentaries on the *Sentences* <note>The *Sentences* of Peter Lombard, the standard theological textbook of the Middle Ages.</note>. 

<margin>Aristotle gives these two primary names, "the One" and "the Good," to God.</margin>
I will also add this: certain Platonists boast unjustly as if they held a mystery unknown to Aristotle when they say that there are two proper names for God, namely "the One" and "the Good," and thus that "the Good" and "the One" exist before "being." For just as we have shown that the Peripatetics are not unaware of how God can be understood as being above "being," we can also show that Aristotle gave these two primary names, "the Good" and "the One," to God. 

For in the twelfth book of his *First Philosophy*, after he has disputed concerning the whole of being and separate minds <note>Or "intellectual substances"—what we might call angels or celestial intelligences.</note>, he asks at last (as if turning after all other things to investigate the properties of God alone) whether, besides the good that exists in the universe of beings—much like the order in an army—there is some separate Good, like a leader of this army. He determines that God is this Good. Consequently, in the same chapter, he proves His unity as a testimony to this, citing that line from Homer after his powerful arguments: **"Let there be one leader, one king."** <note>original: εἷς κοίρανος ἔστω, εἷς βασιλεύς. From the *Iliad*, used by Aristotle to argue that the universe must be ruled by a single prime mover.</note> Where, then, is Aristotle false? Where is he discordant with Plato? Where is he profane? Where does he feel toward God with less honor than is becoming?

### Chapter Five, in which he declares for what reason the Peripatetics ascribe many things to God which the Platonists deny, and teaches how we ascend through four steps to the darkness in which God dwells.

<margin>The first reason of the Platonists must be solved again.</margin>
Let us now resolve the arguments of the Platonists by which they contend—not in the way we agree with, but absolutely—against Aristotle that "the One" is superior to "being." Although their first argument (which said God is the One but not "being") has been sufficiently resolved above, it would be worth the effort to digress further to show why many things are truly affirmed and truly denied of God—not only by different groups, like the Platonists and Peripatetics, but often by the same author. God is all things, and He is all things most eminently and most perfectly. This would not be possible unless...

<summary>Pico argues that Aristotle and Plato both recognize God as being "above Being" and that Aristotle specifically identifies God as both the "One" and the "Good." He asserts that the apparent contradictions between the two philosophers arise from different definitions of "being" rather than theological disagreement.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Pico della Mirandola's "On Being and the One," moving from the definition of God as "the One" to a discussion of how we must understand divine perfection. Having argued that God is above ordinary being, he now begins to explain how human concepts like "life" and "knowledge" must be purified before they can be applied to the Divine.</meta>

<margin>
Twofold imperfection in things.
</margin>
...it should include within itself the perfections of all things, so that it may reject from itself whatever pertains to imperfection in things. We can define whatever has the nature of the imperfect in existing things under two main headings. The first is when something in a thing is less than perfect within its own **genus** <term>genus: the broad class or kind to which a thing belongs</term>. The second is when it is indeed perfect within its own genus, but is not therefore "simply" perfect <note>original: *simpliciter perfectum*. In scholastic philosophy, this means something is perfect in every possible way, not just in one specific respect.</note>, because it only possesses the perfection of one single genus; there are many other kinds of things outside of it, honored with their own perfections, which are not included within it.

<margin>
An example of that which is not perfect within its own genus.
</margin>
<margin>
How sensory knowledge is imperfect knowledge.
</margin>
As an example of the first type: sensory knowledge is not only imperfect because it is *only* knowledge and not, for instance, desire; it is also an imperfect form of knowledge in itself. This is because it requires a dull and physical organ to function, and because it only touches the outer surface of things, failing to penetrate to their innermost part—that is, to their **substance** <term>substance: the essential nature or underlying reality of a thing, as opposed to its outward appearance</term>.

<margin>
How human knowledge is imperfect.
</margin>
Likewise, human knowledge—which is called "rational"—is an imperfect knowledge because it is wandering, uncertain, shifting, and laborious. Consider also the intellectual knowledge of divine minds, which theologians call **angels** <note>In this context, Pico refers to the Neoplatonic "Intelligences" as well as the biblical messengers.</note>;

<margin>
How angelic knowledge is imperfect.
</margin>
even this is an imperfect knowledge. This is at least because it seeks outside of itself what it does not fully possess within—namely, the light of truth which it needs and by which it is perfected. Now consider life:

<margin>
How the life in every body is imperfect.
</margin>
The life found in plants, or rather the life found in every physical body, is not only imperfect because it is merely life and not knowledge. It is also imperfect because it is not "pure" life; rather, it is a kind of "animation" derived from the soul into the body, always flowing away and always mixed with death. Indeed, it should be called death rather than life.

<margin>
When we begin to die.
</margin>
For we begin—in case you did not know—to die the very moment we begin to live, and death is stretched out alongside life; we only first cease to die when we are released from "this body of death" <note>original: *corpore mortis huius*. A reference to Saint Paul in Romans 7:24.</note> through the death of the flesh. But even the life of angels is not perfect; for if the life-giving ray of divine light did not cherish it from within, it would all slip away into nothingness. The same reasoning applies to all other things. Therefore, when you conceive of God as knowing and God as living, first take care that the life and knowledge which are ascribed to Him are understood to be free from all these defects. But even this is not enough.

<margin>
An example of that which is not "simply" perfect, even if it is perfect within its own genus.
</margin>
For there remains that second type of imperfection, of which this is the example: Imagine a most perfect life—one that is entirely and purely life, with nothing mortal about it and nothing mixed with death, needing nothing outside itself to remain stable and permanent. Imagine likewise a knowledge that knows all things, and knows them all at once most perfectly. Add to this that the knower finds all these things within himself, so that he does not seek the truth he knows outside of himself, but is himself that very truth. Even so, each of these—though most perfect in its own category and such that they could not exist outside of God—is still unworthy of God if they are accepted as distinct from one another. For God is all-encompassing and infinite perfection; but He is not all-encompassing and infinite simply because He contains all particular and infinite perfections within Himself. For if that were so, He would not be "most simple" <note>In theology, "divine simplicity" is the idea that God has no parts; His attributes (like goodness, life, and knowledge) are all actually one and the same thing.</note>, nor would the things within Him be truly infinite. Instead, He would be one infinite thing assembled from many things—things that might be infinite in number but would be finite in their individual perfection. To say or even think such a thing of God is profane. But truly, if life (which is indeed most perfect life, but is *only* life and not knowledge) and likewise if desire or will (which is indeed most perfect will, but is *only* will and not life or knowledge) and other similar attributes are placed in God, it follows clearly that the divine life would be of finite perfection. This is because it would possess the perfection belonging to life, but would lack the perfection belonging to knowledge or desire. Let us therefore remove from "life" not only that which makes it an imperfect life, but also that which makes it *merely* life; and do the same for "knowledge" and the other names by which we call God. Then <insert>it follows</insert> that which... <note>original: *tunc que quod*. This is the catchword for the next page.</note>

<summary>Pico explains that God's perfection is not a collection of separate qualities, but a unified "simplicity" where attributes like life and knowledge are identical and absolute. He argues that human and angelic versions of these qualities are inherently limited and must be conceptually "purified" before being applied to the Divine.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Pico della Mirandola's argument from the previous page, where he began explaining how to understand God by stripping away the limitations found in created things. He is now moving toward a "mystical" understanding of God that transcends human language.</meta>

<margin>How God is Being itself.</margin>
...out of all things, what remains will necessarily be such as we wish God to be understood: one, that is, most perfect, infinite, and most simple. And since life is a certain kind of being, and wisdom likewise is a certain kind of being, and equally so is justice; certainly, if you remove from these the condition of particularity and limitation, what remains will not be *this* or *that* being, but Being itself—being simply, being universal, not by the universality of predication <term>universality of predication: a logical term referring to a general concept that applies to many individuals (like "animal" applies to both cats and dogs)</term>, but by the universality of perfection. Similarly, wisdom is a certain good, because this specific good which is wisdom <margin>Augustine</margin> is not that good which is justice. "Take away this, take away that," as Augustine says <note>original: *Tolle hoc: Tolle illud*. See Augustine, *On the Trinity*, VIII.3</note>; that is, take away this particular limitation through which wisdom is a good in such a way that it is wisdom and not the good which is justice. And likewise, justice has the goodness of justice in such a way that it does not have the goodness which belongs to wisdom. <margin>Seeing the face of God in a mirror.</margin> Then you will see the face of God "in a mirror darkly" <note>original: *in enigmate*. A reference to 1 Corinthians 13:12</note>; that is, you will see every good, Goodness itself, simply good, the Good of every good. Just as life is a certain kind of being, so it is a certain kind of unity; for it is a single perfection. <margin>How God is Unity itself.</margin> Likewise, wisdom is a single perfection. Cast away particularity, and there remains not *this* or *that* unity, but Unity itself and Unity simply.

Therefore, since God is He who—as we said from the beginning—is all things once all imperfection is removed; certainly, when you have cast out from all things both the imperfection found within their kind and the particularity of their kind, that which remains is God. God, therefore, is Being itself, Unity itself, Goodness itself, and likewise Truth itself. We have now advanced two steps, ascending toward the darkness where God dwells, purging from the divine names every stain that comes from the imperfection of the things they signify. Two steps still remain, of which one proves the deficiency of names, and the other accuses the weakness of our understanding. These <margin>How God is above being, above unity, above goodness.</margin> names—being, truth, unity, good—speak of something concrete and, as it were, participated <term>participated: in Platonic philosophy, this describes a thing that has a quality (like beauty) by "taking part" in a higher source, rather than being the source of beauty itself</term>. For this reason, we say again that God is above being, above truth, above unity, and above goodness; because He is Existence itself, Truth itself, Unity itself, and Goodness itself.

But we are still in the light; yet God "made darkness His hiding place" <note>Psalm 18:11</note>. Therefore, we have not yet reached God; for as long as <margin>God is above all that can be said or conceived by us.</margin> what we say, understand, and comprehend about God is said to occur in the light, we are speaking and thinking of things that are so much smaller than God as the capacity of our intelligence is smaller than His infinite divinity. Ascending, therefore, to the fourth step, let us enter the light of ignorance; and, blinded by the darkness of divine splendor, let us cry out with the Prophet: "I have fainted in your courts, O Lord" <note>original: *defeci in atriis tuis domine*. See Psalm 84:2</note>. Saying this one thing <margin>The Psalms</margin> about God at last: that He is, in a way both intelligible and ineffable, above all that we can either speak or conceive of as most perfect. Then, placing God most eminently above even that unity, goodness, and truth which we had conceived—and even above Being itself—Dionysius the Areopagite <margin>Dionysius</margin> <note>Dionysius the Areopagite: a 5th-century Christian theologian (then believed to be the convert of St. Paul) who wrote on "Negative Theology," the idea that God is better described by what He is NOT than by what He IS.</note>, looking toward this, after all those things which he had written in his *Symbolic Theology*, in his *Theological Institutes*, and in his works *On the Divine Names* and *On Mystical Theology*, finally at the end of that same book, like one who was already in the darkness and speaking as holily as possible about God, exclaimed after certain other matters pertaining to this: "He is neither truth, nor kingdom, nor wisdom; neither the one, nor unity, nor deity, nor goodness; nor is He spirit, as far as we can know; nor is there any naming of 'Son' or 'Father', nor any other thing from those which are known to us or to anyone else in the world."

<summary>Pico describes a four-stage intellectual ascent to God, moving from specific virtues to abstract perfections, and finally into a "divine darkness" where God is understood to be beyond all human concepts and names. He cites St. Augustine and Pseudo-Dionysius to argue that God transcends even the concepts of "Being" and "Unity."</summary>

<meta>This page continues Pico della Mirandola's defense of the "Four Gates" of theology. He is moving from the first stage (denying that God is a physical body) to the second stage (denying that God is even an intellectual or living being in the way we understand those terms). He is addressing his friend, the famous humanist scholar Angelo Poliziano.</meta>

<margin>First step.</margin>
<margin>Against the Epicureans, Egyptians, Varro, and others.</margin>
...nor is He anything of those things that are not, nor of those things that are. Neither do those things that are know Him as He is, nor does He know those things that are as they are <note>original: *sicuti sunt*. This is a classic expression of "Negative Theology," suggesting God's knowledge and being are so far above ours that they cannot even be compared using the same words</note>. There is neither a word for Him, nor a name, nor knowledge; neither darkness nor light; neither error nor truth. There is absolutely no way to affirm or deny anything about Him. These are the words of that divine man <note>referring to Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, a 5th-century mystic thought by Pico to be a student of St. Paul</note> recorded word for word. Let us gather together what we have said, and we shall see that in the first step we learn that God is not a body, as the **Epicureans** <term>Epicureans: followers of Epicurus who believed the universe was made of atoms and that the gods, if they existed, were physical beings</term> thought, nor the form of a body, as those wish who assert that God is the soul of the heavens or of the universe. The **Egyptians** thought this, as Plutarch writes, as did **Varro**, the Roman theologian. For both groups, this was a great source of Idolatry, as we shall declare elsewhere. But there are even some among the **Peripatetics** <term>Peripatetics: followers of Aristotle's school of philosophy</term> so dull-witted that they confirm this to be both the truth and the opinion of Aristotle. See how far these men fall short of a true knowledge of God! Resting in their prison as if in lime <note>original: *in calce*. Lime was used in mortar; Pico is suggesting they are stuck in the "bricks and mortar" of the physical world</note>, they believe they have reached the heights of God when, still lying on the ground, they have not yet moved a foot toward Him.

<margin>The fifth decade of the concord of Plato and Aristotle.</margin>
<margin>Second step.</margin>
...God is not a perfect life, nor a perfect being, nor even a perfect intellect. We have attacked this profane opinion at length in the "fifth decade" <note>Pico planned a work in "decades" (groups of ten books) to prove that Plato and Aristotle actually agreed on all major points of philosophy</note> of our *Concord*. We learn in the second step—which few attain correctly, and in which we can easily be deceived if we wander even a little from the true understanding—that God is neither life, nor intellect, nor an "intelligible thing" <note>original: *intelligibile*. Something that can be grasped by the mind</note>, but something better and more excellent than all these. For all these names speak of a *particular* perfection, none of which exist in God. 

<margin>Dionysius and the Platonists.</margin>
Looking at this, both **Dionysius** and thereafter the **Platonists** deny that life, intellect, wisdom, and similar things are in God. But since God, in His unique perfection—which is His infinity and His deity—unites and gathers within Himself all the perfection of these things (which in us are many and divided), He is Himself these things. He is not like "one" among many, but the One *before* the many.

<margin>Peripatetics.</margin>
<margin>Parisian theologians.</margin>
<margin>Augustine.</margin>
For this reason, certain others—especially the **Peripatetics**, whom the **Parisian theologians** <term>Parisian theologians: the Scholastic scholars at the University of Paris, known for their rigorous logic and use of Aristotle</term> imitate in almost everything as far as they are able—concede that all these things are in God. In saying and believing this, we not only speak and believe correctly, but we also speak in harmony with those who deny them. This is true if we always keep the words of **Aurelius Augustine** before our eyes: that the wisdom of God is no more wisdom than it is justice, and the justice of God is no more justice than it is wisdom. Likewise, life in Him is no more life than it is knowledge, and knowledge is no more knowledge than it is life. For all these things are one in God—not through confusion or mixing, or as if they were distinct things penetrating one another—but through a simple, supreme, ineffable, and fountain-like unity. In this unity, every act, every form, and every perfection is enclosed excellently, just as in a first and most eminent leader, or in the innermost treasures of divine infinity. Thus, He is above all and outside all, yet He is not only intimate to all things, but more "one" with all things than they are with themselves. Truly, words fail, and what is said is far less than what is conceived.

<margin>To love God.</margin>
<margin>Note.</margin>
But see, my dear **Angelo**, what madness holds us! While we are in the body, we can *love* God more than we can either speak of Him or know Him. By loving Him, we benefit ourselves more, we labor less, and we obey Him more. Yet we always prefer to seek through knowledge—never finding what we seek—rather than to possess through love that which, without love, would be found in vain. But let us return to our point. It is now clearly evident to you how God is sometimes called Mind, Intellect, Life, and Wisdom, yet at other times is placed above all these things. 

<margin>Plato.</margin>
Yet both views are proven truly and harmoniously. Nor does **Plato** disagree with **Aristotle** on this; for in the sixth book of the *Republic*, when he speaks of God (whom he there calls the "Idea of the Good")...

<meta>This page continues Pico’s discussion on the "degrees" of knowing God, moving from the philosophical concepts of the Good and Intellect to a mystical "unknowing." He then transitions into Chapter 6 to address a technical Platonic argument about the nature of matter.</meta>

...places the Good above the intellect and intelligible things <note>In Platonic philosophy, "intelligible things" are realities that can only be understood by the mind, like math or virtues, rather than seen with the eyes</note>, granting the power of understanding to the former and the capacity to be understood to the latter. But here—namely, **Aristotle**— <margin>Aristotle.</margin> often calls God "Intellect," "the one who understands," and "the intelligible." For even **Dionysius the Areopagite**, <margin>Dionysius.</margin> while saying the same thing as Plato, would not deny (even alongside Aristotle) that God is not ignorant of Himself and other things. Therefore, if He understands Himself, He is both "intellect" and "intelligible." For He who knows Himself necessarily knows and is known. And even if we take these as "particular perfections" as I have said—or if, when we say "intellect," we mean a nature that reaches out toward the "intelligible" as if toward something outside itself—Aristotle would no less consistently deny that God is "intellect" and "intelligible" than the Platonists do.

In the **third degree**, <margin>The third degree.</margin> a bit more light shines upon us as we draw near to the darkness. We must not, with impious thought, imagine God to be an incomplete or flawed being—which is what would happen if we called Him either a body, or the soul of a body, or a living creature composed of them. Nor should we make Him a particular kind of thing, however perfect, as those do who speak with human wisdom, such as when we call Him "Life," or "Mind," or "Reason." Instead, we should recognize that He is better than even what "universal names" indicate—names which embrace all things, such as "True Being" and "the Good."

In the **fourth degree**, <margin>The fourth degree.</margin> we come to know that He is not only above those things, but above every name that can be formed and every notion that can be conceived by us. Then, for the first time, we "know" Him in a certain way, when we "unknow" Him entirely. From this, one can gather that God is not only—as **Anselm** <margin>Anselm.</margin> says—"that than which nothing greater can be thought," but that He is that which is *infinitely greater* than everything that can be thought. Thus, the prophet **David** <margin>Psalm.</margin> truly said, according to the Hebrew text: *To You, silence is praise* <note>original: "Tibi silentium laus." This is from Psalm 65:2. Pico notes that the Hebrew version emphasizes that God is so far beyond words that silence is the only appropriate worship</note>.

Let these things be said as a solution to the first argument. From here, a great **window of understanding** <margin>A window of understanding is opened to the books of Dionysius on Mystical Theology and the Divine Names.</margin> is opened for anyone reading the books of Dionysius titled *On Mystical Theology* and *On Divine Names*. Regarding these books, one must be careful: let us neither make his writings out to be less than they are (for they are of the highest importance), nor, while we think all we understand is trivial, should we dream up imaginary and inextricable fables for ourselves.

-> ## Chapter Six, in which he solves the second argument of the Platonists concerning primary matter. <-

As for the objection they raise regarding **primary matter**, <term>Primary Matter: the most basic "stuff" of the universe before it has been given any form, shape, or qualities</term> it is trivial. For matter, insofar as it "is," is "one." Indeed, if they wish to follow the words of **Plato** to the letter, they must grant that matter has less the character of "one" than of "being." For Plato does not want matter to be "nothing" prior [to form]; otherwise, how could it be the "receptacle of forms," the "nurse," a "certain nature," and the other things he confirms it to be in the *Timaeus*? <note>original: *thi meo*. The *Timaeus* is Plato's famous dialogue on the creation of the universe</note>. It is not, therefore, "nothing"—that is, not entirely devoid of being—if we believe Plato. Yet, in the *Philebus*, <note>original: *philebo*. Another dialogue by Plato concerning pleasure and the "Good"</note> he calls this same matter not only "multitude" (which, as they wish, is opposed to the One, just as nothingness is opposed to Being) but "the infinite." 

Now, if a multitude is finite, it does not entirely escape the logic of the "One," because insofar as it is finite, it is "one" [whole]. But an **infinite multitude** lacks the true nature of the "One" just as it lacks a boundary. Therefore, according to Plato, primary matter is "being" more than it is "one." Those who argue against this, in order to prove that the "One" is higher than "Being," used to say that matter was *not* being, and yet was "one." **Iamblichus** <margin>Iamblichus.</margin> <note>Iamblichus was a Syrian Neoplatonist philosopher who influenced how later scholars interpreted Plato and Pythagoras</note>, also a Platonist, in the book he wrote *On the Pythagorean Sect*, calls primary matter "duality," because duality is the first multitude and the [source] of all others...

<meta>This page continues Pico's critique of the Platonic school, specifically addressing their views on "prime matter" and the relationship between "the One" and "Being." He transitions from a technical rebuttal into a broader explanation of the four "transcendentals"—Being, One, True, and Good—which he argues are co-extensive.</meta>

...the root of multiplicities. Therefore, **prime matter** <term>Prime matter (materia prima): the most basic, formless "stuff" that makes up the universe before it is given specific shape or identity.</term>—according to that man who is so great among the Platonists that he is called "divine" <note>Pico is likely referring to Plotinus, the 3rd-century founder of Neoplatonism.</note>—is not only not "one," but is a multitude; indeed, it is the root of all multiplicity found in things. We have said these things while confronting them with their own arguments. However, matter is not entirely devoid of unity, just as it is not entirely devoid of being. It receives its exact unity from the same source from which it receives its being: from **form** <term>Form: the organizing principle or "blueprint" that makes a thing what it is (e.g., the "form" of a chair makes wood into a chair).</term>. I pass over the various affirmative or negative disputes regarding its unity, as these are all very well known to those who have, even once, taken a little walk with **Aristotle**. <note>original: "Aristotele de ambulatiūculam fecerint." ## Chapter seven, in which he resolves the third argument of the Platonists regarding multitude, and shows that to those who say the One is something more common than Being, something must be conceded which Plato denies.

<margin>
Solution to the third argument.
</margin>

<margin>
An argument against the Platonists proving that, according to Plato, the One cannot be superior to Being.
</margin>

**T**hey are most deceived in their third argument. For multitude is not opposed to the "One" in the same way that "non-being" is opposed to "being." For being and non-being have a **contradictory opposition** <note>A contradictory opposition is "black" vs "not-black"—there is no middle ground.</note>; but the former (One and multitude) have either a **privative** or **contrary** opposition, a matter extensively debated by the Aristotelians in the tenth book of the *Metaphysics*. But let them see what ruins they fall into, those who are called Platonists and say the **One** is superior to **Being**. It is certain that whenever two categories are related so that one sits under the other as a more common term, it is possible for something to escape the lower category while still being caught by the higher one. This is exactly why the higher one is called "more common." A ready example: because "animal" is a more common term than "human," it is possible for something to be "not human" while still being an "animal." By that same reasoning, if the **One** were more common than **Being**, it would be possible for something to be "non-being" (or nothing) while still being "one." Thus, "one" would be said of "nothing"—a claim that Plato himself expressly refutes in his dialogue, *The Sophist*.

## Chapter eight, in which he declares how these four—namely Being, the One, the True, and the Good—are in all things that exist after God.

<margin>
Followers of Avicenna. Averroes. Plato.
</margin>

**T**herefore, the truest opinion is this: there are four things that encompass everything: **Being**, the **One**, the **True**, and the **Good**. This holds if they are understood such that their opposites are "nothing," "divided," "false," and "evil." To these four, two others were added—**Something** and **Thing**—by later thinkers who followed **Avicenna** <note>Avicenna (Ibn Sina) was a Persian philosopher whose work blended Aristotelianism with Islamic theology.</note>. Avicenna modified Aristotle's philosophy in many places, which led to great intellectual battles between his followers and those of **Averroes** <note>Averroes (Ibn Rushd) was a Spanish-Muslim philosopher known as "The Commentator" for his strict adherence to Aristotle; he often disagreed with Avicenna's innovations.</note>. But as far as this specific matter is concerned, there is little actual disagreement. They divide what is understood under the "One" into "One" and "Something"—an idea Plato does not reject, as he lists "Something" among these most common terms in *The Sophist*. They also divide what is contained under "Being" into "Being" and "Thing." But we shall pursue these four as we began. These four are in God in one way, and in those things created after God in another; for God has these from Himself, while created things have them from Him. Let us first see how they exist in created things. Everything after God has an **efficient**, **exemplary**, and **final** cause <note>These are types of causes: "efficient" is the maker; "exemplary" is the blueprint or Idea; "final" is the purpose for which it was made.</note>. For from Him, through Him, and toward Him are all things. If, therefore, we consider things as they are established by God as the **efficient cause**, they are called **beings**, because they participate in "being" through His action. If we consider them according to their **archetype** (which we call the **Idea**) by which God founded them, they match and respond to it; thus they are called **true**. For a statue is called a "true" image of Hercules if it conforms to the real Hercules. If they tend toward Him as toward their **ultimate end**, they are called **good**. If, however, each thing is taken absolutely according to itself, it is called **one**. Now, the order among these four is as follows:

<margin>
The order among these four.
</margin>

<meta>This page continues Pico's argument on the "transcendentals"—the universal properties of all things. Having previously discussed the One and Being, he now demonstrates how Truth and Goodness are also equal in scope to Being, responding to alternative views from the Platonic tradition.</meta>

First, each thing should be conceived under the concept of **being** <term>Being (ens): the most basic category of anything that exists.</term>, since an agent first brings each thing into existence before it is anything in itself; otherwise, it would not proceed from the agent according to the whole of what it is. From this, it follows that nothing exists after God <note>In this context, "after" refers to logical or metaphysical priority, not time.</note> which we do not understand as being "from another," "finite being," or "**participated being**" <term>Participated being: a thing that does not exist by its own power but receives its existence from a higher source (God).</term>. To "being" succeeds the "**one**." The third property is **truth**, because after something exists in itself, it must be seen whether it is such as the **exemplar** <term>Exemplar: the divine "blueprint" or ideal pattern in the mind of God according to which a thing is made.</term> to which it was formed. If it is found to be similar to that exemplar, it remains for it to turn itself toward that source—as if toward a relative or kin—through **goodness**.

<margin>Plato.</margin>
Who does not see that these properties are equal in scope? Grant that something exists, and it is certainly also "one." For he who does not say "one" says nothing, as **Plato** says in the *Sophist*. For whatever a thing is, it is undivided from itself and divided from others which are not itself; this is what we understand when we say "one."

<margin>
The True is interchangeable with Being.
</margin>
Or, to use Plato's words, it is "the same as itself and other than others," which he himself confirms in that same dialogue belongs to every single thing. It is also necessarily **true**. For if he is a man, he is certainly a "true man." It is the same as saying "this is not true gold" and "this is not gold"; for when you say it is not true

<margin>Augustine.</margin>
gold, you mean this: it certainly looks like gold and is something similar to gold, but it is not gold. For this reason, **Aurelius Augustine**, defining what the "true" is in his *Soliloquies*, says: "The true is that which is." This should not be taken to mean that "being" and "true" are the same thing; they are the same in reality, yet they are different in reason and definition. Therefore, one should not be defined by the other, but Augustine wanted to express that a thing is called "true" when it is that which it is named and said to be—as gold is "true gold" when it is gold and

<margin>
The Good is interchangeable with Being.
</margin>
not something other than gold. This is, therefore, what he meant by "the true is that which is," though some, not paying attention, have criticized this definition. Similarly, a thing is also **good**, because whatever exists,

<margin>
He disputes against Olympiodorus.
</margin>
insofar as it exists, is good. **Olympiodorus** <note>A 6th-century Neoplatonist philosopher who argued that the Good was superior to Being.</note> is far wrong, in my opinion, in believing he can prove that the "good" and "being" are different things because we desire "to be" simply, but rather "to be well"; and therefore it can happen that if we are in a bad state, we might desire not to be. But—to set aside the question of whether those who are in a bad or miserable state can seek not to exist with a right and natural desire—he does not notice that just as "being" is manifold, so "goodness" is manifold. First, there is the **natural being** of things, such as for a man to be a man, a lion to be a lion, or a stone to be a stone; a natural goodness follows this being inseparably. There are other types of being which can be called "**adventitious**" <term>Adventitious: properties that are added to a thing but are not part of its basic essence, like being "wise" or "healthy."</term>, such as for a man to be wise, to be beautiful, or to be healthy. Just as wisdom and beauty are different "beings" from humanity, so they are different "goods." The goodness by which a man is a man is one thing; the goodness of wisdom, by which he is not just a man but a wise man, is another. Just as these are different beings, they are said to be different. Therefore, just as all things seek the good, so all things seek "to be." First, they seek that goodness which follows natural being, since this is the foundation of the goodnesses that follow; all those others are added to it such that they cannot stand without it. For how will someone be happy who does not exist at all? Truly, that goodness which they attain when they first exist is not enough for them; they desire to reach the remaining ones which might complete and adorn that first one. Just as we truly say that they seek other goodnesses beyond the first, so we can truly say they desire other "beings" beyond the first—because it is one "being" to be happy, and another "being" to be a man. And if someone grants that one might not wish to exist if he were not happy, it does not follow (as Olympiodorus thinks) that the Good and Being are different; rather, it follows that "being a man" is one thing and "happiness" is another, and likewise the "goodness of a man" is one thing and the "goodness of happiness" is another.

<summary>Pico argues that Being, One, True, and Good are "interchangeable" (convertible) concepts that apply to everything that exists. He specifically refutes the Neoplatonist Olympiodorus, arguing that the desire for "well-being" (happiness) over "simple being" does not prove they are separate categories, but rather that being exists in multiple layers.</summary>

...of which a person does not want the first <note>original: "primam"; referring to the "One" or Unity.</note> unless they also possess the second. They are from a good artisan, who impresses his own likeness upon all things that come from him. 

In the **existence** <term>Entitas: the basic quality of being or existing.</term> of things, therefore, we can admire the power of God as the **efficient cause** <term>Efficient cause: the agent or force that brings something into being.</term>; in their **truth**, we can venerate the wisdom of the artisan; in their **goodness**, we can proclaim the generosity of the lover; and in their **unity**, we can look up to the unique **simplicity** <term>Simplicity: in theology, the idea that God is not composed of parts but is a single, unified essence.</term> of the Creator, so to speak. This simplicity has united each thing to itself, and all things among themselves, and yet all things back to Himself—calling each thing to the love of itself, of others, and finally of God.

<margin>Evil and nothingness are interchangeable.</margin>
Let us also examine their opposites to see if they are similarly equal in scope. What we said above shows that "falsehood" and "nothing" are the same thing. If we should say that "evil" and "nothing" differ, both philosophers and theologians will object. For this reason, doing evil is usually called "doing nothing." <margin>Against the error of the Manichaeans.</margin> It is said that evil does not have an **efficient cause**, but a **deficient cause** <note>Ficino follows Augustine here: evil isn't a "thing" created by a cause, but a "falling away" or lack of being.</note>. This confutes the insanity of those who posited two principles—one of good things and another of evil things—as if there were some efficient principle of evil. 

<margin>Nothingness and the divided are interchangeable.</margin>
But to divide a thing is the same as to destroy it. We cannot take away the natural unity of any thing without its integrity ceasing to exist. For a whole is not merely its parts, but that "one" which <margin>Aristotle</margin> springs forth from the parts, as **Aristotle** teaches in the eighth book of the *First Philosophy* <note>The *Metaphysics*.</note>. Therefore, if you divide a whole into parts, the parts indeed remain, but the whole that was divided does not remain; it ceases to exist in **act**, and exists only in **potency** <term>Act and Potency: "Act" is the current reality of a thing, while "potency" is its potential to become something else.</term>. Just as the parts, which were previously in potency, then begin to exist in act; for when they were previously in the whole, they did not have their own unity in act, which they only obtain for the first time when they subsist by themselves, separated from the whole.

### Chapter nine, in which he declares how those four are in God.

Let us examine again how these properties exist in God, in whom they do not exist in relation to a cause, for He has none; He Himself is the cause of all and is from no one. They can be considered in God by a twofold reason: either insofar as He is the cause of others (a distinction which does not apply to created things in the present matter, since God can exist without being a cause), or as He is in Himself. Other things cannot exist without being from Him. 

Therefore, we first conceive of God as the totality of all **act**, the fullness of **being** itself. **Intelligence** follows this in such a way that He is "one," so that no opposite can even be conceived. See how far they wander who imagine many first principles or many gods! Immediately, this is also most true: for what can appear to be and yet not be in Him who is **Being** itself? It follows certainly that He is Truth itself; and He will also be Goodness itself. <margin>Three conditions of the Good according to Plato.</margin> For there are three conditions of the **Good**, as **Plato** writes in the *Philebus*: it must be **perfect**, **sufficient**, and **desirable**. This which we conceive as such will be perfect because nothing will be lacking to Him who is all things; it will be sufficient because nothing will be lacking to those who possess Him, in whom they find all things.

...must be sought: because from Him and in Him are all things which can be sought for any reason. For the cause which is called the **end** <term>Final Cause: the purpose or goal for which a thing exists; in this case, God as the ultimate Good that all things desire.</term> is prior to that which is the **exemplar** <term>Exemplar Cause: the blueprint or ideal form of a thing; here, the divine ideas or Truth.</term>, and the exemplar is prior to the **efficient** <term>Efficient Cause: the agent or force that actually produces an effect; here, God's power bringing things into being.</term>. For example, we first desire to have something to protect us from the harm of storms <note>The "final cause" or goal.</note>; then we conceive the idea of a house in our mind <note>The "exemplar cause" or plan.</note>; and finally, we form it in matter by building it from the outside <note>The "efficient cause" or action.</note>. Therefore, if—as we defined in the previous chapter—Goodness relates to the final cause, Truth to the exemplar, and Being to the efficient cause, God as Cause will first have the character of the Good, then of the True, and finally of Being. We touch on these matters briefly here, for they are otherwise pregnant with many great and difficult questions.

## Chapter Ten: In which he turns the entire discussion toward the conduct of life and the improvement of morals.

<margin>Note.</margin>
But we must take care that we do not debate for the sake of others rather than ourselves. We must ensure that while we investigate the highest things, we do not live in a lowly—that is, unworthy—condition, since it has been granted to us from heaven that we are able to track the very logic of heavenly things. Instead, we should constantly meditate on this: that our mind, to which even divine things are accessible, cannot be from a mortal seed <note>original: "mortali feminio"; likely a scribal error for "semine," referring to human versus divine origins.</note>, nor will it be happy anywhere except in the possession of divine things. The more our mind wanders here as a stranger and a pilgrim, the closer it approaches happiness the more it puts aside the care of earthly things and lifts and kindles itself toward the divine. 

Our present discussion seems to warn us above all that if we wish to be happy, we must imitate the most blessed God, possessing unity, truth, and goodness within ourselves. <margin>Ambition disturbs the peace of unity.</margin> Ambition disturbs our unique peace; it snatches the soul away from itself and drags and tears it into different directions. <margin>The splendor of truth is darkened by pleasures.</margin> Who will not lose the splendor and light of truth in the mud and darkness of physical pleasures? <margin>Greed takes away goodness.</margin> A most thieving greed—that is, avarice—steals goodness from us. For it is the specific nature of goodness to share the goods you possess with others. 

Therefore, when Plato asked why God created the world, he answered himself by saying: "He was good." These are those three things: the pride of life, the lust of the flesh, and the lust of the eyes <note>A reference to 1 John 2:16.</note>. As <margin>John.</margin> John writes, these are "from the world" and are not "from the Father," who is Unity itself, Truth itself, and Goodness itself. <meta>This page concludes the philosophical exhortation of Giovanni Pico della Mirandola's "On Being and the One" and begins the formal "First Objections" raised by his critic, Antonio Cittadini of Faenza (Antonio Faventino). ...we are **one** only if we do not fail to bind together our base senses <note>Original: "curvum sensum," literally "crooked sense," referring to the downward-looking nature of physical desires.</note> and our heaven-gazing reason through a pact of virtue. Otherwise, two conflicting principles reign within us at intervals: while we follow God through the law of the mind at one moment, and then follow Baal <note>A biblical reference to a false god, here representing carnal or worldly idols.</note> through the law of the flesh at another, our kingdom—divided against itself—is surely laid waste. When we do not fall away from our divine archetype through **truth**, it remains for us to be eventually joined to Him by striving toward Him through **goodness**. Since these three—**Truth**, **Goodness**, and the **One**—follow **Being** in a perpetual bond, it follows that when we lack those three, we utterly cease to "be." Even if we seem to exist and are believed to be alive, we are actually dying continually rather than living.

## THE FIRST OBJECTIONS OF ANTONIO OF FAENZA AGAINST THE BOOKLET ON BEING AND THE ONE.

<margin>First objection.</margin>
If any booklet deserves to be titled *On Being and the One*, it must necessarily explain the nature and properties of both "being" and "the one." However, in this little work that recently came into my hands, and which is titled *On Being and the One*, several matters are discussed that are almost foreign to that title. The author’s primary goal is to argue whether, according to Plato, **being** and **the one** follow each other interchangeably <note>This refers to the "convertibility" of transcendentals: the idea that anything that "is" is also "one," and vice-versa.</note>, or whether (as the Academics <term>Academics: The followers of the Platonic Academy, who often emphasized the transcendence of "the One" above all categories of "Being."</term> think) the **One** is more universal than **Being**. But this is not a general treatment of "being" and "the one"; it is merely a discussion of their mutual conversion—and even then, only according to Plato. If a philosopher were to discuss only the question of whether the soul is immortal, he would not be writing "On the Soul" in general; rather, it would be <margin>Second objection.</margin> a treatise specifically on the **immortality** of the soul. Furthermore, the author of the work claims that the Academics believe that, according to Plato, God is not truly and properly "being." This I find greatly surprising. If he means *all* Academics or Platonists (as his wording suggests), and unless he qualifies his statement, his claim may not be free from falsehood. <margin>Themistius.</margin> For Themistius, a notable authority among the Platonists, testifies that the "Idea" which is the principle of all things is, in Plato's opinion, truly and properly **Being** and **One**. Most Platonists do not think the "Idea" is one thing and God the Creator another.

<margin>Third objection.</margin>
Continuing, the author says: "If it can be defended in any way that, according to Plato, the **One** is more universal than **Being**, it must be judged thus: those terms which in Latin are called 'concrete' names <term>Concrete names: In scholastic logic, terms like "white" or "shining" that imply a subject possessing a quality (whiteness), as opposed to the quality itself.</term>—such as *bright*, *shining*, or *being*—signify something external, by whose presence things obtain their name. For whiteness is one thing, and 'bright' is another; a man is one thing, and 'humanity' another. Therefore, 'Being' shall be the name for that in which 'to be' <note>Original: "esse," the act of existing.</note> is one thing and the underlying subject <note>Original: "quod subsistit."</note> is another. God, therefore, who is Existence itself, cannot be considered 'Being,' but rather 'the One,' since He contains and encloses all things." But does not this defense itself lack internal coherence?

<summary>This page concludes Pico della Mirandola's spiritual argument that humans only truly "exist" when aligned with divine truth and goodness, then transitions into the formal academic critiques by Antonio of Faenza regarding the definitions of Being and the One.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the "First Objections" raised by Antonio Cittadini against Giovanni Pico della Mirandola's treatise "On Being and the One." The previous page argued that for human reason to be true, it must align with God, the ultimate Truth. Here, the critic begins a technical scholastic deconstruction of Pico’s claim that God is "The One" but not "Being," using the logic of Aristotle and Thomas Aquinas to challenge the distinction.</meta>

For by the same reasoning that "white" and "man" and "being" signify something different from one another, it must also be that "one," "blessed," "God," and many similar terms signify something different. Therefore God, who is at once unity, blessedness, and deity, could not be called "one," nor "blessed," nor even "God" at all. How then is He not "being," but only "the One"?

<margin>
Third
Confirmation.
</margin>
Furthermore, "being" <term>Being: *ens*, the most general category of existence.</term> is so named because it *is*. Just as it is impossible for someone who sits not to be sitting, it also cannot be that He who truly and properly *is* is not "being." For God says: "I am who I am." <note>Exodus 3:14. Scholastic philosophers used this biblical verse to argue that God's very essence is "to be."</note> It may seem even more remarkable that he <note>Referring to Pico della Mirandola.</note> tries to defend the idea that God is not "being" not only according to Plato, but he even tries to pull Aristotle himself into the same opinion. For in [the relevant] book of the *Metaphysics*, Aristotle divides "being" into "being by itself" <term>Being by itself: *ens per se*, things that exist as independent entities or categories.</term> and "being by accident" <term>Being by accident: *ens per accidens*, qualities like "color" that only exist by being attached to something else.</term>. "Being by itself" is divided into the ten categories <note>Aristotle’s *Categories* (Praedicamenta) are the ten ways anything can be described, such as Substance, Quantity, or Quality.</note>. But the author says that God cannot be placed in any genus <note>A "genus" is a general class. Pico argued God is above all classes, while the critic here debates if God can be classified as "Substance."</note>, just as he thinks Blessed Thomas [Aquinas] has shown. If, therefore, God is neither "being by itself" nor "being by accident," then according to Aristotle, He will not be "being" at all. Furthermore, "being" is separated into "substance" and "accident" according to the most common division. But God is neither an accident nor a substance; for the author says that "substance" is a genus, and God exceeds the limits of any genus. But for my part, I do not see by what reasoning the author is led to ascribe a Platonic opinion to our Aristotle—if, indeed, it even is Plato’s opinion.

<margin>Saint Thomas.</margin>
The division of "being" into "being by itself" and "being by accident" is a division of "complex being," as the Blessed Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas, the 13th-century theologian who harmonized Aristotle with Christianity.</note>—to whom the author grants much authority—subtly writes in that passage. The same is clear from examples: <margin>Aristotle.</margin> for "being by accident," according to Aristotle, is threefold: either an accident is predicated of a subject, or a subject of an accident, or an accident of an accident. All of these involve "complexity" <term>Complexity: *complexio*, a logical term for when multiple concepts are joined in a single statement.</term>. In the same way, those things are called "beings by itself" in which something is predicated that belongs either to substance, or to quantity, or to another genus, provided that what is predicated belongs to the subject by itself—as "white" belongs to Socrates, but not to "man" in general, or to "horse" in other cases. However, the division of "being" into "substance" and "accident" also encompasses God. For it is a division made through affirmation and negation: for "substance" is that which rests upon nothing but exists by itself, while "accident" is that which exists in another as if in a subject. Between these two, there is no middle ground, as Blessed Thomas believes; for indeed, no middle ground can be thought of between "having a subject" and "not having a subject." Therefore, "substance," as it is opposed to "accident," will not be a genus.

<margin>
Fourth
Confirmation.
</margin>
If God is contained in no genus. Furthermore, it is not the undisputed opinion of Aristotle that God is contained in no genus "by Himself" <term>By Himself: *per se*.</term>. For there are some followers of Aristotle who think that God is placed "by Himself" within a category. And I, for my part, believe the distinguished philosopher Boethius <margin>Boethius</margin> was of this opinion; and I could demonstrate, if it were necessary, that this can be aptly gathered from the words of Boethius <margin>Augustine.</margin> and even Augustine.

<margin>Fifth Confirmation</margin>
Again, the author says that "the divided" is the negation of "the one," which he proves by the fact that a thing is destroyed when it is pulled apart and divided. But how can "the divided" be opposed to "the one" as a negation? Between affirmation and negation, there is a contradiction. A chimera <note>A mythical beast used in logic to represent something non-existent or impossible.</note>, for instance, is neither "one" nor "divided"; nor is this statement—"that the diagonal [of a square] is commensurable"—either "one" or "divided." <note>In geometry, it is a proven truth that the diagonal and side of a square are incommensurable. A false mathematical statement, like a chimera, lacks real existence and thus cannot be logically "one."</note>

<margin>Sixth.</margin>
He also thinks that "the false" is the negation of "the true"; though this might be defended in some way, <margin>Blessed Thomas.</margin> yet it is a "contrary" rather than a "negation," as Blessed Thomas shows. For a chimera is neither true nor false, unless we completely abuse the term. For "true" is "that which is"—that is, as he himself explains, that which *is* what it appears and is said to be. Therefore, "false" will be that which *is not* what it appears and is said to be—such as a "false coin." Nothing, therefore, happens to be false unless it *appears*...

Therefore, good and evil will be contraries, which Boethius <note>An influential 6th-century philosopher whose commentaries on Aristotle were standard textbooks in the Middle Ages.</note> also asserts in the *Categories*, whatever others might have said about the matter.

->Response to the First Objections.<-

## GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA SENDS GREETINGS TO ANTONIO FAVENTINO.

**I** read your questions against that little book which I recently published *On Being and the One* <note>original: "de ente & uno"</note> with as much pleasure as they were written by you with both affection and freedom of spirit. I owe you a great deal on account of this service. Indeed, if we either bestowed such freedom upon our friends or more willingly demanded it from them, we would certainly be far better and more learned than we are. But this deadly persuasion has seized the minds of men: that we think we do not please those who are not pleased by our errors. We interpret the free judgment of friends as hatred or moodiness, while we interpret flattery as love and natural goodness. Thus it happens that while we prefer to be praised—even when undeserving—rather than be corrected when we deserve it, we are mocked; we always seek praise, but never deserve it. See how much we err! For almost all praise is always useless, and often harmful. For if it is true, what utility does it bring? If it is false, it surely makes us who are praised insane, and those who praise us ridiculous. Reproof is certainly always useful: if it is just, it rouses us to knowledge; if it is less than just, it rouses us to the defense of the truth. Finally, what else is it to be corrected than to become better through another's labor? Or what else is it for a friend's book to shine under the file <note>The "file" (*lima*) was a common classical metaphor for the painstaking process of editing and polishing a text.</note> than for you to profit from his sleepless nights while you yourself sleep? I cannot, therefore, as I was saying, help but owe you a great deal—you, who have freely indicated to me what you felt about those things in my book which pleased you less. I recognized in your writings, besides your benevolence, that dexterity of intellect which has long been known to me. I immediately began to examine more severely whatever you had noted—not as a father <note>i.e., not as the protective "parent" of the text.</note>, but as a judge—inasmuch as your testimony had already brought me to a suspicion of falsehood. But as I was thinking, several points occurred to me by which those things seemed able to be defended and vindicated from fault. I wanted to write these back to you freely, lest I should perhaps embrace that virtue of yours which I praise less in myself; so that, if I do not imitate your judgment in criticizing those things, I might at least imitate your freedom in defending them. You say that the book is not correctly titled *On Being and the One*, since you do not deal in it with all the natures and properties of

To me, Antonio, it usually seems that two things are set before books as a kind of vestibule: the Title and the Preface. The Title is a short Preface; the Preface is a Title poured out and explained. The title promises a treatise on Being and the One, which...

<meta>This page continues Giovanni Pico della Mirandola’s letter to Antonio Cittadini (Antonio Faventino). Pico is defending his treatise On Being and the One against the charge that his claim—that God is "above being"—is unorthodox or un-Platonic. He clarifies the positions of various Neoplatonists to show that his synthesis of Plato and Aristotle is grounded in traditional interpretation.</meta>

...Moreover, the preface explains why "on being and the one" <note>original: "de ente & uno"</note> must be treated. But if this were done in the title, it is to be feared lest the title of the book becomes a book itself. This could be defended by the precedent of a thousand authors whose prefixed titles to their books would suffer the same accusation. But that question is not of such weight that either you or I should be occupied with it any longer. 

<margin>Solution to the second objection</margin>
You wonder, furthermore, that I said it was believed by the Platonists that God is not, strictly speaking, **being** <term>ens: a technical term for 'a being' or 'that which exists.' In Scholastic and Platonic thought, there is a distinction between 'Being itself' and 'a being' that participates in existence.</term>. Do not wonder at me, but at those whom I, along with you, do not approve in the assertion of this dogma; yet it is most known to all who have read Platonic works that they felt this way—which seems almost incredible to you—and left it written for posterity. 

<margin>Syrianus, Proclus, Plotinus, Themistius</margin>
Syrianus, Proclus, Plotinus, and finally all the extant interpreters of Plato confirm this with one voice. But, you say, **Themistius** (not ignoble among the Platonists) asserts that, according to Plato's opinion, the **Idea** is truly and properly being and one; and the Platonists (either all or most) think the **Idea** is nothing other than the Craftsman God <note>The "Demiurge" or creator figure in Plato's Timaeus.</note>. Wherefore, if the Idea is properly called being, God himself will also be properly called being.

You argue this quite ingeniously, but see whether you do so with enough skill. For they—namely Proclus and Plotinus—confess that the Idea is and is called being; but they contend that just as God is above beings, so he is above the Ideas. 

<margin>Plotinus's opinion on the Ideas</margin>
For Plotinus placed all the Ideas in that Mind <note>The "Nous" or Divine Intellect, the second principle in the Neoplatonic hierarchy.</note> which is closest to God, which he calls the "first being," the "first intelligible," and the "first life," so that God is not the harbor of Ideas, but their source; not their receptacle, but their principle. 

<margin>The opinion of Proclus on the Ideas; Syrianus, Amelius, Iamblichus</margin>
Proclus makes not just one but many orders of minds intermediate between God and the Ideas, whose fullness—imitating Plato's words in the *Timaeus*—he called the **Living Being in itself** <note>original: "per se animal"</note>. I pass over Syrianus, Amelius, Iamblichus, and many others who feel the same. These are the rudiments and, as it were, the nursery-cradle of that doctrine which is considered Platonic. 

But if someone grants you that the Idea and God are not different in reality, you will nonetheless not deny that they are different in reason <note>Meaning they are conceptually distinct even if they refer to the same entity.</note>. 

<margin>Another solution</margin>
This diversity will sufficiently allow that God, insofar as he is the exemplar <note>The perfect pattern or blueprint.</note> of man, horse, or lion, can truly be called **being**; but insofar as he regards nothing outside himself and has no relationship to created things, but remains solitary in the retreat of his own divinity, he exceeds every name of being and has neither name nor opinion, as **Dionysius** says. 

<margin>Dionysius</margin>
Wherefore it is most manifest even among the leaders of the Academy <note>The school of Plato.</note> that God cannot properly be called being; and if anyone grants that the Idea and God are the same in reality, it does not immediately follow that if the Idea is being, God must also be called being properly. 

<margin>Solution to the third objection</margin>
Let us move to other matters, among which this displeases you most: that I said there is a certain way of speaking which, if we follow it, we can truly say that **the One** is higher than **being**. For we can give the name of "the One" to God in such a way that we do not give him the name of "being"; because "being" has the appearance of a **concrete noun** (to use the Latin term) and it signifies that which participates in existence from another—which cannot be said of God, who is **existence itself** <note>original: "ipsum esse"</note>. 

By the same reasoning, you say, he cannot be called "the One," because "one"—namely, in its concrete form—is a noun just as "being" is. I both saw and resolved this question when I was writing; for as soon as I proved that "being" (because it signifies that which is not of itself but through participation in another) cannot be predicated of God, I added that since the name of "the One" is given to God, it follows that we must confess "the One" is above "being." And immediately after this, meeting your objection, I added: "We call God 'the One' then, not so much stating *what* he is, as *how* he is all things that he is, and how all things are from him." 

<margin>Dionysius</margin>
For God is called "one," says **Dionysius**, because he is all things singularly; and again he is called "one" because he is the principle of all things that exist, just as [the one is] the principle of all numbers...

...unity is. I said this there word for word. If, therefore, when we call God "one," we wish to declare what He is, I admit to you that He cannot be called "one" for the same reason that He cannot be called **being** <term>ens: a technical term for 'a being' or 'that which exists'</term>, because both are clearly concrete names. > These names—**being**, **true**, **one**, and **good**—denote something concrete and, as it were, participated. Therefore, we say again that God is above being, above truth, above unity, and above goodness, because He is Being itself, Truth itself, Unity itself, and Goodness itself.

So I said there.

It did not escape me, then, when I was writing, that both **being** <term>ens</term> and **one** <term>unum</term> are equally concrete, and by reason of their concreteness, either neither or both equally should be removed from God. But as I warned above: when we say God is "one" but not "being," we signify not *what* God is, but *how* He is that which He is: namely, because He is all things in the most primary and simple way. This manner can in no way be indicated or represented by the name "being," but it can be by the symbol and title of "unity":

<margin>Aristotle.</margin>
For beings relate to each other as numbers do, as **Aristotle** writes: and of numbers, the most primary and most simple is unity. 

<margin>Solution to the fourth objection.</margin>
You add that you wonder that I wish to defend the idea that God is not **being**, not only according to **Plato**, but also according to **Aristotle**. But if you have run through the book more attentively, I mainly endeavor in this whole work to show that God both is and is called **being** in the proper sense, not only from the dogma of **Aristotle** but also from **Plato**, and consequently that "the one" is not superior to **being**. However, lest those who said God is not "being" but "above being" should seem entirely insane: 

<margin>

</margin>
Among these men—even if **Plato** and **Aristotle** are not included—there is certainly **Dionysius the Areopagite** <note>A 5th-6th century Christian theologian and philosopher whose works were highly influential in the Middle Ages.</note>, who is greater than both. I have tried to prove that there is a certain mode of speaking <note>original: "locutionis rationem"</note> which, if we follow it, will not be out of tune with the truth: namely, that God is greater than the name of "being." This mode is even sometimes used by the **Peripatetics** <term>Peripatetics: Followers of Aristotle's school of philosophy.</term>; though you might shrink from it, you cannot deny it unless you deny the authority of those to whom, in your own opinion, the first place in that family belongs. For who does not know that the division of being into **substance** <term>substantia: that which exists in itself</term> and **accident** <term>accidens: a quality that exists only in another thing, like a color or a size</term> is frequent among the Aristotelians? 

<margin>Thomas.</margin>

These are roughly Thomas's words: 

> God is neither **accident** nor can He properly be called **substance**, both because substance is called substance because it "stands under" <note>original: "substat"; the root of the word 'substantia'</note> and because substance indicates a "what-ness" <note>quiddity</note> which is different from its being. Therefore, that division of being into substance and accident is a division of **created being**. 

So he says. 

<margin>How it has been proved that God can be properly called "being."</margin>
Furthermore, when **Aristotle** says that the primary philosopher deals with "being insofar as it is being" and the causes and principles of being, there are many among the **Peripatetics** who maintain that God is not placed there by **Aristotle** among *beings*, but among the *causes of being*. 

<margin>Solution to the confirmation</margin>

I do not know, however, why you—always an imitator of illustrious authors—now desert the most famous **Peripatetics** for those who place God under a genus, among whom **Boethius** <margin>Boethius.</margin> certainly did not wish to be numbered...

<meta>This page continues Giovanni Pico della Mirandola’s defense of his treatise On Being and the One. Pico is responding to point-by-point objections from an opponent (likely Antonio Civitella) regarding the nature of the "transcendentals"—the philosophical categories of Being, One, True, and Good. He is currently arguing that unity and being are essentially the same, and that their opposites (division and non-being) are likewise linked.</meta>

<margin>Solution to the fifth objection</margin>
...I do not doubt. Finally, you contend that the "divided" is not the negation of the **one**; nor the "false" the negation of the **true**; nor "evil" the negation of the **good**. Indeed, I know that the controversy regarding these oppositions is not an easy one among great authors, and for that reason, I ended the book in which I treated these matters in passing with that very clause. I briefly touch upon all these things here; otherwise, they are the seeds of many and great questions. However, as for doubting that the opinion I followed is less probable or true: the things you object do not move me at all.

You say the **Chimera** <note>In philosophy, the Chimera—a mythical beast made of a lion, goat, and serpent—is the standard example of an "impossible object": something we can imagine but which cannot exist because its definition is self-contradictory.</note> is neither "one" nor "divided." I, however, say that the Chimera we conceive in the mind does not exist precisely because the parts from which we understand it to consist are **divided** in the nature of things, and are not **united**. And just as a thing does not exist if its constituent parts are divided, so also does a thing not only not exist, but *cannot* exist, if its parts are neither united nor can be united by the force of nature.

Therefore, we say the Chimera not only does not exist, but we believe it cannot possibly come to be, for no other reason than that it is not credible that the diverse beasts from which we fashion it would ever merge into a single animal composition. Again, you insist that because a diameter is **incommensurable** <note>This refers to a famous mathematical problem: the diagonal of a square cannot be expressed as a simple ratio of its sides (it is an irrational number). Pico’s opponent used this to argue for a type of "division" that isn't just a simple negation of existence.</note>, it is neither "one" nor "divided." You are mistaken, in my opinion. For by the same reasoning that a thing is **false**, it is necessarily **divided** in itself. For something is detected as false only to the extent that it fights with itself and includes a contradiction. And what else is it to include a contradiction than to be divided within itself? Every **truth**, therefore, is **one**, because it is consistent and harmonious with itself; every **falsehood** is **divided**, because it fights with itself and does not cohere with itself.

<margin>Solution to the sixth objection</margin>
Many have believed that the **false** is the negation of the **true**, which is something that does not escape you either; nor do the arguments you bring forward stand in the way. For as I said, we call "false" that which is not what it seems to be: just as **false gold** is that which seems to be gold but is not gold. And although false gold is not only "not gold" but is also something *other* than gold <note>For example, it might actually be brass or lead.</note>, it happens to it—insofar as it is false—to be something else besides gold; but it is false specifically because it is **not gold**, despite appearing to be. Therefore, it is "false gold" because it does not match the **idea** <term>idea: the perfect, mental or divine archetype of a thing</term> of gold. But because it matches the idea of bronze or silver, it is not *entirely* false; it is only "false gold," just as it is not entirely **non-being** <term>non ens: that which has no existence at all</term>. For although it is not that which is gold, it is nevertheless something else: say, bronze, lead, or silver. 

<margin>What constitutes absolute falsehood</margin> 
However, that which corresponds to **no idea** is entirely and absolutely **false**, just as it is also entirely **non-being**—such as that which we call a Chimera. See, therefore, how they proceed in equal pace: **non-being**, the **divided**, and the **false**. And thus both the Chimera may rightly be called false, and every false thing may rightly be called divided.

<margin>Solution to the seventh objection. Albert. Thomas.</margin>
But that **evil** does not oppose **good** by a "contrary opposition" <note>In logic, a "contrary" is an opposite that exists (like black vs. white), whereas Pico argues evil is a "privation" or "negation" (like blindness is the absence of sight), meaning evil has no independent existence of its own.</note>, as you think: both **Albert** <note>Albertus Magnus (c. 1200–1280), a teacher of Thomas Aquinas and a major authority on Aristotle.</note> teaches when explaining Aristotle's *Categories*, and your **Thomas** <note>Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274). Pico calls him "your Thomas" to appeal to his opponent’s likely Scholastic training.</note> most extensively in the first question of his work *On Evil*. All of which I believe have long been very well known to you.
