-># GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA. ANTONIO CITTADINO.<-

* **Y**ou yourself are witness, most excellent man, to how much I have loved you and always honored you.*
*You can easily remember how diligently and exceptionally I have devoted my efforts to you, if you so*
*wish. But if you now either doubt or in no way believe that you are loved by Antonio, your old friend and godfather, then by Hercules, you have poorly remembered my respect for you. For how could it be that I, who loved and honored you when you were scarcely initiated into philosophy, would not love and admire you now that you are distinguished in learning and integrity? Would that all who have lived familiarly with you had embraced you with an equal benevolence as that with which your godfather has always followed his own Pico. But let us now come to our business. You say that your little book *On Being and the One* <note>original: "de ente & uno"</note> could be aptly titled so, even if the title of the work is short; and although it puts forward a treatise on being and the one, the prologue (which is a more expansive title) explains what kind of treatise it promises: namely, the mutual*
<margin>First objection.</margin> *interchangeability <note>The philosophical concept that "Being" and "the One" are the same thing viewed from different angles.</note> of being and the one. But see, I pray, whether this defense of yours is sufficient. For by the same*
*reason, if a little book were published in which only the immortality of the soul was asserted by the author, it could rightly be titled *On the Soul*. The author of the work, entering into the dispute, would soon perhaps propose the question by asking whether the soul is immortal or not. Indeed, this objection was almost entirely explained in my previous letter, but in my judgment, you responded with nothing. Furthermore, if a question were raised concerning the velocity of motions, as to whether it follows an arithmetic or geometric*
*proportion, and at the beginning of the work the author promises he will take many things from geometry,*
<margin>Second objection.</margin> *the little book could be titled *On Geometry*, even though it was actually concerned with motion. But let us omit these things as if they were trifles. If indeed Themistius <note>A 4th-century philosopher and statesman who commented extensively on Aristotle and Plato.</note>, among the Platonists, being not ignoble, affirms according to the opinion of Plato that the **Idea** <note>In Platonic thought, the "Idea" or "Form" is the perfect, eternal pattern of which worldly things are mere shadows.</note> which is the principle of things is truly and properly **Being**, it should not have been absolutely pronounced that the Platonists, following Plato, think that God is not truly and properly Being; for the Idea is God. You, however, respond that the Idea is one thing and God is another; and even if it were granted that the Idea is God, it does not necessarily follow from this that God is properly and truly Being. For God and the Idea, even if they do not differ in reality <note>original: "re"</note>, differ nevertheless in reason <note>original: "ratione" — meaning a distinction made by human logic rather than a physical difference.</note>. But I would not wish to dispute in this*
*place whether the Platonists think God is one thing and the Idea another, since that question is far removed from the purpose—even though very many authors, both Greek and Latin, following Plato, place the Ideas of Plato in God. I seem to have done enough for the purpose by showing*
*that a certain Platonist, and by no means an ignoble one, asserts according to Plato that the*
*Idea—and therefore God—is truly and properly Being. Nor does that distinction of reason*
*to which you take refuge do anything in this matter. For the "Idea" is a relative term, but "God" is an absolute thing. If, therefore, God is truly and properly Being in that part by which He is referred to externally, how much more ought He to be considered Being by that reason by which He is God and consists in His own nature? For why is the Idea, by that reason by which it is an Idea, truly and properly Being? No reason, I say, can be assigned unless it is said to be truly and properly*
*Being because it truly and properly **is**. Therefore, God, by that reason by which He is God, will much more be truly and properly Being; for He said, "I am who I am" <note>A reference to Exodus 3:14, where God reveals His name to Moses, often used by medieval philosophers to prove God is the essence of Being itself.</note>. Furthermore, it was objected in this way: if Plato...*

<meta>This page continues the philosophical debate between Antonio Cittadino and Giovanni Pico della Mirandola. The discussion focuses on whether God can be properly called "Being" (Ens) and "Substance" (Substantia), or if such terms are too restrictive for the divine nature. Cittadino is challenging Pico's views by citing authorities like Aristotle, Thomas Aquinas, Boethius, and Augustine.</meta>

...nor, therefore, can those be rightly defended who claim that God is not truly and properly **being**, but rather **the one**. Their argument is that the name "being" <note>original: "ens"</note> is a "concrete" term—one that implies a subject possessing a quality—which suggests something distinct from that which is "one." However, if it can be gathered that God is not **being** because He is uniquely everything that exists, then by that same logic, one could argue that God is not **the one**, for "one" is also a concrete name. Furthermore, He would be neither **blessed** nor **God**, as both of these words are also concrete. 

You respond, however, that God is not called "one" as if the substance of God were being pointed out by the name of "one," but rather to explain the manner in which He is that which He is. But I ask: to what purpose is this? You have not yet solved the objection. You say God is not **being** but **the one** because the name of "being" is concrete. If, therefore, "one" is also concrete, must it not be concluded by the same reasoning that God is not **the one**? Nor would He be **God**—a name which pertains to substance just as **being** does. 

Furthermore, if He is "one" because He is uniquely that which He is, why should He not also be called **being**? For in being "one," He is all that He is: namely, wisdom, goodness, and power. He is not called "one" simply because He is alone. Therefore, by the same reasoning, He can be called **being**, even if He is not the only being; for He is, in fact, "most being" <note>original: "maxime ens," meaning the highest or most complete form of existence</note>. 

Besides, that reasoning which was stated thus has not yet been refuted: God truly and properly **is**; and "being" is said of that which "is," <margin>Confirmation</margin> just as "sitting" is said of one who sits. Therefore, God is truly and properly **being**. For He Himself says, "I am who I am" <note>A reference to Exodus 3:14, where God reveals His name to Moses</note>. 

Again, I was amazed that you would defend the idea—also according to Aristotle—that God is sometimes not considered under the name of **being** because He is neither being "through Himself" <note>original: "per se"</note> nor "by accident" <note>original: "per accidens"</note>, and neither "substance" nor "accident." Indeed, I have shown that God is neither being through Himself nor by accident, and that no middle ground can be imagined between **substance** and **accident** <note>In Aristotelian logic, everything that exists is either a "substance" (a thing that exists on its own, like a tree) or an "accident" (a quality that exists in something else, like the color green). Cittadino argues there is no third option.</note>. 

You, however, offer no response to the first objection. Against the second, you cite only one interpreter of Aristotle: namely, **Blessed Thomas** [Aquinas], who says that God is not properly a **substance** because He does not "stand under" <note>A literal translation of the Latin "sub-stare," the root of "substantia"</note> any accident, nor is the essence of God anything different from God Himself. 

But see, most excellent man, whether Thomas might actually bear witness against you. For if the division of "being" into **substance** and **accident** is a division of *created* being according to Blessed Thomas (as you report), then how can it be ignored that there is such a thing as *uncreated* being, which is God? By what reasoning, then, can you maintain—following the interpretation of St. Thomas—that Aristotle thought God is not properly and truly **being**? 

Even if St. Thomas seems in a certain place to deny that God is properly a **substance** (imitating the *Master of the Sentences* <note>Peter Lombard, the author of the standard medieval theology textbook</note> because God does not "under-lie" any accident), it is not for that reason false what I wrote in the earlier letter: that there is no middle ground between substance and accident. St. Thomas himself proves this in many places with effective arguments, and you have not refuted a single one of the points written to you. 

If, therefore, he sometimes denies that God is a **substance**, the very words you cite clearly reveal the man's mind. For "substance" can be said in many ways (which he himself explains more broadly in the first part). Sometimes, "substance" is properly so called because it stands under accidents; for this reason, he denies God is a substance—not simply and absolutely, but he says He is not "properly" a substance because He underlies no accident. Yet "substance" is also sometimes said of that which exists through itself and does not need a subject; in this way, St. Thomas uses the name "substance" sometimes, and indeed frequently. 

Thus, no middle ground can be thought of between substance and accident: for it is a division of both through affirmation and negation. As for the fact that—led by no necessity but of my own accord—I affirmed (following the opinion of Boethius and Augustine) that God is placed "through Himself" in a **category** <note>original: "praedicamento," referring to the ten categories of being defined by Aristotle</note>: I did not say this because I do not hold Blessed Thomas in high esteem, or do not venerate or approve of him. Rather, I said it because the authority of St. Thomas alone is not sufficient to demonstrate that either Aristotle or the Aristotelians thought God is by no means placed in a category. Nor have I, for that reason, defected from the best authors to the wicked and common ones; on the contrary, I follow and approve of the best. Do you make Blessed Thomas equal or superior to Boethius or Augustine? I, for my part, have read them all for a long time and...

<margin>The third principal objection.</margin>
I read daily; nor do I think any man of vigorous intellect either ignores or neglects those things which have been devised by our British scholars—I mean **Swineshead** <note>original: "Suisset." Richard Swineshead (fl. 1340–1354), known as "the Calculator," was a prominent member of the Oxford Calculators at Merton College, famous for applying mathematics to philosophical problems.</note> and his like. To be sure, I do not approve of or admire everything written by them; indeed, I am often accustomed to weaken several of their points—and not a few, by Hercules!—according to the opinion of **Aristotle** and other approved authors. Yet, I cannot help but marvel at the great subtlety of these men and their most acute <term>reasons in physical matters</term> <note>original: "acutissimas in rebus physicis rones." Refers to the "calculatory" tradition of physics that preceded the Scientific Revolution.</note>. Even Aristotle himself, if he were to rise from the dead, would admire them and extol their subtlety in the highest degree, approving it in most cases even if he did not approve of its truth.

You defend, moreover, the idea that the negation of the "one" is the "divided." You say a **chimera** <note>In logic, a chimera represents an "impossible object" composed of contradictory parts.</note> is "divided" because the parts of which it would consist, if it existed, are divided from one another and cannot be united. You think a **commensurable diameter** <note>original: "Dyametrum uero cōmēsurabilē." A classic example of a mathematical impossibility; the diagonal of a square cannot be measured by the same units as its sides.</note> is "divided" because it is divided from itself and is discordant. These are the words you use: "for a thing is detected to be false only insofar as it fights against itself and includes a contradiction." But what else is it to "include a contradiction" than to be divided within itself? Therefore, every **truth** is "one" because it is consistent and harmonious with itself; every **falsehood** is "divided" because it fights with itself and is not coherent with itself.

But see how you can sustain your position. For if something is "one" because it is harmonious with itself and undivided from itself, then falsehood itself and the impossible will be both "one" and "true." I am not saying that this falsehood or that—such as a "chimera" or a "flying stag"—is true, but I am considering the very nature of falsehood and the impossible itself. I shall prove this nature to be both "one" and "true." According to your dogma, a chimera is "divided" because its parts are always divided from one another; it is also divided because it is divided from itself. For a chimera is not a chimera, and by the same reasoning, for a diameter to be commensurable is "divided," for in no other way can it be understood that each of these is discordant with itself and fights against itself. 

But if you look at **falsehood** itself separately, falsehood is falsehood, and the **impossible** is impossible. Neither, therefore, fights against itself; neither is discordant with itself. By the same reasoning, the dead do not fight against themselves at all; for they are dead who are already dead. Therefore, any of these things is "one" and "true" if a thing is "one" because it is undivided from itself. Furthermore, how is it true that everything that is false "encloses a contradiction"? Are there not many things that are false which, by the power of nature or of man, could be true? 

You attempt again to defend the definition of **truth** put forward by you, and you say that the "true" is that which is seen to be what it is, while the "false" is that which is seen to be what it is not. Now, for this reason, you think it can be gathered that falsehood is not the negation of truth. But, by your leave, I would say you have so far said nothing in response to my argument. The argument is this: If the "true" is that which is seen to be what it is, and the "false" is that which is seen to be what it is not, since there is no contradiction between "being seen to be what is" and "being seen to be what is not," then falsehood will not be the negation of truth. For if neither man nor God existed in the nature of things, **Socrates** would not exist. Thus, he would not be seen as what he was, nor as what he was not. Therefore, he would be neither true nor false, but he would be "non-being." Therefore, "non-being" and "falsehood" sometimes disagree.

**Blessed Thomas** <note>St. Thomas Aquinas.</note>, whom you do not oppose, pronounces that truth and falsehood are contraries to each other if they are referred to the mind—upon which your opinion of the nature of truth and falsehood also depends. He says: "true and false estimations are contraries to one another," just as **Aristotle** says. Finally, you deny that **good** and **evil** are contraries to one another, and you do not respond to the reason by which it was proved that they are contraries; nor do you explain how evil is the negation of good. For I said this: I do not deny that those things, especially those which embrace things that do not exist, can be a genus. For in the **Topics** <note>Aristotle's *Topica*, a treatise on the art of dialectic.</note>, it is said by Aristotle that there are no genera or species of non-being. Therefore, **evil**, which embraces all such things, cannot be a genus. How then did Aristotle, that greatest of men, say in the **Categories** <note>original: "p̄dica," referring to the *Praedicamenta* or *Categories*.</note>...

<meta>This page continues the philosophical exchange between Antonio Cittadino, a physician from Ferrara, and the famous philosopher Giovanni Pico della Mirandola. You mention that good and evil are types of contraries. You also say that **Albert** <note>original: "Albertū." Albertus Magnus (c. 1200–1280), a dominant figure in medieval scholasticism and the teacher of Thomas Aquinas.</note>, whom I think holds great weight with you, denies that good and evil are contraries to one another; and that the blessed **Thomas** <note>original: "beatus Tho." St. Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274).</note> feels the same in the first question *On Evil* <note>original: "de malo." Referencing Aquinas's work *Quaestiones Disputatae de Malo*.</note>. Referring to Aristotle's *Categories*, which Boethius translated and commented upon.</note> that good and evil are mutually contrary. 

I say, therefore, once again and I affirm, that good and evil are mutually contrary—not in the way that white and black, or hot and cold are (which are all true qualities), but in the same way as healthy and sick, strong and weak, rare and dense, beautiful and ugly, and many similar things. Nor does the blessed Thomas deny this; rather, that most eminent man, in the first question *On Evil* regarding the solution to the second argument, shows how good and evil—even if they oppose each other by way of <term>privation and habit</term> <note>original: "priuatiōis & hītus." A technical distinction in Scholastic logic: a "habit" (habitus) is a positive quality, while "privation" is the lack of a quality that should naturally be present (like blindness in an eye).</note>—are nonetheless usually counted among the contraries. He confirms this by the authority of **Simplicius** <note>A 6th-century Neoplatonist commentator on Aristotle.</note>. 

Therefore, my objections—which were thought up solely for the sake of searching for the truth and for our mutual charity—do not yet seem to me to be entirely weakened. I ask, therefore, and I beseech you, by that love with which you endeavored to open the truth of the Platonic doctrine to your **Angelo Poliziano** <note>A renowned Renaissance humanist, poet, and close friend of Pico.</note>, the most learned man of our age: that you might also, with the same zeal, untie for us the knots and <term>thorns</term> <note>original: "syrpos." Literally "rushes" or "reeds," used metaphorically by ancient authors to mean a knotty problem or an intricate difficulty.</note> of our weakness. For my part, I am meanwhile entangled in many readings and in my duty of practicing medicine; you, however, who are devoted entirely to contemplation and are able to strive through the four stages into the <term>profound darkness of God</term> <note>original: "ī pfūdā dei caliginē." A reference to "apophatic" or negative theology, where God is understood to be so far beyond human intellect that He is described as a "divine darkness."</note>, will claim light from the darkness with no or very little labor. 

Farewell. Farewell, and be mindful of us. From Ferrara, May 22, 1491.

Just as the previous letter was too brief, or certainly more obscure, in solving your questions regarding that little book I recently published, *On Being and the One* <note>original: "de ente & uno." Pico's famous treatise (1491) attempting to reconcile Plato and Aristotle.</note>;

Now, since you demand this of me, we shall pursue even the smallest details. Through the individual heads of your questions, I will bid you to remember those things which we wrote previously, and I will rouse you where there is a need for a more profound understanding of them. Furthermore, since you have not until now touched upon Platonic commentaries, nor—due to your ignorance of the Greek language—the Greek <term>Peripatetics</term> <note>original: "pipateticos." Followers of Aristotle's philosophy.</note>, I shall lead you through the lines and decrees of the Latins, especially

You add that if he is an "Idea" insofar as he is, then he is a "being"; much more so insofar as he is God, it will follow that he is a "being" and is called so. <margin>Themistius.</margin> 
**Themistius** <note>A 4th-century philosopher and statesman known for his paraphrases of Aristotle.</note>, did not say so—even though I may have ascribed it to the Platonists in common. 

Likewise, you cannot understand how I say God is called "the One," since by this we signify not *that* he is, but *how* he is that which he is. For if he is "One," you say, because he is uniquely all things, why should he not also be called "Being," since for the "One" to *be* is all that he is? For he is not called "One" because he is the only one. Therefore, he can equally be called "Being," even though he is not the only being. <margin>
These things are prefaced for a clearer understanding.
</margin>
As I promised, I will remove every scrap of doubt from you using things already known to you. You know that, according to **Thomas** <note>original: "Thomam." St. Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the preeminent Scholastic theologian.</note>, the essence of a thing is one thing, and its existence is another. The **existence** of a thing is that by which a thing *is*—that is, it exists. The **essence** is that by which a thing attains a certain species, such as that of a horse, or a stone, or a shrub. For this reason, what is called "essence" is also called <term>quiddity</term> <note>original: "quidditas." A Scholastic term derived from the Latin "quid" (what), meaning the "what-ness" or defining nature of a thing.</note> by the more recent scholars, because from the notion of essence, we know *what* a thing is. 

<margin>
Aristotle.
</margin>
Therefore, as **Aristotle** teaches in the second book of the *Posterior Analytics*, since it is one question when we ask, for example, "Is there a rose?" and another when we want to know "What is a rose?", the first question certainly looks to the thing's existence, while the second looks to its essence (or, to use the word of the moderns, its <term>quiddity</term>). 

<margin>
Another preface.
</margin>
Again, remember that according to the opinion of Thomas, all things below God which actually exist are composed of essence and "being" (for that is what he calls existence). 

<margin>
A third.
</margin>
But God Himself is not composed of essence and existence; nor, on the other hand, is He an "essence," but rather He is pure **Existence** itself, from which all other existence of created things is subsequently derived and shared with created essences. Add to this that by this word <term>Being</term> <note>original: "ens."</note> the essence is usually indicated, but by this word <term>is</term> <note>original: "est."</note> the existence is indicated, not the essence. 

<margin>
Thomas
</margin>
The same Thomas teaches you this in the first question *On Evil*, where he says that when we say "this or that is a <term>being</term>," the question of *what* the thing is is being answered (which, as we said above, looks to the essence). But when we say "this **is**" or "this **is not**," we are satisfying the person asking *if* the thing exists—a question which, as we were saying, pertains to existence. 

<margin>
Solution to the argument according to Thomas's opinion.
</margin>
Now, I believe, the entire opinion of the Platonists and the solution to your objection is clear to you. For if God is Existence but not Essence, then just as we truly say "God **is**," so we truly deny that "God is a **being**." 

<margin>
Thomas.
</margin>
I cannot help but wonder why you—even if you have not read the Platonists—insist so much on this argument in your reading of Thomas: "God **is**, therefore He is a **being**." For Thomas himself says, almost word for word, that these two things do not follow from one another ("to be" and "to be a being"), but rather they pertain to entirely different and unrelated questions. Yet why do we need the authority of Thomas here? Who but a fool doubts whether God exists? And again, who but a fool presumes to know, even in the smallest part, *what* God is? Since, therefore, it is one thing to know *if* God is and quite another to know *what* God is, the statements will also be very different: saying "God **is**" is different from saying "God is a **being**." The former asserts that God exists (than which nothing is more certain), while the latter asserts 

<margin>
Note. Politianus, Simonides the poet.
</margin>
something of what God is (about which no one would dare pronounce anything, as nothing is more uncertain). For this reason, our most learned friend **Politianus** <note>Angelo Poliziano (1454–1494), the famous Renaissance humanist and close friend of Pico.</note> answered you most correctly during our dispute when you asked what God was; following the opinion of the poet **Simonides** <note>A 6th-century BC Greek poet. When asked by King Hiero to define God, Simonides repeatedly asked for more time to think, eventually concluding that the longer he meditated, the more obscure the subject became.</note>, he said he did not know what He was. 

<margin>
Solution to the confirmation.
</margin>
Furthermore, the example you bring up about "a person sitting" is far removed from this purpose. These two—"to be a person who sits" and "to sit"—do not vary in the same way that "to be" and "to be a being" vary. 

<margin>
Shows the example is not valid.
</margin>
For I am answering the same question when I say "Socrates sits" as when I say "he is one who sits"—namely, the question where someone asks me about Socrates's posture. Just as when we say "Socrates is white" and "Socrates is pale," the same question is satisfied: namely, "What sort of person is Socrates?" 

<margin>
Solution to the other argument.
</margin>
But the same logic does not apply between "being" and "is," one of which (to press the point again) reveals *what* a thing is to those who ask, and the other reveals *whether* it is. From this it is also clear that if God is called "Being" as an Idea <note>Referring to the Platonic theory of Forms or Ideas.</note>, it does not follow that He retains the title of "Being" insofar as He is conceived as absolute in Himself. For just as He takes on the role of Ideas, so also He takes on the role of essences...

<margin>Solution to the other argument</margin>
Let us come to that point: why God is called "One" even though he is not called "Being." Call to mind what we wrote to you in our first letters. Do you not see what is being said: that by the name of "the One," it is not indicated *what* God is, but *how* he is that which he is? <margin>Solution to the second.</margin>

For "false gold" is false for this reason: because it is not gold; and as far as the definition of the false is concerned, it happens to it either to seem to be, or to be, something other than gold.

See how far you wander: you believe an opinion is confirmed by the testimony of Simplicius which Thomas himself weakens by that same testimony. <margin>Note.</margin>

If you pay attention, you will see why he wishes this to be so: he knows that evil itself is entirely ignorant of the properties of a contrary. For he grants that these can, in some way, obtain the name of "contrary" only insofar as they do not possess the full character of evil, but retain something of the goodness <note>In the philosophical tradition Pico is using, "goodness" and "being" are interchangeable; to exist at all is to have some "goodness."</note> which they have not yet lost.

<margin>He argues against the opponent.</margin>
Therefore, they are contraries in some way only insofar as they are not entirely evil. But if I were to set before you death or blindness, I would ask whether these are "true evils" according to the opinion of Thomas, and again whether they oppose one another by that species of contrariety you describe. I do not see at all what you would answer. For if these are evils, then in the very passage from which you bring forth testimony from Thomas for your side, he would contend with great assertiveness that these cannot possibly be contraries by that very species of contrariety which you bring into the light. With what mind do you affirm that, according to Thomas’s opinion, good resists evil by some opposition of contrariety? Certainly, you ought to have considered this: that what is granted concerning certain "imperfect" evils—because of the mixture of goodness they still retain—must not be transferred to the unmixed and absolute nature of evil itself.

## ANTONIUS CITADINUS SENDS GREETINGS TO GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA.

I have not forgotten you, my dear friend <note>original: "compater" — literally "godparent," but here used as a term of intimate intellectual kinship or "brother-in-arms."</note>, do not doubt it. I remember everything quite clearly, as you will plainly see; although it would be no great loss if the things we discussed in person were to slip away. For all these matters with which you occupy yourself—and with which you keep me, a man who is not exactly idle, busy—are quite trivial. But lest you think I am imitating Nicoletto <note>Nicoletto Vernia (c. 1420–1499), a famous contemporary philosopher at Padua who was known for his controversial views and occasional refusal to engage in certain debates.</note>, who wrote to you that he did not deign to respond to his opponent at all, I will briefly note the solutions to your doubts.

<margin>a. I said it is truly said that "God is." Also, following the opinion of Dionysius <note>Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, a highly influential 5th-century Christian theologian and Neoplatonist whose works suggested God is "beyond being."</note>, I said that God is greater than any name, even this name "God," as he writes in the book *On Mystical Theology*. You have not yet moved Dionysius from his position with your strikes—nor is that a surprise (forgive me for saying so), for he is far stronger than you, even if you might hold his authority in contempt while I used it against you. I also said that it is occasionally granted by those who deny God is a "being" that God is "One." I have explained the reasoning behind their opinion both in my commentaries *On Being and the One* and in two letters to you.</margin>
The conclusions that were once granted by word—unless perhaps you have forgotten—were: God is; God is one; God is not God <note>This is a paradoxical theological statement intended to show that God's nature exceeds the human definition of the word "God."</note>. **c** It involves a contradiction to say that God—that is, the First Being—is not, and yet gold is. Regarding these, I formed several objections and gave them to you in writing. I was waiting, therefore, for you to finally respond to these objections after you had been silent for four months, perhaps entangled in greater business. But you respond only to the first ones, which I had previously formed against the solutions of certain arguments. For you say this first: "I will show you, according to the decrees of the Latins and especially the blessed Thomas [Aquinas], that although God truly and properly *is*, he is not so properly a 'being' <note>term: "ens" (being) vs "esse" (existence) — In medieval philosophy, this distinction is crucial. Citadinus is arguing about whether God has a definable "essence" like a created thing does.</note>." For you say, following Thomas, that God is not an "essence." Likewise, you say that according to him, the word "being" usually signifies "essence" and answers the question "what is it?" while the word "is" itself usually answers the question "does it exist?" Therefore, you conclude that according to Thomas, God is not a "being" if he is neither "existence" nor has an "essence," but merely exists.

<margin>b. I said in my last letter that there is no one who does not know that, both in Thomas and among other Peripatetics <note>term: "Peripatetics" — followers of Aristotle, who famously walked about (peripatētikos) while teaching.</note>, both "being" and "essence" are often accepted as being said of God. But it is enough for me that they sometimes use "being" and "essence" in such a way that it *cannot* be said of God. This is what you ought to be refuting. You will never need to bring more evidence to this matter than is necessary.</margin>
**b** But I ask you, where on earth did you learn in Thomas that God is not an "essence"? For all of Thomas’s thought cries out against this opinion. In the first part of the *Summa*, in the *Summa Against the Gentiles*, in the *Disputed Questions*, in the little book *On Being and Essence*, in the commentaries on Aristotle—in all places, finally, where the subject requires it, he holds and proves that God *is* essence. There is no need to cite the man’s words in a matter so clear. If you deny it, I will recount more than is necessary.

<margin>c. This is an unrefined objection. For the Platonists, when they say this, understand that essence and existence are in God, but they do not differ in Him. But "existence" holds that place in God which "essence" holds in other things, so that for Him, essence is nothing other than existence itself.</margin>
**c** Furthermore, in your own little book *On Being and the One*, unless it has slipped your mind, you previously said: for this reason, according to the Platonists, God is not a "being" because God’s existence is not different from His essence. How, then, following them now and defending them, do you deny that God is essence?

<margin>d. Read the earlier letters and you will see.</margin>
**d** Also, tell me: from what passage of the divine Thomas did you gather that the word "being" mostly signifies "essence," and not also "existence"? For in the fourth book of the *Metaphysics* and the first question of *On Truth*, and elsewhere, he says "being" <note>original: "ens"</note> is so called from "that which is," but a "thing" <note>original: "rem"</note> is so called because it is an essence or has an essence. Also, tell me where in Thomas you were able to learn that the question "what is it?" is reasonably answered if one says: "it is a being"?

<margin>e. This is a rather tasteless argument, since it is one thing for a thing "to be"—that is, to exist—and another to be a "being," as "being" is an essential predicate.</margin>
**e** For it is foolish to ask "what it is" unless it is known "that the thing is," as Aristotle says.

This is demonstrated as follows: Thomas openly says that **being** and **something** are spoken of in two ways. One way is that which has the nature of some category; the other way is that which responds to the question "does it exist?". Now, when asking "does God exist?", the response is affirmative, and that response is not a lie. Therefore, God is **being**.

If we must proceed further, let us say this without departing at all from Thomas: because the response to "does it exist?" is rightly "it is being," it follows that what responds to the question of whether a thing truly and properly exists is "truly and properly being." For just as that which "simply is" relates to that which "simply is," so that which "truly and properly is" relates to that which "truly and properly is." When someone asks whether God truly and properly exists, the reasonable answer is "God [is]"; therefore, He is truly and properly **being**.

Furthermore, Thomas calls $^i$ **something** and **being** (according to the first sense) that which responds to the question "what is it?". Therefore, in both the first and the second sense, God is **being** and **something**. $^k$

Furthermore, if "the true" is "that which it is," then blindness will be true, and death, and falsehood, and "non-being" altogether. For blindness is blindness, and death is death, and falsehood is falsehood; "non-being" also is "non-being." Any of these would be "true" without any mind thinking about them at all.

<meta>This page continues a technical debate regarding the nature of truth, non-existence, and logical contradiction. The author is responding to an opponent (likely Giovanni Pico della Mirandola) concerning whether a "falsehood" is inherently self-contradictory. The discussion uses the "Chimera"—a mythical beast that does not exist—as a standard logical tool to explore how we can make true statements about things that aren't real.</meta>

If a chimera is an animal, then some animal is a chimera; but no animal is a chimera. For every animal exists, and lives, and is <term>simply a being</term> <note>Latin: *simpliciter ens*; something that exists in the most basic sense.</note> and something. For that which does not exist is not an animal, unless the word is used <term>equivocally</term> <note>Used "equivocally" means using the same word with a different meaning, like calling a painting of a person a "man" even though it is just pigment on canvas.</note>. Therefore, a chimera is not a chimera. By the same reasoning, "to be a chimera" is not "to be a chimera." For if "to be generated" is "to be moved," then generation is motion. Therefore, if generation is not motion, then "to be generated" is not "to be moved." By equal reasoning, if "to be a chimera" is "to be a chimera," then a chimera is a chimera. For both are joined; but a chimera is not a chimera, as has already been proven; therefore, "to be a chimera" is not "to be a chimera."

Furthermore, no chimera is a chimera; therefore, it is true that "no chimera is a chimera." Thus, it is false that "some chimera is a chimera." By the same reasoning, it will be shown that a vacuum is not a vacuum since it does not exist, nor is blindness "blindness" if nothing is associated with it <note>This refers to the idea that "blindness" is a privation—a lack of sight in a being that should have it—rather than a "thing" itself.</note>. Non-being is always non-being. For "not to be" is non-being and is true, just as "for a chimera not to be" is both true and necessary. 

Why then was it necessary to fear that you might be refuted if you had simply and absolutely declared that every falsehood is divided in itself? Why was there no need to flee to the refuge of contradiction? 

Next, you frankly confess that my argument—by which I proved that good and evil are contraries to one another—was not "untied" <note>In logical debates, to "untie" or "solve" a "knot" meant to find the flaw in an opponent's syllogism.</note>; but you say it was not untied because no "knot" was present in it. A clever excuse, by Hercules! <insert><gloss>p</gloss></insert> But it is a wonder: if no knot was present, how were you able to "untie" the knot? The words of my argument, which were written to you in my first letters, are as follows: 

"Good, by the very reason that it is good, is to be sought; but evil is to be fled. Seeking and fleeing, however, are contraries to each other, just as uniting and separating are. Therefore, good and evil will be contraries to each other." 

This is something that **Boethius** <note>An influential 6th-century philosopher whose works on logic were standard textbooks in the Renaissance.</note> also asserts in his commentary on the *Categories* <note>Original: *in Praedicamentis*. This is Aristotle's work on the basic kinds of things that exist.</note>. But you respond in this way: "To be" is to be sought; "not to be" is to be fled; it does not follow from this that they are contraries. But I ask you, does your argument not seem similar to mine? <insert><gloss>q</gloss></insert> You might say it this way: "To be," by the reason that it is "to be," is to be sought (that is, the proper nature of being is something sought); "not to be," by its proper nature, is something to be fled; therefore, they are contraries. You would be constructing the argument beautifully. For by this form, we demonstrate that hot and cold, and white and black, are contraries. For the nature of the "hot" is to separate heterogeneous things, while the "cold" is to unite them; the nature of "white" is to disperse the sight, while "black" is to contract it.

<margin>
p You should have said how you have now "untied" it; for it is no wonder not to untie what has no knot. In this, therefore, you might wonder at me: what did I untie in which there was no knot?
</margin>

<margin>
q Why is it not similar, since just as this one has no strength, neither does that one? For if good, by the reason it is good, is to be sought, and evil is to be fled, and if fleeing and seeking are contraries, how do you prove from this that good and evil are contraries? This is what you must prove; yet to prove this, you have never before spoken a word, nor do you do so now. I was right, therefore, to say there was no knot in your argument, because that which you must prove, you not only do not prove strongly, but you do not prove it in any way, nor even attempt to prove it.
</margin>

<meta>This page continues a technical scholastic debate, shifting from the logic of non-existence (the "chimera" on the previous page) to the specific definition of "Good" and "Evil." The author is challenging his opponent's unconventional definitions, which seem to deviate from the standard Aristotelian and Thomistic (Thomas Aquinas) views of the time.</meta>

When you responded in person to my argument, you said that the proper definition <term>definition</term> <note>Latin: *ratio*; in this context, it refers to the essential nature or logical definition of a concept.</note> of the good is not "that which is something to be desired." Yet, this is conceded by all philosophers, especially the Latin ones, and **Aristotle** in the first book of the *Ethics* says that they have correctly defined the good by saying it is "that which all things seek." To those listening, your statement seemed extraordinary.

When the definition of the good was demanded of you, you said that something is good because it is "ordered toward God." But I immediately replied: therefore, God is not good. You then claimed that God is not "a good thing," but rather "Goodness itself." <note>This is a classic theological distinction: creatures *have* goodness as a quality, but God *is* the essence of Goodness.</note> I added: therefore, there is some medium <term>medium</term> <note>A "middle ground" or intermediate state between two opposites.</note> between good and evil; for if God is not "good" (in the categorical sense), He is certainly not "evil" either. 

How, then, can it be defended that "evil is the negation of the good" if a middle ground is conceded? Furthermore, if evil is the negation of good, then "evil" and "not good" are the same thing. For a single thing has only one unique negation. It follows then: if something is "not good," then it is "evil." Thus, an affirmative statement can be gathered from a negation. 

Furthermore, the following does not follow: if evil exists, it is either a <term>privation</term> <note>The absence of a quality that should naturally be present, like sight in an eye.</note> or something deprived. If it is "something deprived," it is a <term>subject</term> <note>Latin: *subiectum*; the underlying thing or person that possesses a quality.</note> and therefore it is also good. If it is a "privation," then it exists within a subject and therefore has being. But whatever has being is, in some way, a "being" and thus "good"; therefore, it is not "not good."

Furthermore, you deny the truth of what **Aristotle** says in the *Categories* <note>Latin: *Predicamenta*; Aristotle's work on how we classify reality.</note>, namely that "good" and "evil" are the <term>genera</term> <note>General categories or "types" that contain other specific things under them.</note> of opposites—a point which neither **Boethius** nor the Latin commentators dare to deny. <margin>ʳ Are you—who usually claim to be a follower of Boethius and a mocker of "barbarians" <note>The "barbarians" likely refers to the older, less-polished medieval scholastic thinkers whom Renaissance humanists often ridiculed.</note>—now laughing at those who, setting aside the Latin interpreters, follow the Greek ones? But even your **Thomas Aquinas** is not only a Latin author, but the foremost among them; he not only cites **Simplicius’s** exposition but approves of it. You, however, not only disagree with Simplicius and Thomas, but you say the Latin commentators do not "dare" to deny it. You are a strange man.</margin>

Indeed, you have cast aside the Latin interpreters and fled to **Simplicius** <note>A 6th-century Greek philosopher whose commentaries on Aristotle were highly influential in the Renaissance.</note>, who says that "good" and "evil" are the "genera of opposites" for this reason: because between opposites, one is always "good" (meaning it is "better") and the other is always "evil" (meaning it is "worse"). Thomas also reports this from Simplicius. 

But if one may oppose Simplicius: Aristotle says in that same place that not only is good the opposite of evil, but sometimes "evil is the opposite of evil." <note>For example, the vice of "cowardice" and the vice of "recklessness" are both evil, yet they are opposites of each other.</note> If Aristotle calls that which is "better" "good," and that which is "worse" "evil," then good and evil will always be opposites. 

Furthermore, if Aristotle says "good" and "evil" are the "genera of opposites," and these are "better" and "worse," then good and evil would be placed in the category of <term>relatives</term> <note>Latin: *relatiua*; things that are defined by their relationship to something else, like "taller" or "smaller."</note>, since "better" and "worse" are relative terms. Yet Aristotle says that "good" and "evil" are not just *in* a genus, but are themselves "genera." <margin>ˢ Who would not be amazed? I was amazed then, when I had not yet perceived your sharp mind; now I am not amazed by many similar things.</margin> <margin>ᵗ And you later confess that you cited this falsely, but you say this is of no consequence. How then does your mind escape me? I confess it escaped me that it was "of no consequence" to ascribe to Simplicius things he does not say. For I believed that he who said "Simplicius says this" was in error if Simplicius never actually said it.</margin>

Finally, you wonder that I affirm "evil" and "good" to be opposites based on the opinion of Saint Thomas, and—what is more—you say I am wandering into error by falsely <margin>ᵗ</margin> alleging Simplicius. I have also said, perhaps falsely, that I can prove evil is an opposite using the testimony of Saint **Thomas Aquinas**.

For this reason, then—by which **Aristotle** separates contraries from the other types of opposition—I affirmed that good and evil are contraries, and I confess it again. Since these have the true definition of evil, he who says that evil is a contrary according to the opinion of **Thomas** errs no less than my fellow countryman who said that **Simplicius** says things which he does not say.

But you say: "I will show you that evil is entirely ignorant of the property of a contrary." For although a certain evil might seem contrary to a certain good (such as "sick" to "healthy," because it leaves behind something of the good), I will nevertheless offer a certain evil which can in no way be opposed to a good by this reasoning: namely, death and blindness. 

But I, for my part, do not know whether they are similar. For if you have read the words of **Thomas** more accurately, it can be clearly understood how neither blindness nor death nor any other evil can take away the good entirely. Blindness takes away sight, and entirely so; but it does not take away life or the body. Death takes away life, which it removes completely; but it does not take away the body nor prime matter <note>The most basic substance of the universe that remains when all specific forms are removed.</note>.

Does **Thomas** not openly admit to you and say that evil is contrary to the good just as sick is to healthy, not as blindness is to sight? Blindness, therefore, insofar as it is evil, leaves something of the good upon which it rests; but insofar as it is blindness, it permits nothing of sight to exist. But what **Thomas** says—that good and evil are opposed like state and privation—is most true. For in that place **Thomas** uses those terms properly...

...calls them privations, not only those that are complete states and perfect privations—which **Aristotle** calls state and privation only in the *Categories* <note>Latin: *Praedicamentis*; Aristotle's work on the basic classification of things.</note>—but more broadly, he declares that all things where one is a <term>state</term> <note>Latin: *habitus*; a positive quality or "having" something, as opposed to lacking it.</note> and the other is a privation (whether complete or partial) are opposed as state and privation. <margin>y In that chimera of yours, you imagine many other chimeras <note>The author is being witty, using the "chimera"—a beast that doesn't exist—to tell his opponent his logic is full of imaginary problems.</note>.</margin>

Do you think a <term>chimera</term> <note>A mythological beast; in logic, it represents something that is "non-being" because it is a physical impossibility.</note> is entirely "non-being"? If you deny it, you must necessarily contradict yourself, since you previously said a chimera is entirely non-being and false. But if you grant that it is entirely non-being, I shall proceed in this way: "non-being" and "evil" are equivalent; therefore, "entirely non-being" and "entirely evil" are equivalent. But a chimera is entirely non-being; therefore, it is also entirely evil. Yet that cannot be; for the concept of a chimera does not involve a logical contradiction. It can, therefore, be created by God.

<margin>z If a chimera can be created by God, this power [of creation] is not in the chimera, but in God.</margin>

Now, what can be created, can exist. To exist, however, is a good. Therefore, what can be created can be a good. But the potential for good is itself good; therefore, a chimera is not entirely evil.

<margin>a The notion of a chimera that I form for myself: insofar as it is something [in the mind], it is good; but the chimera itself, insofar as it is nothing [in reality], is likewise not good.</margin>

Furthermore, a chimera can be understood both by God and by us. It can, therefore, exist in our mind and soul. Therefore, in some way, it can exist. Whatever can exist in some way participates in goodness in some way. Therefore, a chimera is not entirely evil. Furthermore, nothing can be evil unless it is to be shunned; but nothing can be shunned or avoided unless it is known, either by the one who flees or by God who implanted the natural instinct for flight. It is necessary, therefore, that every evil can be known in some way. But knowledge is a certain good; therefore, the ability to be known is also a good. For the potential for good is a certain good. Furthermore—

<margin>b Good and evil, according to you, are contraries, and each of two contraries is something positive. Therefore, that which is good is something positive, and that which is evil is something positive. And according to you, non-being is "good"; therefore, according to you, non-being is something positive. But "something" and "being" are interchangeable; therefore, according to you, non-being is a positive being. See where your chimera has led us!</margin>

—**Aristotle**...

<margin>
c But according to your view, it is a contrary, not a privation.
</margin>
<margin>
d He did not say that evil is good, but that it exists in what is good.
</margin>
<margin>
e It is a privation to the extent that a privation is formally a negation.
</margin>
<margin>
f Re-read your earlier letters and you will see this was shown to you in them, and perhaps more than you might wish.
</margin>

In the fourth book of the *Metaphysics* <note>Aristotle's primary work on the nature of existence.</note>, **Aristotle** says that negations and <term>privations</term> <note>Latin: *privationes*; the absence of a quality that should normally be present, like blindness in an eye.</note> are, in a certain way, beings. Indeed, he even says that "non-being" itself is, in a certain way, "being." The proof of this, he says, is that we say: "non-being is non-being." Now, whatever is "being" in any way at all is also "good" in some way. Therefore, even a **chimera** <note>A mythical beast used by philosophers to represent something that can be imagined but has no physical reality.</note>—in which it is true to predicated the name of "non-being"—is, in a certain way, a being and is good.^c Furthermore, evil is a privation of good. Every privation, however, is a negation of a <term>form</term> <note>The essential identity or "shape" of a thing.</note> in a subject that is naturally suited to possess that form and <term>habit</term> <note>Latin: *habitus*; a stable quality or state of being.</note>. Therefore, nothing can be evil which is not capable of receiving good; and this very capacity or aptitude for the good is itself good. Thus, evil cannot be entirely evil, which is why **Augustine** says that evil is always in what is good.^d 

Furthermore, if evil is a privation of good as you say, how can it be anything other than a negation of good? For the opposition between a privation and a habit is one thing, while the opposition between an affirmation and a negation is another. Furthermore, it is your task^f to show that the "valid reason" you previously made is actually sound—the one where you tried to prove from **Aristotle** and **Thomas [Aquinas]** that God is not "being" <note>Latin: *ens*.</note>. For I have weakened both your points, and it is not enough for you to say: "I know that sometimes the **Peripatetics** <note>Followers of Aristotle’s philosophy.</note> call God 'Being,' but I also know that among those same thinkers, God is sometimes not included under the term 'Being'."^f Show me, I ask you: in what place do either **Aristotle** or the **Aristotelians** judge that God should not be addressed by the name of "Being"?

<margin>
g Pay attention; I will explain shortly. When, through this word "God," you conceive only that which is signified by the name, this word does not function as a predicate, but as a subject. For it is that about which one asks: "What can or should be declared about it?" It is not that which is declared about something else. Therefore, this was not unknown either to **Simonides** or to the tyrant who consulted him. Likewise, when you ask whether "God can be called God," or whether He is "something other than God," I ask you what you conceive by this word "God" when you speak it of God. If you conceive nothing, you do not err, because you are saying nothing. If you do conceive something, I say that God is something other than what you conceive and what you explain through this word "God." For He is above everything that can be conceived by us.
</margin>

Furthermore, if you have the time, explain how you defend the idea that God "is" and is "One," yet God is "not God." For if the word is understood, it is necessary that some description be formed by the mind; once that is given, it follows immediately that "God is God." Nor would the poet **Simonides** <note>Simonides of Ceos, who famously kept asking for more time to think when the tyrant Hiero of Syracuse asked him "What is God?", eventually concluding that the more he thought, the more obscure the answer became.</note> have asked the tyrant for more time to answer the question "What is God?" unless he had grasped a concept and a definition for the word in his mind; for in every inquiry, the first thing is the meaning of the word. 

Furthermore, if God is One, and "the One" is something else than God, then that "something else" can only be God. Likewise, if God exists and is not God, He is something other than God. Therefore, it would be necessary for Him to be something other than Himself. Furthermore, if the reason God is not "God" is because the name of God is <term>concrete</term> <note>Referring to a specific, embodied thing rather than an abstract quality like "Godhead" or "Divinity."</note>, signifying one thing and then another, then one should not concede that "God is" or "God is One." For there is nothing in the nature of things that is "God" by participating in a "Godhead." Finally, you shall show how you either prove or defend the idea that a contradiction is enclosed in saying "God is not" and "Gold is." Such a dispute will be pleasing to me and should not be troublesome to you; for a dispute is the **sieve of truth**, the most sweet food of the soul, having nothing unpleasant about it.

<margin>
h Let us come to your gold, which you do not wish to lose at all, even if God is lost. It is impossible for anything to be if "Being" itself <note>Latin: *ipsum esse*; the act of existing.</note> is not. It is impossible, therefore, for gold to be if God is not. Furthermore, if God is not, then everything is "infinite" <note>In the sense of being "without limit" or "unbounded."</note>. If everything is infinite, then nothing exists, because if the infinite is, the finite is not. But even if the infinite is, the infinite is not, because the infinite destroys itself, just as other things do that contain a contradiction. If nothing exists, gold does not exist. I believe this is enough for you, a man as talented as you wish to be.
</margin>

->Farewell.<-

<meta>This page continues the philosophical investigation into the nature of existence, specifically challenging the recipient's views on how "Being" (existence) relates to "Essence" (what a thing is). # Fourth Objections

->OO<-

<margin>n</margin>
**N**ot for that reason was it said that God is not a "being" because in God, existence <note>Latin: *esse*; the act of being or existing.</note> stands for essence; rather, it is because existence is not something different from essence—which is a very different matter. Otherwise, the very existence of a stone—which for it is its essence—would be neither a being nor good; for the existence of a stone is not essence <note>In scholastic thought, only in God are essence and existence identical; in creatures like stones, they are distinct.</note>, but it is itself for itself, both its own existence and its own essence.

If it is impossible to ask "what they are" regarding negations and <term>privations</term> <note>The absence of a quality that should be there, like blindness in an eye.</note>; since they *do* exist in a sense, it is not sufficient for formulating the question "what is it?" to merely know that the thing being asked about exists. Rather, one must also know *that* it is and *what* it is. Therefore, to someone asking "what is it?", it is ridiculous and irrational to answer "a being" or "something," whether "being" is taken in the first sense <note>Substantial being.</note> or the second <note>Accidental or conceptual being.</note>. If one asks what "sin" is, the question is about the word rather than the thing itself.

If something is a "being," then according to your position, it is a being because its existence is a different thing in reality from its essence. You say humanity is one thing, a man is another; whiteness is one thing, a white thing is another. Therefore, if an **Idea** <note>Referencing the Platonic "Ideas" or eternal forms.</note> is a being, it will be a being because the existence of the Idea is different from the Idea itself. However, the Idea is God; therefore, the existence of the Idea is something different from God. Consequently, in God there would be a real composition <note>A "composition" implies God is made of parts (Essence + Existence), which contradicts the theological doctrine of Divine Simplicity.</note>, not just a conceptual one.

According to the definition of <term>denominatives</term> <note>Words derived from another, like "brave" from "bravery."</note>, "one" is a denominative derived from "unity." Yet, according to your position, God is called "one" by a likeness to unity; therefore, the predication by which the **Platonists** say "God is one" does not pertain to the substance of God. Furthermore, when we say "God is one," you think not *what* He is, but *how* He is is being signified. But "how" (mode) belongs to the category of <term>accidents</term> <note>A quality that can change without changing the essence of a thing (e.g., being tan or sitting).</note>; therefore, the word "one" in God is not substantive, nor does it pertain to the reality. This is because either I have not learned the Platonic sect or I am ignorant of the Greek language; for that is not enough to defend the discipline of the **Academics** <note>The school of philosophy founded by Plato.</note>.

If God did not exist and gold did exist, you say gold would be gold and yet not be gold; therefore, it would be gold. If, then, the definition of truth stands, there will be a truth that fits no Idea. If "Socrates is sitting" is neither true nor false because it is not necessary, I will certainly defend the view that a true affirmation or negation does not exist in every case; for in every case, it is not necessary that one or the other possesses the truth.

If good and evil are in things, but truth and falsity are in the soul, where is your opposition between affirmation and negation? For a negation posits nothing. How is a **chimera** <note>A mythical beast used to represent something that can be imagined but cannot exist.</note> both in things and in the soul if it is entirely non-being and false? Especially since you think that "non-being" and "evil" are interchangeable terms.

If it is true that "blindness is blindness," who would not see that blindness is true? For they are the same thing; once blindness is posited, that which is "blindness being blindness" is posited, and when it is removed, it is gone. For the same reason, **Socrates** and "Socrates being Socrates" are the same, and both are generated by the same generation, and through themselves. So too, God and "God being God" are the same; for both are eternal and the First Truth.

If every false thing is simply "divided" (as you do not deny has been proven), it should not have been said that a "certain false thing" is divided only with this condition: namely, so long as it is false.

<meta>This page continues a rigorous philosophical debate concerning the definitions of "being" and "essence." The author is responding to critiques about how terms are restricted in logic, the authority of classical commentators like Simplicius and Boethius, and the specific metaphysical nature of evil as a "privation" or lack of good.</meta>

For if every man is simply and absolutely **capable of laughter** <note>Latin: *risibilis*; in traditional logic, this was considered a "property" unique to humans: they aren't defined by laughter, but only they can do it.</note>, it is not necessary to add a condition to restrict it, such as saying: "every man is capable of laughter *as long as he is a man*." Nor should such a restriction be added just because not all false things are divided equally, or are equally false; for not even all beings are equally good, yet all things are nonetheless absolutely good.

How it may be concluded that good and evil are contraries will be easily established if you follow this: if "seeking" and "fleeing" are contraries, and if the reasoning behind contrary motions has been sufficiently understood by you.

Why do you wonder if I say that the Latins do not deny Aristotle—whom **Simplicius** <note>A 6th-century Greek philosopher and one of the last great Neoplatonists who wrote influential commentaries on Aristotle.</note> denies, but **Boethius** <note>An early 6th-century Roman senator and philosopher who translated Aristotle into Latin, bridging the gap between Antiquity and the Middle Ages.</note> does not? Should I, for that reason, either fail to imitate Boethius or instead extol the "barbarians" <note>A likely reference to the later medieval Scholastic thinkers, whom Renaissance humanists often labeled "barbarians" for their complex, non-classical Latin.</note>? You call me a "strange man"; but I would call you "marvelous" instead—you who think that because I imitate Boethius while setting Simplicius aside for the moment, I must therefore despise Boethius and follow the barbarians.

If good and evil are contraries, you wish to prove that a **chimera** <note>In philosophy, a "chimera" is a standard example of an impossible object—something that can be imagined but cannot exist in reality.</note> is something that exists in the nature of things. But if it were understood by what reasoning I called good and evil "contraries"—which you either do not yet wish to, or cannot, understand—you would have proved nothing from the example of the chimera.

You marvel greatly that certain **privations** <note>A "privation" is the absence of a quality that should naturally be present, like blindness in an eye.</note> are called "half-full" <note>Latin: *semiplenas*; meaning partial or incomplete.</note> by me, and you try to prove they do not exist in this way: "Evil is nothing; therefore, it is not a partial privation." But I, following your own argument, shall say this: sickness is evil; therefore, it is nothing. Thus, it is not a partial privation. However, sickness *is* a certain privation. Therefore, it is not a partial privation of health or of some good, but rather a "full" and "perfect" one—which cannot happen. Therefore, privations are "half-full" or imperfect, such as sickness, rarity, foulness, or blindness. Sight is "perfect" [as a quality], but [as a privation] it is an imperfect good; for the good that is in the one who sees is not taken away entirely.

If it is true, as you write, that every evil leaves behind something of the good, then the **chimera**—which is entirely "non-being"—and evil things would retain something of the good. If indeed it preserves something of the good, it is not entirely evil, nor entirely a "non-being." Even if the **power** <note>Latin: *potentia*; the potentiality or capacity for something to be brought into existence.</note> by which it can be created and exist lies within God, and the concept by which it can be understood is in the mind, this does not prevent the chimera from being "good" and a "being" in terms of its potential. For there is the power of God, and the chimera is one thing in one sense and another in another. Nor do we deny that the **Antichrist** is "good in potential," whose power to exist is partly in matter and partly in the heavens and in man. Furthermore, how is the chimera—if all thought and the power of God are meanwhile excluded—entirely "non-being" and evil? For in order to be "non-being," it certainly cannot be evil. For evil is a privation that exists in a subject; it is necessary that this subject participates in goodness. Otherwise, it could not be a subject at all. For that which does not exist at all cannot serve as a subject.

You have not yet disproved what I said; and you confirm it by the authority of Simplicius, except you claim Simplicius does not say it. But there was no need to boast for that reason; for I did not say that Aristotle felt that "everything that is" exists either essentially or accidentally, nor did I falsely attribute anything to the **Blessed Thomas** <note>Saint Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the most influential Catholic theologian and philosopher of the Middle Ages.</note> for that reason.

Although every privation is a kind of negation, it is not yet established that there is not one kind of opposition between affirmation and negation, and another between privation and possession. Nor, for that reason, if evil is the privation of good, is it necessary that "evil" and "not good" are interchangeable terms.

Regarding your defense, by which you wish to protect the idea that **"God is not God"**... I [attribute this] neither to the truth nor to the Blessed [Thomas...]

<meta>This page concludes a philosophical rebuttal regarding the naming and conceivability of God before transitioning into a formal letter from Gianfrancesco Pico della Mirandola. The previous discussion focused on logic, definitions, and the nature of "being."</meta>

<sig>oo ii</sig>

I think this is consistent with **Dionysius** <note>Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, a 5th-6th century theologian whose "negative theology" argued that we can only describe what God is *not*, rather than what He is.</note>, for the blessed Dionysius never denied that God is God. But as **Blessed Thomas** <note>Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the preeminent Scholastic philosopher and theologian.</note> interprets it, no name can fully or perfectly explain the nature of God; nor does he think affirmations are attributed to God for any other reason. 

Yet you say that the name of God, if it has a description, possesses the quality of a definition <note>original: *rationem*</note> rather than a predicate. But even if this is granted, the argument stands: let **a** be the definition of the name; let it be said in this way: "God is **a**." For the definition of anything is predicated of that which it defines. Therefore, by simple conversion, "**a** is God." Therefore, "God is God." 

Likewise, you say when it is asked whether God is something other than God or not, one must realize what is conceived by the name of God. Whatever else is given, you say, "I will say it is God," for He is above everything that can be conceived. But does not a solution of this kind contradict itself? For if you confess a proposition of this sort—which is "God is above that which can be conceived"—do you not clearly affirm something about God? Let the definition of the name be exactly that: "that which is above all that can be conceived"; the argument will still hold. Furthermore, it follows that "God is above all that can be conceived; therefore God cannot be conceived." Otherwise, the same thing would be "above itself." Therefore, He could neither be loved nor worshipped.

Finally, you seem to think the power of gold is so great that, whether we wish it or not, by the necessity of reality or the mind, it drags God along with it in this manner: "Gold exists; therefore Being itself exists; therefore God exists." Likewise: "God is; therefore He is infinite. He is infinite; therefore He is nothing." If being is infinite, you say, the finite is not. It is as if you were arguing: "the finite is not; therefore it is nothing." Then: "It is infinite; therefore the infinite is not," for you say the infinite destroys itself. 

Indeed, I think if someone had written such arguments to **Nicoletto** <note>Nicoletto Vernia (c. 1420–1499), a famous professor of philosophy at Padua known for his Averroist leanings.</note>, he would have replied with nothing. Nor shall I oppose anything further, lest I seem to doubt a matter that appears clearer to me than light. If you try to prove your position with these arguments, I truly fear you will lose your gold.

If you wish, my best companion, reply to these objections so that we may now bring an end to this disputation; for we have played enough. Moreover, I would not want you to think I turned to these matters out of hatred or ill-will. I know you remember that before I wrote anything to you, I asked if you were willing. Indeed, I call God to witness that I love and venerate my **Mirandolan** <note>Giovanni Pico della Mirandola (1463–1494), the famous Renaissance humanist and uncle of the author of this letter.</note> companion; if you ever care to put it to the test, you will find I have told no lie.

<meta>This page transitions from the philosophical arguments concerning the nature of God into a prefatory letter by Gianfrancesco Pico della Mirandola. ...acting in the interest of men, I hastened to Florence with the greatest possible speed. I took care by every means I could so that whatever had been noted down by him—although unpolished and unexamined—might be placed into our custody. Our efforts were not entirely in vain; for even if the wills <note>original: *tabule*; legal documents or testaments</note> were not yet opened nor the heir known, the chests were nevertheless opened such that we could inspect and turn over all the commentaries. 

We saw in those scattered paper codices the man's incredible zeal, his reading of every kind, and concepts admirable beyond the grasp of the human mind. Truly, however, in the organizing of his writings there was a lack of care not to be praised; everything was thrown here and there and scattered. But of these things, I shall speak elsewhere. 

While we were unrolling these with diligent care, his little work *On Being and the One* <note>original: *De ente et uno*; a famous treatise by Giovanni Pico attempting to reconcile Plato and Aristotle</note>, published roughly four years before his death <note>original: *occubitum*; literally "falling down" or "death"</note>, fell into my hands together with three letters written by you regarding it and the replies to them. Because of the novelty of the matter, I not only read them through but drank them in—almost, as they say, devoured them. (For I had known by rumor that this had been done, but I did not have sufficient knowledge of what significance had been brought to it). 

I began to think and debate with myself whether I should give that work to the printers publicly with the other works I had gathered and decided to publish, making no mention of your objections; or whether it would be more advisable if it went out into public both attacked by obstacles on one side and fortified by defenses on the other. After a long discussion of the matter, the latter opinion finally settled in my mind. Indeed, it would seem to carry marks of infamy among learned men if the work did not only fear its accusers, but also did not dare to summon them to judgment properly, as if having little faith in its own conscience. 

Likewise, it seemed appropriate for it to go accompanied by the replies, as if with witnesses to defend the cause of innocence. I did not doubt that our counsel would be praised by upright men, since I either had to allow my deceased uncle—a man who certainly deserved the best from me—to be defrauded of some part of his famous doctrine by not publishing such a booklet, or, if it went forth alone, to leave an opportunity for the most wicked vituperations to always find room for accusation. This would happen if I did not summon to the forum those things which had been composed on both sides in many letters, both by objecting and by repelling. 

But when some letters were presented by our friend Christopher Saxolus, both citizen and physician, in which it was signaled to us that you had produced a fourth letter on that business which lacked a response (as you said), the matter was called back into doubt. Once again, being of two minds, I thought my judgment, though already balanced, should be weighed more exactly, since the last accuser was pressing the case and there was no one to act as patron. 

Then a certain urge <note>original: *titilatio*; literally a "tickling"</note> for undertaking the defense entered my mind, though how I might turn myself away from maintaining silence was not immediately clear. On one hand, I was moved by the man’s modesty and his kindness toward everyone, as well as the skill and sharpness of his talent in untying and washing away difficult knots <note>metaphor for complex philosophical problems</note> and inexplicable riddles on the spot. Because of this, I certainly judged that your last letter had not been safely delivered. I thought it would have been easy for him to have written back. If, however, your letters were given to a faithful messenger, they might have perished either through the negligence of the couriers (for that happens often) or by some other chance on the road. 

Finally, it occurred to me that in the explanations of your earlier questions, he had complained that the same points were often repeated by you and the same things often doubted. Because of this, I immediately ran through the main points of your entire controversy, to see if something could be found in the first responses by which I might show that the fourth letter had been sufficiently answered in part.

...done before it was written. For if the rumor had reached them that you had sent a fourth letter to my uncle <note>The famous philosopher Giovanni Pico della Mirandola (1463–1494), Gianfrancesco’s uncle.</note> regarding that controversy to which he had not responded, they would have immediately passed judgment—as is the habit of babblers and the envious—that he had failed to write back for some reason other than a just one.

Otherwise, my dear Antonio, I would have very gladly abandoned this work from the beginning. First, because I abhor controversies, and I would not wish to appear to be initiating one even if I were defending a most righteous cause. Second, so that I might not deviate from the true path of philosophy. I began to walk this path—led by my uncle Giovanni Pico and our friend Giovanni Mainardo <note>Giovanni Mainardo (1462–1536) was a prominent physician and a close associate of the Pico family.</note>—after my time among horses and arms (even if I had caught the scent of certain little flowers of literature since boyhood). For the knowledge of nature should not be used for exhausting literary contests <note>original: *literarios deſudādos agones*; a reference to competitive academic debates</note>, but rather to recognize the Creator of nature Himself. Philosophical meditations should always, of their own accord, invite us to investigate the innermost meanings of the divine words. This is the goal of all studies; by these, the way to heaven is revealed to us, provided we cultivate them not for the sake of catching at our own glory, but so that we may both know our God more easily and love Him more fervently. From there, we may more promptly pursue the things He commanded to be done and flee from the things He taught us to avoid.

Behold, the reason for this burden I have undertaken and my business with you is explained. It is most just that it be seen as such, and therefore you should bear it with an even mind. When, therefore, it was said in this manner that God is not "being," we assert that it was put forward for this reason: because in God, <term>to be<note>original: "esse," referring to the act of existing.</note></term> stands for <term>essence<note>original: "essentia," the "what-ness" of a thing.</note></term>.
