You think these two points are entirely different; I, however, contend that one is the opening and clarification of the other. For when it is said that God is not being because in Him "to be" is not separated from "essence," nothing else is asserted than that "to be" in God is for Him his "essence." Nor is it judged by us through this statement—namely, that "to be" in God is not different from His essence—that there is an "essence" in God, as is clearly seen through the words of the man against whom you argued. 

For my uncle <note>Giovanni Pico della Mirandola.</note> refuted your objection, which concerned this very matter, saying: "For the Platonists, when they say this, do not mean that essence and being exist in God but do not differ; rather, that *to be* holds the place in God that *essence* holds in other things, so that for Him there is nothing other than *to be* itself acting as His essence." 

Perhaps you will change your mind about how completely incongruous you think it is that the "being" of a stone cannot be called "being," if you consider what is said by <margin>Thomas</margin> Thomas Aquinas—who was summoned by you as a judge of this controversy—in the first part of the *Summa*, Question 45, Article 4. Wherefore, by his followers—most notably <term>Capreolus<note>Johannes Capreolus (c. 1380–1444), known as the "Prince of Thomists."</note></term>, when the question of the distinction between <term>being<note>ens</note></term> and <term>existence<note>existentia</note></term> arises—the "to be" of created things is received neither into the number of true beings nor of creatures. If it does not take the name of "being," it undoubtedly does not take the name of "good" either, since being and good follow each other and are reciprocal in their scope.

...to have understood that a question can be formed to which a positive and correct response can be given. First, if you think that a question cannot be correctly formed unless the matter being asked about is such that an answer can be given through it, I do not agree with you.
<margin>Aristotle</margin> For it is the opinion of <term>Aristotle<note>The Greek philosopher (384–322 BC) whose logic dominated medieval and Renaissance thought.</note></term> that one can inquire whether a centaur exists or not, even though a centaur is not the kind of thing that allows for an answer to the question "is it?", since it is a mere fable and a total fiction. Likewise, I oppose you if you believe that the person asking must already know this same thing; for (as we have shown) the person who correctly asks "what is it?" regarding a thing does not need to know more than the fact that it *is*. Therefore, if someone knows a thing is *something*, it is not a ridiculous answer to say "it is something" to a person who is ignorant and asking about it. 

I am not accustomed to teaching those who ask "what a thing is" that it is either "a being" or "something," so that we might answer more fully. It happens that those who have already established that a thing is "something" might still search for what *kind* of being it is. Therefore, we satisfy not only their expressed petition, but also their desire for investigation, when we resolve their conceived but unvoiced questions by anticipating them in our responses. 

As for those words—namely, that if one asks "what is sin," the question concerns the word rather than the reality—these were part of the objection made against you. For since your previous answer did not seem to carry much weight, you argued from the opinion of <term>Thomas<note>St. Thomas Aquinas.</note></term>: specifically, that a thing is called <term>being<note>original: "ens"</note></term> according to the first mode because it is the answer to the question "what is it?", and that one who asks what it is that preserves and moves the world is reasonably answered "God." From these points, you concluded that God is "being" in this first mode. 

The opponent replied: "See how much you are deceived; according to Thomas, <term>evil<note>original: "malum"</note></term> is not the sort of thing that allows us to answer someone asking 'what is it' with 'it is a being.' Yet, to someone asking 'what is sin,' we can answer 'it is evil.' Therefore, your response does not help you at all—namely, that if one asks 'what is sin,' the question is about the name rather than the thing." 

Indeed, the question "what is it that governs the world?" is no more a question of a name than "what is sin?", even though that which governs the world (namely, God) does not have a <term>quiddity<note>original: "quidditas," a technical term for the "what-ness" or essential nature of a thing.</note></term>, as more recent thinkers say. This is most clearly confirmed by everyone except those who place God in a <term>category<note>In Aristotelian logic, "categories" are classifications of types of being. Pico argues God is beyond such classification.</note></term>. 

And as the most holy <term>Dionysius<note>Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite.</note></term>, the prince of our theology after the Apostles, says: 
<margin>Dionysius</margin> there is neither a name nor a definition for Him. Furthermore, this response of yours does not even harmonize with what you said before; previously, you said that evil itself is not "nothing" but something positive, yet now you confess that a question can be formed regarding its name alone.

<margin>Third Objection</margin> You oppose me a third time with these words: "If something is 'being,' then according to your position it is 'being' because its <term>to be<note>original: "esse," the act of existing.</note></term> is a different thing from its <term>essence<note>original: "essentia," what a thing is.</note></term>. For example," you say, "humanity is one thing, a human is another; whiteness is one thing, a white object is another. Therefore, if an 'idea' is a 'being,' it will be a 'being' because the 'to be' of the idea is different from the idea itself. But the 'idea' is God. Therefore, the 'to be' of the idea is different from God. Consequently, there is in God a real composition, not just a conceptual one." To these things, we say an answer has already been given.

<margin>Solution</margin> For when you argued using almost the same means in your third letter, the answer was that the composition of "being" and "essence" in divine matters is <term>conceptual<note>original: "secundum rationem," existing in the mind/reason rather than as physical parts.</note></term>, not <term>real<note>original: "secundum rem," existing in the actual reality of the thing.</note></term>. We therefore deny that the first premise of this <term>syllogism<note>A formal logical argument consisting of a major premise, a minor premise, and a conclusion.</note></term> you bring forward is true.

<meta>Pico continues his rebuttal to Antonio's philosophical objections. On this page, he addresses the technical distinction between "essence" and "existence" and defends the use of the term "One" as a description of God's very substance, rather than just an accidental quality.</meta>

For even if in created things essence differs from being in reality, it does not necessarily follow that whatever can be called "being" in any way must be composed of essence and being (or existence) as if from parts. Therefore, in the Idea—which is the pattern for created things—essence and existence do not come together as things distinct in reality. Rather, we create this composition in the Idea when we consider it as the "exemplary cause" of the essence and the being (or existence) that are found in created things. We apply this same composition and distinction even to the simplest things, and we call it "conceptual" 
<margin>
The Peripatetics
Antipater
Posidonius
Seneca
</margin>
when our intellect has fashioned it. The <term>Peripatetics<note>The followers of Aristotle, named for the "colonnades" (peripatoi) where they walked and studied.</note></term> very frequently use this widely known distinction which, as the author says, was repeated by Antipater, mentioned by Posidonius in his letters, and by Seneca. For that reason, we can say in this way that the "Idea" is conceptually composed of essence and existence, and we can call it a "being"—specifically when we consider it the pattern for creatures that are composed of existence and essence which *do* differ in reality. However, we do not place this composition in God when we contemplate Him not as the pattern for others, but as He enjoys Himself in the deepest inner sanctuary of His divinity.

<margin>
Solution to the fourth objection
</margin>
Fourthly, you say that according to the definition of derivative terms, "one" is derived from "unity." You claim that according to my position, God is called "one" based on a likeness to unity; therefore, the declaration by which the <term>Platonists<note>Followers of Plato, who held that "The One" was the highest principle of all reality.</note></term> say "God is one" does not concern God's substance. Furthermore, you think that when we say "God is one," it signifies not *what* He is, but *how* He is; and a "mode" <note>A way of being rather than the thing itself.</note> belongs to the category of accidents. Therefore, you argue the word "one" is not substantive when applied to God—concluding that either I have not unlearned the Platonic sect or I am ignorant of the Greek language. For you say this is not enough to defend the discipline of the <term>Academics<note>The Academy was Plato's school; "Academics" here refers to later philosophers in that tradition.</note></term>. 

But the response is easy. Since the Platonists have said that the "One" declared of God is substantive and not merely derivative, it has been correctly asserted. And again, it is not inconsistent to assert that He is called "one" because He is like unity. For even if a name is adapted to something based on a property or likeness of some other thing, it does not necessarily follow that the name is not substantive, provided it is taken as a substantive name—one that signifies something standing by itself rather than something attached to another. Indeed, it is so clear that the "one" predicated of God is understood as something standing alone and not merely inherent <note>i.e., not just a quality "stuck" onto Him like a color is stuck to a wall</note> that it needs no proof. You see, then, that the property from which a name is applied does not take away its status as a substantive. 
<margin>
Thomas
</margin>
For your <term>Thomas<note>Saint Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the leading light of Scholastic theology.</note></term>—or rather, *our* Thomas—records in other places as well as in the First Part of his work that the thing the name is intended to signify differs from the source from which the name is derived. For example, he explains that the name "stone" <note>original: *lapis*</note> is applied to signify that substance so named, even though it is called such from a related property—namely, that it "hurts the foot" <note>original: *pedem ledit*. A popular, though linguistically incorrect, medieval etymology of the Latin word for stone, *lapis*.</note>. 
<margin>
John Scotus
</margin>
Wherefore in another place he teaches that it is used by grammarians to write that a "name" denotes a substance along with a quality; <term>John Duns Scotus<note>A major Franciscan philosopher (c. 1266–1308) often contrasted with Aquinas.</note></term> affirms this same thing in the first book of his commentaries on the *Sentences*. Therefore, my dear Antonio, when we speak of the "One" in relation to God, we speak truly and use it as a substantive name; for we both conceive and predicate it as something standing by itself. Again, when we say it is applied from a likeness to unity and its properties, we speak to the truth...

<summary>Pico argues that while the distinction between essence and existence is a conceptual tool we use to understand God, God is actually a perfect, non-composite unity. He defends calling God "the One," arguing that even if the word is derived from a property, it still describes God's essential substance.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the author's defense of Giovanni Pico della Mirandola’s philosophical positions against Antonio’s objections. Having previously discussed the nature of being, the text now moves into the specific logic of God as the "One" and the impossibility of a world existing without a divine foundation.</meta>

<margin>A brief solution from the words of [my] uncle.</margin>
We approach as closely as it is permissible for us because we use a suitable term to point toward that deity, which remains unspeakable and far above all created things. He is the principle of all things that exist, just as "Unity" is the principle of all numbers. From these words, you will also gather the solution to your other argument regarding the "mode"—where you claim it belongs only to the category of accidents—specifically in the statement: **God is one.** You can see how "God is one" signifies substance, and nonetheless, the word "one" remains substantive in God. If you consider the source from which the name is taken and what it is intended to denote, you can recognize a brief solution to your doubt from the words of [my] uncle <note>The author is Gianfrancesco Pico della Mirandola, defending his famous uncle, Giovanni Pico della Mirandola.</note>. He asks: "Why do you say I follow the reasoning of the **Platonists** rather than **Dionysius**, when you have never read Dionysius or the Platonists, even as you boast with a loud voice?" Know that for the Platonists, the "type" of God is Unity, and for <term>Dionysius<note>Dionysius the Areopagite, an early Christian theologian whose works merged Christian thought with Neoplatonic philosophy.</note></term>, God is "uniquely all things." No one could rightly demand a more ready solution. For when it is said that "Unity is the type of God," it refers to likeness and mode; but when it is said that "God is uniquely all things," it refers to His substance. It has been asserted that these two are entirely the same. Furthermore, in the Greek language (which he knew well), an abstract term can sometimes signify a concrete reality using the same word.

<margin>Solution to the fifth objection.</margin>
Not many words are needed to offer a solution to your fifth doubt. He says: "If God did not exist and gold existed, it would be gold and it would not be gold." You add these words: "therefore it would be gold." What if the definition of truth stands? It will be a truth corresponding to no <term>Idea<note>The "Ideas" are the divine patterns or blueprints of all created things held in the mind of God.</note></term>. Add, I pray, these few things which he said followed from his words, and you will recognize how it would be a "truth corresponding to no Idea." What, I ask? An **impossibility**. For an impossibility gives birth to an impossibility, and therefore it is no wonder if you make whatever you wish follow from your impossible proposition. For if God did not exist and gold existed, it would be a truth corresponding to no Idea, since from the impossible, the impossible is generated. Not only dialecticians <note>Logicians.</note> but also theologians agree with this.

<margin>John of Baconthorp</margin>
For if you ask <term>John of Baconthorp<note>original: "Ioannem de bachone". A 14th-century English Carmelite theologian known for his rigorous logical approach.</note></term> the Carmelite whether it could happen that gold exists and God does not exist, he will answer you in the first book of his *Sentences* that no thing whatsoever, of whatever kind it may be, can be understood unless God is understood first. Since God is involved in the understanding of all things, you can gather whether it can be pronounced—beyond all controversy, even among novice logicians—that for gold to exist and God not to exist is an **impossibility**.

<margin>Cardinal of Cambrai</margin>
But we will speak of this again at the end of the work. If you later consult the <term>Cardinal of Cambrai<note>Pierre d'Ailly (1351–1420), a prominent French theologian and logician.</note></term>, you will hear a man trained in every branch of philosophy saying, in his first commentary on the *Sentences*, that a contradiction follows from any impossibility.

<margin>Solution to the sixth objection</margin>
In the sixth place, you said that if "Socrates is sitting" were neither true nor false (as he had asserted because it was not necessary), you could defend the claim that a negation is not true in every case, nor an affirmation, since in any given case one or the other does not have a necessary truth. Solving this objection, we reply that this statement—namely "Socrates is sitting"—does not necessarily determine its own truth or falsehood in itself. It does not follow from this that an affirmation is not true of everything, or a negation is not true. However, if you understand it in the way he himself teaches...

<summary>Gianfrancesco Pico defends his uncle's use of Neoplatonic terminology, arguing that God's status as "Unity" is substantive rather than accidental. He further argues that the existence of any object (like gold) without the existence of God is a logical impossibility that leads to total contradiction.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the defense of Giovanni Pico della Mirandola's philosophical theses. The author, his nephew Gianfrancesco, is addressing logical and metaphysical objections raised by a critic named Antonio regarding the nature of truth, existence, and the distinction between the mind and external reality.</meta>

You will also be able to deny that in any case an affirmation or negation is true in such a way that one part is necessarily true. For he <note>Likely referring to Aristotle or a specific commentator.</note> says that **"I am sitting"** is always either true or false because I am always either sitting or not sitting. And what is called **"me sitting"** is in itself neither true nor false—that is, this proposition does not determine truth or falsehood for itself from its own nature, which is what **necessary propositions** <note>Propositions that must be true by their very definition, such as "a triangle has three sides."</note> do. But since it can happen that it is true when I actually sit, and false when I do not sit, the statement is in itself indeterminate toward either outcome.

<margin>Seventh objection and solution.</margin>
<margin>Aristotle</margin>
Furthermore, you insist against some of his words regarding good and evil, truth and falsehood—which he had claimed exist in things and in the soul—in this manner: "If good and evil are in things, and truth and falsehood are in the soul, where is your opposition of affirmation and negation? For negation posits nothing; how then is a **chimera** <note>A mythological creature used in philosophy to represent an impossible or non-existent thing.</note> in things and in the soul if it is entirely non-being and false, since you think non-being and evil are interchangeable?" But I pray you pay attention and notice: evil and good are pronounced to be in things for the reason that they relate to the things themselves, just as truth and falsehood relate to the soul. For truth and falsehood are not in things, as **Aristotle** writes in the sixth book of *First Philosophy* <note>original: "prime philosophiæ"; this refers to the *Metaphysics*.</note>, but in the mind. Nor does it necessarily follow that a thing which is entirely evil must be a "true thing." Indeed, that "truth" and "falsehood" which Aristotle mentions in that passage are <term>complex expressions<note>original: "complexa"; in logic, this refers to full propositions (sentences) rather than single words or concepts.</note></term>. Likewise, it does not follow that if good and evil are in things, they cannot be opposed contradictorily. This is because evil, which is pronounced to be in things, is not said to be in them in the sense that it is understood to be some "thing" or substance, but because it is observed and considered regarding the things themselves—that is, insofar as a thing is deprived of its perfections. Thus, they are made "not good." A **chimera**, however, is not in things because it is entirely non-being and entirely evil; yet, if it were possible for it to be produced by nature, it would be both a thing and "good." It is "false" only insofar as it has no existence at all and corresponds to no idea. We do not even claim it exists in the soul, except as a "notion" of a chimera; that notion, as a mental thing, is good and true, but it is "false" only insofar as it represents a chimera, since the chimera itself is both nothing and evil.

<margin>Eighth objection with solution.</margin>
After this, you believed you could prove that **blindness** is true—which he <note>Giovanni Pico</note> had denied—even if he had not denied nor conceded that "blindness being blindness" is true. But he would have said these two are very different things. You argued in this way: "If 'blindness being blindness' is true, who wouldn't see that blindness is true? For they are the same thing; for with only blindness posited, the fact of 'blindness being blindness' is posited, and if it is taken away, the fact is taken away." By the same reasoning, you argue that "Socrates" and "Socrates being Socrates" are the same, and both are brought forth by the same act of generation; and even that God and "God being God" are the same, since both are eternal and the **First Truth**. But I, my dear Antonio, contend against this and deny that those things you claim are the same. For if one of those things you bring forward is posited, the other is not necessarily posited. For if only "blindness" is posited, and no intellect is there to consider it, there will indeed be blindness, but there will not be this <term>complex truth<note>A truth that requires a mind to form a statement or proposition about the thing.</note></term> that is "blindness being blindness." This also solves the argument regarding God and the generation of Socrates. For Socrates is generated in himself, but the proposition "Socrates is Socrates" is not generated, since <term>complex expressions</term> are not generated. Even if I were to grant you that they are the same, we still say it does not follow as you concluded, because of the different **modes of signifying**—namely, "complexly" and "incomplexly"—since your conclusion would be of no valid force.

<summary>Gianfrancesco Pico defends his uncle’s distinction between truth (which resides in the mind) and good/evil (which reside in things), refuting Antonio's arguments about the "truth" of non-existent things like chimeras or privations like blindness.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Gianfrancesco Pico della Mirandola's defense of his uncle Giovanni's philosophical theses against the critic Antonio. The discussion has moved into the technical realm of formal logic, specifically focusing on the relationship between names, propositions, and the nature of truth and falsehood.</meta>

This argument—that "blindness" and "the fact that blindness is blindness" are the same thing—is true; therefore, the other point must be true as well. For by the same logic, it would follow that if this is a **complex** <term>complexum: in medieval logic, a proposition or a statement made of multiple parts, rather than a single term</term>, then the other is too. This is absurd, since "blindness" is a **simple name** <note>A single word or concept, not a full sentence.</note>, not a complex one or any kind of **statement**. <margin>Gregory of Rimini</margin> Therefore, it is one thing for "blindness" to be true, and another for the "fact that blindness is blindness" to be true.

And although these points might suffice for my uncle's defense, do not think that there is any lack of further ways to protect and fight for his position. So that a more complete response may reach you, I want you to know that according to the opinion of **Gregory of Rimini** <note>A 14th-century philosopher and theologian known for his "nominalist" views on how language relates to reality.</note>, I could have said that even if, once "blindness" is posited, the "fact that blindness is blindness" were also posited, it does not necessarily follow that they are the same thing. For he denies this logical consequence (and many like it): "If everything else besides God were set aside, God exists; therefore, God is the fact that 'God exists'."

<margin>The Cardinal of Cambrai</margin> The **Cardinal of Cambrai** <note>Pierre d’Ailly (1351–1420), a prominent theologian and logician.</note> also denies all sentences in which something is stated about an infinitive phrase used in a meaningful way. He asserts that such sentences are both false and logically improper, as can be seen in his first book on the *Sentences* <note>The "Sentences" by Peter Lombard was the standard theology textbook of the Middle Ages.</note>.

<margin>Ninth objection and the solution to the objection.</margin>
Next, you complain that "the false" should not have been described as being **divided** <note>In logic, "divided" (sensus divisus) refers to looking at the components of a statement separately rather than as a single unit.</note> with this specific condition: "as long as it is false." You explain your point in these words: "If everything false is simply 'divided'—a point you do not deny has been proven—then there was no need to say that a certain falsehood is divided only on the condition that it remains false."

For if every human is simply and absolutely **capable of laughter** <term>risibilis: the classic logical example of a "proper" attribute—something that belongs only to humans</term>, one does not need to add a condition to restrict it, saying, "Every human is capable of laughter *as long as* they are human." You argue that a restriction shouldn't be added just because not all false things are equally "divided" or equally false; after all, not all **beings** are equally good, yet all beings are absolutely good.

But consider his words carefully, and you will be able to cast aside every doubt. He says that not every "false divided" is equally false, because they are not equally divided. For those things are not [necessarily] false which are not *necessarily and always* false. Antonio, that phrase "as long as" was quietly added because those things are not always and necessarily false; for even though they are false, they can become true and "united" <note>The opposite of "divided" in this logical sense.</note> either through nature or the work of a craftsman—a point you yourself made in your second set of objections.

Nevertheless, as long as they are divided, they remain false. Those things, however, are *always* false which can never return to "friendship" <note>A metaphor for things that are logically impossible or can never be made true.</note>, as is shown abundantly in the response to the second objections. Nor do your analogies about beings and the capacity for laughter support you much. For beings are always and absolutely good. Even though they are not all *equally* good—some participating more in the nature of "good" than others—they are nonetheless always and necessarily good. Insofar as they are beings, they are good, and they cannot become "non-beings" or "non-good" unless they are reduced to nothingness.

But a "false divided" statement, which consists in a **complex** <note>A proposition or sentence.</note>, can easily become "not divided" and true. Therefore, your analogy does not fit. For although not all false things are equally divided, they are nonetheless false insofar as they are not united and not true. Furthermore, this objection should have troubled us very little. For who would doubt that a human (who is absolutely and always capable of laughter) can be described as being capable of laughter *as long as* he is a human? Would learned men really disapprove of the phrase: "A human is capable of laughter as long as he exists"?

<margin>Solution to the tenth objection</margin>
The tenth chapter of your objections brings nothing else against him except the claim that what you said could have been easily established if only the logic of **contrary motions** <note>A reference to Aristotelian physics/logic regarding how things change from one state to their opposite.</note> had been sufficiently understood by him...

<summary>Gianfrancesco Pico defends his uncle's logic by distinguishing between simple terms and complex propositions, citing authorities like Gregory of Rimini and Pierre d'Ailly. He refutes Antonio's objection regarding the "divided" nature of falsehood, arguing that logical conditions like "as long as" are necessary for non-permanent truths.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the logical and philosophical dispute between Gianfrancesco Pico della Mirandola and his critic, Antonio. The previous page discussed the nature of "truth" and "complex statements" regarding blindness. This page shifts to a technical debate over the "contrariety" of good and evil, drawing on Aristotle’s Physics and the interpretations of Simplicius and Boethius.</meta>

But he, unless his memory failed him, complained that you did not prove what you so often claimed to follow—namely, that the contrariety of good and evil is inferred from the contrariety of "pursuing" and "fleeing." He said: if good is to be sought precisely because it is good, and evil is to be fled, and if "fleeing" and "seeking" are contraries, how do you prove from this that good and evil are contraries? This is the very thing you must prove, yet you have never said a word to prove it, nor do you now. He denies the form of your argument. 

Perhaps for this reason—since "seeking" and "fleeing" are not properly **contrary motions** <term>motus contrarii: in Aristotelian physics, motions that move in opposite directions between two opposite states</term> from which contrary terms can be identified—even Aristotle himself assigns a certain contrariety of **changes** <margin>Aristotle</margin> in the sixth book of his *Physics* <note>original: "sexto physicæ auscultationis libro." Aristotle's Physics was often referred to as "Physical Lectures."</note> where the terms are not "contraries" but **contradictories** <note>In logic, "contraries" (like black and white) allow for a middle ground, while "contradictories" (like being and non-being) are mutually exclusive with no middle ground.</note>—namely, **being** and **non-being**. For generation proceeds from non-being to being, while corruption falls from being into non-being. 

But you have once again dragged out this contrariety of good and evil and brought no other proof. Do not doubt that he has carefully looked into the logic of contrary motions "from the very fingernails" <note>original: "ab ipis ut aiunt unguiculis." A Latin idiom meaning to examine something thoroughly or from the very beginning.</note>. Indeed, he has often not only pushed back your arguments against him regarding this contrariety, but even acted against you. In his second letter, he deduced that your proof implies not only that good and evil are contraries, but that **contradictories** are contraries. Second, he turned your own weapons against you in this way: "According to you, good and evil are contraries, and each of a pair of contraries is something **positive**. And according to you, **non-being** is good. Therefore, according to you, non-being is something positive. But 'something' and 'being' are interchangeable terms; therefore, according to you, non-being is something positive."

<margin>Solution to the eleventh objection</margin> When you said in your third letter that he was retreating to **Simplicius** <note>A 6th-century Greek philosopher and one of the last Neoplatonists; he wrote extensive commentaries on Aristotle.</note> and leaving behind the Latin interpreters regarding the opposition of good and evil, he responded as if in amazement. Why should you, who used to be a "Boethian" and a mocker of "barbarians" <note>The "barbarians" likely refers to the late-medieval Scholastic philosophers whose Latin was considered "unpolished" by Renaissance Humanists.</note>, now mock those who, setting aside Latin interpreters, follow the Greek ones? He relies most effectively on the point that you are thinking incorrectly if you believe Greek philosophers should not be magnified. **Boethius** <margin>Boethius</margin> <note>A Roman statesman and philosopher whose translations of Aristotle were the foundation of logic in the Middle Ages.</note>, whom you hold in high price and honor, always held them in the highest honor and used them as both teachers and guides. 

You reply that it is not a matter for wonder, since the Latins do not deny Aristotle, whom Simplicius also does not deny, and so on. But it does not seem to me that Simplicius denies Aristotle, since he interprets him correctly; nor does it appear that the Latin interpreters vary from Simplicius's opinion when they embrace it with their whole mind and follow it in their works. If he was amazed that you denied the Latin commentators follow Simplicius, he would have fallen into an even greater stupor if he had understood you to claim the Latins do not deny Aristotle but Simplicius does. 

Furthermore, Simplicius and those who follow him clearly elucidate Aristotle’s mind when they say good and evil are contraries because one of the contraries always has the character of evil and "deficiency." For this reason, in the first book of the *Physics*, he taught that contraries are always compared according to the logic of "better" and "worse" respectively. He also imitated the **Pythagoreans** <margin>Pythagoreans</margin> <note>Followers of Pythagoras, known for their "Table of Opposites" (the Dualism of Limited/Unlimited, Good/Evil, etc.).</note>, who established two "orders" of things, one contained under good and the other under evil. He frequently used this exposition in his logical books with external examples...

It also defends the use of Greek commentators like Simplicius, noting that even Boethius respected the Greek tradition over Latin interpretations.</summary>

<margin>Thomas</margin>

<margin>Burley</margin>
<margin>Esculanus</margin>
<margin>John Scotus</margin>

<margin>Augustine</margin>
of the Manichaeans, said that no nature is evil; and shortly after, lest there be any ambiguity about what he meant by "nature," he added: "and nature itself is nothing other than that which is understood to be something in its own kind." We have seen that Giles of Rome, in his first book of

He asserts it is nothing but a name. He likewise interprets Aristotle's words on the opposition of good and evil according to [my] uncle's mind, and agrees with the teachings of Simplicius and other worthy interpreters of Aristotle—
<margin>Simplicius</margin>
namely, declaring that they [good and evil] are not proper **genera** <note>In logic, a genus is a category under which species are grouped.</note> but that only of other contraries should "genera" be properly spoken. For one has the character of a positive thing while the other does not; and no
<margin>Gregory of Rimini</margin>
contrary, in itself, is "non-being," but rather some nature and existence. Gregory of Rimini testifies to this same thing in his commentaries on the second book of the *Sentences*: namely, that evil itself is not—to use his language—any "entity," but pure privation. This same thing was felt by that man of most sharp intellect, Robert Holcot, in the first question of his commentaries on the second
<margin>Robert Holcot</margin>
book of theological *Sentences*. Many others have judged the same, whom it would perhaps be tedious for me to cite while writing and for you to read later. It will be enough for the present business to have enumerated these, especially since we must speak of this again when dissolving other objections where mention is made of evil. But to return to where we digressed: of all the Latins, you seem to summon only Boethius to judgment against Simplicius and the other illustrious interpreters. If you deign to count only him among the Latins, he will be a *single* Latin commentator—not "the Latin commentators"—who seems to support your opinion. Add to this that even he, if his mind is properly examined, does not protest against our view, since he neither treats this question exactly nor examines it with final judgment, but only declares what Aristotle's words, strictly and narrowly grasped, demand—which is a habit very familiar to him...

Indeed, it was my intention in this matter to resolve your final objections against my uncle, but to pass over in silence those to which he himself had already responded in some way. Nevertheless, if something does not seem fully clarified by him which you both hope for and demand that I explain, we will attempt to satisfy your desire. We will wander through your arguments, both dissolving them and responding to them with all our strength. For he did not judge it inappropriate for even your smallest word to lack a response. He confesses in his first letters that certain things were omitted to which no response was given, lest he waste words on trivial matters; and some things were treated lightly, as he considered that for a philosopher, things should be indicated rather than [laboriously] explained. I would wish you to interpret these words such that it was not worth the effort—for you, a noble philosopher, against a man most celebrated in both learning and fame—to bring up several points whose controversies are known even to common philosophers. He [my uncle] holds a discourse on the highest things and would not descend to discuss these lowest matters without a loss of the high speculations he had conceived regarding the most difficult subjects. However, concerning this "contrariety" of yours, we shall say something in the following response when we speak of "partial privations" <term>partial privations: (original: "semiplenis priuationibus") the idea that a lack of something, like sight or health, might be only "half-full" or incomplete rather than a total absence.</term>.

<margin>Solution to the thirteenth objection.</margin>
You wonder, moreover, that he marveled at your invention of "partial privations." I believe his wonder was not so much at that time as it was after you tried to prove it again (if indeed your last objections were seen by him). He had said against you: "Evil is nothing; therefore, it is not a partial privation." You, however, pursue his argument in this way: "Sickness is evil, therefore it is nothing. Therefore, it is not a partial privation." But sickness is a certain kind of privation; therefore, it is not a partial privation of either health or some other good, but rather a full and perfect one. This, you argue, cannot happen; therefore, privations are "partial" <note>original: "semiplenæ." Antonio is trying to argue that things like sickness or blindness are "partial" lacks of a quality, rather than a total "nothingness."</note>—such as sickness, rarity, ugliness, or blindness. You say that blindness is a perfect privation of sight, but an imperfect privation of the good. These are your words, verbatim. But I, my dear Antonio, would say freely that these words of yours do nothing against him, which I will review one by one so that you may see more clearly. You say first, from his own words: "Evil is nothing, therefore it is not a partial privation." You are walking on the right path. Again: "Sickness is evil, therefore it is nothing; therefore it is not a partial privation." Thus far you proceed correctly, because sickness, insofar as it is evil, is to that extent "nothing." Again you say: "But sickness is a certain kind of privation, therefore not of health," and so on until the end. In my judgment, with your leave, a falsehood is built upon these words, which we shall endeavor to show. For blindness is not only a "perfect" <note>In this context, "perfect" means "complete" or "total."</note> privation of sight, as you say, but it can also be called a perfect privation of the good, because all that good...

<meta>This page continues Gianfrancesco Pico della Mirandola’s defense of his uncle, Giovanni Pico, against the criticisms of Antonio. The argument here focuses on the definition of "privation" (the absence of a quality) and "evil," drawing heavily on the works of the 5th-century philosopher Dionysius the Areopagite.</meta>

<sig>PP ii</sig>

<margin>
Privation is considered in two ways.
</margin>
<margin>
Dionysius
</margin>
...removes that which it is naturally disposed to remove—namely, sight—which <term>ophthalmia</term><note>An old medical term for severe inflammation of the eye.</note> does not do, although it too may destroy the good it is naturally disposed to take away. However, it can in no way be called the privation of something it is not suited to destroy, whether you call it "half-complete" or "complete." For privation is considered either absolutely—that is, as it relates to a <term>habit</term><note>original: "habitum." In this context, a "habit" is not a routine behavior, but a stable quality or state of being, like health or sight.</note> in general—or it is restricted to a certain and limited kind of being, such as the health of the whole body, the eye, beauty, and other things of that sort. 

In the first way, it does not deprive a particular habit because an "all-encompassing" privation—as **Dionysius** says in his book *On the Divine Names*—is utterly lacking in power. In the second way, which Dionysius calls "singular" (distinguishing it from the universal), it deprives the specific habit it regards. In this manner, such a privation is "complete" regarding the habit it is naturally disposed to harm; it is not a "half-complete" privation of some other thing. For who would dare to say that blindness is a half-complete privation of a man, or of some other good that might be in a man? Therefore, an absolute privation regards a habit absolutely, while a proper and particular privation regards a proper and particular habit and does not exceed its limits. 

Wherefore illness is a complete privation, not a half-complete one, whether you ascribe it to the whole body or to a particular limb. For a fever is a perfect privation of that <term>balance</term><note>original: "temperative." Referring to the "temperament" or balance of bodily humors.</note> which it is naturally disposed to corrupt. Ophthalmia, too, even if it is not a privation of the whole good in the eye, is nevertheless a perfect and proper privation of *some* good, because it destroys all of that good which it is naturally disposed to destroy, even when it does not take away sight, provided the ophthalmia does nothing else. 

**Ugliness** also—because it takes away all that good which it is able to remove, namely the perfect arrangement of parts which is called **beauty**—is a perfect privation; and consider the rest in the same way. We might also say this in excess: blindness, insofar as it is blindness, is an evil; insofar as it is an evil, it is "nothing"; insofar as it is nothing, it is not a "half-complete" privation, because if it were half-complete, it would leave behind something positive, which evil does not do. 

Furthermore, no privation in itself actually deprives one of *every* good; therefore, [by your logic] all privations would be "half-complete" privations. This contradicts your own position, because you contend that some are complete and others are half-complete. This connection is excellent and necessary, and we prove what we have assumed by this argument: since no good would ever be found if a certain total and universal privation were found in the nature of things—as we hinted a little earlier from the words of **Dionysius**. For evil deprives a particular good, since evil exists *within* the good; a universal evil would destroy universal good, if indeed such a thing could be found—which is impossible. And so, conclude that privations of their own habits are always found to be complete, not half-complete.

<margin>
Solution to the fourteenth objection.
</margin>

To the fourteenth objection, which contains several questions, I respond individually. First, I say that not every evil leaves something of the good behind, unless you understand it to be in some <term>subject</term><note>The physical thing or person in which the quality exists.</note> which the evil itself does not regard, or unless you consider that subject according to the habit which is destroyed by the evil itself. Nor did my uncle assert that which is opposite to the habit—which you nevertheless attribute to him and seize upon as a hypothesis he supposedly asserted. For he abundantly testified that some evil is found which completely takes away all the good that is naturally from it, since in the response to the second letter he reminded you of this, writing in this manner: "Certainly you ought to have considered this..."

<summary>This page argues that evil is a "complete privation" of a specific good or quality (habit), rather than a partial or "half-complete" absence. Using Dionysius the Areopagite as an authority, Gianfrancesco explains that while an evil like blindness doesn't destroy a man's entire existence, it is a total destruction of the specific quality of sight.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Gianfrancesco Pico della Mirandola’s philosophical defense of his uncle, Giovanni Pico della Mirandola. It maintains continuity with the previous page's focus on Dionysius the Areopagite's definitions of privation and being.</meta>

<sig>ii qq</sig>

...that what is granted regarding certain imperfect evils—on account of the mixture of goodness they still retain—must not be transferred to the unmixed and absolute nature of evil itself. And so that you may perceive the truth more clearly, I will not hesitate to explain the force of the distinction:

<margin>Evil is understood in two ways.</margin>
Evil can be considered in two ways: first, absolutely and according to its own nature as evil—that is, insofar as it is **nothing**. Second, insofar as it is a <term>privation</term><note>The absence or lack of a quality that should naturally be present in a subject.</note> of a certain good—this is a "particular evil." Evil accepted in this second way leaves behind some subject of goodness; however, the other kind of evil does not do this, as it is entirely <term>non-being</term> and nothing. We call the <term>Chymera</term><note>A mythical beast used in formal logic to represent a "non-entity" or something that is fundamentally impossible and non-existent.</note> such a thing, since it does not regard any subject or <term>habit</term><note>original: "habitum." In this context, a stable state of being or a quality that a subject possesses, such as health or sight.</note>. For this reason, it is called "altogether evil" and is distinguished from the absolute and unmixed nature of evil.

<margin>Dionysius</margin>
As **Dionysius** says in his book *On the Divine Names*: "this evil, because it lacks a subject, is in no way, nowhere, and is a non-existent nothing." Even if a Chymera could be called "good in potentiality" because of the power to produce it which exists in God, it still cannot be named either a "being" or "good." For if this connection—namely, "something is good in potentiality, therefore it is good"—were valid, I think it would turn back upon its author like a blow, forcing him to admit that everything that *ought* to be created by God (but is not yet) and even things that have been destroyed are simultaneously "something" and "not something." For if, according to him, they were both "beings" and "good" by the power of the Creator, then they would necessarily be *something*, since "something" and "good" are interchangeable terms and cover the same ground entirely.

However, I will argue as follows that it could not be "something": "Nothing can be made out of nothing." Before a Chymera is created, according to your view, it cannot exist unless it is created. Therefore, it is created from nothing. Thus, before it was created from nothing, it was not "something." Therefore, a thing cannot be called "absolutely good" simply because of the power of goodness that exists in the Creator; otherwise, to use the language of our <term>dialecticians</term><note>Scholars of logic and argumentation.</note>, a <term>fallacy of the accident</term><note>original: "fallatia secundum quid ad simpliciter." A logical error where a statement that is true only in a specific, limited sense is wrongly applied as a general, absolute truth.</note> would be committed. I intentionally pass over those things asserted against that opinion concerning "eternal <term>quiddities</term><note>The "what-ness" or essential nature of a thing.</note>" (so to speak), and the objects proposed, even if your opinion could perhaps be weakened by those same reasons.

<margin>Averroes</margin>
It is enough for our purpose if we have proved that a Chymera cannot be called good. We can also say that we are following **Averroes** in this matter; he says that "being in potentiality" is not "being," where in his commentaries on the fourth book of the *Metaphysics* (fifteenth division), he stated that "that which is not in <term>act</term><note>original: "actu." In Aristotelian philosophy, "actuality" is the reality or completion of a thing, as opposed to its mere potential to exist.</note> is not being."

As for what you add—namely, that a Chymera is a "being" because, although the power to produce it is in God, the power of God and the power of the Chymera are different in <term>reason</term><note>That is, they are conceptually distinct even if they relate to the same divine action.</note>—I respond: First, I can deny that God's power and the power of producing a Chymera are different in reason. Second, even if it were granted to you for the sake of argument that those powers are different, what would your reasoning prove? A Chymera can in no way be called a "being" on account of a "power to produce itself" existing in God. That power is so far from being able to be called the "Chymera" or "something internal to the Chymera" that they are, in fact, infinitely distant.

Furthermore, you add that if God’s power and our own thought are excluded, the Chymera is not "evil," since evil is a privation that exists in a subject participating in goodness. To this, I would like to respond with the same distinction as a moment ago, since the Chymera...

...[sub]ject, but is absolutely bad, even though it is conceived by us. That is to say, we can declare that the very **notion of the chimera** <note>original: "notionem chymeræ." A mental concept of a mythical creature.</note> which we carry in our mind is "something" and therefore "good" <note>In scholastic philosophy, "being" and "goodness" are interchangeable; if something exists, even as a thought, it has a degree of goodness.</note>; however, we must pronounce that the **chimera** itself is neither "something" nor "good."

<margin>Solution to the fifteenth objection</margin>
Furthermore, you seem to rejoice as if what you brought forward was not disproven, and as if the only response given was that **Simplicius** <note>A 6th-century commentator on Aristotle.</note> did not say that concerning simple things. Likewise, you claim you did not say that **Aristotle** felt every being was entirely either <term>per se</term> <note>In itself; essential being.</note> or <term>per accidens</term> <note>By accident; incidental being.</note>, nor did you ascribe anything to **Thomas [Aquinas]** on that account. Truly, even if so much has been said on this matter by the one we are defending <note>His uncle, Giovanni Pico della Mirandola.</note> that it seems unnecessary for me to speak further—and though I once proposed not to retract what he had discussed—I will nevertheless say this for my uncle's sake out of an abundance of caution: namely, that **Simplicius**, whom you have so often summoned to testify, has more often borne witness against you than my uncle has devised in his responses.

Again, I would like to know whether you have undertaken to defend the idea that, according to the mind of **Aristotle**, not every being is either "by accident" or "in itself." For he, in the fifth book of his *First Philosophy* <note>The *Metaphysics*.</note>, divides being into **being in itself** (*per se*) and **being by accident** (*per accidens*). Finally, they are divided into <term>substance</term> and <term>accident</term>, which were contained in the first branch of that partition, since "being in itself" is divided into ten <term>genera</term> <note>The ten Categories of Aristotle (substance, quality, quantity, etc.).</note>, of which one is substance and the rest are accidents. I would now most gladly be taught by you what sort of "being" that would be which is neither *per se* nor *per accidens*.

And if perhaps you were to say—as you produced in your first objections—that this division into *per se* and *per accidens* is an assignment of <term>complex being</term> <note>A "complex being" refers to a proposition or a combination of terms (e.g., "the man is white"), whereas a "simple being" is a single term (e.g., "man").</note>, I would not hesitate to respond that you truly cannot demonstrate this. You cannot support your opinion with any sentiment of **Aristotle** nor with suitable reason, since in that passage **Aristotle** divides being *per se* into ten genera, of which one is substance and nine are accidents. No one believes these to be "complex beings" when they are distinguished against "complexes," especially since **Averroes** <note>The influential 12th-century Islamic philosopher and commentator on Aristotle.</note> says in that place that "being in itself" is divided according to terms signifying the genera of the <term>predicaments</term> <note>The Categories.</note>, and a term is not a complex being. Also, in the sixth book of the *Metaphysics*, the same **Averroes** says that the first division of being is into *per se* and *per accidens*; however, it could not be the "first" if a division of "complex being" preceded it. Nor is it found in **Thomas's** fifth book of the *Metaphysics* that "complex being" is divided in the way you asserted.

Indeed, it cannot be believed—since being is first partitioned into *per se* and *per accidens*, and that *per se* is sub-partitioned into the ten genera which we have shown to be incomplex—that a division of "complex being" is assigned in that place, since it is necessary that what is divided be predicated of the dividing members. Let these things be said, even if they pertain little to the business at hand, since that dogma of yours seems to me at first glance to be consistent neither with the views of the Aristotelian interpreters nor with reason. But if perchance you prove the contrary, it will be most welcome to have learned something from such a serious philosopher as I certainly judge you to be.

You oppose this, saying it is not established that there is one opposition of affirmation and negation, and another of privation and <term>habit</term> <note>The presence of a quality or state.</note>; and that it does not follow that if "evil" were the privation of "good," then "evil" and "not good" would necessarily be interchangeable. <meta>This page continues Gianfrancesco Pico della Mirandola’s defense of his uncle, Giovanni Pico della Mirandola. The text moves into a technical scholastic argument about the nature of evil as a "deprivation" of good, drawing on Aristotle, Albertus Magnus, Thomas Aquinas, and Anselm, before addressing the 17th objection regarding the mystical knowledge of God and the work "On Being and the One."</meta>

I would like there to be one kind of opposition for <term>privation</term> <note>A lack of something that ought to be present, like blindness is the privation of sight.</note> and another for negation, and I would like him not to have put forward that opposite; but it still follows that if evil is opposed to good as a privation, 
<margin>Albertus Magnus</margin>
it is necessary for "evil" and "non-good" to be interchangeable. For as the great **Albertus** says in the first book of the *Physical Auscultation* <note>Aristotle’s Physics.</note>, privation, insofar as it is privation, does not exist of itself or through itself, because of itself it possesses "non-being." Indeed, it was also asserted by **Aristotle** in the *First Philosophy* <note>The Metaphysics.</note> that privations belong to the category of non-beings, since privation of itself is the other extreme of a contradiction. And therefore, since evil is the privation of good, and non-being follows from this, then insofar as evil is evil, "evil" and "non-good" are interchangeable. For "evil" and "nothing"—as has been proven—are the same; likewise, "nothing" and "non-being" are the same; and similarly, "non-being" and "non-good" are the same because "being" and "good" are the same. For this reason, my uncle said most correctly that negation is a privation to the extent that privation was formally a negation. For even if they differ in this—that one of them, namely contradiction, has no middle ground (as the **Philosopher** <note>Aristotle.</note> says in the first book of the *Posterior Analytics*), while the other may have one in a certain way since it occurs with its opposite regarding the same thing—nevertheless, as far as the present purpose is concerned, they would be the same, since privation of itself is negation and non-being, and posits nothing, as 
<margin>Thomas.</margin>
**Thomas [Aquinas]** proves in many places, most notably in his treatise *On the Four Opposites*. If indeed "non-being" things are "evil," and "evil" things are "not good," you can gather from this that "evil" and "non-good" are entirely interchangeable. And do not believe that illustrious men have been lacking who asserted this: 
<margin>Aristotle. Anselm</margin>
Listen to **Aristotle** saying that "good" is spoken of equally with "being." Add, therefore, by the rule of contradictories, "evil" to "non-being." Listen to the most celebrated theologian **Anselm**, Archbishop of Canterbury, in his book *On the Fall of the Devil*, uttering these words: <note>original: "malum non est aliud q̃ non bonum"</note> "evil is nothing other than non-good." From these things it is most consistently gathered that "evil" and "non-good" follow one another mutually.

<margin>Solution to the objections which were contained in the seventeenth place.</margin>
There would have been no controversies between you and him in the seventeenth place if you had more diligently considered that little book *On Being and the One* <note>original: "de ente et uno." Giovanni Pico's famous attempt to reconcile Plato and Aristotle.</note> and if you had recalled to memory whatever was written in it concerning those steps and that very <term>darkness</term> <note>original: "calligine." A reference to the "Divine Darkness" or "Cloud of Unknowing" in mystical theology.</note> which is granted to those who contemplate. You would have seen that in those first three steps, something can be predicated of God; in the fourth, not at all. 
<margin>Dionysius</margin>
And there, the window of understanding the books of **Dionysius** <note>Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, a foundational mystical theologian.</note> was opened, through which you could most conveniently be advised of this: for he neither denies, nor could he deny, that this statement is true: "God is God," in the way that we are able to both conceive and speak of God—namely, while situated in those first three steps. But he only denies that any predicate can truly explain the nature of God in that 
<margin>Philosophers and theologians</margin>
fourth step of "darkness" alone, which all rightly-thinking philosophers (to say nothing of theologians) would also affirm. Since this name "God," which performs the office of a predicate in this proposition "God is God," not only fails to explain and declare the divine essence and nature, 
<margin>In what order one must proceed in dissolving this objection.</margin>
but is also infinitely surpassed by it, he denied that it could be affirmed of God, keeping in view that fourth step of darkness. Come then, let us examine the words themselves which will testify to the man's mind; afterwards, we will bring forward some points so that it may be seen more clearly whether and how God can be spoken of by us; finally, we will show that your arguments against his words—even taken as they stand—conclude nothing. He had said that it is said...

<meta>This page continues the defense of Giovanni Pico della Mirandola by his nephew Gianfrancesco. Having discussed the nature of evil and privation on the previous page, the text now shifts to the 17th objection concerning the name of God and the "apophatic" (negative) theology of Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite. The argument centers on whether human language can ever truly describe the nature of the Divine.</meta>

...[it can be] truly [said that] God is God; likewise, according to the opinion of **Dionysius**, He is greater than any name, even this name of "God," just as was held in his book *On Mystical Theology*. He had said in another place that when, through this word "God," you conceive only that which is signified by the name, this word does not have the character of a <term>predicate</term> <note>In logic, the part of a sentence that says something about the subject. Here, saying "God is God" is seen as a circular statement that doesn't actually provide new information about His nature.</note> but refers to itself when it is asked what can or should be declared about Him, rather than something that could be declared about another. For this reason, this was not unknown to **Simonides**, nor to the **Tyrant** <note>Hiero I of Syracuse, who famously asked the poet Simonides to define God; Simonides repeatedly asked for more time because the more he thought, the less he felt he understood.</note> who consulted him. For when you ask if "God" cannot be called "God," or if there is something else from God, I ask you what you would conceive through this word "God" that you would declare about God. If you conceive nothing, you would not err, because you would be saying nothing. If you conceive something, you must say that God is something other than what you conceive, and you would explain your concept through this word "God," since He would be above everything that could be conceived by us—so says that author. 

I believed it would be clear to you from these words that there is a most true solution to your doubts on this matter. 

<margin>**Dionysius**</margin>

But you, indeed, contend that **Dionysius** does not deny that "God is God." Read, I pray, **Dionysius** in the final chapter of the book *On Mystical Theology* and the first *Letter to Gaius*, and it will become plain to you that God is greater than every name. Read the same author again in the second chapter of *The Celestial Hierarchy*, and you will understand that this <term>divine man</term> <note>A common honorific for Dionysius the Areopagite.</note> teaches us that the likeness of Divine truth transcends all substance and life; no light can express it, and every discourse, every mind, and every reason is, without any comparison, inferior to the likeness of that truth. From these things, I thought you could weigh the mind of my uncle: namely, that in this way it cannot truly be said "God is God" such that through this name "God," acting as a predicate, that which we strive to conceive through it is declared. It is not that "God is God" could not be said in some way, just as it is said "God is good" or "God is wise," and other predications are allowed with which the sacred books are full, in which something is declared about God in some manner. But His nature is not explained, since it stands at an infinite distance from those concepts, just as my uncle quite clearly taught in the fifth chapter of his book *On Being and the One*. He was not speaking about those words of **Dionysius** which are cited by **Thomas** <note>Thomas Aquinas.</note>, as you supposed, but about those which were cited a little earlier. 

Furthermore, **John of Damascus** writes in the first book of his *Sentences* of theology that certain things said affirmatively about God have the force of a "superexcellent negation." For example, if we call "darkness" in God, we do not understand darkness, but rather that He is not light—or rather, we say He is "above light" and "light itself" when darkness is absent. 

<margin>**Jean Gerson**, Chancellor of Paris</margin>

Treating this same opinion, the most learned and most devout **Chancellor of Paris** <note>Jean Gerson (1363–1429), a prominent French theologian.</note> says: "Therefore, whatever we say affirmatively about God includes some negation." And a little later, he says for this reason that **Dionysius** denies God is "being" but affirms Him to be "above being."

<margin>**Giles**</margin>

**Giles** <note>Giles of Rome (Egidius Romanus), a student of Thomas Aquinas.</note> says in his first book of *Sentences* that God is wise, but not in the way that we understand "wise." Hence, he says this is the reason why **Averroes**, in the twelfth book of the *Metaphysics*, pronounced that these predications we attribute to God are similar to mathematical propositions; in their manner, those things which we understand are in the objects, but not in the way we understand them—just as we understand a line which is in matter, but not by the same logic as it exists in matter. But why should I delay you with many words, when I can make you more certain of this truth we assert with even a few: namely, so that you may know that whatever we predicate of God signifies something far different from what we conceive and declare.

<summary>Gianfrancesco defends his uncle’s claim that God transcends all names and human concepts, citing authorities like Pseudo-Dionysius, John of Damascus, and Jean Gerson to argue that human language about God is always metaphorical or "above being." <margin>
Christ
Dionysius
</margin>

Jesus Christ himself, the power of God and the wisdom of God, says—as the Gospel of John bears witness—that **God is spirit**. Dionysius, in his book *On Mystical Theology*, speaking of God and contemplating the ineffable <term>deity</term> <note>The divine nature or essence of God, often considered beyond human description.</note>, removes many of the predicates <note>Qualities or characteristics assigned to a subject in logic.</note> that we attribute to Him, saying that He is **not even spirit** insofar as we are able to know it. See, therefore, that Dionysius does not wish to deny that God is spirit, but rather that He is spirit in the way that we can understand "spirit." By these final words, he teaches the reader that it is true that God is spirit, so that he might agree with the Gospel of Christ, and yet that He is not spirit in the way we perceive it, lest we believe that the nature of God can be truly expressed by us through any name. 

Indeed, I thought it was not unknown to you how great the authority of Dionysius is, and how highly his most sacred dogmas have been extolled with praise and celebrated by all the theologians who have attended the **Schools of Paris** <note>The University of Paris, the premier center for medieval theological study.</note>. Nevertheless, since your uncle, in his responses to your objections, hinted that during your disputation you did not very willingly admit the sayings of Dionysius, I would have you know that he stood out as the most faithful disciple of **Paul the Apostle** in the faith of Christ. By Paul's help, God willed that Dionysius, having left behind the errors of the <term>gentiles</term> <note>Non-Jewish people; here referring to the pagan Greeks.</note>, should both recognize and follow the truth and be gifted with the crown of martyrdom for the faith of Christ. **Gregory** and **Pope Martin**, in the synod celebrated at Rome against the heretics, said great things of his doctrine; **Damascene** and many others have extolled him with the highest praise. His books were hidden for a long time by heretics from the minds of the faithful, 

<margin>
Constantine
the Philosopher.
</margin>

and there was a report of **Constantine the Philosopher** <note>Also known as St. Cyril, the missionary to the Slavs, who was said to have committed Dionysius’s works to memory.</note> who had committed all his books to memory. If Dionysius had been held in such regard by the many Fathers who fought great wars against the heretics and enemies of the most holy Catholic Church, how much more quickly and easily would they have achieved a triumph over their enemies (which was only done later, slowly and with great, exhausting labors).

But when you intend to prove that God can be called "God" because of the "reason of the name" <note>The logical definition or etymological meaning associated with the word.</note> which is predicated of the name, I say that you labor in vain (my **Antony**). For you are not announcing anything about God, but about this name "God"—which I shall explain more broadly so that it may be understood more clearly. For I ask you: what do you conceive through the letter "a," which you designated for the "reason of the name"? If you conceive nothing, you do not err (to use the words of your uncle). If you conceive something, I ask again if you conceive it as that about which something can be announced. If in this way, you also do not err, because again that "a" will hold the place of the **subject**, not the **predicate**. But if you were to conceive that which is announced about Him, you would wander far from the truth, since God Himself is infinitely greater than 

<margin>
Apuleius
Plato

Even the **Platonist Apuleius** <note>A 2nd-century Roman writer and philosopher; here cited for his Latin translation of Plato’s ideas.</note>, in his book *On the Doctrine of Plato*, calls Him "unutterable" and "unnamable." The words of **Plato** himself on this matter were made into Latin by that same Apuleius: *To have found God is by no means easy; to have understood Him is impossible.* Therefore, let us say that all affirmations about God are "improper," because whenever we wish not only to speak but even to conceive something, He exceeds it to infinity. Indeed, we are not only unable to comprehend God while held in this earthly prison of ignorance and misery, but even when we are established in the heavens in that enjoyment of God by which we are perfectly blessed, we shall not **comprehend** Him, but only **apprehend** Him (to use the words of our theologians).

<meta>This page continues the defense of Giovanni Pico della Mirandola's theological views. While the previous page established that God’s nature cannot be captured by human names—referencing Dionysius the Areopagite—this section addresses the logical challenge of how we can speak of, love, or worship a God who is "unconceivable."</meta>

...it will be forgiven. Furthermore, you believe that these two propositions contradict one another: namely, that **God is above all that can be conceived**, and that **nothing can be affirmed about God**. You argue that if the definition of the name "God" is "that which is above what can be conceived," then the argument for God's existence or nature will fail. But this is resolved when one understands that when it is said that "proper affirmations" <note>An "affirmation" in this context is a positive statement about what something is, such as "God is wise."</note> cannot be brought forward concerning God, it means that no <term>predicate</term> <note>A term or quality assigned to a subject in logic.</note> can be found that represents the nature of God in its entirety. Indeed, this phrase—"above all that can be conceived"—means nothing other than that God cannot be fully grasped by the mind, and that what God is in His essence cannot be known. These words, therefore, do not merely state what God is, but rather that it is impossible to know what He is. Thus, they possess the power of **negating** rather than **affirming**. 

However, even if I granted that these words were affirmations, your argument still would not hold. Otherwise, if someone desired to know about an unknown thing and asked us about its essence, and we responded to the seeker: "It is that which we do not know, which we are not acquainted with, which we have not yet conceived in the mind, nor are able to conceive," that person’s request would not seem to be satisfied. By receiving such a teaching, they would not be able to state anything about that thing affirmatively, but only negatively—unless, perhaps, someone could be found who could explain to others what that thing was which, being entirely unknown to men and beyond the reach of all thought, 

<margin>Simonides</margin>
could not be known or conceived even by himself. Thus, both **Simonides** <note>Simonides of Ceos, a Greek poet. According to a famous story, when the Tyrant Hiero asked him "What is God?", Simonides repeatedly asked for more time to deliberate, eventually concluding that the more he meditated on God, the more obscure the subject became.</note> and the Tyrant who consulted him knew that the name of God represented something of the greatest importance; yet one of them desired to know what God was, while the other admitted he did not know. 

Furthermore, you use the following logic: "God is above all that can be conceived; therefore, God cannot be conceived—otherwise He would be 'above Himself'—and therefore He cannot be loved or worshiped." I respond that God can be conceived in His entirety, exactly as He is, **only by Himself**, and by no other intellect. Yet it does not follow from this that He cannot be loved or worshiped. For we conceive the <term>deity</term> <note>The divine essence or Godhead.</note> to be so great, endowed with omnipotence and surpassing all creatures in every kind of virtue to an infinite degree, that we cannot conceive of Him except through His **effects** <note>In medieval theology, "effects" refers to created things (the world, life, the stars). We cannot see God's "face," but we see His "handiwork."</note>. 

Stirred by this admiration and warmed into a love for Him, we begin to conceive of these effects; we recognize Him as the **supreme good**, and we admire, worship, and love Him. For when the things God has made are perfectly known—to use the words of 

<margin>Themistius</margin>
**Themistius** <note>A 4th-century philosopher and rhetorician who wrote widely on Aristotle.</note>—He turns the minds and voices of all people toward the admiration and praise of Himself. Likewise, we read those things which have been divinely revealed, and being endowed with His grace, we conceive through **faith** that which we cannot naturally conceive in full. Above all things, it is necessary for us to love Him, so that at last—once the riddle of this flesh is broken—we may be able to contemplate Him as He is, with the highest joy of the whole person, which is our ultimate happiness. 

Again, for us to love something, it is not necessary that it be perfectly seen, known, or conceived by us. It is enough if we know that "He is," or "He is such a kind," even if that knowledge is confused and obscure, whether it comes from faith or from His effects. Thus, even a small amount of preceding knowledge, of whatever sort it may be, is enough for us to love such a being. For we can love any thing at all, provided we are not entirely lacking in knowledge of it. As **Gregory** <note>Pope Gregory the Great (c. 540–604).</note> says, the soul learns to love unknown things from the things it already knows. **Thomas** <note>Saint Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), specifically referring to his "Summa Theologiae."</note> also proves in the *Prima Secundae* that something can be loved perfectly even if it is not perfectly known, and he proposes God as an example among others.

<vocab>Simonides, Themistius, Gregory, Thomas Aquinas, Deity, knowledge, love, effects</vocab>

Drawing on thinkers like Simonides, Themistius, and Thomas Aquinas, the text explains that imperfect or "obscure" knowledge is sufficient to spark divine love.</summary>
