<meta>This page continues the defense of Giovanni Pico della Mirandola’s philosophy, specifically addressing his arguments regarding the relationship between the existence of God and the existence of material things like gold.</meta>

<margin>Solution to the last objection</margin>
Finally, you say that your uncle thought the power of gold was so great that, whether we wish it or not, it necessarily draws **God** along with it, either in reality or in the mind. But, my Anthony, he did not merely think this was the power of gold; rather, he was convinced of gold's *impotence*—its lack of power. He believed that **God** is so essential that gold itself could neither exist nor even be understood if **God** were removed. And although 
<margin>John Baconthorpe</margin>
I could refer you to <term>John Baconthorpe</term> <note>original: "Ioannem de bachone"; a 14th-century English Carmelite theologian known as the "Prince of Averroists."</note>, whom we mentioned in the resolution of the fifth objection, you said you did not wish to respond at all when you reviewed your uncle’s arguments—arguments in which he had claimed that "God does not exist" and "gold exists" are mutually exclusive ideas. You did this lest you seem to be groping in the dark regarding a matter clearer than light. Yet, it is my plan to show (perhaps even in your judgment) that it was worthwhile for you to undertake the task of dissolving those arguments if you were able; or if not, at least to set your hands to the work or frankly confess that his assertions were true. These are my uncle’s arguments, which I will now explain: it is impossible for anything to exist if **Being itself** <note>original: "ipsum esse"; a philosophical term for the pure act of existing, which theologians identify with God.</note> does not exist. However, **God** is **Being itself**. Therefore, it is impossible for gold to exist if **God** does not exist. Furthermore, if **God** is not, then there is only the **infinite**. If there is only the infinite, there is **nothing**, because if the infinite is all there is, the finite cannot exist, since the "infinite" destroys itself <note>In this logical context, the "infinite" refers to something without any boundaries or definitions; without a "limit" provided by God, nothing specific or "finite" could take shape.</note>, just as other things do which contain a contradiction. If there is "nothing," then gold does not exist. It is impossible for anything to be if **Being itself** is not, for **God** is that Being, and so on. Since **Being itself**, which is **God** (as no one denies), is that by which not only all things are what they are, but 
<margin>
Thomas
Theologians
Plato
</margin>
also they depend upon Him and are preserved by Him at every moment. This is taught most abundantly not only by all theologians, especially **Thomas Aquinas**, but it was also asserted by **Plato** in the *Timaeus*. It is impossible for gold to exist except by the grace of **Being itself** and by participating in Him. Furthermore, if **God** is not, then there is only the infinite. All beings besides **God** are finite and contained within certain limits. There is no doubt that they hold and possess this limited nature they have through the work and grace of **God**. 
<margin>Plato</margin>
For this reason, they say the followers of **Plato** called **God** the "Limit" <note>original: "terminum"</note> in the *Philebus* <note>One of Plato's dialogues exploring the nature of pleasure and the "good."</note>, because He limits all things by distributing forms as if they were measures. But the **Book of Wisdom** also says that 
<margin>Book of Wisdom</margin>
all things were established by Him in weight, number, and measure. If, therefore, there is no **God**—by whose cause all beings are finite—nothing would be finite; therefore, all would be infinite. If it is infinite, it is nothing, because if it is infinite, it is not finite, since the infinite destroys itself, just like other things that contain a contradiction. Since it has been proven that there is some "One" from whom all things receive their being, and that they are finite, if that One is removed, nothing remains, and nothing is finite. For if something is "infinite," that means it is not limited or defined by that First Principle by whose help all things are both brought into being and given their boundaries and limits. It follows that the infinite does not exist. Therefore, the infinite destroys itself. To say that the "infinite" exists in the sense used here is to say nothing at all; for if a thing is neither finite nor **God**, it is beyond controversy that it is nothing at all. These, Anthony, are the points I have brought forward to open up my uncle's opinion, which perhaps contains other doctrines as well; for it is not given to everyone to attain everything he had conceived. But I believe other meanings also lie hidden under the "bark" of his words <note>A metaphor meaning the literal or surface level of the text.</note>. I am moved by the words with which he ended his response: "I believe these things are enough even for you, a man of such great talent, but let us leave aside the inaccessible things and hold to what we have written while performing the office of an interpreter..."

It draws on authorities like Thomas Aquinas, Plato, and the Book of Wisdom to argue that without God, the universe would be an undefined "infinite" which is logically equivalent to nothingness.</summary>

<meta>This page concludes Gianfrancesco Pico della Mirandola’s formal defense of his uncle Giovanni Pico’s philosophical positions, specifically the metaphysical argument that all existence depends on God. It then transitions into a congratulatory letter from Antonio Faventino.</meta>

<margin>p</margin>
<margin>Aristotle.</margin>
<margin>Averroes</margin>
<margin>Gregory</margin>
<margin>Augustine.</margin>
<margin>Thomas Aquinas</margin>
<margin>John Duns Scotus</margin>
<margin>Giovanni Mainardi</margin>
<margin>Christopher Saxolus.</margin>
...should satisfy you; they will also close my response, once I have first brought forward certain points that both strengthen my uncle’s opinion and confirm as well as clarify the interpretation of his words that I offered earlier. For when the <term>First Cause</term> <note>God, as the ultimate source of all things.</note> is lacking, it is necessary for all those things that proceed from it to perish, as is gathered from the eighth book of Aristotle’s *Physics*. <margin>Arguments to show this.</margin> Furthermore, according to that same philosopher, **God** is the true principle from which all other true things descend; therefore, if **God** is removed, it is necessary for all true things to perish. Moreover, if truths vanish into nothingness, then existing things are likewise not saved from destruction, since they <term>share the same scope</term> <note>original: "aequali ambitu comeent"; a logical principle that "Truth" and "Being" are interchangeable.</note>.

Likewise, if the one who communicates both "being" and "living" to things is removed, who could fail to see that those very things would utterly perish? That **God** grants this to the things themselves is the opinion of Aristotle in the first book of *On the Heavens*, where he adds that this is communicated more clearly to some and more obscurely to others. Furthermore, whatever is governed by the art of the First Cause collapses if that cause perishes. Averroes, in the second book of *The Prime Philosophy* <note>The Metaphysics.</note>, testifies that this entire worldly machine is governed and ruled by the First Cause, under which no one can doubt that gold is also contained and included. I could bring forward many other proofs from the sacred books, such as many from the Gospel itself, many from the most sacred dogmas of the Apostle Paul, and very many from others—such as from **Gregory**, who said that all things would fall into nothingness unless they were preserved by almighty **God**; from **Augustine** in his commentary on *Genesis*; from **Saint Thomas**; and from **John Duns Scotus** in his treatise *On the First Principle*. I deliberately pass over these, since it should be enough to have proved the point by natural reasons—which you seemed to demand—and by the teachings of the pagan philosophers, something you did not believe could be proved by him at all. Therefore, through all these things we have stated, I should think it will be beyond controversy for good minds that all my uncle's opinions have been sufficiently defended, perhaps even in your judgment.

However, I have written these things not to clash with you. Indeed, I wrote them unwillingly, as our friend **Giovanni Mainardi** and **Christopher Saxolus**—a citizen of Mirandola, a physician, and formerly your student—can testify. I also wrote without any hatred. The greatest proof of this for you is that if you judge anything I have committed to paper to be detracting from your honor in any part, I am ready to strike it out and remove it at your discretion before this response reaches the hands of others. I would do this most gladly, as I love you as a man, respect you as a philosopher, and revere you as a Christian. If it should please you to put my feelings toward you to the test, you will perceive that my deeds have weighed as much as my words.

...posterity will see that I have told no lie if you live: may God only grant a longer life. As far as I am concerned, I certainly shall not disapprove of what you have written with such subtlety and sharpness in defense of your uncle. But let there now be a limit to the disputation. For the rest, Illustrious Count, I wish you to think of me as yours, now and always, to use as you see fit. Farewell. ## Gianfrancesco Pico della Mirandola to Antonio Faventino, distinguished philosopher. Hearty greetings. <note>original: "S.P." for Salutem Plurimam.</note>

<margin>i</margin> Your wishes have been satisfied abundantly; my promises to you have been satisfied, since I have removed from our dictations all the words that seemed to carry even a little **sting**. One must pardon the impulse of the mind if, by chance, things were handled more sharply than was appropriate. Something must be forgiven for a just defense, and it must be forgiven all the more because it is a common vice of those who, in their commentaries, either accuse someone or excuse themselves or their friends, to attack those to whom they write with insults, to seek them out with calumnies, to provoke them with reproaches, and to commit other such acts foreign to the duty of a good man. From these things (I summon you as a witness and appoint you as judge), we have abstained entirely, and at your suggestion, we have removed about ten or so somewhat sharp words (while keeping the meanings intact). I would not want you to believe there was any other purpose for composing this little commentary than that we might defend my uncle Pico without offending you. Indeed, I would have preferred that nothing had ever been debated between you, so that every entrance to writing about this matter would have been closed to me and every occasion removed. For the business of letters can only be conducted with the greatest difficulty when placed in an altercation, while still maintaining the honor due to those to whom the words are addressed. Add to this that this duty is hardly performed without a certain <term>agitation of the soul</term> <note>original: "animi tumore"; literally a "swelling of the soul," implying pride, arrogance, or anger arising during debate.</note>, which must be avoided at all costs. As for what you say about the protection of your cause, we say this very same thing about ours. But enough of the controversy so far: let there be (as you correctly wrote) those who read as judges, provided they are learned and not biased toward either side; or, if they are held too ardently by the love of one of us, let love not at least cast a <term>deception</term> <note>original: "praestigium"; an illusion or trick that clouds judgment.</note> over their eyes. For the rest, you attribute much to me, though I deserve little, and you promise great things from me if only I continue to philosophize. But I fear, my Antonio, that I may entirely abstain or perhaps desist from this study of philosophy of which you make mention. I will tell you what I feel about this matter: this business brings much harm and little profit to us who desire it too much. I do not say this to condemn or disparage the many truths, or at least the likenesses of truth, which we acquire for ourselves by philosophizing. But I blame the common use or (to speak more significantly) the **abuse**, which, unless we strive greatly to avoid it and constantly...

<summary>Antonio Faventino and Gianfrancesco Pico agree to end their public philosophical dispute, with Gianfrancesco editing out "stinging" remarks to preserve their friendship. Gianfrancesco expresses growing weariness with the "abuse" of philosophy and the prideful nature of academic altercations.</summary>

<meta>This page continues a letter from Gianfrancesco Pico della Mirandola to Antonio Cittadini (Faventino). Having just discussed removing "stings" from his writing to maintain peace, Gianfrancesco now pivots to a philosophical meditation on the humility required of a Christian scholar, contrasting human "opinion" with eternal wisdom.</meta>

...and [if] we have examined our thoughts with the greatest diligence: for a Christian, ambition creeps into the heart like poison, which later gives birth to death-dealing pride. Whence it often happens that the lovers of this wisdom in which we daily dwell—swollen and puffed up by fleeting glory—altogether neglect that wisdom which is born yet eternal, from which all this flowing and temporary wisdom is derived. 

But let us see, I pray, from what source we are carried away in spirit, and why we estimate ourselves too highly: for how small is our knowledge, when many and even the greatest things silently cry out that we either profess or think ourselves learned in vain and falsely. Undoubtedly, even a simple man, unrefined and unskilled, or a farmer completely ignorant of letters, could ask many questions about things placed right before our gaze and under our eyes, for which an otherwise great philosopher could not give a certain explanation. Indeed, in perceiving those substances entirely separated from sensible matter <note>Referring to "immaterial" things like angels or the soul, which cannot be perceived by the five senses.</note>, how far do we proceed in knowledge? We see them only with the bleary and **owl-like eyes** <note>A common philosophical metaphor: just as an owl is blinded by the sun, the human intellect is blinded by the "light" of supreme truths.</note> of the mind. 

But what shall we say of divine matters? Toward these—not just to know them but even to track them—panting and anxious, we direct our blinking and dim-sighted gaze against what are almost the thickest clouds. Furthermore, have we not received this knowledge of things of ours either from books or from a teacher? What need is there, then, to boast: that we have learned the meditations of others, having drunk them in as if from someone telling a story? But it is a story of nature, placed through various studies into bitter altercations and agitated by various opinions, and for that reason, uncertain. This is revealed most clearly from the very name of **opinion** itself. If indeed we obtain some small bit of knowledge by ourselves, what else is it, I ask, but a certain uncertainty rolled up in a thousand wrappings and entangled in a thousand deceits? I would pursue this business [of criticizing] those who value these studies more vehemently than is appropriate, as if I were angry, if I had not specifically treated this matter in a long inquiry and dedicated a special book to it. 

<margin>Manners</margin> For these reasons, I have decided to turn myself to unrolling those books whose propositions and <term>axioms</term> <note>original: "dignitates." In logic, these are self-evident truths that serve as the foundation for an argument.</note> are set forth, whose conclusions are gathered in a describable <term>syllogism</term> <note>A logical formula where a conclusion is drawn from two premises (e.g., All men are mortal; Socrates is a man; therefore Socrates is mortal).</note> and which return a purified mind—if we have taken care for that. 

But let there now be an end to this literary conflict, and now, finally, to this letter. But see how different the effect has been of both our controversy and those of others: once a debate, conducted either by voice or in writing, is finished, hatreds and rivalries are often practiced among those minds that were at odds; fraudulent wars are plotted; and detractions of honor and reputation gush forth from both sides. 

You, however, and our [beloved] Pico <note>Referring to the author's uncle, the famous philosopher Giovanni Pico della Mirandola.</note> were **co-fathers** <note>original: "compatres." This indicates a "spiritual kinship," likely meaning one was a godfather to the other's child.</note> before the disputation—that is, bound by a spiritual knot. Nevertheless, because of this [dispute], the former concord of your souls has not been dissolved. As for me, while my uncle was alive, I was known to you only by name, and you to me; this defense [of him] has caused a certain treaty of friendship to be struck between us. Take care that it remains stable as long as we shall live; and do what you can, by living rightly and piously, so that it may persevere eternally after this death which we expect. I also shall strive to do the same. Meanwhile, do not be reluctant to experience with what love I follow you. Perhaps I shall provide more abundantly what you have requested than I promised at the conclusion of my defense. For there is nothing so difficult that I would not do it for the sake of more readily deserving [the friendship] of you, a most serious philosopher indeed. 

->From the fortress of Mirandola, 4 January 1496.<-

<meta>This page serves as a formal introduction (Argumentum) by Gianfrancesco Pico della Mirandola to a collection of his uncle Giovanni's works. It transitions from the previous page's philosophical meditation on humility to a specific justification for publishing Giovanni's "lighter" youthful works, including his famous Oration and various letters.</meta>

# Introduction by Gianfrancesco Pico della Mirandola, etc., to the Speech and Letters of Giovanni Pico, his Uncle, etc.

Accept, reader, these studies <note>original: "lucubrationes"; literally "works composed by lamplight," implying late-night scholarly devotion.</note> of Giovanni Pico della Mirandola—works of lighter effort which perhaps he himself would not have published while living, nor would we, had we not been stirred by the frequent encouragements of famous men. You will read first a most elegant speech, dictated indeed with youthful eagerness, but often admired by the more learned for its summit of teaching and eloquence. 

Do not be disturbed if many things are seen at its conclusion which were also inserted into the preface of his *Apology* <note>Referring to the "Apologia," a defense Giovanni wrote after the Pope condemned some of his 900 theses in 1487.</note>; for he published the latter to the world but always kept the former at home, sharing it with none but his friends. In this speech, you will see many of the ancient teachings, previously hidden in riddles and the wrappings of fables, most ingeniously unlocked. You will see his attempt, using both intellectual strength and the charms of rhetoric, to show how the "poetic theology" <note>original: "poetica theologia"; the Renaissance idea that ancient myths and poetry contained hidden divine truths that prefigured Christian revelation.</note> of the ancient sages served as a handmaid to the mysteries of our own theology. By untying the knots of both, he invites men to literary wrestling-grounds <note>original: "litterarias palestras"; a metaphor for public academic debates or disputations common in Renaissance universities.</note>. 

Indeed, at that time he was very active in these contests, which he later abandoned—regarding them as mere preludes and playful battles before more serious studies. He then turned his mind to the labor of those greater works which we have already published and those we intend to publish in the future. 

You will also read several letters (for it would be a most laborious task to collect them all). Some are personal letters written both in his tender youth and his more mature years; others were written after he dedicated his whole heart to God, filled with the most holy advice. You will find that the earlier letters smell most abundantly of both learning and eloquence; the later ones you will perceive to savor sufficiently of both, but beyond these, to breathe most fruitfully the love of Christ.

<summary>Gianfrancesco Pico introduces a collection of his uncle Giovanni’s "youthful" works, including the famous Oration, explaining that they bridge ancient "poetic theology" with Christian mystery. He justifies their publication as a prelude to Giovanni’s later, more spiritually focused writings and letters.</summary>

<sig>QQ ii</sig>

# ORATION OF GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA, COUNT OF CONCORDIA.

I have read, most venerable Fathers <note>Pico is addressing an audience of high-ranking church officials and scholars in Rome.</note>, in the records of the Arabs, that when Abdala the Saracen <margin>Abdala the Saracen</margin> <note>Likely referring to Abdallah Ibn Qutaiba, a 9th-century scholar, though Pico often synthesized various Eastern sources.</note> was asked what was most worthy of wonder on this "stage" of the world, he replied that nothing is seen to be more marvelous than man. To this opinion agrees that saying of Hermes <margin>Mercurius</margin> <note>Known as Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary "thrice-great" Egyptian sage to whom many mystical and philosophical works were attributed.</note>: "A great miracle, O Asclepius, is man." 

When I began to consider the reason for these sayings, those many arguments regarding the excellence of human nature did not fully satisfy me—those things offered by many: that man is the intermediary between creatures, <margin>The dignity of man</margin> intimate with the gods above, king of the lower beings; by the sharpness of his senses, by the inquiry of his reason, and by the light of his intelligence, he is the interpreter of nature; the interval between stable eternity and flowing time; and (as the Persians say) the bond <note>original: "copula"</note> of the world, or rather its marriage song; and according to David, <margin>The Persians</margin> <margin>David</margin> <note>Referring to Psalm 8:5.</note> "made a little lower than the angels." These things are indeed great, but they are not the principal reasons—that is, they are not the ones that rightly claim the privilege of the highest admiration. For why should we not admire the angels themselves and the most blessed choirs of heaven more? 

At last, I seemed to understand why man is the most fortunate animal and thus worthy of all admiration, and what exactly that condition is which he has been allotted in the order of the universe—an inheritance to be envied not only by the brutes but by the stars and even by the minds beyond this world <note>Pico refers here to the higher angelic orders.</note>. It is a thing beyond belief and wonderful. Why should it not be? For it is on this account that man is rightly called and considered a great miracle and a truly marvelous living being. But hear, Fathers, what this condition is, and grant me your attention with kindly ears, according to your courtesy.

Now the Supreme Father, God the Architect, had already built this worldly home we see—this most august temple of divinity—according to the laws of his secret wisdom. He had adorned the region above the heavens with minds <note>The angels.</note>; he had animated the celestial spheres with eternal souls; and he had filled the excremental and dreg-filled parts of the lower world with a multi-formed crowd of animals. But, the work being finished, the Artisan desired that there be someone to weigh the reason of such a great work, to love its beauty, and to admire its vastness. Therefore, when all things were finished (as Moses and Timaeus testify), <margin>Moses</margin> <margin>Timaeus</margin> <note>Pico aligns the Biblical account of Genesis with Plato’s "Timaeus," a common practice in Renaissance Neoplatonism.</note> He finally thought of producing man. 

However, there was nothing left in his archetypes from which He could fashion a new offspring, nor in His storehouses was there anything he could bestow as an inheritance upon this new son, nor was there a seat in all the benches of the world where this contemplator of the universe might sit. Everything was already full; all things had been distributed into the highest, middle, and lowest orders. But it was not in the nature of the Father's power to fail, as if exhausted, in His final birth; it was not in the nature of His wisdom to have wavered for lack of a plan in a necessary matter. It was not in the nature of His beneficent love that he, who was to praise divine liberality in others, should be compelled to condemn it in himself.

Finally, the Best of Artisans ordained that this creature, to whom He could give nothing as his own, should have in common whatever had been unique to each individual. Therefore, He took man, a work of indeterminate image, and having placed him in the center of the world, He spoke to him thus: 

"We have given you, O Adam, no fixed seat, no form of your own, nor any gift peculiar to you alone, so that whatever seat, whatever form, and whatever gifts you yourself shall desire, these you may have and possess according to your wish and your own judgment. The nature of all other beings is limited and constrained within the laws prescribed by Us. You, constrained by no limits, shall define your nature for yourself according to your own free will, <margin>Free will in man</margin> in whose hand I have placed you. I have set you in the center of the world so that from there you might more easily look around at whatever is in the world. We have made you neither celestial nor earthly, neither mortal nor immortal, so that as if you were your own free and honorable sculptor and maker, you may fashion yourself into whatever..."

<summary>This page contains the famous opening of Pico's Oration, where he argues that man's unique dignity lies not in a fixed place in the hierarchy of being, but in his God-given free will to shape his own nature.</summary>

There, as the sacred mysteries hand down, the 

<margin>Seraphim</margin>

<margin>Cherubim</margin>

<margin>Throne</margin>

Therefore, if we are dedicated to the active life and have undertaken the care of lower things with a right examination, we shall be strengthened by the steady solidity of the Thrones. If, being at leisure from actions, we are occupied in the peace of contemplation—meditating on the Creator in His work, and on the work in the Creator—we shall shine on all sides with Cherubic light. If we burn with love for the Creator alone, we shall suddenly be set ablaze in the image of a Seraph by that fire which is all-consuming. God, the Judge of the ages, sits upon the Throne—that is, the just judge. He flies above the Cherub—that is, the contemplator—and cherishes him, as if by hovering over him. For the Spirit of the Lord is carried above the waters: those waters, I say, which are above the heavens, and which in the book of Job praise the Lord with hymns before the dawn. He who is a Seraph—that is, a lover—is in God, and God is in him; indeed, God and he are one. Great is the power of the Thrones, which we attain by judging; supreme is the height of the Seraphim, which we attain by loving. But in what way can anyone either judge or love things that are unknown?

<margin>Moses</margin>
Moses loved the God whom he saw, and he administered judgment among the people as a judge, having first seen these things as a contemplator on the mountain. Therefore, the Cherub in the middle prepares us with his light for the Seraphic fire, and likewise illuminates us for the judgment of the Thrones. This is the bond of the first minds, the order of Pallas <note>The "Palladic order" refers to Athena/Pallas, the goddess of wisdom, signifying the intellectual path of the Cherubim.</note>, the leader of contemplative philosophy. This is what we must first emulate, and seek after, and so fully grasp: so that we may be snatched up to the heights of love and descend, well-instructed and prepared, to the duties of action. But indeed, it is worthwhile, if our life is to be formed according to the model of the Cherubic life, to have before our eyes and ready at hand what that life is, what it's like, and what their actions and works are. Since it is not permitted for us—who are flesh and savor the things of the earth—to achieve this by ourselves, let us approach the ancient fathers, who can provide us with a most rich and certain faith regarding these things, as they are familiar and known to them.

<margin>Paul the Apostle</margin>
Let us consult the Apostle Paul, the "vessel of election" <note>original: "vas electionis"; a traditional title for St. Paul, indicating he was chosen by God to carry His name.</note>, for what he saw the armies of the Cherubim doing when he was raised up to the third heaven. 

<margin>Dionysius</margin>
He will surely answer, with Dionysius <note>Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, a 5th-6th century mystical theologian whose "Celestial Hierarchy" described the ranks of angels.</note> as his interpreter: that they are first purified, then illuminated, and finally perfected. Therefore, we also, emulating the Cherubic life on earth—by restraining the impulses of the passions through moral science, and by dispersing the darkness of reason through dialectic <note>In the Renaissance, "dialectic" referred to the art of logical reasoning and debate.</note>—let us purge the soul as if washing away the filth of ignorance and vice, lest the passions rage blindly or an imprudent reason sometimes go astray. Then, let us fill the well-composed and purified soul with the light of natural philosophy, so that finally we may perfect it with the knowledge of divine things. And lest we be sufficient unto ourselves, let us consult

<margin>Jacob</margin>
the patriarch Jacob, whose image shines sculpted on the seat of glory. This most wise father will advise us—he who sleeps in the lower world but keeps watch in the world above. But he will advise us through a figure <note>A "figure" or "prefiguration" is a symbolic event or person in the Bible that represents a deeper spiritual truth.</note> (for all things happened to them in this way): that there are ladders stretching from the lowest ground to the heights of heaven, divided by a series of many steps, with the Lord sitting at the top. The contemplating angels ascend and descend them by turns. And if we must do this same thing in the angelic...

<meta>This page continues Pico della Mirandola's Oration on the Dignity of Man. Having urged the reader to emulate the Seraphim, Cherubim, and Thrones, he now explains the practical steps of this ascent: using moral philosophy to purify the soul's lower faculties and dialectic and natural philosophy to prepare for the final theological union.</meta>

<page-num>99</page-num>

...must be practiced in our lives by our choices. I ask you, who would touch the ladder of the Lord with dirty feet or poorly washed hands? As the sacred mysteries hold, it is a sacrilege for the impure to touch the pure.

<margin>Foot of the soul</margin>
<margin>Hand of the soul</margin>
But what are these feet? What are these hands? Surely the "foot" of the soul is that most contemptible part by which it rests upon the ground of matter as if upon the earth—I mean the nourishing and dietary power, the fuel of lust and the mistress of voluptuous softness. Why should we not call the "hand" of the soul the irascible power <note>The "irascible power" refers to the part of the soul associated with anger, courage, and spiritedness.</note>, which, as the champion of desire, fights on its behalf and, like a foot-soldier, seizes its prey under the dust and the sun? This part, which gluttonizes while dozing in the shade—these hands and these feet, that is, the whole sensual part in which the enticement of the body resides, and which (as they say) holds the soul by a "twisted neck" <note>original: "obtorto collo". A Latin idiom meaning to drag someone by force or against their will.</note>. Lest we be rejected from the ladder as profane and polluted, let us wash ourselves in moral philosophy as if in a living stream. 

But even this will not be enough if we wish to be companions to the angels running up and down Jacob’s ladder, unless we have first been well-fitted and instructed to be promoted duly from step to step, never to stray from the path of the ladder, and to undertake reciprocal journeys. When we have achieved this through the discursive art <term>the art of logic or dialectic</term>, then, inspired by the Cherubic spirit, philosophizing through the steps of the ladder—that is, the levels of nature—and penetrating all things from center to center: now we shall descend, dispersing the One like Osiris into a multitude by Titanic force; now we shall ascend, gathering the multitude like the limbs of Osiris into one by Phoebian force <note>Pico uses the myth of Osiris—who was torn apart by Titans and reassembled—as an allegory for "Analysis" (breaking a concept down) and "Synthesis" (bringing parts back into a unified whole).</note>; until, finally resting in the bosom of the Father who is above the ladder, we shall be perfected in theological happiness.

<margin>Job</margin>
Let us also ask the righteous Job—who entered into a covenant with God before he was even brought into life—what the Highest God desires most among those ten hundred thousands who assist Him. He will surely answer "Peace," according to what is read in his book: "He who makes peace in the high places" <note>Job 25:2.</note>. And since the middle order interprets the commands of the highest order for the lower orders:

<margin>Empedocles</margin>
Let the philosopher Empedocles interpret for us the words of Job the theologian. He signifies to us that a dual nature is situated in our souls: by one we are raised upward to heavenly things, by the other we are thrust downward to the lower regions—through "Strife" and "Friendship," or war and peace, as his poems testify; in which he complains that, because of strife and discord, he is tossed about in the deep like a fugitive fleeing from the gods.

<margin>Multiple discords within us.</margin>
Truly, Fathers, there is a multiple discord within us; we have heavy and internal struggles at home, more than civil wars. If we wish to avoid these, if we strive for that peace which lifts us so high that we are placed among the exalted ones of the Lord:

<margin>Moral philosophy</margin>
...philosophy alone will first restrain and calm them within us. First, moral philosophy, if our inner man seeks only a truce from enemies, will crush the unbridled outbursts of the "manifold beast" and the rages and angers of the "lion" <note>Pico refers to Plato’s *Republic*, where the soul is described as containing a many-headed beast (desire), a lion (anger/spirit), and a man (reason).</note>. Then, if we take better counsel for ourselves and desire the security of perpetual peace, she will be present and will generously fulfill our prayers. For, having slain both beasts—as if striking a sow in sacrifice <note>This refers to the Roman ritual of "foedus ferire," where a pig was sacrificed to seal an eternal peace treaty.</note>—she will establish an inviolable covenant of most holy peace between the flesh and the spirit.

<margin>Dialectic</margin>
Dialectic will calm the disturbances of reason as it anxiously struggles amidst the conflicts of speeches and the deceptions of syllogisms.

<margin>Natural philosophy.</margin>
<margin>Heraclitus.</margin>
<margin>Homerus.</margin>
Natural philosophy will calm the strifes and disagreements of opinion which vex, distract, and tear apart the restless soul on all sides. But it will calm them in such a way as to command us to remember that nature, according to Heraclitus, was born from "war"—for which reason it was called "Contention" by Homer. Therefore, natural philosophy cannot provide us with true rest and solid peace; this is the gift and privilege of its mistress, most holy Theology.

<margin>Most holy theology</margin>
To her, Natural Philosophy will show the way and lead as a companion. Seeing us from afar as we hurry, she will cry out:

<meta>This page continues Pico's exposition on the ladder of ascent. ...me, and I will give you peace which the world and nature cannot give you. So gently called, so kindly invited, with winged feet like earthly Mercuries <note>In Roman mythology, Mercury (Hermes) was the messenger of the gods, characterized by his winged sandals representing swiftness and the mediation between the divine and earthly realms.</note>, flying into the embraces of our most blessed mother, we shall enjoy the longed-for peace: that most holy peace, an indivisible bond, a friendship of one mind, through which all souls do not merely agree in one Mind which is above every mind, but in an ineffable way become utterly one. <margin>

Pythagoreans
Peace to be desired
</margin>

Let us wish for this peace for our friends, for our century, for every house we enter, and for our own soul, so that through it the soul itself may become the house of God. Then, after she has shaken off her filth through moral philosophy and dialectic—as if through a courtly preparation—and has adorned herself with multi-faceted philosophy as if with regal finery, and crowned the heights of her gates with theological garlands, the King of Glory may descend, and coming with the Father, make His dwelling with her. If she shows herself worthy of such a guest—such is His boundless clemency—she will be surrounded by a golden garment as if by a wedding robe of many-colored sciences, and she will receive this beautiful guest not merely as a guest, but as a bridegroom. 

<margin>
Precious in the sight of God is the death of His saints
</margin>
Lest she ever be separated from him, she will desire to be "dissolved" <note>original: "dissolui". This refers to the Pauline desire (Philippians 1:23) to be released from the body to be with Christ.</note> from her people and her father’s house; indeed, forgetting herself, she will desire to die within herself that she may live in her bridegroom, in whose sight the death of His saints is precious indeed—that death, I say (if it should be called death), which is the fullness of life, the meditation upon which the wise have said is the primary study of philosophy. 

<margin>
Moses
</margin>
Let us also cite Moses himself, who was only a little lower than the fountain-like fullness of the holy and ineffable intelligence from which the angels are intoxicated with their own nectar. We shall hear this venerable judge decreeing laws to us who dwell in the desert solitude of this body: 

<margin>
Thessalian priests
</margin>
Those who are still polluted and in need of moral instruction should dwell with the common people outside the tabernacle under the open sky, meanwhile purifying themselves like Thessalian priests <note>Pico references ancient Greek purificatory rites to illustrate the preliminary stage of moral cleansing.</note>. Those who have already composed their conduct, having been received into the sanctuary, should not yet touch the sacred objects, but first, as diligent Levites in the service of dialectic, let them minister to the sacred things of Philosophy. Then, when they are admitted to these things themselves, let them contemplate—now in the royal palace of the supreme God—the multi-colored (that is, the star-filled) courtly ornament; now the celestial candelabrum distinguished by seven lights; and now the skin-covered elements in the priesthood of philosophy. Finally, having been received into the inner recesses of the temple through the merits of theological sublimity, they may enjoy the glory of divinity, with no veil of any image intervening. This is indeed what Moses commands us, and in commanding, he warns, excites, and exhorts us that we should prepare a path for ourselves through philosophy toward future celestial glory while we are able. Truly, however, not only the Mosaic or Christian mysteries, but also the theology of the ancients shows us the benefits and dignity of these 

<margin>
Secrets of the Greeks
</margin>
liberal arts which I have come here to discuss. For what else is intended by the stages of initiation observed in the Greek mysteries? Those who were first purified by those "februarial" <note>original: "februales". Referring to Februa, the Roman festival of purification.</note> arts (moral philosophy and dialectic) received the "assumption of the mysteries." And what else can this be but the interpretation of nature’s more secret things through philosophy? Then at last, to those so prepared, there came that <term>epopteia</term> <note>original: "εποπτει α". In Greek mystery religions, this was the highest stage of initiation: the direct "beholding" of the sacred objects or truths.</note>, that is, the inspection of divine things through the light of Theology. Who would not yearn to be initiated into such sacred rites? Who [would not wish to set aside] human things...

<meta>This page continues the description of the soul’s mystical ascent. Having purified itself through moral philosophy and dialectic, the soul now reaches for divine "frenzy" or inspiration, moving through the stages of natural philosophy toward the ultimate union of theology.</meta>

...setting all things aside, despising the goods of fortune, and neglecting the body, would one not desire to become a guest of the gods while still dwelling on earth? And, soaked in the nectar of eternity, would not a mortal animal be bestowed with the gift of immortality? 

<margin>Socratic frenzies.</margin>
Who would not wish to be so inspired by those Socratic frenzies <note>original: "Socratici furores"; a reference to the four types of divine inspiration described by Plato in the *Phaedrus*: poetic, mystical, prophetic, and amatory.</note> praised by Plato in the *Phaedrus*, so that by the rowing of wings and feet, he might fly away from here—that is, from this world set in wickedness—and be carried in a swift course to the heavenly Jerusalem? Let us be driven, fathers <note>Pico is addressing his audience of scholars and clergy.</note>, let us be driven by those Socratic frenzies which place us so far outside our own minds that they place our mind and our very selves in God. Let us be driven by them, provided that we have first done what is in our power. For if, through the power of moral philosophy, the emotions have been tuned to the proper measures through due proportions so that they chime together in an unshaken harmony; and if reason has moved itself toward number through the progress of dialectic <term>dialectic: the branch of philosophy that uses logic to investigate the nature of truth and reality</term>, then, driven by the frenzy of the Muses, we shall drink in the heavenly harmony with our innermost ears. 

<margin>Bacchus</margin>
Then Bacchus <note>In this context, Bacchus/Dionysus represents the divine "intoxication" or ecstasy that comes from recognizing spiritual truths hidden in the natural world.</note>, the leader of the Muses, showing us the invisible things of God through his mysteries—that is, through the visible signs of nature—will inebriate us from the abundance of the house of God. 

<margin>Moses</margin>
In this house, if we are entirely faithful like Moses, the most sacred Theology will approach and animate us with a double frenzy. For, raised to her most eminent watchtower, measuring from there what is, what will be, and what has been in an indivisible eternity, and looking up at that primeval beauty, 

<margin>Priests of Apollo.</margin>
we shall become the winged lovers of that beauty and priests of Apollo <note>original: "Phoebei uates." Phoebus Apollo was the god of light, prophecy, and the sun.</note>. Finally, spurred by an ineffable love as if by a gadfly—like burning Seraphim <note>The highest rank of angels, whose name means "the burning ones," symbolizing their intense love for God.</note>—placed outside ourselves and full of divine power, we shall no longer be ourselves, but we shall become He who made us. The sacred names of Apollo, if one examines their meanings and the mysteries hidden within them, sufficiently show that he is no less a philosopher than a prophet. 

<margin>Ammonius. Three Delphic precepts</margin>
Since Ammonius <note>Likely Ammonius Hermiae, an influential Neoplatonist philosopher.</note> has sufficiently followed this out, there is no reason for me to treat it differently now. But let three Delphic precepts <note>The famous maxims inscribed on the Temple of Apollo at Delphi.</note> come to mind, fathers, which are exceedingly necessary for those who are about to enter the most holy and august temple of the true Apollo—not the fictional one—who enlightens every soul coming into this world. You will see that those precepts warn us of nothing else but that we should embrace with all our strength this tripartite philosophy which is the subject of the present dispute. 

First, that saying **nothing in excess** <note>Greek: *mēden agan*</note> rightly prescribes the norm and rule of all virtues through the principle of the "mean," which is the concern of moral philosophy. 

Then that second saying, **know thyself** <note>Greek: *gnōthi seauton*</note>, rouses and exhorts us to the knowledge of all nature, of which the nature of man is a sort of intermediary and, as it were, a blending. 

<margin>Zoroaster, Plato, Pythagoras the Wise. Declaration of the precepts of Pythagoras.</margin>
For he who knows himself, knows all things in himself, as Zoroaster first wrote, and later Plato in the *Alcibiades*. Finally, illuminated by this knowledge through natural philosophy, and now being close to God, we shall address the true Apollo with the theological greeting **Thou art** <note>Greek: *ei*; a reference to the inscription at Delphi which Plutarch and other thinkers interpreted as a recognition of God’s eternal existence.</note>, and we shall call upon him as familiarly as we do happily. 

Let us also consult the most wise Pythagoras, who was especially wise because he never thought himself worthy of the name of a "wise man." He will first command us *not to sit upon a bushel* <note>original: "ne super modium sedeamus"; one of the Pythagorean "symbols" or riddles, meaning one should not remain idle or fail to use one's rational capacity.</note>—that is, we should not lose the rational part by which the soul measures, judges, and examines all things through idle sloth. Instead, we should diligently direct and excite it through the exercise and rule of dialectic. 

Then he will signal two things especially to be avoided: that we should *not urinate against the sun*, nor *cut our nails during a sacrifice*. But after we have, through moral philosophy, "passed out" the flowing desires of overflowing pleasures, and have cut away the "nail-clippings" of the soul—that is, the sharp outbursts of anger and the stings of the spirit—only then may we take part in the sacred mysteries of Bacchus of which we made mention; and then our contemplation, whose father and leader is rightly called the Sun, [will begin...]

<meta>This page continues Pico's argument for the soul's purification. He transitions from the "Socratic frenzies" to a synthesis of ancient traditions—including Chaldean, Platonic, and Christian—to describe how the soul prepares for divine union through the stages of moral philosophy, dialectic, and natural philosophy.</meta>

...we may begin to be free for contemplation. Finally, it will advise us to feed the cock <note>original: "gallum nutriamus"; a reference to Socrates’ last words in Plato’s *Phaedo*, interpreted here by Pico as an allegory for nourishing the divine or rational part of the soul.</note>. That is, that we should feed the divine part of our soul with the knowledge of divine things, as if with solid food and heavenly Ambrosia. This is the cock whose sight the lion—that is, every earthly power—fears and reveres. This is that cock to whom we read in the Book of Job that understanding was given. <margin>Cock.</margin>

At the crowing of this cock, straying man returns to his senses. <margin>Job</margin>
This cock, in the morning twilight, sings in harmony every day with the morning stars as they praise God. This is the cock that the dying Socrates—hoping to join the divinity of his soul to the divinity of the greater world—said he owed to Asclepius <margin>Socrates.</margin> (the physician of souls), having now been placed beyond all danger of disease. Let us review the monuments of the Chaldeans <margin>Chaldeans</margin> and we shall see (if they are to be believed) that through these same arts the path to happiness lies open to mortals. The Chaldean interpreters <margin>Chaldean interpreters</margin> write the word of Zoroaster: that the soul is winged, and when the wings fall off, it is carried headlong into the body; then, as they grow back, it flies back to those above. When his disciples asked <margin>Zoroaster</margin> him by what means they might obtain souls as birds with well-feathered wings, he said: "Water the wings with the waters of life." When they asked again where they might seek these waters, he answered them through a parable (which was the man’s custom): "The paradise of God is washed and watered by four rivers. Draw for yourselves life-giving waters from the same place: the name of the one from the North denotes 'the right' <note>Pico associates the North with moral rectitude.</note>, of the one from the West, 'expiation', of the one from the East, 'light', and of the one from the South, what we can interpret as 'piety'." 

Pay attention and diligently consider, fathers, what these teachings of Zoroaster mean. Surely nothing else but that through moral science, as if by northern waters, we should wash away the filth of our eyes; and through dialectic <term>dialectic: the use of logic and reason to clarify thought</term>, as if by a rule <note>original: "amussis", a mason's level or straight-edge.</note>, we should align their sight to what is right. Then, in natural contemplation, let us grow accustomed to enduring the still-weak light of truth, as if it were the cradle of the rising sun; so that finally, through theological piety and the most sacred worship of God, like heavenly eagles, we may bravely bear the most brilliant radiance of the midday sun. 

These are perhaps those morning, midday, <margin>David</margin> and evening cognitions first sung by David and explained more broadly by Augustine. <margin>Augustine</margin> This is that midday light which inflames the Seraphim <note>The highest rank of angels, associated with fire and love.</note> to the limit and equally illuminates the Cherubim <note>The second rank of angels, associated with knowledge and wisdom.</note>. This is that region toward which the ancient father <margin>Ancient father Abraham</margin> Abraham was always traveling; this is that place where the teachings of both the Kabbalists <margin>Kabbalists</margin> and the Moors <margin>Moors</margin> <note>The "Moors" here refers to medieval Islamic philosophers such as Averroes or Avicenna.</note> have handed down that there is no place for unclean spirits. 

And if it is permitted to bring any of the more secret mysteries into public, even under a riddle: after the sudden fall of man from heaven condemned our head to dizziness, and according to Jeremiah, "death entered through the windows" <margin>Jeremiah</margin> <note>A reference to Jeremiah 9:21, often interpreted by theologians as death entering through the five senses.</note>, affecting the liver and the breast badly, let us call upon Raphael, <margin>Raphael</margin> the heavenly physician. Let him free us using moral and dialectical science as healing medicines. Then, once restored to good health, the "Strength of God"—Gabriel—will <margin>Gabriel</margin> dwell in us. He will lead us through the miracles of nature, pointing out the power and might of God everywhere. Finally, he will hand us over to the high priest Michael, <margin>Michael</margin> who will distinguish those who have completed their service under the pay of philosophy with the priesthood of theology, as if with a crown of precious stone. 

These are the things, most worshipful fathers, which have not only encouraged but compelled me to the study of philosophy. These things I certainly would not have said, were I not responding to those who are accustomed to condemning the study of philosophy, especially in princes or in those who live in moderate circumstances. For now (which is the misfortune of our age) this whole pursuit is held in contempt and insult rather than honor and glory. Thus, this deadly and monstrous persuasion has invaded almost everyone's minds: that one should philosophize either not at all or only a little. As if the causes of things, the ways of nature, the reason of the universe...

<meta>This page continues Pico della Mirandola’s "Oration on the Dignity of Man." Having previously discussed the spiritual preparation of the soul through ancient wisdom, Pico now pivots to a personal defense of his own life’s work. He addresses the critics who look down upon his upcoming public debate (disputation) of 900 theses in Rome.</meta>

...to have the counsels of God and the mysteries of heaven and earth most thoroughly explored and ready at hand before their eyes. Indeed, it has come to this—that there is no one who does not seek some favor or try to acquire some profit for himself. So much so (alas!) that men are no longer considered wise unless they turn the study of wisdom into a mercenary trade. Thus, one may see the modest Pallas <note>original: "pudicā palladē"; Pallas Athena, the Greek goddess of wisdom, used here as a personification of Philosophy.</note>—who dwells among men as a gift from the gods—cast out, exploded, and hissed off the stage. She has no one to love or favor her, unless she, like a prostitute, receives some small payment for her deflowered virginity and brings back ill-gotten coin to her lover’s small chest.

<margin>Note.</margin>
All of these things I say, not without the greatest pain and indignation, directed not at the princes of our time, but at the philosophers. For they believe and preach that one should not philosophize because no wages and no rewards have been established for philosophers—as if they do not show by this one name alone that they themselves are not truly philosophers! 

<margin>Note.</margin>
Since their entire lives are focused on either profit or ambition, they do not embrace the knowledge of truth for its own sake. I will take this upon myself, and I shall not blush to praise myself in this regard: I have never philosophized for any other reason than to be a philosopher. Nor have I ever hoped for or sought any other reward or fruit from my studies and my late-night labors than the cultivation of my soul and the knowledge of the truth I have always so greatly desired. I have always been so greedy and so fond of this truth that, leaving aside all care for private and public affairs, I have given myself entirely to the leisure of contemplation. From this path, no detractions of the envious nor any insults from the enemies of wisdom have been able to deter me in the past, nor will they be able to deter me in the future. 

<margin>What philosophy itself taught him</margin>
Philosophy itself has taught me to rely on my own conscience rather than on external judgments, and to always think not so much about whether I might be spoken of badly, but rather that I myself should not say or do anything bad. I was certainly not unaware, most worshipful fathers <note>The "fathers" (patres) refers to the assembly of high-ranking Church officials, cardinals, and scholars in Rome before whom he intended to speak.</note>, that this very disputation of mine—which you, who favor all the good arts, have wished to honor with your most august presence—would be pleasing and delightful to many, but to many others heavy and annoying. And I know there is no lack of those who have condemned my undertaking before now, and who condemn it currently on many grounds. It is the custom that things done well and holily toward virtue have no fewer—if not more—barking critics than things done wickedly and wrongly toward vice. There are those who do not approve of this whole kind of disputing and this practice of publicly debating on literature, asserting that it serves the display of talent and the showing off of learning rather than the acquiring of education. There are those who do not indeed disapprove of this kind of exercise, but in no way allow it in me. 

<margin>The age of the author.</margin>
They object that I, at this age—being only twenty-four years old <note>original: "quartum f. & uigesimum"; Pico was famously young when he challenged the established scholars of Europe.</note>—have dared to propose a disputation on the sublime mysteries of Christian theology, on the highest points of philosophy, and on unknown disciplines, in this most celebrated city, in the largest assembly of most learned men, and in the Apostolic Senate. Others, while granting me the right to dispute, are unwilling to grant that I should dispute on nine hundred questions <note>The famous "900 Theses" Pico proposed to defend in Rome in 1487.</note>, slandering the act as being as superfluous and ambitious as it is beyond my strength. I would have yielded to these objections at once if the philosophy I profess had so taught me; and even now, with her teaching me, I would not respond if I believed this discussion between us were established for the purpose of brawling and quarreling. Therefore, let all intent of detraction and provocation be gone from our minds—along with that malice which Plato writes is always absent from the divine choir. Let us learn in a friendly manner whether I should dispute at all, and whether I should dispute about so many questions. First, to those who slander this custom of public debating, I shall not say much, since this fault (if it is judged a fault) is shared not only by all of you, most excellent doctors, who have frequently performed this duty with the highest praise and glory...

<meta>This page continues Pico della Mirandola’s "Oration on the Dignity of Man." In the preceding section, he lamented the state of philosophy, which had been reduced to a mercenary trade. Here, he shifts to a vigorous defense of the practice of public disputation—the formal, academic debating of theses—which he believes is the most effective way to sharpen the mind and uncover truth.</meta>

<margin>A useful disputation</margin>
...but with Plato, with Aristotle, and with the most approved philosophers of all ages. For them, it was a certain fact that nothing was more conducive to attaining the knowledge of truth they sought than to be most frequently engaged in the exercise of disputation. For just as the strength of the body is made firmer by gymnastics, so without doubt in this, as it were, literary arena <term>palaestra: a wrestling school or gymnasium for the soul</term>, the powers of the soul become far stronger and more vigorous. I would not believe that either the 
<margin>The Poets</margin>
Poets intended anything else by the celebrated "arms of Pallas" <note>original: "decantata Palladis arma"; referring to Pallas Athena, goddess of wisdom, who is often depicted in armor</note>, or that the Hebrews—when they say that iron <insert>△</insert> is the 
<margin>The Hebrews</margin>
symbol of the wise—meant to signify anything to us other than that these most honorable types of contests are exceedingly necessary for the acquisition of wisdom. Perhaps this is why the 
<margin>The Chaldeans</margin>
Chaldeans <note>Ancient Babylonian astrologers and sages</note>, in the horoscope of one who is to be a philosopher, require that Mars look upon Mercury in a trine aspect <note>original: "Triquetro aſpectu"; an astrological configuration where two planets are 120 degrees apart, traditionally considered harmonious</note>—as if to say that if you take away these encounters, these wars, then all philosophy will be sleepy and drowsy.

But indeed, with those who say I am unequal to this task, the logic of my defense is more difficult. For if I say I am equal to it, I may be branded as immodest and having too high an opinion of myself; if I confess I am unequal, I appear to be under the mark of being rash and ill-advised. See what straits I have fallen into, and what a position I am in, since I cannot promise something about myself without fault, which I then cannot fulfill soon after without fault. Perhaps I could also bring forward that saying of 
<margin>Job</margin>
Job: "The spirit is in all men"; and hear with 
<margin>Timothy</margin>
Timothy: "Let no one despise your youth" <note>1 Timothy 4:12</note>. But I shall say this more truly from my own conscience: there is nothing in us that is great or singular. I do not deny that I am perhaps studious and eager for the liberal arts, yet I neither assume nor arrogate to myself the name of a scholar. 

Therefore, as to why I have taken such a heavy burden upon my shoulders, it was not because I was unaware of my own weakness. Rather, it was because I knew that in this kind of battle—that is, literary ones—it is a peculiar thing that the prize is to be defeated. Thus it happens that even the weakest person should not merely not refuse them, but should desire them of his own accord. For he who falls receives a benefit from the victor, not an injury, because through the victor he returns home more enriched—that is, more learned—and more prepared for future battles. 

Animated by this hope, I, a weak soldier, have not feared to join so heavy a battle with the strongest and most vigorous men of all. Whether this was done too rashly or not, one can certainly judge better by the outcome of the battle than by my age. 

It remains for me to respond in the third place to those who are offended by the large number of proposed topics, as if this burden sat upon their shoulders, and as if I alone—whatever my labor might be—did not have to endure it. This is surely unseemly and far too peevish: to wish to set a limit on another person’s industry. And as 
<margin>Cicero</margin>
Cicero says in that matter: in a thing that is better the greater it is, one should not require moderation. In such grand attempts, it was entirely necessary for me either to fail or to satisfy the requirement. If I satisfy it, I do not see why what is considered laudable in performing ten questions should be considered culpable in performing nine hundred. If I fail, those who hate me will have a reason to accuse me, and those who love me will have a reason to excuse me. For in a matter so grave and so great, it will be more worthy of pardon than of accusation that a young man, with slender talent and small learning, has failed. Indeed, according to the 
<margin>Gorgias of Leontini</margin>
poet: "if the strength is lacking, the boldness will certainly be a credit; in great things, to have even willed is enough." But if in our age many, imitating Gorgias of Leontini <note>A famous Greek Sophist known for offering to speak on any subject</note>, have been accustomed—not without praise—to propose a disputation not only regarding nine hundred questions, but regarding all questions of all arts, why should I not be allowed (even without blame) to dispute about many things indeed, but things that are certain and determined? 

But they say this is superfluous and ambitious. I, however, contend that this was done by me not in a superfluous manner, but necessarily. And if they would philosophize with me...

<meta>This page continues Pico della Mirandola’s defense of his intellectual breadth. Having argued for the necessity of public debate, he now explains his "syncretic" or eclectic approach: rather than sticking to one school of thought (like the followers of Thomas Aquinas or Duns Scotus), he has studied every available philosophical tradition—Latin, Arabic, Greek, and Neoplatonist—to find truth wherever it may be hidden.</meta>

...if they were to consider the method of philosophizing, they would be forced to admit, even against their will, that it is plainly necessary. For those who have devoted themselves to any one of the **families of philosophers**—to **Thomas** <note>Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the leading Scholastic theologian</note>, for instance, or to **Scotus** <note>John Duns Scotus (c. 1266–1308), a major rival to the Thomist school</note>, who are now most widely studied—can indeed put their own doctrines to the test in the discussion of even a few questions. But I have so trained myself that, **sworn to the words of no one master**, I might spread myself through all the masters of philosophy, examine all manuscripts, and recognize all schools. 

Therefore, since I had to speak regarding all of them—lest, if I had defended a private doctrine while neglecting the rest, I might seem bound to that one—it was impossible, even if only a few points were proposed regarding each, that there should not be a great many points brought forward simultaneously regarding all of them. And let no one condemn in me that "wherever the storm carries me, I am driven as a guest" <note>A famous quote from the Roman poet Horace, expressing intellectual independence</note>. 

<margin>
The observation of the ancients
Aristotle
Plato
</margin>
For this was once observed by all the ancients: that in unfolding every kind of writing, they passed over no commentaries they could read. This was especially true of **Aristotle**, who for that reason was called by **Plato** an *anagnostes* <note>original Greek: "$\alpha\nu\alpha\gamma\nu\omega\sigma\tau\eta\sigma$"; meaning a reader or "the reader"</note>, that is, a **reader**. And surely it is a mark of a narrow mind to have confined oneself within a single Porch or Academy <note>Referring to the Stoics, who met in the "Stoa" or Porch, and the followers of Plato's Academy</note>. Nor can one rightly select his own path from among all of them if he has not first become familiarly acquainted with them all. Add to this that in every single family there is something distinguished that is not held in common with the rest.

And to begin now with our own thinkers <note>The Latin Scholastics of Western Europe</note>, to whom philosophy has most recently arrived: 

<margin>

In **John Duns Scotus**, there is something vigorous and analytical. In **Thomas**, something solid and balanced. In **Aegidius** <note>Aegidius Romanus (Giles of Rome)</note>, something polished and precise. In **Francis** <note>Francis of Meyronnes</note>, something sharp and keen. In **Albert** <note>Albertus Magnus</note>, something ancient, vast, and grand. In **Henry** <note>Henry of Ghent</note>, as it has always seemed to me, something sublime and venerable. 

Among the Arabs, there is in **Averroes** something firm and unshakable. In **Avempace** and **Al-Farabi**, something grave and meditated. In **Avicenna**, something divine and Platonic. 

Among the Greeks, philosophy is in general especially brilliant and pure. In **Simplicius**, it is rich and abundant. In **Themistius**, elegant and concise. In **Alexander** <note>Alexander of Aphrodisias</note>, consistent and learned. In **Theophrastus**, weightily elaborated. In **Ammonius**, smooth and pleasing. 

And if you turn to the **Platonists**, to review a few: In **Porphyry**, you will be delighted by the abundance of matter and a religion of many strands. In **Iamblichus**, you will venerate a more secret philosophy and the mysteries of the "barbarians" <note>Referring to the Egyptian and Chaldean wisdom Iamblichus defended</note>. In **Plotinus**, there is nothing in particular to admire because he offers himself as admirable from every side; the sweating Platonists can scarcely understand him when he speaks of divine things divinely, and of human things in a learned, indirect style far above man. I pass over the more recent ones: **Proclus**, luxuriating with Asiatic fertility, and those who flowed from him—**Hermias**, **Damascius**, **Olympiodorus**, and many others—in all of whom that *to theion* <note>original Greek: "$\tau o \theta\epsilon\iota o\nu$"; meaning "the divine"</note>, that is, the **divine**, which is the peculiar symbol of the Platonists, always shines forth. 

Furthermore, if there is any sect that attacks truer doctrines and mocks good causes with the slander of its wit, it strengthens the truth rather than weakening it; and like a flame shaken by motion, it excites rather than extinguishes it. Moved by this reasoning, I wished to bring into the open the opinions not of just one school (as some preferred), but of every kind of learning. I did this so that by this comparison of many sects and the multifaceted discussion of philosophy, that "shining of truth" of which **Plato** mentions in his letters might illuminate our minds more clearly, like a sun rising from on high. What would it be if only the philosophy of the Latins—namely, of **Albert**, **Thomas**, **Scotus**, **Aegidius**, **Francis**, and **Henry**—were discussed, while omitting...

<meta>This page continues Pico della Mirandola’s explanation for his extensive and diverse list of 900 theses. He has just finished arguing that a true seeker of truth must not be bound to a single school of thought, like that of Thomas Aquinas or Duns Scotus, but should instead explore all traditions—Latin, Greek, and Arabic.</meta>

...was it treated by the philosophers of the Greeks and Arabs? Since all wisdom flowed from the **"barbarians"** <note>In the Renaissance context, "barbarians" refers to non-Greek sources of ancient wisdom, such as the Hebrews, Chaldeans, and Egyptians</note> to the Greeks, and from the Greeks to us. Thus, our own countrymen have always thought it sufficient, in their method of philosophizing, to stand upon foreign discoveries and to cultivate the inventions of others. 

<margin>Peripatetics</margin> 
What use was it to have dealt with the **Peripatetics** <note>The followers of Aristotle</note> concerning natural things, unless the Academy of the **Platonists** was also included? 

<margin>Platonists</margin> 
<margin>Augustine</margin> 
Their doctrine regarding divine matters has always been held as the holiest among all philosophies, according to the testimony of **Augustine**; and now, for the first time by me—so far as I know (and may there be no ill will in the word)—it has been brought out into public for examination by debate after many centuries. What would it be to have treated the opinions of others, however many there were, if we, approaching the "banquet" of the wise as if with our **symbols** <note>original: "symbolis"—here referring to a guest's contribution to a shared meal, suggesting that Pico is bringing his own intellectual "dish" to the table</note>, brought nothing of our own, produced and worked out by our own wit? 

<margin>Seneca</margin> 
Indeed, it is ungenerous (as **Seneca** says) to be wise only from a commentary, as if the discoveries of our ancestors had closed the path of our own industry, or as if the power of nature were exhausted in us, producing nothing from itself which, if it does not demonstrate truth, might at least point to it from afar. If the farmer hates sterility in his field, and the husband in his wife, surely the divine mind associated and joined with the soul will hate an unfruitful soul all the more, the more a much nobler offspring is desired from it. 

Therefore, I was not content with common doctrines, but added much from the ancient theology of **Hermes Trismegistus** <note>original: "Mercurius trismegistus"; a legendary Hellenistic figure regarded as the author of the Hermetic Corpus</note>, much from the teachings of the **Chaldeans** and of **Pythagoras**, and much from the more secret mysteries of the **Hebrews**. 

<margin>Hermes Trismegistus</margin> 
We have also proposed many things discovered and meditated upon by ourselves concerning natural and divine matters for dispute. 

<margin>The harmony of Aristotle and Plato</margin> 
We proposed, first, the **harmony of Plato and Aristotle**, believed by many before this but proved by none sufficiently. **Boethius**, among the Latins, promised that he would do this but is not found to have ever performed what he always wished to do. 

<margin>Boethius</margin> 
<margin>Simplicius</margin> 
**Simplicius** <note>A 6th-century Neoplatonist commentator on Aristotle</note>, among the Greeks, professed the same; would that he had fulfilled his promise as well as he made it! 

<margin>Augustine</margin> 
**Augustine** also writes in his *Against the Academics* that there were several who attempted to prove the same thing in their highly subtle discussions: namely, that the philosophy of **Plato** and **Aristotle** is the same. 

<margin>John Philoponus</margin> 
**John Philoponus** <note>original: "Ioannes grammaticus"; a Christian commentator on Aristotle</note> likewise, while saying that Plato differs from Aristotle only for those who do not understand Plato's words, nevertheless left the proof of this to posterity. Moreover, we have added many points in which we assert that the opinions of **Scotus** and **Thomas**, as well as those of **Averroes** and **Avicenna**, which are thought to be discordant, are in fact in harmony. 

In the second place, alongside what we ourselves have thought out in both Aristotelian and Platonist philosophy, we have arranged **seventy-two new physical and metaphysical dogmas**. 

<margin>Seventy-two new physical and metaphysical dogmas</margin> 
If anyone holds these, they will be able (unless I am mistaken, which will soon be clear to me) to resolve any question proposed concerning natural and divine things by a far different method than that taught to us through the philosophy which is read in the schools and cultivated by the doctors of this age. 

Nor should anyone wonder, fathers, that I, in my early years and tender age—during which it was hardly permitted (as some boast) to read the commentaries of others—should wish to bring forward a new philosophy; rather, they should praise it if it is defended, or condemn it if it is refuted. And finally, since they are to judge these our discoveries and our writings, they should not count the years of the author, but rather the merits or demerits of the work itself. 

<margin>A new way of philosophizing through numbers</margin> 
There is also, besides that, another method of philosophizing through numbers which we have introduced. This is an ancient method observed by the **Ancient Theologians**, especially by **Pythagoras**, **Aglaophemus**, **Philolaus**, **Plato**, and the earlier **Platonists**. But in this age, like other noble things, it has grown so obsolete through the neglect of those who followed that hardly any traces of it are found. 

<margin>Plato</margin> 
**Plato** writes in the *Epinomis* <note>A dialogue traditionally attributed to Plato concerning the study of astronomy and mathematics</note> that among all the liberal arts and contemplative sciences, the chief and most divine is...
