<meta>This page continues Pico della Mirandola’s defense of his 900 theses. Having established that he must draw from every school of thought, he now transitions into justifying his use of "secret" sciences—specifically Pythagorean Arithmetic and Natural Magic—as tools for understanding the divine.</meta>

...is to be found in the **science of numbering**. Seeking also why man is the wisest of animals? He answers: because he knows how to count. <margin>Aristotle</margin> Of which opinion **Aristotle** also makes mention in his *Problems*. <margin>Abu Ma'shar</margin> **Abu Ma'shar** <note>A famous Persian astrologer known in the West as Albumasar</note> writes that it was a saying of <margin>Avenzoar</margin> **Avenzoar the Babylonian** that he knew all things who knew how to count. 

These things can in no way be true if, by the "art of counting," they understood that art in which **merchants** are now especially skilled. **Plato** also testifies to this, warning us in a loud voice that we should not understand this **divine arithmetic** to be the same as the **arithmetic of merchants**. Therefore, regarding that arithmetic which is so highly praised: since I seem to myself, after many sleepless nights of study, to have explored it thoroughly, I have promised to respond publicly through **numbers** to seventy-four questions which are considered principal among physical and divine matters, to put this matter to the test.

<margin>Magical theorems</margin> We have also proposed **magical theorems**, in which we have indicated that magic is of two kinds. <margin>Twofold magic</margin> One of these consists entirely of the power and authority of **demons**—a thing, by my faith, to be cursed and monstrous. The other, when well-explored, is nothing else but the absolute **consummation of natural philosophy**. 

When the Greeks mention both, they in no way deem the former worthy of the name of magic, calling it *goeteia* <note>original: γοητεία - sorcery or witchcraft involving the invocation of spirits</note>. The latter they call by its own peculiar name, *magia* <note>original: μαγεία</note>, as if it were perfect and supreme wisdom. 

<margin>Porphyry</margin> For the same word, as **Porphyry** <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher</note> says, in the language of the Persians means "magus," which among us signifies an **"interpreter and worshipper of divine things."** <margin>What 'magus' signifies in the Persian language.</margin> Moreover, Fathers, there is a great—nay, the greatest—disparity and dissimilarity between these arts. 

The former is condemned and cursed not only by the **Christian religion**, but by all laws and every well-ordered republic. The latter is approved and embraced by all wise men and all nations studious of celestial and divine things. The former is the most fraudulent of arts; the latter is higher and holier than philosophy. The former is futile and vain; the latter is firm, faithful, and solid. Whoever cultivated the former always concealed it, because it would result in the ignominy and reproach of the author. From the latter, the highest clarity and glory of letters has been sought since ancient times, and almost always. 

No man who was a philosopher and eager to learn the liberal arts was ever a student of the former. To learn the latter, **Pythagoras, Empedocles, Democritus, and Plato** traveled across the seas; they preached it upon their return and held it as primary among their secret mysteries. Just as the former is proven by no reason, so it is supported by no certain authors. The latter, honored by most illustrious "parents" as it were, has two principal authors: <margin>Zamolxis</margin> **Zamolxis**, whom <margin>Abaris the Hyperborean</margin> **Abaris the Hyperborean** imitated, and <margin>Zoroaster</margin> **Zoroaster**—not the one you might think, but the son of Oromasius.

If we ask <margin>Plato</margin> **Plato** what the magic of each is, he will answer in the *Alcibiades* that the magic of **Zoroaster** is nothing else than the **science of divine things**, in which the kings of the Persians educated their sons, so that they might be taught to rule their own republic according to the pattern of the cosmic republic. He will answer in the *Charmides* that the magic of **Zamolxis** is the **medicine of the soul**, through which, indeed, temperance is brought to the soul, just as through medicine, health is brought to the body. 

In their footsteps later followed <margin>Charondas</margin> **Charondas**, <margin>Damigeron</margin> **Damigeron**, <margin>Apollonius</margin> **Apollonius**, <margin>Hostanes</margin> **Hostanes**, and <margin>Dardanus</margin> **Dardanus**. <margin>Homer</margin> **Homer** also followed, and we shall one day prove in our *Poetic Theology* that he, just like all other forms of wisdom, also concealed this one under the wanderings of his **Ulysses**. <margin>Eudoxus</margin> **Eudoxus** and **Hermippus** followed. Almost all who have scrutinized the **Pythagorean** and **Platonic** mysteries have followed. Among the more recent thinkers who have had a "scent" of it, I find three: <margin>al-Kindi the Arab</margin> **al-Kindi the Arab**, <margin>Roger Bacon</margin> **Roger Bacon**, and <margin>William of Auvergne</margin> **William of Auvergne**. <margin>Plotinus</margin> **Plotinus** also mentions it, where he demonstrates that the magus is the **minister of nature** and not its maker. He approves of this magic...

He also argues that true Arithmetic is a sacred science used by ancient sages to understand the cosmos, rather than a mere tool for commerce.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Pico della Mirandola’s defense of his 900 theses. After distinguishing between demonic sorcery and natural magic, he further defines the latter as a noble pursuit that "marries" the heavens and the earth. He then transitions into a defense of the "mysteries of the Hebrews" (Kabbalah), arguing that Moses received a secret, oral interpretation of the Law on Mount Sinai intended only for the wise.</meta>

### RR ii

...and a most wise man was present: so abhorring the other <note>demonic magic</note> that when he was called to the rites of evil demons, he said it was more right that they should come to him than he to them; and rightly so. For as the former makes man a subject and slave to wicked powers, so the latter <note>natural magic</note> makes him their prince and lord. Finally, the former cannot claim for itself the name of either art or science. The latter, full of the highest mysteries, embraces the deepest contemplation of the most secret things and, eventually, the knowledge of all nature. This magic, calling forth into the light, as if from hiding places, the virtues scattered and sown in the world by the blessing of God, does not so much perform wonders as it diligently serves nature as she performs them. 

Having searched more scrupulously into the "consensus of the universe"—which the Greeks more significantly call *sympathy* <note>original: συμπαθειαν — the idea that all parts of the cosmos are interconnected</note>—and having a clear understanding of the reciprocal nature of things, this magic applies to each thing its own native allurements (which the magicians call *iynxes* <note>original: ιυγγεσ — ancient Greek magical charms or "love-spells" used to draw things together</note>). Thus, it brings out into the public view the miracles lying hidden in the recesses of the world, in the lap of nature, and in the secret storehouses of God, as if she herself were the craftswoman. And just as the farmer marries elms to vines, so the magus **marries the earth to heaven**—that is, he joins the lower things to the gifts and virtues of the higher. 

<margin>
Note:
<gloss>**Natural philosophy**</gloss>
</margin>

Consequently, just as the former magic appears monstrous and harmful, so the latter appears divine and salutary. Most especially because the former, by enslaving man to the enemies of God, calls him away from God; while the latter excites in him such an admiration for the works of God that fervent charity, faith, and hope most certainly follow. For nothing promotes religion and the worship of God more than the constant contemplation of the miracles of God. Once we have well-explored these through this **natural magic** of which we speak, we shall be more ardently animated toward the worship and love of the Creator, and we shall be compelled to sing: "The heavens are full, and the earth is full of the majesty of Thy glory." 

And this is enough regarding magic, of which I have said these things because I know there are many who, like dogs always barking at strangers, often condemn and hate what they do not understand. 

I come now to those things which, unearthed from the ancient **mysteries of the Hebrews**, I have brought forward to confirm the most holy and Catholic faith. Lest these things be thought by those to whom they are unknown to be made-up trifles or the tall tales of charlatans, I want everyone to understand what and of what sort they are, from where they are sought, by which and how famous the authors are who confirm them, and how recondite, how divine, and how necessary they are for our people to defend our religion against the persistent slanders of the Hebrews. 

<margin>
Doctors of the Hebrews:
<gloss>Through these mysteries of the faith, conquer [?] and Divine [things].</gloss>
</margin>

Not only the famous doctors of the Hebrews write of this, but from our own tradition, **Esdras**, **Hilary**, and **Origen** also write that **Moses** received on the mountain not only the Law, which he left for posterity recorded in five books, but also a more secret and true explanation of the Law. They say it was commanded to him by God that he should indeed make the Law public to the people, but that he should neither commit the interpretation of the Law to writing nor make it common knowledge. Instead, he was to reveal it only to **Joshua**, and then he in turn to the other succeeding heads of the priests, under a great religious obligation of silence. 

It was enough to recognize through the simple history now the power of God, now His wrath against the wicked, His mercy toward the good, and His justice toward all; and through divine and salutary precepts, to be instructed in living well and happily and in the worship of true religion. But to make public to the common people the more secret mysteries, the secrets of the highest divinity hidden under the "bark" of the Law and the rough cover of words—what was that other than **"giving that which is holy to dogs and scattering pearls among swine"**? 

Therefore, to keep these things secret from the common crowd and to communicate them only to the "perfect," among whom alone **Paul** says he speaks wisdom, was a matter of divine command, not human counsel. This custom the ancient philosophers most religiously observed...

<summary>Pico defines natural magic as a divine art that unites earthly and heavenly forces, contrasting it with forbidden sorcery. He then introduces the Kabbalah as a secret, oral tradition given to Moses on Sinai to explain the hidden meanings of the Bible.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Pico della Mirandola’s justification for his study of esoteric traditions. Having just finished his defense of natural magic, he now transitions to his second controversial source: the Hebrew Kabbalah. He argues that the greatest philosophers and religious leaders of antiquity—from Pythagoras and Plato to Jesus and the Apostles—purposefully hid their most profound truths from the common public, using a secret oral tradition similar to the one he claims to have found in Jewish texts.</meta>

<margin>Pythagoras</margin> ...they preserved it. Pythagoras wrote nothing except a few small things which he commended to his daughter Dama as he was dying. The sphinxes carved into the temples of the Egyptians warned that mystic doctrines <margin>Plato</margin> should be kept inviolate from the profane multitude by means of the knots of enigmas. Plato, writing to Dion about the highest substances, said: "I must speak in enigmas, lest if the letter should by chance fall into the hands of others, what we write to you might be understood by them." <margin>Aristotle</margin> Aristotle used to say that his books on *Metaphysics*, in which he treats divine matters, were both "published and not published." What <margin>Jesus Christ</margin> more? Origen asserts that Jesus Christ, the teacher of life, revealed many things to his disciples which they <margin>Origen</margin> were unwilling to write down, lest they become common to the masses. This is most strongly confirmed by <margin>Dionysius</margin> Dionysius the Areopagite <note>A Christian theologian and philosopher of the late 5th to early 6th century, often conflated in Pico's time with the convert of St. Paul mentioned in the Book of Acts</note>, who says that the more secret mysteries were poured out by the authors of our religion

"from mind to mind" <note>original: "ex animo in animum"</note>, without letters, through the intervening medium of the word. In exactly this same way, when that true interpretation of the Law, divinely handed down to Moses, was revealed by God’s command, it was <margin>Kabbalah</margin> called "Kabbalah" <note>original: "Cabala"</note>—which is the same among the Hebrews as "reception" is among us. This was because one man received that doctrine from another, not through written records, but by a regular succession of revelations, as if by a hereditary right. Truly, after the Hebrews were restored from the Babylonian captivity by Cyrus, and the temple was restored under Zerubbabel, they applied their minds to repairing the Law. Ezra <note>original: "Esdras"</note>, then the leader of the Church, after amending the book of Moses, clearly recognized that because of the exiles, slaughters, flights, and the captivity of the Israelite people, the custom instituted by the ancestors of handing down the doctrine from hand to hand could not be preserved. He saw that the secrets of the heavenly doctrine granted to them by God would perish, for their memory could not endure for long without the aid of commentaries. He therefore decreed that the wise men who then survived should be called together, and each should bring into the open what he remembered regarding the mysteries of the Law. With scribes employed, these were reduced into seventy volumes (for there were approximately <margin>Ezra</margin> seventy wise men in the Sanhedrin <note>The supreme judicial and ecclesiastical council of ancient Jerusalem</note>). Concerning this matter, so that you do not have to believe me alone, Fathers, hear Ezra himself speaking thus: "After forty days had passed, the Most High spoke, saying: 'Publish the first things you wrote openly, that the worthy and unworthy may read them; but the last seventy books you shall keep, to hand them over to the wise among your people. For in these is the vein of understanding, the fountain of wisdom, and the river of knowledge.' And so I did." These are the words of Ezra. These are the books of the science of the Kabbalah. In these books, Ezra deservedly proclaimed with a clear voice that there is a "vein of understanding"—that is, an ineffable theology of the supersubstantial deity <note>A Neoplatonic concept referring to God as being "above" or "beyond" the traditional category of being or essence</note>; a "fountain of wisdom"—that is, an exact metaphysics concerning intelligible and angelic forms; and a "river of knowledge"—that is, a most solid philosophy concerning natural things. <margin>Pope Sixtus IV</margin> Pope Sixtus IV, who immediately preceded the one under whom we now live happily, <margin>Innocent VIII</margin> Innocent VIII, took the greatest care and study to ensure that these books were committed to Latin letters for the public benefit of our faith. Thus, when he died, three of them had reached the Latins. Among the Hebrews in this time, these books are held in such great reverence that no one is allowed to touch them unless they are forty years old. When I had acquired these books for myself at no small expense, and had read through them with the greatest diligence and unwearied labor, I saw in them (God is my witness) a religion not so much Mosaic as Christian. There I saw the mystery of the Trinity, there the Incarnation of the Word, there the divinity of the Messiah; there I read about original sin, its expiation through Christ, the heavenly Jerusalem, the fall of the demons, the orders of the angels, the purgations, and the punishments of Hell. I read the same things that we find in Paul and Dionysius...

<summary>Pico explains the origins of the Kabbalah as a secret oral tradition given to Moses and later recorded by Ezra in seventy books. He argues that these texts, recently translated into Latin under Pope Sixtus IV, contain profound proofs for Christian dogmas like the Trinity and the Incarnation.</summary>

I wanted to say this so that it might be known what labor and what difficulty I faced: to draw out the hidden meanings of secret philosophy from the thorny thickets of riddles and the hiding places of fables—especially in a matter so grave, so hidden, and so unexplored, without the aid and diligence of other interpreters. And yet my dogs <note>Pico refers here to his critics and detractors who "bark" at his work.</note> have barked that I have accumulated certain trifling and light things for a show of numbers, as if all these questions were not extremely ambiguous and controversial, in which the principal Academies clash; as if I have not brought many things to these very men who carp at me—who believe themselves to be the princes of philosophers—that are entirely unknown and unattempted. On the contrary, I am so far from that fault that I took care to compress the disputation into as few headings as possible. If I had wished to divide and carve it into its own members (as others are accustomed to do), it would surely have grown into an innumerable number. And to say nothing of the rest: who is there who does not know that one dogma out of the nine hundred—namely, the reconciliation of the philosophy of Plato and Aristotle—could have been drawn out by me, without any suspicion of affected number, into six hundred or even more headings, by enumerating point by point all the places in which others think they differ and I think they agree? But certainly (I will say it, though neither modestly nor according to my character), I will say it nevertheless: because the envious compel me to speak, and my detractors compel me, I wished to give proof by this meeting of mine, not so much that I knew many things, but that I knew things which many do not know. So that this might now be made clear to you in fact, most worshipful fathers, and so that my speech no longer delays your desire, most excellent doctors—whom I see with great pleasure prepared and girded for the fight—may it be happy and auspicious! As if the trumpet were sounding the charge, let us now join hands in battle!

<meta>This page marks a transition from the philosophical "Oration on the Dignity of Man" to a more personal, pastoral letter. While the previous page focused on the intellectual synthesis of ancient wisdom and Christian doctrine, this letter is addressed to Pico’s nephew, Gianfrancesco Pico della Mirandola, offering practical and spiritual advice on living a Christian life in a distracting world.</meta>

-> Giovanni Pico della Mirandola to his nephew Gianfrancesco. Greetings in Him who is true salvation. <-

<margin>i</margin>
It is no surprise, my son, that as you depart from me, many opportunities for evil immediately present themselves to disturb you and oppose your resolve to live well. But you should not grieve or be terrified. How much greater a miracle would it be if the path to heaven lay open for you alone among mortals without any sweat—as if now, for the first time, the deceitful world and the evil demon had ceased to exist, or as if you were not still in the flesh, which "desires against the spirit." <note>original: "concupiscit aduersus spīm" — a reference to Galatians 5:17 regarding the conflict between physical desires and spiritual goals.</note> Unless we look out for our salvation with a watchful eye, the world—with the alluring cups of Circe <note>In Greek mythology, the sorceress Circe used drugged wine to turn men into beasts; Pico uses this as a metaphor for how worldly pleasures dehumanize people.</note>—transforms us while we are drunk into the monstrous shapes of beasts. But as James writes, you should even rejoice: <margin>James</margin> "Rejoice, my brothers, when you fall into various trials." <note>original: "gaudete fratres cū itētatōes uarias īcideritis" — James 1:2.</note> And not without reason: for what hope of glory can there be if there is no hope of victory? Or where can there be a place for victory where there is no battle? He who is challenged to a fight is being called to a crown—especially in that fight where no one can be conquered against his will, and where we need no other strength to win than the simple desire to be victorious. <margin>The great happiness of a Christian.</margin> Great is the happiness of a Christian, since victory is placed within his own choice, and the future rewards will be greater than any victor’s wish or expectation. 

Tell me, I ask you, dearest son: is there anything in this life among those things that drive the minds of men toward earthly lusts, for the sake of which many labors must not first be undergone, and many indignities and miseries endured? A merchant thinks he has done well for himself if, after a ten-year voyage, after a thousand inconveniences and a thousand dangers to his life, he has acquired a slightly richer estate. Concerning the "service of this age" <note>term: <term>militia saeculi</term> — refers to both literal military service and the metaphorical struggle for worldly status and career.</note> there is no need for me to write to you; its miseries have already taught you enough, as does experience itself. In earning the favor of princes, in reconciling friendships among equals, in seeking honors—what a mountain of troubles! How much anxiety! How much worry! I can learn these things from you rather than teach them to you; for I, content with my little bit of leisure among my books, have learned from childhood to live within my fortune. Remaining as much as I can within myself, I sigh for nothing and seek nothing outside of myself. 

Therefore, we pursue these earthly things—fleeting, uncertain, worthless, and shared with the beasts—only with exhaustion and gasping; yet we are drawn toward the celestial and divine things (which "eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor heart imagined") <note>original: "nec oculus uidit / neqʒ auris audiuit / neque cor cogitauit" — 1 Corinthians 2:9.</note> while we are sluggish, sleeping, and almost against our will. As if God could not reign or those heavenly citizens could not be happy without us! Certainly, if earthly happiness could be obtained by us while we were idle, someone who dislikes labor might prefer to serve the world rather than God. But if we are fatigued no less—indeed, far more—in the way of sinners than in the way of God, then that cry of the damned must follow: "We are weary in the way of iniquity." <note>original: "Lassati sumus ī uia iniquitatis" — Wisdom of Solomon 5:7.</note> It cannot be anything but extreme madness to be unwilling to labor where one goes from labor to reward, rather than where one goes from labor to punishment.

<margin><unclear>Position</unclear></margin>
I will not mention how great is that peace, and how great the happiness of a mind that is conscious of no wrong and grows pale at no guilt <note>original: "nil cōscire sibi nulla palescere culpa" — Pico is quoting the Roman poet Horace (*Epistles* 1.1.61), describing the "wall of brass" that is a clear conscience.</note>; this, without <margin>A sentence to be remembered</margin> doubt, far outweighs all the pleasures that can be possessed or hoped for in life. For what is there to be desired in the pleasures of the world? While they are sought, they exhaust us; when they are acquired, they fool us; when they are lost, they torture us. Do you doubt, my son, that the minds of the impious are driven by perpetual cares? It is the word of God, which can neither be deceived nor deceive: their heart is like a boiling sea that cannot rest. For nothing is safe for them, nothing is peaceful; everything threatens fear, everything threatens cares, everything threatens death. Shall we then look to these people? Shall we envy them? And forgetting our own dignity, forgetting our homeland and our heavenly Father, shall we make ourselves their slaves, even though we were born free? Living miserably with them, and dying more miserably, shall we at last be afflicted most miserably of all by eternal fires? O, the blind minds of men! O...

<meta>This page continues the letter from Giovanni Pico della Mirandola to his nephew Gianfrancesco. It transitions from general encouragement to a stern warning about the corrupting influence of worldly society and the logical inconsistency of those who claim to believe the Gospel but do not live according to its teachings.</meta>

...blind hearts! Who would not see, clearer than light itself, that all these things are truer than truth itself? Nor do we then do what we recognize ought to be done, but we still hesitate, fruitlessly wishing to pull our feet out of the mud. <note>The "mud" or "mire" is a common metaphor in Renaissance spirituality for the entanglement of the soul in material desires.</note> Do not doubt, my son, that in those very places where you live, countless obstacles will meet you every hour to deter you from your purpose of living a holy and good life, and unless you are careful, they will drive you headlong into ruin.

But among all these, that pestilence is most deadly: to spend your days and nights among those whose life is not only an enticement to sin in every respect, but is entirely set upon conquering virtue. Under the devil as their commander, under the banners of death, and under the wages of <term>Gehenna</term> <note>Gehenna is a term derived from the Hebrew "Ge Hinnom," referring to a valley near Jerusalem; in the New Testament and later Christian writing, it is used as a name for Hell or the place of eternal punishment.</note>, they wage war against heaven, against the Lord, and against his Christ.

<margin>Propheta</margin>
But you, cry out with the Prophet: "Let us break their bonds asunder and cast away their yoke from us." <note>original: "dirūpamus uincula eorum & proiiciamus a nobis iugum ipsorum" — a quote from Psalm 2:3, used here to urge the soul to break free from the social pressures of the wicked.</note> 

<margin>Apostolus</margin>
For these are they whom God has handed over to shameful passions and to a reprobate mind, to do those things which are not fitting; they are full of all iniquity, full of envy, murder, strife, deceit, and malice. They are whisperers, hateful to God, insolent, proud, boastful, inventors of evil things, foolish, faithless, without affection, without a covenant, without mercy. <note>Pico is quoting the Apostle Paul’s description of a fallen society from Romans 1:26–31.</note> Though they see the justice of God daily, they do not understand it; nevertheless, since those who do such things are worthy of death, this applies not only to those who do them, but also to those who consent to the ones doing them.

Therefore, my son, do not wish to please those whom virtue itself displeases. But let that word of the Apostle always be before your eyes: "It is necessary to please God rather than men." <note>original: "oportet deo magis placere q̄ hominibus" — Acts 5:29.</note> And also: "If I were to please men, I would not be a servant of Christ." <note>Galatians 1:10.</note> Let a certain holy ambition seize you, and disdain to have those as the masters of your life who rather stand in need of you as a teacher. For it is far more fitting that they begin to be human beings by living well alongside you, than that you should wish to become shamefully beast-like with them by abandoning your good purpose.

God is my witness, a kind of ecstasy and a certain stupor sometimes takes hold of me when I begin to consider the pursuits of men—or, to speak more significantly, their sheer madness. I know not whether to think on it rather than to grieve, or whether to marvel or to deplore. For it is indeed a great madness not to believe the Gospel, whose truth the blood of martyrs cries out, the apostolic voices echo, miracles prove, reason confirms, the world testifies, the elements speak, and demons confess.

But it is a far greater madness if, while you do not doubt the truth of the Gospel, you nevertheless live as though you did not doubt its falsehood. For if those things are true—that it is most difficult for a rich man to enter the kingdom of heaven—why do we pant for daily accumulated riches? And if that is true—that glory should be sought not from men but from God—why do we always hang upon the judgments of men? There is no one who cares to please God. And if faith is firm within us that the Lord will one day say, "Depart, you cursed, into eternal fire," and again, "Come, you blessed, possess the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world," why do we fear nothing less than Gehenna, or hope for nothing less than the kingdom of God?

<margin>Nota</margin>
<margin><unclear>paucissim.</unclear></margin>
What else can we say but that many are Christians in name, but in reality, very few? <note>margin: "Nota paucissim." — Note: very few.</note> But you, my son, strive to enter through the narrow gate; do not look to what the many do, but to what the law of nature, reason itself, and God himself show you must be done. For neither will your glory be less if you are happy with the few, nor your punishment lighter if you are wretched with the many. 

Now, there will be two remedies especially ready for you against the world and Satan, by which, as if by two wings, you may be lifted high from the valley of tears: <term>elemosina</term> <note>elemosina: Almsgiving or acts of charity. Pico views charity and prayer as the two essential "wings" for spiritual progress.</note>...

He characterizes the wicked society around him as a literal army of the devil and identifies almsgiving and prayer as the primary remedies for the soul.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Giovanni Pico della Mirandola's letter of spiritual advice to his nephew Gianfrancesco. It concludes this letter and begins a new piece of correspondence to the famous humanist scholar Filippo Beroaldo. The transition highlights Pico's shift from spiritual mentor to a humble member of the Republic of Letters.</meta>

<margin>two most healthy remedies</margin> <note>original: "duo remedia saluberrima"</note> **study** and **prayer**. For what can we do without the help of God? Or how will He help us if He is not called upon? But surely He will not hear you calling upon Him if you did not previously listen to the poor man calling upon you. For it is not fitting that God should not despise you, a man, when you as a man have first despised another man. It is written: *In the measure you have measured, it will be measured back to you*; and elsewhere: *Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy.* 

When, however, I invite you to prayer, I do not invite you to that which consists of much speaking, but to that which happens in the secret retreat of the mind, in the innermost parts of the soul, where you speak to God with true affection. In that <term>most lucid darkness of contemplation</term> <note>This refers to a mystical state where the overwhelming "light" of God appears as "darkness" to the limited human intellect—a concept popularized by the theologian Pseudo-Dionysius.</note>, the mind is not only presented to the Father but united to Him in certain ineffable ways which only the experienced know. Nor do I care how long your prayer is, but how effective it is, how burning, interrupted by sighs rather than a continuous series of words spread out in a rhythmic flow. 

If your salvation is dear to your heart; if you wish to be safe from the snares of the devil, from the storms of the world, and from the ambushes of enemies; if you desire to be pleasing to God and finally happy: make sure no day passes in which you do not approach your God at least once through prayer. Prostrated before Him with the humble affection of a pious mind, cry out—not from the tips of your lips, but from your innermost depths—with the Prophet: *Remember not the sins of my youth and my ignorances, but according to your mercy remember me for your goodness' sake, O Lord.* 

Both the Spirit who intercedes for us and necessity itself will suggest to you every hour what you should ask of your God. Sacred reading will also suggest it—which I ask you again and again to keep always in your hands, setting aside now the fables and trifles of the poets. You can do nothing more pleasing to God or more useful to yourself than if you do not cease to *turn the sacred letters with a nightly hand and a daily hand.* <note>Pico is cleverly adapting a famous line from the Roman poet Horace, who advised poets to study Greek models day and night; here, Pico applies the advice to the Bible.</note> For there lies hidden in them a certain living and effective heavenly power which—if the reader treats them purely and humbly—transforms the soul into divine love by a certain wonderful power.

But I have already exceeded the limits of a letter, drawn on by the subject matter itself and by a certain wonderful charity with which I have followed you in spirit, especially from that hour when I was made more certain of your most holy purpose. Finally, I would wish you to be reminded of that which I often spoke with you when you were here with me: that you never forget these two things: that the Son of God died for you, and that you also, even if you live a long time, will soon die. 

<margin>Note</margin> With these twin spurs—the one of fear, the other of love—urge your horse through the brief course of this momentary life toward the rewards of eternal happiness. We neither ought to nor can set any other goal for ourselves than that we may enjoy the infinite good without end in the perpetual peace of the <term>twofold man</term> <note>The "twofold man" refers to the Pauline concept of the "inner man" (spirit) and "outer man" (body/flesh) finally being in harmony.</note>. Farewell. And fear God. Ferrara, May 15, 1482.

## Giovanni Pico della Mirandola to Filippo Beroaldo, Greetings.

<margin>a</margin> <margin>z</margin> I have received from you, most learned Beroaldo, a letter both amiable and erudite, along with many verses that beyond doubt challenge antiquity itself. That gift was most welcome to me. Therefore, thanks to you, I have spent my leisure hours in "good business," and I could not have enjoyed myself more pleasantly or more honorably in any other way. 

Indeed, I would act as an altogether ungrateful man if I wished to repay your excellent works with mine, which are very poor, and to exchange the wit of Catullus for the poisons of <term>Suffenus</term> <note>Suffenus was a poet mocked by the Roman poet Catullus for writing thousands of lines of terrible verse while being very proud of them.</note>. For I am no better in poems than he was, except in this: that I recognize myself to be a Suffenus, and I see what is in the knapsack on my back. <note>An allusion to Aesop's fable where humans carry their own faults in a bag behind their backs where they cannot see them, while carrying the faults of others in front.</note> Yet you demand this: namely, that I give you something of my own writings. And you demand it so insistently that you seem to require it as a right, appearing as though you will not take a refusal with a calm mind. Therefore, even at the cost of...

...zeal, so that if there is any regard for me in your opinion, it may be satisfied. Therefore, you have these two letters: one to **Lorenzo de' Medici**, the other to **Hermolaus** <note>Hermolaus Barbaro (1454–1493), a famous Venetian humanist who debated Pico on the merits of "barbarous" medieval philosophical Latin versus polished classical style.</note> regarding the style of the philosophers. You will read these in such a way as to remember that I have applied myself to these less refined studies with a hurried care and in my spare time—as one who has devoted his primary efforts and, as they say, his <term>serious lamps</term> <note>original: "seriosas lucernas"; a metaphor for late-night scholarly labor.</note> to the philosophers. Among them, I hope I have made the same progress that you have among the rhetoricians and poets. Among those poets (I speak from my heart), I do not see why you should not rightfully claim the first place for yourself. Your **Poliziano** <note>Angelo Poliziano (1454–1494), the preeminent poet and scholar of the Medici circle.</note> is entirely yours; he loves you as much as anyone can. Regarding myself, you can promise yourself nothing that I would not be able to do. Farewell.

-> **Giovanni Pico della Mirandola sends many greetings to Lorenzo de' Medici.** <-

<margin>a 3 1</margin>
I have read, **Lorenzo de' Medici**, your *Rhythms* <note>Referring to Lorenzo’s vernacular Italian poetry.</note> which the native Muses suggested to you despite your tender age. I recognized the legitimate offspring of the Muses and the Graces; but I did not recognize it as the work of a tender age. For who, in your rhythms and the rhythmic joining of your verses, would not see the Graces dancing to the beat? Who, in that melodious and modulated style of speaking, would not hear the Muses singing? Who would recognize a mere youth in your unpretentious charm, your cheerful wit, your honeyed salts <note>A classical metaphor for wit or humor.</note>, your fitting allurements, and your wonderful clarity? Who would see a young man in your prudent arrangement and your most weighty thoughts, dug out from the very <term>inner chambers of philosophy</term>?

I know for certain that I am not "on this list" <note>original: "in hoc albo"; meaning a list of qualified judges.</note> nor am I one to climb up to such a judgment of things. But I would wish it could be said—without suspicion of flattery—what I truly feel about those poems. I would certainly say that there is no ancient writer whom you have not surpassed by a long interval in this style of speaking. Lest you think this is said merely to please you, I will bring you my reasons for this opinion. 

Among you, there are two especially celebrated poets of the Florentine language: **Francis Petrarch** and **Dante Alighieri**. Concerning them, let me first say this in general: there are some among the learned who find <term>substance</term> <note>original: "res"; meaning the intellectual content or "matter."</note> lacking in Francis, and <term>words</term> <note>original: "verba"; meaning the polished style or vocabulary.</note> lacking in Dante. In you—provided one has a mind and ears—neither will be found wanting; in your work, one cannot tell whether the matter is more illustrated by the speech, or the words by the thoughts. 

But let us expand upon the merits of each one individually, as if in books. If Francis were to come back to life, who doubts that he would voluntarily <term>yield the grass</term> <note>original: "herbā datuꝝ"; an ancient Roman idiom for admitting defeat.</note> to you regarding the thoughts? For you are always sharp, weighty, and subtle. He, however, taking much from the common middle-ground, colors his thoughts with words and makes common things excellent through his style of speaking. In that style, let us see what he provides to you, and what you provide to him—though in certain places he may appear "sweeter." But to me, his sweetness seems (if I may say so) "sweetly accidental" and "pleasantly austere." He is flowing and smooth in a uniform way. You, however, grip the mind with majesty and a certain vivid light of oratory. In him, there is an ambitious and excessive diligence; in you, it is rather neglected than affected. He is tender and soft; you are masculine and muscular. He is voluble and melodious; you are concise, full, firm, and modulated. He is perhaps more charming; you are certainly more ample and elevated. He is more "painted," but you are more sinewy. In him, there is something you might prune away; in you, there is nothing redundant and nothing cut short. 

But perhaps I am a bit bold to say that something should be removed from him. It is certainly so, and it seems so to many in whose judgment I trust—for I trust mine not at all. For one can often see him failing where the "Asiatics" <note>A reference to "Asianism," a rhetorical style characterized by being overly florid or wordy, contrasted with the leaner "Attic" style.</note> failed: that is, stuffing in words as if to fill up cracks, and using full and harmonious voices not to decorate, but to prop up the poem like a flute-player’s accompaniment, lest it limp. In you, everything is present: the words are no less necessary for the substance than they are pleasing for the ornament...

<meta>This page continues Giovanni Pico della Mirandola’s letter to Lorenzo de' Medici, written around 1484. Having previously praised Lorenzo's poetry, Pico now engages in a detailed comparison between Lorenzo and the great masters of Italian literature, specifically focusing on the relationship between style (words) and substance (meaning).</meta>

...so that whoever takes away from you, mutilates the work; but whoever takes away from him <note>Pico is likely referring to Petrarch here, comparing his "polished" style to Lorenzo's.</note>, merely clips and cleanses it. Even if we were to grant (though I never will) that the things he wrote are more charming and elegant than yours, it was an easy thing for a man to excel when he did not have to struggle and fight with the weight of the ideas themselves. But those sharp and subtle—and to use a single word—**Laurentian sentences** of yours can hardly be said to reject the "curling irons" <note>A metaphor for artificial stylistic ornamentation or "crimping" of language.</note>, nor do they willingly admit those "cosmetics" <note>original: "fucos"; meaning artificial dyes or rhetorical disguises.</note>. If he had been required to handle the subjects you treat—he whom we read as soft, polished, and pleasant—we would instead read him as thorny, rough, and ungrateful. Indeed, we can see that whenever he attempts something sharp, implicit, or knotty, he fails in style as much as he rises in meaning. But when he displays that "furniture" of his words—his ointments, his curls, and his flowers—he would often be warned, if Castritius <note>Titus Castritius, a Roman rhetorician mentioned by Aulus Gellius.</note> were present, as he warned Gracchus: not to be deceived by the rounded sound and the flow of the verses. Rather, we should look at what lies beneath: what seat, what foundation, what ground supports the words. If you were to do this, you would see that his work is sometimes "void of Epicurus" <note>original: "epicuri uacuum"; a philosophical joke suggesting the text lacks the "atoms" or substance of real thought.</note>, so that either no meaning lies beneath, or what is there is cold and light. In this respect, which is the most important, even if you do not grant him superiority, I do not see at all why he should excel you for the sake of speaking beautifully. Since words could not be more brilliant in your work, and their arrangement is so fitting that they could not cohere better, nor flow more roundly, nor fall more rhythmically in any way.

<margin>Note</margin>
But now let us carefully weigh **Dante** against you, concerning whom many will perhaps create a controversy. For there are many who, in the comparison of writers, do not so much weigh their merits as count their years; they command others to read the ancients with reverence, while they themselves cannot read their contemporaries without envy. Certainly, as far as style is concerned, I think no one will deny you the first place. Dante is sometimes so harsh, rough, and thin, as to be quite unrefined and unpolished; even his own "goldsmiths" <note>original: "aurarii"; likely referring to Dante’s scholarly commentators or devoted admirers who "refine" his meaning.</note> confess this. But they cast the blame for this entirely on the age and the century. You are more refined in your oratory, and he is no more "grand" than you. But they will say he is grander and more sublime in his meanings. I ask: what wonder is it if he speaks [**fari**] <term>to speak</term> on physical [**physica**] <term>natural philosophy</term> matters, since nature itself compels him to this and provides the insights of its own accord?

<margin>Augustine. Thomas</margin>
If the subject is God, the soul, or the blessed, he brings forward what **Thomas Aquinas** or **Augustine** wrote on these things. And he was as frequent and diligent in handling and meditating on these topics as you are in carrying out the greatest public and private business. It was not so much distinguished for Dante to have done this, as it would have been shameful for him *not* to have done it. But it was, beyond a doubt, a work of supreme genius that you yourself manage to turn "physical" <note>Meaning philosophical or natural science topics.</note> matters into things of love; and those things which are somewhat stern in their own severity, you make lovable by the addition of grace. Thus, in your verses, the serious matters of philosophers are so mixed with the playfulness of lovers that the latter gain dignity from the former, and the former gain cheerfulness and grace from the latter. By this union, both have retained what was their own and have shared themselves with each other, so that both possess individually what was previously shared between them. But this is not as admirable as the thing that moved me most: these ideas were introduced by you not as if they were brought in from the outside, but as if they were plucked from the very heart of the subject you are treating. As if, by your "watering of the soil," they seem to blossom naturally, appearing native and not foreign, necessary and not imported, entirely genuine and not grafted. This is what I cannot admire enough, and in this, you seem to me to have surpassed Dante. For even if he flies high, he is lifted by the "wings" of his subject matter; you, though the subject resists and drags you down, are raised on high by the wings of your own genius. And so...

He specifically notes that while Dante relied on theological sources like Aquinas, Lorenzo's genius allows him to elevate "lowly" themes of love with profound philosophical insight.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Giovanni Pico della Mirandola’s 1484 letter to Lorenzo de' Medici. Pico is moving from a general comparison of Lorenzo’s style to a direct contrast with the "Three Crowns" of Italian literature (Dante, Petrarch, and by implication, Boccaccio), arguing that Lorenzo’s work possesses a unique balance of accessibility and philosophical depth.</meta>

...so that you do not depart from the subject matter; but you lift it up with you as much as you yourself have deserved from it, just as it deserved well from Dante. Now one may see the difference between you, Francesco <note>Petrarch</note>, and Dante. I would add this: Francesco sometimes does not live up to his promises; he has something that attracts at first glance, but further on he does not satisfy. Dante has that which sometimes offends at first meeting, but he delights more the one who penetrates his inner depths. Your works have no less in their inner depths to hold the reader than they have in their first appearance to capture them. Add to this that they composed their poems in retreats, in the shade, in the highest tranquility of studies; you sang yours amidst tumults, the noise of the court, the shouts of the forum, the greatest cares, and the most turbulent storms, while being extremely busy. For them, the muses were their ordinary and primary business; for you, a game and a certain relaxation from cares. For them, it was the greatest exhaustion; for you, exhaustion is leisure. Finally, by relaxing your mind, you reached the point where they, straining every nerve of the mind, perhaps did not reach.

But what shall I say of my paraphrase? For why should I not call it mine? Or rather, why is it not mine by right of naming? Finally, why not mine, which although I venerate as yours, I love as mine. I truly admire it, and you in it, from which I gather how far I was from the true praise of your verses, in which I had looked with "nocturnal eyes" <note>Metaphor for dim vision, like an owl trying to see in the sun; Pico admits he did not initially see the full depth of Lorenzo's work.</note> at those things that were greatest and most illustrious. I saw them revealed through you, who alone both could and should do so; you owe it to yourself and to us, lest you cheat yourself of much glory and us of much pleasure. I read it (I call God to witness), most great Lorenzo, not so much for delight as for doctrine. For how many things from <margin>Aristotle</margin> Aristotle <note>original: "Aristotele"</note> are there—specifically from the *Physics*, the books *On the Soul*, *On Ethics*, *On the Heavens*, and from the *Problems*; and how many from <margin>Plato</margin> Plato <note>original: "Platonis"</note>, from the *Protagoras*, the *Republic*, the *Laws*, and the *Symposium*? All these things, although I have read them elsewhere in their own works, I read in your work as if they were new, as if they were better, and transformed by you into some form so that they seem to be yours and not theirs, and in reading them, I seem to learn something. This is the greatest proof that you know these things not from a commentary but from yourself. For most people are accustomed to show more <term>sophistry</term> <note>original: σοφιστεα (sophisteia); here meaning an outward display of learning used to impress others rather than genuine wisdom.</note> in their writing than actual work; when they are about to write something, they treat philosophers like <margin>Note</margin> legal advisors <note>original: "pragmaticos"; technical term for those who provided the substance or "case matter" for orators.</note> suggesting certain dogmas to them, which they shove into their books so they seem like philosophers. But you can easily detect these people. For you see those things are neither rightly arranged nor coherent, and not explained by them, but entangled. And men who are otherwise eloquent appear like infants when speaking of those things. But who would not see that you do not hold these things precariously, but as matters over which you have right and power to turn, act, and treat at your will? You (O happy genius!) have achieved these things in the heat of the Republic, in an active life—things which we, who are not the disciples of philosophers but merely their "tenants" <note>original: "inquilini"; suggesting those who live in a house they do not own, i.e., scholars who merely inhabit the ideas of others without internalizing them.</note>, follow rather than achieve in our shaded and sedentary life.

But what shall I say of the sweetest style of your paraphrase? It seems to me exactly like that of <margin>Caesar</margin> Caesar <note>Julius Caesar’s prose was famously admired by Humanists for its "pure" and unadorned Latinity.</note> in the Latin tongue. For it is speech that is not artificial, not gold-leafed, not twisted, but by its own nature upright, clear, and solid; neither running out at random but keeping its pace; not luxuriant, nor meager, nor wanton, nor unpleasant; sweetly grave, gravely lovable; words selected but not hunted for, illustrious but not painted, necessary, not sought out, not just explaining the matter but placing it before the eyes themselves. I pass over how you always remember your <unclear>persona</unclear> <note>original: "p̃one" (likely *persone*); referring to the consistency of Lorenzo's character or authorial voice.</note>, and how there are seeds of that prudence of yours everywhere...

<summary>Pico della Mirandola argues that Lorenzo de' Medici excels beyond Petrarch and Dante because he integrates profound Aristotelian and Platonic philosophy into his poetry despite the distractions of his public political life. He compares Lorenzo's prose style to the clarity and directness of Julius Caesar, praising its lack of artificial ornamentation.</summary>

<meta>This page concludes Giovanni Pico della Mirandola’s letter to Lorenzo de' Medici (begun on the previous page) and introduces his famous 1485 letter to the Venetian humanist Ermolao Barbaro. This second letter is a cornerstone of Renaissance intellectual history, debating the value of "barbarous" Medieval philosophy versus "elegant" Humanist rhetoric.</meta>

I have followed these tracks with many others, and anyone else far better than I. But I have seen two things especially besides these, which perhaps not many have seen, however sharp-eyed they may be. The first is that she <note>Referring to Lorenzo’s poetic style or Muse</note> hides her riches to avoid envy, holding her flowers in her lap; she does not show them off, nor does she stand tall on her toes, but sits modestly so as to appear smaller. I do not see what the other thing is—for I am not so skillful—but I see it is something most distinctly Laurentian <note>Meaning uniquely characteristic of Lorenzo de' Medici</note>. If anyone could see Lorenzo’s gifts and genius, they would see all of Lorenzo graphically depicted here. But perhaps I have said too much; I have spoken even against my will, for the very sentiment of my mind drew me sideways, as they say, into words. This I will not omit: to urge you with the greatest possible effort that, having stolen some little bit of leisure from governing the Republic, you might devote it to completing your paraphrase—certainly for the honor of yourself and your native tongue, and for the use and pleasure of us all.

->Florence, on the Ides of July <note>July 15th</note>, 1484.<-

### Giovanni Pico della Mirandola to his friend Ermolao Barbaro, Greetings.

<margin>f</margin>
<margin>e</margin>
I certainly, my Ermolao, am unable either to keep silent about what I feel regarding you, or to fail to feel those things which ought to be felt about a man in whom everything is found at the highest level, just as in each individual part. But I wish there were such a grasp in my mind that I might feel about you according to your merits; I wish I had such power of speaking that I might eventually express what I always feel. I know that what I have conceived of you falls infinitely below the heights of your learning. May you also know that whatever we say is far less than what we conceive; know that words are as lacking for the mind as the mind is for the reality of things. And yet, you believe me to be so bold as to hope I might be able to imitate your works, whose greatness I cannot even estimate. All can admire you; so few can imitate you that no one can find fault. And I wish I had such happiness that what I write might represent my Ermolao in some part. For your style itself—to say nothing of the rest—to which you give so little favor, affects and delights me so much. It is so learned, grave, composed, erudite, polished, and ingenious; in it, nothing is exposed, nothing is trivial, whether you look at the words or the ideas. Our friend Poliziano <note>Angelo Poliziano (1454–1494), a brilliant classical scholar and poet</note> and I often read whatever letters of yours we have, whether to others or to us. The subsequent ones always compete with the previous ones, and new graces bloom fruitfully during the reading, so that we have no room to breathe between our constant acclamations. But it is a wonderful thing to say how you persuade and drive the reader's mind wherever you wish. I have experienced this, both at other times and especially in this most recent letter of yours to me. In it, you attack those "barbarous" philosophers <note>The Scholastic philosophers of the Middle Ages, known for their technical but "un-classical" Latin</note>, whom you say are commonly held to be filthy, rude, and uncultivated; people who did not even live while they were alive, much less live now that they are dead; and if they do live now, they live for punishment and disgrace. I was so moved, so ashamed and weary

<meta>This page continues Giovanni Pico della Mirandola's famous 1485 letter to Ermolao Barbaro. Pico has just begun a rhetorical exercise: he is imagining how one of the "barbarous" Medieval Scholastic philosophers (whom the humanists often mocked for their poor Latin) would defend themselves if they were brought back to life today.</meta>

I was thinking <note>The Latin begins "gitabam," likely the end of "cogitabam" (I was thinking) continued from the previous page</note> to myself, as a way to console myself, whether if any of those [medieval philosophers] were to come back to life now, they—men otherwise full of arguments—would have anything with which to defend their cause by some reasoning. Finally, it occurred to me that one of them, a bit more eloquent than the rest, might defend his "barbarism" in as little a "barbarous" way as possible, perhaps in this manner:

"We lived as famous men, O Ermolao, and we shall live hereafter; not in the schools of grammarians and pedagogues <note>Teachers of basic Latin and literature</note>, but in the circles of philosophers and the assemblies of the wise. There, the discussion and debate are not about the mother of Andromache <note>original: "matre andromaches"; a reference to the kind of useless mythological trivia humanists were sometimes accused of obsessing over</note>, nor the children of Niobe, nor light trifles of that sort, but about the reasons of human and divine things. In meditating upon, inquiring into, and unravelling these things, we were so subtle, sharp, and keen that we might sometimes seem to have been too anxious and fastidious—if indeed anyone can be too fastidious or over-curious in the investigation of truth. And if anyone in these matters accuses us of dullness and slowness—well then, please, let whoever he is step forward; he will discover that these 'barbarians' had **Mercury not on their tongues but in their hearts** <note>Mercury was the god of both eloquence (tongue) and cunning intelligence (heart/breast)</note>. They did not lack wisdom, even if they lacked eloquence; and perhaps failing to join eloquence with wisdom is so far from a fault that joining them might even be a sin. 

For who would not condemn and detest curled locks and makeup on an honest maiden? There is such a conflict between the duty of the orator and that of the philosopher that they could not be more at odds with one another. For what else is the rhetorician’s job than to lie, deceive, circumvent, and play tricks? For it is your boast—as you say—to be able at will to turn white into black and black into white; to be able to raise up, cast down, amplify, or diminish whatever you wish by speaking. Finally, you boast of being able to transform things themselves, through the almost magical powers of eloquence, into whatever appearance or shape you please, so that things do not become what they are by their own nature, but appear to the listeners to be what you wanted them to be, even when they are not. Is all of this anything other than pure lying, pure imposture, pure trickery? 

Since rhetoric always either exceeds the nature of the thing by exaggerating or falls short by diminishing, and by holding out a deceptive harmony of words—like masks and phantoms—it mocks the minds of the listeners with flattery. Will there be any affinity between this and the philosopher, whose entire study is occupied with knowing the truth and demonstrating it to others? Add to this that we will have no credibility if, affecting refined words and charms as if we had little confidence in the facts, and not relying on the truth, we seek to draw men to our opinion with these enticements. 

For this reason, it is better to read sacred matters written in a rustic rather than an elegant style; for nothing is more unseemly or harmful in any matter where the knowledge of truth is at stake than that whole elaborate style of speaking. This belongs to legal questions, not to natural and celestial ones. It does not belong to those in the Academy <note>The school of philosophy</note> but to those involved in the Republic <note>Public political life</note>, where what is done and said is weighed on the scales of the common people, and where flowers far outweigh the fruit. Do you not know that 'not all things suit all people in the same thread'? Eloquence is an elegant thing (we admit this), full of allure and pleasure; but in a philosopher it is neither fitting nor pleasing. Who would not approve of a soft gait, expressive hands, and playful eyes in an actor or a dancer? But who would not disapprove, condemn, and detest them in a citizen or a philosopher? If we see a girl with charming manners and a witty tongue, we will praise her [and embrace her...]" <note>The Latin "osculabi" is truncated; likely "osculabimur," meaning we will kiss or embrace her</note>

<meta>This page continues the fictionalized defense of medieval "barbarian" philosophers written by Giovanni Pico della Mirandola in his 1485 letter to Ermolao Barbaro. Although the metadata identifies Angelo Poliziano as the author, Poliziano was the editor who published Pico's correspondence. Here, the "barbarian" speaker argues that a philosopher's plain, unadorned language is a deliberate choice for the sake of truth and modesty.</meta>

...[mur] we shall condemn and prosecute these things in a matron <note>original: "matrona." He is comparing overly ornate speech to a woman who uses too much makeup or jewelry, which would be seen as scandalous</note>. Therefore, it is not we who are foolish, but those who celebrate the Bacchanalia <note>Wild, drunken festivals for Bacchus</note> at the feet of Vesta <note>The Roman goddess of the hearth and symbol of purity</note>. 
<margin>Synesius <gloss>Protheology</gloss></margin>
Those who dishonor the gravity of physical matters and the chastity of things with playful trifles and, as it were, curling irons—truly, what Synesius <note>A 4th-century philosopher-bishop</note> said of a youth can aptly be said of a speech: "A long-haired speech is always a shameless one" <note>original: "comatam orationem semper cinedam." In the ancient world, long, styled hair on a man was often a sign of vanity or effeminacy</note>. Therefore, we prefer our speech to be shaggy-haired, rounded, and unrefined, rather than beautifully coiffed with even a mark or suspicion of impurity. 
And even if everything else were nothing, this is most true: nothing is more different from the purpose of a philosopher in any matter than that which tastes in any way of luxury or pride. 
<margin>Socrates</margin>
Socrates used to say that Sicyonian shoes <note>Expensive, elegant footwear from the Greek city of Sicyon</note> were comfortable and fit the foot well, but they did not suit Socrates at all. There is not the same rule for civic attire and philosophical attire, just as there is not for the table or for speech. The philosopher uses these only for necessity; the civic man uses them also for grace. If the latter neglects grace, he is not a man of the city; if the former affects it, he will not be a philosopher. 
<margin>Pythagoras</margin>
If Pythagoras could live without food, he would even spare the vegetables. If he could explain his thoughts by a look, or at least with less effort than speech, he would not speak at all. So far is he from polishing and adorning his tongue; a thing we must avoid, lest the reader, enticed by a medicated skin <note>A metaphor for makeup or cosmetic powders</note>, linger upon the surface and not penetrate to the marrow and blood—which we have often seen infected beneath a painted face. 
We have seen it, I say, in those "foods" which have come into use for this reason: since there is nothing inside that is not empty and vain, they detain the reader on the surface with various rhythms and harmony. 
<margin>Musonius</margin>
If a philosopher does this, Musonius <note>A Stoic philosopher known for his austere teachings</note> will cry out that it is not a philosopher speaking, but a flute-player singing. Therefore, let it not be held against us as a vice that we did not do what it would have been a vice to do. We ask *what* we are writing, not *how*. Or rather, we do ask "how": namely, without any pomp or floral ornament of speech. We do not want our speech to be delightful, charming, or witty, but useful, grave, and venerable; so that it attains majesty from austerity rather than grace from softness. We do not look for the applause of the theater, or for a smooth or rhythmic closing cadence to stroke the ears, or for one part to be deceptive and another elegant. 
<margin><gloss>for the <unclear>philosophers</unclear></gloss></margin>
But instead, we look for the silence of a few, in wonder, as they look deep into something either unearthed from the inner shrines of nature or brought down from the celestial court to men. Then perhaps something so sharp that there is no room for defense, or so defended that there is no room for argument. Let them admire us, moreover, as sagacious in inquiring, circumspect in exploring, subtle in contemplating, grave in judging, tight in binding arguments, and easy in unravelling them. 
Let them admire in us a brevity of style packed with many great things: beneath plain words, the most profound meanings, full of questions and full of solutions. How fit we are, how well-equipped, to remove ambiguities, to dissolve difficulties, to unroll what is tangled, and with soul-bending syllogisms <note>A form of logical argument where a conclusion is drawn from two premises</note> both to weaken what is false and confirm what is true. 
By these titles, O Ermolao, we have claimed our place until now, and we do not doubt we shall claim our memory from oblivion hereafter. If we are held by the common crowd, as you say, to be dirty, rude, and uncultivated, this is to our glory, not our shame. We did not write for the crowd, but for you and those like you. No differently than the ancients used their enigmas and the veils of fables to keep ignorant men away from the mysteries, we also have been accustomed to frighten them away from our feasts—which they could not help but pollute—by a somewhat rougher bark of words. Those who wish to hide treasures, if they cannot put them away in secret, are accustomed to cover them with trash or rubble, so that those passing by do not discover them—except for those whom they themselves have judged worthy of that gift. Such is the aim of philosophers: to hide their affairs from the people.

He invokes ancient figures like Socrates and Pythagoras to justify this austere, intellectual lifestyle.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Pico della Mirandola’s defense of the "barbarian" scholastic style. He argues that the internal truth of philosophy is far more valuable than external rhetorical polish, using classical metaphors to show that a rough exterior often hides a divine interior.</meta>

## SS ii

Since it is fitting that they should not only be disapproved of, but not even understood by such people, it cannot fail to be disgraceful for what they write to have anything theatrical, crowd-pleasing, or popular—anything that seems to accommodate itself to the judgment of the masses. But do you want me to sketch the ideal of our speech? It is the very same as the Sileni <note>Hollow statues that were ugly and misshapen on the outside but contained beautiful figures of gods within.</note> of our <margin>Alcibiades</margin> Alcibiades <note>A famous Athenian statesman who, in Plato’s *Symposium*, compared the philosopher Socrates to these statues.</note>. For their images had a shaggy, foul, and despicable appearance. But inside, they were full of gems and rare, precious furnishings. Thus, if you look from the outside, you might see a wild beast; but if you look inside, you would recognize a divinity. 

But you will say: "The ears <note>original: "aurae" (literally 'breezes'), here used poetically for the sense of hearing.</note> cannot bear it; now harsh, now gaping, always in an inconsistent texture. They cannot bear barbarian names, names that are almost terrifying in their sound." O delicate one! When you approach flute-players and lyre-players, leave your ears behind you. But when you approach philosophers, leave your vocal sounds behind and return to yourself, into the inner chambers of the soul and the recesses of the mind. Take up those ears of the <margin>Thianeus</margin> man of Tyana <note>Apollonius of Tyana, a legendary 1st-century mystic and philosopher.</note>, with which—since he was not entirely in the body—he did not hear the earthly Marsyas <note>A satyr who challenged the god Apollo to a musical contest and was brutally punished for his pride.</note>, but the celestial Apollo, tempering the melody of the universe in ineffable ways upon his divine lyre. 

If you taste the words of philosophers with *these* ears, they will seem honeyed to you, enough to make Nestor <note>The elder king in Homer’s *Iliad*, famed for speech that flowed "sweeter than honey."</note> envious. But let us leave aside these overly lofty things. Truly, to loathe an unpolished style in a philosopher who is disputing most subtly is the sign not so much of a delicate stomach as of an insolent one. It is no different than if someone, while Socrates was teaching about morals, were to be offended by a loose shoe or a sagging toga, or were to be annoyed by a poorly cut fingernail. <margin>Tullius</margin> Cicero <note>original: "Tullius," referring to Marcus Tullius Cicero.</note> does not demand eloquence in a philosopher, but only that he satisfy us with his subject matter and his doctrine. 

That man, as prudent as he was learned, knew that our task is to compose the mind rather than the diction; to take care that reason does not wander, not the speech. He knew it belongs to us to care for the <term>inner word</term> <note>original: "εν διαθεσει λογον" (en diathesei logon). In Stoic philosophy, this refers to the thought or reason within the mind before it is spoken.</note>, and not the <term>outer word</term> <note>original: "τον εν προφορα" (ton en prophora). The actual spoken or written language.</note>. It is praiseworthy in us to have the Muses in the soul and not on the lips, lest anything sound too harsh through anger or too weak through lust. Finally, let there be nothing discordant from that genuine harmony by which man is tunefully tempered. When <margin>Plato</margin> Plato understood that this harmony is often corrupted by theatricality and poets, he banished all poets from his Republic, leaving it to be governed by philosophers. Surely, those who imitate poets through a wantonness of speaking should be condemned to exile. 

But <margin>Lucretius</margin> Lucretius <note>A Roman poet and Epicurean philosopher.</note> will insist that, even if philosophical meditations do not lack charm by themselves, the austerity of the things themselves must be concealed by its use. Just as wormwood <note>A famously bitter herb used as medicine.</note> cures diseases on its own, yet is smeared with honey so that the unsuspecting age of childhood might be deceived. Perhaps you had to do this, Lucretius, if you were writing your works for children or the common crowd—you, who offered not just wormwood but the most unmixed poisons! But we must hold to a far different reasoning: we who, as I said before, seek not to attract the common crowd, but to frighten them away. We do not offer foul wormwood, but nectar. 

But <margin>Lactantius</margin> Lactantius <note>An early Christian author (c. 250–325 AD) known as the "Christian Cicero" for his polished Latin style.</note> will contend that it is well enough established that truth flows more powerfully into the minds of listeners, even elders, when it is both equipped with its own strength and adorned with the light of speech. If you had been as frequent in sacred letters, Firmianus <note>Lactantius’s middle name.</note>, as you were in fictional lawsuits, you would not have said this; perhaps you would have confirmed our views no less well than you destroyed those of others. Tell me, I ask you: what moves and persuades more strongly than the reading of the Sacred Scriptures? Do they not move? Do they not persuade? <margin>the effectiveness of speech</margin> No, they compel, they agitate, they apply force! You read words that are rude and rustic, but they are alive, they are animated, they are flaming and stinging, penetrating to the very depth of the spirit, transforming the whole man with a marvelous power. <margin>Pericles</margin> <margin>Alcibiades</margin> Alcibiades says he was not moved at all by the elaborate and brilliant speeches of Pericles...

<summary>Pico argues that philosophy should prioritize internal reason over external beauty, using the metaphor of the Sileni statues to describe how a "barbaric" style can hide divine truth. He contrasts the honeyed deceptions of poets and rhetoricians like Lucretius and Lactantius with the raw, transformative power of the Sacred Scriptures.</summary>
