<meta>This page continues Pico della Mirandola’s defense of the "barbarian" scholastic style against humanist criticisms. Having previously compared philosophy to the Sileni—ugly on the outside but divine within—he now invokes Socrates and Heraclitus to argue that truth requires no rhetorical ornament and that the "barbarian" technical language of the schools is a valid form of communication.</meta>

<margin>Socrates.</margin>
<margin>Three things most persuade</margin>
But by the naked and simple words of Socrates—he adds, even if they are inept <note>clumsy or unpolished</note>—one is swept into a frenzy, placed outside oneself, and whether one wills it or not, one must do what he has commanded. But why do I waste words on a settled matter? If the listener is not a fool, what else does he expect from painted speech <note>original: "fucato sermone", referring to speech that is artificially colored or deceptive, like makeup.</note> but a trap? There are three things that most persuade: the life of the speaker, the truth of the matter, and the sobriety of the speech. These are the things that will win credit for a philosopher: if he is good, if he is a speaker of truth, and if he seeks that kind of speaking which has flowed not from the pleasant groves of the Muses, but from the fearsome cave in
<margin>Heraclitus</margin>
which Heraclitus <note>A pre-Socratic philosopher known for his cryptic style; he famously remarked that "Nature loves to hide."</note> said truth lies hidden. But someone will say: "Come now, friend, let us examine these things with our rivalry set aside. Wisdom is something reverent and divine in itself, and it does not need exotic finery. But what harm is there if this [finery] is added? Who denies that things which are becoming in themselves become even more becoming if they are adorned?" My friend, I deny this in most cases. There are so many things whose splendor you would dim rather than illustrate if you added anything to them; they are, of course, in such an optimal state in their own nature that they cannot be changed from it except for the worse. A marble house does not receive painting. If you were to apply a plaster coating <note>original: "opus albarium", a fine white plaster or stucco.</note> over it, you would take away from its dignity and beauty. It is no different with wisdom; those things which are handled by philosophers do not become clearer through a <term>tectorio</term> <note>a decorative plaster or finish</note>, but are obscured. Why say more? Is it not common knowledge that beautiful forms are disfigured by white lead <note>original: "cerussa", a lead-based white pigment used as a cosmetic.</note>? In general, whatever beauty you place on top hides what it found; what it brings with it, it displays. Therefore, if what was there before is better than what is added, it has suffered a loss, not a gain. For this reason, philosophy offers itself naked; visible from every side, she longs to come entirely before the eyes and under judgment. She knows she has the means to be pleasing from every side. As much as you might wish to add to her, just as much do you take away from her form and diminish her praise; she wants to be held as sincere and unmixed. Whatever you mix in, you have thinned; you have adulterated her and made her something else. She stands at an indivisible and point-like center. Therefore, one must not play with tropes or words, nor luxuriate too much, nor be wanton with metaphors, nor be daring with invented words in a matter so serious and of such great importance, in which to take away, add, or change anything would be a disgrace. 

"But," you will say, "come, we grant you this: that it is not your business to speak ornately. But it is certainly your business—though you do not perform it—to at least speak in Latin; so that even if you do not explain matters with flowery words, you explain them in their own proper terms. I do not demand from you a polished speech, but I do not want one that is filthy; I do not want one that is perfumed, but neither do I want one that smells like a goat <note>original: "hircosam", suggesting something rank, neglected, or uncouth.</note>. Let it not be choice, but let it not be neglected. We do not ask that it delight, but we complain that it offends." 

Very well, now you are finally coming over to us. But I ask you, let us find out what this "Latinity" is, which you say alone the philosophers ought to provide and yet fail to pay. If, for the sake of example, someone says in a speech that "man is produced by the sun," our people <note>the scholastic philosophers</note> will say that man is "caused" <note>original: "causari", a technical scholastic term for being produced by a cause.</note>. 
<margin><unclear>argument for the philosophers</unclear></margin>
You will immediately shout: "This is not Latin!" Thus far, you speak truly: it is not spoken in the Roman fashion. But this is even truer: therefore, the argument does not fail. An Arab will say the same thing; an Egyptian will say it; they will not speak in Latin,
<margin>+</margin>
but they will speak correctly nonetheless. For either the names of things consist of arbitrary choice, or of nature. If they are placed by chance—that is, by a community of men coming together in the same opinion, through which they have decreed that each thing be called by a name—then it is called correctly among them. What prevents these philosophers, whom you call "barbarians," from having conspired into one norm of speaking, which is held as sacred among them just as the Roman norm is held among you? Why do you not seek that norm as the "correct" one? You seek your own; there is no reason for this if this imposition of names is entirely arbitrary. But if you do not wish to deign to call it by the name "Roman," call it "Gallic" or "British"...

<summary>Pico argues that philosophy's power lies in its naked truth rather than rhetorical polish, using analogies of marble and makeup to show that ornament obscures wisdom. He further defends the "barbarian" technical language of scholasticism, arguing that if language is based on convention, the philosophers' specialized vocabulary is just as valid as classical Latin.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Pico della Mirandola’s letter to the humanist Hermolao Barbaro. Pico is defending the "barbarian" scholastic philosophers (like Duns Scotus and Thomas Aquinas) against the charge that their Latin is crude and unpolished. He argues that the content of their thought—wisdom—is far more important than the "tongue" or rhetorical style they use.</meta>

...Spanish: or what the common people are accustomed to call Parisian. When they speak to you, it will happen that much will be laughed at and much will not be understood; the same will happen to you when you speak to them. 
<term>Anacharsis commits a soloecism among the Athenians, and the Athenians do so among the Scythians</term> <note>original Greek: "ανάχαρσις παραθηναιοις σολοικίζει. αθηναιοι δε παρα σκύθαις." Anacharsis was a Scythian philosopher famous for his "barbaric" but wise speech. A "soloecism" is a grammatical error or a clash of cultures.</note>. If the correctness of names depends on the nature of things, should we not consult the philosophers—who alone have looked into and explored the nature of all things—rather than the rhetoricians? Perhaps the things the ears reject as somewhat harsh, reason accepts as being more closely related to the reality of the things themselves.

But why was it necessary for those men to innovate language, and if they were born among Latins, why did they not speak in a Latin manner? Could they not, O Hermolaus, while they were reading the laws of the fates and the order of the universe in the heavens—while they were reading the cycles of birth and death in the elements, the powers of simple substances and the temperaments of mixtures? Could they not, I say, at the same time note the properties, laws, and observations of the Roman language in Cicero, Pliny, or Apuleius? They were seeking what was discordant and what was accepted in nature; meanwhile, they did not care for the truth of words. 

Indeed, I now place you in a better position: I grant you that eloquence and wisdom have conspired in a mutual bond. But the philosophers separated wisdom from eloquence; so did the <margin>Philostratus</margin> historians, the rhetoricians, and the poets—a separation of eloquence from wisdom which Philostratus <note>A Greek scholar who wrote about the lives of the Sophists.</note> deplored. You do not doubt that these latter men will live on with celebrated fame, while the former live only in punishment and insult. See what you are doing: <margin>Cicero</margin> Cicero prefers unadorned wisdom to foolish loquacity. In money, we do not ask what mint struck it, but what material it is made of. Nor is there anyone who would not prefer to have pure gold under a German stamp than counterfeit gold under a Roman symbol. 

He sins who creates a rift between the heart and the tongue; but those who are entirely tongue and no heart—are they not, as <margin>Cato</margin> Cato says, mere "mortuary glossaries"? <note>A "mortuary glossary" refers to something that has the words of a language but no life or soul behind them.</note> We can live without a tongue, though perhaps not conveniently; but without a heart, we cannot live at all. He is not human who exists only in the sun of polished literature; he is not a man who is devoid of philosophy. Wisdom, even if inarticulate, can be of benefit; but foolish eloquence is like a sword in the hand of a madman—it can do nothing but the greatest harm. 

Therefore, you will say, statues are commended not for their shape but for their material. And if <margin>Choerilus</margin> <margin>Homer</margin> <margin>Maevius</margin> <margin>Virgil</margin> Choerilus <note>A notoriously bad poet.</note> had sung the same things as Homer, or if Maevius had sung the same as Virgil, would it have happened that the former would be received among the poets as equal to the latter? Do you not see the disparity of the comparison? We too have become accustomed to judging a thing by its appearance, not just its substance. For a thing is what it is because of its form. But one form is required to be received among philosophers, and another among poets. 

<margin>Lucretius</margin> Let Lucretius write about nature, about God, and about providence; and let one of our men write about the same things. <margin>Duns Scotus</margin> Let John Duns Scotus <note>A major medieval scholastic philosopher known for his complex, technical language.</note> write, and let him even do so in verse so that he might be even more "unfit." Lucretius will say that the principles of things are atoms and the void; that God is corporeal; that he is ignorant of our affairs and that everything is carried along by the random collision of little bodies. But he will say these things in Latin and with elegance. John will say that things consist of nature, constituted by their own matter and form; that God is a separate mind, knowing all things and providing for all. Nor, because he sees and governs all things—even the lowest—is his peace disturbed in the least. Rather, as the saying goes, <term>descending, I am not brought down</term> <note>original Greek: "κατιοντα μη κατιεμαι." A Neoplatonic concept: God can involve himself in the lower world without losing his higher perfection.</note>. But he will say it inexpressively, rudely, and not in Latin words. 

I ask: who would doubt which is the better poet and which is the better philosopher? It is beyond all controversy that Scotus philosophizes more correctly than Lucretius speaks ornamentally. But see how they differ: the one has a tasteless mouth, the other a senseless mind. The one is ignorant of the decrees of grammarians (not to say poets), while the other is ignorant of the decrees of God and nature. The one, though most inarticulate in speaking, perceives things that deserve to be praised...

<summary>Pico argues that the "barbarian" technical language of scholastic philosophers like Duns Scotus is superior to elegant but false classical poetry because it prioritizes the "heart" (intellectual truth) over the "tongue" (rhetorical style).</summary>
<keywords>Scholasticism vs Humanism, eloquence vs wisdom, Duns Scotus, Lucretius, Anacharsis, soloecism, philosophy, nature of language</keywords>

...cannot be sufficiently censured; that most eloquent man, in speaking, says unspeakable things. Perhaps those men would assert these things, my dearest Hermolaus, in defense of their own barbarism, or perhaps because of their own subtlety they have much better arguments. I do not entirely agree with their opinions, nor do I think any noble or free-spirited person should. However, I have willingly exercised myself in this matter as if it were a disreputable subject—like those who praise <term>quartan fever</term> <note>A form of malaria; Pico is referring to the rhetorical tradition of "paradoxical encomiums," where authors would write mock-praises of bad things to show off their skill</note>—both to test my own talent and with this specific intention: just as that character in Plato's works praises justice not out of personal judgment, but to stimulate Socrates to give his own praise of justice, so too I might hear the cause of eloquence pleaded by you. I have attacked it a little more license than my own feelings and nature allow, as if I thought it should be neglected or held second to the barbarians. Had I truly felt that way, I would not have nearly deserted them for the sake of eloquence, as I did recently by turning to Greek literature and your never-sufficiently-praised <term>Themistius</term> <note>Hermolao Barbaro had recently published a translation of the Greek commentator Themistius</note>; though I will speak freely what I feel.

<margin>

Elegant
Beautifully placed
</margin>

Certain <term>grammarians</term> <note>Latin: "grammatistæ"; Pico uses this diminutively to mean pedantic teachers of grammar who lack philosophical depth</note> move my stomach; when they have grasped two origins of words, they show themselves off so much, sell themselves so much, and carry themselves around so boastfully that they think philosophers should be considered as nothing compared to themselves. "We do not want these philosophies of yours," they say. And what wonder? Dogs do not want <term>Falernian wine</term> <note>A famous high-quality wine from ancient Rome; Pico implies the grammarians lack the refined "palate" for deep philosophy</note>. But let us close the letter at this point. If those "barbarians" earned any honor or name for themselves through the knowledge of things alone, it is not easy to say what place or what praises you should claim for yourself, you who are the most eloquent among philosophers and—to speak in Greek—the <term>most philosophical</term> <note>original Greek: φιλοσοφωτατοσ (philosophōtatos)</note> among the eloquent. 

->Florence, June 3, 1485.<-

Greetings, most beloved father. Regarding <term>Apollonius of Tyana</term> <note>A 1st-century Neopythagorean philosopher and reputed miracle-worker</note>, I feel nothing other than what you feel, concerning which matter I shall write more to you when there is leisure and things that will perhaps not be unpleasing to you. Regarding the difference in our translation from the Hebrew text in the third chapter of the <term>Book of Genesis</term> where it deals with Eve and the serpent, this is indeed what I think: it is in the Hebrew just as you write, "He shall crush your head," and it refers to the "seed" of Eve, about which it had been said, "I will put enmities between your seed and her seed." However, the <term>Seventy</term> <note>The Septuagint, the ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament</note> and Jerome translated it as "She shall crush your head." But in both cases, the meaning is the same. For when it is said "He shall crush," it regards not so much the person of Eve herself as it does Eve’s posterity. For a person is said to do what they do through their seed. But as for why they preferred to translate "she" rather than "he," I think the reason was to signify that since not only females but also males were to be propagated from Eve, what was said about the seed should be referred back to the feminine source alone. These are the things that come to mind at present on this matter. 

I am working tirelessly on the *Harmony of Plato and Aristotle*. I give it its due time every morning; after the midday hours, I give time to my friends, my health, and occasionally to poets and orators; if there are any lighter studies, the night shares itself with sleep and <term>Sacred Scripture</term>. Please see to it that I do not have to go without your letters for much longer. Greet Beroaldo. Your Poliziano is yours entirely. Farewell, and pray to God for me. 

->Florence, March 20, 1490.<-

## Giovanni Pico of Mirandola to Aldus Manutius, Greetings.

<margin>G.</margin>
<margin>6.</margin>
<margin>m</margin>
I am sending the Homer which you desired, though later than you wished and later than I ought to have sent it. I am so distracted by my obligations, my dear Aldus, that there is no space even to catch my breath. As you already know, I have long since surrendered myself into the service of literature. These studies, like a harsh master, demand such a severe portion of reading and dictating that I can scarcely preserve my own health. As for what you write regarding your own future: prepare yourself for philosophy. But do so under this law: remember that there is no philosophy which calls us away from the truth of the mysteries. Philosophy seeks the truth, theology finds it, but religion possesses it. <note>original: "philosophia ueritatem querit. Theologia inuenit religio possidet" — This is one of Pico's most famous aphorisms, illustrating his view of the hierarchy of knowledge leading toward God.</note> Farewell. From Florence, the eleventh day of February, in the year of grace 1490.

## Giovanni Pico of Mirandola to Hermolao Barbaro, Patriarch of Aquileia, Greetings.

<margin>a</margin>
I hear that you have been elected Patriarch of Aquileia. I congratulate those people on receiving the best of pastors, and the whole Church on gaining a most energetic soldier. To you, I congratulate the opportunity given to illustrate and amplify your virtue. There are generally three ways of living: the civil, the contemplative, and the religious. In the first, we require prudence; in the second, learning; and in the third—the very summit of life—we require holiness in addition to those other two. Your own city has already experienced you as most diligent and prudent in managing the state and handling great affairs. Furthermore, all students of letters love and admire you as the patron and protector of the <term>liberal arts</term> <note>Latin: "bonarum artium"; literally "the good arts," referring to the humanities like grammar, rhetoric, and philosophy</note>. That you will fulfill this remaining role <note>The religious/pastoral role</note> is something we know beyond a doubt, and we rejoice so sincerely that the Church will surely owe no less to you in the future than your city and literature have owed to you thus far.
<margin>+</margin>

## Giovanni Pico of Mirandola to his dear Hermolao, Greetings.

<margin>q</margin>
What should I say this is, my dear Hermolao, that you burden me daily with new kindnesses, as if you owed me something—I, who have long since owed everything to you? A few days ago, my brother Antonio arrived here while returning to our homeland. I asked him, "What is Hermolao doing?" He replied, "This is what he does: he loves you, he praises you, he carries you to the heavens—in my presence, in the presence of others, and before the <term>Pope</term> <note>Innocent VIII</note> himself. And he does this so constantly and so strongly that it is as if he has nothing else to do." Likewise, the friends I have in your location sometimes write to me, especially one, <term>Cosimo de' Pazzi</term> <note>Cosmus Pactius; a high-ranking Florentine clergyman and humanist scholar</note>—a man worthy of your unique affection, to summarize his merits at once. Whenever he writes, he writes of your kindnesses toward me, of your love, and of a certain wonderful inclination of mind, so that I perceive you always speak of me in the most honorable terms. Oh, this unheard-of humanity of yours! You never think you have done enough for a man of words. And if you are such toward me so that you might make me more your own and bind me to you more closely, then you are "acting on what is already done," as the saying goes. I am not able to owe more, nor can I love you more. But such a man you are; you surpass all others in prudence...

### Giovanni Pico of Mirandola to Girolamo, Greetings.

<margin>9</margin>
**U**nless our Angel <note>referring to his close friend, the poet and scholar Angelo Poliziano</note> were writing to you, I would have written more at length; but I do not want my "magpies" <note>original: "picas meas" — Pico is making a pun on his own name, *Picus*, which means "magpie" in Latin. He is humorously suggesting his own prose is mere chatter compared to Poliziano's "Muses."</note> to drown out his Muses, nor do I wish to be an intruder and disturb your pleasure. If he has done a favor by refraining from the injury he could have inflicted <note>This is a playful, rhetorical way of saying Poliziano's excellence might make Pico's own writing look bad by comparison.</note>, you cannot help but credit me for this brevity of letters as a favor—for which you will be most beautifully rewarded if you return very long letters to me in exchange for these very short ones. For nothing is more pleasing to us than your letters; please do not defraud me of them. Otherwise, if you remain silent, I shall return like for like. For I shall then most certainly not be silent, and in that way, I shall retaliate against you quite handsomely. Farewell, and give many greetings in my name to our friend Hermolao, the "delight of the Roman tongue." <note>original: "delitias Romanae linguae" — A reference to Hermolao Barbaro, a Venetian humanist famous for his elegant Latin style.</note>

### Giovanni Pico of Mirandola to his nephew Gianfrancesco Pico, Greetings.

<margin>10.</margin>
**T**hat I have not responded to your letters until now was because certain Hebrew books fell into my hands, upon which I have now been intent for a continuous week, day and night, so much so that they have nearly made me blind. For the one who brought these books here, a certain Sicilian Hebrew <note>This refers to Flavius Mithridates, a Jewish convert and scholar who served as Pico’s primary tutor in Hebrew and Aramaic, and who translated many Kabbalistic manuscripts for him.</note>, is to depart from here in about twenty days. Therefore, until I have extricated myself from them, do not expect even a single letter from me; for I cannot depart from them for a moment, lest they perhaps leave before I have thoroughly examined them all. When I am free from this care, I will overwhelm you with letters, even though you know I have a very occupied mind. If you are ever going to do anything for my sake, see to it by whatever means you can that the Prince of Bari <note>Ludovico Sforza, known as "Il Moro," who held the title of Duke of Bari at this time and later became Duke of Milan.</note> does not require my presence there; for it would disturb all my studies, to which you know how devoted I am and how I care for nothing besides them. It is not quite clear to me whether it would be more troublesome to displease him or myself. Farewell; fear God, and think daily that you are going to die. Ferrara, May 30, 1492.

---

### Giovanni Pico of Mirandola to Marsilio Ficino, Greetings.

<margin>11.</margin>
**T**hose who strive for what they desire from friends with too many words do an injustice to friendship, as if friendship itself were not able to do what the allure of a speech can. Therefore, I shall deal with you simply, as that benevolence which has long existed between us requires. At this time, Iamblichus the Platonist <note>Iamblichus was a Neoplatonist philosopher whose works on theurgy and Egyptian mysteries were central to the interests of the Platonic Academy in Florence.</note> is very necessary for my studies. If you send him to me, you will have bound me to you in perpetual obligation. He will be here for twenty days or a month at most, and then will be sent back immediately by courier. In the meantime, use both my library and all my things as your own. Farewell.

<meta>This page continues the personal correspondence of Giovanni Pico della Mirandola. The tone remains intimate and witty, focusing on Poliziano’s recent work—specifically his Latin translation of the Stoic philosopher Epictetus—and the "philosophical conversion" it has sparked in Pico’s household.</meta>

## Giovanni Pico of Mirandola to Angelo Poliziano, Greetings.

<margin>12</margin>
<margin>n</margin>
My "Loves" <note>original: "amores mei" — Pico is likely personifying his recent writings or poetic works which he had sent to Poliziano for review.</note> declare that they have never been received more elegantly or more cheerfully than they were at your house in these recent days; and having been quite amiably "stabbed" <note>This refers to Poliziano’s editorial corrections, which Pico describes as wounds from a friendly sword.</note>, they congratulate themselves and owe you a great deal. For who would not wish to die by that sword of yours? They grieve, however, that it was done more indulgently than was necessary, and they are at the point of wondering whether your love for me made you blind toward my "Loves." Indeed, they doubt to such an extent that they do not quite trust your judgment in their case, which is otherwise most serious. Let them trust it, however, and let them now claim themselves from their chains; they do not know how to stay at home, and they securely demand their freedom and public appearance.

But what shall I say of the liveliness of your Epictetus? <note>Angelo Poliziano translated the *Enchiridion* (Manual) of the Stoic philosopher Epictetus from Greek into Latin in 1479, dedicating it to Lorenzo de' Medici.</note> O, what a humorous thing, worthy of a laugh from Cato himself! <note>Cato the Younger was a Roman statesman famous for his rigid, humorless Stoicism; Pico suggests the situation is so funny even Cato would laugh.</note> He was scarcely at the threshold when, opening his robe, he said, "Behold the obeloi <note>original: "obelos" — critical marks used by ancient editors to indicate suspicious or incorrect passages in a text.</note>, behold the arrows (if you do not know Greek). Behold me, prepared to strike back if any of you should be so bold!" Who could have restrained their laughter when a Stoic man was joking so charmingly? We certainly abstained from our weapons, both because he was threatening to return any injury, and because his skin had grown so thick <note>A reference to the Stoic ideal of being "thick-skinned" or indifferent to external hardship.</note> that it would not admit such light blows.

Therefore, with the veneration we owed him, we received the old man. When he finally sat down with us, he began to philosophize about morals; and he did so in Latin, not so much because he was among Latins (for there were some in that assembly who knew Greek), but because he himself tasted more brilliantly in Latin through your benefit. Nor did he lose his effort, since he did not stop speaking until he made us into Stoics instead of Peripatetics <term>Peripatetics: Followers of Aristotle, who generally allowed for more emotional expression and physical comforts than the Stoics.</term>. And we all approved of that "apathy" <term>Apathy: From the Greek 'apatheia,' meaning a state of mind where one is not disturbed by passions or emotions; the ultimate goal of Stoic practice.</term>, so that now one may see men who were a little while ago quite delicate now made the most tolerant of all. We can indeed be provoked by others, but harmed only by ourselves; we who never struggle against fate, and who wish for things that are not ours to happen only as God wills. Let us never blame nor accuse those things; let us grieve for nothing, demand nothing, and not know how to be enslaved or conquered.

Let us philosophize in deed, not just in speech; and we who are novices, let us observe ourselves as if we were adversaries. Let us neglect the opinions of others about us and other external things of that kind rather than rejecting them. Let us care for our daily life like travelers in an inn; finally, let us possess those things, but not be possessed by them. Let us love silence, lest anything be vomited up that is not yet digested. Let us rarely provide laughter for others, and never for ourselves. And to embrace the whole of Epictetus in a single word: we have abundantly learned both to endure hardships and to abstain from pleasures.

See how, point by point, we have modeled our life after your Epictetus. See how quickly we have done so, lest in this part too we should not be Stoics—who wish us to be reminded that a man fails as long as he does not make progress. Though I have admired this in others, I admire it most of all in myself. Although I have always spent my time in the Lyceum or the Academy <note>The Lyceum was Aristotle's school; the Academy was Plato's. Pico is saying he was traditionally a follower of their philosophies.</note> and never in the Portico <note>The "Stoa" or Portico was the school of the Stoics.</note>, I was so conquered by the old man's speech that I moved over to his opinion not just with my feet, but with my hands and my whole body.

I am sending to you the catalog of Greek books that are staying with me here, along with Manuel's <note>Likely referring to Manuel Chrysoloras, a pioneer in introducing Greek literature to the Latin West.</note> letter, as your letter requests. I likewise desire the catalog of your own books. Give greetings in my name to the younger Lorenzo <note>Likely Lorenzo di Pierfrancesco de' Medici, a cousin of Lorenzo the Magnificent.</note>, to whom I was going to write, but shame deterred me, lest I seem to compel the man with letters. Farewell.

<meta>This page transitions from Pico's correspondence with the scholar Angelo Poliziano to a letter addressed to Thomas of Milan (Thomas Mediolanensis). While the previous letter discussed serious philosophical works and Stoicism, this letter takes a lighter tone, praising a "fabella" (a little story or fable) that Thomas has dedicated to Pico. It reflects the Humanist interest in "facetiae"—witty, brief stories—and the intellectual challenge of writing elegantly about "humble" subjects.</meta>

### Giovanni Pico of Mirandola to Thomas of Milan, Greetings.

<margin>13</margin>
<margin>q</margin>
**T**hat you have dedicated your little story—and a festive and elegant one at that—to my name was a sign to me both of your learning and your singular goodwill toward me. Each is a weighty reason that urges and impels me to love you. I do not know which moves me more: for just as in love (as the proverb says) it is a crime not to have returned love in kind, so too is it the mark of a boorish or truly wicked character not to have loved a most praiseworthy man, even if you are not provoked to do so. See, therefore, how you do not merely call me to friendship, but drag me with "twin ropes" <note>original: "geminis funibus" — a classical idiom meaning to be pulled by two strong forces at once.</note> as they say; for there is nothing in that little story that does not smell of learning and wit. Nor could you have better earned my favor than by so amiably and generously deciding to dedicate such an excellent tale to my name. So far am I from neglecting or criticizing its subject matter <note>original: "argumentum" — the plot or theme of the story.</note> that I even approve of it with all my might.

For it has always been my opinion—which I think no learned person will dispute—that it requires a sharper wit to write these jests and little stories (provided it is done with erudition and elegance, as you have most abundantly achieved) than to have discoursed ornately on the gravest matters. Indeed, since we judge a statue to be far more beautiful because of the "file" <note>original: "ex lima" — a metaphor for the painstaking process of editing and polishing a literary work.</note> than because of the bronze or gold from which it is made, why should it not be the same when someone says something remarkable about a humble subject as opposed to a sublime one? It is certainly a matter of more work, and therefore even more praiseworthy. For the dignity of the subject matter "flatters" the work of the former; but whatever these latter writers bring forth that is worthy, it is all drawn from the author’s own "storehouse" <note>original: "penu" — meaning the author's internal resources or mental pantry.</note>. Nature diligently assists the former; the latter certainly struggle against nature.

Even if this is so, I will not deny that among these "humbler" subjects I have mentioned, some are wonderfully superior to others. There are some of that genre so flat and so tasteless that they cannot be sufficiently raised up or skillfully seasoned by any force or majesty of words. This fault can never reside in those stories which are stuffed with the charming wit of jests. Truly, I believe those stories should be placed on the highest benches which have a graphic description of ages and characters mixed with the charm of "salt" <note>original: "salium" — a common Latin metaphor for wit or sharp humor.</note>. Your story has all those qualities found in the comic poets, which you have most beautifully imitated in the tale you sent to me. What cleverness is there! What a timely and witty mixture of "salts"! How it delights, how charming it is, how perfect in every way! And if anything appeared a bit "dirty" <note>original: "sordidiuscula" — meaning low-brow or trivial.</note> or weak due to the humility of the subject matter, it raises itself up by the light and dignity of the speech, assuming a brilliance and strength. It is a work (to put it briefly) that clearly demonstrates it was perfected by a most literate man.

But among all other things, that exquisite and fitting observation of manners, ages, and characters is especially close to my heart; in this, I perceive your wisdom from afar, as if from a watchtower—and no mediocre wisdom at that. I wish you could see what a laugh that eighty-year-old <term>prelate</term> <note>original: "antistes" — a high-ranking cleric or bishop. Pico is laughing at the character's greed.</note> provoked in me! No matter how other things turn out, he "rolls this stone" <note>A reference to Sisyphus, suggesting the old man's endless, repetitive efforts.</note> so continuously that he might scrape together money from somewhere—a vice that has always been kin and familiar to the elderly. What shall I say of our <term>parasite</term> <note>In the tradition of Roman comedy, a "parasite" is a stock character who lives off the hospitality of others through flattery and wit.</note>, who, by feigning a family dinner, extorts a meal from a most stingy old man? He "squeezes the pumice stone" <note>original: "pumicem emungit" — a proverb meaning to get blood (or money) out of a stone, or to trick someone who is notoriously stingy.</note>, so to speak, in a most singular way. There is not a word, my dear Thomas, in that little story that does not claim for itself some peculiar prize. But it is not my place to recount everything I have "scented out," nor do I have the kind of nose that smells everything. Let this be certain to you: a more pleasing or more delightful thing has never happened to me. Therefore, I have received the story into this home, and you yourself into my soul. You have, my Thomas, what you—even if you...

Pico argues that writing light, comedic works elegantly is actually more difficult than writing on serious topics because the author cannot rely on the inherent dignity of the subject.</summary>

<meta>This page completes a letter to Thomas of Milan regarding a "festive and elegant" story he dedicated to Pico. ...you should have asked me; friendship between us is mutual, which you yourself (as became a most excellent man) have initiated with favorable omens. It remains that whenever you need my affairs, small as they are, or my labor, you should put my goodwill toward you to the test. Nor shall I (if any opportunity is given) omit any kind of service toward you, since you were the first to do so in the vestibule of our friendship. Farewell.

### Giovanni Pico of Mirandola, Count of Concordia, to his friend Niccolò Leoniceno, Greetings.

<margin>14 i</margin>
I would have already written to you many times, my sweetest Niccolò <note>Niccolò Leoniceno (1428–1524) was a famous Italian physician and humanist scholar known for correcting errors in ancient medical texts.</note>, if your location had been known to me by messenger, by letter, or by rumor. Indeed, I anxiously inquired about this from many, and received uncertain answers from everyone. Finally, in recent days, a letter from Antonio of Faenza—a most serious philosopher—to Tommaso Frignano fell into my hands. From that, I learned you were in Florence, which was very pleasing to me. As soon as I understood this, I sent a letter to you in Florence by courier. The trip was in vain, for he did not find you there.

I grieved greatly; today Thomas indicated that you left Florence and are now in Bologna; I ordered these words to be delivered to you immediately. In these, I will not strive to disclose my goodwill or singular love for you at great length, for you should not doubt my will toward you even a little bit, unless you thought I had forgotten your extraordinary virtue and your services to me—which is not my way. 

I could not help but wonder greatly that, since you have rescued yourself from the city's turmoils to seek a place where you could live both peacefully and pleasantly, you have either forgotten this little town of ours or certainly overlooked it. You seemed, Niccolò, to distrust either my will or my resources; though the latter is less than your merits, the former is greater than you think. It will be pleasing to me if you inform me of your plan, and most pleasing of all if you do not disdain to share my home with me, to rest while others are busy with war <note>original: "cum marte negotiabuntur" — literally "negotiating with Mars," a classical way of referring to military conflict.</note>.

Finally, I am sending "John the Grammarian" <note>likely a manuscript by Joannes Philoponus, a 6th-century commentator on Aristotle highly prized by Renaissance scholars.</note> to you, which was not found for many days but has now been recovered. I am yours and I await you. Farewell, at Mirandola, on the 20th day of July, 1482.

If you love me, take every care to obtain a catalog of all the books found in the library of Saint Dominic <note>The library of the Basilica of San Domenico in Bologna was one of the most important intellectual centers of the era.</note>; send it or bring it with you. Farewell again.

I have built a suburban villa, pleasant enough for the condition of the place and region; I have composed a long poem about it; the house will be sweet to you, and the poem will not be unpleasant. Farewell again.

### Giovanni Pico of Mirandola to his friend Angelo Poliziano, Greetings.

<margin>15 q</margin>
**T**hat you praise me so much in your recent letters: I owe you as much as I am far from being worthily praised. For what is given for free is owed to someone, not what is paid as a debt. Therefore, I owe you everything you write about me, since there is nothing of the sort in me. Since you owed this to me in no way at all, it was entirely a result of your kindness and singular goodwill toward me. Furthermore, if you examine me, you will find nothing but what is thin, humble, and narrow. We are novices and raw recruits <note>original: "tirunculi" — a term for young soldiers or beginners in a discipline.</note>, who have only just moved our feet out of the darkness of ignorance, and have advanced almost nothing. It is kindly dealt with us if...

<meta>This page continues Pico’s correspondence with Angelo Poliziano, finishing a letter where Pico reflects on his own status as a scholar caught between disciplines. It then begins a new letter to Paolo Cortesi, a fellow humanist, discussing the philosophical and emotional value of letter-writing as a means of bridging distance.</meta>

...let me be counted among the ranks of students. The name of "learned man" implies something else entirely, something peculiar to you and those like you; such grand titles do not suit me. Regarding those things which are foremost in literary studies, I have not only nothing fully explored, but so far I have seen nothing except through a lattice <note>original: "pertransennam" — a proverbial expression meaning to see something only partially or through a screen, rather than clearly.</note>. I will indeed strive (as I am doing now) to one day become such as you now proclaim and judge me to be, or certainly as you wish me to be.

In the meantime, I will imitate you, Angelo, you who excuse yourself to the Greeks because you are Latin, and to the Latins because you speak Greek. I shall use a similar refuge, so that I may be approved by the poets and rhetoricians because I am said to **philosophize**, and by the philosophers because I have played the rhetorician and cultivated the Muses. Although, for me, it turns out quite differently than it does for you. For indeed, while I wish (as they say) to **sit on two chairs** <note>original: "geminis sellis sedere" — a Latin idiom similar to "sitting on two stools," implying an attempt to hold two positions at once.</note>, I am excluded from both, and the result is (to put it briefly) that I am neither poet, nor rhetorician, nor philosopher.

You, however, fulfill both roles so completely that it is not clear which you excel in more; you embrace both the Greek and our own Roman wisdom <note>original: "minervam"</note> so beautifully, like a **swan of both languages**, that it is not easy to discern which is learned and which is innate. For even if I stay silent about the Latin—for in this, to whom would you yield first place?—who would believe (as was said of the Emperor Hadrian) that a Roman man could speak Greek so well? Our friend Emanuel used to swear, while reading your works, that Athens itself was not so **Attic** <note>Attic refers to the dialect and pure style of ancient Athens; Pico is saying Poliziano’s Greek is more authentic than the Greeks themselves.</note>. You are the one, my Angelo (let all flattery be set aside), to whom only one or two of our men—not to say no one—can be compared. If there were more such men, these ages would have no reason to envy antiquity.

Apply yourself, I pray, and rescue literature from its decay as much as you can, lest that brilliance of the Roman tongue completely fade away through the injury of the times. Always forge something new that may assist and illuminate the Latin cause. And those works you have at home, let them finally come forth for the common benefit of studies. I indeed love and desire all your works just as I love you yourself—all the more because I have set you before me as a model into which I might be molded. Since all ought to follow such a man, yet few can actually catch up to him. Farewell.

### Giovanni Pico of Mirandola to his friend Paolo Cortesi, Greetings.

<margin>16 b</margin>
You think well, Paolo. Let us send letters frequently, so that we who are divided by the distance of places may certainly be joined by the exchange of letters. It usually lightens the longing for those who are absent if you happen to have a statue or perhaps an image of that person at home. To me, however, there seems to be this difference between an image and a letter: the latter portrays the **mind**, while the former portrays the **body**. The image sketches only the outward parts, but the letter clearly expresses and shapes even the innermost parts. The image represents, as it were, the tunic and clothing of a friend; the letter represents the true friend to us. The image emulates the colors and shape of the flesh as best it can; the letter expresses thoughts, counsels, sorrows, joys, cares, and finally all emotions. And those secrets of the soul which hardly anyone speaks to himself when present, he transmits most faithfully to an absent friend. In short, the letter is a living and effective likeness, while the statue is a dead and mute one.

Therefore, we shall send these images of our souls to one another—you indeed will send what you can in gold and silver, while I will send mine in bronze or clay <note>Pico uses these metals as a metaphor for the stylistic quality of their writing, self-deprecatingly calling his own work "clay."</note>. Thus we shall be beyond all injury of places and times, just as the power of the soul itself knows neither the distances of space nor the delays of time. But truly, how much do I owe you, most dutiful Paolo, for how you...

you invited me to this duty first with such a letter, especially, which so held and delighted me that I cannot remember being more charmed by any reading for many days now. For it is full of eloquence, full of graces, full of love and benevolence. You were perhaps expecting me to say "full of my own praises." Indeed, I was going to say this as well, for I am not so iron-hearted, or if you prefer the term, so much a **philosopher** that I am not delighted by the praises of friends. If these praises are true, they commend me to myself; if they are false, they commend the friend's love and goodwill toward me. Therefore, I shall easily obtain permission from my philosophy to read your letters frequently and with pleasure, even in the parts where they praise me. 

But it is not so easy for me to appear sufficiently civil, or at least not ungrateful, in repaying this duty of correspondence. For an **imperious mistress** <note>original: "imperiosa domina" — here Pico refers to Philosophy, personified as a demanding lady who takes all his time.</note> so distracts me, so demands her daily task <term>pensum</term> <note>original: "pensum" — originally a weight of wool weighed out for a weaver to complete in a day; used by scholars to mean a daily quota of study or writing.</note>, and finally so occupies my whole self that scarcely any part of me is left even for myself. But such is your kindness that you will take even the bad letters I write in good part, and you will think well of my silence when I am still. Poliziano, our shared delight, sends you his greetings.

->Farewell.<-

### Giovanni Pico della Mirandola to Troilo Malvezzi, Greetings.

<margin>17. l</margin>
<note>The first word "Ibellus" is likely intended to be "Libellus" (little book).</note>
Your **little book** <note>original: "Ibellus" [Libellus]</note> regarding the brave <note>original: "de fortibus"</note> affected me with as much pleasure as is usually felt by one to whom the best of luck has befallen. I give you immense thanks for making me a participant in your **nocturnal labors** <term>lucubrationum</term> <note>original: "lucubrationum" — writings produced by lamplight, implying deep study late into the night.</note>, especially such as these. In them, both the subtlety of your disputation and your multifaceted, varied knowledge are easily apparent. One of these deserves praise for your talent, the other for your diligence. I shall give my **trifles** <note>original: "nugas nostras" — a common humanist trope of self-deprecation, calling one's own works "trifles" or "toys."</note>, which you desire, to you very shortly. It is indeed uncertain whether it is more unworthy for you, a very busy legal expert, to be detained by the reading of them, or for a very dear friend to be held in suspense by longing for them. Farewell, and love me. Ferrara, 29 May 1492.

### Giovanni Pico della Mirandola to Taddeo Ugolino, Greetings.

<margin>18. g</margin>
<note>The first word "Ratissimas" is likely intended to be "Gratissimas" (most welcome).</note>
I found your letters **most welcome** <note>original: "Ratissimas" [Gratissimas]</note>, full of love, faith, and charity—not only because you remembered me, but because in them you remind me as a friend that I should remember myself: that is, of good studies and of sustaining the expectation that I have given. Indeed, conscious of my own weakness, I would not dare to promise anything even mediocre of myself. But He, from whom comes every good, the most merciful **Father of Lights**, as He has given until now the source from which men might hope for something from us, so He will give in the future, so that we may not hold such a well-conceived opinion in vain. I am hurrying to Rome, where we shall make a trial of our studies, even at some risk <note>original: "cum periculo" — likely a reference to the theological scrutiny Pico's 900 theses faced in Rome.</note>. If we make any progress, it is God's gift; to Him be the praise and thanks. If we fail in anything, it is our own feebleness; let it be imputed to us. For the rest, I am yours, as one who, on account of the integrity of your life and character, would scarcely yield the first place in loving you even to our **Jerome** <note>original: "Hieronymo nostro" — almost certainly referring to Girolamo Savonarola, the influential Dominican friar who was a close friend to both Pico and Taddeo Ugolino.</note>. Farewell, from Fratta.

## Giovanni Pico della Mirandola to Thomas Medius, greetings.

<margin>19</margin>
I do not remember ever being more soundly delighted than recently, while I was reading your *Epirota* <note>original: "epyrotam" — a Latin comedy written by Thomas Medius in 1483.</note>, a story undoubtedly most witty, both for the festivity of its subject matter and the erudition of its style, challenging even the ancient comedies. **For what shall I say of these modern ones: clearly inept and witless, which easily declare the childishness of their authors.** It was truly worthy to be dedicated by name to Ermolao Barbaro <note>A famous Venetian scholar and diplomat (1454–1493) known for his efforts to "purify" Latin and Greek texts.</note>—I know not whether he is more yours or mine. To him alone I believe all men of letters owe as much as they scarcely owe to antiquity itself. That you did not deprive me of it <note>the comedy</note> was done in accordance with your goodwill toward me, most evident before now. Nor is anything I have of such value that, if I sent it to you in return, I would think the favor fully repaid. I am already gaping in expectation of the new comedy you promised me. Nor is there anything I wish for more than that, except for your arrival here to visit us; which, if I did not have to depart from here within ten days (as I believe you have learned from our Sita <note>referring to a mutual friend or messenger.</note>), I would surely have obtained from you by entreaty. For one can guess from what you have written what pleasantness there will be in our intimacy, what in our living together, and what in those living voices which surely possess a hidden energy <term>energeia</term> <note>original: "energiā" — a Greek rhetorical term for "vividness" or "active force" that makes speech feel alive.</note> which delights the soul more deeply and affects it in wonderful ways, far outweighing all writings. But since this visit is not possible, do not meanwhile expect the subject matter for a comedy from me. I prefer that you bring forth both [plot and style] from your own storehouse, so that the story may taste of Thomas Medius—not mediocrely, but entirely <note>Pico is making a pun on the name "Medius," which means "middle" or "moderate" in Latin.</note>. For I fear that by complying with you, the dullness of my wit might cause a loss; and from whatever it might admit from me, the work would degenerate from its maker. In my own work, there is nothing that is not plain, tasteless, foolish, or common. But these comedies require I know not what secret things: something witty, biting, elegant, and sharp—peculiar to you and the delights of your wit. Therefore, hasten the matter, which will be most welcome to me, so that since I cannot enjoy your presence, I may enjoy you in this way while you are absent. If, as I said before, my departure had not been so swift, we surely would have cultivated both our spirits and our wits together for several days. Farewell.

---

## Giovanni Pico della Mirandola to Marsilio Ficino, greetings.

<margin>20</margin>
You could not have asked back for your Latin "Mahomet" <note>likely referring to a Latin translation of the Qur'an or a polemical work about Muhammad.</note> at a more opportune time than now, when I hope to hear Mahomet himself speaking in his native tongue shortly. For after I have kept watch day and night for an entire month over the Hebrew language, I have turned myself entirely to the study of Arabic and Chaldean <note>Usually referring to Aramaic, the language of the Talmud and Zohar, which Pico studied extensively.</note>, fearing not at all that I shall make less progress in them than I have in Hebrew, in which I can already—not yet with praise, but without fault—dictate a letter. See what the impulse of the soul can do. See what labor and diligence can achieve, even where strength is somewhat weak. Certain books in both languages have animated me, and indeed driven me with a different force to learn the letters of the Arabs and Chaldeans—books which surely came into my hands not by chance or accident, but by the counsel of God and the favor of a divine power toward my studies. Hear the titles and you will be bound by them <note>original: "uadimonium deferes" — a legal metaphor suggesting the reader will be stunned or held to a promise of interest.</note>. These books are Chaldean. If books...

they are not mere treasures; first among them are the oracles of Ezra, Zoroaster, and Melchiar the Magi, in which those things which are circulated among the Greeks as faulty and mutilated are read as whole and complete. Then there is that brief and rough <term>interpretation</term><note>likely referring to a commentary or paraphrase</note> of the Chaldean sages, but one full of mysteries. There is likewise a little book on the dogmas of Chaldean theology, as well as an abundant and divine explanation of the Greeks and Chaldeans. See, Marsilio, what unexpected goods have crept into my bosom! Why should I not think that I have now obtained a <term>Cornucopia</term><note>A "horn of plenty," symbolizing infinite abundance.</note>? But what of the Arabic works? Among these are many inquiries by Muhammad of Toledo <note>original: "maumet toletini"—likely referring to the translator Mark of Toledo or a specific Arabic philosophical text</note>, and by Abulgalem, who studied under Averroes—and, what will touch you more, by a certain Adelandus <note>possibly a reference to a lost or misidentified source Pico links to the Neoplatonic school</note>, who studied philosophy in Egypt under Ammonius, the master of Plotinus. 

Good God, how Pythagorean these are! How full of the dogmas of the ancients and of secret discipline! An effective vow immediately invaded my mind: to be able to unroll and scrutinize these things by myself, without an interpreter. And this is what I am doing now; I roll this stone <note>A reference to the labor of Sisyphus, suggesting a monumental and repetitive task</note> tirelessly and assiduously. This, my Marsilio, is my desire; these are my fires, which promise me—and indeed already provide—a pleasure that is not fleeting or vain, but firm. It is a true image of that future glory "which shall be revealed in us" <note>A quote from the Vulgate, Romans 8:18: "gloria quæ reuelabitur in nobis."</note>. But I return to your letter. Your Muhammad is at Peruna; when I return (for I am away because of the suspicion of the plague), he will go to you immediately. Regarding what you write about Plotinus, I do not quite understand; this I know: I have not forgotten Plotinus, whom I have always judged—and judge now—not only to be held in one's hands, but even to be learned by heart. If you have complained about me at all to either Mithridates <note>Flavius Mithridates, the Jewish convert who taught Pico Hebrew and Arabic.</note> or Pietro Leone <note>A famous physician and book collector.</note>, it cannot be that such a thing was done by you without injury to me, for I have never been injurious to you or your affairs in any part. Yet what that matter might be, I still do not know—willingly I do not know. I am a Pythagorean, among whom nothing is more sacred than friendship; if there is anything that can weaken or diminish it between us (as they say), "let it go to the west winds." <note>A poetic way of saying "let it be scattered and forgotten."</note> Farewell, and love me, who am yours just as much as I once was. From Fratta.

And if it is ever granted—which is the sum of my prayers—to philosophize with you for several days, we shall discuss these things more extensively in person and make some trial of this thought of mine. Farewell, you who are the glory of our age.

->Giovanni Pico della Mirandola to Brother Battista Mantovano, Carmelite, Greetings, etc.<-

<margin>33 [Section mark]</margin>
Greetings, best father. I have not written to you for some time, but meanwhile I have read what you have written—those divine and most holy poems of yours. In them, there is such majesty of content and such splendor of eloquence that words and thoughts seem to vie for the prize between themselves. Happy are you who wish for the best things and are able to achieve them; happy are we to whom it is given not only to read what you have written but also to love you, see you, and speak with you. Here is rich material for me, which would fill not just a letter but a proper volume, if my own weakness or your modesty allowed me to wander into praising your poems. I will say only this: I am so delighted by the reading of your songs that almost daily, when weariness or fatigue overtakes me, I am accustomed to retreat into them as if into a garden. From which such great pleasure always arises in my soul that it desires nothing more than to be fatigued again so that it may be refreshed again. I long for Philostratus's *On the Life of Apollonius* <note>A famous biography of the Neo-Pythagorean sage Apollonius of Tyana, which Pico was eager to study.</note>, if you are finished with it, and also the work of Zacharias the Philosopher; see that I may eventually have the copy you said you obtained in Rome. Furthermore, I ask for the index of your library in Bologna, if it can be done at your convenience. Farewell.

->Giovanni Pico della Mirandola to C. F., Greetings.<-

<margin>[Section mark]</margin>
For a long time, I have debated within myself whether I should deal with you through silence or through letters. This matter, having "handles" on both sides <note>A Greek idiom meaning there are arguments for and against a course of action.</note>, as I judged it first this way and then that, was the reason why I have remained silent with you until this time. For it seemed no less shameless than intrusive to interrupt the ears of a most busy man with these light trifles; and there was nothing at all worthy of you for me to write. On the other hand, if I did not venerate a man distinguished by such dignity as yours, who has deserved so well of me, through letters when I could not do so in person, I was undoubtedly failing in my duty. When my mind had wavered between these for a long time, devotion finally overcame shame and persuaded me that the mark of a bold and reckless man should be endured rather than that of a forgetful or negligent one. Receive me, therefore, [dear] C. P., with that [kindness] with which you always received me when [I was] there...

</margin>

You will wonder, and indeed not without cause, at my response to your letter coming much later than you perhaps desired and than your letter itself deserved. Hear briefly why this happened. At almost the same time I received yours, a truly honest man—though previously unknown to me—was about to travel to you; he said he was doing business in Milan. I thought this a favorable departure, whereby it might happen that through a faithful messenger, my letter would be delivered to you without delay, which was my primary wish. But I <term>struck the south wind</term><note>original: "austrum perculi"—a metaphorical expression for encountering a setback or bad luck, often used in classical Latin to describe a journey gone awry.</note>; for when he had postponed his departure from day to day for a month, he finally left, but with me entirely unaware. Truly, having become more negligent in the hope of a certain messenger, I had nearly forgotten the letter. Now at last, when your letter fell into my hands, it immediately roused me as if I were sleeping and reminded me of the time passed without fulfilling my duty. I grieved (God is my witness) no small amount, and even now I grieve; nor would I wish these things said to excuse myself, but rather to accuse myself. I will easily allow myself to be condemned for negligence, and if you prefer, let it be called a punishment from you.

Now to your letters. I received no small pleasure both from the letters themselves and from the Greek books of which you so generously and in such a friendly manner gave me the use. I value them not so much because their use contributes greatly to my studies, as because we have laid the foundations of a perpetual <term>friendship</term><note>original: "necessitudinis"—this term implies a close, binding relationship or kinship, often used by humanists to describe their intellectual circles.</note> between us. I value this one thing more than the entire library of either Sunandius <note>Likely a reference to a legendary or specific ancient library often mentioned in Renaissance lists alongside Ptolemy's.</note> or <term>Ptolemy</term><note>The Great Library of Alexandria, founded by the Ptolemaic dynasty in Egypt.</note>. For I am so far from neglecting the friendships of learned men that nothing is more a matter of concern or dearer to my heart. I know, moreover, what place you claim for yourself among learned men, since your letter was to me the most evident proof of your learning, erudition, and <term>humanity</term><note>original: "humanitas"—the quintessential Renaissance ideal of refined learning and civilized conduct.</note>. Therefore, if I did not love you greatly, I would truly have forgotten myself and would act far differently than is my custom. I love you, therefore, uniquely, although I have never seen you. I love you so from my soul that I love few others more; so much so that it could eventually lead to our familiarity, but it cannot increase my love. And if there is anything that can be added, it will all be added upon your arrival here, which you voluntarily promised in your letter and which we so ardently seek and impatiently desire. If you provide me with <term>John the Grammarian</term><note>John Philoponus (c. 490–570 AD), an influential Byzantine commentator whose works helped bridge the gap between ancient philosophy and the Middle Ages.</note> on the *Physics* and Aristotle’s *Metaphysics*, you will bind me to you in perpetual service. For I do not have them with me and I am in great expectation of them. **Farewell.**

# Giovanni Pico della Mirandola to Jacopo Feltrino, Greetings.

<margin>26</margin>
<margin>l</margin>
Your letters, if ever they did before, have now delighted me most especially; through them, I have come to know that you hold such an estimation of me that one could not even imagine a better one in a prayer. One thing alone troubled me: that since you noted nothing in those things which I wrote to you, you have raised a suspicion in me that you did not think everything was worthy of note. For I would then have believed that many things had pleased you, had you indicated that some things had displeased you. Thus it happens that I do not sufficiently trust your testimony in my own cause, however highly esteemed it may otherwise be. For you love all our things just as we do; and since, from the innate kindness of your character, you are accustomed to be so toward everyone, this happens to you especially in my affairs—you, from whose fountain flowed everything that is in me. Indeed, I neither cease nor shall I cease to emulate you and to persist in your footsteps. Would that I might catch up to you someday. But I grieve that the distance between our places prevents me from hearing you in person, as you are accustomed to do, treating the deepest matters of philosophy with such gravity. For even if the same things you say can be sent through your letters—which I would most greatly desire to obtain from you—the <term>living voice</term><note>original: "viva vox" — a classical concept suggesting that oral instruction from a teacher is more transformative than written text.</note> nevertheless possesses some unknown quality that more effectively moves and shapes the student. **Farewell.**

# Giovanni Pico della Mirandola to Girolamo Donato, Greetings.

<margin>27</margin>
<margin>a</margin>
I received your letters, which were truly sweet and learned; I was delighted by them no differently than I used to be by your company when I was in <term>Padua</term><note>original: "patauii" — Padua was a major center for Aristotelian philosophy and humanism where Pico studied.</note>, as often as the opportunity of enjoying it was offered to me—an opportunity of which I have always been both eager and most greedy, even beyond your own opinion. For it was not hidden from me how sweet and pleasant the genius of Donato was, overflowing on all sides and filled with all good disciplines and every virtue. But it is certainly so, my Girolamo: it often happens to me that the free and ready ability to obtain that which we most desire makes us sluggish and negligent; for while we hope that what we neglect today can be done quite conveniently tomorrow, it finally happens that from this supine procrastination of ours, a year flows away while we are blinking. But since the matter has turned out this way, you have done quite beautifully to wake me now with your letters, even as I was slumbering in this kind of duty. I shall use this duty toward you more often hereafter, and I would most greatly desire you to be asked to do the same. As for what pertains to your poems, they were indeed with me for several days while I was in Padua. I remember being greatly delighted by the charm of the little book and the most elegant composition of the verses. But unless I am mistaken, they were returned to <note>Girolamo Ramusio (1450–1486), a physician and humanist scholar associated with the Venetian intellectual circle.</note>Ramusio before I departed from there. Concerning other things that belong either to me or to my affairs, hold it as settled that you may use them as your own; otherwise, you would certainly be doing an injustice to both me and our friendship. **Farewell.**

## Giovanni Pico della Mirandola to Angelo, Greetings.

<margin>z 8 c</margin>
Since I have organized my slender muses—with which I played regarding my loves as much as my age allowed—into five small books, I am sending you the first of them. I will send the rest if, in this one, I find you to be a friend and not a flatterer. For they come to you under the law that they may be corrected and even "beaten"; so that they may pay the penalty for their errors with both fingernail and <term>obelisks</term> <note>The "fingernail" (ungue) refers to a poet testing the smoothness of verse, while "obelisks" (obeliscis) were critical marks used by ancient scholars to mark suspected errors in a text.</note>. Therefore, present yourself to them as a fair judge, not an unfair one—that is, severe, not indulgent. For what is a greater injustice than to deceive a friend who promises everything of himself to you? I am not of such a delicate nature that I would loathe the erasures of another, nor do I seem so beautiful to myself that I would ignore or blame a censor. Indeed, perhaps neither you nor anyone else would believe how much these works of mine do not satisfy me; for even in those things which please me more, I fear lest I be like that <term>Suffenus</term> <note>A character from the Roman poet Catullus, known for being a prolific but terrible poet who was oblivious to his own lack of talent.</note>. Surely we are all deceived and do not see the <term>knapsack</term> which is on our back <note>A reference to Aesop’s fable where humans carry their own faults in a bag behind them, out of sight, while carrying the faults of others in front.</note>. Therefore, do not deny your effort in an honorable and noble matter to a most friendly man—especially one who entreats it with such great zeal and from his heart. If I were the sort from whom a favor could be returned to you in such a matter, I would not be silent about that Greek saying: that <term>Lysippus</term> was accustomed to use the work of <term>Apelles</term>, and Apelles that of Lysippus, in turn <note>Lysippus was a famous sculptor and Apelles a famous painter; Pico suggests that even great masters relied on the critical eyes of their peers.</note>. **Farewell.**

## Giovanni Pico della Mirandola to Angelo Poliziano, Greetings.

<margin>a z 9 c</margin>
When I was in Florence in previous years, I left four love elegies with you, which—as is often the case—I had fashioned almost as a boy during that time for the sake of exercising my talent. They were indeed tasteless, unlearned, and light, easily betraying the age and ignorance of the author. You, however, approved of them—not according to the merit of the thing, but according to your own kindness and even indulgence. And for that very reason, so that you might give proof that you approved, you asked for copies. Surely you were not unaware that such things are the sharpest incentives for the minds of youths toward virtue: so that, enticed by the desire for praise, they might soon strive to taste more deeply that little bit of glory they have sampled. For just as strength lies flat and cold in despair, there is no one who doubts that it is raised up and set on fire by hope. But now the defense of age is being removed; and those errors which were previously signed off on will now be turned into a fault against me, because, now being more mature in years, I have not either better purged them or deleted them. Therefore, if you love me, either send back to me whatever poems of mine are with you, or tear them up, or give them to the fire. All those things, more carefully labored over, and many others which have slipped from me during leisure since I left that place, will shortly be entrusted to your <term>file</term> <note>A common humanist metaphor for the process of polishing and perfecting a literary work.</note>. In the meantime, let those things which cannot live without detriment to a friend be condemned by a <term>fatal pebble</term> <note>original: "capitali damnentur calculo" — a reference to the ancient judicial practice of using black stones to cast a vote for a death sentence or a guilty verdict.</note>. Furthermore, I would entirely wish that your <term>Epictetus</term>, and whatever you have translated from <term>Homer</term> up to this day, as well as what you composed concerning <term>Giuliano de' Medici</term> in the <term>mother tongue</term> <note>original: "sermone patrio" — this refers to Poliziano’s famous Italian poem "Stanze per la giostra," celebrating a tournament held by Giuliano de' Medici.</note> and whatever else you have composed in the Latin language, be sent to me. I ask this of you as most earnestly as possible; for I desire it as one who is most impatient. Nor is there any reason for you to refuse because they perhaps have not yet been <term>brought to the navel</term> <note>original: "ad umbilicum... deducta" — an ancient idiom for finishing a book, referring to the wooden roller (umbilicus) around which a finished scroll was wrapped.</note>. Indeed, I now announce and promise to you that all these things will be kept secret with me, if such should be your wish. **Farewell.**

### Giovanni Pico della Mirandola to Marsilio Ficino, Greetings.

<margin>30.</margin>
<margin>m</margin>
**I**t has always been my judgment, most learned Marsilio, that there is nothing we should work harder on than ensuring that we do not, through sloth or laziness, degenerate from the nobility of the soul—that nobility by which, with <term>Trismegistus</term> <note>Hermes Trismegistus, a legendary figure from late antiquity whom Renaissance thinkers believed was a contemporary of Moses and the source of all ancient wisdom.</note> as witness, we are considered next in rank after <term>Jove</term> <note>Pico uses the Roman name for the supreme deity to refer to God.</note>. It has always been my chief aim to acquire for myself the cultivation of the soul and the disciplines of the liberal arts from wherever I could. Although this plan of mine has been most constant since my boyhood, your exhortations so greatly stirred and inflamed me when I was with you in former years; never have I more ardently devoted myself entirely to literature than from that time until this very day. For three years now, Marsilio, I have been occupied among the <term>Peripatetics</term> <note>Followers of Aristotle’s philosophy, named for the "covered walkways" (peripatoi) of the Lyceum where Aristotle taught.</note>, nor have I omitted anything, as far as it lay in my power, to be admitted into the house of the Aristotelians as if I were one of their own family, not unworthy of the name. Although I have not yet fully achieved this—indeed, I am barely in the vestibule—I have nonetheless advanced far enough that I would not hesitate to claim for myself the name of a "student," even if age does not yet allow me to be called "learned" or "erudite."

But since it has always been your opinion, and that of the most learned men, that the <term>Academic</term> <note>Platonic philosophy, named for Plato’s Academy in Athens.</note> way should be mixed with the Peripatetic—since one who reads both will possess the truth more correctly and more richly—I have decided that I must undertake this task. Now, by the strength of my own talent and with as much persistence and diligence as I can muster, I intend to compare Plato with Aristotle, and in turn, through alternating studies, Aristotle with Plato. 

But just as I previously had you as my advisor, so now I need you as my helper. It will be a mark of your humanity and your goodwill toward me not to fail my purpose—and that in a cause so honorable and noble. I believe you will have done this most abundantly if you send me your book *On the Immortality of Souls* <note>original: "de immortalitate aiorm [animorum]"; this refers to Ficino's masterpiece, the *Platonic Theology*, which sought to prove the soul's immortality using Platonic arguments.</note>. With this book as a sort of guide into the Platonic discipline, I hope and trust that I shall make progress. For who would not promise themselves the very greatest things in that branch of learning from a man like Ficino—in whom, if the <term>Pythagorean</term> <note>A reference to the doctrine of metempsychosis, or the transmigration of souls; Pico is suggesting that Ficino is Plato reborn.</note> opinion were true, I would believe Plato himself had come back to life? Only do not fail me; I would plead for this from you at greater length, were it not that the very principle of honor, which you value so highly, pleads this same thing from you. For if our <term>Cicero</term>, the wise <term>Chilo</term>, and the most serious philosopher <term>Theophrastus</term> all believed that one should turn aside from the path somewhat for the benefit of friends, would it not be a disgrace to fail a most dear friend in such an honorable request? See to it, therefore, that what I have long pursued by your encouragement, I may finally attain by your help. For I have no one besides you who can assist me in this matter, since care for Platonic affairs has entirely vanished among the men of our age, just as have many other beautiful and excellent things. Farewell.

---

<margin>n</margin>
**I** am writing to you not because I have anything worthy of you to write, but only so that you might write back. Otherwise, I have no reason for writing, nor any subject. For I have always condemned the opinion of those who [write] to friends...
