...they feel that one must write so that this is paid as a kind of debt to friendship. Truly, this whole business of writing and sending letters back and forth is characteristic of a friendship that is weak and somewhat chilly: one that does not stand firmly enough on its own strength and looks elsewhere for something to sustain it. But for a friendship that has already taken deep root in the very depths of the soul, why, I ask you, does it need the support of letters? I will therefore send mine to you, Hermolao Barbaro, for this reason: to entice your letters, which I desire most greatly, to come to me. You, in return, shall send yours back most abundantly so that I do not desire them in vain. For just as it is the mark of a weak mind to use letters as <term>buttresses</term> <note>original: "tibicines," literally "props" or "supports" used in building to keep a wall from falling.</note> for friendship so that it does not waver, so to show oneself easy and beneficial to friends is a mark of singular generosity and goodwill. Farewell. And please send me Ptolemy’s *Music* <note>Referring to Claudius Ptolemy’s "Harmonics," a foundational Greek text on the mathematical theory of music.</note> if it is not an inconvenience to you; it will be here for only a few days. For what should I not boldly ask of you, to whom I have long since vowed and dedicated everything of mine?

## Giovanni Pico della Mirandola to Hermolao [Barbaro], Greetings.

<margin>a 3Z m</margin>I have never pleased myself more, nor owed more thanks, than at this time, when by a single letter of mine to you I have summoned letters back to me that are so sweet, so learned, and so very much like yourself. If the fact that you were away from Padua while I was there, and that I have missed your companionship for two years, was the reason you wrote these things to me, then whatever that cause may be, it cannot fail to be pleasant to me now. Your single letter has so abundantly not only fulfilled but even exceeded my every wish. For I shall say nothing of the letter's elegance, its charm, its learning, and its sweetness—the mere reading of which repays any favor many times over. How much do you think I value the fact that you give yourself to me as a friend so lovingly, so kindly, and so sincerely from the heart? And—something I would not even dare to wish for—you so generously promise your effort in honoring me from every side. This is a kind of service that I must frankly confess I should not just receive, but even seek out, and I would not blush to do so in your presence. Indeed, not even the Stoics themselves, as you know, approve of <term>apathy</term> <note>original: "απαθιαν" (apatheia). In Stoic philosophy, this isn't "not caring," but rather a state of being free from irrational emotions or suffering.</note>, nor among these feelings which the Greeks call <term>passions</term> <note>original: "παθη" (pathe), meaning emotions or disturbances of the mind.</note> can any be more praiseworthy or honorable than that one—if it is indeed among them—which is called the desire for a good name and glory. Truly, this can be provided to me more abundantly by no one than yourself, in whom all the virtues, as if individually, compete to claim the prize for themselves. And I certainly have no one to whom I would more gladly be indebted. This promise of yours is therefore as pleasing and desirable to me as it is honorable; I rejoice in it most of all because it provides proof of your extraordinary love and most affectionate goodwill toward me. At last I have what I have long desired, and so now I truly triumph. I have, I say, Hermolao Barbaro—the delight of the Latin language and a distinguished storehouse of all the fine arts—as one who is not only well-disposed toward me, but a most intimate friend. You likewise have Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, so devoted to you and so studious of your interests that no one could be more so. In returning mutual favors to you, I may indeed be unequal in ability, for nothing I do could be grand enough or worthy of Hermolao; but if you look at my spirit, it is certainly either equal or superior. Farewell.

## Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, etc.

<margin>^ 33 n</margin>Nothing was sweeter to me than your company while you were here with us, and nothing was more profitable; such is the sweetness of your character and the depth of your learning. But see how sweet and how welcome you were to me while I enjoyed your presence, since now, while you are away, nothing is sweeter to me than the memory of you. But surely, if the seat of friendship is the soul—and we are, above all, our souls, as **Plato** and **Aristotle** write—there is no reason why any distance of place or long intervals of time should be able to create a division between us. I was thinking just now of some other way I might achieve being with you, and nothing else came to mind except that my late-night labor regarding the **sevenfold explanation of the six days of Genesis** <note>This refers to Pico’s famous work, the *Heptaplus* (published 1489), where he provides a complex, seven-layered allegorical interpretation of the creation story in the Bible.</note> should come to you. For if we give birth to books as if they were children, and the greatest part of a father is in his son, I too shall come to you in the one I have sired. Therefore, receive my little son coming to you as cheerfully and willingly as you used to receive me. It will please you, I know, because you love me. I know also that it will displease you for the same reason: for it is the nature of such devotion to look pointedly into the errors of those we love so that we may correct them, and, once looked into, to indulge them lightly so that we do not cause distress.

---

## Giovanni Pico della Mirandola to F.B.C.Th. <note>These initials likely refer to a religious correspondent, possibly "Fratri Baptistae Carmelitae Theologo" (To Brother Baptista, the Carmelite Theologian), referring to the famous Neo-Latin poet Baptista Mantuanus.</note>

<margin>^ 34 s</margin>Greetings, most beloved father. Here is **Apollonius** <note>Likely a manuscript of Apollonius of Tyana, a Greek philosopher whose life was often compared to that of Christ in the Renaissance.</note> for you. Even if I did not owe him to your virtue and your kindness toward me, I would certainly owe him because of the letters in which you demand him, so great is the love and humanity within them. Indeed, it is a mark of the highest love to call someone to the place you have already reached: namely, to the **purgation of the soul** <note>The "purgation of the soul" is a Neoplatonic and Christian concept referring to the process of cleansing the mind of earthly distractions to achieve spiritual clarity or "true happiness."</note>—that is, to true happiness. And it is a mark of the greatest humanity to encourage me as an equal, though you could dictate the law to me as if to a son. But would that it might one day happen in practice that we could philosophize together piously in some retreat. You will see that for me, nothing comes before the joining of **piety with wisdom**. You will see that I am most firmly convinced of this: that there is no wisdom which should blot out the image of **Eternal Wisdom** <note>A reference to Christ, often identified as the "Divine Logos" or "Eternal Wisdom" in theological texts.</note> within us, making us like senseless beasts. I have my guardian angel as a witness that I credit as much to my daily profit in studies as I emerge from them better equipped and stronger for the struggle of purifying the soul. This manifold handling of disciplines, and whatever literature can promise us, colors the skin and makes us more beautiful with a kind of **pigment** <note>Pico uses "pigment" (pigmentum) metaphorically to mean the outward decoration of the mind or rhetorical style, contrasting it with the "inner health" of the soul.</note> on the face. But we cannot hope for a sound, firm, and robust mind from anywhere else than from integrity of life, from character, and finally, from divine religion. Therefore, you compel one who is already willing (if I may put it so) to be even more willing. But also help me with your sacred prayers so that I may achieve both what I wished for and what you so greatly desire me to want. Farewell, most loving father, whom I love uniquely and hold before my eyes. Florence, January 13, 1490. I expect all your news. My **Poliziano** <note>Angelo Poliziano (1454–1494), the famous humanist poet and close friend of Pico and Lorenzo de' Medici.</note>, the delight of all literature, bids me send you his greetings.

---

<meta>This page concludes the first letter to the Venetian scholar Hermolao Barbaro and begins a new correspondence with Andrea Corneo of Urbino. The text transitions from Pico's admiration for Barbaro’s translations of Aristotle and Themistius to a vigorous defense of the contemplative, philosophical life against the pressures of entering public or political service.</meta>

...it would be public: I was in Padua for two years and, though it is hard to believe, I neither saw Hermolao nor was I seen by him, except as I had known him long before by his reputation. So it often happens that while we look down upon an offered opportunity with a certain lazy procrastination, it slips away from our hands like something slippery. I had known of your learning only by rumor; now I have recognized it with these eyes and these ears, while that Roman **Themistius** <note>original: "themiſtium". This refers to Hermolao Barbaro’s famous Latin translation and paraphrase of the Greek philosopher Themistius, published in 1481.</note> spoke from your mouth about the nature of the soul and the first beginnings of things. What riches of expression! What brilliance! What purity of speech! O most distinguished man, O living image of antiquity! It was my frequent prayer that the writings of **Varro** <note>Marcus Terentius Varro (116–27 BC), a Roman scholar known as "the most learned of the Romans." Most of his encyclopedic works on "Divine and Human Antiquities" were lost to history.</note> on divine and human things might one day come back to life, so that we might have someone from whom to learn the principles of nature in Latin. You, indeed, recalling both him and all the most approved authors, have shown yourself to us such that nothing remains for us to desire, except that by translating other Greek works you might both win more abundant praise for yourself and deserve even better from natural history and from all students. All these things, most learned Hermolao, aim at nothing else but that you understand I am your most dear friend; your virtues so kindle me to love and respect you that I yield to no one, not even among your kin, in my affection. This letter shall sanctify a bond of friendship between us, so that we may continually engage in a most honorable contest of mutual love.

->Giovanni Pico della Mirandola to Andrea Corneo of Urbino. Greetings.<-

<margin>q</margin> I received your most recent letter, written on the Ides of October. Those you write of having sent earlier did not arrive; I would have replied immediately had I received them, as I am not slow to write, and in this duty—whether by habit or by nature—I am least of all a slacker. Yet there was no reason for you to fear that our friendship could be weakened even by a long silence. I am a constant friend, not a temporary one. And a friendship is not firm enough if it requires these exchanges of letters like <term>props</term> <note>original: *tibicines*. Literally "flute-players," but in Roman comedy (like Plautus) and architecture, the term referred to structural supports or shores used to keep a sagging building from collapsing.</note> to support it when it is, as I might say in a word from **Plautus**, "nodding" and a bit weak. 

But to come to what you wrote: you urge me toward the active and civil life, saying that I have philosophized for so long in vain—and even to my disgrace and reproach—unless I finally sweat in the <term>wrestling-ground</term> <note>original: *paleſtra*. A Greek term for a wrestling school, used here metaphorically for the public arena of politics and business.</note> of managing and handling affairs. And indeed, my dear Andrea, I would have lost both the "oil and the labor" <note>A common Latin idiom (*oleum et operam perdere*) meaning to waste one's time and effort.</note> of my studies if I were now so minded that I could agree or assent to you on this point. This is that fatal and monstrous persuasion which has invaded the minds of men: either that the study of philosophy is not to be touched by leading men, or that it is to be tasted only with the "tips of the lips" for a display of wit rather than for the cultivation of the soul, even in leisure. They hold that decree of **Neoptolemus** <note>A reference to a line from a lost play by Ennius, where the character Neoptolemus says one should philosophize "only in small amounts."</note> as absolute: either one should not philosophize at all, or only in small amounts. Now, those sayings of the wise are accepted as mere trifles and old wives' tales: the idea that firm and solid happiness lies in the goods of the soul, and that these external things—of the body or of fortune—pertain to us little or not at all. But you will say: "I wish for you to embrace **Martha** in such a way that you do not, in the meantime, desert **Mary**." <note>Pico references the biblical sisters Martha and Mary (Luke 10:38-42), who were traditional symbols for the active life of service (Martha) and the contemplative life of study and prayer (Mary).</note> In this part, I do not...

<meta>This page continues the correspondence from Giovanni Pico della Mirandola to Andrea Corneo. Pico is responding to Corneo’s suggestion that he should leave his private studies to enter the service of a prince. Pico defends his choice of the "contemplative life" over the "active life," a central debate in Renaissance humanism.</meta>

I do not resist, nor do I condemn or accuse those who do so. But it is far from the case that moving from a life of contemplation to a civil life is not an error; nor should one judge it a disgrace or a mark of idleness or a crime not to have made that transition. Why, then, should it be held against someone as a vice? Let him perpetually strive for and pursue virtue itself for the sake of virtue, seeking nothing outside of it. While he searches into divine mysteries and the designs of nature, let him enjoy this **leisure** <note>original: "otio". In the Renaissance, *otium* (leisure/study) was the noble opposite of *negotium* (business/public affairs).</note>, looking down upon and neglecting all other things, since these studies are enough to satisfy the prayers of their followers. 

Therefore, would it be ungenerous, or entirely unworthy of a prince, not to make the study of wisdom a mercenary pursuit? Who could bear or hear such things with an even mind? Certainly, he has never practiced philosophy who has done so only so that he might one day be able to, or wish to, stop practicing it. That man has practiced commerce, not philosophy. 

You write that the time is approaching for me to devote myself to one of the highest princes of Italy. You do not yet know the opinion that philosophers hold of themselves: those who, according to **Horace** <note>original: "oratium". Refers to Horace’s *Epistles* 1.1.106, where the philosopher is called "the king of kings."</note>, think themselves the kings of kings; they do not know how to endure courtly manners or to serve. They dwell within themselves and, content with the tranquility of their own mind, they are sufficient unto themselves. They seek nothing outside themselves. The things that are held in honor by the common people are without honor to them; and they utterly neglect and despise whatever human lust thirsts for or ambition sighs after. 

This is what all men should do, but especially those whom fortune has so favored that they are able to live not only elegantly and comfortably, but even splendidly. Those "great fortunes" indeed elevate and show one off. But often, like a fierce and bucking horse, they throw off the rider. Certainly, they always treat one poorly and vex rather than carry their owner. That **golden mean** <note>original: "Aurea illa optāda mediocritas". A famous concept from Horace regarding the balance between poverty and excessive wealth.</note> is to be desired, which carries us more evenly like a small horse, and being patient of command, truly serves us and does not dominate us. 

Persisting in this opinion, I prefer my little cell, my studies, the delights of my books, and my peace of mind to royal courts, public business, your political pursuits, and the favors of the curia. Nor do I expect such fruits from this literary leisure of mine that I should be tossed and fluctuated in the heat and tumult of public affairs. Rather, it is so that I may finally give birth to the children I am laboring with and—may it be happy and auspicious—put something into the public view that, if not learning, might at least show my talent and diligence. 

And lest you believe that any of our industry or labor has slackened, know that after much effort spent in assiduous and tireless midnight labors, I have learned the **Hebrew** and **Chaldean** <note>term: Chaldean (Chaldaicam). In this period, "Chaldean" usually referred to the Aramaic language, particularly that found in the Bible and the Zohar.</note> languages, and have now also applied my hands to overcoming the difficulties of **Arabic**. These I have always considered, and now consider, to be the pursuits of a leading man. 

But though I have spoken truly and perhaps severely, I nonetheless cherish and venerate those most excellent princes, and especially the high-minded **Ludovico, Duke of Bari** <note>Ludovico Sforza (1452–1508), known as "Il Moro," the powerful regent and later Duke of Milan.</note>, more than any other prince in Italy. I understand that I owe him much for many reasons, and there is nothing so heavy, nothing so arduous, that I would not do (if the opportunity were given to me) for the sake of deserving his favor. But such is their greatness and my smallness that, just as I cannot help but need them, they can in no way need my help or my arrival there. 

I shall set out for **Rome** shortly to spend the winter there, unless some sudden event or new fortune draws me elsewhere. From there, perhaps, you will hear what your Pico has accomplished in his "shadowy and seated" life of contemplation, or what—for I will speak somewhat arrogantly—what he has achieved when you promised him a bounty of other learned men to help him there...

<summary>Pico della Mirandola defends his choice of a private life of study over a career in the service of princes, revealing that he has mastered Hebrew and Aramaic and is currently learning Arabic.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Giovanni Pico della Mirandola’s letter to Andrea Corneo from October 1486. Pico has been arguing against joining the service of a prince, preferring the "leisure" of philosophy. Here, he shifts to more personal matters, including gossip about marriage, his own poetic output, a disloyal servant, and a mutual friend’s scandalous love affair.</meta>

...is lacking in literary matters. In Rome and wherever in the world I may be, those princes will have someone to command, someone whom they might turn at their whim like a **hand-driven mill** <note>original: "trusatilem... mola". Pico quotes the Roman playwright Plautus (*Persa* 22) to describe the grueling, repetitive labor of a courtier compared to a slave turning a millstone.</note> according to their will. 

What you write regarding the matter of a wife, I do not think was said rashly or for no reason. But **I am Davus, not Oedipus** <note>original: "dauus sum/Edippus non sum". A common Latin proverb derived from Terence. Davus is a simple slave, while Oedipus solved the riddle of the Sphinx. Pico is saying "I don't understand your riddles/hints."</note>; nor, if I were, would I wish to be. Whatever it is, if it seems right, explain it more clearly; if not, let it be **Harpocrates** <note>The Greek god of silence.</note>. And as circumstances offer themselves, I take counsel in the midst of arms. 

There is no reason for you to desire my **Tuscan verses** <note>original: "Rhythmos meos ethruscos". Refers to Pico's vernacular Italian poetry, which he eventually burned or suppressed in favor of Latin philosophy.</note>. Long ago I sent a message of divorce to amorous trifles; we are contemplating other things. But I want you to be warned of this too: regarding your **Laura** <note>Likely a reference to a poetic work Corneo was writing, named after Petrarch’s muse.</note>, if you were going to publish it, suppress it for a few more days. For perhaps soon our people will read things about love (see what I am saying) which they have not yet read. And you will be able to note many things that will contribute greatly to your own work. 

Regarding **Alibrana** <note>A servant or associate of Pico who apparently deserted him under poor circumstances.</note>—although he is not worthy for me to speak of him—I will say this: that man has returned bad thanks to a well-deserving master. Nor is there any reason for him to blame his flight on anyone but himself, since he owes almost as much to my household staff—which he cannot deny—as he owes to me. But this is not the first time, as you know, that he has broken faith or mocked his master. I know what he said against me and about me after he fled. But **the elephant does not care about the gnat** <note>A proverb meaning the great are not bothered by the insults of the small.</note>. I am willing to forgive whatever that frivolous man has done wrong for your sake. But let him not abuse my patience in the future, lest I be forced to eventually show myself to him as he undeservedly showed himself to me. 

As for your friend whose affair of love turned out badly, you did your duty in excusing him to our friend Florianus. He indeed has means from history, from poets, and even from philosophy itself to clear himself of the mark of crime; he has means to protect himself by the precedents of great men—of David and especially of Solomon—to say nothing of **Aristotle** <note>Pico alludes to a medieval legend that Aristotle was so infatuated with a woman (Phyllis) that he allowed her to ride him like a horse.</note>. While Aristotle often fell desperately in love with several harlots, he remembered nothing of his own precepts on morals when he performed sacrifices to his beloved woman as if to **Eleusinian Ceres** <note>The goddess of the harvest; Pico is noting the irony of a philosopher treating a lover as a divinity.</note>. 

But your friend does not merely embrace or love these defenses and, as it were, ramparts of his deed; he hates, rejects, and refuses them. He laments his loss; he does not pray away his guilt. He grieves that he sinned; he does not defend it. And to me, he seems for this reason alone to be worthy of excuse by others: because he does not excuse himself at all. Nothing is weaker than man; nothing more powerful than love. Even that invincible and unshaken mind of **Jerome** <note>St. Jerome famously wrote about his struggles with lustful visions of dancing girls while living as an ascetic in the desert.</note>, while it clung entirely to heaven, was present among the dances of girls. What plague could infest a man that love will not tame? If love could do this in the desert, on the ground with bruised limbs, in the fasting of weeks—what can it not do in down feathers, in the shade, in every abundance of delights? 

Add to this that he has now fallen for the first time, being otherwise unaccustomed to and ignorant of such a ruin. He who has suffered shipwreck only once can complain to Neptune. If he strikes the same stone again, let no one stretch out a hand; let no one pity him. Now, he cannot rightly be denied excuse, for he so repents of the deed that he does not think himself worthy of an excuse. But enough of this, since your friend desires that the memory of such a deed not only be recorded in letters in some way, but that his subsequent life cause it to be entirely blotted out. 

Farewell. Christopher was not present when I received yours. Commend me in no common way to your master and the whole **Borromeo family** <note>The powerful Milanese banking and noble family; Corneo was in their service.</note>, whom I have always loved and now love very much. 

At Perugia, October 15, 1486, the year of grace.

## Giovanni Pico of Mirandola sends many greetings to his nephew Gianfrancesco.

<margin>page 37 g</margin>

**Y**our letters were most welcome to me. This is not only because I had heard nothing from you for a long time, but also because they signaled things to me in which I took wonderful delight; since those same things are pleasing to you, I do not doubt they are also most pleasing to God. You should have no doubt either: if you continue on the path you have begun, your reward will be abundant in heaven. 

I have not yet sufficiently determined whether I must go to Rome or not. As far as I can gather by conjecture, I believe it is more likely that I will have to go there; you know the reason <note>Pico was likely referring to his ongoing negotiations with the Papacy to clear his name of heresy charges following his 900 Theses of 1486.</note>. As soon as I am certain of this, I will let you know, lest if you should happen to come here (which I would otherwise very much desire), you might either not find me here, or be forced to return home immediately upon my departure. In the meantime, you can remain at home, unless you feel otherwise. 

But remember this also: you have a wife, to whom you owe your body no less than you owe your soul to God <note>original: "uxorem cui nō aliter corpus tuum q̃ deo ipſam aĩam debes". This reflects the Pauline doctrine found in 1 Corinthians 7:4 regarding the "marriage debt."</note>. Her desires must be satisfied in some part: you must consider what she might crave or be able to crave based on her physical nature and age, and what she might not ask for out of modesty and virtue. For why should I be ashamed to write these things which the Apostle Paul also wrote? There is almost no matter in which I suspect you could be more prone to error. Indeed, our men are greatly deceived when they think their wives are bound and devoted to them, but they owe nothing to their wives—believing they can decide whatever they please regarding themselves at their own whim. Finally, you cannot be entirely your own master, having once submitted yourself to the laws of marriage and chosen to belong to a wife. Nevertheless, you can belong entirely to God, whose favor you earn when, in order to obey His law, you obey yourself less, even in matters concerning God <note>Pico suggests that fulfilling marital duties is a form of religious obedience, even if it takes time away from direct prayer or study.</note>. But I have spoken with you about these things in person at other times. 

As for me, as soon as the air turns to spring—that is, during the first days of Lent—when I have extricated myself from the "salt" of these Greek books <note>original: "græcorum librorũ ſalibus". Pico uses "salt" here to mean the wit, sharpness, or sophisticated nuances of the Greek texts he was translating/studying.</note>, I shall come to Ferrara immediately. In the meantime, press on with the sacred scriptures, especially the reading of the Gospels, which repeatedly brings the soul back to God. Both the world and the Devil never cease to lead the soul away from Him—the former with charms, the latter with deceits—by day and by night. Farewell, half of my soul, and pray to God for me. As soon as I have decided anything regarding my departure for Rome, I will let you know. 

Florence, November 27, 1491.

## Giovanni Pico of Mirandola sends greetings to his friend Jacopo Antiquario.

<margin>38 i</margin>

**A**mong the pleasures I used to take when I was in Florence from the company of **Poliziano** <note>Angelo Poliziano (1454–1494), the preeminent poet and classical scholar of the Medici circle.</note>—a man who is, in my opinion, the most learned of all in our age—it was no small joy that as soon as he received your letters, which were always weighty and elegant, he would immediately give them to me to read. In those letters, I was vehemently delighted both by a certain singular wisdom—for which you are commended by the most prudent men even in the handling of great affairs—and by the refinement and sobriety of your speech. Furthermore, since in several places you made honorable mention of us, not only did your letters please me, but I also took pleasure in myself within them. Naturally, with the testimony of such a great man yielding...

Thus, I was bound to you by a double tie: first by your virtue, and second by the services and even benefits so often bestowed upon me. I thought more than once of thanking you by letter, lest I should seem ungrateful or perhaps unsophisticated toward you. Not because you overwhelm me with excessive praise (which I do not recognize as my own), but because you love me so much that your otherwise steady and robust judgment wavered under the weight of that love. Therefore, I owe you more than I can pay or than you could easily believe; there is nothing so arduous or difficult that I would not do as much for your honor as for my own safety. Since you have possessed me through Politiano until now, but with nothing changed in the situation, you will now bring to light the name of Pico which was hidden beneath. Farewell. From the Ferrarese countryside, June 28, 1494.

## To the most excellent and learned man, Master Jacobus Antiquarius, as to a father.

# Giovanni Pico of Mirandola to Andrea Corneo, sends greetings.

<margin>39</margin>

**M**y wishes have been fully and abundantly satisfied, dearest Andrea. Since I learned from your letters to Christopher <note>Likely Christoforo Landino, the Florentine humanist.</note>—who is most dear to both of us—that you are living there with both comfort and dignity. For this is, and always has been, my greatest wish: that you be well and happy; and I have nothing greater to say than this, in accordance with your merits. I never doubted that this would happen. And this one thing was always clear to me: as long as your tongue survived you, wherever in the world you might be, you would be in a high position. I know (and this is said without flattery) the nobility of your soul, which will suffer nothing base or common. I know your virtues, learning, character, and prudence; all of which will easily lead you wherever you aim. I only fear for your health, which has been oppressed and weakened—rather than broken—by so many diseases from an early age until this day, as you used to tell me. Yet your intellect has moved even that illness, so that it knows not how to be conquered, but with a certain perpetual solidity of its own, it fights strenuously against the blows of fortune. I beg you, take no less account of your health than of your fortunes, since when life fails, those fortunes are nothing. As for the fact that you speak of me honorably before all, you do so out of your humanity and old benevolence toward me; and for that, I owe you as much as one can possibly owe. But I fear lest you unweave your own web... <note>An idiom suggesting that excessive praise might eventually undermine the speaker's own credibility.</note>

<margin>40.</margin>

Our Matthew <note>likely Matteo Bosso (1427–1502), a scholar and regular correspondent within Pico’s circle</note>, a most dutiful man, has both given me many greetings in your words and most clearly declared with what love and benevolence you follow me. He promised, moreover, in your name, your zeal and labor if ever I should happen to need them. I wish I were equal to such kindness, most humane father. For I have always both desired and hoped to be taken into your protection and to be numbered among your own. But to have you meet me halfway so kindly—approaching me with such friendly and generous promises, and calling me (if I may say so, and through you I may) to your friendship—has exceeded both my hope and my every wish. For how great a thing is it to be invited by him, by whom it would have been enough not to be excluded? This thing you have done is worthy of you, even if it is not worthy of me. For according to my merits, I might not have been admitted; but according to your humanity, I could not have gone uncalled.

Therefore, in what way might I explain how much I rejoice for myself, or how much I owe to you, when I cannot even conceive of the extent of it? Certainly, I owe you all the more for these things because you owe me nothing in return. For those things are neither too great nor too many which Matthew and my other friends have reported, estimating me more out of goodwill than out of judgment. But such as I am, or however great, allow me also to be among all those who cultivate and admire your virtues—to say nothing of the rest—through which one can see in you both that which surpasses antiquity and that which cannot be surpassed by posterity. I might say this deservedly, since in you nothing is lacking that is placed in honor, or prudence, or learning. This one thing ought to be desired by all: that through you eventually, according to the wish of Plato <note>original: "iuxta Platonis uotum". A reference to Plato’s famous "Philosopher King" ideal from the Republic, where he wishes for the union of political power and philosophical wisdom.</note>, the highest power might be joined with the highest wisdom. 

But these things are from God; meanwhile, I ask and request this of you: that you provide me an opportunity—not for returning favors, for there is no room for that given your greatness or my insignificance—but for testifying to my spirit toward you, and for witnessing my loyalty and respect. You shall find in Giovanni Pico a man devoted and dedicated to you beyond all opinion; you cannot promise yourself more from him, but you can promise all those things, whatever they may be, which are in him. When you yourself use them, you will bring some of your own splendor to them; and they will become great when they begin to be yours, which, while they are mine, cannot be great. Farewell.

### Giovanni Pico of Mirandola to his Alessandro Cortese, Greetings.

<margin>41. g</margin> Your letters were most pleasing to me. You recently sent them, as you know, not as a stranger to a stranger as you suppose, but as a friend—and indeed an old friend—to a friend, or rather as one well-known to another. For as you write, you knew me previously and deemed me worthy of your love. I likewise have heard of your learning and virtue quite often, both from many others and from our friend Poliziano <note>Angelo Poliziano (1454–1494), the preeminent humanist scholar and poet of the Medici circle.</note>, in whose judgment who would not trust? He established my faith in your integrity, just as my own long-standing benevolence toward you can establish it in yours. Although that goodwill was already at its greatest, know that your letter has added such heaps of affection as few could even conceive in their minds. For what could be sweeter than that letter? What more erudite? How learned it is! How full of love! You subscribe most generously to what our friend Puccio <note>Likely Puccio de' Rossi, a Florentine scholar and diplomat.</note> says of me, speaking more as a friend than with strict truth. Truly, nothing more pleasing could have come to me from you, nor could anything be more honoring than your opinion of me. For all these things, I give you the greatest possible thanks, and I confess that I owe to my dear Alessandro whatever is mine or whatever is in me. I am sending you the letter of mine to Lorenzo de' Medici <note>Laurentius Medice (1449–1492), the ruler of Florence and a major patron of Pico.</note> which you requested.

---

### Giovanni Pico of Mirandola to Domenico Benivieni, Greetings.

<margin>42. f</margin> Greetings, my Domenico, chosen for the lot of the Lord <note>original: "in domini sortem". A play on the word 'cleric,' derived from the Greek 'kleros' (lot/portion). Benivieni was a prominent Florentine theologian.</note>. Your letters were pleasing to me, but it was even more pleasing to learn—both in person from your brother while he was staying here and through letters from our friend Pietro Antonio—that you are of a stronger physical condition and have a better stomach. If you care for all of us, if you care for letters <note>In this context, "letters" refers to the humanities and scholarship.</note>, then take care of your health. I have always been and remain anxious about your health, not only because I love you (and I love you vehemently), but because I love the scholarship which I believe—and indeed certainly know—is at risk alongside you. If your brother reported any of my goodwill toward you, you may have the fullest faith in it; if he said anything of my praises, believe him as little as he loves me much. There is no reason for you to wonder at our little commentary <note>original: "Commentariolum nostrum". Refers to Pico's "Commentary on a Poem of Platonic Love," written to explain a poem by Domenico's brother, Girolamo Benivieni.</note>; when we wished to be at leisure and do nothing at all, we did that, relaxing the mind rather than straining it. It is entirely a prelude to the commentaries we are meditating upon regarding Plato's *Symposium*. There will be something in those at least for you to love and praise, you who love and praise all our things. Concerning the council and the questions <note>Refers to the 900 "Theses" Pico intended to defend in a public disputation in Rome (the Council).</note>, I think your brother has already told you why I wrote that I am working for your sake. I shall do this most gladly when I understand that you have been restored to your primary and hoped-for health from that bodily weakness from which you have suffered until now. I pray and hope for this for you with the same spirit with which you pray and hope for the health of my soul. Farewell. From La Fratta <note>A villa near Vicenza where Pico stayed in 1486.</note>, November 10, 1486.

->Giovanni Pico of Mirandola to Battista Guarini, his teacher, Greetings.<-

<margin>44.</margin>
Why do you furrow your brow? Is it because I have addressed you as "teacher" against your instructions, and thus done you an injustice? If you are not my teacher, I am not rightfully bound by your precepts; if you are my teacher, I rightfully call you "teacher." But why do you reject the student whom you praise so greatly? These things fight against each other, unless perhaps one belongs to love and the other to judgment; and while you preach his praises out of benevolence, you fear his errors out of conscience—lest, perhaps, they bring shame upon you, which you might be able to acknowledge as a praiser but not as a teacher. But I beg you, receive me into a partnership of learning on this condition: that I may admit you into a partnership of our little glory—if there shall be any—while I alone would bear the blows <note>Presumably the "blows" of critical rejection or academic dispute.</note>.

But why do I delay with cold jokes the heat of my joy, which I conceived from your letters and from your so serious and honorable praise? Now at last it smiles upon me. Now my ***Heptaplus*** <note>Pico's famous work, a seven-fold mystical explanation of the first chapters of Genesis, published in 1489.</note> is pleasing to me, since under your public commendation—as if behind the **shield of Pallas** <note>The Aegis of Athena (Pallas), a symbol of divine protection.</note>—it now shows itself invulnerable to rivals. You urge me toward other writings of this kind, which you would do in vain, were it not that while you subscribe to me with such full approval, you had made me far stronger for writing than I was before by instilling little sparks of good hope. For I trust myself so much in your judgment that I have undertaken the burden of explaining the entire **Old Instrument** <note>original: "instrumenti ueteris," a common humanist term for the Old Testament.</note>. To which I am altogether unequal, yet I shall now bear it much more strongly than usual. As for the books, perhaps I would satisfy you better if I had a list of those books which are with you, since many could serve your purpose, which nonetheless you might not need. Your aforementioned virtue has made you most highly commended to **Lorenzo de' Medici**; nor is there ever a mention among us of the learned men of this age without "Guarini" being frequently on our lips, especially when our friend **Poliziano** <note>Angelo Poliziano (1454–1494), the preeminent poet and scholar of the Medici circle.</note> intervenes (and he always intervenes), who grants you as much as...

## Giovanni Pico della Mirandola to Antonio Pizzamano, Greetings.

<margin>45. n</margin>
**N**othing in my whole life has been more pleasant to me than these letters which I recently received from you, full of love, duty, and kindness. So may I be happy—as I do not deceive you—unless perhaps that day was more pleasant when you and **Grimani** <note>Domenico Grimani (1461–1523), later a Cardinal and a famed patron of arts and letters.</note>—I know not whether he is more yours or mine—met me and greeted me in so friendly and honorable a fashion. For although you both took on a persona, as it were, and presented yourselves to me not as you were, but under some charming fiction of names, nevertheless your most sweet character, singular learning, lovely gravity, liberal modesty, noble countenance, and most witty conversation represented the open and true Grimani and Pizzamano to me. Therefore, even if I could be deceived by the naming, I could not be defrauded of the pleasure that was due to me from you. You could disguise your names; you could not disguise your virtue, which betrays itself by its own brilliance and knows not how to hide. That so serious a discussion on physical matters <note>Refers to natural philosophy or physics.</note>, those sharp and intricate arguments, those most refined judgments—whom else could they announce to me but your very selves? I congratulated myself silently as I listened to you, thinking our age had produced not just one Grimani and one Pizzamano, but two of each; but when our friend **Poliziano** <note>Angelo Poliziano (1454–1494), the renowned humanist scholar and poet who was a close friend of Pico.</note> revealed who you truly were, I began to congratulate my own judgment no less than my age, for I seemed to have recognized in you all those things which I had discovered were in you by the most constant testimony of everyone. But see how these praises of yours lead me astray and away from your letter—though the letter itself calls me to the same place, even against my will. But I will restrain myself, lest I seem to wish to satisfy your praises with a "mutual service" <note>original: "mutua opera," a reference to the proverb "scratch my back and I'll scratch yours," implying a hollow exchange of flattery.</note>, with which you have piled many honors upon me. Whether these come from a propensity of the soul or from judgment, I know not whether they bring me more honor or pleasure. I owe very much to that mind of yours toward me, my dear Pizzamano; but please, you too, if ever a trial occurs concerning me—that is, concerning my goodwill toward you—you will find a man so loving of your virtue and so devoted that I would not yield the first place in loving you even to your friend Grimani himself. Farewell. July 9, 1489.

## Giovanni Pico della Mirandola to an Unknown Friend, Greetings.

<margin>46. q</margin>
**W**hoever you are, you shall be ours, since I have learned from the hand <note>original: "syngrapham," a signed bond or written agreement, here referring to a letter or note of introduction.</note> of our **Roberto Salviati** <note>A member of the prominent Salviati family of Florence and a close associate of Pico.</note> that you are most closely joined to him. I read your letters to **Mithridates** <note>Flavius Mithridates, a Jewish convert and scholar who taught Pico Hebrew and Arabic and translated Kabbalistic texts for him.</note> which I could not deliver to him in his absence. I began to love you in those letters, not so much because Roberto loves you, but because I recognized that you love letters and (what is more important) that you are a student of sacred matters and the Law <note>original: "legis," likely referring to the Mosaic Law or Torah in this context.</note>. And since regarding those things which you requested, I felt I could satisfy you in some part...

<meta>This page continues Pico della Mirandola's correspondence, specifically a letter regarding his Hebrew and Chaldean (Aramaic) studies. Pico is writing from Fratta, preparing to travel to Rome, and responding to a scholar's questions about ancient texts and linguistic history.</meta>

...so that our friendship might begin well from here, I wanted to signify to you what I feel. I would certainly do this far more richly if I had those friends of all men—that is, my books—here to consult. But they have already preceded me to Rome as if they were forerunners to their master, and I myself, already **booted and spurred** <note>original: "petalatus iam & caligatus"—a classical idiom for being prepared for a journey</note>, being in readiness [to depart], have written these things to you as familiarly as they were written in haste. 

Regarding what you ask about **Josephus** <note>Titus Flavius Josephus (c. 37–100 AD), a Romano-Jewish historian.</note>, know that the true Josephus is not found among the Hebrews. Instead, there is an "epitome" of Josephus—that is, a certain summary—in which many things are fabricated. Many among the Hebrews have confessed to me that what is read there concerning the **ten tribes** <note>The "Lost Tribes" of Israel.</note> who did not return after the Babylonian captivity by **right of recovery** <note>original: "postliminio"—a legal term for the restoration of rights to those returning from exile or captivity</note> are spurious and adulterated. Therefore, no credit at all is to be given to their Josephus. 

In the Greek Josephus, I know there are certain things that make both faithful and honorable mention of **Christ**. But I would not assert that these are entirely the same as those read in the Latin codices unless I had recently read the Greek copy, of which I have no supply here. 

And to come to those things which you desire concerning the letters of the **Chaldeans** <note>Likely referring to Aramaic or the "square" Hebrew script.</note> and Hebrews: I have often questioned both **Mithridates** <note>Flavius Mithridates, a Jewish convert and scholar who taught Pico Hebrew, Arabic, and Chaldaic.</note> and many Hebrews regarding those things read in **Jerome's Helmeted Prologue** <note>The "Prologus Galeatus," Jerome’s famous preface to the books of Kings in the Vulgate, where he defends his translation and discusses the Hebrew alphabet.</note>, where he writes that the characters of the **Samaritans** and the Hebrews were once the same. They all declare themselves ignorant of this change—the idea that **Ezra**, after the restoration of the temple under **Zerubbabel**, invented other letters which are now in use—and (what is more significant) they hold it as certain that **Moses** and all the ancient patriarchs used the same **points** <note>original: "apicibus"—referring to the strokes or marks of the Hebrew letters</note> which we now use in Hebrew literature. 

This opinion—as it now occurs to me—is given the greatest credit by the science of **Kabbalah** <note>A school of Jewish mysticism; Pico was a pioneer in developing a "Christian Kabbalah."</note>, whose writers (who were in the assembly with Ezra himself) both maintain and prove that Moses concealed divine mysteries under those very characters and shapes of the letters in which we now have the Law written; this could in no way be the case if Moses had used characters different from those we use now. 

To defend Jerome's statement, I have only this one point which I recently read in the commentaries on the book which the ancient father **Abraham** published on creation <note>The *Sefer Yetzirah* (Book of Creation), an early and influential kabbalistic text attributed to the patriarch Abraham.</note>. For while the authors are interpreting those **thirty-two gates** <note>The "32 Paths of Wisdom" in the *Sefer Yetzirah*.</note> which he mentions, they say that number is composed of the **ten numerations** <note>The *Sefirot*, or divine emanations.</note> and the twenty-two letters. However, they say the remaining letters—which are **Mem, Tsade, Pe, Kaph, and Nun** <note>The five Hebrew letters that have a different "final" form when they appear at the end of a word.</note>, and are called "double" letters—were added by the **overseers or prefects**. Perhaps Jerome understood this; his testimony ought to be held as most sacred in all things by everyone, and it is certainly held so by me. 

The Chaldaic alphabet which you seek, you would not have obtained even from Mithridates; nothing is permitted through him, though you might obtain everything from me. For he would not teach me the Chaldaic language by any means unless I were first sworn—and indeed with formal words—not to hand it over to anyone. Our **Girolamo Benivieni** <note>Hieronymus Benivenius (1453–1542), a Florentine poet and close friend of Pico.</note> can attest to this; while he happened to be present while the man was teaching me, the raging Mithridates threw him out. 

But so that you have not written entirely in vain, you may have the Arabic alphabet as a substitute for the Chaldaic, which is sent noted by my own hand. There is nothing left for me to write except that I cannot help but be most fond of you, whoever you are, if I understand that you are most fond of the **good arts** <note>A humanist term for the liberal arts and classical studies.</note>. 

Farewell, from **Fratta**, November 10, 1486.

->Ioannes Picus of Mirandola sends greetings to his nephew, Gianfrancesco Pico.<-
<sig>f</sig>

# Ioannes Picus of Mirandola sends greetings to his nephew, Gianfrancesco Pico.

<margin>47 f</margin>
You are blessed, my son, when God grants you not only that you live well, but that while living well, you are spoken ill of by wicked men—especially for the very reason that you live well. For it is equal praise to be praised by the praiseworthy, and to be disapproved of by the wicked. Yet I do not call you blessed for this reason alone, that this slander is glorious to you, but because the Lord Jesus—who is truthful, or rather Truth itself—affirms that our reward will be abundant in heaven when men speak ill of us and speak every kind of evil against us, lying for his sake <note>original: "propter eum"; Pico is paraphrasing the Beatitudes from Matthew 5:11</note>. This, if you did not know, is an **Apostolic dignity**: to be considered worthy of being defamed by the impious for the sake of the Gospel. Thus we read in the writings of **Luke** <note>Referring to Acts 5:41</note> that the Apostles went out from the presence of the council rejoicing, because they were considered worthy to suffer contumely for the name of Jesus. 

Let us therefore rejoice as well, if we are worthy of such great glory before God, so that his glory may be manifested through our ignominy. And if we suffer anything harsh or troublesome from the world, let that sweetest voice of the Lord console us: **"If the world hates you, know that it hated me before it hated you"** <note>original: "Si vos mundus odio habet, scitote quia priorem me vobis odio habuit" — John 15:18</note>. If the world hated him through whom the world was made, should we—the most lowly of **little men** <note>original: "homuntiones"—a diminutive, self-deprecating term for humans</note>, and, if we weigh our own shames, most worthy of all reproaches—be so distressed if someone disparages or curses us, that we ourselves begin to act badly just so that he might not speak ill of us? 

Let us instead receive these curses eagerly. And even if our happiness is not so great that we might endure lashes, chains, prisons, or swords for the sake of virtue and truth—as our **heroes** <note>Pico refers to the early Christian martyrs as "heroes"</note> did of old—let us think it has gone well enough for us if we suffer at least the insults of wicked men, their detractions, and their hatreds. Otherwise, with every occasion for merit taken away from us, no hope of a reward would remain. 

If men praise you for living well, then your virtue, insofar as it is virtue, makes you similar to **Christ**; but insofar as it is praised, it makes you dissimilar to him, who received the death of the cross from men as the reward for his virtue. On account of this, God—as the Apostle says—**exalted him and gave him a name which is above every name** <note>original: "exaltavit eum, & dedit illi nomen quod est super omne nomen" — Philippians 2:9</note>. It is therefore more desirable to be crucified by the world so that you may be exalted by God, than to be exalted by the world and then be judged by God. For the former crucifies unto life, while the latter exalts unto [worldly] glory; the former exalts to heaven, while the latter judges one to **Gehenna** <note>A term for Hell or a place of fiery torment</note>. 

Finally, if the world applauds you, it can hardly happen that your virtue—which, being directed entirely upward, ought to have only God to please—does not lean a little toward the flattering favor of men. And even if it does not lose its integrity, it nevertheless loses some of its reward; for when a reward begins to be paid on earth, where all things are small, it will be less in heaven, where all things are immense. 

Blessed are the insults that keep us safe, lest the flower of justice wither by the pestilential breeze of **vainglory** <note>original: "inanis gloriæ"</note>, or lest the wages of eternity be diminished for us by the empty contract of popular rumor. Let us embrace these insults, my son, and let us, as faithful servants, take pride with a most holy ambition in the ignominy of the Lord’s cross alone. **"We preach,"** says Paul, **"Christ crucified: a stumbling block to the Jews, and foolishness to the Gentiles; but to us, the power and wisdom of God"** <note>original: "predicamus... Christum crucifixum hebreis quidem scandalum, gentibus stultitiam..." — 1 Corinthians 1:23-24</note>. This wisdom of the world is foolishness before God, and that "folly" of Christ is what conquered the wisdom of the world, through which it pleased God to save those who believe. If you do not doubt that those who disparage your virtue and call the Christian life—that is, true wisdom—"insanity" are themselves insane, then consider how great your own insanity would be if you were moved from the path of a right life by the judgment of the insane. Every error should be removed by correction, not increased by imitation.

<summary>Pico della Mirandola writes to his nephew Gianfrancesco, encouraging him to embrace worldly criticism and "the folly of the cross" as signs of divine favor and authentic Christian virtue. He argues that being hated by the world aligns the believer with Christ and protects them from the spiritual dangers of pride and earthly rewards.</summary>
<keywords>Gianfrancesco Pico della Mirandola, imitation of Christ, Apostolic dignity, vainglory, persecution, virtue, folly of the cross, Christian ethics, stoicism</keywords>

--- Page 320 ---
<meta>This page continues Pico’s letter to his nephew Gianfrancesco. The previous page established that being slandered by the wicked is a sign of "Apostolic dignity." Pico now urges his nephew to ignore worldly critics and focus on the brevity of life and the judgment of God.</meta>

Let them gape, let them howl, let them bark; you, however, continue the journey you have begun without fear. Consider how much you owe to God for their wickedness and misery—He who has illuminated you as you sat in the shadow of death, and who has brought you out from the company of those who wander here and there in the thickest darkness without a guide, joining you instead with the children of light. Let that sweetest voice of the Lord sound always in your ears:

> Let the dead bury their dead; you, follow me. <note>original: "sine mortuos sepellire mortuos suos/tu me sequere"; a quote from Matthew 8:22. Pico uses this to distinguish between the spiritually "dead" worldlings and the "living" followers of Christ.</note>

For those who do not live for God are dead; and in this span of temporary death, they most laboriously acquire eternal death for themselves. If you were to ask them where they are heading, or where they direct their studies, works, and cares—or finally, what end they have set for themselves in the attainment of which they might be happy—they will either have nothing at all to answer, or they will speak words that conflict and disagree with one another, like the ravings of fanatics. For they themselves do not know what they are doing; rather, like those who swim in rivers, they are carried along by the force of ill-borne habit as if by the rush of a torrent. From here, with wickedness blinding them and Satan goading them toward evil, they rush headlong into every crime as blind leaders of the blind, until unforeseen death seizes them, and it is said to them:

> Friend, this night they require your soul from you; but these things you have prepared, whose will they be? <note>original: "Amice hac nocte repetent animam tuam a te/hæc autem quæ parasti cuius erunt"; from the Parable of the Rich Fool in Luke 12:20.</note>

Then they envy those whom they once despised; they praise those they once abandoned. They would wish to imitate those they cannot, whom they preferred to persecute when they were able to follow them. Therefore, my **dearest son**, stop up your ears with wax <note>A classical reference to Odysseus, who plugged his sailors' ears with wax so they would not be lured to their deaths by the song of the Sirens.</note>, and holding as nothing whatever men might say or feel about you, look only to the judgment of God. He will render to each according to his works at his revelation from heaven with the angels of his power, in a flame of fire taking vengeance on those who did not know God, nor obeyed his gospel. These (as the Apostle <note>Referring to St. Paul in 2 Thessalonians 1:9</note> says) will pay the penalty in eternal destruction from the face of the Lord and from the glory of his power, when he comes to be glorified in his saints and to be marveled at in all who have believed. It is written:

> Do not fear those who can kill the body. But fear Him who can cast the soul into hell. <note>A paraphrase of Matthew 10:28.</note>

How much less should you fear those who can harm neither your body nor your soul! If they now disparage you for living according to reason, they would disparage you no less if you abandoned virtue and were overwhelmed by vice—not because vice displeases them, but because the vice of disparaging always pleases them. Flee, if your salvation is dear to your heart; flee their company as much as you can. Returning to yourself, pray often in secret, crying out to the most merciful Father with the prophet:

> To you, Lord, I have lifted up my soul. My God, in you I trust; let me not be ashamed, even if my enemies mock me; for indeed, all who hope in you shall not be confounded. Let those be confounded who act iniquitously in vain. Show me your ways, O Lord, and teach me your paths; lead me in your truth and teach me, for you are God my Savior, and in you will I hope all the day long. <note>Pico quotes Psalm 25 (Psalm 24 in the Latin Vulgate tradition).</note>

Likewise, see that you always meditate upon imminent death. Realize that the time we live is but a point <term>point (punctum)</term> <note>In medieval philosophy, a "point" is the smallest indivisible unit of time or space, emphasizing the extreme brevity of human life.</note>—indeed, less than a point. Consider how evil is that **ancient enemy** <note>A common title for the Devil (Satan).</note> who promises us the kingdoms of the world to snatch from us the kingdoms of heaven; how false are the pleasures that embrace us only to strangle us; how deceitful the honors that lift us up only to cast us down; how lethal the riches which, the more they feed us, the more they poison us; and how brief, uncertain, shadowy, false, and imaginary is everything that includes all these things together...

<summary>Pico encourages his nephew to ignore worldly critics, comparing them to the "spiritually dead" and "blind guides." He uses biblical and classical imagery to urge a focus on the soul’s salvation and the extreme brevity of life compared to eternity.</summary>

<meta>This page concludes a letter from the philosopher Giovanni Pico della Mirandola to his nephew Gianfrancesco. The previous page warned of the dangers of worldly living and the suddenness of divine judgment. This section transitions from the personal advice of the letter to a formal, poetic prayer (the "Deprecatoria") which reflects Pico's deeply spiritual and penitent later years.</meta>

...even if such things flow to us according to our every wish, they can provide [little]. How great are the things promised and prepared for those who, despising present things, sigh for that fatherland <note>original: "patriam"; Pico refers to the heavenly kingdom as the true home of the soul.</note> whose King is Divinity, whose Law is Charity, and whose measure is Eternity. Occupy your mind with these and similar thoughts, which may rouse the sleeper, kindle the lukewarm, strengthen the wavering, and provide wings of divine love to one striving toward heaven; so that when you come to us—which we all expect with great desire—we may see you not only as the man we want, but also as the *kind* of man we want you to be. Farewell. And love God, whom you once began to fear. Bigus <note>Likely Ludovico Bigi Pittorio (c. 1452–1525), a Latin poet from Ferrara and a friend of Pico.</note> salutes you. Ferrara, July 2, 1492.

## Giovanni Pico of Mirandola’s Prayer of Plea to God.

Gracious God, who, to be revered in highest majesty,
Truly holds one divinity in a triple power <note>A reference to the Christian Trinity: one God in three persons.</note>
To whom, above the flaming walls of the high world,
The blessed throng of the angelic choir serves.
Whose omnipotent right hand once created
This immense work, visible to our eyes:
You who twist the heavens, who direct the world with a nod,
From whose command the sent lightnings fall:
Spare us, I pray, the wretched; wash away our filth, I pray,
Lest the just punishment of your fury drive us to ruin.
For if our debts were weighed in an equal balance,
And if the standard of your judgment were severe,
Who could bear the horrific whip of the living Avenger,
And endure his heavy blows?
Not even the Fabric of the World <note>original: "Machina"; a common Renaissance term for the universe or the structured "machine" of the cosmos.</note> itself would withstand your angry right hand—
That Fabric not meant to perish until the final day.
What mind is not condemned from the origin of the first sin? <note>A reference to Original Sin.</note>
Or what mind has not been made guilty by its own crime?
But certainly you are that very one whose nature it is always to spare,
And who holds justice with equal mercy:
You who repay rewards far greater than merits,
And likewise give punishments lighter than the evils committed.
For your mercy is greater than our faults,
And to give to the unworthy is a thing more worthy of God.
Although they are worthy enough, if He deigns to love them—
For He Himself makes worthy those whom He finds unworthy.
Therefore, I pray, look upon your people with a peaceful, pitying face,
Whether you prefer them to be your servants, or rather to be defendants <note>original: "reos"; a legal term for those standing trial.</note>:
Defendants indeed, if you should look upon the crimes of our life...

<meta>This page continues the "Deprecatoria" (Prayer of Plea) by Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, picking up from the previous page's unfinished thought regarding the weighing of human sin against divine mercy.</meta>

...[the work] of an excessively ungrateful mind.
    But if instead you look upon your gifts within us—
    Gifts ennobled by your most excellent blessings—
    We are the very ones whom nature once made your servants,
    And whom holy grace soon after made your own children.
    But (alas!) the indulgence of such a great destiny weighs upon us wretches:
    Those whom grace made children, guilt has made defendants.
    Guilt made us defendants; but let grace conquer guilt,
    So that your honor may increase through our crime: <note>Pico employs the theological concept of the "happy fault" (Latin: *felix culpa*), suggesting that human sin allows for a greater demonstration of God’s mercy and glory.</note>
    For while your wisdom or your power might otherwise
    Be known for displaying their riches to the world,
    A greater glory of goodness shines through our errors,
    And that love shines forth, to be loved above all things:
    The love that could lead the Lord down from high heaven,
    And lift the limbs of the highest God onto the cross;
    So that the blood and water from your side
    Might wash away the filth so poorly contracted from our forefather’s seed. <note>original: "patrio de semine"; a reference to Original Sin inherited from Adam, the "father" of humanity.</note>
    Thus your love and mercy, most gentle King,
    Allow evils to provide the very material for such great blessings.
    O love, O mercy, so well-provided for our needs!
    O goodness, made the servant of your own servant!
    O love, O mercy, so poorly understood in our times!
    O goodness, now almost overwhelmed by our evils:
    Grant, I pray, that there may be a heat in our hearts
    To match this great love that always burns.
    Grant that we may cast off the yoke and lay down the empire
    Of Satan, whom we repent having served for so many years.
    Grant, I pray, that the fires of a frantic mind be extinguished,
    And let your love live within our breast;
    So that when the spirit, having finished its duty of mortal life,
    Shall be led before its Lord,
    Having gained the happy lot of the promised kingdom,
    It may perceive you not as a master, but as a father.

->THE END<-

# Various testimonies of the life, doctrine, and commentaries of Giovanni Pico della Mirandola. Collected from various places, though many from these most celebrated men and others have been omitted.

### Two letters from Brother Baptista Mantuanus, a Carmelite, and a most learned and eloquent theologian, to Gianfrancesco Pico della Mirandola, Count of Concordia, etc., concerning the death of Giovanni Pico, his uncle. <note>Baptista Mantuanus (1447–1516) was a famous Neo-Latin poet and theologian, often called the "Christian Virgil." Gianfrancesco Pico was Giovanni’s nephew and his primary biographer.</note>

<margin>47</margin>
**I**llustrious Lord. Having recently heard of the death of your uncle Giovanni Pico, a most renowned and learned man, I was so struck with dismay in my soul that neither my feet nor my mind could sufficiently perform their duties. I was very nearly moved to complain against both God and Nature: that they should take such a great light from the world so quickly, such an ornament of Italy, such a glory of our age—as if they envied the earthly republic of its goods, and cut him down without any regard for us. They cut him down even while he was growing, while he was flourishing, and while he was nourishing everyone with the most abundant fertility of his genius. But remembering the saying of Paul, where he says "the judgments of God are a great deep," <note>original: "iudicia dei abyssus multa"; a reference to Psalm 36:6, often cited by St. Paul in his theology of divine mystery.</note> I restrained myself, lest I should think ill of God and His works with impious rashness. 

Upon the sunset of this man, literary studies, the knowledge of things, and integrity of character suffered a great eclipse. For in your uncle (as you know), linguistic erudition and the knowledge of human and divine matters were so joined with a holiness of life that in one and the same man I seemed to see Jerome and Augustine brought back to life. <note>St. Jerome and St. Augustine were the premier scholars of the early Church, representing the ideal union of classical learning and Christian faith.</note> And if only he had finished that work *On the Harmony of Plato and Aristotle* <note>original: "de concordia Platonis & Aristotelis"; Pico’s ambitious, unfinished project to prove that the two greatest Greek philosophers were ultimately in agreement.</note> before he passed away! For its title promised the whole philosophy of the ancients and the uncovering of the most hidden matters most worthy of knowing. 

All his small works—those he completed and those he left unfinished—must be sought out with all zeal and diligence; for since they flowed from such a happy genius, they cannot but be most worthy of being read, loved, and adored by all posterity. I would summon you to this duty, were I not certain that you were already sufficiently persuaded and so-minded. This immortal honor was lacking to your family: that alongside its ancient nobility, its abundance of riches and wealth, and its glory in military affairs, there should also be placed the excellence of such great wisdom, so that all things which among mortals are worthy of the highest praise might flow together into your single house. 

It truly befits you, Gianfrancesco, to strive with all your might so that you may possess your uncle's virtue as an inheritance, and that his spirit might be doubled within you, just as the spirit of Elijah was in Elisha. <note>A biblical reference to 2 Kings 2:9, where the prophet Elisha asks for a "double portion" of his mentor Elijah's spirit.</note> This we expect of you; this we require. When you have collected his works, I pray that you make me a participant as well; it will be worth my while to betake myself there for the sake of such great pleasure once I know of it. I will subjoin a couplet in his praise, composed on the spot, even if it might not please. Farewell, best of princes, and love me. At Mantua, the 27th day of November, 1494.

->Giovanni Pico—learned in the heavens, the elements, and God—<-
->Died while still a youth, made holy.<-

<meta>This page continues the correspondence from the Carmelite theologian Baptista Mantuanus to Gianfrancesco Pico della Mirandola, following the death of the latter's uncle, the philosopher Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, in 1494.</meta>

<page-num>49.</page-num>

<margin>I</margin>**llustrious** Count Gianfrancesco, the most honorable delay of your response had made me believe that my letters had perished on the road. While I was therefore determining to send you new ones, and had already begun to write them, your most longed-for, most elegant, and most delightful letters arrived. On the following night—I believe because of what I had been thinking about during the day—as I slept toward dawn (the time when dreams are usually seen as true), the image of your uncle, now deceased, seemed to appear to me. To our shared and greatest pleasure, he discussed many things with me concerning the nature of angels, and the types, names, and duties of spirits of the air, the earth, and even the water. 

When I asked him why he was stuttering (for he seemed to be a stutterer in the dream), he replied that it was a sign of the imperfect and unfinished discourse which he had begun long ago concerning the nature of things and philosophy. <note>Giovanni Pico died at age 31, leaving his massive work "Against Divining Astrology" and other philosophical projects incomplete. The stutter represents the "silence" of an unfinished life.</note> I seemed to be burning with a desire to inquire about many hidden things which are wonderful and unknown to us mortals; and I don't know how it occurred to me first to ask what use amulets and corals were to infants, and other things of that kind which are tied to the necks of little children. He replied that there is sometimes some virtue in these things, and this pertains to <term>natural magic</term> <note>magia naturalis: a Renaissance concept involving the study of the hidden properties of plants, stones, and stars to produce beneficial effects, distinguished from "black magic" or demonic sorcery.</note>; but for the most part, they are condemned customs and superstitions. 

Having said these things, he vanished. Having woken up, I thought long and hard about what we had discussed in our sleep, because they seemed not to be empty things but to have some weight. I write this, however, not because I place any faith in dreams—for that is foreign both to my profession and my nature—but because I cannot sufficiently wonder how it happens that those who sleep can dispute, teach, learn, and often do things which are impossible or certainly difficult for those who are awake. Our souls certainly possess some spark of divinity. If we lived holily and piously, and our minds were not spun around by so many winding paths of business, the separated spirits would have great commerce with us. 

But enough of these things. As for your wish, as you write, to compose the life of your uncle, I both praise it and urge and beseech you to do it more promptly. For this duty is most fitting for you, and must be taken up by you for several reasons: for you are very strong in style and eloquence, which is a gift of nature, industry, and a singular gift of God. Likewise, since you are his kinsman and closely related by blood to such a wonderful man, it happens that you cannot help but share in his glory. Nor should you in any way allow your most illustrious family to lose any of such great ornament and splendor. Added to these things is that his life should be known to no one more than you, whom you had long ago proposed for yourself to imitate. And indeed, most wisely; for he was an extraordinary example of holiness and religion, in whom the light of all wisdom appeared. 

I will say to you, therefore, what Christ said to the apostles: "Gather up the fragments, lest they be lost." <note>original: "colligite fragmenta ne pereant"; quoting John 6:12. In the Renaissance, this was a common metaphor for collecting the scattered writings or memories of a deceased scholar.</note> This must be done all the more studiously as it will be more profitable for us who survive and for future generations. Undoubtedly, although I see he is more to be congratulated because, after such a short voyage, he collected so much spiritual wealth and happily reached port, I cannot however help but grieve with you over the loss of such a great man. 

The death of Giorgio Merula <note>An Italian humanist and historian (c. 1430–1494) who taught in Venice and Milan.</note>—first my fellow student and later my teacher (for we served together under Gregorius Tiphernas <note>A Greek scholar who was instrumental in bringing Greek studies to the University of Paris and Italy.</note>)—has affected me with sadness. But he was already aged and, with his heavy old age, was becoming useless and had finished his duty. [The deaths] of Hermolaus and Politian, two... <note>Referring to Hermolao Barbaro and Angelo Poliziano, two of the greatest scholars of the age, who both died in the same period (1493–1494).</note>

<meta>This page concludes the letter from the Carmelite monk Baptista Mantuanus to Gianfrancesco Pico and begins a new section of letters from the scholar Ermolao Barbaro to Giovanni Pico della Mirandola. The previous text described a dream in which the late Giovanni Pico appeared to the author.</meta>

<sig>XX ii</sig>

The mournful death of illustrious men has brought a heavy grief both to me and to all learned people. But this wound has seated itself deeper: literary affairs have suffered a far greater loss in our Pico. The fields of eloquence mourn; the studies of the mathematical arts have collapsed. All philosophy, and the highest speculations of metaphysics and theology—which he had already begun to amplify and illustrate—will henceforth fall silent. But I stop now, lest I indulge too much in a justified grief. We must rather take care to become like him in the studies and exercises of the sciences, and in integrity of morals and religion, so that, enriched by a similar trade <note>original: "negotiatione"; referring here to the "business" of intellectual and spiritual labor</note> as he was, we may one day arrive where he now rejoices to have reached. I will come as soon as I can, so that I may see and adore the immortal remains of his divine genius which are in your possession. Meanwhile, devote your effort to writing his life story, and love me. Farewell. To your Lordship, to whom I commend myself. At Mantua, the 3rd day of January, 1495.

->Brother Baptista Mantuanus, Carmelite.<-
