->Five letters of Ermolao Barbaro, the most celebrated man and Patriarch of Aquileia.<-

->Ermolao Barbaro sends greetings to Giovanni Pico della Mirandola.<-

<margin>A .50. t</margin>
Truly, Pico, you owe me nothing, neither in terms of silence nor any service on my part toward you; indeed, your letters caused me great blushing. You apologize to me for my own negligence as if it were yours, when instead it should have been redeemed by us at any price. This is the goodness, the candor, and the fairness of your intellect: you recognize the fault of another as your own when you could either avoid it or certainly share it. You are anxious over a mutual offense, though even before the accusation <note>original: "antecategoria"; a legalistic term for a preemptive defense</note> you could have been secure in a better cause. Either both of us are guilty, or you are not. Otherwise, you have already cleared yourself as far as you are concerned. It remains that I myself should give satisfaction. 

But what can best be written by me to you? I shall exhort you to continue to love literature, in which you are most eminent. I will advise you to devote yourself to virtue and good morals, in which you have made such progress that it is difficult to know which part of philosophy you have spent more effort upon: the part containing the theoretical <note>original: "spectatiuas"</note> and instrumental arts <note>the "tools" of philosophy, such as logic and dialectic</note>, or the part embracing dogmatic and moral instruction <term>paraeneticen</term> <note>paraenetic: a style of writing intended to provide moral advice or exhortation.</note>. Altogether, it is a supreme thing and greater than human capacity, which you—owing either to your own genius or certainly to your Maker—have achieved at such a tender age, whereas to hope for such things in extreme old age would be most impudent. 

These things are not yours, Pico; they belong to nature; they belong to God. Yet, if anything is yours, these are most especially yours. See how much less they can be called "yours": the nobility of fortune, health, or beauty—goods in which you yield to no one, just as you yield to no one in those things which are more truly your own. I exhort you to turn your attention here: revolve this day and night—how great a debt you owe to Him who has enriched you to such an extent that you will never be able to repay or even calculate what you possess. Think how much He can do, He who willed that you be able to do these things; how much He loves you, He who chose you for Himself out of so many thousands. You, who while almost a boy <note>Pico was famously a child prodigy who challenged the scholars of Europe at age 23.</note> surpassed old men, and who, not yet an <term>ephebe</term> <note>a youth entering manhood, typically aged 18-20.</note>, turned the assemblies of learned men toward admiration of your learning. Unless you see this, unless you value it, I affirm to you right now and declare with a free voice: you are not yet as great as you truly are. It is an immense and infinite thing that I long ago promised myself regarding you, and continue to promise; but neither speech nor proclamation can keep up with the opinion I have formed of you. I do as people usually do who...

### Ermolao Barbaro to Roberto Salviati, sends greetings.

<margin>a
if.
f</margin>
You suggest, Salviati, if you suspect anything other than my busy schedule was the reason I have not yet replied to you: this is a common and much-touted excuse for silence. But by Hercules, it is so true that unless you accept it, you would seem to deserve poorly of my love, faith, and devotion toward you. All your letters are always most welcome to me, but those especially so in which there is mention and the name of my Mirandola <note>Giovanni Pico della Mirandola</note>. Nothing is more wonderful in literature than that man alone; there is no one whom I would rather see praised, honored, and raised to the heavens. There is no one from whose praise I can less easily depart. In this, I am perhaps excessive, yet I seem so to no one; there is so much praise in him, so boundless, that there is no room left for ambition or flattery. 

I have read his *Apology* <note>Pico's *Apologia*, written to defend his 900 theses against charges of heresy</note>, and in it—why does he attribute so much to me, who deserves so little? Why does he name me with such an honorable preface as if I were an ordinary witness, not to say a Gregory <note>Likely referring to Saint Gregory the Great, an ultimate authority</note>? Especially in that work, than which nothing is more subtle, more powerful, or more acute. However, it is better that I defer my judgment for a while until I have read the whole thing clearly. 

As for what you wish to know about what I am doing, what else can I say except that I study? Public duties <note>Barbaro was serving as a Venetian ambassador</note> certainly take away some of my persistence—or rather, from my studies, but not from my persistence. For I press on more sharply and exact my "task" more severely; I repair with diligence whatever my greater business has taken from me. The more business has increased, the more eagerness and alacrity it has struck into me. Thus, all those holidays which a private man would give to his health, I distribute to public service; and what I lose for one reason, I gather back by another means. 

I believe I have written to you at other times, or that those who have heard it from me told you, that the *Instrument* of Aristotle <note>The *Organon*, Aristotle's collected works on logic</note> (for that is what the Peripatetics usually call his Logic), and likewise the eight books of *Physics*, and his three books of *Rhetoric*, were translated by me into Latin some time ago. My *Dioscorides* <note>Barbaro's massive commentary on the ancient Greek pharmacological text by Pedanius Dioscorides</note> is now finished; the final touch is now being applied by me. The daughter’s dowry is ready; she will be settled very soon <note>A scholarly metaphor: Barbaro refers to his book as his daughter and its publication as her marriage</note>. Then, relieved of that burden, I shall devote myself entirely to Aristotle. Unless God calls me elsewhere, he will go forth finished, at least in the Logic, within about two years from the publication of the *Dioscorides*, along with the commentaries which I have already completed on the *Posterior Analytics*. After...

...I will begin these published works on natural and divine matters: likewise the *Rhetoric* and *Poetics*, equipping all the volumes of that philosopher <note>Barbaro is referring to Aristotle, whom he spent much of his life translating and correcting from the original Greek.</note> according to my strength, partly with commentaries and partly with annotations. Every day I experience the truth of the saying that grasping for everything is the same as grasping for nothing. Farewell. ## Ermolao Barbaro to Giovanni Pico, sends hearty greetings.

<margin>
a
fz
e
</margin>
Three days ago, your *Hexameron* <note>original: "Xameron". This refers to Pico's work on the seven days of creation, more commonly known as the *Heptaplus*.</note> was delivered to me by the effort of Salviati; I read it so greedily that on the very first day, and not even the whole of it, I drank the whole thing in without a breath. Three things in it delight me wonderfully: first, that your speech teaches and moves; it is well known that the ancient theologians in sacred letters, and even the Pythagoreans and Platonists in natural philosophy, observed this, while more recent writers sweat only over teaching. Second, that amidst such a wealth of material and such freedom to plunder <note>A common humanist metaphor for borrowing or citing from earlier authorities.</note>, you keep such chaste and innocent hands; or rather, in this style of writing, you seem to have followed yourself and no other. This is common neither to the ancients nor to the moderns, but is unique and your own. In this, I will open my mind to you: I am so affected that, because those predecessors did not say what you have said, they seem to me to have said almost nothing. Third, I see that you have been initiated into the sacred mysteries not so much of Aristotle as of Plato and his schools; you have brought full drafts from there into this late-night work <note>original: "lucubrationem", a term humanists used for scholarly work produced by the light of a lamp.</note>. I pass over how many excellent things from Plotinus <note>A 3rd-century philosopher and the founder of Neoplatonism.</note> you have touched upon briefly and elegantly, so that whatever is contained in his nearly fifty-four volumes, arranged into six Enneads <note>original: "nouenarios", referring to groups of nine.</note> by Porphyry, you seem not just to have read but to have mastered by heart. Nor can I pass over this: that you conduct yourself as a middle ground between the new and old theologians, such that you neither despise the simple majesty of the former nor are carried away by the ambitious subtlety of the latter. Thus it happens that while you wish to imitate the one, you are able to master the other; you have plucked the best of both kinds. We hope you will do the same in your explanation of the Davidic poem <note>The Book of Psalms, attributed to King David.</note>. Farewell. Venice, the day before the Nones of September <note>September 4th</note>, 1489.

<meta>This page concludes the letter from Ermolao Barbaro to Giovanni Pico della Mirandola dated August 1490 and contains a subsequent letter from March 1491. It also begins a new correspondence from Battista Mantovano to Pico's nephew, Gianfrancesco.</meta>

...is a form of tyranny, though you, following your own brilliance, interpret it as humanity and kindness. They are acting in their own interest; they look to their own accounts; they redeem their own fame—those who support and desire yours. Truly, the less you owe your creditors—that is, your praisers—the more they owe you, since you make them your creditors whether they like it or not. O unheard of kind of debt: for the creditors to exist without there being a debtor! But I am too busy to be able to play with you any longer. But you, how relaxed you are—good gods!—to allow anyone to take a holiday. I pray you have endured my long joke thus far; I do not ask that you admit it, only for a brief little yawn. Farewell, along with my Politian <note>Angelo Poliziano, the famous Florentine humanist and close friend of both Barbaro and Pico.</note>.

### Ermolao Barbaro, Venetian orator and Patriarch of Aquileia, to Giovanni Pico, sends greetings.

<margin>54</margin>
**I**t is well; it is fitting. Since you love me so much, you congratulate me greatly on the Patriarchate of Aquileia <note>Barbaro was appointed to this high ecclesiastical office in 1491 by the Pope, which led to his permanent exile from Venice, as the city-state forbade its citizens from accepting such posts without permission.</note>; you even attribute much greater things to me and prophesy for me more than I could hope for, if I were most ambitious, or deserve, if I were most modest. I know your devotion toward me; I see how much you value me. I recognize the strength of your love; nothing is more certain to me. Would that it might someday be possible for me to live with you, to philosophize about nature, about God, and about holy morals. How much I desire this, and how much of an addition I judge it would be to my prosperity if this should happen, I can neither express, nor would I wish to in this place even if I could. I pray that if you ever judged me worthy of your benevolence, I may be held by you in the same category, and even a better place if possible. Consider Ermolao a priest now, so that you may more closely cherish and hold dear as a soldier of Christ him whom you loved as a secular person <note>original: "paganum seculi," referring to his life before his ecclesiastical appointment.</note>. As for you and your most illustrious virtues, I can no more fail to proclaim, admire, and extol them than you can fail to increase them. If I flatter you or lie to you, let me be a source of contempt to all learned men; for a long time now, amazement at you and your affairs has held me.

Now there is wonder and ecstasy of knowledge. You will read these things patiently, and your heart will not be exalted, nor will you have haughty eyes. For why should you be pleased with yourself, you who know that these good things you possess are not yours, nor from your own savings <note>original: "peculio," a term for the small assets a person in servitude was allowed to hold as their own.</note>, but are granted and belong to the Master? Forgive me. The north wind of truth and the west wind of charity have seized me and carried me away. Farewell. Rome, the day before the Kalends of April <note>March 31st</note>, 1491.

<meta>This page continues the correspondence concerning the works of Giovanni Pico della Mirandola. It concludes a letter from the poet Battista Mantovano to Pico’s nephew, Gianfrancesco, and begins a new letter from the scholar Matteo Bosso to Roberto Salviati regarding Pico's "Heptaplus."</meta>

I have always followed its author with reverence. But in reading it, while I desired to
quench one thirst, another thirst grew: namely, the longing to see the rest. When I 
have attained this through the gift of your favor, I shall consider myself to have 
achieved a great part of my happiness. Your uncle Giovanni Pico has, in my judgment, 
surpassed all the philosophers of our age, especially for these reasons: that while 
others consume their lifetimes only in the dogmas of Aristotle and the Peripatetics 
<note>Followers of Aristotle’s philosophy</note>, he himself, with Herculean audacity, 
has scrutinized the sects and families of all philosophers, both ancient and modern, 
with a marvelous vigor of mind. And whereas the moderns follow no flower of 
oratory, he has so joined philosophy with eloquence that he can be said to have 
restored the ancient and true Academy <note>The school of philosophy founded by Plato, which prized both deep thought and beautiful language</note>. These things 
are worthy of all the greater admiration because he ascended to such a height of 
virtue and glory with such swift study and in so few years. Nor does he seem to have 
sought knowledge, as others do, through labor and study and many late-night 
toils, but to have found it all at once by chance—as usually happens to those 
who, while doing something else entirely, unexpectedly stumble upon a treasure. 
Happy, therefore, is your family for such a student; happy is our age, illuminated by 
such brilliance from this man. Farewell, most worthy prince, and remember how 
much you must strive so that you may be held a worthy imitator of your uncle. I 
hate these distances between places, for I long to be with you, so that you might 
share in my studies and I in yours. Again, fare well and fear God. 
Mantua, October 29, 1494.

### Matteo of Verona, Canon Regular, to Roberto Salviati, sends greetings.

<margin>SG i</margin>The interpretation of the six days in which God created all things, written by 
our Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, which you sent to me as a gift—inscribed and 
noted by him as the *Heptaplus* <note>From the Greek "Heptaplous," meaning "sevenfold"; Pico’s work explaining the creation story in Genesis through seven layers of meaning</note>—even if it is clearly of such a kind that it cannot 
easily be skimmed and understood at the same time by a reader, nevertheless, the 
beginning of the work so inflamed and drew me that, eager for the end and 
hardly catching my breath, I did not so much taste it as certainly devour it, 
though it must finally be chewed over with more diligent study and by a longer 
lamp. It seemed to me that our Giovanni here not only is skilled and wise in 
all philosophy and whatever is contained within the laws of nature, but even 
raises himself above human things, flying through the sublime. He has turned 
hidden mysteries and heavenly sacraments toward mystical senses and 
allegories, which those of our time who are considered wise and learned 
scarcely notice or pass over entirely unattempted. Here he explains the most 
difficult and celestial matters, and—as much as the subject allows—opens, 
discloses, and illuminates them more brightly than the sun. And what is 
wonderful: while still a youth and living in the secular world, he joins himself 
closely with the likes of Dionysius, Hilary, Damascene, Augustine, Ambrose, 
Jerome <note>A list of major early Christian theologians and "Church Fathers"</note>, and other such most holy and rare men of old. All posterity will 
admire him when envy has grown quiet and the passing days have established 
his authority. For what we believe the supreme God will give him...

->From a letter of Ermolao Barbaro to Giovanni Pico.<-

<margin>57</margin>
Your genius is illustrious and clearly divine, Pico: for since those things which you write are the best, you nevertheless express and shape the works of others (which are of the worst quality) so that they seem to be yours (which are the best). For I consider it a matter of <gloss>o</gloss> greater <margin>o worth, I reckon:</margin> worth to lower oneself and descend than to strive for lofty heights. For while the latter is more honorable, the former is certainly more laborious and a work of greater effort. Therefore, whether you believe our writings to be such that you should spend effort imitating them, or whether you do this for the sake of putting me in your debt: in both ways I owe you very much. I intend to return the favor at some time; I do not want to say "when I am able" (for I shall never be able), but when you yourself or your family think I am able. For such is the goodness and humanity of your whole family that you are accustomed to credit as a benefit that which is not one. Wherefore, I shall act for my own benefit if I leave both the manner and time of reclaiming the favor to you, so that in the clearing of accounts every <term>false reasoning</term> <note>original: "paralogismus," a piece of illogical or fallacious reasoning</note> and deception may proceed not from me but entirely from you. 

Indeed, what you wrote about the plan of your studies and wished to communicate with me has affected me with the greatest pleasure. I have congratulated this century for a man of such learning that he knows almost nothing <note>A paradoxical compliment: Pico’s knowledge is so vast it encompasses everything, yet he remains humble</note>, and of such care that he seems to know nothing at all. I see you are an excellent poet and a most eminent orator. I notice that you, previously an <term>Aristotelian</term> <note>A follower of the philosophy of Aristotle, which dominated medieval universities</note> philosopher, have now also become a <term>Platonic</term> <note>A follower of Plato, whose works were being rediscovered and translated during the Renaissance</note> one. I see that you have not only learned Greek letters—which alone were lacking in you and without which you would have been nothing—but have mastered them. And you did this with such ease and speed that neither do you remember that you were once ignorant of Greek letters, nor could you persuade others of it; this is something I proclaim about my friend Girolamo Donà <note>Girolamo Donà (c. 1457–1511), a Venetian humanist, diplomat, and close associate of Ermolao Barbaro</note> no less gladly than truly. I would exhort you to these letters so that you might hold them as plainly and familiarly as Latin, but you do not need spurs, etc.

For when I myself, in a certain corner of my mind within a letter to you—as if occupied with something else and only in passing—attacked the "barbarian" <note>original: "barbaros." It was a work comprised of many thousands of lines, explained and unfolded: an elegant, learned, and elaborate work. You finished it with such great speed that, had I not possessed a most thorough perspective on the riches of your genius, I would have believed this argument had been prepared by you long ago, just so you could bring it forth at the first available opportunity. But so that the matter might turn out both more witty and more pleasant for me, you—a most charming, refined, and most "Latin" <note>original: "latinissimus." This refers to Pico’s mastery of pure, classical Latin style, contrasting with the "barbarians."</note> man—defend a barbarian against a barbarian. You did this as if an enemy were standing up for an enemy, a companion against a companion, pretending to stand and act as an advocate against your own self. And so forth.

Greetings. Certainly, the laws and the subject matter of the work do not demand a hurried opinion prepared for the present moment. But at the same time, it can be said that it is almost a miracle that Pico, most learned, most eloquent, and most Christian, has achieved all these things at such an age. I owe you very much.

It does not escape me—nor did it ever escape me while you were spending your life in Padua—Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, how great the excellence of your genius was, and how great your eloquence. You have indicated this more clearly in many matters always, but especially in this, your most learned narration on Moses <note>The *Heptaplus*.</note>. Indeed—to speak for myself—you have not only confirmed my entire opinion of you, which I had long ago conceived as being the best, but you have also nourished and increased it in a wonderful way, and raised it to the very summit. Truly, I was so delighted in reading this work of yours that I think nothing more excellent or more worthy could be held; it is something that ought to be read or heard by everyone. For while many things worthy of praise are recognized in this most brilliant work of yours—things which are powerful not only when joined together but even individually—this in particular stands out: that you have spoken (as that famous man says) with a divine, not a human, mouth. Furthermore, you have attained such facility in explaining the enigmas of Moses, which Jesus Christ seems to have granted to you alone—who are otherwise well-deserving of Him—and to no one else. For I am not ignorant...

this is a gift from some celestial nature rather than something attained by any lower power. ->Girolamo Donato to Roberto Salviati. Greetings.<-

**I** was provoked by you in affection with great enchantments just a little while ago by the sweetest gift of the *Heptaplus* <note>Pico's *Heptaplus* (published in 1489) is a seven-fold interpretation of the first chapters of Genesis.</note>. Then by your most recent, kind, and elegant letter: either one could have been enough to fulfill all the requirements of friendship. To this was added our Seraticus <note>Likely a mutual friend or messenger.</note>, a man as upright in character as he is elegant in letters; for his sake as well, I cannot help but love you greatly. From this, I prefer to be privately conscious of how much I owe to your kindness rather than writing it to you. The benevolence of Pico toward me, already perceived before, deserves to be judged even more pleasing to me on the strength of your testimony. I know how much I ought to value being loved and praised by that man in whom the rewards of learning and character have combined with the greatest glory of our age. It is more fitting to admire his *Heptaplus* than to judge it. That style of writing delights me wonderfully: I see no richer harvest of both doctrine and erudition from any source other than the Sacred Scriptures. But that boldness is successful in very few men, among whom is my Pico. Greet him as much as you can in my name; for this very reason I am most dear to myself: because I love him vehemently. You, Salviati, shall promise yourself as much from me as is fitting to be provided by a most friendly and well-wishing man. Farewell. Milan, October 25, 1489.

->Battista Guarini to the most learned prince Giovanni Pico della Mirandola. Greetings.<-

<margin>61.</margin>
**O**ur Pictorius <note>Likely a messenger or minor scholar associated with the court.</note>, with his usual rather quick pace, brought your little gift to me in recent days. ### Cristoforo Landino to Roberto Salviati, greetings.

<margin>q</margin>

**H**ow pleasing, how delightful, and how distinguished your gift was to me, I do not believe I could express even in a second Iliad <note>The writer suggests that even an epic poem as long as the Iliad would be insufficient to describe his gratitude.</note> in proportion to the magnitude of the thing. For what could proceed more appropriately from you—at once a most liberal man and a most learned gentleman—or be brought more expectedly to me, who am most greedy for letters, than that exact <term>Heptaplus: Pico della Mirandola's famous sevenfold commentary on the seven days of creation in Genesis.</term> on the Genesis of Moses by our Pico? He is easily the prince of all letters and teachings in our age, and this work is wonderfully composed. 

For although we see this subject treated learnedly, distinctly, and eloquently by countless Hebrews, many Arabs, and not a few Greeks and Latins—so much so that I believed not a word more could be added—he himself, beginning the entire matter with a nearly new argument and arriving by an unusual path at the same things that seemed already well-trodden and common to everyone, has described them in such a way that even the most learned admire them as if they were new and unheard of. 

Because of this, he has carried me—who until now have never stepped outside the borders of Tuscany—through all the regions and tracts of the earth. I was carried by no horse, conveyed by no beasts of burden, but drawn along by the perpetual vehicle of his reason. With no trouble, he led me forth; and leaving the continent behind, I was carried across all the seas by his narration as if in Neptune's chariot—not on Arion’s dolphins <note>In Greek myth, the poet Arion was rescued from the sea by dolphins after being cast overboard.</note>, let alone on human ships. 

These things could indeed seem great and incredible to everyone. But there are other things that are greater and worthy of even greater admiration. For lifted up from the waters—I know not whether by swan's feathers, or by the wings of Daedalus or Pegasus—I arrived through all the air, through all the ether, to the very summit of corruptible things, with him not merely leading but carrying me up. It is a thing truly worthy of extreme amazement: to have traveled through this lower and elemental world, but to have reached much further into the celestial world! I penetrated the first orb of the Moon, then of Mercury and Venus; I saw the rays of the Sun; I felt the fires of Mars; and finally, I came to know the health-giving rays of Jupiter and the heavy rays of Saturn. Then, at last, I reached that eighth sphere, shining with burning stars. And all these heavens...

<meta>This page continues the introductory letter from the Florentine humanist Cristoforo Landino to Robert Salviati, prefacing Giovanni Pico della Mirandola's *Heptaplus*. Landino reflects on his deep reading of the work and uses a playful etymological analysis of Pico's names to praise his intellectual prowess.</meta>

...observed to revolve not by a simple and uniform motion, but by a triple and threefold one. Yet who is unaware that all these things fall under our senses? Moreover, he <note>Referring to Pico della Mirandola.</note> allowed me to soar into the **third world** in such a way that, with all senses lulled to sleep—for these hinder rather than help such an inspection—I might traverse these vast spaces with the mind alone. For indeed, by the mind alone are they traversed. And I would indeed have beheld and looked through it, but its sight, like an owl's eyes in the sun's rays, becoming blind, could not withstand such great splendor. 

Therefore, whatever in this kind of pilgrimage—or to speak more truly, a **return to the homeland**—either lay hidden from me or escaped my eyes, the guide himself <note>Pico.</note> is not to blame; rather, the fault is easily found in the one to whom it was shown. For the divine genius of **Giovanni Pico della Mirandola** both promises and delivers that it will demonstrate all things. 

What is there, then, my **Robert**, that I should not confess I owe to you, having been enriched by so great a gift from you? As soon as I began to taste it, such a greed was at once awakened in me, and such a love for feasting on the sweetness of this food, that, impatient of any delay, I entrusted nothing to be chewed by the jaw, but like a most greedy bullock, I devoured the whole solid mass. But when, through continued reading, I had gone through the whole matter, and like that same beast, having gathered it in my stomach and calling it back to my mouth, I ruminated upon it more carefully; then indeed a wonderful sweetness appeared, and then a stupor such as never before came upon me. 

But you will say: "Did you not admire the man's learning before?" I did admire it, because he was so involved in all disciplines that he seemed to excel in each individual one. No topic escaped him when disputing in physics, none in mathematics; and in metaphysics and every kind of theology—whether you seek that which was stirred up by **Hermes** <note>original: "mercurio." Landino refers to Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary founder of Hermeticism, which Pico integrated into his philosophy.</note> and brought to perfection by **Plato**, or our own **Christian theology**, the most excellent and truest of all—these ages of ours, and even several before them, have seen nothing more learned than him. 

But lest you think (a fault by which most of us are troubled) that he separated eloquence from wisdom—does he not describe everything most weightily, most abundantly, and moreover most elegantly? He can now, by his own best right, be numbered among those ancient orators. I used to admire these things about him to such an extent that I thought nothing could be added to such discovery. But having read through his ***Heptaplus***, I have now begun to wonder how I ever admired those earlier things in comparison. 

Therefore, I believe it happened neither rashly nor by some chance, but by God's command, that this divine man should be distinguished by these three names. For **Giovanni** <note>original: "Ioannes" (John).</note> is interpreted as either "the grace of the Lord," or "in whom is grace," or "to whom a gift has been made by God." Who would not see that he could not have attained the learning he has reached without the special and greatest grace of God? 

In the **woodpecker** <note>original: "pico." Landino makes a pun on Pico’s surname and the Latin word for woodpecker, *picus*.</note> we know there is such hardness of the beak and strength of the head that you will find no wood, however bony (so to speak) or stony, that this bird does not pierce; and in it, he skillfully carves out a hiding place where he may withdraw and build his nest. In the same way, therefore, nothing from all the disciplines is so difficult for human intellect to know that he himself, by pounding, has not penetrated even its hardest parts, nested there, hatched his young, and brought them forth. 

Since indeed all things in this man are to be **wondered at** <note>original: "miranda." A pun on his title, the Count of "Mirandula" (Mirandola).</note>, who would not think he should be called **Mirandula**? For this reason, just as I congratulate you, who enjoy his constant friendship, so I grieve for myself—for myself, I say, who consider myself unhappy in this respect, because on account of many and necessary...

<summary>Cristoforo Landino praises Pico della Mirandola's "Heptaplus," arguing that Pico's intellect transcends the physical senses to grasp divine truths. He uses symbolic etymologies of Pico's names—John (grace), Pico (the industrious woodpecker), and Mirandola (wonderful)—to illustrate his genius.</summary>

...my busy schedule does not allow me to stick by his side day and night, though I desire it most ardently. For if it were permitted, I would never leave the side—I do not say of an old man, but of a young man; I mean a youth in whom all wisdom and all learning is as mature and gray-haired as an elder’s. <note>Landino employs the "puer senex" (old-souled youth) trope to praise Pico’s precocious genius.</note>

You, however, to whom fortune has offered far greater **leisure** <note>original: "ocium," referring to scholarly retirement or time for study.</note>, and to whom nature has granted an excellent intellect—which your long-standing practice in all the liberal arts and frequent usage has since increased and polished—enjoy this good gift fallen to you from heaven. Drink from this most fertile fountain, or rather, this immense ocean; and drink so much that it may suffice to quench not only your present thirst but every future thirst as well. Reflect then upon yourself; calculate and argue with yourself how very few mortals have ever received so much good.

The great **Alexander** <note>Alexander the Great.</note> boasted that he had lived in the time of such a great philosopher as Aristotle. But to you, it has been given by your most happy fate to have lived familiarly with both an **Aristotle** and a **Plato** at once; and such an Aristotle and Plato that in them, besides the ancient doctrine of the **Academics** <note>The followers of Plato.</note> and **Peripatetics** <note>The followers of Aristotle.</note>, we see our own Johns, Dionysiuses, Augustines, Jeromes, Thomases, and other lights of this kind shining back. Therefore, from these things, conclude how much you ought to love either yourself or him for this, my best **Robert**; for fortune herself has offered this to you, and you, by your own prudence, have succeeded in making yourself particularly intimate with this man. Farewell. November 22nd. <note>The Latin date "x. Kalen. Decembris" (the tenth day before the Kalends of December) corresponds to November 22nd.</note>

->### Alessandro Cortesi to his Pico, Greetings<-

<margin>63 e</margin>
<note>The letter 'e' in the margin serves as a guide for an intended decorative initial 'E' for the word 'Ego'.</note>
<insert>I</insert> have never in my whole life received greater pleasure than recently from your letters; and although I had believed the very highest things of you, you have nevertheless (I confess) surpassed my opinion of you. Indeed, you have surpassed it so far that although your glory is already spread far and wide, I now consider those boundaries too narrow. Let us speak more openly and far from the flattery from which illustrious souls always shrink. What is there in you that is not extraordinary? What is not worthy of admiration? Individual qualities could honor any man, but in you, all have been brought together equally. From everyone (if I may say so) you, as one man, have stolen every charm. <note>original: "omnes ueneres," literally "all the Venuses," a metaphor for intellectual and aesthetic graces.</note> And although your ancestors reached a point that few could easily reach unless born of them, you have nevertheless turned out so great that you seem to return more grace to them than you received. While old age brings authority to others, youth extols your dignity; and what others surpass by time, you have overcome by invincible virtue.

In my judgment, you are placed beyond every gamble of genius <note>meaning his talent is a certainty, not subject to the "roll of the dice" or doubt.</note>, and as I search through Greek praises, I find no one to whom I may deservedly compare you. To sum up, one may believe that someone equal to you existed at some time, but it is not possible to see one in this present age. Let all the gifted men grant me pardon: they are all far surpassed by this one Pico. Nature’s kindness has so cherished him that it must seem a wonder even to her that such a great abundance of all praises has been gathered into one man. Why do you blush? Or do you think I am being false? I would indeed yield if you attributed this to love, which is painted blind. But I have witnesses: my friend **Poliziano** <note>Angelo Poliziano, the renowned poet and scholar.</note>—who is deceived only regarding me—and others even more substantial. And although he increases his riches of gold daily, as I hear, no less than his riches of speech, I congratulate him equally and give him thanks. I wish that he might possess the **horn of plenty** <note>The Cornucopia.</note>, since he is not unmindful of hospitality...

->### Girolamo Donà to his friend Giovanni Pico, greetings.<-

<margin>64.</margin>
Those parts which should have been mine, you have taken all for yourself, most learned Pico: accusing yourself of negligence toward me, and seeking an excuse in that very crime of which I am most guilty toward you. It seems too little to you to excel others in genius and erudition, unless you also conquer—not only others but even yourself—in modesty and kindness. But indeed, I pray, embrace the gifts of these virtues in such a way that you leave us some opportunity to fulfill our own duty, lest while you claim all these parts for yourself, we be considered inhuman and uncivil. In this matter—such is my impudence—I no longer excuse my negligence but rather accuse your kindness. Because you write that you have established not a temporary but a perpetual friendship with me, I understand that I owe you much for that reason alone; but truly you also seem to have defined friendship correctly for me: since if it is temporary, it can no longer be friendship. Know this: I have set that friendship apart among the choice of my ornaments. For what can come to me more illustrious than not only to be praised but also to be loved by such a great man?

I see that our **Hermolao [Barbaro]** <note>Hermolao Barbaro (1454–1493), a prominent Venetian humanist and diplomat.</note>, through an incredible tranquility of learning and a care for his studies through **diligence** <term>philoponia: love of labor or industriousness</term>, is especially learned in utility—something supreme and rare which letters can hope for while he is safe. I preserve his companionship—which you envy me so much—in the same storehouse as your friendship. Moreover, I judge nothing so **wonderful** <term>thaumaston: marvelous or admirable</term> that you cannot attain it by your genius and erudition, especially since I hear you have moved there <note>Likely referring to Pico's move to the outskirts of Florence to study.</note>; a plan I praise so much that I could not praise it more. For **nothing is sweeter than to know everything** <note>original: "ouden glykyteron ē pan eidēnai"</note>. I envy you **Poliziano** <note>Angelo Poliziano, the famous poet and scholar.</note>, a man of the most fertile and eloquent genius, whose *Rusticus* <note>A didactic poem on country life published by Poliziano in 1483.</note> I recently read; he seemed to me the splendor of our age and <note>blank space in original</note>. I ask you to promise these things of me to him in my own words: things which can be expected from a most friendly man. I use you as a messenger in inaugurating my goodwill with him, relying on your kindness...

## Filippo Beroaldo to Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, Greetings.

<margin>c</margin>
**C**enaturus <note>Latin: "About to dine." The marginal 'c' indicates the missing initial letter for the start of the letter.</note> at the home of **Minius Roscius** <note>Domenico Rossi, a refined Bolognese scholar and senator.</note>, who is most polished in literary studies and the greatest ornament of our senate, I was reading the plays of **Plautus**, which overflow with the most sophisticated wit, when your letter was brought to me—exceedingly learned, polished, and sharp. Immediately setting aside the comic charm, I began to read your most delightful writings with haste. Good gods, how much grace, how much erudition, and how much majesty we found within them!

A great reputation had preceded **Giovanni Pico**, but he was found to be even greater; nothing trite, nothing trivial resonates in your writings. The matter matches the words, and the words the matter, perfectly. You speak Latin purely. You use a splendid and magnificent eloquence. You possess a <term>dialect</term> <note>original: "Dialecton"; here referring to a particular literary style or manner of speaking.</note> full of pleasantness and clarity, and a most abundant supply of the finest words. Your thoughts are frequent and well-rounded; you express the feelings of your mind so clearly and elegantly that the immortal gods seem to have given to you alone what they have granted to very few: namely, to think the best things and to say the best things. And you encompass this no less in verse than in prose.

**Livy** and **Homer** write, almost by divine inspiration, that the gods have not granted all things to one man. This is why we often read of some who flourished by excelling in eloquence, and others endowed with erudition, but very few have stood out as both eloquent and erudite at the same time. For this reason, the two peaks of the Roman tongue are cited as **Terentius Varro** and **Marcus Tullius Cicero**: from the former, knowledge of things was sought; from the latter, knowledge of words. One is called most learned in every respect by **Terentianus**; the other is called most eloquent by all.

As **Seneca** excellently says, that happiness of genius deserted **Virgil** in prose; **Cicero** wrote poems with no grace and no charm, clearly with the Muses unwilling and resisting. But you are both most learned and most eloquent; you who are powerful in verse as well. You write things worth reading; you are skilled in things that must be written. You can deservedly be called a foster-child of the Muses; for you have not, like many, drunk only one or two of the Muses' mixing bowls, but like a second **Apuleius**, you have drained every bowl, and especially that clear and nectar-like bowl of <term>philosophy</term> <note>original: "philosophiae"</note>, which very few touch even with the tips of their lips, and barely greet from the threshold.

Oh, great fecundity of mind! Oh, most blessed richness of immortal genius, which has forged such virtues in **Pico della Mirandola** while still a boy, still a youth; which has poured in so many various disciplines and implanted such gifts of the soul. He who is a mere recruit in age is a veteran in erudition. Proceed, most learned man, as you have begun; ensure that as the years increase, your knowledge grows, your genius matures, and your memory becomes more vigorous and supportive. You, who in your youth are the glory of our age and an example of virtue. 

What sort of man will you be in old age? **Papinian** <note>A celebrated Roman jurist.</note> is called by **Spartianus** "the asylum of the law" and "the treasury of legal learning." You shall be called by us the "asylum of the liberal disciplines." To us, whenever something hidden in literature...

<summary>Filippo Beroaldo praises Giovanni Pico della Mirandola for his rare ability to master both eloquence and deep philosophy, comparing him favorably to classical figures like Cicero and Varro.</summary>
<keywords>Filippo Beroaldo, Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, eloquence vs. erudition, humanism, classical comparisons, philosophy, Apuleius</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Filippo Beroaldo’s letter to Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, emphasizing Pico’s mastery of both Latin and Greek and his effortless command of all branches of knowledge. It then introduces a new letter from Bartolomeo Fonzio to Roberto Salviati regarding Pico’s "Heptaplus."</meta>

you will encounter an inner treasury; or rather, to speak more truly, you are already a treasury yourself. All things, even the most hidden in literature, are at your hand; everything presents itself readily. That "circle of learning" <note>original: "orbis ille doctrinae"; the Greek concept of *encyclopedia* or a well-rounded education.</note> which is praised by the learned seems to be in your service. Both Greek and Latin letters are handmaidens to you. You are permitted to nourish your genius now with this meditation, now with that, for one is the seasoning of the other. And just as various and changed seeds recreate and restore the earth, so the changing of studies refreshes and delights the mind. You may gladden your talent with the sweeter studies of poetry if it ever tires from the more austere dogmas of philosophy. 

You, finally, stand at the citadel and peak of the noble disciplines, while we sweat barely on the first slope. You have climbed the narrow path of virtue with a giant's stride; we attempt to climb with the pace of a tortoise or an ant, and we labor on rough paths, now slipping, now nodding, and stumbling. I write what I feel; I feel what I write; my pen agrees with my mind. I am moved by an incredible desire to see you together with **Poliziano** <note>Angelo Poliziano (1454–1494), the brilliant Florentine humanist and poet.</note>; a desire I shall satisfy within a very few days. For **Minius Roscius** <note>Domenico Rossi, a Bolognese nobleman and scholar.</note>, who is most fond of all men of letters and who pursues us both especially with a wonderful love, is coming there during these Easter holidays to fulfill his vows. 

I shall accompany the man. Then it will be possible to join right hands in turn and enjoy mutual conversation. Then I, a mere man of letters and grammarian, shall approach, address, and greet you, the most learned of men. Then I, who seem wise here, will perhaps mutter there, or like a goose among swans, I will sound off with a noisy clatter. Meanwhile, farewell, asylum of letters; love me in return, and greet the most missed **Poliziano** in my name. 

Bologna, the sixth day before the Ides of March [March 10], 1486.

->**Bartolomeo Fonzio** to **Roberto Salviati**<-

<margin>66 f</margin> **G**reetings. Indeed, I have never read anything with greater pleasure, **Roberto**, than your **Pico** <note>Referring to a work by Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, likely his *Heptaplus*.</note>, which I read last night for two reasons: both because it was sent by you, a most friendly man, and because I love the author of the work for himself—whom I thought it would be a disgrace not to have read by now. Through your kindness, I have truly obtained what I most desired. I give thanks to you for such a gift, and I vehemently congratulate him for having published such a work, which ought to be celebrated by all of Christendom. In it, I truly doubt whether to wonder more at the numerous and great discoveries of things, or at the incredible order within such variety, or at such great elegance of speech in such laborious descriptions. 

For what I might mention regarding the *Heptaplus* <note>Pico’s work *Heptaplus* (1489), a mystical and philosophical commentary on the seven days of Creation.</note>—which most commends authors of such works—is that there is no loquacity, no swelling of pride, and a singular modesty in all things, without any suspicion of envy. Would that I could have returned a similar gift to this most sweet and desired one of yours, so that you might see my mind toward you more clearly. But what I could do, I have done: I have sent to you, first of all, the oration I recently delivered at Buda to King **Matthias Corvinus** <note>Matthias Corvinus (r. 1458–1490), the King of Hungary and a famed patron of humanists.</note>. 

When you have read it yourself, you shall also give it to your **Pico** to read. I judge him to be the most outstanding in every kind of learning among all those of our age whose writings I have seen thus far. Farewell, and continue to love me in return.

### Battista Guarini to the most learned prince Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, Greetings.

<margin>67</margin>
<margin>n</margin>
I do not yet concede that the lawsuit should be settled in your favor. For I can easily turn those clever traps of yours <term>turning back against you</term> <note>original Greek: αντιστρέφοντα (*antistrephonta*), a logical term for an argument that can be reversed against its proponent.</note>. If I am your teacher, why do you not obey me? If I am not, why do you call me teacher? I do not refuse this title because I despise you as a student—you, whom I declare to be my own teacher—but because I both venerate and proclaim your learning. In this learning, I am conscious that I have promoted you not by the prayers of my talent, nor by the mark of a crossed pen, nor by little wax marks, nor finally by an obelisk or asterisk. <note>Guarini refers to the specialized marks used by classical editors to flag errors or noteworthy passages; he is saying Pico’s brilliance owes nothing to his own red-penning.</note> But we seem to have fallen into a new kind of judicial case, while you strive to assign to me that possession <note>The "possession" refers to the credit for Pico's immense knowledge.</note> which I am trying to assign to you. What case of the orators ever had a plaintiff or defendant of this kind? I, my Pico, will never <term>yield the prize</term> <note>original: *herbam porrigam*, a Roman idiom meaning to pluck grass and hand it to a victor as a sign of surrender.</note> to you in this fight unless we first settle on good terms: since you will not submit otherwise, each of us shall be judged equally as both teacher and student to the other. 

But jokes aside, let us deal with serious matters. Both your **Heptaplus** <note>Pico’s famous sevenfold narration of the six days of Genesis, published in 1489.</note> and you yourself can rightly be pleased with your work. Since you have won every vote of learned men, so that not even the slightest hint of envy appears in the record. It is to be hoped that the same will be more easily granted to you in your other writings, especially once experience is added, which is usually considered the best teacher in writing. As for what concerns me, I rejoice greatly that I am spoken of by that praised man, and one who should be praised by everyone and everywhere: **Lorenzo**. <note>Lorenzo de' Medici (1449–1492), the "Magnificent" ruler of Florence and patron of the arts.</note> Especially with the addition of **Poliziano's** <note>Angelo Poliziano, the leading poet and scholar of the age.</note> judgment, whose copious and secret reading of multifaceted discipline I so embrace that I admire it, and so admire it that I shall not cease to commend it. Thus it happens that I consider it like a triumph to be placed by him beyond the "gamble of learning." 

As for your asking for an index of my books, that is laborious for me and useless; it will be enough if you attend to my requests as time permits. Now, I desire **Martianus Capella** and **Seneca’s** *Natural Questions*, provided the manuscripts are corrected. For those that are here among us <term>need the work of a Sibyl</term> <note>meaning the manuscripts are so corrupted or messy they would require a prophetess to decipher.</note>; if I can buy them in printed form, it will be more pleasing to me; if not, they will return to you after a short stay. Farewell, my hope and the hope of the liberal arts; continue to love me. Ferrara, the 5th of December, 1489.

### From a letter of Hermolao to Giovanni Pico.

<margin>67</margin>
<margin>q</margin>
Indeed, I love these letters of yours because they flow, because they are not affected, and because they—I will not say do not know care—but rather they reject it. That is, they do not accept care by design, and they shut out anyone who wishes to approach or intrude upon them with artificiality. So it is that there are indeed traces of diligence deep within them, but they are in a way repressed and repudiated. I am not so skilled that I can look into your genius and estimate its magnitude and fecundity. I seem to see—and perhaps I am not mistaken—where you are aiming and directing your path, and indeed where you will soon arrive. Nothing is more noble than that natural talent of yours, nothing more remarkable; and if it may be said once, even if a bit harshly, nothing brings forth more vigor—if indeed it should even be called "talent" <note>Hermolao suggests Pico's "talent" is so fully realized it has surpassed the status of mere potential.</note>. For it has already produced fruits that should not be despised even by those of mature age and the most practiced learning. Come now, how great, as I hear, is your spirit in poetry! What felicity! What strength! Finally, what nobility and splendor in every act, especially in literature!

Hermolao Barbaro follows with a tribute to the natural, unforced elegance of Pico's writing style.</summary>

How is it that when you act the philosopher: what memory, what great subtlety, what speed of mind you show, which accords so well with the vigor of your whole body. ### From a letter of Hermolao Barbaro to Giovanni Pico.

<margin>
70
</margin>
<margin>g</margin>
I have congratulated this age on a man of such great learning that he knows almost nothing <note>The Latin *nihil fere nesciat* (knows almost nothing not) is a double negative meaning he knows everything.</note>; and with such great care that he seems to know nothing at all <note>A compliment to Pico's humility; despite his vast knowledge, he acts with the modesty of one who knows nothing.</note>. I see that you are an excellent poet: and that you are, or soon will be, a most eminent orator. I notice that you were first an Aristotelian philosopher, but now you have also become a Platonic one. I see that you have not only learned but have drunk deeply of Greek letters <note>The "Greek letters" refers to the study of the Greek language and its literature.</note>—which alone could have been found lacking in you, and without which you would have accomplished nothing. You did this with such facility and speed that you yourself no longer remember, nor could you persuade others, that you were ever once ignorant of Greek. This is something I say no less willingly than truly about my friend Girolamo Donato <note>A Venetian nobleman and fellow humanist scholar.</note>. I would urge you and the rest.

### From a letter of Jacopo Antiquario to Angelo Poliziano.

<margin>n</margin>
Do not, therefore, allow the offspring of your long incubation to waste us away in expectation; rather, accept Pico as a guarantor for the security of your name, for his whole life is full of glories. I hope with all my prayers that you will be received by him into his circle of friends. I always adore his footsteps. Whatever is born at home from that <term>flock of fattened birds</term> <note>original: *altilium cohorte*. Antiquario uses a metaphor of poultry-raising to describe Poliziano’s refined literary works.</note> should be sent out to be looked at, read, and learned by heart; you will hold everyone fast by your strings who is said to possess some likeness of virtue or harmony. Farewell.

### Angelo Poliziano to his friend Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, Greetings.

<margin>
71
</margin>
<margin>a</margin>
I have laughed almost always (perhaps too immodestly), but I have always burned with a desire for perpetual fame, so much so that surviving glory was considered as nothing in comparison. But since what I was writing hardly promised even the survival of my name, you appeared, Pico, who provided what I could not. You did this by dedicating your commentary *On the One and the Being* <note>original: *De uno et ente*. This was Pico's famous attempt to reconcile the philosophies of Plato and Aristotle, arguing they were fundamentally in agreement.</note> (for so you titled it) to me. In this work, you call back the streams running through the <term>Lyceum</term> <note>The school of Aristotle.</note> and the <term>Academy</term> <note>The school of Plato.</note> to a single source. And since philosophy is more a single thing than a twin, you also join it to our theology. What <term>grass of Glaucus</term> <note>original: *glauci gramen*. In mythology, the fisherman Glaucus became an immortal sea-god after eating a magical grass. Poliziano is saying Pico’s dedication has made him immortal.</note> should I now seek, since I am to live forever through you? But I shall live with you as well; and posterity will one day tell that there was once a certain Poliziano whom the great Pico himself—the light of all learning—held in such high esteem that he did not hesitate to dedicate his most beautiful book on the most sublime matters to him. Therefore, I give you thanks for my immortality—but they are immortal thanks. Farewell.

# Marsilio Ficino of Florence to Germain de Ganay, President of Paris, sends greetings.

<meta>Original text: S.D. (Salutem Dicit), a standard Latin greeting.</meta>

YY iiii <note>This is a signature mark used by early printers to keep the pages in order during binding.</note>

<margin>
a
JZ
c
</margin>

You wish to be more certain regarding the death of Pico della Mirandola, which, as it seems to you, remains uncertain; you wish, Germain, to grieve more surely. For since you have until now grieved heavily over this ambiguous loss, once you have been made certain, you will soon—as I believe—grieve most heavily of all. Perhaps it was better to mourn a doubtful loss than to be tortured by a certain one. Alas, what do you ask, my most beloved Germain? I myself would rather remain in doubt. Nor can I, at this moment, make you more certain without tears. This past November, on the very day that the great King Charles of the French entered our city of Florence, our dear Mirandola left us. He affected the learned with almost as much grief as the King, in the meantime, gave joy to the city. Thus, the provident genius of the place balanced the joy of the people with the groans of the scholars; and in exchange for an extinguished philosophical divinity, it kindled a royal light. This was done perhaps so that Florence would not seem too dark on that day: the light of Mirandola was extinguished on earth and returned to heaven. For Pico migrated from this shadow of life with such cheerful security that he seemed, beyond any doubt, to be returning from a kind of exile to his heavenly fatherland.

You desire, furthermore, to know what Pico composed in the past, or what he was composing lately. He wrote the *Hexameron* <note>original: "Exameron"; a commentary on the six days of creation, published as the Heptaplus.</note>, the *Apology*, and a treatise *On the One and the Being*, as well as several letters. Whatever he had composed regarding love during his fervent youth, he later condemned with a more mature judgment and wished to be entirely destroyed; it cannot be published without doing him an injustice. Indeed, I knew the last will of that pious man. For in age Pico was like a son to me, in familiarity a brother, and in love truly my other self. He was laboring daily on three things: the harmony of Aristotle with Plato, commentaries on the Sacred Scriptures, and the *Confutations of the Astrologers*. All these were disputed with as much eloquence as subtlety. But as clear as they were in style, they were sketched in such new and obscure characters <note>This refers to Pico's notoriously difficult handwriting or shorthand.</note> that they could hardly be read by him. Therefore, they have not yet been finished or revised by him, nor can they be transcribed by others, unless perhaps they can divine his meaning. For if they could be transcribed, we would not miss our Pico so much as one who is absent, nor would we even suspect he was gone. But his pious nephew, Giovanni Francesco, powerful in both letters and intellect, strives daily to rescue these works from darkness into the light, and he is writing the life and deeds of his uncle. Receive, finally, this epigram of ours concerning him: "High priests very rarely grant the more secret mysteries to the eyes, and immediately hide them away again; thus God showed to mortals the divine philosopher Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, ripe in the thirtieth year of his age."

So that you may be aware of the rest of the loss to literature that occurred this autumn in Florence: our friend Angelo Poliziano, most learned in the Latin and Greek languages, departed from this life in the September immediately preceding Pico's death, in the fortieth year of his age. He had already published his *Miscellanea*, the *Sylvae* <note>A collection of occasional poems.</note>, and certain declamations and letters—all composed with sharpness and elegance. He also daily noted down many things necessary for elegance in the same uncertain characters as Pico, so that in both men a grave loss to literature has occurred. 

March 23, 1494. <note>In the Florentine calendar, the year began on March 25th; by modern reckoning, this is 1495.</note>

# Marsilio Ficino of Florence to Gianfrancesco, Count of Mirandola and Concordia, sends greetings.

<margin>e</margin>
I sent a brief letter to France regarding the death and the praises of Pico after your departure. You may, however, gather extensive and singular praises of Pico from my many writings throughout the years: especially from the later books of my letters. There are now twelve of these in print. You may also find them in my preface to Plotinus <note>Plotinus was a 3rd-century Neoplatonist philosopher whom Ficino translated and admired</note>, in the book *On the Sun*, and in my commentaries on the *Timaeus* and *Parmenides* <note>Two significant dialogues by Plato</note>. Please accept this epitaph for him: "The High Priests very rarely allow the more secret mysteries to be seen by eyes, and they immediately hide them away again. Thus God held out to mortals the divine philosopher Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, mature in his thirtieth year." Let the epitaph end here. God seems to have given Giovanni Pico the most abundant goods of soul, body, and fortune—if only He had granted a longer span of life. But it is not right to accuse Providence even in this. For if God had led him to the summit, beyond the powers of nature, in the shortest time, he perhaps could not have progressed to anything better. On the other hand, the shifting nature of the world does not allow one to remain at the same peak. And his perfected virtue would not tolerate a slide back toward the worse. But you yourself have written of these and other such matters better and more extensively in your *Life of Pico* <note>Gianfrancesco wrote a famous biography of his uncle</note>—not so much to illuminate him (for who could add light to the sun?), but rather to clear away the clouds and bring his hidden works, which are most worthy of light, into the clear. Therefore, both mortals will wonderfully commend your great piety toward your uncle, and God will judge it worthy of no small rewards.

->On the first day of November, 1495.<-

## Twelve rules of Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, partly for awakening and partly for directing men in spiritual combat.

**The first rule:** If the way of virtue seems hard to a man because we must continually fight against the flesh, the devil, and the world, let him remember that whatever life he chooses—even according to the world—he must suffer many adversities, sorrows, inconveniences, and labors.

**The second rule:** Let him remember that in worldly matters, the fight is longer, more laborious, and more fruitless; in these, labor is the only end of labor, and finally, there is eternal punishment.

**The third rule:** Let him remember that it is foolish to believe one can reach heaven except through a struggle of this kind, just as our head, Christ, did not ascend into heaven except through the cross; nor should the condition of the servant be better than the condition of the master.

**The fourth rule:** Let him remember that this combat is not only to be endured with difficulty, but even to be desired—even if no reward were to come to us from it—solely so that we may be conformed to Christ our God and Lord. And as often as you use force against any of your senses by resisting some temptation, think of which part of the cross of Christ you are being made conformable; for example, when resisting gluttony you afflict your sense of taste, remember that he was <note>original: "felle potatum & aceto"</note> given gall and vinegar to drink. <meta>This page continues the "Twelve Rules" of Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, specifically detailing the final spiritual strategies for the Christian "soldier." The previous page introduced the context of Pico’s death and the beginning of these devotional rules.</meta>

...If you restrain yourself from the seizure of any thing that pleases you, think of His hands fixed for you to the wood of the cross. And if you resist pride, remember Him who, though He was in the form of God, took the form of a servant for you and was humbled even unto death on the cross. And when you are tempted by anger, remember Him who was God and the most just of all men, yet when He saw Himself treated like a thief, mocked, spat upon, scourged, and afflicted with every insult, and counted among thieves, He never showed any sign of anger or indignation; instead, bearing everything most patiently, He replied to all most gently. And so, by running through each point individually, you may find that there is no suffering that does not, in some part, make you conform to Christ.

**Fifth rule:** that you should not trust in those twelve weapons <note>Pico previously outlined "Twelve Weapons of Spiritual Warfare" including the love of God, the brevity of life, and the uncertainty of death</note> nor in any other human remedy, but in the power of Jesus Christ alone, who said: "Have confidence, I have overcome the world" <note>original: "confidite ego uici mundum"; from John 16:33</note>; and elsewhere: "The prince of this world is cast out" <note>original: "Princeps mundi huius eiicitur foras"; from John 12:31</note>. Therefore, let us also trust in His power alone: both to be able to conquer the world and to overcome the devil. And for this reason, we must always seek His help through prayer and through the prayers of His saints.

**Sixth rule:** remember that when you have conquered one temptation, another is always to be expected; for the devil always circles about, seeking whom he may devour. Therefore, it is necessary to always serve in fear and to say with the prophet: "I will stand upon my watch" <note>original: "super custodiã meã stabo"; from Habakkuk 2:1</note>.

**Seventh rule:** that you should not only avoid being conquered by the devil when he tempts you, but that you should conquer him. This happens when you not only do not sin, but from the very thing by which he had tempted you, you take the opportunity for some good. For example, if he offers you some good work of yours so that you might fall into vanity, you should immediately think of it not as your own work, but as a gift from God; humble yourself and judge that you are not grateful enough to God for His benefits.

**Eight rule:** that when you fight, you should fight as if you are about to win and then have perpetual peace; for perhaps God will give this to you by His grace, and the devil will no longer return, having been put to shame by your victory. But when you have won, behave as if you are soon to fight again, so that in the fight you are always mindful of victory, and in victory, you are always mindful of the fight.

**Ninth rule:** that however much you feel yourself well-fortified and ready on all sides, you should nevertheless always flee the occasions for sinning; for as the wise man says: "He who loves danger will perish in it" <note>original: "q̃ amat piculum pibit in illo"; from Ecclesiasticus 3:27</note>.

**Tenth rule:** that in temptations you should always resist at the very beginning and "dash the little ones of Babylon against the rock" <note>A metaphor from Psalm 137:9; the "little ones" or infants represent the very first stirrings of sinful thoughts, and the "rock" represents Christ. It means to kill off bad thoughts before they grow into actions</note>. The rock, moreover, is Christ; for a remedy is prepared too late <note>original: "sero medicina paratur"; a common Latin proverb meaning it is better to prevent an illness than to cure it</note>.

**Eleventh rule:** remember that although the fight may seem bitter in the very conflict of temptation, it is nevertheless far sweeter to conquer the temptation than to go toward the sin to which it inclines you. In this, many are deceived, because they do not compare the sweetness of victory to the sweetness of the sin. Instead, they compare the struggle to the pleasure. And yet a man who has experienced a thousand times what it is to yield to temptation ought to try, at least once, what it is to conquer temptation.

**Twelfth rule:** if you are tempted, do not believe yourself to be forsaken by God, or to be little pleasing to God, or insufficiently just and perfect. Be mindful that after Paul saw the divine essence, he suffered a temptation of the flesh, which God permitted him to be tempted by, lest he be tempted by pride. In this, a man ought also to notice that Paul, who was...

<meta>This page continues the spiritual commentary on the Psalms, specifically moving into a line-by-line exposition of Psalm 16 (Psalm 15 in the Vulgate). It follows the previous discussion on guarding against pride by using the words of David and the Apostle Paul as a shield.</meta>

...he has bestowed many benefits upon you. And these three things are in God: first, because for his service nothing new is received that is not good for us, both as to the soul and as to the body; for to serve him is nothing other than to tend toward him: that is, toward the **highest good** <note>original: "summum bonum"; the ultimate source of happiness and the final goal of human existence in Christian philosophy.</note>. Similarly, he himself is the best, most beautiful, and most wise: and he possesses all the conditions which usually move us to love someone and serve them freely. Furthermore, he has bestowed upon us the greatest benefits, since he both created us from nothing and redeemed us from hell through the blood of his son.

---

### PRESERVE me, O Lord. <note>original: "CONSERVA me domine"; the opening of Psalm 16:1.</note>

If anyone who is perfect wishes to acknowledge his state, he faces one danger: that he may become proud of his own **virtue**. Therefore David, speaking in the person of a righteous man about his state, begins with this word: **preserve me**, which, when rightly considered, removes every occasion for pride. For he who can acquire something by himself can also preserve it for himself by himself. He, therefore, who asks to be preserved by God in a state of virtue signifies by this that he did not acquire that virtue by himself from the beginning. Moreover, he who remembers that he has attained virtue not by his own power, but by the power of God, cannot be proud of it, but is rather humbled before God according to that saying of the **Apostle** <note>St. Paul.</note>: *What do you have that you have not received? And if you have received it, why do you boast as if you had not received it?* <note>1 Corinthians 4:7. Pico uses this to emphasize that all human excellence is a gift from God.</note> There are, therefore, two phrases which we ought always to have in our mouths: one, namely, *have mercy on me, O God*, when we remember our sins; the other is *preserve me, O God*, when we remember our virtues.

---

### BECAUSE I have hoped in you. <note>original: "QVONIAM speraui in te"; the second part of Psalm 16:1.</note>

This is the one thing that causes us to obtain from God what we ask: namely, when we hope that we shall obtain it. And if we observe these two conditions—that we never ask from God anything except those things which are salutary <note>conducive to salvation or spiritual health.</note> for us, and that we ask for what we seek ardently with a firm **hope** that God will hear us—our prayers will never be in vain. Therefore, when we do not obtain something, it is either because it is harmful to us—for we do not know what we should ask for, as **Christ** says—and **Jesus** said: *Whatever you ask in my name will be given to you.* For this name, **Jesus**, signifies "Savior"; and therefore nothing is asked in the name of Jesus except that which leads to the salvation of the one asking. Or he does not hear us because, even if we ask for good things, we do not ask well; that is, we ask with little hope. For he who hopes timidly, asks coldly. Therefore **James** said: *But let him ask in faith, nothing wavering.* <note>James 1:6.</note>

---

### I SAID to the Lord: You are my God. <note>original: "DIXI domino deus meus es tu"; Psalm 16:2.</note>

After he has fortified himself against pride, he begins to describe his state. The entire state of the righteous man consists in this word: *I said to the Lord: You are my God.* Although this word seems common to almost everyone, there are few who can truly say it. For a person holds as "God" that which he holds as his **highest good**: and we hold that as the highest good which, if we possess it alone even if other things are lacking, we think ourselves happy; and which, if it alone is missing even if we have all other good things, we think ourselves miserable. Thus the greedy man says to his money: *You are my God*, because even if he lacks honor, health, virtue, and friends, as long as he has money, he is content. And if he has all those good things we mentioned but lacks money, he thinks himself unhappy.

--- Page 346 ---
<meta>This page continues the line-by-line commentary on Psalm 16 (Psalm 15 in the Vulgate numbering). Having previously discussed the need for humility and God's protection, the author now examines why God alone is the true object of worship and contrasts the focus of the righteous on the "heavenly homeland" with the "idols" of the wicked.</meta>

The glutton is likewise a slave to his excess <note>original: "crapulæ"; refers to the physical or spiritual sickness following over-indulgence.</note>, the incontinent man to his lust, and the ambitious man to power or glory. Each says: **You are my God.** Consider, therefore, how few are able to say: **I have said to the Lord, you are my God.** For only he can say this for whom God alone is enough; so much so that if all the kingdoms of the world were offered to him—both heavenly and earthly goods—he would not offend God even once to obtain them. In this saying, therefore, consists the entire state of the righteous man.

## BECAUSE you have no need of my goods: <note>Psalm 16:2</note>

He gives the reason for his proposal: why, specifically, he says to the Lord alone: **You are my God.** The reason is that God alone does not need our goods. There is no creature that does not need other creatures, for they are imperfect, as **philosophers and theologians** <note>This likely refers to the Scholastic tradition, such as Thomas Aquinas, who argued for the interdependence of the created order.</note> prove. For if those others did not exist, these would not exist; if one part of the universe is destroyed, the whole universe is destroyed, and once the whole is destroyed, all parts are destroyed. All creatures are parts of one universe, but God himself is not a part of this universe; rather, he is the **principle** <note>original: "principium"; the first cause or source from which all things originate.</note>, depending on nothing. God acquired nothing from the fact that he created the world, and he would lose nothing if the whole world were annihilated. Therefore, God alone does not need our goods. We ought to feel ashamed to take for a god that which lacks our goods—which is the case for every creature. Furthermore, we ought not to take anything for a god—that is, for the **highest good** <term>Summum Bonum: the ultimate source of all value and happiness, which philosophers identified with God.</term>—unless it is that in which the highest good resides. But in no creature is there every good. Therefore, to the Lord alone we must say: **You are my God.**

## TO THE SAINTS who are in his land. <note>Psalm 16:3</note>

After God, we ought to love most those who are most closely joined to God, such as the angels and the blessed in the **homeland** <note>original: "patria"; a common theological term for Heaven as the true home of the soul.</note>. Therefore, after he said to the Lord: **You are my God**, he adds that God...

## HE HAS MADE WONDERFUL his wills. <note>Psalm 16:3</note>

That is, he made his loves and his desires wonderful toward the saints who are in his land. This refers to the **heavenly homeland** <note>original: "cæleſti patria"</note> which is called the land of God and the **land of the living**. Truly, if we considered how great is the happiness of that homeland and how great is the misery of this world, and how great is the goodness and charity of those citizens, we would always desire to depart from here to dwell there. When we meditate on these and similar things, we must always take care that our meditations are not fruitless. Instead, from every meditation we should always acquire some virtue. Specifically, from the goodness of that higher homeland, we ought to acquire this virtue: that we not only bear death bravely and patiently when our hour comes (or if it must be faced for the faith of Christ), but that we even desire it of our own accord, wishing to depart from this **valley of miseries** <note>original: "ualle miſeriaų"; a common medieval reference to the earthly life, often called the "valley of tears" in prayers like the Salve Regina.</note> so that we may reign with God and his saints in that happy homeland. Since the righteous man has thus described his state—that his whole heart is set upon God and he despises earthly things—he then speaks from on high about the state of wicked men, saying:

## THEIR INFIRMITIES have been multiplied. <note>Psalm 16:4</note>

By **infirmities**, however, he understands **idols** <note>original: "idola"; the commentator notes that while the Latin Vulgate used "infirmates" (weaknesses/infirmities), the Hebrew source uses a word for idols here.</note>, and thus the **Hebrew text** <note>original: "textus hæbreus"</note> has it. For just as the good man has one God whom he worships, so the wicked have many gods and idols, because they have many pleasures, many vain desires, and various passions which they serve. It is for this reason that they seek many pleasures.

It contrasts the virtuous longing for the "heavenly homeland" with the wicked man's devotion to various "idols" of pleasure and ambition.</summary>
