<meta>This page continues the line-by-line commentary on Psalm 16 (Psalm 15 in the Vulgate numbering). The author is contrasting the restless, circular path of the wicked with the focused, inheritance-based joy of the righteous. The previous page ended with a discussion on why God alone is sufficient for the soul.</meta>

...because they find nothing that brings them peace: and therefore they walk in the circle of their own dominion <note>original: "in circuitu imperii"; this is likely a play on or a typo for Psalm 12:8 (Vulgate 11:9), "the wicked walk in a circle" (*in circuitu impii ambulant*). The author suggests the wicked are trapped in a repetitive, worldly cycle.</note>: and he adds afterwards that they cried out: because, namely, they rush headlong and thoughtlessly after their own desires. From this we are taught that we ourselves should run no less quickly toward virtues than they run toward vice; nor should we serve our Lord less diligently than they serve their own lord, the devil. The righteous man, however, considering the state of the wicked, firmly resolves—as we always ought to do—to by no means wish to follow them: and he says:

### I WILL NOT gather their meetings of blood: nor will I be mindful of their names. <note>Psalm 16:4</note>

He speaks of "blood" for two reasons: first, because idolaters used to perform their ceremonies around the gathered blood of victims; second, because the entire life of the wicked, having abandoned reason, follows sensuality, which is situated in the blood <note>In medieval physiology, the "blood" was often associated with the "animal" or "sensual" nature of man, as opposed to the "spirit" or "reason."</note>. Moreover, he says that he not only refuses to sacrifice to idols, but does not even want to name them. This is said and done to show that the perfect man must abstain not only from illicit pleasures but even from licit ones, so that he may be more fully carried into heaven and devote himself more purely to the contemplation of divine things. And because someone might believe it to be foolishness to deprive oneself of all pleasure, he adds:

### THE LORD is the portion of my inheritance. <note>Psalm 16:5</note>

It is as if he were saying: do not wonder if I leave all other things behind to possess God, in whom all other good things are finally possessed. This should be the voice of every good Christian: "The Lord is the portion of my inheritance." Because we Christians, to whom God himself is promised as an inheritance, ought to blush to desire anything besides Him. And because it might seem to someone a matter of presumption to dare to promise these things to himself, he adds:

### YOU ARE he who restores my inheritance to me. <note>Psalm 16:5</note>

As if to say: "Lord my God, I know well that since I am nothing in respect to you, I cannot ascend by my own strength to possess you. But you are the one who will draw me to you through your grace, and you are the one who will give yourself to me to be possessed." Let the righteous man then consider how great this happiness is, that God has fallen to him as an inheritance; he adds:

### THE LINES have fallen for me in excellent places. <note>Psalm 16:6. "Lines" (original: *funes*) refers to the measuring cords used in ancient times to mark out plots of land for inheritance.</note>

For in ancient times, portions and lots were divided by ropes. And since there are many who, although called to this happiness—as all Christians are—nevertheless value it as nothing, and frequently exchange it for some trivial pleasure, he therefore adds:

### MY INHERITANCE is excellent to me.

As if to say: just as the inheritance is excellent in itself, so I personally consider it excellent. All other things in respect to it—as Paul used to say—I consider as dung <note>original: "ſicut ſtercora"; a reference to the Apostle Paul in Philippians 3:8.</note>. Moreover, because having this light of understanding—so that a man may know the happiness given to him—is a gift of God, he adds:

### I WILL BLESS the Lord who has given me understanding. <note>Psalm 16:7</note>

A man often judges according to reason that he should serve God, yet sensuality and the flesh resist. A man is truly perfect when not only his soul but also his flesh is carried toward God, according to that saying: **My heart and my flesh have exulted in the living God** <note>Psalm 84:2 (Vulgate 83:3).</note>; therefore he adds:

<summary>This page provides a commentary on Psalm 16:4-7, explaining that the righteous man rejects the sensual "blood" of the wicked in favor of God as his sole inheritance. It emphasizes that choosing God over worldly pleasures is a gift of divine "understanding" rather than human strength.</summary>

<keywords>inheritance, sensuality, blood, Psalm 16, idolatry, Paul the Apostle, divine grace, measuring lines, spiritual joy</keywords>

--- Page 348 ---
<meta>This page concludes the line-by-line commentary on Psalm 16 (Vulgate 15). The author moves from the internal struggle against desire to the ultimate hope of the resurrection, interpreting the Psalmist's words as a prophecy of Christ’s victory over death, which then extends to all believers.</meta>

### AND EVEN UNTO the night my reins have rebuked me. <note>Psalm 16:7</note>
That is, the reins <term>renes: literally "kidneys," but used biblically to refer to the seat of deep emotions and hidden desires</term> themselves—in which there is usually the greatest inclination toward lust <term>concupiscentia: the tendency of human nature toward worldly or sinful desires</term>—do not only incline me toward evil, but rather rebuke me. That is, they hold me back even until the night; that is, to the point that they even spontaneously afflict the body itself. For "night" is often used to signify affliction. He then shows the root of such self-denial and says:

### I SET God always in my sight. <note>Psalm 16:8</note>
For if anyone were to always have God before their eyes as a rule for all their actions—and in all their works sought neither their own utility, nor glory, nor pleasure, but only to please God—they would shortly emerge perfected. And because the one who acts thus always prospers in all things, he therefore says:

### HE IS at my right hand, that I be not moved.
He shows then how great the happiness <term>felicitas: the ultimate state of blessedness or well-being</term> of the righteous man is: because he will be happy forever, both in soul and in body; therefore he adds because of these things:

### MY HEART is glad. <note>Psalm 16:9</note>
That is, my soul is joyful, knowing that after death heaven is prepared for it.

### AND MY FLESH shall rest in hope.
That is, although the flesh itself does not rejoice yet—as if it were to receive its perfected state immediately after death—it nevertheless rests in the grave with this hope: that it will rise again on the day of judgment with its soul, immortal and most splendid. And he declares all of this in the following verse; for because he had said the soul was rejoicing, he adds the reason:

### BECAUSE you will not leave my soul in hell. <note>Psalm 16:10</note>
And because he had said that the flesh rested in hope, he adds the reason, saying:

### NOR WILL YOU suffer your holy one to see corruption.
Because that which was corruptible shall rise incorruptible; and because Christ was the first who entered paradise and opened life to us, and was the first who rose again—and his resurrection is the cause of our own resurrection—therefore these things we have said about the resurrection are understood principally of Christ, as Peter the Apostle declared <note>A reference to Peter’s sermon in Acts 2:25–31, where he quotes this Psalm as a prophecy of Jesus.</note>. Secondarily, they can be understood of us insofar as we are members of Christ. He alone did not see "corruption" because his body did not decay in the tomb. Since, therefore, the way of living well leads us to the perpetual life of the soul and body, he adds:

### YOU HAVE made known to me the ways of life. <note>Psalm 16:11</note>
And because the whole happiness of this life consists in the fitting vision and enjoyment of God, he therefore adds:

### YOU WILL FILL me with joy with your countenance.
And because this happiness will last forever, he adds:

### DELIGHTS at your right hand even to the end.
He says "at your right hand" because our happiness is completed in the vision and enjoyment of the humanity of Christ, who sits at the right hand of Majesty on high; according to that saying of John: This is the whole reward, that we may see God, and him whom you have sent, Jesus Christ. <note>original: "Haec est tota merces ut uideamus deum et quem misisti Iesum Christum." This is a paraphrase of John 17:3, which usually reads "This is eternal life..." rather than "This is the reward..."</note>

->The End<-

<summary>This page concludes the commentary on Psalm 16, interpreting the text as a roadmap for the righteous—from the discipline of the flesh to the hope of bodily resurrection through Christ. The author emphasizes that the ultimate reward of a holy life is the eternal vision of God and Christ.</summary>

## Baccio Ugolini to Roberto Salviati, Greetings.

<margin>74 m</margin>
**M**ore than anyone, Roberto, the learned rightly love you, for you have always honored them with a certain marvelous passion; and all students love you, whom you assist not only with your labor but with your resources so they may more conveniently make progress. For my part, even if I am not to be numbered among the learned or even the studious, I nevertheless confess that I owe you a great deal, because through you the abundance of a truly divine work has been made available to us—even to those of us farther away—recently published by Pico della Mirandola, a man truly to be admired above all who are or ever were. My friend Poliziano—himself another miracle of our age—rightly calls him no longer "Pico" but his own "Phoenix," nesting in the sacred laurel of the Medici <note>Poliziano frequently used the "Phoenix" metaphor for Pico to signify his unique, self-taught, and incomparable genius</note>. You have taken care that his book concerning the seven-fold narration of the six days of Genesis <note>This is the "Heptaplus," Pico's mystical and philosophical explanation of the creation story in the Bible</note>—a true advancement of philosophy and the Christian religion, dedicated to my patron, the great Lorenzo de' Medici—should be most diligently printed, as well as transmitted to diverse and distant places, and held as a gift by the many people who were eager for its reading. Among these, it fell to me as well—through your friend Vittorio Caiano, a man of much humor, great sweetness, and wit—to obtain this desired gift. This dedication of yours to famous men, this dutiful liberality toward all lovers of virtue: who would not praise it and follow it with a most grateful heart? He who is at odds with all humanity and a stranger to the habit of letters must undoubtedly be considered a fool. For no one could have consulted the public utility more lovingly, more rightly, or more swiftly. Therefore, I would wish you to be especially certain of this: that you have undertaken this task for no small reward, since you have gained from it both the favor of good men and no mediocre glory. Farewell. Naples. March 26, 1490. <note>original: "vii. Kal. aprilis. Mcccclxxxx."</note>

## Giuniano Maio to Roberto Salviati, Health and Greetings.

<margin>75 q</margin>
**B**ecause you have taken care that the divine work of Giovanni Pico della Mirandola should be printed with no less care than he himself composed it, I think much gratitude is owed both to your diligence and to his divine learning. To you, because you did not allow such a sublime work to lie hidden in the darkness of oblivion; and because by this one labor you have looked out for the perpetuity of your friend and the common utility of all. To him, however, because he was deterred neither by the authority nor the sanctity of the ancient men who narrated these same things, nor did he follow in the footsteps of others, but illuminated those same things with a certain light of his own...

--- Page 350 ---
<meta>This page continues the series of commendations for Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, transitioning from a letter by Baccio Ugolini to excerpts from the "Miscellanea" of Angelo Poliziano. The text emphasizes Pico's youth, his role as a "miracle of the age," and his efforts to reconcile philosophy with scripture.</meta>

For when this work—so profound <note>original: "reconditū," meaning hidden or abstruse</note> and removed from the knowledge of many—first came into my hands, I began to read it most diligently. It did not merely bring me pleasure combined with admiration, but it truly uplifted my soul as I contemplated its sublimity. I have never seen or heard anything more admirable or more clearly explained. Indeed, his genius stands above the sharpest minds of all others; he is skilled in an incredible investigation of the sciences and already possesses a knowledge of all things beyond what is believable. Especially at this age, having only just passed through puberty <note>Pico was famously young, often called a child prodigy of philosophy</note>, he has attained such a notice of things as was not permitted even to the most learned and those advanced in years to reach. Therefore, I shall never fear to name him the sacred home of all good arts and sciences, and the miracle of our age—especially when I read more closely the profound meanings of the work, the progress of things devised by few men, the revealed hiding places of nature and of God, and finally the secret riches of the Supreme Architect <note>God</note> now brought into the open. I know of nothing more admirable I have ever heard, nor anything deeper I have read. Since a peace has now been entered into between the philosophers and Moses—who were weaving the craftsmanship of the world by such different paths—certain joined treaties of nature and of God are now understood without controversy. But I reserve this to be repeated more deeply and explained more wordily at another time. 

I come to you, my dear **Robert** <note>Roberto Salviati, a Florentine patron and friend to the humanists</note>, a truly eminent man, whom I love uniquely because of your writings; though they are few, they show such a specimen of your virtue that they promise and offer a no less fruitful harvest of genius to come than the current pleasing hope of their "little flowers" <note>original: "flosculoz," likely referring to an anthology or early poems</note>. Know, therefore, that your **Junianus** <note>Juniano Maio, a Neapolitan humanist</note>, if you give me anything hereafter from your writings to me, will be no less a herald of your affairs than a lover of you for that very reason. **Victorius** <note>Vittorio Marcello</note> likewise proclaims the excellence of your genius and your learned refinement in these letters, so that I am provoked to desire and proclaim the same. I ask one thing, however: that you do not cease to follow with your humanity—which you have shown and embrace—the one whom **Victorius** has invited to love by his flattering encouragements. Wherefore you will rouse my sluggishness to write to you more often, provided you do not despise our efforts. And if, from the words of our **Victorius**, you do not disregard my friendship, you will provoke me to follow you with every duty by the bond of necessity. For there is nothing I would prefer more than to contend in mutual love and the exchange of letters with noble and learned men. Your **Mirandola**, whom you proclaim as a pillar of humanity—and I myself dare to call him the "delight of nature"—return him to me as a friend, for I desire to be loved by him, and give him greetings from me. 

Farewell. From **Naples**. The day before the Nones of June <note>June 4</note>, 1490.

***

### From the Preface of the *Miscellanea* by Angelo Poliziano.

Concerning that man, to be admired above all others, I no longer say "Pico" <note>original: "pico," a pun on the Latin word for woodpecker</note>, but—as I myself am accustomed to call him—rather a **Phoenix**, who now nests in your **Laurel** <note>original: "Lauru," referring to Lorenzo de' Medici, whose name Laurentius is derived from the laurel tree</note>. My expectation of him is indeed so great that I would dare to sing along with **Propertius**: *Yield, you Roman writers; yield, you Greeks!* <note>original: "cedite romani scriptores cedite grai," a famous line from Propertius suggesting a new work surpasses all previous classical literature</note>

***

### Also from Chapter 14 of the same work.

As the same **Giovanni Pico della Mirandola**—my one friend who is utterly and from every part the most blessed of all men—proves and shows in that singular and admirable work in which he teaches that the Psalm translated by the **Seventy** <term>the Septuagint: the ancient Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible</term> responds to the Hebrew truth, especially by that argument of the notations. This is so that the Jew can no longer insult us or object that we sing things in the Temple at every hour which we ourselves do not consider to be faithfully translated.

Such a man also is this **Giovanni Pico** of mine, from the Princes of Mirandola, most perfect...

### Also from Chapter 94 of the same work <note>Referring to Poliziano’s *Miscellanea*</note>.

Pico—this Mirandola here, a man who can never be praised enough—and I sometimes spent our leisure hours scouring the ancient commentators on the **Old Testament** <note>original: "instrumenti sacri veteris," a common humanist term for the Hebrew Bible</note>; primarily the Greeks, such as **Diodorus**, **Philo**, **Gennadius**, **Aquila**, **Origen**, **Basil**, **Didymus**, **Isidore**, **Apollinaris**, **Severianus**, and many others of that kind. Pico, just as he does with all the opinions of the Latin writers, compares these most diligently with the views of the **Hebrew** and **Chaldean** <note>original: "chaldeoz," referring here to Aramaic</note> interpreters. He sifts and weighs everything: from which the truth might be drawn out, obscurity removed, faith strengthened, or impiety refuted.

### From the book *On Ecclesiastical Writers* by Abbot Johannes of Sponheim <note>Johannes Trithemius (1462–1516), a famous German abbot and pioneering bibliographer</note>.

**Giovanni Pico**, an Italian by birth, Count of Mirandola and Lord of Concordia: a man most studious in all good literature. Just as he is most noble in his illustrious blood, so he is most noble in his truly divine genius. Surrounded by a great company of every kind of art, he is worthy and best deserving of the Muses' pursuit. He is the most learned philosopher of our age and a most sharp debater. He wrote several things in a most elegant style, which our age will have cause both to approve and, even more so, to admire; by these works, he has rendered the memory of his name and glory eternally worthy.

### From the *Compendium of Revelations* by the most learned and holy man, Brother Girolamo Savonarola of Ferrara, of the Order of Preachers <note>Savonarola was the famous Dominican reformer of Florence and a close associate of Pico in his final years</note>.

**Count Giovanni of Mirandola**, a man singular in our times for his genius and manifold learning.

### From the second commentary on Propertius by the most learned and eloquent man Filippo Beroaldo of Bologna: regarding that verse, *“Not so many Achaemenians,”* etc. where *“Susa”* is written instead of *“Etruscan.”*

I read this written in a manuscript <note>original: "codice"</note> belonging to **Giovanni Pico della Mirandola**, a man worthy of being remembered for centuries. Endowed with many-yoked disciplines <note>i.e., multiple fields of study</note>, he adorns the glory of our age. To him can be applied what Terentianus wrote of Varro: Pico is a man most learned from every side. He not only esteems but vehemently loves you, my **Memmius** <note>likely a student or dedicatee of Beroaldo</note>, as a learned man himself and one most noble; he speaks honorably of you and holds the best opinion of you. After his severe studies, he is accustomed to rest in the reading of **Propertius** as if in a most pleasant inn. He agreed with me in reading this passage and showed me that in his own manuscript, it was written as **Susa** and not **Etruscan**, and so forth.

->**THE END.**<-

**Benedetto d'Ettore of Bologna** carefully printed these small works of **Giovanni Pico della Mirandola**, Count of Concordia. He applied all his strength, skill, and diligence so as not to wander from the original <note>original: "archetypo"</note>. At **Bologna**, in the Year of Salvation **1496**, on the **20th day of March**.

# Giovanni Francesco Pico della Mirandola to the Most Sacred Father Oliverio Carafa, Bishop of Sabina and Cardinal of Naples. Greetings.

<margin>a</margin> We read, most distinguished father, that Apollonius of Tyana <note>original: "Pollonium thyanæū." A 1st-century Greek philosopher and miracle-worker whose life was chronicled by Philostratus and often compared to Jesus in late antiquity.</note>, when he was about to set out on that journey later made famous by Philostratus to pursue learning, wished that he might find and recognize good men; and he also requested this of the Sun with many prayers. This wish can certainly be praised without fault, just as the prayer to the sun need not be blamed; for the learned and the unlearned masses alike proclaim this, led by the innate light of knowing the truth, to say nothing of the strongest reasons and the testimonies of divine eloquence.

But if such a gift is to be wished for and demanded from God the Best and Greatest, those people should undoubtedly rejoice most of all who happen not only to recognize good men but to find them within their own family and bound to them by the bond of blood—to discover them rather than to seek them out—and thereby to gain some of the fruits produced by the friendship of good men. I do not deny nor hide that this divine benevolence has happened to me, since I found within our domestic walls Giovanni Pico della Mirandola—my father Galeotto’s brother—a man truly worthy for whom Apollonius might greedily search beyond the Caucasus and the <term>Brahmans<note>The priestly class of India, often idealized in Renaissance texts as ancient keepers of wisdom.</note></term>, and even to the opposite side of the world; and I have been overwhelmed by many kindnesses from him. While he lived with us, I judged that I should return like for like as much as I could; but after his death, I decided that the duties I had undertaken ought to be repaid all the more, since his glory and the utility of his studies were at risk, and the Church was suffering no small loss.

For this reason, I have committed several of his works to writing, and through long and anxious searching, I have seen to it that his works, having been gathered by us, be transcribed into many copies. I have labored most intensely in restoring the books that fundamentally overturn all divinatory astrology, since they had been sketched in such characters <note>Gianfrancesco is referring to Giovanni Pico’s notoriously difficult handwriting, which was rapid and full of personal abbreviations.</note> (as was the man's custom) due to his speed in dictating and writing, that they seemed to take the form of any language other than Latin. They were so smeared with erasures that it was not easy to distinguish what should be considered deleted and what should be considered corrected. Furthermore, they were so torn and shredded in so many parts that it was judged they could scarcely be transcribed by the author himself.

I have long reflected on to whom I should destine and inscribe these books (if they are not treasures rather than books) now that they have been brought back to life and, as it were, recently recalled from destruction. You occurred to me, most sacred prelate, from whom I could in no way turn away. For to whom could I more fittingly and honorably dedicate the literary monuments of this most learned man and kinsman than to you? Especially those works which refute the errors opposed to our <term>Christian<note>The original uses a Greek-Latin hybrid "χρianæ" (Christiane).</note></term> religion, since you are powerful in learning, and because of Giovanni Tommaso Carafa, Count of Maddaloni, my father-in-law (to whom you are bound by the closest kinship), you are also joined to me in relationship; and you hold that office among men of the religion itself which is closest to the supreme <note>A reference to Carafa's high standing as a Cardinal, second only to the Pope.</note>.

Accept them, therefore, willingly; and when you steal some leisure from handling the greatest affairs, I beg you to read them. In that reading, you will simultaneously learn and rejoice that the astrological art—or to speak more correctly, that plague which, having risen with savage madness, was raging to our destruction while concealing its poison behind a deceitful brow—has been most powerfully extinguished by the work of Giovanni Pico, my uncle.

->Farewell, most distinguished father. From Mirandola, June 28.<-

# Gianfrancesco Pico della Mirandola to the lovers of truth.

<margin>a</margin> <note>The small letter 'a' in the margin is a guide for a rubricator to add a decorative initial 'A' at the start of 'Amatores' (Lovers).</note> Lovers of truth, rejoice; and you also, who labor with the desire of illuminating and amplifying it, gladden your hearts. Behold, there now come forth into the public the **Disputations against Astrologers** by Giovanni Pico della Mirandola—that very Pico at whose sublimity of mind and all-encompassing learning almost the entire world has already stood in awe. These are Disputations, I say, which will cause the haters and attackers of truth to grieve; and those who devote their labor to the vanity of astrology for the sake of extorting money, they will be forced either to wail and be torn asunder, or to abandon their error. 

Nor should it diminish your solid joy that he—called to God by a death immature for us but timely for himself <note>Giovanni Pico died at the age of 31 in 1494. Gianfrancesco suggests the death was "timely" for Giovanni's soul but "immature" for the world.</note>—did not wipe and polish these books with the *final file* <note>original: "extrema lima." A common classical metaphor for the final editing or "polishing" of a literary work.</note>, nor bring the final epilogue, which was to be the conclusion of the whole work, from the *anvil* <note>original: "ab incude." Another metallurgical metaphor for the process of drafting and refining text.</note>. That is perhaps lacking for the more abundant ornament of the work, but not for the reader's perfect benefit. 

And although elsewhere this tree of vanities and all superstitions has indeed been exploded and detested by the oracles of the prophets, and stripped of its leaves, hissed at, and even struck in some part by the axes of our theologians and philosophers—both Greek and Latin, as well as the <term>barbarians<note>In the context of Renaissance Humanism, "barbarians" usually refers to the medieval Scholastic thinkers or non-Latin authors like the Arabs, whose Latin translations were considered unrefined.</note></term>—it remains. Let it also be granted that it was uprooted and displaced by imperial laws and pontifical decrees; nevertheless, by human curiosity it has often been brought back and replanted in its original pit, supported and strengthened. So much so that it was never entirely eliminated or brought to utter destruction by the strongest instruments of reason. 

But now, our Pico has utterly burned this unlucky tree from root to trunk, from trunk to branches, and from branches to leaves, with the most rushing fire of true philosophy and true theology, and with the unique inventions and meditations of that incomparable genius. He has reduced it to ash, which he has dispersed with such a rapid blast of eloquence that any supporter or promoter of astrology (unless they be out of their mind) must either cry out in grief over its death or exult in joy once the vanity has been cast away and scorned. 

Come then, learned men of all nations, arm your souls with these reasons; support yourselves with these testimonies, both human and divine. With these—as if with the heaviest double-edged axes and ignited torches—you must strike down, crush, tear up, and exterminate any sprouts of the cut and extinguished tree that might perhaps sprout again, hidden within the bowels of the earth by the fault of a poorly cultivated field.

# Table

In summary, these are the contents of the individual books of the **Disputations against Astrologers** by Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, the prince of letters.

**In the First Book:** The preface; also, how astrology was condemned by philosophers, prophets, emperors, and popes; and what sort of men they were who wrote on astrology.

**In the Second:** The uselessness, falsity, and ignorance of the profession as a whole, and the negligence of the practitioners of our time. Also, why they occasionally predict the truth, even though the profession itself is false.

**In the Third:** The arguments approving the truth of astrology are brought forward; afterward, they are diluted and turned back against the astrologers.

**In the Fourth:** That the things astrologers believe are not caused by the heavens; also, that things not caused by the heavens are not signified by them; and that their "questions" or "interrogations" <note>original: "interogationes." In astrology, this refers to Horary Astrology, where a practitioner answers a specific question based on the moment it is asked.</note> are empty.

**In the Fifth:** Great circles, the revolutions of Saturn, and great conjunctions <note>original: "magnæ coniunctiones." The alignment of Jupiter and Saturn, which medieval astrologers believed signaled major historical shifts or the rise of new religions.</note> are disproved.

**In the Sixth:** The following are demolished: houses, signs, aspects, <term>obsessions</term> <note>planetary configurations where a planet is "hemmed in" by others</note>, and <term>combustions</term> <note>when a planet is so close to the sun that its influence is supposedly "burned up"</note>, retrogradations, the head and tail of the dragon <note>the lunar nodes</note>, <term>antiscia</term> <note>points on the zodiac that are mirror images of each other across the solstice points</note>, commanding and obeying signs. Also, exaltations, <term>triplicities</term> <note>groupings of three zodiac signs belonging to the same element</note>, faces, terms, <term>dodecathemoria</term> <note>the division of a single zodiac sign into twelve smaller parts</note>, ninth-parts, <term>monomoiria</term> <note>the study of individual degrees of a sign</note>, the properties of degrees, parts, and <term>climacteric years</term> <note>critical years in a person's life, often multiples of 7 or 9, believed to be governed by celestial cycles</note>.

**In the Seventh:** It is contained that the beginnings of fate—whether particular or universal, and whether of a man or any other thing—cannot be properly captured; also, that the time in which something will happen cannot be defined through <term>directions</term> <note>a method of calculating future events by "moving" planets at a rate of one degree per year</note> or any other way; and the manifold error regarding the fixed stars.

**In the Eighth:** That the number of spheres is uncertain; and however many are established, the error of the astrologers is certain. Also, regarding the errors concerning the difference between constellations and signs; and regarding invisible constellations.

**In the Ninth:** It concerns the uncertainty of the hour of birth and other beginnings; and regarding errors in the division of houses, signs, places, and the motion of the planets; the motion of the eighth sphere and directions.

**In the Tenth:** The arguments of the astrologers with which they strive to strengthen their dogmas are reduced to five types; all these are shown to be ineffective and, moreover, ridiculous.

**In the Eleventh:** That astrology cannot be grasped through experience; or if any experience could be gathered, it has not yet been achieved.

**In the Twelfth:** That it was not obtained through revelation; also where it was born, increased, and nourished, and how it was propagated.

## The table of chapters for the whole work begins

The **First Book** is not divided into several chapters; rather, in a single chapter, it casts down astrology by the authority of philosophers, prophets, emperors, and popes.

In the **Second Book**, the following are contained: the uselessness and falsity of the profession; the ignorance and negligence of its practitioners.

**Chapter One:** That this art is uncertain even by the judgment of its own leaders.

### In the Third Book, the arguments favoring astrologers are presented and refuted.

**Chapter i** What was covered in the preceding book, what is to be done next, and in what order.
**Chapter ii** Five reasons by which astrology seems to be capable of being strengthened.
**Chapter iii** The first reason is turned back against them, and it is shown that the heavens are a universal cause and not responsible for the variety of individual things.
**Chapter iiii** In what way the heavens act through motion and light, and how they are the universal cause of meteorological elements, minerals, and living things.
**Chapter v** That besides the common influence of motion and light, no peculiar power exists within the heavenly bodies.
**Chapter vi** That the light of the moon, like that of the sun, is vital; and neither produces cold or humidity except by accident.
**Chapter vii** That the dogmas of astrologers cannot be defended as <term>Ibn Ezra</term> <note>original: "Auenazra." **Chapter viii** An objection against those things which have been said.
**Chapter ix** The objection is resolved, and it is shown that neither specific nor individual differences of things depend on the motion of the heavens.
**Chapter x** That stars other than the sun and the moon either do nothing at all or act upon us very little indeed.
**Chapter xi** By what means the same stars can act on us differently at different times.
**Chapter xii** Which variety of effects can be traced back to the heavens and which cannot.
**Chapter xiii** That the sun performs many things which astrologers mistakenly believe are done by other stars.
**Chapter xiiii** How the power of the moon varies, and that certain "lunar days" are observed through true superstition.
**Chapter xv** That the tides of the sea can be attributed to a cause other than the moon; and even if they are attributed to it, it does nothing to help the case for astrology.
**Chapter xvi** Galen’s opinion regarding <term>critical days</term> <note>original: "creticis diebus." In ancient and medieval medicine, these were specific days during an illness when a patient was expected to either recover or take a turn for the worse; Galen linked these to lunar cycles.</note>, which refers them to the moon, is refuted.
**Chapter xvii** That the cycles of the <term>humors</term> <note>The four bodily fluids (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile) believed to control health and temperament.</note> are not to be referred to the motions of the stars.
**Chapter xviii** That the misfortune of an eight-month birth is not to be ascribed to Saturn.
**Chapter xix** Why sailors, physicians, and farmers predict the truth more often than astrologers.
**Chapter xx** That not everything predicted by astrologers depends on the <term>primary qualities</term> <note>original: "primis qualitatibus." The Aristotelian qualities of Hot, Cold, Moist, and Dry, which were the building blocks of the physical world.</note>.
**Chapter xxi** That neither the harms of the elements nor the injuries to our bodies originate from the heavens.
**Chapter xxii** That the variety of human talents and characters does not depend entirely on the primary qualities.
**Chapter xxiii** That neither wars nor external events depend on the primary qualities.

**Chapter xii** The origin of antiscia <note>points of equal daylight on either side of the solstices</note>: and how Ptolemy did not use them in forecasting, and how much Maternus and Haly <note>referring to Firmicus Maternus and Haly Abenragel, famous astrological authors</note> went astray regarding them.

**Chapter xiiii** A refutation of the reasons that certain astrologers assigned for the "exaltations" <note>specific degrees where a planet is thought to have maximum power</note> of the planets.
**Chapter xv** The arguments of astrologers regarding trigons <note>triplicities, or groups of three zodiac signs belonging to the same element</note> and the rulers of trigons: and, in passing, the "sex" of the signs is refuted.
**Chapter xvi** Regarding faces, terms, dodecatemories <note>divisions of a zodiac sign into 12 parts of 2.5 degrees each</note>, the Babylonian "nine-parts," and monomoiries <note>individual degrees of a sign</note>: how little they are supported even by the testimony of Ptolemy himself.
**Chapter xvii** Regarding feminine, bright, and dark degrees: and other things of that kind which Ptolemy ignored, and on which other astrologers do not agree.
**Chapter xviii** Where the "Parts" <note>calculated mathematical points like the "Part of Fortune"</note> originated, and how much astrologers conflict with one another in measuring them.
**Chapter xix** The theory of dodecatemories is exploded, and their Egyptian authors are rejected along with their "climacteric years" <note>critical or dangerous years in a person's life, often every seventh or ninth year</note>.

->The seventh book contains [arguments] concerning the initial hour, directions, and the fixed stars.<-
**Chapter i** What has been discussed so far and what is to be discussed in this book.
**Chapter ii** That the "fatal hour" <note>the exact moment of destiny or birth</note> is ambiguous, if indeed it exists in all things which are completed over time rather than in a single moment: and especially in humans, in whom the "birth-chart" <note>original: "genitura"</note> seems to have little power.
**Chapter iii** That Ptolemy attributed more to conception than to birth, yet Ptolemy's own reasoning proves that nothing should be attributed to either.
**Chapter iiii** By what paths astrologers track "universal events" <note>large-scale events like plagues or wars</note> and how little they are based on reason.
**Chapter v** That an astrologer cannot predict in which region of the world a particular fate will happen, since they are uncertain which region is subject to which sign or planet.
**Chapter vi** That a single "beginning" cannot be established upon which the fates of the whole year depend: since different beginnings of the year are set by different people, and according to the Hebrews, the year begins in autumn rather than spring.
**Chapter vii** Regarding "directions" <note>a predictive technique where a planet is "directed" to a significant point</note> and other ways by which they define the times of future events: how inconsistent they are and how astrologers disagree among themselves in these matters.
**Chapter viii** Just as they adopt useless things, so they omit necessary ones; and how much they err concerning the fixed stars.
**Chapter ix** That the dogmas of astrologers regarding the fixed stars conflict both with each other and with the truth.
**Chapter x** That astrologers are also deceived regarding the planets: and a repetition of what has been discussed so far.

# BY GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA, COUNT OF CONCORDIA, ON DISPUTATIONS AGAINST ASTROLOGERS.

## PREFACE

<note>Guide letter 'h' provided for an intended large decorative initial 'H'.</note>
H

omer and Caecilius, <note>Caecilius Statius was a Roman comic poet; Homer is the legendary Greek epic poet.</note> most ancient poets, proclaim that those enemies are the worst who circumvent us under the guise of friends. No sentiment can be spoken that is truer, nor any rule prescribed that is more beneficial. Yet why do we need the testimony of poets? Since Divine Truth <note>A reference to the teachings of Christ in the Gospels.</note>—the teacher of our lives and morals—has warned us to avoid wolves in sheep's clothing and cautioned us not to judge by appearances. Indeed, this is the one kind of enemy that can neither be turned away nor overturned, and whom we ourselves do not wish to overcome; instead, we run to meet them, we kiss them eagerly, we welcome them, and we stand with them against our own selves, rather than against them as we ought. 

This is surely a deception that costs us dearly; it must be looked into more deeply and examined longer; it should not be rashly admitted, nor immediately driven away. But once the fallacy is detected, it must be rejected all the more fiercely, just as it crept in more covertly toward our destruction under the pretext of being helpful. Nor should those evils be considered less which do not seem to be the worst; because they are sometimes mixed with good things, they harm us all the more fatally. Just as they are admitted more easily through the hope and mixing in of the good, so once admitted, they occupy what they have invaded more tenaciously and retain it more powerfully. 

In the same way, if poison is served in pure wine, although wine is by its nature a very healthy thing, it nevertheless disguises the malice of the poison with its own flavor, and by its own strength, it drives the poison into the veins and the innermost parts more quickly. This must be observed throughout all of life, but especially in the arts and the branches of learning. Among these, the most pernicious are those which—though they are deceptions or some other kind of vanities—have nevertheless held out some lure of falsehood so that they might claim for themselves the name of science or art. 

Whether that lure was grasped from antiquity through fictional authors, or from great promises—the bait of human curiosity and greed—or from some false color and appearance of probability. For sometimes, as Aristotle testifies, false things are more probable than true ones, especially to the common people and the multitude, whose nature has always been to err, to be deceived, and to understand nothing. 

What then is more destructive? What is more irrepressible? Than when error itself creeps into us under the title of wisdom, so that (as the saying goes) we take pains to <term>be insane with reason</term> <note>original: "cum ratione insaniamus". This is a famous quote from the Roman playwright Terence, suggesting the dangerous use of logic to justify madness.</note>. This is nothing other than dismissing the counsel and the mind—whose sole innate power is to drive away falsehood—so that the lie itself turns out more honorable by the mind's testimony, more robust by its power, and better protected by its defense. Furthermore, there is no hope left for health when nature itself assists the disease. 

This, as I was saying, happens through the madness which, under the appearance of either art or science, circulates and sells itself to the people. It is not less insane because it feigns wisdom on the surface; rather, the more deceptive it is, the more treacherous. Just as among physicians, none rave (so to speak) more deliriously than those who maintain a serious face during their delirium. This is the characteristic stain of all superstitions, which profess nothing other than to hand down the rules for going mad. But above all others, astrology has claimed this title for itself:

<summary>This preface introduces Giovanni Pico della Mirandola's critique of astrology, arguing that it is a dangerous "superstition" that masquerades as a legitimate science. He warns that falsehoods appearing rational or beneficial are the most destructive because they bypass our natural defenses against error.</summary>

<header>Preface</header>

# Preface

...just as among those very superstitions, of which it is rightly considered both mother and nursling, it holds the first place. When I speak of **astrology**, however, I do not mean that which measures the masses and movements of the stars by mathematical reasoning—a certain and noble art, most honorable in its own merits, and greatly approved by the authority of the most learned men. 

But rather, I mean that which pronounces what is to come from the stars through the fraud of mercenary lying—an art forbidden by both civil and pontifical laws, yet retained by human curiosity, laughed at by philosophers, practiced by charlatans, and suspected by every good and prudent man. Its professors were once called by the ethnic name **Chaldeans** <note>original: "chaldei"; the ancient Babylonians were famous for star-gazing, and their name became a shorthand for "astrologer" or "soothsayer" in the Roman world.</note> or, from the profession itself, **genethliacs** <note>original: "genethliaci"; from the Greek word for "birthday," referring specifically to those who cast birth charts or horoscopes.</note>. Soon, so that they might be honored by a common name, they called themselves "mathematicians" and "astrologers," as if this too were one of the liberal disciplines which spoke about the stars with reason. They separated themselves from that true mathematics only by this distinction: that the name of **astronomy** was given to the former, and **astrology** to the latter. This was done with an excessively wicked zeal for invading another's title; for indeed, "astrology" is the name of another art, as we shall declare. 

But this divinatory art, always laboring with this ambition to be named after the stars, we shall deign to call by both names—and in imitation of that art which treats the motion of the stars, we shall call it "astrology" for astrology, and "astronomy" for astronomy, appropriately enough and according to its merit. 

Whatever is decided about the name, I, supported both by reasons and by the judgments of the wisest men, would not hesitate to affirm that among the deceptive arts <term>prestigious arts <note>original: "artes prestigiosas"; here meaning "prestige" in its original sense of trickery, illusions, or sleight-of-hand.</note></term>, there is none that more greatly deceives the credulous and unskilled, or which, by deceiving, does more harm to those it has persuaded. It is all the more deadly than other superstitions because it seems to approach closer to the truth. For while other superstitions display marks of their own madness and levity on their very face, and hardly impose on anyone except the utterly sightless, this one—holding and nourishing its insanity in its very heart and core—puts on the hope and appearance of wisdom. 

It is as if you look from a distance or through a lattice <note>original: "per transennam"; a classical idiom for seeing something partially or through a screen.</note>, you might be captured by its form; but if you bring a searching eye closer, you would see it as a mere shadow or a kind of ghost, and you would detest this deception of darkness under the open light. So it is, certainly; so it shall become clearer than light through the most manifest reasons that there is no greater deception, none more ruinous. 

From afar, it displays the sky and the planets, whence you might easily believe that in such a sublime and lucid spectacle, everything could be most truly foreseen. But soon, when you consider more attentively, you see that the mirror is so high that images of earthly things do not ascend to it, and so bright that our weakness grows dim at its glare. Then, when you come closer, you will see woven into its robe <note>original: "peplo"; a reference to the ceremonial robe or veil of Athena, here used metaphorically for the "fabric" of the heavens.</note> monstrous images instead of celestial ones, and stars transformed into animals, and a sky full of fables—nay, instead of the true sky, a counterfeit sky, not made by God but fashioned by astrologers. 

Thus it appears equipped with every support of proven dogma, carrying around books titled with great names, and so many reasons for its decrees, and—beyond reason—experiments corroborated by such long-lasting observations and such diligent notes, received then from the use of so many centuries and the approval of so many ages. It is a wonder how, through these mists and clouds, it presents a beautiful, venerable image of itself, full of serious authority to the eyes of the unskilled. But when you have dispersed these shadows and illusions with the ray of reason and diligent treatment, you will see that in those books there is nothing...

<summary>Pico della Mirandola distinguishes between legitimate mathematical astronomy and "divinatory" astrology, which he characterizes as a fraudulent and harmful superstition. He argues that astrology masks its irrationality by stealing the terminology of science and using the majesty of the heavens as a deceptive front.</summary>

<keywords>astrology, astronomy, superstition, Chaldeans, genethliacs, mathematical reasoning, deception, Giovanni Pico della Mirandola</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the "Preface" (Proœmium) of Pico della Mirandola’s critique of astrology. He has just defined the difference between mathematical astronomy and the "fraud" of divinatory astrology. Here, he begins to list the specific ways this "art" deceives and corrupts society.</meta>

# Preface

...balanced: among the authors, there is no authority; in their reasonings, nothing rational; in their experiments, nothing harmonious, nothing constant, nothing true, nothing credible, nothing solid. Instead, everything is conflicting, false, vain, and ridiculous—to such an extent that you would scarcely believe the authors themselves gave credit to what they were writing.

Indeed, regarding its vanity, you will not easily find an art that offers more hope to its gold-seekers <note>original: "aurariis"; likely referring to those greedy for wealth or those who treat astrology like alchemy.</note> or promises greater and more desirable things. It presents itself as the preserver of **Prudence**, claiming to stabilize our conjectures of the future through certain foreknowledge; it also claims to serve **Philosophy**, whose greatest part—concerning the heavens—is (as they would have it) clearly resolved through celestial influence. It is hardly necessary to speak of **Medicine**, **Navigation**, or **Agriculture**, since this art not only predicts the future for these fields but even claims to draw down the powers of the heavens to earthly things. By this means, they claim the works of all arts are most effectively achieved, and the masters of all arts may easily obtain whatever they wish. 

This art persuaded the ancients, but it has even persuaded the moderns <note>original: "neotericis"; Pico is referring to the thinkers of his own 15th-century context.</note> that it confers a great deal of authority and benefit to religion—both to religion in general (if the gods please! <note>original: "si diis placet"; a sarcastic classical idiom equivalent to "god help us."</note>) and specifically to the Christian faith. To put it simply, having imitated its master <note>Pico here likens astrology to the Devil/Satan.</note>, it promises the kingdoms of the world to those who worship it, and to those who taste its "wood" <note>An allusion to the Tree of Knowledge in the Garden of Eden.</note>, it promises a rivalry with divinity and the knowledge of good and evil. 

But this art is not the convenient tool for the uses of life that it promises; it is, in fact, the most pestilential fraud of all. It is the very thing, as we shall demonstrate, that corrupts all philosophy, adulterates medicine, weakens religion, gives birth to or strengthens superstitions, fosters idolatry, takes away prudence, pollutes morals, defames the heavens, and makes men miserable, anxious, restless, and slaves instead of free men. In almost all their daily affairs, it makes them plainly unfortunate.

Since I seemed to have explored and discovered this for myself, I thought I would be committing a <term>piaculum</term> <note>A sin or crime requiring a religious sacrifice to expiate.</note> that could be atoned for by no sacrifice if I remained silent or concealed it. I felt I must attempt, to the best of my ability, to wrench this poison from the hands of the credulous—especially in this age, when more than ever before, people of every age, rank, and sex are blinded by this fraud. 

However, one must fight all the more for the truth as many more are known to oppose it. Just as we desire to benefit everyone, we wish to please only the good. The judgment of the multitude holds no weight where reason and the consensus of the learned stand against it; we do not look for the popular breeze, but for the light of truth and the public utility.

->The Preface concludes.<-

<meta>This page transitions from the general Preface to the first formal book of the treatise. Book One

# THE DISPUTATIONS OF GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA, COUNT OF CONCORDIA, AGAINST ASTROLOGERS: BOOK ONE.

<margin>Laws of the Emperors.</margin>
<margin>Oracles of the philosophers.</margin>
<margin>Sanctions of the Popes.</margin>
<margin>Teachings of holy men.</margin>
<margin>Philosophers. Mathematicians.</margin>
**F**irst of all, I want the reader to know: it was not my own invention or audacity to reject and refute astrology. Rather, from earliest antiquity, it has always seemed so to sound judgments: that this is no true profession, as it brings so many troubles and so much madness to mankind everywhere under the pretext of science and utility. For this reason, it is eliminated by the laws of Emperors <note>Original: "caesarum legibus"; Pico refers to Roman legal codes, such as the Theodosian or Justinian codes, which often banned "mathematicians" or diviners.</note> and the wise as harmful to civil life. Furthermore, it is condemned by the oracles of the prophets, the sanctions of the Popes, and the voices and teachings of the holiest men as pestilential to morals and piety. Here, by philosophers and mathematicians—those who have learned to speak from wisdom and not just from books—it is either utterly despised or refuted as false, useless, impossible, and unfriendly to philosophy. This fact, which others either do not know or deny, we shall declare in this book before the matter is argued by reason; so that after such esteemed accusers, this accusation might not bring envy upon us, but rather might serve as a defense for men of honest character, if any should undertake to defend it. We shall begin our introduction with the philosophers, whose authority is greater than that of the lawmakers, and whose path is usually more common than that of the prophets.

<margin>Pythagoras.</margin>
<margin>Democritus.</margin>
<margin>Favorinus.</margin>
<margin>Panaetius.</margin>
<margin>Carneades.</margin>
<margin>Bion.</margin>
<margin>Epicurus.</margin>
<margin>Plato.</margin>
<margin>Aristotle.</margin>
That Pythagoras placed no faith in astrology is attested by the author Theodoret, and Diogenes Laertius and Plutarch have also indicated this. Of Democritus, it is famously said that while no one looks at what is before their feet, he scrutinizes the regions of the sky <note>This is a play on the famous anecdote of a philosopher falling into a well while gazing at stars.</note>. Favorinus the Academic and Panaetius the Stoic attacked it; it is laughed at by Seneca and refuted by Cicero. And who is ignorant of Carneades disputing against it, or the philosopher Bion, who was hostile to diviners? If it surpasses all madness, such that even the insane Orestes <note>A mythological figure driven to madness by the Furies; Pico suggests astrology is a deeper madness than clinical or divine insanity.</note> would not approach it, how much madness does astrology contain, to which even Epicurus, despite his many delusions, could not assent? Plato and Aristotle, the princes of philosophy, thought it unworthy even to mention in their entire philosophy, condemning it more by their silence than any voice or writing could. For those who feel otherwise, I ask them to answer why, in the whole course of their commentaries—where either the properties of the heavens were to be explained or the causes of lower things sought—they never brought forward anything astrological? Did they not think it concerned a philosopher to study the primary and most noble parts of the universe—the moving bodies that in turn move others—the most effective causes without which nothing in nature can happen or be known, if they were believed to be such as astrologers claim? To know only certain universals about them, as the leaders of philosophy wrote, when specific things could be understood, would be the mark not of a philosopher, but of an imperfect one. Why then did Aristotle leave his books *On the Heavens* <note>original: "de caelo"</note> so meager? Where he could have said so many splendid things—and if he could, he should have—indicating to us the effects, properties, and knowledge of the stars and planets? Why, in the books of the *Meteorology* <note>original: "metheorologicis"</note>, while scrutinizing the causes of comets and winds, is he always forgetful of astrological matters? Why, in the books *On the Generation of Animals*, does he never refer twins, nor portentous and monstrous births, nor sex, nor childbearing, nor form, nor qualities to the stars, nor even mention in passing that they could be so referred? Why does Plato do the same in the *Timaeus*? Why, before Plato, did Timaeus himself, the Pythagorean, in his book *On Nature*—where Plato says he was both a philosopher and an astronomer—do the same? Why also Ocellus Lucanus?

<summary>Pico begins Book One by arguing that his rejection of astrology is supported by a long tradition of authority, including Roman law, the Church, and ancient philosophers like Aristotle and Plato, who notably omitted astrological explanations from their scientific works.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the opening argument of Book One. Having stated that astrology is rejected by law and religion, Pico now turns to the intellectual giants of antiquity—Plato and Aristotle—arguing that their silence on the "science" of astrology proves its illegitimacy.</meta>

# Book One

-> a iii <-

...in the book *On the Universe* <note>original: "de mundo"; a work long attributed to Aristotle, though scholars now believe it was written by a later follower.</note>: even by the testimony of Plato himself, the most eminent figure in philosophy. Did these men despise these matters as if they were trifles? If they were true, nothing could be of greater importance. Or were they not despised, but simply unknown? Yet they lived in Egypt and Babylonia—could they have failed to understand these things that are so frequently discussed among the philosophers there, and known to every common person? Certainly, they would not have thought it outside their own profession (as we have said) unless they were ignorant of what their profession actually was. It would be as if one believed a philosopher’s duty was to investigate the tiniest properties of ants, but thought they should not consider Jupiter and Saturn—especially since reason demonstrates, and observation teaches, the truth regarding them, as the astrological writers so vehemently contend. 

What else, then, can be said, except that Plato and Aristotle were of the opinion that the celestial causes of which the astrologers speak do not exist? They did not believe astrology was either an art or a science; otherwise, it would have been mentioned alongside the others. Instead, they viewed it as one of the trifles—or rather, the frauds—of traveling performers, in the same category as <term>geomancy</term> <note>divination by interpreting markings on the ground or patterns formed by tossed handfuls of soil.</note>, <term>hydromancy</term> <note>divination by means of water.</note>, sleight of hand, and incantations, none of which the ancient philosophers included among the sciences and arts. 

For if astrology were a true art, it would depend upon natural science, just as medicine does. A physician borrows the knowledge of the nature of shrubs, herbs, and animals from the philosopher so that he may use them to restore health to bodies; in the same way, an astrologer should learn the powers and properties of the stars from the philosopher so that he might use them, and teach how to use them, for prediction. Those who think that "divinatory" astrology is a part or the goal of mathematical astronomy—and believe it has more in common with that than with natural philosophy—will later be shown just how far they are deceived.

<margin>That the naturalist considers the stars.</margin>
For now, we only remind the learned of a fact that is beyond controversy: it belongs to the philosopher to know everything concerning the substance and order of the stars. The task of measuring their motions and masses is delegated to the astronomer. To the astrologer is left the task of 
<margin>What the astrologer does.</margin>
foreseeing the future from their condition and position—if, indeed, we grant that such a craftsman as an "astrologer" even exists.

Therefore, it would be an act of inexcusable sleepwalking for Plato and Aristotle to remain silent and give no indication of these matters, which they should have treated with the utmost precision. This silence is most admirable in the works of Plato, who dealt with a wide variety of subjects and every kind of doctrine, and also in Aristotle’s *Problems*. In that book, where he proposes questions concerning mathematics and all the arts and disciplines—bringing forth solutions from every kind of doctrine, even the most ancient—the word "astrological" is never found to breathe a sound. The same is true in the *Eudemian Ethics* <note>Aristotle's treatise on character and virtue, named for his pupil Eudemos.</note>, where he discusses good fortune. If we are not sufficiently moved by this evidence, let us listen to the disciples of both philosophers, who testify to the very opinion that their masters expressed to us through their silence.

<margin>Plotinus mocked the astrologers.</margin>
Plotinus is held to be of the highest authority in the Platonic school. Porphyry <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher and the primary biographer/editor of Plotinus.</note> writes that after Plotinus had devoted diligent effort to astrology, he finally realized the vanity of the art and the falsehood of its predictions, and thereafter stripped the astrologers of all credit. For this reason, in a book dedicated to the subject—titled *On the Influence of the Stars*—he resolutely laughed at and refuted the dogmas of the astrologers.

<margin>Maternus.</margin>
Firmicus Maternus <note>A 4th-century Roman lawyer and astrologer who wrote the 'Matheseos Libri VIII'.</note>, taking this poorly, tells many lies regarding Plotinus’s death, as if Fate had taken its penalty from him. But those claims are easily understood to be utterly false from the accounts of Porphyry himself, Plotinus’s disciple, who plainly and faithfully describes the nature of the disease from which he died, the cause, and why he departed from Rome.

<margin>Origen condemned astrology with many arguments.</margin>
Origen, known as "Adamantius" <note>A title meaning 'man of steel,' referring to his indomitable character.</note>, who was as eminent in the philosophical sect as he was in all other disciplines, frequently and with many arguments mocked astrological vanity. Perhaps superstitious men might value his testimony less because he was also a Christian; but Eudoxus was no Christian. He was a student of Plato, 
<margin>Eudoxus.</margin>
lived in Egypt, and was considered the prince of astronomers in his time; yet he believed nothing in it...

<summary>Pico argues that the silence of Plato and Aristotle regarding astrology proves they considered it a fraudulent superstition rather than a science. He supports this by citing Plotinus’s active refutation of the practice and dismissing the retaliatory claims of the pro-astrology writer Firmicus Maternus.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Pico's systematic dismantling of astrology's intellectual credibility. Having previously argued that the silence of Plato and Aristotle on the subject implies their rejection of it, he now cites a "who's who" of major Peripatetic, Islamic, and contemporary scholars who explicitly condemned the practice as a fraud or a logical impossibility.</meta>

# Book One

<margin>Alexander.</margin>
Regarding the astrologers who left writings predicting the fates of men from their births: Alexander of Aphrodisias, the supreme authority in Aristotelian philosophy, in writing his book *On Fate* to the emperors Severus and his son Antoninus, both rejected the necessity of fate and remained silent on astrological matters. Perhaps the very mention of fate draws people toward it, or even leads them astray. Nor, perhaps, did he have any other purpose in laboring over his commentary than to use philosophical reason to correct the mind of Emperor Severus, which was inclined toward such superstition.

<margin>Averroes everywhere tears astrology to pieces.</margin>
Averroes <note>The 12th-century Islamic philosopher Ibn Rushd, famous for his commentaries on Aristotle.</note>, a celebrated philosopher of the same school and a serious evaluator of natural things, everywhere tears astrology to pieces, damns it, and attacks it. For in his *First Philosophy* <note>original: "prima philosophia"; referring to the study of Metaphysics.</note>, he calls the opinion of astrologers concerning celestial "images"—under which they believe earthly animals of similar form are subject—fabulous. Once this is removed, the greatest part of astrological superstition collapses. He also says elsewhere, while explaining the *Cantica* <note>The "Poem on Medicine."</note> of Avicenna, that astrology is contrary to philosophy; elsewhere, that almost all the dogmas of astrologers are false; and that the art itself is entirely vain and weak. Likewise, in his books against Al-Ghazali <note>original: "Algazelem"; referring to Averroes's work *The Incoherence of the Incoherence*.</note>, he asserted that those artificial images into which astrologers think they can draw the virtues of heaven are utterly ineffective.

<margin>Avicenna proves that the future cannot be foreseen by astrologers.</margin>
Avicenna <note>The Persian polymath Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037).</note>, a great man in all disciplines, proved with many reasons in the final part of his *First Philosophy* that the future cannot be foreseen by astrologers. Therefore, no faith should be placed in their predictions. I omit Henry of Hesse <note>original: "Henricum ex Assia"; a 14th-century theologian and mathematician at the University of Paris.</note> and many illustrious moderns in the Academy of Paris who pursued this vanity in dedicated works. Indeed, the greatest part of philosophers have despised it rather than refuted it, just like other <term>itinerant arts</term> <note>original: "artes circulatrices"; refers to the tricks of street performers and peddlers.</note>, old wives' tales, and the delusions of charlatans.

But it is worth noting that astronomers themselves have also rejected this profession. This could not have happened unless they were aware of its manifest falsehood, since otherwise, for those most skilled in the movements of the heavens, as much knowledge, glory, and profit would accrue to them as there was faith and authority in astrology. But that Eudoxus of Cnidus whom we recently cited was supreme in mathematics, and Aristotle relies on his judgment in astronomical matters. Yet this most prudent legislator—for he wrote laws for his citizens—and a distinguished physician under Philistion and a philosopher under Plato, nevertheless warned us not to believe astrologers and committed this to writing. Thus, mathematical reasoning had demonstrated the truth to him, and his teacher Plato had also convinced him. Panetius is the authority that Cassander and Archelaus, though they excelled in astronomy, never used this kind of prediction. Scylax of Halicarnassus, although most learned in all mathematics, repudiated this whole genre of divining through the stars.

Let us come to the moderns: Nicolaus Oresme <note>A significant 14th-century French philosopher and mathematician.</note>, both a most sharp philosopher and a most skilled mathematician, also attacks astrological superstition with indignation in a specific commentary. He thought nothing was more deceptive, nothing more detestable, and nothing more pestilential to all ranks of people, but especially to princes.

<margin>Giovanni Marliani.</margin>
Giovanni Marliani in our own age was—and was considered—the supreme figure in mathematics. He not only always abstained from these predictions but had even begun to write about their falsehood in his final years; although he was long-lived, he was cut off by death before he could finish it. This man, who was not at all boastful, used to say he possessed the most certain demonstrations against the astrologers.

<margin>Luchinus</margin>
Our friend Luchinus, himself an excellent mathematician, related this to me more than once, as did others.

<margin>Paulus of Florence.</margin>
Paulus of Florence <note>Likely Paolo dal Pozzo Toscanelli (1397–1482), the mathematician and cosmographer.</note>, most learned in Greek and Latin, in medicine, and especially in mathematics—whenever he was asked about this profession, he always asserted it was uncertain and deceitful. Among other things, he cited the evident evidence of his own experience: although he had already completed eighty-five years of life, he had found no "vital constellation" <note>A planetary configuration indicating a long life.</note> in his own birth chart, which he had examined most diligently. I could bring forward many of those who are still living, both philosophers and astronomers...

<summary>Pico provides a catalog of historical and contemporary intellectuals—including Alexander of Aphrodisias, Averroes, Avicenna, and Nicolaus Oresme—who rejected astrology as a fraudulent or illogical practice. He emphasizes that even master astronomers and mathematicians, such as Eudoxus and Marliani, found no truth in astrological prediction.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Pico’s survey of intellectual authorities who rejected astrology. Having discussed ancient philosophers like Alexander of Aphrodisias and medieval thinkers like Averroes, he now turns to his own contemporary circle of Italian humanists—Marsilio Ficino, Angelo Poliziano, and Niccolò Leoniceno—to show that the most learned men of his own day also view astrology as a fraudulent or purely "poetic" pursuit.</meta>

# Book One

...feeling the same. But I do not know if they wish to stir up envy against themselves among men who believe they are powerful over heaven and fate. Furthermore, our Marsilius <note>Marsilio Ficino (1433–1499), the leader of the Platonic Academy in Florence and a mentor to Pico. Although Ficino practiced a form of "natural magic," Pico here portrays him as a skeptic of judicial astrology.</note> wrote effectively against them, following the tracks of Plotinus. <margin>Marsilius.</margin> In interpreting and explaining Plotinus, he greatly aided, increased, and illuminated the Platonic cause. And if, looking out for the health of men, he sometimes gathers certain aids for himself from the heavens, he desires that such a thing be possible rather than actually believes it. I can testify most faithfully to the mind of this man, with whom I am on familiar terms; I have had no one who more often or more effectively encouraged me to expose this fraud. Nor is there ever a richer occasion or harvest of laughter for us whenever we joke together about the vanity <margin>Poliziano. Nicolaus Leoniceno.</margin> of astrologers, especially if a third party intervenes: Poliziano <note>Angelo Poliziano (1454–1494), a brilliant poet and scholar in the Medici circle, known for his sharp wit.</note>. He is always present as a wonderful mocker <note>original: "exhibilator," literally "one who hisses off the stage."</note> of all superstitions. 

Perhaps the judgment of our Nicolaus Leonicenus <note>Niccolò Leoniceno (1428–1524), a famous physician and humanist at the University of Ferrara, known for correcting errors in ancient medical and botanical texts.</note> on this matter should not be concealed. Although he faithfully masters mathematics—as he does all the liberal sciences—he nevertheless judges this "prophesying" astrology to be so vain that he does not even think those who wrote about it (especially the more learned ones) actually believed the things they were writing. If you ask the reason why they wrote it, he responds that it was partly due to greed, and partly the result of the ignorance of princes. 

For, he says, when those excellent men were laboring day and night in measuring the movements and bodies of the stars—which is what mathematical astronomy <term>mathematica astronomia</term><note>The scientific study of planetary positions and cycles, which Pico distinguishes from "divinatory" astrology.</note> does—there was no reward for them from princes. Those rulers, you see, cared nothing for how large the stars were, or with what speed they revolved through the spaces of heaven. When the astronomers saw this, lest they remain impoverished of earthly things while scrutinizing heavenly ones, they devised a clever deception to bind the minds of princes to them and make them lovers of their profession. 

They invented the idea that the fortunes of all people, but especially of princes, depend on these stars: specifically their children, their lives, their power, their victories, and their health. They claimed that because they had observed the heavens for a long time, they had thoroughly learned and explored what good things the stars promised or what adversity they announced. Furthermore, they claimed to have remedies at hand by which foreseen evils could be repelled and good things confirmed. They argued that if a "fortunate hour" were noted, certain images could be fashioned from materials that shared a kinship with those heavenly natures; through wonderful mechanisms, a power would be drawn down from the stars into these objects, making men most happy and kings powerful. Merely by touching or wearing these items, they would easily obtain whatever they desired. 

To make all these things more believable, they added that the more secret mysteries of this art had been revealed to them by divinity—just as one reads in Maternus <note>Firmicus Maternus, a 4th-century author of a major astrological handbook, the *Mathesis*.</note> that Petosiris and Aesculapius <note>Legendary founders of astrology and medicine; Petosiris was a semi-mythical Egyptian priest-astrologer.</note> received many things from the most powerful deity Mercury. Then indeed the illiterate and curious princes, who were most greedy for the things being promised, were easily led to believe them, to support the practitioners, and to stimulate these studies more and more every day with rewards. Our Leonicenus speaks and thinks this seriously, and it is not far from the truth regarding astrologers.

But we must especially beware lest astrologers creep into our trust by writing volumes falsely attributed to great authors—a practice they share with every superstition. For since the things they predict cannot be confirmed by reason, they seek to catch credit for their errors by attaching the names of most famous and ancient men to these books of fables, whether they themselves believe these things to be true or merely want them to be believed by others. To this category belongs the book *On the Properties of the Elements*—in which great conjunctions are discussed—and the book *On Secrets* addressed to Alexander. <margin>The book *On the Properties of the Elements* and *On Secrets* are falsely attributed to Aristotle.</margin> These are attributed to Aristotle through no fault or merit of that good philosopher. Similarly, the magi circulate the books of Plato *On the Cow* <note>The *Liber Vaccae* (Book of the Cow) was a notorious medieval Arabic grimoire of "low magic" falsely attributed to Plato.</note> and those they call the *Institutions*, which are more execrably filled with dreams and fictions, and are no less alien to Plato than these "medicines" are distant from Plato's integrity and wisdom. Thus of old the heretics called Gnostics used to show off books of Zoroaster <note>Pico is likely referencing Porphyry’s *Life of Plotinus*, which mentions Gnostics using forged Zoroastrian texts.</note>, in which they founded their heresy...

<summary>Pico recounts how his contemporaries Ficino, Poliziano, and Leoniceno mocked astrology, with Leoniceno suggesting the "art" was a fraud invented by astronomers to secure funding from ignorant princes. He also warns against forged texts attributed to Aristotle and Plato used to give astrology a false veneer of authority.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Pico's argument that astrology relies on fraudulent texts.
