# Book One

...they seek to make their works venerable by claiming the antiquity of Zoroaster <note>A legendary ancient Persian prophet often claimed by Renaissance magicians as the founder of astrology and magic.</note>. Porphyry <note>A 3rd-century Neoplatonist philosopher.</note> demonstrated through many arguments that these writings were new and invented, rather than belonging to Zoroaster. Those who are unskilled in "humane letters" <term>humane letters (humaniores litterae): the study of classical literature, grammar, and history, which humanists used to detect forgeries</term> are easily deceived and ensnared by these lies, even if they are otherwise learned. It is precisely through these studies—by recognizing the phrasing and character of a text—that we immediately identify the author and discern the forged from the legitimate. Indeed, the superstitious fictions of our current astrologers, which are now in circulation, are so far from any resemblance to the truth that they are obvious even to a common person. 

For who could be led to believe that the book *On the Old Woman* <note>original: "De Vetula." This was a famous 13th-century poem falsely attributed to the Roman poet Ovid.</note> is truly by Ovid? In that work, wonders are predicted concerning "great conjunctions" <term>great conjunctions: the rare alignment of Jupiter and Saturn, which astrologers believed signaled major historical shifts</term> and the Christian law. Roger Bacon <note>Roger Bacon (c. 1214–1292), a pioneering English scientist and friar who, despite his brilliance, was a firm believer in the power of the stars.</note>, that great patron of astrology, uses the testimony of no other writer more willingly—unless perhaps he brings forward Artephius <note>A legendary author to whom many alchemical and magical texts were attributed.</note>, who reveals countless other secrets. Among these is the claim that a man’s life, talent, and circumstances—all of them—can be known beforehand through an inspection, not of the stars, but of his urine <note>original: "lotio." Pico is mocking the overlap between medical uroscopy and astrological divination.</note>. 

Bacon also places great faith in that "Ethical Philosopher" <note>Aethicus Ister, the purported author of a bizarre and largely fictional "Cosmography."</note> whose book on cosmography is said to have been translated by Jerome. The text is so ridiculous it could not be more so, yet it is frequently cited by our Roger in his letter to Pope Clement. I am almost led to believe that Bacon himself composed a certain booklet titled *On the Errors of Students of Theology*. In the first volume of that work, he charges theologians with the "error" of confirming the mysteries of religion more from Aristotle and other philosophers than from the authors we just named: Aethicus, Artephius, Ovid’s *On the Old Woman*, and similar poets. 

This book is falsely attributed to Albert <note>Albert the Great (c. 1200–1280), a teacher of Thomas Aquinas and a polymath often wrongly associated with the occult.</note>, but most deceitfully so, since he never mentioned these dreams in his genuine theological writings. Rather, the work should rightly be attributed to Bacon; his other writings clearly show he held such opinions, as they are always teeming with the "oracles" and testimonies of those authors. If he could believe those, it is no wonder he could also believe in astrology. 

Indeed, this class of superstitious men is so shameless <note>original: "frontem perfricuerunt," a Latin idiom meaning to rub the forehead to remove the blush of shame.</note> that they even circulate books on necromantic images under the name of Thomas Aquinas. It is therefore less surprising that they possess some "Rings of Ptolemy," or that they forge astrological books for Aristotle which Ptolemy <note>Claudius Ptolemy, the most famous astronomer of antiquity.</note> never wrote. By the same boldness or ignorance, many attribute a short work by a certain man of York <note>original: "Eboracensis." Likely referring to John of York or another medieval English writer.</note> to Albert. They also cite books by Hippocrates <note>The famous Greek "Father of Medicine."</note> on prognosticating illness from the course of the stars. I believe Hippocrates was ignorant of these when he wrote the *Prognostics* explained by Galen and celebrated throughout Greece—or, if he did know them, he supposedly set them aside as "secrets" to be shared only with those properly initiated. 

I pass over what Al-Kindi <note>A 9th-century Islamic philosopher and astrologer.</note> and others mention regarding rains and "interrogations" <term>interrogations: an astrological practice of casting a chart to answer a specific question</term>, citing Pythagorean and Aristotelian authority. There is also a book titled *On Governance* <note>The "Secretum Secretorum," a wildly popular medieval forgery claiming to be Aristotle's advice to Alexander the Great.</note> attributed to Aristotle, in which they speak in such a way about the heavens. If only they had not attributed such profane things to holy men, or made Saint Jerome the translator of a book on incantations! Though, if they have defamed the very angels, they can easily do so to men; they claim some of these delusions were handed down by the angel of Adam, others by Solomon's angel, and others by the guardian angel of Tobias. 

But let us return to the astrologers, leaving aside these related errors. Aristotle showed in a single word what he thought of this class of men when, in his *Problems*, he categorized the astrologer alongside the mime and the conjurer <note>original: "praestigiatore," a sleight-of-hand artist or trickster. Pico refers to a section in the pseudo-Aristotelian *Problems* (30.1) where such types are grouped together.</note>. 

But you will say: "Even if those ancient philosophers did not write those specific books, those who *did* write on astrology were still philosophers—men like Albumasar, Ptolemy, Haly, Abenzagel, Julius Firmicus, and countless other Latin, Greek, and 'barbarian' authors of great learning and talent." 

You, sir, have timely warned me not to...

He specifically critiques Roger Bacon for relying on these "ridiculous" forgeries and notes that true philosophers like Aristotle viewed astrologers as mere entertainers or tricksters.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Pico della Mirandola’s critique of astrology’s intellectual foundations. Having previously argued that astrologers rely on forged "ancient" texts like those of "Zoroaster" or pseudo-Ovid, Pico now turns his focus to the most famous authorities in the field—Ptolemy and Albumasar—to show that even the "greats" were poor philosophers who lacked logical rigor.</meta>

# Book One

...I would say this only against you: that astrology has been neglected by true philosophers. Furthermore, whoever has written about it has philosophized either not at all or very poorly. Therefore, leave us to our Pythagoras, our Plato, and our Aristotle, if it please the gods; and you, keep for yourselves your Abu Ma'shar, your Al-Qabisi, your Ibn Ezra, and your Al-Zarqali <note>Pico lists several famous medieval Islamic astrologers: Albumasar, Alchabitius, Abraham ibn Ezra, and Abenzaghel. He views them as inferior to the "true" Greek philosophers.</note>. It will be clearly demonstrated how far all of these were from a philosophical mind. We shall openly show that they resort to the most mythical fables, assert things that have no basis in reason, speak contradictions, and overturn their own arguments. Such things are entirely alien to a philosopher, whose most specific duty is to believe nothing and affirm nothing that cannot be demonstrated by either evidence or reason. But come, let us say something here to establish that the authors of astrology were either mediocre or bad philosophers.

<margin>Ptolemy’s standing in scholarship.</margin>
Furthermore, they will easily grant that Ptolemy is the "prince" of the others. Indeed, he is the most learned of the astrologers and, as far as mathematics is concerned, a man of the greatest genius. However, regarding the "casters of birth-charts" <term>birth-charts (genethliacos): the practice of predicting a person’s life based on the stars at their birth</term>, he is, as they say, the "best of the worst." How he handled philosophical matters—with what level of judgment—he sufficiently indicated both in the prefaces to his great composition, which he calls the *Almagest* <note>original: "Almagestum." Ptolemy's 2nd-century masterpiece on the motions of the stars and planets.</note>, and in the books of the *Apotelesmaton* <note>original: "apoteclesmatō." Better known as the Tetrabiblos, Ptolemy's primary work on the influence of the stars.</note>.

<margin>Ptolemy’s opinion.</margin>
For at the beginning of his mathematical books, he divides "contemplative philosophy" into three types, following the opinion of Aristotle: the theological, the natural, and the mathematical. Then, explaining the reason for this division, he says that all things consist of three elements: matter, form, and motion. These can be separated from one another in thought, but not in reality. From these three, therefore, those three types of philosophy are derived: the theological from motion (since the cause of the first motion is none other than God); the physical from matter; and the mathematical from form.

<margin>Against Ptolemy.</margin>
This is Ptolemy’s opinion, in which any slightly learned person would not doubt there are as many errors among good philosophers as there are words. For not all things consist of those three. If he means "natural things" when he says "all things," then how will philosophy itself be concerned with these, when it is later divided into those three types: physical, divine, and mathematical? Moreover, nothing among natural things consists solely of motion, although nothing is made or remains without motion; but let us grant him this turn of phrase. Aristotle himself, whom he approves—how will he allow the "theological" category to arise from motion? For even God himself, insofar as He is the author and cause of the first motion, is investigated by the philosopher, not just the theologian.

<margin>Against the same author.</margin>
The rest of his points are either false or easily seen as the inventions of a man little skilled and poorly trained in philosophy. Indeed, in the books of his "four-part work" <note>original: "quadripartitos." The Tetrabiblos.</note>, more notable and evident errors appear. For instance, he believes the Moon is "moister" because moist vapor ascends from the Earth to the Moon (which is closer to the Earth than the other stars). By the same logic, he claims Saturn is "dry" because it is further removed from these vapors. He also claims Saturn is "cold" because it is far from the sun's heat; that Jupiter is "temperate" because it is placed in the middle between cold Saturn and burning Mars; and many other things of this kind concerning the properties of the stars, which philosophers would sooner hiss off the stage than bother to refute. And although his Arabic commentator <note>Haly Abenrodan (c. 998–1061), an Egyptian physician and astrologer who wrote a famous commentary on Ptolemy.</note>, blushing at his master’s error, tries to twist Ptolemy’s words into another meaning, Ptolemy himself does not allow himself to be defended or excused, as he asserts, affirms, and repeats these things so often that no doubt remains about his meaning.

<margin>The nature of Albumasar.</margin>
Indeed, learn about all of them from this one example, and judge the worse ones by the best. Almost second after Ptolemy is held to be Albumasar <note>Abu Ma'shar (787–886), one of the most influential astrologers of the Middle Ages.</note>. He was neither a philosopher nor a logician, and he was unskilled in mathematics. He was, in fact, a professor of the art of grammar, and—as Abenrodan <note>Haly Abenrodan.</note> tells it—he turned to astrology from writing histories. Even in his own profession, you may know how "true" he was from the fact that he thought Ptolemy the astrologer was one of the kings of Egypt who succeeded Alexander the Great—as if there were not more than five hundred years between those kings and the man himself...

<summary>Pico criticizes the philosophical credentials of astrology's greatest authorities, specifically attacking Ptolemy's flawed logic regarding the division of science and his unscientific explanations for planetary influences. He also dismisses the influential Arab astrologer Albumasar as an uneducated grammarian who committed massive chronological errors.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Pico della Mirandola’s critique of the famous authorities of astrology. # Book One

...years intervened; since the Ptolemaic kings flourished four hundred years before Christ, <margin>In what time Ptolemy lived.</margin> while Ptolemy the astrologer wrote under Hadrian and Antoninus <note>Ptolemy the scientist (2nd century AD) is often confused by some with the earlier Ptolemaic dynasty of Egypt; Pico is clarifying the timeline to show that the "prince of astrologers" was not as ancient as some claimed.</note>. Behold how wondrous it is that a seeker of the highest things and a faithful observer could show such sleepiness or sluggishness of mind in so obvious a matter? How much he erred in astrological matters, and with what blatant and confessed lies he persisted as if they were truths, we shall declare later. Why should I mention [Julius Firmicus] Maternus <margin>The character of Maternus.</margin> <note>A 4th-century Roman official and astrologer whose work was a standard textbook in the Middle Ages.</note>, who hallucinates even in the basics of arithmetic? He writes what Mercury decrees when it occupies the "midheaven" in a nighttime birth-chart, as if Mercury could ever be more than forty or so degrees away from the Sun, or as if the Sun at night were not always more than seventy degrees from the midheaven. I pass over many other things in which you will always find a man of much talk and very little wisdom.

Now, if Mallius <margin>The character of Mallius.</margin> <note>Marcus Manilius, author of the 1st-century astronomical poem Astronomica.</note> were not a poet, good God, with what laughter would we pursue him! He says those celestial images [constellations] he imagines are started by a few stars rather than completed ones, for fear that if more fires were lit there, the world would burn in a conflagration.

<margin>The character of Bonatus.</margin> I do not descend to the more recent ones—common and ignorant men—to whom, as if to rightful owners, almost this whole profession has devolved. Among them, Bonatus <note>Guido Bonatti (c. 1210–1296), the most famous medieval Italian astrologer, whom Dante famously placed in the Eighth Circle of Hell.</note> is of the primary authority. He is not only ignorant of philosophy, but he clearly raves and is delirious. Read his first book *On Judgments*, in which he prefaces the work. I lie if you do not judge the man worthy of hellebore <term>hellebore: a plant used in antiquity as a remedy for madness or insanity</term>. He constructs—where he is least foolish—certain reasons by which he tries to prove astrology is true; what shall I say of them? They are false, indeed more childish and ridiculous than can be said.

Indeed, the one argument he thinks is most effective is that the **quadrivium** <term>quadrivium: the four mathematical arts of medieval education—arithmetic, geometry, music, and astronomy</term> would be destroyed if astrology were removed. For he says it is one of the four mathematical arts. See how he does not even know what this very thing is that he professes? For this "divinatory astrology" <note>original: "astrologia diuinatrix"</note> which we are refuting is as far from that which is numbered among the mathematical arts as light is from darkness, or as truth is from a lie. And while this one, which usurps the prediction of the future, cannot stand if that former and truer one [astronomy] is removed, the logic does not work in reverse: if the divining one is taken away, the mathematical one is not also removed. This is so clear, even to those who have touched the first elements of these arts, that to declare it further would be superfluous.

Ptolemy himself, in the prefaces of the *Apotelesmaton* <note>The Tetrabiblos, Ptolemy's work on astrology; the Greek title means "Effects."</note>, after he speaks of the twofold astronomy, nevertheless refers his discourse to the former and mathematical part, saying thus: "The first indeed..." <note>original Greek: "το μεν πρωτον"</note> and what follows.

If by chance this profession has not displeased certain people of otherwise good judgment, it is not immediately good just because some good person did not disapprove of it; for even good men are not always good in every respect, and few achieve the prerogative of being learned in all measures. And if I must say something paradoxical <note>original Greek: "παρα δοξον"</note>: not all learned philosophers are always philosophers.

But it is also necessary to remember that there are certain truths against which some desire of ours resists; and there are others against which there is no resistance. In the first category [where desire resists] are contained all things concerning morals and many theological matters; in the second [where there is no resistance] is the greatest part of what concerns physical and mathematical things. Furthermore, it is manifest that this truth we are treating—concerning the **vanity of astrology**—belongs to the first category, because the vice of curiosity innate in man fights against it. Since this curiosity is the most powerful of all, being proper to man insofar as he is man, it sometimes causes many people either not to have the leisure to investigate this truth, or to approach it unwillingly even when it has been found. And just as many, after having treated of the philosophers...

<meta>This page continues Pico della Mirandola's systematic dismantling of astrology’s credibility. Having previously criticized the errors of individual authors like Ptolemy and Manilius, he now addresses the psychological reasons why people remain attracted to astrology despite its lack of evidence, before moving into a theological critique based on the Hebrew prophets.</meta>

# Book One

...most evident arguments against greed, yet men still gape after the accumulation of wealth. In the same way, even after it has been established for most that the things astrologers say cannot possibly be true, that innate curiosity for the stars is hardly torn away from them. If we, being greedy for news, listen even to tall tales with pleasure, we similarly feel a certain delight toward those who measure the future, even when we sense the astrologers are lying. To this is added the fact that an excessive love of ourselves always infatuates us; for whatever pertains to our prosperity or adversity, we easily hope for, easily fear, and are prompted by a blind desire to seek out those things even where we know they cannot be found. What of the fact that this widespread and long-standing consensus creates a prejudice? Many think that astrology must be *something* simply because so many believe it; yet it never occurs to them to look deeper and see what foundation this matter has, or what solid firmament lies beneath it. Therefore, you will find that almost everyone held by this vanity was either a poor philosopher or certainly a poor astrologer; for the former prevents them from seeing the errors, and the latter prevents them from judging them. In short, it may have pleased some when merely tasted, but it never satisfied the palate of a true philosopher when fully drunk. For it has something on its surface that entices, appearing great, plausible, and useful; but when you look more deeply into it, you see that all is false, uncertain, and mythical—born either from no evidence at all or from certain very weak conjectures, about which we shall discourse abundantly and at length in the following books.

<margin>
Some were deceived by the similarity of names.
</margin>
But perhaps this also deceived some: that there are similar names among both philosophers and astrologers, which might lead one to believe they were the same people who wrote both philosophical and astrological works. For instance, there is an Albumasar <note>Abu Ma'shar (787–886 AD), a famous Persian astrologer whose works were highly influential in medieval Europe.</note> among the philosophers and likewise among the astrologers; but although the Latin language confuses these names, they are distinguished differently among the Arabs. For the one who is a philosopher is called Abumašar, while the astrologer is called Abuasar. Likewise, Abubater <note>Likely referring to Abu Bakr (Ibn Tufail), the 12th-century philosopher.</note> wrote on predictions of nativities, and another by the same name wrote philosophical works, especially the book on how one becomes a self-taught philosopher <note>The famous "Philosophus Autodidactus" or "Hayy ibn Yaqdhan," an Arabic philosophical novel about a feral child who discovers God through reason.</note>, which I translated from Hebrew into Latin <margin>A book translated from Hebrew into Latin by the author.</margin> last year. But that author was Al-Thabibi, while this one was the son of Tripdis. There is a similar affinity of names in many cases, despite a great disagreement in both their times and their professions. Enough regarding the philosophers; let us move on to the prophets, that is, to the oracles of the Old and New Law, beginning with Isaiah. <margin>Testimonies of the prophets.</margin>

He, therefore, when threatening future destruction to the Babylonians—among whom this sect especially flourished, which is why astrologers were even called "Chaldeans"—and while summoning King Cyrus of the Persians (whom he called "Anointed" even two hundred years before he was born) to fight against them, addressed the city of the Chaldeans to be desolated in this way:

> Let the augurs of heaven now stand and save you, those who contemplated the stars and computed the months so they might announce what was to happen to you. Behold, they have become like stubble; fire has consumed them, nor shall they deliver their own soul from the power of the flame.

And a few verses before this, he had rebuked them for this celestial observation thus:

> This wisdom and knowledge of yours shall deceive you; evil shall come upon you, and you shall not know its origin; and calamity shall fall upon you which you shall not be able to atone for. <note>Quoting Isaiah 47:10–13. Pico uses this to argue that if the "experts" of the stars could not see their own destruction coming, the science is useless.</note>

In these words, the divine prophet accuses the astrologers of a double rashness: one is thinking that they can foresee the future from the heavens; the other is thinking that, once foreseen, they can either ward off evils or secure good things. "Evil shall come," he says, "whose origin you shall not know"—that is, which neither Mars nor the cold star of Saturn shall have signaled to you. Furthermore, you will not be able to atone for the falling calamity—that is, to repel it from you by the "election of hours," <term>election of hours: the practice of choosing an astrologically auspicious moment to begin an action</term> astrological images, <note>Astrological talismans or amulets engraved with celestial symbols intended to harness planetary power.</note> or other superstitious contrivances. It is worthy of attention that we should use these points to refute the responses of those who wish to be both Chaldeans and Christians at the same time. For they are accustomed to say, not simply...

<meta>This page continues Pico della Mirandola’s philosophical and theological attack on astrology. He has just explained that curiosity and self-love lead people to believe in the stars despite a lack of evidence. # Book One

...that astrology is condemned by the saints and prophets. But <insert>they claim</insert> it is only condemned insofar as they attribute vices or virtues to the heavens, or bind human events to fatal necessity. They argue that since even "good" astrologers refute these errors, those holy men did not abhor the science of astrology itself, but only the mistakes of certain astrologers.

Let Pierre d’Ailly <note>Petrus Alliacensis (1351–1420), a French cardinal and scholar who famously tried to harmonize astrology with theology.</note> and whoever else protects themselves with this defense tell me: did it pertain to human morals that the King of the Persians waged war on the Assyrians? And even if it does not involve morals, why did the prophet believe that such a thing could not be foreseen by even the greatest astrologers? If those astrologers had been in the error of thinking that future events must happen by necessity, they would not have been blamed for failing to avert a coming calamity through their rites—a calamity they themselves would have believed could not be averted, since they thought everything happened by necessity.

Furthermore, by no right judgment are good arts condemned just because certain evil people abuse them. Otherwise, we would first have to condemn the reading of the Sacred Scriptures, from which so many heresies and so much madness have been confirmed by certain ignorant and proud men. Philosophy would likewise have to be condemned, since one philosopher says the soul is mortal, while another says there is only one soul for all people. Some deny that God provides for humanity; others claim there is no religion at all. By this logic, all good things would be overturned, as there is nothing so good that human nature cannot abuse it.

Therefore, those who defend themselves this way are indirectly and gravely slandering the judgment of the Church—which they are ashamed to openly despise. They must be forced to either repudiate this vanity entirely or admit they are deviating from their ancestors, the leaders of the Church. For by whatever reason those leaders condemned astrology, I ask: did they condemn it justly or unjustly? They do not wish to say it was unjust. If it was just, why do you not also condemn it along with them?

"But we do condemn it," they will say, "and we also condemn those errors for which astrology displeased them." But I ask this: why does it not displease you for those same reasons? For it is clear—and we will soon show—that the Church fathers did not forbid astrology in part, but followed after it to abhor the whole thing entirely. You contend this was done because of certain errors. So be it. But answer this: is the whole thing rightly rejected because of those errors? If it is right, why do you not do the same? Instead, you approve what they condemned; you defend what they attacked; you spread what they forbade; and you teach publicly what they wished to remain unknown.

Or is it as d'Ailly says—that because astrology could have hindered the growing faith, the first doctors of the nascent Church pursued it, but now that the Church is "adult," it no longer harms but is even greatly profitable? This will be refuted later. We will clearly demonstrate that it is as pestilential now as it was then, a fact which experience itself still demonstrates. They argue it was not the practice that was condemned, but its abuse. Why, then, did they not condemn philosophy itself, but only the impiety of certain philosophers? Why did they not condemn astrologers, but astrology itself? Clearly, it is because in philosophy, any error is the fault of the practitioner; but in astrology, the profession itself is the fault. Following their authority along with reason, we—when disputing against the impious—have refuted the errors of philosophers, not philosophy. But here, we refute not just astrologers, but astrology, because astrology itself is an error.

But let us return to the testimony of the prophets. God speaks to us through Moses: "The nations listen to soothsayers and diviners; but you have been instructed otherwise by the Lord your God." In place of what we read as "soothsayers," <margin>Achinas.</margin> the Hebrew text uses the word *nihonen* <note>original: "nihonen"</note>. Achinas <note>Likely referring to Rabbi Akiva, a major Jewish scholar, though Pico's transliteration varies.</note>, the greatest teacher of the Hebrews, says this refers to those who calculate times and observe lucky and unlucky hours...

<summary>Pico argues that astrology is inherently flawed and was rejected in its entirety by the Church and the Prophets, refuting Pierre d'Ailly's claim that only its "misuse" is problematic. He draws a distinction between philosophy, which is a valid pursuit prone to individual error, and astrology, which he considers an error in its very essence.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Pico della Mirandola’s argument that the Church Fathers and Biblical prophets were not merely condemning "bad" astrology, but the entire practice itself. He explores the different names given to astrologers throughout history and cites several authoritative sources to prove that the science of the stars is both religiously dangerous and intellectually empty.</meta>

# Book One

<b>

For that term comes from <note>There is a blank space in the original manuscript here, likely intended for a Greek root word like *hora*</note> which signifies an "hour": Jerome <note>Saint Jerome (c. 347–420 AD), the scholar responsible for the Vulgate Latin translation of the Bible.</note> translated them as "augurs" <term>augurs: ancient Roman diviners who interpreted the will of the gods through signs, like the flight of birds</term>. But even in the book of Isaiah, we see astrologers referred to as augurs. Indeed, the specific name "astrologer" was not used in the Sacred Scriptures. For the language itself has various expressions, and that particular superstition has been assigned different names at different times. In the old days, they were called "Chaldeans" <note>A term originally referring to the people of Babylonia, who were famous for their astronomical observations, but which became a synonym for "astrologer" in the Roman world.</note> and "casters of horoscopes" (*genethliaci*); in Augustine's time, they were called "mathematicians" and "wanderers" (*planetarii*); now, they are commonly called "astrologers" everywhere. 

As for what Jerome translated in that place and elsewhere as "diviners," <margin>Ibn Ezra</margin> the Hebrew word is *chilem* <note>original: "chilem." Pico is likely discussing the Hebrew root *halam*, which relates to dreaming or binding, or *h-b-r* (horoscoping), though the OCR spelling here reflects his specific source.</note>: which Ibn Ezra—himself an astrologer—says is a general term for all diviners, but is a more specific name for astrologers. And who is ignorant of that saying of Jeremiah? <margin>Jeremiah</margin> *Do not fear the signs of heaven which the nations fear.* <note>Jeremiah 10:2. Pico uses this to argue that celestial signs should not hold power over a believer's heart.</note> Why then should a Christian man either rejoice or grieve at the judgments of astrologers, from whom Isaiah tells us there is nothing to hope for, and Jeremiah tells us there is nothing to fear? Rather, through both of them, the Divine Truth affirms that this entire profession is, as Ambrose <note>Saint Ambrose (c. 340–397 AD), the Bishop of Milan and a mentor to Augustine.</note> says, "absurd to seek out," since what they promise is impossible. 

<margin>Ambrose</margin> Hence the Lord of Heaven says in the book of Job: <margin>Job</margin> *Do you know the order of heaven, and can you set its logic upon the earth?* And further down: *Who shall declare the logic of the heavens?* <note>Job 38:33 and 38:37.</note> For the error of the astrologers is twofold: first, they subject many things to the heavens that do not actually depend on them; and second, even if the heavens do cause certain effects, they cannot be foreseen by men in the way they think—as these words brought forth from Job demonstrate to us. And since the Doctors of the Church refute both points equally, how can it be said that they only disapprove of astrology because it takes away free will or introduces the necessity of fate? 

<margin>Testimonies of Augustine</margin> Does not that famous reasoning of Augustine concerning twins tend toward stripping them of all foreknowledge of the future? <note>Augustine famously argued that twins born moments apart often have vastly different lives, which should be impossible if their destinies were dictated by the stars at the moment of birth.</note> In his *Enchiridion* <note>A handbook on Christian faith, hope, and love.</note>, did he not say that the mere observation of times—thinking this hour lucky and that one unlucky—pertains to a great sin? Even though in this "choosing of hours and days," we are exercising our freedom rather than having it taken away. 

But it is certain: astrology displeased them in every respect, although especially in that part where it subjected religion and morals to the heavens. In that regard, they cursed it; everywhere they refuted it. In that regard, they judged it impious; everywhere they judged it vain. Here they called it blasphemous; everywhere superstitious. Here they called it abominable; everywhere ridiculous. Therefore, Augustine, in his book *On Christian Doctrine*, said that those called "casters of horoscopes" (*genethliaci*) belong to a "pernicious superstition," not only because they think our actions, but even the outcomes of our actions, proceed from the stars. And in his book of *Confessions*, speaking of the "wanderers"—that is, the astrologers—he says that Christian and true piety expels and damns them. 

When explaining that passage of Moses: *Let the stars be placed for signs and seasons,* <note>Genesis 1:14.</note> Augustine says it does not mean "signs" that are vain to observe, but signs necessary for the uses of life, such as those observed by sailors, farmers, and craftsmen of that kind. <margin>Basil</margin> In the same place, Basil <note>Basil of Caesarea (330–379 AD), a leading Greek theologian.</note> said that astrology was a "most busy vanity"; <margin>Ambrose</margin> Ambrose called it "useless and impossible"; <margin>Theodoret</margin> Theodoret <note>Theodoret of Cyrus (c. 393–457 AD), a central figure in early Christian theology.</note> said it was refuted even by the philosophers; <margin>Chrysostom</margin> Chrysostom <note>John Chrysostom (c. 347–407 AD), famed for his eloquent preaching.</note> called it "vain, false, and ridiculous." Let us read Bardesanes, Euselaus, Didymus, Apollinaris, Tertullian, and countless other apostolic men. To put it simply: we see that the Hebrews, the heretics, and the pagans alike have pursued this race of men with a censorious rod. 

<margin>Bardesanes</margin> <margin>Euselaus</margin> <margin>Apollinaris</margin> <margin>Tertullian</margin> Because of this, Augustine wondered why, even though Didymus <note>Didymus the Blind (c. 313–398 AD), a scholar from Alexandria.</note> and these testimonies refuting the astrologers were read with such frequency in the churches, the meeting-houses were still full of our people who would receive the "proper times for doing things" from the "mathematicians" <note>Here used in the historical sense of "astrologers."</note>. He said the same to the people when commenting on the sixty-third Psalm...

<summary>Pico identifies the various names used for astrologers across history (Chaldeans, mathematicians, etc.) and uses the authority of Church Fathers like Augustine, Jerome, and Ambrose to argue that astrology is a "pernicious superstition" that should be entirely rejected by Christians.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Pico della Mirandola’s survey of historical and ecclesiastical condemnations of astrology. Having previously discussed the various names for astrologers, he now turns to specific examples of repentance and the formal prohibitions issued by Church Fathers, Popes, and Councils.</meta>

# Book One

...when he was preaching, he produced a repentant mathematician <term>mathematician: in this period, the term "mathematicus" almost always referred to an astrologer or someone who cast horoscopes</term> who had renounced his profession, no differently than if some Jew or pagan had received the bath of regeneration <note>original: "regenerationis lauacrum," referring to baptism</note>. How beautifully the same author, interpreting John <note>Likely referring to Saint John Chrysostom, a 4th-century Church Father known for his eloquent preaching</note>, warns us of our madness: we enter the homes of astrologers as free men, only to leave as slaves; by purchasing their lies, we pay out our own freedom to them. Indeed, in the book *On the Nature of Demons*, he expressly states that after the coming of Christ, no one is permitted to interpret anyone’s horoscope <note>original: "genituram," a birth-chart</note> from the heavens. <margin>Jerome</margin> Jerome says that seeking the courses of the stars and searching out future events from them is among the "reproaches of Egypt"—that is, the remnants of idolatry. <margin>Severianus</margin> Severianus, in the book he wrote on the seven arts (which Roger <note>Likely referring to Roger Bacon, a 13th-century friar and scientist</note> falsely cites as if it were by Cassiodorus), after speaking of true astronomy, says: "Then those matters which pertain to foreseeing the future ought to be so unknown that they should not even seem to have been written; for they are, without doubt, contrary to our faith." These are his words exactly.

<margin>Abhorrence of astrology through ecclesiastical decrees.</margin> 

If the opinion of such great and excellent men moves no one, at least let the papal authority deter them, which so strictly forbids this profession to our people. <margin>Alexander III</margin> For instance, Alexander III <note>Pope from 1159 to 1181</note>, the Supreme Pontiff, required a certain priest to abstain from the ministry of the altar for a full year because he had attempted to investigate a theft from a church by using an astrolabe <term>astrolabe: an ancient instrument used to calculate the positions of stars, often used by astrologers to determine "lucky" or "unlucky" times</term>—even though the same pontiff testifies that no magic or other superstition had been admitted there. <margin>Synod of Martin</margin> In the Synod of Pope Martin, it is written: it is not for true Christians to observe either the courses of the moon or stars, or the empty fallacy of signs, for the purpose of building a house or joining in marriage. Moreover, under the name of "soothsayers" <term>soothsayers: or "haruspices," those who predict the future by inspecting entrails or other omens</term>, the astrologer is pronounced anathema <note>A formal curse or excommunication by the Church</note> <margin>Gregory</margin> by a decree of Gregory the Younger. <margin>Council of Toledo</margin> And in the Council of Toledo: if the practitioner is a priest or deacon, let him be relegated to a monastery to pay the penalties of his crime there in perpetual detention. <margin>Augustine</margin> For as Augustine teaches in his book *On the Nature of Demons*, those who observe days and hours in conducting their business and works are usually designated among our people under the name of "soothsayers." In this passage, that part of astrology which deals with "elections" <term>elections: the astrological practice of choosing the most auspicious moment to begin a task, like a wedding or a journey</term> seems especially noted.

Who then among Christian men (for my speech is now addressed to all) would dare to defend, follow, or extol astrology—prohibited by law, condemned by prophets, mocked by saints, and forbidden by pontiffs and holy synods? But if you oppose me by citing Albert the Great <note>Albertus Magnus (c. 1200–1280), a famous scholar and theologian who was often associated with the study of nature and the stars</note>, that most excellent theologian who was nevertheless a supporter of astrologers, I will first remind you that many things are attributed to Albert which are not actually his—a point I touched on above. Then, if you should perhaps object by citing the book *On Licit and Illicit Things* <note>Known as the *Speculum Astronomiae*, a text often attributed to Albert that defends certain types of astrology</note> in which he rejects magicians but approves of astronomical authors, I will reply that although many think that is a work of Albert’s, neither Albert himself nor the title of the book confirms this. Indeed, the author—whoever he may have been—deliberately and by profession hides his name. Why? Because many things are read in it that are unworthy of a learned man and a good Christian. For example, the claim that images can be made by which not just one man, but even a whole city may become unhappy or unfortunate; or that magical books should not be cast away because they might one day be useful to the Church. This is clearly against the judgment of the Church itself, which commands those books to be burned and utterly exterminated wherever they are found. For by what reason will it be useful to keep books intact which it would have been most useful never to have been written? Either Albert did not write these things, or if he did, it must be said with the Apostle: "In other things I praise you; in this I do not" <note>A reference to 1 Corinthians 11:2, "I praise you... but in this following matter I do not praise you."</note>. Just as it is a mark of envy to seek what to condemn in great men rather than what to extol, so it is a mark of madness to be unwilling to condemn them where they have failed.

<summary>Pico cites various Church authorities, including Popes and the Council of Toledo, to show that astrology is formally condemned as a "reproach of Egypt" and a form of slavery. He also addresses the pro-astrology writings attributed to Albert the Great, arguing they are either misattributed or simply wrong.</summary>

<meta>This page concludes the first book of Pico della Mirandola's "Disputations Against Divinatory Astrology." Having established the religious and patristic arguments in the preceding sections, he now focuses on the critique of fellow theologians like Pierre d'Ailly and concludes with the legal prohibitions established by the Roman Emperors, specifically Justinian.</meta>

# Book One

->b ii<-

...ought to be imitated. I will praise in Pierre d'Ailly <note>Petrus Aliacensis (1351–1420), a French cardinal and influential theologian who attempted to reconcile astrology with history and theology.</note> his dedication to literature, his practical experience, his extensive reading, and the fact that he wrote and treated certain theological matters with skill and subtlety. However, as for his attempts in one small work to reconcile astrology with history, and in another with theology—seeking to prove it "true" in the first and "pious" in the second through reasoning—I certainly do not praise him. Instead, I condemn, curse, and detest it. For we can defend no position that is more false or more hostile to religion. Since we will discuss this matter at length in the following books, nothing more needs to be said here. In those pages, we will provide ample evidence, even for astrology's supporters, that those booklets are enemies of religion and so full of historical and astrological errors that our old saying might apply: "If you wish to remove the error, remove the book."

We have spoken of philosophers and prophets; what remains are the civil laws—that is, the commands and judgments of the Emperors and legal experts. <margin>Testimonies of civil law.</margin> Their primary goal is to serve the common good, so that human life may be lived well and happily. Since life is improved above all by the "good arts" <note>This refers to the liberal arts and useful sciences</note> and disrupted by harmful ones, these rulers took the greatest care to ensure that the good arts flourished while the harmful ones were, as much as possible, eliminated from the cities. To achieve this, they established rewards and honors for those who taught the good arts, while decreeing public disgrace and punishments for the harmful ones—the more dangerous they judged the art to be, the more severe the penalty.

Therefore, no one who has read the legal codes of Emperor Justinian <margin>Justinian</margin> is unaware of what he thought of astrologers. In these laws, the "art of the mathematicians" (for this is what the astrologers called themselves <note>original: "mathematicorum." In the Roman and Medieval periods, "mathematicus" was a common synonym for an astrologer.</note>) is forbidden as something abominable. The Emperor commanded that no one should consult a mathematician, but rather that the "curiosity for making such judgments should be silenced forever for all people."

If anyone did consult a mathematician, they were threatened with the "penalty of the head" <note>original: "capitis poena," referring to capital punishment or the death penalty.</note>. Surely that most wise Emperor, who relied on the laws and judgment of so many learned men, would not have decreed this unless experience had proven that this profession was not only useless for daily life but truly ruinous to mankind. The most blessed Justinian himself so loathed this class of people that if any mathematician were caught within his imperial court, he would pay the price for his audacity with the most extreme tortures, even unto the rack <term>rack: an instrument of torture, known in Latin as the "eculeus," used to stretch the body to extract confessions or punish crimes.</term>. Finally, speaking of this superstition, the Emperor declared that those who teach such things and those who study them share in the same guilt. Even before the time of Justinian, do we not read that all mathematicians were frequently expelled from the city of Rome? We shall demonstrate this clearly at the conclusion of these disputations.

<margin>Conclusion of this book.</margin> 
Therefore, if all right reason is either guided by prudence, perfected by philosophy, or illuminated by the rays of divine splendor, then astrology must surely be struck down by every sound judgment. For it is a practice that the most prudent lawmakers have banished, the most learned philosophers have refuted, and the most holy and divine men have loathed.

### End of the first book of the Disputations of Giovanni Pico della Mirandola against the astrologers.

<summary>Pico concludes Book One by condemning the pro-astrology writings of Pierre d'Ailly and citing Emperor Justinian's severe legal prohibitions against astrologers as proof of the practice's harmful nature. He summarizes that Law, Philosophy, and Religion all stand united against the "superstition" of astrology.</summary>

<header>Book II</header>

# GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA’S DISPUTATIONS AGAINST ASTROLOGERS, BOOK THE SECOND.

---

## Chapter 1: That this art is uncertain, even by the judgment of its own leaders.

<margin>f</margin>
But lest we fight with authority alone, we shall demonstrate in this entire work, by certain reasoning, that this superstition was rightly rejected by the holy fathers because it is most opposed to religion; that it was usefully forbidden by laws because it is useless—indeed, even harmful—to life; and that it was rationally refuted by philosophers because they recognized it as false and uncertain. And although it seemed we should begin by demonstrating it to be false (since it would immediately be rendered useless as well), I thought I should act differently: namely, that before I disputed its falsehood, I would show the lovers of astrologers that even if this profession were such as they themselves make it out and affirm it to be, no benefit would come from it to the "outer man," <note>The "outer man" refers to one's physical body, wealth, and worldly status.</note> while to the "inner man" <note>The "inner man" refers to the soul, intellect, and moral character.</note> it brings not only the greatest damage, but even destruction. 

Before we approach this, we must first say certain things from which we may understand how much the supreme leaders of the astrologers themselves attribute to their own profession. Ptolemy, <note>Claudius Ptolemy (c. 100–170 AD), the most influential astronomer and astrologer of antiquity.</note> therefore, in the first book of his *Apotelesmaton* <note>original: "apotelesmaton" — better known today as the Tetrabiblos, the foundational text of Western astrology.</note>, after saying that the judgments of astrologers are often lies due to the fault of the one predicting, nevertheless adds these words—which we have chosen to translate literally because they are poorly handled in the common translation and worse in the translation of Avenrodan, <note>Ali ibn Ridwan (c. 988–1061), an Egyptian physician and astrologer whose Latinized name was Avenrodan; his commentary on Ptolemy was standard in the Middle Ages.</note> and are badly explained by him. But when they are faithfully translated, they will require no explanation: 

"Truly, it is clear that even if someone has investigated these disciplines by following their footsteps correctly as far as possible, it is still necessary that he should err very often. This is not only because of those things we mentioned above, but rather due to the very nature of the matter, or because our own weakness is greater than our ability to be equal to the magnitude of such a great profession. For indeed, since every contemplation that deals with the qualities of matter seeks what is likely <note>The Latin implies probability (verisimilia) rather than absolute certainty.</note> rather than deciding anything as absolute truth, this is especially characteristic of that discipline which is, as it were, confused from many dissimilar parts and depends upon the ancient configurations and aspects of the wandering stars <note>The planets.</note>. For those observations concerning the events of things which were noted by the ancients, we apply to our own age whenever matters stand in the same way. But who does not see that it can happen that those very configurations and aspects may be more or less similar to one another over long circuits of time? So that unless a perfect harmony of all things in heaven returns to the same state—especially if you also add the Earth—it seems one should not even hope for it, unless perhaps someone vainly and boastfully prides himself on grasping and knowing things which either cannot be fully grasped by their own nature, or certainly not within that span of time granted to human senses. Thus it happens that when dissimilar examples are proposed, one may err even in things previously known. And in looking at those things which happen regarding the nature of things surrounding us, nothing else is difficult; but in the birth-charts <term>genituris</term> <note>A "geniture" is a birth horoscope used to predict an individual's fate.</note> themselves and in the private comparisons of individuals, causes fall in that are neither small nor slight, by which each person's own character is shaped. For even the differences of seeds <note>Pico/Ptolemy refers here to biological heritage and ancestry as factors that override the stars.</note> have the greatest influence..."

[These factors] are effective for the specific properties of a species: since even if the surrounding environment <note>original: "corpus ambiens" — the air or celestial spheres surrounding the Earth.</note> and the boundary are the same, nevertheless each of the seeds holds the greatest weight for the universal shaping of its own peculiar form: for instance, in a human, a horse, and others. The places of birth also bring no small distinction. For even if the species of the seeds is the same—namely the human race—and the state of the environment surrounding all things were the same, those who are born still differ greatly in their bodies and souls due to the diversity of regions. It also matters greatly for varying the acts of life, even if other things are equal, what foods each person uses or what customs they follow. Unless each of these factors were contained within the cause of the surrounding environment (which possesses this power most of all), so that they themselves were a part of the cause of why things are as they are, then they could have a very different effect altogether. In this, let those hesitate who think they can do all things—although these factors are clearly not the same—merely by discerning them from the motion of the heavenly bodies alone. 

These are the words of Ptolemy, who also, in the first proposition of another book titled *The Fruit* (commonly called the *Centiloquium* <note>original: "centiloquium" — a famous collection of 100 astrological aphorisms formerly attributed to Ptolemy.</note>), speaking of the science of astrology, says this: "It cannot be that one who is knowledgeable can pronounce the particular forms of things, just as the senses do not receive the particular, but rather a certain general form of the sensible thing." He adds that the practitioner must use conjecture in these matters, for only those inspired by a divine spirit can predict particulars. These are his words to the letter, though they are found differently, and in a faulty and corrupted state, in the common manuscripts. 

But it is also the undisputed opinion of the Arabs and Hebrews who write on astrology: that whatever the star has promised can nevertheless fail to happen, both because the material might not be fit for receiving the influence, and because human affairs depend mostly on our own free choice; and because a particular fate can be overcome by the power of a more universal opposing fate; and because divine providence, more powerful than all fate and greater than the heavens, sometimes orders things to happen differently than the ordinary revolution of the sky would have achieved. While these ideas are scattered here and there among the astrologers, you will read them all together in Abraham ibn Ezra <note>original: "Auenazrā" — a 12th-century Jewish polymath and influential astrologer.</note> in the first chapter of his *Book of Nativities*.

## Chapter II: That the observations of times, which they call "Elections," are useless: by the testimony of one astrologer, by reason, and by experience.

<margin>Auspices are useless.</margin>
Now, if these things are true, let the astrologer show what benefit life might gain from his predictions. He will perhaps answer that the benefit is twofold. First, he says it is true that the hour can be taught in which we ought to take our "auspices" <note>original: "auspicari" — picking a starting time for a task.</note> for our actions, so that what we are about to do may turn out happily. The second benefit is when he predicts what is to come, from which comes this utility: that we may abstain from those things in which we have learned we will be unhappy, and conversely, we may undertake those in which our birth hour promises us happiness. 

But come, let us examine both, starting from the one proposed in the first place. And since our dispute is with the astrologers, let us use those very assumptions which are considered most true among them. Therefore, in the matter which you are about to do by choosing a time, either the constellation of your birth made the heavens favorable to you, or unfavorable. If it is unfavorable, "auspication" <note>The act of picking an auspicious moment.</note> is of no use according to the opinion of Ptolemy; therefore, you will always undertake that matter unhappily, and you will always happily abstain from it. If the heavens are favorable, there is no need for any "election" <term>Election: The astrological practice of "electing" or choosing a specific moment to begin an enterprise to ensure a successful outcome.</term> of hours, but your own choice is sufficient for you; since you will then most happily undertake that matter when—

<margin>Experience.</margin>
I pass over the testimony of experience itself, than which nothing is more certain and nothing more consistent. For experience makes it manifest every day that those who observe this vain distinction of times are the ones least successful in conducting their affairs. On the contrary, those who reject such superstition and use only choice and prudence as their guides are far more successful. For who

<margin>Francesco Sforza.</margin>
in our age was more fortunate than Francesco Sforza <note>Francesco Sforza (1401–1466), the mercenary who became Duke of Milan and founded a major dynasty.</note>? Yet he always held all astrologers either in hatred or contempt, let alone

<margin>Zoroaster</margin>
employing them as advisors in his military or domestic affairs. Among the ancients, who was more powerful in astrology, in magic, and in every superstition than Zoroaster? And yet

<margin>
Ninus.

Ninus <note>The legendary founder of Nineveh.</note>—who was certainly neither an astrologer nor a magician—defeated and killed him in war. Pompey placed the greatest faith in the responses of diviners; Caesar placed none. The former met with adverse fortune, the latter with happy and joyful success. Who is ignorant of the fact that Emperor Justinian—the exterminator of astrologers, as we have seen—was most successful at home and in war? On the contrary, the Emperor Julian <note>Julian "the Apostate" (r. 361–363 AD), who attempted to revive paganism and was famously interested in divination.</note>, an enemy of the Christian name and a most curious observer of all superstitions, lost both his life and his empire in a short and unhappy span. I could, however, name one or two learned astrologers, friends of mine, for whom faith in this vanity—according to which they had established their way of life—resulted in either their ruin or no small detriment. But I do not wish to defame men who are otherwise good, nor to violate the laws of sacred friendship in a matter not strictly necessary for the truth. But if only it had not taken away one man's inheritance, and another's homeland and life! If only it had not made many foolish and insane with vain hope, and many miserable with fear. May God not look upon my own sins, just as I have seen no one more lacking in those things which astrology promises its followers than those who have devoted themselves entirely to astrology and who hunt for the favor of the heavens every single hour through its means. A certain great man known to me changed his way of life, resulting in no small loss of his prior fortune, because of this counsel; he was moved especially by the astrological hope that in his new profession he would attain great successes through celestial favor. But when he experienced a fortune that grew more adverse every day, he used to say that he had been deceived by Mars—unwilling to say what was truer: that he had been deceived by astrological vanity. The same man died shortly after, in a truly miserable death, which he himself had not foreseen from the heavens. For he was preparing many things and striving for great goals, like one who had set for himself long limits of life yet to come. I could recount many things of this kind, but my mind recoils from narrating those things which I can hardly remember without tears.

...to have known; and since these errors have fallen upon very dear friends, they demand compassion from me rather than rebuke. But I wish that this reluctant refutation—the names of old friends being withheld—might benefit my living friends. I appeal to them by all the rights of friendship that exist between us, by their fortunes, and by my prayers for their happiness: I would have them warned and asked again and again never to entrust themselves to the advice of this vanity <note>original: "vanitatis" — here referring to the "empty" or "vain" practice of astrology</note> in their affairs. Let them hold it (if they like) as if it were a **poetic fable** over which they may laugh, play, and joke; let them not hold it as a leader or a mistress of life. 

Instead, where the health of the body must be considered, let them consult doctors; where external matters must be looked to, let them use the eyes of **prudence and reason**. Divine wisdom teaches us both of these: it says both that the physician was created by the Most High for our necessity <note>A reference to the biblical book of Ecclesiasticus (Sirach) 38:1: "Honor the physician... for the Lord created him."</note>, and it says that prudence must be preserved by man so that he may be rescued from the evil way. We find no such thing written about astrology. We have proved its profession to be so useless that we would grant it only as much as the astrologers themselves think should be granted. For when it is subsequently proved that it possesses no truth, it will be beyond all controversy and sufficiently clear—as we have tried to prove here—that it is most dangerous to entrust our affairs to the advice of astrologers. If ever something happens correctly according to their predictions, it is not to be attributed to their "reasoning" (of which they have none), but to **recklessness and chance**.

# Chapter III: Astrology is not useful for deciding what should be done or what should be avoided.

<margin>a</margin> Again, as we were saying above, an advantage for astrology can be imagined: namely, that we pursue that which the astrologer has ordered us to follow, and conversely, that we flee from those things which he forbids. We demonstrate that this is either superfluous or harmful. For what he predicts pertains either to the body or to external and fortuitous events. 

In those matters which pertain to the body, if they concern health, I ask whether the judgment of the physician agrees with the judgment of the astrologer, or if it is instead different. If both feel the same, the astrologer brings you nothing that the physician could not provide alone. If they disagree, which one, I ask you, do you think should be followed? Surely, if you reject the physician and entrust yourself to the astrologer, you will pay the penalty for your **insanity**. 

Similarly, in conducting affairs, I ask whether prudence advises the same thing that astrology advises. Or do these judgments completely oppose each other? If they are in harmony, why should we seek in the heavens that which is within us? If they disagree, who could rightly or rationally defend an action if, in the conduct of affairs, **prudence** is abandoned—which is nothing other than the "right reason of things to be done"? <note>original: "recta ratio rerum agendarum" — This is the classic Scholastic definition of prudence (providentia/prudentia).</note> 

But these things will be clearer through examples. Suppose an astrologer predicts that <term>Mars</term> <note>In ancient medicine, the planet Mars was associated with the "choleric" humor (yellow bile) and heat.</note> threatens you this year with a <term>tertian fever</term> <note>original: "tritaeum" — a fever that returns every third day, typically associated with an excess of bile.</note>. He claims that bile is being stirred up by the power Mars holds in its annual revolution; therefore, one should use cold remedies and establish a way of life to counter the heat of Mars. Now, as for this very thing he announces from the heavens: either the same signs will be demonstrated by the condition of your body (upon which the physician’s conjecture relies), or they will not. If the signs are present in the body, this will be enough evidence for you to guard against future ill health. If they are not present, I ask: do you think it right that when there are no signs of seething bile...

<margin>Example in external affairs</margin>
But pale and thick urine <note>original: "lotium" — urine analysis was a primary diagnostic tool in humoral medicine to identify imbalances</note>, a sluggish pulse in the veins, a face marred by paleness, lethargy of the limbs, and other signs of that kind which physicians use as indicators, will show the dominance not of bile <note>Mars was associated with yellow bile and "choler."</note>, but of phlegm <note>original: "pituite" — one of the four bodily humors, associated with coldness and moisture</note>. Yet you would still have bile evacuated because an astrologer has imagined a threatening Mars in the sky for you. Why? Not even a "prudent" astrologer could advise you correctly; for even if he truly pronounces those things about Mars, your own natural temperament, the general disposition of the year itself, or the way of life you have long practiced may have turned you toward the opposite. Ultimately, the astrologer sees only one cause that might affect this—and that is a remote and universal one. The physician judges not only from specific and nearby causes but perceives the matter itself through the senses; he holds that which results from the combination of all causes at once, as the evidence of present nature itself demonstrates it. I pass over the fact that even those who favor the judgments of astrologers are not so insane as to think those judgments are less prone to error than the judgments of physicians. Let us propose a similar example in the handling of external affairs: namely, that a mathematician <note>In the Renaissance, "mathematicus" was a common term for an astrologer.</note> advises a prince not to go to war with his enemies because Mars is not sufficiently favorable to him. I ask whether, at the time he gave this advice, the prince had no just cause for war; or if there was a cause for war, was there no occasion or opportunity for victory? Or rather, was a just cause for war not lacking, and were all the instruments for victory at hand? If you grant the first case, he will rightly not go to war—but led by prudence alone. Even if the mathematician were completely silent, the result would be the same. If you grant the second case, not even the astrologer himself—unless he were acting in his own interest—would judge that one should abstain from war. And if the prince did abstain, what would that be other than to abandon sensory evidence and reason for the sake of conjecture?

### Chapter IV: That astrology is not useful to religion, as Roger Bacon and Pierre d'Ailly believed.

<margin>
Opinion of Roger
Bacon and Pierre
d'Ailly.
</margin>
<margin>a</margin>
Even if it is useless for life, perhaps it is useful for religion? This is what both Roger Bacon and Pierre d'Ailly <note>Roger Bacon (c. 1214–1292) and Pierre d'Ailly (1351–1420) were prominent medieval thinkers who believed planetary cycles could help explain the timing of religious events.</note> seem to have thought. The latter [d'Ailly] held this primarily for two reasons.
<margin>Pierre's first reason</margin>
The first is that from the astrological calculation of the "great conjunctions" <note>Alignments of Jupiter and Saturn, which were thought to signal major shifts in history and religion.</note> (as they call them), the truth might be obtained regarding the number of years from Adam to Christ—a matter of great dispute among ecclesiastical texts.
<margin>Second [reason]</margin>
The second reason is that the oracles of the prophets might be confirmed if the testimony of astrological prediction were added to their predictions. For since every truth is consistent with every other truth, the truth of astronomical science must necessarily be in harmony with theological truth. Indeed, they believe it serves theology as a handmaid to a mistress, especially since the "invisible things of God are seen through those visible things which have been made" <note>A paraphrase of Romans 1:20.</note>, and nothing among those things is more noble than the heavens. From this comes the word of David: *The heavens declare the glory of God, and the firmament proclaims the work of his hands* <note>Psalm 19:1.</note>. d'Ailly, as if to prove this opinion by his own work, wrote a small book divided into twenty theorems which he calls "words." In this book, there are clearly as many errors as there are words. Its title is *On the Harmony of Astrology and Theology* <note>original: "De concordia astrologiae & theologiae"</note>—as if he had never read Paul exclaiming, *What fellowship has light with darkness? Or what part has Christ with Belial?* <note>2 Corinthians 6:14-15. Pico is arguing that divine truth and "vain" astrology cannot coexist.</note> In that work, he strives to achieve those two things we mentioned: namely, to show that what the divinely inspired prophets foretold was also pre-signified by the heavenly constellations, and then to investigate the calculation of years from Adam to Christ based on the dogmas of astrologers. # Book II

->The concordance of astronomy and history:<- in which he strives to relate the seven greatest <term>conjunctions</term> <note>A "conjunction" occurs when two or more celestial bodies appear close together in the sky. Astrologers believed the meeting of Saturn and Jupiter marked major historical shifts.</note> noted from the beginning of the world to those events which are gathered from histories as great and wonderful in the middle ages. From this, he intends to confirm the dogma of the astrologers, who claim that great changes in human affairs, laws, and kingdoms always occur as a result of those great conjunctions. Indeed, I would have wished that he had written things which I might praise rather than refute; for I love him as a man of letters and I venerate the office he held in the Church. But perhaps I shall even do him a service if I can use this just refutation to erase, as much as lies within our power, anything he wrote that was incautious or untrue regarding the Church, since such things are undoubtedly found to be both false and harmful.

<margin>The cause of d’Ailly's error.</margin>
Moreover, ignorance of astronomy—above all else—led this otherwise learned man into error. Having exercised himself in the study of theology in the most celebrated University of Paris, he began only as an old man to take a small taste of this art. He was enticed by that magnificent appearance of the art regarding "greatest differences"—things which human curiosity desires to know above all else. Before he had reached the point of detecting the weakness of the dogma through careful examination, he wrote too hastily those two small works <note>original: "opuscula"</note> which he later retracted once he became a little more skilled. Then he wrote many things in that booklet which he calls the *Elucidarium* <note>meaning "The Clarifier" or "The Manual of Enlightenment"</note>, even though there is much darkness within it. If anyone unrefined in astronomy reads these booklets, he will marvel at them all the more for the fact that he understands them less.

<margin>Where he took his dogmas from; d’Ailly’s ignorance is uncovered.</margin>
But anyone who has made even moderate progress in that art will judge him to have been a writer rather than an astrologer; and whatever he says seems more to have been read by him than understood in its marrow. Almost everything he writes is taken word-for-word from Roger Bacon, Abraham the Jew <note>Likely the scholar Abraham ibn Ezra.</note>, Henry of Mechelen, Albumasar <note>The Latinized name of the Persian astrologer Abu Ma'shar.</note>, and some "Summa" by a certain John the Briton. That he was extremely eager but insufficiently skilled in astronomical matters can be known from this: in that very *Elucidarium* (which is his most corrected work), he says in Chapter 11 that when he was writing those things, we were in the "airy <term>triplicity</term>" <note>In astrology, the twelve zodiac signs are divided into four "triplicities" based on elements: Fire, Earth, Air, and Water.</note>—specifically in the year of Christ 1404—and that we would remain in it for sixty-one more years until the year 1465. At that time, he claimed, there would be a great conjunction of Saturn and Jupiter with a change from the airy to the watery triplicity. In truth, however, that change had already occurred nearly forty years earlier, in the year of Christ 1365; at that time, on the twenty-ninth day of October, Saturn and Jupiter were together in the seventh degree of Scorpio. From then until now, they have always joined in the watery signs. Our d’Ailly, however, was still waiting for something to happen that had already occurred nearly a hundred years before!

<margin>Book on the True Calculation of Times.</margin>
As for the other benefit which he thought came from astrology—namely, the gathering of the true number of years <note>i.e., historical chronology</note>—we have abundantly refuted this in the book we wrote titled *On the True Calculation of Times*. Even if it did help the Christian state, that part of astrology would not belong to the branch we are refuting here (which deals with the prediction of the future); rather, it would belong to true astronomy, which is one of the liberal disciplines, whose task it is to calculate times and measure the motions of the stars by mathematical reason. But this is not the place for refuting his errors; that we shall do in the following books. For there, regarding the "concordance of philosophy and theology," we shall show that those things announced by the prophets are neither caused nor signified by the heavens; and thus, even if astrology were true, the prediction

# Book II

...nevertheless, these things do not pertain to it. However, we shall show that those who argue that some things are beyond nature and thus exempt from the heavens—while contending that other things are natural and are both caused and foreseen by the heavens—are saying nothing at all, even though they seem to be saying something. Indeed, the prophetic oracles are so far from being usefully confirmed by the decrees of astrologers that nothing could be more powerful or effective in weakening religion. Furthermore, we will show that those who have attempted to do this have always been found to be liars and ignorant of astronomy, and in their historical profession, they wander far from the truth. 

Broadly speaking, we will expose the vanity and falsehood of their dogma not only regarding divine laws and miracles, but also regarding other changes in human affairs which many have wished to predict from "great <term>conjunctions</term>" <note>A "conjunction" occurs when two or more celestial bodies appear close together in the sky. Astrologers believed the meeting of Saturn and Jupiter marked major historical shifts.</note>. On this point, we shall enter into a pure contest with Albumasar <note>Abu Ma'shar (787–886 AD), a Persian astrologer whose works were foundational to Western medieval astrology.</note>, the author of that error, along with Hiero his interpreter, Abraham the Israelite <note>Abraham ibn Ezra (c. 1089–1167), a polymath who wrote extensively on astrology and biblical exegesis.</note>, and John of Oxford. We shall unravel the entire book of Pierre d'Ailly from the beginning—the book in which he wished to do the same regarding the "concordance of astrology and historical narrative." Following it from the first conjunction he notes to the very last, we will demonstrate that nothing he said regarding either celestial or earthly matters is sound or close to the truth. We will show that not one of those seven conjunctions he notes happened at the time he thinks it did; rather, his account is vastly different from the actual history of events and true chronological calculation.

But let us also see whether those arguments he later brought forward have any truth: namely, that "all things harmonize with one another" and "the heavens declare the glory of God" <note>original: "caeli enarrant gloriam dei," a quote from Psalm 19:1.</note>. To be sure, that first statement is most true, but it should have been accepted with the understanding that since astrology is false, it cannot harmonize with theological truth. The Apostle Paul teaches that the testimony of David <note>Referring to the authorship of the Psalms.</note> should be referred to the celestial minds of the astrologers who announced that glory of God, about which it is later written: "The law of the Lord is perfect, converting souls" <note>original: "lex domini immaculata convertens animas" from Psalm 19:7.</note>. 

Even if the phrase is referred to the visible sky, what logic is there in this: if the heavens declare the glory of God, does it follow that they favor the glory of God that astrologers fabricate about the sky? But he says, "His invisible things, and His power and divinity, are understood through visible things" <note>A reference to Romans 1:20.</note>. Yet this is the task of the philosopher, whose proper role is to ascend from the order, motion, and nature of the heavens to the invisible, divine Architect of the heavens. If the astrologer sees anything in the heavens, it is against his will; he turns his eyes away from the sky and back down to the earth. Only the philosopher contemplates invisible things from the visible.

### Chapter V: How harmful and pestilential astrology is to the Christian religion.

As I survey everything on all sides and scout the enemies of the Church, I do not see any other source from which more supplies and more weapons are provided against the truth than from this profession. For from here, there is a headlong and very easy slide into impiety, into bad religion, into heresies, into vain superstition, and into corrupt morals and irrevocable malice. 

From where else will impiety better arm itself against the weapons of religion than by claiming that divine miracles—by which all religion is chiefly confirmed—must be referred back to the heavens? If you present the example of martyrs despising death, or the few, poor, and unlearned apostles subjecting the world to the law of the Gospel, or even people being recalled from the underworld <note>Pico refers here to the miracle of resurrection (raising the dead).</note>—events too great to be human and too good to be performed by a demon—they will diminish the power in these events, claiming that nothing could have done them except for the course of a star or a celestial influence which only they recognize. If someone says this, will it not be a safe haven for religion...
