# Book II

...to bring to the roots of religion: if it persuades, does it not drain it of life and utterly uproot it? Which, if you say this is not a fault of the art but of its professors <note>Pico is addressing the common defense that astrology is a valid science and only the "bad" astrologers make mistakes.</note>—I will admit it is so, in that they wander within their own profession. For I was not saying this was an error *of* astrology, but that it is easy to slip from it into this error. Nor, if astrology were true, would I desist from this task of turning men away from that danger; since no truth is to be confirmed by lies. But since it is false, its falsehood will be usefully exposed; for if it were thought to be true, it could generate in the minds of the unlearned such a grave pestilence. Especially when you see all professors of some art holding the same vanities, it is hardly possible that the blame is not truly attributed to the art itself. 

Indeed, among the principal writers of astrology, I have read no one who does not subject religion and all laws—like other human affairs—to the constellations of the stars. Ptolemy, in the second book of the *Apotelesmata* <note>original: "apoteleſmatõ", also known as the Tetrabiblos, the most influential ancient Greek text on astrology.</note>, understands that the fact that one deity is worshiped among this nation and another among that one arises from nowhere else than from the varying nature of the stars and signs presiding over those peoples and nations. Nor far from that passage, a certain Greek interpreter of Ptolemy says the miracle of Moses—who crossed the Red Sea with his people on dry feet—was done because he observed the ebb and flow of the sea. As if the Hebrew people did not cross unharmed in those same waters at the same time that Pharaoh, with his astrologers, was drowned! Or as if Joshua did not cross the Jordan on dry feet, in which no tides, no reciprocal movement of waves is imagined by them. But all these and similar trifles we have sufficiently refuted elsewhere.

<margin>Albumasar</margin>
Albumasar the Arab derives the law of the Saracens, his own, ours, and all laws equally from heaven, so that he pronounces from the constellation itself which constellation made which law, and how many years each is to last. In which matters, what part of astrology or truth is found, we shall declare later.

<margin>Henry</margin>
His interpreter, Henry of Mechelen <note>A 14th-century philosopher and astronomer.</note>, was so delirious that he even found a ship in the sky according to which Noah built that ark of his; a discovery which Pierre d'Ailly <note>Alliacensis.</note> greatly admired as if it were a divine invention. Finally, that they reduce the Law to the order of those things which happen by natural course and the movement of heaven can be known from this: that they wish it to be known from heaven how many revolutions of years will occur from the "ascendant" of a law until its fall.

<margin>Haly</margin>
And Haly Abenzagel <note>An 11th-century Arab astrologer.</note>, to say nothing of the others, pronounces the fertility and sterility of the year from there; such that if the "ascendant" <note>The sign of the zodiac rising on the eastern horizon at a specific moment.</note> of the law is applied to the place of Jupiter or Venus, it will be a fertile year; conversely, if to the places of unlucky stars.

<margin>Abraham</margin>
Abraham the Jew—not the one called Ibn Ezra, as Pierre d'Ailly falsely believed, but the one they call *Nasi*, that is, the Patriarch—did he not attempt to refer the Mosaic law, the exodus of the Jews from Egypt, and whatever happened to the people under the law to various inept and indeed ridiculous conjunctions? But would that only those we have mentioned had failed to see the light of this truth amid the shadows of a bad religion; would that our own people were not so blind in the splendor of the Gospel, thinking no better than those others about our religion and theirs.

<margin>The error of Bonatti himself</margin>
That insane man Bonatti <note>Guido Bonatti, a famous 13th-century Italian astrologer.</note> says that the Lord Jesus used the "election of hours" <note>An astrological practice of choosing the most auspicious time to start an activity.</note> when, in response to the apostles advising Him not to return to Judea, He replied that there are twelve hours in a day. For, he says, He chose for Himself an hour in which they could not harm Him—as if He did not prostrate them when He wished, and as if He did not remain hidden while passing through them better in the light of day! I pass over how rashly and blasphemously he speaks of the divine family of Francis, and how he fabricates that the miracle of divine love was the work of Mars. But why do we seek remote examples, if to these which daily regarding the events of years...

# Book II

...are published abroad by prophecy; do they not say that the Christian law is perfected by the teachings of Christ and Mercury? And that it received its purity from the religion of Jupiter and from a Virgin? Thus Christian men read these things with their eyes and without indignation; and in the prefaces of I know not what theorist disputing many things against Gerard: was it not even written, when there was a debate about choosing a new Pope, that one must pray devotedly that the Mercurial star might temper the choice with its holy ray? (For they say our law is subject to Mercury; and therefore he called the men of Christ "men of Mercury"—something I do not know how any Christian man can hear with steady ears.) <margin>Roger Bacon.</margin> Roger Bacon was carried so far that he did not hesitate to write that Christians err by not keeping the Sabbath as a holiday and refraining from work in the Jewish rite; since that day is Saturn’s, which star is considered little suited or fortunate for conducting affairs. In these words, he accuses not only our people but also Moses; indeed, he openly turns the prophet into an astrologer, teaching that what Moses established regarding the Sabbath holidays did not have the reason of some divine mystery, but of an astrological dogma. If anyone weighs all these things with a correct examination of judgment, they will see that the piety of true religion is offended by no greater error than this; since it is equally impious to think there is no religion at all, and to derive it from the heavens by some fatal necessity. But if there is any religion to be embraced by an astrologer, he will be more prone <margin>Idolatry. Heresies. Superstition. Varro. Geomancy. Magic. Chiromancy.</margin> to idolatry than anything else, so that he might especially worship and revere those gods from whom he thinks all good and evil things come to men. 

Now, where do we think the heresies of the Manichaeans <note>original: "manicheorum". An ancient religious movement that taught a dualistic struggle between Good (Spirit) and Evil (Matter), often denying human free will.</note>, which take away freedom of choice, emanated from, if not from this false opinion of the astrologers regarding fate? Concerning superstitions, there is no controversy that they all proceed from astronomy <note>In this context, Pico uses "astronomia" to refer to the divinatory practice of astrology.</note>, and Varro <note>Marcus Terentius Varro (116–27 BC), a celebrated Roman scholar and writer.</note> confirms that they are all contained by it like its foster-children. All writers call Geomancy <note>original: "Geomantia". A method of divination that interprets markings on the ground or the patterns formed by tossed handfuls of soil or rocks.</note> the daughter of astrology. Mages think the use of this art so necessary to them that they call astrology the "key to magic." Palm-readers <note>original: "Chiromantici".</note> map out seven mounds in the palm of the hand according to the number of the planets, from which future things are foreseen through the lines seen there. But we shall pursue these follies one by one; when, after the mistress and queen [astrology] has been overthrown, we shall trample the rest of the crowd of superstitions in our path. But it is clear enough that she gives birth to them all and they cannot stand without her, because there is no superstition that does not use the selection of days and hours, which astronomy alone teaches them; so that what is said in Ecclesiastes can be said of her: "Vanity of vanities, astrology and every superstition is vanity." <margin>Morals.</margin> Concerning morals, it is not necessary to say more, since it is clear enough that no greater protection can be given to vice than if the heavens are thought to be its author; and that nothing makes us fear hell less or hope for happiness less. If these things are undoubtedly true, then even if that profession [astrology] were true, what truth would it be more useful to be ignorant of? And since it is false, what falsehood is more usefully attacked? Which task I have embraced with a desire for helping religion and protecting the truth.

# Book II

...events that refute them. For how few of those things predicted by them actually happen? Or if something does happen, why should it not have happened <note>Pico argues that coincidence is not proof of an underlying science</note>? For this reason, I am all the more accustomed to wonder at some who, in disputing against this art, always raise this objection: "If their art is not true, why are their predictions sometimes true?" An astrologer considers it a great success if, when we object to the falsehood of his predictions, he can satisfy us with even a few [that were right]; he is far from thinking he can take an argument against us from this point. 

<margin>Ptolemy</margin> We have cited above the words of Ptolemy <note>Claudius Ptolemy, the 2nd-century author of the *Tetrabiblos*, the foundational text of Western astrology</note> attempting to resolve this question, in which we saw that he cast the lies of astrologers not only upon the astrologers themselves—as being insufficiently skilled or diligent—but also upon the art itself, which he admitted is uncertain and most prone to deception. 

<margin>Porphyry</margin> Porphyry <note>A 3rd-century Neoplatonist philosopher who wrote extensively on oracles and the stars</note> himself says that the responses of oracles were discovered to be false; for those divinities announced those things from celestial causes which they had explored. However, the announcement derived from them is deceptive. But if the demons <note>In the Platonic sense, *daimones* are intermediary spirits, not necessarily "demons" in the modern evil sense</note> themselves, from whom nothing of celestial matters is hidden, are deceived while perceiving the future therefrom, what, I ask, shall we judge concerning men? Even those who are and have been the most excellent in this art (if it is an art at all) have never touched even a thousandth part of it. 

Finally, among all the arts which by their nature may fall short of the truth, the judgment of none is more uncertain; and I believe the astrologers themselves will not deny this. For they say that the **free choice** <term>arbitrium</term> <note>original: "arbitrium"; refers to human free will, which Pico argues can override "fated" celestial influences</note> of man causes many things to happen otherwise; and the flux and instability of matter often frustrate the works of celestial actions; and one fate is turned or hindered by another. 

Indeed, if you examine human affairs diligently, you will find almost nothing in which one of these things we have mentioned does not change an outcome even truly foreseen from heaven. For it is characteristic of man to arrange his affairs by choice and reason; and that which is annexed and bound to matter on all sides is vehemently liable to its change. Furthermore, since nothing exists in isolation, almost all men depend on one another in turn, so that there is no one whose fortune cannot be harmed or helped by the fortune of another. Thus, a fortunate son will share in the father's misfortune and even an unhappy end; and an unfortunate man will obtain a happy outcome from the good fate of a parent. And a servant, though little favored by his own birth-chart <term>genitura</term> <note>original: "genitura"; a horoscope or birth-chart determined by the stars at the moment of birth</note>, will fare happily under a fortunate master. Thus, the fate of the soldier follows from the fate of the commander; and the fortune of the sick man from the doctor; and conversely, that of the doctor from the sick man; it will happen now one way, now another. 

From all these things, it is declared how often it must be that what a mathematician <note>In this period, "mathematicus" was often a synonym for an astrologer</note> has predicted for someone does not happen, even if that profession were true—let alone that the truth of the profession could be proven from the "true" predictions of these practitioners. 

<margin>A strange and great disagreement among astrologers.</margin> What of the fact that there is such great disagreement of dogma among the authors of this art? It is necessary that either all or the greatest part of them speak lies about the future. They themselves greatly admire and venerate certain ancient Egyptians, Indians, and Babylonians as if they were high priests of celestial mysteries; they sound their names daily in the ears of the unskilled with puffed-out cheeks as if they were divinities. But if those ancients were true, then you cannot be true astrologers, you who have only the books of the juniors to imitate, which differ in every way from that ancient discipline. 

<margin>Ptolemy against the Egyptian astrologers.</margin> For Ptolemy, your father [of the art], everywhere censures and tears apart the astrology which belonged to the Egyptians; sometimes saying it is little consistent with reason, other times attacking it with other proofs, which is easily established by anyone reading his books of *Apotelesmaton* <term>Apotelesmaton</term> <note>original: "apotelesmaton"; a Greek term for astrological effects or outcomes, often used as a title for Ptolemy's *Tetrabiblos*</note>. 

<margin>Disagreement between Chaldean and Egyptian astrologers.</margin> Nor indeed did Ptolemy alone differ from them, but they likewise disagreed among themselves: the Indians from the Chaldeans, the Egyptians from the Chaldeans; since they differ from each other, and from these, and from all other astrologers.

<summary>Pico argues that astrology is inherently unreliable because human free will, the randomness of matter, and the interconnectedness of human lives override celestial influence. He further notes that even the "fathers" of astrology, like Ptolemy, constantly contradicted their predecessors, undermining the art's claim to be a stable science.</summary>

...the Indians, and after all these, the Persians. Nor is Greek astrology any more in agreement with itself than it is with the barbarian <note>In the Renaissance, "barbarian" often referred to non-Greek and non-Latin sources, particularly Arabic, Persian, and Indian authors</note> traditions, since what Ptolemy rejects, Dorotheus <note>Dorotheus of Sidon, a 1st-century author of a famous instructional poem on astrology</note> embraces; and Paul <note>Paul of Alexandria, a 4th-century astrologer</note> thinks one thing, Hephaestion <note>Hephaestion of Thebes</note> another, and others think and opine differently still. Nor will you find any one of them who does not claim to gather the reliability of his outcomes from the authority of experience. 

<margin>
Discord among the Arabs themselves and with the Greeks.
</margin>
Do the Arabs not also fight among themselves and with the Greeks? Furthermore, just as Ptolemy rejects that ancient astrology, so Albumasar <note>Abu Ma'shar, the most influential Persian astrologer of the Middle Ages</note> rejects the astrology of Ptolemy to such an extent that he says nothing can be read in his books that is found to be consistent with either reason or experience. Conversely, Avenrodan <note>Ali ibn Ridwan, an 11th-century Egyptian commentator on Ptolemy</note> says that no one in astrology has spoken with reason except Ptolemy; and if you look at the sayings of others, you will find them far removed from the truth, while Ptolemy’s words can in no way be found to be false. 

<margin>
Discord of the Hebrews with the Greeks and Arabs.
</margin>
The Hebrews also disagree, and the first among them, Abraham Ibn Ezra <note>A 12th-century Jewish polymath and astronomer</note>, dissents from Ptolemy and has often torn Albumasar to pieces—indeed, they reject and repudiate his entire book, which in Latin is titled *On Great Conjunctions*. Therefore, if the followers of Ptolemy are true, must not the ancient Arabs who followed them necessarily be lying? And if those books which these men boast of were held in such admiration by all, why did they produce the truth? Must not Ptolemy and Albumasar necessarily have been objects of laughter in their own centuries? And others similarly, who deviated entirely from their decrees. 

And yet, you will find it has always been the case that among every nation and in every age, there were always men who said that true things were predicted by astrologers—which happened not through the truth of their dogmas, but by chance. Nor was there ever a lack of those who held this fallacy in mockery, contempt, or even hatred. 

<margin>
Note
</margin>
But whatever the case was in previous centuries, certainly in our own time the truth of their teachings cannot be confirmed by the professors [of the art], since they follow mostly bad authors and do not understand the good ones. Furthermore, they perform their duty so negligently that they are ignorant of many things they ought to know; they even omit more things that should be considered, sparing themselves the labor and hurrying toward the pursuit of money. 

If I had intended to teach astrology here rather than to refute it, I would pour out my hand against the errors of the younger men who profess this art. But that is not my plan. Nevertheless, it may be worthwhile to note a few things so that it becomes more manifest that they cannot predict the truth, even if the teachings of the astrologers were perfectly true.

### Chapter VII. On the ignorance of the astrologers of our age.

These predictions of men are either universal—as when they predict future good or evil in general from the chart of the year, from an eclipse <term>defectu: an eclipse, literally a "failing" of light</term> of the sun and moon, or from the conjunctions of the higher stars—or they are particular, such as when they divine something about a private fate from an individual’s own birth chart <term>genitura: a horoscope based on the moment of birth</term>. 

In the first kind, nothing is more effective than an eclipse of the lights, from which, as if from the most universal causes, the most universal changes of the lower things occur. In the other, nothing has more weight than the "equation," which is usually done regarding the span of life and the number of years. In both, the modern <note>Pico uses "neoterici" to refer to contemporary or recent writers</note> and barbarian writers err wonderfully, though their authority is most powerful among our astrologers. 

<margin>
Ptolemy
</margin>
Ptolemy writes in the second book of the *Apotelesmaton* <note>The Greek title of Ptolemy’s foundational work, the *Tetrabiblos*</note> that in an eclipse of the sun, two things must be observed above all: namely, the place in which the sun is eclipsed, and the "angle" that closely follows that place; for example, if it is in the ninth region of the heaven...

<summary>Pico highlights the chaotic lack of consensus among Greek, Arabic, and Hebrew astrologers, arguing that their mutual contradictions prove the art is based on chance rather than science. He also attacks the incompetence and greed of contemporary astrologers who fail to follow even the basic rules of their own authorities like Ptolemy.</summary>

Book II
c ii

...if the eclipse occurs, the angle of the tenth house is to be observed; if in the eleventh or twelfth, the angle of the rising <note>The Ascendant</note>; however, because in that place the Greek text reads **the following center** <note>original Greek: "tou epomenou kentrou"</note>, which means the subsequent angle, the common translation instead has "the preceding angle." From this, a completely contrary meaning is derived, giving the barbarians <note>Non-Greek/Latin authors, specifically Arabic sources</note> an opportunity for error. Thus, John of Ashenden <note>A 14th-century English astrologer</note>, in that work commonly called the *English Summa*—which holds primary authority among our people—after a long and perhaps argumentative investigation, finally concludes according to the opinion of Ptolemy that the angle to be observed should not be the one that follows, but the one that precedes the place in which the eclipse of the light <note>The Sun or Moon</note> happened. 

That this is entirely contrary to the opinion of Ptolemy is clear from what we have said; namely, that in the Greek it is written **following**, which means "subsequent," not "preceding." But also, a little later, Ptolemy himself, explaining which angles these are, named the meridian of the sun and the rising angle. 

<margin>John of Ashenden.
Greek interpreter.
Commentary on Ptolemy.</margin> 
In this, the Greek interpreter <note>Possibly Proclus or another ancient commentator</note> reminds us that the western angle is omitted, as it cannot follow the place of an eclipse unless the sun were obscured beneath the earth—and when that happens, they do not think it has the power to produce future effects. But if the *preceding* angle were to be observed, then the rising angle should have been omitted by Ptolemy, because it cannot precede the eclipsed sun unless it is beneath the earth; and the western angle would have to be included, which, whether the eclipse occurred in the eighth or ninth house of heaven, would always be found to run ahead and precede it. From this error, the entire method of prediction is changed, since in predicting they look to nothing more than the nature and state of the stars dominating both the place of the lights and that specific angle. When one angle is taken for another, there will also be a different and distinct ruler. And according to the diverse nature of the ruling star, the pronouncement regarding future events will always be different, or even contrary.

<margin>Haly Abenzagel.
Hylegh.</margin> 
Regarding the prediction of the span of life, I will show in a few words that these little diviners see nothing. Haly Abenzagel <note>'Ali ibn Abi al-Rijal, a prominent 11th-century Arab astrologer</note>, the oracle of the astrologers of this age, says in the fourth part of his work that, according to the opinion of Ptolemy, there are five <term>hylegh</term> <note>The "giver of life" or "aphetic" point in a birth chart</note>. For this is how they speak: the Sun, the Moon, the horoscope, the "Part of Fortune," and the place of the full or new moon that most recently preceded the birth. Besides these five, they say the planets holding power and authority in those five places must be considered. In the next chapter, speaking of that which they call <term>Alchochoden</term> <note>The "giver of years," a planet used to calculate the length of a person's life</note>—

<margin>Alchochoden.
Ptolemy.</margin> 
which is the giver of years—he says: "Ptolemy says the planet that has the most authority in the <term>hylegh</term> becomes the <term>Alchochoden</term>, whether it aspects it or does not aspect it." And so he repeats many things many times about this <term>Alchochoden</term> as being the opinion of Ptolemy. Our astrologers, who follow him and other barbarians, persist in the same error. They investigate in every birth chart which planet is the <term>hylegh</term> and which is the <term>Alchochoden</term> according to the opinion of Ptolemy.

<margin>A most evident error of the astrologers.</margin> 
But in truth, in Ptolemy himself, this <term>Alchochoden</term> is as much a non-entity as a goat-stag <note>A "hyrcoceruus," a mythological hybrid used in logic to denote something that does not exist</note> or a chimera. Read all his books, read all his interpreters, read even the barbarian translations, and you will not find that word or any word corresponding to it in his writings. For that opinion—which makes the <term>hylegh</term> one thing in birth charts and the giver of life and years, which they call <term>Alchochoden</term>, another—belongs to later writers. Neither Ptolemy nor those more ancient than he ever imagined such a thing. He first enumerates the places which he calls <term>aphetic</term> <note>From the Greek 'aphetes,' meaning "releaser"</note>, which the Arabs call <term>hylegh</term>; in Latin, we can call them "dismissory" <note>Dimissoria</note>, so named because from there the course of life takes its powerful beginnings, as if from the starting gates of a race.

<summary>Pico identifies a critical translation error in Ptolemy's work regarding which astrological "angles" to observe during an eclipse, arguing this mistake invalidates the predictions of famous astrologers like John of Ashenden. He further critiques the Arabic concept of the "Alchochoden" (giver of years), asserting it is a late invention entirely absent from Ptolemy's original Greek texts.</summary>

II

...and those places are known to be above the earth, or connected by some affinity to the setting point or the horoscope <note>the Ascendant, or the point of the zodiac rising on the eastern horizon</note>. Then he establishes the *aphetae* <term>Aphetae: From the Greek "aphetes," meaning "releasers." In astrology, these are the specific points or planets used to determine the length of a person's life.</term>, that is, the "dismissors" themselves, who, from those places as if from prisons, bestow the impulse of life by their own—if I may put it this way—breath. He intends these to be: the Sun, the Moon, the horoscope, the Part of Fortune, and the wandering stars <note>the planets</note> predominating in those places. Besides these, among which all the "hylegial" factors <note>points used to calculate life expectancy</note> are numbered, he makes no other distributor of years except that which these *aphetae* we mentioned bestow; he thinks these years can be increased or drained by the commerce <note>the influence or "aspect"</note> of happy or unhappy stars. 

The barbarians <note>A term Pico uses for non-Greek/Latin sources, particularly Arabic and Persian astrologers</note> and our own modern astrologers, besides these *Aphetae*—which they call *Hylegh* <term>Hylegh: A Persian/Arabic term for the "Giver of Life," roughly equivalent to the Greek "Apheta."</term>—believe there is another factor, also supposedly according to the opinion of Ptolemy, who determines the spaces of living, whom they call *Alchochoden* <term>Alchochoden: An Arabic term for the "Giver of Years," the planet that rules the Hylegh and determines the specific number of years a person will live.</term>. Regarding this matter, as I was saying, Ptolemy himself says nothing anywhere; yet based on their own interpretation of his opinion, they seek, dispute, and define many things about it. And they do not only err in this, upon which the whole substance of the matter depends.

<margin>Haly</margin>
But they also err in the enumeration of the *hyleghs* themselves, since Haly <note>Haly Abenragel, a famous 11th-century Arabic astrologer whose "Book on the Judgments of the Stars" was a standard medieval text</note> says that the places of the preceding new moon or full moon were placed among them by Ptolemy. Yet Ptolemy never judges that this should be done, whether the birth be nocturnal or diurnal. What of the fact that this Haly accuses Ptolemy of being at odds with himself, and boasts greatly over this assessment of Ptolemy—in which he says no one ever opposed him—and gives great thanks to God, the revealer of secrets? He says that Ptolemy contradicts himself because he does not enumerate the eighth "place" <note>the Eighth House, traditionally associated with death</note> among the *hylegial* places, on the grounds that it does not "behold" <note>form an astrological aspect with</note> the horoscope.

<margin>The error of Haly</margin>
Yet in selecting the *Alchochoden*, Haly thinks it makes no difference whether it "beholds" the *hylegh* or not. Why do you talk nonsense, barbarian? Or what are you dreaming of? Where in Ptolemy did you read about the *Alchochoden*? But I know that this term has deceived him and all the others. Ptolemy places among the *hylegia* those planets ruling in the remaining *hylegial* places; but these men think they are something entirely different from the *hylegia*. They act as if the other four—Sun, Moon, Horoscope, and Part of Fortune (to which they also falsely added the new and full moon)—should alone have the character of the *hylegh*, while the planets ruling those places would separately determine the years. 

And since Ptolemy never said regarding the ruling planets that it was necessary for them to "behold" the *hylegia*, they wondered why he did not think those two (namely, the two they think exist: the *hyleg* and the *Alchochoden*) should be joined in a partnership of aspect. Yet it is no fault of Ptolemy if he did not seek a partnership of aspect between things that are one and the same <note>Pico argues that for Ptolemy, the "giver of life" and the "ruler" are not two separate entities requiring a connection.</note>. For in his work, whenever the Sun or Moon are *hylegial*, there will never be another planet besides them as the disposer of life. He uses a ruling planet only when the other *hylegia* have no authority in the granting of years. When this is the case, no "commerce" can be left for the vital planet with any *hylegh*, because—namely—none besides it is found. 

I do not know how they failed to understand this from Ptolemy's words, or how none of them detected this. But they have all gone off into this error in flocks, so that there is no one who does not search for the *Alchochoden* and the *hyleg* "according to the opinion of Ptolemy." See how "true" the dogmas of the astrologers are, and how they are able to predict truths about the span of life! Especially when, to the errors we have mentioned, a very great one is added: that they prescribe the number of years for the planet that is the giver of life, according to that common saying among them that there are so many "greater" years of the Sun, so many "lesser," so many "mean"; so many for the Moon, so many for Mars, and so on for the other stars—even though Ptolemy and...

He argues that this reliance on "barbarian" (Arabic) innovations has led to fundamental errors in how astrologers predict a person's lifespan.</summary>

# Book II
## II

...he rejects that Egyptian opinion, saying it has no reason; and where he speaks of the span of life, he counts the years not from the nature of the planets but from the number of parts of the equatorial circle, according to the place of life—that is, the "divider" <term>Divisor: In astrology, the planet or point that 'divides' or governs a specific period of life.</term>—and another "lethal" or "killing" point among those intercepted. To this point, the course of a life already growing weary first stumbles heavily. Thus, when the *aphetes* <note>the "releaser" or life-giving point</note> is placed between the boundary <note>the horizon</note> and the heights of heaven, that progression is maintained which the Greeks call *actinobolia* <note>original: "ακτινο βολιαμ"</note>, which means "radiant projection." But when it has declined from the height toward the west, we use a calculation conducted in both directions which they call *horiaian* <note>original: "ωριαιαυ"</note>, which we can call "hourly." 

Our astrologers are so ignorant of all these things that even if they were to read them, I have no doubt they would think they were hearing of monsters. And yet we are so miserably gullible regarding their predictions—as they promise us the old age of Nestor <note>A legendary Greek king who lived for three generations</note>—that we forget the Lord's voice <note>original: "Dominicæ uocis"</note> commanding us to be ready, since we know neither the day of our death nor the hour. If they threaten a short life, we are tortured by anxiety day and night; the voice of a single "rabble-rouser" <note>original: "rabulæ," referring here to a deceptive astrologer</note> snatches all the joy of life away from us. 

Haly <note>likely the Arab astrologer Haly Abenragel</note> says that if a fortunate planet is in the horoscope, it adds its "lesser years" to the years of life according to Ptolemy's opinion; and yet, as I was just saying, in Ptolemy's work there are no "planetary years"—neither greater, mean, nor lesser. When Ptolemy speaks of adding years, he follows an entirely different path, using the division of hours, which I believe Haly did not understand. But it is not necessary to pursue every single point; otherwise, the book would grow to an immense size. 

Now, in those very questions they call "interrogations" <note>Horary astrology, where a chart is cast to answer a specific question</note>, do they not also err so remarkably that from one error the entire system of answering is perverted? For it is a common "preamble" among them that the seventh house of the chart—that is, the West—is given to the matter being asked about. And yet Ptolemy commands that this place be given not to the matter being consulted, but to the Mathematician <note>the astrologer</note> who is being consulted. The Indian mathematicians also observed this, so much so that when the West and the "Lord of the West" <note>the planet ruling the sign on the western horizon</note> were in a bad state, they would not answer the question, fearing an error. I could list six hundred errors of this kind, were I not focused instead on declaring their entire profession to be in error. For recently, when comparing Ptolemy’s books with barbarian and Latin authors, I found that almost everything had to be "pierced with the spit" <note>original: "uerubus confodienda," a metaphor for marking errors or deleting text</note>.

### Cap. VIII. On the negligence of the astrologers of our age, which is so great that even if astrology were true, they themselves could not be true.

Indeed, how great is their negligence! You will find few among them—even those who have a method for calculation (which the greatest part of them lack)—who do not flee to ephemerides <note>tables of planetary positions</note> to find the true position of the stars. <margin>Bonatus.</margin> Bonatus <note>Guido Bonatti, a famous 13th-century Italian astrologer</note> testifies to this in these words: "The wise men of this art use the *Almanach*," for so the Arabs call the ephemerides. Those who do this must necessarily speak hastily and omit many things, which weakens almost all the truth of their predictions. For there is almost never any mention of the "latitude" <note>the distance of a planet north or south of the ecliptic</note> of the planets; when this is ignored, where will the astronomer not err? Where will he not lie? If we believe the true decrees of this art, the stars are thought to have the greatest power when they are positioned at the beginnings of the twelve houses of heaven...

<summary>Pico criticizes modern astrologers for their ignorance of Greek technical terms and for misinterpreting Ptolemy’s methods regarding life expectancy and horary questions. He highlights their dependence on pre-calculated tables (almanacs) and their failure to account for planetary latitude.</summary>

...especially in the cardinal points. For in those cases, when the stars are present, the astrologer will think they are not; and when they are not, he will think they are. This happens because he observes only that movement which follows a straight progression, but fails to perceive the **declination to the side** <term>latitude: the distance of a star or planet north or south of the ecliptic, the sun's apparent path</term> of the stars. For when a star turns either toward the north or toward the south, it rises more slowly or more swiftly depending on the part of the zodiac sign in which it is placed. Thus, you will sometimes think a planet is above the earth when it is actually below it; or you will think it has already set when it is still visible and appearing above the horizon. 

While this creates errors in every prediction, it causes them to fall away from the truth most significantly when they investigate the hour of birth based on the hour of conception. If it happens that the moon is very close to the west, it could be thought to have already set when it is still above the earth; and conversely, it might be thought not to have sunk yet when it is actually hidden below the eastern horizon. This mistake can cause them to wander astray by many days from the actual hour of conception. Who can correctly determine the radiations of the planets if the latitude is ignored? Who will correctly measure the "walking of a star"—which is called *proödos* in Greek and commonly named **direction** <note>original: "directio"; a technique used to predict the timing of events in a person's life</note>? 

Since every declination of a star from the path of the sun makes the event of a thing happen several years faster or slower, there is also a great slip in the arrangement of the fixed stars, since they are commonly placed in the spot to which they are carried by a straight-line progression. They altogether fail to consider in what part of the sky they either set or rise in different regions, or at what points they begin to shine upon the remaining **houses** <note>The twelve divisions of the sky representing different areas of human life</note>. Furthermore, the *ephemerides* <note>astronomical tables showing the daily positions of celestial bodies</note> often show the location of the planets with very little reliability, not only through the fault of the copyists, but often through the fault of the author, who was either not diligent enough or not skilled enough. 

I will pass over the fact that different astronomers use different tables, which are sometimes insufficiently exact. Even when an astronomer has made his own diary with few errors, they differ greatly in this current age. Everyone now rejects the tables of **Ptolemy** <note>The 2nd-century Greco-Egyptian whose 'Almagest' was the standard for over a millennium</note>. A large part of the more learned follow the **Alfonsine tables** <note>13th-century tables prepared in Toledo under Alfonso X of Castile</note>, but it is now clearly established that there is falsehood in their foundations. 

Nor are they any less "sleepy" <note>metaphorically: careless or lazy</note> in choosing the horoscope and in grasping the beginnings of the twelve remaining heavenly places. I have seen many who were of no small skill and of good name in that profession use some little table of their own for distributing the twelve houses (as they call them) regardless of the sky under which the person was born whose birth-chart they were about to inspect. If they ever wish to be diligent, they might note the difference in **climate** <note>the latitudinal zone</note>, which is the only thing Alfonso shows them; beyond that, they will hardly investigate anything more exactly. 

Who now observes the declinations from the equator, the circumferences of the planets, and the various heights in the smaller circle, or the changes of longitudinal motions in the eccentric circle when judging birth-charts? How many things do the younger practitioners not know about **equating the days** <term>Equation of Time: the adjustment needed to account for the difference between solar time and clock time</term>? How many things do they say incorrectly? 

We have said all this so that it may become clear that this art of predicting cannot be confirmed with any reliability. Even if it consisted of the truest reasoning, the truth about the future cannot be known because of the fault, ignorance, or negligence of the practitioners. If this does not persuade you that faith should not be given to astrology, let us at least be persuaded by that epigram: **no faith should be given to irrational astrologers** <note>original: "αστρολογοισ αλογοισ" (astrologois alogois). Pico is using a Greek pun: 'astrologoi' means 'speakers of the stars,' while 'alogoi' means 'without reason' or 'irrational.'</note>.

### Chapter IX. That what astrologers say rarely happens, shown by both foreign and domestic examples.

If they were sane, if they were speakers of the truth—even if not in everything, but in most things—they would not only have avoided being expelled from cities and always held in mockery by every wise man, but they would be held in the highest honor...

He argues that even if astrology were a valid science, the incompetence and negligence of its practitioners would make accurate prediction impossible.</summary>

<page-num>II</page-num>

## Book II

-> Book II <-

...would have been the case in every age among all nations. Such is the curiosity of men for **foreknowing the future**, especially those things that pertain to themselves. There is such a great reputation and esteem for those who provide this service, yet we read of statues being erected and public honors decreed for philosophers, doctors, poets, and emperors, but we never read of such for astrologers. Instead, we more often read of them being cast out, ridiculed, or even turned into the subject of popular fables, so that the allegories of these stories—usually drawn from common sense and life—contained a rebuke of this vanity among the ancients. 

For those who interpret **Homer** <note>The Greek epic poet; Pico refers to the tradition of "allegoresis," where myths were read as symbols for natural or moral truths.</note> allegorically say that by the story of **Icarus**—who, committing himself to the thin air with artificial wings, was plunged into the sea—it is the astrologers who are signified. They say that these men, lifting themselves into the sky on the wings of a rash profession, fall into a **sea of lies** when they predict what is to come based on their celestial dogmas, by which they seem to be elevated. 

Why should we need other testimonies or conjectures when daily experience itself testifies to us in this matter? For if astrology can provide the truth anywhere, it ought most especially to be able to do so in predicting **changes in the air**: namely, rain, drought, heat, cold, winds, hail, and earthquakes. In these matters, they are daily caught in such falsehoods that the actual state of almost no day ever corresponds to their predictions. 

<margin>Pandolfo Collenuccio</margin>
I observed this during this winter in my suburban villa where I wrote these things. I noted every significant change in the air each day, having placed the decrees of the astrologers before my eyes. As I hope the heavens remain healthy and favorable to me, out of more than **one hundred and thirty days** of continuous observation, I saw no more than six or seven days that were such as they had foreseen in their books. I believe my friend **Pandolfo Collenuccio** <note>Pandolfo Collenuccio (1444–1504) was a famous Italian humanist, historian, and jurist.</note> remembers—a man consulted in the law but most ingeniously learned in all literature—how much laughter a certain mathematician in **Bologna** gave us on this subject. That man commanded us to expect "most copious rains" on a day which the most bright sun rendered entirely clear and serene. 

<margin>Ambrose</margin>
**Ambrose** <note>Saint Ambrose (c. 340–397), Bishop of Milan and a Father of the Church.</note> says in the *Hexameron* <note>original: "Exameron"; a treatise on the six days of creation.</note> that when there had been talk some days prior about rain that was said to be needed, someone said: "Behold, the **new moon** <term>neomenia: the beginning of a lunar month, often used by astrologers to predict weather</term> will give it." Nevertheless, no rain fell until it was granted by the prayers of the Church, making it manifest that rain is not to be hoped for from the beginnings of the moon, but from the providence and mercy of the Creator. 

Through his words, both the vanity of astrology and the efficacy of religion are proven by the facts themselves. Therefore, those who are less capable of reason and have enslaved their faith to these men can assert their freedom in this way: let them ask them repeatedly about the state of the air. When they find that these men say false things almost always, they will easily perceive that if these **scoundrels** <note>original: "nebulones," a pun on "nebula" (cloud), implying both "cloud-men" and "worthless fellows."</note> lie so much about the clouds, they will predict false things much more in judging the fates of men and nations. For in the latter case, the predictions concern things that are less subject to the heavens and are far more difficult and laborious to foresee. 

<margin>A healthy teaching.</margin>
As for what they babble daily in their mercenary prophecies regarding the **birth charts** <term>genituris: horoscopes calculated for the moment of birth</term> of men, if anyone were to examine them, he would see that they lie much more than when they answer regarding the quality of the air. Unless I feared the vice of being inept while pursuing the ineptitudes of others in too much detail, I could bring forward many birth charts of both the living and the dead—unhappy charts for the fortunate, and the most fortunate charts for the utterly miserable. In this matter, I truly lie about nothing, for I know that the **Divine Truth** (under whose banner this expedition fights) neither needs nor delights in our lies. But I will be content with certain domestic examples...

<summary>Pico argues that astrology fails in its most basic test—weather prediction—citing personal observations and an anecdote involving Pandolfo Collenuccio. He concludes that if astrologers cannot predict the weather, they certainly cannot predict the complex fates of human beings.</summary>

I would especially wish to warn those who, having received promises of a long life from the **mathematicians** <note>In the Renaissance, "mathematicians" was a common term for astrologers because of the calculations involved in casting horoscopes.</note>, forget the voice of the Gospel warning us to be vigilant, lest the "day of the Lord" catch us unprepared. Take **Pino Ordelaffi**, the prince of Forlì, to whom my sister **Lucrezia** was married: in the very year he died, **Girolamo Manfredi**—an astrologer of singular reputation in our age—had promised him total safety and a long life. It is hardly surprising that Manfredi failed to foresee the deaths of others, since he could not even foresee his own. For although he passed away this last summer, in his public prediction for that year (which turned out to be fatal for him), he repeatedly promised that he would have many wonderful things to say in the following year. I do not know how he will now redeem his pledged word, unless perhaps, from heaven, he now looks down upon earthly things more truly than he once looked up from earth at the heavenly ones.

<margin>
Pietro Attendolo.
Eleanor, his niece.
Costanza, his brother's wife.
</margin>
**Pietro Attendolo**, an ingenious young man who was married to **Eleanor**, the daughter of his brother Galeotto, died last year, killed by the distress of a sudden and unexpected disease. Yet the astrologer in whom he placed the greatest trust had predicted no such thing, but had instead promised him a secure life. Then there is **Costanza**, the most beloved wife of my brother **Antonio**; she died in Rome two years ago, to the public grief of almost the entire city. Has she not also testified to us the vanity of this art? In the year she left us mourning, she had received from the astrologer a promise not only of prosperous health, but of a most happy life. Not forgetting this, even as she was breathing her last and holding the hand of her weeping husband (by whom she was uniquely loved), she said: "Behold, how true are the prophecies of the astrologers!"

<margin>
Seneca
</margin>
On the other hand, for my brother Antonio himself—good God!—what evils, what masses of trouble, how many dangers did astrology threaten him with this year? And yet, having experienced no injury from the heavens, he has lived with his family safe, his wealth preserved, and his health intact, tossed by no shaking of misfortune or danger. And lest you think our astrologers alone are liars, know that the same happened to the ancients. **Seneca** <note>Lucius Annaeus Seneca (4 BCE – 65 CE), a Roman Stoic philosopher.</note>, in a certain passage mocking the most wicked **Claudius Caesar**, introduces **Mercury** among the gods procuring Claudius's death. To tear down that vanity in passing, among other reasons why Mercury persuades the gods to end the Emperor's life, he says: "Let it be done out of pity for the **Chaldeans** <note>Another common term for astrologers, referencing their supposed Babylonian/Mesopotamian origins.</note>, who have already been burying him for so many years." For the mathematicians used to predict every single year that Claudius would die, yet he did not die so easily. When I read this, it brought to mind

<margin>
Cicero.
</margin>
our own little soothsayers, who also "bury" the **Roman Pontiff** <note>The Pope.</note> every single year. **Cicero** <note>Marcus Tullius Cicero (106–43 BCE), Roman statesman and orator.</note> writes that it was predicted to **Pompey**, **Crassus**, and **Caesar** by the Chaldeans that none of them would die except in old age, at home, and in great glory. Therefore, that most wise orator says it seems a wonder to him that anyone exists who believes those whose predictions he sees daily refuted by reality and events.

### Chapter X: Why astrologers sometimes predict the truth.

But sometimes what they have predicted does happen. Yet since there are many more things that do *not* happen, why should we not judge that they have stumbled upon the truth by chance? For there is no "art" so much like an old wives' tale, or of such vain superstition, that it cannot be proven "true" by that same argument—namely, because what was predicted from it occasionally happens. Indeed, there is no art that does not achieve this, even one you might make up for yourself at random and by accident. Therefore, let them tell me by what reasoning they are moved: do they think every art of divination is true, or...

...rather than many vain and false ones? If many are false, I shall prove those "true" ones by the same argument: namely, why it occasionally happens that what they foretold actually occurs. If I show they believe in contradictions, it is because the various arts of divination do not give the same response regarding the same matters. For I have often tested this hundreds of times: when I had cast a <term>geomantic</term> <note>Geomancy was a method of divination that interpreted patterns of points made in the earth or on paper.</note> figure and mapped an astrological chart for the same question, one outcome appeared to me in the marks and another in the stars. 

If anyone happens not to believe this, let him try it himself and consult a <term>Chiromancer</term> <note>A palm reader.</note>, an **Astrologer**, and a **Geomancer** regarding the fate of the same man; he will see that almost always something different is signaled in the lines of the hand than what will be pronounced either from geomantic marks or from astrological planets. And if he looks to the actual outcome of the matter, he will find truth more often where he least expects it. This is either because chance has more power where there is less reason, or because spiritual wickedness <note>A reference to demons or fallen spirits who, according to medieval theology, enjoyed deceiving humans through occult practices.</note> more willingly mocks us in those matters. 

Yet a manifold deception aids the predictions of **Astrologers**, explaining why they are so often thought to be proven right by the reliability of their <term>outcomes</term> <note>original: "apothelēsmaton" — a Greek term for the effects or results of the stars.</note> when, in fact, they are not. For if they must speak about the past to show that such things happened as the heavens signified, they lack nothing to ensnare the minds of the unlearned. This is because there is no position of the stars, no birth-chart, in which a complex constellation of both favorable and unfavorable significance cannot be found. 

This is especially true since they have fashioned no fewer stars for themselves in the heavens than God formed there from the beginning. Therefore, regarding past events, they will always have a basis to defend their positioning; for they will rarely fail to find in the planets whatever they want. Nevertheless, they make people both happy and unhappy in many ways, having—it seems—more jurisdiction over heavenly things than earthly ones. Thus, the location of the sky, or the goodness or malice of a sign, or the radiation of another star, or "love" with the Sun, or "hatred" or "friendship" with the <term>horoscope</term> <note>The "horoscope" here refers to the Ascendant, the specific point of the zodiac rising on the eastern horizon.</note> will always support them. 

Or if, in the end, these do not satisfy, they will implore help from the "non-wandering stars" <note>The fixed stars, as opposed to the planets (the "wandering" stars).</note>—among which they themselves never cease to wander into error. Or if even these do not satisfy, there will be ready at hand for them

<margin>The cunning of astrologers.</margin>
either the "images of the Indians," or the "parts of the Egyptians," or the <term>antiscia of Firmicus</term> <note>A complex technique involving "shadow" points of planets, popularized by the 4th-century astrologer Julius Firmicus Maternus.</note>, or the <term>twelfth-parts</term> <note>original: "dodecathemoria" — a method of dividing each zodiac sign into twelve smaller sections.</note> of the Chaldeans, or something entirely fabricated by them. In these things, they glory all the more as if they were "hidden dogmas," the more they are false and invented.

<margin>The opinion of Euripides.</margin>
In predicting future things, they have less opportunity for deception, although they do not lack for it even here. For they guess many things by observing the earth—as the saying goes—rather than the heavens, remembering that well-known line of **Euripides**: *The best prophet is he who guesses well.* <note>original: "qui coniiciet is uates optimus esto"</note> Generally, they announce things that almost cannot help but happen, or at least cannot be thought *not* to have happened. They utter many things ambiguously, in the manner of oracles, always including some exception by which the prediction can be diminished, increased, or obstructed. Thus, if it happens, you cannot say it was not predicted; if it does not happen, they are nonetheless thought to be truthful. You will rarely hear anything specific or certain from them; and when they do dare such a thing, they are proven right either by chance (which is very rare) or they are refuted by experience (which is very frequent).

<margin>Eulogy of the temple of Apollo.</margin>
But it happens as that man said concerning the temple of **Apollo**: that the things said correctly are remembered and celebrated, while no one records the errors. This is because those who favor these arts do not want the errors known, and those who despise them are entirely ignorant of both the successes and the failures.

<margin>Augustine’s opinion on true astrological predictions.</margin>
Furthermore, we must not overlook what **Augustine** says and what reason suggests: that through the hidden breathing of demons, which they suffer without knowing it, they occasionally attain the truth.

### Book III

...which they would not otherwise achieve. This is thought to happen if, through a marvelous prediction, they pronounce some specific deed or word <note>Pico is distinguishing between general predictions (e.g., "it will rain") and highly specific ones that seem impossible to guess.</note>—a feat which **Ptolemy** <note>Claudius Ptolemy (c. 100–170 AD), the most famous astronomer/astrologer of antiquity, whose "Tetrabiblos" admitted that astrology deals in generalities rather than specific certainties.</note> himself testified that the art of astrology cannot provide. 

But someone will wonder how they can experience this unknowingly, and yet we should think that whatever they predict, they do so through demonic inspiration. Indeed, this can happen in many ways, about which I will remind the astrologers by using a similar case. For it is admitted among them that one astronomer is more "fortunate" than another in attaining the truth, even when both possess equal talent, learning, and diligence. Let them tell me then what this "being fortunate" is, if they do not seek the truth by any path other than the dogmas of the art. For he who holds those dogmas equally or even better would not, however, be equally fortunate in predicting the truth. 

Furthermore, this is nothing other than the fact that, since various constellations almost always occur regarding the same matter, and conflicting or diverse opinions of authors occur regarding the same constellation, the mind of the predictor is turned from heaven toward the true opinion. Thus, by attempting many things, he stumbles inadvertently upon the truth. Therefore, this same thing could also be done by the hidden and latent inspiration of a demon, by which someone's actions are guided even if he does not perceive himself being acted upon. Since this is the case, how it happens need not be explained more extensively now. 

But divine power and wisdom do not only allow demons to do this; they even allow them to bring about through their own works what had previously been falsely predicted, so that it becomes true. No punishment is more fittingly demanded by supreme justice than that those proud minds which do not submit to divine truth should then bind their faith and liberty to the lies of a scoundrel and a <term>sycophant</term> <note>original: "sycophantae" — here meaning a deceiver or a cheat.</note>. But I think we have said enough already as to why those triflers sometimes seem to babble and spread some truths. Nevertheless, as we said from the beginning, we must not labor greatly over this matter, since, according to the testimony of **Favorinus** <note>A skeptical philosopher of the 2nd century who wrote a famous critique of astrology.</note>, that part which they predict truly—whether by chance or by cunning—is never found to be even one-thousandth of the parts they lie about.

### The end of the second book of Giovanni Pico della Mirandola's Disputations Against Astrologers.

# GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA'S DISPUTATIONS AGAINST ASTROLOGERS: BOOK THREE.

## Chapter One: What was done in the preceding book and what is to be done next, and in what order.

<insert>W</insert>e have resolved <note>original: "soluimus"</note> the question of the public who repeatedly ask concerning astrologers: from where does the faith in their responses come, if there is no solidity in their profession? I mentioned a question which the more accurate and learned do not use. To those learned men, it is well known that what the astrologers say does not happen often, but rarely, and as if you might say, by accident. Nor, if their predictions do come true, can it be concluded that the art is necessarily true—just as it is not necessarily false simply because they very often lie in their predictions. For indeed, false things can be pronounced from true precepts, not so much because of the art...

### Book III

...complete falsehood <note>original: "omnimodam falsitatem"</note> [rather] than an uncertainty of opinion and **conjecture** <term>cōiecturalemque</term>: so that we may overlook either the **ignorance** <term>ignorātiam</term> or the **negligence** <term>īdiligētiā</term> of the practitioner. Just as, on the contrary, true things [derived] from false ones [come] not from the truth of the dogma, but from the cunning of the speaker, or luck, or chance, or the hidden promotion of **foreknowing** <term>prænoscientium</term> spirits <note>Pico refers to "numinum," often interpreted here as daemons or spiritual entities believed to have access to future knowledge.</note> who predict, or other causes which we sufficiently explained in the previous book. 

But if anyone cannot be persuaded, let him recall to memory how much we discussed a little while ago—hopefully without hatred or envy—concerning the carelessness and the errors of the astrologers of our age. Nor can he be led (unless he desires to be deceived) to think that **whenever** <term>quotiēs</term> they attain the **truth** <term>ueritatē</term>, it was discovered by them through skill rather than found by chance. 

The following treatise will entirely settle this dispute. In it, it will be demonstrated that the things they **predict** <term>p̄di/cunt</term> from the sky either have no **causes** <term>cās</term> or signs there by which they are effected or **indicated** <term>indicētur</term>; or if they do happen from there, they happen differently than the astrologers believe; or if they happen in that way too, they do not come from those causes in the sky nor from those origins of things on earth. Then, even if all these things were granted, certainly these origins and those causes cannot be apprehended by men; or, if they can perhaps be apprehended, they have not yet been **discovered** <margin>inuentas</margin>.

When all this has been demonstrated, I think it will be beyond controversy for good minds that whenever an astrologer happens upon the truth, it can be reduced to no cause more truly than to the truth of the profession—which is clearly false on so many counts, relying on no reasons of truth, but **fictitious** <term>cōmentitia</term>, deceptive, and therefore by its very nature clearly lying. 

Therefore, let us now approach the refutation itself, examining first what constitutes the sum of the whole matter: whether the heavens effect what these diviners pronounce from the heavens. This will be handled by us in such a way that in this book we defend that the heaven acts upon us only by motion and light; that beyond these, other more hidden <note>occult</note> influences are imagined in vain. Furthermore, from that light of the **stars** <term>syderū</term> and motion, nothing else is **communicated** <term>cōmunicari</term> to the **passive** <term>patiēti</term> matter <margin>disponens</margin> than **motion** <term>motū</term>, **light** <term>lucē</term>, and **heat** <term>calorē</term>. 

This heat, I say, both **consumes** <term>cōsumātē</term> **bodies** <term>corpa</term> through a general **influence** <term>influxu</term>, and **disposes** <term>disponētē</term> **bodies** <term>corpa</term> capable of **life** <term>uitā</term> toward the **functions** <term>functōes</term> of life. [We argue] that this flows from **all** <term>oībȝ</term> the stars, even though it is not **admitted** <term>cōfessū</term> by **all** <term>oīum</term> that the outflows of the **planets** <term>planetarȝ</term> reach us as well. **Whatever** <term>qc̄q̄</term> the stars are said to bestow upon **inferior things** <term>rebȝ inferioribȝ</term> <note>The "sublunary" world of Earth, beneath the Moon.</note> beyond these is neither **proven** <term>pbari</term> by **reason** <term>rōnē</term>, nor **demonstrated** <term>cōuincī</term> by **experiments** <term>expimētis</term>, nor persuaded by the authority of the leaders of philosophy. 

Indeed, all these things stand in the way of our understanding that the power of the celestial bodies reaches **sublunary** <term>sublunaria</term> bodies in any way beyond these **common** <term>cōmunes</term> influences. 
<margin>
Timaeus <note>Plato's dialogue on the origin of the universe.</note>
Alexander of Aphrodisias <note>Famous commentator on Aristotle (c. 200 AD).</note>
Porphyry <note>Neoplatonist philosopher (c. 234–305 AD).</note>
Plotinus <note>Founder of Neoplatonism (c. 204–270 AD).</note>
Psellus <note>Michael Psellus, Byzantine polymath (11th century).</note>
</margin>
Therefore, the peculiar properties of things, even corporeal ones—whether those that **follow** <term>cōsequant̄</term> the species or the particular thing—do not have their origin from the stars, **except** <term>præterq̄</term> by reason of a universal principle, but from the proper nature of those things and their proximate and kindred causes. 

And we shall make this very opinion of ours more **certain** <term>asseueratam</term> and **probable** <term>probabilemq;</term> by no other arguments than those very ones which the astrologers use against us. When this has been sufficiently explained, we shall **proceed** <term>deueniamus</term> in the fourth book to that discussion: so that if we grant to the astrologers that hidden powers exist in the rays beyond the effect of light and heat, from which **men** <term>homīes</term> and the **rest** <term>reliquaq;</term> of nature can specifically receive various gifts and powers, we may nevertheless make it certain—by the clearest reasons and the consensus of all the more illustrious **philosophers** and **theologians** <term>theologorumq;</term>—that those powers which they imagine do not exist in them, nor from those things which they divine from the sky. Having **completed** <term>confectū</term> this, we will retreat to the individual...

### Book III

...to the things we have spoken regarding those who prophesy from the stars, we will add this and leave it as a most firm testament: that those things which are not caused by the heavens are not signified by the heavens <note>original: "quæ non fiunt a cælo / a cælo non significari"</note>. That is to say, those things for which celestial bodies are not the causes, cannot have celestial signs. Therefore, there is no reason why they could be foreseen from the sky. Now, as we set out to do first, let us see with what arguments they attack us—those who contend that all things are bound, led, and governed by the stars—so that we may soon not only repel these same arguments, but, relying on divine aid, drive them back upon the adversaries themselves with greater force than they came.

## Chapter II: Five reasons by which astrology seems to be strengthened.

<margin>r</margin> <note>Likely shorthand for "Ratio 1" or the first reason.</note>
The reasons by which astrologers attempt to persuade us that whatever changes occur in the sublunary world—but also the diversities of all things, accidental events, and the characters and talents of men—depend on the stars, are primarily these. There is one voice of **theologians** <term>Theologorū</term> and **philosophers** <term>philosophorū</term> that the lower world is governed by the heaven in such a way: This is taught by that most common sentiment of 
<margin>Aristotle</margin>
**Aristotle** <term>Aristotelis</term> <note>Pico refers to the Aristotelian view that the "unmoved mover" acts through the celestial spheres to influence the Earth.</note> that this lower world is necessarily contiguous to the motions of the upper world, so that all its power is governed from there. So too 
<margin>Augustine</margin>
**Aurelius** <term>Aurelius</term> **Augustine** <term>Augustinus</term> said that these grosser bodies are ruled and moved through more subtle bodies <note>A reference to Augustine's *De Trinitate*, where he discusses the hierarchy of physical and spiritual substances.</note>. Who then, they ask, would doubt that any changes whatsoever in earthly matters are caused by the movements of the superior bodies? This is demonstrated even by experience itself through the changing seasons of the year, from the approach and retreat of the sun toward us: from which the condition and habit of all living things varies, while the heaven tempers the fields, while it varies the crops, and both gives and takes them away. 

But even in the daily revolution, the sun changes the qualities of the air: warming or drying more or less at noon, morning, or evening, and leaving it to moisture and cold at night. Who is ignorant of how much power the moon has over all bodies, especially those that are more fluid? Causing the tides of the ocean, rising and falling, it moves the sea and sends it into the lands and brings it back; but even the animals submerged in the straits, enclosed in the "prison" of their shells, vary their bodies according to the motion of the moon. Even the **critical days** <term>Crisimı</term> <note>original: "Crisimı dies"; these were specific days in an illness when a patient's condition was expected to change, traditionally linked to lunar cycles.</note> observed by doctors follow the motions of the moon and the sun. We see that when the moon is full, new, or halved, storms are often stirred up and humors are agitated in bodies. From this, many observations have been accepted by shepherds, sailors, and farmers regarding the motions of the moon—observations confirmed by manifold experience over many centuries past. 

Why then, if we perceive the more manifest impressions of the luminaries and their authority in changing lower things, should we believe the remaining stars to be idle and ineffective? Or that their powers do not reach us—even if they are more hidden—by which the bodies subject to them are affected in various ways? Those who are skilled and prudent in these matters can foreknow certain more secret things about future events, just as doctors, shepherds, farmers, and sailors predict their own affairs. 

<margin>Third reason</margin>
Furthermore, no one would deny that the state of the air and the storms vary according to the position and placement of the stars, since heat, cold, dryness, moisture, and whatever impressions occur on high are generated by celestial motions and influences. But if drier breaths enclosed in the bowels of the earth move the ground [earthquakes], if causes in the air arise from either the excess or defect of those four qualities, if either excessive moisture or dryness causes the high price of grain—whether when fruits are gathered or sown—and in turn, a moderate and timely state of the air brings fertility: Who will deny that not only storms...

...changes and earthquakes. But also plagues and various kinds of diseases in men and in cattle: [they are said] to proceed from the healthiness of regions, and from fertility or sterility. Furthermore, if we too are composed of these same qualities and of a bodily temperament <term>temperatura</term> <note>The specific balance of physical qualities and "humors" in a person's body.</note>, and our characters and talents are varied while our freedom remains intact, why can it not be that inclinations are created in us toward anger or gentleness, and toward other good or bad effects, by the stars—either by arousing or restraining the **bile**, **blood**, **phlegm**, or **black bile** <term>humores</term> <note>The "Four Humors" of ancient medicine. It was believed that an imbalance of these fluids determined a person's temperament: choleric, sanguine, phlegmatic, or melancholic.</note>, which those emotions for the most part accompany? Why can it not likewise be that dry and hot impressions of heat, by sharpening the bile in us, excite us to strife, quarrels, insults, and enmities? From whence come wars, slaughters, and devastations; from whence are impious kingdoms changed? 

After this, **Ptolemy** <term>Ptolemæus</term> <note>Claudius Ptolemy, the 2nd-century author of the *Tetrabiblos*, the foundational text of Western astrology.</note> concludes thus: if the 
<margin>Ptolemy</margin>
stars create a diversity of body and soul, this is then derived toward those things which are external but have an affinity with them—such as a wife and wealth with the body, or dignity and honors with the soul. This is the principal reasoning of Ptolemy; nor does he anywhere approve of the stars as the "effectors" of all things in any other way than through the efficiency of the **primary qualities** <note>The four basic qualities: hot, cold, moist, and dry.</note>, by producing which they consequently produce all other things. For this reason, he brings forward no other causes for why **Saturn** does this, **Jupiter** does that, or **Mars** works another thing, other than that Jupiter is a hot and moist planet, Saturn is dry and cold, and Mars is more dry and burning. He feels the same way about the "wandering stars" <note>The planets.</note> as he does about the "non-wandering stars" <note>The fixed stars of the constellations.</note>: judging the fixed stars by the nature of the planets, and the planets by the nature of the primary qualities. Indeed, some might leave behind these primary qualities and flee to "occult" or hidden powers—more eminent forces—which it is not fitting to doubt exist in the celestial bodies in great number and efficacy. 

<margin>Fourth Reason</margin>
If we behold any singular and excellent gifts in earthly things, we are accustomed to think of them as gifts of heaven—qualities which are not "elementary" <note>Derived from the four elements: earth, air, fire, water.</note> (from which those bodies are formed), but which follow rather from a power infused into them from the heavens. How much more, then, will those most noble bodies—with such clear light, such vast mass, and such rapid motion—not lack such powers and properties? Or in what way, if they are transmitted to the earth along with motion and light, will they not be the producers of marvelous effects among us? 

<margin>Fifth Reason</margin>
Finally, there is the course of human affairs, concerning which the divination of astrologers seems to persuade people everywhere of the power of the heavens and fate, even those who are unwilling. In these affairs, variety itself is most familiar and frequent; then we see many things happen above the strength of our mortality, many things beyond reason and merit, and most things outside the order and established condition of human life—for which it seems no causes can be found anywhere other than in the heavens. 

One man is born fit for **philosophy**, another for **poetry**; another, despising letters, handles either civil business or arms more willingly and successfully. From whence comes this variety of talents? There is one who counts riches as nothing; there is another who would sell his soul for profit. This one is sober, that one a scoundrel; this one is 
<margin>Alexander</margin>
bold, that one fearful—from whence comes such great dissimilarity in character? **Alexander** <note>Alexander the Great.</note> conquered the East as quickly as he saw it: from whence came the 
<margin>Aristotle</margin>
impetus of such great fortune? What force unlocked the secrets of nature for **Aristotle**, his 
<margin>Plato</margin>
teacher? What force for **Plato**, and before them for **Pythagoras**, **Socrates**, and the rest? This reasoning is too great for these things to be believed to have sprouted from the earth. 

Again, what does the astrologer not ascribe to these "fortuitous courses"? That an innocent 
<margin>Pythagoras Socrates</margin>
man is condemned, while a guilty man is gifted with rewards; that the industry, skill, talent, and learning of many are made to fail, while the laziness and wickedness of others are enriched. A pirate, bloodied by slaughters, amid a thousand perils of sea and land, finally dies at home among his own in old age; while a most gentle man, most ready to serve, is mindlessly cut down by the swords of those who did not even wish it.

<meta>This page transitions from the astrologers' arguments (that the stars govern all human behavior and fate) to Pico della Mirandola’s systematic rebuttal.
