# Book III

...dear; then there are those monsters of intellects and portents, some delighting even in foul things—or, to put it simply once and for all, those who stray from the laws of humanity. Does this not seem to testify to a certain force and the necessity of a fatal power <note>original: "fatalis potentia." This refers to the concept of an inescapable destiny or "fatum" that overrides human will.</note>? These are the circumstances with which mortal life is filled, persuading many that these successions of good and evil things, deserved or undeserved, and such a great variety of matters, are produced by the motions of the stars, whose impulses fragile and fleeting mortality can hardly or never resist.

### Chapter III. The first argument is turned back and it is shown that heaven is a universal cause and not to be referred to the variety of individuals.

<margin>Even if the arguments of the astrologers are granted, it does not follow what they contend. The first argument is turned back.</margin>

**N**ow, we have striven not only to weaken these arguments of the astrologers but even to bolster them, so that they might not complain of being defrauded. But first, we wish the reader to know that even if these arguments were granted, it would not necessarily follow that any "astrology" <note>In this context, Pico is attacking "judicial astrology"—the practice of predicting specific human events—rather than astronomy.</note> could exist, as will become clear in the following books. However, we do not grant them those points; rather, we take strong arguments against them from those very same premises. For regarding the first argument, as soon as the astrologers say that every lower motion depends on the motion of the heaven, they immediately contradict their own dogma. From this follows a principle well-worn among philosophers: that heaven is the **universal cause** <term>causa universalis</term> <note>A general force (like sunlight) that provides the necessary conditions for life but does not dictate the specific form that life takes.</note> of lower effects. A universal cause, however, does not distinguish between effects, nor is it asked why this or that happens; instead, one looks to **proximate causes** <term>causae proximae</term> <note>The immediate, local factors—such as genetics, environment, or individual choice—that determine specific outcomes.</note>, which are various and different according to the variety of effects. And since among these causes one does one thing and another does another, the universal cause does all things with all of them. Since this is clearly apparent in things different in nature and species, it is a wonder how they do not understand that the same must be much more believed regarding the variety of individuals. For the more a thing is particular and draws its origin from matter, the less it can be referred back to a cause that is supreme, formal, and universal. 

And who does not see that heaven generates a horse with a horse, and a lion with a lion? Is there any position of the stars under which a lion is not born from a lion, or a horse from a horse? By the same reasoning, why would heaven not produce different children from different parents, even if under the same or a similar constellation? Experience itself proves this, since we sometimes see those born in the same hour, and under the same inclination of the heaven, to be most diverse in fortune, talent, and body. In this matter, the astrologer cannot avoid the blow. For they are accustomed, when the birth of twins is held against them, to flee to the **wheel of Nigidius** <note>A famous analogy from the Roman scholar Nigidius Figulus. He spun a potter's wheel and marked it twice with ink; though the marks seemed to be in the same spot, the rapid rotation meant they were actually far apart. Astrologers used this to explain why twins born minutes apart have different fates.</note>, upon which it is impossible to mark the same place twice with ink. But even here he explains himself poorly, since they themselves cannot track that rapid motion from which such a great difference of fate would arise as they wish. Therefore, while he tries to defend the efficiency of heaven, he falls into other snares, so that he must unwillingly confess that he cannot have knowledge of that efficiency. 

Furthermore, we do not only hold against them those twins where one comes out after the other (the brief delay of which provides them some small handle for an answer), but rather those born at the same moment from different parents within the same latitude and longitude of the same region. For these births, the astrologer must describe the same **theme of heaven** <term>thema caeli</term> <note>A horoscope or birth chart showing the positions of the stars at a specific moment.</note> and must pronounce the same things, both regarding what will happen after the hour of birth and what happened to them even within the mother’s womb—as they are thought by him to be conceived at the same hour, just as they were born at the same hour. Regarding these, I ask, what will the astrologer answer? For when the constellation is exactly the same, will the fate of both not appear different? Can he say anything else—unless he is insane—except that those celestial "breaths," universal in their power and potency, are determined and distinguished by proximate and secondary causes? If this is so, how will they render a cause for every variety of individuals based on the stars at the hour of birth...

<summary>Pico begins his rebuttal of astrology by arguing that the heavens act only as a "universal cause," which provides general life-giving energy but does not determine the specific differences between individuals or species. He mocks the "Nigidian wheel" defense used to explain twins, pointing out that children born at the same moment to different parents have vastly different lives despite sharing the same horoscope.</summary>

# Book III
<margin>d ii</margin>

...they promise. They claim that one man is snow-white and another black; this one is short of stature, that one tall; this one of dull wit, that one clever; this one pleasing to all, that one a nuisance; this one destined for philosophy, that one born for trade; this one rich, that one poor; this one short-lived, that one long-lived. Yet this entire variety of individuals, all sharing the same hope, is far less a result of the heavens than is the diversity of the species themselves under that same genus. For example, the fact that nature produces now a lion, now a human, now a donkey, now an elephant—just as these specific differences follow from their immediate causes, so do those individual differences follow either from the variety of seeds (if we consider bodily qualities or natural talent) or from education and free will (if we consider the soul’s faculties), or from the resources of parents, personal choice, prudence, and opportunities (if we consider external and accidental circumstances).

### Chapter IV. How heaven acts through motion and light, and how it is the universal cause of meteorological elements, minerals, and living things.

As the universal cause is more divine and eminent than particular causes, so do we think of heaven more truly and honorably than the astrologers do. To make the reason for this universal efficiency more apparent, and to explain more clearly what heaven does and does not accomplish, we must begin from a higher point: discussing the nature of heaven and its actions toward inferior bodies. Heaven is a natural body, the most perfect of all natural bodies. Since motion and sensible qualities follow a natural body, it is fitting that the most perfect motion and the most perfect of sensible qualities belong to the most perfect natural body. No motion is more perfect than circular <term>orbicular: moving in a perfect circle</term> motion, and no quality perceptible to the senses is more perfect than light. These, therefore, shall be the properties of the celestial body. Furthermore, the heaven exists in an incorruptible substance, since its motion and quality have no contrary; and because it is the most perfect body, it must also occupy the first place—that is, the highest—to which the primary motion is owed. Now, that which is first in any category is the cause of the rest contained within that series, even if not all things share the same relationship to the cause. Therefore, that which is moved by the first motion moves all other moved things, and if it were to cease, the others would no longer move—just as in the "lesser world" <note>original: "minore mundo." This refers to the Microcosm, the ancient and medieval idea that the human body is a small-scale map of the entire universe.</note>, if the motion of the heart ceases, all motions of the animal must necessarily perish.

<margin>Aristotle</margin>
On this account, Aristotle rightly said in the eighth book of his *Physics* <note>original: "physicae auscultationis." This is the standard Latin title for Aristotle's "Physics," which explores the principles of nature and motion.</note> that the motion of the first heaven is the "life" of all things; for indeed, the most evident and common operation of life is internal motion. Therefore, this is one dignity and efficacy of heaven toward the lower world: that through its indefatigable agitation, all other motions are both ordered and excited. That this efficiency is universal, and does not distinguish lower motions by this principle, is evident enough; for just as it cooperates with a clod of earth falling downward, so it does with a flame moving itself upward, and with all other types of motion.

<margin>
The action of heaven is through universal motion.
</margin>

The other prerogative of heaven concerns light. Since light is the highest quality of bodies, and indeed the first grade of life for corporeal nature—and since the highest points of a lower order almost always reach the extremes of a higher order—it must follow that light possesses a certain perfecting power over bodies and contains something vital. It is not that light itself lives or brings life, but it most greatly prepares and disposes a body capable of life to receive that life.

<margin>
How heaven acts upon us through light.
</margin>

For there follows upon light, as its proper characteristic, a certain heat—not a fiery heat, nor an airy one, but a celestial one, just as light is the proper quality of heaven. This heat, I say, is most effective and healthy, penetrating all things, nourishing all things, and moderating all things. This is the primary gift of heaven by which bodies are perfected and living things are disposed toward life. Beyond the agitation of circular motion, this light and heat are necessary not only to be carried down to us and imparted to the earth in more or less degree through a wonderful seasonal opportuneness, but also so that we, having been moved, might be [disposed] to heat...

<summary>Pico argues that heaven is a "universal cause" that provides the general conditions for life—motion, light, and heat—rather than a "particular cause" that determines individual human fates. He uses the Aristotelian model of the cosmos to show that heaven's role is to sustain the general order of nature.</summary>

# Book III

...makes them more fit, which constantly emanates from the perpetually moving body. We perceive the force of this most beneficent heat in the whole corruptible world, in things both incomplete and finished, both inanimate and animate. For it contains and preserves the elements just as their place and form do; like an artist, it surrounds all things, but also diffuses itself intimately through all. And just as it is the privilege of the "first motion" <note>The *Primum Mobile*, or the outermost sphere that moves all others in ancient astronomy.</note> that other motions cannot turn without it, so it is with this first sensible quality: without it, other qualities can do nothing. Therefore, if they were deprived of celestial heat, neither could cold act as coldness, nor heat as hotness. For that sidereal heat is not contrary to cold in the same way the heat of fire or air is; rather, it contains all elemental qualities by a "simple eminence" <note>A philosophical term meaning it possesses the power of all qualities in a higher, more unified form.</note>, just as the nature of heaven contains every body, just as circular motion contains all motions, 

<margin>
Pythagoreans
The error of some
</margin>

and just as light contains all heats. As the Pythagoreans would say, it is like how unity <note>The number one.</note> contains all numbers. Thus, those are mistaken who deny that cold elements can be preserved by the heavens unless the stars also influence them with "coldness" in addition to heat. Their argument would have weight if the heaven preserved hot things with a heat of the same nature and logic; but instead, it preserves all things equally—hot, cold, moist, and dry—by its own unique quality. This quality is none of those four elemental qualities, yet it includes them all within itself—not as they appear in the elements, but as a manifold concluded in unity by a principal power through which it governs them. 

<margin>Whence they are deceived</margin>

It governs them so that it unites each thing to itself by preserving it, preserves the whole within them by moderating all, and produces new things from them by mixing them all together. Truly, the name "heat" is deceptive, because when we hear it, we immediately understand something opposed to coldness. Yet elemental heat is closer in nature to that celestial heat than elemental cold is, just as it is also more "perfect" in the hierarchy of nature. But nothing prevents celestial heat—being exalted above the properties of both elements—from embracing the power of both. 

<margin>A suitable comparison.</margin>

Consider brilliance <note>original: "candore"</note>: we see it as something opposed to dark or black color. Yet no one would deny that a black color is preserved and made effective by the brilliance of light just as much as a white color is. This is true even though the white color is closer to the nature of light and almost shares a common name with it, so that it is sometimes called "bright." Finally, if the substance of heaven (as the first body) most perfectly contains every body in its power, its own unique quality must necessarily contain every corporeal quality in power and perfection. This is what we call "celestial heat," the offspring of light. We call it heat both because it warms vitallly and because, among all properties of the elements, heat is closest to it. 

<margin>
Celestial heat, with proximate causes, generates all qualities of bodies.
</margin>

Thus, when it descends from its celestial condition, it exercises the operation of heat most of all, as we shall later explain. Therefore, if this heat contains all qualities of inferior bodies in perfection and power, it will both generate and nourish them all alongside their proximate <note>Direct or immediate</note> causes. It is like <term>seminal heat: "calor seminalis," the life-giving warmth in a seed or embryo that directs its development</term>; though it is called heat, it governs, digests, preserves, shapes, and moderates all the matter of the fetus, whether that matter be hot or cold. 

Therefore, if anyone asks me whether heaven produces coldness by itself or by accident, I will answer: if you ask what heaven produces by its own nature with no mediating cause, only heat is produced by itself, and other qualities by accident—just as heat itself makes things cold by accident <note>For example, how heat can evaporate moisture and leave a surface cold.</note>, as we shall explain in the following chapter. But if you ask how it acts as a universal cause with secondary causes: it acts by itself as much for coldness as for heat, and for dryness as for moisture. It generates water with water no less than it generates fire with fire. Nor could water generate more water without heaven's influence any more than fire could generate fire. When heaven generates the substances of the elements, it also generates their resulting properties; thus, with water it produces coldness, and with fire, heat. And if we were to deny that heaven produces anything other than heat by itself, those absurdities would follow which Thomas <note>Likely Thomas Aquinas, the influential medieval theologian.</note> mentions regarding coldness, dryness, and mo[isture]...

<summary>Pico argues that "celestial heat" is a universal, life-giving force that transcends the elemental opposition of hot and cold. He explains that heaven acts as a primary cause that enables all physical properties to exist and interact, much like light allows all colors to be seen.</summary>

<margin>
The vain exhaustion of certain interpreters of Aristotle.

For when he says the elementary bodies filling this space, he calls it the "sublunary world" <note>The region of the universe below the moon, subject to change and decay, consisting of the four elements.</note>, not including the very things that inhabit this world along with the elements. This is most clearly evident from the flow of the speech: for after he said it had been determined by him in previous books that there are four bodies below the heaven—Fire, Air, Water, and Earth—he then adds: "Since, therefore, the whole world around the earth consists of these bodies whose properties we are about to describe, this world is by necessity continuous with the superior orbits, so that all its power may be governed from there." Therefore, the "world" whose every power he said is governed by the superior body is this very mass of the four elements, since no other world is continuous with the superior orbits; nor was he about to discuss the properties of another world in that book, in which certainly there is no mention of plants or animals, but only of those things which happen in the elements, such as comets and other impressions, and whatever common passions of air and water occur, as he himself states in the preface shortly before. Therefore, let our diviners cease to hold out this testimony of the philosopher in their annual prophecies as a decoration and strength for their fraud, since in that very book the most wise Aristotle detracts from astrology, while he seeks the causes neither of rain, nor earthquakes, nor other effects of this kind in the stars, but in the matter; according to the variety of that matter, and not the diversity of the constellation, the sun's heat affects them in different ways. So this is how matters stand regarding meteorological impressions.

# Book III

<margin>Objection and Solution: The Opinion of the Platonists</margin>
...thus, by the power of those rays of heat, they are organized and formed. Nor does it stand in the way that we said this heat proceeds from light, even though light does not reach certain subterranean places where the most precious mixtures <note>The author is referring to minerals and gemstones, which were thought to be "mixtures" of elements matured by heat.</note> of this kind are generated. For even if that opinion of certain Platonists were not true—that light penetrates all bodies, though it may not be seen in the densest bodies where it is compressed, or in the thinnest where it is dispersed—it certainly cannot be denied that the heat diffused from light can reach where the light itself does not. This is just as the heat of a fire can be felt through a wall even though the flame itself cannot be seen. Thus, there is nothing to prevent the light shed upon mountains and caverns from failing to enter the interior (being repelled by the opacity and density of the body, which are not suitable conditions for receiving light), while it still sends its heat within. For although such bodies cannot be illuminated by the heavens, they can still be heated, even more so than those that are thin and transparent. How such a mixture of things is made by the heaven, and again by secondary causes <note>In scholastic philosophy, "secondary causes" are the natural laws and physical agents through which God or the Heavens act.</note>, we shall discuss in the solution to the fourth argument. The remaining things are those that live by the breath of this heat; for as we concluded a little earlier, since this quality holds the highest rank in bodies, just as it has the power to perfect the bodies we have described, so it is observed most closely to bind together life and the body respectively. Therefore, in all living things, between

<margin>How the heaven is the cause of living things</margin>
this which is seen as a thicker dwelling <note>Referring to the physical body.</note> and the soul, the source of life, there is a medium which we call **spirit** <note>technical term: <term>spirit</term> (Latin: *spiritus*), a subtle, invisible substance—often compared to a vapor—that was believed to circulate through the nerves and arteries to connect the physical body to the soul.</note>. This is a very thin and invisible body, most closely related to that starry light and heat, in which life is chiefly present and through which the soul unfolds and diffuses its powers into this visible and earthy body. 

<margin>Spirit is a certain medium between the body and the soul</margin>
Thus, in the seminal matter, there lies hidden this kind of spirit, whose mystery that more divine power—the architect of living works—uses in place of the soul; it flows into the water and propagates the seed of generation into the matter it has occupied. However, these spirits are not useful for generating bodies, or preserving them, or performing the duties of the senses, if they are deprived of the help of the celestial spirit (that is, the heat we have mentioned). Because that celestial heat is more mobile, purer, and more effective, it strengthens the weakness of the lower spirit and, through its commerce, makes it more akin to the soul. 

<margin>The heaven is not proved to live because it nourishes living things</margin>
Therefore, it is no longer an argument that the heaven "lives" simply because it nourishes living things with its rays. For all these things live by their own souls, and through them, the power of the soul is propagated into the seeds, with the heat of heaven supporting them—not as a life-giver, but as something that disposes them most conveniently and closely toward life for the reasons we have stated. No one would say that the power of seeing (which comes from the soul) is "in" the light or "because" of the light, even though we cannot see without light. Whether the life of the heaven can be proved by other reasons has been discussed by us in the *Concord of Plato and Aristotle* <note>original: "concordia Platonis & Aristo." This refers to a common Renaissance philosophical project of reconciling the seemingly contradictory views of Plato and Aristotle.</note>. Thus it is clear:

<margin>The Concord of Plato and Aristotle</margin>
In the corporeal world, nothing indeed happens without the heaven; however, whether this or that specific thing happens, that is not from the heaven alone, but from secondary causes, with all of which the heaven produces such things as they are born to make, whether those causes pertain to the species or to the individual.

### Chapter V. That no peculiar power exists in the celestial bodies besides the common influence of motion and light.

<margin>Whether the celestial spheres act upon us by heat</margin>
Now, the outpouring of this heat is common to all stars, if it follows the universal celestial nature just as light does. But it is doubtful whether this applies to the spheres themselves; for if they are not luminous, they are not propagators of this heat. If they are luminous (as they are), but because of their thinness the light is invisible to us, it might be equally ineffective, as Avicenna <note>original: "Auicenna"; Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), the Persian polymath whose works on medicine and philosophy were standard texts in Europe.</note> writes in the *Book on the Heaven*. Regarding the stars themselves, which come under our sight, there can be no doubt, unless we take away from them their celestial nature and the gifts of light. Therefore, besides motion and light (and the life-giving heat that comes from light), do other influences come down to us from the stars? Or do other effective corporeal qualities reside in them? We have seen none, as we shall see more clearly in the following...

...effects, experience shows: since through motion and its heat-producing light, the heaven seems to be able to sufficiently fill everywhere. <margin>The opinion of certain people.</margin>
are accustomed to decreeing that all stars which shine are indeed producers of heat by a certain general property common to all; but then, that specific powers belong to them, so that this star bestows dryness, that one cold, and another moisture. Thus, nights during a full moon are warmer because the more abundant light heats more. Nor does this prevent the moon from cooling or moistening the air by its own specific influence. I therefore ask them whether they believe this heat—which they admit is common to all stars just like light—is the kind we have described as containing all four qualities <note>The four primary qualities of Aristotelian physics: hot, cold, moist, and dry.</note> in a most eminent way, and therefore productive of all things along with fertile causes, while being in itself merely diffusive; or rather, do they not believe the other qualities are contained in it, but heat only? And that cold, as a thing different from heat, flows from some other particular power of a certain star? Whichever they choose, they fall, unless I am mistaken, into no small inconveniences. If they answer the first, I will press them thus: it does not belong to anything by its own proper nature—if they wish it to be said this way regarding the stars—that something specific and more imperfect should belong to it than what belongs to it from its more common nature. For a more specific difference 
<margin>An effective reason.</margin>
always adds a degree of perfection to the universal difference; but that quality which contains every quality is more perfect than that which is only productive of cold. Therefore, if that perfect quality is owed to the stars by a common and general condition, a cold-producing influence will not be owed to any star by its own proper nature. Thus, the other branch of the division remains, in which they must necessarily be no less stuck; for nothing belongs to a thing by its own nature that is repugnant to those properties belonging to it from its common nature. Just as if it belongs to a man, insofar as he is an animal, to have sensation, the same man cannot, insofar as he is a man, have insensitivity <note>Original: "stupiditas," meaning a lack of sensory perception or the state of being "numb" like a rock, rather than low intelligence.</note> belong to him. Or if, insofar as he lives, it belongs to him to have an internal principle of motion, how could it be that, insofar as he is this or that specific living thing, some reason of inanimate immobility could be appropriate? On the contrary, the particular degree distinguishes that which is in the common nature. For if it belongs to a living thing absolutely to be moved not only from without but from within, it must necessarily belong to the nature of an animal (which is a species of living things) to be the internal principle of some operation; and again to the rational nature (which is another species) to be the internal principle of another operation. Therefore, by a similar example, if that life-giving heat follows the celestial nature insofar as it is celestial, a power productive of cold and dryness (which are qualities contrary to life) will not follow the peculiar nature of any star. Thus we argue against them. However, the arguments of the opposing side are partly resolved,

Just as we also resolved the point that many things are generated in these places by celestial action where the light of the heaven nevertheless does not reach. <margin>Galen:</margin>
**Galen** asserts that just as the moon does not illuminate, so it does not affect us in any way during its conjunction <note>When the moon is positioned between the Earth and the Sun.</note>. For this reason, he calculates the month as twenty-six days and twelve hours—which are the number of days in which the moon's light reaches us with efficacy—while for about three days it remains hidden under the sun's rays. However, the moon meeting the sun acts upon us in the same way as someone who "acts by doing nothing": for by depriving bodies of its light, it harms them; but when that same moon is waxing <note>literally "adolescent"</note>, it nourishes them more fully and fills them more succulently. But if we believe that the moon possesses its own proper light, albeit very dark and thin—whence it does not entirely escape our gaze even in conjunction—it can be believed that it retains some of its efficacy even from that light.

### Chapter VI. That the light of the Moon, like that of the Sun, is vital; and that neither produces cold or moisture except by accident <note>In natural philosophy, an "accidental" effect is a secondary result rather than an essential property of the cause.</note>.

**S**o then, if (as we have said regarding each individual thing) this celestial heat is the universal craftsman of corporeal things, and it is not otherwise: why should we believe that other breaths are inspired into earthly bodies by the stars? Let us not give either more to those superior bodies, or less to the inferior ones, than is proper. Only let the reader recall this to memory: whatever is shared by a better nature with a lesser one necessarily becomes somewhat different and lesser than it was in its first origin. This happens both because of the source from which it exits and because it is admitted only according to the capacity and condition of the recipient. It is diminished partly because it is mixed with a foreign and alien nature, and further because the recipient, being of a lesser sort, is also affected by many-sided impressions from elsewhere; it necessarily draws in and confuses that which it received from a better place with a sewage-heap of many other affections. Likewise, there is no doubt that this very thing happens to this celestial heat whenever it is received into the sublunary mass, so that it falls short of its own natural action and perfection. This occurs in two ways: for although it is always healthful by its own nature, through the weakness of the recipient it sometimes turns out to be harmful; and while it produces no elementary quality <note>The qualities of the four elements: hot, cold, moist, and dry.</note> (being diverse from them by its own property), it nevertheless degenerates into elementary nature toward the actions of the elements—especially heat, to which it is most similar in nature as well as in name. Therefore, it often acts not so much as a celestial force, but rather as fiery and elementary heat is accustomed to do. That these things do not happen from the heat by its own nature, but by the fault of the matter, is clear from this evidence (to omit reason for a moment): that when among sublunary bodies it finds matter kindred to itself, it is always found to be beneficial and only life-givingly heat-producing. 
<margin>Aristotle. Avicenna.</margin>
For indeed, there is no matter more like it than the spirit, and especially the human spirit <note>In medieval medicine, the 'spiritus' was a refined vapor from the blood that acted as the bridge between soul and body.</note>, which is a thin, clear, mobile, bloody vapor; it corresponds in proportion to the heaven, as **Aristotle** and **Avicenna** write. The heat of the heaven always so cherishes and strengthens this spirit that it is almost to the spirit what the spirit itself is to the thicker body. If it harms it sometimes, it harms it for no other reason than the weakness of the recipient. The sign of this is that by the same ray the weak is harmed and the stronger is fortified; so that here also that saying is true: "to him who has shall be given, and from him who has not shall be taken away even what he has." <note>original: "habenti dari / nō habēti auferri & id qd hēt"; a reference to the Gospel of Matthew 13:12.</note> Therefore, it is not from the sun that harm comes—since otherwise it would not have profited another—but from the weakness of the matter, which collapses in its own sickness under the weight of such great goodness. Otherwise, those things which are equal to the sun's rays, the more they are sunned, the more they obtain life and vigor. For this reason, let no one think that either devouring heat or dryness (which is contrary to life) flows from the sun, just as neither suffocating moisture nor excessive flux and numbing cold flow from the moon. For if this were so, the waxing moon would not assist the innate generative power in things by which bodies are invigorated and grow alongside it; nor would the full moon...

It posits that harmful effects like excessive heat or cold are not properties of the stars themselves but result from the weakness or "sickness" of the earthly matter receiving the influence.</summary>

# Book III

<margin>Hippocrates. Aristotle.</margin>
Hippocrates writes in his first book *On the Eight-Month Birth* <note>original: "de octimestri partu"</note> that a knowledge of the lunar cycles would be useful for making both males and females fertile. Nor would Aristotle be speaking truly when he says the moon is, as it were, a second, smaller sun, and that it contributes to all generation and perfection. For how could these things be true if the moon's light were not by its own nature nourishing, vital, and fertile, just like that of the sun and the other stars? In all of these bodies, this quality exists, just as the celestial property is common to them all. 

But (as we were saying) this celestial heat, just as it sometimes becomes excessive due to the weakness of the thing receiving it, so too through the elementary nature into which it descends, it almost turns into elementary heat—so much so that you would not easily recognize it as celestial, except in those spiritual corpuscles <note>In ancient science, these "spirits" were subtle fluids or gases that carried life and sensation through the body.</note> which we have shown to be most similar to heaven among all bodies. For, once infused into these, it perfects every mixture and everywhere serves the works of the soul being perfected. However, when it falls upon hard, rough, thick, watery, or dross-filled bodies, it degenerates from its celestial property and acts much like elementary heat usually does: if this heat is more powerful, it burns, dries out, and reduces a thing to ash; on the other hand, if it is thin and meager, it causes a flow and dissolves moisture.

Thus it happens to celestial heat according to the conditions of the matter it acts upon: hence the opinion arose that the sun creates dryness and the moon increases humidity. This is because the sun's heat is more burning, while the moon's is more lukewarm. But in suitable and related subjects, the sun’s ray will not dry up healthy moisture, nor will the moon generate useless or harmful humidity; instead, both stars will work according to their own nature. Although the moon acts more mildly where the sun acts more intensely, it happens to them differently by "accident" <note>In natural philosophy, an "accidental" effect is a secondary result or a byproduct rather than the essential nature of the cause.</note>, through the perfection of foreign matter: for the sun to dry, and the moon to moisten. 

For when the sun's rays reach us more closely—as in the northern signs of the zodiac or at more direct angles, such as at midday—or when they meet in concave, harsh, and resistant spaces, they are squeezed and repelled, and they break apart with an igneous property which they acquire by such violence or intersection. Thus they dry and scorch the bodies they strike. Conversely, the moon, with its meager and thin heat, if it touches a humid and fluid body, it dissolves the moisture found within it and makes it more fluid. The moon does not itself bring that cold and watery humidity; rather, by its own heat, it dissolves, calls forth, and spreads the humidity it finds already existing in a watery and cold body.

For this is the nature of heat: if it is stronger, it consumes the moisture it calls forth from bodies; if it is weaker, it calls it forth but—because it is the same healing heat but weak—it fails in the effort and does not consume what it has called forth. Thus, by accident, the moon moistens excessively, and the sun dries. But both also create cold by accident: for as Aristotle writes, both are principles of cold and heat, and the movement of these stars governs the boundary of both the beginning and end of those qualities. 

How this is to be understood, the same author declares elsewhere. For he says the sun creates winter and summer throughout the whole year; the moon does the same throughout the month. But the difference is this: for the sun, this happens through its approach and departure; for the moon, it does not happen in this way, but rather one effect occurs during the waxing light and another during the waning light. Thus, the sun departing far from us leaves us to the cold, and so it is said to "make" cold; so too the moon, when it is repeatedly stripped of its light at conjunction <note>The new moon phase.</note>, is said to make things cold—not because it brings cold, but because it protects us from the nighttime chill less than at other times.

Furthermore, it is worthy of examination that Aristotle, in those same books *On the Generation of Animals*, says the times of the waning month are more humid and colder; yet it is commonly agreed that moisture dries up as the moon grows old. I would resolve it this way: when the moon is waning, humidity flourishes, not because it comes from the moon, but from the lower elements which the moon resists less, being weakened in heat and hiding for the greatest part of the night. Therefore, that humidity is also watery, unhealthy, and excremental <note>Referring to waste fluids or "superfluities" in the body.</note>. Hence, as the new moon approaches, many vapors are raised, signifying rain, and menstrual flows often occur more fully, as Aristotle [says] in...

It also resolves a contradiction in Aristotle regarding why the waning moon appears to coincide with increased humidity and cold.</summary>

histories and writes *On the Generation of Animals* <note>original: "de animalium generatione"</note>: indeed, when the moon is waxing, humidity increases, either because the moisture that was already present in bodies becomes more fluid, or because a more life-giving moisture is added through the benefit of the approaching lunar heat. For this is what Aristotle thinks: that because of the lunar increases, sea urchins and living things of that kind become fuller for no other reason than this: since they are cold—being those that lack blood—when they are filled with the moon’s more abundant light, they grow warm in a more vital way and thus digest <note>The author uses the term "concoct," a historical medical term for the body’s "cooking" or processing of nutrients and humors using internal heat.</note> better; hence they necessarily become juicier and more robust. 

Therefore, humors flow both when the moon is waxing and when it is waning, but they are of different kinds: good humors flow when it waxes, and bad ones when it wanes. From this it is clearly evident that the moon does not cause moisture because it is cold and wet (for such moisture increases when the moon is waning), but because it is healthfully and life-givingly warm. When bodies become more moist and robust under the abundance of its light, they do not become more moist in any other way than through the force of heat and the help of a nourishing power which assists them; it is a property of this heat to call forth humors from the innermost parts to the extremities. 

For this reason, bloodletting <note>original: "sanguinis missio"</note> is also most conveniently performed then; thus the astrologer Haly Hamec <note>Likely referring to a medieval Arabic authority like Haly Abenragel, whose works were central to European astrology.</note> was greatly mistaken when he said that veins should be cut while the moon is waning. Therefore, let us firmly conclude that the humor which increases along with the moon—and increases in its flow because of it—is a most healthy humor, not one that weakens the body with its flow or kills it with cold, but one that makes it firmer and more lively. This is attested by that experience confirmed by the faith of all doctors: that those who fall ill at the beginning of the month bear the assault of the disease more strongly, and that those who have been given up for dead and are already at their last breath can scarcely have life leave them while the moon is rising. 

However, both the sun and the moon can make things cold, not only by depriving us of light but by affecting us (although this also happens by accident). The sun does this when it either kills through excessive drying, or draws out the vital heat, or generates rains from the watery vapors of the sea—which it stirs up more than it can dissolve—or by stirring up winds, or even for other reasons. The moon, however, through its thin heat, makes the pores of the body more open and thin, and by its own rays, it lets the nighttime cold—which has also been thinned by those rays—enter into us more abundantly. 

For this is the reason many are deceived into thinking the moon is cold: that numbness and coldness, I say, that comes to those sleeping under the lunar rays. The weaker ray of the star makes a path into the body for the cold that has occupied the air from the earth and water during the night. In this way, therefore, the rays of the stars—which by their own nature only heat healthfully—can both make things cold and, falling sometimes on hard bodies and sometimes on those dripping with watery thickness, dry them or moisten them. They are also sometimes harmful, not through their own fault, but through the weakness of the receiver.

### Chapter VII That the dogmas of the astrologers cannot be defended as Ibn Ezra thought if all stars are considered hot.

<margin>
A certain solution.
Abraham
</margin>
But someone might say it would be enough for the astrologers if, in this way, this star produced dryness or that one moisture, and others produced other qualities. For even Abraham Ibn Ezra <note>original: "Abraam auenazra," a 12th-century Jewish polymath and famous astrologer.</note>, a great figure in the astrological profession, contended that the stars are only producers of heat, and that nothing else could be believed about bodies that are luminous and in perpetual motion. However, he says some stars are called "cold" because they do not impart as much heat to us as is sufficient for our temperament. Thus Saturn is accused of cold because, being placed far from the earth and smaller than Jupiter, it warms lower nature more lukewarmly than it ought; and for that reason, when it is the lord of a birth <note>original: "geniturae dominus," the planet that holds the most influence over a person's horoscope at the moment of their birth.</note>, it signifies death not because of an impressed cold, but because of a lack of heat. 

<margin>
Refutation.
</margin>
I, however, praise Ibn Ezra for thinking correctly about the heat of the stars, but he loved his profession too much, and did not see that its dogmas necessarily conflict with that truth. For let what he said about Saturn proceed, that it is considered cold because it is only slightly warm and therefore kills; in the rest...

# Book III

...because that reasoning does not hold up, nor does it apply consistently to Saturn; for although it is a planet with little heat, it creates moisture by accident—as we have already explained—rather than drying things out. Yet some astrologers still contend that Saturn is dry. Furthermore, would it not then clearly follow that all the stars that are fixed <note>referring to the "fixed stars" in the firmament as opposed to the "wandering" planets</note> and fall below the first magnitude are colder than Saturn, since they are both smaller than it and further from the Earth? For stars are only considered "cold" in the sense that they possess very little heat. If that were the case, the **Heart of the Lion** <note>original: "cor leonis"; the star known today as Regulus</note> would be a cold star, yet it is judged by astrologers to be the most flaming of all. Moreover, if we wish to examine the planets themselves according to this principle accepted by **Ibn Ezra** <note>original: "Auenazra"; Abraham ibn Ezra (c. 1089–1167), a celebrated Jewish scholar and astrologer</note>—namely, which star heats us more and which heats us less—we will find nothing that agrees with the sayings of the astrologers.

<margin>Three things produce the intensification of heat.</margin>
For there are generally three things that produce an intensification of heat: the **magnitude** of the light, its **density**, and its **proximity**. However, it has not been precisely explored how much magnitude outweighs density, how much density outweighs magnitude, or how much proximity outweighs either one or both of them. Therefore, for those who wish to reason this out, the matter will remain uncertain. Nor can our senses judge it, since they do not perceive the rays of any other celestial bodies except for the Sun and the Moon. This is the primary obstacle for astrologers: their entire art is nothing if the power of celestial rays remains ambiguous. 

Indeed, to those willing to follow conjecture, it will appear entirely different from what the astrologers have determined. For if we consider physical mass, the rays of **Mars** would be thought less hot than those of **Saturn** or **Jupiter**. If they respond that Mars is hotter because its light comes from a closer point and is more compact, I would say it is in no way believable that these factors could have such a great effect. Furthermore, regarding the smallness of its disc: should Saturn, which is nearly fifty times larger, be numb with cold while Mars burns with heat? This would only make sense if the smallness of a body's size subtracted very little from the efficacy of its light. 

On the contrary, if an abundance of light combined with proximity adds so much power, we would be cherished more by **Venus** than by any other star except for the Sun and the Moon. This occurs when the **kindly Venus** <note>original: "alma... cytherea"; Cytherea is a poetic name for Venus, derived from the island of Cythera</note>, smiling with her nectar-like light, shines far and wide, for she alone among all the stars is able to cast a shadow. Nor is any star closer to the Earth; for according to common opinion, the Earth does not exceed the width of the orbit of Venus. Yet most astrologers condemn her to "coldness," just as they do not doubt that Jupiter and Mars far surpass all others in heat. If they return to the visual size of the body, their reasoning is once again weak; for while Jupiter's disc is not much larger than that of Venus (considering its vastness), and it is not much closer to the Earth, they nevertheless define Jupiter as being far more heating than Venus, and Saturn as far less. Indeed, they claim that the bodies of Venus and Jupiter are nourishing, while Saturn kills with its coldness.

### Chapter VIII: Objection against what has been said.

And suppose someone says that the differences between these rays are neither known to astrologers, nor can they be known—but that this belongs to a different question. Now we must see if there could be such a diversity in the rays themselves: so that while every ray is warm by nature, and even life-givingly warm, one compared to another might be called "cold" or "contrary to life" due to the abundance or scarcity of light, or perhaps its thinness or efficacy. Likewise, one might be called "dry" and another "moist," whether this happens by its own nature or through contact with the matter of the elements <note>The four elements: Earth, Air, Fire, and Water</note>. 

For there is nothing to prevent this: although the heavens are a universal cause, yet because of their continuous motion they behave differently at different times. Through the various positions of the stars, they cooperate differently with inferior <note>Earthly or physical</note> causes. Thus, not all variety of effects arises from the inferior things themselves, but also from the varying disposition of the universal cause itself—especially if the stars differ from one another not only in the quality or quantity of their light, but also in their other gifts and more peculiar properties.

# Book III

...which the fourth reason put forward against us. For then it seems possible that through motion and heat, which are common to all stars insofar as they are celestial bodies, that common efficiency is also owed to heaven. But through influences <term>influxus</term><note>The medieval concept of "influence" (literally a "flowing in") suggested that a physical or spiritual force emanated from the stars to affect earthly events.</note> which follow the particular natures of the stars, something more particular may happen; and likewise, through the various relationships of the same star to other stars and to the locations of the sky, it might vary the figure, position, and condition of earthly bodies—altering the works of inferior causes <note>The "inferior causes" are things on Earth, like biology or environment, as opposed to "superior" celestial causes.</note> in no small way. Thus, the first argument of the astrologers still stands, referring even this very diversity of effects back to celestial things.

### Chapter IX: The objection is resolved, and it is shown: neither the specific nor the
### individual differences of things depend on the movement of heaven.

A timely objection, bringing to mind many things we object against them: and it is often the case that a bad cause loses more ground the more it defends itself. On the contrary, truth, like fire, the more it is shaken, the more it shines. We shall therefore satisfy this objection. We will first declare what diversity exists in celestial influence, whether according to the diverse nature of multiple stars, or according to the various and revolving changes of the same star. And we will say about these things what evidence or natural reason prescribes by necessary demonstration. For the extent to which our adversaries err requires more work than can be done in passing. Therefore, it will be treated in the following books; here it will be enough to explain how one constellation can differ from another constellation, and we will see how much authority that diversity has in varying the effects in the lower world. From this, what we ourselves intend will be confirmed: that the primary, substantial, and almost the entire distinction of things comes from secondary causes <note>natural, earthly processes</note>; and the fallacy of the astrologers will be more exposed as they claim to predict such distinctions from celestial causes. We have said that heaven acts on us through motion and light. Through motion, it is believed to do three things: to move, to heat, and to bring light. This third point must be treated later, when we discuss light. But as for what they say about heating by motion, it is a difficult question and must be discussed separately in books of philosophy: for it pertains little to the astrological matter. Indeed, how heaven moves things through its own motion we have explained above: namely, that all movements depend on the first motion, just as all the movements of an animal depend on the heartbeat.

Let us see, therefore, as far as motion is concerned, whether different stars move differently, and whether the same stars move differently at different times; then we shall look at light. The movements of the stars differ for three reasons: First, that some move faster, others slower. Second, that some have more movements, others fewer. <margin>Aristotle</margin> Third, by the position of the region in which they move, because some occupy higher seats and travel through larger spaces. **Aristotle** does not think that the multitude or fewness of movements pertains to the diversity of the things affected or moved. Rather, he believes that by the dignity of the movers, it happens that a nobler being attains its end with few movements, whereas an ignobler one does so only with many. Concerning their speed and slowness, nothing is sufficiently explored. For <margin>Macrobius, Ibn Ezra</margin> **Aurelius Macrobius**, imitating the ancients, affirms that all planets proceed at an equal pace; an opinion which **Ibn Ezra** <note>original: "Auenazra"; Abraham ibn Ezra (c. 1089–1167), a polymath whose astrological works were widely cited.</note> will support, placing the Sun, Venus, and Mercury in the same sphere, separated only by the positions of their epicycles <note>small circular paths centered on a larger orbit</note>. However, <margin>Alpetragius</margin> those who make them unequal are at odds with one another. For **Alpetragius** <note>original: "Alpetragius"; al-Bitruji (died c. 1204), an astronomer who challenged the Ptolemaic system.</note>, who thinks some are faster, asserts they are actually slower; others, on the contrary, observe the time of restoration <note>the time it takes for a planet to complete its circuit</note>. This must necessarily deceive, unless one examines the proportion of the delays and the spaces more carefully. But however the matter stands: if indeed they heat by motion, then by faster motion they heat more...

<meta>catchword: light</meta>

...will make warm. As for that primacy of movements we were mentioning, this can create no variety, since inferior movements depend on the movement of heaven. Insofar as that first and circular movement is such, it matters not whether it is slower or swifter. A stone would not move downward, nor fire upward, if the heaven were at rest; but the stone does not descend faster, nor the fire ascend faster, because the heaven revolves more rapidly. It only receives from there the impulse to be moved, as if by a universal nature animating <term>vegetante</term><note>Meaning to give life or "vegative" power to a process.</note> every movement. The movement receives its specific kind from its own substance, its decrease <term>remissionem</term> and increase <term>intentionem</term> <note>Terms from medieval physics referring to the intensity or "stretching" of a quality.</note> from the mover, from impetus, from shape, and from other similar conditions. Therefore, Saturn will not move us differently because it moves more slowly, nor Mars because it is considered faster; for what the astrologers say—that slower planets bestow their gifts later—will be refuted afterward. For now, we maintain that nothing else is given by them through their movement except that we ourselves are also moved. This certainly happens no differently from them, whether they are driven around more slowly or more swiftly. Furthermore, concerning the same planet, there is no reason to doubt that we are moved by it in different ways because it moves differently at different times; for it is a firm dogma of philosophers that celestial movements are always similar to themselves and equal, and stars cannot halt or turn back their course, even though it may appear so to us. This appearance is attributed by mathematicians <note>original: "mathematicis"; in this period, the term usually referred to astronomers and astrologers.</note> to eccentric circles, or to diverse movements striving against one another, or to other things of that kind. The only diversity could be that, when carried through the lowest parts of their epicycles <term>epicyclorum</term> <note>Small circular orbits centered on a larger orbit, used in Ptolemaic astronomy to explain planetary motion.</note>, they might affect us more favorably as they are closer—yet this disagrees more with the decrees of astrologers than it agrees, as will be explained more widely in what follows. Concerning the dignity and rank of the movers or the bodies that are moved, the question is whether they all do the same thing equally in these things that happen, or whether one mover does one thing and another another.

<margin>Question: An Opinion</margin>
For there are those who think that everything which happens is done by the proximate cause <term>proxima causa</term><note>The direct, immediate cause of an event, such as a parent being the proximate cause of a child.</note>, and that superior things do nothing other than move that proximate cause to act. With so many intermediate causes placed by nature between them, it is not that one does one thing and another does another, but so that the thing is effected in its own order, since an effect cannot be produced except by a related cause. And that proximate cause is too ineffective, due to the bonds of matter by which inferior things are more tightly bound, to move without being moved itself. Since it cannot be moved directly by the most noble and supreme causes, it was necessary for as many intermediate causes to intervene as there were degrees of dignity in the order of causes. Therefore, these people believe the same thing is done by so many causes, not because one claims one part of the work and another another—since they are bound together by an essential link—but so that they may do the same thing, one of necessity being moved by another in a threefold series.

<margin>Another opinion.</margin>
There are others, on the contrary, who would have it that the superior and inferior cause do not do the same thing in what is produced, but that according to the degrees of perfections which the substance of the work contains, the work also depends gradually on causes differing among themselves in the perfection of their order. Therefore, the more common nature in the work belongs to the more common cause—that is, a cause as much more universal as it is more excellent in its power of effecting. And thus, things that are made have the fact that they *are* from God; the fact that they are *substances* from the cause that follows next; again, that they are *bodies* from the one after that, until one arrives at the thing's own species and nature, which is referred to its own particular and proximate cause. But whichever of these we believe, it is clear that not only individual differences but even the specific differences of things do not come from the heavens, insofar as we are considering this efficiency of movement.

## Chapter X: That stars other than the sun and moon do nothing, or certainly very little, to affect us.

We have spoken of motion; it remains to speak of light. But first, we must observe certain differences between the action of stars on us through movement and that which occurs through light. The light of the former...

<meta>This page continues the technical dismantling of astrological theory. Having previously discussed how physical movement alone cannot account for the diversity of earthly life, the author now distinguishes between the "power" of celestial movement (spiritual or intellectual) and the "power" of celestial light (physical), arguing that only the Sun and Moon have a demonstrable physical impact on the sublunary world.</meta>

# Book III

Its power comes from the mover—more from the soul <note>In Aristotelian and Neoplatonic thought, the celestial spheres were believed to be moved by "Intelligences" or souls.</note> than from the physical body being moved. The power of a planet comes from the body of the planet itself; that of the spheres <term>sphærarum</term> belongs to the spheres rather than the stars, while the power of the stars is believed to belong to the stars rather than the spheres. In the former case, lower things depend on higher ones, since there is no doubt that the planets are subject to the movement of the first orb <note>The *Primum Mobile*, the outermost sphere that carries all others in its daily rotation.</note> and, along with the rest, the sun is driven around. Regarding light, on the other hand, it is the opinion of almost all consenting philosophers that not only the moon but also the rest of the stars are illuminated by the sun. Furthermore, higher things move us more when the rest are moved by their power; but regarding the influence of light upon us, if other conditions are equal, the influence is more powerful from a closer location. However, it is not clear—as we shall demonstrate—whether the lights of the higher bodies act upon us at all, or only those of the moon and sun. The others, up to this point, do not reach us with any efficacy, either due to the smallness of the shining bodies or their distance. Regarding movement, there is no doubt that (as we have said) the higher things are more powerful. From all of this, one can gather what is said by the philosophers: that by a certain essential order and series, a "chain of causes" <note>original: "cathenam causarum"; a reference to the Golden Chain of Homer, often used by Neoplatonists to describe the hierarchy of being.</note> is woven together and hangs downward. This relates mostly to the efficiency of movement, since this assembly and order of causes is understood to exist more in the moving souls than in the bodies. It is characteristic of this order that second things depend on the first, and a higher cause has more strength and power than any of the lower ones—not so that the higher ceases while the lower acts. Yet we do not deny that the heat of the sun stands as a cause for "seminal heats" <note>The vital heat within living seeds and organisms that allows for generation.</note> in the essential order of the higher world. But that order is not extended any further; therefore, we do not find here that "complication of causes" led from the first to the lowest through intermediate steps of which they speak. Rather, in the movers—insofar as they are movers—this series is found more completely. However, in both cases, a four-fold <term>quaternarium</term> progression is observed. In movement, the first place is held by that sphere or universe which revolves by the daily agitation, from which that movement is communicated to all other things. There follows the chorus of planets running in the opposite direction over the poles of the zodiac <term>signiferi</term> <note>Literally "the sign-bearer," the belt of the heavens containing the twelve signs.</note>. In this, there are no further steps to be distinguished, since they neither move one another nor are they moved by one another. Therefore, like a single movable thing, just as it is carried away by the "first mover," it also moves by its own specific movement—which is called the movement of "Diversity" by Plato <note>Refers to the *Timaeus*, where Plato distinguishes the "Same" (the outer heaven) and the "Different" (the planetary paths).</note>. It moves the ether, I say, and the highest air, from which, by each degree, the movement reaches us and the lower bodies, while all the particular movements of natural things are enlivened <term>vegetantur</term> from there. Regarding light (by which I always mean the heat flowing from light), the sun is the source of the entire influx—the eye of the world. It illuminates the moon; the moon affects the air; the air affects all bodies that live in and under the air. But consider this diversity: we are moved by the first mover through the planets, and we are illuminated by the sun differently than by the moon. We review all these things primarily so that, before we discuss the differences in "sidereal flows" <note>The supposed influence or "fluid" emanations from the stars.</note>, we may recognize that it is not established whether these superior influxes—whatever they may be—actually reach our region. What astrologers believe about certain tiny stars could just as well be believed about all the planets except the sun and moon. Since the primary objection to this opinion might be that celestial bodies are the "essential causes" of lower things—an order in which no link can be missing—I wanted to declare that this order belongs to the "moving virtues" rather than the illuminating bodies. For astrologers cannot argue that God created the stars in vain if their "breaths" <term>afflatus</term> are not felt; they themselves freely admit this very point about other things. Otherwise, they might think this sublime candelabra, radiating with so many lights, was made primarily so that by bringing light to our eyes at night, it might illuminate the dens inhabited by light-fleeing moles.

<margin>The Solution</margin>

But why, you will ask, are there so many stars if one sun and moon suffice us? This was fitting for the celestial nature, this order of things...

# Book III

<margin>The reasoning of Averroës</margin>
<margin>The reasoning of Averroës <note>Averroës (1126–1198) was an influential Andalusian philosopher known for his commentaries on Aristotle.</note> is turned against the astrologers</margin>
<margin>Three things that make the action of light effective on us</margin>

<margin>Those three things meet in the sun</margin>
<margin>The size of a star</margin>
<margin>Of the largest fixed stars</margin>
<margin>Jupiter, Saturn, Mars, Sun</margin>
<margin>Venus, Mercury</margin>
<margin>Confirmation of this opinion by Aristotle</margin>
<margin>Aristotle</margin>

...the perfection of the entire universe demanded this; nor does it follow that if all things do not illuminate us, they cannot have some other use or benefit for us. Averroës argues in this way: "The sun and moon act upon us, therefore the rest do as well, since they are all of the same nature." I like this style of argument, and it tastes of Aristotle, who also argues thus: "The moon does not move by its own motion, but with its sphere, which its spots <note>The "spots" on the moon were used as evidence that the moon itself does not rotate independently of its celestial sphere.</note> prove; therefore, the same must be judged of the rest, since the nature of all celestial things is one." It is as if we, following in these same footsteps, were to gather this: "The sun heats, therefore the moon does too, because they are all of the same nature." And we would indeed be right to conclude this, insofar as reason proves the conditions of all are the same when considered absolutely in themselves; but when you compare them to other things, the reasoning falters because they are not compared in the same way. For if the sun, by its own nature, is destined to do the same things as Saturn, it does not follow that both do the same thing *toward us*, because one is compared to us as near and the other as remote. 

Thus, those who would say that only the sun and moon act upon us have reasons they may offer for their suspicion, even though the same nature exists in all celestial bodies. For three conditions of a shining body primarily make the action of light effective upon us: **size**, **density**, and **proximity**. All of these meet excellently in the sun; for it is nearest to us (especially if it is placed just above the moon, as the ancients and, after Ptolemy, Geber and Theon contend) and is of such a vast body that it exceeds the largest of the stars by more than a ratio of one and a half <term>sesquialtera</term>. Furthermore, it is seen with the densest light, the most radiant of all. The moon is so close to our regions that it cannot fail to affect them, from which it also follows that its light is necessarily effective, being almost no different than solar light. You will not find these conditions in the others in such a way that what you grant concerning the sun and moon, you must also grant concerning the rest. 

But perhaps the very distance will stand in the way of the lights of the eighth sphere <note>The sphere of the "fixed stars," the most distant part of the visible universe in this model.</note>, even the largest ones. That same distance will stand in the way of the stars of Saturn and Jupiter, which are reported to be smaller than the fixed stars, even if they are closer to the earth. For the largest fixed stars are said to contain the mass of the earth one hundred and seven times; but Jupiter only ninety-five times, and Saturn only ninety-one. These things are not said with total precision, yet if we follow experience, we see that those fixed stars—even though they are of such vast magnitude—do not have their rays felt at night, even if Saturn and Jupiter shine upon us with them above the horizon. Mars decreases far more in body than it approaches in position, for it has a ratio to the earth only a little larger than one and a half; so that one sun could contain nearly a hundred Mars-sized bodies. Indeed, the sun is one hundred and sixty-six times larger than the earth. Therefore, why would he be saying something absurd who, witnessing the powers of the sun upon bodies by his own senses, believes it possible that the powers of the star of Mars do not reach these things, being so much smaller and also more remote from the earth? He might believe the same of the star of Venus, perhaps even more remote from us than the sun is, and certainly far smaller than the earth itself (of which it is thought not even to be a twentieth part); for Mercury is smaller than the moon, just as it is also more distant from us. 

Therefore, why is it a wonder if this planet is felt so little, since it is also so rarely seen?—though astrologers are accustomed to attribute a great deal to it. But Aristotle also seems to support those who think this way; for when he deals with motion, he mentions all of them, as in the book *On the Heavens*, and especially the highest motions, as in the final part of the *Physics*—namely, because all bodies are moved by these motions. But when he speaks of that life-giving heat that nourishes things and brings about generation, he speaks either of the sun alone (as when he said that "man is generated by man and the sun") or of the sun and moon, as in the books *On the Generation of Animals*...

# Book III

<margin>Pico’s opinion. <note>Giovanni Pico della Mirandola (1463–1494) was a famous Italian Renaissance philosopher who wrote a massive critique of astrology, which the author is referencing here.</note></margin>

<margin>The opinion presented above is most aptly clarified.</margin>

...makes mention [of this], so that if anyone should contend that this was Aristotle's opinion, they could not be refuted by any of his philosophical sayings. We do not assert the former as much as the latter: that whatever reaches us here below from the other stars is extremely thin and minute. For example, if perhaps by the nocturnal lights of the stars the air becomes somewhat **milder** <note>original: "mittescat", meaning to grow soft or mild</note>, making it better suited for the generation of life. 

However, if someone were to attribute all generation to the Sun alone, they might decide that what the Sun performs by day through its own light, it also performs by night through light reflected off the Moon—as if from a mirror—from which it is bounced back to the Earth. Nature most wisely arranged these turns, because earthly weakness cannot constantly endure the rays of the Sun. Therefore, by night, it receives them through the Moon, more broken and weaker, and thus more suited to its own infirmity; so that things are neither completely abandoned by life-giving light, nor do they collapse under its full intensity. 

In the same way, the Sun returns to us more healthfully in early spring after being far away all winter, than if it had lived near us constantly. Our fragility is so overwhelmed by the "goodness" of the heavens if it is excessive, that not even the Moon herself always reflects the solar rays to us in her entirety, but now sparingly, now abundantly, according to her **alignments** <note>original: "schematīsmis", referring to the geometric angles between celestial bodies</note> with the Sun. Divine care has so ordered these things for our benefit, since for that same reason it did not fill the star closest to us [the Moon] with its own light. 

If you survey all of nature, you will see no evidence given by her that lower things are nourished by any heat other than that of the Sun. While we do not stubbornly defend this—and we do not refuse to admit the stars into a partnership in this duty, as many philosophers believe—we nevertheless refute the astrologers who think that in any birth (if human births pertain to the stars at all), the primary rule should sometimes be granted to other planets, setting aside the Sun or the Moon, whether the birth was by day or by night. They even think that the Sun itself can be overwhelmed by the rays of others and negatively affected, as if it were simply one of many, reduced to the common rank. 

But of these things later; for now we only advise that those who believe the other stars can do more than the Sun in altering lower things are refuted more by evidence and the senses than those who contend they can do almost nothing—attributing this entire illumination and **life-giving force** <term>vegetationem</term> <note>From the Latin "vegetatio," meaning the power to give growth and animation, typical of the "vegetative soul" in Aristotelian biology.</note> of the lower world to the **solar torch** <note>original: "phœbeæ lampadi," literally the lamp of Phoebus Apollo, the sun god.</note>, from which the lunar lamp is also lit for us by night.

<margin>Those who attribute nothing to the stars seem more correct than those who attribute much.</margin>

### Chapter XI. In what way the same stars can act on us differently at different times:

But let us grant the astrologers—since we ourselves do not greatly deny it—that something flows down from all the stars upon us. It remains to be examined what their objection required: whether they always bestow the same thing, or whether different stars bestow different things; and if not the same, let us see if the lower effects are also varied by that diversity. 

In their fourth argument, they try to prove that there are specific powers for each star besides motion and light, based on the nobility of the heavens and the powers of certain bodies thought to come from the heavens; we shall dismantle these arguments there. Here, however, they assert the diversity of the stars themselves as a reason: that since star differs from star, and light and motion are common to all, they must necessarily have certain specific properties besides these by which they differ from one another. 

But Paul said: *star differs from star in glory* <note>A reference to the Apostle Paul in 1 Corinthians 15:41.</note>. What then if, just as circular motion is common to all, yet they differ in motion so that this one moves faster and that one more slowly (though not even this is conceded by all)? It is the same with light: namely, that they agree in having light, but differ in the conditions of that light, as the light of one star is denser or more abundant, while that of another is rarer or thinner. For there will be those who believe that a star is more different from its own sphere than one star is from another; yet they do not differ in any other way than...

<margin>Paul the Apostle. Opinion.</margin>
