# Book III

...[overwhelmed by] density and thickness, so that if this is accepted, it will consequently be thought that their action upon us varies in no other way than this: those that are denser, larger, and closer pour out more light and heat; those that are rarer, smaller, and more remote pour out less. Finally, the **breath** <note>original: "spiramen," referring to a celestial emanation or influence</note> from all of them is the same—consisting of hot light and shining heat—from which health, life, and nourishment for bodies flow. They differ only in that the influence is breathed into us more thinly from some and more abundantly from others; from some at close range and from others from afar. 

Furthermore, regarding what we shall decide about a star through the perpetual rotation of its motion: it is truly the opinion of the **Peripatetics** <term>Peripatetics: Followers of Aristotle's philosophy, so named because Aristotle often walked about while teaching.</term> that stars do not change their quality, but only their location—except for the Moon, which, shining with borrowed light, is illuminated more or less depending on its turnings toward the Sun. Therefore, through the turning it makes away from the Sun, it reflects light to us more or less abundantly, and heat along with its light. Thus, it almost abandons us at the **New Moon** <note>original: "nouilunio"</note> because the side facing us is deprived of light; it nourishes and warms us more at the **Full Moon** <note>original: "plenilunio"</note>. Just as it warms more when waxing and less when waning—a variety that cannot exist in the other stars, which shine with a stable and proper light of their own. For this reason, of almost all the changes that frequently occur in bodies, if there is a heavenly cause, it is usually attributed to the Moon; because she herself is changeable not only in position but in quality, she affects us most closely. 

For the other planets, change occurs only through the movement of their locations. From this, the variety of their influence is nothing other than they affect us more intensely or more weakly insofar as they migrate here and there, becoming closer or more remote to us. Their motion is twofold: **universal** and **proper** <note>Universal motion is the daily rotation of the sky from East to West; proper motion is the individual planet's movement along the zodiac from West to East.</note>. The universal motion carries them toward us daily, lifting them above the earth, and daily snatches them away, leading them toward the setting. From this arises the first diversity of action: from the peak of the sky, they hurl the strongest rays because they fall more perpendicularly. Therefore, the more they approach the **zenith** <note>original: "culmini," the highest point</note>, the more powerfully they affect us; the more they descend from there, the more weakly.

<margin>Whether stars submerged beneath the earth can have any power over us.</margin>

Whether they can do anything to us when merged beneath the earth must be discussed. Indeed, when they are near the **horizon** <term>finitore: An old astronomical term for the horizon, which "finishes" or bounds the visible sky.</term> and not yet completely snatched from our sight, they can certainly do something, though very little, through rays reaching us at an angle. But when they are hidden deep in the shadows of the earth and are taken further away from us, if I believe they can do nothing, my senses will support me and reason will not oppose it—if indeed anything else can be believed. 

<margin>Avicenna, Albert.</margin>

Truly, what we have owed [to reason] up to this point is that nothing reaches us from heaven unless light is the carrier. This is what **Avicenna** <note>Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), a Persian polymath whose works on medicine and philosophy were standard texts in European universities.</note> also said in his books on **meteorology** <note>original: "metheorologicis"</note>, calling light the "vehicle" of all celestial virtues; and **Albert** <note>Albertus Magnus (c. 1200–1280), a famous German scholar and bishop who sought to reconcile Aristotelian science with Christian faith.</note> confirmed this in his book *On Sleep and Waking*. Therefore, just as light does not reach us then, neither will any virtue reach us. We shall say that the Sun alone is present for us even at night for this reason: that it creates a sisterly substitute, shining upon us through the splendor impressed upon the Moon. Unless, perhaps, it could also be said that since the upper air is continuous with the lower air, the lower air is somewhat nourished by the presence of the Sun there, so that it would be much colder if there were no Sun at all to illuminate any part of the air. 

But if this effect exists, eyes and touch will report that it is almost nothing. If any **astrologers** <note>The author uses this term here with a tone of skepticism regarding their "dreams."</note> have dreamed up powers for themselves which the whole mass of the Earth does not block, they should at least not be so delirious, even in their sleep, as to not concede that these virtues are imprinted upon us more purely and effectively when they are poured out through the surrounding air alone, than when the entire thickest density of the blunt Earth must be pierced through by them. Those who do not concede this, they think, are defended from insanity [only by their own logic]. For they think that the powers of the stars in the **twelfth house** <note>The "twelfth house" in astrology is just above the eastern horizon; the author argues it is absurd to think stars here are "weak" while stars deep under the Earth are "strong."</note>—which, rising nearest to the East above the horizon, is only one "mansion" away from the summit—are sluggish, idle, and weak, while the same stars at the bottom of the earth have the most vigor and efficacy. But we will deal with their errors later; for now, we treat only what ought to be decided by reason. We have spoken of the universal motion...

<header>Book III</header>

# Book III

...universal. By their own motion <term>Motu proprio: The independent movement of a planet through the zodiac, as opposed to the daily rotation of the heavens.</term> the planets are carried now to the south, now to the north <note>original: "aquilonem"</note>; which even the fixed stars are believed to do, according to the opinion of more recent thinkers. The Sun does the same, not because it deflects from the orbit it has once occupied, but because that orbit is oblique, making it now closer to us, now more remote: closer in the north, and more remote in the south. From this, another variety of influence <note>original: "influendi"</note> is born, since there is indeed greater efficacy in rays inclining toward us, and less when they recede toward the south. Beyond these and similar things, any other diversity imagined in the action of the stars is utterly vain and irrational. Such is the case among the astrologers, who think that the same star is affected in various ways according to the twelve signs of the zodiac it passes through, or by its relation to fixed or wandering stars at certain intervals—which they call **aspects**—and that it thus acquires the most diverse powers for influencing us. Against this error, the entirety of Book VI will prepare itself; here, at the beginning of this chapter, we will merely set against them the authority of the **Peripatetics** <term>Peripatetics: Followers of Aristotle's philosophy, who focused on physical and observable causes.</term>, who deny any change in the stars other than their position, except in the case of the Moon. For if they only exclude change that is corruptive or harmful, they ought not to have excluded the Moon, since it is necessarily changed by the Sun. 

<margin>Whether the Moon receives the rays of other planets just like the Sun’s.</margin>
However, as we shall see, astrologers do not free the stars from changes that weaken them—if not in their substance, then in their powers and faculties. But we will discuss this later. Let us drive away the idea that the Moon receives the rays of other planets in the same way it does the Sun's. Indeed, it appears probable because the Moon's nature is a vessel for incoming light rather than being bright itself; and being the lowest of all the heavenly bodies, it seems less prepared for this. Truly, neither greater authority nor the senses themselves support this; for if the Moon is joined with the Sun, and at that time it is placed opposite the rays of Jupiter or Mars—from which it ought to reflect their light more fully to us—it is acknowledged to possess nothing of their rays or light. We touch upon this question because if it were to draw light from the others as well, the planets would become more effective toward us for this reason: their power would be joined to the Moon and transmitted through it to us, whereas on its own, it might reach us less. But if this were to happen, it would happen 

<margin>That the conjunction of the Moon with the stars is unfortunate rather than fortunate.</margin>
altogether differently than the astrologers think. For they believe the Moon transmits the rays of that star most strongly when it is found together with it. I, however, have no doubt that the further the Moon departs from a star, the more of that star's light is communicated to us through it. The less the distance, the less light; and it is least of all, or certainly nothing, when there is no distance between them. I am moved to this by evident experience: when joined to the Sun, the Moon does not transmit the Sun's rays to us, with the bulk of its body especially causing this obstacle. How much less, then, the rays of others, which are far thinner than the solar ones and more remote from the Moon? See how greatly they are deceived who believe a day or a birth <note>original: "genituram," referring to a natal horoscope</note> is fortunate when the Moon meets with **benefic stars** <term>Benefic stars: Traditionally Jupiter and Venus, thought to bring good fortune.</term>, and unfortunate when with **malefic ones**. For the Moon "meeting" them is nothing other than their influence being intercepted from us by the density of the Moon. Perhaps, however, there is some reason to think that a morning planet has some prerogative in changing things below, 

<margin>Whether a new force grows from the mixture of rays. Plotinus.</margin>
because, rising before the Sun, it claims the air for itself before it is entirely occupied by the Sun. But if this is so, it can hardly have great importance. It remains to be examined whether a new force grows from the mixture of rays, producing a new effect that individual rays would not produce on their own. **Plotinus** <note>A major Neoplatonic philosopher (c. 204–270 AD) who argued that celestial souls influence the world through contemplation and natural law rather than "mixing" physical rays.</note> denies that this "tempering" or mixing can happen to rays so that a new power or form springs from their union. I think this is because rays are not bodies like liquids, nor are they qualities fixed to bodies in such a way that they are received into bodies to be stained by them or changed from their own nature. Wherefore, it is likely to this philosopher that what happens to many qualities does not happen to rays: that they are sometimes changed by some combination or mixture into another form growing out of all of them—especially since this does not happen without the destruction of the simple and particular qualities that flow together.

<meta>This page continues the argument against the complex systems used by astrologers. The author is moving from a general critique of "aspects" (the angles between planets) to a specific philosophical distinction between "substantial" influences—the universal laws of nature—and "accidental" influences, which are the minor variations caused by local conditions or the specific timing of a birth.</meta>

Book III

...but to happen: something that no one will easily imagine occurring in rays. For even if we grant the astrologers that rays are mixed, or that heat flows from them, we have been accustomed to the idea that all rays are mixed together, rather than being "unsociable" <note>original: "asymbolos"; here meaning rays that refuse to blend or interact.</note> as if they were not at all united with others through those positions which they now call **aspects** <term>Aspects: In astrology, specific angles between planets (like 90 or 180 degrees) believed to create harmony or conflict.</term>. Therefore, the mixture of the present hour, moment, year, month, or day does not vary from the radiant mixture of any other time, except for those reasons by which we have already explained that the actions of the stars vary: so that there is one temperament for the night and another for the day; one when the stars recede toward the south <note>original: "meridiem"</note>, and another when they incline toward the north <note>original: "aquilonem"</note>; from which alone the intensification and weakening of heat arises.

---

## Chapter XII: Which variety of effects can be traced back to the heaven and which cannot.

<margin>In the mixture of rays there is something substantial and something accidental. Substantial things in the heaven.</margin>
Let us consider the mixture of all rays in the air; in it there is something we might call **substantial**, and something largely **accidental**. The substantial part is that there is one light or one heat gathered or resulting from all the lights of the heaven; and this is indeed perpetual and unchangeable. But the fact that this specific ray is more intense in it now, and another is weaker, is accidental; it changes repeatedly due to the constant motion of the celestial bodies. 

The reason for this distinction of ours is easily seen. For in the heaven, which we know to be the source of this heat, something can be called "substantial"—just as we say substantial things are those that follow the substance of a thing inseparably. Such things are the incorruptible body, the circular figure which is the first of all shapes, the movement in an orbit, and the light that nourishes all things with its heat. And if indeed the stars have their own powers, those powers of the stars are also substantial. Conversely, there is something in the heaven and stars that is as variable as it is accidental, such as the change of position in all the stars, <margin>Accidental</margin> and the changing phases of light in the moon. 

Therefore, those things in the mixture of rays that follow the substantial things of heaven, we call **substantial**; those that follow the accidental, we call **accidental**. For example, the fact that the power of Saturn, Jupiter, the Sun, and the others are present in the mixture is substantial; but that some are more intense and others more weak due to the variety of their rays is called accidental. 

Thus, Socrates was aided by that superior power—which is certainly not a changeable power (otherwise it would not always be present to the causes doing all things as it is seen to be)—aided, I say, by that power, he generates a human being insofar as he is a human. But he generates *this* specific human being insofar as he comes from *this* seed and from *this* matter. Therefore, if you look at this individual substantial condition, nature, or character of the effect, any constellation is indifferent. 

However, because of the diversity of the constellation—that is, the varying state and relation of the stars to the earth—more or less heat is poured into the air. Through this different mixture of rays, a new proportion and measure of warm light results. This is what is accidental in the celestial things, and it likewise creates diversity in the accidental results. For instance, if someone says that a better conception occurs during a full moon, or that the fetus grows more as the moon waxes, or that seeds are better affected under a temperate state of the sky and thus a better offspring is procreated—this is the kind of diversity that can exist in the generation of substances due to the varying positions of the stars. We call this "accidental" and "external" because, as we have declared, the specific and substantial mark of the conceived fetus depends on its own most immediate source and its own substantial matter. 

Furthermore, even for accidental properties, the "accidents" <term>Accidentia: In philosophy, properties that a thing can lose without ceasing to be what it is, such as hair color or height.</term> of the seed and the matter do more than the external disposition of the surrounding air, as daily experience makes manifest. <margin>Aristotle</margin> So much so that Aristotle says if a son is not shaped according to the seeds of the parents and does not derive his likeness from there, he must be numbered among **monsters** <term>Monstris: In ancient biology, a "monster" was any birth that deviated from the natural likeness of the parents, not necessarily something frightening.</term>. Therefore, nothing shall hinder us from making the stars only universal causes, and seeking the distinction of effects from secondary causes; for the varying disposition of the stars works through the changes of the air, or the bodies, or the parents...

<summary>This page argues that while stars provide a universal, unchanging "substantial" power (like light and heat), the specific differences in people and things come from local matter and biological seeds. The author uses Aristotelian logic to claim that astrology's "aspects" are merely accidental variations of air temperature rather than direct controllers of human destiny.</summary>

# Book III

...can vary the disposition of those to be generated in some way; for as we have said, this external influence is a very general change. However, those things which pertain to the **substance** and the most intimate qualities undoubtedly draw their origin more properly from specific causes, and for that reason, they can in no way be foreseen from the heaven. This is certainly true in the case of physical bodies which are "perfect substances" <note>original: "perfecta substantia"; in medieval philosophy, this refers to a complete, individual being like a human or animal, rather than just a raw element.</note>, for all of which there are immediate **efficient causes** <term>Efficient cause: The agent or force that actually brings something into being, like a builder for a house.</term>—or something proportional to them, as in things generated from decay or inanimate mixtures, which we shall discuss in the solution to the fourth argument. 

But the heaven can produce changes in the air—such as heat, cold, moisture, and dryness—without any intermediate cause. It does this entirely and universally. From its own nature, it provides a healthful warmth, while other effects occur "by accident" <note>meaning as a secondary result</note> according to the condition of the material. Just as by one and the same heat mud hardens and wax melts, and under the same sun linens become white while they are being washed, yet the face of the one washing them is turned dark. 

Furthermore, since this is an **accidental change**, that which we have called "accidental" in the celestial constellation has the greatest power: that is, the positions and attitudes of the stars. From these, the strength of the rays is intensified or weakened; and for that reason, heat grows stronger in the air to a greater or lesser degree. Specifically, because of the varying path of the sun, the four seasons of the year change; and the rising and setting, the ascending and descending of the sun produce nearly these same four changes throughout the day. 

Between these primary qualities of bodies and inanimate mixtures, **meteorological impressions** <note>original: "metheorologicæ ipreſſiōes"; phenomena like rain, snow, or thunder.</note> hold a kind of middle ground. The heaven is their efficient cause, and the lower elements are their material. Hence, their diversity depends more on the celestial disposition than the diversity of "perfect" bodies does. Thus, thunder usually occurs in spring and autumn, hail in summer, and snow and rain in winter. These four qualities are not absolute; sometimes a ray falling upon matter moves it by its own power, but they congeal from the lower matter. Therefore, they vary greatly according to the condition of that matter, as will be explained more fully in the treatise on the third argument.

But perfect substances—which possess not only matter but also their own specific **efficient cause**—receive whatever is substantial and specific to them from their own specific causes. The heaven acts only as an "immobile influence" <note>a constant, background force</note> cooperating as a universal cause. It does produce some external and very general changes, but about these, even astrologers can say nothing. This is because such changes depend neither on the celestial causes they have invented, nor on the hour of birth, but on other principles, as we shall declare later. For now, we are only investigating what the heaven does and what it does **not** do.

Therefore, understanding these things we have discussed, **Aurelius Augustine** <margin>Augustine</margin> <note>St. Augustine of Hippo (354–430 AD), who famously argued against astrology in "The City of God."</note> said it was not entirely absurd to think that certain "stellar breathings" <note>original: "afflatus quoſdā ſydereos"; influences or flows of energy from the stars.</note> might have power over the differences in physical bodies alone. He did not assert this as fact, nor did he accuse those who thought otherwise; rather, he lessened the blame of those who held such an opinion, pronouncing it "not altogether absurd." To explain how this should be understood regarding physical differences, he added: "Just as we see the seasons of the year vary with the approach and retreat of the sun, and certain kinds of things increase or decrease with the waxing and waning of the moon—such as **sea urchins** and **shellfish**, and the wondrous **tides of the ocean**." 

In these words, you see nothing listed that contributes to the generation of a perfect substance. He teaches that these physical differences should not be referred to the stars, but rather he immediately reminds us of the "proximate" or immediate causes, adding: "What is more physical than the sex of a body? And yet, under the same position of the stars, twins of different sexes could be conceived." <margin>Hippocrates</margin> Confirming this same sentiment a little earlier, he had approved of **Hippocrates** <note>The ancient Greek "Father of Medicine."</note> who gave the reason from specific and secondary causes why two brothers might fall ill and recover at the same time. <margin>Posidonius</margin> However, he did not approve of **Posidonius** <note>A Stoic philosopher who tried to use astrology to explain medical conditions.</note> who tried to trace this back to their constellation.

The author cites St. Augustine's examples of twins and shellfish to demonstrate that biological realities like gender and health are independent of birth charts.</summary>

# Book III
# III

<margin>Words of Augustine in Book 5 of *The City of God*</margin>
Referring to this similarity, he says that a medical explanation is much more acceptable: that just as the parents were physically affected while they were conceiving, so the "first seeds" <note>original: "primordia"; the initial biological sparks of life</note> of those conceived could be affected. Thus, following their initial growth within the mother’s body, they would be born with equal health. Furthermore, being nourished in one house with the same foods—where medicine testifies that the air, the location, and the quality of wine and water are very powerful in determining whether the body is well or poorly received—and being accustomed to the same exercises, they would possess such similar bodies that they would even be moved to fall ill at the same time and from the same causes. But to refer this to the constitution of the heaven or the stars when they were conceived or born, I know not what kind of "insolence" <note>original: "insolentiæ"; Augustine uses this word to describe the arrogance of astrologers claiming to know God's secrets through the stars.</note> it might be. These are the words of our Augustine which we have woven into the text. However, many, understanding only this much from what is frequently used by our writers, think that because differences in bodies pertain to celestial influences, Augustine believed all diversity in physical effects comes from the heaven. Consequently, they think that with Augustine’s agreement, astrologers can prophesy about these things. They are little mindful that nothing can be called so purely "physical" as the **temperament** <term>Temperament: In ancient medicine, the specific balance of the four humors (blood, phlegm, black bile, yellow bile) that determines a person's health and personality.</term> of the body itself; yet those seeking the causes of this temperament in the heaven are branded with the mark of "insolence" by Augustine.

## Chapter: XIII The Sun performs many things that astrologers think are done by other stars.

**P**ressing back against the first argument of the astrologers, we have declared in a long but necessary digression how the action of the heaven and the celestial bodies might affect us, and how it might vary, whether we consider the stars themselves or the material receiving their influence. From this, it has been made clear that the heaven is a **universal cause**, and that the distinction of effects—especially those that are primary and substantial—should not be sought from there. Now, in a proper order and taking it step by step through what we have discussed, we shall set our hands to solving the **second reason** <note>The second major argument used by astrologers to justify their craft.</note>. This reason is as follows: since it is observed that the dispositions of inferior bodies vary according to the different positions of the sun and moon relative to us, they contended that the same should be believed regarding other things and planets. For, they say, the turns of the four seasons vary through the "solar circuits," and the state of all bodies varies both from that change and through the increases and decreases of the moon.

Therefore, they think two things can be gathered from this. First, that just as we see sea urchins, shellfish, the ocean, and the moisture of bodies change according to the cycles of the moon—and the earthly mass in general changes through the annual and daily revolution of the sun—we should likewise agree that all other things are bound to and governed by the stars. Second, that the manifest power of the sun and moon in changing "sublunary" <note>Anything below the moon, i.e., the Earth and its atmosphere.</note> matter should compel us to believe the same about the rays of the other stars; that is, that there is also a great power in them, however hidden, for changing things and affecting them in many ways.

We shall make it clear that neither conclusion follows. Indeed, we shall show that these very examples they bring forward actually favor those who think otherwise. Before that is done, we shall provide a reason for all those observations based on the principles already established, so it may be clear that we are not led by arguments or experiments to feel any differently about the efficiency of the stars and the change of celestial virtues than what we have written so far, guided by natural reason. Nor in the meantime shall I cease to taunt the many fallacies and many errors of the astrologers encountered along the way. Let us begin, therefore, with the works of the sun. The approach and retreat of the sun varies the seasons of the year; this we would even affirm under oath if necessary. But the **obliquity of the zodiac** <note>The tilt of the Earth's axis (or, in their view, the sun's path) which creates the seasons.</note> causes this, not the "nature" of the signs. That is, the sun does not burn in Leo because it is the "Sign of the Lion," or the "House of the Sun," or a "Hot Sign," as the astrologers fabricate; but because when the sun is positioned there, it is closer to our air and has been heating it for six months already.

# Book III
# III

Otherwise, the heat is most intense in <term>Cancer</term><note>The zodiac sign associated with the summer solstice in the northern hemisphere.</note> even though, according to the astrologers, Cancer is neither the **house** nor the **exaltation** <note>In astrology, a "house" (domicile) is a sign where a planet has maximum control, and "exaltation" is a sign where it has specific strength. The Sun’s house is Leo and its exaltation is Aries.</note> of the sun; nor is it a "fiery" sign, but an "aquatic" one. Likewise, in <term>Aries</term>, the sun restores the world, calling forth flowers and increasing the growth of seeds; for then, first returning to us, it inspires bodies with a fruitful and pleasant warmth. Indeed, it is a mere fable of the astrologers that Aries is the "exaltation" of the sun—as if the sun did not do the exact same thing in <term>Libra</term> (the sign opposite to Aries) for other peoples <note>A reference to the inhabitants of the southern hemisphere, for whom Libra marks the beginning of spring.</note> as it does for us in Aries. Namely, while it recedes from here, it approaches them. Therefore, the sole cause of all the variety that occurs with the seasons is the greater or lesser distance of the sun from the lands we inhabit; from this, we participate in more or less of its heat. From this also, thunder occurs in the spring; for when the sun reaches Aries, the winter humidity is dissolved by the heat of the air. Consequently, much evaporation is lifted upward into the air <margin>Why thunder occurs in spring</margin> by the "laws of the clouds," from which thunder and lightning proceed. If the astrologers also understand this, what is this "sleepiness" or desire to deceive, that they define Aries as a sign that stirs up rain and thunder—as if the nature of that sign itself operated this way? They would not say that the Moon in Aries causes thunder in any way if they were able or willing to observe that this happens not by the power of that sign, but by the action of the sun reaching that sign. By a similar fallacy, it was written by <term>Ptolemy</term> <note>Claudius Ptolemy, the 2nd-century author of the *Tetrabiblos* (here called the *Apotelesmaton*), the foundational text of Western astrology.</note> in his books on the effects of the stars, that the Moon in Aries, if it causes disease, produces especially "white leprosy" which the Greeks call <term>alphos</term> <note>original: "αλφους"; a skin condition characterized by white patches, often equated with vitiligo.</note> and is commonly called <term>morphea</term>; in Cancer, it causes <term>mentagra</term> <note>A pustular eruption on the chin or face.</note> which the Greeks call <term>lichens</term> and is commonly called <term>impetigo</term>; in Libra, it causes leprosy; and in Capricorn, freckles. For this reasoning is drawn from the state of the air when the sun is carried through those signs: that is, from the quality of spring, the time when the sun is in Aries; of summer, when it is in Cancer; of autumn, with Libra; and of winter, when it runs through the sign of Capricorn—provided that those types of diseases match the conditions of those seasons. Indeed, vitiligo easily invades and occupies the surface of the skin at that time because humors are especially redundant in that part of the year; summer causes "mentagra," which arises from drier and sharper matter; in autumn, leprosy is expected, if indeed it is considered an infection of **black bile** <note>original: "atræ bilis"; one of the four humors in ancient medicine, associated with melancholy and skin disorders.</note>; and freckles are expected in winter, which are generated from colder and more humid excesses. It is, therefore, the height of "slowness" <note>intellectual dullness or stubbornness</note> to ascribe to the signs—under which the sun is carried during those times—that which is caused by the sun heating the air more or less according to the variety of its position. Or, if they understand this, but act as if they do not, so that they might think other planets in these same signs operate in the same way, let us conclude that the fixed diversity in the seasons of the year happens from nowhere else than the approach and retreat of the sun due to the obliquity of the zodiac. If not all summers are equally hot, nor all winters equally freezing, this happens <margin>Why not all summers are equally hot.</margin> according to the disposition of matter, which has the greatest momentum in the air—as evidenced by the senses and by Ptolemy. Nor is it necessary to refer this to the heaven, except as if to a universal cause of every bodily thing, as can be understood from **Aristotle's books on Meteorology**. Thus, the fact that in the same summer the heat is more intense on some days and weaker on others is not required by the position of the sun itself. A change in the lower regions causes it: for example, a wind stirred up somewhere, or a flooding of rain, or something of this kind that happens far from us, such that we do not see the cause itself, yet we nonetheless experience its force redounding with effect even unto our own sky.
But if some planets are hotter than others, those that are less hot can, by accident, generate rains and cover the sky with clouds when humors are dissolved but not consumed; from which heat fails and cold is intensified. On the other hand, those that are hotter lead toward dryness and heat...

# Book III
# III

It is not far from our principles to admit that for the change of the air, the various "dominions" of the stars might contribute something: provided that we understand no other dominion here than that a star is closer to us or illuminates us with more direct rays. However, since we suspect that if anything does reach us from the higher stars <note>In the cosmology of this period, the "higher stars" refers to the planets further from Earth, such as Saturn and Jupiter.</note>, it must be altogether very weak—especially regarding those qualities we can perceive with our senses—the causes of storms are, for the most part, not found in the heavens, whether we look at the stars according to the opinion of the astrologers or the philosophers, as we have defined them. It seems that this whole matter, which is often taken from or attributed to the actions of the <term>luminaries</term><note>The "luminaries" are the Sun and the Moon.</note>, should instead be referred to the nature of matter itself. Indeed, the luminaries themselves change things—one by its position alone <note>The Sun.</note> and the other also by its changing light <note>The Moon and its phases.</note>—but neither does so because of the nature of the zodiac signs they pass through, nor the places where they reside, nor the planets with which they are aligned, as will be made manifest in what follows. 

For instance, consider how the **Persian Sea** is agitated and swells with waves when the Sun enters <term>Virgo</term> and especially when it reaches <term>Sagittarius</term>, yet is calm and navigable when the Sun is brought to <term>Pisces</term> and especially <term>Gemini</term>. Conversely, the **Indian Sea** is calm under Virgo and Sagittarius, but navigable under Pisces and Gemini. This does not arise from the "quality" of the signs, but from the physical position of the Sun and the condition of the material world. Even the astrologers admit this.

<margin>
A non-superstitious observation of times which is useful for sailors.
</margin>

Therefore, an observation of these times by sailors would be useful and not superstitious, provided it is based on the nature of the sea they navigate. Sailors even observe specific days on which they declare one must abstain from sailing. If these days have a cause from the heavens, they can have it from nowhere else but the Sun. This is because the observation of these days is fixed and perpetual, and thus can only be referred to the Sun, whose relationship to the Earth is almost always exactly the same at those same times each year. This cannot be referred to other constellations in any way, as they are never found in the same positions relative to the same bodies <note>The author argues that because the planets move at different speeds, their configurations never repeat exactly on the same calendar days, unlike the Sun’s seasonal path.</note>. 

For example, the days always suspected by sailors are:
*   **March:** 1st, 7th, 15th, 17th, 19th, and 25th.
*   **April:** 5th, 6th, 12th, and 20th.
*   **February:** 6th, 12th, 15th, 17th, 19th, and 20th.

Sailors always use this invariable observation and say that during these days, great changes in the sea usually occur, moving either toward calm or toward storm. Since the outcomes are uncertain, those who abstain from sailing act more securely, lest a change for the worse should happen. This practice, therefore, cannot be reduced to the "positions of the stars" which astrologers note and command us to observe; for during those same parts of the year, those astrological configurations do not return in a similar way, but are most dissimilar. Indeed, the astrologer will sometimes predict those very days—which captains always suspect—as being harmless and most lucky for navigation. Conversely, the astrologer might predict as most dangerous those hours which the sailors do not fear at all, simply because of the varied state of the Sun and the mixed ranks of the planets.

Because of this, a sailor will not approve of astrological rules, which are entirely hostile to his own practical principles. Since the sailor's rules are proven daily by long experience and the use of a sublime art, they provide the most abundant evidence of the vanity of astrologers. 

<margin>
There can be a double cause for the "malice" of those days.
</margin>

Moreover, those "dangerous" days can have a double cause: one from the Sun and the other from the water. Just as the humors <note>The four bodily fluids (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile) believed to control health and temperament.</note> of our body have their own periods in which they are moved, so too might the Ocean. It is known with evident certainty that the Sun, according to the moments of its approach toward or retreat from us, changes the disposition of both the sea and all bodies. 

The reader should also be warned that when those who write on rural and nautical matters note the seasonal variety by the "rising" and "setting" of fixed stars—such as <term>Arcturus</term>, the <term>Pleiades</term> <note>original: "vergiliarum"</note>, the <term>Hyades</term>, and others—it is not because these stars themselves have an influence that must be avoided or sought. Even the astrologers do not truly say this, as they hold that fixed stars are ineffective unless they occupy the "angles" of a chart. Rather, these stars serve as a visible sign for the unlearned and unlettered masters of those arts, so that they may recognize the time, which is neither perpetual nor...

## Book II
# III

And it was found better to observe them clearly in their rising and setting than when the stars were hidden. Furthermore, nothing gains more authority and respect among the unrefined common people than what is written by physicians: that winter illnesses are cured in summer, and summer ones in winter; sometimes those that attack in winter leave in spring, or those in spring depart toward autumn; and finally, that whatever happens at any time of year is ended by its opposite. This is because, namely, the quality of these seasons differs according to the Sun's proximity or distance from the lands. However, what they say about the **Moon** regarding <term>critical days</term><note>In ancient medicine, "critical days" were specific points in an illness where a patient was expected to either recover or take a turn for the worse, often linked to lunar cycles by astrologers.</note> is vain and irrational; but we shall speak of this later when we discuss the Moon.

From these same progressions of the Sun comes the varied condition of both inanimate things and all living creatures under the different inclinations of the heavens. Although all humans are born of the same earth, the customs of peoples and the disposition of their bodies vary in different regions. We ought not to imagine that other constellations, other signs, or other planets are responsible for the places beneath them; the Sun is always carried between **Cancer** and **Capricorn** <note>The Tropics of Cancer and Capricorn, which mark the northernmost and southernmost latitudes where the Sun can appear directly overhead.</note>.

Therefore, whoever lives between the <term>equidial circle</term><note>The Equator.</note> and the summer solstice necessarily inhabits the hottest region. Those positioned under the North <margin>Man is born everywhere</margin> <margin>Southerners</margin>, being furthest from the Sun, live in the coldest; and those between them in a temperate region. And since the eastern part of the heavens is more effective, the power of the Sun is greater there than in the western part; from this, a reason can be given for everything concerning the "property of things" as far as it pertains to a celestial cause. For gems, spices, and everything of that kind require more celestial heat and are produced in the East and South; likewise, lions, tigers, and elephants are found in those same lands, along with other animals that require powerful heat to be generated, to live, and to remain in their vigor.

Only man is born and preserved everywhere on earth because of the wide "latitude" of his nature under a multiform habit—though this variation has given some philosophers the vain suspicion that one man might differ from another by a <term>specific difference</term><note>In logic and biology of this era, a "specific difference" would imply that people of different climates were actually different species, a view the author rejects.</note>.

Therefore, those who inhabit the southern part, the more they breathe hot air, the colder they are internally <note>This refers to the theory of "antiperistasis," where the body’s internal temperature was thought to react to the external environment by intensifying its opposite.</note>. For this reason, they are timid, effeminate, and—as proven by ancient and modern experience—born to serve <note>This reflects the "Climate Theory" common in Renaissance thought, which suggested that climate dictated the political and moral character of a people.</note>. <margin>Northerners</margin> These things happen because immoderate heat relaxes the body so much that it draws out and consumes the greatest part of the internal heat; thus, when the heat is drawn to the surface of the body and leaves the inner chambers, it produces blackness in the skin and leaves timidity in the heart.

On the other hand, those who live under a cold sky toward the North are spirited, brave, and fair-skinned for the opposite reason. Truly, both peoples—whether those who are mostly under the Sun or those who are moved furthest from it—possess little of what is human and are hardly sociable due to the excess of heat or cold, by which they deviate from that moderate temperament in which our nature is primarily situated. <margin>Error of the Greek astrologers</margin> Both groups are also savage and wild, partly for the common reason we mentioned, and partly because one is fierce while the other is fearful.

It is not, therefore, as the Greek astrologers fabulate: that because the harmful planets **Saturn** and **Mars** dominate the extreme climates, those people are more savage; nor is it because Saturn rules the Southerners that they are timid and short-lived, or because Mars rules the Northerners that they are more warlike. This is a fiction about which even other astrologers do not agree; some do not assign Mars to the Northerners, but rather the **Moon**. Using neither Mars nor the Moon, we provide the proper reason for the condition of both peoples from the Sun alone—a reason which the trifler is more likely to dream up for himself than a philosopher. Saturn also dominates in **India**, as they say, and yet people there are long-lived; why then would Southerners be short-lived on account of Saturn...?

### Book III
# III

...overflowing with fragility: why are they timid? For even there <note>Referring to the southern regions mentioned on the previous page.</note>, the most ferocious beasts are born; although **Aristotle** <note>Aristotle (384–322 BCE) discussed how climate affects the temperament of nations in his work "Politics."</note> writes that all things in the North are more virile. But the human average suffers extremes most painfully. Just as the stomach is warmer in winter than in summer, so those living under excessive heat grow cold within; they have barely finished their thirtieth year of life before being worn out by old age, as **Avicenna** <note>Avicenna (Ibn Sina, c. 980–1037) was a Persian physician whose "Canon of Medicine" was a standard textbook in Europe for centuries.</note> relates. Those in the North, dwelling in a frozen seat, are hot in their innermost principal members, with heat trapped within and having much thicker blood; they are as much stronger than Southerners as the latter are more ingenious due to the subtlety of their spirits and blood. Middle nations, being neither dull through a lack of blood nor through its thickness, are made more prudent and wise for ruling, and are—if I may say so—more truly human.

This general variety of earth's inhabitants comes from the celestial circulation; to which many specific qualities are added from the <term>sublunary</term><note>In ancient science, the "sublunary" sphere is the region of the universe below the moon, made of the four changing elements (earth, air, fire, water), as opposed to the unchanging heavens.</note> disposition of lands, air, and water. For instance, one region might be half-rotted by marshes or stagnant waters, besieged by foggy nights; another by harsh winds, or raised up by mountains. I have dwelled on these more than necessary. These qualities pass from the earth to the air, and the air itself has its own properties, different in different places, as <margin>Panaetius</margin> <note>Panaetius (c. 185–109 BCE) was a Stoic philosopher who studied the relationship between the environment and the human soul.</note> says—not sought from the heavens, but held from its own principles. These differences in the air can more or less affect bodies; it is ambiguous how much they change the inhabitants through their breaths, as is evident through the things they eat, which everyone knows become harmful or healthy solely by the condition of the waters and air.

Hence the first diversity of bodies is due to the celestial impression from the Sun, which is immediately followed by the manner of living. At the same time, <margin>From where the variety of intellects and customs arises</margin> depends both on the habit of the body and on education, the foundation of habit, which approaches the strength of nature. Then come laws, which carry the greatest weight in this matter—so much so that if properly enacted, they can make fierce nations most gentle, and conversely, they can enervate the strongest, or easily turn the best into the worst if the laws are bad. From this, the <term>freedom of will</term><note>Latin: "arbitrii libertas." The author argues that human choice and legal systems are more powerful than the "destiny" suggested by stars or climate.</note> is most clearly declared against all natural necessity.

<margin>Example.</margin>
The Gauls were once infamous for the love of boys, if we believe **Ptolemy** and **Aristotle**; yet now, by the benefit of Christian law and the most holy Prince, **King Louis** <note>Likely referring to Saint Louis IX of France, famed for his Christian piety and legal reforms.</note>, they abhor this crime more than any nation under heaven. Nor should one rely on the examples of a single people, since the preaching of the Gospel has changed the customs and institutes of almost the entire world from what they were originally. Furthermore, <margin>The quality of the region does much for acquiring skills</margin> that one might first happen upon: such as devoting oneself to trade and navigation if the city is conveniently by the sea; or to letters if near an academy; or to military service if troubled by hostile neighbors or internal civil factions.

There are those whom fertility and abundance make idle and pleasure-seeking, while scarcity and sterility make them laborious, industrious, and diligent. But indeed, some <margin>The response of the astrologers</margin> might respond: "We do not deny these things, but we assert and proclaim them along with you! However, we contend that there are other properties in these places, namely from private influences and a peculiar constellation—for the <term>trine</term><note>A "trigon" or trine is an astrological aspect where planets or signs are 120 degrees apart, thought to influence specific regions of the earth.</note>, for the planet, for the sign to which the region is subject, for the disposition of the heavens under which the city's foundations were laid, or under which its empire, or king, or tyrant grew strong."

<margin>Refutation</margin>
Therefore, even if what you say were true, it does not follow that our views cannot also be true. But I do not think, most excellent diviners, that from the things I have mentioned it follows that what you imagine cannot exist; rather, it is so that we may understand that the cause is fully explained by what we have said...

...can be explained by the every-sided diversity of both places and nations, so that it is not at all necessary for me to seek other causes. For the following pages will demonstrate that those causes which you astrologers introduced above are both false and legendary. However, while we were disputing those factors to which you yourselves attribute the diversity of peoples and regions, it was expected that someone might ask what, then, is the cause of such great variety. Therefore, before we overturned the false causes, it was necessary to demonstrate the true ones, so that from this, your unnecessary theories might be understood—which later shall be refuted as fictitious and impossible. 

Thus, we did not introduce that life-giving heat of the heavens—about which we have discussed so much above—nor the efficacy of the sun, simply to tear down your arguments; nor did we introduce the idea that rays are intensified or relaxed according to the distance or proximity of the stars to us for that reason. Rather, before we refuted your fabricated trifles and showed that a change of stellar power based on locations, signs, and aspects <note>In astrology, "aspects" refer to the angular distances between planets (like squares or trines) believed to influence their power.</note> is imagined by you most absurdly, I wished to make it known—on the authority of philosophers, the testimony of the senses, and the judgment of reason—that whatever the force of the heavens effects in us can be most sufficiently achieved through the common <term>influx</term><note>A technical term in medieval science for the "flowing in" of celestial power or light into the earthly realm.</note> of light, which is healthfully warm and emanates continually from an eternally moving body. Therefore, to imagine other powers or "stellar influences" upon bodies is superfluous; and after this, it can be more easily declared that those things you have imagined are no longer merely superfluous, but insane.

### Chapter XIV. How the power of the Moon varies: and that certain days of the moon are observed with true superstition.

<margin>Ptolemy's opinion on the operations of the moon</margin>
We have shown from the works of the Sun that the dogmas of the astrologers are not necessarily proven. The same must be done regarding the works of the Moon. **Ptolemy** <note>Claudius Ptolemy (c. 100–170 CE), the most influential astronomer and astrologer of antiquity.</note> says in his <term>Apoteleſmata</term> <note>original: "apoteleſmatis"; another name for Ptolemy's "Tetrabiblos," the foundational text of Western astrology.</note> that from the <term>interlunion</term> <note>The "new moon" or the period between moons when it is invisible.</note> until the moon is halved, it is more effective at producing moisture; from then until the full moon, it produces heat; from the full moon until it is halved again, dryness; and then until the conjunction, cold. Thus, he claims the moon has the nature of Spring and Air in its first quarter; Summer and Fire in its second; Autumn and Earth in its third; and Winter and Water in its fourth; and that it most strongly excites the qualities of these seasons in bodies at those times.

<margin>Refutation</margin>
That division is more "pretty" than it is natural and true. For such is the condition of heat that when it is weak, it does not move moisture—being barely felt, it has no efficacy. But when it has some power, it begins to dissolve and melts more diffusely as it becomes more powerful, unless it grows so strong that it consumes the very moisture it caused to flow; for then it dries out and does not moisten. But the heat of the moon, being very thin, is never so intensified that it dries things out. Instead, it increases within those limits by which it moistens bodies with heat, rather than parching them. Thus, it follows that the more light the moon has, the more moisture it produces, just as it produces more heat. Conversely, just as it is deprived of light, it likewise moistens and warms less. Therefore, it would follow the nature and quality of Spring from the first quarter to the full moon, rather than from the new moon to that first quarter; for the nature of Spring is defined as moist. Nor can it look back <note>original: "reſpī" (likely *respicere* or *respondere*).</note> toward winter from the second quarter to the conjunction...

### Book III

...represent: autumn from the full moon to the <term>quadrature</term><note>The "quadrature" refers to the moon's quarter phases, when it is at a 90-degree angle from the sun.</note> itself: for indeed autumn is dry and winter is humid. The moon, once it has been full until it is half-full, produces moisture; and from then until the <term>conjunction</term><note>The "conjunction" is the New Moon, when the moon and sun align in the sky.</note> it dries things out—namely, because its moistening effect ceases. For this reason, timber that is meant to last is cut then. Therefore, Ptolemy spoke much more correctly in his book

<margin>Ptolemy in the book of the hundred announced Experiments.</margin>
of one hundred aphorisms <note>original: "centum enunciatorum," referring to the *Centiloquium*, a famous collection of astrological observations attributed to Ptolemy.</note> when he said that from the first lunar quadrature (the point at which it departs from its meeting with the sun), the moisture of bodies flows until the second quadrature, but in the remaining times it decreases. Not only does the reasoning we have stated prove this, but experience itself bears witness: for as the moon increases, there is an addition of moisture; as it decreases, there is a lessening. This is because not only the quality of its light but also its motion works toward this increase or decrease. For this reason, when it begins to rise after departing from the sun until it is half-illuminated, it moistens and warms more than when, possessing the same amount of light at the second <term>dichotomy</term><note>The "dichotomy" is the phase where exactly half the moon's disk is illuminated (the half-moon).</note>, it tends toward the conjunction; this is because in the former the light is increasing, while in the latter it is failing. This is the whole of lunar astrology,

<margin>Why the time of the waxing moon is suitable for planting.</margin>
observed usefully and naturally by physicians, farmers, and sailors. For they have generally considered the time of the rising <note>waxing</note> moon to be suitable for planting, so that the seeds, nourished by a greater abundance of moisture, may themselves grow more quickly.

<margin>Why the waning moon is for cutting timber.</margin>
But they consider the waning moon the time for cutting timber, because then all wood is drier and thinner, and therefore does not rot as easily or become consumed by <term>decay</term><note>original: "carie," referring to wood-rot or wood-boring insects.</note>. Conversely, if any wood is taken when the moon is increased in light—at which time moisture overflows—it easily rots and is ruined.

<margin>Verification of certain sayings of Hesiod.</margin>
For this reason, Hesiod rightly praises the ninth day of the moon for planting trees, as well as the thirteenth,

<margin>Plutarch</margin>
since, as Plutarch says, the power grafted into the roots is spread by the now-fuller light. Yet he makes the same time unsuitable for casting seeds, because the cast seed desires rain more, so that it may rot <note>break down its outer shell</note> and germinate. Furthermore, he denies that the sixteenth day is fit for planting because the failing light does not sufficiently draw out the buds.

<margin>Explanation of a certain passage of Virgil.</margin>
Therefore, when Virgil said "the seventh after the tenth is lucky both for planting vines" and so on, it should not be understood to mean the seventeenth day; for that day is not at all lucky for planting vines due to the diminished light. Rather, he either judged the first seventh day that comes after the tenth to be better (that is, the fourteenth day), on which full moon vines are not unluckily planted; or, what is more consistent with reason, he praised two separate days—the seventh and the tenth—but the tenth more so; which is why he says "after the tenth, the seventh is lucky." For this is how the matter stands: on the seventh day, the half-moon supplies enough heat and moisture to the roots of the plants, but the tenth day does so even more abundantly. Truly, the seventeenth day could not have been denoted except through ignorance or error, since that day is fit not for planting trees but rather for cutting them, which Hesiod also hand down—namely, for the reason we stated: decreasing moisture. Therefore, at that time, timber is prepared for building ships, which must endure for a long time.

<margin>Proclus</margin>
Moreover, as for the Greek poet’s command to bring the fruits of the harvest to the threshing floor at that time, there is a reason for this: as Proclus writes, winds are usually stirred up after the full moon, by which the chaff and the husk are separated from the grain. Just as the cause and reason for these works are easily recognized in these days, so too can other lunar days be assigned to certain works...

# Book III

...are more suitable for reasons that are not so obvious: even though they arise from those natural principles we mentioned. For indeed, a portion of such great light can harmonize with one thing in a suitable proportion, while it will be discordant with another. In this category, perhaps, are those things that Hesiod <note>Hesiod was an ancient Greek poet (c. 700 BCE) whose work *Works and Days* contains many traditional agricultural rules.</note> prescribes: castrating lambs on the sixth moon; oxen and pigs on the eighth; and mules on the twelfth. He says the sixth and sixteenth are opportune for fathering males rather than females, but the tenth is for females. Truly, he orders calves to be castrated in autumn during a waning moon for a well-known reason: they fear the flow of humors when emasculating, and therefore require a dry time and a dry moon. For this reason, they even forbid much drinking for the castrated animal.

Likewise, there is an evident reason why Hesiod says the sixth and sixteenth are more opportune for fathering males than females, but for females the fourteenth: because, as we have repeated quite often, moisture increases with the light. Therefore, at the full moon, the "excrements of generation" <note>This refers to reproductive fluids (semen and vaginal moisture), which ancient science believed were "surplus" humors or "excrements" of the blood.</note> will drip with more moisture, from which comes female offspring rather than male.

In this manner, you can reduce other things handed down by Hesiod to natural causes. However, he does mix in some things—though quite few—from old superstition; but there is nothing anywhere that supports the astrologers as "governors" of fate.

<margin>Sailors</margin>
Likewise, from these shifts of arriving light in the moon, sailors can usefully observe many days without superstition, since that variation of light has great power in changing the state of the air. Therefore, they prudently abstain from sailing during the <term>new moon</term> and <term>full moon</term>, when storms are most frequently stirred up during these times.

<margin>Physicians</margin>
Physicians themselves also rightly advise the sick by observing the days of the moon’s increase and growth, lest the flowing humors escape their notice more or less, especially in an afflicted body which, being destitute of its own strength, becomes more vulnerable to external harm. For example, to open a vein <note>Bloodletting, or phlebotomy.</note> while the moon is "waxing" <note>original: "adolescente luna," literally "the moon growing up."</note> might be avoided, whereas a <term>cupping glass</term> <note>original: "uentosa," a medical instrument used to create a vacuum on the skin to draw out "wind" or humors.</note> might be used when the moon is failing rather than waxing; this perhaps has a rational basis. For the incision of a vein expels fluids but also draws them in. Therefore, when the humors are bubbling and expanding toward the extremities of the body at the beginning of the month, more material than is proper might be drawn out and removed—unless one says that the works of medicine are always more successful when they harmonize with the progression of nature. But let these things be left to the judgment of physicians. Whatever they observe beyond these things, however, possesses a manifest vanity, as will become clear in what follows.

### Chapter XV. Whether the tides of the sea can be referred to a cause other than the moon, and even if they are so referred, how astrology is not aided by it.

<margin>The opinion of the Saracens according to the mind of Adelard</margin>
Regarding the ebb and flow of the sea, it is a complex question, although it seems to everyone that this proceeds from the moon. Adelard <note>Adelard of Bath (c. 1080–1152), a 12th-century English scholar who translated many scientific works from Arabic into Latin.</note>, following the opinion of the Saracens <note>In this context, "Saracens" refers to medieval Islamic scientists and philosophers.</note>, both recounts and approves this cause for the sea's approach and retreat: "When," he says, "the arms of the sea themselves—namely those which, placed between land, divide the land masses—hasten to meet and flow together with a swift impulse, it happens both because of the intervening mountains and because of the land itself—"

### Book III

...so that they are brought back from that same course while they are failing, and so that they are recalled by the position of the place itself to where both paternal and natural motion impels them. The moon, however, is not the cause: otherwise, this same thing would happen in the seas closer to the torrid zone <note>The "torrid zone" refers to the Earth's equatorial region, which ancient geographers believed was too hot for habitation.</note>; since they are no further from the moon—as to why they would not feel its power—nor is the nature of the waves thought to be less humid: and yet, there is no reciprocation <note>The author uses "reciprocation" to describe the ebb and flow of the tides.</note> there: namely, because the cause we mentioned is missing, which is the mass of the earthly site gaping with converging parts. **This opinion of his is not greatly different from the likeness of truth: since the parts of every element are carried by a natural inclination toward their own wholeness.** What wonder is it, then? If the present oceans, separated in place by intervening lands, strike the shores as they approach while they long to run together: and likewise move backward, repulsed by the obstacle: when this cause is removed (as happens in the southern sea), we see that these tides do not appear. Thus, someone might say that this manner of approaching and receding is natural to water, not insofar as it is water:

<margin>Another opinion.</margin>
But insofar as it has parts of the principal element, divided and separated by the obstacle of the earthly mass. If this reasoning does not satisfy someone, let him hear another: the astrologers <note>In this period, "astrologers" (*astrologi*) often referred to what we would now call astronomers or natural philosophers who studied the heavens to explain earthly physics.</note> confess that such recurrences do not happen in all waters, even marine ones: but only in those where the deep earth is hard, rough with frequent movements, and unequal: where the water is indeed plentiful: which neither increases by the addition of rivers, nor diminishes by their departure: but has held a long-lasting seat there with a thick density: Wherefore it becomes a receptacle (and a breeder of many vapors, neither thin nor easily blown away: which from their parents—that is, the watery earth and the earthy water—and from the heat of the sky, derive that well-known bitterness and saltiness: because fountains and rivers, and even certain seas, do not have these conditions and sources: therefore they say these tides do not appear in them: However, a sufficiently clear and sufficient cause for the marine reciprocation could appear to anyone from this: if indeed from such earth and water, vapors of the kind we described, and winds, are repeatedly stirred up: from which a wind and a tumult arise in the water: especially because from that motion and impulse, and the mixing of vapors, it grows hot: wherefore it seeks a wider place in which to spread itself out. There is added a third cause of motion, the reflection of winds plucking at the surface of the water toward its lower parts: which, becoming entangled with the winds breathing from there, drive the waters into the upper regions with an effort: then the waters necessarily swell, overflow, and surge while they are erupting, and are likewise rejected and pushed back: having rolled back, they create their own approach <note>That is, the high tide or "accession."</note>. Again, when that force burns out as the vapors are dissolved: they subside and are leveled: and contracting themselves in the narrow spaces, they depart from the occupied places: which generation of vapors and winds, according to the nature of the sea, just as it is almost perpetual, so too its dissolution is perpetual: it seems a sufficient cause for the continual reciprocation. ...the water returns cold which had previously arrived warm: which Adelard <note>Adelard of Bath (c. 1080–c. 1152) was a 12th-century English natural philosopher known for bringing Arabic scientific knowledge to the Latin West.</note> indicates to us.

And those defending this opinion can indeed provide a reason why certain larger seas do not reciprocate <note>original: "reciprocant"; the author uses this to describe the ebb and flow of the tide.</note>, even though winds and vapors are present. For the same effect surely happens to them as well; but the vastness of the open sea and the distance of the shores removes the appearance of the "approach" and "retreat" <note>The high and low tide.</note>. Thus, it might rather be well said that the waters appear to do this: that they are alternating—that is, a fluctuating tide rather than a reciprocating one. If these things are in harmony with natural reason, and if they are in harmony with experiments, why should they be judged as lacking probability? Or why is it necessary to add, besides these causes, the motion of the moon—drawing the waters with it, both downward and on high—especially since those things do not correspond which must necessarily correspond? For instance, that tides should become more abundant when the moon is increased in light <note>The full moon.</note>, when it is faster in its course, when it is closer to the earth, when it declines toward the north from the path of the sun, or when it is positioned in the northern signs of the zodiac. On the contrary, tides are thinner <note>Weaker or lower.</note> when the moon behaves differently than what we have said.

<margin>Abu Ma'shar.</margin>
Furthermore, it is not apparent what can be objected against those who think this way, except for the "concordance" <note>The synchronization or harmony.</note> of the waters with the moon in both their ascent and descent. This objection (if what Abu Ma'shar <note>Abu Ma'shar (787–886) was a hugely influential Persian astronomer whose "Greater Introduction to Astrology" was a standard textbook for tide theory.</note> confesses is true) I do not know how it could be sufficiently raised. For he writes that the beginnings of the approach and retreat are not the same everywhere, even where there is no variation in the boundary <note>Likely referring to the horizon or the latitude of the observer.</note>; rather, it sometimes happens in practice that at the time the waters recede in a certain place, they are then beginning their approach elsewhere. He himself does not hide that this has given many people cause for suspecting that those motions do not depend on the movements of the moon. Although he tries to give a reason for this diversity so as to defend the moon as being no less the cause, it follows nonetheless that an argument for the moon cannot be taken from there. Rather, an opportunity for contradiction is provided; for these things differ greatly among themselves: the lunar cause is clearly confirmed by the timing of the tides, yet is not clearly refuted by them.

<margin>Another opinion of Alpetragius.</margin>
Alpetragius <note>Alpetragius (al-Bitruji) was a 12th-century philosopher in Islamic Spain who challenged Ptolemy’s planetary models.</note> brought forward a celestial cause for this motion, yet not from the moon, but truly from the "diurnal motion" <note>The daily rotation of the heavens from East to West.</note> by which all things are moved—but lower things less so. For the sphere of fire is rotated in a circle; a disordered motion occurs in the air, which in the water ends in the approach and retreat.

<margin>That this question is irrelevant to astrology.</margin>
Indeed, I dispute all these things more as a philosopher investigating the true cause of that effect than to contradict astrologers; since in this matter, nothing is added to or taken from astrological affairs, whether we refer these approaches and retreats to the courses of other stars or to the moon. Since this itself is (as Favorinus <note>Favorinus of Arelate (c. 80–160 AD) was a skeptic philosopher who famously argued against the validity of astrology.</note> most truly said) more of an astrologer’s fallacy: who, when they have seen certain earthly things situated among men being moved by the sense and guidance of celestial things—such as how the ocean, like a companion of the moon, ages and grows young along with it—from this, they clearly [take] for themselves an argument...

# Book III

...they prepared themselves to persuade us, so that we might believe all human affairs—both small and great—to be led and governed as if bound to the stars and constellations.

---

<margin>The opinion of Roger Bacon</margin>
For let it be that the tides come from the moon—which we ourselves also willingly and easily believe—what does that weigh in favor of the astrologers or against us? For it is not understood from this (as some think) that the stars act not only by motion and light, but by <term>occult influxes</term> <note>Hidden or supernatural "flows" of power from the stars; the author argues tides are physical, not magical.</note>; as when the moon, positioned beneath the bottom of the earth, moves the waters, even though its light cannot reach them then. Roger Bacon <note>Roger Bacon (c. 1214–1292) was an English Franciscan friar and philosopher who emphasized the study of nature through experience.</note>, in a letter to Pope Clement V <note>Original: "Clementem quintum." Historically, Bacon wrote his scientific works for Pope Clement IV; the author may be mistaken or referencing a specific edition.</note>, wished to provide a cause based on light in the following manner.

For he says that when the moon rises over the sea of a certain region, the lunar rays fall at oblique angles; therefore they are weaker, and for that reason they rouse vapors from the depths of the sea which they cannot consume—vapors, I say—swelling the waters with bubble-like tumors, so that they expand from their channels, just as fire placed under a cooking pot evaporates the water, causing it to foam over the rim of the vessel. Therefore, while that attraction of boiling vapors lasts, the water flows from its beds. But when the moon approaches its summit <note>The zenith, or its highest point in the sky.</note>, the rays become more direct and thus stronger as it ascends; these eventually become so powerful that they are equal to the task of dissolving the vapors. For this reason, Roger says, the "approach" <note>The incoming tide.</note> becomes sluggish as the moon nears the meridian <note>The imaginary line in the sky the moon crosses at its highest point.</note>; when it declines, the waters also immediately decline. Just as in that same pot: when the heat has grown stronger and the vapors are consumed, the liquid subsides and retreats to the bottom of the vessel.

After this, he raises the proposed question: namely, in what way the moon retains its moving power as it travels from the west to the bottom of the earth <note>The opposite side of the world during the night.</note>. For then the waters rise just as they do when the moon is striving from its rising toward the summit. And yet, as he admits, no force of rays can penetrate through the middle of the earth. He thus resolves the matter in this way:

The highest heaven, he says—whether it be the eighth or the ninth <note>In the medieval geocentric model, the stars and planets were carried on nested transparent spheres.</note>—is necessarily dense, since it terminates our sight, which is terminated only by something dense. Accordingly, it is necessary that the lunar rays stretched out to that place are reflected to the opposite side. Therefore, if the moon moves from the west to the bottom of the earth, its power will be active in another opposite quarter of the heaven, and it performs by a reflected ray what it did while moving from the east toward the summit. This is Bacon's discovery, in which he takes such great pleasure:

He also describes Bacon's unique theory that tides occur when the moon is on the opposite side of the Earth due to rays reflecting off the edge of the celestial spheres.</summary>
