-># Book III III<-

...so that he may first boast that the <term>flood and ebb</term> <note>Original: "accessus atque recessus." Literally the "approach" and "retreat" of the sea.</note> of the tide have given a logical account of themselves in opposite quarters; yet in his words there are as many shameful errors as there are words.

<margin>Confutation of Bacon. First reason.</margin>
First, he contradicts—I would not say experience—but certainly <term>Aboafari</term> <note>Likely referring to the Arab astronomer Abu Ma'shar (787–886), known in the West as Albumasar, who wrote the influential "Greater Introduction to Astronomy" which discussed tides.</note>, whose interpreter he makes himself. Aboafari teaches that the vigor of the flood tide occurs when the moon reaches the highest point of the sky, and does not slacken until she begins to descend. On the contrary, Bacon thinks that the closer the moon comes to the highest point, the more the flood tide is slackened, because the vapors are dissolved by the hotter light.

<margin>Second reason</margin>
Nor did he see that the moon's light is never so intense that it could consume marine exhalations; indeed, it cannot even raise up such great ones as are needed to move the tides.

<margin>Third reason.</margin>
But if he should obstinately deny this, he must admit, even against his will, that for several days around the new moon there would be no ocean tides; for at that time there is either no lunar light or it is so thin that no amount of impudence could claim it is sufficient to produce so many vapors in the sea and then dissolve them.

<margin>Fourth</margin>
Finally, why are the rays of the descending moon not stronger than those of the ascending one? Why does the descending moon recall the waters, while the ascending one pours them out? And why are the rays not weaker when they are just declining slightly from the highest point than when they are first rising? Why does he create an ebb there and a flood here?

<margin>Fifth</margin>
For if, as he himself believes, the vigor of the rays suppresses the flood tide with more intense heat, then the weakness of those same rays must increase it. Finally, who would believe that in the reflected rays of the moon running beneath the earth there is such great power that they can even consume the raised-up vapors? Or if they cannot do that, what is the cause of the ebb when the moon is carried below the <term>horizon</term> <note>Original: "finitorem." The boundary line of the observer's vision.</note> according to Bacon's foundation? Why should the waters recede when the moon departs, but approach when it rises from the east?

<margin>Another opinion</margin>
Therefore, let Bacon keep these inventions of his for himself. If such an effect pertains to the moon, let us refer it to its motion, which the movement of the ocean imitates by a silent consensus of nature; therefore, it rises with the rising moon and falls with the falling moon.

<margin>Thomas</margin>
He who says this seems to agree with the view of <term>Thomas</term> <note>Saint Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the famous Scholastic philosopher and theologian.</note> in the book *On the Occult Works of Nature* <note>Original: "de occultis operibus naturae." A treatise exploring phenomena that lack an obvious physical explanation.</note>. Nor should we think that these tides are an actual increase or decrease in the volume of the waters. But rather, as the words themselves express—"approach" and "retreat"—it is not a matter of the sea being increased or diminished, but of the sea extending itself in a rise and contracting in a fall. We say these things regarding the daily and nightly tides; for if there are some seas (as has been written by certain authors) that are always in a state of flood while the lunar light increases—namely, from the <term>conjunction</term> <note>Original: "coitu." The New Moon, when the sun and moon are aligned.</note> to the full moon—and again in retreat when it decreases from the full moon until the conjunction, those do not follow the motion of the moon in its sphere. They follow instead the motion, if I may put it this way, of the light in the moon, decreasing and increasing in it equally; the variation of which can also vary somewhat the tide that occurs daily. But the observations handed down on this matter do not agree: for both the Egyptians and those who sail to the West [observe] from the noon of the first day of the lunar month until the eleventh...

...they said that for one day the <term>flood tide</term> <note>Original: "accessus." The approach or rising of the tide.</note> is invigorated; from the eleventh to the eighteenth part and part of the following day, it is weakened. From then until the twenty-sixth, it is again intensified, and then slackened right up to the start of the month. However, whenever the flood is greater, the <term>ebb</term> <note>Original: "recessus." The retreat or falling of the tide.</note> is smaller, and vice versa in a swapped proportion. There are others who say this truth is discovered in the waters of rivers flowing from springs, which on the aforementioned days are either extended or drawn back to their sources. Concerning the sea, however, it is reported differently by the Easterners, who do not even agree among themselves. For there are some who report that in the first and last <term>decan</term> <note>A "decan" is a period of ten days used in ancient astrology and timekeeping.</note> of the month, the flood tides diminish; in the middle, they grow; which seems to have this reasoning: that they grow with fuller light and decrease when the light fails. Others say it is not continuous for many days—that the tides either increase or fail—but that it happens on only one or two days, whether when they are intensified or when they are slackened.

<margin>Aboafar</margin> **Aboafar** <note>This refers to Abu Ma'shar (787–886), a Persian astrologer known in the West as Albumasar. His "Greater Introduction to Astronomy" was a primary source for medieval tidal theory.</note> makes four phases in this manner: the first after the <term>conjunction</term> <note>The New Moon, when the moon and sun are aligned.</note> when the moon begins to recede from the sun until it is half-full; then he says the flood is diminished in that proportion by which the moon departs from the sun, so that when it reaches the <term>quadrature</term> <note>Original: "quadrangulum." An astrological aspect where the moon is 90 degrees from the sun.</note> they are weakest; the second phase from then until the full moon, at which time they are gradually intensified so as to reach the highest point at the full moon; the third from the full moon until it is again halved, with the flood decreasing along with the light; the fourth from then until the conjunction. 

<margin>Against Aboafar</margin> Then indeed, he claims the floods become more violent immediately so that at the lunar conjunction they are most violent. But this can have no logical basis, if indeed this difference in light (as far as the proposal is concerned) is "much," "little," "increasing," or "decreasing." If the flood occurs with either "much" or "increasing" light, the fourth observation is false; if with "little" or "decreasing" light, the second is false. If with "much" but "decreasing" light, the third is false; if with "little" but "increasing," the first is false. Truly, whichever of these traditions is preferred, it is clear we are not forced to devise any new power in the moon besides motion and light to explain why it moves the sea; for all the reported variations in the flooding and ebbing of the sea can most evidently have their cause either from the variation of the motion of the rising or declining star, or from the losses and increases of light.

***

### Chapter XVI: Galen’s opinion regarding critical days, which refers them to the moon, is refuted.

<margin>c</margin> That the <term>critical days</term> <note>Original: "Crisimos" or "dies cretici." In ancient medicine, these were specific days during an illness when a "crisis" would occur, determining if the patient would recover or die.</note>—which in Latin you might call "judiciary days"—are referred to the moon, I certainly do not doubt is as false as it is superstitious; this must be explained more broadly. **Galen**, the authority among physicians for this opinion, in the third book of *On Critical Days*, mentions a twofold lunar influence: one comes from the sun, from which the moon receives its light; the other from the more oblique signs <note>The signs of the Zodiac.</note> which the moon traverses by its own motion each month. Then he posits, according to the opinion of astrologers and as if proven by experience, that in opposite positions and at right angles, great commotions are stirred up by the moon.

# Book III

...which he contends is true both in its relationship to the sun and to the zodiac signs, even when no account of the sun is taken. Regarding the sun, because when the moon is <term>halved</term> <note>original: "diuidua." Referring to the quarter phases (First and Last Quarter).</note>—which occurs in places nearly <term>quadrangular</term> <note>original: "quadrāngulis." In astrology, this refers to a "square" aspect, or 90 degrees of separation.</note> from the <term>conjunction</term> <note>The New Moon, when the sun and moon are at the same point.</note>—and again when it is filled—which is in the <term>opposite</term> <note>The Full Moon, 180 degrees from the sun.</note> places—it changes the state of the air and the weather. Regarding the zodiac signs, it works in this manner: whatever begins while the moon is positioned, for example, in Taurus, a change in that matter will always occur when the moon subsequently reaches Leo, Scorpio, or Aquarius, which are the places <term>tetragonal</term> <note>original: "tetragona." Another term for a 90-degree square aspect.</note> or adverse to Taurus.

He confirms this by the authority of the Egyptians, who assert that if at the moment of someone's <term>nativity</term> <note>original: "genitura." A birth horoscope.</note> in Aries (to use an example) favorable stars were seated, the person born will fare well whenever the moon passes through either Taurus or the square or opposite signs; conversely, they will fare poorly if unfavorable stars were there. From this, Galen thinks the cause of <term>critical days</term> <note>original: "creticorum dierum." In ancient medicine, these were specific days during an illness when a "crisis" or decisive change occurred.</note> becomes most evident. For the seventh and fourteenth days are especially "critical." The moon reaches the fourth sign from the one it held at the start of the disease on the seventh day, and it reaches the opposite sign on the fourteenth day, since the moon completes its <term>restoration</term> <note>original: "restitutionem." The sidereal month, or the time it takes the moon to return to the same place among the stars.</note> in nearly twenty-seven days and a third part of a day. Therefore, since the moon excites commotions in these quadrangular and adverse places, it causes them on these days—namely the seventh and fourteenth—on which those places are reached, so that the turmoil of the disease is also stirred up. This leads to health if the illness turns favorably, or to death if it turns destructively. 

However, because Galen thought the twentieth day was "critical" rather than the twenty-first (which Archigenes <note>A prominent Greek physician of the 1st/2nd century AD.</note> believed), he worked hard to provide a reason why the twentieth day itself might also be considered a "seventh" day. First, he showed this by a proof that was neither absurd nor difficult. For the course of the moon is completed in twenty-seven days with eight hours added. If you divide this into four <term>weeks</term> <note>original: "ebdomodas." From the Greek "hebdomas," a grouping of seven.</note>, each "week" will consist of six days and twenty hours. Therefore, three such weeks will contain twenty days and twelve hours; thus, the twenty-first day—which is the third "weekly" marker in the lunar course—will belong partly to the twentieth natural day and partly to the twenty-first. For its twelve hours will end the twentieth day, and the remaining hours will begin the twenty-first. And so the critical commotion will occur on the twentieth day as the moon reaches the second quadrangle within the third "week." 

Again, it does not escape the same logic if the crisis is delayed until the twenty-first natural day, which usually happens in <term>acute</term> <note>Short-term and severe.</note> illnesses, just as it happens in more <term>chronic</term> <note>Long-term.</note> ones, with the cycle running through even numbers in the former and odd numbers in the latter. After Galen himself had said this—which <margin>Peter of Abano</margin> **Peter of Abano** <note>original: "aponenſis." Refers to Pietro d'Abano (c. 1250–1316), a famous physician and astrologer who wrote the "Conciliator."</note> later reported as if it were his own discovery—he devised a new fiction by which he would not make the critical influence equal for both days, as Archigenes did. Instead, he gathered that the entire twentieth day was critical, and the twenty-first was not. Thus he invented the idea that the time in which the moon returns to conjunction with the sun is twenty-nine days and twelve hours, which is commonly thought of as a month. Let us subtract the days in which the moon does not appear, being overwhelmed by the sun's rays, since then it has no power to transform lower things; there will remain twenty-six days and twelve hours. For it is hidden for nearly three days. Let us add these days, which is the space of the shining moon, to the days in which it traverses the signs, which he calculates as twenty-four days and twenty hours; the total will be...

# Book III

...fifty-three days and twenty hours: the half of which is twenty-six days and twenty-two hours. Galen considered this span of time to be a reasonable measure for the placement of **critical days** <note>original: "dies creticos." In ancient medicine, these were specific days during an illness—such as the 7th, 14th, or 20th—when a patient's condition was expected to take a decisive turn for better or worse.</note>. He saw that this was half of the combined time in which the moon both traverses the zodiac and is illuminated by the sun, as if it encompassed two powers of lunar influence: that which comes from the zodiac signs, and that which comes from the sun. It is probable that both of these cause a commotion in diseases. 

This number was later called the **medicinal month** <note>original: "mensis medicinalis."</note> by subsequent authors on Galen's authority; just as they call the cycle of twenty-nine days the month of **conjunction** <note>original: "coniunctionis." The synodic month, measured from New Moon to New Moon.</note>; the cycle of twenty-six days and twelve hours the month of **manifest vision**; and the cycle of twenty-seven and one-third days the month of **traversal** <note>original: "peragrationis." The sidereal month, the time it takes the moon to return to the same position relative to the stars.</note>. 

Through this invention, Galen achieved what he wanted against **Archigenes** <note>A famous Greek physician whose theories on the timing of disease crises often clashed with Galen's.</note>. For if the entire [medicinal] month is 26 days and 22 hours, each individual **week** <note>original: "hebdomodae." Literally a group of seven, but here Galen calculates a "medicinal week" as roughly 6 days and 17 hours.</note> of this month will consist of six days, seventeen hours, and a half-hour. Therefore, half of the month is thirteen days and eleven hours. Consequently, the hours from the first until the seventeenth of the seventh natural day will pertain to the seventh day of the medicinal month, and for that reason, they will be **critical**. The remainder of that day will belong to the eighth medicinal day. 

Furthermore, the fourteenth natural day will have only its first eleven hours belonging to the end of the fourteenth medicinal day; its preceding thirteen hours will be counted with the thirteenth natural day. However, since any medicinal week consists of six days and seventeen and a half hours, it is clear that the third week ends on the twentieth natural day, with only four and a half hours overflowing into the twenty-first. 

And so, Galen accomplished what he primarily desired, and for whose sake he fabricated this whole commentary: to show that the twentieth day, by a far greater margin than the twenty-first, should be considered **critical** by a logical progression of weeks. Yet, Galen took this labor upon himself for nothing. It was not necessary, for the twentieth day was already sufficiently defended by the time of the moon’s **traversal** through the zodiac—especially since he himself does not deny that the twenty-first is also a critical day, particularly in acute diseases. 

We have not recounted these things to act as a judge between Archigenes and Galen (which would exceed our purpose), but rather to ensure that no one thinks we have failed to fully address the matter. We have shown that critical days cannot be referred to the moon simply by its power received from the sun or the zodiac signs alone; Galen introduced a kind of "mixed" influence to specifically trigger these critical days. Perhaps Galen did not actually do this, or if he did, he could not have done so reasonably. For if we say, with him, that the moon rouses commotions when it is in **square** <note>An astrological aspect of 90 degrees, often considered tense or "active."</note> or opposite positions to its starting sign, and again when it is illuminated by the sun's rays at **right angles** or opposite positions: 

<margin>First reason.</margin> we cannot expect these events from the moon except at those specific times when it stands in one of those positions—if, that is, the outcome is expected from those causes. For if it produces such effects at both times according to the habit and constellation of each period, we cannot believe that the power of both constellations is mixed together at a time when neither of those constellations is actually found.

# Book III

...argument, since that time is the half of the sum of both times counted together. <note>The author is finishing a calculation from the previous page: Galen arrived at his "medicinal month" by averaging the time the moon takes to orbit the Earth relative to the stars and relative to the sun.</note> Indeed, we do not even know if we are ourselves or among the "Orestes" <note>original: "non scimus nos esse non sumus etiam inter & horestes." A classical allusion to the madness of Orestes, suggesting that following Galen’s logic leads to total confusion or delusion.</note>. Therefore, if Galen thinks this "arousing power" exists in the weeks and half-weeks of this medicinal month of his, and not in the weeks or halves of the month in which the moon is actually illuminated by the sun or traverses the signs of the zodiac, he is misleading us. This is because the power of that invented month cannot be reduced to any astrological **influxes** <note>original: "influxus." The "flowing in" of celestial power or influence onto the terrestrial world.</note>—that is, it corresponds neither to the **quadrate** <note>original: "quadrata." An astrological aspect where two bodies are 90 degrees apart; a "square."</note> nor to the opposite signs, nor to the quadrangular and opposite configurations of the moon with the sun. For to claim that their power is preserved and stays constant at a time when those configurations do not exist is, as I have said, utterly absurd and a total fiction. 

Those who have wanted to defend Galen and simultaneously match the **critical days** <note>original: "creticos dies." Specific days of an illness where a major change occurs.</note> to the cycles of the moon have been unable to stand by their promises. Instead, they defend now this point, now that; never both at once. For if it is asked why the fourteenth day is a critical day, they retreat to the month of the moon's **traversal** <note>original: "peragrationis." The sidereal month (approx. 27.3 days).</note>, because on that day the moon reaches the opposite signs. This reasoning fits a portion of the medicinal month—if indeed its second week ends on the thirteenth natural day, leaving eleven hours of that week pertaining to the fourteenth day. For as we have said, any week of Galen’s month is six days, seventeen and a half hours. Therefore, the thirteenth day ought to be called "more critical" than the fourteenth, since the thirteenth possesses thirteen "critical hours" while the fourteenth has only eleven. At this point, abandoning the power of their "mixed" and artificial month, they flee back to the actual spaces traversed in the zodiac. 

<margin>Second argument.</margin>
On the other hand, so that they may make the twentieth day a critical day, they do not use the month of traversal, but Galen’s [artificial] month. Furthermore, if someone falls ill the day before the moon is in **conjunction** <note>original: "coeat." The New Moon, when the moon and sun are at the same longitudinal position.</note> and has his seventh day as a critical day, how will that result from the influence of power—whether received from the sun or from the zodiac signs? For according to Galen himself, during the greatest part of those days, just as we have not seen the moon, it has not affected us with solar power. It is therefore necessary here too that they turn to the signs, as if the influx from the power of a **quadrate** <note>A 90-degree angle between the moon's starting position and its current position in the zodiac.</note> alone made that seventh day critical for the patient. 

<margin>Third argument.</margin>
I pass over the fact that Galen’s month is entirely artificial and not "struck from the mint of nature." <note>A metaphor meaning it is not a naturally occurring phenomenon.</note> For it is forged as if the moon were always hidden by the sun for three days. But sometimes it is seen in the morning before the sun rises, and in the evening of that same day it appears with a "razor-like" face <note>A very thin crescent moon.</note>; this is both shown by experience and testified by **Al-Farghani** <note>original: "Alphraganus." A famous 9th-century Persian astronomer whose works were standard textbooks in Renaissance Europe.</note>. Furthermore, Galen determines the space of the lunar motion as if it always moved at the same pace, and not sometimes faster and sometimes slower, as is demonstrated in astronomical calculations. 

Therefore, let Galen keep his month to himself. So that he does not force it upon us too importunately, let us concede to those who prefer that certain days be critical, while rejecting **Archigenes** <note>Galen's rival physician.</note>. I firmly assert that these days are ruled by no cycles of the moon, whether we estimate the power as being received from the sun or from the signs. For that power which is from the sun is indeed solid and natural (as we have declared), but critical days cannot pertain to it unless we were always attacked by diseases at the New Moon. Otherwise, the half-moon would not correspond to the seventh day, nor the full moon to the fourteenth—the times in which the quadrangular and opposite configuration to the sun rouses the **humors** <note>The four bodily fluids (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, black bile) believed to govern health.</note>. What remains is the power from the zodiac signs. As the following pages will declare, this power is non-existent; but even if it were, it would in no way relate to the critical days in the way they describe. For if they argue from experience that a "commotion" occurs on the seventh day, and again on the fourteenth, and that during these days the moon is in quadrate or opposite signs, they conclude that those commotions follow from this change of signs.

# Book III

<margin>Rebuttal of the argument</margin>
We argue against this as follows: a stirring of the humors occurs on the seventh day, and again on the fourteenth; yet throughout these days, the moon is often neither in a <term>quadrate</term> <note>original: "quadratis." An astrological aspect where two celestial bodies are 90 degrees apart, thought to cause tension or change.</note> position nor an opposite one. Therefore, that stirring is not provoked by this change of signs. Which side relies on truer assumptions is a doubt to no one who is not entirely ignorant of lunar motions. For when the moon is carried through the lower parts of its <term>epicycle</term> <note>original: "epicicli." In Ptolemaic astronomy, a small circle the moon moves along while that circle itself orbits the Earth.</note>, it moves more swiftly and reaches the quadrate signs on the sixth day, and sometimes the opposite signs on the thirteenth. However, when it is carried through the upper parts more slowly, it does not reach the quadrate position before the eighth or ninth day. 

If one were to respond that for this very reason those days sometimes also become <term>critical days</term> <note>original: "creticas fieri." Days of significant change or "crisis" in a disease, such as the 7th or 14th.</note>, they would have a point if the humors were stirred on the eighth or ninth day specifically when the moon’s course is slow. Conversely, they should be stirred on the sixth day when it is fast, and on the seventh when it is at a middle pace. But observation does not teach this; rather, it frequently happens in practice that even with a slower moon, a "judgment" or crisis of the disease occurs on the seventh day, and sometimes on the sixth. Yet, the actual stirring of humors may be delayed until the eighth or ninth. Noting this, many physicians have utterly denied that this order observed by nature in diseases depends on lunar cycles. Nothing induced those who reported otherwise to do so except either a love for astrological matters or the authority of Galen. We shall soon discuss how much weight such authority should carry in this matter.

<margin>
The opinion is falsely ascribed to Hippocrates and Avicenna. Celsus. Asclepiades.
</margin>
Furthermore, some of the <term>modern authors</term> <note>original: "neotericis." Scholastic or contemporary writers of the author's era.</note> falsely claim that Avicenna and Hippocrates held this opinion. For Hippocrates indeed never said a word about this. Instead, he likely related this order of days to numbers which nature is accustomed to observe willingly—a point noted by Celsus and Asclepiades. As for Avicenna, when he recalled the opinion relating these things to the moon, he said: "There is much ambiguity in these sayings." He then rejected the question, as its investigation did not belong to the physician; indeed, it would rather be a hindrance to him. Therefore, let Galen’s authority prevail among us when deciding which days are critical and how the patient is to be treated 

<margin>
To what extent Galen is to be believed in certain matters.
</margin>
when they either appear or are foreseen. For in this duty of the physician—a profession in which Galen excelled—we, with the consensus of the learned, truly approve of him as "divine" and admire him. But when the *cause* of those days is investigated, this is a work of higher philosophy. In that realm, Galen's opinion should be regarded neither as a definitive judgment nor even as a testimony of great weight.

<margin>
Maimonides. Avicenna.
</margin>
Indeed, what <term>Moses the Egyptian</term> <note>original: "Moses ægyptius." Referring to the famous philosopher and physician Maimonides (1138–1204).</note> and Avicenna—great men and great supporters of Galen in medicine—report, contains more in the "branches" of knowledge than in the "roots." Truly, Galen is laughed at by experts in logic for his "fourth figure" of <term>syllogisms</term> <note>The "Galenic figure," a controversial fourth pattern of logical argument added to Aristotle's original three.</note>, and in philosophy he so often stumbles and fails to perceive the strongest reasons that a philosophical judgment is found lacking in him by many. He cannot understand how, if the soul survives and is immortal, it ceases to function when the brain is not yet dissolved. He says he was exhausted by this question from a certain Platonic thinker—as if a sailor, surviving a wrecked ship, does not stop sailing! Nor does he understand what is demonstrated by philosophers: that universal notions of things are grasped by our intellect alone, and not by the capacity of brute animals. It is not the time to recount how he falters in the knowledge of time itself. For we are not here to discuss Galen’s philosophy; we have only tasted these points to confirm the judgment of Maimonides and Avicenna on the matter, and simultaneously to warn that no one should be deceived by his authority into accepting superstition. For in this very astrology of which we treat, the calculation of lunar motion shows him to be insufficiently skilled. Nor does <term>Pietro d'Abano</term> <note>original: "Apponensis." A prominent 13th-century physician and astrologer who sought to reconcile Greek/Arabic science.</note> defend him, except by saying that in Galen’s age the logic of celestial motions had not yet been clearly explored. Therefore, let his credibility in medicine be as great as it possibly can be; but as for what pertains to other doctrines, let us remember to deal more cautiously with the man. It must be examined...

...more carefully what he has handed down, and whether it harmonizes with experience, with reason, or with the opinions of others. And indeed, we have proved that what he put forward concerning <term>critical days</term> <note>original: "creticis diebus." Specific days in the course of a disease, like the 7th or 14th, when a "crisis" occurs that determines if the patient lives or dies.</note> appears to agree with the facts themselves; yet it will become clear to those who examine them that these same ideas do not even have the color of reason. For what reason is there that the moon—when it has reached the fourth or seventh sign from the place where it was when the disease first struck—should stir up an agitation in the <term>humors</term>? <note>The four vital fluids (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, black bile) believed to govern health.</note> Galen denies that he will provide a reason; instead, he puts forward the authority of the Egyptians. We shall remind him of his own sixth book of *On Simple Medicines*, in which he notes the "madness" of the Egyptians; why their authority should also falter among us will become known in the final two books.

For now, let us say this: the changes of bodies according to these lunar courses could not have been faithfully observed by the Egyptians, to whom the actual courses of the moon were not faithfully known. For <term>Hipparchus</term> <note>An ancient Greek astronomer (c. 190–120 BCE) who discovered the precession of the equinoxes.</note>, on the island of Rhodes, was the first to observe them more accurately, although he did not quite reach the truth, to which <term>Ptolemy</term> <note>The most influential astronomer of antiquity (c. 100–170 CE), whose geocentric model lasted 1,400 years.</note> later came closer; although he, in turn, did not satisfy the desires of the Spanish astronomers.

<margin>Reasoning of the Moderns</margin>
The <term>Moderns</term> <note>original: "Neoterici." Refers to contemporary 16th-century scholars or late medieval authorities who attempted to reconcile astrology with medicine.</note> have devised a reason that not only fails to agree with the truth, but does not even fit the position they defend, nor the words of Galen which they follow. It is of this sort: <term>quadrate</term> <note>Signs 90 degrees apart.</note> or opposite signs have contrary qualities. Quadrate signs differ in both qualities, or at least the active ones: for example, Aries differs from Cancer in both qualities, since Aries is a hot and dry sign, while Cancer is moist and cold. Taurus differs from Leo, but not in both qualities, for they agree in dryness; however, they disagree in the "active" quality, as Taurus is cold and Leo is hot. Likewise, opposite signs always disagree in at least one quality. They say it is a common refrain among astrologers that <term>quadrangular</term> <note>A "square" aspect.</note> and <term>diametrical</term> <note>An "opposition" aspect, 180 degrees apart.</note> radiations are contrary and combative.

These things having been established, they conclude that when the moon reaches places "hostile" to those it held when the disease first invaded, it follows that a battle arises between the disease and the body's nature. But we, having considered what they say, will speak thus: you think this is the reason the moon produces critical days: because if, for example, it was in Taurus when the disease seized the person’s nature, it ought to produce a contrary effect when it reaches a "contrary" place. Thus, it will cause nature to rise up against the disease; from this comes the fight and the trial, with victory leaning toward one side or the other. Moreover, the moon will be in a "contrary" place when it reaches Leo or Scorpio. But it will reach Leo on the seventh day and Scorpio on the fourteenth.

Therefore, on these days, the signal for war will sound for the disease and nature. But why will it not do the same on the third day when it reaches Gemini, which differs even more from Taurus than Leo does? Why not on the twelfth or thirteenth day when reaching Libra, with which Taurus again agrees less than it does with Scorpio? Why not on the fifteenth day, entering Sagittarius, which disagrees with Taurus just as much as Scorpio and Leo do? 

I know what they will answer: that there is no connection of <term>aspects</term> <note>Geometric angles between planets or signs that astrologers believe transmit influence.</note> between these specific signs. But I did not wish to lead them anywhere else—not to object that this logic of aspects is worthless (which we shall do in the sixth book), but to show that even if there is some validity to it, it nevertheless does not serve the question at hand. For that theory is observed between two planets, whose rays they believe cannot combine to complete an effect—whether they agree or disagree—unless they are configured with specific intervals toward each other, such as the <term>hexagon</term> <note>60 degrees; also called a sextile.</note>, the <term>triangle</term> <note>120 degrees; also called a trine.</note>, the <term>quadrangle</term>, and the <term>diameter</term>. But here, we are not comparing the moon to other planets; we are only noting its return to a place...

...is carried to a position contrary to that which it previously occupied. Although astrologers will deny that a star placed in Gemini is linked by an <term>aspect</term> <note>original: "aspectum." In astrology, an aspect is a specific angular distance between two points in the zodiac (like 90 or 120 degrees) believed to create a positive or negative influence.</note> to a star placed in Taurus, they will nonetheless not deny that this place is contrary to the other. Now, if the moon produces an effect contrary to the first because it has reached a place of contrary quality—for instance, if it stirred up a disease while in a cold and dry sign, why, when it is placed in hot and moist signs, does it not stir up nature *against* the disease? Whether that sign is calculated as the sixth, the second, or any other number you prefer? This is entirely ridiculous; it is not something that could be said by a man looking for the truth rather than defending a preconceived position. 

But if they contend that the power lies in these aspects, they must consequently also grant that when the moon reaches <term>trine signs</term> <note>original: "trigona signa." Signs that are 120 degrees apart. In traditional astrology, this is considered a harmonious and beneficial angle.</note>, it will confirm and strengthen the disease. For just as <term>square signs</term> <note>original: "quadrata signa." Signs 90 degrees apart, traditionally associated with tension, conflict, or "discord."</note> are discordant, so trine signs are concordant. Why, therefore, if square signs rouse nature against the disease because of their contrary quality, will trine signs not rouse the disease because of their concordant quality? Add to this that since the moon is carried there roughly on the eleventh day, the eleventh ought to be deemed harmful; yet it is numbered by physicians among the healthy <term>critical days</term> <note>original: "creticas." Specific days in the progression of an illness where a "crisis" occurs, traditionally deciding if a patient will recover or decline.</note>.

<margin><unclear>Enumerate</unclear></margin>
Finally, it will be most manifest to anyone considering it that the observations of critical days handed down by physicians cannot have their logic based on the moon’s motion. For they say that bad agitations happen on these days: the sixth, eighth, twelfth, tenth, sixteenth, and eighteenth. Let them give a reason for these from the moon if they can! For it would be more fitting for the sixth and eighth to frequently be good days, as we were saying, since the moon reaches a <term>square aspect</term> on those days. But why is the tenth or twelfth not bad, on which the moon is not in places linked by any aspect to the sign of the illness? Why are the seventeenth and thirtieth counted among the healthy days? 

And what logic is there regarding the moon, which has power every three days until the twentieth day, and after the twentieth day every seven days—not every four—such as the twenty-seventh, thirty-fourth, and forty-first? When you exceed these, "twentieth" critical periods are found, such as the sixtieth, eightieth, and one-hundred-and-twentieth. Why then is there a circuit of months and years? Just as all these things do not have a cause from the moon, so they cannot have one from the sun, nor from any other constellation. For those constellations are not found to be fixed or similar or concordant on those fixed days; instead, they vary in a marvelous way and maintain no order that could correspond to the order in the agitations of diseases, which is mostly preserved by nature. 

Thus, one may marvel at <term>Pietro d'Abano</term> <note>original: "apponensem." <margin>See the shameful error of Pietro d'Abano, the Conciliator.</margin>
He is too forgetful of himself, having previously said that the turns toward health on the seventh day occur because of the nature of the square—which supposedly opposes the sign of the disease. How, then, does he now also give a reason for the malice of the sixth day from a square? It is clear, therefore, that all these things have other causes. But it deceived them that the seven-day and fourteen-day marks seemed to coincide, though even there, as we said, they do not truly match.

# Book III

<margin>Avicenna</margin>
...long-lasting: as **Avicenna** <note>Avicenna (Ibn Sina, c. 980–1037) was a Persian physician whose "Canon of Medicine" was the most influential medical text in the Middle Ages.</note> writes: they are often accustomed to being resolved in the seventh month, the seventh year, the fourteenth, or the twenty-first. I do not, however, approve of those who superstitiously observe numbers here; rather, I say that the courses of nature are mostly fulfilled in things in this way, not because of constellations corresponding to these times (for none are found), but because of a hidden property and condition of those matters in which it usually happens this way. For we see nature so arranged:

<margin>Galen</margin>
as **Galen** <note>Galen of Pergamon (129–c. 216 AD) was the preeminent physician of the Roman Empire; his theories on "critical days" dominated medical practice for over a millennium.</note> himself writes, that acute diseases are moved through odd days, while slower and longer-lasting ones through even days. Relate these to the moon; relate them to the sun and stars if you can! Why then should we refer the agitation on the seventh day in acute diseases to the <term>square signs</term> <note>original: "tetragona signa." These are signs 90 degrees apart in the zodiac. Astrologers believed that when the moon reached a "square" position from where it started at the beginning of an illness, it caused a crisis.</note> through which the moon is carried? Especially since that rule is not even constant; indeed, some of the younger physicians speak against the opinion of Galen and others who flee to the moon for explanations. They argue that if someone falls ill while the moon is in Aries, they ought to have the <term>critical day</term> <note>original: "creticam diem." Derived from the Greek *krisis*, this refers to a specific day during an illness when a sudden change occurs, leading to either recovery or death.</note> on the eighth day, because that is when the moon reaches the "square" of Cancer. And they respond that it indeed ought to happen this way if the lunar motion is taken into account; but the agitation actually occurs on the seventh day because of the nature of the disease, which, when it is acute, moves through odd days until the fourteenth day. 

Finally, what has been truly observed by medicine concerning critical days is not only not confirmed by astrological matters, but is actually weakened by them; so it serves as the greatest argument that the affections of bodies do not depend on the causes which astrologers introduce. For if there were no fixed order or status in these days—but now this day was critical, now that one, and again among the critical days one was harmful at one time and another healthy at another—no wonder would rouse us to investigate the cause, with the changeable diversity of the matter alone satisfying us. But since certain days are not always but *mostly* critical—and some mostly lead toward life and some toward death—this order seems to require a certain and rarely changeable cause. Galen concludes from this that the cause is in the heavens,

Signs thought to represent stability and slowness.</note> would do so more slowly. 

These things would not happen similarly for every sick person, even if they were under the same constellations, but differently for different people according to the condition of their own birth charts. I pass over the figure whose angles **Ptolemy** <note>Claudius Ptolemy (2nd century AD), the author of the most famous ancient textbook on astrology.</note> commands us to observe—whether they derive from favorable or unfavorable rays—so that we may predict the disease from there; which indeed the most ignorant believe pertains to critical days. If physicians took all these things from astrologers, it would not mostly be the days that the medical art intended, but one person would have one critical day and another person another. Nor would it be a fixed rule that the sixth day kills with "tyrannical cruelty," while the seventh sets one free with "royal kindness." Instead, the seventh day would be counted among the harmful constellations, and the sixth among the healthy ones. If this should happen occasionally, it ought not to be said to be from heaven, where they seek the cause of that which occurs with...

# Chapter XVII. The periods of the humors are not to be attributed to the movements of the stars.

<margin>First argument.</margin>
Neither should anyone believe that the periods of the <term>humors</term> <note>The four humors—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—were the fluids believed to control health and temperament. Imbalances caused specific types of fevers.</note> in fevers are to be attributed to the movements of the stars; for example, that <term>black bile</term> <note>original: "bilis atra." Associated with quartan fevers, which recur every fourth day.</note> should cease for two days and be aroused on the fourth because it is under the influence of **Saturn**, whose motion is slower than the others. For by what reason is <term>blood</term>—assigned to **Jupiter** by astrologers—continually rotting without any pause? Since Jupiter is not the fastest of all; rather, if one estimates the time it takes to return to its starting point, he is the slowest of all after Saturn. Why likewise is the motion of <term>red bile</term> <note>original: "rubrae bilis." Also known as yellow bile; associated with tertian fevers occurring every third day.</note>—ascribed to **Mars**—a little slower than the motion of black bile? For it ceases for six hours less: since that one [black bile] lies dormant for forty-eight hours, while this one [red bile] is stilled for thirty-six; yet the star of Mars is much faster than Saturn. 

Furthermore, it is a decree of the astrologers that the works of stars with slow motion are more long-lasting the slower they are. Since, therefore, if the motion of <term>phlegm</term> <note>original: "pituita." Associated with quotidian (daily) fevers.</note> returns sooner than red bile—for that one returns after six hours, this one after thirty-six—because the **Moon**, exciting the phlegm, is faster in motion than Mars, who excites the bile. Why, I ask, if this were true, does the agitation of bile not affect the patient for longer than phlegm? Seeing that the former lasts only twelve hours, while the latter lasts eighteen. For (if we stand by the precepts of the astrologers) the works of Mars ought to be more long-lasting than those of the Moon, since the motion of the latter is clearly faster than the former. 

But if, on the other hand, we wish to refer all these periods to the Moon alone—as being predominant over all the humors—the astrological reasoning upon which they lean will falter no less. For they say that phlegm, because of its kinship with the Moon and water, almost imitates the movement of the waters; they flow and ebb with a middle delay intervening:

<margin>Second argument.</margin>
but it is a small delay, such as necessarily falls between directed motions. Thus phlegm leaves only six whole hours of rest. But this could better suit the blood, in which, just as in water, a continuous heat is found, in which the little delay separating the flow from the ebb does not well correspond to an interval of six hours: in which the entire flow or ebb itself is driven. But in blood there could be a greater similarity, the motion of which they themselves—the supporters of this opinion—do not deny is interrupted in perceptible little delays. 

But let us follow the rest. They say black bile, because it differs most from the nature of water, moves in a manner contrary to phlegm: namely, ceasing for up to two whole days. But to me, indeed, it seems that water has more in common with earth than with fire, whether you look at location, quality, or motion—conditions than which no others can weigh more. Therefore, the same judgment will apply to humors compared to the elements: so that the motion of red bile [fire] ought to be more different from the motion of phlegm [water] than that of black bile [earth].

<margin>What sort of man Peter of Abano was.</margin>
But truly, none of the illustrious and ancient physicians attributed the circuit of fevers to these causes. The first who attempted this was **Peter of Abano** <note>Petrus Apponensis (c. 1250–1316) was a famous Italian physician and astrologer who attempted to reconcile medical science with celestial influence. He was posthumously condemned by the Inquisition.</note>, a man born to amass more things than to digest them; indeed, the more ignorant usually admire him more intensely where he talks the most nonsense.

# Book III

<margin>d</margin> While we are discussing these matters, it comes to mind that astrologers are accustomed to ascribe the misfortune of an **eight-month birth** to **Saturn**. I must speak of this in this place, but briefly, so it does not seem that by failing to refute it, we are forced—even against our will—to concede that we are gripped by the rays of the most hostile stars. While I willingly concede that we are influenced by them, I do not willingly concede that we are gripped by them in such a way that we are held captive; for I believe that influences glide down from heaven in such a way that I do not think anything harmful proceeds from it. The sum of the matter is this: astrologers are deceived if they believe those born in the eighth month do not live because individual planets preside over each individual month of carrying the womb. They claim that because **Saturn** rules the first month, he also rules the eighth—and as a cold and dry planet, he possesses qualities contrary to life. First of all, those handed-down successions of planetary rule have no rational basis (as will be stated elsewhere in its proper place), and the fact that an eight-month birth does not live has an entirely different explanation. There are those who believe the fetus attempts to exit in the seventh month and is injured in the effort; if it then exits in the eighth month, having not yet been restored to its health, it is not usually long-lived. But I side instead with **Hippocrates**, who in the treatise he wrote on the *eight-month birth* <note>original: "octimestri partu"</note> says the reason it often does not survive is that the carrying of the womb is difficult in that month.

<margin>Hippocrates</margin> At that time, pregnant women find themselves in a more serious condition, and suffer I know not what heavy weights and discomforts in the <term>matrix</term> <note>The uterus or womb.</note>; and if they give birth, being overwhelmed by the double labor of birth and sickness, they become extremely weak. From this, the fetus itself is necessarily made feebler and rarely lives for long. This opinion is supported by the fact that if women are found who are more vigorous and stronger, they usually give birth even in the eighth month to children who will survive—such as **Avicenna** writes are found in Spain and **Aristotle** in Egypt. I have added the Greek words of Hippocrates himself on this matter, lest—since this book is not commonly available—it be believed that I fabricated it: **"I speak concerning eight-month birth,"** <note>original: "περί οκτα μήνου γεμέσιν φημί" (peri okta mēnou genesin phēmi). Hippocrates was the most famous physician of ancient Greece.</note> and what follows.

Second, the testimony of the <term>good arts</term> <note>Practical sciences such as medicine and navigation that rely on empirical observation.</note>—medicine, agriculture, and navigation—which employ astrological observations in their works. <meta>This page continues Pico della Mirandola's systematic dismantling of judicial astrology. # Book III

Thus we have rejected both in such a way that we might strike back at them with the same weapons, showing—as we were saying a little while ago—that from the works of the sun and moon and from the observations of those practical arts, it is rather gathered what the astrologer denies than what he affirms. There remains a third point, which was taken from the common predictions of those same practitioners, as if we were being too unfair by granting no foreknowledge of the future to astrologers skilled in the whole heaven, when even any unrefined master or common person sometimes achieves it. For we see many things concerning rains, illnesses, cattle, and the daily grain supply being predicted by the common people with the reliability of the outcome. Why then, they ask, could those who have explored the celestial causes more thoroughly not predict those things more rightly, as well as other more secret things? This is what we must refute at present; or rather, as is our custom, we shall cast the argument back at them, which we will explain briefly and with no trouble. 

For if true things are predicted by them without any regard for the rules of astrology, who would not say that their conjecture is flimsy? It would mean that the things they omit or are ignorant of are not necessary, but superfluous; not more secret, but more false; not dogmas, but fictions. But **Ptolemy** <note>Claudius Ptolemy, the most influential astronomer and astrologer of antiquity</note> says that those who do not know astrological matters are sometimes deceived. What of the fact that astrologers are deceived even more often? It is concluded, therefore, that astrologers have less grasp of "astrological" matters than those who are not astrologers at all. 

Indeed, it cannot be denied that what doctors say about the sick, farmers about the grain supply, sailors about storms, and shepherds about their flocks corresponds more to the truth than what is predicted about these same things by astrologers. The reason is immediately at hand: since the astrologer looks at signs that are not signs and contemplates causes that are not causes; moreover, he is deceived. For he looks at the celestial disposition, which is only a universal cause and does not produce variety in lower things except according to the condition of the material and the lower efficient causes. 

However, that is not even the celestial disposition he looks at, but a disposition invented by him in the heaven through the most vain and fabricated rules, consisting not of nature but of the arbitrary will of astrologers. For, as we shall demonstrate, that father of men and god of gods <note>Referencing God as the Creator</note> did not make images, signs, parts, **antiscia** <term>antiscia</term> <note>points on the zodiac that are equidistant from the tropics, used in astrology to determine "shadow" influences</note>, **dodecatemoria** <term>dodecatemoria</term> <note>a division of each zodiac sign into twelve equal parts of 2.5 degrees each</note>, houses, and other such things in heaven; rather, it is the astrologer, the deceiver of men and defamer of the gods, who has lied about these things in the heaven. 

Therefore, it is no wonder if that art cannot foreknow any future thing by certain reason. But the craftsmen we mentioned rely on true, natural, proper, and proximate causes and signs; and therefore they rarely fall away from the truth. Instead, through true pre-sentiments of the future, they both build faith in their methods and practice their arts with success and good fortune. Read the books of *Prognostics* by **Hippocrates** <note>The famous Greek physician of the 5th century BCE</note>; you will never find him seeking the future state of a patient among the stars. He was one who knew these things were sought more reliably from urine <note>original: "ex lotio"</note> than from a star, and were foreknown more certainly from the pulse of the veins than from the motion of the spheres. 

Skilled navigators do not foresee storms from **Jupiter**, **Saturn**, **Venus**, **Mars**, or **Mercury**, but from a cloud, from the winds, and from every condition of the air. Their skillful discipline is confirmed everywhere by experiences; from the breath of the slightest breeze or from a tiny cloud scarcely visible, the navigator understands an imminent storm, of which no omen or sign was yet apparent to the eyes of others. Nor do they only understand that it is coming, but from which direction it will be stirred up, how it can be avoided, and how it can be overcome.

<summary>Pico argues that practical professionals like doctors and sailors are more accurate than astrologers because they study real, physical causes (like pulse or wind) rather than the "fictional" divisions of the heavens created by astrologers.</summary>
<keywords>epistemology, causality, Hippocrates, Ptolemy, medical prognosis, navigation, weather forecasting, celestial signs, antiscia, dodecatemoria</keywords>

--- Page 446 ---
<meta>This page continues Pico della Mirandola's argument from the previous page, where he began to contrast the practical, observation-based predictions of common laborers with the theoretical, often-failed predictions of astrologers. He is building toward a refutation of Ptolemy's claim that celestial knowledge improves practical forecasting.</meta>

# Book III

...the judgment of astrologers will fail entirely. Thus shepherds, farmers, and even the uneducated common folk often foreknow the state of the weather, not from the stars, but from the disposition of the air itself and from those impressions made in the upper atmosphere. For this reason, they are rarely deceived: predicting the weather <note>original: *aerem*, literally "the air"</note> from the air, just as doctors judge a patient by the patient's own condition—that is, from their own internal principles—and not as astrologers do from remote, common, and universal causes; indeed, what is worse, from fictitious, imaginary, and fabulous ones. Therefore, let no one think that farming will be made better, medicine more effective, or navigation safer if these things are handled by men who are well-versed in and observant of astrological matters. Rather, this would be the ruin and destruction of those arts; for they would be called away from certain rules to uncertain ones, from truths to fabrications, and by the mixing in of false dogmas, the solidity and truth of every already-proven experiment would be undermined. 

This can be sufficiently argued—even without yet understanding the reasons by which the vanity of astrology becomes known—from what we said at the beginning of this work: that the greatest masters of those arts, who were especially successful in practicing them, did not merely fail to include astrological observations in their works, but either ignored or even refuted them. <margin>Columella.</margin> **Columella**, whom we have cited elsewhere, that most precise writer on rural matters, in the passage where he is about to hand down the precepts for observing the seasons, mentions his own late-night study <note>original: *lucubrationis*</note> against the astrologers. He says: "these things which we have treated with 'coarse Minerva' <note>the Latin idiom *pingui Minerva* refers to plain, practical common sense or "rough-and-ready" wisdom</note> are true; but those things which the **Chaldeans** <note>a common historical term for astrologers</note> most imprudently promise are false, and have been refuted by us elsewhere." 

Therefore, when **Ptolemy** <note>Claudius Ptolemy, the 2nd-century author of the *Tetrabiblos*, the foundational text of systematic astrology</note> argues that "farmers foresee many things about the state of the air, so we must foresee more and more certain things the more we surpass them in knowledge of celestial matters," Columella would deny that truth follows from such a conclusion. For this "astrological wisdom" by which they supposedly surpass farmers is not wisdom at all, but folly. It is not that they know more than farmers; they simply invent more things, using the magnitude of the subjects they lie about to mask the absurdity of their profession. Doubtless, human life would have received astrology into a most honorable place along with the other arts if it actually made such good and necessary practices as farming, medicine, and navigation any better. But its vanity and deceit, having been frequently detected by the wisest lawmakers, forced them to banish it from cities with the strictest prohibitions, as we declared in the first book; this was done lest it infect good minds and good arts alike with its secret poisons. 

How much astrology is surpassed in foreseeing the future by these common arts we mentioned can be seen from this: there is a wonderful agreement among sailors, farmers, and shepherds regarding their forecasts, but among astrologers, there is nothing of the sort. This is so true that **Abofalar** <note>A Latinized reference to Abu Ma'shar, a famous 9th-century Persian astrologer often cited by Pico</note> does not hesitate to begin a journey without his traveling hat <note>original: *non petasatus*; the *petasus* was a wide-brimmed hat used by travelers to protect against sun and rain</note> on the very day Ptolemy has predicted a flood of waters.

### Chapter XX: Not everything predicted by astrologers depends on the primary qualities

We now wish to examine what things might depend on the primary qualities <note>In Aristotelian physics, these are Hot, Cold, Wet, and Dry</note>, since the third argument of the astrologers seemed to require it. Even Ptolemy proves that whatever happens is caused by the stars in no other way than this, as his <term>apotelesmatic</term> <note>derived from the Greek *apotelesma*, referring to the "effects" or "outcomes" of the stars; these are books concerning astrological influences on earthly events</note> books declare. All astrologers always retreat to this point whenever they defend themselves, claiming either that they say nothing superstitious (on the grounds that it proceeds through the tracks of nature), or that they say nothing for which a manifest [reason cannot be given].

<summary>Pico argues that practical experience in farming and sailing provides more accurate weather predictions than astrology, citing the Roman writer Columella as a proponent of practical observation over "Chaldean" fabrications. He concludes by noting the internal contradictions between famous astrologers like Ptolemy and Abu Ma'shar.</summary>

Having previously argued that practical observation (like that of farmers) is superior to astrological theory, he now attacks the "physical" defense of astrology—specifically the claim that stars influence us through the "primary qualities" (heat, cold, moisture, and dryness) as proposed by Ptolemy.</meta>

# Book III

e <note>This "e" is a signature mark, used by early printers to keep the folded sheets of the book in the correct order.</note>

...reason cannot be given. For they almost always take refuge in these <term>qualities</term><note>The four "primary qualities" of Aristotelian physics: heat, cold, moisture, and dryness.</note> whenever they are asked why Jupiter does this, or Saturn does that, or why one planet produces one effect and another something else. In that part of the work where the principles of astrological dogma are refuted, it will be shown that in this matter they speak with little consistency, both with themselves and with the truth. Indeed, they seek this refuge for themselves in vain, for many things besides what we have said make this clear. Among these, the first point that occurs is this: it would follow that in the lot of fate, the time of year in which one is born would matter more <margin>First reason.</margin> than any other variation of the constellation. This is because the season does more to increase or decrease the primary qualities than any other position of the stars or mixture of their rays. Thus, summer days are always hotter than winter ones, even if **Saturn**—no matter how much he may be stiff with cold or sluggish—is dominant in the summer. Conversely, winter days are always colder than summer ones, even when **Mars** burns and "rages, flaming, in the middle of heaven" <note>original: *ardet mars medioque furit flammatus olympo*</note>. If the difference in fate arises from cold, heat, dryness, and moisture prevailing to a greater or lesser degree, it follows that everyone born in winter is doomed to a perpetually "cold fate" compared to those born in summer—especially if (as they must necessarily defend) these people are more influenced by this quality of the air, thus affected from heaven, than by the condition of the seed and the immediate matter of their conception.

<margin>Second reason</margin>
Furthermore, if **Ptolemy** maintains this—which is for him the very foundation of natural astrology—that the rays of the planets produce all else through the primary qualities, he ought not to prophesy concerning the character or the fortune of men from any other source than from that constellation which produces and demonstrates the physical constitution <note>original: *corporis habitum*, the "habit" or "disposition" of the body</note>, since everything else follows from this. Likewise, in universal prophecies, only one thing would need to be inspected: what the future state of the air will be. Once this is inspected, the rest would be revealed, since all other things are arranged according to the measure of heat, cold, dryness, and moisture. But neither others nor Ptolemy himself act in this way; they often say things about character in a private birth-chart, or about accidental events, which do not correspond in the least to the temperament of the body—at least not by the logic through which other things are usually referred to these qualities. Nor will the things they pronounce about the character, the plague, the grain supply, or wars for the whole year be consistent with the weather; for they investigate these things from the most diverse constellations. This will be easily established for anyone reading both astrological books and the prophecies of astrologers. Therefore, let them not hold up this facade and "honorable decoration" of a natural method to cover their superstition—claiming that human affairs are subject to the stars only insofar as the disposition of the air and the body depends on heaven through the primary qualities. For while Ptolemy, in introducing the art, asserted this as if it were possible, in the process and explanation of his dogmas he neither observed it, nor could he have observed it while keeping the professional "oaths" <note>original: *iuribus*, meaning the established rules or rights of the profession</note> of his trade. Otherwise, as I was saying, astrology would consist of only a few points: it would only have to speak about the disposition of the air and the habit of bodies. Anyone could then guess the rest for themselves from these few given rules. But there are countless things in the books of Ptolemy and others which can in no way derive their origin from the primary qualities of matter.

### Chapter XXI: Neither the harms of the elements nor the damages to our bodies are from heaven.

From what we have just said, that point which was brought forward in third place above for the assertion of astrology can easily be rejected: namely, the claim that if the changes of the air are caused by the stars...

<summary>Pico argues that if astrology were truly based on the physical "qualities" of heat and cold as Ptolemy claims, then the season of birth would matter more than any star, and astrologers would only ever predict physical health, not character or fate.</summary>
<keywords>Ptolemy, primary qualities, Aristotelian physics, Saturn, Mars, winter vs summer, physical temperament, astrological methodology</keywords>

--- Page 448 ---
<meta>This page continues Pico della Mirandola's systematic dismantling of astrology. In the previous section, he argued that the seasons (based on the Sun's position) have a far greater impact on physical "qualities" like heat and cold than any other planet. Here, he moves to a more philosophical argument: the heavens are a source of order and "harmony," and therefore cannot be the direct cause of earthly disasters or "discord."</meta>

# Book III

...therefore, do pestilences, <term>cataclysms</term><note>Massive floods or disasters.</note>, fires, and the high price of grain [follow from the stars]? We deny it; for it does not follow. On the contrary, he who says this is ignorant of what the heavens are. For what else is heaven in the whole of bodily nature than the containing force in any particular body, which prevents it from flowing apart or being dissolved? Just as the heart in an animal is the source of that power by which the integrity and the order of the <term>mixture</term><note>The specific balance of elements and qualities that makes up a living thing.</note> are preserved, and the injury of invading elements is repelled. 

Let him know, therefore, that he who attributes the excess of elements—from which fires and cataclysms happen, and from which high prices, disease, and pestilence arise—to the heavens, errs no differently than one who refers the diseases, vices, and ailments of our body to the very power of nature that governs the body. It is the role of that power to cure these things, not cause them; to soothe them, not stir them up. 

If these things are true, another point is clear: it is one thing for primary qualities to exist, and another for the withdrawal or damage of those qualities to happen by heavenly influence. We might as well deny the difference between the laws and magistrates of a city and the crimes committed within it, [falsely] claiming that those crimes originate from the work of a good prince. 

So, though a philosopher might grant that whatever is orderly and natural in the elements has the heavens as its author, I do not know by what reasoning he would concede that their deficiencies also come from there, or that they vary from nature’s prescription and laws. It is rather the dogma of the philosophers that the elements remain within their boundaries and, content with their own rights, do not cause trouble for the world, precisely because of the heavenly nature which rules and moderates the fluid and erratic number of corruptible things.

<margin>Objection.</margin>
But, you will say: "Once you grant me that some stars cause cold and others heat, does it not follow that when cold stars predominate, the cold elements grow strong, and when hot stars predominate, the hot ones do? And if that is said, might it not also happen that by a great convergence of cold constellations, the coldness of the waters might so overflow that the earth is submerged in floods? Conversely, when the hot stars are very powerful, fires occur."

<margin>First response.</margin>
The response is easy, and not just one: first, concerning the "dominion" of planets and signs which the astrologers have invented—it will be shown later how false these claims are. Why, I ask, would any planet so rule the heavens as to produce monstrous things in this world, especially evils? 

<margin>Second.</margin>
Since the work of heaven springs from the <term>conspiracy</term><note>original: "conspiratio." In the ancient sense, this means a "breathing together" or harmonious cooperation of all parts.</note> of all the lights, that entire higher <term>harmony</term> is always so tempered that just as all things within it are in concord, so through it nothing ever sounds discordant in the lower world. In this lower world, whenever something harsh or discordant is heard, it should not be attributed to the touch of heaven, but to those four strings of the <term>sublunary lyre</term><note>A metaphor for the four elements (earth, air, fire, water) that make up our world below the moon.</note>. These strings, made of disordered and impure matter, are sometimes found to be stubborn when struck by the heavenly <term>plectrum</term><note>A tool used to pluck a stringed instrument; here, the influence of the heavens.</note>, which always moves them toward rhythm and concord. 

<margin>Third.</margin>
After this, it must be considered more subtly: if various stars are set in charge of various elements, they are set in charge so that the elements themselves might be perfected. Therefore, any element will be more perfect when touched, the more powerful its presiding star may be. But if the perfection of the parts does not conflict with the perfection of the whole—indeed, when the whole is weakened, the parts are as well—it will not belong to the perfection of an element for its nature to overstep its order and seize upon the others. 

An element is only "perfect" when it has deflected nothing from the order and course of nature; it can deflect from that path just as much by exceeding its bounds as by failing them. For this reason, if **Mars** <note>The planet associated with heat and fire.</note> presides over fire, it is not fitting that anything should be done by the star to the quality under its influence that does not agree with good order and the laws of nature; not...

<summary>Pico argues that the heavens are a source of cosmic order and harmony, acting like a heart or a musician. He contends that earthly disasters like floods or plagues result from the "stubbornness" of earthly matter rather than the intentional influence of the stars.</summary>
<keywords>celestial harmony, sublunary lyre, four elements, Mars, astrological critique, primary qualities, cosmic order, nature's laws</keywords>
