<meta>This page continues Pico della Mirandola's argument that the heavens are a source of perfect order. Having previously argued that the Sun's seasons are more impactful than planetary positions, he now asserts that earthly disorders—like disease or birth defects—cannot originate in the perfect heavens, but must arise from the "stubbornness" of physical matter.</meta>

# Book III

...it would be less the duty of the heavenly governance to restrain what is rioting than to rouse what is sluggish. Therefore, it can be granted that the four primary qualities <note>The building blocks of the physical world: heat, cold, moisture, and dryness.</note> come from heaven; but nevertheless, their failures, transgressions, and riots are not from heaven. Instead, they arise from the disordered motions of matter, which does not obey the laws of heavenly discipline in every way. For this reason, I believe that neither 
<margin>Plato.</margin>
Plato in the *Timaeus* <note>original: "Timeo"</note> nor 
<margin>Aristotle.</margin>
Aristotle in the *Meteorology* <note>original: "Metheoris"</note> ever attributed those temporary tyrannies of the elements to any force of the constellations. 

<margin>The damages to our bodies do not have their causes in heaven.</margin>
It is clear from what has been said that not only the harms caused by the elements, but by the same logic, the damages to our bodies and to other living things do not have their causes in heaven. Indeed, the heavens—which are the most notable of all bodies for their reputation for order and beneficence—ought not to produce those things which are rather the works of rioting or failing matter. 

Therefore, what we said about the elements can likewise be said about the <term>humors</term><note>The four bodily fluids (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile) believed to control health and temperament.</note> in our body that correspond to them. If Saturn presides over black bile, Mars over red bile, and others over the blood and phlegm, there is no work of these planets more important than to bridle these qualities and keep them within the harmonious arrangement of life. Nor, when Saturn is at his most powerful, will black bile be stirred up to destroy the others and undermine the whole; rather, it will behave in a more orderly, composed, and better way. 

The same must be said of red bile when Mars reigns. Since their rays and their very nature are beneficent and healthy, they do not act like a destructive fire. Instead, they act just as the "innate heat" <note>The vital warmth believed to be the source of life in a body.</note> within us works correctly, guided by the hand of the soul toward a certain end for the health of the living being. In this way, those vital lights—the instruments of the inner mind of the soul—never act for destruction, but always for the benefit and well-being of the bodies subject to them. Saturn will never pour anything into the black bile (if indeed he presides over it) that is not orderly or that is faulty; therefore, he will not excite it to the destruction of the animal, but will moderate it for its preservation. 

<margin>Death is not from heaven.</margin>
Nor will the humors derive a reason from their stars to act more violently when those stars prevail, but rather to act more moderately and vibrantly. Death is not from heaven. Rather, death comes from matter with its own defect, whenever a quality has degenerated so much that it cannot sustain the discipline of the presiding star, but either wanders off in excess or fails through weakness. 

But our soothsayers <note>Astrologers.</note>, who make themselves both the interpreters and the patrons and defenders of heaven, refer not only diseases caused by the excessive irritation of primary qualities to the stars, but also the very vices of blindness and deafness. And what is more detestable, they even blame the stars for <term>monsters</term><note>In the Renaissance, "monsters" (monstra) referred to congenital birth defects or biological anomalies that deviated from the "natural" form.</note>; nothing more absurd can be said or thought. For what else are monsters than the "sins of nature"? No philosopher has ever attributed these to an <term>efficient cause</term><note>The primary source of change or action; Pico argues heaven is an "indefatigable" cause that cannot fail, unlike matter.</note>—especially one that never fails—but everyone attributes them to matter. 

Nor has anyone been so delusional as to say that monstrous births occur through a fault of the "forming power" <note>The biological force believed to shape an embryo.</note>. That power, being guided by the hand of God, commits no fault; rather, they blame the matter, which, due to its position, quantity, or quality, is poorly formed and is insolent and rebellious against its maker. But it is a far greater insanity to condemn the power of heaven than the power of the seed. The power of heaven can err and fail all the less because nature itself is more powerful, a mistress, and more closely joined to the Creator, by whom this lower "seeding power" is ruled and formed. It is therefore extremely absurd to think that the movements and configurations of the heavenly bodies (if indeed those configurations change the effectiveness of the planets) ever go or are arranged in any way other than what the natural tenor and orderly course of the lower world requires...

<summary>Pico argues that the heavens are perfect and orderly, meaning they cannot be blamed for earthly disorders like disease, death, or birth defects. These "sins of nature" are instead caused by the inherent flaws and rebelliousness of physical matter.</summary>
<keywords>Aristotle, Plato, humors, black bile, Mars, Saturn, birth defects, efficient cause, nature, matter vs spirit</keywords>

--- Page 450 ---
<meta>This page continues Pico della Mirandola's critique of astrology in Book III. Having just discussed how the four humors relate to the planets, he now argues that even if the heavens influence our physical makeup, they are not responsible for moral failings, individual character quirks, or the chaos of war.</meta>

Where does this order reside—the transgression of which is a monstrosity? Where does it have its origin, if not in heaven? Or how do the heavens hear their own voice well enough? Why do men ascribe a thing that is evil, disordered, and unnatural—whose origin is vice and weakness—to the primary causes of nature, which are the best, most 
<margin>Averroes</margin>
ordered, and most powerful of all? Therefore, **Averroes** <note>A 12th-century Islamic philosopher from Spain whose commentaries on Aristotle were foundational to European science.</note> said truly: that whoever believes that **Mars** or any other star, however it is positioned, harms bodies, believes things that are foreign to all philosophy. But certainly, no oppression does more injury to heaven than astrological superstition. For whatever we do against reason through the fault of our will, or whatever happens in the physical world outside of order due to the vice of recklessness or the frailty of matter, astrology attempts to blame entirely on the stars. It does not think their dignity is safe unless even the most unworthy things are attributed to them.

### Chapter XXII: The variety of intellects and characters does not depend entirely on the primary qualities.

Truly, even if the stars do not cause the bad conditions of the body, do they at least cause the differences between bodies? I do not mean those that are diseased, faulty, or accidental, but those within the limits of nature’s integrity, which differ from one another by the ratio of their <term>temperament</term> <note>The specific "mix" of the four primary qualities (hot, cold, moist, dry) that determines a person's physical and mental makeup.</note>. For it seems to follow that if the stars are the authors of the four primary qualities—for example, that bodies born or conceived under **Saturn** are drier and colder, warmer under **Mars**, more moist under **Venus**, and so on—then a diversity of intellects and mental affections usually follows this diversity of temperament. We are not forced by these, but we are provoked by them. But this topic will be treated more extensively later. 

For now, let us see whether the dissimilarity of intellects and characters can be born from this. For while it is true in some way, it is false in another. It follows that the manner of the qualities dominant in the body does indeed influence the emotions; for instance, boiling bile <note>Yellow bile, associated with fire and Mars.</note> makes people more prone to anger, <term>phlegm</term> <note>Associated with water and the moon; thought to cause sluggishness.</note> makes them sluggish, blood makes them more cheerful, and <term>black bile</term> <note>Associated with earth and Saturn; thought to cause melancholy.</note> makes them sad. But this is quite general and does not always correspond to the evidence, nor does it satisfy the more hidden and specific conditions of one's intellect. 

I said it does not always correspond to the evidence because one can sometimes find men who are very similar in the temperament of their bodies, yet very different in their interests—not because of a choice they made, but by a natural inclination. I have seen a beastly cruelty beneath a virginal face; and beneath a grim and disdainful expression, a mild and lovable gentleness. Others, through the grace of their brow and the beauty of their face, present perpetual joy while boiling within with sorrows and feeling loathing for themselves. Others, whom you would judge to be plain slaves of **Saturn** <note>Meaning they look naturally gloomy or "saturnine."</note>, brighten everything with cheerfulness and wit. These traits are powers that can grow from sources other than the primary qualities, by the general consensus of philosophers—that is, things which are neither the primary four qualities themselves, nor their daughters or appendages. We shall declare a little later that many things predicted by astrologers regarding the diversity of characters cannot be traced back to these qualities at all.

### Chapter XXIII: Neither wars nor external events depend on the primary qualities.

But it is truly too ridiculous to claim that if the stars can produce cold, heat, and other qualities, they can also produce wars and seditions, or that they can overturn cities and change the course of the impious. The reasoning for this position is no less ridiculous. For they say that when bile is stirred up in the bodies of kings and princes by a more burning heat of the mind, they become more eager to either avenge or inflict injuries. O blessed **Italy**, flourishing in perpetual peace, if only you were allowed to have phlegmatic princes! This great and divine good could be achieved at a small cost: a single ointment...

<summary>Pico argues that astrology insults the divine order of the heavens by blaming stars for human "vices" and material accidents. He further contends that human character and complex social events like war cannot be reduced to simple planetary "temperaments" or bodily fluids.</summary>
<keywords>Averroes, primary qualities, temperament, humors, bile, phlegm, Saturn, Mars, Venus, astrology, human will, Italy, philosophy of nature</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Pico della Mirandola's critique of astrology in Book III. Having previously argued that the heavens do not dictate moral character, he now turns his focus to the causes of war and the distinction between physical "humors" and external "fortune," specifically challenging the logic of the famous ancient astronomer Ptolemy.</meta>

<page-num>III</page-num>
# Book III

...bringing forth a <note>original: "mactabilem," implying slaughter or destruction</note> deadly spirit; yet if it were rightly divided among the princes, those who are more warlike would bring peace to the whole world for us. Who would not refute such things—or rather, laugh at them? As if this were ultimately the cause of wars, and not rather greed more than anger: not lust, not the occasion or hope of seizing power. Do not rivalries and hatreds—which the astrologers attribute to **Saturn** rather than **Mars**—and sometimes even the love of justice itself, stir up wars and tumults? As if the mind of kings were not more often a god according to their bile <note>In ancient medicine, "bile" (choler) was the humor associated with anger and a "hot" temperament.</note>. 

<margin>Causes of wars.</margin>
Now God exercises the good toward virtue; now He punishes the wicked through the service of the wicked, whom He often employs as executioners in cleansing the republic, acting as visible demons. Truly, although the astrologers say ridiculous things here, they nonetheless seem to be saying *something*. But as for external matters, 

<margin>External things.</margin>
which do not vary at all according to our humors—how will they relate them to those four primary qualities <note>The four qualities are hot, cold, moist, and dry.</note>? How can exile, honors, wealth, poverty, children, a wife, friends, and enemies be linked to them? **Ptolemy** says they have an affinity with the soul and the body: honor and 

<margin>Ptolemy</margin>
<margin>Question.</margin>
dignity with the soul, and a wife and wealth with the body. What is this "affinity," O **Ptolemy**? That these chance events follow the condition of the soul or the body? Or is it what you are accustomed to say: that if the influence of **Mars** 

<margin>Solution.</margin>
makes someone bilious, it also inflicts wounds and a violent death upon him, because the heat of the bile incites one to brawls and to arms, in the midst of which death itself familiarly dwells? 

<margin>Refutation.</margin>
But we usually consider it to be the work of the stars especially when a gentle man, living in leisure and insulting no one, is nonetheless dragged by some fatal force, as if against his will, into dangers, onto swords, and into enmities. Likewise, a warlike man—a "stirer of hornets," as the saying goes—full of days and unharmed, may pass away at home among his own people. Why then does the former man, destitute of Martian heat, nevertheless perish by the sword (which is the work of **Mars**), while the latter dies in peace, though he himself is almost hotter than **Mars**? Furthermore, they might be able to offer some connection between these things and what is within us, such as how they refer to the "habit" of the body; but by what reasoning could things like a wife, wealth, honors, and other things of this kind follow the differences of the body and soul? Certainly, one cannot even dream of this. 

For this reason, **Ptolemy** himself, in the first chapter of his book *Apotelesmaton* <note>Known today as the *Tetrabiblos*, the foundational text of Western astrology.</note>, where he constructs his reasoning on the efficacy of the stars, concludes nothing other than that the diversity of the body (and of the soul, insofar as it is attached to the body) follows from the stars in some way. Regarding fortuitous events, he adds nothing in that place; for he writes as follows: *Any person will therefore be able to say what the state of the air surrounding us will be at any time. But he will also understand the proper habit and temperament of any man by drawing an argument from the state of the air when he was being formed. Therefore, he will be able to say what sort of body and what sort of soul he would be allotted. Then, he will foresee how he will fare in the course of time: namely, that a future disposition of the air, agreeing with a body of such a temperament, will lead to its health, or, if the occasion is dissonant, will cause disease and sickness.* These are **Ptolemy's** words, in which, as is apparent, there is no mention of external things. 

Soon after, however, in the next chapter, where he repeats what was said and connects it to what follows, he adds external things as if he had already proven them—perhaps thinking he could deceive a reader who had already forgotten the reasoning by which that conclusion was said to be deduced and proven. Therefore, even if we grant to **Ptolemy** that the primary affections of matter—moisture, dryness, cold, and heat—are changed according to the condition and state of the stars, we will by no means concede that the stars are what cause the various accidents of human life.

<summary>Pico argues that while stars might plausibly affect physical temperament (humors), they cannot be responsible for external life events like wealth, marriage, or death in war. He specifically critiques Ptolemy for logically leaping from physical effects to predicting "fortuitous" life events without proof.</summary>
<keywords>Ptolemy, Mars, Saturn, war, humors, temperament, Tetrabiblos, fortune, primary qualities, bile</keywords>

# Book III
<meta>catchword: inq/ (continuation of "inquiry")</meta>

## Chapter XXIV: That hidden powers do not exist in the heavens through which they produce hidden properties of lower things, but only heat and life-giving light.

It remains to be discussed whether, besides the effective power of those <term>primary qualities</term><note>The "four primary qualities" of Aristotelian physics: hot, cold, moist, and dry.</note>, there are more hidden and eminent powers in the stars through which they can do many things that they cannot achieve through those primary qualities alone. For example, by its own particular property, the **magnet** draws iron; the **peony** <note>original: "peonia"; in Renaissance medicine, the peony was widely used to treat "the falling sickness" or epilepsy.</note> helps those suffering from epilepsy; and in other things, there are other powers inherent in them that are both nobler and more effective than the first affections of matter. 

<margin>Refutation</margin>
The fourth argument of the astrologers contended this, asserting that it is impossible for the stars not to abound with powers of this kind if—as almost all philosophers say—earthly things obtain such gifts by the benefit of the stars; and since the stars are the noblest of bodies, they must necessarily be endowed with the noblest gifts. 

But neither the nobility of these bodies, nor the fact that the hidden and wonderful powers of earthly bodies are said to come from them, is an argument by which we are forced to believe that such virtues—that is, some power other than what we have called **life-giving heat**—reside in the celestial nature. For, to address the last point first, they do not correctly understand the saying that lower bodies "receive their powers from heaven" to perform things that cannot be achieved through the four primary qualities. Those gifts and powers flow from the innermost principles of the bodies themselves—that is, from their **forms** or **essences**. Furthermore, just as heaven is said to have given the form from which motion follows, so it is said to give them such virtues. 

Yet the diversity of these virtues arises not from a diversity of constellations, but from the **mixture** of elements, from whose varying proportions different forms result. This actually pertains to the dignity of the heavens: for those things which are divided among a multitude in the lower order are possessed by the superior order in a single, more eminent act. Therefore, if this sublunary crowd of decaying bodies—so multiform, so numerous, weak, tumultuous, particular, and narrow—is compared to the celestial body, which is eternal, unfailing, simple, vast, and universal, it is most consistent with reason that whatever power or perfection is cut up and distributed among the lower parts originates from that first body. 

But the celestial bodies bestow all these various and manifold powers equally through their unique gift of **light** and **heat**. 

<margin>The great dignity of light.</margin>
This gift, communicated more or less through the sequence of the stars, creates their order among themselves rather than a difference in kind. Nor should we search further for what this gift or property might be; we have said often that it does not need a demonstrator, as it demonstrates itself and all other things with it: namely, **light**. 

<margin>God is the true light.</margin>
Light is evident to all; flowing from a moving body and breathing forth heat, it reveals to us the nearly hidden mystery of divinity: it represents **Power** in motion, **Wisdom** in light, and **Love** in heat. By these, He moves, illustrates, creates, perfects, and preserves all things—that first God, the first of all. Just as heaven is the first among all bodies, what more do we desire in heaven, or what seems to us to be lacking for the supreme perfection of physical nature and its rule over the lower world, besides this prerogative of a triple efficacy hanging in a certain order from a single body? 

To be marked and distinguished by many different properties is a claim to the dignity of an *imperfect* nature; it actually detracts from a *perfect* one. To the perfect, as I have said, it is proper to possess gathered together in one what lower things possess separately and in parts. This is a privilege which, if it did not belong to the perpetual motion of the body and its heat-giving light, certainly besides it... <note>original: "inq/," likely a catchword for "inquiritur" (it is inquired) or "inquit" (he says) continuing on the next page.</note>

<summary>Pico argues that stars do not possess "occult" or magical powers; rather, they influence the Earth solely through motion, light, and heat, which mirror the divine attributes of power, wisdom, and love.</summary>
<keywords>astrology, light, heat, primary qualities, occult properties, magnetism, divine attributes, Aristotelian physics</keywords>

# Book III
<margin>h ii</margin>

...it would be necessary to seek <note>The text here completes a thought from the previous page regarding whether we must look for a specific "hidden" power in the stars.</note> something else in heaven that, by a single act, might encompass and embrace the power of any corruptible bodies whatsoever. But if this is found fully within light and heat, there is no necessary labor in inventing others. Indeed, it is undoubtedly found there, since without heat no corporeal thing can either generate or exercise its functions once generated. Take away heat itself and its warmth: the **peony** will not help those with the <term>falling sickness</term><note>epilepsy</note>; **hyacinth** <note>original: "iacynthus"; likely referring to the gemstone, which in medieval lapidaries was thought to stem the flow of blood.</note> will not stop blood; nor will **rhubarb** draw out bile. And just as the efficacy of all things that act upon us would cease if they were not stirred by the fuel of our own internal heat, so too would the power of those bodies—and the very heat of living things—cease, unless they were both cherished separately and joined together by celestial heat. 

Therefore, the act and perfection of whatever powers are implanted in earthly things is this very heat-producing light, insofar as it is hot; just as the perfection of all heat is light, insofar as it shines. And just as colors cannot be seen, nor can eyes see, except by the benefit of this light, so too can the gifts of any bodies whatsoever neither subsist in themselves nor affect one another if they are destitute of the help of that motion and heat. Therefore, just as it pertains to the dignity and beauty of the heaven—which flashes with a single native splendor of light despite such a great diversity of colors—so it belongs to its perfection to have possessed one single power in place of a manifold number of material powers. This single power is nobler than all others, just as light precedes all colors; and it is their perfect constitution, just as light is the perfect constitution of all colors. Nor should we think it detracts from the dignity of heaven if we deny these particular gifts to the stars, any more than we believe the heaven itself to be **yellow**, **blue**, **leek-green**, or **purple**. While such variety is beautiful and necessary in earthly things, it is neither possible nor becoming in the stars.

### Chapter XXV: Even if a proper and individual power is granted to each star, it is nonetheless a universal power.

<margin>
Let these be
the dogmas
of the
astrologers
</margin>
Now, if someone should contend that besides this property of motion, light, and heat common to all, each star has its own particular **influence**, I will not greatly resist him, although I could. But I will remind him that these diverse powers by which they differ from one another still agree in this: that they are all **celestial powers**. Furthermore, whatever is in heaven—even if it is something "particular" when compared to the totality of celestial things—is nonetheless **universal** when referred to the things beneath the moon (even if it seems very narrow). When I say "universal," I wish it to be understood in this way: that it enclosed within itself the entire perfection of the corruptible world. Otherwise, it will not be "celestial," as has been declared in part already and will soon be explained more broadly. 

If this is granted, those peculiar gifts of the stars will not help the cause of astrology at all. There will indeed be one property of **Jupiter** and another of **Saturn**, but Jupiter will not, for that reason, produce a different effect among us than Saturn; therefore, both will be able to do all things equally through this property of theirs. I will not deny that the **Jovian** power differs from the **Saturnine**. But there is no power of lower bodies that the Jovian power does not contain, generate, preserve, make effective, and perfect just as much as the Saturnine, and vice versa. I will say first why this is so, and then how diversity of both property and action remains in both despite this commonality. The nature of heaven seems unable to be explained more aptly or briefly than if you say that **heaven is the unity of all bodies**. Indeed, there is no multitude that does not depend on its own unity; nothing in the universe exists that is not derived from a single, as it were, fountain-head.

He further asserts that even if stars have individual "influences," these powers are universal rather than specific, meaning no single star governs a single earthly outcome.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the argument regarding the nature of celestial influence. Having previously argued that light and heat are the primary instruments of the stars, the author now moves to a metaphysical explanation of how the "First" or "Head" of a category (like the Heavens) contains all the powers of the "Body" (the earthly realm) in a unified, superior way.</meta>

# Book III
->ii d<-

And just as in an army every legion looks to its own prefect, while the entire army is referred back to a single general: so too every series of things, through a commonality of kind, is in harmony with itself. It has its own principle <note>original: "principium"; in this context, it means a source, origin, or governing cause.</note> from which it is derived, by which it is nourished, ruled, and contained. Since there are many such principles, they are ultimately reduced—like a multiple unity—to the most simple unity of the First Principle. Moreover, just as every number is in some way contained within the number one, and an entire city within its king, and a whole army within its general: so too is all the power and perfection of a "flock" (so to speak) contained within its own principle. Truly, that which is divided, incomplete, unfinished, or unlimited in that "gregarious" condition—if I may call it that—flourishes in the "Head" within a singular embrace of a certain unlimited unity: pure, effective, and perfect. Thus, it is said that nothing of the subsequent "body" is in the "Head," yet conversely, the whole body is said to be in the "Head." <note>This reflects the Neoplatonic idea that a cause contains the effects of its subordinates in a higher, more unified form than the effects themselves possess.</note> 

So it is with God, who is first among all that exist: He is none of the things that exist, and yet again He is all things through the eminence of His primary nature and all-encompassing power. From what principle, then, shall the corporeal <note>physical/material</note> genus depend, if not from that which is the first body in both location and dignity? This, however, is the **heaven**. Truly, therefore, as we were saying, the heaven shall be the unity of all bodies. Regarding the heaven, one might deny all things that belong to other bodies, yet one might also affirm them. They are denied because that which is formed in those lower bodies has various limits, and that which is discrete, multiple, and imperfect in them possesses neither those characteristics of form nor that same diversity when it is in the heaven. Yet all those things are affirmed of the heaven at once—not through the potential of matter, but through the magnitude of its power <note>original: "uirtutis"; referring to the inherent efficacy or "virtue" of a thing.</note> and the sublimity of its original nature. 

If this is the nature of the heaven, it certainly applies to every celestial thing. One should not think that while the whole heaven contains the total perfection of the inferior bodies, a specific part of heaven contains only a specific part of them. That would be no privilege for the heaven! Rather, any part of heaven is the entire inferior world—excluding those things that are *in* the world but not *of* the world. <margin>Allegorical opinion of the Pythagoreans.</margin> <margin>The distinct "seas" of the moon.</margin> <margin>God is the true light.</margin> The Pythagoreans seem to have signified this through a certain allegorical opinion of theirs, by which they were accustomed to affirm that this entire sublunary <note>The region below the moon, i.e., the Earth and its atmosphere.</note> region is itself a single star. They also claimed that in any star of the heaven, there exists everything that is seen in our own region: thus, in the **moon**, there is a distinction of the four elements, as well as valleys and mountains, and even the plants and living creatures that are found among us. Likewise in **Venus**, **Mercury**, and the rest of the stars. 

By this "type" <note>symbol or figure</note> they certainly declare nothing other than what we intended to prove: that there is no star in heaven that does not encompass the whole of what exists beneath the moon. Otherwise, they would not be of a "celestial nature," if the following assumption and proof does not fail: that nothing is more truly called the celestial nature than the "unity of corporeal nature." Furthermore, this would be a privilege worthy of heaven: that with such vastness and an innumerable number of lights, it should embrace the goods of this narrow sublunary space. Therefore, in the power of any star whatsoever, there resides every power of perishable bodies. Nor do the powers of different stars differ in that some preside over certain things and others over others; for all of them preside over everything. Nor does a higher star excel a lower one by a wider embrace (that is, by containing more things), but rather by a more noble embrace—containing the same things as the lower star, but in a far more unified and eminent manner. This same principle can be seen in the "separate minds" <note>Angels or pure intellects detached from matter.</note> and in the cognition of living beings. For just as every body depends on the heaven, so every power that participates in cognition depends on the **Intellect**. I call it "Intellect," not meaning our own human reason, which...

<summary>Pico explains that the Heavens act as a "Head" or "Unity" that contains the powers of all earthly things in a superior, unified state. He uses the Pythagorean allegory of stars as inhabited worlds to argue that every single star exerts influence over the entire earthly realm, rather than being restricted to specific parts or objects.</summary>

<page-num>III</page-num>
# Book III

...it is said: but of the angels, whom the philosophers call Minds and Intellects. This Mind is sufficient unto itself for understanding, needing nothing below it; nor does it look into anything beneath itself to perceive what it understands. It is not deceived, nor does it labor. And that which, in every kind of knowledge, is distributed among various powers, the Mind possesses through a single power, far more excellently than it exists in those others. It beholds the truth within itself and touches it as present with the certainty of a sense. It holds that truth within itself through an imaginary faculty as things slip away; it foresees the causes and species <note>original: "species"; here meaning the essential forms or "blueprints" of things.</note> of things, both corporeal and incorporeal, with rational perspicacity—yet it is not itself rational, or sensual, or imaginary, but rather possesses an intellectual property of a nobler condition. It collects what is perfect in those lower faculties and rejects what is imperfect. 

For in us, physical knowledge is one thing, mathematical another, and divine knowledge <note>This refers to "Metaphysics," which was historically called "Divine Science."</note> yet another. For physical reasoning follows along with the senses; mathematical reasoning with the phantasia <note>original: "fantasia"; refers to the faculty of imagination that bridges the gap between the senses and the higher intellect.</note>; and divine reasoning with the mind and intellect. Furthermore, there is no mind, even the most lowly, that does not see in its own light every truth which we either barely reach or surely pant after through those sciences and arts. 

Come then, let us compare these things to the physical realm. These arts and sciences are within us; in all of knowing nature, there are various kinds of cognitions, just as there are various privileges of different virtues <note>original: "uirtutum"; in this context, "virtue" means a specific power or inherent property of a thing.</note> in the multitude of bodies. All knowledge is a certain participation in intellectual light; every physical power is a certain participation in a celestial faculty. However, just as that light shines more evidently in reason, so this faculty shines more perfectly in the spirit of the heart. 

These things being established, let us see whether someone might rightly say that if intellectual rays flow down from those Minds, some would be those that create physicists and not mathematicians; others mathematicians and not divines; and others divines rather than physicists or mathematicians. And thus this light would be like those studies, depending on the diversity of the nature of the "breathing" minds, and not from rays proceeding from that same mind by its own counsel and will. I think he will judge more rightly who believes that there is nothing of this sort: that any of those Minds could not give largely of everything; and that it grants these things not by its own liberty (in the manner of the stars) but by its nature. 

And if it happens that this gift is received rather than that, it should be attributed not to the giver (who is equally liberal in all things) but to the capacity and condition of the receiver. If, as we have said, the star stands in relation to the corruptible body—as far as our present purpose is concerned—just as the Mind stands to failing knowledge, it must likewise be said that any star can give of itself whatever the subject body, whatever it may be, is born to receive. Thus, the diversity of the hidden influence <note>original: "afflatus occulti"; a term for the subtle, invisible breath or spiritual flow from the heavens.</note> is caused not by the star that breathes it (as the astrologer thinks), but by the diversity of the matter being breathed upon. 

I have called it a "hidden influence" because the action of a star, beyond light and heat, can be diverse according to the intensity or relaxation of the ray, as we explained above. But in these hidden properties through which the star, as it were, propagates itself and pours out its own (so to speak) species and images: just as that intensity and relaxation do not appear there, so we are not persuaded to posit any diversity of action. But you will say: "Surely the power of Jupiter and that diffused species is different from the power of Saturn?" I admit it; but it does not follow that it will produce a different thing, since there is nothing in the sublunary world <note>The realm of Earth, located beneath the sphere of the Moon.</note> that either one cannot produce.

<meta>This page continues the philosophical critique of astrology by Giovanni Pico della Mirandola. Picking up from the previous page's discussion on how the "Mind" or intellect interacts with lower forms, Pico now focuses on the physical mechanism—or lack thereof—by which planets influence the material world. He explores the Aristotelian concepts of matter and form to show that even if stars had specific roles, the diversity of life on Earth stems from the nature of the "receiver" (the earthly object) rather than a complex "message" from the stars.</meta>

# Book III

What then is the diversity of action? Each does the same thing: but one does it in one way, another in another: the nobler power in a nobler and more eminent way. Although I do not know if we should so determine concerning these virtues: whether perhaps a lower power is more effective upon us—not because it is closer in location, but because it is more related in nature <note>Pico is suggesting that "like affects like"; things on Earth might be more influenced by earthly forces than by distant celestial ones.</note>—but this inquiry is for another work. Here we only affirm: if, besides light and heat, each star is granted its own property, it can be defended that all stars act as universal causes, so that they produce no diversity among lower things by their own power alone. 

We could, however, grant them some particular power by restricting, namely, the sidereal <note>term: "sidereal" (sideream). Relating to the stars or constellations.</note> power. And we could grant it in such a way that it would nonetheless not help the astrologers: as if we were to grant that all stars always work the same way in all things, but not that all things receive that work in the same way; but rather one thing in one way, another in another, following this example. Any body consists of **matter** and **form** <note>These are the two fundamental components of any object in Aristotelian philosophy: "matter" is the raw stuff, and "form" is the essential nature or blueprint that makes it a specific thing.</note>: let someone suppose then that the matter stands thus: that the three minor stars—the **Moon**, **Venus**, and **Mercury**—deal with what pertains to matter, with divided duties. For instance, the Moon might rule the matter itself, but it is disposed toward form by Venus and Mercury: by Venus through quantity—while order, figure, composition, and the due beauty of parts are established—and by Mercury through quality, while it puts on the appropriate qualities with a moldable mobility for the form to be received. 

And let us suppose the qualities of the remaining form are from the three superior stars <note>In the traditional geocentric model, Saturn, Jupiter, and Mars were "superior" because they were further from Earth than the Sun, while the others were "inferior" or "minor."</note> in this manner: so that the nature of the form itself is from **Saturn**; that which gives being and life to living things is from **Jupiter**; and that which moves and excites from within to action is from **Mars**. But that any thing should diffuse itself, and through that diffusion make itself known and propagate, will be referred chiefly to the **Sun**, whose works seem to be both to overcome the matter from which it produces something like itself, and the act of generation itself, and manifestation. 

What if, therefore, the works of the planets differed? We even grant this voluntarily: not because we are compelled by reason, nor by the reliability of experiments, nor by the authority of **Plato** or **Aristotle**, but even then, all diversity of lower things would be not from heaven, but from lower causes. This is because that celestial influence acts in its own way always in all things, in the same manner, but with the effect varied: partly by the immediate causes, and partly by the disposition of matter. It is better to place the cause in these lower factors rather than placing particular virtues in the stars, since no reason persuades us of even these universal ones. I do not deny that one might suspect otherwise concerning some things without sin <note>original: "piaculo"; a religious transgression or sin.</note>, and even with the authority of the learned; but as the following book will show, if there are any such influences, they are not those which the astrologers say, nor are we affected by them in the way they believe.

## Chapter XXVI: Epilogue of this book, with a rejection of certain arguments of the astrologers against those arguing against them.

<margin>e</margin>
We have examined all the natural changes of lower things which seem to be the works of heaven: for we shall speak of the fortuitous <note>original: "fortuitis"; refers to things happening by chance or luck rather than natural law.</note> accidents of men in the solution of the fifth reason. Nor was there found in those changes anything that favored the astrologers, but rather an opportunity was given to object to many things, so that they may regret having stirred up this **anagyris** <note>original: "anagyrin"; referring to the "stinking bean-trefoil." This is a classical Greek proverb for "stirring up a stink" or causing one's own trouble by meddling.</note>. For what else do we conclude but that sublunary <note>term: "sublunary" (sublunaria). Literally "under the moon"; refers to the Earth and its atmosphere, the realm of change and decay.</note> bodies are affected by the rays of the luminaries? But they are affected by no other influence than heat, and no other heat than vital heat; nor would that action be changed in any way other than by the position of the star, irradiating us more either from nearby or directly. From these principles, we have rendered the reason for all effects: whichever ones they provide by the reliability of experience as witness to their dogma...

He concludes the book by asserting that stars influence the world only through vital heat and light, not through the complex "meanings" claimed by astrologers.</summary>

# Book III

...brought [proofs]; in rendering which it became clear that astrology was not confirmed by those observations, but rather weakened; and it was everywhere uncovered that they <note>The astrologers.</note> either were deceived or were deceiving. Thus it appeared that it is falsely believed by them that the sun has a drying power, or the moon a healthily moistening and cold power; it is falsely imagined that there is in the moon a hidden power beyond motion and light which calls back and pours out the sea <note>Referring to the tides.</note>; falsely that Saturn is made the culprit for the harm of an eight-month birth <note>A common ancient belief held that babies born at eight months rarely survived because they were ruled by the "malefic" planet Saturn.</note>; falsely ascribed to the signs <note>The signs of the Zodiac.</note>, as if they were of diverse virtue and power, whereas it is only through the variety of the sun’s placement that its rays work; and falsely that critical days and the periods of fevers are referred to the motions of the moon or other stars. Finally, it was so far 

<margin>
Argument of the astrologers
Another argument
</margin>
from the case that an argument for faith in the decrees of astrology could be taken from these changes caused by the sun and moon, that it instead leads into a no small suspicion of falsehood. For they argued thus: if someone sleeps under the moon, a numbness takes over the limbs; and at the same time **sea urchins** are filled up; therefore, it cools and moistens. Sense attests that the sun is scorching; therefore it is dry. 

<margin>
He retorts with the first point of Aristotle.
</margin>
We, on the other hand, press on thus: the moon fills the sea urchins; therefore it is hot. We have demonstrated this from **Aristotle** <note>Pico is likely referencing Aristotle’s *Parts of Animals*, where the growth of shellfish is linked to heat.</note>; those sleeping under it are numbed by cold; therefore it is hot. We have explained this 

<margin>
Hippocrates
Solution to the second argument.
</margin>
by clear reason, namely, how that happens. In the full moon, it favors conceptions, nourishes bodies; as it grows it strengthens and enlivens: therefore it is hot. We have proved this from **Hippocrates** <note>The famous Greek physician often cited in debates about the moon's influence on the human body.</note> and from evidence itself. Concerning the sun, we likewise appeal to experience, by which it is clear that by its rays every breath of life is made living; this indeed is not the property of a dry power, but of a healthily hot one. Nor was it difficult to declare how the sun, either by accident, dries or burns, or indeed even cools; 

<margin>
Another reasoning of the astrologers.
</margin>
[or how] the moon is said to be the cause of cold and moisture: although each star, by its own nature, is only the author of life-giving light and heat. They likewise gathered this: we see our bodies are manifestly changed by the sun and moon; therefore we must not doubt the influences of the other stars. But this very thing draws us into doubt concerning the others, precisely because we see this regarding the sun and moon: for we find the dispositions of bodies varied by them in such a way that we judge the remaining stars to be <term>asymbolic</term> <note>original: "asymbolas"; from the Greek, meaning they contribute nothing or have no share in the physical effect.</note> rather than called into a share of the work. Since, as the moon’s light decreases, moisture in bodies is always diminished, and it always increases as the moon waxes. Why then, if what the astrologers think about the efficiency of the other stars is true—why, I say, do the humble planets, when they are dominant and make up for the loss of lunar light, not increase moisture? So that we might sometimes, by the benefit of the stars, dine on succulent oysters even during the new moon? Why, in turn, does that fullness of the dryness of **Saturn** and **Mars**—usurping the law of the sky according to astrological rules—never dry out bodies and protect logs from rot [when the moon is full]? Therefore, these observations favor those who take away the power of the planets rather than those who affirm it; just as they favor those who attribute no efficacy to the timing of cutting wood rather than those who attribute the most. Otherwise, since the sea is moved by the moon—as they wish and we ourselves do not deny—why does it not move the sea more when placed in "watery" signs than in "fiery" ones, or less in "dry" ones than in "moist" ones? Or why does the moon not make more abundant tides when joined to "moist" planets than to "drying" ones? And how, if what they predict about the <term>twelve places</term> <note>original: "duodecim locis"; refers to the twelve houses of an astrological chart.</note> which they call **houses** is true, does it harmonize with this: that as the moon rises from the horizon and approaches the summit, it acts more strongly on the ocean? And thus it acts more strongly from the **twelfth house** than from the <term>horoscope</term> <note>original: "horoscopo"; in Pico's time, this specifically meant the Ascendant, or the point of the Zodiac rising on the eastern horizon.</note>, in which place they say all stars languish and become the weakest of all?

<summary>Pico disputes the physical evidence for astrology, arguing that the moon's effects on tides and shellfish are due to its life-giving heat rather than "moisture," and that planetary influences should be consistent if they were real.</summary>

# Book III

...they affirm power; rather, therefore, these experiments stand with us against them, rather than being claimed as proof for the astrologers' opinions—unless, as **Favorinus** <note>Favorinus of Arelate (c. 80–160 AD) was a philosopher who famously argued against the validity of astrology.</note> used to say, and as we also touched upon above: because the ocean, as a companion of the moon, grows old and young along with it, they think this is an argument to persuade us that all human affairs, both the smallest and the greatest, are led and governed as if bound to the stars and constellations. But it is far different, and as that same man used to boast while mocking the astrologers, it is too clumsy and absurd: just because the tide of the ocean agrees with the course of the moon, we should also think that some legal business a man might happen to have with his rivals before a judge regarding a **water duct** <note>Latin: *aquae ductu*. Pico is contrasting a massive natural force (the tides) with a trivial, specific human legal dispute to show the absurdity of astrological determinism.</note> is itself also governed from heaven as if by some rein.

## Chapter XXVII

It remains for us to dissolve the final argument sought from human events: in which some things so far exceed our powers, or happen so far beyond merit and reason, that they seem to establish the force of a fatal decree and celestial power. We shall solve this for the present by showing that all these things have sufficient causes among ourselves, and that nothing appears in all of them that requires heaven as an author. This is to say, there is nothing in the course of human affairs from which a suspicion ought to arise that the deeds of men are sufficiently ruled and governed [by stars]. For in the beginning of the following book, no longer merely dissolving but now arguing, we shall teach especially that these things—in which those men think they recognize the force of fate—are in no way done by heavenly influence. These are, in short, two great things: namely, the good and the bad. Let us speak first of the great things: these pertain either to the soul or to external matters. Thus, they were objecting to us both the **success of Alexander** <note>Alexander the Great, whose rapid conquests were often attributed to "Fate" or "Fortune" by astrologers.</note> and the genius and learning of his teacher.

<margin>Why Aristotle was a consummate philosopher.</margin>

Let us begin, therefore, from those things which pertain to the soul. You admire in **Aristotle** a consummate knowledge of natural things; I admire it along with you. "The cause is heaven," you say, "and the constellation under which he was born." I do not agree—not only for the common reason that many were born under the same star who were not Aristotles—but because, besides the heaven (which is a universal cause under which both **Boeotian pigs and Attic philosophers** <note>A traditional proverb: Boeotia was legendary for its "thick" air and supposedly stupid inhabitants (pigs), while Athens (Attica) was the center of philosophy. Pico argues that since they both exist under the same sky, the sky cannot be the cause of their difference.</note> sprout alike), there are proximate causes proper and peculiar to Aristotle, to which we may refer his singular progress. First, as he himself says, he was allotted a **good soul**; and this certainly did not come from heaven, since the soul is immortal and incorporeal—as he himself demonstrated, and even the astrologers do not deny. Then, he was allotted a body suitable to serve such a soul; nor did this come from heaven, except as from a common cause, but rather from his parents. He chose to philosophize. This was the work of the principles we mentioned: that is, of the soul and the body, and it was of his own **free will**. He progressed in philosophy; this was the fruit of the purpose he embraced and of his own industry. But many who philosophized more than he did had equal zeal and labor. The cause was the teaching of his master <note>Plato.</note> and the good fortune of the age in which he was brought forth, which was full of the monuments of the ancients; yet these were not so perfected that there was no labor left for beginning and completing the noble arts, nor was material lacking. But he progressed far more than his contemporaries and his disciples. He had been allotted not a better star, but a better **talent** <note>Latin: *ingenium*, referring to natural mental capacity.</note>. Nor is talent from a star, since it is incorporeal, but from God, just as the body is from the father, not from heaven. Concerning which we speak so much more honorably than the astrologers...

<summary>Pico argues that celestial phenomena like tides do not prove that human legal or personal affairs are predestined. He specifically refutes the idea that Aristotle's genius was caused by the stars, attributing it instead to a good soul, free will, parental biology, and a lucky historical era.</summary>

# Book III

## ## Book III

...how much more divine and eminent a universal cause is than particular causes. For if the genius of a human—whether **Aristotle** or some other philosopher—exceeded common understanding, the cause of this would not be something inferior (such as a celestial body, which is merely physical), but something better: that is, divine. Just as **Socrates** <note>Socrates famously claimed to be guided by a *daimonion*, a private divine voice or "present deity," rather than the stars.</note>—who in my opinion was the greatest of all philosophers—attributed his wisdom not to his birth-stars, but to a present deity. Therefore, we give more credit to the heavens than is proper if we derive the divinity of our souls from those physical rays; conversely, we give the heavens less than its due if we attribute individual physical differences to it as if it were a specific, particular cause. 

Indeed, it is altogether less than decent when we ascribe our own deformities and the failures of our minds to the stars. This is one of the main reasons people flee to the stars for answers: because there appear in many men certain discordant desires that seem to go against the laws of humanity. Because these desires seem to have an external rather than an internal human cause, and because that cause is powerful, they assume it must be "stellar." 

But I would ask those people: why does a pregnant woman often crave to eat earth and charcoal more than any kind of exquisite food? If they find the cause of this monstrous desire in the condition of the fetus rather than a star, I will remind them that the cause of the things they wonder at should likewise be sought in the temperament of the body rather than in the heavens. I might even suggest the influence of wicked demons, but I would still lead them away from physical celestial bodies. 

Certainly, beyond the disposition of the body, I can demonstrate with a very true example how much habit contributes to these kinds of portentous afflictions. 

<margin>
See a monstrous example of lust.
</margin>
There still lives a man known to me of a monstrous and unheard-of lust. He is never aroused to **Venus** <note>In this context, Venus refers to sexual desire or activity.</note> unless he is beaten; and yet he contemplates this crime in such a way, and so desires the cruel blows, that he scolds the one beating him if they act too slowly. He does not fully achieve his wish unless blood breaks out, and the more violent lash tears the limbs of this most guilty man. The miserable man begs for this service with the highest prayers from whatever woman he visits; he even provides a whip the day before, hardened for this duty by being soaked in vinegar. He suppliantly demands to be beaten by the prostitute, and the harder he is struck, the more fervently he warms up. He pursues pleasure and pain at an equal pace—a man discovered who finds physical delight in the midst of torture. 

Because he is not otherwise a bad man, he recognizes and hates his own disease. Since he has been a friend of mine for many years, he freely revealed what he suffered. When I diligently inquired into the cause of such an unusual plague, he said: "I became accustomed to it as a boy." And when I asked the cause of the habit, he explained he was raised with most wicked boys among whom it was agreed that, through this license of striking one another as if it were a price, they sold their mutual shame in a shameful exchange. 

I have not suppressed this story—though it may be harsh for refined ears—so that we might recognize by this very evidence how much habit can influence these passions. We should not immediately accuse heaven as if such things could have no earthly cause. For if an astrologer heard of this, he would say that Venus had been condemned in the man’s birth chart, and perhaps whipped by the threatening rays of **Mars**. <note>Mars was traditionally associated with violence and cutting; an astrologer would link a "whipping" fetish to a negative alignment between Venus (sex) and Mars (violence).</note>

<margin>
Whence Alexander had such great fortune in warlike affairs.
</margin>
Let us turn to external matters, in which **Alexander** <note>Alexander the Great.</note> was pre-eminent. Whence did such great and sudden success in his affairs arise, if not from heaven? The answer is easy: from the virtues of Alexander, of which he had many that are necessary for a commander: fortitude, liberality, endurance of labor, military skill, outstanding learning, and others which I need not enumerate here...

# Book III

## ## Book III

...necessary: from the army he obtained, which was highly trained under his father **Philip**, and most warlike due to the benefit of that region; he was also most beloved by them because of his generosity and his example of virtues. His success also came from the cowardice of the peoples he overcame; for this reason, his uncle said he had "fought against <margin>Fortune.</margin> women." It came from **Fortune**, which holds great power in matters of war. Indeed, when I say **Fortune**, I do not mean the sky/heavens, but that cause which **Aristotle** mentions in the second book of his *Physics* <note>Aristotle defines "fortune" or "luck" as an accidental cause in the realm of things that happen for a purpose but occur by chance.</note>, and which we commonly call fortune and are accustomed to express in these words: "so luck brought it," "so it happened," "so it fell out." It is through this that those playing with dice either throw what they want or what they do not want; this is that so-called "blind" power which, besides those causes we have mentioned and similar ones, created the **Caesars**, the **Sullas**, the **Augustuses**, and the **Alexanders**. This power does not depend on the heavens by itself, nor is it the same thing as **Fate**, nor does it detract from divine providence. What it finally is, or might not be, must be discussed at length in the next book; it is not appropriate to say it here, where we—as an astrologer—shall overwhelm with his own weapons none other than <margin>Thomas.</margin> **Thomas Aquinas**, whom these astrologers think is highly in their favor <note>Pico often uses the authority of St. Thomas Aquinas to show that even great theologians limited the power of the stars over the human will.</note>. As for what pertains principally to what is being treated here: I deny that anything on earth is made or seen to be so great that it deserves the heavens as its author. For indeed, the miracles of the mind, as we have said, are greater than the heavens; but the miracles of fortune and the body (as great as they may be) are found to be very small when compared to the heavens. As <margin>Favorinus.</margin> **Favorinus** <note>Favorinus of Arles, a philosopher whose skeptical views Pico often quotes to emphasize human dignity.</note> rightly said: "Nothing is great on earth except man; nothing is great in man except his mind and soul." If you ascend to this, you transcend the heavens; if you incline toward the body and look up at the heavens, you see yourself as a fly, and something even less than a fly. 

Just as in that black line of ants, there are some who excel others in strength and size; there are victories, wars, peaces, duties, labors, poverty, and riches. To us who contemplate them, these things are all tiny and, in the end, are nothing. In the same way, our little bodies, our fortunes, our kings, our provinces, wars, treaties, and marriages are absolutely nothing if compared to the heavens. Compared to the heavens, the entire earth—one tiny portion of which men divide among themselves with fire and sword—is but an indivisible point. 

Therefore, the magnitude of earthly things is not such that they could not be the work of anything other than the heavens. If the things among us that are considered "worthy" are not worthy of the heavens, how much more unworthy are those things which are even done shamefully by us? Such as the scandalous being raised to dignity, or **Socrates** perishing by the judgment of a "star-gazer" <note>original: "stellicatoris." This likely refers to the "judge of the stars" or an astrologically-inclined accuser, highlighting the injustice of a wise man killed by those following superstition.</note>, and many enormous things of that kind which we see and suffer every day. In these things especially, **Maternus** <note>Firmicus Maternus, a 4th-century author of a famous astrological handbook, whom Pico frequently attacks.</note> says that **Fate** and the necessity of celestial decree shine forth. I would gladly ask him, along with other astrologers: why are they so eager to impute our errors to the stars? And why, when we ourselves sin, do we more willingly accuse the heavens than ourselves? As if it were either a miracle that we, who are prone to evil from youth, should err, or as if those heavenly bodies—which always serve the commands of the best God in an unchangeable order—could ever err. 

They say "the innocent are condemned, and the wicked are bestowed with rewards." By which leaders, I ask? Just ones or unjust ones? If by just ones, even the heavens will not be enough to explain such a miracle; if by <margin>Aristotle.</margin> unjust ones, what need is there for the heavens, when the malice of man (which despises the heavens) is sufficient? **Aristotle** asks in his *Problems*: "Why are the good almost always poor?" and although he brings forward many causes, both true and clever, he brings none from the heavens. For <note>original: "q. f. scitet sentes & tribulos"</note> as is known, it is not the heavens that germinate thorns and thistles, but the <margin>Objection.</margin> earth. Yet a cautious and prudent man, who was especially fleeing from danger, runs into it; he escapes...

# **GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA'S** DISPUTATIONS AGAINST THE ASTROLOGERS: BOOK FOUR

### Chapter One: The method observed in disputing thus far and to be observed hereafter; then, even if we grant to astrologers what theologians grant most highly, astrology is nonetheless nothing.

<margin>The author's method of disputing is remarkably persuasive</margin> This is generally our custom in disputing: if the adversary proposes something that can be granted without impiety and can also be reasonably denied, we do not simply deny it, even if it is such that, once conceded, it does nothing to prove the point he contends. And so, proceeding through this sequence until we reach the greatest claim he can make, we show that even if that were granted (which we have shown could rightfully be denied), the conclusion he expects still does not follow. For in this way, the whole matter under dispute is explored through its particular parts, and the adversary understands how many things he receives as a gift while defending a certain and absurd opinion. Since these things are false for many reasons, or certainly doubtful, yet regardless of how they stand, they cannot be entirely false if we follow this custom.

When dealing with astrologers, we first argued that only the rays of the **Sun** and the **Moon** have the power to change lower things. <margin>How that method was observed in this disputation</margin> That the other stars have no influence on us, either because of the distance of their rays or their weakness. In the second place, if it were granted to them—not by force, but as a concession—that something flows down from all the stars into us, we showed that this flows from all of them only with differences in intensity and relaxation: that is, light with life-giving heat. But cold, humidity, and dryness do not emanate from them.

Thirdly, even if they produced the four primary qualities <term>Primary Qualities</term><note>In ancient and medieval science, these were the four basic building blocks of the physical world: Heat, Cold, Moisture, and Dryness.</note>, it would not follow that the diversity of "impressions" <note>Atmospheric phenomena like rain or wind.</note> made in the heavens came from them. Or if it did, it still does not mean that pestilences, floods, or conflagrations come from them—much less that external things subject to chance and fortune are governed by the stars through the power of those four primary qualities. Fourthly, if the stars were believed to be the authors of those primary conditions—that is, having the power to heat and cool, or to moisten and dry—no other gifts besides these should be attributed to them through which they could effect things that cannot be done by the power of those qualities alone.

Finally, whatever virtues and properties the stars might have, they are so universal that none could fail to encompass the true condition and power of lower bodies. Therefore, they act upon all things together, which is the characteristic of a universal cause <term>Universal Cause</term><note>A "universal cause" is a broad influence—like the sun providing light—that affects everything at once, whereas a "particular cause" is a specific event or choice that affects only one thing.</note>. But the diversity of what happens and what occurs takes its origin entirely from immediate causes, whether they be free <note>Referring to human free will.</note>, natural, or fortuitous. All of these things we have undertaken to defend with that purpose...

<summary>Pico concludes Book III by citing Aristotle on the nature of chance and begins Book IV by outlining his "concessionary" debate strategy, systematically dismantling the idea that stars exert specific control over earthly events.</summary>

...so that astrologers may understand, when they feel otherwise and assert things not confessed or manifest, that they say things confirmed neither by certain reasons, nor evident experiments, nor the authority of **Plato** or **Aristotle**. Instead, these things are placed in ambiguity: just as they are defended by some, so they are attacked by many. If all astrology relied on these [ambiguities], and if it did not place even more untrustworthy foundations for itself, it would not be entirely ruinous to me, but merely tottering—that is, my opinion of it would waver rather than fall. But even if we grant to astrologers as much as the theologian **Thomas Aquinas** <note>Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the influential Dominican friar and philosopher whose "Summa Contra Gentiles" Pico cites below.</note> and many philosophers contend can be granted—not without reason pushing back—they will still receive far less than is necessary for them to receive, if some form of astrology is to be defended as existing not only among us, but by its own nature even among the angelic minds themselves.

<margin>What Thomas grants to astrologers</margin>
For Thomas will grant them the maximum that can be granted without an open slander of the truth: namely, that the "outpourings" <note>Original Latin: *defluuia*, referring to the celestial influences or emanations believed to flow from the stars to the Earth.</note> of all the planets reach us with power, and that different stars have different properties—not only heating, cooling, moistening, and drying, but more hidden <term>occult</term> <note>In the Renaissance, "occult" referred to properties that were not immediately apparent to the five senses (like magnetism), rather than "magic" in the modern sense.</note> properties. From these, the crowd of earthly things receives various gifts; thus, not every property possessed by humans and the rest of lower physical nature comes from their immediate causes, but some even come from the heavenly bodies.

<margin>There is no astrology even if this is granted</margin>
Even if we precariously grant all of this to the astrologers, we will show that this "art" will still not exist, even if it prophesies mostly from the stars about those things which can happen or be indicated—even if all those things we mentioned actually occur. Thus, the current dispute will utterly overturn that astrology which was shaken or brought to its death in the previous book, leaving behind any hope of peace or indulgence.

## Chapter II: Fortuitous things do not come from the heavens.

<note>Initial letter 'F' missing; space likely left for a rubricated drop cap.</note>ortuitous things <note>Original Latin: *Fortuitæ res*, things happening by chance or luck.</note>, by which we call men fortunate or unfortunate through good or bad outcomes, are primarily those which are thought of as "fated" and hanging from a heavenly decree; thus they are the greatest part and most powerful subject matter of astrological predictions. For things that have immediate causes in themselves, such as conditions of the mind and body, do not seem to require a superior and more hidden cause as much as those things which we say happen randomly or by chance—since they seem to happen without an immediate cause. Such things include: sailing or traveling successfully or unsuccessfully; engaging in trade; finding treasure while digging the earth; encountering bandits or wild beasts; pleasing the king; escaping danger; obtaining good or bad servants; entering a house just as it is about to collapse; and other things of this sort which happen to wretched and truly sick mortals <note>Pico is likely referencing a poetic trope regarding the fragility of human life.</note> beyond their planning and beyond their expectation. Regarding these matters, since they are entirely out of our hands and come upon us from the outside, we most desire to hear the opinion of astrologers. Otherwise, one might know the condition of their body from a mirror or a physician, just as they know the quality of their mind from themselves—if indeed they have a mind. But what we call "fortuitous" are those things which human curiosity most seeks through the divining arts. Therefore, we will prove that these can in no way be foreseen from the sky, and by no other reason than that used by **Thomas Aquinas**—especially in that place where he seems to favor the opinion of astrologers: namely, in the third book of *Against the Gentiles* <note>Original: *Contra Gentes*. Pico refers to Book III, Chapter 92, where Aquinas discusses whether celestial bodies cause human fortune.</note>, where he seems to say that men are made both fortunate and unfortunate by the heavens. That reasoning is as follows:

<margin>The reasoning of brother Thomas</margin>
The power of a heavenly body does not act by intellect or choice, but just as nature acts; it is the property of nature to tend toward one thing. Therefore, an effect which is not "one" <note>In Aristotelian logic, a "natural" effect must be a single, unified result of a cause, not a coincidence of two unrelated events.</note> cannot be produced by a natural cause by itself...

<summary>Pico argues that even if we grant Thomas Aquinas's view that stars possess hidden physical properties, astrology remains a failed science. He begins Chapter 2 by asserting that "chance" events, which astrologers claim to predict, cannot be caused by the heavens because natural causes produce unified, not coincidental, effects.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Pico's critique of astrology, specifically focusing on the philosophical definition of "accidental" or "fortuitous" events. In the previous page, he began addressing Thomas Aquinas's views on celestial influence; here, he uses Aristotelian logic to argue why the stars cannot be the cause of "luck" or "chance" occurrences.</meta>

<page-num>4</page-num>
<header>Book</header>

...can [be]: but those things that concur by accident and happen to coincide with one another: these are not truly "one," but only "one by accident" <note>Original: *per accidens*. In scholastic philosophy, this refers to a coincidental connection rather than a natural, essential unity.</note>. Therefore, a concurrence of this kind, which we usually call "fortuitous," can have no natural cause through itself <note>Original: *per se*—meaning a direct, primary cause</note>; but rather, a celestial natural cause [is not possible], as we were saying. Therefore, the heavens cannot be the cause of such fortuitous things through themselves. 

<margin>An example of the same</margin> 

He adds an example to this, which simultaneously demonstrates how the heaven is not a direct cause of these events, but only an accidental one. He says: someone is prompted by the heavens to dig a grave; it happens that there is a treasure in that grave. Therefore, while digging the grave, he finds the treasure. This finding was not caused by the heaven except by accident—since it is only by accident that the grave and the location of the treasure are the same place. For prompting a person to dig a grave in which treasure is hidden so that he may find the treasure belongs to a **rational and intelligent cause**, whose property it is to relate and order one thing to another. It does not belong to a **natural cause**, which is only directed toward one specific outcome as we have said—and no one will deny that a celestial ray is such a natural cause.

### Chapter III: How God is the cause of fortuitous things; how angels are; how the heavens; how we are; and how fortune is.

Since mention is being made of fortuitous things, it will be worth the effort to explain more deeply what their causes are according to the philosophers and theologians. For from what we have said so far, it might be estimated that we are merely referring to "blind chance" and "recklessness," and that astrologers should not be blamed for trying to preserve order and certain causes even in these extraordinary events—so that nothing in nature happens recklessly or without a legitimate cause. 

If any such cause must be considered, that which the astrologers accept seems most likely to be chosen: namely, the heavens. For they judge that nothing below the heavens is so powerful over all things that happen under the heavens; nor do they look above the heavens [to God], because many things seem to happen unworthily, beyond merit and reason—things which suggest a certain necessity of a physical cause rather than the providence of one who chooses. Therefore, to push away these doubts, it will be useful to discuss certain matters more broadly regarding these things, so that after we have shown that these cannot be governed by the heavens, we may open up from where and how they *are* governed. 

<margin>What are called fortuitous things.</margin> 

We say that "fortuitous" things are those that happen **outside the intention of the one acting**. For this reason, **fortune** is only spoken of in human affairs, which alone are done by counsel and reason. 

<margin>Example.</margin> 

An example like the one we used above: a farmer proposes to dig the earth, thinking of the cultivation of the soil, not a treasure. It happens that he finds a treasure; we say it was done "fortuitously," nor do we give any cause for the found treasure other than **fortune**. By "fortune," however, we do not mean a deity or a nature, or any thing that is entirely a cause of such an event; rather, we only exclude a direct cause by saying it was "done by fortune," as if we were to say: "it happened by chance, not from some specific cause." For the digging of the earth cannot be called the cause [of finding the treasure], nor is the earth, insofar as it is earth, the cause of the location. But it happened that the same spot of earth was simultaneously the hiding place of the treasure. Therefore, if you ask by what cause it happened that this man dug up the treasure, there is none to bring forward; since not one cause, but a fortuitous concurrence of many causes brought this about. 

Therefore, those who denied that fortune exists in things were in error; an opinion which **Aristotle** <note>The Greek philosopher (384–322 BC) whose logic dominated Renaissance thought.</note> tears down in the second book of his *Physics* <note>Original: *physicæ auscultationis*—literally "Lectures on Nature," the standard title for Aristotle's Physics.</note> and the sixth book of his *First Philosophy* <term>First Philosophy</term> <note>Aristotle’s own term for Metaphysics, the study of the fundamental nature of reality and first causes.</note>. They were in error, however, not because they thought that things which are unforeseen and fortuitous to us...

<summary>Pico argues that fortuitous events, like finding treasure while digging a grave, cannot be caused by the stars because natural causes act uniformly and lack the intelligence to coordinate separate coincidences. He begins to define "fortune" using Aristotelian logic as a concurrence of independent causes rather than a mystical force.</summary>
