<meta>This page continues Pico's argument regarding the nature of chance. Having previously established that natural causes (like the stars) cannot be the direct cause of coincidental events, he now transitions to explaining how these events, while seemingly "random" to humans, are actually part of a higher order governed by God, angels, or spiritual powers.</meta>

<page-num>4</page-num>
<header>Book 4</header>

<note>The text begins mid-argument, discussing how higher intelligences perceive what we call "luck."</note> One might think that these things could be known to higher minds; for this reason, nothing is "fortune" in an absolute or simple sense. Rather, one might think that events of this kind necessarily have a proximate cause <note>A "proximate cause" is the immediate, direct reason something happens.</note> through themselves. Yet, those who think this do not understand how something that is **one by accident** <note>original: *unum per accidens*. This refers to a "coincidence"—two things happening at once that have no natural connection, like a man being both a musician and a soldier.</note> does not require a single, direct cause. 

For example, there is no single cause for the same man being both a musician and a warrior. Otherwise, if they existed together because of some specific cause, they would have a natural order between them derived from that cause. However, things that happen to each other by chance—such as a warrior being a musician, or a musician being a warrior—it is clear that these have no inherent order. Therefore, such a coincidence has no active cause "through itself" <note>original: *per se*</note>, but only "by accident." 

In this way, the **Peripatetics** <note>The "Peripatetics" were the followers of Aristotle's school of philosophy.</note> correctly defend the existence of chance and fortune, thereby removing "necessity" from human affairs. However, 

<margin>Another detestable error</margin> 

some among them err more detestably than those who take away chance by denying it. They claim that these things happen by chance in a way that implies no counsel from a higher cause and no providence. Indeed, this most pestilential error sprouts from the root of impiety, by which it is believed that human affairs are either not known by the higher beings, or if they are known, they are not cared for. This error will be refuted elsewhere with arguments, where there will be a dispute against impious philosophers. For now, let it be rejected as a false judgment, based on the authority of all theologians and the entire family of philosophers, including **Aristotle**, the prince of the Peripatetics. In his books on morals—both where he discusses happiness and where he discusses "good fortune"—he clearly asserted that men, and especially the wise, are an object of care to the gods. He also stated that all sensible things, past and future, are known to God, and that we are directed by Him in these matters. He confirmed this also in the book *On the Universe* <note>original: *de mundo*</note>, 

<margin>Aristotle's book *On the Universe*, worthy of wisdom.</margin>

a book certainly worthy of Aristotle's wisdom, which he concluded with that Platonic sentiment regarding divine justice as if with the finishing touch of an oracle. 

If, therefore, the gods care for human things—for we speak in this way so as to include **guardian angels** and the ordered ranks of intelligent causes serving the counsel and providence of the true God—if, I say, this is true, no one will doubt that men are often prompted by them to do things which were not foreseen or foreknown by the man himself, but which were arranged by those spirits with the wisest foreknowledge. 

The most common example is that of **two servants** sent to the same place by their master so that they might meet, though they themselves are ignorant of the master’s will. Their meeting and concurrence is unexpected and "fortuitous" to the servants themselves, but it was foreseen and pre-arranged by the master. Likewise, a guardian angel, caring for the benefit of a poor farmer, can invite him by hidden impulses to dig in a certain place where the angel knows there is a treasure. Thus, what was "fortune" for the poor man was "counsel" for the angel. 

<margin>Augustine</margin> 

Reflecting on this, **Aurelius Augustine**, in the fifth book of *The City of God*, says: "We say that those causes which are called fortuitous (from which 'fortune' also takes its name) are not non-existent, but hidden; and we attribute them either to the will of the true God or to that of certain spirits." He said "of certain spirits" because this can be done by both good angels and evil ones, although the evil ones cannot do everything that the good can, nor do they have the same goal. For the good, the goal is the common good of men; for the evil, it is harm. However, the divine goodness frustrates their malice by ordering and reducing to good whatever they have perpetrated with an evil will. 

But these matters are discussed more widely elsewhere. 

<margin>Definition of fortune assigned by Proclus.</margin>

**Proclus** the Platonic, in his commentaries on the *Timaeus*, for the same reason as Augustine, defined **Fortune** as: "a power of the mediating spirits <note>original: *demonicam potestatem*. In Neoplatonism, a "daemon" is a mediating spirit between gods and humans, not necessarily an "evil demon."</note> that gathers together causes that were otherwise separated from one another." This does not differ from the Peripatetic determination which says that fortune is a cause producing an effect "by accident" within human choice; however, one looks at the more remote and hidden cause, while the other looks at the proximate and known cause. For Proclus spoke of "mediating power" because the Platonists call all minds placed between humans and the higher intellects by that name...

<summary>Pico reconciles Aristotelian "chance" with Divine Providence, arguing that what humans perceive as random luck is actually the result of higher spiritual beings (angels or "daemons") coordinating events. He cites Aristotle, St. Augustine, and Proclus to prove that God cares for human affairs through these hidden causes.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Pico's argument that astrology cannot account for coincidental "lucky" events. He provides a specific thought experiment involving a character named Lucius to demonstrate that while a physical cause (like a star) might move a person's body, only an intelligent cause (like God) can coordinate that movement with an external event to create what we call "good fortune."</meta>

<page-num>4</page-num>
<header>Book 4</header>

...removed from our knowledge. Let us illustrate with examples how this happens and what role the heavens play in these matters. Let us take an example. Lucius was at home and had no business to attend to outside; yet he decided in his mind to go out. As soon as he left the house, the house collapsed. You would call him lucky for having avoided such imminent danger in this way. 

If you ask a secular philosopher <note>original: *male pio philosopho*, literally an "impiously-minded philosopher," likely referring to those who exclude divine providence from their physics.</note> for the cause of this, he will answer that it happened by chance and that no other cause should be sought. But if you ask an astrologer, he refers this to some benign radiation from a lucky planet, by whose help Lucius was defended from ruin. However, he is mistaken for the reason explained above: because inciting Lucius to leave so that he might not perish under the ruin requires the planning and reason of an intelligent agent. 

No ray of Jupiter or any other star possesses such reason. The only thing the heavens could do is make Lucius's mind more inclined toward movement than toward rest—just as this could also result from his own physical temperament, by which some men are naturally more sedentary and others more prone to walking. Thus, if any constellation was the cause of this good outcome, it would be from those that make us vigorous and active—which they call "Martian" <note>Influenced by the planet Mars, associated with energy and movement.</note>—rather than some "beneficent" force acting as a defender against evil, as is often claimed. 

Indeed, a physical ray cannot coordinate two independent things: the act of leaving and the protection from the ruin. Just as it was lucky for Lucius, who chose to leave for the sake of a walk, to escape the danger of death, so too for a constellation (if we assume such a thing helped him move) it is entirely accidental and unintentional that it freed him from the ruin. 

Consequently, even if an astrologer identifies what celestial influence is then flowing into Lucius, he knows nothing except that Lucius will be eager for movement and walking. But the fact that he would flee the house and the danger simultaneously cannot be foreknown by any birth chart <term>thema: a horoscope or astrological map of the sky at birth</term> or by any logic. 

Therefore, only one cause remains for which this event could be foreseen and not be a matter of chance: the Divine <note>Referring to God or Divine Providence.</note>, nudging Lucius's mind from within and instigating his departure so that he would not perish under the house about to fall. This deity understands that the house will fall and can coordinate Lucius's exit toward that specific end. 

Regarding a physical ray, neither can be said. For this reason, no philosopher has ever defined fortune as a decree of the heavens, or a result of one's birth, or anything drawn from astrological dogma. Instead, they referred it either to chance itself—the unexpected meeting of causes—or to intellectual causes coordinating things by their own counsel, which escape the limits of our own foresight. 

Thus, that great leader of philosophers, Aristotle <margin>Aristotle.</margin>, when discussing at great length what "good fortune" and "bad fortune" are, and what it means to be lucky or unlucky, does not mention celestial constellations when making his determination—nor even in his inquiry and debate. This is because he did not think the opinion of the "nativity-casters" <term>genethliaci: astrologers who predict a person's life based on their birth chart</term> was even worth a philosopher’s doubt. 

Instead, he believed it should be numbered among the delusions of charlatans, among fables and stage-tricks, rather than among the serious controversies of philosophy. Therefore, Aristotle himself, in that treatise after a diligent examination of the whole question, defines it thus: when things go well for us by chance, it usually happens in two ways. Either we stumble into a good outcome completely unawares, or we are led toward it by an impulse of the mind without conscious planning or deliberation. We are so ignorant of the reason for this impulse that we follow it obstinately, as if "by oar and sail" <note>original: *rhemo veloque*, an idiom meaning with all one's might or at full speed.</note>. 

He thinks the first type should be attributed to chance, and the second to divine motion, by which the will itself is inclined through hidden impulses. Those who experience this usually say: "My mind has a presentiment of I know not what," or "I cannot want otherwise," or "I am being pulled here," or "My mind will not focus on anything else." And so, while they can give no reason for their own plan, they are nevertheless so set in their pleasure and so fixed in their mind...

<summary>Pico uses the story of Lucius escaping a falling house to argue that astrology cannot predict "luck," as stars only influence physical impulses, not the coordination of events. He concludes by citing Aristotle, who attributed such "gut feelings" or lucky escapes to divine intervention rather than the stars.</summary>

# Book IV
<page-num>Book 4</page-num>

<margin>
Aristotle, who [speaks] correctly concerning God and the soul.
</margin>

...correctly assert. In this place, the philosopher Aristotle <note>Pico often cites Aristotle to provide a rational, philosophical foundation for his theological arguments, here focusing on the idea that God is the ultimate "unmoved mover" and source of all knowledge.</note> affirms that all things are known to God—as we said above—and that nothing is more sublime than God from which our will could be moved. He states that this is a great argument for immortality. From all of this, it can be gathered that human affairs happen sometimes by **chance**, sometimes by **nature**, sometimes by **choice**, and sometimes by **divine counsel**. 

For although nothing happens outside of God’s counsel, we distinguish these categories so that we may say things are done **divinely** which human minds, if left to themselves, would not accomplish, but which they do when moved by a specific impulse of the divine power. This is in addition to that general assistance of the highest power which is present to all things, and without which nothing—not even the smallest thing—can exist or happen. Thus, although it is characteristic of man to act by **choice**, he is nonetheless sometimes ruled by **nature** when, surrendered to the movements of bodily affections <note>original: *affectionum corporalium*, referring to physical urges or emotions like anger or hunger that can bypass logical thinking.</note>, he does not wait for the judgment of reason. 

These things are explained by one example: a king declares war on his neighbors. Perhaps the nature of the king is warlike, greedy, or restless; perhaps he is led not so much by passion as by reason, or by the law of claiming what is his, or for the sake of repaying an injury, or for other reasons. Beyond all these, a special counsel of God can intervene—always just, always rational—though its justice or reason is not always open to everyone. It is the counsel of God, I say, that both animates the heart to undertake war and arms it for victory as He pleases. This is the way the prophet Jeremiah speaks: 

->*Behold, I will send and take all the families of the north, says the Lord, and Nebuchadnezzar the king of Babylon, my servant; and I will bring them against this land, and against its inhabitants, and against all these nations round about.*<- <note>Jeremiah 25:9. Pico uses this to show that even a pagan king can be a "servant" or tool of God's plan without knowing it.</note>

And in Isaiah: 

->*Woe to Assyria, the rod of my anger! The staff in their hand is my indignation. I will send him against a deceitful nation, and against the people of my wrath I will command him, to take the spoil, and to take the prey, and to tread them down like the mire of the streets. But he will not think so, nor will his heart so estimate it.*<- <note>Isaiah 10:5–7. This reinforces the idea that human actors have their own motivations (greed/war), while God uses those actions for a higher purpose.</note>

### Chapter 4: That if anything is done by us that seems to exceed our powers, it should not be attributed to the heavens, but rather either to angels or to God. And therein many things concerning fate, and how divine providence does not take away our freedom.

But when something is done by a man that seems to exceed his powers, our mortal nature is usually shaken by unusual and admirable events. Overcome by the magnitude of these things, we suspect the force of a more powerful cause acting in the man and through the man, which exceeds the capacity of human strength. 

By this suspicion, those who have only "eyes of flesh" <note>original: *carneos tantum oculos*, meaning a purely physical or materialistic perspective.</note> are swept away toward the heavens <note>The physical stars and planets.</note>, than which they see nothing greater and feel nothing more powerful. They are so possessed of a "bad mind" <note>original: *malae... mentis*, suggesting a spiritual or intellectual error.</note> that they refer these events to a cause that is mindless and devoid of knowledge—the stars—to which they believe even the full counsel of the human mind is not sufficient. 

But if they should respond that those things are indeed arranged and ordered by God, but are fulfilled by God *through* the heavens and the stars (whose power and efficacy are so great), they are proven to be speaking most absurdly. For if these causes intervene between God and us, just as they are lower than God, so they ought to be higher than men. It is not fitting that things performed by reason and counsel—as our human actions are—should be arranged by the First Author <note>God.</note> through irrational bodies <note>The stars, which Pico argues are physical objects without minds.</note>.

# Book IV
<page-num>Page 4</page-num>

[...of the] king: but just as He [God] rules and moderates the elemental mass—as something inferior—through the celestial realm, which is better: so it is fitting for human affairs to be governed not by the mystery of bodies <note>The "mystery of bodies" refers to the influence of physical stars and planets, which Pico is arguing against.</note> but of **angels**, who by nature and dignity are the mediators between us and God. Therefore, when you descend from God to the earth, descend through heaven; when you descend from God to <margin>Prophets</margin> men, descend through angels. Thus, we see the angels of the Persians, the Greeks, and the Hebrews providing for their peoples in the writings of the prophets. And in <margin>Plato.</margin> Plato, and among all the Platonists <note>Followers of Plato’s philosophy who believed in a hierarchy of spiritual beings.</note>, we find "local gods" set over cities, kingdoms, and men. These beings were also <margin>Isidore the Elder.</margin> mentioned by Aristotle, by the elder Isidore, and after Isidore, by <margin>Clement of Alexandria</margin> Clement of Alexandria in his *Stromata* <note>A work of early Christian philosophy; the title means "Miscellanies."</note>. 

Nor should it disturb us that sometimes certain things seem to happen to us unworthily or unjustly, causing us to more willingly resort to the cause of "natural necessity" <note>Referring to the idea that things happen because they *must* due to physical laws or fate, rather than by a divine plan.</note> rather than a deliberate plan. For it would surely be ridiculous if the lowlier slaves of a city presumed to judge the plans of their prince; much more ridiculous—or rather, sacrilegious—is our rashness in claiming for ourselves the judgment of the "first order" and of divine wisdom. This wisdom extends the eye of providence and the ray of its goodness not merely to the utility of one man, one family, or one city, but to the entire world; and not just to the present age, but to all ages equally. 

Do we little men—nay, we owls, we moles, truly asses, and truly oxen, and indeed judging like those of the "seventh rank" <note>original: *septimi*. This likely refers to those furthest removed from the "First Cause" (God) in the Neoplatonic hierarchy, representing the lowest level of understanding.</note>—call God to an examination? We who more often judge not even with that tiny bit of judgment we possess, but rather from the "sickness of the mind," complaining that whatever is done is "unjust" simply because we ourselves would not wish it to be done. 

Who would not have loudly exclaimed that God was "sleeping" when the just **Joseph** was being sold by his brothers? Who would not say there is no God when that same man received prison as the reward for his chastity? But look at him soon after: a king in Egypt, or second only to the king. See him redeeming his father and his entire family from famine. See him noble in prophecy. You will not then deny that those earlier events were done by God, through which, in their own proper order, these later things were eventually reached. 

But if you look even higher, you will understand that the matter was led from that impious trade [the selling of Joseph] to this end: that the entire people descending into Egypt, and long worn down there by the Egyptian kings, should be so gloriously asserted into liberty by **Moses**. God’s power was confirmed by so many prodigies and manifested by so many oracles: in Pharaoh, in Egypt, in the Hebrew people, through the Law, and through so many miracles of divine majesty—sometimes through benevolence, sometimes through justice. These events prefigured those ineffable mysteries of the divine incarnation that would come in the future under **Jesus**. 

Truly, only a madman could be led to suspect that anything happens without reason in human affairs. Only such a person would believe that we are governed not by the best and wisest God, but either by an evil demon (as the <margin>Manicheans</margin> Manicheans <note>A dualistic religion that believed the world was a battleground between a good God of light and an evil god of matter.</note> believe), or by the necessity of the stars' revolution (as the **astrologers** believe), or by haphazard chance and rashness (as many who philosophize poorly believe). 

Furthermore, whenever you perceive wars and slaughters being stirred up, the devastation of cities, and the overturning of kingdoms: do not think—like those charlatans—that the cause is a "mixture of two rays" <note>An astrological term for a planetary conjunction or aspect.</note> or a shadow interposed in its natural course between the sun and the moon. Instead, recognize the **counsel of God**, either punishing the wicked or testing the good. This is why that famous leader [Attila] was called the "**Scourge of God**" <note>Attila the Hun (c. 406–453), whose invasions of the Roman Empire were seen by Christians as a divine punishment for sin.</note>; and another closer to our own age said he was not a man, but the "wrath of God and of the world."

# Book IV

<margin>Herodotus.</margin>
...devastation. That wise Persian in the writings of Herodotus <note>A reference to a story in Herodotus's *Histories* (Book 9), where a Persian guest at a banquet in Thebes foretells the coming destruction of the Persian army.</note> spoke rightly when, dining at a banquet in Thebes, he revealed that he had a certain premonition of the future slaughter of his people. For when a Theban urged him to report this to the commander of the army and to discourage him from an undertaking that would have such an unhappy outcome, he replied that it was inevitable for a man: what God has ordained must come to pass. For this reason, he believed his own words—specifically his warning to the commander—would not be believed, since God had so decreed it. Consequently, he too followed Mardonius <note>original: "Maridonium"; a Persian general during the Greco-Persian Wars.</note> because they were bound by necessity. It is pleasing that he spoke of a necessity born not of the stars, but of **divine counsel**. If anyone chooses to call this "fate," Augustine says they will "think rightly, though they speak poorly" <note>original: "rectius sentiet quam loquatur"; Augustine argued that while the word "fate" is often used superstitiously, if one means the "will of God," the underlying thought is correct.</note>.

<margin>On fate. Augustine. Fate is understood in four ways.</margin>
Furthermore, this term "fate," as far as can be gathered from the monuments of the ancients, is accepted in a fourfold sense: either fate is **nature** itself; or it is a **series and order of causes** producing all things by a necessary connection; or it is the **constitution of the stars** at the moment someone is born, conceived, or begins a task; or it is the **execution of the divine plan**, a certain and inevitable success.

<margin>The first mode.</margin>
The first meaning is accepted by Alexander of Aphrodisias <note>A celebrated Greek commentator on Aristotle (c. 200 AD).</note> in his book *On Fate* addressed to the Emperors Severus and Antoninus. For he grants that the fates exist in such a way 

<margin>Alexander</margin>
that fate is nature itself, which is a principle distinct from choice. Therefore, by "fate," fire heats, water is wet, and the sun shines. So too, when someone dies from a dissolution of the body's temperament <note>The balance of "humors" or physical qualities that kept a person healthy in ancient medicine.</note>, he dies by fate. However, if he is thrown from a horse or killed by swords, 

<margin>Virgil.</margin>
he does not die by fate. In this manner, Virgil says of Dido as she prepared a violent death for herself: *But because she perished neither by fate nor by a deserved death* <note>original: "Sed quia nec fato debita nec morte peribat"; from the *Aeneid*, Book 4. This implies her suicide was outside the natural span of her life.</note>. Astrologers, however, would have most especially cast that kind of death back onto fate. Thus says Demosthenes.

<margin>Aristotle</margin>
And indeed, no one would deny fate in this sense, just as no one denies nature. In this way, Aristotle also, in the fifth book of his *Physics* <note>original: "physicae auscultationis"</note>, spoke of "fatal generations"—that is, those which happen according to nature. Nor is there any doubt that when we understand fate in this way, many things happen **beyond fate**, just as many things happen beyond nature, either by chance or by our own choice, or, as 

<margin>The second mode of fate. Alexander</margin>
Alexander of Aphrodisias himself says in that same place, by the counsel of the gods. Those, however, who introduced the second opinion, considered that nothing happens in nature that does not happen by necessity, if one were to embrace all causes at once. For those who say many things happen outside of necessity defend this in both natural and "arbitrary" <note>Refers to things involving *arbitrium* or free will.</note> matters. In natural things, they argue that not everything which happens naturally happens by necessity, since the work of nature can be hindered. In arbitrary things, they argue that our choice and will are free. Their opponents, conversely, insist: in natural things, if something is hindered, 

<margin>Refutation of the second mode.</margin>
it is necessarily hindered, because even that hindrance comes from a natural cause, which must eventually be traced back to the supreme nature—that is, the heavens. They claim the heavens act by necessity. But they are deceived; for while the hindrance may have had a natural cause, it was one that itself could either be or not be, and could have been hindered while it was acting. Therefore, that contingent <note>In philosophy, a "contingent" event is one that is possible but not certain; it could happen or not happen.</note> hindrance was not necessary. And if you press us again regarding that hindrance—namely, that its natural cause would likewise, naturally and necessarily, either be hindered or not—I reply to you: if you believe the world is eternal, or that it will proceed to infinity from a contingent cause...

<summary>Pico defines the four historical meanings of "fate," focusing on the Aristotelian view of fate as "nature." He argues against the idea that every event is a necessary result of a causal chain, asserting instead that many things happen through free choice or chance.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Pico della Mirandola’s philosophical investigation into the four definitions of "Fate." He is currently refuting the idea that everything is bound by a "first necessary cause" in nature, arguing instead that natural events are contingent and that human will remains free even under divine providence.</meta>

# Book IV

...a contingent cause: among which the order is always accidental. It will never arrive at a single, first, necessary cause from which necessity might be imposed upon everything following it. This is because no such cause exists within the realm of natural things; not even the celestial cause <note>The influence of the stars and planets.</note> is of this kind, since its operations are easily obstructed by both physical matter and other competing lower causes. 

However, if you agree with theological truth regarding the creation of the world, you will escape that **troublesome regression** <note>A logical "infinite regress" where one cause requires another forever; Pico argues God is the starting point that breaks this loop.</note> and arrive at the first contingent institution of things, through which necessity is removed rather than confirmed. Some argue that our "elections" <term>elections: the act of choosing or exercising free will</term> bring about necessity even more irrationally, claiming the will chooses nothing that has not been pre-judged by reason, and that it is not in our power to judge or will as we do. But these people rely on false assumptions, as has been shown by others and will be explained by us elsewhere.

<margin>The third mode of fate is to be refuted throughout the whole work.</margin>
These specific matters require their own separate treatments. Furthermore, they do not greatly pertain to the refutation of the astrologers, whose "third interpretation of fate" is what must be refuted throughout this entire work. This third view differs from the first opinion because it makes the celestial nature the origin not only of natural things, but also of **fortuitous** <note>original: "fortuitarum"; things that happen by chance or luck.</note> events. This view thinks poorly of lower causes and even worse of celestial ones. For although the heavens exist by nature, those "constellations" which astrologers invent—based on the positions of stars, locations, signs, houses, and the like—are not natural causes; they are **fictitious**. The operation of the heavens does not depend on a single initial moment <note>Such as a birth chart or the moment of a project's start.</note>, nor are they responsible for things that belong properly to lower causes, as we have already declared and as the following pages will further clarify.

<margin>Approval of the fourth interpretation of fate.</margin>
There remains the **fourth meaning of fate**, which is theological in the same way the first was physical. Both, however, are true: it signifies the series and order of causes depending on **divine counsel**. Under this definition, our liberty is in no danger. We ourselves are among these causes; in this **dance of fate** <note>original: "chorea fati"; a striking metaphor suggesting humans are active participants in the cosmic order, not just passive victims.</note>, we do not merely suffer or endure, but we act. Whether you focus on God’s **foresight** or His **providence**—that is, whether you consider His mind foreknowing all things or His will disposing all things according to His pleasure—no harm is done to our free actions. For if we consider providence, why should I not freely do what God foresaw I would do? If what He foresaw will indeed happen, then I will certainly freely do what He foresaw I would freely do.

<margin>Our liberty is not taken away by God's prescience or providence.</margin>
Furthermore, because what occurs is what He willed—and He willed me to be **free**—I shall act freely in whatever I do, unless He Himself were to take my liberty away. Certainly, God not only foreknew our wills but also pre-ordained them. When Gregory of Nyssa and John of Damascus <note>Two influential early Christian theologians (Church Fathers) from the 4th and 8th centuries.</note> seemed to deny this, they did so only to offer a warning.

<margin>The opinion of Damascene and Gregory of Nyssa is explained.</margin>
While other things happen through the divine will, our choices are arranged by that will in cooperation with our own. Thus, not only the outcomes of our thoughts, but the thoughts themselves, our counsels, and our purposes are in God's hands. It is written that the hearts of kings are in the hand of God, but in truth, He moderates the hearts of all. In matters that pertain neither to vice nor virtue, He inclines the will as He pleases to fulfill His decrees. At other times, He works the virtues within us, both beginning the work and perfecting what He has started. Sometimes, when people move from virtue toward vice, He turns them back toward justice, either applying the "teacher’s rod" <note>A metaphor for divine discipline or trials.</note> out of mercy, or crushing the one who is dazed <note>original: "hallucinatus"; wandering or blinded by error.</note> through His justice. He always makes all things either good or, at the very least, occasions for good. We have said this much concerning fate, providence, and the governance of human affairs because these things are useful to know in their own right, and also for **uprooting the vanity of astrology**.

<summary>Pico distinguishes between astrological fate (which he calls fictitious) and theological fate (divine providence). He argues that God’s foreknowledge does not eliminate human free will, as God wills for humans to act freely within the cosmic order.</summary>
<keywords>Fate, free will, divine providence, astrology, Gregory of Nyssa, John of Damascus, celestial causes, contingency</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Pico della Mirandola’s refutation of the "third mode of fate" (astrological determinism). On the previous page, he argued that natural events are contingent and that the stars do not impose necessity. Here, he transitions to the importance of human "prudence" and divine providence over the "rays" of the planets.</meta>

...necessary: so that when we see something happen or occur that seems either greater or more orderly than can be attributed to mere chance or human effort, we should recognize therein not the power of physical rays <note>original: "corporalium radiorum"; the author refers to the "rays" or influences that astrologers believed emanated from the planets</note>, but the care and power of divine counsel and angelic ministry working alongside human liberty. 

It is clear from what we have said how future events can be foreseen, and how they can be guarded against when they are evil. For if human affairs happened only by chance, no foreknowledge of the future would be possible. However, since they occur through human and divine counsel, human reason is able to make some conjectures about them. Only those inspired by the divine, however, can foresee them with absolute certainty—a fact confirmed by the predictions and oracles of the prophets. Those who are **prudent** <term>prudence: in this context, "prudentia" refers to practical wisdom and the ability to make good choices</term> are closest to the prophets, though they remain at a very great distance from them. 

Hence the saying of Euripides: *The best seer is the one who guesses well.* <note>original: "Qui bene coniectauerit is uates optimus eſto"</note> Thus, in securing a happy outcome and avoiding misfortunes, the most vital thing is to make God favorable to oneself through purity of mind, pious works, and most holy vows. After this, a man should look out for himself through his own **prudence**. For although fortune <note>In the sense of "luck" or "random chance."</note> may have much power in many matters—and the disposition of the certain divine will has the most power, or rather, total power in all things—it is nevertheless necessary that a right way of living carries great weight in these affairs. Otherwise, we would have to say this gift of reason was bestowed upon us by God in vain. 

Therefore, that famous author <note>A reference to the Roman poet Juvenal.</note> said rightly that no divinity is absent if there is prudence, but that it is we who make "Fortune" a goddess and place her in the heavens. For this <margin>Plato</margin> reason, Plato, in his letter to the Syracusans, recalled that Homeric saying: *The gods took away his mind.* <note>A common phrase in the Iliad regarding those who act foolishly.</note> He suggested that men themselves cast away the mind granted to them, rather than the gods taking it. This is confirmed by that sentence of Euripides, who said that fate is the "daughter of the soul." 

If we therefore establish our lives prudently through natural reason, and secure divine benevolence through pious religion, we may avoid all superstitious vanity. Otherwise, he who hopes to either foresee the future or guard against evils through astrological observations will hear Isaiah speaking to him: <margin>Isaiah</margin> *Evil shall come upon you, and you will not know its dawning; and calamity shall fall upon you which you will not be able to expiate.* <note>Isaiah 47:11. Pico uses this to argue that astrology cannot protect one from divine judgment or unforeseen disaster.</note>

### Chapter V: Neither the past nor matters pertaining to others can be foreseen from any constellation.

Even if the astrologers happened to have some answer regarding fortuitous events—though they can offer nothing either true or even likely—what, I ask, will they answer regarding those things which precede the hour of birth? That is, in what way will they claim that an **efficient cause** <term>efficient cause: the primary agent that brings something into being</term> can be later than its own effects? 

What should we think of those matters which are not only prior to the birth, but also foreign to it? These have their causes not in the constellation of *this* specific birth chart <note>original: "genitura"</note>, but elsewhere. For example, astrologers attempt to pronounce judgment on the natures and fortunes of parents, grandparents, and older brothers based solely on the hour in which a son is born. These relatives and their lives are both prior to that child's constellation and foreign to it; they have held their own order and dependence of fate from their own specific constellations long ago (if, of course, we were to believe that any fate comes from the heavens at all). In the same way, regarding the one who is born, how...

<summary>Pico argues that human prudence and divine providence, not the stars, govern life, and ridicules astrologers for trying to predict a family's past or an elder's fate from a newborn's birth chart.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Pico della Mirandola’s refutation of astrological determinism. Having previously argued that natural events are not strictly dictated by celestial rays, he now focuses on the logical contradictions of "natal" astrology—the belief that the stars at the moment of birth determine physical traits or the fate of one's parents.</meta>

<page-num>IV</page-num>

# Book I

The natal constellation supposedly accomplishes this: that which the infant received many days before the day of birth. For they <note>The astrologers.</note> predict from the **horoscope** <term>thema geniturae: a birth chart or map of the heavens at the moment of birth</term> whether the one being born is male or female, crippled or whole, beautiful or deformed, and regarding other bodily conditions of this kind. Yet concerning all these things, the die had already been cast <note>original: "iacta alea erat"; a reference to the famous phrase of Julius Caesar, meaning the outcome was already determined by biological conception.</note> before the infant was released from the mother's "womb-pouch," <note>original: "bulga"; a rustic or satiric term for a sack or the womb, quoted here from the Roman satirist Lucilius.</note> as Lucilius says. By what logic do astrologers claim for themselves the prediction of all these things? A cause cannot be posterior <note>Coming after.</note> to its effect; nor are things foreseen from heaven in any way other than how an effect is known in advance from its cause. 

<margin>Haly Avenroda. A beautiful imagination.</margin>
**Haly Avenroda** <note>Ali ibn Ridwan (c. 988–1061), a famous Egyptian physician and astrologer who commented on Ptolemy.</note>, in explaining the *books of effects* <note>Ptolemy’s *Tetrabiblos*, the foundational text of Western astrology.</note> by Ptolemy, wished to show—as if solving this very question of ours—in what manner the fates of parents could be foreseen from the horoscopes of brothers and sons. He says that a woman does not conceive every time she joins with a man, but only then when that hour falls whose constellation accords with the constellation of the parents. And since those things which agree with a third thing must also agree with each other, if the horoscopes of all the children agree with the constellations of the parents, then the children’s charts will also agree among themselves. Therefore, they will mutually signify each other’s fates; thus, the nature and fortune of the parents are demonstrated from the horoscope of the brother or the son.

<margin>Refutation.</margin>
Truly, in this astrological "subtlety," I do not know what I should first refute or laugh at. A woman (he says) does not conceive except at an hour when the position of the stars agrees with the stars of the parents. Therefore, the deeds of the parents should be foreseen not from the hour the child is born, but from the hour he is **conceived**. 

<margin>
First reason.
Second.
Third.
</margin>
Furthermore, since the father was born under one sky and the mother under another, how can a single constellation [at the moment of the child's conception] correspond to such diverse constellations? Or, if they think this can happen through some variation of the stars, how will the horoscopes of so many children correspond to the horoscopes of both the father and mother at once? For the significance of the parents must be sought from the same stars and the same regions of the sky in every case. The fortune of the father and mother is investigated by them from the fourth and tenth **houses** <term>places: "locis," referring to the twelve divisions or "houses" of an astrological chart</term> of the sky; likewise from the Sun, Saturn, Venus, and the Moon. 

The arrangement of these in the horoscopes of births is almost always varied and manifold, matching the variety of the children. Do you think that all this variety can avoid differing from the constellations of the parents? It is as if something could fail to disagree with another thing when it first disagrees with itself! Otherwise, it would happen that the same father must necessarily be both fortunate and unfortunate at once: for instance, if one of his sons has the "fourth house" illuminated by favorable rays, while another son has it besieged by unfavorable ones. 

<margin>The response of the common crowd of astrologers.</margin>
To avoid this, the common crowd of astrologers is accustomed to saying that the fates of parents are foreseen not from the horoscopes of all the children, but only from that of the **first-born**. But that refuge is immediately taken away from them regarding the horoscopes of brothers, which they were just trying to show agreed with one another because they all supposedly harmonized with the parents' constellations. 

But why is it necessary to laboriously refute something so evidently frivolous? For by what reason is it defended that a woman only conceives if the one then conceived is destined to be born at an hour whose constellation will be of such a kind as to signify the lot and nature of the parents to an astrologer? It is as if heaven and all of nature were at their service! As if nothing can happen in the universe except in such a way that an astrologer can divine it. Furthermore, how do they solve the point in which the entire force of our argument lies: that an effect cannot be produced by the hour an infant is born, when that effect was already present in the brothers...

already preceded long before in the parents. For we will later refute the opinion of those who say that things are not *produced* by this matter, but only *signified* by the stars. For now, we are disputing against those who believe that the heavens are the *cause* of those things which are predicted from the sky—which is what both **Ptolemy** <note>Claudius Ptolemy (c. 100–170 AD), the most influential astronomer/astrologer of antiquity.</note> and all the masters of that art have believed.

## Chapter VI

### That future events occurring long after the present cannot be produced by the current constellation.

Observe that not only past events—if we consider it rightly—but even those which are to be in the future long after this time, cannot be produced by the present **constellation** <term>constellatio: the specific arrangement of stars and planets at a single moment</term>. This is, however, a very familiar and frequent claim in the predictions of astrologers. For where does one not read among them that a planet in the "oriental" <note>Rising in the East or appearing before the sun.</note> position provides what it promises in the first part of life, and in the "occidental" <note>Setting in the West or appearing after the sun.</note> position in the last? Or that the planet which occupies the **horoscope** <term>horoscopus: here meaning the Ascendant, the sign rising on the eastern horizon</term>, or is the ruler of the horoscope, gives its gifts quickly? That shortly thereafter, the one who possesses the rights of the "tenth place" <note>The Midheaven, or Medium Coeli, representing career and public life.</note> gives its gifts; while the one who is present at or presiding over the "occident" <note>The Descendant, the western horizon.</note> gives them late; and later still the one who was located in the "bottom of the sky" <note>The Imum Coeli, the lowest point of the chart.</note>? And they say countless other things of this kind. Finally, they attest to this: that what the constellations are going to do is not done *while* they are constellations, but rather many years after they have existed. 

Indeed, no example of this wonder appears in any power or natural action (such as they admit the celestial action to be)—namely, that a thing should be considered more effective when it *is not* than when it *is*. Nor does a celestial **influx** <term>influxus: the "flowing in" of power from the stars into the terrestrial world</term> remain in the body like a medicine.

<margin>Response</margin>
But they will perhaps respond that even if that position of the stars has passed, the power nevertheless remains "poured into us," which in its own time—according to the nature of the agent and the suitability of the **matter** <note>In Aristotelian philosophy, "matter" is the physical substance that must be ready to receive a specific "form" or change.</note>—will finally bring its effects into the light.

<margin>Refutation</margin>
I, however, regarding what pertains to the nature of the acting cause, object to them what I objected before: that while the nature and condition of the effect vary according to the condition and various power of the agents, it is equally common to all causes that they produce what they are going to produce more effectively *when they exist* than when they have already ceased to exist for a long time. 

Regarding the **matter**, if they say by chance that one who is born is not immediately made a king or a philosopher even though the heavens promise it, because his age is a barrier, this might seem not to be absurd. But when his age *is* capable of those offices which the birth-stars promised, why does the effect not happen then? For its sufficient cause has already preceded it, and the matter is present, fit and suitable. 

But they say either that the effect ceases for as many years as the planet was distant by degrees of the signs from such a place, or because it held such a place in the **theme of the sky** <term>thema caeli: a horoscope or birth chart</term>; that it cannot provide its benefits except late. This belongs to the choice and judgment of a rational nature dispensing its gifts at whatever time it wishes, rather than a natural cause; such a thing neither is, nor can be, a natural cause. Furthermore, if the heavens indeed gave what they promise immediately, but the disposition of the matter caused the delay, it would not be the task of the astrologer (who considers the heavens) to foreknow the times of events, but rather the task of one who knows the state and condition of the matter. Thus, he would hear from the astrologer *what* is to happen, while he himself would demonstrate to the astrologer *when* it will happen. 

Likewise, regarding their response that a force derived from the heavens is preserved after the constellation passes, I would wish to know from them: where exactly is it preserved? Certainly either in the matter, or in the inferior and secondary causes. Whichever of these (or both) they choose, let them know that neither in the "tide" of flowing and ebbing matter, nor in such a varied and changeable multitude of particular causes, can a celestial power remain the same and stable for such a long time.

<summary>Pico argues that it is logically impossible for a momentary astrological alignment at birth to cause events decades later, as natural causes are most powerful when they are actually present, not long after they have vanished.</summary>

->Book IV<-

## Chapter VII: Concerning the taking of auspices which they call "elections" / how vain and impossible the opinion of the astrologers is.

<margin>I</margin> It is also pleasing to inquire of them regarding that part of astrology which is thought to be most useful for life: which concerns the taking of auspices, commonly called **elections** <term>electiones: the practice of choosing a specific hour to act based on planetary alignment to ensure success</term>. That is, in what way do they understand it to be brought about by the heavens that what we undertake at one particular hour is done successfully, but what is done at another happens to us unsuccessfully? For while all these things are easily said and have a surface appearance of probability, when they are examined more carefully, they are found to be empty and impossible. If someone, they say, begins a journey under such a **constellation** <term>constellatio: the specific arrangement of stars and planets at a single moment</term> of the sky, he will have a favorable travels; he will be kindly received by the king; he will increase his family wealth. Conversely: if at another hour he mounts a horse or boards a ship, he will experience difficult paths and a dangerous voyage. Nor will he achieve, in the end, the purpose for which he undertook the journey or sailing. I confess I do not perceive how all these things are caused by the heavens; let them teach me if they can. Let it be that **Jupiter** <note>Jupiter was traditionally considered the "Greater Benefic," the planet of luck, wealth, and favorable outcomes.</note> casts his rays upon the earth from the ninth region of the sky; they will call this a fortunate constellation for beginning a journey. I ask of them: does this fortunate outflow and "breath" affect the men themselves who are about to set out, or rather the action of the men traveling—that is, the mounting of the horse, or the leaving from the house, or any of those things which are the necessary beginnings of a journey?

If they answer the first—that it affects the men—then those men will be "breathed upon" by the star's benefit even if they do not then first take the journey, whenever it has been their purpose to set out. This is especially true since, according to the astrologers' own opinion, a constellation does not provide what it promises precisely at the moment it exists, but often after a long interval of time. If they answer the second—that it affects the action—they will surely be forced into many delusions in order to protect their position, as they explain to us how that "Jupiter-influenced" mounting of a horse can spread a soft path for the feet, drive away robbers from the road, and, by scattering the clouds, make the sky calm with diffused light. Nor will they have little trouble in explaining how that "outflow" is retained while a journey of perhaps many days is being completed. For there should be a justified suspicion that a power does not descend from heaven upon a man mounting a horse only for it—by a reciprocal logic—to ascend back to heaven the moment he dismounts, as if the traveler always needs a "new Jupiter" every time he has to jump back into the saddle. For to dream of some primordial force consisting of nothing, rooted nowhere, which makes the whole journey soft and happy for you, belongs to men who are sleepwalking or even raving; they weigh nothing of what they speak, giving off a futile sound without a mind behind it.

Let us see again if they fall into the same difficulties in those things which are our "works" rather than our "operations." <margin>Ptolemy</margin> It is the opinion of **Ptolemy** <note>Claudius Ptolemy, whose "Tetrabiblos" was the foundational text for medieval and Renaissance astrology.</note> that if, at the founding of a city, **Mars** <note>The planet associated with war, violence, and iron.</note> occupies the **mid-heaven** <term>medium coeli: the highest point in the sky at a given moment, representing authority and public life</term>, the princes of that city will for the most part perish by the sword. Let Ptolemy explain to us exactly where that blood-stained radiation of Mars is received, which is destined to kill so many subsequent princes by the sword in the course of time? If he wants it to be received in the prince who is then building the city, I will ask how those stones—the foundations of the city—thrown and dug into the ground by the prince's command, could bend and derive those celestial rays (which were turning elsewhere) onto that prince? And how does that harmful influence descend to his descendants and the successors of the kingdom as if by hereditary right, when its "receptacle" <note>Pico is mocking the idea that a physical object like a foundation stone could "capture" a planetary ray and then pass its "poison" down through generations of people who weren't there.</note> has perished and its origin has passed away?

<summary>Pico ridicules the astrological practice of "elections," arguing that it is logically impossible for a fleeting planetary alignment to physically influence a long journey or haunt a city's future rulers through its foundation stones.</summary>

<margin>Haly</margin>
Truly, I do not see how they can respond without blushing to those who ask what power this could have. For perhaps someone will say that it is not in the prince himself—the founder of the city—but rather in the city itself, in the very first stones upon which it is to be raised, that this pestilence is received; as if by a certain pestiferous breath of **Mars** <note>Mars was traditionally associated with war, destruction, and "pestilential" heat.</note>, it will breathe upon all the princes of that city. This war-bringing finding must also be confirmed, they say, by the testimony of **Moses** <note>original: "mosayco testimonio"</note>, who once showed us the expiation of a **leprous house** <note>A reference to Leviticus 14:33–53, where Moses gives instructions for cleansing a house infected with a "leprous" mold; astrologers apparently interpreted this as a celestial or elemental corruption of the building materials.</note> through prophetic inspiration. But I fear that the earth heaped on top and stamped down upon those first stones might not prevent that Martian **foul vapor** <term>mephitim: a noxious, suffocating, or life-threatening atmospheric vapor</term> from exhaling; or, if it should exhale at all, it would surely attack the needy and the poor, who are more susceptible to pestilence, rather than the prince of the state himself. For if he happens to live in some suburban villa, I believe he will not perish by the sword—especially if it is separated from the city by many miles—lest that Martian vapor be smothered along the way by lime, rubble, and waste, and fail to arrive there intact and effective. But the glory of the Academy of **Plato** and of **Aristotle** will be at risk among philosophers; for though they perceived so much in their books on the republic regarding the founding and happy governing of a city and state, they left us nothing written about such a "useful" and "necessary" caution. If we weigh all these things seriously and not as a joke, we will see that **Haly** <note>Haly Abenragel, a famous 11th-century Arabic astrologer.</note>, the interpreter of **Ptolemy** and himself a supreme astrologer, rightly judged this part of astrology concerning "elections" to be frivolous and ineffective.

### Chapter VIII: That astrologers subject our mind to the heavens, though as they are cunning they try to disguise it.

<margin>The cunning of astrologers.</margin>
<margin>Astrologers subject our mind to the heaven.</margin>
Thus far it has been demonstrated that none of the physical and temporary things—over which the heaven is thought to have the greatest jurisdiction—depend on the heaven in the way the astrologers imagine. For it is not those things which are accidental, nor those which pertain to others, nor those which are either in the past or far in the future, that are successfully brought to pass by the observation of certain hours. If the heaven does not effect these things in such a way that they can be foreseen through the heaven, how much less can it effect those things which are **incorporeal** <note>Non-physical or spiritual realities, such as the soul or the intellect.</note>, concerning which astrological superstition does not blush to make pronouncements? For under this category are included the diversities of character and intellect, and whatever works and properties belong to our soul; it includes things pertaining to **demons**, to superior minds, to **God**, to the efficacy of prayers, to the secrets of conscience, to the state of the future life, and other things of this kind. Concerning all these, this "mercenary" <note>original: "nugiuendū" - literally a "seller of trifles" or a huckster.</note> class of men spreads a thousand dogmas of prediction with the most arrogant rashness. And indeed, I shall begin with **character** <term>moribꝫ (mores): the habits, morals, and personality traits of an individual</term>, which they think vary in men according to the variety of the birth constellation. But when they are pressed on this point, they are accustomed to hide what they truly feel; pouring out many words about **freedom of choice** <note>The theological concept of "Liberum Arbitrium" or Free Will.</note>, they warn that we should not think our liberty is compelled by the stars, from which we supposedly receive only a "propensity" and a certain "invitation," which it is within our choice either to follow or decline. I will therefore first uncover the fraud of this defense, bringing forward many of their own dogmas from which it will be clear that they subject the mind itself to the heaven, even where it does not depend on the body. Afterward, we shall declare that the diversity of character and intellect cannot be referred to celestial causes even in the way they claim. Therefore, if they do not think the differences of the human soul come from the condition and position of the stars except insofar as the body is affected in one way or another, then the soul also...

...that **prayer** <note>original: "oratio"</note> should change nothing? This is not only a matter of the soul inclining toward the body, but of one living in the body in such a way that—being full of God and with the mind inhabiting its innermost shrines—one does not even feel oneself to be living in the body. Furthermore,

<margin>Second point.</margin>
on the part of the **Sun**, they presume they will judge the secrets of the conscience of a person regarding gods and men; yet nothing is placed in the hand of the soul and our freedom in this way—not even so that they are open to angelic knowledge, nor are they subjected to such power. Finally, if the partnership

<margin>Third point.</margin>
of the body joins the soul to heaven, how do they predict its state when it is placed outside the body based on a celestial constellation? For it is common among them to say there are two planets who are authors of happiness: **Venus** and **Jupiter**, but with different duties: so that Venus bestows the happiness of the present life, and Jupiter that of the future. After **Maternus** <note>Julius Firmicus Maternus, a 4th-century Roman author of the most extensive astrological handbook from antiquity.</note> recounted many of these things which are

<margin>Maternus.</margin>
provided by **Saturn** being positioned in **Leo**, he then adds this: "But when they have attained all these things, they shall die at a great age, and their soul shall pass away, joined to the gods in heaven. For Saturn, positioned in Leo, recalls the souls of those who lived thus on earth—liberated from innumerable narrow straits—to heaven and to the first beginnings of their origin." These are his words. From this, I wish it to be understood not only that this astrological superstition spreads even to the suspicion of impiety, but also how much faith can be placed in the writers of this art—as if they had committed these things to writing only after they were proven by experience and use! We know beyond a doubt that when they were writing, they had no experience of the future life. For if they perhaps learned these things from their deceased followers, a constellation could more easily be understood to send one to the underworld rather than to the heavens. For although they think that by praying at a certain hour they can obtain from God what they wish, I would not easily believe—unless they changed their dogma—that they would obtain eternal happiness from Him. And they certainly believe what we have said. For that most legendary **Albumasar** <note>Abu Ma'shar (787–886), a Persian astrologer whose works were the primary source of astrological theory for the Middle Ages.</note> writes:

<margin>Fourth point.</margin>
that whoever prays to God when the **Moon** is joined to **Jupiter** with the **Head of the Dragon** <note>The "Head of the Dragon" refers to the North Node of the Moon, a mathematical point where the Moon's orbit crosses the ecliptic; it was considered highly auspicious.</note> will obtain whatever he asks from God. And will there still be philosophers,

<margin>Albumasar.</margin>
will there be theologians whom these things please? Do they think that they and the astrologers they follow sufficiently understand what God is, or what prayer is? This insanity of theirs in this place is not so much to be refuted as it is to be cursed, since it has been sufficiently refuted by those things we have discussed elsewhere regarding prayer against the impious. But as for **Peter of Abano** <note>Petrus Aponensis (1250–1316), a famous physician and philosopher often accused of magic and heresy for his astrological views.</note>, whose writings I read, as often as I do, that

<margin>Peter of Abano.</margin>
saying of **Heraclitus** comes to mind: <term>πολιμαθεια νοον ου φερει: much learning does not teach understanding</term>. He himself writes that at that hour of which we were speaking, he sought knowledge from God, and after that day he progressed greatly in it. I do not have the leisure to measure how much this "new Solomon" has progressed in it. I certainly believe that whatever he progressed was no more than what can be accomplished by human steps. But however the matter stands, I would advise this Peter to credit all his progress to his own industry and talent, rather than to that "Jovian" <note>Referring to the planet Jupiter, associated with wisdom and success.</note> prayer of his; let him not stubbornly defend it, lest good judges be forced to deny that he has made any progress in good literature, rather than believe he would ever assent to such a vain superstition. I would likewise advise all astrologers in common: since Jupiter is so favorable to them, let them acquire for themselves so much wealth and resources by a single prayer at a happy hour that, needing nothing of our money hereafter, they might finally stop mocking the minds of the unskilled with so many daily lies for the sake of squeezing out money.

# Book IV

## Chapter IX: Human character is not created by the heavens.

<margin>The opinion of some</margin>
<margin>Refutation.</margin>
Let us consider **character** <note>original: "moribus"; refers to a person's habits, morals, and natural temperament</note>: whether it can be defended by right reason that the cause of these things also lies, in some way, in the heavens. Perhaps, if we believe that neither the rational part of the soul suffers the force of heaven, nor our liberty is compelled, there will be nothing left for either philosophy or piety to deny: that the various pursuits of men and the many types of natural talents arise from various **stellar influences** <note>original: "afflatibus"; literally "breathings" or "inspirations" from the stars</note>. This would be because the condition of the body is affected by them, while the dignity of the soul and its freedom of choice remain safe. But he who thinks this is far mistaken. For even to suggest that the sensory part of the soul alone is so affected by the **Sun** that it has a propensity toward some disgrace is both contrary to reason and greatly opposed to piety. For whatever is produced by natural causes—especially those which keep the laws prescribed for them immutably by the Creator of nature—must be attributed both to the Author of nature who so established it, and to nature itself. Whatever power or property the stars possess was granted to them by God, the principle of nature, according to the consensus of both philosophers and theologians. Even the foolish hardly deny that God is the greatest and wisest; yet what sort of goodness or powerful wisdom would this be, to use the mighty hand of heaven to bend a human being—however free, yet still weak—toward that side to which you would least want him to decline?

<margin>Second reason</margin>
Furthermore, it would make the best servants <note>i.e., the stars, which obey God's laws perfectly</note> the authors and ministers of evil; though they themselves never transgress the King’s commands, they would be the ones most inviting and impelling others toward transgression.

<margin>Third reason.</margin>
Finally, what kind of natural order, what consensus, what wise institution is this? That those things which the reason of nature would not want to happen are nevertheless diligently brought about by those who are the great, powerful, best, and principal parts of nature. Furthermore, he who commits a sin does not "do" something; rather, he

<margin>Fourth reason</margin>
**fails** <note>In Scholastic philosophy, sin was often viewed as a "privation" or a failure to act, rather than a positive action in itself.</note>. Therefore, he who invites one to sin invites one to fail, which is not appropriate for higher "efficient" causes, which are always active and never "failing." It is, therefore, a most absurd dogma of the astrologers to think that we have an inclination toward theft from one position of the stars, toward incest from another, or toward fraud and homicide from others. For all of nature—especially the superior part joined most closely to the Divine Mind—may perhaps favor the observation of natural and divine law, but it can in no way hinder or oppose it. Let them therefore shut their profane mouths! Let them not say that **Venus** joined to **Mars** calls us to adultery, or that those same planets placed in masculine signs excite us to the "nefarious intercourse of males" <note>A reference to homosexual acts, which were heavily stigmatized and categorized as "against nature" in Renaissance thought.</note>. Nor should they say that Mars occupying the ninth part of the sky makes people irreligious, or that other constellations entirely provoke us to other disgraces. Let them impute their crimes to themselves, not to heaven, nor to "filthy matter"; and let them not think that the stains of an unjust soul emanate from the purest fountains of nature.

<margin>The solution of some.</margin>
But can this objection perhaps be resolved? As some think, we might say that the powers of all the stars are good and healthy, but when they are received in us, they degenerate through the vice of the material; and the influences which were beneficial occasionally turn out to be noxious and harmful. Thus, from **Mars**, fortitude of soul and "Herculean" effectiveness are provided. But, either through a vice of the body in which **red bile** <note>original: "bilis rubra"; associated with the choleric temperament, which was thought to cause anger and violence</note> boils over too much, or through the fault of a soul abusing the celestial gift, those impulses are sometimes turned toward cruelty and injustice. Likewise, from **Saturn**, height of mind, depth of counsel, and the investigation of hidden things and a love of **contemplation** are infused. However, because these same things found a sluggish vessel, or through the fault of the free will of the recipient, they make the soul deceitful...

<summary>Pico argues that the stars cannot be the cause of human sin or character flaws, as this would imply God (the creator of the stars) is the author of evil. He refutes the astrological claim that planetary alignments cause crimes like theft or adultery, insisting that moral failure lies in human will, not celestial influence.</summary>

--- Page 477 ---
<meta>This page concludes the argument that human character and moral failings cannot be blamed on celestial influence, focusing on the contradictions within astrological doctrine regarding "good" and "bad" planets. It then transitions into Chapter X, which addresses the origins of laws and religions.</meta>

...filthy, uncultivated, superstitious, and even dangerous in its **madness of imagination** <note>original: "lymphationis"; a term for a frantic or hallucinatory delirium</note>. They say that by **Venus** we are made prone to cheerfulness, benevolence, and civil elegance, yet we abuse that instinct toward wickedness, luxury, and dishonesty. We are incited by the **Sun** toward magnanimity, but we abuse that impulse toward ambition; and so it goes for the rest of the planets.

<margin>Refutation:</margin>
But truly, someone might say these things as a defender of astrology rather than as an astrologer himself. For it is among the very first and most acknowledged principles of the astrologers that some planets are **good** and others are **bad**. If the things just said were true, then all planets would be equally good by their nature, and all would be called bad for the same reason. For there is no **influence** <note>original: "afflatus"; literally a "breathing" or "blowing upon"</note> so healthy that it cannot be infected, changed, or disturbed by the matter and condition of the one receiving it. If they themselves wish for there to be no planet so bad that great goods cannot come from it, and none so good that great evils cannot arise, they nevertheless do not attribute this diversity of effects to the matter or the reception of the ray, but to the varying state and position of that same star in the heavens. 

Therefore, they say that if **Saturn** holds his own house, his own **exaltation** <note>original: "altitudinem"; a specific sign where a planet's power is heightened</note>, or his own **bounds** <note>original: "fines"; specific degrees within a zodiac sign</note>; if he is mixed with good **aspects** <note>original: "radiationibus"; literally "radiations" or rays</note>; if it is a daytime birth—then he makes men contemplative, pious, and wise. But indeed, if he is received in a less favorable position, they say this very same planet degenerates into an evil condition: if he is poorly placed, if joined with **Mars**, if in bad **configurations** <note>original: "schematifmis"; from the Greek 'schemata'</note> to the Sun, he makes men demonic, filthy, envious, and liars. 

Nor do they ever contend that when Saturn is so situated in the heavens, any good can be expected from him. Therefore, he who defends astrology in such a way clearly ignores what he is defending. What we have said of Saturn should be understood of all the planets; for they are also accustomed to say that **Mars**, when not favorably disposed, incites to ambition, to lack of self-control, and to a lust for tyranny—not because the vital spirit of the one being born becomes too hot or too cold, thereby making the good fire of heaven either sluggish or consuming, but because Saturn, Mars, and the Sun, when they are so positioned in heaven, pour such evils into those being born out of their own nature and property. This is what the astrologers write and believe. 

Nor does anyone who denies this defend astrology any more than someone who **corrects a book with a sponge** <note>a classical metaphor for erasing something entirely</note>; he takes away both the doctrine (as we have declared) and the truth of every prediction, if it does not depend on the observation of celestial influence, and if the disposition of matter not only diminishes or increases the celestial influence, but changes it and makes it something entirely different.

### Chapter X: Bad laws, just like good ones, are not subject to the heavens.

From this, the opinion of those who deny that good laws are subject to the heavens (arguing they depend on divine power) but concede this for bad laws (since they have nothing that exceeds the powers and capacity of nature) is refuted. For just as the loftiness of truth prevents good laws from being subjected to corporeal causes, so too does the wickedness of bad laws prevent them from being referred to the best causes, which are most obedient to the best God. In general, experience itself sufficiently demonstrates that religions—both good and bad—do not depend on the heavens. For some refer the origin and variety of religions to the stars, which rule over cities and provinces by their own right, as they believe. Others refer them to...

<meta>This page continues the critique of astrological determinism regarding human history, moving from the influence of planets on individual character to their supposed influence on the rise and fall of entire religions and laws. # Book IV

...the **great conjunctions** <term>great conjunction: a rare alignment of the superior planets, Jupiter and Saturn, which medieval astrologers believed signaled major historical shifts, such as the birth of prophets or the fall of empires</term>, as they call them, of the superior planets, especially of **Saturn** and **Jupiter**. This is indeed the opinion followed by the Arabs and the Latins who follow in the footsteps of the Arabs.

<margin>Ptolemy.</margin> Ptolemy seems to have approached this view, though (as we will explain later) he never actually made any mention of those "great conjunctions." But in the second book of his *Apotelesmatika* <note>original: "apoteleſmatõ"; the Greek title of Ptolemy’s influential work on astrology, commonly known as the *Tetrabiblos*</note>, he says that among those Asians who live toward the east and the south, they worship **Venus** and **Saturn** because they fall under the **triplicity** <term>triplicity: a group of three zodiac signs belonging to the same element; here, the "Earth" signs of Virgo, Taurus, and Capricorn</term> of a dry quality—that is, Virgo, Taurus, and Capricorn—which he believes are ruled by Saturn and Venus. On the other hand, those who live between the south and the west hold Venus and **Mars** as deities because they are subject to the humid triplicity, over which he places **Mercury** and Venus along with Mars.

However, both opinions are—as we were saying—refuted by the sheer evidence of facts and outcomes. For if a religion is born by the power of some great conjunction, then once that power is exhausted, that religion ought to vanish as well. But there is no conjunction of stars whose power is imagined to last—even by the astrologers’ own calculations—for as many years as the worship of idols, the Mosaic religion, and the Christian religion have endured. For about five thousand years, the world remained in the darkness of idol worship. What conjunction, I ask, or what **Great Years** <note>original: "maximi anni"; a theoretical cycle after which all celestial bodies return to their original positions, often spanning thousands of years</note> of any star, can claim for themselves such vast spans of time? 

The rites and observances of the Mosaic law are still in force among the Hebrews today, and they have flourished for three thousand years or more. What constellation is so strong and so long-lasting that it does not allow a religion to be extinguished even after its political power <note>original: "imperio"</note> has vanished? A theologian will provide the true causes for these things, consistent with his own doctrine; an astrologer can provide no such causes from the heavens. If this variety of religions were derived from the stars, we would see them vary every day and change quite frequently. 

The astrologers themselves, sensing this and gathering it from the principles of their own science, defined time limits for every religion. But since religions have overstepped those limits, they have shown by the evidence of the facts themselves that they depend on something other than the stars. Now, that opinion of Ptolemy—which assumes that just as different stars dominate different places and nations, there are also different religious rites in those places—is even more thoroughly refuted by experience. 

For the same stars preside over those provinces lying between the east and the south as presided over them in the past. Yet, Venus and Saturn are no longer worshipped there as they once were. Why did those deities rule over them then? Surely, as Ptolemy himself writes, because the earthly triplicity (Taurus, Virgo, and Capricorn) governs those regions, and Venus and Saturn govern that triplicity. That was his belief. But this partitioning of the world and its regions under various triplicities is perpetual and not temporary. Therefore, the celestial influence will always be the same as it once was. Why then, O Ptolemy, does the same religion not endure today in those same locations? 

Finally, let us conclude this entire dispute by asking Ptolemy himself: if, by the varying presidency of the stars, different stars were once worshipped among different nations, by the power and force of which star is it brought about that today almost no stars are worshipped in any region of the whole world?

But not even this can a birth constellation effect, since both the body's...
