The child possesses the constitution and appearance <note>original: "habitum & figuram"</note> that he carries with him from the womb before he even leaves that womb. For this reason, these traits must be numbered among those things we discussed in the eighth chapter, which cannot be predicted through the **birth** <term>nativity: the specific moment of birth used by astrologers to cast a horoscope</term> they use. This is because those traits precede the birth; they are instead determined by the conception or the condition of the woman. But if the seed is not yet present then, the **constellation** <term>constellation: here meaning the specific alignment of stars at a given moment</term> under which the seed was created should instead be observed—though we will address this later. Therefore, if the disposition of the body can be foreseen and predicted, it could certainly be done more effectively from the hour of conception than from the hour of birth, from which it is impossible. Whether it is even possible from the hour of conception will be examined in the following books. 

For now, it is demonstrated that **astrologers err** when they pronounce—based on the hour of birth—whether someone will be born with a short or tall body, fat or lean, strong or weak, maimed or whole, natural or monstrous. Indeed, a person acquires all these conditions long before they are sent out into the public world from the mother’s womb, already formed and completed. Therefore, just as these traits are not created by a constellation which they have already preceded, so too they cannot be predicted by a **mathematician** <note>original: "mathematico"; in this period, the term often referred specifically to astrologers</note> through the observation of that constellation. 

We have disputed the timing of conception elsewhere; for now, we wish the reader to know that even the greatest astrologers believed that things pertaining to the temperament of the body depend on <margin>Haly</margin> **proximate causes** <note>Haly: likely Haly Abenragel, a famous 11th-century Arab astrologer</note> and the lower heavens beneath God. As **Haly** writes, they even asked for pardon <note>original: "veniam"</note> for themselves if they should fail to reach the truth in predicting the disposition of the body. 

<margin>Epilogue</margin> Let us, therefore, summarize this entire dispute concerning the efficiency of the heavens: if the heaven is a **universal cause**, then the variety and distinction of particular things do not come from it. Even if we were to grant that there are powers in the heaven that produce particular properties, they are not of the kind that astrologers prophesy. For it seems there is no reason why:
*   Chance events should be traced back to natural causes.
*   Things that are evil should be traced back to the best authors <note>referring to God or the celestial bodies as perfect creators</note>.
*   Things that proceed from reason and counsel should be traced back to principles acting by natural necessity.
*   Incorporeal things should be traced back to bodies by means of a **ray** <term>ray: the "influence" or "emanation" astrologers believed planets beamed down to Earth</term>.
*   Things already past, or those far in the future, should be traced back to a present constellation.
*   Things pertaining to others should be traced back to our own birth chart <note>original: "genituram"</note>.

Furthermore, it is utterly absurd and most foreign to all philosophy to seek the origin of things in the stars when you can see their own manifest and sufficient causes right here among us: in the powers of inferior bodies, in the diversity of minds, in emotion, counsel, opportunity, and habit—and in the varied meeting of things and causes flowing together from every side. Such an origin is not found in the stars, nor does the nature and condition of the things being done, or of the heaven itself, allow it to be so. 

This is the fact: all philosophers whose study and labor is occupied in investigating the causes of things—while they borrow true causes from medicine, mathematics, and every art and science—never use astrological causes. We declared at the beginning of this work <margin>Favorinus, Carneades, Posidonius, Timaeus, Pythagoras, Aristotle, Plato, Plotinus, Averroes, Avicenna</margin> that this was the practice of **Favorinus**, **Carneades**, **Posidonius**, **Timaeus**, **Pythagoras**, and even **Aristotle**, **Plato**, **Plotinus**, **Averroes**, **Avicenna**, and the good followers of both their schools.

### Book IV

...varieties and outcomes of human affairs. However, it does not immediately follow that these things cannot be foreseen and predicted from the heavens. For even if the **stars** <term>stars: the Latin "sidera" refers to any celestial body, including planets</term> do not cause these things at all, they might still signify and portend them. Indeed, there are those who have held the opinion that events do not happen by the power of celestial bodies—except in matters of general influence—but since they depend on their own immediate and proper causes, they are nonetheless indicated by the heavens before they occur. 

<margin>Refutation.</margin>
In this way, through the passage, station, and retreat of the planets, the future might be known—just as birds, whether by flying or standing still, signify the future with their wings or voices without even knowing it themselves. But in truth, 

<margin>First reason.</margin>
the famous astrologers never believed this themselves, nor does any reason agree that we should believe it. For when something is a sign of another thing by nature (and not by human convention) and is a physical body, it is either the **cause** of the thing it signifies, or the **effect**, or both the sign and the thing signified proceed from the same common cause. If anyone thinks something should be added to this—as if there were a connection distinct from these—claiming it is necessarily and inseparably linked to the cause, he is greatly and far mistaken. This is because such a connection and accompaniment cannot happen for any other reason than that the cause produces the one before it produces the other, or that whatever moves the cause to act also stirs this sign at the same time. We concede that both of these are referred back to a common cause. 

Come then, let us see which of these is more naturally suited to the heavens, if the future is indeed signified by the heavens. Certainly, the motions and arrangements of the heavens are not the **effects** of lower things; and these thinkers deny they are the **causes**. It remains, then, for them to say that the state and disposition of the heaven, and what is believed to be indicated by it, proceed from the same cause—just as a **rainbow** <note>The author uses the rainbow as a classic example of a "natural sign" that indicates weather without causing it.</note> sometimes portends clear weather, not because it creates the clear weather, but because the cause of the rainbow is also the cause of the clear weather. But no physical cause can be found that is superior to the heaven and which therefore creates the dispositions of both the heaven and lower things at once. 

<margin>
That divine minds are not the causes of earthly outcomes without the efficiency of the heaven.
</margin>

<margin>First reason.</margin>
Will there then remain an incorporeal cause? For perhaps it might seem possible to say that the outcomes of human affairs are created by the **divine minds** <term>divine minds: in Renaissance philosophy, these were often identified as angels or "intelligences" that moved the celestial spheres</term> themselves as they revolve the celestial bodies; and while they occur, they are indicated to us by the very state of the heaven which they move, as if by certain nods or gestures. Truly, whoever says this is surely close to the fables of the poets. How will he avoid the following problem? It would mean that those things which men themselves cannot do without the guilt of a crime—such as urging and impelling this man to homicide, that one to adultery, or another to theft—are being done by divine minds.

<margin>Second reason.</margin>
I set aside the fact that all philosophy abominates the idea of physical things being created by incorporeal causes without an intervening physical cause. Furthermore, why would those 

<margin>Third reason.</margin>
born at different hours be born with a different fate, if the author and cause of fate is not the position of the heaven (which varies by the hour), but the Author of the heaven—who is immobile, always equal to Himself, and like Himself? 

<margin>
Fourth reason.
Thomas.
</margin>
Finally, as **Thomas** <note>A reference to St. Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the influential medieval theologian who argued against hard fatalism.</note> argues: since the effects of the same cause indicate one another, they must proceed from the same principle and in the same manner. But the motion of the heaven and the disposition of lower bodies and affairs do not proceed from superior causes in the same way. The heavens move in an immutable and necessary order, while human affairs move in a variable order that can fall out either way by chance—following the nature of the things being moved and governed. Divine principles do not change this nature but preserve it; otherwise, they would not be guiding nature, but destroying it. Therefore, the heaven cannot signify lower things except insofar as a cause signifies its effect...

# Book IV

<margin>Thomas</margin>
points out his own view: regarding those who, while admitting they cannot win by reason, nevertheless contend that the stars are signs—they do not understand their own voice <note>original: "vocem suam ignorant," meaning they don't realize the logical implications of their own argument</note>. And this, **Thomas Aquinas**—a man of the weightiest judgment who usually asserts nothing rashly—pronounced with certainty in his *Summa Theologiae* <note>Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274) was the preeminent Catholic theologian of the Middle Ages; his *Summa* sought to harmonize faith with Aristotelian reason</note>. This "signifying" role might be said of comets, of "trajections" <term>trajections: shooting stars or meteors</term>, and other things of this kind that occur in the heights <note>original: "in sublimi," referring to the upper atmosphere where such phenomena were then believed to occur</note>; these may be stirred up by the stars to signify what the cause of those stars is about to do, without the phenomena themselves being the cause. But this can in no way be said of the stars themselves, since (as we were saying) no superior physical cause can be found above them. Moreover, 

<margin>Second main reason</margin>
those who think this way introduce the necessity of fate, even if they do not wish to. For if the stars are the *causes* of lower things, it is possible for the effect prompted by their influence to fail to occur—either because the physical matter is resistant, or because a particular cause diverts the general influence elsewhere. However, if they are *signs*, since they were instituted by nature to signify, their signification will be as true as their true nature. Otherwise, why were they instituted by God to signify? Are the works of He whose works are perfect meant to deceive or lie? If they do not lie, then whatever is signified by them must 

<margin>Third reason.</margin>
necessarily come to pass. Finally, if they are numbered among causes, it is not contrary to their nature to be in that order of causes which can be hindered, changed, or overcome. But if they are considered signs, they cannot be held as lies, lest He who described the notes and letters of the future in the "heavenly book" (as they call it) 

<margin>Fourth reason.</margin>
be considered either deceitful or ignorant. Furthermore, if the heaven does not indicate by doing, but indicates that which it does not do, it remains that what *other* causes do is indicated by the heaven. Therefore, does it indicate what all causes do, or only what some do? If only some: why, I ask, does it indicate the works of these and not those? If indeed it indicates all equally, there will be no remaining causes by which what was demonstrated could be prevented from happening. Therefore, what was portended will necessarily occur. If we say this, we not only oppose 

<margin>Astrologers have denied the necessity of fate</margin>
the truth (as we have demonstrated elsewhere), but we also oppose the astrologers themselves. For the Egyptians, and **Ptolemy**, and every famous astrologer has always thoroughly denied the necessity of fate <note>Ptolemy’s *Tetrabiblos* argued that astrology provides warnings, not unavoidable destinies</note>. They declare this especially in their treatises on "interrogations" <term>interrogations: a branch of astrology (horary) where a chart is cast to answer a specific question</term>. Since they do not say every question is legitimate—but only those that proceed from an impulse of the soul moved by the heavens—and since they admit many questions are not of this kind (namely, those born from our own reason and counsel), they clearly declare they do not admit the necessity of fate. Moreover, if such necessity were introduced, all the utility of astrology would perish, which is chiefly placed in this: 

<margin>Fifth reason</margin>
that we might avoid foreseen evils and confirm or increase good things. Finally, if the stars are signs and not causes of lower things, that part of astrology commonly called "elections" <term>elections: the practice of choosing an auspicious time to begin an endeavor, like a wedding or a voyage</term> is removed beyond controversy; for in that practice, we seek celestial favor to help *bring something about*, not merely signposts to satisfy curiosity.

Regardless of which opinion the astrologers prefer—that is, whether they want the stars to be causes of lower things or only signs and not causes—that part concerning "questions" <note>interrogations</note>, which they use most of all, would necessarily be fundamentally destroyed. For the nature of this...

# Book IV

<page-num>IIII</page-num>

->Header: Book<-

<margin>The foundation of this branch of astrological interrogations.</margin>
The basis of this branch of astrology is the idea that our minds are moved by celestial configurations, at least within the imaginative faculty. They claim that when the mind is stirred by these stars to desire knowledge of a particular matter, if one then consults an astrologer, the arrangement of the heavens at the exact hour of that consultation portends the very thing the seeker wished to know. Therefore, they argue that an astrologer is able to provide true answers to those inquiring about any matter whatsoever. 

Let us, therefore, ask those who claim to be able to resolve every inquiry: are the stars merely signs of earthly things, or are they also causes that signify by their actual influence? If they are merely signs, then the impulse of our desire to ask a question does not come from the stars. Instead—as those who hold this opinion say of other things—the impulse is produced by its own internal causes, even if it is merely indicated by the stars. Thus, the movement of our desire would not claim a celestial constellation as its origin or cause, but rather the imaginative power itself, our own choice, the appetitive force of the mind, and those external things that provoke our senses and thoughts. 

However, if they respond that the stars *are* causes and that lower things are signified by them (just as effects are demonstrated by their cause), how will they defend the idea that the configuration of the heavens appearing at the hour of consultation is the *cause* of those things about which the astrologer answers the questioner? For those things have either already happened long ago, or perhaps will never happen at all—in which case they ought to have no cause in the present sky. 

<margin>A quite witty mockery.</margin>
To be sure, they will say Mars is in the West, which will not permit them to answer the truth! But if they can manage to get him to at least allow them to hear the truth, I will respond—even to those who do not ask—with absolute truth regarding these inquiries. 

<margin>Where this branch of astrology was born.</margin>
It seemed to the astrologers that they gained too little prestige—and, what pressed them more, too little profit <note>original: "quæstus," referring to financial gain</note>—if they only pronounced fates for each person based on the time of their birth or the annual revolution of the sun. To understand these, a person only needed to visit them once in a lifetime or once a year. Yet, our curiosity desires to know many things daily about which the astrologers could provide no answer. Consequently, the art lost much of its authority among the unlearned <term>unlearned: the original "idiotas" refers to laypeople or those without formal education, rather than a lack of intelligence</term>, and the practitioners lost a great deal of money. 

From this, they persuaded themselves—or at least others—that they could clearly foresee whatever was asked based on the hour the question was posed, provided that the person asking was moved by a "natural impulse" and had not simply chosen to ask on a whim. In this way, they beautifully vindicated themselves from any infamy of falsehood. For if the answer they gave was refuted by the facts, they would claim it was not because the astrologer was untruthful, but because the question had not been "effective" or sincere. But if the responses happened to match the events, then why shouldn't they be regarded as oracles on earth? 

By these arts and fallacies, this class of triflers <note>original: "nugiuendum," describing people who deal in worthless or trivial things</note> mocks the ignorant, since nothing more dissonant with reason can be said or thought than what they have devised concerning this fallacy of interrogation. For even if I grant them that my desire to know about an absent person, for example, comes from the sky, what logical sequence leads to the conclusion that the constitution of the sky at the hour I explain my desire to an astrologer must immediately be of a kind that reveals the status of that absent person? Where is this "correspondence" or "treaty" between our desire and the thing we wish to know? 

<margin>The response</margin>
If they perchance respond that the same celestial power which brings about that distant event also "twitches" our mind at the same time and warns us of the thing happening—

<margin>The refutation</margin>
—firstly, it would follow that these impulses would only strike us...

# Book IV

->Book IV<-

...only these desires assail us when the matter itself has occurred. And yet, they believe that effective interrogations can be made concerning things that happened long ago, or will happen in the distant future, or even things that will never happen at all. Furthermore, if we were to grant their premise, we should not look at the configuration of the heavens at the hour we consult the astrologer, but rather at the very first moment the desire to ask the question invaded us. This is because—according to them—it is the same or a similar constellation that both produces the event and awakens in us the desire to know it. If one must be "rationally insane," this would be a far more reasonable claim than what the astrologers actually say: namely, that we must observe the time of the inquiry itself, rather than the moment when the concern for inquiring first troubled us. 

Then, as we were saying, if any kinship or "consensus" can exist between these things, it can only be between the event that occurred and our desire, which might both seem referable in some way to the same or a similar constellation. However, the hour in which we actually consult the astrologer can vary due to a thousand causes—meaning we might meet the astrologer sooner or later. For instance, his house might be far away, or someone might delay us on the road, or other random occurrences of this sort might intervene. These chance delays change the hour of the question, and therefore change the configuration of the heavens upon which the astrologer bases his answer. But the astrologers care nothing for these facts; it has long been their habit to always say and believe things that possess no reason or stability whatsoever.

### Chapter XIV: Divine miracles are neither performed nor signified by the heavens, but miracles are indicated by miracles, just as natural things are indicated by natural things.

<margin>Greatest insanity.</margin>
<margin>A book against the impious.</margin>
But would that they were insane only to this extent, and did not also believe that divine miracles—which exceed the capacity of all nature—were performed by the natural rays of the higher bodies <note>The "higher bodies" refer to the planets and stars in the celestial spheres.</note>. We have shown above that they are mired in this error, demonstrating that they attribute divine religion to the power of the stars: both the law which God once promulgated to the Hebrew people through Moses, and that which Christ later proclaimed to the world through the apostles. So too with that flooding <note>original: "eluionem"</note> of the entire world under Noah, and other divine miracles of this kind produced in sacred history; they have ascribed them all to their own constellations. In this matter, they undoubtedly seem more insane than those who refuse to concede these things ever happened at all. For they believe these events occurred as narrated, yet claim they were effected by natural causes—and no greater insanity can be imagined than to think an act performed *above* nature was achieved by the *forces* of nature. 

We have already proved, in our disputes against the impious, that the divine law consists of things that exceed the forces of nature. The same can easily be demonstrated regarding the universal cataclysm <note>The Great Flood of Noah.</note>. Nothing is more repugnant to nature than that it should plot its own destruction; therefore, nature would never inflict such an injury upon itself from which it could not recover by its own power. If it could not happen by a natural course—such as when the waters rose fifteen cubits above the peaks of all the mountains—then it was not nature’s purpose to submerge the entire earth in a flood to destroy every living thing. And if Noah, with his family and every kind of animal, escaped that shipwreck while shut inside a single ark for twelve months, this too was beyond nature. If these things are not caused by the heavens, they cannot be foreseen from the heavens. For as we proved a little while ago, the heavens do not signify what they do not cause. There is a specific reason why these things are not portended by the stars, even if we were to grant that other things (which do not exceed nature's capacity) are performed or indicated by the heavens. For there is...

<meta>This page continues the author’s theological dismantling of astrology. While the previous page focused on the logical absurdity of "interrogative" astrology (predicting the future based on the moment a question is asked), this page shifts to a higher philosophical and scriptural level. The author argues that "natural" things—like the stars—cannot be used to predict "supernatural" events—like miracles—because the two realms are fundamentally distinct in God's order.</meta>

<page-num>IIII</page-num>

->Book IV<-

As we have declared elsewhere, the order of things established by God for the natural course is so enclosed within its own boundaries, and separated from those things which are performed by divine power and will beyond nature <note>original: "praeter naturam," referring to the supernatural or miraculous</note>, that if all these miracles were removed, nothing would be missing from the natural world, and nothing would be left over. Now, the heavens and whatever occurs in the heavens according to the common course are among those things that exist according to nature. Therefore, if any movement or arrangement of the stars—which is owed to them by their natural condition—signifies something in the future, this significance and indication ought to be held and described among natural things.

But if we say that any of these signs portend things that happen *above nature*, this absurdity follows: if God leaves nature to its own conditions and does not perform anything above it, nature itself would be found false and a liar. In such a case, God would have established something in the stars in vain and superfluously, since there would still be signs of future things in the stars that would never happen—because the things being signified are those "beyond nature" which we just assumed were removed. If the signs themselves are natural things, we must say that when supernatural things are removed, the signs themselves are neither taken away nor deprived of any perfection due to them.

Therefore, if God has disposed from eternity to perform some miracle, He did not insert the signs of that miracle into natural things in such a way that the significance belonged to the "reason" or natural logic of those things. Instead, He willed that natural things be signified by natural signs, and miracles by preceding miracles.

The Great Flood <note>original: "Cathaclismum"</note>, which was to occur by the miracle of divine justice, was signaled to the world by Noah, who was divinely inspired and to be divinely saved. The leading of the Hebrews out of Egypt and the giving of the Law were testified to more by the miracles performed by Moses with the divine rod—witnessed even by the magicians and astrologers of the Egyptians—than by any stars. That the Promised Land was to be subjected to the people of God—and the wonders God was to work there above the laws of nature—was indicated not by any natural configuration of the heavens, but by the swiftest motion of the sun being restrained by the hand of the Creator <note>A reference to the Book of Joshua, where the sun stood still during a battle</note>. To pass over the crossing of the Jordan on dry feet and the walls of the city <note>Jericho</note> destroyed by the sound of trumpets: the life of Hezekiah <note>A biblical King of Judah whose life was extended by 15 years as a sign from God</note> prolonged by divine power was demonstrated not by the "benign irradiation of Jupiter" running its course in the right order, but by the miracle of the sun moving backward.

When the oracles, divinely inspired beyond the nature of the human mind, announced the wonder of the Word made flesh <note>The Incarnation of Christ</note> and the Virgin’s childbirth, a thousand wonders were testified to in the heavenly and earthly bodies themselves. While that immense and new star rose for the Lord, later, when He was failing on the cross, the sun failed while the moon was full, contrary to the order of nature <note>During a solar eclipse, the moon must be "new"; a full moon eclipse is physically impossible in the natural order</note>. By these signs, divine miracles are both demonstrated and confirmed—miracles which can neither be performed by the natural state of things nor is it appropriate for them to be indicated by it.

### Chapter XV: That no constellation can be understood as the Star of the Magi; and an explanation of certain scriptures that might seem to support astrology to the unskilled.

Now, since we have come to the mention of the star that showed the Magi the birth of Jesus, it would not be out of place to warn the reader not to suspect that this star favored the opinion of astrologers. It is not as if that star were nothing other than a heavenly constellation—the "index of a born prophet"—known and explored by those in the East who were, as is thought, exceedingly skilled in heavenly science. However, the very text of the Gospel leads us away from this error most evidently; speaking of this star, it says: *And behold, the star which they had seen in the East went before them, until it came and stood over where the child was.* <note>Matthew 2:9. The author argues that natural stars do not "walk" in front of travelers or stop over specific houses.</note>

<summary>The author argues that natural astrology cannot predict or explain biblical miracles, as miracles are "beyond nature." He uses examples like the sun stopping for Joshua or the Star of Bethlehem to show that divine signs are unique acts of God, not movements of the planets.</summary>

<page-num>IIII</page-num>

->Book IV<-

...perceived. <note>The OCR "puer" is likely a fragment of a word like "perceptum" or "percipitur" continuing from the previous page.</note> Which no one, unless they are insane, will think should be understood as referring to the stars and configurations of the heaven. Therefore, that star <note>The Star of Bethlehem</note> was **manufactured** and **temporary**: it was not a perpetual and natural star created for that duty by the Creator, through which it was signified that the King of the Jews was born. Perhaps the Magi understood it in this way: just as they were later warned in dreams to avoid Herod and return to their homeland by another way.

But we must likewise be careful not to be disturbed by certain expressions of the Scriptures: as when we read in Paul that the Son was sent in the **fullness of time**;
<margin>Paul.</margin>
and in the Gospel where the Lord says, *Now is your hour and the power of darkness*, and elsewhere, *My hour has not yet come*. For the superstitious man will think that the constellations of hours and times are being signified. But you, ask him: Does he think the time for eating is when he becomes hungry, regardless of what the constitution of the heaven might be at that time? And when he has labored enough, that it is time for the body to be cared for? And when he has slept enough, that it is the time for waking?

If he says that all these things have their own "time"—not because of the constellation of that time, but because of the nature of the thing itself which is done, and for the occasion and opportunity of doing it—then it is the same for other things which God performs above nature, and which men perform by their own freedom. Although these require no constellations to occur, they must necessarily happen at some time, and it is more fitting and convenient for them to happen at this time rather than that. It was fitting for the Son of God to be sent at the time he was sent; before then, it was not fitting. The cause is not in the heaven, but in the purpose of God and the "requirement of things" <note>original: "exigentia rerum," the logical necessity or suitability of circumstances</note> about which theologians write much, as far as they were permitted to penetrate the secret of divine counsel through the evidence of the Scriptures.

Likewise, it was fitting that after he was born he was not killed immediately; but at the time it was expedient, he surrendered himself to the hands of the wicked, and that was "the hour and the power of darkness." The same must be understood in other matters, which is clearly declared to us from one passage in the Book of Genesis. For there, when God promises the land of promise—so called from the fact—to Abraham, He says: *Know that your seed shall be a stranger in a land not their own, where they shall be afflicted for four hundred years, but in the fourth generation they shall return here.*

If only this much had been written, the astrologer would boast that the divine promise could not have been fulfilled until, after the passage of so many years, a certain disposition of heaven was reached which would bring about that event. But you, see what the prophet adds from the person of God: *For the iniquities of the Amorites*, He says, *are not yet full up to the present time.* See, therefore, what was being waited for: not a conjunction <note>original: "copulatio," referring to an astronomical conjunction</note> of Jupiter and Saturn, or any other sidereal constellation, but the **fullness of iniquity** among the Amorites. By this, divine justice—by whose laws human affairs are governed, and not by fatal necessity—might both deservedly expel them and introduce the seed of faithful Abraham there.

### Chapter XVI. That those things which surpass the powers of nature, even regarding what they contain in themselves that is natural, cannot be signified by the heaven.

Unless I am mistaken, it has now been sufficiently demonstrated that divine miracles are neither caused nor signified by the heaven; although, as far as their efficiency is concerned, the words themselves indicate this and it needs no proof. However, most recently, **Girolamo Benivieni** <note>A prominent Florentine poet and close friend of Pico della Mirandola</note>, a man of sharp and perspicacious intellect, was asking: since in these things which happen above nature there is sometimes also something natural, could they perhaps be signified by the stars from that perspective?

He concludes by beginning a discussion with Girolamo Benivieni on whether the natural elements within miracles can be predicted by stars.</summary>

-># Book IV<-

<margin>Pierre d'Ailly</margin>
...that some constellation indicated the incarnation of God; nevertheless, it could be shown that he was a law-giving man and one about to promulgate good laws. I replied that these things could not be signified by the stars in this way, nor could they happen because of them in the manner that Pierre d'Ailly <note>original: "Alliacensis" — Pierre d'Ailly (1351–1420) was a French cardinal and theologian who famously attempted to harmonize astrology with Christian history.</note> believed. For he thought there was no other way to defend from the charge of impiety those who sought the causes of such miraculous and divine things in the stars, than by saying these things depend on the heavens—not insofar as they are above nature, but insofar as there is something natural in them. 

Truly, he who says this says nothing, just as he who says a man is made by a constellation says nothing if he does not also say a rational nature is made by it. For if the constellation does not produce that which is rational in a man, there is no reason why it should be said to "make" a man any more than it makes a lion. Therefore, if you take away from divine miracles that which is proper to them, and leave only those things which they have in common with countless other things, there is no reason why you should seek the unique cause of that effect so diligently in the heavens. 

Indeed, those who investigate the horoscope <term>birth; original: "genesim"</term> of Jesus do not strive to know why he was in the womb for nine months like other men, or why he was of good physical condition, or why he had long hair, or why he was poor, or why he was a Jew; for the lives of all mortals abound with these common conditions. Rather, they seek a cause in the stars for those things which were exceptional and unique in Him, which they believe to be both exceptional and unique. But those things are the works of God above nature, not the works of the heavens: such as that he was born of a virgin; that he was both man and God; that he was Lord in his true homeland <note>Heaven</note> and a pilgrim in the flesh; that he was the performer of miraculous works; that he was by right the Lord of the world; that he was the judge of the living and the dead; that he was the author and dispenser of divine grace; the expeller of idolatry; the conqueror of demons; the author of virtues; the expeller of vices; the peace of the world; and the manifestor of truth. 

If you do not seek these things, you seek nothing; if you do seek them in the stars, you seek them impiously. Therefore, the refuge that Pierre d'Ailly prepares for astrologers—so they might say divine miracles are caused by heaven, but not insofar as they are miracles—is no refuge at all. Nor can these things be signified by the stars for that reason (as our friend Girolamo <note>original: "Hieronymus" — likely Girolamo Savonarola, the influential friar and Pico's close associate</note> asked of us); for if the order of things that proceed from God above nature were removed, there would remain, as we said above, these signs of the heaven tending toward those effects in some part—but the effect itself would no longer exist. Therefore, those signs are vain and deceptive, just as it was demonstrated above that nothing of the sort exists in the celestial nature.

V
Book

# THE FIFTH BOOK OF GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA’S DISPUTATIONS AGAINST THE ASTROLOGERS

### Chapter 1: That the decrees of astrologers regarding great conjunctions are profitably refuted; and how those who wished to judge the great changes of lower things through them have been found to be liars.

<margin>The opinion of the astrologers.</margin>
<insert>B</insert>ut many are led away from that truth by the fallacy of astrologers, who persuade the unskilled that there has never been a change of laws, no arrival of prophets, and no wondrous event in human affairs which a <term>great conjunction; original: "magna... coniunctio" — a rare alignment of the outer planets, specifically Jupiter and Saturn, believed by medieval scholars to signal major historical shifts</term> of the higher stars—especially Saturn and Jupiter—did not precede. When they discuss this matter in their charts before their followers or the unlearned as if it were a certain and conceded fact, and running through many thousands of years, they say: "This is the constellation that caused the Flood; this one brought forth Moses; that one preceded the arrival of Jesus; this one preceded the law of Muhammad." There is almost no one who is not moved by this, and who is not forced either to agree with their opinion or at least to doubt the truth.

<margin>How profitably this opinion is refuted.</margin>
Therefore, since this profession harms religion most in this area, I wish to confront this pestilence before we tear up the very foundations of the art itself. For astrologers err so greatly in this place that even if they were correct in all other matters, they still could not be defended here—not only because they predict things that undoubtedly do not fall under the governance of the heavens, but because the very rules they use in predicting contain the most manifest errors in both history and astrology. Before we show this by reason, experience itself can make it certain enough for those who may not fully perceive the force of arguments; for all who have wished to divine anything from these constellations regarding the change or success of sects and laws have been found to be false and liars.

<margin>Refutation through experience.</margin>
Long ago, the <term>mathematicians; original: "mathematici" — in this context, the term refers specifically to astrologers</term>, when the faith of Christ began to sprout, said it would not last more than [a certain number of] years; yet from its beginning, the 1,494th year is now unfolding <note>This identifies the date of Pico’s writing as 1494, the year of his death.</note>.

<margin>Albumasar.</margin>
<note>original: "Albumasar" — Abu Ma'shar (787–886 AD), a Persian astrologer whose works were foundational to medieval European astrology.</note> Albumasar, either the author or the inventor of this error, said that the same law—that is, our [Christian] law—would remain for 1,460 years, because, forsooth, there are that many years in what they call the "greatest years of the sun." Those years have passed, and the law has not passed away; for "Heaven and earth will pass away, but the words of the Lord will not pass away" <note>A reference to Matthew 24:35.</note>. Yet he predicted no less true things—or rather, more "true" lies—about his own law, that is, the law of Muhammad.

<margin>The error of Abraham the Jew.</margin>
<note>original: "Abraā iudeus" — likely referring to Abraham ibn Ezra (c. 1089–1167), a famous Jewish scholar and astrologer.</note> Abraham the Jew said, from astrological observation, that their Messiah would come in the year of Christ 1464; for then, he claimed, that position of the stars would first return under which Moses had once led the people out of Egypt and given the law to those he led. I, having been born in the year immediately preceding that one, and now being in my thirtieth year, have learned by experience the falsehood of that prediction.

<margin>The error of Arnald.</margin>
<note>original: "Arnaldus hyšpanus" — Arnaldus de Villa Nova (c. 1240–1311), a famous physician and religious reformer.</note> Arnaldus the Spaniard, a noble physician indeed but one leaning a bit too much toward superstitions, threatened us with the Antichrist in the year of grace 1345, based on astrological vanity and many other added reasons. More than 148 years have flowed by since that time, and as yet there is no Antichrist, except such as there were many even in the time of the Apostles. The younger ones, as often as they [predict] the arrival of a false prophet to us from some conjunction of the superior planets...

1

<margin>The error of d'Ailly and the astrologers of his time.</margin>
...then they announced: especially from that <term>conjunction; original: "coniunctio"</term> of Jupiter and Saturn in Scorpio ten years ago; yet no false prophet has appeared to the world since then, except for these astrologers themselves. Pierre d'Ailly himself writes that in the year the general <term>Council of Constance; original: "cōstātīæ... cōcilium"</term> was celebrated, the astrologers predicted that there would be no peace in the Church. Instead, they claimed the destruction of religion and dissensions were signaled because Jupiter was in the first house in the figure of the year and in retrograde. And yet, that great <term>Schism; original: "scisma"</term>—than which none was ever greater in the Church nor longer-lasting, having been established for forty years—was extinguished in that very first year, with the accustomed peace and tranquility restored to the Church. This certainly should have been enough to move d'Ailly himself to place no further faith in this vanity; for he, perhaps persuaded by those astrologers, feared that the Schism would bring the <term>Antichrist; original: "antixp̄m"</term> upon us shortly thereafter. There were other predictions of theirs concerning laws and sects which I could recount that were later proven false by the events themselves; but I think these suffice, since there are no others in that art of such great authority as those held by all astrologers whose predictions we have shown to be refuted by actual experience. Now, let us descend to the arguments.

## Chapter II: By what ways astrologers pass judgment on greater matters: and the rejection of the "great circles."

<margin>Four ways by which astrologers investigate great matters.</margin>
Astrologers are accustomed to investigating the great changes of lower things by four primary ways through the higher planets—especially Jupiter and Saturn when they are together, which they call a **great conjunction**; through **great circles**; through **Saturnian revolutions**; and through the **approaches and retreats of the eighth sphere**. We shall show all these ways to be irrational, false, and impassable. By doing so, we will not only achieve what we first sought here—to prove that the impious and rash things they publish about religion and laws are false—but every judgment regarding the great changes of the world will also be weakened. I will begin with the refutation of the **great circles** and the revolutions they call **Saturnian**; once these are rejected, the entire discussion of this present book can then range freely against the great conjunctions.

<margin>The second order.</margin>
<margin>The opinion of astrologers regarding great circles.</margin>
They imagine that each of the planets, and likewise each of the signs, holds dominion over the world for **three hundred and sixty years**. When these years are finished, they say a new **great circle** begins, over which the planet closest to the previous one and the sign which follows the previous sign likewise preside. Thus, whatever the nature of the dominant sign and star may be, such things happen in that span of years. When a new circle starts, they claim many things are renewed in lower affairs, and the condition of our world is always changed according to the nature of the ruler.

<margin>Under which circle we live according to the astrologers.</margin>
<margin>Albumasar.</margin>
Then, if anyone asks them where we are or in what circle we live now—that is, under which ruler—they answer: **under Leo and the Moon**. They prove it in this way: <term>Aoniar; note: likely referring to the Persian astrologer Al-Andarzaghar</term> writes in his *Book of Nativities* that a new great circle began at the time of that conjunction of Jupiter and Saturn by which they claim the **Flood** <note>original: "cathaclifmum"</note> was foretold. That conjunction preceded the Flood, as they say, by two hundred and seventy-nine years. Aoniar says that Saturn presided over this circle among the planets, and Cancer among the signs; <term>Albumasar; note: Abu Ma'shar (787–886 AD), the most influential medieval astrologer</term> also said this in the first book of his *Great Conjunctions*, in the first chapter. Therefore, taking these points as the pivot of their whole calculation, they conclude from the number of years he provided that our Lord Jesus was born when the one hundred and forty-first year of that circle was turning—the one which followed the one we mentioned under...

<margin>Reasons beyond [the previous]</margin>
I could object here to how flimsy the conjecture is that moves them to call a "Great Cycle" a space of as many years as they have imagined there are parts in the heavens <note>Astrologers often divided time into cycles of 360 years, mirroring the 360 degrees of a circle</note>. <margin>Second.</margin>

<margin>Third.</margin>

<margin>Albumasar and Eusebius</margin>
For <term>Albumasar; original: "Albumasar"</term> <note>Abu Ma'shar (787–886), a highly influential Persian astrologer whose work shaped medieval European thought</note>, the author upon whom they chiefly rely, counts 2,228 total years from the beginning of the world to the Flood. Let us, therefore, take the number of years from Adam to the Flood according to the opinion of Albumasar, against whom we are arguing. It is clear that from the <term>conjunction; original: "coniunctione"</term>—the one which they say foretold the Flood and with which a new cycle simultaneously began—there remained 1,947 years back to the creation of the world. This is because the conjunction preceded the Flood itself, as we were saying, by 279 years. Let us then divide that number [1,947] by the number of the Great Cycle—that is, by 360 parts. It will be plain that five whole Great Cycles are produced, and then there remain 147 undivided years. Because of this, the beginning of a "Great Cycle" must necessarily be placed in the 1,408th year of the world. If that number of years is part of another preceding cycle, it must necessarily be said that 213 years of a cycle passed *before* there were any years at all—that is, before the very beginnings of the world. Nothing could be said that is more clearly insane. 

<margin>How delirious the astrologers are.</margin>
But certainly, there is nothing more thoughtless than this class of men, nothing more naturally or professionally inclined toward lying and deceiving. They invent things for themselves to protect their dogma and to perform sleight-of-hand for the unlearned; this is their "soldiery" and their vanity. But let the power of truth always prevail, so that something eventually follows that is either false, or entirely impossible, or self-contradictory—that is, repugnant to their own words and dogma. While paying no attention to this, they produce, scatter, and are equally forgetful and lying; this is the vice of ignorance and sluggishness. An example is right at hand in the matter we are discussing. For in order to persuade by whatever reason they could that the great <term>Deluge; original: "inundatiōem"</term> of the world proceeded from the heavens, they added a childish fiction of a Great Conjunction, claiming a new cycle began with it, under which the world was to be renewed...

<margin>A true calculation from the beginning of the world to our own years.</margin>
It must not be overlooked that if these "Great Orbs" <note>Cycles of 360 years used by astrologers to predict historical shifts</note> were indeed necessary, whatever the astrologers say through them would have to be false, since they stray so significantly in calculating their progression. For they believe that this current cycle—in which they claim we are in the one hundred and ninety-fifth year—is the nineteenth orb since the beginning of the world, and the fourteenth since the Great Flood. By this reasoning, they place the **Lion** <note>the zodiac sign Leo</note> and the **Moon** in charge. But this cannot be so unless we count six thousand, eight hundred and thirty-eight years from the beginning of the world to our own time. This exceeds the true calculation of years by more than one thousand and four hundred years, as we have proven in our own treatise *On the True Calculation of Times* <note>original: "de uera tēporu ſupputatiōe"</note>. Furthermore, even if we follow other histories—namely the Latin ones, which compute a greater number of years—we still find fewer than those these men arrogantly claim for the completion of their orbs. No historical record exceeds approximately six thousand and seven hundred years; yet these men are caught adding nearly one hundred and forty years to those figures just to defend their theory of the orbs—a theory I believe has already been sufficiently refuted by the scriptures.

### Chapter III: That the Saturnian revolutions invented by Albumasar are contrary to both history and reason.

<margin>r</margin>
Next are the <term>Saturnian revolutions; original: "saturniis reuolutiōibus"</term> <note>Cycles based on the time it takes the planet Saturn to return to the same point in the zodiac, roughly 30 years</note>. Indeed, <term>Albumasar; original: "Albumasar"</term> <note>Abu Ma'shar, a highly influential 9th-century Persian astrologer</note> alone seems to have imagined these for himself, and since his time, others have not made much use of them. But let us see what they are, what moved Albumasar to create them, and how much he has strayed in this matter, as is his habit in others. He believes that when Saturn has completed ten periods—which takes nearly three hundred years—great events then occur in human affairs. He was moved by this conjecture because he occasionally found in his histories that something significant happened after this number of years; from this, he established the dogma that ten revolutions of Saturn bring about a change in lower <note>earthly</note> things. 

But look first at how much he has strayed in this very historical conjecture. "After **Alexander**," he says, "when three hundred years had passed, there appeared **Aielasor** son of Bel, who built palaces; and after another three hundred years, appeared **Jesus**, our leader." 
<margin>Years from Alexander to Christ.</margin>
By this reasoning, there would be six hundred years from Jesus to Alexander. It is established beyond all controversy that this is utterly false, since no history counts even four hundred years from Christ back to Alexander; even **Alphonso** <note>King Alfonso X of Castile, who commissioned the Alfonsine Tables</note> in his astronomical tables counts no more than three hundred and eleven. 

Now we see the foundations upon which these principal authors of astrology prop up their miraculous dogmas. The same Albumasar says that after Jesus, once ten Saturnian revolutions were completed, a law arose which is a "middle" between the <term>Nazarenes; original: "nazarenos"</term> <note>Christians</note> and the pagans (for so they call the nations). Now, we know for a certainty that no law arose after Christ before **Muhammad** <note>original: "Maometē"</note>; however, I suspect these Arabs understood the sect of the **Manichaeans** <note>followers of the prophet Mani, who combined elements of Christianity, Zoroastrianism, and Buddhism</note>, who are also called <term>Minin; original: "Minin"</term> among the <term>Talmudists; original: "Talmutiſtas"</term> <note>Jewish scholars of the Talmud; "Minim" is a Hebrew term for heretics</note>. 
<margin>An attack through reason.</margin>
This heresy gained strength not only after ten revolutions were finished, but even before the ninth revolution of Saturn was completed. Even if he had drawn all this from a faithful history, that would be no reason to create a dogma that ten periods of Saturn produce such things; otherwise, I could invent a thousand such dogmas for myself. For the Hebrews say that the first temple built by **Solomon** lasted for four hundred or a few more years. Then the second temple, built under **Darius**, lasted no more than ten years more than that—that is, four hundred and ten years. From its destruction, for nearly the same number of years, they composed their laws in **Babylon**. Let us make a dogma from this: that the fourteenth revolution of Saturn always brings a great change to the Saturnian race of the Jews. We would be speaking with more probability than Albumasar.

### Chapter IV. The order of things to be discussed & the dissenting opinions of astrologers regarding great conjunctions.

<margin>The order of things to be said.</margin> There remains the matter of the "access and recess" <note>An astronomical theory, now obsolete, suggesting the celestial spheres "trepidated" or wobbled back and forth</note> of the eighth and ninth spheres; and there remains the matter of **Great Conjunctions**. But let the former be examined in the following book. For now, let us turn to the great conjunctions. It will be worth the effort to first report what the astrologers themselves think about these things, so that what we bring forward in refutation may be more easily understood. This narration itself will not be without the utility of refutation, as we shall see them disagreeing on these matters to such an extent that it is not yet clear among astrologers which is the *greatest* conjunction, which is the *greater*, and which is the *middle*. In this matter, the controversy is not merely about a name; from this arises a great diversity of predictions, as some command us to expect events from the greatest, others from the middle, and others from the minor conjunctions.

<margin>Common opinion. Great conjunction. Greater.</margin> The common opinion, therefore, which Al-Qabisi <note>original: "Alchabitius"; a 10th-century Arab astrologer</note> and Leopold <note>Leopold of Austria, a 13th-century astronomer</note> pass down, and Abu Ma'shar before them, is of this kind: a **Great Conjunction** is when Jupiter and Saturn are joined together, which happens every twenty years. A **Greater Conjunction**, however, is when a shift occurs from one triplicity <note>original: "triplicitate"; a group of three zodiac signs belonging to the same element: Fire, Earth, Air, or Water</note> into another, and they meet at the thresholds of a new triplicity. They say this happens approximately every two hundred and forty years; for within the boundaries of one trigon <note>original: "trigoni"; another term for the elemental triangle formed by three signs</note> they are joined twelve times, and then a transition is made to the sign of the next trigon—not the first one, but the second one from where they joined. For example, if they both departed from Capricorn <note>an Earth sign</note>, they do not meet first in Libra <note>an Air sign</note>, but in Aquarius <note>another Air sign</note> in that triplicity.

<margin>Middle. Greatest.</margin> A **Middle Conjunction** is that which is completed every thirtieth year by Saturn and Mars in Cancer. The **Greatest of all** is of Jupiter and Saturn in Aries, which occurs after nine hundred and sixty years.

<margin>The opinion of Masha'allah. Greatest.</margin> Masha'allah <note>original: "Meſſala"; an 8th-century Persian-Jewish astrologer</note>, disagreeing with these men, says in his book on conjunctions that the **Greatest Conjunction** is that of the three "superiors"—that is, Saturn, Jupiter, and Mars. From this, he expects the changes of "sects" <note>religious movements or laws</note>, the transfer of kingdoms, and the arrival of prophets—not from the conjunction of Jupiter and Saturn in Aries, as the common crowd of astrologers believes. <margin>Greater. Middle. Great.</margin> He makes the next conjunction after this (the **Greater**) that of Jupiter and Saturn; the third (**Middle**) of Saturn and Mars; the fourth (**Great**) of Jupiter and Mars. Let us now see how much both positions err.

### Chapter V. Planets joined in great conjunctions have no more power than when separate: and these great conjunctions are a new invention born from a bad understanding of Ptolemy.

<summary>Pico outlines the conflicting definitions of planetary "conjunctions" used by medieval astrologers like Abu Ma'shar and Masha'allah, noting that even proponents like Pierre d'Ailly eventually retracted these theories.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Pico della Mirandola’s systematic dismantling of astrological "Great Conjunctions." Having previously noted the inconsistency of modern astrologers, he now challenges the physical and philosophical logic of planetary alignments, specifically the conjunction of Jupiter and Saturn.</meta>

->Book V<-

<margin>First reason.</margin> I would like to learn from them why they think Jupiter and Saturn do greater things when they are together than when they are separate and each exercising their own specific powers. For while the mixing of different types of rays indeed creates a new effect—one that a separate and distinct influence would not produce—we can find no reason why it should create a *greater* effect. In fact, we are more inclined to believe that the result is something less than what each planet would achieve if acting alone. For if the planets that come together possessed the same property and produced the same effects, then surely the addition of a second ray would double the effect. But since they are of contrary and clashing natures—as are Jupiter <note>Considered "the Great Benefic," associated with growth and warmth.</note> and Saturn <note>The "Great Malefic," associated with cold and restriction.</note>—one necessarily hinders the other. While they mutually restrain and bind their powers through the diversity of the mixture, it follows that we can expect nothing from them but mediocrity, just as all things resulting from the mixing of extremes are weakened. It is just as they themselves are accustomed to say when Saturn and Mars are together: although both are harmful and both are "malefic" <note>A term for planets believed to have a negative influence on human affairs.</note>, because they have different ways of causing harm, no greater or more remarkable evil arises from their conjunction. Instead, the powers of one are broken and weakened by the other, so that neither can do harm while each strives to do harm according to its own natural condition. Therefore, it is not entirely certain that if earthly events are subject to the heavens, greater and more lasting things happen when the "superior stars" <note>The outer planets: Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn.</note> are joined than when one of them—while the others are <margin>Second reason.</margin> weakened—attains perhaps more strength and power than usual.

Even if we were to grant them that joined planets do more than separate ones toward the great changes of this world, we would not attribute this to the conjunction of Jupiter, Saturn, or Mars. Rather, we shall prove, both by logic and by the authority of the greatest astrologers, that other stars hold the primary power in these matters. For none of the ancients ever judged universal changes in the world by these "great conjunctions," as they call them. Maternus <note>Julius Firmicus Maternus, a 4th-century Roman lawyer and astrologer.</note>—though a most diligent investigator of astrology—says nothing of them; nor does Paul <note>Paul of Alexandria, 4th-century author of the *Introduction to Astrology*.</note>, nor Hephaestion <note>Hephaestion of Thebes, a 5th-century astrologer.</note>, nor Theophilus <note>Theophilus of Edessa, an 8th-century scholar and court astrologer.</note>, nor Astaxarchus, nor Ptolemy himself. Ptolemy’s testimony alone will be enough for us here, so that we do not use too few well-known witnesses against them. In the second book of his *Apotelesmaton* <note>original: "apotelesmaton"; better known as the *Tetrabiblos*, the most influential astrological text of antiquity.</note>, when teaching the way universal and world changes may be foreseen, he refers them all solely to the eclipses <note>original: "defectus"</note> of the Sun and Moon. Nothing more reasonable could be said; for universal and great effects ought to be referred to those causes which are most universal and effective. It is confessed by all that among the planets, only two are of universal effectiveness: the Sun and the Moon (whose light is nothing other than the light of the Sun brought to the Earth through her, as if through a mirror, so to speak). Therefore, if any celestial power must be considered the origin and cause of great and universal effects, none should be considered more so than these stars.

As for what Messalla <note>Masha'allah ibn Athari (c. 740–815), a Persian-Jewish astrologer influential in the Middle Ages.</note> says—that great things are done by Jupiter and Saturn because they have a slower motion—he proves what he denies rather than what he affirms. For it is the consensus of everyone that a faster motion is owed to a nobler and more powerful body. Therefore, those who defend the roles and dignity of the superior stars—lest they be thought weaker because they return to their place more slowly—are accustomed to prove by the proportion of the circles they travel that they are faster than many others, even if they appear slower due to the length of their periods. But I know what they will say about Ptolemy: that this was omitted by him in the book...

<summary>Pico argues that the conjunction of Jupiter and Saturn produces mediocre rather than "great" effects because their contrary natures cancel each other out. He asserts that ancient authorities like Ptolemy prioritized solar and lunar eclipses over planetary conjunctions for predicting major world events.</summary>

->Book V<-

...of the *Apotelesmaton* <note>Original: "apotelesmaton." This refers to Ptolemy’s *Tetrabiblos*, the foundational text of Western astrology.</note> lest he betray the mystery. For so writes Haly <note>Haly Abenragel or Haly Heben Rodan, famous Arabic commentators on astrological texts.</note>, his interpreter. But in the *Centiloquium* <note>A collection of 100 astrological aphorisms formerly attributed to Ptolemy, but now recognized as a later medieval compilation.</note> (for so they call it), they claim he gave many proofs of this matter, since in the fiftieth "word" <note>Aphorism or short decree.</note> of that book he commands that we should not forget the conjunctions of the planets, in which there is great efficacy. Likewise, in both the fifty-eighth and the sixty-fourth words, he warns us of these same things, handing down great precepts about them, distinguishing between the greatest, the middle, and the smallest conjunctions.

<margin>Refutation.</margin>
Indeed, I would wish for nothing more than for them to answer me: so that from this it may become clear to everyone that whatever of their dogmas seem greater and more admirable have sprouted either from vain opinions or from a false understanding of ancient authors. For as to their claim that Ptolemy remained silent about this in his book of *Apotelesmaton* lest he betray the mystery—far be it from me to deny he was silent; rather, I do not even believe it was mentioned by him in the *Centiloquium*. In that work, he certainly spoke no more of those conjunctions than he did of the death of Priam <note>The legendary last king of Troy; Pico uses this as an example of something completely irrelevant to the text.</note> or the war of the Trojans. We shall subsequently reveal how they perverted many of that author’s pronouncements, and how many errors have propagated one after another from a single source. Ptolemy’s fiftieth word stands thus in the common edition used by them: *Do not forget that there are one hundred and twenty conjunctions among the wandering stars; for in them is the greater knowledge of things that occur in this world, observing increase and decrease.* In the Greek, it is thus: *Lest we overlook the one hundred and nineteen conjunctions. For in these is placed the joining of things that happen in the world, both of generation and corruption.* First, the barbarian <note>Pico uses "barbarian" to refer to the medieval Arabic and Latin translations which he considered linguistically and intellectually inferior to original Greek sources.</note> interpretation attributes more to these conjunctions than Ptolemy does, for in his version, there is no claim that there is "greater knowledge" of things in the world than that which comes from them.

<margin>The Opinion of Ptolemy.</margin>
Furthermore, even if we set that aside, the meaning of the statement is nothing other than that we should not look solely at the property of each individual star. Instead, we should know that from their conjunction, various power-producing effects of various things arise—a point that no one denies and which must be granted by all astrologers. But Ptolemy certainly did not say that we should attribute the greatest changes of the lower things <note>Earthly or "sublunary" events.</note> to the conjunctions of the superior stars. Rather, if his words are read and understood correctly, they will indicate the opposite opinion to us. For he did not say there are one hundred and twenty of these conjunctions (as is commonly read), but only one hundred and nineteen. This is because he does not count the conjunction of the Sun and Moon among them, as it possesses peculiar privileges and a singular prerogative in great and universal changes. He reduces all the rest into a single number and order, such that among them, no one conjunction would excel another by any singular condition. Not noticing this, the barbarian expositors—as if the conjunction of the Sun and Moon had been omitted by a scribe's error—added it back, believing that one should read "one hundred and twenty" and not "one hundred and nineteen," which all the Greek manuscripts have. Thus, not content with corrupting the sense, they even falsified the reliability of the literal text. Let us move on to other matters. Ptolemy writes in word fifty-eight in this manner: *the place of the conjunction in which place [the planet] was with the Ascendant in Spica...* <note>Spica is a bright star in the constellation Virgo, often used in horoscopes.</note> and word sixty-four is of this kind: *in the smallest conjunction the difference of the middle conjunction, and in the middle...*

<margin>Poor understanding of the 58th and 64th words.</margin>
*...the difference of the greatest conjunction.* The Arabs and Latins think that in both places, Ptolemy understands the conjunction of Saturn and Jupiter. But no one would be so deceived if they had ever read the Greek authors of astrology—and especially Ptolemy—with their eyes open. For indeed...

# Book V

<margin>The meaning of the fifty-eighth word <note>Original: "Sententia verbi quinquagesimi octavi." Pico refers to the 58th aphorism of the *Centiloquium*.</note></margin>
We use the term "conjunction," which in Greek is *synodus* <note>Original: "synodus" (σύνοδος). While it can mean any meeting, Pico argues that in an astronomical context, it specifically refers to the New Moon.</note>. When this word is used on its own, it is always understood as the joining of the Sun and Moon, unless a specific addition is made to show whose conjunction it might be—such as Venus and Mercury, or Jupiter and Saturn, and the other planets. Therefore, since Ptolemy spoke of "conjunction" in both statements without adding anything further, it is perfectly clear to anyone who is not entirely ignorant of Greek literature that he intended it to be understood as the conjunction of the luminaries <note>The "luminaries" are the Sun and the Moon.</note>, and not of other stars. And so, the meaning of the former—that is, the fifty-eighth word—is this: that once we have carefully observed the sign and place where the conjunction of the Sun and Moon occurred during the revolution of the year, we should then look for the effect. This happens when the "perfection" <note>Original: "perfectio," usually translated as "profection" in astrology. This is a technique where a point in the birth chart is moved forward by one sign per year or month to predict timing.</note> of the year—distributed through the months—reaches that place where the sign succeeds the previous one in the order of ruling power. For that conjunction of the Sun and Moon, occurring before the year's turning, will have signaled the outcome to us. Indeed, Ptolemy uses these meetings of the luminaries above all others to investigate the events of the entire year, a fact known to anyone who has turned the pages of his *Apotelesmatic* <note>Original: "apotelesmaticos." This refers to Ptolemy's *Tetrabiblos*, his main work on the effects of the stars.</note> books.

<margin>
Errors of the common translation in word 58.
</margin>
However, in the common translation of this aphorism, many things have been added, omitted, or altered. For instance, instead of "conjunction," they read "minor conjunction," even though no distinction between "greater" or "minor" is added in the Greek manuscripts. Furthermore, they extend the term of the "perfection" to many years, whereas Ptolemy makes no mention of this, speaking only of the events of a single year, as we said; yet the text seems to favor the astrologers' view in their eyes. 

Now, regarding that last statement where the "greatest," "middle," and "smallest" conjunctions are distinguished: many do not understand what kind of distinction this is in a conjunction of the luminaries. But this is easy and open to those who have stayed awake by Ptolemy’s lamp without yawning. Since he attributes everything to the conjunctions of the Sun and Moon, he then distinguishes them into three types and orders.

<margin>Explanation of word 64.</margin>
First, he places those which cause an eclipse of one of the luminaries. Through these, the events of not just one year, but sometimes many years, can be foreseen. For this reason, we call them the "greatest," because the stars are then most "joined"—differing neither in the longitude of their place nor in their latitude <note>In an eclipse, the Sun and Moon are aligned not just on the horizontal plane (longitude) but also the vertical plane (latitude), meaning they physically overlap from our perspective.</note>—and they portend the most distant future events. 

<margin>
What are the greatest conjunctions according to Ptolemy?
</margin>
<margin>What are the smallest?</margin>
<margin>What are the middle?</margin>
On the other hand, according to him, the "smallest" are those which occur every month; these indicate to us the disposition of only a single month. The "middle" ones are those which immediately precede the Sun’s entry into the four tropical signs <note>The "tropical signs" are Aries (Spring), Cancer (Summer), Libra (Autumn), and Capricorn (Winter).</note>: Aries, Cancer, Libra, and Capricorn. From these, the entire following season of the year is indicated to us—be it spring, summer, autumn, or winter. 

Therefore, because the "universal" disposition indicates something that the "particular" following it distinguishes and determines, he said that the middle conjunction is the greatest "difference" <note>Original: "differentia." In this context, it refers to the primary variation or change in the year's quality.</note>, while the smallest is the least. To give an example: if the conjunction of the Moon and Sun immediately preceding the spring equinox shows us the future quality of the spring, we should then know that this quality is both increased and decreased according to the nature of the conjunctions that happen in each of the following months in their fixed revolution. And the relationship that these monthly conjunctions have to those four seasonal ones, the seasonal ones have to the "greater" and rarer meetings and joinings of the eclipsing stars. This is Ptolemy’s opinion on the greatest, middle, and smallest conjunctions. These "barbarians" <note>Pico's term for medieval Arabic and Latin astrologers who he believes corrupted classical knowledge.</note>, not understanding this, have manufactured for themselves the most beautiful dreams about the conjunctions of Saturn and Jupiter—which return as "greatest" after nine hundred and sixty years, "middle" after two hundred and forty, and "smallest" after twenty years. This interpretation, besides what we have already said...

# Book V

It cannot even be expressed, because the greatest conjunction among them encompasses the mean and the least ones. Therefore, the effect of the greatest conjunction cannot be determined through those smaller ones, through which that [greatest] one is accomplished over many revolutions of centuries. What then did Ptolemy say? That the mean is the difference of the greatest, and the smallest is the difference of the mean? This is that fiction born from a false understanding of a single author, in which these men boast so much and by which they pride themselves, glorying in the fact that their entire religion is bound to the stars. By this, they subject the most holy laws of the prophets, the coming of divine miracles, to the powers of the stars and the fates. Certainly, they never show themselves to be more childish, or are found to be more ignorant and ridiculous.

### Chapter VI: That the principal astrologers have used mean conjunctions, not true ones; and other errors of theirs concerning the same.

<margin>Response.</margin>
**B**ut perhaps some of the astrologers will say: "Suppose we did not understand Ptolemy; what if, just as a storm sometimes drives a ship into a harbor, so this error has led us to the truth? Whatever Ptolemy and others felt, experience has confirmed that no great change of laws or kingdoms has ever occurred which some conjunction of the higher stars <note>The "higher stars" refers to the outer planets, specifically Saturn and Jupiter.</note> did not precede; nor has any alignment of this kind ever occurred without such changes in inferior matters following it." It is well if they acknowledge the "storm"—we shall see about that "harbor." For if they have raved so wildly in great matters, we shall see how much they hold up when they have tried to make experience out of these lowest things. We shall first declare this in general, and then we will show more clearly than light that every "great conjunction" any astrologer has marked and related to the events of wonderful things is false, falsely calculated, and falsely related to its effects.

<margin>First reason.</margin>
In the first place, all authors of this doctrine do not use true conjunctions, but <term>mean conjunctions</term> <note>Mean motion is a mathematical average of a planet's speed, whereas "true motion" accounts for its actual, varying speed in the sky.</note>—that is, fictitious and imaginary ones. So that everyone may clearly understand this, I will state what true motion is and what mean motion is.

<margin>What true motion is and what mean motion is.</margin>
The wandering stars <note>Original: "erraticae stellae," the classical term for planets.</note> are not carried through the zodiac with an even course; that is, they do not always pass through equal parts of the zodiac in equal intervals of time. Therefore, those who wished to measure their motions and organize their countless paths invented a uniform motion for each planet, so that from this fictitious and uniform motion they might more easily reach that unequal and true motion.

<margin>Ptolemy.</margin>
Ptolemy calls that fictitious motion "periodic"; the younger [astrologers] call it "mean," because they use it as a kind of middle ground to investigate the true [position]. When we seek the place of a planet from a calculation of motion, we again use mean motion—sometimes, indeed, not because that "mean" indicates to us the place where the planet actually stays, but so that from it we may seek its true seat by an easier method and logic. For a planet is never exactly where it is found to be through mean motion, because it never actually moves that way. But this was devised by astrologers, as I said, so that the truth might be attained from there with a certain order. I was saying, therefore, that those who judge the future by <term>great conjunctions</term> <note>Alignments of Saturn and Jupiter, occurring roughly every 20 years, and shifting "triplicities" every 200 years.</note> use mean conjunctions, not true ones. For when they say that after twenty years Jupiter and Saturn are joined, and after two hundred years they meet at the beginnings of the <term>triplicities</term> <note>Groups of three zodiac signs associated with the four elements: Fire, Earth, Air, and Water.</note>, and then after 860 years they meet in the boundaries of Aries—this is completely false if we look at true motions. It is true, however—though not exactly—if we look at those mean ones, which are fictitious and false, and invented by mathematicians for the ease of teaching. Thus, because what is called "mean motion" is different from what we reach through "true motion," it can even happen that the sign of the conjunction is assigned to one place—for example, in Pisces—while it actually occurred in Aquarius. And the time varies so much that if we are dealing with conjunctions occurring after 240 years, the true one sometimes...
