# Book V

<margin>The insanity of astrologers.</margin>
<margin>The most prominent authors of astrology used "mean" conjunctions.</margin>
...even though the mean precedes the true by a hundred years. It is apparent from the tables to anyone calculating correctly that Jupiter and Saturn, in the year of grace 1226 <note>1226 AD</note>, migrated from the earthly triplicity <term>triplicity: a group of three zodiac signs associated with one of the four elements (Fire, Earth, Air, Water)</term> into the airy triplicity in Aquarius. According to the logic of their "mean motion" <note>Mean motion is a simplified mathematical average of a planet's speed, whereas "true motion" reflects its actual, irregular position in the sky.</note>, they were supposed to remain there for two hundred and forty years; and yet, after about one hundred and forty years—that is, in the year of grace 1365—after a change was made from the airy to the watery triplicity, they met in Scorpio. They were thereafter always found together in watery signs and did not return to the airy ones. What insanity is this, then, to fight against the open truth? And to use things so shamelessly false and fictitious that, while there is absolutely no agreement among them regarding the constellations, they nevertheless refer the outcomes of human affairs to them with blind recklessness. That which is not, has never been, and never will be, they nevertheless consider to be the cause of things that are. Certainly, nothing is more delirious than this vanity, into which all the leading authors of astrology have fallen. For **Albumasar** <note>Abu Ma'shar, a 9th-century Persian astrologer whose works were foundational to medieval European astrology.</note>, the prince of this doctrine, in that book titled *On the Great Conjunctions*—which is much celebrated among astrologers—always used mean conjunctions, never the true ones. Furthermore, **Abraham** <note>Likely Abraham bar Hiyya, a 12th-century Jewish philosopher and astronomer whose work "The Scroll of the Revealer" (Redemption) linked astrology to the coming of the Messiah.</note>, in that work titled *Redemption*, although he seeks one or two conjunctions from true motion, he thereafter always flees to the mean ones, making no mention of the true ones at all.

<margin>Alliacensis.</margin>
**Alliacensis** <note>Pierre d'Ailly (1351–1420), a French cardinal and theologian who attempted to reconcile astrology with sacred history.</note>, in his treatise *On the Concordance of History and Astrology*, although he asserts there are seven "greatest conjunctions," he brings forward only mean ones, and no true ones. Many others, always suffering from the same disease in the same way, do the same; we shall discuss all of them individually later. Indeed, these points could suffice for us, so that we might show there is nothing in what they say, if the very constellation from which they predict is itself a nothing.

<margin>The fiction of the astrologers.</margin>
For since these "mean" conjunctions—which is to say, non-existent ones—do not correspond to the truth for them (that is, they do not fall at the times when the astrologers would most want them to), they manufacture another refuge for themselves, defending their prior insanity with a new folly. For they have imagined that the things they portend do not follow immediately after these conjunctions—indeed, not even quickly—but rather after many years: a hundred, or two hundred, or even more than these.

<margin>Refutation</margin>
See how greatly they are deceived in this matter! For it is not the nature of a powerful and effective cause to begin what it is going to do late, but rather to finish late; it should begin either immediately or quickly. Therefore, the power of these conjunctions is either effective or weak. If it is effective, it cannot cease for a long time without acting; if it is weak, it cannot last long enough to finally act at some late point. A great force tames and overcomes whatever prohibits or resists it.

<margin>Another refutation</margin>
A weak force vanishes and dissolves itself into thinness over a longer stretch of time. Furthermore, during this interval of time, new conjunctions are always occurring; their nature, as the astrologers themselves say, is to "erase" the previous ones, since a succeeding constellation strikes down the preceding one. Hence, if an eclipse of the luminaries occurs at a certain time of year, they are accustomed to say that the fate which was received from the beginning of the annual revolution ceases. Why, therefore, does it not also cease at the following conjunction, especially one of a different property and nature? Why would it not expunge that first one? Yet they want the effect to belong to that first conjunction, even though it follows three hundred years later, with so many various mean constellations intervening. No one would say this—neither a philosopher, nor even a man who is not of the most extreme slowness of mind. This error is increased in a marvelous way by another inexpiable error: for in the very computation of times they err so significantly that a conjunction which they sometimes think will last for two hundred...

# Book
<page-num>V</page-num>

<margin>The cunning of astrologers.</margin>
...years, a certain event preceded it. But that event actually preceded the time of its occurrence by one thousand four hundred years: as will be demonstrated in the following chapters of this book. In these matters, the unlearned and ignorant are indeed caught in lies. But see also how cunning these most elegant diviners are: so that an opportunity for deception would never be lacking, they have linked their own decrees together in such a way that, whenever something somewhat marvelous happens, they can refer it back to some preceding conjunction. For they have said, in order to achieve this, that the power of a single conjunction <term>conjunction: the meeting of two planets, usually Saturn and Jupiter, in the same degree of the zodiac</term> lasts until the very hour of the next one; thus, whatever happens in the middle can always be referred back and attributed to some conjunction. Nor did they see their own ruin in this fallacy: for if it remains the case among them that there is no great effect without a great conjunction, and no great conjunction appears without an effect, while they try to ensure that such causes are not absent for such events, they necessarily cause such causes to be frequently exhausted without such events. For great and wonderful things do not always happen because of them; indeed, those things which they say are caused by great conjunctions do not even happen frequently. And yet, as they themselves wish, the power that produces them remains uninterrupted in a continuous succession. These things are said in general against those who speak with impious rashness about future events based on these great conjunctions; now let us examine everything in detail.

### Chapter VII What order is to be followed, and that d’Ailly felt one thing at one time and another at another.

<margin>Pierre d'Ailly</margin>
Let us begin with the "greatest conjunctions" which **Pierre d’Ailly** <note>Pierre d’Ailly (1350–1420) was a French cardinal and scholar who wrote "On the Concordance of History and Astrology."</note> collects in his treatise on the concordance of history and astrology. Here, he intends to confirm the astrologers' claim that such conjunctions never occur without a great change in earthly affairs. And yet, he himself disagrees with this entire "concordance" of his in his *Elucidarium* <note>A later work where d'Ailly was more skeptical of certain astrological techniques.</note>; while he uses Saturnian revolutions and the greatest conjunctions there, he openly confesses for once that they have no foundation and were not calculated by him. This makes it all the more surprising that he has a praiser in a matter in which he himself did not approve of himself. But because he occasionally moved arguments against himself that were insufficiently true—since some are unnecessary and some poorly expressed—let us gather a few but effective points by which that entire treatise may be plainly cut down. Then we shall proceed to refute the other conjunctions which **Abraham** <note>Abraham Ibn Ezra (1089–1167), a Jewish polymath and astrologer.</note> and **Albumasar** <note>Abu Ma'shar (787–886), a leading Persian astrologer of the Middle Ages.</note> and many others, and d’Ailly himself following them, put forward in the *Elucidarium*. Truly, since it will be necessary to speak often of the calculation of times, I thought it necessary to preface certain things. From these, it should first be shown that when there is doubt about dates, the judgment of this matter does not belong to the astrologers, as d’Ailly thinks, but to history; then, when there is variety among historical writers, which one should be followed by right. Regarding these things, I will say a few words here and in passing, since we have disputed this extensively in that specific work we wrote concerning the true calculation of times.

### Chapter VIII That the division of eras is not to be sought from astrology as d’Ailly thought, but from history.

<margin>Opinion of d'Ailly.</margin>
<gloss>a</gloss> **Pierre d’Ailly**, in his book on the concordance of astrology and theology, thinks that the number of years from the beginning of the world to these times can be detected and reduced to truth by astrological reasoning—matters which sacred or foreign histories have put forward variously. "For if," he says, "you have the investigated *thema* <term>thema: a horoscope or birth chart</term> of the world's own birth, you will be able to gather from it the first conjunction of Saturn and Jupiter from the beginning of the world by calculation." But if you then track down the next conjunction nearest to your own years, the interval which was between...

# Book V

<margin>His opinion in the *Elucidarium*</margin>
That first and last interval of time will be drawn out from the calculation of the intervening conjunctions. This is what he [Pierre d’Ailly] felt at that time: but in the *Elucidarium* <note>original: *elucidario*, a work by the 14th-century cardinal and scholar Pierre d'Ailly</note>, he plainly confessed that there is no astrological way by which we might find anything certain regarding the doubtful number of years. Therefore, not even the greatest astrologers ever attempted this or promised it from their art. But since he says these things, I do not know why he persists again in that opinion that the ultimate question regarding the calculation of times should be referred to astrologers; and that whatever is found in histories concerning the "Year of the World" <note>original: *annus mundi*, the date calculated from the biblical creation</note> that differs from them <margin>Against d'Ailly.</margin> ought to be corrected and punished according to their opinion. We will briefly show that this can be defended by no reasoning. For an astronomer can—if he has a true position of the stars that once was, and again has another recent one—determine by a most certain reason how much time must necessarily have passed in between them. But how will this help him? If the time of some past event is uncertain. For suppose someone says three thousand years have passed from Christ to us; let another say one thousand and four hundred. In settling this dispute, what will be the duty of the astronomer? You will say he will show that between the stellar position under which Christ was born and that which is held now, three thousand years could not have passed, but only one thousand four hundred. But what slowness, what dullness is this: that you do not see you are assuming as certain the very thing that is in question? For the astrologer does not know what stellar position Christ was born under unless he first learns from history at what time he was born. Let us go to more remote times. Alfonso <note>Alfonso X of Castile, sponsor of the influential Alfonsine Tables</note> counts <margin>Alfonso and Albumasar.</margin> three thousand one hundred and two years from the Deluge <term>Deluge: the biblical flood of Noah</term> to Christ. Albumasar <note>a famous 9th-century Persian astrologer</note> feels the same, whom he [Alfonso] followed; all history opposes this number. D’Ailly thinks all histories are in error rather than the astrologers. By what reason, I ask? Is it because the time between the conjunction that preceded the flood and Christ is reached through so many cycles of years? No one denies this to them. But where did they learn that this conjunction happened as many years before the flood as they think? Could they know this from anywhere else but history? Truly this is so manifest that unless I had seen d’Ailly's slip here, I would think I was wasting words on a superfluous matter. For how ridiculous, I ask, was their opinion when they said we could be made certain about the years of the world from the first conjunction at the beginning of the world? They gathered that first conjunction from the "birth of the world" <note>original: *mundi genitura*, the hypothetical horoscope of creation</note>, as if we could doubt the years of the world, for which we have established not only in what year, but even at what hour it began. Therefore, let no one doubt that the timing of events must be sought from the great history of things; in this matter, astronomy must be a pupil, not an arbiter. For I will grant Alfonso that so many thousands of years before Christ there was such a position of the stars as appears from his tables; but I will not grant that the Deluge or any other past event happened at that time, unless a faithful history demonstrates this to me.

<margin>All astronomers have erred in the calculation of times.</margin>
Moreover, all astronomers have erred vehemently in this calculation of times, which will become more manifest in its proper place. This could have happened to them for no other reason than that they adhered to false histories. For the Latin astronomers followed the Arabs, but those [Arabs] are the most prone to fables. And if any received histories from Greek or Latin writers, a foreign translation violated most things. While this happens easily in every matter among foreign peoples who lack letters, it happens most easily in the notation of numbers, in which even the most accurate diligence of scribes almost always hallucinates <note>original: *hallucinatur*, meaning to wander or make errors</note> something. Therefore, true and faithful histories must be used, among which no Christian will doubt that Sacred Scripture is to be preferred above others; but neither will a Hebrew or a Saracen <note>Saracen: a term used in the Renaissance for Muslims</note>. Furthermore, regarding those things that happened before the Deluge, the nations will either have that history—that is, the Mosaic one <note>referring to the books of Moses/Genesis</note>—or they will have none to follow, since among others nothing is found preserved in writing concerning those times, unless somewhere in the sacred vo...

# Book V

Regarding the luminaries, the Greek edition <note>the Septuagint, the Greek translation of the Old Testament</note> disagrees with the Hebrew truth <note>original: *hebraica ueritate*, referring to the Masoretic Hebrew text</note> in this measurement of years; no one of sound judgment can prefer the faith of a translator over the author himself. This is especially true since not only does Jerome <note>the translator of the Latin Vulgate</note> side with the Hebrew numbering, but Augustine also thinks one should side with it. Although Augustine gladly follows and approves of the old translation <note>the Septuagint</note>, nevertheless, when he mentions this varying calculation of years, he says that the reliability of the history must be sought from that language from which what we have was translated. Thus, while Augustine might think that what is different in the Septuagint is a mystery rather than an error of history, he still does not doubt that the literal truth resides with the Hebrews.

### Chapter IX: The summary opinion of Pierre d’Ailly in the book which he titled *On the Harmony of Astrology and History*

Now that we have briefly laid these foundations concerning the true calculation of times, let us come to those "greatest conjunctions" of the astrologers—or rather, to their greatest follies. We shall begin from those which Pierre d'Ailly <note>Petrus de Alliaco, a prominent 14th-century theologian and cardinal</note> collected in his treatise *On the Harmony of History and Astrology*. In that work, he used the following order. He assumes two principles: the first concerns the number of years from Adam to Christ; the second concerns the birth chart <note>original: *themāte genituræ*, a horoscope for the moment of creation</note> of the world itself. He says that 5,344 years flowed from Adam to Jesus: specifically, 2,242 years from Adam to the Flood, and 3,102 years from the Flood to Jesus.

In the first constitution of the world, he claims the stars were so placed in the heavens that the first part of Cancer formed the horoscope <note>the Ascendant, or the point rising on the eastern horizon</note>. The very highest point of the sky <note>the Midheaven</note> possessed the first part of Aries. Mercury was in the fifteenth part of Gemini in the twelfth region of the sky; Venus occupied the eleventh region in Taurus. Both luminaries <note>the Sun and Moon</note> were positioned so that the nocturnal one <note>the Moon</note> was in Taurus, while the diurnal one <note>the Sun</note> shone at the nineteenth part of Aries in the middle and highest part of heaven. Saturn was in Aquarius in the house of death <note>the 8th House</note>; Jupiter held the ninth place of heaven in Pisces. Mars stayed in Scorpio and in the fifth seat from the horoscope, in which same place—but in Sagittarius—was the Dragon’s Tail <note>the South Node of the moon</note>. The following figure puts this entire arrangement before your eyes.

<margin>
The first greatest conjunction.
</margin>

With these things so established, he concludes with no effort that the first "greatest conjunction" of Saturn and Jupiter occurred from the beginning of the world in the beginning of Aries after 320 years. After this, he enumerates six others, always with an interval of 960 years (by an error of "mean motion" <note>a simplified calculation of planetary movement that assumes constant speed</note>). Thus, it follows that the seventh "greatest conjunction" from the beginning of the world occurred in the year of grace 735, after which the eighth will follow in the year 1694. Having distributed these, he gathers from histories the most memorable events which occurred in those middle spaces of time—that is, between one conjunction and another.

...nor is the "greatest conjunction" required: this is because of those nine hundred and sixty years, in which time interval whatever happens that is significant and memorable, they think it should be referred to the preceding conjunction after which it—namely, the event—occurred. And because something great and memorable is always found within this span of years, they consider their theory confirmed. They claim that these greatest conjunctions do not happen without a massive change in earthly affairs. In this, d’Ailly seems to have fulfilled what he promised in another book: to show that the truth of history harmonizes with the truth of astrology. This is the summary of the whole book, this its order, and this its foundation.

### Chapter X: That d’Ailly erred in many ways; and even if his assumptions were granted, he still does not prove what he intends.

<margin>First reason. Second reason. Third reason. Fourth reason. Fifth reason. Sixth reason. The horoscope of the world <term>genitura mundi</term> <note>A theoretical astrological chart calculated for the exact moment of the world's creation.</note> described by d'Ailly is false and impossible. Refutation of another horoscope of the world. Abraham.</margin>

**T**o begin with, let us grant his points about the conjunctions, the timing of events, and the world’s birth chart; let us finally give him everything he demands. What kind of "confirmation of astrology through history" is this? What if we were to show that no nine hundred and sixty years have ever passed without the world seeing some great change in created things, or some shift in the human condition? I ask you to describe this span of years starting from other dates—not, for example, from the year 320 of the world, which was the time of the "first conjunction," but starting from the year 500. Count those nine hundred and sixty years which revolve from one conjunction to another. You will find no fewer varieties of wars, laws, prophets, plagues, and diverse events of many kinds occurring in that long stretch of time. Why did you not always trace the series of these deeds back through every two hundred years from the time of that conjunction of yours? This is "thick-witted" <note>original: *Pinguis hic nimis minerua*, a Latin idiom for a crude or unrefined approach.</note> reasoning if this is how we harmonize astrology with history. 

Furthermore, those conjunctions were not "true" but "mean"—which is to say they are false and non-existent. <note>In astronomy, "mean motion" refers to a simplified average speed of a planet, whereas "true motion" accounts for its actual, variable speed in the sky.</note> Nor should they be referred to those specific times, even if we accept them as mean motions. Nor is the number of years from Adam to Christ what he thought it was; the true calculation exceeds his by more than one thousand four hundred years. Nor did those deeds or events happen at the times he believed they did. 

Finally, the birth chart he describes for the world is shown by astrological reasoning to be not only doubtful or false, but plainly impossible. Since that whole booklet can be corrected with a single strike of the pen, no one is ignorant—and he himself does not deny—that those were mean conjunctions, not true ones. But if the birth chart of the world, from which all others are derived, is impossible, then those calculations based on mean motion will necessarily be found false as well. 

As to whether it is impossible, we want Mercury to interpret for you: in that specific figure <note>the birth chart of the world</note>, Mercury is placed fifty-six degrees away from the Sun. Yet Mercury would swear by all the gods and goddesses that it has never moved even a finger's breadth further than twenty-nine degrees away from the Sun. <note>Mercury is the closest planet to the Sun and never appears more than about 28 degrees away from it from Earth's perspective; d'Ailly's chart is therefore astronomically impossible.</note> This is an error that is all too evident and unpardonable. He also considers that to be the primordial figure of the world which he asserts in his *Elucidarium*, a work burdened with marvelous illusions. It is attributed to the Chaldeans and the Ishmaelites, whom the Divinity supposedly made privy to this mystery. In that chart, Mercury is placed in the first part of Gemini, and the Sun in the first part of Aries. This would mean Mercury is separated from the Sun by sixty degrees, which any astronomer will deny is possible. 

But let us return to those conjunctions which (as I was saying) are found to be false and impossible once the first figure of the heavens, from which all others were gathered, is removed. There is also the fact that there is no conjunction in Aries after nine hundred years (as Abraham the Spaniard <note>Abraham bar Hiyya, a 12th-century Jewish philosopher and astronomer from Spain.</note> teaches in his sixth book titled *The Redemption of Israel*). Furthermore, the events he refers to those conjunctions did not even happen at the times he thinks. For not from the world...

### Chapter XI. That the astrologers disagreed both among themselves and with the truth regarding the conjunction of the flood; and even if everything they ask for were granted, they still do not prove what they contend.

**L**et us pass on to the other great conjunctions noted by others with a bit more diligence, though not so much that they avoid the mark of madness, let alone error. It is clear, therefore, that at the time of the universal flood there was no such conjunction as they suppose; and even if we grant them the number of years they want, there were instead during those times constellations from which one would expect burnings by fire rather than an inundation of waters.

## Chapter XII. On the conjunction of Moses and the prophecy of the Messiah which the delirious Jew Abraham [concocted].

<margin>
Abraham the Prince.
Abraham Avenezra.
The fiction of Abraham.
</margin>
**A**braham the Prince (as he is titled among the Hebrews) <note>Refers to Abraham bar Hiyya (c. 1070–1136), a mathematician and astronomer known as "Savasorda."</note>, whose student was Abraham Avenezra <note>Abraham Ibn Ezra (c. 1089–1167), a polymath whose astrological works were highly influential in the Latin West.</note>, composed a book which he entitled *On the Redemption of Israel*. The purpose of that work was to use the astrological path to investigate the time of the coming Messiah. Beginning from the birth of Moses, he invented some specific positioning of the stars for himself (of the kind we were discussing), involving a coupling of Saturn and Jupiter. To this alignment he refers Moses, the kingdom of Israel, and the Law given to the Jewish people—even though (as they usually do) he wraps his writing in the most religious words to protect his books from the fire, and he himself often denies saying what he is actually saying. Having formed this constellation under which the kingdom and Law of the Hebrews supposedly arose, he found a similar one 2,859 years after Moses (according to his own calculation), which is the year of Christ 1464. He commanded that the Messiah be expected then. In that year, Saturn and Jupiter were together in Pisces, and twenty years before the others—that is, in the year 1444—they were together in Cancer. Following either of these conjunctions, he pronounced by astrological assertion that both the arrival of the Messiah and all those wonders expected through the Messiah would occur.

<margin>
Refutation.
First reason.
</margin>
But since this has already been sufficiently refuted by reality itself—fifty years having now passed since the first conjunction and thirty since the second—the fable he tells about Moses can also be sufficiently weakened. We should not believe that the constellation gave them a kingdom, since it did not return a kingdom to them when it recurred. Nor does it seem to have brought forth Moses, since it returned to us with its powers completely spent, bringing us no prophet.

<margin>
Second reason.
Jews expelled from Spain.
</margin>
Furthermore, not only did the Hebrew people not begin to fare more happily after those conjunctions, but they were overwhelmed by calamities almost no less great than those under Titus or Hadrian. Recently, all the Jews were expelled from the whole of Spain by that most Christian King [Ferdinand II]—who can certainly never be praised enough <note>Pico refers to the Alhambra Decree of 1492. As a man of his time, he views the expulsion as a triumph for his faith, though he notes the human suffering it caused.</note>—where they had been most powerful in number, wealth, and authority. They themselves do not deny that they have suffered almost nothing more sad or bitter than this expulsion. Many were taken by shipwreck, very many by pestilence, and the greatest part of them were consumed by hunger. Even to us Christians—while the glory of divine justice in such a great calamity was a delight—the extreme suffering of these men nevertheless evoked compassion and grief.

# Book V
<page-num>V</page-num>
<header>Book</header>

...is the Messiah: this is that redemption which Abraham <note>Likely referring to Abraham Aven Ezra (c. 1089–1167), a scholar whose astrological works Pico frequently critiques.</note> promised them based on the "Mosaic constellation." Lest it be believed that he divined better regarding past events than future ones, let us look at that conjunction to which he attributed the coming of Moses, and see how plainly false and ridiculous he is. For that conjunction, by which he believed Moses was born, occurred many years after the death of Moses; and even if we grant him his timing, it signified nothing of the sort he imagines. 

<margin>Third reason</margin>
Let us look at the timing; but first one must know that in this year, which is 1494 from Christ, the Hebrews count 5,253 years from the foundation of the world <note>The Jewish calendar *Anno Mundi* (AM). Pico is comparing various chronological systems to spot inconsistencies.</note>. 

<margin>Calculation</margin>
Therefore, they calculate 3,760 years from the creation to Christ. Since that Abraham says Moses was born after three years had passed from that conjunction—which he says occurred in the year of the world 2,365—it follows that it occurred 1,395 years before the time of Christ. But in truth, by a correct calculation, the years from Moses to Christ are found to be 1,509. Therefore, that conjunction was 130 years **after** Moses was born. 

The number of years is demonstrated as follows: 

<margin>Calculation of the years from Moses to Christ.</margin>
* From Moses to the first building of the Temple (from the third book of Kings, which is the first of Samuel among them) <note>Pico is referencing the biblical chronology in 1 Kings 6:1, noting the different naming conventions of the books in the Hebrew vs. Latin Bibles.</note>: **479 years**.
* From that first building to the restoration of the Temple under Darius: **512 years**.
* From Darius to Christ are counted: **518 years**.

The sum of all these is the number I mentioned: **1,509 years**. But that conjunction preceded Christ by 1,395 years, and thus it occurred 130 years after the birth of Moses. However, that constellation was not so "miraculous" or "prophetic" that we must fight over the timing. For he says that Jupiter and Saturn were joined in the year of the world 2,365, on the 25th day of the month of Adar <note>The twelfth month of the Hebrew civil year, roughly February/March.</note>—that is, February—in the first part of Pisces according to <term>mean motion</term> <note>The calculated average position of a planet, assuming a perfectly circular orbit at a constant speed.</note>. But according to <term>true motion</term> <note>The actual observed position of a planet in the sky, accounting for its elliptical orbit and varying speeds.</note> in that same year, they were together in the twenty-fourth part of Aquarius. 

<margin>Fifth reason</margin>
Let him first explain, then, which conjunction he chooses to prefer, to which he might chiefly refer the kingdom of the Jews and the Mosaic law: that "mean" one in Pisces, or this "true" one in Aquarius? If he says the true one, he will contradict himself and other astrologers, for that was among the <term>minor conjunctions</term> <note>A meeting of Jupiter and Saturn that does not result in a change of "triplicity" (the element of the zodiac signs), which astrologers considered less significant.</note>, since it did not happen at the beginning of a <term>triplicity</term> <note>A group of three zodiac signs belonging to the same element (fire, earth, air, or water).</note>. 

Such conjunctions, as he himself writes in the same passage, do not signify changes of laws or the coming of prophets, but rather the fertility or scarcity of the harvest, or perhaps the transfer of an empire—but only between relatives and those within the fortunes of a single nation; indeed, they keep themselves within the boundaries of the same family. Furthermore, in the <term>theme</term> <note>A natal chart or astrological diagram.</note> of the conjunction he describes, Aquarius (in which Jupiter and Saturn were located) filled the **seventh house** of the heavens, not the ninth or tenth, by which kingdoms, laws, and the beginnings of new wisdom are signified. 

And if anyone should contend at all that this Aquarius rained down Moses to us from his urn in heaven, let him tell me, I pray: why did no Moses descend from heaven in the year of our Lord 1226, when Jupiter and Saturn were joined in Aquarius with a change of triplicity? That was a conjunction to be numbered among the "greatest," yet no people were led out of Egypt, no law was given, and the world saw no miracle of those things that happened under Moses in the desert. But it seems that Abraham did not particularly note the conjunction that was in Aquarius; rather, he called that conjunction which was in Pisces the "conjunction of the Jewish kingdom and the Mosaic law."

<summary>Pico uses historical chronology and astronomical definitions to prove that the planetary conjunctions used by astrologers to explain the life of Moses actually occurred over a century after his birth. He further argues that the specific alignment in Aquarius was astrologically "minor" and should not, by the astrologers' own rules, signify a major religious or political shift.</summary>

...and he does something similar regarding that conjunction in Pisces which comes 2,859 years after the other, from which he commanded the Messiah to be expected as if he were a second Moses. Why should we spend more time refuting this? Since it is one of those which they call "mean" <note>In medieval astronomy, "mean" (mediis) refers to a calculated average position of a planet, as opposed to its "true" or observed position in the sky.</note>—that is, things which are effectively nothing, being merely invented and imaginary constructions of our own. I can never sufficiently marvel at the insanity of astrologers, which I have so often mocked and censured, for the way they refer the outcomes of earthly affairs to these "causes" which they admit are nothing and have never actually existed or will ever exist, as if they were true causes. 

Nor do I know why Avenezra—who says no faith should be given to Albumasar <note>Albumasar (787–886 AD) was a Persian astrologer whose "Great Conjunction" theory influenced much of the Middle Ages.</note> because he uses mean conjunctions—did not say the same about this teacher of his, who throughout his entire booklet always deals with mean conjunctions. These are the ones that occur after 239 years when a migration occurs from one <term>triplicity</term> <note>A group of three zodiac signs belonging to the same element (Fire, Earth, Air, or Water).</note> to another. And in that initial "prophetic" conjunction of his, he is incredibly ridiculous. For he describes the "theme of the heavens" <note>A birth chart or horoscope.</note> at that hour in which Leo holds the <term>horoscopus</term> <note>The Ascendant, or the point of the zodiac rising on the eastern horizon.</note>; Saturn and Jupiter are guests in the seventh house in Aquarius; and the Sun runs through the summit of the midheaven in Aries. Pisces occupies the ninth region <note>The Ninth House in an astrological chart, traditionally associated with religion, law, and prophecy.</note>. Since every indication of laws and prophets is sought from that ninth house, he had little success because no planet was found within it. 

But this astrologer, a man of "admirable subtlety," transported the Sun, Jupiter, and Saturn—the first from the tenth house and the others from the seventh—to the ninth! For he says: "By mean motion, Jupiter, Saturn, and the Sun (even if the Sun is in the tenth by the division of the houses), if we nevertheless observe the number and sequence of the signs, will be in the ninth; for Aries is the ninth sign from Leo, and the ninth house is the ninth from the ascendant." Do we really think anyone is more "subtle" than these craftsmen of lies? I should respond that I do not know whether to be indignant at such stupidity—such madness—or rather to grieve for the loss of unrefined minds who pass down these things in writing as if they were not understood, and sometimes even magnify them. Such people usually go from error into superstition, and from superstition they gradually rush into infidelity. 

Tell me, I pray, "admirable" Abraham: at that hour, were Saturn and Jupiter in Aquarius, or were they in Pisces? "By mean motion," you say. But what is this other than saying they were *not* there? And if the Sun from the tenth house portended power, how could it simultaneously indicate the splendor of the Law from the ninth? For neither can the ninth be turned into the tenth, nor the tenth into the ninth, nor can the same planet be in both places at once. But I have said too much about these things, since against stupid opinions—

### Chapter XIII: The Christian law is ascribed to various mean conjunctions by various people, and even without astrological reasoning.

<margin>The Christian law is ascribed to various conjunctions and always "mean" ones.</margin>
<margin>Arguments omitted.</margin>

Some refer it to that which occurred in the sixth degree of Aries six years before Jesus was born; others to that which happened in the last part of Cancer, twenty years before the former one. ...it has been declared that saying these conjunctions are "mean" <note>In medieval astronomy, "mean" (mediis) refers to a calculated average position of a planet, as opposed to its "true" or observed position in the sky.</note> is no different than if we said they are non-existent; for what does not exist certainly can neither act nor indicate things that are. And if he <note>Avenezra</note> brings forward any true conjunction after the birth of Christ, I will marvel at nothing unless we are to believe that the heavens stood still after He was brought into the light. Otherwise, it was necessary for Jupiter, Saturn, and the other planets to repeatedly come together and separate from one another. But no astrologer ever said that these conjunctions have power over things that have already passed; rather, they say their effects precede them by many years, but never follow them—which is reasonably stated. For if events are caused, the cause cannot be later than the effect; if they are signified, it is useless for celestial signs to signify that an event will happen which has already occurred.

### Chapter 14. That the commonly cited horoscope [of Christ] is not true; nor can it be judged from it that He would die a violent death or be a great prophet.

<margin>A wicked fabrication.</margin>
<margin>Albumasar.</margin>
<margin>First reason.</margin>
<margin>Second reason.</margin>
<margin>That Mars was not in the eighth house.</margin>
<margin>Objection</margin>
<margin>Solution</margin>
<margin>That a violent death is not portended by the horoscope of Jesus.</margin>

**I**t is common to disturb some people that these petty diviners babble about the horoscope of Jesus himself. For they say He was born with the first face of Virgo (this is how he calls the <term>decans</term> <note>original: "decanos"; These are ten-degree subdivisions of a zodiac sign, each with its own symbolic "face" or image.</note>) ascending, of which Albumasar <note>A famous Persian astrologer (787–886 AD) whose works were widely translated into Latin.</note> writes that in it there is a beautiful maiden carrying two ears of grain in her hands and nursing a boy whom a certain nation calls "Jesus." Thus he thinks the miracle of the Word made flesh is confirmed by the science of astrology, which supposedly found the Virgin and Jesus among the images of the sky. I am not greatly angry with them here, since they are accustomed to confirm their own dogmas with such testimonies, and they think we will gladly receive these things to corroborate our own dogmas. But Christian truth does not need these fables and long-winded tales; compared to it, the serious works of philosophers are almost fables. Who has seen these images? To whom has a more hidden reason revealed them when the senses were silent? Where did either Ptolemy or any ancient author ever mention them? They are the purest nonsense and fabrications of the Arabs, even if they refer them to idols—against which we will dispute more extensively in the following book.

But the Lord Jesus was not born with that sign of Virgo ascending (as they say); otherwise, He would have appeared in the light nearly two hours before midnight, whereas we have received from Church tradition that He was born at midnight. Therefore, it was not the third degree of Libra (as someone says), but rather the tenth that occupied the <term>horoscope</term> <note>original: "horoscopum"; In ancient astrology, this term specifically refers to the "Ascendant," the point of the zodiac rising on the eastern horizon.</note> when the most desired of all children was born. From this, it is shown to be false what they spread with blasphemous voices—that in that horoscope Mars was in the "house of death" <note>The eighth house of an astrological chart, traditionally associated with the manner of one's passing.</note>, from which He was destined to die by the punishment of the cross. For Mars could not have been in that place unless we made Virgo the ascendant, which we have shown is greatly different from the hour of His birth. 

But someone will insist: if we remove Mars from that part of the sky, we will place him in the west <note>The descendant or 7th house.</note>, where he would threaten dangers of a violent death. I, however, departing not at all from their own decrees, will show that the end of a violent death is not portended by that horoscope. For although Mars in the seventh house might bring the newborn into danger of life, Firmicus Maternus <note>A 4th-century Roman author of a major astrological compendium.</note> nonetheless writes that this misfortune is diminished if it is a nocturnal birth. Likewise, if Mars is in his own house, or terms, or at his own exaltation; and even if he were found in the eighth house (from which no clearer sign of death exists), the benevolence of Jupiter resists the malice of Mars—whether Jupiter is in the ascendant, or the ascendant itself is in the house of Jupiter or Venus, which auspicious star joins itself to Jupiter by aspect. Not just one or two of these, but clearly all of them are found in the horoscope of Jesus. For He was born by night, not by day; and Mars was in Aries (that is, he was in his own home <note>original: "in suis laribus"</note>); and the ascendant was Libra, the house of Venus, which Jupiter illuminated almost exactly by degree; then, he joined Venus, positioned in Aquarius, to himself in a friendly society by a <term>trine</term> <note>An astrological aspect where planets are 120 degrees apart, considered very harmonious.</note> aspect. Add to these the Moon, which rules the night; you will see that in a nocturnal birth, she was happily situated and held the house of death, which necessarily signifies a good death.

<margin>A similar conjunction [occurred] to the conjunction of Muhammad, which created no law.</margin>
Nor is there any need to spend many words refuting the one who prophesied about that law <note>The "law" refers to the religion of Islam</note> from that same constellation, since experience itself has already proven him wrong. ## Chapter XVI: On the Prophecy of the Antichrist—How Some Have Already Been Proven Liars and Others Will Be Proven Liars in the Future

<margin>Arnaldus</margin>
If we have caught them being false, vain, and ridiculous in what they have said concerning past religions, we should not think that any more faith should be granted to the trifles of these scoundrels when they speechify with a certain "prophetic authority" about the Antichrist, the end of the age, and other future things of this kind. For events have already rejected some of them: such as Arnaldus <note>Arnaldus de Villa Nova (c. 1240–1311), a physician and reformer who predicted the end of the world</note> and several others who say that in the year of our Lord 1345, because of that conjunction of the three superior planets in Aquarius, or in the year 1464, because of Jupiter and Saturn joined in Pisces, some threatened us with a Messiah of Abraham <note>A reference to Jewish messianic expectations linked to astrology</note> and others with the Antichrist. I have no doubt that those who have deferred these things further into the distant future will be refuted by posterity with the same argument, because the reality itself will refute their prophecy until that day comes, unknown even to the angels. When our Lord Jesus denied that this day was for us to know, he "unloosed the fingers" of all bold men with a single voice, <margin>Augustine</margin> as Augustine says <note>Augustine used the phrase "unloosing the fingers" to describe God stopping those trying to calculate the date of the end of the world on their hands</note>.

## Chapter XVII: How Flimsily Astrologers Prove There Can Only Be Six Religions, and Why the Law of the Hebrews Should Be Called Jovial or Solar Rather Than Saturnine.

But hear by what a beautiful fiction they collect all past religions and the one that will be under the Antichrist into one bundle (so to speak). Jupiter, they say, signifies religion; it signifies one religion or another based on its embrace with one or another star. There are six stars besides Jupiter, and therefore there are six types of religions, of which there will be no more, nor have there been fewer. For Jupiter with Saturn makes the religion of the Jews; with Mars, the religion of the Chaldeans who worship fire; with the Sun, the religion of the Egyptians who worship the "heavenly host," that is, the stars; with Venus, the religion of the Saracens <note>Muslims</note>; with Mercury, the Christian religion; and with the Moon, that which is to be the last of all under the Antichrist. This is that "subtle and profound" invention which <margin>Roger Bacon</margin> Roger Bacon uses most especially in his letter to Clement <note>Bacon's *Opus Majus* sent to Pope Clement IV</note>, and which <margin>D'Ailly</margin> Pierre d’Ailly <note>A 15th-century cardinal and theologian</note> also used in his treatise *On the Concordance of Astrology and Theology*. In this, I first marvel that they have so far forgotten their own dogma: they were always accustomed to saying that religions are made or signified only from the union of the superior stars (especially Saturn and Jupiter), yet now they descend all the way to the Moon, which is to produce some Antichrist for us. If they want to count the types of religions according to the number of planets, they must either remove a planet from the sky or beg for more planets from somewhere else; otherwise, the number will not match. For either they accept idolatry as a single religion, or they wish to accept each type of idolatry separately in that number, according to the various rites and worship of those who served idols. If they prefer the former, they must remove [the others] from the midst...

...one planet: because there will not be one religion for the Egyptians and another for the Chaldeans <note>The "Chaldeans" were synonymous with Babylonian astrologers and sages in Renaissance thought</note>, but one and the same: that is idolatry. Wherefore, there will only be five religions: Idolatry, Mosaic <note>Judaism</note>, Christian, Mahometan <note>Islam</note>, and—if I may put it this way—Antichristian. If the types of idolatry are to be accepted separately, there are almost as many religions on earth as there are stars in the sky. But if they are thought to be reduced to those five heads <note>Pico is critiquing the common astrological schema of five historical religious eras</note>, then some who worship fire and others the heavens would have a great grievance against those demons, for they would be indignant at being left out of this division, seeing as they are worshipped particularly and almost exclusively in idolatry. For "all the gods of the nations are demons" <note>A common citation of Psalm 96:5</note>; wherefore they must necessarily make at least three types of idolatry: of the heavens, of demons, and of elements. Thus, they will be forced to seek out another error for themselves from somewhere among their friends—I meant to say "error," that is, a "planet" <note>A pun on the Greek word *planētēs*, which means "wanderer" or "error"</note>—so that eight might be found to match the number of religions.

But also, they always have a poor understanding of all the kings they speak of. For the worship of the celestial bodies was specific to the Chaldeans, as **Iamblichus** <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher (c. 245–325 AD) who wrote on the Egyptian mysteries</note> writes, while the Egyptians were more occupied with the worship of demons; wherefore, they should give the Sun to the Chaldeans instead of Mars, and provide the Egyptians with the devil along with some planet.

It would be easy to show that they fight against the truth everywhere, for they have always been poor friends to it. But why do they so often disagree with themselves so unwillingly? For they will not find their own dogmas to be sufficient if they consult reason. Why should the Hebrew law be "Saturnine" rather than the Christian? Rather, the former should be referred to the Sun or Jupiter, and ours to Saturn. For **Saturn**, as some say, does not bestow physical goods but takes them away; instead, he gives spiritual things and things that are not seen. The Mosaic law both promised and bestowed physical goods; ours takes them away rather than offering them, and promises and provides spiritual things and whatever is not seen. 

Saturn does not produce kings of the people, commanders of armies, wealthy men, or those noble for their many offspring and naturally fond of women—such as all the princes of the Hebrew religion: Abraham, Jacob, Moses, Joshua, Solomon, David. Instead, he makes people ignoble, poor, hermits, haters of pleasures, meditating on eternity, and despising physical things. Such a man—if he is to be assigned to any planet—is our leader and commander **Jesus Christ**, and such were the apostles, martyrs, monks, and Christians, by whose life, doctrine, and blood our religion was increased, born, and confirmed. Therefore, if they were to speak consistently with their own decrees, we should be called Saturnine, and the Hebrews should be called Solar or Jovian <note>Governed by Jupiter</note>.

But what drew them into that opinion was the observance of the **Sabbath**; since that day is considered Saturn's day among them, it seemed most fitting to those who said the Jews were a "Saturnine" people because they venerated Saturn's day above the others. Led by similar conjecture, they are also accustomed to saying our religion is "Solar," because we observe the day of the Sun, which we call the Lord's Day.

<margin>Albumasar</margin>
But why are we not instead associated with the day of **Mercury**, since they also subject us to Mercury? For they used to give the Sun to the Egyptians and Mercury to us. And **Albumasar** <note>The Latinized name of the Persian astrologer Abu Ma'shar (787–886 AD)</note> says that Jupiter with Mercury signifies the Christian law, although he also said the same thing about the Sun. For to err or to change one's opinion is no vice among those who are so persistent in the errors and movements of the planets; stunned by that rapid vertigo of the heavens they inspect, they can hardly ever stand firmly on their feet.

But however it may be, they have marvelous reasons with which to confirm these inventions of theirs. For they did not refer us to Mercury at random, but because, as **Roger Bacon** <note>The 13th-century English philosopher and scientist who explored astrology and optics</note> says, Mercury has multiple movements and is difficult to understand, so he claims for himself the Christian religion, whose dogmas are found to be almost incredible and most difficult to know. Others, younger ones, have devised something else: since Mercury is the "librarian of the gods," and there is a great abundance of books among Christians, therefore, they say, this religion should rightly be judged Mercurial. This is the "admirable wisdom" of the astrologers! They have forgotten, it seems, the libraries of the pagans, and they have seen almost no books of the Arabs or the Hebrews until now.

Book VI
A

# THE SIXTH BOOK OF THE DISPUTATIONS OF GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA AGAINST ASTROLOGERS.

### Chapter one.

-> In what order one must proceed in demolishing the foundations of the astrologers. Also, that it is impossible for all the stars to ever be restored to the same positions in which they once were. <-

<margin>e</margin>
**W**e have departed from the order and plan established for our treatise, in which the roots of the astrologers were meant to be pulled up first, before we cut down those pinnacles of the <term>great conjunctions</term> <note>The "Great Conjunctions" of Saturn and Jupiter were believed by astrologers to signal major historical shifts, such as the birth of prophets or the fall of empires.</note>, the great orbs, and other things of that kind; for once the roots were removed, those heights would necessarily collapse. For who would put faith in those who announce the change of kingdoms and religions through great conjunctions? It has already been established that those signs—Aries, Leo, Cancer, Sagittarius—in which they think the meeting of Jupiter and Saturn brings these things about, are either non-existent, or if they are of such a kind, they are not in that part of the heavens in which they are calculated. Furthermore, it is established that Saturn, Jupiter, and the rest of the planets do not cause events or the changes of things in the lower world. Even if they did cause them, nothing has been discovered about their efficient power, nature, or property, either by reason or by experience. And since one thing follows from one conjunction and another from another (if indeed anything follows from them), these things cannot be judged by men among whom the very first rudiments of that art are still in dispute. For we shall see in those matters which will be discussed later that it is not yet agreed what hour should be considered for the conjunction: whether the beginning of the year in which it happened, or rather the time when the stars themselves actually meet. Furthermore, we shall see that they can attain neither of these times, which is why the <term>horoscope</term> <note>In this context, the "horoscope" refers to the "Ascendant," the specific degree of the zodiac rising on the eastern horizon at the moment of the conjunction.</note> of the conjunction is left in doubt. Likewise, even if the horoscope were established, nothing is yet certain regarding the method of arranging the <term>theme</term> <note>The "theme" or "thema" is the technical layout of the astrological chart.</note>, but it remains uncertain where the beginnings of the <term>twelve places</term> <note>These are the "Houses" of the zodiac, which astrologers use to divide the sky into twelve sectors governing different aspects of life.</note> are correctly established; and even when these are established, the virtue of the place itself—what is the beginning, the middle, and the end—is not clear to them. When these things are ignored, just as the region of the sky where they join is unknown, so too what the conjunction will produce cannot be known, since almost every variety of significance is reduced to the nature and property of the places which they call "houses." And because in these great conjunctions they are most accustomed to observe which planet is <term>exalted</term> <note>original: "exaltetur." Exaltation is a specific state where a planet is thought to be at its most powerful within a certain sign.</note> over the other, we shall see that they still do not know what that "exaltation" is which they commonly call "elevation." And since it likewise matters greatly which planet chiefly rules the place of the joining of the superior stars or the eclipse of the luminaries, we shall see that all those rights, commands, and authorities of the planets are so controversial that there is almost no part of any sign to be found whose prince and lord is definitely established among astrologers. But it is not necessary to enumerate here all the foundations of that art which will be demolished later. Along with these foundations (as I was saying before), all those things must also fall which they dare to pronounce regarding divine miracles through great conjunctions and other things of that kind. And because they would most greatly offend the integrity of religion with this part of their craft, every delay in removing this plague seemed like an eternity—especially since it seemed this part could be most effectively refuted while the rest of the astrological system was still intact and unshaken, if this claim regarding great conjunctions were proved false; thus, where they seem greatest and strongest, they might rather be defeated. Now returning...

He lists several technical uncertainties in astrology, such as the calculation of houses, planetary exaltations, and the timing of conjunctions.</summary>

# Book VI

<margin>The error of Albumasar and others</margin>
...from where we diverged, we will proceed to root out the first foundations of that art in consecutive order. Nor indeed should we pass over in silence the common error among astrologers into which **Albumasar** <note>Abu Ma'shar (787–886), a Persian astrologer whose works were central to the transmission of Greek and Indian astrology to the Latin West.</note> and many others fell, thinking that eventually all the stars will be restored to their original places such that a completely identical arrangement of the heaven and the same position and relationship of all celestial bodies among themselves would be found as once existed. From this, they believe it will come to pass that the same things which once were will exist again among us: the same men, the same events, the same animals, and the same condition for all lower things. Some deeper "astrologer-mystics" <note>original: *astrologomiſtæ*</note> thereafter, examining these things more profoundly, are accustomed to whisper in the ear of their collectors: "this is that resurrection of the Christians which the Hebrews also hope for and the Muhammadans." They claim those prophets were surely the greatest astronomers, but they hid these mysteries from the common people and the uneducated. For they thought there was a common number of years and days for the world with which the locations of the planets and stars could be certified, and when that number is complete, all stars will have returned to the same point; and because of this, all things will return as they were. 

For our part, it is not necessary to rebuke this insanity at great length; for **Haly** <note>Ali ibn Ridwan, an 11th-century Egyptian physician and astrologer who wrote famous commentaries on Ptolemy.</note> himself, in his exposition of the first book of the <term>Apotelesmata</term> <note>Also known as the *Tetrabiblos*, the foundational text of astrology by Claudius Ptolemy.</note>, following the opinion of **Ptolemy** who says the same, rebukes this idea with indignation, and says there is no one skilled in arithmetic to whom this error is not evident. 

<margin>An impious and detestable dogma.</margin>
<margin>Haly and Ptolemy</margin>
<margin>Nicole Oresme</margin>
Then, after him, **Nicole Oresme** <note>A 14th-century French philosopher and mathematician (c. 1320–1382) who argued that the ratios of celestial movements were likely irrational, making a perfect recurrence of stellar positions mathematically impossible.</note>, a most sharp philosopher and diligent mathematician, in his treatise *On the Proportions of Proportions*, demonstrated by mathematical reasons that this opinion—thinking that the same position of the heaven and stars which existed at another time could ever return—is false and impossible. I have judged that the reader should be delegated to him, as he has sufficiently fulfilled this task, so that we do not do again what has already been done, a thing we have nowhere done until now.

## Chapter II. By what things astrologers say the influences of the stars vary; and that all these things are entirely absurd.

The great, or (to speak more truly) all foundations of astrology are removed, if it is sufficiently proven that nothing is done by the heaven nor indicated of which the astrologers profess a prediction from celestial observation. Moreover, among the reasons we used against them, there was one most powerful concerning the momentary change of celestial powers which they invent. We touched upon this in the previous dispute, but we have rightly deferred its explanation until this place; for it both requires its own peculiar treatment and carries great weight in uprooting astrology. For from this, it is confirmed not only what has been proven so far—namely, that particular changes of lower things are not effected by the stars—but also that if those things do proceed from the heaven, they nevertheless proceed in such a way that they cannot be detected or signified by any celestial observation. 

<margin>The opinion of astrologers concerning the variation and powers of the stars</margin>
It is therefore what the astrologers say: that this kind of virtue and power of the stars and planets is different at every hour and moment, while they are either in other places of the heaven—which the moderns call <term>houses</term> <note>The twelve divisions of the sky in a natal chart, supposedly governing different areas of life like wealth or health.</note>—or in other <term>signs</term> <note>The twelve divisions of the zodiac (Aries, Taurus, etc.).</note> of which they invent twelve to be found; or the planets themselves, separated by a certain interval of space, are joined to each other by various radiations, which they commonly call the <term>aspects</term> <note>Specific angular relationships between planets, such as a "conjunction" or "opposition," believed to alter their influence.</note> of the planets. These are the principal ways (to omit certain more recent ones) by which they think the flow and power of the celestial bodies are changed: namely, the diversity of the house, the sign, and the aspect. Unless these things are defended by them, they cannot protect the dogma of the efficiency of the stars—that every change and diversity of lower things proceeds from the stars—since if those stars always have the same and immutable power (as we think of all except the moon)...

<summary>Pico attacks the concept of the "Great Year" (the cyclic return of the stars to the same position), citing Nicole Oresme to prove it mathematically impossible. He then begins a critique of the "houses," "signs," and "aspects" that astrologers use to claim varying celestial influences.</summary>

-># Book VI<-
<margin>A ii</margin>

...[we would argue] that necessarily either the same or similar effects would always proceed from them. For they cannot refer the diversity of effects to lower causes <note>Earthly or "sublunary" factors, such as geography or individual biology.</note> as we ourselves do, unless they also confess with us that they can divine nothing from the heaven regarding this diversity—since, in that case, the heaven would not be considered the author and cause. Therefore, it is necessary for them to find as much variety among the causes in the heaven as there is variety in the effects of lower things. In this matter, the multitude of stars does nothing to support them;
<margin>Variety of things</margin>
for however many stars and planets there may be, they are all present at the birth of anyone. For this reason, no explanation could be asserted as to why they would bestow things differently on some and not the same on all, unless they were to fabricate a multitude of reasons why the power and efficiency of the stars should be one thing at one time and another at another. From this, it could then be gathered why things happen or arise differently at different times: because the state of the stars would then receive a different condition from the heaven. Regarding this, they claim they can prophesy because they have the state of the stars known and explored at any given time. However, this is what we shall refute in the present book, since nothing can be thought more absurd or more remote from all reason than that there should be such inconstancy and mutability in the nature of the superior bodies <note>The "divine" planets and stars, which Aristotelian philosophy held to be unchanging and perfect.</note> as is certainly seen in the lower things of the heaven—things which are, in their own nature, mostly fluid and changeable. For what is this so "shape-shifting" change
<margin>General change</margin>
and chameleon-like <note>original: *Chamaleōtis*</note> inconstancy? That even in a brief interval of time, those most divine bodies are never found to be similar to themselves or endowed with the same gifts? Let them say, I pray, whether they think those properties of **starry influences** <term>defluxuum: the "flow" or emanation of power from a planet to the Earth</term> proceed from the very nature and substance of the stars, or rather from some force sent in from the outside? Whether drawn from the twelve "places" of heaven <note>The astrological houses.</note>, or from the signs <note>The Zodiac.</note>, or from their mutual **radiations** <term>aspects: the geometric angles, such as squares or trines, between planets</term> upon one another. If they answer the first, they cannot change those properties unless the very substance of the stars is also changed—which I do not think even they will concede. If they prefer the second, then the celestial bodies would be the most ignoble of all bodies, doing almost nothing from their own nature, but performing everything according to a force and influence rushing in from the outside. For a physical substance is more perfect the more its resulting operation issues from the innermost substance of the one acting. And these things we have said generally and universally; for the vanity of their opinion will shine forth most clearly when we examine in detail the ways in which they think the virtues of the stars are changed. In examining these, we shall follow the sequence of their errors and fables. This we now proceed to do, beginning with the twelve houses of heaven, through whose diversity they fabulously devise that the influence of signs and stars is not only strengthened or weakened, but rendered entirely and fundamentally different.

## Chapter III: The Houses of the astrologers, which rest on no foundation; and how astrologers fight among themselves in explaining their powers.

No one who is not entirely unrefined in this art is ignorant of the twelve houses celebrated among astrologers.
<margin>d</margin>
To these, it seems to me, almost every significance and property of the **influences** <gloss>emanations</gloss> is ultimately referred by them. For if you ask about the nature of any planet—what it produces or of what thing it is considered the giver and author—they will answer nothing definite or certain, unless they know the nature of the **house** <note>In astrology, a "house" is one of twelve divisions of the sky relative to the horizon at a specific moment.</note> in which the planet is found. Thus, almost everything they are accustomed to say in general about the properties of planets seems to fall into categories that have multiple meanings under a common term. For what is more general in the definition of a planet than that it be "good" or "bad"—that is, the author of happiness or unhappiness? And yet even this is not firm or always the same among the stars. For in a "bad place" <note>An "unfortunate" house, such as the 6th, 8th, or 12th houses, associated with illness or death.</note>, a good planet <note>A "benefic" like Jupiter or Venus.</note> does harm, and in a "good place," a bad one <note>A "malefic" like Saturn or Mars.</note> is thought by them to be beneficial. Finally...

<summary>Pico argues that astrology is logically inconsistent because it attributes earthly-style "inconstancy" to the perfect, unchanging heavens. He begins a specific critique of the twelve astrological houses, noting that astrologers use them as arbitrary "foundations" to explain away why planets don't always produce the same effects.</summary>
