<meta>This page continues Pico's critique of the logical inconsistencies in astrological theory. He has just finished arguing that if stars were the true causes of earthly diversity, they would need to have internal variety themselves. He now focuses on how astrologers claim a planet's character changes radically based on its "house" or position in the sky, using Jupiter and the authority of Julius Firmicus Maternus as his primary examples.</meta>

-># Book VI<-
<sig>A</sig>

<margin>Maternus</margin>
Jupiter—to speak of one planet as an example for all—when located in the East <note>The Ascendant, or the point of the zodiac rising on the eastern horizon at the moment of birth.</note> differs so much from himself when he has migrated slightly above the East into what they call the twelfth place of the heaven, as fire differs from air or water, or as a hare from a donkey, or a donkey from an elephant. For in the East he always decrees the greatest goods; yet in the twelfth house, which is adjacent to the East, he often decrees great evils. It is especially characteristic of Jupiter to bestow resources and riches; yet when placed in the third and eighth [houses], he frequently dissipates the inheritance, even though by his own nature he makes men noble and wise. If he holds the eighth place, he will make men ignoble, and those whose fury—as Maternus <note>Julius Firmicus Maternus, a 4th-century lawyer and astrologer whose work *Mathesis* was a primary source for medieval and Renaissance astrology.</note> says—erupts into insanity. Finally, what is more characteristic of Jupiter than to be considered a beneficial star, since he is named both the "greatest of the fortunate planets" and the "great happiness of the heaven"? Yet Maternus says that when situated in the third place, he is neither good nor evil. Furthermore, when located in the sixth place, he decrees the greatest evils. Giving a reason for this matter, Maternus adds: "For the sixth place has its own particular prerogative of malice, and

<margin>Refutation</margin>
whatever star is in that place (that is, the sixth) will borrow the greatest powers for decreeing evils from the vice of the location." So he says. Let us therefore ask the astrologers: whence comes such a great, sudden, and perpetual "deluge" <note>original: *diluuio*; used here metaphorically to mean a washing away of the planet's essential nature or an overwhelming inconsistency.</note> in divine bodies? By the firmness and immutability of their substance, these bodies should rightly be believed to be most tenacious of their own proper nature and always similar to themselves. Truly, only two ways can be imagined by which this could happen. One is that we understand various forces and powers to be inherent in those "places," which they then flow into the stars placed within them—which the quoted words of Maternus seem to signify. The other is that we should not think the planet itself receives anything from elsewhere or is affected differently, but rather that the power and efficiency of its rays are varied, just as the projection of rays to the earth is varied according to the different habits of the star's position. Whichever they prefer to say will prove their insanity. For if they answer that powers of this kind flow from the "place" to the planets, we shall ask: what do they feel regarding "place"? Do they mean what some ancients held, that place is an empty space <note>A vacuum.</note>

<margin>Aristotle</margin>
separated from bodies? Or do they mean what Aristotle <note>The philosopher defines "place" in his *Physics* as the inner boundary of the containing body.</note> held: the innermost surface of the surrounding body? If they mean space and an interval, let them admit along with the same philosophers that an interval of this kind has no such virtues or properties, since natural forms follow actual substances, not mere dimensions and empty gaps. If they mean the innermost surface of the surrounding body, it is possible that some power resides in this "place" just as it does in a body—specifically, the body whose surface it is, by which the surrounded body is then affected. But what are these bodies whose extremity is considered the "place" of the stars? Certainly, whatever they are called—whether the outermost sphere of all <note>The *Primum Mobile*, the highest heaven that carries the others.</note> or the one joined and closest to each star—no part of such bodies would fail to circle the East, the West, the summit of the heaven, and the bottom, and all other places in the revolution of a single day. Therefore, if the virtue comes from those physical parts, the virtue of the East would not always be the same, nor would that of the West. Rather, through the nature of that physical body currently located there, the virtue itself would change. Finally, this cannot be said by them for another reason: because the twelve <term>signs</term> <note>The constellations or divisions of the zodiac (Aries, Taurus, etc.).</note> which are said to be in the <term>houses</term> <note>The twelve fixed segments of the sky relative to the observer's horizon (1st House, 2nd House, etc.).</note> other than the houses themselves—just as planets are in houses and in signs—are described by them as being in the highest sphere of all. These signs are also said to borrow their powers and nature from the house in which they are located, just as the planets do. For they say that Aries does not do the same things in the East as it does in the West; the same is said of other signs which are taken to be in the eighth sphere <note>The sphere of the fixed stars.</note> (if there is none higher) or in that which is considered the highest sphere. Therefore, since these are surrounded by no other body, there is nowhere for us to imagine this "virtue of the houses" to exist, except in immobile space and intervals occupied by bodies. But that is either nothing at all, if we believe Aristotle,

<summary>Pico challenges the astrological doctrine of "houses," arguing that it is logically impossible for fixed locations in the sky to possess inherent powers that radically alter a planet's essential nature. He uses Aristotle's definition of place to show that if these powers were physical, they would move as the heavens rotate, rather than staying fixed at points like the East or West.</summary>

<keywords>Jupiter, houses, Maternus, Aristotle, eighth sphere, zodiac signs, celestial physics, Ascendant, planetary influence</keywords>

--- Page 515 ---
<meta>This page continues Pico’s critique of the astrological "houses." On the previous page, he used the example of Jupiter to show how astrologers claim a planet’s character changes completely based on its position. Here, he argues from the principles of optics and natural philosophy that a change in position can only change the intensity of an effect, not its fundamental nature, and highlights the glaring contradictions between different astrological traditions.</meta>

-># Book VI<-
<sig>A iii</sig>

...or if there is anything there, it is marked by no character of either efficacy or specific property. Therefore, to imagine diverse powers in these places (that is, in the different positions of the signs and planets) by which the stars placed there are affected, is completely foreign to all reason. Nor would they speak with less absurdity or ridicule if they were to use the other side of the defense: namely, that because of the diversity of position, the planets look upon us with a different face, and their rays are sent down into the earth differently, and this creates a diversity of effects. For anyone who has even tasted the rudiments of optics <note>The study of light and vision, which in the Renaissance was a branch of geometry and physics.</note> and philosophy will easily understand how absurd this is: since there is no one who does not know that the quality of an effect is distinguished by the quality of the ray and by the nature of the radiating body, not by the different circulation of the ray. This [position] can be the cause for the same effect becoming more or less intense. A ray of the Sun, in whatever manner or position it is cast upon us, always heats and always illuminates; but when it is nearest or in a straight line, it illuminates more and heats more. Yet when it descends either obliquely or refracted, or from a more remote place, it does the same thing as the straight or near ray, but it does so to a lesser degree. No other diversity can occur in the effect except that which follows the very intention and remission <note>Increasing and decreasing intensity.</note> of heat and light.

Therefore, it is an insane dogma of the astrologers who think that the twelve signs of the heaven and the planets, when positioned here, provide for our brothers or make them miserable, but when they have proceeded a little further, they have no power over brothers and no significance, but instead either give or take away riches; in one place they reconcile friends, in another they rouse adversaries against us—even though nothing of the nature of the sign or the planet has changed, but only a variety of position has occurred. However, as we have said, whether this position makes the rays nearer to us, or draws them more powerfully into the earth, or joins or separates them from the rising [horizon], or mixes them more or less with the vapors of the earth: it can perhaps sharpen or blunt the force of the ray, but it certainly cannot change its nature. Therefore, it cannot change the thing that the ray produces; it will perhaps work upon the species of the effect without changing it, either more firmly and effectively or perhaps more weakly, since powers and properties—whether they are like those of the elements or those that are more hidden—follow the nature and species of the thing. Therefore, if the nature is not changed into another, the properties themselves can in no way be changed so that they become different things.

But if they should respond that it is so because of experience, some faith might perhaps be held, if an experiment could be produced regarding these things that would prove it, or if they agreed among themselves in the same opinion. But since different authors ascribe different properties to the same places, they strip away the authority of faithful testimony from their own observations.

<margin>The Arabs and the Latins; the Egyptians and Ptolemy</margin>
The Arabs and the Latins <note>Medieval European astrologers who followed Arabic sources like Albumasar.</note>, following in the footsteps of the Arabs, contend that the quality of servants is indicated by the sixth place. The Egyptians and Ptolemy <note>Claudius Ptolemy, the 2nd-century author of the *Tetrabiblos*, the most influential astrological manual of antiquity.</note> contend it is from the one that is distant from the sixth of all, that is, from the twelfth. They seek adverse health, whether a defect or a disease, from that place; yet Ptolemy does not seek it from the sixth place, but from the seventh and the first, because he never uses the sixth in his <term>astrological judgments</term> <note>original: "apotelesmatis," referring to the casting of horoscopes or predictions.</note>. He always uses these, contrary to the crowd of astrologers, who, omitting those, seek every significance of this kind from the sixth.

<margin>Discord regarding children; Ptolemy; Manilius</margin>
Regarding which children anyone will have in the future: the Arabs and Latins pronounce from the fifth place. Ptolemy uses the tenth and eleventh, and when nothing is extended for anyone's life, he uses the fifth and fourth equally. Paulus Alexandrinus <note>A 4th-century astrological writer.</note> observes the same thing. Mallius <note>Likely Marcus Manilius, author of the 1st-century poem *Astronomica*.</note> suspends the fortune of children and the prayers of parents from the East <note>The Ascendant.</note>. Porphyry <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher and astrologer.</note> says children are signified especially from the tenth [house], because from that part souls are sent down into bodies—and thus he beautifully confirms one fable with another fable. Ptolemy accepts the fortune of parents from no place. The Arabs from the fourth and sixth; Heliodorus <note>An astrologer, likely the brother of Ammonius.</note> also.

<margin>Porphyry; Abenzagel</margin>
Others, as Abenzagel <note>Possibly a corruption of an Arabic name like Ibn Abi al-Rijal (Abenragel).</note> reports, even from the ninth. The second place for the Alexandrian is especially...

<summary>Pico argues that changing a planet's position can only alter the intensity of its effect, not its fundamental nature, and points out that major astrological authorities (Ptolemy, the Arabs, and the Latins) contradict one another on which "houses" govern specific life events.</summary>

<sig>A iii</sig>

...on the matter of business <note>original: "περὶ πράσεως λόγου"</note>: and they signify sudden hopes; among younger people, almost none of these occur: but of riches, for which however there is no judgment regarding any of the twelve places by Ptolemy in his *Apotelesmatics* <note>The *Tetrabiblos*, Ptolemy’s famous work on the "effects" of the stars.</note>, nor by Secundus, nor by anyone else: though Heliodorus receives the signification of them even from the third house.

<margin>On marriage</margin>
Almost all predict marriage from the West <note>The 7th House, where the sun sets.</note>; Heliodorus even from the Midheaven <note>The 10th House, the highest point in the sky.</note>; Ptolemy ignores both.

<margin>On travel</margin>
They judge travels from the ninth and third regions. Heliodorus also examines the seventh for this. Ptolemy treats both this house and those others with equal contempt.

<margin>On parents</margin>
Heliodorus judges concerning parents from the fourth place; Maternus <note>Julius Firmicus Maternus, a 4th-century Roman astrologer.</note> from the tenth; Ptolemy judges from neither.

<margin>On friends</margin>
They foresee friends from the eleventh house; Heliodorus even from the third; Ptolemy from neither the eleventh nor the tenth.

<margin>On religion.</margin>
The rest take religion from the ninth house. Likewise, Mallius <note>The Roman poet Manilius, author of the *Astronomica*.</note> from the seventh, which he also calls the "Port of Pluto" <note>A poetic reference to the setting point of the zodiac, leading to the underworld.</note>; this is the name of the second house among the Egyptians. This same man places Saturn in the fourth place, contrary to the opinion of others who place him in the twelfth. For if we unroll the works of Mallius—who says he has sometimes imitated the dogma of the ancients, and than whom no one older exists among the Latins as a narrator of celestial matters (or, to speak more truly, as a narrator of fables)—we find his system of the twelve places to be so different from every opinion now reported that the entire method of prediction is completely changed. He placed Mars in the setting, where others decreed the first seat under the setting for others. What of those other twelve celestial places handed down by Mallius? Are they not different from all the astrology now in our hands? Do they not vary every method of prediction?

> Clinging to the house. What limit there is for slaves, what

# Book VI

...and with a brow that weighs and settles disputes:
When a judge, in truth, calls for nothing more than himself,
Whatever eloquence achieves among the proposed laws—
It has granted all this into one single part <note>The "part" or "temple" being described here is the Seventh House, associated by Manilius with the law and the setting sun.</note>.
And however the ruling stars behave, so it flows forth.

<margin>The Fifth</margin>
The fifth degree is dedicated to marriage through the signs.
It also holds partners and companions; and at the same time,
It is joined to a bond that unites similar friends.

<margin>The Sixth</margin>
In the sixth seat, a rich abundance is counted,
As well as the safety of one's possessions; of which the one 
Advises how much use may occur, the other how long it lasts:
As the stars incline their powers and govern the temples.

<margin>The Seventh</margin>
The seventh is considered dreadful for its harsh dangers,
If the stars located through the signs provide a bad omen <note>Manilius’s Seventh House is the "occident" or West; while others saw marriage here, he often saw the end of life or legal strife.</note>.

# Book IV

*Or let him seek Bacchus <note>original: "Bacchum"; a poetic reference to wine or the harvest.</note> flowing through the rich new wine.*
*In this part, days and these moments will be given,*
*If the stars following through the signs agree well.*

So far Manilius, whose opinion clearly differs from all astrology now in use. Yet I believe he has not yet been understood by any of those who call themselves his interpreters and followers. In such a great variety of opinions, what faith can be placed in experience? Especially since another, greater problem is added: the way in which the beginnings and ends of the "houses" <note>The twelve divisions of the sky in a horoscope.</note> ought to be divided has not yet been established. Different authors feel differently, as we shall declare in another book; yet this ought to have been explored and settled before any observation regarding their specific properties was even begun. It is so far from being certain or established that no observation can even be claimed which would force us to turn away from the truth with compelling arguments. Whatever Ptolemy and the others believed, we conclude—with the evidence of reason forcing us to this—that it is ridiculous and false either that there are any specific properties in those locations, or that the influence and effectiveness of the planets are changed by the diversity of those places.

### Chapter IV: On the twelve signs; that they were invented by mathematicians for the ease of calculation. Also, that astrologers have erred in many ways regarding the same.

<margin>1</margin>
<margin>Albumasar</margin>
Indeed, they maintain this division and the boundaries of the signs as if they were prescribed by the laws of nature. They think two planets have more "commerce" <note>Astrological relationship or influence upon one another.</note> even if they are twenty degrees <note>original: "partibus"</note> apart, provided they are placed in the same sign, than if one holds the final degrees of Aries and the other is found in the first degrees of Taurus, even though they are separated by the smallest space. Between these latter two, not even a finger's breadth of interval falls. 

But if someone should contend that this number of signs comes from nature—and was not invented by mathematicians for ease of calculation, but established by philosophical reason such as that which Albumasar <note>Abu Ma'shar (787–886 AD), a highly influential Persian astrologer.</note> offers—namely, 
<margin>Against Albumasar, Haly, and Avenazra</margin>
that there are twelve signs because there are four elements, each of which is divided into three parts (the middle, the first, and the last): I could certainly respond that this reason is no less ridiculous and frivolous than the mathematical one. But that the authors of this division were not moved by such a conjecture at all can be easily demonstrated by reason, just as we declared above by the testimony of Haly and Avenazra <note>Haly Abenragel and Abraham ibn Ezra, significant medieval astrological authorities.</note>. For even if that conjecture holds for the signs, what will be said about the distribution of signs into thirty degrees <note>original: "partes"</note>? What of the partition of degrees into sixty minutes <note>original: "minutias"</note>? What philosophical reason will they bring for these? Or how will they justify things made by mathematicians who thought there were no properties of nature there, but were simply seeking numbers more convenient for calculating? 

This is where the lapse of the astrologers occurs, or a certain opportunity for deception, when they decree upon these things as if they had entirely separate powers, and as if nature, rather than human choice, had divided them from one another. For it is well known that they ascribe various properties both to different degrees and to the minutes of the same sign. Hence they proclaim some degrees to be "bright," others "dark," others related to the Sun, others to Mars, and others to other planets. They also tell such fables about the minutes themselves, 
<margin>Aesculapius, Maternus</margin>
as Aesculapius <note>A legendary figure often associated with early Hermetic and astrological texts.</note> wrote in the *Myriogenesis* <note>A lost work (meaning "The Ten Thousand Births") detailing the influences of the smallest divisions of the zodiac.</note>, which Maternus <note>Julius Firmicus Maternus, a 4th-century Roman astrologer.</note> concealed as a mystery. In that work, he supposedly handed down what property every single minute of influence held. But just as human will alone made the second partition for the sake of calculation, so too was the primary division of the whole zodiac into twelve signs.

<summary>Pico argues that the twelve signs of the zodiac and their subdivisions into degrees and minutes are arbitrary mathematical conventions created for ease of calculation, not natural divisions with inherent physical properties. He critiques authorities like Albumasar and Manilius for their inconsistent and unproven systems of celestial influence.</summary>

<page-num>VI</page-num>

-> # Book VI <-

the division did not receive its origin from elsewhere: in whatever way the division of these things is understood, we have declared that they possess no efficacy. Thus, the insanity of the astrologers is refuted here—those who think that by the condition of a sign which a planet has traveled through, that planet is changed. For they establish the **houses** and **altitudes** <note>Also known as "exaltations," where a planet is thought to be most powerful.</note> of the planets according to these signs, not according to the **images** <note>The actual constellations or clusters of stars in the sky.</note> which we showed in the previous book can only be thought of by us and have no solidity. Perhaps for this reason, the Chaldeans <note>Ancient Babylonian astronomers/astrologers.</note>, who did not use "signs," also created no houses for the planets. For among them, Leo was not the domicile of the Sun, nor was Cancer the Moon's, nor Libra and Taurus for Venus, nor Pisces and Sagittarius for Jupiter, and so on for the rest. Instead, they observed only the altitudes of the stars, related not to the signs but to the images. Thus, for them, Saturn possessed nothing in Capricorn or Aquarius, but held authority only in Libra and Scorpio. For although these are two signs, they were judged as one image among the Chaldeans. Otherwise, if Ptolemy and others referred the houses of the planets to the images (which they do not do), the ratio would not square; for with the stars constituting the image of Taurus, Mars has the greatest affinity, even more than any other planet, yet he is said to be "debilitated" in the sign of Taurus. Therefore, the <term>houses</term> <gloss>domiciles</gloss>, <term>altitudes</term> <gloss>exaltations</gloss>, <term>bounds</term> <gloss>fines</gloss>, <term>triplicities</term> <gloss>triangularitates</gloss>, <term>monomoiria</term> <gloss>individual degrees</gloss>, <term>decans</term>, <term>faces</term> <gloss>idropoſopias</gloss>, and the rest of such affinities of the planets with parts of the Zodiac receive their power from these signs. Since it has been clearly enough proved (as I think) that no force can come to the planets from these signs if the things are entirely imaginary, not natural, and not effective, one must marvel at those who wished to fortify the astrological opinion regarding the "similarity" of the planets. They say the planets "smell" of the qualities of the Zodiac in which the seeds of things are dispersed, just as plants reflect the flavor of the earth.

<margin>Panaetius Plotinus</margin>

But this comparison is unlike the reality: for while plants are nourished by the earth and therefore reflect that flavor of the earth, the planets are not nourished by the Zodiac (even though all kinds of "animals" <note>A reference to the living figures represented by the zodiac constellations.</note> are there). Nor are they fixed to the zodiac like the roots and shoots of the earth; rather, they are separated by an immense chasm and interval. For this reason, <term>Panaetius</term> <note>A Stoic philosopher known for doubting astrology.</note> and <term>Plotinus</term> <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher.</note> especially mock them, who think a "contagion" could reach the stars from the Zodiac across such a great distance of space.

<margin>Whence they were deceived</margin>

We are moved not so much by the space that lies immensely between them, as by the nature of the things themselves. Since true and natural bodies cannot be affected in any way by imaginary ones, and the shining stars cannot be changed by non-shining ones (not to say by "nothing"). But it is easy to see what deceived them here: for since the Sun, placed in **Leo**, heats the lands more violently, and the same Sun coming to **Aries** as if renews the world, it seemed to them to have a kinship with Leo and Aries. Because by traveling through those signs it is rendered stronger, and we experience its greater power every year, they established Leo as the domicile of the Sun and Aries as its kingdom. Led by this conjecture regarding the Sun, they thought a similar thing should be decreed for the other signs: that they could do more in one sign and less in another. And with very beautiful reasoning, they distributed two houses to each planet except the Sun and the Moon, for whom one royal house each would be enough. For regarding the Sun, when they had decreed for the reason given that it should obtain Leo for a house, in which it might exercise its greatest strength in burning heat, it seemed reasonable that the next house should be thought of as the Moon's, as she approaches us more. Indeed, her circle is also closest to us; therefore they assigned **Cancer** as the domicile of the Moon. However, according to the position of the spheres in which the planets are carried, they distributed two to each of the others. For instance, to **Mercury**, which is believed to be adjacent to the Moon, they gave **Gemini** on one side and **Virgo** on the other; to **Venus**, **Taurus** on this side and **Libra** on that; here **Aries** and there **Scorpio**... <insert>to Mars</insert>

<summary>Pico critiques the astrological system of planetary "houses," arguing that these assignments are based on poetic imagination and false analogies rather than physical reality. He specifically points out that the signs of the zodiac are mere geometric divisions that cannot physically influence the planets across the vast void of space.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the critique of planetary houses and the zodiac. <page-num>VI</page-num>
<header>Book VI</header>

<margin>The foundation is destroyed</margin>
...they bestowed [Scorpio] on Mars; Pisces and Sagittarius on Jupiter; and Aquarius and Capricorn on Saturn. With these persuasions, they did not even establish their dogmas on the basis of rhetorical probability, yet these ideas were handed down by their successors with such authority that they are received as if they were greater than oracles. In these matters, see first how criminal it is—and how full of ignorance and sluggishness—the very point on which the rest of their system depends. For the fact that the Sun heats us more when it is in Leo happens not from the nature of the **sign** <note>The 30-degree mathematical division of the zodiac.</note> it travels through, but occurs because of its position and placement; from that location, it strikes the earth more directly in the regions closest to us. Otherwise, if the quality received from the sign itself produced this effect, it would do the same among all nations, since the signs are the same for everyone. But in truth, at the same time the Sun burns the lands situated to the North while positioned in Leo, it is cold for those who live in the South; conversely, for those southern peoples, the heat is intense when the Sun reaches Aquarius—the sign under which it pours out ice and watery rain for us. Specifically, this is because the more it approaches us, the further it is distanced from them; and on the other hand, its path turns back toward them whenever it departs from us. 

But if they contend that they are led not so much by this reasoning as by other "experiments" <note>In this context, "experiments" refers to empirical observations or recorded case studies.</note> by which it has been observed that a planet has more or less power in one place than another, there might perhaps be some faith in this if the founders of the art had passed down consistent truths. Wherefore, even regarding the new professors of the art, I mention the "experiments" of the Chaldeans <note>Ancient Babylonian astronomers/astrologers.</note>—those masters who they claim observed the heavens for so many thousands of years in the open plains—they gave no credit to these **houses** <note>The specific zodiac signs where a planet is said to be most "at home" or powerful.</note> as we said above. Why then did they, in such diligent and long-lasting observations, never find Mars to be strong in Scorpio and weak in Taurus, or Saturn powerful in Capricorn and weak in Cancer? 

Let the same be understood for what is said of the rest. And since the same sign is divided into so many **bounds** <term>fines: specific degree ranges within a sign ruled by different planets</term>, so many **decans** <term>decani: 10-degree divisions of a sign</term>, so many **monomoiria** <term>monomiriis: degree-by-degree divisions used in Egyptian astrology</term> among the Egyptians, and **dodecatemoria** <term>dodecathemoriis: 1/12th subdivisions of a sign, or 2.5 degrees each</term> among the Chaldeans, and there is no agreement among them concerning these "bounds"—Ptolemy <note>The most influential astronomer/astrologer of antiquity.</note> neglects the decans, which the Indians and Egyptians divide differently; the Arabs do not know the monomoiria; the Greeks mock them; yet the Egyptians use them in every prediction. I pass over the use of dodecatemoria which is frequent among the Chaldeans. However, as Maternus <note>Julius Firmicus Maternus, a 4th-century Roman astrologer.</note> writes, a planet provides in its own bounds what it provides in its domicile, and in its decan what it grants in its bounds and house—or at least things very close and similar to them. 

Since these things are so, what faithful and consistent "experience" can there be? In whatever part of the Zodiac a planet travels, whether they are referred to a new sphere or rather described in the eighth, in that same part one person wants Saturn to rule, another Jupiter, and another some other planet. And here some use signs they think move, while others use those that do not move. Concerning these conflicting opinions, nothing is so settled or decided that Abraham <margin>Abraham</margin> <note>Abraham Ibn Ezra (c. 1089–1167), a celebrated Jewish scholar and astrologer.</note> in his book *On Nativities* even instructed that a double **theme** <note>A horoscope or birth chart.</note> be made: one for the moving signs, the other for the immobile ones. By this variety of the horoscope, the whole reasoning of their predictions is changed. Thus, all authority of their "experimentation" is weakened; we will demonstrate later that no such experience can be had in these matters, or if it could, it has not yet been obtained.

### Chapter V: What the opinion of astrologers is concerning aspects, and what part is rational.

<margin>c</margin> We have now refuted the opinion of astrologers regarding the signs and the twelve places of heaven. There remains the third way in which they fable that powers and influences are changed, which is commonly named **aspects** <note>The geometric angles between planets, such as 60 or 90 degrees.</note>. For they think that if Saturn, for example, is sixty degrees away from Jupiter—that is, by two whole signs—it affects and moves the lower things differently than if it were ninety degrees away from the same star.

<summary>The author critiques the inconsistency of astrological "houses" and subdivisions like decans and bounds, noting that different cultures (Egyptians, Chaldeans, Greeks) cannot agree on them. He argues that the perceived power of signs like Leo is due to seasonal geography rather than the stars themselves.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the critique of astrological foundations, moving from the signs of the zodiac to the theory of "aspects"—the specific geometric angles between planets that astrologers claim alter their influence.</meta>

# Book VI

...which is an interval of three signs. Again, they say that at a distance, Saturn and Jupiter behold each other in a **hexagonal radiation** <note>original: "exagona radiatione"</note>, which they call the **sextile** <term>sextile: An aspect where two planets are 60 degrees apart, considered harmonious.</term> aspect; because the intervening space is a sixth part of the Zodiac. In another instance, they look at each other from a **square** <note>original: "ex quadrato"</note>, because they are separated from each other by a fourth of the Zodiac. Similarly, they claim there are other properties for both stars if one is distant from the other by one hundred and twenty degrees, from which the **trine** radiation—that is, the threefold aspect—emerges. Otherwise, if they are simultaneously opposed from the diameter <note>the **opposition** aspect, 180 degrees apart</note>, or meet in the same site or place <note>a **conjunction**, 0 degrees apart</note>. And what we have said about Jupiter and Saturn should be understood as applied to all of them: so that through the various distances between them, their power and efficiency are always changed. Indeed, they claim they are changed to such an extent that when they are distant by certain intervals—that is, in trine or sextile—their entire outflow is good and salutary. On the other hand, when established at a certain distance—that is, either quadrangular <note>square</note> or opposite—they possess the most harmful strength of rays, or at least are always minimally beneficial. They also claim that from this diversity of intervals, not only the goodness or malice of the outflow changes, but also the very type and reason for their operation. These are the delusions <note>original: "deliramenta"</note> of astrologers regarding the aspects of the planets, which any philosopher, upon hearing them, will immediately condemn even without anyone else refuting them. For by no reason can it be defended that from the mere diversity of distance and interval, the nature and property of two causes conspiring toward the same end should be so greatly changed. But first, I ask them this: do they want these things they say about aspects to refer to the planets themselves, or only to the effects of the planets?

<margin>A two-part argument</margin>
That is, when they say Jupiter is "provoked" by Mars with quadrangular rays, or Venus is "cherished" by the trine radiation of Jupiter, do they mean that the actual bodies of the planets are moved by such good or evil affections? Or do they mean that those bodies suffer nothing from each other and feel none of these changes, but rather that what they do toward us, and in what way they move the subject bodies <note>the physical things on Earth</note>, is signified by this kind of speaking? For whether they answer this way or that, they fall into a thousand snares and a thousand difficulties on all sides.

<margin>That planets do not harm each other</margin>
For if they think the planets are moved by each other and, as if practicing friendships and hatreds, now cherish each other in a friendly embrace, and now pursue and invade in a hostile manner with the points of their rays, not only will divine Job cry out...

<margin>Job, Aristotle</margin>
...at whose house we read that God "makes peace in his high places" <note>Job 25:2; Pico uses this to argue that there is no "conflict" or "hostility" between celestial bodies.</note>. But also his own Aristotle and the whole family of **Peripatetics** <term>Peripatetics: Followers of Aristotle's philosophy, which held that the heavens were perfect and unchanging.</term>, among whom it is certain that superior bodies are changed only by variety of place. Those qualities found below the moon neither arrive there nor depart from there. But if they wish to concede those qualities entirely, certainly regarding "noxious" qualities, if they concede them, it seems they should be exploded from every assembly of philosophers; since those who think there is something in that celestial homeland that can inflict or sustain injury seem to be entirely ignorant of the nature of the heavens. Therefore, if any **passion** <note>In ancient philosophy, a "passion" is any state of being acted upon or undergoing change.</note> is to be admitted in the stars, it should at least be no other than what should be called a **perfection** rather than a passion; as when the moon is illuminated by the sun, she then "suffers" from him in no other way than one who receives a benefit suffers from the one who gives it. Therefore, for a star to be harmed or obstructed or infected by a star, or to become weaker or worse—and from beneficial to be rendered noxious, from powerful to be made infirm—is as far removed from all truth as all the nature of celestial things is removed from all evil. But if the stars can suffer injury, surely those which are more noble and perfect ought not to suffer it from the ignoble; so that at least one may conclude that not all things can be mutually affected and moved by all, but certain ones by certain others, so that some only act while others suffer; otherwise, how do they not blush at the Sun, the ruler and king...

<summary>Pico attacks the astrological theory of "aspects" (geometric angles between planets), arguing that it is philosophically absurd to suggest that perfect celestial bodies can harm, weaken, or hate one another based on their distance.</summary>

# Book VI

...of the planets; and just as it is the highest source of light, so too is it the highest source of celestial power. Yet they <note>The astrologers</note> do not reduce it to the same order of numbers, lest it too should either wither, conquered by the rays of others, or turn out to be only equally beneficial, since all the power of the planets is derived from it, and it would suffer from its own weapon (as the saying goes). But let us set aside all these things which perhaps do not seem absurd to them, and let us establish, as they wish, how the planets are affected and moved. Let them answer what reason they have that stars which are very close do not move each other, yet once they are made more remote, they begin to perceive one another and suffer mutual influence. For that is how they are accustomed to define **aspects** <term>aspects: The specific angular distances between planets that astrologers believe trigger an influence.</term>. For if Jupiter holds Cancer and Mars holds Leo—between which signs nothing lies—they say the stars of Jupiter and Mars are **unconnected** <note>original: "asyndeta"</note>; that is, joined by no connection of rays or aspects. But then, when Mars is made much further from Jupiter and has traveled to Virgo, they will think that Mars participates in Jupiter and Jupiter in Mars. What could be said that is more absurd or more remote from all philosophy? For it is a very common principle that everything which acts upon another does so more effectively the closer it is to the recipient.

<margin>
Aspect is nothing other than radiation.
</margin>

This thing which the moderns call "aspect," since it is nothing other than "radiation"—as it was also called by the ancients—that is, the propagation of its own light and power onto another (and, so to speak, a certain **illumination** <note>original: "elucidatio"</note>), how shall it be ineffective on bodies that are closest, but effective on those furthest away? What persuades them that just because a ray is poured out from a more remote or a closer distance, it turns out to be of one nature or another? Since (if we follow true reason) no other diversity can arise from this except that the ray is fixed into the recipient planet more weakly or more strongly. But why its very property should be changed can be neither imagined nor even thought up. For even if, through the diversity of the interval, either the number of intervening parts is varied, or the planets themselves obtain a different geometric figure relative to one another, nonetheless, the power of natural things is not varied by a diversity of numbers and figures. This is because natural powers do not come from numbers and figures, but from natural forms; and through the diversity of these forms, the figures themselves—stable and innate ones—are moved and varied, not the accidental ones that arise from motion.

<margin>
That different radiations do not produce different effects.
</margin>

No less do difficulties arise if they think the diversity of radiation should be considered not in the bodies of the planets, but in their effect; namely, that the stars suffer nothing from one another, but the different reasoning of the distance between them causes the flowing rays to be mixed differently, and therefore various effects arise from the diversities of the mixture. If they should answer this, we could first object on the authority of **Plotinus** <note>Plotinus (c. 204–270 AD), a founding philosopher of Neoplatonism, who argued that while the heavens might signal the future, they do not cause it through physical rays.</note> that rays flowing down from heaven cannot be so mixed with each other that a new power or form arises, since they are neither bodies, nor liquids, nor qualities fixed to bodies. Nor are they received into bodies in the manner of such things, such that they might be stained by them or changed in some way from their own condition by the state of the substance. For it seemed likely to that philosopher that what happens to many qualities does not happen to rays: namely, that from some thickening or mixture they are sometimes changed into another form coalescing from all of them. This usually happens only with the destruction of the simple and particular qualities flowing together toward the same point; one will not easily imagine this in the case of rays. But let us grant them that rays are mixed, provided they show us how the rays that flow together from stars at various distances from each other are mixed differently. For only this diversity (as we were saying above) can arise: that those which come from the closest and most joined...

<summary>The author argues that astrology contradicts natural philosophy because it claims planets have no influence when adjacent but gain influence when distant. He further uses the philosopher Plotinus to argue that celestial rays cannot "mix" like liquids to create new effects.</summary>

The author is refuting the idea that physical distance or geometric shapes (aspects) should logically govern how celestial bodies influence one another, arguing that if rays come from the same source, their power shouldn't change just because of the angle they form.</meta>

...emanate from these bodies; these would mix better and more intimately, whereas those which proceed from separate and more remote places would cohere with more difficulty. This, however, does not please those who allow no interaction <note>original: "comertiū," referring to astrological commerce or influence</note> between the rays of planets located in adjacent signs; yet they allow the greatest interaction between those that have emanated from stars separated by a vast and immense region of the sky. Furthermore, if the ratio of either the diametrical opposition, or the quadrangular, or the triangular figure creates a difference in the **property** <term>property: The inherent power or specific quality of a planetary ray.</term> of the rays, this cannot be defended unless we say that the bodies of the planets change their condition based on that variety of figures. For the power and property of a ray comes from nowhere else than from the nature of the radiating body. Nor is that variety of figures located anywhere other than within the bodies themselves from which the rays descend to us; and the further they recede from there, the less they preserve that relationship of figures among themselves, until, touching the earth, they meet in a cone. Thus, those rays which flowed from opposite sources flow together into a unity of coalescence when they reach us. Therefore, when they are mixed, they are no longer entangled in triangular or quadrangular **schemes** <note>original: "schematis," referring to the geometric layouts of aspects</note>, such that the nature of the mixing could be changed by that variety of shapes. But astrologers will be forced to retreat to this argument: they must claim that there is a specific property in the rays because the stars from which they emanated were arranged in such a relationship of figures to one another. And so, finally, they will either say that the stars vary their nature according to the variety of configurations—which has been refuted—or, if the stars themselves do not vary, they will be forced to confess that the power of the rays flowing from them remains the same and unchanged.

### Chapter VI: Various reasons for aspects are recounted and refuted.

The ancients, whom *Maternus* <note>Julius Firmicus Maternus, a 4th-century Roman lawyer and astrologer.</note> imitates, derived the reasoning for **aspects** from numbers. They argued that stars were said to be joined by a certain number of parts <note>degrees</note> which, when multiplied by a specific number, would equal the total parts of the heaven. Thus, they say a diametrical radiation <note>an opposition, 180°</note> occurs at an interval of one hundred and eighty parts, because that number doubled makes the full number of three hundred and sixty parts. Likewise, a **trine** <term>trine: An aspect of 120 degrees, considered very harmonious.</term> consists of one hundred and twenty parts, because if you triple these parts, you again complete all the parts of the sky. 
<margin>
Refutation
</margin>
The square radiation <note>a quadrature, 90°</note> requires ninety parts, which if you [quadruple] <note>The text says "double," but mathematically implies the fourfold sum to reach 360</note>, you collect the sum of three hundred and sixty. The **hexagon** <term>hexagon: Also known as a sextile, an aspect of 60 degrees.</term> is computed at sixty parts, which are the sixth part of all the parts. But this reasoning is far too drowsy and lazy. For by the same logic, they should create an aspect at seventy-two degrees, since multiplied five times they complete three hundred and sixty degrees; they should do the same at forty-five degrees, since this number is the eighth part of all the degrees of the heaven. But *Abu Ma'shar* <note>original: "Aboasar," a famous Persian astrologer of the 9th century.</note> says those numbers have another prerogative, because they not only count the parts of the sky but also the number of the **signs** <term>signs: The twelve 30-degree divisions of the Zodiac.</term> when multiplied. For in the hexagon, two signs are counted; in the trine, four; in the quadrate, three; in the diameter, six. For twice six, and thrice four, and four times three, and six times two all finish the number of twelve signs. But this confirmation is also frivolous. For by similar reasoning, stars that are distant by thirty parts would be configured with each other, 
<margin>
Rejection of Ptolemy's mathematical reasoning
</margin>
because if you look at the number of parts, you have a twelfth part of the heaven, and if you look at the signs, you have their twelfth portion as well. Finally, the reasons brought from geometric figures by *Ptolemy* <note>Claudius Ptolemy, the most influential astronomer/astrologer of antiquity.</note> do not prove the proposition, since even these harmonies of figures do not produce different properties in natural things. But those who use them fall into that error condemned by *Aristotle*: treating mathema...

Now, the 
<margin>Ptolemy’s natural reason</margin>

That is, the planets bound together in those **schemes** <note>original: "schematis"</note> are so disposed that if one is in a feminine sign, the other is also in a feminine one; if one is in a masculine sign, the other is likewise in a masculine one. Conversely, the square <note>90°</note> and opposite <note>180°</note> radiations are malevolent because they emerge from signs of different kinds. <margin>First reason</margin>

<margin>Second reason</margin>

<margin>Third</margin>
Finally, whatever their condition might be, the planets cannot be changed by them, which 
<margin>Fourth</margin>
we shall demonstrate. For now, let us not dispute these points. Instead, let us show most evidently how these arguments fight against themselves. For if what he assumes is true, then the **opposite radiation** <note>the opposition aspect</note>, which is considered most malevolent, ought to be numbered among the good ones, since it too occurs only in signs of the same kind. For Aries and Libra are of the same kind; 
likewise Cancer and Capricorn, and all others which gaze upon each other across the diameter <note>the 180° opposition</note>. It is quite 
surprising that Ptolemy did not see this, so that in a matter so open and manifest, a man 
<margin>Fifth</margin>

If he had remembered what he himself said elsewhere, he would have seen that this reasoning does not proceed but is contrary to his own precepts. For in the third book of that same work <note>Ptolemy's *Tetrabiblos*</note>, he thinks that between signs not only of the same sex but even of the same quality, there is sometimes not a hexagonal (that is, good) configuration, but a square (that is, bad) one—as when they are "oblique," which is to say of **short ascension** <term>short ascension: Signs that take less time to rise over the horizon, which distorts their geometric relationship.</term>. Likewise, those which are of different kinds may have not a square but rather a hexagonal affinity, so that he would compose a square radiation between Gemini and Aquarius, but a hexagonal one between Taurus and Aquarius. If this is true, how can the goodness or malice of the configurations arise from the affinity or discord of the signs? This is a difficulty that must be faced by all those who measure the spaces of radiations not by the **zodiac** <note>original: "signiferi," the sign-bearer</note> but by the parts of the equator—which the majority of astrologers observe. Yet all of them (being wonderfully inconsiderate) when they must give a reason for the malice or goodness of the aspects, reason from nowhere else than from this kinship or diversity of signs. 
<margin>Another reason from Albumasar</margin>
Albumasar <note>original: "Aboasar," the influential Persian astrologer</note> brings another reason for the aspects which he thinks is natural: saying that the **opposition** is confirmed by the fullness of light which the Moon attains when it is opposite the Sun. The **square** power appears in the motion of the planets from their **apogee** <note>original: "apside," the point furthest from Earth</note>, for when they are ninety degrees away from it, they change their course. The **Trine** is seen in the superior planets which, when removed from the Sun by one hundred and twenty parts, move backward if they were previously moving forward, or move forward if they were previously retrograde. The quantity of the **Sextile** <note>original: "exagoni"</note>, he says, fits the half of the diameter of the circle, as well as the quantity of the distance of the houses of Venus from the houses of the luminaries <note>the Sun and Moon</note>. 
<margin>Confutation</margin>
Thus, he has poorly stitched together one **patchwork quilt** <note>original: "centonem," a garment of scraps</note> from a thousand rags: seeking the opposition from the Moon, the square from the apogee, the trine from the superior planets, and the sextile from Venus. And all of it is poorly done by everyone. For what reason is there that, because the Moon is filled with the Sun's light across the diameter, all planets should be coupled by this distance—not only to the Sun, but even among themselves? # Book VI

<margin>Paul and Porphyry</margin>
<margin>Another reason for aspects devised by certain moderns</margin>
<margin>Refutation</margin>
...they change their course at the Sun's **trine** <note>a 120-degree angle</note>: why should this interval have the power to change the forces of the planets, not only the superior ones <note>Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn</note> but also the inferior ones <note>Venus and Mercury</note>; and not only in relation to the Sun, but when measured between the planets themselves? Furthermore, that rule is not even constant among the superior planets. For Mars, as **Paul** and **Porphyry** <note>Paul of Alexandria (4th century) and Porphyry (3rd century), influential astrological writers</note> write, sometimes halts to begin its retrograde motion when it is eighty-four degrees away from the Sun, positioned in the preceding signs, not only without waiting for the expected trine, but without even completing the **square** <note>a 90-degree angle</note>. But if they derived the power of the trine from that change of the superior planets in relation to the Sun's trine, it should have been numbered among the "bad" rather than the "good" radiations. This is because every superior planet in the Sun's trine is "unlucky," if we believe Paul and **Heliodorus** <note>another 4th-century astrological authority</note>. For he says, <note>original Greek: αστερεσ στηριζοντεσ κακοι</note> *stationary stars are bad*; that is, that all stationary planets are bad and unlucky, whether they are in their first station or their second. But all these things are of such evident shallowness that they need not be refuted with more words. Finally, a different reason was devised by certain **moderns** regarding musical consonances, from which they hand down that the rays of the planets sometimes harmonize with each other and sometimes are dissonant, according to a certain similarity to musical harmony. For they say it is proven among musicians by both reason and experience that the third and fifth notes harmonize with the first, but the fourth and seventh do not at all. What if, therefore, planets at equal distances from one another are found to be sometimes in good harmony and sometimes in bad? The **hexagonal** radiation <note>the sextile aspect, 60 degrees</note> corresponds to the third note; the **trigonal** <note>trine, 120 degrees</note> to the fifth; the **quadrate** <note>square, 90 degrees</note> to the fourth—since as many signs intervene here as notes intervene there. These things are certainly "pretty," and they have an appearance of probability to those who have only "greeted philosophy from the threshold" <note>a metaphor for those who have only a superficial understanding of a subject</note>. But we—to set aside these similarities between such diverse types of things—shall declare that these reasons have no efficacy and that the comparison and similarity do not hold up. For among musicians, if a voice does not harmonize with another, it is dissonant; among astrologers, many spaces (if I may put it this way) are "mute" to each other: that is, they neither harmonize nor are they dissonant. For example, the second note is numbered by musicians among the dissonant no less than the fourth, seventh, or eleventh. But among astrologers, the second sign from the first is not discordant, but emits no "voice" <note>meaning it forms no recognized major aspect</note> at all. The fifth and seventh signs emit a certain voice, but not a harmonious one. Furthermore, there is an even greater difference: the sixth note among musicians harmonizes just as much as the third, yet among astrologers, the sixth sign is entirely distinct from the first <note>it forms an "inconjunction"</note>. Then, in music, the eighth note harmonizes as if it were the same sound <note>the octave</note>; the eighth sign does not recognize the first, nor can the eighth note represent the appearance of a conjunction, which is better represented by notes of the same tone. Therefore, in this so-called "pretty" similarity, one finds entirely more dissimilarity than similarity.

### Chapter VII: What deceived them: nor was experience held concerning aspects.

But in truth, those who first invented that dogma were not even led by reasons of this kind; rather, a certain conjecture based on the observed Moon deceived them more. For when they saw the Moon, which borrows its light from the Sun, placed in different positions relative to the Sun—whether it was very close or receding—it was seen to change its shape. They transferred this same principle to the rest of the planets: that all of them, through their various distances not only from the Sun but also from each other, would change their condition and state. You may easily notice from this that they were led to this opinion from nowhere else. For they established neither more nor fewer, nor any other configurations of the planets among themselves, than those which the Moon undergoes in relation to the Sun in the signs...

# Book VI

<margin>
Five configurations of the moon in relation to the sun
</margin>

There are five celebrated configurations of the moon in relation to the sun: when it is seen either joined with the sun <note>the New Moon or conjunction</note>, or horned <note>the crescent moon</note>, or divided <note>the half-moon or quarter</note>, or bulging, or full. To these, an equal number of configurations devised by astrologers for the planets correspond: when they are together at the same time, or when they regard each other with a hexagonal <note>the sextile aspect, 60 degrees</note>, or quadrangular <note>the square aspect, 90 degrees</note>, or triangular <note>the trine aspect, 120 degrees</note>, or opposite radiation. For conjunction corresponds to conjunction; then the hexagonal radiation corresponds to the horned figure, which is first seen in the moon when it is sixty degrees distant from the sun. It is called by the Greeks *conoides* <note>original: "conoides," meaning cone-shaped</note>; the hexagonal radiation between planets was established by the astrologers using that same number of degrees. Likewise, the moon is then "divided"—called *dichotomos* in Greek <note>original Greek: διχότομος, meaning "cut in half"</note>—when ninety degrees lie between it and the sun; when the stars themselves are separated by this same space, they are said to be composed in a "square" configuration. They derived the triangular radiation from the likeness of the "bulging" moon, which is first seen in that shape when it is removed one hundred and twenty degrees from the sun; it is called *amphikyrtos* by the Greeks <note>original Greek: αμφίκυρτος</note>, which we can call "bulging" or "gibbous." That the opposition itself corresponds to the full moon, everyone understands. And since the moon, according to the diversity of its shape, is also accustomed to change physical bodies in different ways, they established the same rule for all the planets: namely, that because of this variety of intervals between them, they would also affect "inferior" things <note>objects on Earth, in the sublunary sphere</note> in various ways.

By which conjecture of consequence (if they were led by this, as I suspect), it can easily be understood how much they are deceived. Indeed, the moon changes its properties of influence just as it changes its shape through its various distances from the sun; because it receives light from the sun, it is illuminated more or less on the side that faces us, depending on its position and relationship to the sun. And from this it happens by natural reason that, because of the increase or decrease of light, it not only presents itself to us with a different appearance, but it also changes the physical qualities of our bodies and those of other things. For who does not know that the moistures of bodies are dissolved by heat? Who, again, does not know that light is the cause of heat? From this it is clearly gathered that the more light the moon has, the more the bodies of inferior things (to which it is closest) are heated; and by a following logic, the moistures within them more greatly liquefy and resolve. In this way, that pronouncement of Ptolemy will be true: that from the moon's first "square" <note>the first quarter</note> until the second, the moistures of bodies flow out, because during that time the parts of the moon facing the earth enjoy more abundant light. 

Hence those experiments proven by the studies of farmers: that timber cut when the moon is full of light quickly rots; conversely, that which is cut when the moon is waning is preserved immune from rot and the defect of decay. This is because moisture is most conducive to putrefaction, and as I said, moisture increases and decreases in bodies simultaneously with the waxing and waning of the moon's light. 

<margin>
Turning the argument back against the one arguing
</margin>

But truly, to transfer these changes of the moon—which alone is subject to this kind of alternation of light—to the planets, which always shine with their own and unchanging light, is utterly insane. It is rather permitted to argue from the contrary: if the moon changes us in different ways according to its measure of light (because it is illuminated more or less due to the diversity of its position), it follows that for the planets—just as their light does not change—so their property of influence should not be changed. Their light is neither impoverished nor diminished by various distances, whether in relation to the sun or to each other...

<summary>The author critiques the astrological practice of basing planetary "aspects" (like the trine or square) on the phases of the Moon, arguing that while the Moon's light affects Earthly moisture, the planets shine with constant light and thus cannot be compared to lunar phases.</summary>

# Book VI

->VI<-

...look down upon us. But let them always look upon us and other earthly things in the same way. Whether they have been led to this opinion as we suspect, or moved by the conjectures we first encountered, it is clear that they rely on the most trivial and ridiculous arguments. If, perhaps lacking confidence in these, they allege "experience" as their proof—which is the sole refuge for <margin>That astrologers cannot appeal to experience.</margin> those abandoned by reason—we can equally appeal to experience, by which their <term>apotelesmata<note>original: "apotelesmata," referring to the completed results or effects of the stars on human affairs</term> are daily refuted. But let them answer this one thing: what true and faithful experiments have been held regarding these matters, about which there is such great controversy among them? For instance, one astrologer might determine a place to be a "square" <note>an aspect of 90 degrees</note>, while another contends it is a "trine" <note>an aspect of 120 degrees</note>. And what one <margin>Discord</margin> considers a <term>hexagon<note>original: "exagonum," the sextile aspect of 60 degrees</note></term>, there may be someone who wants it to be a "square"; or indeed, what is a trine to one person will be a "diameter" <note>the aspect of opposition, 180 degrees</note> to others. Since this matter will be discussed at length below, we refer the reader to that place. For now, we are also reminding the reader that they differ not only in prescribing the boundaries of these "radiations" <note>the lines of influence between planets</note>, but also in their very nature. So much so that <margin>Paulus, Heliodorus</margin> Paulus and Heliodorus write that a hexagon—which is between signs that are not equally distant from either the equinoxes or the <term>tropics<note>the points of the solstices</note></term>—has the nature of an opposition. Furthermore, they claim that an opposition is not harmful, but occupies a middle ground between good and bad aspects. Similarly, Ptolemy thinks neither the square is inherently bad nor the trine inherently good. Thus, it is clear enough that no authority of "experience" supports them; in the face of such diverse opinions, each master contends that this "experience" supports him with equal faith and equal authority.

## Chapter VIII: What is said about "obsession" conflicts with what is said about "aspects."

Besides those figures and aspects we have mentioned, there are other positions of the stars, both in relation to each other and to the sun, by which astrologers think the powers of things are affected and their properties changed. Among these are some that seem to contradict those earlier rules. For they say a planet is "obsessed" <note>or "besieged"</note> whenever the rays of harmful stars surround it on both sides. The Greeks call this condition <term>emperichesis<note>original: "$\epsilon \mu \pi \epsilon \rho \iota \chi \epsilon \sigma \iota \nu$," likely a corruption of "emperischesis," meaning a surrounding or enclosure</note></term>. For example, if Jupiter holds Libra, while Mars holds Virgo and Saturn holds Scorpio; or even if Jupiter is placed therein, and Mars shoots rays from Taurus into Virgo and Scorpio, then they will call Jupiter "obsessed." I ask them, therefore: do the planets move and affect each other when located in adjacent and neighboring signs? If they say no, "obsession" is eliminated, because a ray reaching Virgo will not harm a star placed in Libra. Just as a ray sent to Scorpio would not, since Scorpio and Virgo are signs neighboring Libra. But if they grant that they do, then the logic of "aspects" is worth nothing, as it depends entirely on the idea that planets affect each other at specific intervals, while suffering nothing from one another at other distances. If they respond that it happens differently in "obsession" because the rays are on both sides, this is the very point where their insanity is most manifest. It is as if they think what usually happens to men happens to stars: that a pursuing enemy from behind does not harm a fleeing man <margin>Response / Refutation</margin> provided there is an open field ahead to escape, yet he would be caught by the pursuer if another stood in front blocking the path of flight. By this example, they suggest that if Mars occupies Virgo, it does not reach Jupiter located in Libra; yet it will reach him if Saturn stands opposite Jupiter in Scorpio. What kind of consistent discipline is this, then, where you call neighboring signs "unconnected" <note>original: "asindetae," from the Greek for "unjoined"</note> and "averted" <note>original: "apostrophae"</note>—meaning stars placed in them have no communion with each other and nothing flows from one to the other—and yet...

<sig>B iii</sig>

<summary>The author critiques the inconsistency of astrological theories, noting that astrologers frequently disagree on the nature of "aspects" (angles between planets). He specifically highlights the logical contradiction between the rule of "aspects" (which requires specific distances) and the concept of "obsession" (where neighboring signs supposedly influence a planet).</summary>

# Book VI

->VI<-

...yet you would say a planet is "besieged" <note>original: "obsessum," a condition where a planet is positioned between two "malefic" or harmful planets</note> if it is infested by the harmful rays from the nearest signs. For you would not concede that Jupiter is harmed by Mars if Saturn were removed; yet with Saturn added, you would concede it—especially since Saturn arrives in such a way that he himself cannot harm Jupiter. But it is certainly as we were saying: a mere likeness has led these men astray, as if they were imagining a person surrounded by enemies with no way out to safety.

### Chapter IX That planets situated under the sun's rays are not ill-affected, or "combust," as the astrologers say.

<margin>First reason</margin>
They also rave regarding planets compared to the sun, which they claim are ineffective and ill-affected when positioned under its rays—as if the stars too could not bear the light of the sun, or as if their "heads" were too weak and they grew sick if they were "sunned" too much. And yet, all celestial light, and especially solar light, is beneficial. If it is sometimes harmful to earthly things, that happens only because of a defect in the matter it hits. No such defect of matter exists in the stars. Therefore, the more they enjoy the light of the sun, the more vigorous and effective they become—especially since the sun, compared to the stars, acts as a universal cause, whose nature is <margin>Second reason</margin> to confirm the particular nature of things rather than to weaken it. But if the "silent moon" <note>original: "luna silente," referring to the New Moon or the period when the moon is not visible</note> seems to be deprived of its benefit to lower things, the reason is different: because the part which faces us is stripped of light when it is joined to the sun. This does not happen to the other planets, which shine with their own light; therefore, it does not follow that they are less able to transform lower things when the sun's rays are poured around them.

<margin>Third reason</margin>
Furthermore, if they stubbornly defend the idea that the power of the stars can be oppressed and drained, this ought to happen even more when the planets are more powerful and closer to the sun—both of which they usually deny. For if a planet joins the sun exactly <note>original: "partiliter," referring to a conjunction within the same degree and minute</note>, they claim it becomes most effective. Then, they say the sun does not harm a star occupied by its rays in Aries or Leo—even though they decree the sun to be most powerful in those places. For they say the sun "receives" the star as a guest in its own home, since Aries is the sun's <term>exaltation<note>original: "altitudo," the sign where a planet's influence is most elevated</note></term> and Leo is its <term>house<note>original: "domus," the sign a planet naturally rules</note></term>. They claim no good host brings injury to a guest—as if (a mistake they make everywhere) these celestial bodies should be treated in a human fashion, and as if the sun poured out its light and heat not by natural necessity, but by some sort of personal choice and will.

### Chapter X If we wish to follow reason and even the authority of certain astrologers, retrograde planets appear stronger than those in direct motion.

<margin>d</margin>
Finally, anyone who examines the decrees of the astrologers will see that everything has been derived either from a certain human likeness (as we said), contrary to the nature and dignity of celestial things—not by philosophical reason but by almost poetic license—or from mere fables and arbitrary fabrications, such as what they hand down regarding the "images" <note>the constellations</note> which we shall discuss below. Or they arise from certain mathematical occasions which, while used correctly by mathematicians, have been perversely transferred by <term>horoscope-casters<note>original: "genethliaci," those who predict fates based on birth charts</note></term> to this profession of divining. They have erred most greatly in the division of the Zodiac. But that division will be disputed later in its proper place. Now, we deal with the kind of error where they think the efficiency of the planets is either diminished or strengthened, and even that the very nature of the effects varies, according to those diversities of motion which mathematicians devise: such as when they proceed in <term>direct motion<note>original: "directo cursu," the standard eastward movement of a planet</note></term>, or when they are <term>retrograde<note>original: "retrogradiauntur," appearing to move backward in the sky</note></term>, or when they stand still in <term>stationary<note>original: "statiua," the point where a planet appears to stop before changing direction</note></term> slowness. For they say a planet acts weakly when it is retrograde, and effectively when it proceeds. They even say it is prosperous while moving forward, yet the very same planet is harmful if it moves backward...

<summary>Pico della Mirandola argues that astrological concepts like "combustion" and "retrogradation" are based on flawed human metaphors rather than natural philosophy. He contends that proximity to the sun strengthens rather than weakens celestial bodies.</summary>

# Book VI

<margin>Heliodorus.</margin>
...he continues: in which matter, seeing what could be said against the astrologers, Heliodorus <note>Heliodorus (c. 4th century AD) was an author of an influential commentary on the "Introduction" of the astrologer Paul of Alexandria.</note> raised a question against himself in his book of commentaries on Paul of Alexandria, which I shall explain using his own words rather than anyone else’s, including the solution by which he thought he resolved the question—though he actually complicates it further. His words in Greek are as follows.

We have translated this into English, rendering it almost word for word:

It is necessary to know that although the planets are said to move unequally in reality, yet in the heavens nothing is unequal, nothing is disordered; rather, all order and all equality are found within them. But it belongs to our estimation <note>our perspective from Earth</note> that they appear to move unequally and sometimes even to stand still; for in reality, they neither stand still nor ever slow down or reverse their motion. But it happens that they appear to do so because of the position of the eccentrics and epicycles <term>epicycles|In the Ptolemaic system, small circles on which planets moved, while the center of the epicycle moved along a larger circle called a deferent. This was used to explain why planets occasionally seem to move backward (retrograde).</term> upon which they move, as Ptolemy <note>Claudius Ptolemy (2nd century AD), whose "Almagest" defined the geocentric model of the universe.</note> taught us in his composition. And if anyone should object: "How then are the outcomes <note>original: "apoteleſmata," the predicted effects or judgments of a star</note> different, if something either increases or decreases by their motion, or if they are said to be stationary, when in truth they neither stand still nor move unequally?" We respond that the outcomes—that is, the answers given by astrologers—do not occur specifically because of that inequality or stationing of motions, but because it happens then that the planets, carried in their epicycles, either become closer to the Earth or move further away.

These are the words of Heliodorus, from whom we accept it as not only conceded but attested and confirmed that the "stations" <note>the points where a planet appears to stop moving before changing direction</note> of the planets achieve nothing insofar as they are stations—that is, they do not change the effectiveness of the planets. Likewise, neither do the retrogressions <note>backward motion</note> nor the direct motions, insofar as they are such things. Rather, from these, different things are pronounced because of what happens during these differences of motion: either the planets approach the Earth or they move further away. Since he stated this has a natural reason, they might affect us differently when they are close than when they are distant. This we certainly concede; but if for that reason they observe the planets as direct, stationary, or retrograde, a contrary dogma would have to be established: namely, that retrograde planets would be more effective than when they are carried in a direct course, and weaker when they are direct—if indeed the only thing observed in these is a greater or lesser distance from the Earth. For as Haly <note>Likely Haly Abenragel or Haly Heben Rodan, famous medieval commentators on Ptolemaic astrology.</note> writes while explaining Ptolemy, all reason attests that the closer a planet is to the Earth, the more strongly it changes us and the more powerfully it affects us. But every planet, when it moves backward, is closer to the Earth; conversely, when moving direct, it is further away. Therefore, a retrograde planet ought to have been judged stronger, not—as they have decreed—weak and infirm.

### Chapter XI
The Head and Tail are intersections of imaginary circles, endowed with no natural power, which the ancients did not use in predicting; nor do the moderns agree on their powers.

<margin>What the head and tail are.</margin>
Regarding the "Head and Tail of the Dragon" <note>The lunar nodes: the two points where the Moon's orbital path crosses the ecliptic (the Sun's path). They are not physical stars but mathematical points.</note> to which the crowd of astrologers attributes so much—who does not see that these are empty and fabricated things? But as we said before, here the astrologers often slip into error: whatever they find noted by the mathematicians as necessary methods for measuring motions, they misuse all these things in predicting, as if they were equally natural and endowed with a power of influence. Yet the reality is far different, since they invent and devise many things in the heavens to serve mathematical numbers and measures that are otherwise founded on no stability of nature. We showed this in the signs, which Ptolemy does not think of as mobile, being intercepted by the solstices and equinoxes; we showed it in the division of the minute parts of the signs. Now he seeks the same in the Head and Tail; for they are nothing other than the intersections of two circles, which are mere points, or the junction of two lines...

<summary>The author argues that planetary stations and retrograde motions are optical illusions caused by orbital geometry and, if distance were the only factor, retrograde planets should be considered stronger, not weaker. He also dismisses the "Head and Tail of the Dragon" (lunar nodes) as mathematical abstractions rather than physical entities with astrological power.</summary>
