# Book VI

...conceived in the mind: introduced by mathematicians so that they might distinguish ecliptic locations <note>Points where the path of the Moon or planets crosses the Sun's path (the ecliptic).</note>. Yet there is no power there, no quality or natural efficacy, such that it could be transferred in any way to natal astrology <term>genethliacam|The branch of astrology concerned with casting horoscopes based on a person's birth.</term>. Certainly, they can do nothing unless a planet positioned there decrees something better or worse based on the suitability of the location; but these points themselves, noted separately, can have no power to rule or change physical bodies. The distinguished astrologer Abraham Ibn Ezra <note>Abraham Ibn Ezra (c. 1089–1167) was a celebrated Jewish scholar, poet, and astrologer.</note> saw this, writing in the first book of his *Astrological Reasons* as follows: "They have likewise said that the Head of the Dragon is exalted in Gemini, and the Tail in Sagittarius. But this is empty, because the Head and Tail signify neither good nor evil. For they are merely the connections of two circles; however, the Moon is observed when she is in them: because when she is placed in the Head, she is more invigorated for the reason that she is closer to us; conversely, she is weaker in the Tail, because there, turning toward the south, she is further away from us. The same happens to the rest of the planets when they are found in the Head or Tail, except for the Sun, which has no declination toward either part." Now, since you know from the tables of the law <note>The mathematical tables used by astronomers.</note> that the Head and Tail, noted separately, can neither harm nor help, who...

<margin>Maternus</margin>
...many others would think otherwise. Thus spoke Ibn Ezra. But neither does Ptolemy ever use them in predicting, nor will you find the ancients using them from the works of Maternus <note>Julius Firmicus Maternus, a 4th-century Roman lawyer and astrologer.</note>, in whom there is no mention of the Dragon’s Head and Tail. If the ancients occasionally speak of them, they do so only as a certain location and position. Hence, there was a difference of opinion among them: for to the older authors...

<margin>Heliodorus.</margin>
...both locations seemed evil because of the ecliptic <note>original: "eclypticam"</note>, that is, the path [of eclipses]; furthermore, they established both equally among the unlucky places. Heliodorus, in his treatise <term>Concerning Children|<note>original: "περί τέκνου"</note> "Peri teknou," a common title for astrological chapters on progeny.</term>, says that if the locations signifying children are free from the unfortunate planets and the ecliptic nodes—that is, the Head and Tail—it is fortunate. More recent astrologers, if the Head is in the place of children, will announce children "like young olive shoots around the table" <note>An allusion to Psalm 128:3, illustrating the promise of many healthy children.</note>, led by a different conjecture than that which we reported above from Ibn Ezra: that planets are more effective in the Head because they are closer to us. Indeed, that reasoning holds when a planet is *in* the Head; although a planet leaning toward us even before reaching the Head ought to be considered stronger by the same logic. But when no star is found within it, what can it either give or take away? It is a point designated by us solely in the mind. For as to the suspicion of some that a certain power is "left behind" there by the Moon, no astrologer has ever said this, nor is it physical—if you consider the nature and light of the heavenly bodies—nor even astrological, since the Moon travels through the Tail just as well. It is therefore only a site and mere position, about which both the Arabs and the Latins eventually decreed as if it were a star itself, to the point that they think this Head even adds years to one's life...

<margin>Discord of astrologers.</margin>
...and governs a certain part of one's age: and is "exalted" in Gemini: and has the nature of Venus and Jupiter; while the Tail, conversely, has the nature of Mars and Saturn. In this matter we see how much they disagree with the truth itself. But it is a wonder how much they even disagree with themselves, sometimes calling it the knot and bond of all heavenly happiness. Yet elsewhere...

<margin>Al-Qabisi.</margin>
...they say it is good with the good, and with the evil it increases whatever evil it finds. Elsewhere they speak of it as if it were entirely evil. For Al-Qabisi <note>Al-Qabisi (Latinized as Alchabitius), a 10th-century Arab astrologer.</note>, in whose work are the laws we just recounted, also commemorates this among the misfortunes of planets, if they should be with their "Heads." For every planet has its own Head and its own Tail.

He points out the contradictions among various authorities like Ptolemy, Maternus, and Al-Qabisi regarding whether these points are auspicious or malevolent.</summary>

# Book VI

...among the Arabs called *Genzauar* <note>A corruption of the Arabic term *al-jawzahar*, referring to the lunar nodes.</note>: or when they involve the Head and Tail of the Dragon. This is the specific name for the Head and Tail of the Moon. In these places, it is said she fares as poorly at the Tail as she does at the Head. In his book on nativities, the same author makes the Moon "climacteric" <note>A critical or dangerous point in life, believed to be influenced by planetary cycles.</note> when it connects to the Head; in the principal houses of life, he counts both the Head and Tail equally. Abraham <note>Abraham Ibn Ezra, the 12th-century Jewish scholar.</note>, as we mentioned, claims the Moon is invigorated when located in the Head. We saw above that Heliodorus <note>Likely Heliodorus of Alexandria, an early writer on astrology.</note> numbered these among the malefic stars. He likewise includes them in his treatise on "climacterics" regarding the Sun, Moon, the Ascendant, and the Part of Fortune. Thus, what they have put forward regarding this Head seems to have been produced with no "head" at all—or certainly no heart. Yet they everywhere maliciously call it the "Head of the Dragon," so that it might ring in credulous ears with greater reverence, as if possessing the authority of a deity.

### Chapter XII: The origin of antiscia: that Ptolemy did not use them in forecasting: and how much Maternus and Haly went astray in this matter.

<margin>From whence Hipparchus [derived] antiscia.</margin>
On the occasion of the words of a certain mathematician, they similarly erred regarding **antiscia** <term>antiscia|Points in the zodiac that are equidistant from the tropics, sharing the same length of day and night.</term>. For when the Sun is positioned in those degrees where the days are equal to days and nights to nights, Hipparchus and the ancients—because of the reciprocal equality of days and nights—called them "antiscia," as if you were to say "equals from the opposite side." The practitioners of our "divination" claimed these degrees were equal in virtue and power—an equality that no one fails to recognize as born of base ignorance. 
<margin>Refutation of antiscia: Maternus is most ignorant of the whole mathematical art.</margin>
From the equality of day and night that occurs when the Sun traverses them, they transferred themselves to an equality of power. But I wish to accuse Maternus <note>Firmicus Maternus, a 4th-century Roman lawyer and astrologer, author of the *Mathesis*.</note> above all others as the propagator of this error—though he should be pardoned as one who is most ignorant of the entire mathematical art. He says that Ptolemy attributes the highest importance to the decrees of the antiscia. I am not surprised, for though I have read all of Maternus diligently, he never gave me any indication that he had actually read Ptolemy himself. 
<margin>Ptolemy does not use antiscia in judging.</margin>
Regarding what pertains to antiscia, Ptolemy never uses them in making decrees or pronouncements—whether you search his *Centiloquium* <note>A collection of 100 astrological aphorisms traditionally attributed to Ptolemy, though likely of later origin.</note> or his *Apotelesmata* <note>Ptolemy's major work on astrology, also known as the *Tetrabiblos*.</note>. Only in the first book of the *Apotelesmata*, where he relates the opinions of others **on the sympathy of the signs** <note>original: "περι τησ συμππαθειαστων ζῳδιων" (*peri tēs sumpatheias tōn zōidiōn*)</note>—that is, on the affinity and consensus of the signs—did he use these words among the principles themselves: "Again, they say that whatever points are equally distant from either of the tropics are of equal power, because the Sun placed in them makes days equal to days and nights to nights." When he had said this, as if forgetting it afterward—like one who did not approve of it—he never brings it up again. He never mentions not only the name "antiscia" (which otherwise appears nowhere in his work) but not even the thing itself: that is, this affinity and consensus of parts equally remote from the tropics. As for the fact that in a certain place in the *Centiloquium* it says a planet often extends its strength to where it is not, to want to transfer this to antiscia and **dodecatemoria** <term>dodecatemoria|The division of each zodiac sign into twelve smaller parts of 2.5 degrees each.</term> is too forced and reckless—especially since in his entire discipline Ptolemy mocks one of these (the dodecatemoria and other things of that kind) and neglects the other (the antiscia of which we speak). Indeed, by that precept, he wished to indicate nothing to us other than **schematographia** <note>original: "σχηματογραφιαν" (*schēmatographian*)</note>: that is, the power of configuration and radiation through which planets do many and effective things according to the opinion of astrologers, and especially Ptolemy, in places where they are not. 
<margin>Maternus did not understand what antiscia are.</margin>
For he himself observes almost nothing else in the constellations except phases and configurations—or certainly nothing else more than those. But our Maternus did not even understand what "antiscia" meant; he promised to explain their hidden reasoning elsewhere, as if it were a matter not already explained to any mathematician, or one that could not be explained in three words.

<summary>The author critiques the astrological concept of "antiscia" (zodiacal points of equal day length), arguing that while they have astronomical basis, their use in forecasting is a misinterpretation of Ptolemy. He specifically attacks Firmicus Maternus for his lack of mathematical understanding and for falsely claiming Ptolemy's endorsement of the technique.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the author’s critique of astrological "antiscia" (shadow-points or reflections across the solstice axis). He is specifically targeting the technical errors of medieval astrologers like Abenzagel and the linguistic misunderstandings that led to false theories about planetary influences.</meta>

# Book VI

...cannot be: but you may judge his ignorance from the fact that he uses a very unskillful manner of speaking, stating that **Mars**, positioned at the fifth degree of **Gemini**, "sends an antiscion" into **Cancer**. He would not speak this way if he understood what an **antiscion** <term>antiscion|From the Greek for "opposite shadow." It refers to a point in the zodiac reflected across the axis of the solstices (Cancer/Capricorn). If a planet is at a certain distance from a solstice, its "reflection" is its antiscion.</term> actually was. For an antiscion is neither a ray nor a light that can be "sent," nor is "sending an antiscion" anything other than a planet reaching a degree of equality. Therefore, skilled experts would rather speak this way: that the *epoch* of Mars—that is, the part of the zodiac it occupies—has its antiscia in such a part of Gemini, or (what amounts to the same thing) that Mars is in the antiscion of Gemini. Anyone who says Mars "hurls" an antiscion into Gemini will be hissed at and mocked by true mathematicians.

<margin>The error of Abenzagel</margin>
But **Abenzagel** <note>Likely referring to the 9th-century Arab astrologer Abu Sa'id Shadhan, known as Abenzagel in Latin.</note> also slipped up in many ways. In the first book of his commentaries, while explaining certain aphorisms, he writes that degrees equidistant from the equinoxes possess the same power as those equidistant from the tropics (namely **Cancer** and **Capricorn**). However, the ancients did not say this regarding distance from the equinoxes, but only from the tropics, which is why the name "antiscia" was applied to them. Abenzagel should not have failed to see this, since circles drawn on either side of the equinoxes are indeed equal. It is necessary that parallels equidistant from them be equal to each other; however, they are not semicircles equal to one another in the way that happens with those equidistant from the tropics. From this [tropical symmetry] comes that "agreement" of the antiscia. He also errs, along with many others, in counting the relationship of a degree to its antiscion-degree among those they call "aspects." From this, they conclude that a star placed in one of these points has power in the other, just as it would if they were in hexagonal <note>The sextile aspect (60 degrees).</note>, tetragonal <note>The square aspect (90 degrees).</note>, trigonal <note>The trine aspect (120 degrees).</note>, or opposite positions.

<margin>The error of the Greeks and barbarian astrologers</margin>
An error arose here because what the Greeks call *shapes* <note>original: "σχηματα" (schēmata)</note>—that is, "figures"—the barbarians <note>A term often used by Renaissance scholars to refer to non-Greek or non-Latin medieval sources, particularly Arabic ones.</note> and our own writers call "aspects." Among the Greeks, however, signs are said to "behold" each other, not because they are "linked together" (which is how our writers interpret "aspect"), but because of what is called in Greek *from the illuminations* <note>original: "εκ των φωτισμων" (ek tōn phōtismōn)</note>. This means they emerge and set from the same points. Because this happens in signs that are equally separated from the tropics (as they are on the same parallel line), the majority of astrologers call these antiscion signs *seeing* <note>original: "βλεποντα" (bleponta)</note>. The Arabs, and later the Latins, adopted this into a meaning where they misuse the very name of "aspect." And so it happens: an error in words often gives birth to an error in facts.

<margin>An error in words often gives birth to an error in facts.</margin>
Thus, it has been sufficiently declared how varied the observation of antiscia is among astrologers (if any truth were allowed by fate), and how much both the Arabs and Latins have dreamed up regarding these things, contrary to the opinion of the ancients.

### Chapter XIII: Astrologers were equally deceived regarding "commanding" and "obeying" signs.

From this same category comes that observation of sheer stupidity—or perhaps deception—concerning "commanding" and "obeying" signs. For mathematicians called the signs in which the Sun is positioned to make the days longer than the nights *commanding* <note>original: "προσταττοντα" (prostattonta)</note> when compared to the signs in which light is overcome by darkness in equal proportion. These opposite signs, which bring more darkness than day, they called *obeying* <note>original: "υπακουοντα" (hypakouonta)</note>. Moved by the literal meaning of the names, the **Genethliaci** <term>Genethliaci|Casters of birth charts (nativities).</term> decreed that a person whose birth chart had a "commanding" sign on the horizon <note>The Ascendant or rising sign.</note> would be destined to rule over someone who had an "obeying" sign as their ascendant. It was as if that nickname of "commanding" and "obeying," established by mathematicians, actually pertained to social status, rather than merely indicating the inequality of days and nights occurring under those signs.

<summary>The author critiques astrologers for confusing astronomical symmetry with mystical influence, specifically attacking the misuse of "antiscia" and the literal interpretation of "commanding" and "obeying" signs as indicators of social power.</summary>
<keywords>antiscia, Abenzagel, Mars, Gemini, Cancer, aspects, Greek terminology, commanding signs, obeying signs, Genethliaci, solar symmetry</keywords>

Having previously critiqued "antiscia" and the "houses" of the planets, he now moves to "exaltations," arguing that these were originally astronomical observations of planetary height (apogee) that were later misinterpreted by astrologers as signs of mystical power.</meta>

Book VI

# Chapter XIV: Refutation of the reasons that certain astrologers have assigned for the exaltations of the planets.

<margin>Praise of Pliny</margin>
And as for where that opinion concerning the heights or **exaltations** <term>exaltation|In astrology, a specific sign and degree where a planet is thought to perform with its greatest strength, supposedly due to the sign's compatibility with the planet's nature.</term> of the planets emanated from—and how they rushed headlong into this through a certain mathematical pretext—I have been reminded by that most diligent writer of natural history, to whom all antiquity and all posterity are indebted; for he rescued the former from barbarism and the latter from death <note>Referring to Pliny the Elder, whose *Natural History* preserved much of ancient Roman and Greek science.</note>. He, therefore, in his second book, treating the question of why the same stars appear higher at some times and lower at others, adds the following after certain other points:

"Another cause of their heights is that they have their highest **apsides** <term>apsis|The point in an orbit where a celestial body is at its maximum distance (apogee) or minimum distance (perigee) from the center of its orbit.</term> from their center in those signs: **Saturn** in the twentieth degree of **Libra**, **Jupiter** in the fifteenth of **Cancer**, **Mars** in the twenty-eighth of **Capricorn**, the **Sun** in the nineteenth of **Aries**, **Venus** in the twenty-sixth of **Pisces**, **Mercury** in the fifteenth of **Virgo**, and the **Moon** in the fourth of **Taurus**." So he says.

From this, anyone who is not slow-witted can easily gather that either it was once so, or it was believed by those then devoted to stellar science, that the stars positioned in the aforementioned parts were removed at the greatest height from the center of their apsides. For this reason, those degrees or parts were called the "heights" of the planets. This gave an opportunity to the **genethliaci** <term>genethliaci|Casters of birth horoscopes; from the Greek word for "birthday."</term> to abuse the term "height," as if it were not a height of *location*, but of *nature* and *power*. 

For astrologers do not say that planets are **exalted** anywhere else than in those parts where we have shown they were thought, according to ancient astronomy, to be at their greatest distance from their centers. However, the reader should know that a flaw is found in the common manuscripts of Pliny, and the words that follow have become established with the numbers swapped; where the mark for ten <note>original: "denarii"; referring to the Roman numeral X used to signify ten.</note> belonging to **Venus** was transferred to the **Sun**, so that in the Sun the twenty-ninth part is read instead of the nineteenth, and in Venus the sixteenth instead of the twenty-sixth. 

<margin>Error in Maternus</margin>
For there is also a fault in **Maternus** <note>Julius Firmicus Maternus, a 4th-century Roman astrological writer.</note>, where we read that Venus is exalted in the twenty-seventh part of **Pisces**. 

<margin>Porphyry</margin>
For it ought to be written as the "twenty-sixth" according to **Porphyry** <note>A 3rd-century Neoplatonist philosopher who wrote a commentary on Ptolemy's astrology.</note>. There is also some variation in that ancient astrology assigns the fourth degree of **Taurus** to the Moon, while a later age assigns the third—whether this is a difference of opinion or the fault of scribes, who very often hallucinate in the notation of numbers. Similarly, in Saturn, it should not be the twenty-first, but the twentieth that is read, on the authority of that same Porphyry, a matter which was also mentioned in my second book.

I no longer doubt it is clear to sound minds how the exaltations of the planets crept into divinatory astrology. But when the dogma reached posterity and that original reason for the dogma was made obsolete by changes in theoretical stellar discipline, posterity devised other reasons for themselves by which they thought the opinion had been persuaded to their predecessors—some offering one reason, others another (as often happens in making excuses)—but they are truly flimsy and ridiculous. 

<margin>Ptolemy’s reason and its refutation</margin>
**Ptolemy** says that the **Sun** is exalted in **Aries** because when it reaches it, its power begins to appear more clearly. But (as we said above when speaking of the "houses"), this is not caused by the quality and nature of the sign, but by its position. It does not begin to be stronger because it travels through **Aries**, but because it begins to approach us. Therefore, if the Sun pours its seasonal warmth into your gardens upon arriving at that sign, it is not to be spread abroad that it is being raised into a "kingdom" or placed in its "height." For if that were the case, it would surely be lacking in other regions, from which it happens to be further away in **Aries** and closer when it is under **Libra**. 

But let us look at the other planets as well. The Moon's "sublimity" is in **Taurus**, because if she is joined with the Sun in **Aries**, her power will first appear in **Taurus**. O, what a most effective reason! As if, if she were joined with the Sun in **Taurus**, the same thing would not happen in **Gemini**; or if joined in **Gemini**, in **Cancer**; and if in **Cancer**, the same in **Leo**!

The author critiques the logical inconsistencies of Ptolemy and others who tried to invent mystical reasons for these specific zodiacal degrees.</summary>

...and so it is concerning all the rest: so that we may wonder at Ptolemy, who was not ashamed to write such things. Truly there are other reasons given, such as because the Moon is closest to the Sun and the Moon's triangle is lateral <note>Referring to the geometric "aspects" or triangular relationships between signs in the zodiac.</note>.

<margin>Refutation</margin>
But Ptolemy does not think the Moon is closest to the Sun; nor should we conjecture height from the triangle, nor from the "house," nor height from the triangle: nor should we determine the "terms" <term>terms|In astrology, specific subdivisions of a zodiac sign ruled by different planets, used to refine a planet's influence.</term> or the "decan" <term>decan|A subdivision of a zodiac sign consisting of ten degrees, each with its own planetary ruler.</term> from any of these things. For these categories are distinct, so that to each should be owed its own authority in its own proper matter.

Furthermore, if he puts forward the argument of the triangle, why will **Mercury** not rather be exalted in **Gemini** than in **Virgo**? In **Gemini**, the logic would also fit, as it would be nearest to the exaltation of the Sun, from which **Mercury** is usually but a short distance away. This is what **Aboafar** <note>Also known as Albumasar (787–886 AD), a leading Persian astrologer whose works were highly influential in Medieval Europe.</note> also tries to preserve in that reasoning of exaltations.

<margin>Aboafar</margin>
But **Virgo** suits **Mercury**, says Ptolemy: because it is dry, and under **Virgo** the dryness of autumn appears. But we have already said concerning the nature of the signs that this change of the four seasons does not proceed from the stars themselves; rather, the Sun placed in **Virgo** will produce for other regions of the Earth what it produces for us when placed in **Taurus**.

<margin>On the exaltation of Mars</margin>
Furthermore, if this seasonal logic was being observed, why was it established that **Mars** must necessarily rule there—a planet under which the world swelters, just as under **Virgo** it now withers? Now **Mars** is a most burning planet, which they nevertheless wish to be exalted in **Capricorn**, a sign under which we are constrained by cold, frost, and ice.

But they say **Capricorn** is toward the south, and the southern part is warmer. This is what we object to you astrologers: that levity and inconstancy of your reasons (if indeed these are to be called "reasons"). For concerning the same sign, for your convenience and according to your whim, you discourse now as if it were hot, now as if it were cold. And soon you will call the same sign neither hot nor cold, but rather moist or dry. In the division of the signs, you make **Capricorn** earthy (and therefore dry); yet when it is transferred to **Mars**, it is counted among the burning things; and when it is called the house of **Saturn** (the most frozen of stars), snows and rains are recorded to occur under it.

<margin>On the height of Jupiter</margin>
But if **Capricorn** is granted to **Mars** as if it were a hot sign, by similar reasoning **Cancer** ought to be numbered as most cold. If so, it certainly will not have **Jupiter** as its king, who is supposedly exceedingly powerful in life-giving heat. But there is a hiding place ready into which they may crawl. For

<margin>Ptolemy</margin>
Ptolemy says **Jupiter** rouses the northern winds; therefore, a sign positioned toward the north suits him. But first, other astrologers cannot take refuge here, as they deny that winds of this kind are roused by **Jupiter**. Furthermore, neither is Ptolemy excused, because by similar reasoning he ought to have sent **Mars** to the west, not to the south, since he thinks western winds (not southern ones) are excited by **Mars**. I pass over the fact that **Gemini** and **Leo** also incline toward the north; why, therefore, is **Leo** not rather the exaltation of **Jupiter**? The heat of **Leo** does not suit **Jupiter**, says **Averrodan** <note>Likely Ali ibn Ridwan, an 11th-century Egyptian physician and astrologer famous for his commentary on Ptolemy.</note>; on the contrary, it suits him more than the coldness of **Cancer**. Add to this that **Leo** is the triangle of **Jupiter**, a "diurnal" and "masculine" sign; likewise **Jupiter** is masculine and diurnal. **Cancer**, meanwhile, is designated among the feminine, nocturnal, and aquatic signs—all of which are removed from the nature of **Jupiter**. Therefore **Leo** suits him altogether more than **Cancer**.

<margin>On the exaltation of Venus and Saturn.</margin>
Concerning **Venus** and **Saturn**, they rave no less: they say the height of **Saturn** is **Libra** because **Saturn** is contrary to the Sun. **Venus** is said to be exalted in **Pisces** because she is moist, and under **Pisces** the moisture of spring begins. But indeed, we have often said already that those qualities of the seasons do not follow the nature of the signs themselves, but rather the position of the approaching and receding Sun. Concerning **Saturn**, they speak as usual for their own convenience. For here they make him the opposite of the Sun, but elsewhere **of the same form** <note>original Greek: "symmorphon"</note>: that is, they preach that he is of the same condition as the Sun. They claim that the "father" is signified by both planets and that both are "oriental" <note>Rising in the east before the sun.</note>. Both are masculine; both are diurnal. But ne[ither]...

# Book VI
C

...Truly many things could be dictated if we were to pursue all other matters of this kind in detail. Others, lacking confidence in these [arguments], have devised a new reasoning, certainly shorter but entirely ineffective: namely, that the exaltations of the planets are located in signs forming a "triangle" <note>An aspect of 120 degrees, also called a trine.</note> or a "hexagon" <note>An aspect of 60 degrees, also called a sextile.</note> with their primary houses, except for **Mercury**. If you ask why they preferred the hexagon for the **Moon**, **Venus**, and **Mars**, but the triangle for others, they answer that the triangle is more suited to the diurnal <note>Planets traditionally associated with the day, such as the Sun and Jupiter.</note> and more powerful planets. However, for the nocturnal ones, which belong to the "sect" <term>sect|An ancient astrological classification dividing the planets into two teams: the Diurnal sect (led by the Sun) and the Nocturnal sect (led by the Moon).</term> of the **Moon**—which the Arabs call *aiz* <note>original: "aiz" – likely a Latinization of the Arabic term *hayz*, referring to a planet being in its preferred sect and gender.</note>—the hexagon is used *because of the weakness of the ray* <note>original: "δια το ασθενεσ τησ ακτινοσ"</note>. 

<margin>Refutation.</margin>
But they are mistaken regarding **Mars**, since it is not numbered among the nocturnal planets because it is weak, but rather so that the vigor and efficacy of the "martial ray" might be restrained by the nocturnal cold. Nor can it be said to belong to the sect of the **Moon**, since it is a masculine planet which disagrees with the **Moon** in both qualities <note>In ancient physics, the Moon was cold and moist, while Mars was hot and dry.</note>; it is considered nocturnal for a reason entirely contrary to the **Moon**. For the **Moon** is so classified because of a similarity of nature; **Mars** because of a dissimilarity to the lunar nature and to **Cancer**, being opposed in **Capricorn**, just as it is opposite **Taurus** in **Scorpio**. 

But even if that conjecture were to stand, let them answer this: why a "right-handed" triangle rather than a "left-handed" one? Why a left one rather than a right? Indeed, why for **Jupiter** is it the left? For **Saturn** and the **Sun**, the right? And since a planet has two "houses" <note>Most planets were assigned two zodiac signs as their homes; for example, Jupiter rules both Sagittarius and Pisces.</note>, why is the triangle taken from one rather than the other? For instance, since **Jupiter** finds a home in **Sagittarius** and **Pisces**, why should it be exalted in **Cancer** rather than **Leo**? Especially since it has more affinity with **Sagittarius**—as the astrologers say—and furthermore (as we were saying before), **Leo** is far more suited to it than **Cancer**. 

Finally, so that you may understand all such conjectures to be inventions of later followers, and not at all the foundation laid by the first teachers of this dogma: you can see this from the fact that they provide no reason why a planet is said to be exalted in a specific *part* <note>The specific degree within a sign.</note> of a sign, rather than just in the sign itself. I have demonstrated the reason for this above from ancient astrology. For this reason, **Aboasar** <note>Also known as Albumasar (787–886 AD), a highly influential Persian astrologer and astronomer.</note> says it was difficult for the whole community of astrologers to find this; and he himself, lest he seem to say nothing at all, anxiously distorted many things on this matter with an overly perverse and legendary subtlety. 

Therefore, it is undoubtedly clear that this dogma concerning the "altitudes" of the planets was received by the practitioners of nativities <note>original: "genethliacis" – those who cast birth charts based on the moment of birth.</note> based on the occasion we mentioned of the ancient discipline, which thought that the planets were at their maximum distance from their centers at these degrees. How vain this observation is, everyone now understands: not only because they transferred a name pertaining to location and position to a matter of nature and power, but because in that matter, ancient astronomy was perhaps excessively deceptive during its early and insufficiently explored beginnings. Even if they had decreed those things as true then, that reasoning does not suit posterity, since the apsides <term>apsides|The points in an orbit where a planet is closest to or furthest from the center of its motion.</term> and what are called the "apogees" <term>apogees|The point in a planet's orbit where it is furthest from the Earth. The author argues that because these points move over centuries, old astrological rules no longer apply.</term> of the wandering stars have changed.

### Chapter XV. The arguments of astrologers regarding triangles and the rulers of triangles, as well as the sex of the signs, are refuted.

Indeed, let us not think that astrologers only rave when an opportunity is given, as if they were unable to go astray without a leader. They play false most often where there is no one to lead them astray. For regarding these exaltations, they almost certainly owe it to the mathematicians <note>In the Renaissance, "mathematicians" often referred to astronomers or those who calculated planetary positions.</note> that they are out of their minds—though they owe it even more to themselves, lest we defraud them of any injustice. But what are commonly called "triangles" or "triplicities," they themselves gave birth to; nor did mathematics help them in any way in this place. Since the matter depends on the fact that they make certain signs fiery, some earthy, some airy, and some watery, we shall first compel them to give an account of these things: and how this which is...

# IV Book VI

<margin>Elemental qualities cannot be assigned to the signs.</margin>

->**Book**<-

We shall now examine whether it can be well-defined that this planet's triangle <note>Also called a "triplicity," a group of three zodiac signs belonging to the same element.</note> belongs to this element, or that one to another. Tell me, then, you most wise men and interpreters of the heavens: by what logic have you distributed these qualities of the elements among the signs in the sky? **Avenrodan** <note>The Latin name for Ali ibn Ridwan, an 11-month-century Egyptian physician and astrologer.</note>, a great authority in your discipline, refers the nature of the signs either to the Sun or to the stars. To the Sun, in that the nature of a sign is said to be whatever the effect of the Sun is while passing through it—which is how the "movable" signs <note>The cardinal signs: Aries, Cancer, Libra, and Capricorn.</note> are called equinoctial or solstitial, while the others are called fixed or common. Or to the stars, if the virtues of the stars residing there are attributed to the sign. I see neither reasoning fitting your division. For if we follow the effects of the Sun, Cancer would be fiery, not watery; just as Sagittarius would be watery rather than fiery. Aries would not be fiery, but Taurus would abound in moisture and heat <note>Associated with spring</note> rather than cold and dryness, and thus the condition of almost all signs would be changed; nor would they be permanent (as you desire). If it refers to the stars, they are constantly migrating from their seats <note>A reference to the precession of the equinoxes, which causes the physical stars to move out of their namesake zodiac signs over centuries.</note>. Or do you think the reasoning of **Al-Kindi** <note>An 9th-century Arab philosopher and astrologer.</note> is stronger? He argues that since there are four principal signs in the <term>Zodiac|The circle of twelve signs through which the Sun, Moon, and planets appear to move.</term>—two equinoctial and two solstitial—the four primary qualities of the elements are assigned to these four: fiery to Aries, watery to Cancer, airy to Libra, and earthy to Capricorn. Then, because a "triangular radiation" <note>The trine aspect of 120 degrees.</note> falls upon corresponding places, the signs forming a triangle with any sign are rightly judged to have inherited a similar nature. But neither does this reasoning hold up. For in referring the four properties of the elements to the signs, there could be two ways of ordering them: one by the kinship of the sign and the element, and the other by the very position of the elements, so that the first is given to the first, the second to the second, and so on. If they observed the first—that hot things correspond to hot, and cold to cold—they ought to have given fire to Cancer, as I said, and air to Aries. If they followed the second, they should have given air to Cancer, which is second after fire.

<margin>Against the reasoning of Al-Kindi.</margin>
<margin>Al-Kindi's reasoning. Refutation.</margin>

> But **Al-Kindi** says the opposites—heat and cold—must be given to the sign of the second season, which is Cancer. On the contrary, they should then be given to Libra, which is opposite to Aries. But if they say water should be placed next to air because it is more effective in itself, they will make the nature of the signs more complicated than wise.

Furthermore, if an active quality like coldness—not a passive one like moisture—belongs to Cancer, why is it categorized by them among the feminine and nocturnal signs? Why not rather among the diurnal and masculine? They observe this even in the planets, for there is no more reasonable way to distinguish sex in the heavens than by active and passive qualities. For this reason, they called Jupiter, the Sun, and Mars "masculine," in which heat excels, and Saturn, in which cold excels; they called the Moon and Venus "feminine" because they are moist. Thus, water and fire were also called masculine even by the Egyptians for the stated reason; air and water were feminine. Therefore, the astrologers should have counted the watery signs—namely Cancer, Pisces, and Scorpio—among the masculine, not the feminine. Yet they did the same for all of them. Conversely, they decreed the airy signs to be masculine, even though moisture is the proper quality of air. Astrology, therefore, fights against itself in these matters and overthrows itself, raving here as it does everywhere.

<margin>That there are no masculine and feminine signs.</margin>
<margin>See the foolish reasoning of Ptolemy.</margin>

Indeed, so that we may not digress from the subject at hand, what are these lightest of trifles? To discern sex in the heavens by such a conjecture! Moved by this, they established six masculine signs and six feminine signs, so that the first is male, the next female, and so on through the ranks, always one male and the other female. For if this had to be done, it ought to have been done by the nature of the signs, not by a fatal and vain sequence of "first, second, and so on." Hear from **Ptolemy** what logic this has:

> Night, he says, follows day, and women cling to men; therefore, a feminine sign must be placed next to a masculine one.

Against which reasoning...

# Book VI
->C ii<-

This is not something to be debated, but rather laughed at—unless, perhaps, we are to take it seriously when we investigate whether the night comes before the day, or the day before the night, so that perhaps the nocturnal signs should have been given priority. Is it the case that the day follows the night, or the night the day? For it is written, *the evening and the morning were one day* <note>original: "factum est vespere & mane dies unus." This is a reference to Genesis 1:5.</note>, because the Hebrews established the beginnings of time from the night. But truly, we have too many duties to allow us to waste many words on such trifles.

Nevertheless, even for **Ptolemy** <note>Claudius Ptolemy, the 2nd-century author of the *Tetrabiblos*, the most influential manual of astrology in the West.</note> himself, this diversity of sexes is of great importance; he reports that it matters quite a bit whether a planet is found in a masculine or a feminine sign. But if they contend that this dogma is proven by experience, I ask: by whose experience? Their own, or that of the ancients? If it is their own, they do not have the gray hair <note>A metaphor for ancient wisdom or long-standing authority.</note> to grant them such great authority. If it belongs to the ancients, well, a large portion of the ancients thought differently. Many established the order starting from the **horoscope** <note>In ancient astrology, the "horoscope" referred specifically to the Rising Sign (the sign on the eastern horizon), not the whole chart.</note> so that the rising sign was always masculine and diurnal, and the rest were divided by turns in the following order. Others made four signs diurnal: Aries, Cancer, Leo, and Sagittarius; four nocturnal: Gemini, Libra, Capricorn, and Aquarius; and four "promiscuous" <note>Mixed or indeterminate.</note>: Taurus, Virgo, Pisces, and Scorpio. Antiquity often exploded these accepted opinions. Hence, there is this passage from ancient astrology:

> There are those who prefer to call diurnal those signs which rise as masculine,
> And feminine signs to rejoice in the night's far-flung shadows.
> These are people who speak much to themselves, though nothing points the way.

In this place, it is a wonder how much a certain common interpreter of that poet raves. Read likewise those more rational men—if indeed one can ever be insane with "reason"—who called all the fiery and watery signs "diurnal" and the remaining six "nocturnal," namely the earthy and airy ones. Likewise, if it pleases Ptolemy that "masculine" and "diurnal" follow one another, then those will be masculine, and these feminine. Thus the poet sang:

<margin>
These verses are commonly read in a corrupted state, like many other things, but they were corrected by **Poliziano**, whose faithfulness in emending books is proven: his diligence is supreme, and his erudition is rare.
</margin>

> For the sign of the Archer and the swift Lion,
> And the one looking back at its own back with its golden fleece <note>The Ram, Aries.</note>,
> Then the Fish, the Crab, and the Scorpion with its sting;
> All these are called "diurnal" under a similar lot,
> Whether neighboring in place or at equal distances.
> The others, neither sharing the same number nor alternating in position,
> Are said to be nocturnal, cast into just as many places in between.

There were also those who felt differently, which is why he adds:

> Some have even said six continuous signs are diurnal,
> Being the turns of Castor <note>The Gemini twin.</note> which start from the leading sign
> Of the Fleece-Bearer <note>Aries</note>; while six from the Scales <note>Libra</note> appear nocturnal.

Let them cease, therefore, to plead the "faith of ancient observations," from which they differ as often as the whole of astrology differs from the truth. Moreover, this could also be thrown back at them: if they judged that a masculine sign must be established in the first place, it remains uncertain which sign is truly "first" and "masculine," just as it is uncertain which sign is the initial one, as we declared above. For to some, Cancer seemed first; to others, Capricorn; yet both of those are feminine according to these men. But perhaps it was not necessary to mock these fables at such length, though it was worth the effort to incidentally refute this fable of distinguishing celestial signs by sex. We turned aside to this point specifically to show that they fight amongst themselves regarding Cancer: since it is watery...

# Book VI
->C ii<-

...and would make it feminine, even though coldness is considered among the active qualities, not the passive ones. But if the primary division is granted to those signs at the tropics and the equinoxes, the logic of this distribution will not hold for the other signs. Indeed, they engage in **circular reasoning** <term>circular reasoning: a logical fallacy where the proof assumes the truth of the very thing it is trying to prove</term>, which is a disgrace in the art of logic. For in this matter, when they try to prove that the **trine** <note>original: "trigona." In astrology, a "trine" is an aspect of 120 degrees, usually considered harmonious because the signs belong to the same element.</note> signs are of the same nature, they take as their argument that the trine radiation belongs to places that naturally agree with each other; then, when they intend to prove that the trine radiation is harmonious, they assume that it falls upon places that share the same nature.

Let **Al-Kindi** <note>Al-Kindi (c. 801–873 AD) was a pioneering Arab philosopher who wrote extensively on astrology and science.</note> therefore be silent now. There remains the opinion of **Abraham ibn Ezra** <note>A 12th-century Jewish polymath and one of the most famous astrologers of the Middle Ages.</note> <margin>The reasoning of Abraham ibn Ezra</margin> who claims the reason for these qualities comes from the shapes of the constellations and the properties of the animals depicted in them: for example, Pisces, Cancer, and Scorpio are called "cold" because they represent the names and figures of aquatic creatures. The sign of Leo is "hot" because of the nature of the lion, and so on for the rest. But this reasoning is either worthless—if there are no such images in the heavens, as we have already demonstrated—or it is false, if the images that are there are confused with the mathematical signs, a confusion we also refuted above. 

Finally, since the position of these figures changes over time, this distinction of the signs would be merely temporary, rather than immovable and perpetual, which is what all astrologers (including Ibn Ezra himself) want. **Aries** would not even be a "fiery" sign in our own time, since the image of **Pisces** has now occupied almost the entire area, the image of Aries having already shifted to the twenty-fifth degree <note>This refers to the "Precession of the Equinoxes." Because the Earth wobbles, the stars in the sky (the constellations) slowly shift away from the calendar dates of the zodiac signs.</note>.

But if there are no trines, there are also no **Trigonocratores** <margin>That the rulers of the trines—the "lords of the triplicities"—are nothing.</margin>—that is, the "lords of the triplicities," as they call them. Even if we were to grant them their existence, the astrologers define their rules, as usual, without any reason. For they will not deny that if it is good for a planet to be in a certain sign, it must be bad for it in the sign directly opposite—this is clear in the "houses" and "exaltations" of the planets. If this is a point most firmly confessed among them, how could they forget their own astrological dogma and claim that the same three planets rule in opposite trines? I am speaking of the Earthly and Watery triplicities, where they claim **Mars**, **Venus**, and the **Moon** rule. **Taurus** is opposite to **Scorpio**; **Virgo** is opposed to **Pisces**; **Capricorn** lies across from **Cancer**. And yet, those who rule in Taurus, Virgo, and Capricorn also rule with "trine power" in Cancer, Pisces, and Scorpio. Nor, if you ask astrologers why Mars is "fallen" in Cancer, will they answer anything other than because he is "exalted" in Capricorn; and why is he afflicted in Taurus? Because, they will say, he has his home in Scorpio. All these things, therefore, fight against each other and prove themselves false through their own contradictions.

Add to this that in the first triplicity, <margin>Albumasar. Alchabitius.</margin> **Albumasar** <note>Abu Ma'shar, a 9th-century Persian astrologer whose works were standard textbooks in medieval Europe.</note>, **Alchabitius** <note>A 10th-century Arab astrologer whose "Introduction to the Art of Judgments of the Stars" was highly influential.</note>, and all the Latin authors decide that **Saturn** rules along with Jupiter and the Sun; yet in that very triplicity, Saturn is in "exile" in Leo, is "fallen" in Aries, and finds nothing of his own in Sagittarius. "But," they say, "he is a daytime planet like Jupiter and the Sun." True, but he is also cold, while both of the others are considered hot. And if, when discussing exaltations, they assigned **Libra** to Saturn only because it was opposite to the nature of the Sun, why then does he have a kingdom in Aries? Why is he associated with the Sun as a lord of the triplicity against the very nature of those signs, as if he were perfectly suited to the Sun’s nature? There are many more examples of this kind, but to pursue each one would perhaps be unnecessary, and certainly for me it is tedious and nauseating.

If they appeal here to the "reliability of experience," I appeal again to the "discord of such experiences." For the Egyptians make only two rulers of the triplicities, as can be understood from the *monomeria* <note>A technical term for the division of signs into individual degrees, each with its own planetary ruler.</note>. <margin>Albumasar. Alchabitius. The Latins.</margin> Others establish three, and these then disagree among themselves. For in the first triangle, Albumasar, Alchabitius, and the Latins want Saturn to rule; but **Ptolemy** <note>The famous 2nd-century author of the *Tetrabiblos*.</note> wants it to be Mars.

<margin>Ptolemy.</margin>
On the contrary, in the second book, Ptolemy assigns Saturn; the Arabs and nearly all the Latin writers assign Mars; but in the fourth book, Ptolemy makes him—that is, Mars—the lord. He assigns two subordinates, as if they were secondary lords: the Moon by night and Venus by day. Others equate Mars with Venus in lordship; they do not want Mars to command except by night, and Venus by day; then the Moon is the second authority with them both by day and by night.

<margin>More recent authors</margin>
<margin>Ibn Ridwan</margin>
More recent authors say that the opinion of the Arabs and Latins is confirmed by the experiences of the Latins. **Ibn Ridwan** <note>original: "Auenrodan." Ali ibn Ridwan was an 11th-century Egyptian physician and astrologer known for his commentaries on Ptolemy.</note> himself (not to mention the Greeks) affirms that all effects support the opinion of Ptolemy. I pass over many points on which they fight over these same **triangles** <term>triangles: also known as triplicities; groups of three zodiac signs belonging to the same element (Fire, Earth, Air, Water)</term>, since they were dealt with above. However, it is clear from this that even the **Great Conjunctions** <term>Great Conjunctions: the rare meeting of Jupiter and Saturn, which astrologers believed signaled major historical shifts as they moved between the triplicities</term> are dissolved insofar as they depend on this migration through the triangles—not to mention other dogmas of the astrologers that draw their credit and origin mostly from these very triangles.

## Chapter XVI: Concerning faces, terms, Babylonian twelfth-parts, and ninth-parts, and what part remains firm, even by the testimony of Ptolemy himself.

<margin>In Ptolemy there are many faces.</margin>
It remains to refute the faces and the **terms** <term>terms: specific degrees within a zodiac sign that were assigned to different planets, affecting their strength</term>, so that everything regarding the affinity of planets with the signs may be addressed. For just as we have overturned the houses, cast down the exaltations, and obliterated the triangles, there is no great trouble in refuting these: for there are no "faces" even according to Ptolemy; and the same is true for the Greeks, who call them **decans** <term>decans: ten-degree segments of a zodiac sign, each ruled by a specific planet; there are three per sign</term>. But the Greeks use decans for the signs, while faces belong to the planets. Ptolemy, therefore, rejects these faces, thinking them unworthy of mention or of any use in **horoscopes** <note>original: "apothelesmatis," referring to the calculation of astrological outcomes or judgments.</note>. Since they cannot support these with any reasons, they might perhaps claim "experience"—unless consistency failed them in this place too.

<margin>Various faces of various authors.</margin>
<margin>First decan of Taurus</margin>
<margin>Second</margin>
<margin>First of Gemini</margin>
For the Indians want certain "faces" for the planets, the Babylonians (whom the Arabs imitate) want others, and **Maternus** <note>Julius Firmicus Maternus, a 4th-century Roman lawyer and astrologer.</note> wants still others. The first **decan** <term>decan: a 10-degree subdivision</term> of Taurus wears the face of Mercury according to the Babylonians, but the face of Venus according to the Indians, and Jupiter according to Maternus. The second is the Moon's according to some, Mercury's to others, and Mars' to still others. The first of Gemini belongs to Jupiter for the Chaldeans, Mercury for the Indians, and Mars for Maternus. To avoid going through all of them in detail: the Babylonians followed this method, giving the first decan of the beginning—that is, of Aries—to Mars, because that is the house of Mars. However, following the order of the planetary spheres, they assigned the first decan of any sign to the "head of the family"—that is, the lord of the house—and the remaining two to the lords of the signs of that triangle. Maternus’s invention is entirely arbitrary, yet he claims "ancient tradition." When anyone weighs this, they should also realize that they did not decree these dogmas by true observations or the reliability of experiments, but rather gave the credit of "experience" to weak and trivial conjectures of this kind. We will dispute these matters and the "experiments" themselves much more extensively later on.

They used this twelfth-part, but not the one Maternus ascribes to them. **Manilius** <note>original: "Mallius," likely referring to the Roman poet Marcus Manilius.</note> and **Porphyry** <note>A 3rd-century Neoplatonist philosopher who wrote an introduction to Ptolemy's astrology.</note> mention them, and even Ptolemy mentions them, but only to mock them. # Book VI

the first part belongs to the lord of the sign: because it was mobile from that triangle: so that the first ninth part of Aries belongs to Mars: for Aries is a mobile sign; the first of Leo is likewise Mars: because Aries is the mobile sign from the fiery triangle. They place the following parts in the series of the following signs: so that if the first is Mars, whose house is Aries, the second is Venus, the third is Mercury: because the former has Taurus as a house, and the latter Gemini. The Egyptians, on the other hand, numbered each individual part: which they called <margin>On the Egyptian monomoiria</margin> **monomoiria** <term>monomoiria: a system where each of the 30 degrees of a zodiac sign is assigned a specific planetary ruler</term>; and they assigned those to the planets by the order of the triangles: so that the first part of any sign was the monomoiria of the planet which is the lord of that triangle: a nocturnal one if the birth is nocturnal, a diurnal one if diurnal; the second part to the second lord of the same triangle; the third to the lord of the triangle of the following sign, and so on: yet in such a way that the same planet would not obtain a monomoiria twice in one sequence. <margin>Refutation of all these by the words of Ptolemy.</margin> All these "anatomies" and "dissections" of the signs I shall refute with no other words than those of **Ptolemy** himself; for he said all these things are "not based on nature but on vainglorious reasoning" <note>original Greek: "ου φυϲικον αλλα κεροδοξον λογον" (*ou physikon alla kenodoxon logon*). Ptolemy uses this to dismiss arbitrary astrological systems.</note>: that is, having no physical reason, but being a vain ostentation; nor could he have defined them more correctly. For the more these things possess audacity and are fabricated with greater license, the more wonderful and great they seem to the unrefined and unskilled. Nor was there any other reason why <margin>Why Albumasar is considered great in astrology.</margin> **Albumasar** <note>original: "Aboasar." Abu Ma'shar (787–886), a famous Persian astrologer whose works were highly influential in Medieval Europe.</note> was held to be a great man in astrology—a man otherwise ignorant of mathematics—than that nothing seemed to him insufficiently rational; instead, he heaped together the fables of everyone at once, rejecting nothing and scorning nothing. Therefore, he seems to have betrayed more secrets than others because he recorded more fables. There remains the matter of the **bounds** <term>bounds: also called "terms" (fines); subdivisions of a zodiac sign where different planets are said to have influence</term>, which I shall refute briefly in no other way than by the discord among those still litigating over these bounds. For Ptolemy prescribes some; the Egyptians others; the Babylonians others; the Indians others; and some other astrologer mentioned by Albumasar remembers others. According to his opinion, he puts forward wonders in the *Great Introductory*; the younger writers adhere to the Egyptians, the Greeks follow Ptolemy, and with them **Ibn Ridwan** <note>original: "Auenrodan."</note>; others also have their own followers. Therefore, not only are there no signs, but even if signs were something, these affinities of the planets with the signs—so that they have a house here, a kingdom there, and bounds elsewhere—are frivolous, fabulous, conflicting, and fabricated. Nor do only the Latins disagree on these things, but also in the comparison of the systems themselves. For the common crowd gives the first parts to the **house**, the second to **exaltation**, the third to the **bounds**, the fourth to the **triplicity**, and the fifth to the **face** <term>face: also known as a decan; a subdivision of a sign into ten-degree increments</term>. Ptolemy places the house in the first spot, the triplicity in the second (as pleases **Haly** <note>likely Haly Abenragel, an 11th-century Arab astrologer</note>), the exaltation in the third, and the bound in the fourth; he ignores the face. The Chaldeans have no houses; the Egyptians add monomoiria to everything; the Indians have ninth-parts; the Babylonians have **dodecatemoria** <term>dodecatemoria: the division of a single zodiac sign into twelve smaller parts</term>; they do not place triplicity with the houses. **Firmicus Maternus** <note>original: "Maternus." A 4th-century Roman lawyer and astrologer.</note> attributes more to height <note>referring to exaltation</note> than to the bounds, and more to the bounds than to the houses. "For," he says, "the stars rejoice in the first place when positioned in their height; in the second place in their bounds; in the third in their houses." Therefore, the dogmas of the astrologers are most vain, which they neither confirm with reasons nor with experiments: for they play with the former, and do not agree on the latter.

# Book VI

We have refuted those divisions of the signs which they attribute to the planets: such as the claim that here Mars is exalted, and there the Sun. They claim one "face" <note>In astrology, a "face" or decan is a 10-degree subdivision of a zodiac sign.</note> belongs to one planet and another to a different one; this is the **monomoiria** <term>monomoiria: an ancient system assigning each of the 30 degrees of a sign to a specific planetary ruler</term> of this planet, and that of another. Similarly, they divide them into triplicities, bounds, ninths, and **dodecathemoria** <term>dodecathemoria: the division of a single zodiac sign into twelve even parts of 2.5 degrees each</term>. Now we must treat those things which they have handed down concerning the degrees themselves in an absolute sense: such as those they call "shining," others "dark," others "fortunate," others (as they say) "pit-like" <note>original: *puteales*. These were specific degrees thought to represent "pits" or "wells" that weakened a planet's influence.</note>, and others "sickly" (which they call <term>alzernena: a Latinization of an Arabic astrological term referring to "lame" or "impeded" degrees</term> **alzernena**); some they call male, others female. But satisfaction was given for the most part on these matters above; now we shall add this: **Ptolemy** <note>Claudius Ptolemy (c. 100–170 AD), the most influential astronomer and geographer of antiquity.</note> considered all these things too, yet his interpreter **Ibn Ridwan** <margin>Firmicus</margin> <note>original: *Auenrodan*. An 11th-century Egyptian physician and astrologer who wrote famous commentaries on Ptolemy.</note> seems to grant them only this much: that astrologers should only observe these degrees if they have actually found truth in them through experiments.

But what faith can be placed in such an experiment? Especially since six different opinions are reported concerning which degrees are male and which are female. <margin>Abu Ma'shar</margin> For you will read them described one way in the works of **Firmicus** <note>Firmicus Maternus, a 4th-century Roman lawyer and astrologer.</note>, another way in **Abu Ma'shar** <margin>Ibn Ridwan</margin> <note>original: *Albumasar*. A leading Persian astrologer of the 9th century.</note>, another way in **Ibn Ridwan**, and yet another in **Al-Qabisi** <margin>Al-Qabisi</margin> <note>original: *Alchabitius*. A 10th-century Arab astrologer.</note>. **Abraham** <margin>Abraham Ibn Ezra</margin> <note>Likely referring to Abraham Ibn Ezra, a 12th-century Jewish polymath.</note> varies in most of these points. Furthermore, those who make the twelfth part of each sign alternately male and then female disagree entirely with all of these, basing the first parts on the gender of the sign itself. I omit those who place twelve degrees out of thirty in the gender of the sign, the following twelve in the opposite, and then divide the remaining six into equal portions.

Regarding the "bright," "dark," and "obscure" degrees, another opinion first arose among the ancients based on the position of the stars: for they called that part "bright" in which a star was located, and they believed this was perpetual because they thought the stars did not move. Therefore, they erred if they agree with **Hipparchus**, **Ptolemy**, and the rest of the later authors without looking at the origin of the dogma. For even though they contend that the stars *do* move <note>This refers to the "precession of the equinoxes," where the positions of stars slowly shift relative to the zodiac signs over centuries.</note>, they still define the same degrees as "bright" and "dark" that the ancients did. In this matter, such great confusion was born among them, and such a perversion of things and words (as explained above), that nothing could be less reliable than their "experience" in these matters.

The same error was made by them regarding the degrees they call "fortune-increasing." We have declared the error there too; you will find these degrees noted quite differently in **Al-Qabisi**, differently in **Abu Ma'shar**, and differently in **Ibn Ezra** <note>original: *Auenazra*.</note>. The same diversity is found in the "pit-like" degrees, which none of the ancients established. <margin>The lie of Abu Ma'shar</margin> Nor can **Abu Ma'shar** avoid the charge of lying when he claims he is following the opinion of the Egyptians while describing them. For **Hephaestion of Thebes** <margin>Hephaestion of Thebes</margin> <note>A 5th-century Egyptian astrologer who synthesized Hellenistic and Egyptian traditions.</note>, who was highly skilled in all Egyptian astrology, lists many of those very degrees which **Abu Ma'shar** calls "pits" among the "bright" degrees: such as the sixth degree of Aries, the fifth of Taurus, the thirtieth of Gemini, and the twenty-second of Cancer, among many others in other signs. What of a certain Doric astrologer who called himself the "Scrutinizer"? He feels entirely differently about these properties of degrees than all the ancients, and for his dogma he alleges nothing other than the "faith of experience"—namely, that events do not match the words of the ancients. Let them match his own then! Therefore, this observation of various degrees is vain, unfaithful, and inconsistent—condemned not only by us but by **Ptolemy** as well.

<margin>Refutation.</margin>
...it will end; a part will be there as a signifier of some matter, to be observed no differently than the planets or the stars. What can be imagined more delirious than this rule? Not only because there is no natural power in the heavens where there is no star, no light, nor any other natural quality—just as there is certainly none in that degree where that calculation terminates—but also because this enumeration is devised at one's whim and can have no physical reasoning. **Abu Ma'shar** <note>original: *Aboassar*. A 9th-century Persian astrologer whose works were fundamental to medieval European astrology.</note>, that most trifling man, wished to provide a cause for parts of this kind, which none of the ancients had done. Yet he spoke in such a way that, in his extreme loquacity, he says nothing at all.

<margin>Abu Ma'shar's reason.</margin>
For the sum of his words is finally this: when there are two planets signifying the same thing, the distance between them also has the power of signifying, but that distance is to be measured from the **horoscope** <note>In this context, "horoscope" refers to the Ascendant, the degree of the zodiac rising on the eastern horizon.</note>. This is because future goods or evils are <term>known: *sciātur*</term> by identifying the place to which the signifier of one’s affairs arrives from the horoscope. For example, since the Sun and Saturn are the stars of parents, the interval by which they are separated <term>from each other: *inuicē*</term> is to be counted from the ascendant; in the degree where that number falls, the future signification concerning parents will reside, as if the power of the Sun and Saturn were in <term>a certain: *quendā*</term> way joined together. 

This is the "subtlety" of Abu Ma'shar, in which he assumes the very thing that is denied, and which we primarily mock: namely, that such a distance has such power that the end of a similar interval drawn from the <term>ascendant: *ascendēte*</term> possesses some power of effect. He ought to have provided a reason for this; since he does not do so at all, it is not a reasoned opinion but a mere narrative. This narrative, as we have seen, is not only ineffective because it proves nothing regarding the matter in <term>question: *quæritur*</term>, but it is also false and repugnant to the principles of the astrologers themselves. For the original authors of the "parts" (as we have just said) first created parts for the <term>planets: *planeta/*</term> themselves, not for things and events; that was an idea devised later by their successors. 

What place does the reasoning of Abu Ma'shar have regarding the parts of the planets? He says that parts are taken from the interval of two planets <term>signifying: *significatiūm*</term> the same thing, especially since the distance of no planet <term>except: *præterq̄*</term>

A lost Greek astrological work attributed to Hermes.</note>. Rather, the calculation is taken from the planet whose part <term>is sought: *quæritur*</term> and the part of one of the other luminaries <note>The "luminaries" are the Sun and the Moon.</note>. 

<margin>Abu Ma'shar</margin>
For he takes the "Part of Venus" from the part of the Sun and Venus; here we noted in the first book that Abu Ma'shar and **Al-Qabisi** <margin>Al-Qabisi.</margin> <note>original: *Alchabitius*. A 10th-century Arab astrologer and mathematician.</note> were deceived. He takes the Part of <term>Mercury: *Mercu/*</term> from the part of the Moon (which is called the **Part of Fortune**) and <term>Mercury itself: *ipsogz mercurio*</term>, where they also erred. He takes the Part of Mars from Mars and the Part of Fortune; the Part of Jupiter from the part of the Sun and Jupiter; and the Parts of the Sun and Moon from <term>each other: *inuicē*</term>, as is manifest to everyone. Nor does he want other things to be signified through these parts <term>than: *quã*</term> that which each planet, whose part it is said to be, signifies. 

Add to this that the "parts of things" <note>The author distinguishes between parts assigned to planets and parts assigned to specific life events, like the "Part of Brothers" or "Part of Marriage."</note> are not taken from the planets that signify those things according to the astrologers. For indeed, Mars signifies brothers among all of them; and yet the "Part of Brothers" is taken from Jupiter and Saturn, and is <term>never: *nunquã*</term> taken from Mars. Furthermore, all the ancients derive the "Part of Marriage" from Saturn, a planet they intended to have no association with marriage.

Therefore, that fabrication of Abu Ma'shar is not only flimsy and trifling, assuming the very point under dispute, but it is also alien to the opinions of the authors of the dogma itself. ...to the more ancient authorities, the eastern degree—that is, the **horoscope** <note>Also known as the Ascendant; the point of the zodiac rising on the eastern horizon at the moment of birth.</note>—corresponds to the Sun. Because the Moon is considered to be nearly equal to the Sun, they wished there to be another horoscope responding to the proportion of the Moon. They judged that this should be established in no other place than at the same distance from the eastern horizon as the Sun is distant from the Moon in any given birth chart. They called that place the **Lot of Fortune** <note>original: *κληρου τυχησ* (klērou tychēs)</note> for a reason we shall mention shortly. Ptolemy himself teaches this in the third book of his *Judgments* <note>original: *apoteleſmatum*. Referring to Ptolemy's *Tetrabiblos*.</note>, reminding us also that all antiquity agreed that the Part of Fortune should be as far from the horoscope as the Moon is from the Sun. <margin>Whence the name of Fortune's Lot</margin> Nor is there any variation in the opinion of those who, in nocturnal births, calculate from the Moon toward the Sun instead; for these same people turn from the ascendant toward the preceding signs. Thus, they end at the same place as those who, calculating from the Sun to the Moon, count according to the sequence of the signs. I suspect the reason for the name is this: since they had made two "horoscopes" as it were, one for the Sun and one for the Moon, they assigned the lot of the body and soul to the former (the true and solar one), but to the latter (the lunar and accidental one) they assigned the "Lot of Fortunes"—that is, of those things which are outside of ourselves. Thus, from the first, we ourselves might receive our fate, and from the second, those things which are "ours" might be allotted. For this reason, the lunar horoscope is called the **Lot of Fortune**, and Ptolemy judges fortunes from no other source more than from this.

Commonly, these "lots" are called **parts** <note>original: *partes*</note>, though in the works of Maternus <note>Firmicus Maternus, a 4th-century Roman lawyer and astrologer.</note> they are called **places** <note>original: *loca*</note>. Once this had been accepted, a certain **Hermes the Egyptian** <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure to whom many mystical and astrological texts were attributed.</note>, having little regard for the reasoning of the earlier institution, thought that lots for all the planets should be made following the same example. Thus, he established lots for Saturn and the rest in a book titled *The All-Virtuous* <note>original: *παναρετω* (Panaretos)</note>. He called the Part of the Sun the **Good Spirit** <note>original: *αγαθου δαιμονα* (agathou daimona)</note>, that is, the "good god" or "daemon"; that of Jupiter, **Victory** <note>original: *νικησ* (nikēs)</note>; of Mercury, **Necessity** <note>original: *ανακνη* (anankē)</note>; of Venus, **Love** <note>original: *ερωτα* (erōta)</note>; of Mars, **Boldness** <note>original: *τολμασ* (tolmas)</note>; and of Saturn, **Nemesis** <note>original: *νεμεσιν*</note>. In arranging these, he observed this method: he took each part from the distance of the planet itself to which the part belongs, to the part of either the Sun or the Moon. Specifically, he used the Sun's part for Venus and Jupiter, and the Moon's for the rest. Where the Sun's part was to be used, the calculation was made from it in a day-time birth; but in a night-time birth, it was from the planet to the part. The opposite was done where the Part of Fortune was used. But he also commanded that the calculation for all of them be led from the horoscope, because he saw this was done by the ancients for the Part of Fortune, and by its example, he devised the rest. He paid little mind that the conjecture (whatever it may be) which moved the ancients to establish a Lot for the Moon does not apply to the remaining planets. For the other planets do not have that same equality or kinship with the Sun that would require something to correspond to them in the place of a horoscope, just as the rising east corresponds to the Sun.

But if only this license for invention had stopped at those borders! <margin>Paulus Alexandrinus added four parts</margin> For **Paulus Alexandrinus** <note>A 4th-century astrological author.</note>, some centuries younger than the Hermes we mentioned, added four parts to the parts of the planets—not relating to the stars now, but to things: specifically, for parents, children, brothers, and marriage. This invention provided the occasion for such further delirium that, by devising an infinite number, they designated a "part" in the heavens for almost every piece of rubbish. <margin>An infinite number of parts; the Chaldeans did not use parts</margin> For you may read in all the Arabic and Latin authors of parts for **chickpeas, beans, lentils, barley, onions**, and a thousand things of this sort. I am moved to believe that the **Chaldeans** <note>Ancient Babylonian astrologers, often cited as the ultimate authorities by later writers.</note> used no parts, not only because they were an Egyptian invention, but because **Porphyry** <note>The 3rd-century Neoplatonist philosopher who wrote an introduction to astrology.</note>, when writing his astrological instructions according to the opinion of the Chaldeans, mentions parts nowhere. <margin>Porphyry</margin> Ptolemy, besides the Part of Fortune, [omitted] the rest...

<summary>The author traces the history of astrological "Lots," explaining the logic behind the Part of Fortune before criticizing later astrologers like Hermes and Paulus Alexandrinus for inventing excessive and "delirious" parts for every mundane object.</summary>
