<meta>This page continues the author's critique of the "Lots" or "Parts" in astrology. Having just discussed the origins of the Lot of Fortune, the author now demonstrates the utter chaos and lack of consensus among astrological authorities regarding how these points are calculated, using this disagreement to prove they are arbitrary inventions rather than scientific observations.</meta>

<page-num>VI</page-num>

# Book VI

<margin>
Abu Ma'shar.
Astrologers cannot resort to experience because of the disagreement of authors.
</margin>
...everyone loathes it: though he would have examined it even more correctly if he had realized that the **horoscope** of the Moon <note>A reference to the "Lot of Fortune," which was often called the "Lunar Horoscope" by ancient authors.</note> and whatever they devise regarding it is vain and arbitrary. But his error seems pardonable when one considers the depths into which the license of astrologers has fallen with futile rashness, following the example of a single Part. The reason why they maintain the distances between two planets, and why they calculate that distance from the horoscope, is now clear: namely, because they found it done this way in the case of the **Part of Fortune**. This was done by the ancients because it was sought as a kind of "second horoscope." Therefore, it had to be placed at a distance to the east corresponding to the distance the Sun had moved from the Moon. Later, being ignorant of the origin of this doctrine, they fabricated fables there, such as those **Abu Ma'shar** <note>original: "Aboafar," the Latinized name for the influential Persian astrologer Abu Ma'shar (787–886 AD).</note> relates.

If they say they were moved by experience <note>original: "experimentis," meaning empirical observation or trials over time.</note> rather than by reason, I will reply as I have always done: there is no authority in "experience" when men of equal authority do not agree on the facts. This happens in the matter of the "Parts" just as it does in every astrological doctrine.

<margin>
Opinion of Heliodorus and Maternus.
</margin>
First, nearly every author places the Part of Fortune in a different location. While **Ptolemy** <note>The most famous astronomer/astrologer of antiquity (c. 100–170 AD).</note> commands it to be calculated from the Sun to the Moon whether the birth occurs by day or by night, others affirm that in a nocturnal birth, one must calculate from the Moon to the Sun.

<margin>
Opinion of Al-Qabisi and Abu Ma'shar.
</margin>
As for the **Part of Venus**, **Heliodorus** and **Firmicus Maternus** <note>A 4th-century Roman lawyer and astrologer.</note> calculate it from the **Part of the Demon** <note>Also known as the Lot of Spirit; the solar counterpart to the Lot of Fortune.</note> to Venus by day, and the reverse by night. **Al-Qabisi** <note>original: "Alchabitius," a 10th-century Arab astrologer.</note>, following Abu Ma'shar, calculates it from the Part of Fortune to the Part of the Demon at night, and from the Demon to Fortune by day.

<margin>
Another opinion of Haly Abenragel.
</margin>
**Haly Abenragel** <note>original: "Abenzagel," likely referring to the court astrologer of the kings of Castile.</note> takes it from Venus to Fortune, both by day and by night.

<margin>
Opinion of the Arabs.
</margin>
Regarding the **Part of Parents**, the Arabs take it from the Sun to Saturn in a day birth, and from Saturn to the Sun in a nocturnal birth. 

<margin>
Another of Heliodorus.
</margin>
Heliodorus says that if Saturn is hidden by the Sun's rays, whether it be night or day, one should proceed from Mars to Jupiter. For the **Part of Siblings**, Maternus calculates from Jupiter to Saturn at night, but the Greeks do so from Saturn to Jupiter by day.

They disagree in a marvelous way concerning the **Part of Marriage**. If you seek the husband's lot, Al-Qabisi always counts from the Sun to Venus. Heliodorus also goes to Venus, but starts from Saturn. Maternus, following the opinion of the ancients, commands that by day we go from Saturn to Venus, but by night we start from Venus; yet he himself testifies that he has proven in many birth charts what others also teach: that it should always be calculated from the Sun to the Moon in both day and night births. 

If we examine the birth chart of a woman, Maternus commands the calculation to go from Mars to Venus by day, and from Venus to Mars by night. Others always go from Venus to Saturn; Abenragel says this is the opinion of Vellius, while Al-Qabisi attributes it to **Hermes** <note>Refers to Hermes Trismegistus, the mythical founder of alchemy and astrology.</note>. Abenragel himself approves of always taking it from the Moon to Mars. Others always go from the Sun to Mars. They disagree similarly in the rest of the Parts, but it would be tedious to pursue them all.

The Arabs calculate the **Part of Travel** from the Lord of the Ninth House <note>The house traditionally associated with long journeys and religion.</note> to its first minutes; the Greeks calculate it from the Sun to Mars. For the **Part of Inheritances**, the former go from Saturn to the Moon, but the latter from Saturn to Venus. For the **Part of Servants**, the former go from Mercury to the Moon, while the latter go from Mars to the Moon.

All the ancients calculate the **Part of the Mother** from Saturn to the Moon, then counting the number from the horoscope, as the ancients were accustomed to do in all things. The Arabs seek it from the Moon to the first minute of the **Eighth House**; they then add as many degrees as Saturn has traveled through the sign in which he is located. Whatever sum the calculation produces, they take that amount from the beginning of the sign where Saturn is, through the subsequent signs.

But we are not so idle as to record all their fables. This much is certainly clear to anyone: these doctrines do not rely on faithful experience, but are dogmas which each man has fashioned according to his own judgment.

<page-num>VI</page-num>

# Chapter XIX: The theory of the Twelfth-Parts is exploded, and their Egyptian authors are rejected along with their climacteric years.

<margin>What the twelfth-part <term>dodecathemorion</term> is that is discussed here.</margin>
By the same reasoning, the insanity of the **Twelfth-Parts** <note>original: "dodecathemorior," referring to the *Dodecathemoria*, a system where each 30-degree zodiac sign is divided into twelve 2.5-degree segments, which are then mapped back to the twelve signs.</note> should be hissed off the stage. I do not mean that "twelfth-part" we mentioned earlier—which is simply a twelfth portion of any sign—but rather the version handed down by **Maternus** <note>Julius Firmicus Maternus, a 4th-century Roman lawyer and astrologer.</note> and the Greek writers in this manner: "Whatever star you wish," they say, "seek its twelfth-part; calculate its degree twelve times over." Whether that planet is in the tenth, fifth, or any other degree of a sign, you take the total sum of that calculation and divide it into individual signs of thirty degrees each. You begin the count from the start of the sign in which the planet is currently located; wherever the final number lands, that sign shows you the location of the Twelfth-Part.

<margin>Example.</margin>
For an example of this, place the Sun in the fifth degree and fifth minute of **Aries**. If you multiply five by twelve, it makes sixty; the five minutes multiplied by twelve make one full degree, and thus the total is sixty-one. You give thirty degrees to Aries (where we said the Sun was), thirty to **Taurus**, and the Twelfth-Part will be found in the first degree of **Gemini**. Once this is discovered, what could be imagined more vain or futile? For through these numbers, no power of the planet and no quality is actually transmitted into that specific part of the sky.

<margin>Refutation. Paul of Alexandria, because he found these things to be false, devised another calculation.</margin>
If it is claimed that observation shows events correspond to these parts, I will point to **Paul of Alexandria**, a most weighty authority among the Egyptians (whose invention this mostly was). He himself attests that such observations were found to be false. For this reason, he introduced a new method against the opinion of all the ancients: that those degrees should not be multiplied by twelve, but by thirteen. The ancient calculation did not work for him because it was false and fabricated. And because multiplying by thirteen occasionally happened to match what he was looking for, he established a dogma from a single success, as is the custom of astrologers.

<margin>Against the Egyptians.</margin>
These are those "mysteries" of the Egyptians, whose opinions the superstitious common folk adore like oracles, even though their doctrine possesses nothing of the divine and is ridiculous even to the semi-learned. Indeed, if there were such a thing as astrology, the Egyptians would be the least deserving of the name "astrologers." They were ignorant of the true and natural things in the heavens—that is, the motions of the stars and planets—as we shall discuss below. In their predictions, they relied more on these deceptive dreams than on the actual stars. **Heliodorus** writes that **Hermes Trismegistus** <note>original: "Mercurium trimegistum," the legendary Hellenistic figure associated with the beginning of hermetic wisdom and astrology.</note>, who first discovered the degrees of the planets, opened the way so that predictions could be made through those degrees alone, without looking at anything else. It is remarkable how much weight they gave to both **monomeries** <note>The individual degrees (1/30th) of a zodiac sign.</note> and Twelfth-Parts in every prediction.

<margin>Ptolemy, the wisest of astrologers.</margin>
For this reason, **Ptolemy**, the most prudent of astrologers, notes them indirectly. He says he will hand down his teachings "not through lots and numbers without rational cause" <note>original Greek: "υπ δια κληρου και αριθμων απαιτιολογητων" (hypo dia kleron kai arithmon anaitiologeton).</note> which are all "superfluous triflings of the many and hold no persuasive reason" <note>original Greek: "περιττος υποτων πολλων φλυαρομεμα και μη πιθαιμον εχονται λογον" (perittos hypo ton pollon phlyaromema kai me pithanon echonta logon).</note>. When he mentions "numbers," he is targeting both the Twelfth-Parts we are criticizing and those who create **climacteric years** <note>Critical or "dangerous" years in a person's life, believed to be governed by the numbers 7 and 9.</note> from the observation of numbers alone, such as the **enneadics** <note>Cycles of 9 years.</note> and **hebdomadics** <note>Cycles of 7 years.</note>. From this comes that superstition, so troublesome to many old men, concerning the **sixty-third year** <note>7 multiplied by 9; often called the "Grand Climacteric," feared as a year of great illness or death.</note>; they dread it more than a snake or a tiger. The common people sin here with a pardonable error, but who would excuse those who wish to be known as philosophers?

->End of the sixth book of the Disputations of Giovanni Pico against the astrologers.<-

He now shifts his strategy: even if we grant for the sake of argument that the stars influence human life, he intends to prove that astrologers still cannot accurately determine the exact moment that "fate" begins.</meta>

<page-num>VII</page-num>

# BOOK SEVEN OF GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA’S DISPUTATIONS AGAINST THE ASTROLOGERS.

<margin>Continuation of this book with the preceding ones.</margin>

### Chapter 1. What has been disputed thus far: and what is to be disputed in this book.

**Hitherto**, we demonstrated that astrology is a nullity by stripping away the <term>efficiency</term> <note>original: "efficientia," referring to the "efficient cause" in Aristotelian philosophy—the agency or power that actually produces an effect.</note> of the stars. We showed that this could be argued reasonably based on philosophy, the dignity of the stars, the condition of lower things, and the reliability of experience. Furthermore, we proved that even if the stars did produce what astrologers believe they do, these things nevertheless happen differently than they have devised; consequently, no knowledge of that "efficiency" or of future events is possible for them. Now, our task is this: even if we were to grant that these things are produced from heaven, and in the manner they have fashioned—that is, that all things receive their fates from heaven from their primordial hour—we must declare that it is nonetheless impossible for them to know the "making" of any particular thing. For this to be possible, it is first necessary for them to have investigated with absolute certainty which hour is the "fatal" one for each person; in the discussion of the present book, we shall teach that this cannot be known, or at least is certainly not known by them. And since various beginnings are established for various things, we shall first dispute the beginning of man, declaring that beginning to be ambiguous—and that whatever it may be, it is certainly not what is supposed by the astrologers.

### Chapter II. The fatal hour is ambiguous (if such a thing exists) in all things that are not completed in a moment but over time, and especially in humans, in whom the <term>geniture</term> <note>original: "genitura," the astrological chart or the moment of birth/conception.</note> seems to have little strength.

<margin>
A question concerning the beginning of a thing.

A thing receives its fate when it begins to be made.
</margin>

**There is**, in determining the beginning of any thing which is not consumed in a moment but over time, an inextricable question: whether that "fatal" time is when the craftsman first attempts to make it (whatever <term>efficient cause</term> <note>The actual force or agent that brings a thing into being.</note> it may then obtain), or rather when it is finished. Or, if it is not completed all at once but by parts, whether the different parts also have different fates. For whatever we say has its own reason to support it. For if a craftsman sets his hand to the work successfully, how can the work be unsuccessful if the craftsman works successfully? For the success of both the worker and the operation is achieved if the work turns out well and according to the worker’s wish. Furthermore, if fate is from the stars through "efficiency" rather than just through "signification" <note>Pico distinguishes between stars actually causing events (efficiency) versus merely acting as signs of events (signification).</note>, when should a thing rather receive its fate than when the stars produce it through other intermediate causes? It seems, therefore, that the "fact" depends on that hour in which the craftsman first attempts to make the thing. On the contrary: how shall a thing receive a fate before it exists? Or how shall it be said to exist by us when it first *begins* to be made so that it might exist at some future time? Finally, a thing is what it is because of its species and its <term>form</term> <note>In philosophy, the "form" is the essential nature or "blueprint" that makes a thing what it is.</note>, which is established at the very last moment. Therefore, is not that moment rather the fatal one—the moment when it first begins to be what it is, and when it can stand by its own nature and firmness apart from the cause by which it was being made? Thus, we shall more reasonably trace the fates of things not from the hour they are being made, but from the hour they begin to *be*. Again, if different parts are finished at different times, why does each part not receive the decree of its own fortune from its own time? Especially since experience...

<summary>Pico begins Book VII by arguing that even if stars influenced fate, it is impossible to determine the "fatal hour" of a thing's beginning. He questions whether fate is sealed at the start of a process, at its completion, or piecemeal as parts are created.</summary>
<keywords>astrology, fate, fatal hour, efficient cause, geniture, origins, philosophy of time, Giovanni Pico della Mirandola</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the opening of Book VII. Pico is developing a skeptical argument: if astrology depends on a "fatal hour" (the exact moment fate is sealed), it is impossible to practice because there is no consensus on when a human life actually begins—at conception, at the formation of the heart, at the infusion of the soul, or at birth.</meta>

<page-num>VII</page-num>

# BOOK VII

...be proven; otherwise it occurs in various parts of the same thing. For even in the body of the same man, some members will sometimes be healthy while others are ill; and some part of the same city will be prone to ruins and fires, while nothing of the sort happens to the remaining parts. Why, therefore, is it not more reasonable for each individual thing to be moved and governed by its own proper constellation, rather than for subsequent matters to draw the condition of fate from some past and perhaps abolished principle? 

And let these things indeed be said universally about all things; now let us examine the same particularly in man, concerning whose fatal origin (if any such exists) much and inextricable ambiguity necessarily arises. 

<margin>What hour deserves to be called the fatal hour of man.</margin>

For what shall we rather establish when so many of his beginnings are seen, and all of them worthy of primacy? Do we judge that fatal point of time to be that which is first among all in time—that moment when the man first joins with the woman? 

<margin>Various beginnings of man.</margin>

Or is it not that indeed, but rather when the seed from the male increases in the womb? Or are these indeed like fluids and necessary antecedents? Shall we instead establish the first beginning of human formation when the seminal power itself approaches the purest part of the female discharge and constitutes it—that is, collects it into a fetus, just as milk is joined and thickened by rennet? <note>original: "coagulo." This is a classic Aristotelian analogy where the male seed acts like rennet (the enzyme used to make cheese) to "curdle" or stabilize the female material into a physical form.</note> Or is even this not yet the beginning of man, but rather when all parts of the body are present in potentiality within the conception? Or when it is already enveloped by membranes or the afterbirth? 

Or does nature begin to commence the man when the heart is first actually separated, by whose power that which is being born—now like a son emancipated from his father—begins to be governed by itself, as Aristotle, the interpreter of nature, taught? 

<margin>Aristotle, the interpreter of nature.</margin>

For to this principle great force and authority is owed, since the heart is both the first thing formed, and in the distinguishing of the other parts, while there is movement in all of them, nevertheless growth is distributed from the heart. Thus (if we must tell fables along with the astrologers), just as the power implanted in the heart subsequently unfolds the whole man with other parts cooperating, so the solar power first "drunk in" by the heart might subsequently unfold the whole power of fate? 

Or rather, is it from this: that the fate of the heart and life is the principal one, but the disposition of any individual member undergoes the condition of its own private fate especially from the hour in which it is formed? For to those considering and weighing everything rightly, it appears highly reasonable that if, for example, the <term>luminaries</term> <note>The Sun and the Moon, which astrologers believed governed specific organs, such as the eyes.</note> preside over the eyes, their condition and mixture should depend on the disposition of the luminaries at the time the eyes are being formed, rather than from that which preceded long ago when the seed filled the womb, or what is to follow afterward when, with the eyes already finished, the infant is about to come forth from the mother's womb. This point should be understood as being said of the remaining members by equal reasoning.

But if, setting aside all these things we have said, another beginning more outstanding in authority and efficacy were sought, what indeed shall we bring forward as more reasonable than that by which the soul is shared with the fetus? For it is then that it begins to be a man, and having attained the full rationale of substance, it then consists of its own matter and form. And if fate proceeds from the hour in which a thing first *is*, then certainly no other shall be judged the fatal hour of man. 

If, however, we must depart from this opinion, there will be great probability in the idea that bodily things are referred to the seminal principle, things of the soul to the <term>animation</term> <note>The "animation" or ensoulment: the moment the rational soul was believed to enter the body.</note> itself, and things which are external and of fortune to that moment, perhaps, when having exited the enclosures of the womb, man first enters this field in which fortune plays. 

<margin>A ninth mode of beginning, mixed from several.</margin>

Finally, from this various and knotty ambiguity concerning the human beginning, perhaps those who are divine <note>Pico likely refers to theologians or those with spiritual insight, as opposed to natural philosophers.</note> will extricate themselves; philosophy, which relies only on reasons, can in no way rightly explain itself...

***

<summary>Pico challenges the foundations of astrology by listing several possible "moments of origin" for a human being—conception, organ formation, ensoulment, or birth—arguing that if we cannot identify which moment seals a person's fate, astrological predictions are impossible.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Pico’s critique of the "fatal hour." He is currently arguing that astrologers prioritize the moment of birth over the moment of conception or animation not because birth is more influential, but simply because it is easier to observe.</meta>

# BOOK VII

However, someone wishing to affirm something will affirm nothing less than what the astrologers have decreed: that the fates of a human being depend on the hour of birth. Yet, the astrologers were not led to this opinion by reason. Rather, because they thought they could more easily track this starting point, they granted it the primary role. For this reason, even after birth, they are usually willing to grant some importance to conception, since they hope that something can occasionally be known from it. But the other stages, which are certainly the most powerful principles—especially when the fetus is animated <note>The "animation" of the fetus refers to the traditional philosophical belief in the moment the soul enters the body, often thought to occur well after conception.</note>—they have entirely rejected. Why? Because these moments are completely unknown to them. If they conceded that human fates depended on those hidden moments, they would not be able to claim for themselves any power of divining fate. 

But let us pass over the rest and ask by what reason birth should be preferred to conception and the animation of the fetus. If we give the primary role in establishing fate to the beginning that is first in time, there is no earlier principle than the seminal principle <note>The moment of conception.</note> from which all other things proceed. If a stage is preferred not for being first in time but for its efficacy and dignity, then the time of the fetus's animation should be preferred above all. Birth is both the last of all these stages and has either no efficacy or very little; it neither initiates, nor makes, nor completes the person, but only reveals the one who has already been initiated and completed.

### Chapter III: That Ptolemy attributed more to conception than to birth, yet Ptolemy's own reasoning proves that nothing should be attributed to birth.

<margin>
Ptolemy gave more weight to conception than to birth.
</margin>

Indeed, if the words of Ptolemy himself are weighed seriously, we will see that he was led by the force of reason to give more weight to conception than to birth—even though he attempted to build up many arguments for the efficacy of birth to favor his own profession <note>Ptolemy was the foundational authority for medieval and Renaissance astrology; Pico is showing that even the "master" of the craft contradicts the common practice of his followers.</note>. His words in the third book of the *Apotelesmata* <note>original: "apoteleſmatū." This refers to Ptolemy’s *Tetrabiblos*, the most influential astrological textbook of antiquity.</note> are as follows: 

"When some temporal beginning of a man is established, naturally that beginning will be when the seed is admitted into the generative womb; but potentially and by accident, it is when the infant comes forth at the hour of birth. Therefore, those who have grasped the hour of the admitted seed by chance or observation should rather follow that in discerning the properties of body and soul, considering the configurations of the stars active at that time. For once the seed is disposed at the beginning with a certain quality by the influence of the surrounding air—even though the times of subsequent development vary—nevertheless, because it naturally adopts for itself only material that is proper and related to it, when it has been developed, it will even more closely resemble the disposition of its first quality." 

These are Ptolemy's words, verbatim. Here it seems to me that he pronounces most clearly and assertively, without any doubt, that the first, natural, and most effective beginning of a human is the admission of the seed. He says that one must adhere most closely to this when predicting the vicissitudes of life, both regarding the body and the soul. After he asserted this, he then accurately and anxiously resolved the objections that could be raised regarding the changes the seed undergoes. But because he knew his art was in danger if he denied the possibility of predicting fate from any other source, he added to what we have said the following: "But those who are ignorant of the hour of the seminal beginning—which is usually unknown—for them it is necessary to follow the beginning of birth." 

Let us weigh these words before we add others. He says the hour of birth should only be used when the hour of conception is unknown. Regarding the hour of conception, he said it is <term>προσήκει</term> <note>transliterated: "prosēkei"; meaning "it is fitting" or "appropriate."</note> to adhere to it. But regarding the hour of birth, he did not say it was fitting, but <term>ἀναγκαῖον</term> <note>transliterated: "anankaion"; meaning "necessary" or "compulsory."</note>—that is, it is a necessity for those who do not know the hour...

<meta>catchword: q̃ (which)</meta>

<summary>Pico argues that birth is a secondary, "accidental" moment that merely reveals a person, whereas conception or animation are the true beginnings of life. He cites the famous astronomer Ptolemy to show that even the highest astrological authority admitted conception was the superior point of measurement, using birth only as a desperate fallback when the moment of conception was unknown.</summary>
<keywords>Ptolemy, Tetrabiblos, conception vs. birth, animation of the fetus, seminal principle, fatal hour, skepticism</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Pico’s argument that astrologers focus on the moment of birth only because the moment of conception is difficult to observe. He is now examining Ptolemy’s own writings to show that even the "father of astrology" admitted birth is merely a secondary sign reflecting the primary influence of conception.</meta>

# Book VII

<sig>D ii</sig>

conceived. And for those wishing to divine concerning a person's fate, they must necessarily take refuge in the moment of birth, so that it might appear clearer than light that Ptolemy descended into this opinion not willingly, but compelled by necessity. He treats the hour of birth as a "second plank after a shipwreck" <note>original: "secundam post naufragium tabula" — a common Latin metaphor for a desperate fallback plan or a last resort.</note> (as the saying goes). Having spoken thus far for the sake of reason, he soon strives as much as he can to demonstrate that this principle of birth is also valid, lest he abandon his profession; for which reason he adds the following concerning it:

<margin>Ptolemy's Words</margin> "And this is also a most great principle, and lacking only in this first respect: that from conception, those things which happen before birth can also be foreknown. Furthermore, if someone calls that [conception] the principle, but this [birth] *following the flow* <note>original: "κατα ῥοὴν" (kata rhoēn), meaning something that follows downstream from a source.</note>—that is, *after* the principle—then this one will indeed be second in time from that one. But perhaps it will be more perfect in power. For by right, that first generation will not be denied to be that of the human seed, while this one is of the man; for the infant then receives many things which it did not have before while in the womb, and those things are proper to the nature of man. Likewise, although the hour of birth might seem to contribute nothing of itself to making the one who is born such-and-such, it nevertheless causes him to come forth into the light with a configuration of the heavens related to his origin. For nature, after it has perfected him, only gives the impulse to go out when the disposition of the stars is similar in form to that which shaped the fetus from the beginning. Therefore, it is reasonable that the arrangement of the stars at the hour of birth also has significance for these matters—not because it is the cause of them, but because by necessity and according to nature, it is similar in power to that which is the cause."

These words of Ptolemy have been faithfully recited by us. In them, the first thing to see is that what the interpreter Avenrodan <note>Avenrodan refers to Ali ibn Ridwan (c. 988–1061), a famous Egyptian physician and commentator on Ptolemy’s "Tetrabiblos."</note> says is entirely false: that Ptolemy speaks hesitantly in the earlier words where he discussed the efficacy of conception, but asserts firmly in these last ones where he demonstrates that the hour of birth has the power of signifying.

<margin>Error of Avenrodan</margin> On the contrary, in the former he affirms everything, excepting nothing and doubting nothing; while here he says nothing without adding a particle of doubt, interposing now "nearly," now "perhaps." And finally, when he is about to end his whole dispute, he has no other reason to defend the hour of birth as a signifier of fate than his attempt to persuade us that it is similar to the seminal principle <note>The "seminal principle" refers to the biological and astrological state at the moment of conception.</note>. He is so far from denying that the authority to determine what kind of person the one born will be resides in conception, that he concedes no more to birth in this matter than that it be found similar to and in agreement with conception.

For that opinion common among astrologers—and even believed by the interpreter of Ptolemy—that the hour of conception signifies only what happens to the fetus in the mother's womb, is easily understood to be born from a false understanding of Ptolemy's words.

<margin>The common opinion is criticized.</margin> For he did not say that only those things are signified by conception, but also those things which birth cannot signify. Ptolemy says, "Conception excels birth in this: that through it, even those things which occur before delivery can be foreseen." If it were only those things, he never should have added the word "also," nor should the first principle be thought to excel the second on that account, since the span of a whole life is far greater than governing the rudiments of a still raw and unformed fetus.

Therefore, if Ptolemy relies on those words uttered so doubtingly and hesitantly—that the power of the second principle is "perhaps" more effective than the first, and that this is "nearly" the principle of the human seed while that other is the principle of the man—he clearly dissents not only from reason but from himself. From himself, because (as I was saying) he could not defend the authority of fate in the beginning of birth unless he devised an affinity between birth and the seminal principle; and when he later hands down instructions concerning sex and other conditions of the one being born, he says these are foreknown from conception rather than from birth. From reason, both because of many things we have said above, and because it is greatly beyond reason for us to call conception the principle of the seed and birth the principle of the man; since when the seed has filled the womb, it does not then become [the man], but begins...

<summary>Pico critiques Ptolemy and his commentator Avenrodan, arguing that birth is only used in astrology as a "second plank" or fallback because conception is hard to measure. He demonstrates that even Ptolemy admitted birth’s astrological power is merely a reflection of the more fundamental moment of conception.</summary>

# Book VII

...be abolished when nature applies her hands to the fabrication of a man. For this reason, just as that [conception] is the principle of a human being's generation, so this [birth] is the principle of the woman's state ending. <note>original: "corrumpendi" — in the philosophical sense, "corruption" is the end of one state of being (the fetus) as the "generation" of another (the infant) begins.</note> Or, if you call birth the principle of the human being because the child then first possesses many things which it did not have in the womb: well, those things do not pertain to the *substance* of the being, which is already made and finished, but rather to the labor of the delivery. This is true unless we speak of certain qualities that are not even unique to humans; for if we were to time the start of a man's fate from such things, the "seed" of that fate would arise much later than the time of birth: for instance, when he begins to speak (and is no longer an infant), or when he begins to think, to deliberate, and to reason. For immediately upon being born, a child has nothing uniquely human except its wailing.

Therefore, Ptolemy—the most prudent of astrologers—would not have insisted on these points if they were false and frivolous, though he may have put them forward hesitantly, lest he be thought an entire deserter and prevaricator <note>A "prevaricator" here refers to someone who betrays their own profession or legal duty.</note> of his own profession. Nor indeed can there be much stability in those arguments which propose that the birth-chart is linked to the conception, or those which add some force to the birth-chart in deciding fate. For the sum of their entire power is referred back to a certain "consensus" <note>This refers to the "Trutine of Hermes," a method used by astrologers to calculate the time of conception based on the time of birth.</note> which is said to exist between the birth and the conception. 

<margin>Confutation of Haly.</margin>
But what is this "consensus"? What is this similarity? Haly <note>Ali ibn Ridwan (c. 988–1061), a famous Egyptian astrologer and commentator on Ptolemy.</note> responds that the Sun at the hour of birth is always found in a sign that is either the seventh, ninth, or tenth from the sign it was in at the hour of conception. Is this, then, that "similarity"? O ridiculous vanity! As if any point in time would not "consent" to another point in time by this logic; for the Sun, at any given time, must necessarily be at some numerical distance of signs from where it was at another time. 

Or is what they say about the Moon more probable? They claim that the place where the Moon is when we are born was the <term>horoscope</term> <note>In ancient astrology, the "horoscope" refers specifically to the Ascendant, or the degree of the zodiac rising on the eastern horizon, not a daily forecast.</note> of our conception; and the place where the Moon was at conception becomes the horoscope of our birth. But this is a false fiction of the astrologers, as will be demonstrated later. Even Haly Auenrodan, <note>Another name for Ali ibn Ridwan.</note> explaining Ptolemy in a treatise on this very question, says that he has found this rule to be sometimes true, but sometimes false. 

But come now: even if it were true, there is no way that fictional "consensus" between both hours could be more evidently refuted. For if you investigate the hour of conception according to that rule of the astrologers and set up a <term>theme</term> <note>A "theme" (thema) is a technical term for a cast astrological chart or map of the heavens.</note> for that time, you will find the disposition of the heavens and stars to be always different from it, signifying entirely different things than what will appear to those calculating the hour of birth. 

<margin>Haly says the efficacy of fate is in the hour of conception.</margin>
But why do we waste more words in confuting trifles? Haly, a distinguished astrologer, openly confesses in the book he wrote *On Elections* that the efficacy of deciding fate lies in the hour of conception. But because this hour is unknown, he says astrologers have taken refuge in the hour of birth. And when they are pressed on the matter of the birth of twins, whose fortunes are different, they are accustomed to say that sometimes a difference in their conceptions varies their fortune. Yet, if the hour of conception only disposes those things which happen inside the womb, it would follow instead that those whose conceptions were different could have a similar fortune, but their birth could in no way be the cause.

## Chapter IV: By what ways astrologers track universal fates and how little they relate to reason.

<margin>d</margin>
We have spoken of the beginning of particular fate—how uncertain it is and by what false reasoning it was established by astrologers. It remains to speak of "universal" fate: from whence the fates of cities, nations, kingdoms, and the world in general are pronounced. This too (if it be granted that any such thing exists) is in a state of ambiguity and uncertainty, and has been wrongly defined by our astrologers. 

<margin>The threefold way of astrologers for presaging universal things.</margin>
They are accustomed to proceed by roughly three ways to predict universal changes: either from the great <term>eclipses</term> or <term>conjunctions</term> <note>A "conjunction" occurs when two or more planets appear in the same sign of the zodiac, which astrologers believed signaled major historical shifts.</note> of the higher stars or luminaries; or from the disposition of the heaven when the Sun enters the first minutes of <term>Aries</term>, <note>The sign of Aries marks the Vernal Equinox (the start of Spring), which astrologers considered the "natural" beginning of the year.</note> which they have established as a kind of beginning of the year; or from...

<summary>Pico argues that astrologers only use birth charts because the moment of conception is impossible to track, even though they admit conception is the true start of fate. He mocks the "Trutine of Hermes" and begins investigating how astrologers try to predict the fates of entire nations and cities.</summary>

<page-num>VII</page-num>
<header>Book VII</header>

<margin>The insanity and impiety of astrologers.</margin>
...the peculiar principles of cities, kingdoms, and nations: that is, from the hour in which a city was built, or a kingdom instituted, or a law given to a people by which they live and are governed. That all these things are for the most part frivolous has been shown above; not only when the entire efficacy of the stars is rejected, but also when we weaken the whole logic of predicting from <term>great conjunctions</term> <note>Alignments of major planets, particularly Jupiter and Saturn, which astrologers believed signaled major historical shifts.</note>. We have declared it a vain thing to expect something from these, or from eclipses of the luminaries, long after they have occurred. Then we uncovered the impiety and insanity of astrologers, who subject the law of heaven to fate, and subject nations to the fate of their own "law"—and how vain it is to decree a "birthday" for the building of a city or the receiving of a kingdom, as if it were a natural thing. Now, even if we were to concede that there is some fate for all things, we are going to show that nothing certain regarding the fatal principle of these things can be defined, or has thus far been defined by astrologers. First, in taking the <term>auspices</term> <note>The practice of seeking omens or signs to determine the future success of an endeavor.</note> for a city’s fate from the "throwing of the stone," <note>Referring to the laying of the first stone or cornerstone of a city.</note> by what logic are they moved? For they are scrutinizing the fates of a *state* rather than a *city*. That moment ought rather to be observed when the built city began to be inhabited, and to be ruled and contained by its own laws. Regarding the fortune of a king, there is likewise great discord among them: some think it depends on the hour the king is instituted or chosen, while others think the enthronement or the coronation is what should be inspected. But let us pass over these as if they were minor points, since even Haly <note>Haly Abenragel (Abu l-Hasan 'Ali ibn Abi l-Rijal), a famous 11th-century Arab astrologer whose works were widely translated into Latin.</note> believes the fate of nations, cities, and kingdoms depends not so much on these things we were saying, but on the principles of the great and universal constellations—concerning which we shall soon dispute with them "with feet joined" <note>original: "collato pede" — a Latin idiom for close-quarters combat or hand-to-hand fighting; Pico means he will engage them directly and rigorously.</note>.

<margin>The fates of a city are not reasonably divined from the laying of the first stone.</margin>

# Chapter V: That the astrologer cannot predict in which region of the world some fate will happen, since it is uncertain among them which region is subject to which sign or planet.

<margin>Reasons passed over.</margin>
In those "great conjunctions" (as they call them): if eclipses of the sun and moon stir up as many changes as the astrologers fabulate, I do not contend that point here. Yet, I contend that nothing can truly be predicted about them by astrologers. This is not only because of those conjectures that can be raised—such as the <term>horoscope</term> of a great conjunction being uncertain, or whether it belongs specifically to the year in which it occurred—and not only because they arbitrarily observe the beginning and middle of an eclipse while ignoring the rest of the time. Even if the logic of the beginning alone were held, let all these things be granted to them; let us make no suit over these points, for we can press them more effectively elsewhere, from which the total uncertainty of predictions of this kind may be demonstrated. For there are four "heads" <note>Main categories or points of inquiry.</note> of such predictions: first, what is predicted to happen; second, in what kind of thing; third, at what time; fourth, among which nations and in what places and regions.

<margin>The four heads of these types of predictions.</margin>
But if there is almost no change of affairs, no event—either prosperous or adverse—that does not happen in some part of the world among some peoples at whatever time it comes, then every prediction of this kind will be vain and futile unless they have explored this last point: namely, in what place and what part of the lands those wonderful changes are going to occur. Concerning this, however, they define it such that it is expected in those regions which are "subject" to the sign in which such a conjunction of stars or eclipse of the luminaries occurred. And not only those under that exact sign, but either under that sign or at least a sign of the same <term>triplicity</term> <note>A group of three zodiac signs belonging to the same element (Fire, Earth, Air, or Water).</note>. This is the "undoubted opinion" of all astrologers on this matter. From this it is gathered that nothing can be truly divined concerning the fate of any region unless it is first established to which sign and to which planet that region is subjected—just as a man's fate cannot be pronounced if the time of his birth is unknown. But if, concerning the distribution of lands under various signs and planets, everything among astrologers is uncertain...

<margin>By what means, according to astrologers, it can be known in what part of the world some effect is to be expected.</margin>

D iii

He further argues that astrological geography—assigning specific countries to specific zodiac signs—is entirely arbitrary and uncertain.</summary>

# Book VII

<margin>
Discord of the astrologers regarding the lordship of the planets and signs over the regions of the world.
</margin>
...it is most evident that their predictions concerning such matters must necessarily be highly uncertain. He who has read the books of Ptolemy and Albumasar <note>Abu Ma'shar (787–886 AD), one of the most influential Persian astrologers in the medieval West.</note> accurately will easily understand this: for there is no doctrine in which astrology agrees with itself less. Ptolemy, in his *Book of Effects* <note>Referring to the *Tetrabiblos*, Ptolemy’s foundational text on astrology.</note>, says that the fiery <term>triplicity</term> <note>Groups of three zodiac signs associated with the same element—fire, earth, air, or water.</note> presides over the North; the earthly over the South; the airy over the East; and the watery over the West. Julius Firmicus [Maternus], an emulator of ancient opinions, followed this. Yet Ptolemy himself, in the second book of that same work, seems either to explain it differently or to change it somewhat, assigning the fiery triangle not so much to the North as to those lands situated between the North and the West; the earthly to those between the East and the South; the airy to those between the East and the North; and placing the watery between the West and the South. From all these, the things Albumasar writes are as distant as the East is from the West. For in the sixth book of his *Great Introduction*, he wanted the fiery triplicity to rule not the North, as Ptolemy did, but the East; he contends that water rules the North itself (to which Ptolemy assigned fire); and the air which Ptolemy assigned to the East, Albumasar assigns to the West. Paulus Alexandrinus holds the same in his *Instructions on the Art of Prediction*.

<margin>
Opinion of Albumasar.
</margin>
But this same Albumasar, as if forgetting himself, writes things in his first book of *On Great Conjunctions* that are as different from what he wrote in his *Introduction* as those were from the doctrine of Ptolemy. For in that place, he assigns not the fiery triplicity (as the Greeks did with Ptolemy and Maternus), nor the watery (as he himself did elsewhere along with many Arabs), but the airy. And the water he had previously given to the North, he then ascribes to the opposite region—that is, the South. For the West, he says that neither water (as Ptolemy claimed) nor air (as he himself claimed elsewhere) rules, but rather earth. What can be more contradictory than these opinions? Who can make himself the judge of them, since neither reason nor experience can show the truth here?

<margin>
Another opinion of the same Albumasar.
</margin>
<margin>
Henry approves the latter opinion of Albumasar; Alchabitius, Abraham, Zael, Saphar, and Messala.
</margin>
Henry of Mechelen <note>A 13th-century scholar and commentator on astrological texts.</note> says this latter opinion of Albumasar is the truest and confirmed by many experiences. On the contrary, Alchabitius, Zael the Israelite, Abraham Avenezra, Saphar in his *Isagogics*, and Messala <note>Masha'allah ibn Athari, an 8th-century Persian-Jewish astrologer.</note> approve that which he wrote in the *Introduction*. Haly Abenrodan, rejecting both, prefers the opinion of Ptolemy above all. I pass over how the ancients dissented among themselves on these matters—the Egyptians from Hipparchus, and Ptolemy from Hipparchus; I will demonstrate this with a few examples. For to Aries, the Egyptians subjected ancient Babylon and the Arabia bordering Egypt. Ptolemy subjected Britain, Gaul, Germany, Sarmatia, and Palestine to it. Hipparchus and the most ancient of astrologers, with supposedly more exact reasoning, subjected different regions to different *parts* of the sign: and so to the left shoulder of Aries they assigned Babylon; to the right, Thrace; to the sides of Armenia <note>original: "τωσ τησ armeniæ τοισ πλευραισ"</note>, Arabia bordering Egypt; and over the provinces and the south <note>original: "των δ’ επαρχει και νοτω"</note>, Persia, Cappadocia, Mesopotamia, Syria, and the Red Sea. And so there is similar discord regarding the other signs. The Egyptians, Hipparchus, and Ptolemy disagree no less than Albumasar disagrees with Ptolemy—and even with himself. From this it is clearer than light that nothing certain can be pronounced by astrologers regarding where among nations and lands some event is to occur, since they have nothing certain or proven concerning this division of nations and lands under the signs.

### Chapter VI: That a single beginning cannot be established upon which the fates of the whole year depend; also that various beginnings of the year are established by various people, and according to the Hebrews, the year begins in autumn rather than spring.

It remains for us to speak about the beginning of the year. That a single one cannot be established from which the state of the whole year is predicted is so expressly confirmed by Ptolemy that I shall use his own words to prove it. He writes thus in the second book of *On Effects*: "In a circle..."

He argues that since these experts cannot agree on the basic "map" of astrological influence, their predictions for nations and cities are meritless.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the seventh book of Pico della Mirandola’s "Disputations Against Divinatory Astrology." Having established that astrologers disagree on how the stars govern different regions, Pico now moves to the "beginning" of the year, arguing that the choice of when to start an astrological forecast is entirely arbitrary and lacks a consistent natural basis.</meta>

<page-num>VII</page-num>

# Book VII

No one can simply conceive of a single starting point in the <term>zodiac</term> <note>The circular belt of the heavens, divided into twelve signs, through which the sun, moon, and planets appear to move.</note>; yet those points are rightly established as principles which are determined by the <term>equinoxes</term> and <term>solstices</term>. These are four in number: two equinoctial and two solstitial. Nor is there room for hesitation as to whether any one of these four should be prioritized. For if you look at the circular nature of the heavens itself, none of them will hold the privilege of being a unique starting point. However, those who have written on these matters use them in different ways, assuming each of the four as a starting point, moved by their own natural reasoning and consensus. For each of these parts has something peculiar and excellent about it, by which it seems to claim for itself the authority of a beginning and a new year.

For instance, at the <term>vernal equinox</term> <note>The spring equinox, around March 21st.</note>, the day first begins to become longer than the night; and at that time of year, the world abounds in moisture—a quality and nature which (as we said above) is most prevalent in every beginning of things being born. The prerogative of the <term>summer solstice</term> is this: that the day is then extended to its highest peak and completion; then indeed among the <term>Egyptians</term> the <term>Nile</term> floods and the <term>Dog Star</term> <note>original: "canicula"; the star Sirius, whose rising coincided with the hottest part of summer.</note> rises. In the <term>autumnal equinox</term>, all the fruits are gathered and the seeds of the earth are sown. At the <term>winter solstice</term>, after the shortest day, the light then first begins to increase.

What seems more convenient and in harmony with nature to me is this: that in the observation of the year’s events, we use those four starting points by observing the conjunctions or oppositions of the **Sun** and **Moon** that occur just before them, and especially <term>eclipses</term>. In this way, from the starting point taken from <term>Aries</term>, we may foresee what the Spring will be like; from <term>Cancer</term>, the Summer; from <term>Libra</term>, the Autumn; and from <term>Capricorn</term>, the Winter. These are the words of <term>Ptolemy</term> <note>Claudius Ptolemy (c. 100–170 AD), the most influential astronomer and astrologer of antiquity.</note> exactly. From these it is apparent—and believed and proved by him—that no single beginning can be established from which the fate of the entire year might be foreseen.

<margin>
The error of Avenrodan and the moderns.
</margin>
Thus, I cannot wonder enough at both <term>Avenrodan</term> <note>Ali ibn Ridwan (c. 988–1061), an Egyptian physician and astrologer who wrote a famous commentary on Ptolemy.</note>, his interpreter, and the younger astrologers who repeatedly claim that <term>Ptolemy</term> gives more weight to the <term>vernal equinox</term> in beginning the year than to the start of autumn or the solstices. For just as he says the <term>vernal equinox</term> has no reason to deserve a special privilege as a beginning, he does exactly the same for the others; and after he shows that the authority of a "beginning" exists in all of them, he decides that no one point has more importance than another. Instead, he decrees that all are to be observed equally, asserting that this is more convenient and in harmony with nature than if one of them were observed while the others were neglected. 

Indeed, each point has its own reason why it might rightly be considered a beginning of the year. This is why different nations began their year from different points. The <term>Egyptians</term> began from the [summer] solstice; the <term>Romans</term> from the winter [solstice]; others from the autumn—that is, from the entry of the **Sun** into <term>Libra</term>. 

<margin>
Various judgments of the year among various peoples.
</margin>
They even observed the hour in which the sun traversed the twentieth part of <term>Scorpio</term>, believing that hour held the most efficacy and weight for predicting the states and changes of the air—a practice followed by <term>Saphar</term> and <term>Aoniar</term> <note>Latinized names for Arabic astrologers, likely Jafar (a disciple of Abu Ma'shar) and Al-Anwari.</note>. Some others, following the opinion of the <term>Egyptians</term>, want those four principles considered, but not so that everything is observed in all of them. Thus, when the **Sun** enters <term>Aries</term>, they consider the state of the **Sun** itself; when it enters <term>Cancer</term>, they look to **Jupiter**; when <term>Libra</term>, **Saturn**; and when <term>Capricorn</term>, **Mars**—because all these stars are thought to rule in those signs.

<margin>
The fabrication of Albumasar.
</margin>
<term>Albumasar</term> <note>Abu Ma'shar (787–886 AD), the most famous Persian astrologer of the Middle Ages.</note> invented another dream for himself: that if the **Sun** enters the first minutes of <term>Aries</term> and a "fixed" sign is found as the <term>horoscope</term> <note>The ascendant, or the sign rising on the eastern horizon at a specific moment.</note>, the forecast for the entire year may be rightly pronounced from that single celestial arrangement. If it is a "common" sign, two starting points for the year are established; if it is a "mobile" sign, four. These ideas are vain and arbitrary; they are supported neither by reason, nor by the authority of the ancients, nor by experience. But if anyone should wish to confirm the opinion of the astrologers by the creation of the world—arguing that the future fortune is known from the entry of the **Sun** into <term>Aries</term> because of that reason...

<summary>Pico argues that there is no natural "first day" of the year in the zodiac, noting that different cultures and astrologers (like Ptolemy, Avenrodan, and Albumasar) disagree on whether to start with the spring equinox or other seasonal points. He dismisses these varied astrological systems as arbitrary inventions lacking empirical evidence.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Pico della Mirandola’s critique of the "starting point" of the year in astrological practice. He is currently dismantling the argument that the astrological year must begin in the spring (Aries) because that was allegedly the moment of Creation. He uses Hebrew scripture and historical authorities to show that the "beginning" is a matter of religious or civil convention, not a fixed law of nature.</meta>

<page-num>VII</page-num>

# Book VII

...it follows: because God created the world at that time; so that the turnings of the years are nothing other than the revolutions of the world's birth. This, however, is very easily and immediately refuted. For if we follow the "birth" of the world, it will be just as uncertain when the beginning of the year should be established as it is uncertain at what time of year the world was instituted. For even among the Hebrews, from whom we received the account of the world's creation, there is nothing certain and defined on this matter; some contend it began in spring, others in autumn. And if one opinion is to be preferred, they lean rather toward believing it was founded in autumn. 

<margin>
The year more reasonably begins in autumn than in spring, according to the Hebrews.
</margin>

For regarding what is written—that the same month in which <term>Passover</term> <note>original: "phase"; from the Hebrew *Pesach*.</note> was celebrated would be the first month among the months of the year—they maintain this was said for the sake of the solemnities to be celebrated. Therefore, if that was the greatest, first, and primary solemnity (from which their exit from Egypt followed, which was the first benefit of God toward the people), then all other things followed. In all other matters, however, they made the beginning from September. This seems to be confirmed both by many passages of the sacred scriptures and by the ancient customs of the Jews. For it is written in Exodus that <term>Skenopegia</term> <note>The Feast of Tabernacles or Sukkot.</note>—that is, the festival of tabernacles—is celebrated at the "exit of the year" <note>The end or turning point of the year.</note>; and those were indeed celebrated in the middle of September. 

And in the book of Nehemiah it is written: "and it happened in the month of <term>Casleu</term> <note>Kislev, roughly November/December.</note> (which is December among the Chaldeans) in the twentieth year"; then it happened in the month of <term>Nisan</term> (which is April) in the twentieth year. But if the month of Nisan (April) were the head of the year, it should have been written as the twenty-first year, not the twentieth <note>Pico's logic is that if the new year started in April, the year count would have increased between December and the following April.</note>. 

Furthermore, since the law provided that in the seventh year (which was the <term>Sabbatical year</term>) they should neither reap the fields nor sow, if the head of the year were April, it followed that what they had sown during the October of the sixth year, they would not be permitted to reap in the following summer. Therefore, this summer would belong to the seventh year if its beginning were taken from the spring; if that were the case, the seeds entrusted to the earth in the sixth year would perish. This disadvantage did not follow for one establishing the year from September. I omit what <term>Lersiensis</term> <note>Likely referring to a specific medieval commentator or perhaps a corruption of a name like "Dionysius."</note> wrote in his computation, and <term>Bede</term> in his *Book of Times*, and <term>Josephus</term> in the first book of *Antiquities*, and <term>Jerome</term> in his letter on solemnities. 

<margin>
Lersiensis, Bede, Josephus, Jerome.
</margin>

Jerome, also explaining Ezekiel, says that October is the first month and January the fourth. From all of which it is clear—whether we conjecture anything from the creation of the world, or follow the reasoning and authority of the ancient astrologers—that the astrologers are entirely in error when they contend that the fate of the whole year can be pronounced from the entry of the sun into <term>Aries</term> <note>The first sign of the zodiac, marking the spring equinox.</note>.

### Chapter VII: On directions and other methods by which they define the timing of future events, what parts they consist of, and how astrologers disagree among themselves in these matters.

Just as they err in auspiciously forecasting the fates of the year (if any such forecasting of fate were granted), so they err in defining the time when that event shall occur which the initial hour promised. For in this matter too, they use frivolous, false, and vain suppositions and methods that are in no way consistent with nature. Among these, the first and most powerful is concerning the "directions" of the planets and the parts of the zodiac. (For it pleases them to call them so, that we may be better understood by those with whom we dispute.) We shall, therefore, briefly expose those foundations that rest on false and ridiculous bases, after first declaring the intended opinion of the astrologers. 

Suppose, then, the <term>horoscope</term> <note>The Ascendant; the point of the zodiac rising on the eastern horizon at the moment of birth.</note> of some birth is the fifteenth degree of Leo. Let <term>Saturn</term> be placed at the sixth degree of Virgo. It is clear that Saturn is joined to the horoscope neither by <term>aspect</term> <note>A specific angular relationship between planets (like a square or trine) that astrologers believe transmits influence.</note> nor by any other thing; therefore, he ought not to harm it. But they think that eventually, by "direction," the horoscope will reach Saturn, and in the year it reaches there, the danger of disease from Saturn hangs over the native. They say it reaches there by this reasoning: that in each year, single parts of the signs are attributed to us, though according to the proportion of the <term>anaphoras</term> <note>The "ascensions" or the time it takes for a degree of the zodiac to rise above the horizon.</note>. But this is nothing to the matter now at hand.

<summary>Pico argues that the astrological "New Year" in spring is arbitrary, citing Hebrew tradition that suggests the world was created in autumn. He then begins to critique "directions," a technical astrological method used to predict the timing of future events like illness.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Pico della Mirandola’s systematic dismantling of astrological methods. Having previously questioned the "starting point" of the year, he now turns his critique toward the specific technique of "directions," which astrologers use to predict the timing of events in a person’s life.</meta>

# Book VII

They say, therefore, that in the first year of life, the degree in which the <term>horoscope</term> <note>original: "horoscopus"; in this context, it refers to the Ascendant, or the specific degree of the zodiac rising on the eastern horizon at the moment of birth.</note> is located is the one "owed" to that year. Therefore, if a good planet is present in that degree—either by its physical body or by its rays—it bestows its benefits in that year. Conversely, if a harmful planet is there, it brings evils. In the second year, the second degree from the first responds; in the third, the third, and so on.

For this reason, if **Saturn**, for example, occupied the twenty-first degree from the Ascendant, that part would correspond to the twenty-first year of age, such that the year would be infested by Saturn’s rays. Thus, when they wish to foresee in what year something good or evil might happen to a person at birth, they measure the degrees between the principal places of the <term>nativity</term> <note>original: "geniturae"; the birth chart or the configuration of the stars at the moment of birth.</note> and the bodies or rays of the good or evil stars intercepted between them. Based on that number of degrees, they prescribe the number of years after which that event should be expected. This is their position on <term>directions</term> <note>original: "directionibus"; a predictive technique in astrology where degrees of the zodiac are mapped to years of life (often 1 degree = 1 year).</note>, from which **Ptolemy** and the whole crowd of astrologers pronounce the span of a life and all the falls and turns of fortune.

What could be thought of as more trivial? What could be more irrational? First, that distribution of degrees to years: can anything be more fancifully imagined? It is conceived on no foundation of science or reason, especially since they sometimes say years are indicated by these degrees, and sometimes days (as it happens to suit them). This might perhaps have some probability if the partition of the degrees themselves were from nature; however, that partition depends entirely on the whim of the mathematicians, who divide the <term>Signs</term> into thirty parts rather than twenty for no other reason than that the number thirty is more convenient for arithmetic divisions—as will be demonstrated to us by the testimony of the astrologers themselves in the next book.

But how can **Saturn** hurt me when it was found in the sixth degree of **Virgo** (as was recorded) when I was being born, even if we grant them that its influence pertains to me in the twenty-first year of my life? For when Saturn pertains to me, it will not be there; and when Saturn is there, that part will not pertain to me.

<margin>Response.</margin>
To this they might say that perhaps, just as clothes infected by a <term>pestilence</term> <note>original: "pestilentia"; Pico is comparing astrological influence to the contemporary medical theory of "miasma" or "contagion" lingering in physical objects.</note> do not lose their poison for some time, the same thing happens to the parts of heaven: they retain the contagion received from an evil star for a long time.

<margin>Refutation.</margin>
Therefore, because that degree was already infected by Saturn when I was born, it pours that harmful force back into me even after many years. They will defend this position quite prettily and subtly; and indeed, if the conversation were with philosophers, I would bid them remember that the quality of light does not cling to the subject but departs with the body from which it is diffused. Furthermore, as **Avicenna** says in the *Meteors*, for all celestial impressions, light is both the vehicle and the fuel.

<margin>First reason. Avicenna in the first book of the *Meteors*.</margin>
But let them answer me: since other planets move through that same degree in the many intervening years, do they think that ingrained virus can be abolished or diminished by the arrival of saving lights?

<margin>Second [reason].</margin>
Furthermore, if the qualities received and accepted from the planets endure in the regions of heaven and are preserved for more than a brief space of time, then in judging events, one should not only observe which planet is found in which place of heaven—either in the revolving year or the hour of birth—but also who traveled through those same places in the preceding years.

<margin>Third [reason].</margin>
Finally, that fiction of "directing" is nothing other than subjecting things not only to the <term>constellations</term> that exist, but to those that *could* exist.

<margin>Fourth [reason].</margin>
For what else is it to say that the **Moon**, which was struck by <term>sextile</term> <note>original: "exagonis"; an astrological aspect where two planets are 60 degrees apart, usually considered harmonious.</note> rays from the **Sun** at my birth, will nonetheless produce misfortune there eventually from a <term>square</term> <note>original: "quadrato"; an aspect where planets are 90 degrees apart, usually considered challenging or "unfortunate."</note> aspect? The Moon was certainly not under that aspect when I was born; it would have been so only if it had been positioned much further from the Sun by many intervening parts of heaven. Because it will have traveled through those parts—by which it was distant from that square radiation—after so many years, that calamity will be inflicted there. But that constellation did not exist at my birth, even if it is to exist sometime afterward.

<summary>Pico critiques the astrological technique of "directions," arguing that mapping degrees to years of life is a mathematical whim rather than a natural law. He specifically mocks the idea that a planet's "influence" can linger in a point in space like a contagious disease long after the planet has moved on.</summary>

# Book VII

<margin>
Other ways by which astrologers think the times of events can be foreseen.
</margin>

...Yet this matters nothing to me; for if I have any fate, it was that past arrangement of the heavens that gave it to me. It is clear, therefore, how absurd, how false, and how inconsistent the practice of **directing** is—a practice used daily by astrologers. What foundation do they have? From where was it derived? They have not yet, I think, called it back for consideration and examination. 

Besides "directions," they also use the **dominion of the planets** to foresee the timing of events. They have invented a system where the planets take up the "empire of life" in a certain order. From this come the "centers" of the **Chaldeans**; the <term>Firdaria</term> <note>original: "fridariæ"; a Persian system of planetary periods where different planets take turns ruling over specific spans of years.</note> of the **Persians**; the "nines" of the **Indians**; the <term>decans</term> <note>original: "tecates"; likely referring to the Egyptian/Ptolemaic decans, which are ten-degree divisions of the zodiac.</note> of **Ptolemy**; and from here the <term>aphoresis</term> <note>original: "aphoria"; a technique for "releasing" time-periods from a specific point in the birth chart.</note> and the "interceder"; the "ten-year periods" of the **Egyptians**; the <term>chronocrators</term> <note>original: "cronocratores"; literally 'time-lords,' planets designated to rule over specific periods of life.</note> of the **Arabs**; and whatever other things of this kind others have dreamed up according to their whims. 

All of these err in this inconsistency: they define the stars in such a way that a particular planet rules us for a certain number of years. When that time is finished, it hands over the "rudder of government," as if by hand, to the succeeding planet, according to the order of the spheres or the <term>climates</term> <note>The ancient geographic zones used to determine the length of daylight and astrological strength.</note>. This successor, having administered its jurisdiction for the time granted to it, then yields the right and power to the next star. This is entirely foreign to all natural reason. For no cause can be reasonably assigned why this planet, rather than another, should rule over these lower things at this specific time, unless it is because the disposition of matter is better suited to the impressions of one rather than the other, or because the star itself has a more effective relationship to us—such as when it is carried above the earth while others are below, or when it turns toward the North and becomes closer to our regions, or shoots more direct rays onto the earth.

If we were to agree with the astrologers about the good or bad condition of things based on the diversity of places, signs, and radiations of that planet which possesses more authority and power in the heavens than the others at that time—this is the only thing that can be said based on a natural method. But the rest are fictions and fables: for instance, if we say that **Jupiter** now presides over earthly things because in preceding years **Saturn** presided (whom Jupiter follows in the order of the spheres), or that **Taurus** rules this year because **Aries** ruled the previous year—as if the shifts of earthly magistrates were to be found among the stars! 

If they say that "experience proves it," there might be some faith in it if they could at least agree among themselves on this distribution of times. But since one attributes those same years to the **Moon**, another to **Mars**, and another to **Jupiter**, should not the credibility of "experience" be stripped from all of them equally? For each one claims it for his own opinion amidst such a great variety of opinions.

<margin>
The opinion of the Egyptians and Maternus.
</margin>

The **Egyptians**, whom **Firmicus** <note>referring to Julius Firmicus Maternus, a 4th-century Roman author of the 'Mathesis,' one of the most comprehensive textbooks of ancient astrology.</note> follows, give the administration of life to each star in an equal partition of 10 years and 9 months, in this order: in a daytime <term>nativity</term> <note>original: "genitura"; the birth chart or the specific moment of birth.</note>, the **Sun** takes the first decade; in a nighttime one, the **Moon** takes it. After that decade, the one that was in the second place in the nativity according to the course of the signs becomes the ruler, then the third after the second, and so on. But whoever is allotted the decade, although he is the lord of the whole time, he divides the entire substance of the decade among all the stars, starting with himself and handing it over to those placed in order after him. First, however, comes whichever was second in the <term>theme</term> <note>original: "themate"; the layout or scheme of the birth chart.</note>. 

The sum of years which the seven planets moderate, according to their opinion, is seventy-five years with three months added; when these are completed, a return is made again to the first planet. Many others collect the same number of years and start similarly from the Sun if someone was born by day, or from the Moon if by night. They also create one principal lordship of the times, but make others participants in the dominion by a "vicarage" succession. They call this distribution <term>Firdaria</term>. Hence the common saying among the younger practitioners that someone is "a prince of the Firdaria of Jupiter." Yet they disagree greatly with the Egyptians, for in the succession of the planets they do not observe the places of the birth chart, but rather the order of the spheres, making the Sun the center...

<summary>Pico attacks the various systems of "time-lords" (Chronocrators) and Firdaria used by different cultures, arguing that their conflicting rules and lack of physical basis prove they are arbitrary fictions rather than science.</summary>
