<page-num>VII</page-num>
->Book<-

Furthermore, they do not assign an equal amount of time to each planet: but for the **Sun**, they assign ten years; for **Venus**, eight; for **Mercury**, thirteen; for the **Moon**, nine; for **Saturn**, eleven; for **Jupiter**, twelve; for **Mars**, seven; for the <term>Head</term> <note>The "Head of the Dragon" or North Node of the Moon.</note>, three; and for the <term>Tail</term> <note>The "Tail of the Dragon" or South Node of the Moon.</note>, two. Even <term>Abraham ibn Ezra</term> <note>original: "Auenazra"; a famous 12th-century Jewish scholar and astrologer.</note> himself, in his *Book of Astrological Kings*, admits he does not know what reasoning could possibly support this. On the other hand, in appointing the ruling planet, the **Persians** give an equal portion to any of the planets, so that the ruling planet governs the first seventh of its time alone; the second part with the second planet from it; and the third part with the third. However, the **Egyptians** make this distribution unequal, decreeing nineteen months for the **Sun**; thirty for **Saturn**; twelve for **Jupiter**; fifteen for **Mars**; eight for **Venus**; twenty for **Mercury**; and twenty-five for the **Moon**. This they subdivide again, so that from its thirty months, **Saturn** imparts six days to the remaining planets, and the others do the same with their own months, as **Hephaestion** teaches—though <term>Firmicus Maternus</term> <note>A 4th-century Roman lawyer and author of the 'Mathesis,' one of the last great astrological handbooks of the Roman Empire.</note> was ignorant of this. But there was another disagreement between the Persians and Egyptians: the former count the Head and Tail [of the Dragon] among the <term>time-lords</term> <note>original: "cronocratoris"; planets or points designated to rule a specific period of life.</note>, while the Egyptians do not. From all of this, it is clear that after the first decade, the governor of the years will rarely be the same according to the Persians as it is according to the Egyptians. 

<margin>The Opinion of Ptolemy</margin>
**Ptolemy**, however, disagrees with both, establishing "lords of the ages." He has the **Moon** govern the first four years; **Mercury** the next ten. Then, following the natural order: **Venus** governs eight; the **Sun**, nine; **Mars**, fifteen; **Jupiter**, twelve; and **Saturn** the remainder of life. Yet, when he seeks an exact and peculiar distribution of times for each individual <term>birth chart</term> <note>original: "genituræ"; the arrangement of stars at the moment of a person's birth.</note>, he adds yearly, monthly, and daily periods to those principal time-lords. But for Ptolemy, the entire "hinge of fate" turns on these matters; there he censures those who make only one time-lord for life, hinting at the **Egyptians** and **Dorotheus**. If anyone follows this opinion of Ptolemy, they will define the distribution of times in a way that is always vastly different from the Egyptians and Persians. This makes it all the more pleasant to mock the astrologers of our own age.

<margin>A notable error of the astrologers of our time</margin>
These modern astrologers, not understanding that they are measuring the same thing, treat **Ptolemy's** <term>divisions</term> <note>original: "tecates"; here likely referring to specific divisions of time or the zodiac used to assign planetary rulers.</note> and time-lords as if they were the same as the Persian <term>Firdaria</term> <note>A Persian system of planetary periods.</note> and the Egyptian decades. They want to use them all at once, as if they were not diverse and contradictory systems for the same subject. But among these various matters, the opinions are not at all consistent. **Indian** astrology knows nothing of Firdaria, nor decades, nor Ptolemaic divisions, nor time-lords; instead, it divides life into nine parts (not seven like the others). Regarding these, it pronounces an order according to the layout of the "places" in the chart: so that the first part of the years is ruled by the constellations belonging to the **twelfth house**. The second part belongs to the <term>horoscope</term> <note>The 1st House, or the sign rising on the eastern horizon.</note>; the third to the **second house**; the fourth to the **ninth**; the fifth to the **tenth**; the sixth to the **eleventh**; the seventh to the **sixth**; the eighth to the **seventh**; and the ninth to the **eighth**. 

<margin>The opinion of the Arabs</margin>
Not only do they disagree with others in this dispensation of times, but they even clash in the partitioning of the houses themselves, dividing them according to the degrees of the zodiac (which they call "equal houses"). The **Arabs**, imitating **Andruzagar**, judge three parts of life through the <term>triplicity rulers</term> <note>original: "trigonocratores"; the planets that rule over the four elements (Fire, Earth, Air, Water) in the zodiac.</note>. Regarding the matters signified by each of the twelve houses, they judge the first and future status from the first ruler of the triplicity; the middle status from the second; and the final status from the third. But if the triplicity has only two rulers, as we mentioned in the first book—or if perhaps a single birth chart has only one disposer—even if one rules by day and another by night, a great part of life will be left without any governor at all. But there are no...

<meta>This page continues Pico della Mirandola’s critique of the various systems used by astrologers to divide a human life into periods ruled by different planets. Having dismissed the Persian and Egyptian methods on the previous page, he now turns to the Chaldean system and the contradictory opinions of several famous astrological authorities before attacking the logical inconsistencies of their star catalogs.</meta>

<page-num>VII</page-num>
<header>Book VII</header>

<margin>The opinion of the Chaldeans.</margin>
These <term>triplicity rulers</term> <note>original: "trigonocratores"; planets that rule the four groups of zodiac signs associated with the elements Fire, Earth, Air, and Water.</note>—even if it were granted that there are three thousand of them—and their successions as deputies in governing a life, are utterly ridiculous. But the invention of the Chaldeans is clearly different from all these; they use neither "decennials," nor "fridaria," <note>Astrological systems for dividing life into periods of years ruled by specific planets.</note> nor the "nines" of the Indians, nor triplicity rulers, but rather the **angles** of the birth chart. They investigated the first part of life from the first angle <note>The Ascendant or Eastern horizon.</note>; the middle part from the peak of the highest heaven <note>The Midheaven or Zenith.</note>; and the last part from the west. Concerning death, and even those things that happen after death, they would pronounce judgment from the fourth place of the theme <note>The 'Imum Coeli' or bottom of the sky, often associated with the end of life and the grave.</note>. But they further subdivided that previous three-part division: so that the <term>cadent house</term> <note>original: "apoclima"; houses that "fall away" from the main angles, considered weaker in influence.</note> of the ascendant—which you might call a "downward slope"—indicated the pains of labor and what happens in the mother's womb; the <term>ascendant</term> <note>original: "horoscopus"; the point of the zodiac rising on the eastern horizon at birth.</note> itself indicated the birth and the first years; and the <term>succedent house</term> <note>original: "epanophora"; the house that "rises up" after an angle.</note> of the ascendant was the remainder and final part of that first age. Again, the cadent house of the mid-heaven indicated the first parts of middle life; the mid-heaven itself the middle; and its succedent house the final parts. They did the same in the fourth house: so that the house declining from it signified the events leading up to death; the fourth house itself signified death; and its succedent house signified what might happen after death. 

I have set out to explain these opinions so that the contradictions between them might be recognized, and because no trust should be placed in such "experiments"; at the same time, the vanity of these arbitrary dogmas, leaning on the most flimsy conjectures, is laid bare. For why should we give the first part of life to the East and the middle to the highest heaven, since middle age follows the first, but the mid-heaven does not follow the East—it precedes it? <note>Pico is pointing out a logical flaw: in the daily rotation of the sky, a star hits the Midheaven before it hits the Ascendant, so using them in the reverse order for the stages of life is astronomically backward.</note> But one should not labor in refuting these opinions, which refute and destroy themselves. If I were to go on recounting the dreams of them all, there would be no end.

<margin>The opinion of Messala.</margin>
**Messala** <note>Mashallah ibn Athari (c. 740–815), a Persian Jewish astrologer and astronomer.</note> governs the first half of life by the eastern sun, and the second by the western.

<margin>The opinion of Hemus.</margin>
**Hemus** <note>Likely a reference to a classical or Arabic source, possibly Haly or Hermes.</note> assigns it differently: to the planets located in the upper hemisphere—whether they are in the east or west—and the other half to all those under the earth. **Vellius** <note>Vettius Valens, a 2nd-century Greek astrologer.</note> by another fiction ascribes the first part to the **Moon** and the other to the lord of the second house. **Albumasar** <note>Abu Ma'shar (787–886), a leading Persian astrologer in the Abbasid court.</note>, the most myth-making of them all, says the first part refers to the **Lot of Fortune** and the second to the lord of that Lot. Others say still other things, but it is not necessary to pursue them all. Read **Hephaestion** <note>A 4th-century Egyptian astrologer.</note> in his book on the *Apoteclesmata* <note>Astrological effects.</note> of **Ptolemy**. Read **Abenzageles** <note>Possibly the 10th-century Arab astrologer Al-Zarqali.</note>; and besides those we have recounted, you will find many other opinions there, all fighting amongst themselves over this matter. Thus, essentially, each man composes a fable for himself according to his own whim. Yet people who are too gullible surrender their faith to these as if they were oracles or responses of prophets; we entrust our hopes, fears, anxieties, joys, and—what is more ruinous—the very direction and government of our whole lives to these most trifling and deceptive street-performers.

### Chapter VIII: How they adopt fictions for their efficacy, yet omit necessities; and how greatly they err concerning the fixed stars.

<margin>The error of astrologers in neglecting almost infinite fixed stars.</margin>
Just as they adopt many fictional things such as we have mentioned—which have no natural existence and thus no influence, such as signs, houses, imaginary figures, the **Tail** and **Head** <note>The lunar nodes.</note>, "parts," <term>twelfth-parts</term> <note>original: "dodecathemoria"; a subdivision of each zodiac sign into 12 parts.</note>, "ninths," and others of this kind—so too they omit things that are primarily necessary, and decree many false and contradictory things about those they do use. For just as things lacking light are ineffective, so no light in the heavens is ineffective. Yet while almost innumerable stars shine in the eighth sphere <note>The realm of the fixed stars in the medieval geocentric model.</note>, they use only one thousand and twenty-two. When this is objected to them, some resolve it one way, some another. **Peter of Abano** <note>original: "Petrus Aponensis"; a 13th-century physician and astrologer who tried to reconcile Greek, Arabic, and Christian thought.</note> says in his *Elucidarium* that this presents a difficulty in the art, but not an impossibility...

...nevertheless shows it to be so: and responding to this, he seems to concede that those stars are indeed necessary for knowledge, if a perfectly fated constellation is to be comprehended. And because this is difficult, he therefore professes that the art itself is difficult. But we contend that it is impossible for all of them to be grasped; and even if this were possible, the astrologers who have not yet achieved this will not truly predict future events from the sky.

<margin>Defense of others.</margin>
Others, hiding in a somewhat safer refuge, say that those stars they omit are ineffective. For [they claim] all the greater stars have the power of determining fate, and while these have been explored by astrologers, the rest are omitted: in which, due to the smallness of their bodies, there is almost no significance.

<margin>Refutation.</margin>
<margin>First reason.</margin>
But they are easily dragged out of these hiding places. For if they never observed these stars, what can they assert about their nature—whether they act or do not act, whether they change things or do not change them?

<margin>Second [reason].</margin>
And if they respond that they are convinced by the smallness of the body: what body in the sky will be considered small compared to the earth? Or, to speak more correctly, compared to those things which, placed on earth, are thought to be governed from heaven?

<margin>Third [reason].</margin>
Likewise, it would be ineffective and weak if you compare the nature of celestial and earthly bodies to each other: in one, everything is sublime, powerful, and great; in the other, everything is humble, weak, and tiny.

<margin>Fourth [reason].</margin>
Add that perhaps many of these stars, which they say are neglected because of their smallness, are not surpassed by the globe of Mercury or the Moon. For among those they do observe, some are thought to be no larger than Mars or Venus.

<margin>Fifth [reason].</margin>
Furthermore, if perhaps individual smaller stars do not have great power, nevertheless a gathering and assembly of many of that kind will have the greatest power; as with those which make the **Milky Way** thick with so many lights: if individual ones can do little, how will it be thought that they all together can do little?

<margin>Sixth [reason].</margin>
Moreover, often in a musical melody, if one small note is withdrawn, the harmony is dissolved; while that which by itself would be heard little, makes all the others be heard more tunefully. The whole ornament of the heavens is mutually connected and in agreement: it has nothing that ceases, nothing superfluous, nothing useless. Therefore, whatever smallest part you take away, the whole integrity that the total made immediately perishes. Among <term>haulers</term> <note>original: "helciarios"; men who pull boats along a river using ropes.</note>, a man who is not strong can still add usefully to the pull; if his hand is missing, the pulling might not happen. So the ignorance of even one single star can undermine the truth of fate; and it is not possible that they be omitted by them—almost without number—without committing a grave error.

<margin>How lightly Bonatti says the astrologer uses all the stars.</margin>
**Bonatti** <note>original: "Bonatus"; Guido Bonatti (c. 1210–1296), the most famous Italian astrologer of the 13th century, whom Pico frequently targets.</note>, perhaps fearing these things (if he saw them so clearly), says: "The astrologer uses all the stars," even if he does not explain them all by name. For he uses the twelve signs, under which almost all stars are included. But who would say this—not yet an astrologer, but a <term>madman</term>? <note>original: "lymphaticus"; literally "seized by nymphs," used to describe someone in a state of frenzy or delusion.</note> Since the signs called "the twelve" have a width of degrees outside of which stars are innumerable on both sides; and if any within those same lines are extended with any sign, they respond that they are of the same virtue.

<margin>Response.</margin>
<margin>Refutation.</margin>
First, I will ask how he can assert things about unknown matters? If he says this is proper to astrologers, I will not disagree, and I will call upon the astrologers themselves, among whom the **constellations** themselves, rising with the signs, portend one thing, and the **signs** with which they rise portend another. Otherwise, the signs they use are immobile, while the constellations change their place. There will therefore be one nature or another for the same constellation responding to different signs in the same place and sign.

<margin>Another flightiness of Bonatti.</margin>
But even Bonatti himself, I think, noticing the insanity of his response, immediately digressed to another point; and since he saw it could hardly be denied that knowledge of all the stars pertains to the astrological matter—of all of which the astrologers nevertheless did not have knowledge—"What then," he said, "if we astrologers do not know the whole of astrology?" Predica...

# Book VII

Christian teachers do not know all divine matters, yet they preach about them daily to the common people. In this matter, see how little "this good Bonatus" <note>original: *Bonatus*. This refers to Guido Bonatti (c. 1210–1296), the most famous medieval Italian astrologer, whose work Pico frequently critiques as the pinnacle of superstitious practice.</note> is actually deceived. For if someone investigates the nature of the stars for the sake of knowledge—which is the goal of the philosopher—they have achieved something even by knowing a single star. But if someone professes to be an astrologer, they seek not so much a knowledge of the stars as a knowledge of the future through the stars. Such a person achieves absolutely nothing unless they possess knowledge of all those stars from which the future might be foreseen. But the future is foreseen from those things by which it is caused; and it is caused

<margin>Example in philosophy and medicine.</margin>
by all of them. Therefore, it is also foreseen from all of them. Thus, anyone who does not know them all—though he may perhaps know some—will never foresee the future from the stars. Consider an example in medicine and philosophy: the philosopher seeks the powers of herbs so that he may understand them; the physician seeks them so that he may heal diseases by their virtue. If a philosopher discovers even one, he is a philosopher, though an imperfect one, since he possesses some knowledge of the things he seeks. But let us suppose there are ten species of herbs—or whatever number you prefer—necessary for driving away all diseases, such that if one is missing, no flaw of the body can be cured. If someone is skilled in nine of these but ignorant of one, he is not merely an "incomplete" physician; he is no physician at all. While he may have some knowledge, he can provide none of the healing that a physician professes to give. In the same way, a man cannot be called an astrologer if he cannot speak of the fate of even a single person by inspecting their birth chart. For if fate is composed of the mixed influence <note>original: *afflatione*, literally a "breathing upon" or celestial "wafting."</note> of all the stars, how will he foresee it? He cannot know what each individual star effects, nor what the joined temperament of them all produces. Regarding theology, however, the logic is different: because just as it is not possible to know it perfectly, so too it is not necessary. We are able to believe, to know, and to persuade many things concerning it; and it is almost as impossible to know nothing of it as it is to know everything. For it is no less denied to those with eyes *not* to see the sun than it is to look deep into its center. But enough has been said in refuting the trifles of this most illiterate peddler <note>A final jab at Bonatti.</note>.

### Chapter IX: The doctrines of astrologers regarding the fixed stars conflict both with each other and with the truth.

<note>Small guide letter 's' visible in the margin for the initial.</note>
But the astrologers do not only err in being ignorant of most stars; even concerning those they think they have explored, they have established the most conflicting and false dogmas. For there are times (as I shall show) when they decree the stars to be more effective than the planets, and times when they decree them to be less powerful and effective. In this matter, they both fight amongst themselves and disagree with the truth on both sides. They promise an "ordinary" happiness (so to speak), according to the capacity and condition of the one being born, based on a "good state" of the planets; but from the non-wandering stars <note>The "fixed stars" of the constellations, as opposed to the "wandering stars" or planets.</note>, as Ptolemy says, they expect <term>unexpected misfortunes</term> <note>original Greek: παραδοξουσ ατυχιασ (*paradoxous atychias*). Pico is quoting Ptolemy’s *Tetrabiblos*.</note>—that is, successes greater than anyone could imagine. I, however, contend that greater things can be provided by the planets than by the fixed stars, supported both by Proclus <note>Proclus (412–485 AD), a Neoplatonist philosopher who wrote a commentary on Plato’s *Timaeus*.</note> in his commentary on Plato’s *Timaeus* and by reason itself. For a more sublime position does not indicate a more sublime nature for the non-wandering stars, since the sun, the moderator of all things, has many stars placed above it—certainly all of them except the moon.

<margin>First reason.</margin>
Furthermore, let this be an argument for why we judge the planets to surpass the fixed stars: many spheres serve a single planet, while only one sphere serves many fixed stars. Thus, the entire army of those stars together might overcome the power of a single celestial body; yet, individual stars cannot surpass individual planets. But if you look at the size of their bodies, the sun...

<margin>Second.</margin>
Beyond controversy, the Sun is greater than all others; likewise, Jupiter and Saturn are greater than all the rest if you except certain more principal ones. However, power is not understood to be greater based solely on the vastness of these celestial bodies. For it has not been proven that Jupiter is more powerful than Saturn just because he is larger; and since 
<margin>Third.</margin>
Mercury is the smallest of all the stars, he nevertheless possesses (as they themselves would have it) the most power in every birth chart <note>original: *genitura*, referring to the astrological figure of a person's birth</note>. Nor, likewise, do they rank the Moon above Venus, 
<margin>Fourth.</margin>
even though she is exceeded by the Moon in the size of her body. Finally, that bright star situated at the "Heart of the Lion" <term>Regulus (Cor Leonis)</term>, which is called the *Queen* by the Latins and the *Basilisk* <note>original: *basiliscus*, meaning "Little King" in Greek</note> by the Greeks; although it is not of the first magnitude, it is nonetheless judged by them to be of the first authority and power. They certainly consider it more noble because it does not deflect from the path of the Sun <note>The ecliptic, or the Sun's apparent path across the sky</note>. By this same reasoning, the planets are more noble than the stars because they deviate less in either direction from that same path. 
<margin>Fifth.</margin>
Added to this is the testimony of antiquity, which calls the planets <term>Cosmocrators</term> <note>From the Greek *kosmokratōr*, meaning "world-ruler"</note>—as if you were to say "rulers of the world"—a title with which they did not deign to name the fixed stars.

But I wish they would at least maintain their own dogma, and not speak so often of those same stars—which they claim are the makers of marvelous works—as if they were weak and feeble. For they say the stars effect nothing unless they occupy the <term>angles</term> <note>The *cardines*, or the four most powerful points in a horoscope: the Rising, Setting, Midheaven, and Lower Midheaven</note> or at least the beginnings of the "houses," or are joined to one of the luminaries <note>The Sun and the Moon</note>. And thus, those to whom they attributed so much power above, they here take away so much from their virtue that the stars effect nothing by themselves, unless they are supported by the vigor of their location or the help of a most powerful star. 
<margin>How the astrologers have fallen.</margin>
For this rule, they offer neither a cause nor any probable reason. Instead, they have perhaps fallen into error through a false understanding of a certain ancient saying. For the ancients, as <term>Maternus</term> <note>Julius Firmicus Maternus, a 4th-century Roman author of the *Mathesis*, a massive astrological compendium</note> teaches, used to say regarding the Zodiac signs that when they were found "naked" of stars, they had no efficacy, except for those occupying the four angles. This teaching, which was originally taught regarding the signs as the <term>mansions</term> and lodgings of the stars, they have also transferred to individual stars. Unless, perhaps, they astutely established this dogma so that they would not be tormented by a miserably inextricable task: for if the reason for fate had to be explained by *every* star, it would be a burden no man could overcome, and they could not easily persuade the credulous. 

Otherwise, what is the reason for their opinion? Is it because a star is in a more remote place? But how much closer to us is Saturn? 
<margin>The error is revealed by reasons.</margin>
Or what is such a great prerogative of an "angle" that in it stars not only act, but do admirable things? And yet, nothing hindering them despite the vastness of the distance, as soon as they have declined a little from that angle, or reached it "naked," they do nothing at all. This is said even though the <term>eleventh house</term> <note>Historically called the "Good Daemon," associated with friends and hopes</note>, rising toward the heights of heaven, would seem more powerful for action than the fourth house situated below the middle of the earth.

But it is certainly as we said: the labor deterred them. They did not want their art to seem so difficult that it could easily be judged impossible. For as for the "slowness of motion" they are accustomed to cite as an excuse, slowness supports nothing; a star’s ray is fixed all the more strongly, and clings more constantly, the longer the star itself lingers in the place from which it is cast down. What of the fact that these theories also fight against themselves? For there is a dogma concerning a slower planet that it gives "late" whatever it gives, but what it has given lasts and remains for a long time. On the contrary, concerning the fixed stars—which they are accustomed to say have the slowest motion of all—they decree that they bring the greatest happiness indeed, but happiness that ultimately ends in calamities. Therefore, their gifts do not linger long, just as they are not long preserved. But just as they are always far from the truth, so they disagree with themselves everywhere, although we do not pursue every instance. For someone could also ask them why, just as with the planets...

...[stars] among themselves: thus, since they did not consider the intervals and aspects between the stars and the planets, or between the stars themselves; Johannes Regiomontanus <note>Johannes Müller von Königsberg (1436–1476), a famous German mathematician and astronomer who criticized earlier astronomical tables</note>, noticing this, says that their aspects might perhaps be more perfect than those of the planets. For these are not fleeting and momentary like the planets, but rather stable and perpetual. Other objections could be raised on these points, but let us move on to the consequences.

### Chapter X: That astrologers are also deceived regarding the planets; and a summary of what has been discussed so far.

How much they are deceived even regarding the planets themselves has been sufficiently demonstrated above. They repeatedly think that the planets' properties (in which they seem to err as much as they do with the "non-erratic" <term>fixed stars</term>) and powers are not only increased and decreased, but even become different and diverse based on the variety of their locations, the condition of the [zodiac] signs, their configurations <term>schematisms</term>, and the multiple relationships among them all—as well as the various names for their motions, whether stationary, progressing, or retreating <term>retrograde</term>. We have most clearly shown (unless I am mistaken) that these claims are far from all truth, far from reason, and far from the dignity and nature of celestial things. 

We also criticize the way they prescribe that the planets and those twelve signs rule in turns, as if authority were passed from hand to hand by some impious right of succession over different things and times. They certainly do not so much measure the celestial bodies by human standards as they lie about them <note>original: *non tam metientes certe quam mentientes*. Pico is using a wordplay between "measuring" and "lying"</note>. Furthermore, we have laughed at and, along with Plotinus <note>A major Neoplatonic philosopher (c. 204–270 AD) who argued that the stars are signs but not causes of human affairs</note> and his contemporaries, struck out the idea that they command one to expect the effect of some planet for as many years as it happened to be distant in degrees of a sign from some location. Upon this, they devise a thousand falsehoods, conceived with no foundation in science. 

Therefore, let us summarize the entire preceding discussion: it seems that astrologers speak plausibly when they say that lower things are governed by celestial ones; but they are soon caught being false, vain, and detestable—that is, neither pious nor philosophers. This is because they believe, preach, and assert that particular things can be produced from universal causes: evil from good, tiny things from great ones, accidental things from orderly ones, incorporeal things from corporeal ones, arbitrary things from necessary ones, artificial things from natural ones, and things already past from things present, or things now present from those past. 

If all these things were caused by the heavens, astrologers would assign no fewer causes than the celestial ones themselves. Yet they remain silent about the true powers of the constellations and stars that are actually in the sky, while accepting many properties concerning things that are not true. And since they possess only a tiny part of the truth, they themselves add many fabricated things such as we have mentioned in the present book: "places," "houses," "images," "nodes," "antiscia" <term>points of the zodiac that have equal daylight duration</term>, "twelfth-parts" <term>dodecathemoria; 2.5-degree subdivisions of a zodiac sign</term>—fictitious, ineffective, and imaginary things with no basis in the reality of nature. If a wise man can put his faith in these things as if they consisted of true natural solidity, simply because they supposedly rule us, then I confess that I undoubtedly have not yet understood what it means to be wise.

# BOOK EIGHT OF THE DISPUTATIONS OF GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA AGAINST THE ASTROLOGERS.

### Chapter One: That the number of celestial bodies—which, according to astrologers, possess the power to determine fate—is uncertain.

i

Among all the things that one who professes the science of the stars <note>astrology</note> must know, that which we were just discussing might be considered the easiest: namely, how to judge what the "fatal hour" of any given thing might be. But if astrologers have not attained this knowledge, nor are they able to attain it, how can they hope for more difficult things? For it is much more difficult and a task of greater effort to have a full understanding of the number of celestial bodies from which the force of fate reaches us, so that in describing a "fatal constellation," nothing imaginary is added and nothing truly effective is omitted. In the discussions of this present book, we shall reveal that this knowledge is otherwise useful and necessary for them to know, yet impossible to obtain. Thus, they cannot predict the truth, not only because they do not clearly foresee the motions and positions of the stars <note>original: "stellarum"</note> and do not have them all fully explored (which we will object to in the following books), but because it is not even established among them yet which bodies these are whose positions must be inspected and whose properties must be investigated. Indeed, they fail so significantly in what their professional art promises that they do not even know what those things are, the knowledge of which is necessary to them. 

For if they say we are deceived or that we bring these charges through malice, I shall compel them with a divine voice and ask them to tell me something about the number of the stars. When I question them, I realize not only that the stars cannot be counted by them based on what is visible, but that it is not even certain whether there are other stars in the sky beyond those we see, which escape both our senses and our reason. <margin>Favorinus against the birth-casters.</margin> The philosopher Favorinus <note>A 2nd-century philosopher and orator</note>, in that elegant speech of his against the "genethliacs" <term>those who cast birth charts</term> recorded in the works of Gellius <margin>Gellius</margin> <note>Aulus Gellius, author of "Attic Nights"</note>, said he wondered how it could be clear to anyone as a fixed rule that the planets—which Nigidius <note>Publius Nigidius Figulus, a Roman scholar and contemporary of Cicero</note> calls "wanderers"—are no more numerous than is commonly thought. For it could be that there are certain other planets of equal power which humans cannot see, either because of their overwhelming brightness or their extreme height. 

<margin>Alpetragius</margin> Certainly, as Alpetragius <note>Nur ad-Din al-Bitruji, an influential 12th-century astronomer from Al-Andalus</note>, a most wise man in celestial matters, says: there is still motion in the heavens that is unknown; there may also be a body there to which that motion primarily belongs, which has not yet been detected by any observation of the art. Many and various motions of the celestial bodies have been devised by the younger generation which were unknown to the ancients (as they themselves believe) and were finally detected by a long duration of observations. By this example, it is made manifest that other motions may still lie hidden from mathematicians, either because of their slowness or obscurity, or some other appearance—motions which posterity itself will one day come to know through even longer observations. 

I do not wish to speak here of epicycles and eccentrics <term>complex geometric models used to explain planetary paths</term>, nor of the multitude of spheres serving the planets, which is uncertain among all astronomers; for perhaps they will deny that the power to determine fate resides within these bodies. However, one must not remain silent about how much ambiguity exists regarding the spheres above the planets, and how uncertain this "divinatory astrology" is rendered by it. For some say the eighth sphere—which contains the stars that do not wander <term>the fixed stars</term>—is the highest...

<meta>This page continues the opening of Book VIII. Pico is challenging the astronomical foundations of astrology by questioning the number of celestial spheres. He transitions from a general claim about the uncertainty of the stars to a specific historical and technical critique of how medieval "modern" astronomers misinterpreted Ptolemy regarding the existence of a ninth sphere.</meta>

### Book VIII

...they make the outermost sphere illuminated: others have placed a ninth sphere above it: others even a tenth. <margin>Opinion of the Egyptians and Chaldeans.</margin> The astronomers of the Egyptians and Chaldeans judged that there was nothing above the eighth sphere: they were followed by Plato, Aristotle, Hipparchus, and Ptolemy. This is something the younger <note>Pico refers to the "neoterics" or "moderns," the medieval scholastic and Arabic astronomers</note> perhaps did not believe, but this is how the matter stands. In Ptolemy's system, there is no ninth sphere: this can easily be understood from his *Great Composition* <note>original: "magna compositione," referring to the *Almagest*</note>. <margin>Reason for the error of the moderns.</margin> Many, however, are deceived for this reason: they think that everyone who has discovered that the eighth sphere moves from west to east must necessarily fall into the opinion of a ninth sphere. Therefore, since both Ptolemy and Hipparchus admit this motion, these moderns do not doubt that the invention of the ninth sphere belonged to those very men by whom that motion was first recorded. <margin>Another reason.</margin> Add to this that Ptolemy uses both mobile and immobile signs: while they make the figures <note>the constellations</note> of the eighth sphere mobile, they also relate the positions of the planets to "immobile signs." Therefore, it seems certain and beyond doubt to them that, besides the signs of the eighth sphere which move, there are other signs in Ptolemy’s work which do not move except by the motion of the whole world; and they think these exist nowhere else but in a ninth sphere above the eighth. 

But they are very much and long deceived: for the motion of the stars from west to east does not necessarily lead to the conclusion of a ninth sphere. And as for what is argued regarding immobile signs, it is most clearly shown that Ptolemy was content with only the eighth sphere—<margin>Ptolemy describes immobile signs in the eighth.</margin> a fact I marvel was neither noticed nor understood by those men. For Ptolemy describes these immobile signs in the eighth sphere itself; he would not have done this if he had devised another higher one. His words in the second book of the *Great Composition* are these: "We shall make use of the names of the signs for the twelve parts of the <term>oblique circle</term> <note>the ecliptic</note> itself, as if their beginnings are taken from the tropical and equinoctial points. Thus, we shall call the <term>dodecathemorion</term> <note>original: "dodecathemorion," meaning a twelfth part of a circle</note>—that is, the twelfth part which extends from the vernal equinox toward the following parts of the whole sphere—'Aries'; the second, 'Taurus'; and so on in succession according to the order of the twelve signs handed down by us." 

These are the words of Ptolemy, who also teaches the same in the first book of the *Apotelesmatika* <note>The *Tetrabiblos*, Ptolemy's primary work on astrology</note>: that the parts of the zodiac to which the planets are referred begin and are determined by the solstices and equinoxes as the primary points. Since these four points are fixed and unmoved, the division of the signs established by them is also fixed and immobile—even though the figures <note>the constellations</note> from which those names were transferred move continually, and as time passes, their beginnings and ends are found in different places. Therefore, these immobile signs in Ptolemy's work are not in a higher sphere; rather, they are described by four fixed and immobile points of the eighth sphere itself. If he had conceived of another sphere above it, he would never have remained silent about this great discovery in his *Great Composition*. 

<margin>Johannes Saxoniensis is mocked.</margin> It is pleasing, moreover, to mock Johannes Saxoniensis <note>John of Saxony, a 14th-century astronomer known for his work on the Alfonsine Tables</note>, who, in his commentaries on Alchabitius <note>a 10th-century Arab astrologer</note>, strives to prove that signs of the ninth sphere must be used according to the opinion of Ptolemy. In confirmation of his opinion, he asserts certain words of Haly <note>Ali ibn Ridwan, a famous commentator on Ptolemy</note> regarding "bright" and "dark" degrees—which he believed were not the words of Haly, but of Ptolemy himself. However, those are the words of the commentator, not the author; anyone can easily understand this not only from the Greek copies but even from the common <note>Latin</note> translation. See what faith can be placed in these men regarding heavenly matters, when they are caught examining their own authors with such sleepy and blinking eyes! What of the fact that not only Ptolemy, but no one for more than a thousand years...

<page-num>VIII</page-num>

# Book VIII

<margin>Alfonso was the first to calculate the positions of the planets relative to a ninth sphere. The reason why the moderns were moved to this.</margin>
...[he] is found to have followed, using a ninth sphere. **Alfonso** <note>King Alfonso X of Castile, who sponsored the influential Alfonsine Tables in the 13th century</note> was the first to calculate the locations of the planets according to a ninth sphere, to which all the **moderns** <note>neotherici; refers to the medieval scholastic and Arabic astronomers</note> have adhered. The ancients used only the eighth. Even **Leo the Hebrew** <note>Gersonides, a 14th-century Jewish mathematician and philosopher</note> and **Proclus the Platonist**, both most excellent mathematicians, contend that the eighth is the highest of all. From this opinion, the moderns differ, asserting by no vain conjecture that another sphere is superior to the eighth; for two motions toward completely opposite parts cannot exist within the same body of its own nature. Therefore, since it has been discovered through true observation that the **wandering stars** <note>planets</note> do move from west to east <note>precession</note>, and yet that sphere with the rest is rolled from east to west <note>diurnal motion</note>, they think it necessarily follows that the former motion—which is completed in one revolution over many thousands of years—belongs to the nature of the sphere of the stars itself. The other motion, which is completed in the space of a single day, is shared with the eighth sphere by another and therefore higher globe, just as it is with the **planets** <note>original: "eronibus," a variant of "erronibus," meaning the planets or wanderers</note>, sweeping all the stars with it from east to west, even as they are carried by their own motions from west to east. This suspicion, born not from nothing, is nonetheless refuted by others in many ways.

<margin>Various solutions. First. Second. Leo the Hebrew. Third. Fourth.</margin>
For there are those who deny that the stars move from west to east—though there are certainly both observant men and mathematicians who say there is a single diurnal motion of the ether which is one and not divided into spheres but continuous; they say all stars, both fixed and wandering, are carried from west to east by their own motions. **Leo the Hebrew** attributes that motion to a certain lower sphere, not a higher one. Others, constituting the whole heaven as a kind of living being made of all the spheres as if they were limbs, say there is one motion: that which is owed to the whole heaven by some universal motor, while others are owed to the individual spheres according to their diversity by their own diverse motors. Therefore, that which we call the **diurnal motion**, since it is common to the other spheres, belongs no more to the eighth than to any other; rather, it arises from a certain common motor of the celestial universe. For this reason, it is not necessary to imagine another sphere to which that motion belongs, nor does it follow that the same sphere has two motions of its own, since one is granted from its commonality with the rest of heaven, and the other from its own nature, not by the same motor. Let us place all these things in the middle <note>i.e., present them for consideration without taking a side</note>, affirming only this: that nothing undisputed or certain can be asserted regarding these matters. Instead, the whole discussion returns to probable and **metaphorical** <term>translatitios; arguments adapted from one context to another, often lacking direct proof</term> arguments, many of which, being ambiguous on both sides, leave us at last in uncertainty. But if we think we must concede to the reasoning by which a ninth sphere is confirmed, we must also agree with those who have devised a tenth above the ninth, since the logic for both dogmas is nearly the same. For the former, to stubbornly defend the idea that no more than one motion belongs to one sphere of itself, introduced the ninth when they discovered the eighth was turned by a double motion. The latter, having detected a triple motion, were led by the same conjecture to introduce a tenth. **Alfonso**, **Campanus**, **Leopold**, and **Messahala** believed this; they also attribute this opinion (however falsely, as did Albert <note>Albertus Magnus</note> who followed it) to **Ptolemy**.

<margin>Alfonso. Campanus. Leopold. Messahala.</margin>

## Chapter II: If there is another sphere above the eighth, ancient astrology is false; if there is none, modern astrology is false; and even if there is a ninth, it is entirely necessary for it to collapse.

<margin>All ancient astrology falls if there are two spheres.</margin>
From such a varied and manifold variety of opinions, it is easy to see how uncertain the **divining art of astrology** <note>astrologia diuinatrix</note> is made. For if there are two other spheres above the eighth, all ancient astrology is false, for they relied on useless and imperfect observations, being ignorant of the most powerful parts of heaven. Since the spheres...

<page-num>VIII</page-num>

# Book VIII

...those spheres cannot be ineffective, since the highest excels the others in the speed of its motion, and excels in both the loftiness of its place and the vastness of its mass. If, on the other hand, there is no sphere beyond the eighth, then the entire astrology of the **moderns** <note>original: "iuniorum"; Pico refers to the medieval astronomers who followed the Alfonsine tables</note> is nothing; for you describe the twelve signs in the ninth orb: if that orb is non-existent, what authority will it have in determining fate?

Moreover, whether the ninth sphere exists or not, all astrology of our age is known to waver, not only from the inconsistency of the difference between calculations but from being controversial and self-contradictory. For let them answer me this: do they think that celestial influences <term>afflatus; the "breathing" or flowing of power from the stars to Earth</term> reach us from the entire sky? Or only from those parts that flash with visible light? 

First, if they concede the former—that the whole sky has influence—then by that reasoning not only the planets but also the orbs that carry the planets would be included in the participation of the fatal decree. Yet the astrologers do not observe these carrying-orbs; they think there is no efficacy in them for changes in the lower world. 

Second, if they answer that such power exists only in stars shining with a beam of visible light, they must also concede that no outflows <term>defluxus; the downward flow of astrological power</term> from the ninth sphere reach here; for it is either non-existent or endowed with invisible light, and is distinguished neither by stellar rays nor by any variety of lights. Rather, it is either completely transparent—whence it is called the **watery** or **crystalline heaven**—or it is spread with a light so thin and rare that it is as many believe of the other planetary globes. 

Therefore, either every sphere must be observed, <margin>Bonatus</margin> or that ninth one (even if it exists) must be disregarded. This is what **Bonatus** <note>Guido Bonatti, the most famous 13th-century astrologer, whose "Book of Astronomy" was a standard text</note> believed, affirming that nothing placed above the eighth sphere pertains to the astrologer. 

And yet, in that ninth sphere, the twelve signs are described by everyone; these signs have not just some, but the greatest authority in the year's constellation. This is not only regarding what they bestow by their own powers, but because, in the changing powers of the planets, the primary roles are assigned to the signs by everyone. 

Therefore, wherever they turn, they fall into inextricable traps: they either omit many spheres that should not be omitted, or by admitting one that is ineffective, they corrupt the truth of every constellation. Even if they were to extricate themselves from this, they will be held completely by an unbreakable bond. For even if we granted as much fixed virtue and efficacy as you wish to the ninth sphere, the predictions of all the **moderns** will still be proven false. For it cannot be denied that the virtue and property of that sphere is different from the influences of the eighth. 

Yet they, regarding the ninth as if it were the same as the eighth, have handed down nothing else regarding the signs of the ninth sphere than what had been handed down by the ancients regarding the signs of the eighth. This was certainly either from great stupidity or malice: either they did not see that the nature of different spheres cannot be the same, or seeing this, they nevertheless wished to persuade others of it. 

For it appears likely enough that they managed to deceive others because once the ninth sphere was devised, if they had to deal with the influence of a brand-new orb, their profession would necessarily have had to cease for many ages while the nature of the newly discovered orb was verified by many experiments. This is something that deceitful and ambitious men could by no means endure. Therefore, they transferred to the parts of the ninth sphere the same names by which the ancients called the parts of the eighth—as if the nature itself were communicated along with the name!—and they produced exactly the same dogmas about those signs that their predecessors had. 

Thus they describe **Aries**, **Taurus**, **Gemini**, **Cancer**, and the rest of the signs in the ninth sphere, and they say they do the same things which the ancients wrote were done by signs of the same name, but in a different sphere: that is, the whole... <note>The text cuts off here at the catchword "totam", indicating the start of the next page</note>

<summary>Pico argues that modern astrology is logically bankrupt because it assigns the powers of the ancient zodiac (8th sphere) to a newly-invented 9th sphere without any experimental proof, simply to save the profession from obsolescence.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Pico’s critique of the "ninth sphere." He argues that modern astrologers are committing a logical and physical error by applying ancient rules (written for the fixed stars of the eighth sphere) to an invisible ninth sphere. <page-num>VIII</page-num>

<margin>The difference between the ninth and eighth spheres is no less than that between Jupiter and Saturn.</margin>
...defending an imposture solely by a shared use of names. In this matter, if they are deceiving us, it is a crime; if they are themselves deceived, it is madness. They err no differently than if they were to transfer the name of Jupiter to Saturn and then believe that Saturn had actually become Jupiter; and when they ought to be prophesying about Saturn, they instead announce those things which the ancients taught that Jupiter portends. For we should not consider the difference between the eighth and ninth orbs to be less than that between Jupiter and Saturn, if we evaluate both their motions and the quality of their light—the primary ways by which celestial bodies are distinguished. For between those two planets, the only apparent difference is that one is slower than the other, and that the light of one is either darker or brighter than the light of the other. 

But how much greater is the difference between those spheres! One of them <note>The eighth sphere of the fixed stars</note> moves by its own nature with the slowest motion, while the other <note>The ninth sphere, or Primum Mobile</note> is carried along with the swiftest motion of all. Furthermore, the one is radiant and conspicuous with a manifold army of stars, while the other, having either no light or only invisible light, does not fall under our gaze or eyes. Finally, if they claim a vastly different efficacy for different parts and even tiny subdivisions of the same sphere, how can the efficacy of entirely different spheres be the same? And if two spheres had the same nature, would not God, the craftsman of nature, have made one of them in vain? 

And if, as I have said, they do not agree in motion, nor light, nor position, nor mass, what other commonality of nature is there between them? Let the machine of the universe be examined on all sides: in all the globes of the elements or the heavens, a manifest diversity will always appear. Therefore, if a ninth orb has been devised unlike the others, it must necessarily be of a different nature from the eighth. Thus, the instructions that **Ptolemy** and other ancients gave concerning the signs and parts of the eighth sphere cannot possibly apply to the signs of the ninth sphere. Yet, since all the **moderns** <note>original: "iuniores"; referring to medieval astrologers who adapted Ptolemy's work to new astronomical tables</note> do exactly this, their prophecies—even if they were practicing a true art—can only strike upon the truth by mere chance.

### Chapter III: That the images differ from the signs, although they share the same names.

<margin>u</margin>
But indeed, whatever is decided concerning the number of the spheres, we shall briefly demonstrate that the twelve signs themselves—to which both the ancients and the moderns attribute so much that the sum and hinge of all astrological prediction turns upon them—are actually fictional and non-existent. Furthermore, even if those signs were real, we shall show that the astrologers have handed down false and conflicting dogmas about them; therefore, those divinations which depend on them (and indeed they all do) are utterly deceptive. 

But it is first necessary to advise the reader that the twelve **signs** are one thing, and the **images** <term>imagines; the actual visible constellations or groups of stars</term> are another, even though they agree in number and name. I say that these are entirely different things, even according to those who—either ignoring or neglecting the ninth sphere—place the division of the signs in the same space where the forms of the images are conceived. For the **signs** are established as immobile and fixed, bounded by the **equinoxes** and **solstices**; thus the beginning of the sign of **Aries** is always taken from the vernal equinox. However, the beginning of the **image** of Aries is calculated elsewhere at different times, just as the stars from which it is formed are continually carried from west to east <note>This refers to the precession of the equinoxes, where the stars appear to move slowly in relation to the seasonal points</note>. In this matter, a large part of the astrologers have slipped, thinking that because they relate the planets to the eighth sphere, they must necessarily use moving signs. For they did not understand the words of **Ptolemy** in the first book of his *Apotelesmatika* <note>original: "apoteleſ."; the Greek title for Ptolemy's *Tetrabiblos*</note>, who held the contrary view. His words in Latin are as follows: "Let us not overlook this, which is worthy of note: since..."

<meta>This page continues Pico della Mirandola's systematic dismantling of astrological theory. Having previously argued that astrologers confuse the eighth sphere (the fixed stars) with the ninth sphere (a mathematical construct), he now focuses on the "twelve signs" of the zodiac, arguing they are human inventions for measurement rather than physical realities with inherent powers.</meta>

# Book VIII

And it is reasonable to set the beginnings of the <term>twelve signs<note>original: "dodecathemorum." From the Greek for "twelve parts."</note></term>—that is, the twelve signs of the zodiac—and their "limits" or "terms" <note>In astrology, "terms" (fines) are specific degrees within a sign traditionally ruled by different planets.</note> at the tropical and equinoctial points; this is also what the most important writers have indicated. For from what we have said above, it is clear that their natures, powers, and relationships have their cause in the tropical and equinoctial points, and not in anything else. Therefore, if we establish other starting points, we would be forced either to stop using the natures of those signs in our predictions, or, if we do use them, we would fail to reach the truth because the intervals of the zodiac, from which their powers arise, would be discarded and altered. This is the opinion of Ptolemy <note>Claudius Ptolemy (c. 100–170 AD), the most influential astronomer and astrologer of antiquity.</note>, whose view
<margin>Second difference.</margin>
had to be explained before it was refuted, since it has been poorly understood or ignored by very many people. The first difference is therefore clear: between the "images" and the "signs." The former <note>The images or constellations</note> move, while the latter <note>The mathematical signs</note> do not move. Even if the signs are described as being in the eighth sphere <note>The sphere of the fixed stars.</note>, there is a second, most evident difference: the images have unequal sizes, whereas the signs are equal to one another. Each of the signs contains thirty degrees, but among the images, some stretch across fewer degrees and others across many more. Since, therefore, the signs are one thing and the images another, we shall refute both with their own specific reasons. And first, we shall inquire concerning those
<margin>By no reason can it be demonstrated that there are twelve signs distinct in power.</margin>
signs: what reason demonstrated to the astrologers that there are twelve distinct natures there, different in their powers and properties—and why exactly twelve, neither more nor fewer? Abraham Ibn Ezra <note>original: "Abraam auenazra." A 12th-century Jewish polymath and astrologer.</note>, at the beginning of his *Book of Reasons*, says that some things said about the signs are proven, while others are established by arbitrary choice. Immediately declaring which of these are most prominently put forward as arbitrary, he mentions the division of the zodiac. For he asks: why are the divisions of the signs set specifically at 360 parts? Because this number is more convenient for divisions. Ali ibn Ridwan <note>original: "Haly auenrodan." An 11th-century Egyptian physician and commentator on Ptolemy.</note> writes the same thing when explaining Ptolemy's books on the effects of the stars: "We have divided the circle into twelve parts, which are called signs, and each sign into thirty parts, which are called degrees, and any thirtieth part into sixty minutes, because these numbers are found to be more suitable for divisions." With what better words can I bring them to account than their own? They are so ignorant of the nature of things and the consequences of reason that, because those who measure the movements of the stars divided the circle into twelve parts for the convenience of the number, they have established a dogma from this. They claim those twelve parts possess various powers and properties, as if their distinction arose from the nature of the heaven itself, rather than from the choice of mathematicians. It happens that if they are described as being in the eighth sphere—as Ptolemy, the Egyptians, and all the masters of the signs intended—no physical reality or solidity of nature corresponds to them; they can only be 
<margin>Origen.</margin>
conceived and grasped by the mind. For this reason, Origen <note>A 3rd-century Christian theologian who engaged deeply with Greek science.</note>, steeped in the teachings of the Egyptians, called these signs "intelligible" <note>Meaning "perceptible only to the intellect," rather than "sensible" or physically visible.</note> and perceivable by reason alone. For there is no part of the eighth sphere in which an equinox or a solstice always occurs; rather, they occur in different parts at different times, just as that sphere is carried along by its own motion from west to east <note>A reference to the precession of the equinoxes, where the stars seem to drift away from the equinoctial points over centuries.</note>. Therefore, those points in which we understand an equinox or solstice to always occur depend on no physical reality, but on our thought alone. These points can certainly serve mathematicians for finding the motions and calculating the positions of the planets, but they cannot be established as the origins of virtues or the principles of any "influences."

He cites astrological authorities like Ibn Ezra and Ibn Ridwan to show that even they admit the 360-degree system was chosen for its mathematical properties, not its natural reality.</summary>

# Book VIII

<margin>
A greatest argument for the inconsistency of this art.
</margin>

The <term>Chaldeans<note>In this context, "Chaldeans" refers generally to ancient Babylonian astrologers, often cited as the founders of the craft.</note></term>, in their observations, used the images of the sun but did not use the mathematical "signs" in their predictions. From this, the great weakness and inconsistency of this art is clearly recognized: for those things which the consensus of astrologers considers to be its first and strongest foundations, the followers of the Chaldean profession—who were the most famous in predicting the future—regarded as nothing at all. <term>Haly Abenrodan<note>Also known as Ali ibn Ridwan (c. 988–1061), an Egyptian Muslim physician and astrologer whose commentaries on Ptolemy were standard textbooks in the Middle Ages.</note></term>, noticing this to some extent, says: "The signs are <term>mansions<note>original: "mansiones." Dwellings or specific sectors of the sky where planets 'reside.'</note></term> that do nothing; rather, it is the fixed stars within them that act." But then, why does the sun run through them all every year? And why do they receive their names from the operations that the sun performs while positioned within them? Likewise, concerning the fixed stars that are in the same part of a sign: if their power remains, then for the entire time—whether a hundred years according to the ancients or seventy according to more recent writers <note>This refers to the rate of "precession," the slow shift of the stars relative to the equinoxes. Ancient astronomers debated how many years it took for the stars to move one degree.</note>—the power of that sign would be the same as the power of the star dwelling there. But if the star were moved to another part, its power would also be transferred to that other part. These are his words. Indeed, his opinion—both from what has been cited and from his words elsewhere—is known to be this: the parts of the zodiac themselves, if the influence of the stars is excluded, have no power to produce effects. However, when they say that one sign has one property and influence and another has another, they claim this truth is based on two reasons: either because

<margin>
Haly Abenrodan, Claudius Ptolemy, and others. <unclear>A few things</unclear>.
</margin>

the stars meeting in that part of the sign are endowed with such power that the efficacy of the "guest" becomes that of the "host" <note>An astrological metaphor: a planet (the guest) takes on the character of the sign (the host) it is currently occupying.</note>; or because the sun, arriving at that sign, performs such works. In this way, the <term>equinoctial signs<note>Aries and Libra, where the day and night are equal.</note></term> and the <term>solstitial signs<note>Cancer and Capricorn, marking the longest and shortest days.</note></term>—namely Aries, Cancer, Libra, and Capricorn—are called "movable" because the sun, positioned in them, changes the season of the year. In contrast, the signs next to them are "fixed," because during the time of the year the sun traverses them, the state and quality of the air do not change. Similarly, Ptolemy says that Aries causes thunder and lightning not because of any power situated in that part of the zodiac, but because when the sun is placed in Aries, it is the vernal equinox; this time of year, by its own quality, stirs up changes of this kind in the air. For the heat of the sun approaching us dissolves the moisture of the immediately preceding winter and raises many vapors; when clouds are formed from these and run into one another, their mutual collisions emit flashes of lightning. This is Haly Abenrodan’s opinion on the power of the signs, and nothing could more strongly confirm what we wanted to show: namely, that the parts of the zodiac intercepted by the equinoxes and solstices—in which Ptolemy says the principal power consists, and which all astrologers except the Chaldeans use—have no power of their own to produce effects. For while Abenrodan desires to explain and declare Ptolemy’s opinion, he "drowns his thread in the river of truth," so to speak, and—even if unwillingly—completely obliterates and wipes it out. For he asserts that the parts of the circle effect nothing, and that the things thought to be done by them are actually stirred up by the operation of either the sun or the stars acting in those parts. But in truth, the Egyptians, Ptolemy, and the whole crowd of astrologers ascribe permanent and immobile properties to the signs, which do not fade away or change even if the sun or stars depart. Otherwise, Ptolemy ought to have handed down a different nature of the signs than what had been delivered long ago by the Egyptians. But even those who came after Ptolemy should have written something different if the power of the signs changes as the stars migrate. Yet not even a syllable has been changed; the same things regarding the nature of the signs are produced by those who wrote recently as were found in the works of <term>Petosiris and Nechepso<note>original: "Petosiras & Cechipsos." Legendary founders of Hellenistic astrology (2nd century BC) to whom many foundational texts were attributed.</note></term>. Yet it ought to happen that the properties which once belonged to Aries should eventually belong to Taurus, and those which were of Scorpio should at some time belong to Sagittarius, and so on for the rest, since [the stars move].

<summary>Pico argues that astrologers like Haly Abenrodan and Ptolemy inadvertently admit that the "signs" of the zodiac have no inherent power, attributing celestial effects instead to the sun's seasonal heat or the fixed stars. This creates a logical crisis for astrology: if the stars move but the definitions of the signs remain static since ancient Egypt, the entire system becomes obsolete.</summary>

# Book VIII

<margin>
Astrologers are ignorant of logic. They rave like children.
</margin>

The stars that once ran their course in **Aries** are now moving into **Taurus**, and those which once occupied **Scorpio** will, with the passage of time, migrate toward **Sagittarius**. Now, regarding what is said about the sun—<note>original: "iesu bone"</note> good Jesus!—how vain and trifling it is that an effect is attributed to a "sign" when it actually proceeds from the power of the sun positioned there, and not from the sign itself. This is almost as if they said a chair inspires the power of debating because a philosopher sitting in it is accustomed to debate; and likewise, as if they expected <term>syllogisms<note>Logical arguments where a conclusion is drawn from two premises.</note></term> from a footstool because of the person sitting on it. In this same way, because the sun placed in Aries stirs up thunder and changes the winter's frost with the spring temperature, the "planet-watchers" <note>Astrologers.</note> decree that when the moon is in Aries, thunder is to be expected, and that Aries is the author of **mobility** <note>In this context, "mobility" refers to changeability or the initiation of new states.</note> in all things. Nor do they notice that if thunder occurs when the sun is in Aries, the same does not follow for the moon and other planets. This is because that effect comes not from the nature of the sign, but from the heat of the sun, which lifts up watery vapors to the heights—the material of clouds—from which thunder and other things of that kind are later produced. Since this power of heat is not in other stars, what is caused by the sun will not be caused by them, even if they are placed in the same sign. For the fact that the sun does this more in Aries than in Aquarius is not due to the properties of the signs, but the position of the place; namely, that in Aries it is closer to us. Therefore, things near us are more affected by its rays during that time, and thus, placed in the same sign, it effects different things in different regions during that time. But they do not know the first rudiments of <term>dialectics<note>The art of logical reasoning and investigation of truth through discussion.</note></term>, in which we are taught to distinguish what is essential from what is accidental. I only wish they were merely poor logicians and did not clearly rave like children. For who would not call it insanity rather than error to think that—because the season of the year changes when the sun is in Aries (let us stick with that example)—therefore whatever you begin while the moon is positioned there will not be steady or firm, but fluid and changeable? And because, while the sun occupies **Leo**, in the middle of summer, the quality of the air does not change but remains the same, they think Leo is a "fixed sign"; therefore, they think whatever one begins under it will be long-lasting and immovable. From this comes that marvelous dogma: while the moon is traveling through Leo, one should neither put on new clothes for the first time nor cut them. They say that due to the quality of the "fixed sign," those clothes will last a long time—by which meaning it seems either a disease or some other evil cause is implied, on account of which you cannot use them. For clothes that you actually use cannot help but be worn out and cannot last forever. Who, hearing these things, could not help but think they were either invented by storytellers for a laugh or are the ravings of the insane? Or by what arts will those people be removed from their errors, to whom such things can seem not only not absurd, but true? Philosophers, when debating with those who feel no shame and resist even the first principles at first sight, are accustomed to force them into their own overthrow—that is, to show that what they say is not so much firmly proven as it is self-contradictory. And so let us attack them by the same path, since it does not seem absurd to them that Aries has the power of making things "mobile" just because the sun entering it changes the season of the year. Let us at least obtain this from them: that they do not move from their position, as if they were born under Aries, but hold and defend their dogma. If they do so, we ask them: are these signs—which they call "mobile," "fixed," and "double"—themselves immovable? Or do they move along with the constellations <note>The actual groupings of stars in the sky.</note>? If they answer that they are mobile, then they themselves are moved away from their own signs. For to initiate summer, autumn, winter, and spring is the characteristic not of mobile signs, but of immovable ones; and the properties they give to the signs—that they are mobile, fixed, or double—are derived from the aforementioned variety of the seasons. Therefore, not for others...

<summary>Pico ridicules astrologers for attributing seasonal changes to the zodiac signs themselves rather than the physical heat and proximity of the sun. He argues that their failure to distinguish between essential causes and accidental associations makes their "science" a form of logical insanity.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Pico della Mirandola’s critique of astrology from Book VIII. He is currently arguing that astrologers commit a logical fallacy by confusing mathematical "signs" of the zodiac with the actual constellations or "images" they are named after.</meta>

<page-num>VIII</page-num>

# Book VIII

They seek these properties for the signs, which are always imagined as immovable within their designated places in the circle. But if they say these signs are immovable, it follows that they no longer align with the location of the **images** <note>The "images" are the actual groups of stars (constellations), whereas "signs" are the twelve 30-degree divisions of the sky used by astrologers.</note>, which have shifted their positions along with their stars over time. If this is the case, how can they justify attributing properties derived solely from the *shape* of the image to these different mathematical signs? 

Take **Aries**, for instance. They call it "movable" <note>Also known as a "cardinal" sign, marking the start of a season.</note>, "equinoctial," and "short-lived"—all of which are conditions of the immovable sign. Yet, in the next breath, they say it is "four-footed," "weak-eyed," and "lustful"—traits that belong to the figure of the ram (the image), not the sign itself. They use the same name for two things that differ in nature, location, and properties. 

And so I do not need to go through every single detail: the whole crowd of astrologers, when they divide the signs, label some as "common," others "fixed," and others "movable." Again, they call some "straight" and others "oblique." These are, as I said, conditions of the immovable signs. Yet they also use these distinctions: some signs are "human," others "feral," some "aquatic," others "terrestrial," some "mute," others "vocal," some "sterile," and others "fertile." All of these come from the **images**, not the signs; for these traits do not follow any mathematical position in the circle, but rather the nature, form, and likeness of the figure. 

What is this great sluggishness or sleepiness of mind, that they seem to mix and confuse such diverse things, deceived only by a shared name rather than by nature? Furthermore, that one sign is considered "hot," another "earthy," another "airy," and another "watery," is a concept certainly taken from the images and transferred with the same recklessness to the signs. If the state of the circle were considered based on its immovable points, Aries should be judged "airy"—that is, hot and moist—rather than "fiery" (hot and dry), since the spring opens with a hot and moist quality. 

Even **Ptolemy** <note>Claudius Ptolemy (c. 100–170 AD), the most influential astronomer and astrologer of antiquity.</note>, when giving the reason why we usually begin the year with Aries in a circle that has no beginning, answers that it is because in the first age of all things, moisture abounds, which is the quality of the spring that we begin with Aries. So then, O Ptolemy: if Aries is the first sign because moisture is owed to the first age, do you think it is a dry sign or a moist one? If it is dry, then it is not the first; if it is moist, why is it called "fiery" by your people? 

Finally, as I intended to prove, these distinctions of cold, dry, hot, and moist distributed among the signs seem to be accepted from the condition of the **images** rather than from the signs. Even **Auenazra** <margin>Auenazra</margin> <note>Abraham ibn Ezra (c. 1089–1167), a celebrated Jewish scholar and astrologer.</note> confesses this in his *Book of Astrological Reasons*. For thus they established **Cancer**, **Scorpio**, and **Pisces** as cold, having weighed the nature of the animals whose names they bear. For the same reason, they called **Aries**, **Leo**, and **Sagittarius** hot. They called **Gemini** and **Aquarius** "airy" because of their human likeness, as that quality dominates most in humans. Likewise, they called **Taurus**, **Capricorn**, and **Virgo** "earthy," both because of the power of their sex and, in the case of Virgo, because of the ear of grain she carries in her hand. 

Therefore, they attributed this power, taken from the various properties of the images, to the signs. In this matter, the good Ptolemy does not merely nod off; he wanders completely astray, moving back and forth from the sign to the image in the same passage. I shall demonstrate this clearly, along with the unpardonable error of **Haly** <note>Ali ibn Ridwan (c. 988–1061), an Egyptian physician and astrologer who commented on Ptolemy.</note> in explaining Ptolemy’s words. 

Ptolemy's words in the second book of his <term>Apotelesmaton<note>Ptolemy's *Tetrabiblos*, the foundational text of Western astrology.</note></term> are these: "The <term>dodecathemorion<note>A 'twelfth-part' or sign of the zodiac.</note></term> of Aries is generally thunderous and hailing." <note>original Greek: βροντώδες και χαλαζώδες</note>. That is: "In detail, however, these things happen more or less according to the nature and property of the stars that are within it." <note>original Greek: το δε μερος γενοιτο μαλλον απο της του κριου των πλανωμενων αστερων ιδιοτητος</note>. And he adds: "For its preceding part causes rains and winds; the middle part a temperate atmosphere; and the final part heat and pestilence. Then, those parts which turn toward the North cause heat and corruption; those toward the South cause frost..."

He highlights contradictions in the works of Ptolemy, Ibn Ezra, and Haly regarding whether signs like Aries are moist or fiery.</summary>
