<meta>This page continues Pico della Mirandola's systematic deconstruction of astrological logic. He has been arguing that astrologers mistakenly attribute the characteristics of physical star-groups (images/constellations) to the abstract mathematical divisions of the sky (signs). Here, he focuses on how precession—the slow shift of stars relative to the seasons—proves that these two concepts have become detached, rendering traditional astrological "rules" for signs like Aries and Taurus scientifically invalid.</meta>

<page-num>VIII</page-num>

...equinoctial and somewhat cold. I interpret these words of Ptolemy in this way: that what he pronounces regarding **Aries** in general refers to the immovable sign in that location. This cannot be denied, since that is the place where the equinox occurs. For this reason, Ptolemy said it was thundering <note>original: "βροντωδεσ" (brontodes)</note> and hailing <note>original: "χαλαζιωδεσ" (chalaziodes)</note>, because all these weather patterns usually arise before the spring season. Furthermore, regarding what he adds subsequently about the differing effects of its parts according to the nature of the stars existing within them: **Haly** <note>Haly Abenragel, an influential 11th-century Arab astrologer whose commentaries on Ptolemy were standard textbooks in the Renaissance.</note> believes this is also said of the parts of the *sign*, as I will soon demonstrate. However, I will show more clearly than daylight, from Ptolemy himself, that this was said of the **image** <note>The "image" is the actual group of stars forming the shape of the Ram, while the "sign" is the 30-degree mathematical slice of the sky.</note>. As much as Ptolemy erred in establishing this dogma, Haly erred just as much in his explanation of Ptolemy. Haly thinks Ptolemy's words should be understood thus: that the stars Ptolemy claims are in those parts were actually in those parts of the *sign* at the time he was writing; and that the property belonged to the sign then, but as the stars shifted to a new location over time, the property would be transferred elsewhere. This interpretation by Haly might seem plausible if Ptolemy had done for other signs what he did for Aries—specifically, if he had not provided the names of the stars he places in those parts. But since in **Taurus** he explicitly names certain stars, he reveals both his own error and the error of his interpreter simultaneously. This is because those stars, in Ptolemy's time, were not in the part of the *sign* where he places them, but rather in the part of the **image** 

<margin>Words of Ptolemy.</margin>
in which they are, were, and always shall be. His words regarding **Taurus** are as follows: "The sign of Taurus generally brings both qualities of air [warm and cold]; it is, however, somewhat warm. Specifically, the preceding parts—especially where the **Pleiades** are—stir up earthquakes, winds, and 

<margin>Pleiades.</margin>
clouds; the following parts, where the **Hyades** are, cause lightning and thunderbolts."

<margin>Hyades. The Vergiliae.</margin>
Come now, who does not see that these things are said by Ptolemy regarding the **image**? In its "preceding" parts are those stars which our people call the *Vergiliae* <note>The Roman name for the Pleiades, often associated with the start of the growing season.</note>; in the "following" parts are the Hyades, for which the name **Aldebaran** <note>Aldebaran is the brightest star in Taurus; Pico is noting that different translations use different names for the same celestial region.</note> is read in the common translation. The Hyades are located in the crown, the horns, and the whole head; the Pleiades, however, are between the end of the bull's body and the tail of Aries (a place they call the "point of cutting off"). These occupy the preceding and following parts respectively because the constellation of the Bull rises and sets backward. But if these descriptions were applied to the *signs*, there would be no truth in them: in Ptolemy’s time, the Pleiades were not in the *sign* of Taurus at all, but in Aries. This is easily recognized by anyone from his *Great Composition* <note>Known today by its Arabic title, the *Almagest*, this was Ptolemy's definitive work on astronomy.</note>. Since Haly ought to have read that work—and surely did not doubt that the same man wrote both books—I cannot marvel enough at how he hallucinated so badly in such an obvious matter. He explained Ptolemy's words as being about the location of stars in the signs, and left it written that the Pleiades were in the first parts of Taurus at that time. This error was followed by Haly, **Leopold** <note>Leopold of Austria, a 13th-century astronomer.</note>, and the "Ascadensian" <note>John of Eschenden, a 14th-century English astrologer and author of the *Summa Anglicana*.</note> in the work they call the *English Summa*, and finally by later writers like **Bonatus** <note>Guido Bonatti, the most famous Italian astrologer of the 13th century.</note>. But the greater error of these men is that they follow Haly in saying Ptolemy spoke of stars placed in those specific parts of the sign, yet they do not update the positions; they say the same thing as Ptolemy even though the stars have shifted by more than twenty degrees since his time. Thus, what we wished to prove is clear: astrologers imprudently contradict themselves by mixing up the properties of signs and images (if such properties even exist) as if they do not differ in location, nature, or parts.

But come now, even if the signs have no power, are the **images** themselves actually anything? For perhaps here the astrologers will not seem to be raving, nor to rely on fictional things and arbitrary...

He argues that while stars themselves are real and natural, the shapes we impose upon them—like the Ram or the Lyre—are purely human inventions, varying by culture and whim, and therefore cannot be the source of objective "powers" or "influences."</meta>

# Book VIII
## F ii

<margin>Pedro de <unclear>Luna</unclear></margin>
<note>original: "Pedro de Luna" — likely a reference to Antipope Benedict XIII or a specific contemporary commentary Pico is refuting.</note>

...contraries, when those images, each with its own lights, stars, and rays according to the nature of the power of the stars, have very great influence, who will deny it? But I do not doubt at all that the astrologers are raving here; since even if the stars from which the images are fabricated are both true and natural, nevertheless that very constitution of the images from the stars is neither true nor natural, but false and entirely imaginary according to the whim of those fabricating them, and without any hope of probability. For who will not immediately judge: that if the power of one star is great, that of many conspiring together as one would not be greatest? But reason, returning to itself, sees that there is nothing there except the "conspiracy" of the stars mentioned by us. For certainly there is no mixture by fusion <term>coalitus</term> <note>A technical term in Aristotelian physics referring to things growing together or fusing into a single substance.</note> there: how then do many stars, distinct in nature and separated by the immense vastness of great spaces, unite into one property?

I know what they will answer: that they come together in that likeness of one image, which is evidence of some occult affinity; so that just as a single figure is drawn from one species, so there might be one native property in these from all those of the same thing. But indeed, this might perhaps be something (though it would not achieve what they want), if those images appeared there expressed and perfected with very true markings; but since they are fashioned by our own judgment—as I shall show—and it is just as convenient for anyone to form for themselves tigers and elephants there as it is dogs and hares (as they wish), it is clear that the argument taken from the figure is, like the rest of the astrologers' <unclear>fost</unclear> <note>The OCR 'fost' is likely a fragment of "commenta" (fictions) or "facta" (deeds/claims).</note>, vain, arbitrary, and legendary. But if they contend that those figures exist there not by the whim of those looking, but by nature, I will not appeal to the reliability of experience so much as to the reasons and testimonies of the astrologers themselves. For **Abraham Abenazra** <note>Abraham Ibn Ezra (c. 1089–1167), a celebrated Jewish scholar and astrologer whose work Pico frequently cites to point out internal contradictions in astrology.</note>, an authority of great weight among them, in the second edition of *On Astrological Reasons* (for he wrote two books on the same subject), being about to give an account of these images, writes in these words:

<margin>That different people fabricated different images for themselves in the same place.</margin>

"Which we have translated thus according to the sense: **Ptolemy** calls the 'falling vulture' <note>original: "vulturem cadentem" — an ancient name for the constellation Lyra, based on the star Vega.</note> the **Lyre**; nor is it surprising, since just as anyone can change the figure for himself, so also the name. For the heaven is spherical; therefore there is nothing in it why you should establish the beginning of something in this place rather than another; but just as some stars are joined to others by the eyes according to one's judgment, so different images are made. We, therefore, shall relate them in the way they have been handed down." These are his words. 

Nothing can confirm my opinion more truly and effectively: since there is nowhere a beginning or an end in the parts of a circle, you can start an image for yourself from whatever star you prefer, and also end it at whichever you wish. Nor is there any doubt that, through the diversity of the beginning and the boundaries you have prescribed for yourself, and through the number of stars you have either included or excluded, you will forge various images from the same material—especially since one person represents different forms to himself from these same stars, as Abraham declared regarding the vulture and the lyre, and you can declare the same regarding others. For they did not even agree on the number of those more celebrated images of the zodiac; but while some made twelve, the **Chaldeans** <note>A common Renaissance term for ancient Babylonian astrologers.</note> made eleven of them, constituting one out of **Libra** and **Scorpio** <note>In older systems, Scorpio's claws were considered the scales of Libra, making them a single constellation.</note>. For what forbids it, since an equal power of "daring anything" <note>A reference to Horace’s *Ars Poetica*: "Painters and poets have always had an equal right to dare anything."</note> is granted to all in this celestial painting? And even **Albumasar** <note>Abu Ma'shar (787–886), a leading Persian astrologer of the Middle Ages.</note> himself, who professes to give reasons for the dogmas of astrology in all things, when he comes to the images, brought forward no other reason than that **Aratus** <note>Greek poet (c. 315–240 BC) whose poem *Phaenomena* described the constellations; Pico considers him a writer of myths rather than a scientist.</note> described them thus—as if Aratus were not the most legendary of all, he who (as **Cicero** says) [wrote] astrological...

<summary>Pico argues that constellations (celestial images) are arbitrary human inventions rather than natural physical realities, citing the fact that different cultures and astrologers like Ptolemy and Ibn Ezra disagree on their shapes, names, and even the total number of signs in the zodiac.</summary>

# Book VIII

<margin>
See this outstanding madness.
</margin>
...someone wrote a celestial alphabet <note>Pico is likely referring to the *Alphabet of Akiba* or similar Kabbalistic works that claim the Hebrew letters can be seen in the arrangements of the stars.</note> while being utterly ignorant of astrology. For if you compare the sphere of Aratus <note>Aratus was a Greek poet whose work *Phaenomena* described the constellations; his "sphere" represents the classical Greek celestial map.</note> with the "barbaric" sphere <note>The "barbaric sphere" refers to non-Greek astronomical traditions, such as those of the Egyptians, Babylonians, or Hebrews.</note>, you will see that they often disagree and clash with one another. These shapes are fashioned according to human whim and painted upon the heavens; they rest upon no solidity of doctrine or reason. The masters of the Hebrews, just as the astrologers find their images, strive to find their own "alphabet" in the stars—that is, the marks and elements of their own language. If they happen upon credulous eyes, they can persuade people of this no less plausibly than astrologers can persuade people about their images. What more can be said? Every form and every figure is there, and yet no form or figure is there at all; they all exist by the power and will of men, but none by the act of nature or truth. 

If our "diviners" had at least fixed some likenesses of great and sublime things there in the narrow spaces of the sky, I might be more easily led to believe they were the works of God rather than human works contrary to nature. But when I consider His counsel and wisdom, I do not see why He would not have, or could not have, marked that temple of divinity—those halls of heaven—with better images than those of irrational animals, monsters, or even lifeless things. For what is there besides bears, dragons, hares, and dogs? And things which are inanimate, such as arrows, ships, and triangles? Add to this severed heads flowing with gore and madness, and a maiden relegated to torture <note>This refers to the constellation Andromeda, who in mythology was chained to a rock as a sacrifice.</note>—to say nothing of the Hydra and the Centaur. If nature does not allow such things, why did she describe these patterns for herself in the heaven? Truly, I think it the greatest madness of all to be led to believe that these were formed there by the institution of nature and divine counsel. A good priest or a high-minded king would be ashamed not to have better paintings in his temple or palace. 

Otherwise, what was the counsel of Nature in establishing these? Was it so that she might govern lower bodies of the same kind through these superior images? Would she breathe celestial music into whichever men she wished via the Lyre? Would she generate and preserve those animals which are among us—which are born and perish daily—through the animals that are up there? Are monsters "opportune" there, though none exist in nature? And why are innumerable animals described there when no others are? For what privilege do dogs and bears have, that they should have two leaders or overseers in heaven, while elephants, tigers, and innumerable species of animals have no divine power in heaven by which they are ruled? But enough of these things; for a philosopher, it is not only shameful to believe them, but even unworthy to refute them.

<margin>
A Doubt.
The Response.
</margin>
But if someone should ask me why, in this license of fabrication, the supporters of astrology stooped to these images rather than others, I will respond that he seeks a rational question which is sought in vain in these matters, as they were established by no reason. However, it is easy to see what led them to many of these. For I think the names of the images ascribed to the parts of the Zodiac were derived from the works of the sun, which occur primarily when the sun is found in those parts. 

For example:
<margin>
Cancer. Leo.
Taurus.
Gemini.
Virgo. Aries.
Libra.
Scorpio.
Sagittarius.
Capricorn.
Aquarius. Pisces.
</margin>
The name **Cancer** [the Crab] was given to that part of the zodiac in which the sun, having been placed there, begins to retreat in the manner of a crab. 
The next part is **Leo** [the Lion] because of the excessive height of the heat. 
Another part is called **Taurus** [the Bull] because when the sun reaches it, the earth is plowed by oxen. 
**Gemini** [the Twins] follows it, because then all things are "germinating" <note>original: "germinando" — Pico is using a folk etymology, linking Gemini to the Latin word for budding or sprouting.</note> by budding. 
Under **Virgo** [the Virgin], the earth, parched by the sun's heat, brings forth nothing <note>The "Virgin" is here interpreted as "barren" or "unproductive" due to the late summer heat.</note>. 
Under **Aries** [the Ram], the fields are clothed in a "fleece" of flowers; for this reason they placed that animal at the "head" <note>original: "capiti" — Aries is the "head" or start of the astrological year.</note> because of the similarity to a head of hair. 
**Libra** [the Scales] equates the nights and days to one another, hanging them as if in a balance. 
When the sun reaches **Scorpio** [the Scorpion], then the air first stings with cold. 
Soon after, under **Sagittarius** [the Archer], it strikes us with the stings of more vehement colds and winds. 
In **Capricorn** [the Goat], the reason is manifest: because from there the sun begins to climb upward again like a goat. 
In **Aquarius** [the Water-bearer] and **Pisces** [the Fish], it pours out rains in abundance...

# Book VIII

...therefore: led by these sorts of similarities, they were able to manufacture these images rather than those in various parts of the sky, easily pulling the stars into the effigy of that nature whose name they were going to impose on that part for some reason. 

<margin>The fictions of the poets.</margin>
The fictions of the poets were added, many of them inventing for pleasure or to win favor; just as Conon the Egyptian mathematician first "saw" monsters and the hair from the head of Berenice <note>Conon of Samos was a court astronomer who claimed a lost lock of Queen Berenice II's hair had been placed among the stars, creating the constellation Coma Berenices.</note>. But it is not worth the effort to investigate more diligently and explore the insanities of others, as long as it is sufficiently clear to those who do not wish to be delusional that these are not the works of nature, but the trifles of inventors or the delusions of dreamers. So that finally I may rightly define these inventions: they arose from corrupt philosophy and the fables of poets, to which all astrologers nevertheless attribute as if they were the truest things and formed (so to speak) by the finger of God; so that it is scarcely believable into what superstitions this insanity has led them. 

<margin>Dogmas arising from those fictions.</margin>
"Do not give medicine," they say, "when the moon is placed in Taurus, because that animal ruminates; therefore the medicine will cause vomiting." "When you build a house, beware lest Scorpio occupies the fourth place, because many scorpions will abound in that house." He who is born when Corona <note>The "Northern Crown" constellation.</note> is rising will be a king; he [born] with Lyra [will be] a musician; and a thousand other things of this kind from which you may see that they were most thoroughly persuaded that the true effigies and natures of all these things are in heaven, from which wonderful powers flow down to us in decreeing fate. 

<margin>Whence the superstition of manufacturing images arose.</margin>
Finally, that whole superstition of manufacturing images <note>Pico refers here to the practice of making astrological talismans—medallions engraved with celestial symbols at specific times to capture star power.</note> sprouted from that insanity: namely, that by forming an image in some similar metal, they think the metal is breathed upon by that celestial virtue. However, these figures are neither in heaven, nor if they were, would they descend here because of that carved image; and even if they did descend, it would profit us nothing, as Averroes proves against Algazel <note>A reference to the philosophical debate between Averroes (Ibn Rushd) and Al-Ghazali regarding the nature of causality and the influence of the heavens.</note>. But we will discuss these matters more extensively in a specific treatise later.

### Chapter VI: That the invisible images are known neither by sense nor by reason, and that their authors—who were not Chaldeans or Indians, but only Arabs—fight among themselves.

<margin>d</margin>
Someone might certainly wonder at the insanity of the astrologers in manufacturing the most fabulous images which we have attacked so far, if they had not dreamed up others much more ridiculous. For they report that in each decan <note>A "decan" is a ten-degree subdivision of a Zodiac sign. Each sign has three decans, often associated with specific mystical imagery.</note> or "face" of any sign there are certain images—invisible, to be sure, but consisting of the solidity of the truest nature; those who hear this cannot help but break into laughter. 

<margin>Look at these most fabulous trifles.</margin>
They are of this kind: In the first face of Cancer, they say, there ascends a handsome youth, well-dressed, but having something of crookedness in his face and fingers, with the rest of his body like a horse and elephant, with white feet, hanging various kinds of grain and leaves of trees above himself. In the first face of Leo there ascends a tree of a very high root, in whose branches a dog sits, and a man dressed in noble but filthy clothes, weeping, and sad about his parents. Others similar to these in other decans of the signs are described by them.

<margin>Abu Ma'shar.</margin>
Of all these things, as if they were most effective matters, Abu Ma'shar <note>Abu Ma'shar (787–886), known in the West as Albumasar, was the most influential Persian astrologer of the Middle Ages.</note> makes mention in the sixth book of his *Great Introduction*. Ibn Ezra <note>Abraham ibn Ezra (c. 1089–1167), a celebrated Jewish scholar and astrologer.</note> mentions them in that book to which he gave the title *The Beginning of Wisdom*. 

<margin>Pietro d'Abano, Michael Scot.</margin>
Pietro d'Abano, Michael Scot <note>D'Abano (1250–1316) and Scot (c. 1175–1232) were major medieval scholars who integrated Arabic astrological traditions into Latin science.</note>, and many Arab and Latin astrologers mention them. When I had heard a little about these things long ago, I thought they indicated by these images what any decan of a sign would do; not that they thought these figures were actually there in heaven. But approaching their books, I recognized it was far otherwise. For they think and assert and contend that these images are most truly in those decans, the makers of wonderful effects among us. Indeed, Albumasar says they occasionally perform things similar to their forms: but often...

<summary>Pico criticizes the belief that constellations and astrological "decans" have inherent natural power, dismissing them as poetic fictions and psychological delusions. He specifically mocks the bizarre, invisible imagery associated with the decans by medieval astrologers like Abu Ma'shar and Ibn Ezra.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Pico della Mirandola’s systematic dismantling of astrological claims. Having previously mocked the arbitrary nature of the zodiac constellations themselves, he now turns his focus to the "faces" or "decans"—smaller ten-degree subdivisions of the signs—arguing that the images associated with them are inconsistent, culturally biased, and ultimately fictional.</meta>

# Book VIII

<margin>Mockery of this fiction.</margin>
...and other things entirely different: And if lynxes <note>Lynxes were proverbially famous for their keen eyesight in the Renaissance; Pico argues that even supernatural vision could not see what astrologers claim to see.</note> had established this dogma, I might be led in some way to doubt whether things had been open to their eyes which escape our own sight. But when these men spread abroad such admirable mysteries, I find no faith that can support them, since they have no other eyes than those men usually have. Yet men do not see these things; we do not read that they were snatched up into heaven with a philosopher, nor could any reason demonstrate these things to those situated on earth. Those who call themselves philosophers should blush; they are not ashamed to write down such trifles, which an old woman could scarcely persuade a two-year-old infant to believe as fables.

<margin>Discord among astrologers regarding these invisible images.</margin>
Add to this that they do not all imagine the same images, but some imagine one thing and others another. Here, indeed, one says that in the first face of Aries <note>A "face" or "decan" is a 10-degree segment of a zodiac sign. Each sign has three.</note> a woman rises, resplendent with light, having the tail of a sea fish. Another says there is no beautiful woman there, nor a fish, but an Ethiopian, about whose eyes there is doubt as to whether they are black or rather red; he is of a certain stature and is clothed in a white cloak. In the third face of Gemini, some say there rises a golden pipe, a barking dog, and a dolphin. Others contend that none of these things are there, but rather a man seeking arms with which to clothe himself, protected by a shield and equipped with a quiver. In the third face of Scorpio, the Arabs say there is a horse and a hare. The Indians say neither horse nor hare, but a dog, a boar, and a leopard. Others say there is no beast at all, but perhaps a man bent on his knees—if it is permitted to interpret these mysteries—praying to God on behalf of the astrologers, that He might at last restore their sanity and free them from this madness. For what else are they but insane, who devote themselves to such fallacious trifles, which are not even possible, and believe and agree with them?

---

<margin>Abraham the Jew. The Arabs are the most fabulous inventors of this error.</margin>
You see how Abraham the Jew <note>Abraham ibn Ezra (c. 1089–1167), a famous Jewish scholar whose astrological works were widely read in the Latin West.</note> and astrologer, in his book *On Nativities*, confesses that these images are ridiculous rather than true; he says this cannot be refuted because no monuments of the Indians have been handed down to us by trustworthy authors. 

<margin>The custom of the Arabs.</margin>
But this is a peculiarity of the Arabs: whatever commentaries they themselves invent, they sign with the names of illustrious authors, many of which we commemorated in the first book of these disputations. 

<margin>Maternus. Hephaestion. Paul. Teucer. Porphyry. Mallius Maternus.</margin>
Therefore, since Petosiris <note>An Egyptian priest-astrologer to whom many foundational texts were attributed.</note> and certain masters of astrology still exist among the Egyptians; since, besides Maternus, there exist Hephaestion of Thebes and Paul of Alexandria—all of them interpreters of astrology—it is easily known from them that no mention of these images exists in Egypt. The same is clear concerning the Chaldeans on the authority of Teucer of Babylon <note>An astrologer likely from the 1st century AD who wrote on the "paranatellonta" (stars rising alongside the zodiac).</note>, who wrote on the effects of the decans and the images rising with them. It is also clear from the testimony of Porphyry, who wrote astrological institutions according to the opinion of the Chaldeans. I shall pass over Mallius and Maternus, both of whom report the dogmas of the Chaldeans to us. Regarding the Greek authors, only those who have not read Greek can doubt; for nowhere among any Greek writer is there mention of these images.

<margin>The error of Haly in ascribing these to Ptolemy.</margin>
Thus we ought greatly to accuse Haly <note>Ali ibn Ridwan (c. 988–1061), a commentator on Ptolemy.</note> for ascribing this error to Ptolemy. For when, in the ninety-fifth word of the book titled *The Fruit* <note>The *Centiloquium* or *Karpos*, a collection of 100 astrological aphorisms falsely attributed to Ptolemy.</note>, Ptolemy says—<gloss>that is, those things which rise together with the individual decans of the signs</gloss>—that he wishes to indicate the will of the native and what art he will pursue, the expositor Haly thinks that by "co-rising images" those invisible ones of which we have spoken are to be understood. He does not know what they are called among the Greeks—<gloss>that is, they are called 'co-rising' [paranatellonta]. For among them they are called this</gloss> <note>The text ends abruptly here as Pico prepares to explain the Greek term *paranatellonta*, which refers to real constellations that rise at the same time as certain zodiac degrees, as opposed to the "invisible" or imaginary images of the Arab tradition.</note>.

<summary>Pico criticizes the arbitrary and contradictory images assigned to the "faces" of the zodiac by different cultures, arguing they are modern inventions rather than ancient truths. He asserts that legendary Egyptian, Chaldean, and Greek authorities make no mention of these figures, blaming Arab commentators for the confusion.</summary>
<keywords>decans, faces of the zodiac, Abraham ibn Ezra, Haly, Ptolemy, Teucer of Babylon, Petosiris, cultural discord in astrology, Greek vs. Arab astrology</keywords>

<meta>This page concludes Pico della Mirandola’s eighth book and begins the ninth. He specifically attacks the attempt by certain astrologers to "legitimize" Christianity by claiming the birth of Jesus was written in these celestial images. # Book IX

Namely, those thirty-six images outside the zodiac <note>original: "signiferum," literally the "standard-bearer," a common Latin term for the zodiac belt</note>, of which fifteen are toward the south and twenty-one tend toward the north. About their properties and nature, Ptolemy writes in the first book of his *Apotelesmaton* <note>Ptolemy’s famous work, more commonly known as the *Tetrabiblos*</note>. He never mentions any other images in that place or elsewhere except those he constructs from visible stars—the very ones we argued against in the previous chapter. He uses the same expression in the following passage when he says things must be considered in the eclipses of the luminaries <gloss>that is, things rising together / which</gloss> he indicates when treating the same opinion in the second book of the *Apotelesmaton*, explaining what kind of things are said to be "rising together" <note>original: "coorientia," or *paranatellonta*, stars or constellations that rise at the same time as a specific degree of the zodiac</note>. From these, when he says the will and the art a person will profess are indicated, he teaches what Mallius Maternus <note>Pico is likely referring to the 4th-century Roman astrologer Julius Firmicus Maternus</note> and the Greek writers explained: that he who is born when the Ship <margin>Mallius Maternus.</margin> is rising together with the sun is destined to be a sailor; he who is born with the Lyre, a musician; he with the Charioteer <note>original: "emotho," likely a corruption of "Heniochus," the Greek name for the constellation Auriga</note>, a driver; and so on for the rest.

But Porphyry also says in his *Introductions* that the "type"—that is, the figure and form—of the <term>zodiac sign <note>original: τῳ ζωδιῳ (tō zōdiō)</note></term> <gloss>that is, of those rising together</gloss> <gloss>that is, of those rising together</gloss> consists of a composition of stars. From this we understand that these things called "rising together" are no other images than those composed of stars. I have been more lengthy in declaring this because I hear that the Greek man Trapezuntius <margin>The error of Trapezuntius:</margin> (for his book has not reached us) followed the explanation of Haly <note>Ali ibn Ridwan, a medieval Arabic commentator on Ptolemy</note> in his commentaries on Ptolemy’s *Centiloquium*. The "barbarian" Albumasar <note>Abu Ma'shar, a highly influential Persian astrologer</note> could have turned them away from this error; he affirms that, according to Ptolemy's opinion, no images rise from the decans except those visible ones situated to the south and north and composed of stars.

However, I wish to recall to mind what we said in the third book against those who say the Lord Jesus was born <margin>The error concerning the birth of Jesus, criticized above</margin> when the first face <note>A "face" or "decan" is a 10-degree segment of a zodiac sign</note> of Virgo was rising, in which there is a virgin nursing a boy called Jesus. For it is established that this image of a virgin nursing a boy is among those mythical images we have mocked. Even though they do not imagine such an image there, but rather another which Albumasar says the Indians invented—whoever weighs in his mind how vain and ridiculous such an invention is will be ashamed to wish to confirm the truth of the Gospels with these astrological ravings. This was procured by a demon for no other reason than that this plague might be received as if it were a friend and supporter of religion. But let them keep their own trifles to themselves; when such things are summoned, the <term>Christian <note>original: xp̄iana (Christiana)</note></term> truth is not confirmed, but rather weakened and polluted.

->The end of the eighth book of Giovanni Pico della Mirandola against the astrologers.<-

# THE NINTH BOOK OF THE DISPUTATIONS OF GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA AGAINST THE ASTROLOGERS.

### Chapter One: A summary of what has been accomplished so far, what must be done in the following books, and from where we should begin.

It has been demonstrated so far that astrology is nothing, because those things about which it pronounces do not depend on the heavens except by accident, or as if from a remote and universal cause; neither of which produces particular knowledge of events. It has likewise been declared that even if those things were caused by the heavens, they would not happen in the way astrologers believe: that is, from a certain initial moment; then...

<summary>Pico concludes his debunking of the "images" associated with zodiac decans, specifically rejecting the use of astrology to validate the birth of Christ. He then begins Book IX by summarizing his core argument: that celestial influence is too general to predict specific human events.</summary>

--- Page 578 ---
<meta>This page transitions from the end of Book VIII to the beginning of Book IX. In the previous section, Pico concluded his critique of the "decans" or "faces" of the zodiac, arguing that the specific images assigned to these degrees are purely imaginary. Now, in Book IX, he shifts his focus to the technical impossibility of casting an accurate horoscope, starting with the difficulty of determining the exact moment of birth.</meta>

[Even] if this were also granted, it would certainly not be from these causes which they use in their predictions, none of which are true or natural if we were to have a sure examination. For when they use stars and planets, they increase, decrease, or change them according to locations, signs, intervals, and other things of that kind which we have declared to be false and ineffective. Therefore, they either introduce bad causes—that is, fables—or they infect good ones with a mixture of bad. Now we must act to declare that even if they considered all those factors, they are nonetheless of such a kind that they cannot be known by them; or if they can be known, they do not yet possess that knowledge.

<margin>Three things necessary if future events are to be known.</margin> 
There are three things necessary to know if true things are to be predicted about future matters. First, that the initial hour of any thing be faithfully recorded. Second, that we exactly comprehend the state of the heavens and stars at that hour. Finally, that we understand through true reasoning or experiments observed without deception what that position of the heavens and stars actually produces. In the two following books, we will begin to show that none of these things can be known, or that what they have known until now has not existed. We will start from the primordial hour <note>The exact moment of beginning, such as a birth or the founding of a city</note>, the knowledge of which is primary and necessary; nor can the rest be rightly established if anything in it is either ambiguous or erroneous. This applies to men (their nativities <note>original: "geniturarum," referring to the birth-moment or birth-chart</note>), or cities and kingdoms, or the constellation of a year. Let us begin with nativities.

# Chapter II. An astrologer can neither always know the certain hour of birth, nor investigate it by a true rule.

<margin>Birth cannot be truly known except by an instrument.</margin> 
<margin>Not always by an instrument.</margin> 
<margin>Instruments deceive.</margin>
The astrologer cannot have the moment in which someone is born fully explored, unless by chance he is summoned when the infant comes forth to measure the heavens with an astrolabe <note>A portable instrument used by astronomers and navigators to measure the altitude of celestial bodies and solve problems of time and position</note>. But this happens very rarely; nor can it always be done even if we wish it, such as at night, in cloudy weather, or when no mathematician is present. Moreover, since it is very easy to slip up, as Averroes <note>The 12th-century philosopher Ibn Rushd, who wrote extensively on Aristotle and Ptolemy</note> testifies in his commentaries on Ptolemy <note>The 2nd-century author of the *Tetrabiblos*, the foundational text of Western astrology</note>: for if the instrument is not most exact—and perhaps there is none that perfectly matches the moment of birth upon inspection—the calculation of the specific horoscope <note>original: "horoscopi," here meaning the exact degree of the zodiac rising on the eastern horizon</note> will waver. 

But even if there is a true investigation of the hour by the astrolabe, as we were saying, this happens very rarely. What is common and almost constant is that the parents or the "master of the birth" tell the astrologer that such-and-such was the hour of birth. The astrologer himself admits this is not to be trusted, for it is usually deceptive; therefore, they call it the "estimated" or "suspected" hour—concerning which there is suspicion and no certainty. For sundials lie; and as for clocks <note>original: "horologia," which could refer to water-clocks or early mechanical timekeepers</note>, even if they do not fail, they still do not show the small intervals that fall between the hours. Add to this that common hours do not begin from sunset as mathematical reasoning requires, but when the air begins to grow dark, which happens long after the sun has dipped below the horizon <note>original: "subfinitorem," the boundary line of the sky</note>, especially when the sun is placed in "oblique signs" <note>Signs of the zodiac that rise at an angle to the equator, taking longer to set or rise depending on the latitude</note>. Since these linger longer in the west, sometimes a full hour of night has passed before the air grows dark. 

Finally, the astrologers confess this along with us, but they have applied a remedy so that their divination is not endangered. For even if that which they call the "estimated hour" is not true, they say that unless it differs greatly from the truth, they have a method for finding the true one. Therefore, they say that initial uncertainty is no obstacle. If those men were wise, we would only object that a method or science cannot be given to determine whether a particular event occurred at a specific moment or not. <margin>General refutation of all investigations of birth.</margin> Therefore, there is no method by which we may be made certain at what moment John or Paul was brought forth into the light. But this does not seem absurd to them—nor perhaps does the fact that in any given day, let alone hour, there are many small particles of time in which no one can be born in a certain region...

<summary>Pico begins Book IX by outlining the three requirements for accurate astrology—knowing the exact time, the exact celestial state, and the true effect of that state—before arguing that the first requirement is impossible to meet due to the inaccuracy of human reports and timekeeping instruments.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Pico’s critique of the "primordial hour." Having established that human memory and clocks are unreliable for recording the exact moment of birth, he now attacks the mathematical "rectification" methods astrologers use to "correct" those recorded times to fit their theories.</meta>

IX

# Book IX

This is very easily demonstrated. For if I am said by my parents to have been born at the first hour of the night, and the astrologer—denying that this hour fits his method <note>Pico is referring to "rectification," a process where astrologers adjust the reported birth time so the resulting chart "works" or matches the person's life events.</note>—asks whether I was born earlier or later: I ask whether someone else could have been born at that same first hour of the night under that same inclination of the heavens? If they say this is impossible, it follows, as I was saying, that there are many parts of any given hour in which a human being simply cannot be born. I say "many parts" of any hour because almost no time of birth given by those consulting them fits the rules of the astrologers; instead, it is always changed by them to either a preceding or subsequent part of the hour. 

But if they concede that someone else *could* have been born at that time in that region—even if I was not the one born then—let us say that "Antonius" was born at that first hour of the night. I then ask: if Antonius provides the astrologer with that hour, which we have now established as his true time of birth, will the astrologer judge it to be true or false? If he judges it true, he ought by the same reasoning to have judged mine true when it was offered, since it fits his method no better now than when John <note>Likely referring to a specific person in an anecdote or a generic name for a client.</note> offered it. If he judges it false, then a man born at a true hour is being assigned a false one. Therefore, the dogma is false, through which a most true hour is rejected as if it were false.

<margin>Third argument.</margin>
Furthermore, those who have handed down this kind of teaching say that the <term>Zodiac sign</term><note>The 30-degree division of the sky (e.g., Aries, Taurus) rising on the eastern horizon.</note> shown by the estimated hour should not be changed, but that the specific part of that sign which is most essentially at the <term>horoscope</term><note>In this period, "horoscope" referred specifically to the Ascendant, or the exact degree of the Zodiac rising on the eastern horizon at the moment of birth.</note> should be declared by their method. Yet the estimated hour is often measured from a sign precisely when a person is born while the very last or very first parts of a sign are rising; in such cases, their method will not correct the error but will instead confirm it. It is clear from these reasons that there is no way to track down the "horoscope" when it is uncertain. Now let us show that if any other method could perhaps be devised, those which the astrologers have handed down are most patently deceptive.

### Chapter III: Ptolemy’s dogma, which they call *almuseli* or *animodar*, is refuted by both authorities and reasoning.

<margin>Ptolemy's dogma.</margin>
**P**tolemy, in the third book of his *Apotelesmaton* <note>The "Apotelesmaton" is the Greek title for Ptolemy's *Tetrabiblos*, the foundational textbook of Western astrology.</note>, hands down a dogma of this sort. He commands that the New Moon or Full Moon immediately preceding the birth be observed. Then, one must find the planet that had the most "authority" <note>Technical term for "essential dignity" or planetary power.</note> over the place where that conjunction or opposition occurred. Finally, once the <term>theme</term><note>A birth chart or map of the heavens.</note> has been arranged, whichever <term>cardinal point</term><note>The four angles of a chart: the Ascendant, Descendant, Midheaven, and Imum Coeli.</note> that dominant planet is closer to, they fix that location to the same numerical degree which that ruling planet held in its own sign; they fashion this as the cardinal point for the entire birth. All astrologers decree this to be the foundation of the entire art of predicting effects. This is that decree which they call <term>almuseli</term>, or sometimes <term>animodar</term> <note>These are Latinized versions of Arabic terms for the rectification of a birth chart to find the "true" degree of the Ascendant.</note>. In this, the younger generation trembles at the opinion of Ptolemy, having wrongly understood his meaning above.

<margin>Refutation of Ptolemy's dogma, which they call *almuseli*.</margin>
Now Ptolemy himself is examined, against whom I can first oppose a great weight of authorities. For **Abraham the Jew** <note>Abraham ibn Ezra (c. 1089–1167), a renowned Jewish scholar, poet, and astrologer whose work Pico frequently cites.</note> says that he observed many births with the most exact astrolabes in those regions where the longitude and latitude were acknowledged and explored; yet he never found any planet whose degrees and minutes (from the signs they occupied) corresponded to the degrees and minutes of the Rising <note>The Ascendant.</note> or the Mid-Heaven, nor did they vary by less than half an hour from the most true hour of birth already discovered by the senses.

<margin>The madness of some: Abraham was 900 years later than Ptolemy.</margin>
Those who say that **Ibn Ezra** <note>original: "Auenazrā"</note> did not write these things with sound judgment are truly ridiculous, as if he had a dispute with Ptolemy over a kingdom! He lived some nine hundred years after Ptolemy, and in determining the "giver of years" <note>The *Hyleg*, or the planet used to calculate the length of life.</note> and many other matters, he does not prefer the opinions of others over Ptolemy. But **Alchabitius** <note>Al-Qabisi, a 10th-century Arab astrologer and mathematician.</note> also writes in his own commentary that he has demonstrated that the true rising degree can by no means be found through that calculation.

<margin>Henry</margin>
**Henry Bate** <note>Henry Bate of Malines (1246–1310), a scientist and astrologer.</note>, a disciple of Albertus Magnus, examining his own birth chart—even though...

<summary>Pico argues that the mathematical methods used by astrologers to "rectify" or correct birth times (such as Ptolemy's Animodar) are logically flawed and contradicted by historical experts like Abraham ibn Ezra. He highlights the absurdity of discarding an observed birth time in favor of a calculated one that fits a preconceived theory.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Pico’s critique of the "animodar" and other birth-time rectification methods. Having argued that these mathematical "corrections" are arbitrary, he now focuses on the logical inconsistencies when comparing births in different geographic locations and begins a specific attack on the "Trutine of Hermes" method relating birth to conception.</meta>

# Book IX

<margin>Aoniar.</margin>
...disguising his name and calling himself a "servant of God." "Let us dismiss," he says, "the <term>animodar: a mathematical method used by astrologers to 'rectify' or find the exact degree of the Ascendant based on the position of the New or Full Moon preceding birth</term> of Ptolemy as something rejected by the wise." Others do not delete the dogma but rather correct it, as Aoniar does, disagreeing in no small way with Ptolemy. Still others fight over its interpretation. When it is asked which place the planet is closest to, some want discrete quantity to be observed, while others want <margin>Antonius de Monte Ulmo.</margin> continuous quantity, such as **Antonius de Monte Ulmo** <note>A 14th-century Italian astrologer and magician known for his works on the "occult" causes of birth.</note>. However, setting aside the authorities who oppose Ptolemy, I am accustomed to declaring the falsehood of this doctrine in the following way: 

Let Lucius be born in **Rome** and Fabius in **Florence** at the same hour and the very same moment. It is clear to astrologers that the horoscope <note>In this context, "horoscope" refers to the *Ascendant*—the specific degree of the zodiac rising on the eastern horizon.</note> will not be the same for both because of the different inclination of the heaven under which they are born. And yet, if we undertake the calculation according to Ptolemy's instructions, we will make the horoscope the same for both of them, provided that the preceding Full Moon or New Moon occurred in the same part of the sky for both regions. Because of this, the "ruler of the chart," possessing the same degree of the sign in both cases, will define the "angles" <note>The four critical points of a chart: the Ascendant, Descendant, Midheaven, and Imum Coeli.</note> with the same numbers in both births. But this is refuted by the evidence of the facts and the senses. Therefore, the doctrine is false, and I marvel that Ptolemy, a supreme mathematician, did not see through it.

### Chapter IIII: That the investigation of the exact horoscope through conception is falsely ascribed to Ptolemy by the Arabs; that it is irrational and rejected by many astrologers.

<margin>Another doctrine of the moderns.</margin>
Among the moderns, another method has been found for searching for the horoscope based on the hour of conception, to which they attribute great value. It is of this sort: they take it as a conceded fact from the tradition of the ancients—and especially from a statement in the fifty-first aphorism of Ptolemy’s *Book of a Hundred Sayings* <note>Pico is referring to the *Centiloquium*, a collection of 100 astrological aphorisms traditionally (though likely falsely) attributed to Ptolemy.</note>—that the position of the Moon at birth was the horoscope at conception. Conversely, they hold that the position of the Moon at conception is the horoscope of the birth. Having established this, they hand down a method by which they think they can detect the position of the Moon when the seed filled the womb; once this is found, they gather that a similar degree was ascending at the hour of birth.

However, the occasion for their error was a faulty translation of Ptolemy’s books. <margin>The occasion of their error. A faulty translation of Ptolemy.</margin> For he never wrote about the "degree" in this matter, but only about the "sign." His words in the place mentioned above are these: <note>original: "επι..." [Pico quotes the Greek text of the Centiloquium]</note> "In the time of birth, establish that *sign* as the horoscope of conception; where the Moon was at conception, make that the horoscope of the birth or its opposite." 

Ptolemy did not think, therefore, that the horoscope could be found precisely to the degree by this route. This is why in his books on *Judicial Astrology* <note>Referring to the *Tetrabiblos* (or *Apotelesmaton*), Ptolemy's primary astronomical-astrological work.</note> where he investigates this, he makes no mention of this decree. Otherwise, if he had understood it to refer to the "degree"—which we have shown to be false from his own words—he would have thought it extremely easy to find the hour of conception. Today, the moderns provide this hour with no great trouble to anyone desiring it, using a method they claim belongs to Ptolemy. 

How, then, does Ptolemy himself say in the third book of his *Judicial Astrology* that the female principle of conception <note>original: "επιπλεου" (epipleon)</note> is "mostly or for the most part" unknown? And he says that when knowledge of it is attained, it happens either by <note>original: "συμπτωματι" (symptomati)</note> "chance"—that is, by a fortuitous accident—or by observation. He certainly should have added "by art" <note>original: "ευτεχνωσ" (entechnos)</note>—that is, skillfully—if he believed that this could be detected by some art or method. 

<margin>No ancient handed down a way of investigating conception for women.</margin>
When he says it is known by chance or observation, the Greek interpreter explains that it is "by chance" when it happens that a woman feels the reception of the seed (as **Cleopatra** <note>Likely referring to a pseudo-epigraphical medical writer of the time, not the famous Queen.</note> teaches), and "by observation" if a man intentionally notes that time when, having had intercourse with a woman once, he thereafter abstains, and the passing months then declare that the intercourse was fruitful. Besides these, none of the ancients handed down any other way to explore that time clearly, much less did they wish to investigate the hour of birth from it.

<summary>Pico critiques the "animodar" method by showing it fails to account for geographic differences between births. He also attacks the "Trutine of Hermes" (relating birth to conception), arguing it is based on a mistranslation of Ptolemy and ignored by the ancients.</summary>
<keywords>Ptolemy, animodar, rectification, birth time, conception, Trutine of Hermes, Centiloquium, Antonius de Monte Ulmo, astrology vs geography</keywords>

He is specifically addressing the "Trutine of Hermes" (the Scale of Hermes), which attempts to link the moment of birth to the moment of conception.</meta>

# Book IX

<page-num>IX</page-num>

<margin>Hephaestion. Porphyry.</margin>
For what the Arabs say, claiming that **Hermes** <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure to whom many foundational astrological and alchemical texts were attributed.</note> commanded this rule, is a fable; just as they most lyingly attribute many other things to the same author (as we noted in the first book). In fact, regarding what the Egyptians handed down on this matter: **Hephaestion** <note>Hephaestion of Thebes, a 4th-century astrologer who attempted to synthesize earlier Egyptian and Greek traditions.</note> relates it, as does **Porphyry** <note>A 3rd-century Neoplatonist philosopher who wrote extensively on astrology.</note>, who says that this very precept read in **Ptolemy** was the invention of **Petosiris** the Egyptian <note>A legendary Egyptian priest-astrologer; his name was often invoked to give authority to astrological texts.</note> in these words: <term>But Petosiris...</term> <note>original Greek: "Ο ΔΕ πετοσιρις"</note> and what follows.

<margin>Petosiris.</margin>
<margin>The error of later writers.</margin>
<margin>Dogma disproven by experiments.</margin>
<margin>Abraham Ibn Ezra.</margin>
<margin>Immanuel.</margin>
Petosiris, however, says that the zodiac sign in which the moon was at the time of conception is the horoscope <note>In this context, the Ascendant or rising sign.</note> at birth, or its opposite. Furthermore, he claims that whichever sign the moon occupied at the time of birth was the horoscope of the conception. But in the same place, Porphyry reports two other modes from the opinion of **Antiochus** and certain others for tracking the sign in which the moon was at the hour of coitus <note>intercourse</note>; yet no mention was ever made of the specific degree. Indeed, the very chapter in which these are written is titled <term>On the Seminal Sign</term> <note>original Greek: "περὶ σπορίμου σημείου"</note>; that is, concerning the seminal sign of the moon which they designate as the sign the moon held when the seed was admitted into the genital place. Hephaestion of Thebes also narrates three other Egyptian methods different from these, which Porphyry mentions, by which they would investigate the same thing: namely, which sign was ascending at the hour of coitus. Here, Hephaestion warns us in express words that one does not arrive at the specific degree of the horoscope by these paths, but that it is tracked <term>roughly</term> <note>original Greek: "παχυμέρως"</note>; that is, with a "thick Minerva" <note>A Latin idiom, *crassa Minerva*, meaning a rough or unrefined estimation rather than a precise mathematical one.</note>, as is commonly said. He states that for determining the exact degree, there is only one method, which Ptolemy handed down in the third book of the *Apotelesmatika* <note>The *Tetrabiblos*, Ptolemy's foundational work on astrology.</note>.

However, this is the same method we refuted in the previous chapter. But as we said, the more recent authors fell into error because, in the Arabic translation which the Latins follow, the interpreters hastily put "degree" instead of "sign." Moreover, regardless of what the authors wrote, what is the underlying logic of this dogma? Or by what observation could this ever be detected? They answer that the calculation responds: because from the location of the moon at the hour of birth, one understands how many days the infant was in the womb. If you count these days backward, you arrive at the hour of conception, and by that time you find the moon’s location to be the same one that ascends at the time of birth. 

But I ask this: who teaches us to define the length of stay in the womb based on the position of the moon? Neither Ptolemy, nor any of the ancients, nor even your "Hermes" revealed this. There is no other answer you can give except that those durations in the womb *must* be defined that way if the dogma about the exchange of the Ascendant and the moon's place at conception and birth is to be true. Therefore, you demonstrate in a circle: proving the truth of the dogma by the fact that it matches the observed durations in the womb, and then claiming the durations must be observed that way because otherwise the dogma would not be true. If it were that easy, anyone could "confirm" any dogma they liked.

But if perhaps you dare to assert this by experiment—by actually observing and comparing the time of birth and conception—you are lying with impunity, for such acts occur without witnesses. Even your own experts, who most strongly contend for this, deny that the precept corresponds to reality. **Abraham Ibn Ezra** <note>A famous 12th-century Jewish polymath and astrologer.</note> says that he observed it five times and it failed three times; he attributes these failures now to Mars, now to Venus, now to Mercury. I think if he had observed it ten times, he would have blamed all the other planets as well. For **Immanuel the Hebrew** <note>Immanuel Bonfils, a 14th-century astronomer and mathematician.</note>, a follower of Ibn Ezra, having tried it twice using the same corrected methods Ibn Ezra favored, found that it varied from the true time of birth by seven days. **Abu Ma'shar** <note>A prominent 9th-century Persian astrologer, known in the West as Albumasar.</note>...

<summary>Pico critiques the "Trutine of Hermes" by showing it was a misattributed invention of Petosiris and relies on circular reasoning regarding the duration of pregnancy. He cites noted astrologers like Ibn Ezra and Immanuel the Hebrew to show that the method fails empirical testing.</summary>

# Book IX

<margin>
Sedis.
Avenrodan.
Johannes Saxo.
</margin>
**Sedis** <note>Likely referring to Sahl ibn Bishr, a 9th-century Jewish astrologer known in Latin as Zahel or Sehel.</note> believes that the method of the astrologers can be deceived by five degrees, as his disciple relates. Which, if true, helps us not at all, since we are concerned only with the [exact] degree. Likewise, **Avenrodan** <note>Ali ibn Ridwan (c. 988–1061), a famous Egyptian physician and commentator on Ptolemy.</note>, a great commentator on Ptolemy among these men, testifies that Ptolemy often lies. **Johannes Saxo** <note>John of Saxony, a 14th-century astronomer who wrote widely-read commentaries on astrological texts.</note>, the interpreter of **Alchabitius** <note>Al-Qabisi, a 10th-century Arab astrologer.</note>, considers it entirely false and vain, and utterly useless, asserting that it is impossible for an uncertain degree of the horoscope to ever be made certain through it—which he demonstrates at length through the example of a proposed nativity.

### Chapter V. Messahallah's fiction is refuted, along with five other methods for determining the horoscope recounted by Paulus Alexandrinus.

<margin>
The fiction of
Messahallah.
</margin>
**T**hese are generally the methods accepted by most astrologers. **Messahallah** <note>Masha'allah ibn Athari (c. 740–815), a Persian Jewish astrologer who was one of the founders of Baghdad.</note> thought up another fiction, but it has been rejected by everyone as being of perfect futility. For he commanded that the time of the moon from the new moon to the full moon—or conversely from the full moon to the dark moon—be considered as if it were a single hour. Then, whichever of those preceded the birth, the space occurring between that moment and the time of the birth should be compared to the total distance of the moon’s waxing or waning. Whatever the proportion of these intervals might be, that part of a <term>temporal hour</term> <note>Temporal or "unequal" hours divided day and night into twelve parts each; thus, an hour's length changed depending on the season.</note> should be taken; provided, however, that we observe this: that a male should never be born in an even hour, nor a female in an odd one. Later generations laughed at this, proving by experience that males and females are born in the same hour. I, however, do not merely consider the vanity of this one opinion, but judge the whole of Messahallah from this.

<margin>
See the fine
deduction of the
folly of the
astrologers.
</margin>
For while to slip, err, and be deceived is proper to man, yet to write such shameful things, to rely on ridiculous matters, to present fables as dogmas, and to speak what the evidence of things everywhere refutes, is certainly not the mark of a man—if man’s proper gift is reason. But I do not judge Messahallah alone so much as I judge all astrologers by him; for he is of the first rank among them, and you will not easily find wiser men in that family of thought. For the priests of this "sacred discipline," the "admirable" Egyptians, what great fables have they devised regarding this matter!

<margin>
Five other
ways of the
Egyptians
recounted by Paulus.
The First.
</margin>
**Paulus Alexandrinus** <note>A 4th-century author of an influential introductory text on astrology.</note> reports five methods—different from the three already mentioned—which they use to investigate the truth of the horoscope by its specific degree; good God, how varied, crude, futile, and false they are! The first is of this sort: "Look," he says, "at the <term>epoch</term> <note>The position of a celestial body at a specific moment.</note> of the sun in a daytime birth, or of the moon in a nighttime birth; and whatever planet holds the <term>monomiria</term> <note>A system where each of the 30 degrees of a zodiac sign is assigned to a specific ruling planet.</note>, make that same planet's monomiria which is closest to the suspected degree the true horoscope."

<margin>
The Second.
The Third.
</margin>
The second, whether it be day or night, inspects only the position of the moon; the rest is similar. The third, which provided **Ptolemy** the occasion for his own dogma, considers the full moon or new moon closest to the birth. Then it looks at the <term>despot</term> <note>original: "despotem," meaning the planetary lord.</note>, that is, the lord of the house in which it occurs, and the <term>onocraton</term> <note>original: "onocratorem," a technical term for the ruler of the bounds or "terms."</note>, that is, the lord of the bounds. It sees which is stronger in the birth constellation and which possesses more authority in it, and from that, it calculates the ascending degree.

<margin>
The Fourth.
</margin>
The fourth merely inspects the highest lord of the degree—namely, the degree in which the sun and moon either join or are opposed after the infant leaves the womb. However many <term>bounds</term> <note>fines: specific subdivisions of a zodiac sign ruled by different planets.</note> that planet possessed in the ascending sign, that many degrees of the same sign are thought to have already appeared in the East.

<margin>
The Fifth.
</margin>
The last observes not only the birth but the conception; that is, which of the two times—full moon or new moon—preceded it. However, it commands that the <term>dodecathemoria</term> <note>The division of a sign into twelve parts of 2.5 degrees each.</note> of the degrees in which those events occurred be calculated and observed, to see in which planet's <term>monomiria</term> <note>individual degrees.</note> they fall; so that whichever planet is better placed in the <term>theme</term> <note>The birth chart or figure.</note> has the judgment of measuring the horoscope.

<margin>
Heliodorus.
</margin>
Writing on how they might investigate the time of conception, **Heliodorus** <note>An ancient astrological writer, often associated with the work of Paulus Alexandrinus.</note> says they counted backward nine months from the birth, as if the time of carrying a womb were always equal—showing themselves to be the most ignorant people everywhere.

# Book IX
<sig>G</sig>

...those most divine Egyptians are found. I could, however, object to many things in which those particular dogmas are at fault. But that one reason is enough for those of us striving for brevity, by which we also rejected the dogma of Ptolemy <note>Claudius Ptolemy (c. 100–170 AD), the most influential astronomer and astrologer of antiquity.</note>: for whichever method from the aforementioned we follow, we will always produce the same horoscope for those who were born at the same time but in a different region, even though it is established among all mathematicians, beyond any controversy, that the horoscope must be different.

### Chapter VI. The beginnings of cities, kingdoms, factions, and laws are unknown, and there is no art handed down by astrologers by which they can be investigated.

**I**t is clear from these points that a birth hour is never clearly known except by chance; furthermore, because it deviates [from the truth], it cannot be restored by any art. Since that "truth" of the hour is not real, the truth of the prediction cannot stand. Nothing true, therefore, can be said by the <term>genethliaci</term> <note>From the Greek *genethliakos*; those who cast birth charts or nativities.</note> who testify with one voice that the exact degree of the horoscope is the hinge of the birth, the bond of the whole fate, and the foundation of all <term>apotelesmatica</term> <note>The study of astrological effects or outcomes.</note>. Nor, indeed, is there better reliability in the beginnings of cities and kingdoms, the knowledge of which is far more difficult to scrutinize than that of individual nativities. For who recorded these? Which writer of histories observed them? If their reliability and diligence gave us the day a city was restored or founded, they would surely be considered magnanimous. It was the custom to celebrate the "birthday" of Rome, but no more is certain to astrologers from that than that the moon was in the <unclear>first part</unclear>—that is, in Libra—when it was being founded.

<margin>Paolo the Florentine.</margin>
In the letters of **Paolo the Florentine** <note>Paolo dal Pozzo Toscanelli (1397–1482), a famous physician, mathematician, and cosmographer who corresponded with Pico.</note>, physician and mathematician, I found two different times noted for the restoration of the city of Florence: one in the year of grace 801, the other in 802. Consequently, the constitution of the stars is entirely different. I believe that many of the urban constellations commonly circulated are fictions derived from the [supposed] outcomes of the cities, just as **Julius Firmicus** <note>Julius Firmicus Maternus, a 4th-century author of a major astrological compendium.</note>
<margin>Julius Firmicus.</margin>
fakes those of the ancients—of Paris, of Plato, and of others—which he himself testifies regarding the "nativity of the world" <note>Original: *mundi genitura*. Firmicus famously provided a chart for the beginning of the universe.</note> that he provides. Furthermore, they want that moment to be of great weight when a new faction begins to prevail in a city; when a tyrant occupies a city; when sedition occurs among the common people; when civil discord is born; when a foreign nation invades a kingdom; or when new laws are established and new decrees promulgated. Who but a diviner <note>Pico implies a true prophet, not a technical astrologer.</note> shall provide the horoscope for these things, since one must have these times before we can divine? Finally, even if some moments of these times could be obtained, they will surely not deny that they would be less exact and less certain than those of individual nativities. Therefore, if they think the latter need "correction" and cannot be used otherwise, this would be much more necessary in the former—yet they teach no method for emending them. For the methods we mentioned are applied only to the nativities of men. Therefore, all their pronouncements about the fates of cities and kingdoms were maimed and deceptive, since they want these to depend on those primordial moments which they either are completely ignorant of or have received from unreliable or unprecise traditions. Men should not now fear death, exile, or poverty, nor should cities fear destruction or pestilence, when these most daring triflers threaten such things in their widely published annual booklets.

### Chapter VII. It is still uncertain among astrologers how the houses should be divided, how far their powers extend, and which signs should be used.

**I**t remains to speak of the beginnings of the year, and of the great conjunctions and eclipses. For observing the moment they occur, they prophesy from there the fates of republics.

<summary>Pico argues that since precise birth times are impossible to determine, astrologers cannot accurately predict the fates of individuals, let alone cities or kingdoms. He highlights the conflicting historical dates for the founding of Florence and Rome to prove that political astrology is based on guesswork and fiction.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Pico della Mirandola’s critique of astrology, transitioning from the uncertainty of birth times to the mathematical chaos of house division. # Book IX

...and of universals. It will therefore be shown that such times cannot be apprehended by them without the slip of error; indeed, this will become clear from what follows when we show that the movements of the planets are still uncertain and have not been captured by any irreproachable calculation. Thus far, then, let us say how uncertain the "fatal hour" is for any given thing—if indeed there are fatal hours for things, as astrologers especially believe; for we demonstrated above that there are no such fatal hours, and if there are any, they are different from what these men think. Now let us make this clear: even if they could obtain the times for a predicted omen through the power of the stars, they still could not know the state of the heavens at that hour. First, therefore, is the task of arranging the <term>theme</term> <note>A "theme" refers to the celestial figure or birth chart used for a prediction.</note> into twelve predetermined places which they call "houses": where, 

<margin>Discord among astrologers in the division of houses.</margin>
in what great darkness the astrologers are shrouded, and how much they clash with one another over a matter entirely unresolved, no one is ignorant who has touched the books of the mathematicians. Some distinguish these places by six circles, one of which, revolved through the point of the East, creates the <term>seventh hinge</term> and the <term>horoscope</term> <note>The "horoscope" here refers specifically to the Ascendant, or the degree of the zodiac rising on the eastern horizon.</note>; another, the meridian itself, delineates the highest and lowest points of the ether; others, intercepted in the four middle places, are drawn through four points and marks: the arcs of the semi-diurnal and semi-nocturnal arcs divided into three equal portions. But all these circles pass through the poles of the world; an opinion widely accepted which I refuted above.

<margin>Abraham</margin>
Abraham Ibn Ezra <note>Abraham ibn Ezra (c. 1089–1167), a celebrated Jewish scholar and astrologer.</note> teaches in the construction of the astrolabe—and then elsewhere as well—to divide the houses so that we designate six circles, of which one is the horizon, another the meridian itself; by these, the four <term>cardines</term> <note>The "hinges" or most powerful points of a chart: the Ascendant, Descendant, Midheaven, and Imum Coeli.</note> are immediately established. He orders the other four to be drawn through the marks of the intersection of the horizon and the meridian, and the division of the parts of the equator falling between the East and the meridian into three equal portions. He strongly approves of this method, though the name of its author is suppressed.

<margin>Johannes Regiomontanus.</margin>
Johannes Regiomontanus, the most sublime and learned mathematician of our age, was not satisfied with Campanus <note>Campanus of Novara (c. 1220–1296), who proposed a widely used system of house division.</note> and brought forth his own new calculation for this partition, otherwise similar to Ibn Ezra’s; but he differs greatly in this: he uses a certain artificial circle for the equator which he called the "vertical circle." From this, a different measurement and different boundaries of the places emerge. Johannes wrote copiously in confirmation of this dogma, relying on many mathematicians as well as the authorities of ancient astrologers.

<margin>Ludovico the Hermit, a most exact calculator.</margin>
Others divide it differently still; and our friend Ludovico the Hermit <note>Ludovico da Reggio, a contemporary of Pico known for his mathematical precision.</note>, a diligent and most exact calculator, was accustomed to prove that none of the methods we have mentioned agree with the sayings of Alcabitius <note>Alcabitius (Al-Qabisi), a 10th-century Arab astrologer.</note>. What of the fact that many think these same places should be divided by the degrees of the zodiac which they call "equal"? They use either this path alone (which we noted above the Indians did for the most part) or they receive both divisions equally: both the one that varies according to <term>anaphoras</term> <note>The rising times of the signs of the zodiac.</note> and the one that regards only the degrees of the zodiac. 

<margin>Abraham the Spaniard, Henry.</margin>
Abraham the Spaniard <note>Likely referring to Abraham bar Hiyya or a specific teaching of Ibn Ezra.</note>, the teacher of Ibn Ezra, and Henry of Valens observe this, pronouncing no less from the place in which a planet is located by an equal distribution of degrees than from where they are noted by the common method of division. Furthermore, even if it were established where the beginnings and ends of the places should be set, there remains another doubt that again calls everything back to uncertainty: for they do not agree on whether the power and efficacy of a place is enclosed within the space of the designated area. But Ptolemy begins five degrees before the preceding parts of the signs; others extend it by only three parts. The sages of the Egyptians say the beginning of the place, which is commonly called the <term>cusp</term> <note>original: "cuspis"; the boundary line between two houses.</note>, is not the beginning but the middle, and as it were, the center of its power...

<summary>Pico attacks the fundamental lack of consensus among astrologers regarding "house division," citing various conflicting methods from authorities like Ibn Ezra, Regiomontanus, and Ptolemy. He argues that if the experts cannot agree on where a "house" begins or ends, their predictions are mathematically baseless.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Pico della Mirandola's critique of the mathematical foundations of astrology.
