<page-num>IX</page-num>
<header>Book IX</header>

...spread: for which reason they extend fifteen degrees above that place and as many below it. If we observe that almost all these varieties of opinion are fortified by either equal reasoning or authority, we will at least confess by this very uncertainty that the entire method of pronouncing judgment by the stars (if such a thing exists) is in doubt. For when the divisions of the places are varied, the entire constellation is varied: since (as we were criticizing above) the stars change their nature, influence, and property among astrologers according to the change of location. And what is most significant, they assign to those places—which are joined and coherent in position—conflicting and contrary conditions. For in the first place and the twelfth, which follow one after another: what could be more diverse? Or in the sixth and seventh, or again the fifth and sixth, the eleventh and twelfth, and again the ninth and eighth, and so on for the rest. Moreover, it often happens that one <term>mathematician</term> <note>In this period, "mathematician" often referred specifically to astrologers or those calculating celestial positions.</note> will place a planet in the sixth house, while another contends it is in the fifth, which will entirely change the whole prediction; and one will judge it to be in the ninth, while another says it belongs to the eighth. Therefore, this entire distribution of places—the root and foundation of all <term>apotelesmatics</term> <note>The art of predicting the effects or outcomes of celestial movements; essentially, the practice of making astrological forecasts.</note>—remains uncertain. Following this is the concern over which signs we ought to use: where there is a tangled and inexplicable question concerning the movable and immovable signs, and concerning the eighth, ninth, and tenth spheres. This is not the place for us to speak of this matter, as it has been treated abundantly above.

<margin>Abraham the Jew creates a double chart.</margin>
Abraham the Jew <note>Likely referring to Abraham ibn Ezra (c. 1089–1167), a celebrated Jewish scholar whose astrological works were widely translated into Latin.</note> instructs that a double <term>theme</term> <note>A "theme" refers to a celestial figure or birth chart.</note> be made, as one who did not believe the controversy could be settled. Because of this doubt, it will be uncertain which signs are assigned to which planets; but from what we treated before, it is also uncertain which places are assigned. Thus every astrological pronunciation hangs here: everything, therefore, is doubtful, uncertain, and unproven.

### Chapter VIII: That it is extremely difficult to very accurately track the positions of the planets, and concerning the fallacy of instruments.

<margin>Andreas Sommariva</margin>
Having divided the places and distributed the signs, there remains the labor of establishing the <term>epochs</term> <note>Reference points in time used for astronomical calculations.</note> of the constellations and stars: that is, indicating at which degrees and minutes the fixed and wandering stars are found. This is a task which the unrefined and unskilled think they can perform very easily; the most learned hesitate and distrust it, for they know how great the difficulty is in truly attaining the positions of the planets—something judged by many to be not only laborious but impossible. Andreas Sommariva <note>An Italian mathematician and astrologer active in the late 15th century.</note>, a serious mathematician, begins his book thus: "Whether the movements of the stars can be known, I do not know; but that they are not yet known, I hold most certainly." He offers such a reason for his opinion: since those who measure the movements of the stars must necessarily first define the location of a star, in which they behold it by means of an instrument; and once the location of the star is found, they use it as a foundation to arrange the calculation of its course. If the location is truly grasped, the future calculation of the movement will be true, for they rely on mathematical reasoning, which is least likely to deceive. However, the detection of the location is not entirely faithful, simply because the instrument fails. For no matter how vast a mechanical instrument may be, it cannot suffice for divisions that are actually perceptible to the senses—which are necessary for avoiding error—if one considers the distance of any star from the observer’s location, and then the ratio of that proportion by which the circumference of the universe exceeds the circumference of the instrument. Therefore, since the senses cannot grasp the relationship of the parts of a very small physical instrument to the parts of the whole (as if to immense things), the location of a star cannot be observed without deception. To be sure, perhaps the error will be hidden, but over time...

<summary>Pico argues that the fundamental "houses" of an astrological chart are based on arbitrary and conflicting systems, rendering all predictions uncertain. He further cites the mathematician Andreas Sommariva to claim that human instruments are too small and imprecise to accurately measure the vast movements of the heavens.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Pico della Mirandola’s argument regarding the unreliability of astrological data. While the previous page focused on the difficulty of dividing the "houses" of the zodiac, this page moves to the physical tools of the trade, arguing that even the best astronomical instruments and the most famous scholars of the past—from Ptolemy to Gersonides—could not agree on basic celestial measurements due to the inherent fallibility of human observation and mechanical tools.</meta>

<page-num>IX</page-num>
<header>Book IX</header>

<margin>Confirmation through the opinion of Haly.</margin> <note>Haly likely refers to the Arabic astronomer Haly Abenragel or the commentator Ali ibn Ridwan.</note>
...will become more evident in its progression, with the star always receding further from its true place with each return <note>original: "restitutionibus," referring to the completion of a celestial cycle.</note>. Ptolemy confirms this; for this reason, he commands that astronomical numbers be restored every two hundred years due to the fallacy of instruments. He argues that over such a stretch of time, the fault of the old observation is uncovered and must be corrected by new observations. Even these will not be beyond blame, but they will at least be free of errors that can be perceived by the senses at that time. When these again deviate significantly after many revolutions have passed, they are reduced back to the truth by a new correction, as far as is possible. Thus, the tables of Ptolemy, the prince of astrologers, have been considered useless for many years now; for the studies of more recent men repeatedly correct these observations. As we said before, no construction of any instrument, no matter how skillful or subtle, and no size so vast, can report the location of a star with faultless reliability.

<margin>Abraham the Jew. Astrolabes with a diameter of nine spans.</margin> <note>Abraham the Jew refers to Abraham ibn Ezra, a prominent 12th-century scholar and astrologer.</note>
Abraham the Jew reports in his book *On the Use of Tables* concerning two <term>astrolabes</term> <note>A portable tool used by astronomers to solve problems relating to time and the position of the Sun and stars.</note> constructed with the highest reasoning, and of such great size that the diameter of each extended nine spans <note>A "span" is a measure of length, roughly the width of an outstretched hand.</note>. When the two Berseschit brothers <note>Likely referring to the Banu Musa brothers, famous 9th-century Persian scientists.</note>, who were makers of instruments, observed the altitude of the sun together as the sun entered <term>Aries</term>, both instruments did not report the same thing; instead, they varied by two minutes from each other. Henry Baten of Mechelen, a man preeminent in this art as in all mathematics—for he wrote a noble treatise on the construction of the astrolabe—thinks it is either impossible or, as he says, next to impossible for an instrument to be made that is in no way deceptive. While he was in Paris, he reports that he saw two very large <term>quadrants</term> <note>An instrument used to measure angles up to 90 degrees, often fixed to a wall for stability.</note> arranged with miraculous skill to observe the maximum altitude of the sun at noon—that is, at the summer solstice. On one instrument, the position was found to be sixty-four degrees and forty-two minutes. On the other, it was the same number of degrees, but zero minutes. Therefore, there was an error of forty-two minutes in one of the two.

<margin>Error of forty-two minutes.</margin>
See how even those who gather a horoscope of a birth by an instrument can be deceived; we have testified above that we were also warned of this by Avenrodan <note>Ali ibn Ridwan, an influential Egyptian physician and astrologer.</note>. Likewise, Baten, whom we just cited, proves in his *Mirror of Natural Things* across many thousands of verses that neither Ptolemy, nor Geber <note>Jabir ibn Aflah, a 12th-century Spanish-Arab astronomer.</note>, nor Albategni <note>Al-Battani, one of the greatest medieval astronomers.</note> could investigate the size of the diameters of the sun and moon more certainly than through eclipses; for he argues that the reliability of instruments regarding that matter would be suspect.

<margin>The eyes can be deceived in many ways.</margin>
I pass over the many ways in which Ptolemy (in his *Great Composition* <note>Commonly known as the Almagest.</note>) and Alhazen <note>Ibn al-Haytham, the pioneering scholar of optics.</note> (in the seventh book of *On Vision*) teach that the eyes can be deceived when observing the locations of the stars. For even if the air is considered clear and cloudless, something prevents the wind from blowing in a way that is not felt. Yet the philosopher Aristotle writes that when the east wind blows, the stars appear larger.

<margin>Leo devised a new instrument.</margin>
Leo the Hebrew <note>Levi ben Gerson, also known as Gersonides, a 14th-century philosopher and astronomer.</note>, a distinguished man and celebrated mathematician, as if having little faith in the ancients, devised a new instrument <note>This refers to the "Staff of Jacob" or "Jacob's Staff," used for measuring angles between stars.</note>; we have seen his mathematical rules <note>original: "canones"</note> for it, which are excellent in their mathematical subtlety. Nevertheless, when he had observed two fixed stars twice in the same year with it, he says the former observation differed from the latter by two degrees, which he thinks should be attributed to the state of the air.

### Chapter IX: Various opinions on the motions of the planets, the inequality of the year, and the maximum declination of the sun.

<margin>h</margin>
From this, perhaps, has been born such a great diversity of opinions among authors concerning the motions of the stars. For if the true locations had been discovered with non-deceptive instruments, they would not have erred in measuring the duration of the return <note>The time taken for a planet to return to its starting position.</note>, nor would they have disagreed with one another. Ptolemy, in his *Great Composition*, calls the motion of the sun the most manifest of all...

He notes that atmospheric conditions and mechanical errors make it impossible to achieve the precision required for reliable horoscopes.</summary>

...we ought to measure by a more [certain measure]: but here, in truth, nothing will show us more clearly how the path is certainly explored than the traditions written about it by the princes of astronomy, which are most conflicting among themselves.

<margin>Opinions of the ancients.</margin>
Those older than Hipparchus <note>Hipparchus (c. 190–120 BCE) was a Greek astronomer often called the father of trigonometry.</note> wanted the solar restitution <note>The "restitution" of the sun refers to the time it takes for the sun to return to the same point in the sky, completing one solar year.</note>, by which the year is completed, to consist of three hundred sixty-five days plus a quarter part of one day. Others added only the quarter part. Hipparchus, writing in the one hundred seventy-eighth year after the death of Alexander <note>Alexander the Great; the era of Alexander was a common chronological marker.</note>, calculating from his own observations and those of the Chaldeans <note>The "Chaldeans" here refers to Babylonian astronomers.</note>, calculated that less than a quarter of a day should be added; however, he did not work out exactly how much was lacking.

<margin>Another opinion; Opinion of Hipparchus.</margin>
Ptolemy, two hundred eighty-five years after him, defined that part [of the day] as a three-hundredth. Albategni <note>Al-Battani (c. 858–929), a major Arab astronomer.</note>, observing the heavens seven hundred forty-three years after Ptolemy, found the motion of the sun to be faster; therefore, he found it fell short of that quarter part by a one hundred and sixth part of a day.

<margin>Opinion of Ptolemy. Opinion of Albategni.</margin>
Thebit <note>Thabit ibn Qurra (c. 826–901), who proposed the theory of "trepidation" or the oscillation of the equinoxes.</note> said the year consists of 365 days, 6 hours, 9 minutes, and 12 seconds.

<margin>Opinion of Thebit.</margin>
Then there is that great diversity where some think all years are equal, such as Ptolemy and Alfonso <note>Referring to the Alfonsine Tables commissioned by Alfonso X of Castile.</note>. Others think they are unequal, such as Azerchel <note>Al-Zarqali (1028–1087), an Andalusian astronomer.</note>, Baten <note>Al-Battani.</note>, and Isaac the Israelite <note>Isaac Israeli ben Joseph, a 14th-century Spanish astronomer.</note>, whom others of the younger sort follow. They argue that the sun returns to the place from which it departed sometimes sooner and sometimes later. They claim the cause of this inequality is that the eighth sphere <note>The sphere of the fixed stars, which was thought to move independently of the planetary spheres.</note> is not always carried from the west to the east, as Ptolemy and many others think, but is sometimes carried from the east to the west. Therefore, by its motion, when it moves toward the same part to which the sun is turned, the sun’s motion becomes faster; when it moves to the contrary part, it becomes slower. Hence, at different times, the year is observed to be now longer, now shorter.

<margin>Ptolemy, Alfonso, Azerchel, Baten, Isaac.</margin>
And that Isaac whom we cited, in the book titled *Yesod Olam* <note>original: "iesodola"; Hebrew for "The Foundation of the World."</note>, wrote in the year of grace 1310 (which was the year 5070 of the world for the Hebrews) that he thought the years were at their shortest, so that they could not be shortened further; but already time appeared such that by the motion of the eighth sphere, they were beginning to be lengthened very gradually.

<margin>Opinion of Isaac regarding the years of his time.</margin>
Between that which could be the longest and the one, on the contrary, which is the shortest, the average duration is 365 days and 5 hours. Then, dividing the hour into one thousand eighty parts <note>This refers to the *Chelek* (plural *chalakim*), the traditional Hebrew unit for time-keeping in the calendar.</note>, it has nine hundred ninety-six parts, then 48 minutes, of which any one is the seventy-first part of one of those 1080 parts.

<margin>Average year.</margin>
<margin>See the inconsistent calculation.</margin>
I remember that I also read this customary and meticulous calculation in a very ancient writer of the Hebrews, Rabbi Ada bar Ahaba <note>A 3rd-century scholar associated with the calculation of the Hebrew calendar.</note>, son of Ada and Abraham. Finally, that the motion of the sun is detected in ambiguity is shown by those who find the time noted in the tables exceeds [reality] by more than half an hour; which Andreas Summarius reports and is daily declared by the evidence of the senses.

<margin>Adabarba the most ancient.</margin>
Henry of Mechelen <note>A 13th-century philosopher and astronomer.</note> also, in the book he wrote called *The Mirror of Natural Things*, asserts that in eclipses, whether you look at the location, the hour, or the quantity, one who follows the numbers of the movements of either Ptolemy or Albategni will err. Paolo of Florence <note>Paolo dal Pozzo Toscanelli (1397–1482), a famous mathematician and cosmographer.</note>, a distinguished mathematician, when he had observed the entry of the sun into Aries with the most diligent annotations, found it to be faster than the time defined in the tables by a third part of an hour.

<margin>Paulus of Florence.</margin>
Alliacensis <note>Pierre d'Ailly (1350–1420), a French cardinal and scholar.</note> also reports in the *Elucidarium* that when the entry of the sun into the vernal equinox was observed at Paris in the year of our Lord 1364, the Alfonsine tables were found to fall away from the truth.

<margin>Alliacensis.</margin>
But if they are blind in such great light—that is, in the motion of the sun, which is the most manifest of all—where if anything is erred, it is necessary to err in the rest as well, what then will happen regarding the motion of Mercury? This planet almost never shows itself to the eyes of mortals. Sosigenes <note>The astronomer who advised Julius Caesar on the calendar.</note>, the teacher of Alexander of Aphrodisias, reports that it cannot be distant from the sun by more than twenty-two degrees. Theon, Paul, Heliodorus, and Porphyry say twenty-three; Ptolemy even says twenty-eight. Concerning the motion of this planet, a certain distinguished mathematician confessed that nothing had been discovered by him. Furthermore, Mars...

<margin>Various opinions on the distance of Mercury from the sun.</margin>

<margin>Ptolemy; Al-Battani!</margin>
...[it] was slower by almost one hour and thirty minutes <note>original: "minutiisq; triginta" refers here to minutes of time/arc; Pico is highlighting the compounding disagreements between historical authorities.</note> than they thought, which he himself had discovered—a matter in which the diligence of later generations ought to be even more exactly vigilant. He also recorded the maximum declination <note>Declination is the angular distance of a celestial body north or south of the celestial equator.</note> of the sun from the equator, observed by himself, as twenty-three degrees and thirty minutes. However, 

<margin>Arzachel.</margin>
Ptolemy recorded the same degrees but fifty-one minutes. Al-Battani <note>Al-Battani (c. 858–929), known in Latin as Albategni, was a pioneering Arab astronomer.</note> recorded thirty-six [degrees] and thirty [minutes]. Arzachel <note>Arzachel (c. 1028–1087) was a prominent Arab Muslim astronomer based in Toledo.</note> 

<margin>Abraham Ibn Ezra.</margin>
set forth more than twenty-three. Finally, Abraham Ibn Ezra <note>Ibn Ezra (1089–1167) was a distinguished Jewish scholar and polymath.</note>, a supreme mathematician, affirms in his sixth book *On Revolutions* that it is impossible to find the part which is in the horoscope <note>In this context, the "horoscope" refers to the Ascendant, the specific degree of the zodiac rising on the eastern horizon.</note> when the sun enters the first part of Aries. Therefore, the time at which it reaches Aries can be detected neither by a certain calculation of motion, as he says, nor clearly by any kind of instrument.

<margin>Ibn Ridwan.</margin>
Avenrodan <note>Ali ibn Ridwan (c. 988–1061), an Egyptian physician and astronomer.</note>, explaining Ptolemy, also aptly confesses this. The same frequently cited Ibn Ezra, whenever he was to calculate anything by precise reasoning, used three kinds of tables <note>term: <term>canonum</term> (tables/rules) — astronomical tables used to calculate the positions of celestial bodies.</note> as he writes: those of the Greeks, of Ptolemy, and of the Indians, all of which varied among themselves and determined the planets at different positions.

<margin>Plutarch.</margin>
Plutarch, who lived after Ptolemy and was a contemporary of Aemilius the Roman—a supreme mathematician under Trajan—says in his *Roman Questions*: "Even at this time when astrology has reached its peak, the inequality of times has nevertheless conquered the skill of mathematicians, and very often eludes and escapes their numbers and calculations."

<margin>Aemilius.</margin>

### Chapter X: That an error of a single degree, or even of a single minute, sometimes produces many errors; and that the astrologer cannot judge through revolutions of either years or nativities, nor through great conjunctions.

From this uncertainty of celestial motions, who does not see that the whole of divinatory astrology is undermined? For if it slips by one degree, it must necessarily fall from all truth. It will happen that the part of the sign in which the star is found is changed, and the "bounds" <note>term: <term>fines</term> (bounds/terms) — specific degrees within a zodiac sign ruled by different planets.</note> are often 

<margin>The bounds are changed.</margin>
altered—to which all confess a power equal to or even greater than the houses—and sometimes the "exaltations" which they 

<margin>Exaltations</margin>
prescribed for specific parts; certainly the "monomyriae" <note>term: <term>monomyriae</term> — an astrological system assigning a specific influence to every individual degree of the zodiac.</note> will always vary, and sometimes the borders of the 

<margin>Monomyriae.</margin>
decans <note>term: <term>decani</term> — ten-degree divisions of a zodiac sign.</note>; and if a planet holds the last parts of a sign, it can happen that an error of one part transfers it from sign to sign: and the Moon, 

<margin>Decans.</margin>
which would have been in Taurus, might become in Gemini; while she is lucky in Taurus, she is unfortunate in Gemini. 

<margin>Sign.</margin>
Furthermore, it will be changed from a masculine part to a feminine one; from bright to dark; from dark to gloomy; from a "pit" <note>term: <term>puteo</term> (pit) — specific "degrees of depression" or misfortune in ancient astrology.</note> to a height; from "full" parts to "empty" ones; from sickly to most happy. Finally, since there is a different property for every degree among astrologers—nay, even for minutes, whose distinct properties 

<margin>Aesculapius.</margin>
Aesculapius <note>Referring to the mythical or legendary figure often cited in Hermetic and astrological texts.</note> handed down in the *Myriogenesis*—if the planet's location is varied by a degree or minute, will the power and influence of the star not be changed much by the error? And just as an error of a degree sometimes changes the sign, so an error of a minute sometimes changes the degree. But it will also sometimes deceive regarding the "houses" <note>original: "locis" (places), which in astrology refers to the twelve houses of the birth chart.</note> due to the slip of one degree: so that what might be in the West is placed underground; and what pertains to the horoscope is thrust back into the darkness of the twelfth house. In the "dodecatemoria" <note>term: <term>dodecatemoriis</term> — the division of each zodiac sign into twelve micro-signs of 2.5 degrees each.</note>, an error of one degree will cause a deviation of twelve degrees; nor, if the starting point <note>term: <term>epocha</term> — the reference point in time for astronomical calculations.</note> of the star is held incorrectly, will any of the "lots" (which they call parts) <note>These are mathematical points in a chart, like the "Part of Fortune."</note> be correctly established. Add the fallacy in aspects <note>original: "radiationibus" (radiations), referring to the angles or "aspects" planets make to each other.</note> from the variation of only one part: since it does one thing if the aspect is exact, another if applying <note>moving toward an aspect</note>, and another if separating <note>moving away from an aspect</note>. Add the gravest sin of all in "directing" the rays of the planets, as they say: if the astrologer slips by one part, an error of one year will result from it. But these are the highest and greatest, almost shameful errors in that profession; which, nevertheless, if you compare them to other mistakes, will seem small—those which they must necessarily incur when the initial hours...

<meta>This page continues Pico's critique of astrological precision. While the previous page focused on the discrepancy in measuring the solar year, Pico now examines how these errors ripple through the calculation of the "beginning of the year" and "great conjunctions," undermining the entire practice of casting horoscopes.</meta>

<page-num>IX</page-num>
<header>Book IX</header>

<margin>The beginning of the year.</margin>
From the motions of the planets, they derive what we had postponed saying until this point. Let the beginning of the year, therefore, be established at the sun’s entry into the first minutes of Aries <note>The "vernal equinox," which astrologers use to mark the start of the astrological year.</note>. Furthermore, if, as we have seen, they are mistaken by more than half an hour, the resulting constellation <note>The "theme" or birth chart of the year.</note> will be entirely different; such a significant variation will occur. No less an error will happen if the year is inaugurated not from the sun’s entry into Aries, but from the full moon or new moon preceding the year. Nor do I see why Ibn Ezra <note>Abraham Ibn Ezra (c. 1089–1167), a celebrated Jewish scholar and astronomer.</note> and Avempace <note>original: "Auerodan"; likely referring to the philosopher and astronomer Ibn Bajja.</note> think that error can be avoided in the former case but not in the latter, since the hour of syzygy <margin>Error of Ibn Ezra and Avempace.</margin> cannot be clearly grasped unless the motion of both luminaries <note>The Sun and the Moon.</note> is correctly understood. This is also what Henry Bate of Mechelen <note>original: "Marchliuensis"; a 13th-century scientist and astrologer.</note> objects to regarding Ibn Ezra: namely, that they do not correctly define the annual revolutions of nativities because they begin from the sun's return to the same place at a time of restoration <note>The "solar return," used to predict a person's year ahead.</note> that has not been properly investigated. How will they correctly establish the Ascendants of the "great conjunctions" <note>The rare meeting of Jupiter and Saturn, which medieval astrologers believed signaled major historical shifts.</note> if the motions of Jupiter and Saturn are not exactly understood? Abraham [Ibn Ezra] thinks we are so far from a perfect knowledge of these that he pronounces it a great achievement if we even know the *day* on which they should be found together. To this opinion is added that of John of Saxony <margin>John of Saxony.</margin>, who says it was done for this reason: so that the Ascendant of a great conjunction is not taken as that which rises at the hour of the actual conjunction, but rather what was rising at the beginning of the turning year in which it occurred. Thus, he protects one error with another error. But the Ascendant of a conjunction does not cease to be what it is simply because it is unknown to us. Therefore, it should rather have been said that we cannot know what the conjunction will produce because the horoscope <note>The Ascendant or rising sign.</note> cannot be known, rather than inventing a false one because the true one is ignored. For what does a conjunction have to do with the horoscope of a year that perhaps began many months earlier? Or what is the logic that we observe the Ascendant of eclipses <note>original: "deficientiū luminariū"</note> but not that of a conjunction? Finally, even if it were granted that the Ascendant of the year holds power over the conjunction, they will not deny that the conjunction's own Ascendant is of equal or greater momentum. Since an entirely different constellation arises from that Ascendant, and they are ignorant of it, they must necessarily waver in predicting the effects of the conjunction. I set aside the fact that the Ascendant of the year is equally uncertain, according to the same author, Ibn Ezra. From all this, the shameful error of Abu Ma’shar <margin>Ibn Ezra.</margin> <note>original: "Aboasaris"; Abu Ma'shar (787–886), one of the most influential Persian astrologers.</note> is clear; in the first book of his *Great Introduction*, he said it does not matter if an astrologer errs by one degree. By this statement, he clearly showed he did not understand the very astrology he was defending. Thus, it is no longer true to say that astrology is accused by many out of ignorance, when in fact it is only condemned once it has been thoroughly looked into; it is only loved by those who have merely greeted it from the doorstep.

### Chapter XI: Conflicting opinions on the motion of the eighth sphere; the distance of the head of Aries in the eighth from the head of Aries in the ninth; and the solar apogee.

Observe that until now we were speaking only of the motion of the planets, which are perhaps better investigated. But who will faithfully report the motion of the "fixed" stars? All of astrology confesses that their power is great—indeed, primary and wonderful. Who will correctly place the fixed stars in a chart? Or who will deny that an error of a single degree has no momentum at all, when there is only one degree in which they are believed to be effective—that is, either in the "angles" <note>The four most powerful points of a chart: the Ascendant, Midheaven, Descendant, and Imum Coeli.</note> or the luminaries? But we have them all in our astrolabes <note>term: <term>astrolabium</term> (astrolabe); a handheld astronomical instrument used to tell time and map the stars.</note> and in the tables of numbers described everywhere in common use. This is precisely what I was warning about when we began to dispute these matters: these things seem very easy to trivial astrologers whose doctrine comes from a few paltry scraps of paper. But to the more learned and skilled, they are inextricable. When these experts approach the more remote writings, they see that masters of equal authority disagree on these matters as much as the east is distant from the west. The Egyptians, Chaldeans, and indeed all ancient opinion thought that the wandering stars <note>The planets.</note> moved with only one motion, which...

He highlights contradictions between major authorities like Ibn Ezra and Abu Ma'shar to show the field's internal inconsistency.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Pico’s investigation into the inconsistencies of astronomical measurements. Having previously discussed the solar year, he now turns to the "precession of the equinoxes"—the slow shift of the stars over centuries—and highlights the total lack of consensus among ancient and medieval authorities regarding this motion.</meta>

<page-num>IX</page-num>
<header>Book IX</header>

<margin>The work of Hipparchus.</margin>
...what we call the daily motion. <term>Hipparchus</term> <note>A Greek astronomer of the 2nd century BCE who is credited with discovering that the positions of the stars shift slightly over time.</note> introduced another motion by which the stars were swept along from west to east, just like the wandering stars <note>The planets.</note>. Let this, therefore, be the first controversy to be raised: whether they move by their own motion or not. The more recent astronomers will say there is no controversy, since it is not surprising that something observed by later generations was not yet able to be detected by the ancients. However, there are also those among the more recent who defend the opinion of the ancients, as they do not doubt that those who thought otherwise were mistaken. 

<margin>Proclus, most skilled in all mathematics. Proclus censures Ptolemy and Hipparchus.</margin>
<term>Proclus</term> <note>A 5th-century Neoplatonist philosopher and scientist.</note>, who lived long after <term>Ptolemy</term>, was the most skilled of all in mathematics; this is easily declared by his astrological suppositions, his treatise on the <term>sphere</term> <note>A standard textbook on the geometry of the heavens.</note>, the composition of the <term>astrolabe</term>, his commentary on <term>Euclid</term>, and the many other things he wrote. In his commentaries on the *Timaeus* <note>Plato’s famous dialogue on the origin of the universe.</note>—as he also does elsewhere—he censures <term>Hipparchus</term> and <term>Ptolemy</term> because they thought the non-wandering stars <note>The "fixed stars," as opposed to the planets.</note> revolved around the poles of the <term>zodiac</term> <note>original: "signiferi"; the "sign-bearer" or the belt of the ecliptic.</note> toward the east, moving one degree every hundred years. Instead, he argued we should yield to the Egyptians and Chaldeans <note>Ancient Mesopotamian astronomers known for their long records of observations.</note>, who in their long-lasting observations recorded no such thing, especially since the senses testify to ancient tradition so clearly that one cannot agree with <term>Ptolemy</term> without being blind <note>original: "exoculatus"; literally "de-eyed."</note>. 

For if they move, he says, upon the poles of the <term>zodiac</term> as <term>Hipparchus</term> and <term>Ptolemy</term> think, it would necessarily follow that in these regions the <term>Great Bear</term> <note>The constellation Ursa Major.</note> would sink toward its setting by a significant amount; yet from the time of <term>Homer</term> until now, it is said to be "never-setting." Furthermore, <term>Canopus</term> <note>One of the brightest stars in the night sky, visible only from southern latitudes.</note> ought no longer to be visible, since for those living in the third <term>climate</term> <note>A geographical division of the Earth based on the length of the longest day.</note>, that star completes only a brief period above the horizon. 

<margin>Posidonius.</margin>
For those who inhabit <term>Rhodes</term>, it grazes the eastern horizon, as <term>Posidonius</term> <note>A Stoic philosopher and astronomer (c. 135–51 BCE).</note> writes. Since, therefore, the Bear still appears as "never-setting" today—just as it always appeared so many centuries ago—and <term>Canopus</term> has preserved the same position, it is proven by the evidence of the senses that the motion of the fixed stars introduced by the more recent astronomers is false. 

If they perhaps object that the calculations of the motions of the planets are gathered correctly by the testimony of the senses by those who, in arranging the numbers and setting out the tables <note>original: "canonis"; the astronomical tables used for calculation.</note>, assume the motion of the fixed stars, <margin>A double response.</margin> he says the objection is dissolved in two ways. First, because even those who omit that motion of the fixed stars in calculating the motions of the planets say things consistent with appearances; and while they establish tables for the revolutions of the stars while making the non-wandering stars immobile, they nevertheless reach a result that matches the truest reasoning. Second, because it is well known that a truth can be gathered from false suppositions; therefore, just because the result matches the senses, it does not mean the underlying assumptions are true. 

<margin>Abraham Ibn Ezra.</margin>
That most learned philosopher and mathematician <term>Abraham Ibn Ezra</term> <note>A 12th-century Jewish polymath.</note>, though he often mentions both opinions—one making the non-wandering stars mobile and the other making them immobile (which he ascribes to the Indians)—he never passes judgment. Instead, he leaves the matter undecided, so that in his book on nativities <note>A work on casting birth charts.</note>, he instructs that a double chart be made: one as if they moved, and the other as if they did not move. And although I define nothing on this matter myself, except for this one thing: that nothing certain can be defined; nevertheless, it is very true that the fact that the supporters of the opposite dogma do not agree at all among themselves favors the opinion of the ancients. 

<margin>Ptolemy, Hipparchus, Arzachel, Isaac, Thebit.</margin>
For <term>Ptolemy</term>, following <term>Hipparchus</term>, thinks they always move from west to east. <term>Arzachel</term> <note>The Latinized name of the 11th-century Arab astronomer al-Zarqali.</note> the Moor believes that after they have proceeded a certain distance, they return from east to west—a view followed by <term>Isaac</term> the Israelite <note>Isaac ibn Sid, a key contributor to the Alfonsine Tables.</note>, who says it was observed with the most certain experiences. <term>Thebit ben Chorat</term> <note>Thabit ibn Qurra (9th century), who proposed the theory of "trepidation."</note> wipes out that motion, having devised another which inclines toward the south and the north. Recent astronomers, approving the discovery of <term>Thebit</term>, also admit the opinion of <term>Ptolemy</term>, carving up the <term>eighth sphere</term> <note>The celestial sphere containing the fixed stars.</note> with a triple motion. Then, those who agree with <term>Ptolemy</term> that they advance toward the east and do not change course, nevertheless fight over the speed of the course, thinking it false that one degree is completed in a hundred years. For <term>Averroes</term> <note>original: "Auerodan"; the 12th-century philosopher and commentator.</note>, <term>Moses the Egyptian</term> <note>The famous philosopher Maimonides.</note>, and <term>Ibn Ezra</term> after...

<summary>Pico argues that the fundamental astronomical concept of the "precession of the equinoxes" is mired in contradiction, citing Proclus's defense of the ancients and the wildly differing theories of medieval Arabic and Jewish astronomers. He concludes that because the experts cannot agree on whether or how fast the stars move, astrological predictions based on these positions are inherently unreliable.</summary>

<header>Book IX</header>

<margin>Albategni</margin>
Some records state that the space of one degree is crossed in seventy years. <term>Albategni</term> <note>The Latinized name of al-Battani (c. 858–929), a pivotal Arab astronomer.</note> later claimed it took sixty-six years, making the stars move faster than <term>Ptolemy</term> had suggested by a ratio of nearly one and a half. 
<margin>Paulus Flor.</margin>
<term>Paulus Florentinus</term> <note>Paolo dal Pozzo Toscanelli (1397–1482), a famous Florentine mathematician and cosmographer.</note> asserted that they revolved even more swiftly than Albategni had said. Who shall judge between these opinions? The younger astronomers say, "We have detected the positions of the stars with reliable instruments, and therefore we cannot be mistaken." But what was it, then, that deceived those ancients? They did not lack instruments, nor was their skill in the craft any less than yours. It is commonly said in these times that the <term>movable Aries</term> <note>The point in the sky where the sun crosses the equator in spring (the vernal equinox), which shifts over time.</note> is distant from the <term>immobile Aries</term> <note>The actual physical constellation of stars called Aries.</note> by twenty-five degrees. But <term>Auenazra</term> <note>Abraham Ibn Ezra (c. 1089–1167), a celebrated Jewish scholar and astrologer.</note>, in his *Book of Astrological Regents*, 
<margin>Auenazra.</margin>
records that the distance was eight degrees when he was writing. Indeed, he wrote in the year of grace 1153; therefore, he preceded our own time by more or less three hundred and forty years. Accordingly, if we follow the motion recorded by Albategni (which is swifter than the others), the stars would have proceeded by no more than five degrees in the years that have passed since Ibn Ezra; thus the distance today would not be twenty-five degrees, as they say, but thirteen. Was Ibn Ezra then mistaken? He had both the theory and the instruments at his disposal. <term>Moses the Egyptian</term> <note>Maimonides (1138–1204), the preeminent Jewish philosopher.</note>, in that book titled *Misnecota* <note>The *Mishneh Torah*, Maimonides' code of Jewish law.</note>—which you might call in Greek <term>δευτερωσιμ</term> <note>original: "deuterōsim"; meaning "repetition" or "second law."</note> or in Latin the "Second Law"—says near the beginning of the first part that at the time of the <term>cataclysm</term> <note>The biblical Flood of Noah.</note> the movable Aries coincided with the immobile one. Since then, he says, the eighth sphere has always moved toward the east by one degree every seventy years. 
<margin>Time of the Flood.</margin>
Therefore, since the waters flooded the earth in the year of the world 1656, and we are now living (as the more accurate calculation teaches) 
<margin>Years from the beginning of the world.</margin>
roughly 5,300 years from the creation of the world, there will be about 3,600 years or thereabouts from the Flood to our own time. In that many years, the eighth sphere would have moved more or less fifty-two degrees; this would be the distance of the movable Aries from the immobile one. <term>Isaac the Israelite</term> <note>Isaac Israeli ben Joseph (14th century), author of the astronomical work *Yesod Olam*.</note> writes that both signs coincided in the year 560 after the birth of Christ. <term>Pietro d'Abano</term> <note>A 13th-century physician and astrologer.</note>, in his *Elucidarium*, records that this happened in the year of Christ 260; this calculation disagrees with the previous one by three hundred years. <term>Angelus of Mantua</term> and many more recent authors 
<margin>Ange. man.</margin>
contend that this same coincidence occurred in the fifteenth year of grace, with a few months added. The same is reported by <term>Isarith</term> <note>Likely referring to Isaac ben Sid, one of the compilers of the Alphonsine Tables.</note>, a more recent figure; 
<margin>Isarith.</margin>
when he had calculated the positions of the sun and moon relative to the eighth sphere, he found that the new moon of the month of March—exactly 5,224 years from the beginning of the world—was near the fourteenth part of Pisces. Yet <term>Angelus</term>, calculating that same new moon relative to the immobile signs (since he used the tables of <term>Emanuel</term> 
<margin>Tables of Emanuel</margin>
which he entitled *Baal Cuaphaim* <note>The *Ba'al Ha-Kanafayim* ("Lord of the Wings") by Immanuel ben Jacob Bonfils, c. 1350.</note>), found it in the twenty-eighth degree of Pisces. If one follows the <term>Alphonsine Tables</term> <note>The most famous medieval astronomical tables, sponsored by Alfonso X of Castile.</note>, it would be in the twenty-seventh part and fourteen minutes. From this, it would be concluded that the movable signs were distant from the immobile ones by thirteen or fourteen degrees. Now, that man wrote a few years before our own age, which is why he says it is a marvel to him that the <term>Oxford Tables</term> <note>The "Tabulae Oxonienses," likely the 14th-century tables used at Merton College.</note> record the star located between the horns of Aries (which is the beginning of the movable Aries) as being distant from the immobile Aries in the year of grace 1360 by twenty-four degrees and fifty-seven minutes. During those times—about forty years later, I find—both that 
<margin>When Isaac and Roger Bacon flourished.</margin>
Isaac and <term>Roger Bacon</term> <note>The 13th-century English friar and philosopher.</note> flourished; each of them thought that in his own age, the immobile Aries varied from the movable one by no more than ten degrees. For both of them followed <term>Azerchele</term> <note>Al-Zarqali (c. 1029–1087), an Arab astronomer from Toledo.</note> regarding the maximum distance that could occur between them...

# Book IX

<margin>Epilogue of reason</margin>
...judged the parts to be ten: a point which <term>Isaac</term> <note>Likely Isaac ben Sid, a 13th-century Spanish-Jewish astronomer who helped compile the Alfonsine Tables.</note> declared had been reached in his own time. Why, then, would the movement begin to approach that time again, the motion having rolled back in a reverse direction toward the west? Let us therefore conclude: either the <term>thematic instruments</term> <note>Specialized tools like astrolabes or quadrants used to calculate the "thema" or birth chart.</note> do not deceive, or they do. If they do not deceive, how did Isaac and <term>Rogerius</term> <note>Possibly Roger of Hereford, a 12th-century English scientist.</note>, while observing the stars of the <term>movable Aries</term> <note>The point of the spring equinox, which slowly moves against the background of the fixed stars.</note>, judge them to be removed no more than ten degrees from the equinox? Yet, if the opinion of the <term>Oxford tables</term> <note>The *Tabulae Oxonienses*, astronomical tables used in England in the 14th century.</note> or of more recent scholars is true, the stars were moved from that point by more than twenty-three degrees. This makes an error of thirteen degrees strikingly evident. 

If these instruments *do* deceive, how do our own experts know they are not also deceived, especially since the leading men in this art differ with such a great variety of opinions? If anyone thinks they can decide between these views, they do so by brute impulse rather than by any true judgment of the heavens. Therefore, whoever offers a definitive opinion on the locations of the <term>fixed stars</term> <note>Latin: *non erraticarum*, literally "the non-wandering ones," distinguishing the stars from the planets.</note> might perhaps avoid error by sheer luck, but they will never achieve certainty through reason. 

Nor should we overlook that <term>Proclus</term> and <term>Ptolemy</term> deny that the <term>apogee</term> and <term>perigee</term> <note>The points where the sun is furthest from and closest to the Earth.</note> of the sun move at all. However, there is what the astronomers call in their <term>barbarous tongue</term> <note>Pico often uses "barbarous" to refer to Arabic-derived technical terms which Renaissance humanists found unrefined.</note> the <term>aux</term> <note>The apogee.</note> and the <term>opposite aux</term>; the more recent scholars claim these *do* move. <term>Leo the Hebrew</term> <note>Levi ben Gerson (Gersonides), a 14th-century philosopher and astronomer.</note> rebukes these moderns, defending the original opinion of Ptolemy. I pass over their ignorance regarding the <term>equation of days</term> <note>The correction needed to account for the fact that solar days are not all exactly 24 hours long.</note>, over which they clash like swordsmen. From this arises the greatest uncertainty in casting <term>horoscopes</term> <note>Specifically the calculation of the "Ascendant," the point of the zodiac rising on the eastern horizon at birth.</note>.

<margin>Proclus. Ptolemy.</margin>
<margin>Leo the Hebrew agrees with Ptolemy.</margin>

### Chapter XII: On <term>Directions</term>, regarding which there are many conflicting opinions among astrologers.

<margin>The work of the moderns</margin>
**B**eyond all these issues, there remains the inextricable labor of arranging the "rays" (or <term>aspects</term>) and the points which Ptolemy calls <term>aphetes</term> <note>The "giver of life," a planet or point used to determine a person's lifespan.</note> and <term>peripachos</term> <note>A technical term related to the "killing" degree or the end of life; often spelled *anareta* in other texts.</note>—commonly known as <term>directions</term>—which must be counted exactly. On this topic, the mathematicians pierce one another with mutual wounds; no single authority has been able to stand firm, nor has the experience of so many ages been able to settle any single point. 

The opinion of the more recent scholars is that the most exact "radiation" is composed from <term>ascensions</term> <note>The way signs of the zodiac rise over the horizon, which varies based on geography.</note>—right, oblique, and mixed—according to the variety of locations. But a problem arises: if someone is born in a region where the <term>pole</term> is raised forty-eight degrees above the horizon, and the first part of Capricorn is in the horoscope (the Ascendant), a <term>trine</term> <note>A harmonious 120-degree aspect.</note> aspect would fall in the sign of Cancer. However, we know that Cancer is directly opposite to Capricorn <note>An opposition is 180 degrees, not 120; Pico is highlighting a mathematical absurdity in their systems.</note>.

<margin>A reason against this theory.</margin>

<margin>The opinion of Henry Baten.</margin>
<term>Henry Baten</term> <note>A 13th-century Flemish astronomer and astrologer.</note> observes the configuration of planets based on their places: he holds that a "trine" is simply whatever occupies the fifth house from the Ascendant, regardless of the zodiac sign; he does the same for the other aspects. <term>Albategni</term> <note>The Latinized name of al-Battani (c. 858–929), a prominent Arab astronomer.</note> counts the intervals by the degrees of the zodiac, which they call "equal degrees," unless a star has drifted to one side or the other; though the number varies little for that reason. It does not change by more than thirty minutes, even if the star has drifted by ten degrees. This was the method followed by <term>Johannes Regiomontanus</term> <note>A famous 15th-century German mathematician and astronomer.</note>, and it was also taught by <term>Abraham</term>, the chief teacher of <term>Ibn Ezra</term>.

But if you argue that experience has proven that charts must be composed through <term>ascensions</term>, <term>Ibn Ezra</term> will resist you for a long time; he will say a thousand times that they must be established by equal degrees based on many observations. There are others who always use "right ascensions," a practice they falsely attribute to Ptolemy, as we showed above. 

Furthermore, Ptolemy does not take into account the <term>latitude</term> <note>A planet's distance north or south of the sun's path (the ecliptic).</note> of planets, except when they are physically joined. <term>Abenzagel</term>, however, uses latitude in every aspect except the opposition. <term>Aboafar</term> <note>Abu Ma'shar, a famous 9th-century Persian astrologer.</note> uses it even in the opposition, for which others criticize him. I will not even start on how much they disagree on the "orb" of influence—how far the power of an aspect extends. Some say three degrees; some prefer five; for the Moon, some say up to twelve degrees; others, like <term>Porphyry</term>, say thirteen. 

This is an equal question and an inextricable disagreement among mathematicians regarding <term>directions</term> (to use their own jargon). For the Egyptians always used the local ascensions of their region. <term>Dorotheus</term>, in directing the first part, always agreed with right ascensions...

<margin>Opinion of Albategni.</margin>
<margin>Johannes Regiomontanus.</margin>
<margin>Abenzagel. Aboafar.</margin>

<margin>Abraham [Bar Hiyya]. Ptolemy.</margin>
<term>Abraham</term> <note>Likely Abraham Bar Hiyya, a 12th-century Jewish mathematician and astronomer from Barcelona.</note> testifies very often that these methods correspond to experience. <term>Ptolemy</term> <note>The most influential astronomer of antiquity (2nd century CE).</note> and almost all later authors in the East held that when a star is positioned in the east or west, it should be calculated through the <term>ascensions of the region</term> <note>The time it takes for a sign of the zodiac to rise above the horizon at a specific geographic latitude.</note>; if positioned in the fourth or tenth house, through the equator; but in the intermediate places, through a mixture of both. <margin>Almeon.</margin> <term>Almeon</term> <note>Likely Al-Ma'mun, the 9th-century Abbasid Caliph who sponsored major astronomical works, or possibly the astronomer Al-Bitruji.</note> feels the same in the seventh chapter of his fourth treatise on <term>directions</term> <note>A predictive technique in astrology where a planet's position is mathematically "moved" to a new point to determine when a future event will occur.</note>. <margin>The opinion of Abu Ma'shar.</margin> <term>Abu Ma'shar</term> <note>The famous 9th-century Persian astrologer known in the West as Albumasar.</note> directs through the degrees of the zodiac; for in the eighth "difference" of the second treatise of his *Book of Great Conjunctions*, he directs the Moon to the location where the <term>malefic stars</term> <note>Usually Mars and Saturn, considered to bring bad luck or hardship.</note> join together. <margin>Avenezra.</margin> <term>Avenezra</term> <note>Abraham Ibn Ezra, a 12th-century polymath and influential astrological commentator.</note> feels the same in his book titled *The Beginning of Wisdom*, confirming this also by the authority of <margin>Another opinion.</margin> <term>Al-Battani</term> <note>An 8th-9th century Arab astronomer (Albategni) who refined Ptolemy's measurements.</note>. There are others who think that in both cases—both for extending "rays" and directing stars—one must use both the degrees of the zodiac and the proportion of the rising times; <margin>John of Seville.</margin> this seems to be what <term>John of Seville</term> <note>A prolific 12th-century translator of Arabic scientific works into Latin.</note> intended in his *Introductions*. Indeed, in the second part of his four-part work, in the chapter on the <term>First House</term> <note>The "Ascendant," representing the self and the beginning of the life in a horoscope.</note>, he carried out this very method. <margin>Other.</margin> Others extend the "rays" through the degrees of the zodiac, but calculate the directions through the <term>ascensions</term> <note>The rising times of the signs.</note>, which <margin>Ibn Ridwan.</margin> <term>Mashallah</term> <note>An 8th-century Persian-Jewish astronomer (Messahala).</note> as well as Ptolemy (according to <term>Ibn Ridwan</term> <note>An 11th-century Egyptian physician and astrologer (Avenrodan) who commented on Ptolemy.</note>) seem to have supported. <margin>Abraham the Jew.</margin> Conversely, <term>Abraham the Jew</term> <note>Likely referring to Ibn Ezra again, or another contemporary authority.</note> brings forward the same reasoning for both operations: that the <term>charts</term> <note>Schemata: the visual layouts of the horoscope.</note> should be composed by equal degrees, and that one must direct through those same degrees. I will pass over how much they disagree regarding which direction a planet should be led; one can see in the <term>Apotelesmatics</term> <note>The *Tetrabiblos*, Ptolemy's foundational work on astrology.</note> where Ptolemy differs from others, <margin>Ibn Ridwan.</margin> with Ibn Ridwan explaining a good deal of it. But we shall not discuss here the great difficulty faced by those who think <term>mixed ascensions</term> should be used in carrying out these teachings. For the most learned men have judged that Ptolemy taught this neither correctly nor sufficiently. <margin>Paul the German.</margin> <term>Paul the German</term> <note>Paulus de Middelburgo, a prominent mathematician and court physician who later became a bishop.</note>, a distinguished mathematician who now lives with <margin>Guidobaldo, Duke of Urbino.</margin> <term>Guidobaldo, Duke of Urbino</term> <note>A famous patron of the arts and sciences in Renaissance Italy.</note>, a most scholarly prince, once wrote that he had never seen anyone who could correctly direct a star to a <term>trine aspect</term> <note>An angle of 120 degrees between planets, considered highly favorable.</note>. He also denies (as should have been mentioned above) that the current tables of planetary latitudes are reliable. From all this, one can see how wide a door is opened for errors in determining the initial hours—whether for births, for cities, or for constellations—and in arranging the <term>theme</term> <note>The birth chart or horoscope.</note>, whether the <term>angles</term> are being established, the places defined, the signs divided, or seats assigned to stars (whether fixed or wandering), or whether the charts are being composed or the <term>aphetes</term> <note>The "giver of life," a specific point in a chart used to calculate life expectancy.</note> are being numbered. The truth concerning these things and mathematical certainty still lies unexplored, hidden in <term>Heraclitus's cave</term> <note>A variation on "Democritus's well," suggesting that truth is buried in a deep, dark, and inaccessible place.</note>.

# THE TENTH BOOK OF THE DISPUTATIONS OF GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA AGAINST THE ASTROLOGERS.

### Chapter One: An epilogue of those things which have been completed thus far, and what must be done in the following books.

<margin>m</margin> We have already cast down the matter of astrology by many degrees, since it has been declared that the fates of all lower things neither hang from heaven, nor are they signified by it. Even if they did depend on it, it would be according to a knowledge of nature, rather than the astrologers' fictions. Both of these points are confirmed by the perpetual and stable condition of the celestial bodies, which—always equal to itself and similar to itself—does not change like a <term>chameleon</term> based on the power of its locations or distances. Next, we showed why it is impossible for us to understand what the heaven might do or judge...

Book X begins by summarizing his progress in proving that the heavens do not control or signify human fate.</summary>

...we were denying: then, why it is part of our human weakness that we can neither know what those fatal hours <note>The specific, supposedly "destined" moments of birth or events.</note> are, nor in the celestial choir <note>The "chorus" or collective arrangement of the stars and planets.</note> in whose hands the power of deciding fate is placed. Certainly, whatever they have handed down concerning these things deviates entirely from reason. For they have created beginnings that are not truly beginnings, while omitting the real ones. Either through ignorance or negligence, they use the most powerful celestial forces to make predictions based on fictional and legendary causes; since no truth belongs to these causes, they have no power to actually effect anything. 

After this, a third point was declared: even if they found no fault in the things we have mentioned, they still have not achieved what they hoped. Instead, they have only revealed a path that is impassable and cannot be crossed by human footsteps. This is what they must achieve: to track the initial hours of birth and to follow the status and every position of the celestial beings they have imagined at every single moment. We argued in the previous book that neither of these can be known. But even if they could provide these details, they are so far from fulfilling their task that they haven't even begun their true duty. For the labor proper to an astrologer—once the <term>theme</term> <note>original: "themate"; the technical layout of a horoscope or birth chart.</note> has been established (which is the work of a mathematician)—is to investigate what that specific constellation actually does. This is the most difficult task of all. If these claims were supported by reason, astrology would be a science; if by experiments, it would be an art. But since it is supported by neither reason nor experiment, it is neither art nor science. It is instead a form of rashness, an unstable deception—the most legendary fiction of hucksters. Therefore, we shall first strip the astrologers of their authority of reason, and then of their claim to experience.

### Chapter II: The reasons of the astrologers are empty and ridiculous.

<margin>Aristotle. Plato.</margin>
**G**eneral facts about the stars were handed down by Aristotle, Plato, and other philosophers relying on reason: their eternal substance, their circular motion, and other things of that kind. However, they never handed down the specific properties of the stars. Reason indicates nothing about them that could be called <term>physical</term> <note>original: "physica"; here referring to "natural philosophy" or the study of the physical nature of things.</note>. In contrast, with the corruptible earthly things we deal with, which we sense closely and know intimately, we only recognize their peculiar "gifts" or qualities through their outcomes and effects. But the "reasons" the astrologers have contrived to prove their dogmas are so far from reason that nothing more irrational can even be imagined. For they are not only lacking in proof (being inferior even to the rhetorical arguments of public speakers), but they are false, futile, conflicting, flawed, and ridiculous. By examining them, let us make each one clear in order.

### Chapter III: The double principle by which astrologers decide which house is stronger is false; even if it were true, their conclusions do not follow.

**W**e shall begin with the reasons by which they try to prove the properties of the <term>places</term> <note>The twelve "houses" of an astrological chart.</note>; yet we declared above that neither their properties nor their distances can truly be known. First, we will deal with the *quantity* of the power of these places. Second, we will deal with their *quality*, declaring everywhere that the principles they rely on are false; and even if they were true, the conclusions they want do not follow from them. There is a double "preamble," so to speak, by which they define who is stronger or weaker in a certain place. 

The first principle is that those places prevail which are connected to the <term>horoscope</term> <note>The Ascendant, or the point rising on the eastern horizon.</note> by an affinity of radiation—namely the <term>trine</term> <note>An aspect of 120 degrees.</note>, the <term>quadrangle</term> <note>A "square" aspect of 90 degrees.</note>, or the <term>sextile</term> <note>An aspect of 60 degrees.</note>. Conversely, a place is considered "lazy" or "cast down" if it is not so joined. 

The second principle is that the "hinges" (which they call <term>angles</term> <note>The four most powerful points in a chart: the 1st, 4th, 7th, and 10th houses.</note>) possess the primary power. Second in power are the places "succeeding" the hinges. Third are those that decline from them, which in Greek are called <term>apoclimata</term> and the barbarians <note>In this context, non-Greeks or Latin speakers using crude translations.</note> call "cadent." First, then, these principles are false; or, if they are granted, most of the things the astrologers derive from them conflict both with each other and with the principles themselves. The falsity of the principles is demonstrated thus:

<meta>This page continues Pico’s critique of the "houses" in astrology. He moves from questioning their existence to showing that the physical reasons astrologers give for their power are logically inconsistent and contradicted by their own authorities.</meta>

<page-num>X</page-num>
<header>Book X</header>
<sig>H</sig>

The effectiveness of the <term>houses</term> <note>original: "locorum"; the twelve divisions of the sky used in a horoscope.</note> cannot be attributed to anything other than the relationship of a position to the <term>horizon</term> <note>original: "finitorem"; the boundary line between the visible and invisible hemispheres.</note>: so that any star is thought to be more effective in a position where, being placed above us, it acts more powerfully. A philosopher, persuaded by natural reason, will grant this immediately. An astrologer is also forced to grant this: since that power of the houses is either sought from the nature of the space itself, or from that relationship to us which we mentioned. It cannot be derived from the space alone; not only because there is no natural force in that space (as we have shown above), but because if I were to say it was, the <term>horoscope</term> <note>The "Ascendant" or the point of the zodiac rising on the eastern horizon.</note> and the division of the houses would be exactly the same regardless of the region. If specific parts of space had their own properties by which they affected the stars placed within them, they would not vary according to the sky, but would be the same for everyone. However, this entirely contradicts the whole of astrology, which decrees that the same star located in the same part of space is in the <term>Ascendant</term> for me, but in the second house for others, the twelfth for others, the third for others, and the eleventh for others, according to the different inclination of the sky. In that case, the inclination would not be what matters, but rather the nature of the space, from which these properties would follow, rather than its relationship to us; for that nature is not changed by the slope of the sky, while the relationship to us is always changing.

But if it is granted that a house is more effective when a planet situated there acts more strongly upon us, those foundations regarding the <term>angles</term> <note>The four most powerful houses in a chart: the 1st, 4th, 7th, and 10th.</note> and the horoscope immediately collapse. First, any place below the earth would be weaker than all those above the earth; nor would the fifth or fourth house be preferred over the twelfth or eighth. Furthermore, among those above the earth, whichever rises higher above the horizon would be judged more powerful; therefore, the twelfth house would prevail over the first. <margin>Ptolemy</margin> The astrologer <term>Aschedelus</term> <note>Richard Swineshead, a 14th-century English mathematician and philosopher known as "the Calculator."</note>, the author of the *English Summa*, conceded this, trusting in utterly indissoluble reason rather than the authority of all other astrologers.

But Ptolemy also saw this reasoning, and following it in the first book of the *Judgments* <note>original: "apoteleſmatō" (Apotelesmaton), the Greek title for Ptolemy's Tetrabiblos.</note>, he established that the most powerful of all places is the <term>Midheaven</term> <note>original: "medii caeli"; the highest point in the sky.</note>, because the rays of the planets positioned there affect us most powerfully. <margin>The opinion of Ptolemy differs from other astrologers.</margin> Next to that in power he placed the eleventh house for the same reason, while he claimed the weakest planets are those halfway between the West and the bottom of the earth. However, these things contradict other astrologers, the greatest part of whom place the East <note>The Ascendant.</note> before all other places; such as <margin>Messahallah, Firmicus, Abu Ma'shar, Ibn Ezra.</margin> **Messahallah**, **Firmicus**, and **Abu Ma'shar**. Although **Ibn Ezra** agrees with Ptolemy, he does not make all the "angles" primary, but rather prefers the eleventh house to all except the highest. 

Finally, if these sayings are maintained, they would make a planet in the fifth house the weakest, since it is midway between the fourth and seventh houses. Also, in his third book, when speaking about the span of years, Ptolemy prefers everything above the earth to those things below the earth. But forgetting what he had said before, he prefers the East to the eleventh house. Then, following the astrologers, he rejects the twelfth house for a certainly flimsy and false reason: because, he says, the thicker and dark vapor of the earth, exhaling from moisture, disturbs and weakens its descending power. Surely, if this reason holds, a person born in foggy weather will always be born unhappy, as all the planets for them will be under darkness, as if placed in the twelfth house. Furthermore, why would a star positioned in the East not suffer from this more? Or could the light created above have already lifted the watery fumes, but not yet been able to dissipate them? This might perhaps work for the Sun; but at midday, what star residing in the twelfth house would be hindered by watery air? Therefore, he more correctly observed in his first book only that the Midheaven would be the most powerful among other places, being more or less intense as it is closer to or further from the summit. This is the only thing that can be said naturally, if we weigh only the effectiveness of natural forces. For to claim that any specific influence has its own property...

Here, he points out the logical contradictions in how astrologers assign power to these houses based on their distance from the horizon or their geometric relationship to one another.</meta>

Perhaps a place can exist in the west that does not have a mid-heaven <note>The "Midheaven" or *Medium Coeli* is the highest point in the sky at a given moment.</note> (if anyone has ever held such distinctions); but as for what a planet is going to do to act strongly, what else will be the cause than the power of diffusing its rays onto the <term>horizon</term> <note>original: "finitorem"; the line where the sky meets the earth.</note>? It is, therefore, exceedingly foolish to say a fixed star is powerful in the fourth house while hiding under the very bottom of the earth, yet if it were to shine almost in the highest part of the heaven, it would have no strength because it does not touch the <term>pivot</term> <note>original: "cardinem"; one of the four "angles" or cardinal points of a chart: Ascendant, Midheaven, Descendant, and Imum Coeli.</note> in its parts. No one will ever persuade any man that a planet in the twelfth house is not "vital" <note>In astrology, the 12th house was traditionally "bad fortune," while the 5th was "good." Pico is mocking the lack of physical logic in these assignments.</note> simply because it is placed in the fifth; for it is far more reasonable that the fifth house be called the "seat of shadows" than the twelfth. No one will be persuaded that we are more strongly affected by the sun when it is still twenty-five degrees distant from the east than when, having slipped by a single degree, it is submerged into the west—even though in the former case it belongs to the <term>Ascendant</term> <note>original: "ascendente"; the point rising in the east.</note>, and in the latter to the sixth house. Much less will they persuade anyone, unless they lack all sense, that a planet is more powerful in the fourth house under the middle of the night than if it occupied the eighth or twelfth house. For the <term>trigonal connection</term> <note>A "trine" or 120-degree aspect, considered harmonious.</note> with the horoscope is rejected based on what we said above concerning the intervals of rays; so that if we wish to follow right reason, the <term>succession</term> <note>original: "anaphora"; the house that rises immediately after the one preceding it.</note> of the horoscope pertains more to its power than the house of "Good Fortune" <note>A traditional name for the 11th house.</note> which is distant by so many spaces. But if such a connection has any weight, why will a place joined to a better pivot not be more powerful?

<margin>
The decrees disagree with the principles.
</margin>
Furthermore, with reason teaching us and various astrologers agreeing, the highest pivot [the Midheaven] is the best of all. Therefore, the sixth house, which is <term>triangular</term> <note>forming a 120-degree trine aspect</note> to it, ought to be numbered among the good houses; by the same reasoning, the ninth should be good due to its affinity with the ascendant. Up to this point, we have seen the falsehood of their principles; now let us see how their decrees disagree with those very principles. For the eighth house is not always "bad" simply because it is disjointed from the ascendant; since a planet located there often fosters the east with a trigonal ray. Similarly, in the second house, a <term>hexagonal radiation</term> <note>A "sextile" or 60-degree aspect.</note> sometimes reaches the horoscope. Therefore, what they conclude is not universally true unless the places are divided by the degrees of the zodiac; but they do not accept this, and therefore their conclusions amount to nothing. Let them also answer whether, since affinity with the ascendant and the angles makes a place "good," a single privilege is sufficient, or if both are needed. If one is enough, the eighth house will be good as it follows the west; if both are required, the second house will be bad as it is severed from the ascendant.

<margin>
Heliodorus.
</margin>
Heliodorus <note>An ancient commentator on astrology, likely referring to the 4th-century writer associated with Paul of Alexandria.</note> likewise writes, following the opinion of Paul and others, that "bad" and "unfortunate" planets do more harm and injury when in "decline" <note>original: "decliviis"; houses that fall away from the cardinal pivots.</note>, even though they usually say that the lowest place is by its nature <term>ineffective</term> <note>original: "α πρακτοσ" (*apraktos*); idle or powerless.</note> and ought to dull bad rays just as much as good ones.

### Chapter IV: The arguments of astrologers by which they strengthen their dogmas can be reduced to about five kinds, which are indeed weak and ineffective.

Let us now examine the errors by which they "prove" the properties of the houses: that this one signifies brothers; another, parents; another, friends; this one, death; another, enemies. Truly, lest I find myself rebuking the same things too often, I will first refute certain general types of arguing which astrologers use whenever they are about to prove something. Then, overturning the foundations of each dogma bit by bit, we will simply point out from which of these already-criticized categories the argument is drawn.

<margin>
Five heads to which all the argumentation of astrologers is reduced.
</margin>
This will be handled in the appropriate places: so that, given their principles and their form of reasoning, we may show that what they think follows does not, in fact, follow. There are generally five "heads" to which you may reduce every astrological proof. The first can be called the argument from the **order of numbers**; the second, from **parabolic similarity**; the third, from **mathematics**; the fourth, from **astrological principles**; the fifth, from **dialectics**. From the order of numbers, they argue thus: the first <term>climate</term> <note>A geographical zone or latitude.</note> is subject to Saturn; the second to Jupiter; the third to Mars; because Saturn is the first...

<meta>This page continues Pico's critique of the mathematical and logical inconsistencies in astrological systems. He focuses here on the arbitrary associations between planets, zodiac signs, and the "houses" of a horoscope, as well as the historical uncertainty regarding the physical order of the celestial spheres.</meta>
