<meta>This page continues the critique of classical astronomical and astrological theories, specifically focusing on the properties of planets as described by Ptolemy and countered by Aristotelian (Peripatetic) logic.</meta>

# Book

### [On the Nature of the Planets]

[The planet] is carried above the hot spheres of Mars and the Sun: therefore it especially heats. Venus is as moist as the Moon, for by the abundance of its light, it draws many of the Earth's vapors to itself. It also derives a heating power from the Sun, to which it is very close. Mercury, because it always clings to the Sun, possesses the property of drying; yet from its proximity to the Earth and its border with the Moon, it possesses the power of moistening. Thus Ptolemy <note>Claudius Ptolemy (c. 100–170 AD), an influential mathematician and astronomer whose works formed the basis of medieval astrology and astronomy</note> reasons in the first book of the *Apotelesmaton* <note>original: *apoteleſmaton*; this refers to the *Tetrabiblos*, Ptolemy's foundational text on the effects of the stars</note>. 

Even if he cannot be persuaded by the Peripatetics <note>Followers of Aristotle's philosophy, who argued that the heavens were made of a "fifth element" (aether) and were not subject to earthly change or weather</note> that the heavens are free from these physical affections, he should at least understand from the very things he himself demonstrated: the Earth is too far from the Moon for the Earth's vapors and breaths to reach it. These vapors are thought by physicists to be raised no higher than sixteen stadia <note>A stadium was a Greek unit of distance; sixteen stadia is roughly 1.8 to 2 miles. The author is arguing that earthly evaporation cannot reach the planets</note>, let alone be raised intact all the way to the Moon, Venus, or Mercury. 

Furthermore, because of its proximity to the Sun, Venus would be more dry than it is moist from earthly mists, since it is closer to the Sun than to the Earth; nor can the force of earthly moisture be compared with the power of the Sun. Add also that Mercury is closer to the Earth and therefore farther from the Sun [than Venus], which should make it more dry than moist. How then does he agree with himself when attributing moisture to Venus, while the Moon is so near to the solar fire and yet heats so little that it is considered cold by many? And if Saturn is stiff with cold though it is less distant from the Sun [than the stars], would not the entire multitude of fixed stars be bound by numbing icy cold, since they are even further away? Yet they declare many of those stars to be of a fiery nature. Therefore, Ptolemy's reasoning is not only false but inconsistent with itself, as is often the case with false arguments.

Others argue from the colors of the planets, a point which Ptolemy also touched upon regarding Mars. These people say that the philosophers lie when they think the elements have no share in color or flavor. They claim the color of water is white and its flavor is sweetness. To the earth, they assign a dark color and a bitter flavor—though others deny this, contending it is sweet, for if it were bitter, the earth would produce no growth. Then, they admit fire has no flavor but is red in color. They say air lacks both color and flavor, but admits various foreign colors. 

In the planets themselves, they say there are no flavors, but there are multiple colors from which we can easily explore their natures. For they say the darkness in Saturn shows an earthy property and comes from black bile <note>original: *trebili* / *atra bili*; one of the four humors in ancient medicine, associated with melancholy and the element of earth</note>. In Mars, the redness bears witness to a fiery quality and red bile. Venus radiates with yellow and white: from the yellow, it is understood to be hot, and from the white, moist. Since these qualities are not equal, they indicate a temperament of nature similar to the condition of air and blood <note>Referring to the "Sanguine" temperament, which was thought to be hot and moist</note>. A similar conjecture is made regarding Jupiter. In the Moon, the fact that it is white shows moisture, while its touch of darkness demonstrates it is cold. The color of Mercury changes repeatedly: now it appears green, now dark, now it turns to another aspect. However, it favors darkness more, whereby it is rendered more conforming to earthy dryness. 

So they reason, though quite contrary to logic; for colors follow the mixing of elements, of which there is none in the celestial bodies. Nor does Aristotle say that celestial things participate in color, except insofar as light is a kind of color. Truly, if color indicates some property of a mixture, then light will also indicate the nature of the shining body, since the conjecture is based on color which is thought to emerge differently according to the variety of the mixture. Therefore, since color is nothing other than the evidence of light...

# Book X

<margin>
Refutation of the error of Abu Ma'shar.

Abenzagel.
Alchabitius.
Abu Ma'shar.
Ptolemy.
</margin>

[Abu Ma'shar] <note>Abu Ma'shar (787–886 AD), known in Latin as Albumasar, was a leading Persian astrologer whose works were foundational to Western astrology.</note> believes that the nature of the planets can be known from the primary qualities <note>The four "primary qualities" are heat, cold, moisture, and dryness, which Aristotelian physics used to describe all matter.</note> they produce; this is also what Ptolemy advised. For this reason, Saturn is found by experience to be the author of cold and dryness, for these qualities are seen to flourish in bodies when Saturn is the <term>ruler of the year<note>In astrology, the "Lord of the Year" is the planet determined to have the most influence over a specific year's events and weather.</note></term>. The same observation is made regarding Mars and the rest—whichever elemental affection they influence in earthly bodies. From these influences, the whole nature of the planet is clearly conjectured. Since cold and dryness, the works of Saturn, are adverse to life, Saturn is judged to be a "malefic" and "unlucky" star. Mars is also considered malefic because of its burning heat and immoderate dryness. On the contrary, Jupiter and Venus are said to be "benefic" stars because of their nature of heat and moisture, by which qualities life is preserved. He argues similarly for the others, referring everything at last to those four qualities: cold, moisture, heat, and dryness.

But this type of reasoning depends entirely on experiments. For he does not prove by reason that Saturn produces cold rather than heat—as those we just refuted were attempting to do—but rather by "experience," as if it were a fact discovered by the evidence of the senses. Many philosophers, however, think this is utterly false, asserting that no star is a producer of cold or dryness. Even among those who agree, there is no consensus on which star produces which quality; this is especially ambiguous regarding the Moon and Venus. Indeed, Abenzagel <note>Likely referring to the 11th-century Arab astrologer Ibn al-Zarqallu or the physician Ibn Ridwan.</note> and Alchabitius <note>Al-Qabisi, a 10th-century Arab astrologer and mathematician.</note> think Venus is cold, while Abu Ma'shar and Ptolemy think she is hot. Ptolemy thinks the Moon is hot, while others think she is cold. They also do not agree on Mercury. Furthermore, if these observations were made while a planet was "ruling the year" (as Abu Ma'shar wants), how can they possibly agree? There is such an ambiguity of opinions in choosing the "Lord of the Year" that there are nearly as many future "Lords" as there are astrologers to announce them.

### Chapter 14: If we grant that planets produce primary qualities, it does not follow that some should be considered harmful and others healthful.

And so, whether led by such experiments or by the primary reasons brought forward, even if we grant what they say about the primary qualities, nothing more is achieved than a discovery of the influence of the stars in changing the state of the air, rather than an influence on the bodies themselves through these primary affections. Truly, it does not follow that some stars are healthful and others harmful, nor can the proper and peculiar gifts of the stars be gathered from this. First, if the star of Saturn represents the nature of earth, and Mars represents the nature of fire, why is either one "evil"? Neither earth nor fire is evil; they provide innumerable uses for life, without which nature could not exist. 

In the bodies of living creatures, black and red bile <note>Referencing the four humors (blood, phlegm, yellow/red bile, and black bile) which were thought to dictate human health and temperament. "Red bile" refers to yellow bile (choler).</note> are not harmful but necessary; they are no less useful for undergoing certain duties than blood or phlegm. If they are said to harm by excess, then in that same way blood and phlegm harm if they increase beyond measure. If the logic of the "particular world" (which we call Man) <note>The "microcosm," the idea that the human body reflects the structure of the universe (the macrocosm).</note> is properly investigated in relation to the "universal world," we shall recognize that it is an injustice to ascribe an excess of any quality in the human body to the stars. For it is believed that the elements remain within their bounds and are contained by prescribed law—not causing trouble for the world—because of the celestial nature which governs and moderates the fluid and wandering matter of corruptible things. Why, therefore, by that same reasoning, would it not be the role of the heavens to restrain and curb the qualities in our bodies for the continuous arrangement of life, rather than losing the rest and ruining the whole through the superfluous arousal of one quality? Therefore, if Saturn is in charge of black bile—since nothing emanates from heaven that is not ordered and life-giving—he will not excite it to the destruction of the animal, but will moderate it for its preservation; nor will black bile receive from its star a reason to become more violent...

...acts: but in a more moderate and lively way. For the matter of these things is a certain heap of elements; the efficient cause is the heaven: but the efficient cause gathers into one those things which are mixed, and tempers all things under the peace of a single community, moving one thing by one part of the heaven and another by another, if those things are subjected to different stars; yet all the stars breathe together in unison toward the harmony of the whole along with the heaven. Therefore, let no one be deceived, so that when he hears that Saturn is set over red bile <note>original: "rubræ bili". Usually, Saturn is associated with black bile and Mars with red bile; the author may be citing a specific claim or there may be a scribal error here, as he correctly pairs them later in the page.</note>, he suspects that anything happens from the star that is not suited to good order and life. For the duty of the celestial prefecture should be understood as no less to restrain what is tumultuous than to rouse what is sluggish. 

<margin>Death is not from the heaven but from nature.</margin>

Nor is death from the heaven but from nature; it occurs when, by its own vice, each quality has so degenerated that it cannot sustain the discipline of the presiding star, but either wanders immoderately or fails by being sluggish. This is what I have warned the reader once and again: that no profession does more injury to heaven than astrological superstition. 

<margin>No profession is a greater injury to heaven than astrology.</margin>

For whatever we do beyond reason through the fault of our will, and whatever happens in nature beyond order through the vice of rash and unstable matter—astrology seeks to impute all of it to the stars. It does not think their dignity is safe unless we credit them with every most unworthy thing. 

Therefore, let the reasoning be gathered thus: the four qualities <note>Heat, cold, moisture, and dryness.</note> do not harm bodies but benefit them when they are moderate and tempered; and they proceed from the stars in no other way than in such moderation. Therefore, the stars cannot be called harmful simply because these qualities proceed from them. First, neither Mars nor Saturn can be called "evil" for the reason that the latter stirs up black bile and the former red bile in bodies; for neither of these is harmful to life if it does not exceed its limits and measure—rather, they are necessary to it. Indeed, so far is it from overflowing fatally by the authorship of heaven, that it is precisely from the heaven that it is contained within its prescribed limit. We spoke of this matter abundantly in the third book, where we proved that the evils of the body do not proceed from heaven. 

But even if the heaven did strengthen qualities of this kind beyond measure, it would not immediately follow that Mars and Saturn are "evil" planets for everyone; instead, those excesses would be healthy for some. For the rays of Mars would temper a cold old man, and one who is overheating would be reduced to a proper state by the cold of Saturn. Therefore, an astrologer could not judge a man in whose <term>horoscope<note>Latin: "genitura", the configuration of stars at the moment of birth.</note></term> he saw a powerful Saturn to be subject to the discomforts of black bile, nor pronounce one whom Mars breathed upon more than others as liable to the heats of <term>choler<note>Red bile, associated with a fiery or angry temperament.</note></term>, unless he knew what nature had written for them or had explored it through experience. 

Since the astrologer neither knows nor investigates this, but examines good and bad fortune only from these excesses of qualities, it is clear that he will always be turning in doubt. It is likewise clear that what they say is true: a "fortunate" planet is sometimes changed into an "unfortunate" one, and an unfortunate into a fortunate one. For Jupiter sometimes harms and Saturn benefits; this happens in no other way than through the condition of the matter <note>The physical makeup of the person or object being influenced.</note>, and not through the variety of locations, distances, and signs. If those signs were the cause of this kind of change, the astrologers' own decrees would be found most faulty, provided they uphold their position on the primary qualities. For Mars in Aries, as it will heat more, so it should harm more—which they themselves deny. For they say, "Mars does not destroy his own house" <note>An astrological rule stating that a planet is strengthened and acts "better" when it is in the zodiac sign it "rules" (its "house").</note>; and universally, any star occupying its own house, or term, or exaltation is considered "happy" by them. Yet who would doubt that Mars heats more in Aries? Since Aries, as they wish, is a "fiery sign." Likewise, Saturn would be thought harmful in Capricorn and happy in Aries, contrary to their...

...opinion: when in Capricorn, the cold and dryness of Saturn—qualities by which he is thought to cause harm—are intensified, the heat of Aries will moderate that rigor. For he will be more fortunate when he moves retrograde <margin>Al-Kindi</margin> (which people do not usually think) than when he moves in a direct course; because, as Al-Kindi <note>original: "Alchindus". By the same logic, Mercury in Virgo will harm us with excessive dryness; and the heat of the Sun, combined with the heat of Leo, will attack us more violently than is proper. Yet the Sun will affect us more moderately and healthfully if his ray is diffused upon us tempered by the mixture of a cold sign. 

Thus, in many ways, this reasoning concerning the primary qualities <note>The "primary qualities" are the four physical building blocks of the universe in ancient science: heat, cold, moisture, and dryness.</note> is repugnant not only to truth but also to the dogmas of the astrologers themselves. For there are still many things besides what we have said that we might object to them: as if we were to ask why there is no star ruling over phlegm <note>original: "pituitæ". One of the four "humors" or bodily fluids believed to govern health and temperament.</note>, just as Saturn commands black bile <note>original: "atræ bili"</note>, Mars commands red bile <note>original: "rubræ"</note>, and Jupiter commands the blood? If they say the Moon or Venus rules over it, then Venus and the Moon would have to be numbered among the "unfortunate" planets, since <margin>Ptolemy</margin> an excess of phlegm harms life no less than black or red bile. 

Furthermore, if the Moon is defined as Ptolemy <note>Claudius Ptolemy, the 2nd-century author of the *Tetrabiblos*, the foundational text of Western astrology.</note> defines her, she will seem to have the character of an unfortunate star by every reckoning. For she is (as he likes it) of little heat but much humidity; and no temperament is more liable to putrefaction than this. Therefore, if a planet is judged harmful or healthful based on the influence of its primary quality, the Moon will be harmful—the producer of a dissolving and corrupting mixture—and far more harmful than Mars and Saturn, who, if they do not infuse the best natural qualities, at least infuse qualities that only harm when they are not moderate. 

But that which descends from the Moon is, by its very nature, immoderate through the weakness of its heat, with its moisture flowing and being neither sufficiently "cooked" <note>In ancient science, heat was required to "concoct" or mature substances; a lack of heat led to "raw" or corrupt fluids.</note> nor condensed. <margin>Ptolemy</margin> Yet Ptolemy himself numbers her among the fortunate stars, leaning on the authority of the ancients. <margin>Abu Ma'shar</margin> And Abu Ma'shar <note>original: "Aboafar". Referring to the influential 9th-century Persian astrologer Abu Ma'shar al-Balkhi.</note> even contends that she is more fortunate than Jupiter. From whom I would also gladly ask this: since the Sun is hotter than Mars, and with dryness joined to it, why is Mars considered "unfortunate," while the Sun is thought to be the first among the "fortunate" stars? 

For Abu Ma'shar defines it thus, placing the Sun in the first place among the authors of happiness, the Moon in the second, Jupiter in the third, Venus in the fourth, and Mercury in the fifth—concerning whom he seems to disagree with himself, since he wants Mercury to be dry by its own nature and to savor of the nature of the earth more than the others. Therefore, if he followed his own principles, he ought to count Mercury among the harmful stars. 

But others disagree both among themselves and also greatly with Abu Ma'shar himself; for a large part of them make the Moon, the Sun, and Mercury "middle" <note>original: "medios". That is, neutral or ambivalent, depending on their placement.</note> between the harmful and the beneficial, all of whom, as we have seen, Abu Ma'shar makes beneficial. <margin>Heliodorus</margin> Heliodorus <note>Likely Heliodorus of Alexandria, an astrological commentator.</note> and Paul <margin>Paul</margin> <note>original: "Paulus". Referring to Paul of Alexandria, a 4th-century astrologer.</note> also count Mercury among the healthful stars. Ptolemy makes the Moon healthful, but Mercury and the Sun of a "middle" condition; so that even this discord among them might not a little overturn that opinion and make the uncertainty of their art plain. 

Add that if that supposition about the primary qualities were true, then out of the twelve celestial signs, six would beyond controversy be entirely unhappy and unfortunate: namely, all the fiery signs and all the earthy signs, since those qualities abound in them on account of which they accuse Mars and Saturn of misfortune. But it would even be nine rather than six, since in the watery signs as well, there is (as they think) a deadly humidity joined with cold; and it is not like the humidity in the airy signs, or such as exists in Jupiter, Venus, and the "airy" planets—which is vital and prolific—but rather an aquatic and flowing humidity dominates. This is absurd for a double reason: first, the heaven—the greatest of all bodies and the most beneficial—would be condemned in its largest part; and unhappy signs would be the "houses" <note>In astrology, each planet has a "house" or "domicile" in the zodiac where its influence is strongest.</note> for the happy stars.

...just as Pisces and Sagittarius are given to Jupiter, and Taurus to Venus; these assignments should be distributed based on a natural kinship. Finally, if they call these planets "fortunes" and those "misfortunes" <note>original: "fortunas... infortunia". In traditional astrology, Jupiter and Venus are known as the "Benefics," while Saturn and Mars are the "Malefics."</note>, because life-giving qualities come from the former, while corruptive and harmful ones come from the latter—even if we concede this point most generously—it will accomplish nothing more than relating this "happiness" or "unhappiness" to the state of the physical body, which is balanced and composed by those primary qualities. But as for external events and accidental successes, how can they defend deriving those from this system? This is especially true if the arguments we brought against that opinion above are not extremely weak. 

Lastly, even if everything we have just said were set aside, there is no doubt that those who wish to explain the influence of the stars based on these primary qualities <note>The "primary qualities" are heat, cold, moisture, and dryness—the building blocks of Aristotelian physics.</note> act with too little skill and consideration. Yet every single astrologer does this; even those who boast that they can provide "natural causes" for the dogmas of this art ultimately turn to nothing other than these elemental properties. But in truth, if there are indeed specific and particular influences of the stars, these do not follow such qualities, but rather follow the hidden and truly celestial properties belonging to each star. To these properties, people often refer whatever things in earthly matters seem to rise above elemental nature (while remaining within the limits of the body). In these things, we sometimes see many gifts and virtues that not only do not arise from the mixture of elemental qualities but even disagree with it. For example, myrobalans <note>original: "mirobolani". A type of fruit (like a plum or cherry) used in medieval and Renaissance medicine, thought to have specific healing powers beyond its physical temperament.</note>, despite having a cold and dry temperament and appearing more suited to causing death than life, are believed by a privilege of their secret nature to have a marvelous efficacy in prolonging and invigorating life. 

It is much the same for Jupiter and Saturn, and indeed all the superior nature, if (as astrologers believe) they flow into us. Even if this planet is judged cold and dry and that one hot and moist, we must think that they perform many of their most important actions not through these qualities, but through other hidden powers of their rays. This is true both because such a nature is more fitting for them, and because the works attributed to them by astrologers cannot be referred to those qualities and properties, as we have demonstrated. If this is the case, it is clear by reason that those qualities cannot be grasped—which is what we undertook to prove in this section. The path of experience remains, which will be discussed at length in the following book.

### Chapter XV: The arguments of astrologers regarding the lords of days and hours, and the years of the planets, are ineffective; furthermore, astrologers often use circular reasoning <note>original: "demonstratione circulari". A logical fallacy where the conclusion is used to prove the premise.</note>.

<margin>c</margin> We have refuted every way in which they trust they can prove the universal properties of the planets: whether from the positions of the celestial spheres and the location of the Earth, or from the colors of the stars, or from the influence of the four primary qualities. There remain those arguments by which they gather some more specific conditions of the planets. These are elicited either from parabolic similarity, from astrological rules, or from the order of the spheres. They use the spheres, for instance, in the lordship of days and hours; for, giving the first hour of the day to the Sun (for the sake of example), they give the remaining hours to the planets that follow in sequence according to the position of the spheres. From this, the distribution of the days is born: a day is ascribed to that planet which happens to fall on the first hour of that day through the preceding hourly division. However, these things are amply refuted by what was stated above, where we showed how futile this mode of arguing is, and how it again places in doubt...

...the arrangement of the orbs: we have declared that the imagined succession of command in the heavens is vain. Besides these points, we can also ask the astrologers this: what reasoning showed the Chaldeans and Egyptians—the authors of this superstition—the very first day of all time? For they cannot use the authority of Mosaic law <note>The Law of Moses, specifically the creation account in Genesis.</note> unless they also believe that, according to that same law, astrologers and all diviners must be utterly exterminated. 

<margin>Refutation.</margin>
They reason from astrological charts when they say a certain planet bestows a specific number of years of life because it possesses that many <term>bounds</term> <note>original: "fines". In ancient astrology, 'bounds' or 'terms' are specific degrees within a zodiac sign ruled by a particular planet.</note> in the zodiac. It is just as uncertain to take this data from the "bounds" as it is to prove the number of years from them. Even if what they claim about these bounds were true, there is—as Ptolemy <note>Claudius Ptolemy (c. 100–170 AD), the most influential astronomer and astrologer of antiquity.</note> notes—no logical consequence that would allow the spans of our lives to be decreed by them. Furthermore, they often err in these matters by using circular reasoning: in one place they try to prove the number of years from the number of the bounds, and in another, they gather the number of the bounds from the years.

<margin>The beginning of the year</margin>
They begin the year from Aries because it is the first of the signs. Yet they usually try to show that it is the first in a continuous circle by arguing that we begin the measurement of time from it! In the same way, they argue that the second place in the order corresponds to Jupiter because he "acts and portends," and then claim that Jupiter "acts and portends" specifically because he corresponds to the second place. You will find many examples of this in their books, but some are far more ridiculous.

<margin>Why the moon bestows 108 years and the sun 120 according to Abu Ma'shar.</margin>
This is especially true if you come across the books of Abu Ma'shar <note>Pico writes "Aboafaris," referring to the 9th-century Persian astrologer Albumasar, whose works were foundational to medieval astrology.</note>, in whose writings I recently read that the Moon bestows one hundred and eight years, while the Sun bestows one hundred and twenty. He claims the Moon falls short of the Sun’s life by twelve years because the Moon has no power until it has moved twelve degrees away from the Sun. It is no wonder that Abu Ma'shar boasts of having given a full rational account of astrological dogma—since there is nothing so irrational that it does not appear "rational" to him.

<margin>Why the minor years of the sun are 19.</margin>
There is equal insanity when they say the "minor years" of the Sun are nineteen because the luminaries <note>The Sun and the Moon.</note> are joined in their mean motion by this number <note>Pico is referring to the Metonic cycle, where the phases of the moon recur on the same days of the solar year every 19 years.</note>. In this, there is nothing common, nothing connected, and no logical sequence between the premises and the conclusion. Yet they argue: "After this number of years, the Sun and Moon meet in mean motion; therefore, the Sun gives that many years when it gives its fewest." This is as if someone were to say: "A human is born with two eyes; therefore, a human is also born from exactly two parents."

They use symbolic similarities in the same way: "The Moon is the gate of heaven; therefore, it signifies the mouth." For a gate is, in a sense, the mouth of a house, and the mouth is the gate for food and speech. Likewise, they say the beard belongs to the same star <note>The Moon.</note> because it renews itself repeatedly just like the moon. They subject the ears to Saturn because they occupy the high parts of the head, just as Saturn himself is high in the heavens. By that same reasoning—namely, that he is the highest—they say Saturn produces tall men, even though this does not fit his nature, which is defined as dry and cold <note>In the humoral theory of the time, cold and dry qualities were associated with contraction and shrinking, which should logically produce short stature, not tall.</note>.

These are the "reasons" of the astrologers by which their celestial dogmas are propped up. I would not call them reasons, but rather opportunities for error or for playing around. Once heard, the vanity of their dogma is as obvious as the firmness of truth usually is when it is made known. Therefore, it would have been better for them to hide these things behind a veil or in a chest, like the secret rites of a cult <note>original: "orgia".</note>, leaving behind a suspicion of mystery. Instead, by wishing to appear rational, they have signed their own accusation with their own hands. Hearing these reasons is nothing other than understanding exactly what led the astrologers into error.

# THE ELEVENTH BOOK OF THE DISPUTATIONS OF GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA AGAINST ASTROLOGERS.

## Chapter One: From those things which have been proven thus far, it is evident that astrology is not confirmed by experiments; then the same is proven by many reasons.

If they could not grasp the nature of the celestial bodies by reason—which we have already demonstrated—could they perhaps have done so through experience? And even if they are ignorant of *why* something happens, have they learned through observations *that* it happens, so that if astrology cannot claim the name of a "science," it might still hold the privilege of being an "art" and a "true tradition"? For this would mean it could predict the truth whether it arrived at it through <term>syllogisms</term> <note>A form of logical reasoning where a conclusion is drawn from two premises.</note> or through experiments. It matters little for the purpose of divining how the result is reached, provided it is reached. 

Astrologers, however—like every <term>monstrous art</term> <note>original: "ars prodigiosa". Pico refers to "arts" that claim to deal with omens or supernatural feats but lack a natural basis.</note>—usually defend themselves under the title of "experience," retreating into it as if into a sanctuary whenever they speak of or promise some reason that is beyond belief and filthier than dung. They think they can immediately extricate themselves from the snares of all logic if they simply say they have "experienced" it so. We shall therefore take away this refuge from them too—a refuge which only those think is valid who are more accustomed to speaking with their lips and hearing with their ears than thinking with their hearts. 

For if anyone has thoroughly investigated and meditated upon what experience actually is, and by what paths it can be acquired regarding the influence of the stars, he will certainly not doubt that the peculiar powers and specific operations of the stars are just as inscrutable to man through experiments as they are through reasons. Indeed, this can be made clear enough from the previous books: for if there is either no fate from heaven, or if such fate depends not on the initial hour of birth but on the kinship of the matter, it is obvious that no path is left for experiments. Since the moment when each star first breathed upon you is as uncertain as it is utterly unknown, so too is the unique condition of that primary matter. 

But even if someone were to make the <term>seminal hour</term> <note>original: "horam seminalem". The moment of conception, which some astrologers argued was more important than the moment of birth.</note> the fatal one, the astrologers themselves will not deny that the opportunity for such observation would be far too hidden. Even granting that the time of birth is sufficiently observed: how could there be a faithful observation if it is not even established (as we have declared) which and how many celestial causes are to be observed? Nor can they determine with any reliability the form, condition, or position of those causes they *think* they understand at any given moment. Furthermore, they do not possess an exact time of birth from the <term>master of the birth</term> <note>original: "domino geniturae". The planet considered to have the most influence over a person's life based on their birth chart.</note>, nor can they correct any errors in timing by some method. 

Moreover, if they fail in these matters (and we have shown they always fail), the authority of the entire observation necessarily collapses. Now, even if they did not fail in those points, we shall demonstrate in the present book that no experiments regarding the heavens are possible. Let us grant, then, to the <term>genethliacs</term> <note>original: "genethliacis". Astrologers who specialize in casting horoscopes based on the moment of birth.</note> that they hold the hour of birth faithfully and the state of the heavens at that hour as accurately as possible. I ask: what decree of heaven does such a constellation produce or signify? By what means do they think they have reached this through experience? Since experience is gathered by multiple and frequently repeated observation of the same thing, but the same constellation—as the more learned prove—either never returns, or—as the ancients believed—it will not return except after many thousands of ages. Perhaps they will respond that particular constellations return and are repeated...

<summary>Pico begins Book XI by challenging the astrological claim that their practice is based on "experience" or empirical observation, arguing that the astronomical complexity and the rarity of repeating planetary alignments make such data collection impossible.</summary>

...more often, even if the restoration of the whole and absolute constellation does not occur, they claim they can gain knowledge of those particular parts through repeated observations. From these collected experiments, they say the future can be predicted in good faith. This might be explained by an example: suppose someone is born with Aries in the <term>horoscope</term> <note>The "horoscope" (horoscopante) here refers to the Ascendant, or the sign rising on the eastern horizon at the moment of birth.</note>, with the star of Mars placed therein, and Saturn occupying the <term>seventh card</term> <note>The "cards" or "angles" are the four most significant points in an astrological chart: the Ascendant, Descendant, Midheaven, and Imum Coeli.</note>. Then, while other things are arranged in their own way, another person is born with an otherwise different <term>nativity</term> <note>A "nativity" (genitura) is an individual's birth chart or the specific planetary arrangement at their birth.</note>, but similar in what pertains to Mars and Saturn. The astrologer, although not able to observe the whole constellation twice, can nonetheless observe that specific part. Since this happens frequently, repeated observation creates an "experiment." This is perhaps how they defend themselves; but it is a poor defense, inconsistent with their own principles.

<margin>Refutation.</margin>
For a particular constellation produces a different effect when it is part of a different whole. Furthermore, the substance of the entire judgment comes not so much from the parts as from the whole—that is, from the <term>harmony</term> of all the parts acting together, which produces something unique and specific that no single part, nor even all parts taken together, could produce. Indeed, the whole is something different from the sum of its parts, resulting from the proportion of the mixture. Therefore, such an observation, from which they collect their experiments, will be imperfect. For it is imperfect because it fails to grasp the whole, and it is deceptive because it considers the same part without considering it within the same whole. 

This reasoning draws its strength from nowhere more than from the precepts of the astrologers themselves, who assert that everything happens through the mixing of stars, and that the lot of fate is determined not by their individual powers, but by the combined complex of all of them and their shared union. Therefore, if in one or two nativities you have seen the subject torn apart by calamities when Mars and Saturn were in the primary angles looking at each other from <term>opposite sides</term> <note>original: "ex diametro". This refers to an "opposition," an astrological aspect where two planets are 180 degrees apart.</note>, you cannot—as if a rule had been proven—announce calamities when the same thing happens at another time. For there is nothing to prevent that constellation, under a different tempering of other stars, from combining in such a way that it either does no harm at all, or perhaps even produces something entirely different from what it had done in other nativities with different mixtures of rays. 

If we agree with the astrologers that human affairs are governed by fate, we might point to what experience reveals every day: that the most fortunate people often have the "unluckiest" charts, and the most unfortunate have the "luckiest." Thus, although particular constellations might seem to portend good or bad luck based on past observations, the harmony of the total temperament itself—never before seen, unknown, and unexplored—can produce a different result now than what those parts portended elsewhere, either alone or in a different mixture. Realizing this, the most ancient astrologers did not hand down the dogmas of this art in any other way than by explaining the particular nativities they had observed and finally comparing them with the outcomes—not so much to show what Saturn or Jupiter did, but what such a complete constellation produced.

<margin>Maternus</margin>
<margin>Ptolemy.</margin>
<term>Maternus</term> <note>Julius Firmicus Maternus, a 4th-century lawyer and astrologer who wrote the "Mathesis," an influential astrological textbook.</note> attempted this in some way in the sixth book of his commentaries, following the example of the Egyptians. However, <term>Ptolemy</term> <note>Claudius Ptolemy (c. 100–170 AD), the most famous astronomer and astrologer of antiquity, author of the "Tetrabiblos."</note> accuses them of failing to reduce the art to a <term>method</term> <note>A systematic or scientific approach.</note>, even though they were pursuing something infinite and incomprehensible. Therefore, Ptolemy turned himself toward explaining universal rules and the simple powers of the stars, believing that once these were known, a <term>genethliac</term> <note>original: "genethliacum". An astrologer who specializes in casting birth charts.</note> could finally judge the specific mixture through his own conjecture.

<margin>Ptolemy is to be accused.</margin>
But although he rightly accuses the ancient astrologers, he himself is no less rightly to be accused. For the ancients correctly saw what needed to be done, but they erred in thinking it was possible; for it is an infinite task that can be reduced neither to an art nor a method. Furthermore, no use comes from it, since the same constellation is never restored. Thus, Ptolemy focused on what *could* be done rather than what *ought* to be done...

<summary>Pico argues that astrological "experiments" are invalid because they focus on individual planetary alignments rather than the whole sky, which never repeats. He critiques both the ancient Egyptians and Ptolemy for trying to create a science out of these unique, non-repeating celestial events.</summary>

Anyone thinking this could happen would have wandered too far astray if he believed that true predictions could be made from those similar rules. Perhaps this is how it happened, as <term>Ibn Ezra</term> <note>Abraham ibn Ezra (c. 1089–1167), a celebrated Jewish scholar and astrologer whose works were widely read in the Renaissance.</note> writes, that the rules of <term>Ptolemy</term> <note>Claudius Ptolemy, the 2nd-century author of the *Tetrabiblos*, the "bible" of Western astrology.</note> never agree with actual outcomes and experiments. But Ptolemy is less to be blamed for this because, as we showed in the second book, he plainly confessed that this art is based on opinion, conjecture, doubt, and deceit.

So, having brought the theme into the open, let us press the <term>nativity-caster</term> <note>original: *genethliacum*. An astrologer who specializes in birth charts.</note>. Here is something for you, O Astrologer: if all other things were granted to you, the most powerful and chief thing in producing an effect is the specific outcome of the whole <term>harmony</term>. It is from this harmony that the fortune of the person born most properly depends. Since neither reason nor observation has given you knowledge of this, how can you explain the truth of fate? For you are deceived if you think the efficiency of the whole is nothing other than the collection of what the individual parts produce. 

This would only be true in things that are merely heaped or stuck together, whether they are bodies or qualities; but it is not true where they are mixed and grow together into another form. 

<margin>Example</margin> This is a principle that all astrology believes regarding the rays of the stars. Just as someone has not truly experienced the properties of <term>theriac</term> <note>A famous ancient medical concoction or "universal antidote" made of dozens of ingredients. Pico argues that you can't understand the medicine by looking at the ingredients in isolation.</note> by merely observing the powers of the individual things from which it is made, so too, he who has had experience of the parts of the sky separately does not understand what the present "army" of the heavens produces. 

It is not only the relation of part to part—that is, star to star—but the state and condition of absolutely all the stars among themselves that chiefly produces what is unique to the newborn. Just as a person's own individual and unique nature is not born from a mere confluence of accidents, but is an incommunicable and private allotment of a peculiar substance. 

What if they cannot even attain knowledge of a single star through experience? 
<margin>Reason.</margin> Since nothing ever works in isolation, but everything always works with others, it follows not only that any star can only be defined by its relationship to others, but that it cannot be discerned by any knowledge separated from the others. For from the whole constellation, you will see the course of such a life and such events proceeding; but since all the stars are performing all those things together, you will not be able to know which star was the author of which specific thing, unless you have first grasped the nature of each individual star through reason or some other way. 

<margin>Proposed Solution</margin> But if you say you will observe it this way: that when you see some men with similar fates, you will argue that the fate comes from that specific part where their charts harmonized, and you establish this through frequent observation... 

<margin>Refutation.</margin> <note>original: *Confutatio*</note> I respond that this way of conjecturing is far too deceptive. First, because a similar state of a star can produce a different result in a different mixture, and a dissimilar state can produce the same result. Second, because the same fate may not have the same cause, since according to the opinion of astrologers, the causes of the same effect in the sky are almost innumerable. 

This whole matter will be clearer with an example: Peter is born with Jupiter placed in <term>Pisces</term>; Paul is born with Jupiter similarly situated. They live with completely different constellations otherwise, and they have different fates, characters, talents, and health; they are equal only in their fortune of accumulating wealth. Is it permitted here to conjecture that the giver of riches is Jupiter placed in the second house in Pisces? 

Certainly not. For that which was common to them in fate—namely, the abundance of riches—could have come from different celestial causes, not from common ones. Even if in the one's <term>nativity</term> <note>A birth chart.</note> the lord of the <term>horoscope</term> <note>The planet ruling the sign rising on the eastern horizon.</note> bestowed power on the sun occupying a <term>card</term> <note>A "card" (cardinem) or "angle" is one of the four most powerful houses in a chart (1st, 4th, 7th, 10th).</note>, while as the other came into the light, the <term>Lot of Fortune</term> <note>original: *pars fortunae*. An Arabic part or mathematical point in a chart used to signify prosperity.</note> held the East with a favorable radiation from its own lord.

<summary>Pico argues that astrology is logically impossible because planetary influences blend into a "harmony" that cannot be understood by looking at individual stars. He uses the example of Peter and Paul to show that the same outcome (wealth) can arise from entirely different astrological configurations.</summary>

...joined together: either in one <term>nativity</term> <note>original: *genesi*. A birth chart or the moment of birth.</note> the planet of the fortunate shone in the first <term>angle</term> <note>original: *cardine*. The four most powerful points in a horoscope: the Rising, Midheaven, Setting, and Lower Midheaven.</note>, while in the other, Mercury, situated in that same place, borrowed its power from a fortunate and angular planet. Or even if, when Peter was born, Venus resided in the fifth house and held power in the first, while at Paul's birth, the <term>luminaries</term> <note>The Sun and the Moon.</note>—weakened by no low positions—regarded each other favorably; even then, according to the opinion of the astrologers, the same fortune of wealth would not come to both from that same "face" of the stars. A varied fortune can happen to different people in that matter, even if the star that produces it was in a similar position in their nativities. For one thing, the condition of a single star cannot be entirely the same unless the whole constellation is exactly the same. Furthermore, a contrary power could be present in the other person's chart, either overwhelming or dulling the effectiveness of the star there. It is clear, therefore, that from the joined and mixed influence of the stars, we cannot discern by any observation which

<margin>Third Reason.</margin>
star specifically grants what gift. For this reason, we cannot define the powers and natural properties of the stars as known through experiments. Another reason for this insurmountable difficulty is added, even if each star acted individually: since their effects can be reversed, interrupted, or frustrated in many ways by the condition of lower and surrounding causes. No one, unless they are reckless and of a shaky judgment, would assert: "These things happen because this star is situated so; therefore, when it is situated that way again, a similar outcome must be expected." For that star might have been about to produce a different thing by its own nature, but the work is changed by the individual's <term>private fate</term>, or the universal fate of the region, or the soul, or the prince, or the city, or the family, or the household; or by what came before, such as parents, grandparents, and great-great-grandparents; or the <term>free will of the one born</term> <note>original: *arbitrium nati*. Pico famously argued for human dignity and free will over celestial determinism.</note>; or the disposition of the air through which the celestial influences are transmitted to us; or stubborn matter; or a more immediate cause that is not convenient or suitable for the higher motions. Since all these things can change the efficiency of the stars as they please, how can an argument be safe if we interpret the nature of the stars 

<margin>Refutation of a silent rebuttal</margin>
by what has happened? This is especially true since the things we have mentioned are always so closely linked to the operations of the stars that an event cannot be traced back to a star as its sole origin, even if we have noted it happening often. Those who think that observations made by the Egyptians, Chaldeans, or Arabs in their own regions have the status of universal dogma seem to be hopelessly deceived. That is, they think these rules will be equally valid in every region, when in fact it is necessary for them to happen entirely differently—if indeed the things they hand down and which experience itself demonstrates are true. For in the changes of the air, we see quite clearly that from the same constellation, different weather is stirred up in different places: calm here, violent there; snow here, clear skies there; winds in one place, and rain in another.

<margin>Phavorinus. Confirmation by the authority of Paul of Alexandria.</margin>
It is therefore quite inconsistent to think that in the birthing of human bodies and in the successes of those born (if indeed these things come from heaven) the same stars would not work differently because of the different curvature of the sky in different places. <term>Phavorinus</term> <note>A 2nd-century philosopher known for his skeptical arguments against astrology.</note> also threw this objection at them, which we shall confirm by the authority of <term>Paul of Alexandria</term> <note>A 4th-century astrological author; Pico uses the astrologers' own authorities to undermine their "science."</note>. In his *Introduction to Astrological Effects*, he writes that nativities in Egypt are especially happy when <term>Aquarius</term>, holding the principal places, is well-disposed; this is because the region of Egypt is subject to Aquarius. From this, it might be said that Mercury in Aquarius breathes happily upon the talents of the Egyptians; yet <term>Firmicus Maternus</term> <note>A 4th-century Roman lawyer and astrologer.</note> recorded that Mercury is humbled and fares poorly in any house of Saturn <note>Aquarius is traditionally ruled by Saturn.</note>. It is clear, therefore, by the testimony of a singular astrologer, that the same observations will not be equally valid in every region (even if any faithful observations could be made in a specific region), which does not happen...

He highlights that astrological "laws" are often just local observations (e.g., in Egypt) that do not apply globally.</summary>

...we have already demonstrated by many reasons. And if Hippocrates, the father of physicians, <margin>Hippocrates</margin> said that experimentation in medicine is deceptive, no one but the most unlearned would deny that in astrology it is most deceptive of all.

## Chapter II: If any experience could be gained regarding astrological dogmas, it has not yet been gained.

<margin>a</margin> Up to this point, our aim has been to prove that no length of time, and no human industry or learning, can acquire experimental knowledge regarding the more secret powers of the stars. Now, lest that point be perhaps less than persuasive, we will demonstrate this at least most clearly: if such experience *could* be acquired, it has not yet been acquired. For by our previous arguments, this much is certainly established: we must admit that knowledge of all such things is extremely difficult and cannot be completed except through the revolution of many ages. 

Therefore, we shall first refute those lies of the astrologers by which they claim—partly to appear expert, partly to appear truthful—to possess observations spanning many thousands of years. Then we shall show that whatever observations they do have are, by their own words, deceptive. The philosopher Favorinus <margin>Favorinus</margin> <note>A skeptical philosopher of the 2nd century who wrote against the Chaldeans.</note> says in Gellius: "That discipline of the Chaldeans <note>original: *Chaldaeorum*. A term used synonymously with astrologers in antiquity.</note> is not as ancient as they wish it to appear." And Cicero <margin>Cicero</margin>, following the authority of Panaetius <note>A Stoic philosopher who was one of the first to reject astrology.</note>, says: "For when they say the Babylonians spent four hundred and seventy thousand years <note>original: *quadraginta septuaginta milia annorum*. This refers to the astronomical—and likely exaggerated—timelines claimed by Babylonian priests.</note> in testing and experimenting on whatever children were born, they are lying." No author we have says this either could be done or was known to have been done. 

These are his words. Let us, beginning deeper, prove their impudence. Whether the world is eternal, as certain philosophers wish, or created in time, as Divine Truth teaches, let us leave this most attested fact: no observations older than four thousand years could have reached those who handed down the science of the stars. For it is certain even to those philosophers who believed in the eternity of the world that through great changes of the elements, the seas dry up and lands are flooded; once the dwellings of lands and men are changed, an ocean exists where there was land, and land exists where there was ocean. Not only sacred historians, but also the philosopher Plato <margin>Plato</margin> and foreign writers, have often mentioned such floods and conflagrations. It makes no difference whether the world is new or if a change in circumstances robs us of the memory of past things. 

Let us therefore examine from histories how ancient these celestial observations could have been. Varro <margin>Varro</margin> <note>Marcus Terentius Varro, a Roman polymath considered the most learned man of his time.</note>, the most learned of the Romans, when about to weave the most ancient history possible, began from the reign of the Sicyonians. Trogus <margin>Trogus</margin> <note>Trogus Pompeius, a Roman historian of the 1st century BC.</note>, either slightly earlier or a contemporary, began with Ninus <note>The legendary founder of Nineveh.</note> himself, who waged war with Zoroaster and was a few years older than the patriarch Abraham. Thus, those who write that Zoroaster flourished five thousand years before the Trojan War are caught as myth-makers, since not even that many years are counted from Abraham to our own times. 

What reason is there, then, why both Trogus and Varro—having professed to write the most ancient histories—did not start deeper? It is because due to the world’s novelty, <margin>Note: The following names are markers for the text above</margin> or at least its renewal, there were either no records or they were completely obliterated. For although they wished to write ancient and even "first" histories, they wished to write *true* ones, not the fables of Herodotus <margin>Herodotus</margin> and Diodorus <margin>Diodorus</margin>, whose words these most impudent storytellers usually use to bolster their "observations of so many thousands of centuries"—as if Diodorus in his title...

<summary>Pico argues that the claims of astrologers to possess tens of thousands of years of data are historical fabrications, noting that reliable historical records (according to Varro and Cicero) do not extend beyond four thousand years due to geological catastrophes or the world's recent creation.</summary>
<keywords>Babylonian observations, Cicero, Varro, Zoroaster, historical reliability, floods and conflagrations, ancient history, Chaldeans</keywords>

# Book XI

<margin>Porphyry<br/>Confirmation through Porphyry's testimony.<br/>Another confirmation by Hipparchus and Ptolemy.</margin>
Even if Herodotus <note>A 5th-century BC Greek historian often called the "Father of History," but also the "Father of Lies" due to his inclusion of legends.</note> were not considered the greatest teller of fables by the common consensus of literature, let us set such matters aside. In our own case, there is the most evident testimony of Porphyry <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher (c. 234–305 AD) who wrote extensively on philosophy and science.</note>. He says that the observations of the stars which Callisthenes <note>The historian and relative of Aristotle who accompanied Alexander the Great on his conquests.</note> sent to Greece from Babylon at the time of Aristotle and Alexander—which the Chaldeans had recorded—contained observations spanning only one thousand nine hundred and three years. If you count back those years from the time of Alexander, you will find they end at the time of the patriarch Abraham, or only slightly earlier. Hipparchus and Ptolemy, the princes of astronomy, when they bring forward the observations of the ancients to establish their doctrines, bring forward none older than those made under King Nebuchadnezzar among the Egyptians or Babylonians. Hipparchus flourished about six hundred years after that king's reign, and from Hipparchus's time until our own, more than one thousand six hundred years (or thereabouts) have now passed. Therefore, they boast mendaciously and fabulously of having observations from so many ages; and that those observations they do possess are necessarily false can be easily demonstrated. For they either began at the time of Ptolemy, or they were lost by those who preceded Ptolemy. If the continuity of such observation began after Ptolemy, there has not been enough time to perfect the observation, a fact which they themselves will not deny. If they rely on the experiments of the ancients—namely those handed down by the Egyptians or Chaldeans—who can doubt they are deceptive? For there can be no faithful observation of the heavens among those who did not correctly understand the motions of the heavenly bodies. No one who has even touched the books of the mathematicians is unaware that in this matter the Chaldeans and Egyptians alike erred greatly. Ptolemy censures them everywhere in his *Great Composition* <note>original: *magna compositione*. Known more commonly by its Arabic-derived name, the *Almagest*, this was the definitive astronomical text for over a millennium.</note>, as does Hipparchus. Nor would anyone easily believe how late in time the human race began to understand anything correctly regarding the motions of the heavens.

<margin>Thales.<br/>Eudemus<br/>Callimachus<br/>Plutarch<br/>Pythagoras.<br/>Euripides.<br/>Solon.<br/>Proclus.</margin>
Thales was the first to predict an eclipse of the sun, according to the authority of Eudemus <note>Eudemus of Rhodes, a pupil of Aristotle and historian of science.</note>. And Callimachus says that Thales was the first discoverer of the Little Bear <note>Ursa Minor, used for navigation by the Phoenicians.</note> by which the Phoenicians sail. He also divided the year into three hundred and sixty-five days. Plutarch asserts that the obliquity of the zodiac <note>The tilt of the Earth's axis relative to its orbit, which causes the seasons.</note>—the first discovered fundamental of stellar science—was thought out by Pythagoras, although a certain Euripides of Chios <note>Likely a reference to Oenopides of Chios, a 5th-century BC astronomer; "Euripides" may be a transcription error in the original or the source.</note>, younger than Pythagoras, boasts that it was first discovered by himself. Before Solon flourished in Greece—and he flourished about six hundred years before the time of Christ—everyone thought the lunar month was exactly thirty days. Solon was the first to correct this error, as Proclus writes in his commentary on Plato's *Timaeus*. But if they were erring so significantly regarding the motion of the moon, which is so easy and familiar to us, what must be thought of the motions of the other stars, which are more hidden and slower?

<margin>Ptolemy.</margin>
But there is no need for conjecture here. Let Ptolemy’s book titled the *Great Composition* be read, and it will be clear beyond suspicion that all the ancients were "as far apart as the whole sky" <note>original: *toto caelo*. A Latin idiom meaning "completely wrong" or "poles apart."</note> regarding the motions of the heavens. Regarding the motion of the nearest star which we were discussing, you will find that nothing discovered by the ancients was not only far from the truth, but not even close to it.

<margin>The time of Hipparchus.</margin>
Hipparchus was the first, on the island of Rhodes about two hundred years before Christ, to observe the course of the moon more truly. But even so, he did not reach total clarity, which is why he is corrected by Ptolemy. Ptolemy indeed came closer to the truth than Hipparchus, but in such a way that he still did not reach it; he was subsequently corrected by the Spanish astronomers <note>A reference to the Alfonsine Tables, produced in 13th-century Spain under Alfonso X.</note>. Even regarding the motion of the sun, by which they measure all others, they still grope blindly; antiquity certainly never attained it. Indeed, the Egyptians wandered excessively out of orbit, thinking that the solar restoration <note>The completion of a full solar year.</note> occurs after three hundred and sixty-five days and a quarter of a day plus a thirtieth; for more accurate subsequent observations have taught that even the quarter is not fully completed <note>A reference to the fact that the tropical year is slightly shorter than 365.25 days, necessitating the Gregorian reform later in history.</note>.

<summary>Pico argues that astrologers' claims of ancient records are fraudulent, noting that reliable Greek observations only began around the time of Thales and Solon. He demonstrates that even great astronomers like Ptolemy and Hipparchus had to correct the massive errors of the Egyptians and Chaldeans.</summary>
<keywords>Porphyry, Callisthenes, Aristotle, Alexander the Great, Nabuchodonosor, Hipparchus, Ptolemy, Thales, Ursa Minor, solar year, lunar month, Almagest, Alfonsine Tables</keywords>

He transitions from questioning the age of Chaldean records to arguing that the basic tools of astronomy—like the sundial and the astrolabe—were invented much later than the supposed "ancient" observations of the Egyptians.</meta>

# Book XI

<margin>Theophilus.</margin>
<margin>Anaximander, inventor of the gnomon.</margin>
<margin>Pythagoras.</margin>

How, therefore, could the wisdom of the Egyptians have made reliable experiments regarding the fate of the year, when they were so errant concerning its very beginning? In that matter they were quite ridiculous: for they inaugurated the year, as **Theophilus** <note>Probably Theophilus of Antioch, an early Christian writer who discussed chronology.</note> reports, as soon as the Nile first began to flood Egypt. **Anaximander**, as **Favorinus** writes in his *Universal History*, was the first to invent the <term>gnomon</term> <note>The upright part of a sundial that casts a shadow.</note>, with which he might mark the solstices and the equinoxes. Furthermore, no one who has read his books is unaware that the astrolabe was the invention of **Ptolemy**. **Pythagoras** was the first to say that the evening star and the morning star were the same body <note>original: "vesperum atque luciferum"</note>, following the authority of **Parmenides**; and **Pythagoras** did not precede Christ by more than five hundred years. 

But let us return to the motions of the planets, which were so little explored by the ancients that **Hipparchus** said so few observations of the ancients exist regarding the five planets (excluding the sun and moon) that he could not affirm anything certain about them from his own findings. **Ptolemy** was the first who seemed to say something certain about them, although the following age, through the benefit of time, has corrected him in many places. In the reckoning of the "ascensions"—which the Greeks call <term>anaphoras</term> <note>The rising of a zodiacal sign above the horizon.</note>—how far from the truth were all those in Egypt who practiced divination by the stars! Both **Ptolemy** in the first book of his *Apotelesmata* <note>The "Tetrabiblos," Ptolemy's foundational work on astrology.</note> and **Apollinarius** in his commentaries have testified to this; and **Apollonius** of Laodicea, in a work of five books dedicated to this subject, censured their errors. 

Who then, considering these things, would doubt that no true experiment regarding the influences of the stars could be held among the Egyptians or Chaldeans? For they had explored neither the ascensions of the signs, on which the greatest part of this art depends, nor the motions of the planets. It is as if they could faithfully test what a planet was doing in a certain place, when the planets were always in a location where they least expected them; for the motion of the wandering stars was entirely unknown to them, if we believe Ptolemy. 

But if they erred, as is undoubtedly clear, then the Greeks err who follow them; the Arabs err who follow the Greeks; and the Latins err who follow the Arabs and the Greeks, and who predict future events based on their rules and "experiments." For they think they put forward nothing with greater authority than that which they confirm by the authority of the Chaldeans and Egyptians. Hence names like **Aesculapius**, **Hermes**, **Nechepso**, and **Petosiris** <note>Legendary figures to whom many occult and astrological texts were falsely attributed.</note>—all empty names—are scattered like mists before the readers, as if these men were not the most ignorant of the science they professed, if **Hipparchus** and **Ptolemy**, the chief authors of astrology, have handed down the truth to us. Why then did **Ptolemy**, in the first book of the *Apotelesmata*, as if to give credit to his words, turn to the experiments of the ancients? He himself could scarcely begin to find the truth in his own time, when the science of the stars was then for the first time tolerably investigated. **Peter of Abano** <margin>Peter of Abano.</margin> excuses the wandering **Galen** regarding the motions of the moon thus: 

<margin>Galen and Ptolemy.</margin> 
"**Galen** did not write these things exactly, for they were not yet understood; <margin>contemporaries</margin> yet **Galen** was not prior to **Ptolemy**, but a contemporary." 

Therefore, let us conclude the whole dispute thus: if any astrology that has been written relies on the "experiments" of the ancients, it is fallacious, because they lacked a method and reason. And since these things are also ambiguous for the moderns, as we have shown above, they were hardly manifest to antiquity—which is even more fallacious for the younger practitioners, who lacked both method and time.

->**The end of the eleventh book of the Disputations of Giovanni Pico della Mirandola against the astrologers.**<-

<header>Book XII</header>

### THE TWELFTH BOOK OF THE DISPUTATIONS OF GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA AGAINST THE ASTROLOGERS.

## Chapter One: Faith is not to be granted to astrology as if it were a revelation.

<margin>The first reason</margin>
**I**f neither reason supports the fables of the astrologers, nor can any trust be established through experiments, what is left? Why should a wise man surrender himself to them? Shall they be considered oracles? And shall we accept as divine those things which we have refuted as irrational? They act like the astrologers themselves, who, if anything is done by men that defies reason, attribute it to the stars. Shall we then, by a similar example, attribute the ravings of men to the gods? But if perchance this persuasion has seized anyone, let him know that it is of no benefit to him

<margin>The second reason</margin>
to have divine revelations of this kind, since—as we have seen—there is such great disagreement in the decrees of astrology. Nor has it yet been revealed whether that "wisdom" which the gods breathed upon us as a singular gift for our merit is the astrology of the Chaldeans, or rather of the Egyptians, the Jews, Ptolemy, or the Arabs. Therefore, that divine beneficence helps us not at all while that most true wisdom, received from heaven, lies hidden in the filth <note>original: "colluuie"</note> of our own lies.

<margin>The third reason</margin>
Nor has any <term>Lydian stone</term> <note>A touchstone used to test the purity of gold; here used metaphorically as a standard for truth.</note> been sent down from above by which the legitimate might be distinguished from the counterfeit. But if I am speaking with Christians, I would ask whether they think it was revealed by God, or rather by a demon. It cannot be said to be from God, since the Sacred Scriptures—the interpreters of the divine voice—forbid it. If they answer "by a demon," then no faith is due to a demon, whom God called the father of lies. Hence the madness of those is refuted who fabricate the story that this science, like all others, was conferred by God upon **Adam**, from whom it passed down through the hands of men to **Noah**. They claim that **Methodius** <note>Methodius of Olympus (d. 311), an early Christian bishop and author.</note> reports that Noah’s son **Ionicus** predicted many future things through this art; and that through the sons of Noah who survived the **Great Flood** <note>original: "Cathaclismo"</note>, it reached the patriarch **Abraham**, who taught it to the Egyptians (according to the testimony of **Josephus** <note>Titus Flavius Josephus, a 1st-century Romano-Jewish historian.</note>); and from the Egyptians it passed to the Greeks, and from the Greeks to the Latins. Thus they devise for themselves a quite beautiful succession, convenient for ensnaring the ignorant, but everywhere false and deceitful to the more learned.

<margin>The fourth reason</margin>
<margin>Methodius.</margin>
For concerning what they say about Adam—unless this too was a revelation—by what testimony do they prove it? Does it follow that because we believe he mastered all sciences by the gift of God, he mastered this one too? Certainly it would follow if this were also a science—if it were not vain, not false, not ridiculous, and not repugnant to the principles of true doctrines, and (as we were saying) not repugnant to God. But it is not even worthy of a human inventor. Let us come to **Ionicus**: **Methodius** indeed writes about him, but he is an insufficiently reliable author. For he is not the one whom Saint 

<margin>Jerome, Peter</margin>
**Jerome** mentions among famous men; that one was from Patara <note>Pico writes "parcharenfis", likely referring to Methodius of Patara.</note>, while this other is entirely different, cited occasionally by **Peter Comestor** <note>A 12th-century theological writer; Pico implies he is uncritical in his choice of sources.</note>, in whom no moderately learned person would fail to notice a lack of discrimination regarding good authors. But neither does Methodius say that Ionicos predicted anything; moreover, what weight can the authority of an obscure writer have regarding this Ionicos, when even **Moses** himself p<unclear>...</unclear>

<summary>Pico argues that astrology cannot be a divine revelation because its practitioners disagree on its rules and the Bible explicitly forbids it. He mocks the "historical" lineage that claims astrology was passed from Adam to Noah and Abraham as a fabricated story used to trick the uneducated.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Pico's systematic dismantling of the "divine origin" myth of astrology. Having previously questioned the lineage of this knowledge, he now focuses on the claim that the patriarch Abraham was the one who brought this science to Egypt, arguing instead for a distinction between mathematical astronomy and superstitious divination.</meta>

<header>Book XII</header>
<meta>catchword: Nevertheless</meta>

...the prophet <note>Refers to Moses, the traditional author of Genesis.</note> counts only three sons of Noah: Shem, Ham, and Japheth. <margin>Josephus, Philo.</margin> Neither Josephus nor Philo <note>Philo of Alexandria, a Jewish philosopher.</note> mentions anyone else besides these; nor does any Hebrew writer, whether a chronicler or an interpreter of the Mosaic law. Let us believe Josephus when he says that Abraham passed on astrology to the Egyptians—but not that superstitious, divinatory kind so common among idolaters (which is condemned by Moses and the prophets), but rather the kind practiced by those who worship the true God, the "God of Abraham." For those idolaters claimed they were following the traditions and precepts of Abraham. Instead, he taught that mathematical science of the motions and habits of the stars, the use of which was frequent and necessary for the Hebrews to observe the fixed times of their ceremonies. Hebrew records testify that the tribe of **Issachar** was specifically assigned to this study. This cannot be learned without arithmetic, since it consists almost entirely of numbers and measurements. Josephus writes that Abraham demonstrated this alongside astrology to the Egyptians; if Josephus had meant that divinatory kind, he would have been utterly mistaken, since he says that the Egyptians received this astrology (which Abraham first showed them) from the Chaldeans. However, it is clear from earlier accounts that the Egyptians created their own specific astrology for predicting the future, which has almost nothing in common with the dogmas of the Chaldeans. Furthermore, Ptolemy teaches in his *Great Composition* <note>original: "magna compoſitione"; refers to the *Almagest*, the most influential ancient astronomical text.</note> that only a few Chaldeans practiced the branch concerning the motions of the stars, and from them it flowed to others. Therefore, Josephus understood nothing other than this mathematical science. Moreover, **Boasar** <note>Likely referring to the Arab astrologer Abu Ma'shar.</note> is to be laughed at; he says in his own place that the sons of Noah, when they came into Chaldea, disseminated this science, yet he himself rejects the Chaldean opinion regarding the boundaries of the planets as being "divinely held." <margin>Fifth reason.</margin> But one should not spend so much effort in refuting these trifles, since anyone but the most dull-witted understands that these are the ravings of men who grant such credit to their own dreams that they confirm things they have brought forth without any reason by claiming the authority of Adam. For let them answer this: why did other arts and sciences not come down to us through such a succession, but were instead thought out by the talents of posterity and perfected by diligent study? Or did we receive this gift of divine providence only in astrology, as if it were more useful than the rest? Truly, that providence—which does not usually sleep—would have been dozing; you would not fail to notice that this divinatory art is preserved for us in vain unless the mathematical part were also preserved, without which we cannot use the former correctly. For it is of no use to have discovered the powers and natures of the stars unless you can note, by exact calculation, the habits, form, and position of the stars at every single hour. Since only mathematics provides this, this too should have devolved to us by hereditary tradition from the first father <note>Adam.</note>, if divine providence did not wish for the use of such "salutary" divination to be missing from our lives.

## Chapter II: What sort of people the Egyptians and Chaldeans were, among whom astrology was born.

**H**ere are rejected those who worship these trifles—which are so unworthily and so falsely fabricated about the heavens—as if they were nonetheless received from heaven. When anyone reads these things with insight, he sees their nature so clearly that no suspicion of celestial inspiration remains; this, I think, is evident enough from what has already been said to even the dullest person. Nevertheless...

<summary>Pico argues that while Abraham may have taught the Egyptians astronomy for calendrical purposes, he did not teach them the "superstitious" art of divination. He further mocks the idea that astrology is a divine secret passed down from Adam, noting that the necessary mathematical tools for it were never perfectly preserved.</summary>
