<meta>This page continues the transition from the historical legends of Abraham to a sociological and geographical critique of the two cultures most associated with astrology: the Chaldeans and the Egyptians. Pico begins to dismantle the prestigious "ancient wisdom" traditionally attributed to these peoples.</meta>

<page-num>XII</page-num>
<header>Book XII</header>

It will not be useless, reader, to consider in a single view from where this **pestilence** <note>Pico frequently refers to judicial astrology—the practice of predicting human fate from stars—as a "pestilence" or "disease" affecting the mind.</note> was born and spread throughout the world: that is, by what authors it arose, by what persuasions it was received, by what authority it was confirmed, and by what fuel it has increased and persevered to this day. For this will also be not entirely ineffective for stripping away its credit and exposing its vanity. It was born, therefore, from **Chaldean** <note>Ancient inhabitants of Mesopotamia, famous in antiquity for star-gazing.</note> and **Egyptian** parents, about whom something must be said before we speak of the vanity of the thing itself.

Both nations were especially studious and skilled in two things: **idolatrous religion** and **mathematics** <note>In this context, "mathematics" refers specifically to the measurement of celestial movements (astronomy), which was often inseparable from astrology at the time.</note>. They were invited to this by the opportunity of their location; for they inhabited open fields and wide plains, from which there is an easy and more accurate view of the stars. In the former case—that is, why they were occupied with and honored for vain and superstitious ceremonies beyond other nations—this was due to their antiquity, because of which they were the first to practice the worship of the gods, and were as parents to others and, by necessity, masters of religion. Furthermore, as we have shown elsewhere, this was also due to their lack of skill in **physical reasoning** <note>Natural philosophy or science based on cause and effect.</note> and the crudeness of their minds.

For mathematics indeed does not make men wise; wherefore among the ancients it was a study for boys. Rather, if tasted moderately and with reason, it builds a path to philosophy; but if someone gives himself entirely to it alone, it gives birth to the greatest occasions for error in philosophy, as **Aristotle** <note>The Greek philosopher (384–322 BCE) whose works formed the basis of university education in Pico's time.</note> testifies. Therefore, the Egyptians and Chaldeans were—as far as I can reach by conjecture—of a disposition little suited for wisdom, which is even now seen in the men of those regions. Even if the chance of study had been taken from them, nature should not have taken away their natural capacity.

<margin>Solution to the doubt.</margin>
Nor indeed should that deceive us which once deceived me as a youth: the celebrated wisdom of the Egyptians and Chaldeans among the ancients, even **Plato**. It is recorded that **Pythagoras**, **Democritus**, **Eudoxus**, **Plato**, and many others visited them for no other reason than for the sake of acquiring wisdom. Indeed, they claimed that celebrated and divine name of "wisdom" for themselves solely from their knowledge of ceremonies and the way of worshiping the gods. Among all nations, and even among all good philosophers, there has always been this persuasion: that the highest wisdom consists in religion. 

Wherefore Plato, Pythagoras, and many others—seeing correctly that the truest philosophy lies in the knowledge of divine things—descended to the Egyptians with a greed for learning whatever seemed more hidden or sacred among them, since the fame was that the Egyptians were especially skilled in this. They also went down to learn mathematics, which those I just mentioned—Pythagoras, Democritus, and Eudoxus—drank in greedily. 

Nevertheless, that title of "wisdom" and the prerogative of a more secret discipline came to the Chaldeans and Egyptians from nowhere else than from their mastery and teaching of the worship of divine powers. Whether those teachings were approved by the good philosophers who heard them or not, we have discussed elsewhere. We assert only this: that the Greek philosophers who philosophized correctly received **nothing** of that primary natural philosophy which is demonstrated by reason from the Egyptians; they received only what pertained to ceremonies and mathematics. A proof of this is that if the subject is mathematics or "mysteries," we see the Chaldeans and Egyptians cited and their opinions always brought forward; but in the philosophical reasonings of Plato and Aristotle, their names are nowhere to be found. If you say that **Thales** <note>Thales of Miletus (c. 624–545 BCE), often called the first Greek philosopher.</note> philosophized in Egypt, I will not deny it—since he even learned from them that "water is the principle of all things."

<summary>Pico argues that the "ancient wisdom" of the Chaldeans and Egyptians was limited to religious ritual and basic mathematics, rather than true rational philosophy. He asserts that while Greek thinkers visited these nations for astronomical data, they did not derive their logical or scientific frameworks from them.</summary>

# Book XII

<margin>Iamblichus.</margin>
<margin>Thales.</margin>
<margin>Demetrius.</margin>
<margin>Averroes.</margin>
I believe the Egyptians were led into this opinion by nothing other than seeing their region blessed and made fertile by the flooding of the Nile. For this reason, they even inaugurated their year from the river’s outflow through Egypt. <note>The Egyptian calendar began with the heliacal rising of the star Sirius, which signaled the annual flooding of the Nile.</note> Their minds were truly quite unrefined and therefore susceptible to superstitions. Nothing rejects and scorns such things more than the vivid force of the intellect when joined with sound doctrine; thus, they were easily led by demons into every kind of madness. If their religion was anything other than superstition—and <term>Iamblichus</term> <note>Iamblichus (c. 245–325 AD) was a Neoplatonist philosopher who wrote "On the Mysteries of the Egyptians," defending their religious practices.</note> largely admits they were deeply occupied with the worship of evil demons—it follows that while they were famous for the name of wisdom in matters of religion, the wiser they were said to be, the more foolish they actually were.

Nevertheless, as was said above, the commerce of the Greek philosophers with them was always more for the sake of <term>mathematics</term> <note>In this period, "mathematics" often referred to the study of the stars (astronomy and astrology) as well as geometry.</note> than for their superstitions. Thales, in a letter to Pherecydes, says regarding Egypt: "I went down with Solon so that we might see the priests and astronomers," saying nothing of philosophy. He also said he learned geometry from them. Demetrius says that Democritus went to the Egyptians to learn geometry. Occasionally Democritus, as well as Plato, and even Pythagoras, were called "monstrous" <note>The Latin *monstrosus* here implies something strange, unnatural, or deviating from the norm, likely referring to their adoption of foreign or esoteric ideas.</note> by the prudent. 

But Plato, displaying that blameless intellect of his which was sufficient for his age, never defiled his own work with the "leaven of Egypt," <note>original: "fermento nusquam temeravit." Pico uses the metaphor of leaven/yeast to suggest that Plato did not let Egyptian superstition ferment or corrupt his own Greek philosophy.</note> though he gave antiquity its due honor and the title of religion. Likewise, Eudoxus followed the Egyptians in true astronomy, but he did not agree with them in their <term>divination</term> <note>The practice of foretelling the future (judicial astrology).</note>. But, lest we wander too far, we conclude thus: the Egyptians and Chaldeans were most occupied with idolatrous superstition and greatly devoted to mathematics, but they exercised themselves very little in the rest of philosophy. 

Nor should anyone be moved by what <term>Averroes</term> <note>The 12th-century Islamic philosopher from Spain, famous for his commentaries on Aristotle.</note> says—that philosophy was once perfect among the Chaldeans. For he is not speaking of the Chaldeans whose memories or monuments have reached us, but speaks from that opinion which, believing in the eternity of the world, claims these arts have been both abolished and restored infinite times among various nations. Nor should it be held against us that we do not approve of the Chaldeans as a whole, from whom **Abraham**, a divine man, originated. Abraham was not "Chaldean" in spirit, though he is sometimes called a Chaldean due to the proximity of the regions. As was said by Plato: "In a nation that is mostly evil, if someone good is born, he is the very best." Nor did Abraham obtain his privilege so much by nature as by divine grace. But let us return to astrology; it is easy to see what led the Egyptians and Chaldeans into this matter, now that we have said enough about their studies and characters.

### Chapter III: What led the Chaldeans and Egyptians to the opinion that human affairs happen by fate and can be foreseen from the stars.

**S**o it is that whoever has immersed themselves entirely in any one discipline will most willingly refer all things to it. This is not so much due to ambition—to make it seem they know everything through that art—but because it truly appears that way to them. This happens by habit, just as it does to those traveling through the snow: to them, everything else usually appears white, because the habit of brightness has already been received by the eyes, transforming everything else into itself. Likewise, those who love desperately see the face of the beloved, or something of them, in whatever they encounter; the entire imaginative faculty is brought under the rule of a single image of the loved one. He who is a theologian, and nothing but a theologian, refers all things to divine causes; the physician refers them to the condition of the body; the physicist to the natural principles of things; and the mathematician...

<summary>Pico argues that the Egyptians and Chaldeans were driven by their environment and "unrefined minds" toward superstition and astrology. He asserts that while great Greeks like Plato and Thales studied their mathematics, they wisely rejected their religious errors.</summary>
<keywords>Egyptians, Chaldeans, Iamblichus, Thales, Plato, Averroes, Abraham, superstition, mathematics vs. philosophy, intellectual bias</keywords>

Pico continues to trace the cultural origins of astrology by looking at the Chaldeans and the intellectual shortcomings of early civilizations that allowed astrological "errors" to flourish.</meta>

# Book XII

...regarding the figures and numbers which the <term>Pythagoreans</term> <note>Followers of the Greek philosopher Pythagoras, known for the belief that numbers are the fundamental reality of the universe.</note> used to practice. For this reason, since the ancient Chaldeans were constantly diligent in measuring celestial motions and observing the courses of the stars—and since nothing else occupied their minds more—all things were stars to them. That is, they willingly referred all things to the stars; this should be understood as applying to the Egyptians as well.

When, therefore, they approached this inclination from their profession, the conjectures which we narrated and refuted in the third book <note>Pico refers back to his earlier arguments where he dismantled the theoretical foundations of astrological influence.</note> emerged: such as the idea that lower bodies are moved by superior ones; that the stars cannot fail to have the greatest powers of influence; and how much the sun and moon are seen to dominate our bodies and the air. When similar thoughts occurred to minds already inclined in that direction, they were easily led to believe that whatever happened to men—whether pertaining to the body, the soul, or fortune—proceeded from celestial causes. They believed that by knowing and exploring these causes, the future events and conditions of all things could be known beforehand.

For natural science was not yet so well understood by them that they sufficiently grasped how a universal cause differs from particular ones, and what the role of each was. They did not understand what was appropriate to celestial substance or what was repugnant to it; they did not know what is called "essential" <note>original: *per se*</note> among the <term>dialecticians</term> <note>The practitioners of logic and formal reasoning.</note>, or what is "accidental" <note>original: *ex accidenti*</note>; nor did they see how great the dissimilarity is between the works of nature and those of art. They failed to see what might be a sign of another thing even if it were not its cause. Thus, stirred by these reasons, they failed to recognize that even when proximate causes are inactive, one should not ascribe particular diversities to a common cause. Nor did they realize that just as they did not consider the heavens to be equal to God in goodness, they should not impute their own faults to the stars, nor derive from them the punishments for the evils of the soul and body. Nor did they understand that the nature of the body does not recognize the causes of things happening by chance at the same time, such that their coincidence should be referred to it. Nor did they think that new powers flow from heaven into works of art, as if art could penetrate to the innermost substance of a thing. Or, if these things were not done by heaven, they believed they could still be signified by it, even though they were neither effects nor causes of one another, nor did both proceed from the same origin in the same way.

Since they were ignorant of all these things—partly because a perfect philosophy was not yet developed, and partly because they had not yet investigated these matters—is it any wonder if, with so many things pulling them toward error, they were led astray? They were influenced first by the conjectures we mentioned, which were indeed ineffective, but which held great probability for the common people and those unrefined in philosophy. Then came that constant habit and, as it were, familiarity with the stars; to all of which was added the innate curiosity of humans to know the future. For those things we desire to happen, we easily believe to be possible.

Added to this was the vice of the age and the persuasion toward divination deeply rooted in human minds during that time; they greedily followed a thousand modes and types of it, far less probable than this one and possessing more madness—such as <term>pyromancy</term> <note>divination by fire</note>, <term>geomancy</term> <note>divination by patterns in the earth</note>, <term>astragalomancy</term> <note>divination by dice or small bones</note>, and other "old wives' trifles" <note>original: *anilia nugamenta*</note> of that sort, among which the error of the astrologers could be considered the highest wisdom. 

Add that it agreed marvelously with the idolatry to which they were subject, so that they thought the gods they worshiped were the authors of all things—not only good things, but evil ones too. For there was also this teaching in idolatry: that some gods were beneficial and others harmful, so that even from this, contrary to the reasoning of philosophy, they considered some stars good and others evil. Add to this the opportunity for glory and profit which the <term>astronomers</term> <note>Pico uses this term here to refer to those who study the heavens for the purpose of prediction, rather than pure science.</note> saw prepared for themselves, if they thought the future could be foreseen from the courses of the heavens, which they investigated with great labor but perhaps for meager pay. 

To all these things, add the frauds of wicked demons then ruling the world most strongly, who pushed their minds—already inclined toward this error for the reasons mentioned—with even more hidden instigations. They did this both by perverting the judgments of the minds enslaved to them and by sometimes confirming their predictions or moving them to predict.

He argues that they mistook celestial signs for causes and were driven by a human desire to profit from predicting the future.</summary>

...what would happen, or carrying out what had been predicted by them. I do not doubt that all these things together were the reason why the opinion first arose among the Egyptians and Chaldeans—men devoted to superstitions and idolatry, most occupied with celestial motions, and skilled in one part of philosophy <note>Pico means they were skilled in observation but lacked the higher logic to interpret those observations correctly.</note>—that the future could be foreseen from the state of the stars. The world easily accepted this opinion because of curiosity and ignorance; the astronomers confirmed it most willingly in the hope of gaining profit and glory.

# Chapter IV
## On how they happened upon those things which they established as necessary to observe in predictions.

<margin>We have seen</margin> among which peoples and how this error—that human affairs are caused or indicated from heaven—was first born. It is easy to see how, in turn, they arrived at these astrological dogmas which they use in predicting. For they were not led to these things by true reasoning, as we have demonstrated (for how could they be, since there is no true reasoning for a lie?). Furthermore, we do not explore the properties of things joined to us in place and nature otherwise than by their operations <note>Pico is arguing that we only know the nature of things by watching how they actually function; the astrologers skip this step and jump to conclusions.</note>. Nor were they led by experience; otherwise, they ought to have ceased from predicting for many ages, since experiments of this kind are completed beyond controversy only by long-lasting observations and those repeated very often.

What conjectures, then, did they follow? Partly those taken from the mathematical studies they were engaged in, and partly from certain parabolic similarities, than which nothing more deceptive could be imagined. But either they themselves were deceived, being unrefined in philosophy and logic, or they thought the ignorant common people could be deceived. Nor did a more likely path satisfy those hastening toward the profit and glory of divining as much as the easier and readier path did. Thus they first established that these fates of men depend on the hour of birth, then because it generally seems to the common people that a man is "made" when he is born. Also because other beginnings, whether of conceiving the fetus or of giving life <note>original: "aiandi" — referring to the animation or "ensoulment" of the fetus in the womb.</note>, were more uncertain than those to be observed in predicting.

They accepted these from the mathematicians <note>In the Renaissance, "mathematician" (mathematicus) was often a synonym for an astronomer or astrologer.</note>; first, because when measuring the motions of the stars, they divided the oblique circle <note>The ecliptic, the path the sun appears to follow through the stars.</note> into twelve parts for ease of counting, and again by the same reasoning, they divided each of the parts into thirty, and each thirtieth into sixty. They took up this division as if it were made by nature and not by human choice. And they decreed that there were as many powers of influence and diverse properties as the number of parts they had fashioned for themselves. Then, according to the number of the signs, they divided twelve "places" <term>houses</term> <note>The "houses" are twelve divisions of the sky relative to the observer's horizon, distinct from the signs of the Zodiac.</note>: six above the horizon <note>original: "finitorem" — the limiting line or horizon.</note> and six below, just as six signs revolve above the earth and six below. 

Thus, by a great error, it was determined that one must observe primarily in which place and in which sign a planet was located; for they believed planets acquired powers for influencing differently according to the variety of the place and sign. After this, whatever diversities they noted in the motions, they also judged to be noted in the operations of the stars, as if the power and appearance of their efficiency were varied by them. Thus they decreed a planet does one thing when it moves forward, another when it moves backward <term>retrograde</term>, and another when it stands still <term>stationary</term>. Then they decreed that different things happen according to the conjunction or distance of the stars from one another. They observed certain distances in particular, which they measured; they had detected some more significant changes at certain intervals, such as the <term>trine</term> interval <note>original: "trigonum" — an aspect where two planets are 120 degrees apart.</note>, because in it Saturn and Jupiter, when configured with the Sun, always move backward; just as sometimes Mars does in the <term>square</term> <note>original: "quadrangulo" — an aspect where two planets are 90 degrees apart.</note>, while they saw that Mercury and Venus are never removed from the Sun beyond the <term>sextile</term> <note>original: "sexangulum" — an aspect of 60 degrees.</note>. They thought, therefore, that these distances of the stars were to be observed when they presented themselves to one another in trine, sextile, or square radiation, as well as in opposition, for which there is an evident reason, especially since in these configurations...

He argues that astrologers chose the "easier path" of the birth hour for predictions because it was more convenient than tracking conception or animation.</summary>

they observed the phases of the moon change in relation to the sun: becoming **crescent-shaped** at the sextile <note>A 60-degree angle between celestial bodies.</note>, **halved** at the square <note>A 90-degree angle.</note>, **swollen** <note>Also known as a gibbous moon.</note> at the trine <note>A 120-degree angle.</note>, and **full** at the diameter <note>The 180-degree opposition.</note>. Just as they had imagined certain intersections of circles <note>The lunar nodes.</note> to be a necessary thing for measuring motions—but a vain thing for determining influences—so too they applied these to the decrees of the fates, calling them the **Head** and the **Tail** <note>The "Head and Tail of the Dragon," or Rahu and Ketu, points where the moon's path crosses the sun's path.</note>. Finally, they followed these mathematical quantities—positions, locations, points, and distances—as if they were forces and the "breathing" of the rays, rather than looking at the natural qualities of those rays. But they did not notice this error due to their ignorance of physics; nor could they avoid it if they wanted there to be different constellations in the sky at every single moment, which might vary the life, fortune, manners, and character of men being born one after another.

## Chapter V
## What those observations indicated: by what conjectures they defined them.

[S]o they received from the mathematicians what was to be observed, but with a perverse intention. This was also an occasion for error among the ancients (if we believe **Aristotle**) while they judged natural things as if they were mathematical things. It remained after this to investigate what these signs, stars, motions, and aspects themselves signified or effected when they were found arranged in one way or another. Here they acted upon the lightest and most deceptive conjectures, which we shall recount. Regarding the signs, they first devised this: it was an undisputed fact to the Egyptians that all things consist of the four elements <note>Earth, Air, Fire, and Water.</note>. Since they had already accepted the twelve signs of the zodiac for the reasons we mentioned, a division seemed convenient to them: that these too should be distinguished by the four elements. By repeating these elements three times, the full number of signs is filled.

<margin>Where the trines come from.</margin>

<margin>Plato. Where aspects come from.</margin>
And since they believed that the first bodies were **fire** and **earth**—representing the circumference and the center—for fire was the highest body to them, and then **air** and **water** came in between as the middle elements (as **Plato** also shows in the *Timaeus*). Therefore, they established the first sign as fiery, the second as earthy, the third as airy, and the fourth as watery. Then, returning with a similar sequence, the fifth was fiery, the sixth earthy, and so on. From this it happened that those signs which were distant by a triangular interval <note>A 120-degree aspect, or trine.</note>—that is, with three signs in between—were judged to be of the same nature. Thus the fifth sign returned to the nature of the first. Those at a hexagonal distance <note>A 60-degree aspect, or sextile.</note> were partly related and partly discordant, but more related, since the first was fire and the third was air. But those at a square <note>A 90-degree aspect.</note> were utterly adverse, since fire and water are completely discordant. Thus arose the fiction that a triangular radiation was "good," the square was "bad," and the hexagonal was mostly neutral. Some, however, think the square is better, and that the opposition <note>A 180-degree aspect.</note> is also "bad," because stars so positioned look at each other from the opposite side. Some even want this middle quality for the signs, looking at the qualities in them as in others. For there are signs which agree in one quality but disagree in another. It is clear from this how these decrees gave birth to one another; and things which, when heard in isolation, leave a suspicion of some reason, immediately become contemptible once their origin is revealed. For if that first foundation is shaky and weak—namely, the number of twelve signs introduced by the whim of those calculating (as astrologers admit)—then everything built upon it is ruinous. Indeed, very many things sprout from that one root: for from there come the trines <note>original: trigona</note> which claim a large part of astrology for themselves. From these come the "lords of the trines" <note>term: triplicity rulers</note>—that is, the masters of the threefold sets—from whom the later Chaldeans received the rationale for the "bounds," the Egyptians the **individual degrees** <note>original: monomirias</note>, and the Arabs the theory of **great conjunctions**.

the greatest doctrines: **Ptolemy** <note>Claudius Ptolemy (c. 100–170 AD), the most influential astronomer and astrologer of antiquity.</note> and all others (though some in one way and some in another) gave the distribution of the parts of the world and its regions under the signs. They assigned this **trigon** <note>A group of three zodiac signs belonging to the same element.</note> to the east, that one to the west, another to the south, and another to the north. From this, predictions about the fate of the year greatly depend, so that we might know from which region an event will come. But let us return to the other properties of the signs: for we have sufficiently uncovered the mystery of their distinction into elements; having pulled back the veil, we found nothing but the **purest nonsense** there. They therefore devised other things from what the sun, sliding beneath the signs, performs within them. From this, they divided them into **fixed**, **movable**, and **common** [mutable]; others they named from the parts of the circle, as if they would be similar in nature not just in image, but in their very powers. Hence they called some **human signs** and others **brute** [animal signs]: because this sign, **Aquarius**, is figured as a youth himself, while that one is called **Aries** [the Ram]. Thus almost all the doctrines born concerning the signs come either from the work of the sun, or from the name of the images, or from the division by elements which <margin>have been refuted. Whence the nature</margin> he immediately judges to be a unity upon hearing.

<margin>of the planets</margin>
They judged the **nature of the planets** from their colors, as **Abu Ma'shar** <note>Latin: Aboasar; a famous 9th-century Persian astrologer and astronomer.</note> testifies that this is the conjecture of the "universal astrologers," and likewise for the **fixed stars**. For they said all reddish stars were of the nature of **Mars**, such as the Eye of the Bull [Aldebaran] or the Heart of the Scorpion [Antares]. But that these things are as irrational as they are false has already been sufficiently <margin>Whence the nature</margin> demonstrated. They introduced the **affinities of the planets with the signs** little by little: first, I believe, the <margin>of the fixed stars.</margin> **exaltations** <note>The specific degree in a sign where a planet is thought to have its maximum power.</note> were invented among the Chaldeans, regarding which we wrote in Book VIII, because <margin>Whence the affinity of planets and signs.</margin> stars placed in those degrees were furthest removed from the center of their orbits. The Egyptians added the **houses**, first accepting the conjecture regarding **Leo**, under which the power of the sun was seen to increase. Starting from that principle, <margin>Whence the exaltations.</margin> they distributed the remaining signs to the other planets according to the order of the spheres, as we have seen. We have already said what introduced the **trigons**. The division of the signs created **terms**, **decans**, **dodecatemoria**, **ninths**, and **monomoiria** <note>These are all technical subdivisions of the 30-degree zodiac signs into smaller segments, some as small as 1 degree (monomoiria).</note>. Since these seemed too vast to be granted to the power of only one planet while excluding others, they drew lines through them in various and manifold ways. They wanted these boundaries to belong to one star, and those to another. Because every different conjecture decided this differently, five different opinions about these "terms" or "boundaries" arose, over which they still **clash without end**. Some divided the signs into **decans** (that is, into three parts); others into nine; others into twelve. But all did so by their own whim, with no reason. For who could call it "reason" that any sign must be divided into twelve parts because there are twelve signs? Or into three parts for the sake of the perfection of the number three? Or into nine because a new sign agrees in quality with the first—for instance, **Sagittarius** with **Aries**, **Capricorn** with **Taurus**, and so on for the rest? Even **Ptolemy**, though an astrologer, laughed when he read these things. But those "divine" men—the Egyptians, Indians, and Chaldeans—embraced them as if they were the **first philosophy**.

<margin>Where the properties of the Places [Houses] come from.</margin>
Let us come to the **Places** [Houses] <note>The twelve divisions of the sky relative to the horizon at a specific moment.</note>, whose properties they defined by a certain similarity. For example, because the **Midheaven** is the highest point, they thought it signified things that are "sublime": impious kingdoms and powers—as if a man does not descend within himself rather than ascending. The **First House** [Ascendant] indicates one being born from the womb; the **Seventh House** indicates adversaries because it is directly opposite the first; the **Twelfth House** indicates prison and darkness, because when the sun arrives at that place, the vapors are stirred up but not yet dissolved, and the air, as it were, grows dark. But it is not necessary to pursue all the things we mentioned above; it is enough to recall to memory how the oracles of this "stellar and celestial discipline" came forth step by step. They are wonderfully connected to one another, with **fable everywhere extending a hand to fable**. Thus, when they decided that the **trine** [120 degrees] and **sextile** [60 degrees] intervals were good...

->## Book XII<-

they determined, and likewise for the good planets—Venus and Jupiter, as well as the Sun and the Moon—that since the good <term>rejoice</term> <note>In astrology, "joy" (Latin: gaudium) refers to a specific house where a planet’s influence is said to be strengthened or most comfortable.</note> in good things, they said **Jupiter** rejoices in the eleventh house and the **Sun** in the ninth, because one is in <term>sextile</term> <note>An aspect where two points are 60 degrees apart.</note> and the other in <term>trine</term> <note>An aspect where two points are 120 degrees apart.</note> to the <term>ascendant</term> <note>Latin: horoscopo; the point of the zodiac rising on the eastern horizon at the moment of birth.</note>. They placed the **Moon** in the third house and **Venus** in the fifth, because they are distant from the ascendant by similar intervals. They gave the better and more powerful locations—namely, those above the earth—to Jupiter and the Sun, while giving those below the earth to the weaker ones. By the same reasoning, they wanted **Mars** to rejoice in the sixth house and **Saturn** in the twelfth, since these are "bad" places just as those planets are "bad."

I do not doubt that many properties were then attributed to these places by them based on the nature of these planets. Thus, in the ninth house, they placed **prophecies**, which the Sun is believed to give. In the third, **short journeys**, just as the Moon completes her circuit in a shorter time than all other stars. In the twelfth, **sorrow**, according to the condition of Saturn, as well as **hidden enemies**. In the sixth, **slaves** and **diseases**, due to the nature of a harmful but effective and active planet. In the fifth, **joys, children, and pleasures** fell to Venus; they established her as the ruler of these things by no greater judgment than the brightness, radiance, and beauty of the star. From this comes that phrase: *the nurturing one, laughing nectar from above* <note>original: "alma superne nectareum ridens." Likely a poetic description of Venus as the goddess of grace and beauty.</note>. For the ancients, believing her the goddess of elegance and charms, used such demonstrations to weave a deceptive web, as if from a spider.

If you look at it from a distance, the false size of the threads and the lure of the novel texture might deceive you; if you look closely, you would despise it; if you touch it with your hand, you would break and dissolve it. Their descendants increased the invention; the figment was even more robust to the ancients because the fraud of its origin was more hidden, and—as always happens—authority was gained through age. Nor have we said everything; we have only demonstrated the method of invention—that is, the slippery path of error. Everything else was based on the same example of the flimsiest conjectures, leaning on a thin and most dissimilar <margin>Retrocession.</margin> similarity to earthly things.

Such are the ideas that planets are "lucky" when they move forward and "unlucky" when they move in **retrocession**, or even when they are believed to stand still. It is as if, when moving backward, they "deny" what they had promised; when moving forward, they "expedite" what they pledge; and when halting, they "delay" what they bestow. <margin>Eclipse of the luminaries</margin> They claim that an **eclipse of the Sun or Moon** produces great calamities. For these things terrify above all because the cause is unknown, as if the gods were either deserting or rejecting us. They say that a person being born when stars are at their <term>apogee</term> <note>The point in an orbit farthest from the Earth.</note> is exalted, because that place is the highest. Who introduced the "parts" of the Moon, then of other stars, and finally even of **oats and beans**? This error was explained in Book Eight.

But after they founded these dogmas on conjectures of this sort, they began to observe the <term>genitures</term> <note>Birth charts or the moment of birth.</note> of those being born. If once or twice by chance the dogmas seemed to correspond to the experience, there was no longer any doubt, and no greater authority existed. For instance, if by some chance someone born while **Mars** occupied **Scorpio** became famous in war, it was held as certain that Scorpio was the "home" of Mars—as if it were not a vastly different thing for Mars to be positioned thus, and for someone warlike to be born from Mars. As we have said, they could not faithfully test anything in the celestial motions while wandering so far from the truth. Therefore, they also noted whatever had happened to the subject of someone’s <term>theme</term> <note>A horoscope or astrological chart.</note> and established rules and canons from it. This was never a path of true experimentation, but rather chance and rashness serving as their "reason." I see that for others—and even for the same people observing at other times—things turned out differently. Thus it happened that almost as many types of astrology emerged as there were observers; hence that confusion and conflict of opinions which we followed at length in the previous book.

From these trifling conjectures, it grew through deceptive experiments; fostered...

->## Book XII<-

L ii

...by the vice of the age, and nourished by the curiosity of men, everyone is greedy to know their own future. They believe such things are most truly sought from the heavens; for how many among the common people—or even among the scholars—realize that these things are not rightly sought from the heavens? To this was added the enthusiasm of princes, who, through ignorance, believed everything, and through greed, hoped for everything. If ever happiness was pronounced to them from the sky (and it was *always* pronounced), they did not want astrology to be overturned any more than they wanted that happiness to be overturned. These astrologers predicted true things from time to time—sometimes by chance, sometimes by cunning, and sometimes with the help of a demon—using the methods we have already explained. For who would not occasionally succeed if they predict many things? Yet, despite the cheers and applause, a thousand lies were immediately buried in oblivion. 

Furthermore, much faith and authority were granted to them by oracles, which not only approved of that art but actively practiced it. For example, when **Apollo** was asked whether a male or female child would be born, he responded "female," because the Moon was moving toward Venus at the moment of conception. What greater testimony for a profession could there be than to have the gods as its authors?

<margin>
How demons approve of astrology.
In how many things astrology causes harm:
To Religion.
It patronizes vices.
To the good arts.
To Philosophy.
To Medicine.
To Prudence.
Astrology as a cover for other superstitions.
</margin>

Namely, the wicked demons—so named not only by our own writers but also by the **Platonists**—knew how much poison they were administering to the world under the guise of a single superstition. Once it had penetrated deep into the veins, it first took away faith from religion, which is the highest good of men. It did this by making everything depend on a fatal necessity from the heavens, as if there were no miracles and no divine foreknowledge of the future, but rather that everything occurred by the force of the constellations. 

Next, it provided a defense for vices, suggesting they descend into us from the heavens. It then infected the "good arts"—namely, **medicine** and **philosophy**. While it did not entirely overturn them (just as it did not overturn **theology**), it nonetheless contaminated them. It converted philosophy from true reasoning into fables, and medicine from natural and effective remedies into vain observations and the <term>dotage of old women</term> <note>Latin: "anilia deliramenta"; a common Renaissance phrase used to dismiss unscientific or superstitious folk beliefs.</note>. Thus, it became a single plague of perverse superstition, fatal to both body and soul at once. 

They saw **prudence** go to ruin, for now astrology was consulted for what should be done, at what time, and by what method; meanwhile, a most stupid vanity sat at the helm of life, holding the tiller in its hand. Finally, the demons hoped for what eventually happened: that this one art, by drawing authority from the heavens and from <term>mathematical calculations</term> <note>In this context, "mathematics" (mathematicis) specifically refers to the complex geometry and arithmetic used by astrologers to cast horoscopes.</note>, would provide a cover for the less-disguised fraud and the less-obvious weakness of other superstitions. They hoped that those other superstitions would not be thought vain if they appeared to be the followers, appendages, and foster-children of "celestial doctrine." For, as we showed in the first book, there is no superstition that does not acknowledge astrology as either its ally, its parent, or its leader. Is it not, therefore, a worthy cause for which the most harmful demons would themselves become astrologers? They would provide everything necessary so that this pestilential persuasion might daily take hold of human senses and interests. For who would doubt—even a follower of **Porphyry**—that demons used the rules of astrologers in their oracles for no other reason than to deceive, or rather to create a foundation of faith for their deception?

<margin>
Porphyry.
Where superstitious medicine originated.
</margin>

For **Porphyry** <note>Porphyry of Tyre (c. 234–305 AD), a Neoplatonic philosopher who, while interested in the supernatural, often expressed skepticism about the reliability of oracles.</note> himself says that the oracles lied whenever they gave responses based on astrological dogmas—which would not have happened if those dogmas were true. Since astrology claims to be the foreteller of the future, how could the demons, who are most skilled in natural things, not be hidden within it? Grown strong with these fuels and fortified by these protections, it deeply occupied the **Egyptians** and **Chaldeans**, and immediately gave birth to "superstitious medicine" among them. For some writer in Egypt recorded which <term>decan</term> <note>A "decan" is a subdivision of a zodiac sign, covering ten degrees. There are 36 decans in total, and in ancient "hermetic" medicine, each was thought to govern a specific part of the body or a specific disease.</note> caused which disease, and which decan’s power could cure it. This matter was held in secret and among the mysteries, as if this partition of the decans were not arbitrary—though we have demonstrated it is indeed arbitrary—and it was thoroughly mocked and neglected by...

# Book XII

...by **Ptolemy**. <margin>Magic: whence and what it is.</margin> From this point, magic immediately spread, which is nothing other than a combination of idolatry, astrology, and superstitious medicine. <margin>Books on the true faith against seven enemies</margin> These are superstitions which I have refuted individually in my books *On the True Faith Against the Seven Enemies* <note>Pico refers here to a lost or projected work of his, intended to defend Christianity against various opposing ideologies.</note>.

## Chapter VII. How Astrology passed from the Egyptians to others.

<margin>a</margin>
Astrology came to the Greeks from the Egyptians and Chaldeans, but through low-status authors. For it did not enter the **Lyceum** <note>The school of Aristotle</note> or the **Academy** <note>The school of Plato</note>, except for the houses of traveling charlatans. Nor did it enter the **Stoa** <note>The school of the Stoics</note>, although **Thales** <note>Often considered the first Greek philosopher</note> tried to admit it harmoniously. <margin>Epicurus. Ptolemy.</margin> Nor could **Epicurus**, who believed in atoms and the void, believe in astrology. **Ptolemy** was the first—one hundred and forty years after Christ—to cultivate it with a good reputation in literature, but more sparingly than the others. He seemed to want to set a limit on that madness rather than favor it. However, the authority of this one man—always a mathematician <term>mathematicus: in this period, the term often specifically referred to astrologers or those who cast horoscopes</term> and rarely a philosopher—has persisted against the opposing judgments of so many famous men in both mathematics and philosophy. The name of **Ptolemy** swept some Greeks into error who were otherwise inclined toward superstition, such as **Porphyry**, whose excessive effort in the worship of demons and superstitious care was condemned by both his teacher **Plotinus** and his disciple **Iamblichus** <note>These three were the primary figures of Neoplatonism; Pico emphasizes their internal disagreements over the occult</note>. From the Greeks, it passed to the Arabs with even greater authority, as they marveled at whatever they found written by the Greeks and looked up to that empty hope of antiquity in the names of the Egyptians and Chaldeans. However, just as the most prudent of astrologers, **Ptolemy**, purified it of the barbarians' influence and trimmed it as much as he could, <margin>Ptolemy. Abu Ma'shar.</margin> a certain grammarian and historian named **Abu Ma'shar** <note>original: "Aboasar," an influential 9th-century Persian astrologer</note> took it from the Greeks and filled it with countless trifles and fables. He made astrology nearly as much worse than **Ptolemy's** astrology as astrology itself is worse than the good arts. <margin>Note.</margin> He was a man made for empty loquacity, almost entirely ignorant not only of philosophy but also of astronomy, and was mocked by every learned astrologer. Yet he was popular with the masses, among whom he who says the most is great, rather than he who says the best. During those times, the study of mathematics—and indeed of all philosophy and disciplines—grew in Spain. <margin>Alfonso</margin> While **Alfonso** <note>King Alfonso X of Castile (r. 1252–1284), who sponsored the "Alfonsine Tables" of planetary movements</note> reigned there, he was most diligent in mathematical numbers and the calculation of celestial movements. He also loved that divining vanity, though he was otherwise uninitiated in the studies of philosophy. For his sake, many monuments of that art from the Arabs and Greeks reached us, primarily through **John of Seville** and **Michael Scot**, a writer of no weight and much superstition. <margin>Albert.</margin> **Albert** <note>Albertus Magnus (c. 1200–1280), a titan of medieval theology and science</note> first embraced these things because they were new; for he was born in those times. I believe he approved of them as a young man rather than as an old one, just as he published magical things as a youth but detested them in his mature age, living a most holy and blameless life in the monastery. Nevertheless, as time went on, through the long duration of tradition, the multitude of writers, and a certain affinity between mathematical astronomy and names as well as subject matter, it almost came into dispute: was it a science without deception or a superstition? <margin>Note.</margin> Truly, although it has been accepted by the masses for so many centuries (whose nature is to know nothing), and cultivated by the superstitious (whose knowledge is madness), and sought by the curious with no judgment, it has always been—as we showed in the first book—mocked, refuted, and overthrown by the prudent, by philosophers, and by most holy men.

<summary>Pico traces the historical transmission of astrology from Egypt to Greece and eventually to the Arab world and Medieval Europe, arguing that while it gained popularity through figures like Abu Ma'shar and King Alfonso X, it was consistently rejected by the greatest philosophers.</summary>
<keywords>Ptolemy, Abu Ma'shar, King Alfonso X, Albertus Magnus, Porphyry, Neoplatonism, history of astrology, Arabic science, John of Seville, Michael Scot</keywords>

<meta>This page concludes the twelfth and final book of Pico della Mirandola's massive critique of astrology. It summarizes the historical opposition to astrology across different civilizations—Hebrew, Greek, Roman, Arabic, and Scholastic—before ending with the printer's colophon.</meta>

# Book XII

For at the time when [astrology] was growing strong alongside the worship of idols in Egypt and Chaldea, and with the madness of all vanities, among the Hebrews—the worshippers of the true God—it was condemned by the voice and writings of **Moses**, **Isaiah**, **Jeremiah**, and other prophets. When it came to Greece, it did not please **Pythagoras**, according to the testimony of Diogenes <note>Diogenes Laertius, author of "Lives and Opinions of Eminent Philosophers."</note> and Theodoret. The **Platonists** and **Peripatetics** <note>Followers of Aristotle</note> did not even think it worthy of being spoken about, regarding it as one of those itinerant charlatan arts. **Eudoxus of Cnidus**, a most wise legislator (for he wrote laws for his citizens) and a great philosopher under Plato—indeed, by the consensus of all, the prince of mathematics in his age—affirmed that astrologers should in no way be believed, and left this in writing. Cassander and Archelaus, distinguished mathematicians <term>mathematici: while this can mean "astrologers," here Pico uses it for true astronomers to show that even experts in the stars rejected divination</term>, did the same some years later; as did **Panaetius** and **Carneades**, serious and true philosophers. Whenever those diviners came to Rome, whether from Egypt or Babylon, the famous Roman foresight removed them from the city with the strictest laws. Thus under **Tiberius**, **Vitellius**, **Diocletian**, **Constantine**, **Gratian**, **Valentinian**, and **Theodosius**, they were forced either to abandon their profession or suffer the penalties of that profession. Why **Hadrian** was delighted by their tricks is clear enough: for by a certain natural inclination he loved Egypt so much that nothing Egyptian could fail to please him. Yet at that same time, **Favorinus** aptly and **Plutarch** indirectly—both men of the gravest judgment—criticized them. Soon after, although under **Ptolemy** it seemed somewhat honored, it was immediately brought into disrepute by the judgments of **Plotinus** the great Platonist, **Alexander of Aphrodisias** the distinguished Peripatetic, and **Origen**, most eminent in all branches of learning. When it came to the Arabs, it occupied <note>original: "detinuit," implying it held their attention or trapped them</note> **Abenzageles** and **Aboafares** <note>These refer to Arabic-language authors, likely including Abu Ma'shar, whom Pico views as inferior thinkers.</note>, who were neither men of logic nor philosophers. But it did not occupy **Averroes** or **Avicenna**. Where indeed it first appeared in the University of Paris, it was with difficulty that the curious were prevented from consigning it to destruction under the flames. When some years later **Roger Bacon** and certain others tried to make it respectable, most learned men resisted them: **William of Auvergne**, Bishop of Paris, and after him **Nicole Oresme**, an excellent mathematician, and **Henry of Hesse**, and **Jean Caton**, and **Brenlanlius** the Briton <note>Likely referring to the English scholar John Bredon.</note>. They detested astrology not only in the part where it harms religion, but in its entirety, as something vain and false. Therefore, it never so obtained the status of a legitimate art that it became an established rule. For there was always some champion of truth to speak against it. **The End.**

---

->Benedictus Hectoris of Bologna diligently printed these **Disputations** of **Giovanni Pico della Mirandola**,<-
->Count of Concordia and prince of letters, against the astrologers, applying<-
->his full effort so that it would not deviate from the original manuscript.<-
->At Bologna, in the year of salvation 1495, on the 16th day of July.<-

# Corrections for the Book Against Astrology

We have noted these errors so that the book might go forth more correctly. If you, the reader, encounter passages that have not been corrected, know that they either seemed too minor to us to be beyond the ability of a semi-learned person to fix, or too laborious for us to wipe away in a short time. Certain things were also omitted that were not necessary for a true understanding of the matter. Nevertheless, since the commentaries on foreign languages <note>original: "linguarū peregrinarū," referring to the Greek and Hebrew sources Pico cited</note> suitable for this work were not at hand while the book was being corrected, you may, if you wish, fill in the gaps for a more polished version of the book by consulting those commentaries.

### Ludovico Maria Sforza, Duke of Milan, etc., Count of Pavia and Angera, and Lord of Genoa and Cremona:

We consider it appropriate that those who seek to be of use to all others through their own labor and expense should themselves also feel that their purpose pleases great princes, and that they be willingly assisted where there is a need. Therefore, since Benedictus, a bookseller of Bologna, has indicated that he has printed the collected works of Count Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, and has furthermore petitioned us—since there will be no lack of those who, either attracted by the hope of profit or by a desire to harm him, might perhaps hereafter print these same works elsewhere—that we might wish to provide that neither others in our dominion be allowed to print them, nor those printed elsewhere be sold except for his own.

We have decided that his petition ought to be granted. We therefore command and decree that no one hereafter shall be permitted, for the next two years, to print the aforementioned works of Count Giovanni Pico in our dominion, or to bring those printed elsewhere into our jurisdiction, except those which the said Benedictus has printed. But if anyone should dare not to obey this our will, let him know that, besides the loss of all such books, he will also incur heavy penalties. Given at Como under the witness of our seal, on the 7th day of July, 1496.

-> B. CHALCUS <note>Bartolomeo Calco, Secretary to the Duke of Milan</note> <-

**Ludovico Maria Sforza, called Anglus** <note>a title used by the Sforza family to claim descent from the mythical hero Anglus</note>**, Duke of Milan, etc., Count of Pavia and Angera, and Lord of Genoa and Cremona: We consider it fitting that those who seek to be of use to all others through their own labor and expense should themselves also feel that their purpose is pleasing to great princes, and that where there is a need, they may be willingly assisted. Therefore, since Benedictus, a bookseller of Bologna, has indicated that he has printed the collected works of Count Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, and has furthermore petitioned us—since there will be no lack of those who, either lured by the hope of profit or by a desire to harm him, might perhaps print these same works elsewhere—that we might wish to provide that neither others be allowed to print them in our domain, nor those printed elsewhere be sold except for his own: we have decided that his petition must be granted. We therefore mandate and proclaim that no one hereafter is permitted, for the next two years, to print the aforementioned works of Count Giovanni Pico in our domain, or to bring into our jurisdiction those printed elsewhere, except for those which Benedictus himself has printed. If anyone should dare not to obey this our will, let him know that, besides the loss of all such books, he will also incur heavy penalties. Given at Como, under the faith of our seal, on the 7th day of July, 1496.**

->B. CHALCVS<-
<note>Bartolomeo Calco, the influential Secretary of State for the Duchy of Milan.</note>

<meta>This page continues the legal deliberations of Thomas Fastoli, a 14th-century auditor of the Roman Rota, regarding ecclesiastical appointments and the complexities of papal "graces" or favors.</meta>

# Thomas Fastoli.

...by whose power a person called to a dignity was provided for <note>An ecclesiastical "dignity" refers to a high office such as a deanery or archdeaconry.</note>, if a revocation of graces <note>A "revocation of graces" was a papal decree cancelling previously granted favors or appointments.</note> occurs, is it said to be withdrawn regarding a prebend <note>A "prebend" is the portion of the church's revenues granted to a canon as a stipend.</note> that becomes vacant later?

### QUESTION 44.

<margin>1</margin>
**AND** first, it was doubted regarding this: does the revocation extend to this prebend? And it was said by Lord Aegidius <note>Likely Aegidius Bellamera, a prominent canon lawyer.</note> that it would not be extended, arguing from the chapter *si cui* in the section *non sic autem* under the title "On Prebends" in the Extra <note>The *Liber Extra*, a primary collection of Canon Law.</note>, where the case seems to involve the revocation of a benefice. However, some, such as Lord Durandus, wished to distinguish whether the prebend was annexed to the dignity or not. In the first case, the revocation would not take place; in the second, it would. This follows what is held in the title "On Prebends" in the chapters *quia sæpe* and *super eo*. Supporting this distinction is the first response in the said chapter *si is cui*, where in the matter of the Bonifacian reservation <note>Legal rules established by Pope Boniface VIII regarding the reservation of benefices for papal appointment.</note>, a distinction is made between annexed and non-annexed prebends. There it says, "to one not annexed," etc. And thus it seems that the same distinction should be observed in the second response. But for that reason, he seems to touch upon the non-annexed dignity/prebend there because if it were annexed, it could not become vacant before the vacancy of the dignity. And for the same reason, the second response must be understood as referring to a non-annexed one, so that even if it is not annexed to the dignity, the reservation does not take place. According to this, the aforementioned distinction does not apply in this case. Hence, the majority adhered to the opinion of Aegidius.

---

### SUMMARY.

<margin>1</margin> The clause "to be preferred" <note>original: *anteferri*</note> is a departure from common law: and therefore it should not be extended beyond its specific terms.

Does the phrase "and of prebends of those resigning or dying," etc., extend to prebends and stipends becoming vacant through the deprivation <note>Removal from office as a punishment.</note> of a canon?

<margin>2</margin> Civil death is not equated to natural death, except in cases expressly stated by law.
<margin>3</margin> Words must be reduced to that sense which the words would generate for those who understand them correctly.
<margin>4</margin> In case of doubt, interpretation must be made according to what commonly happens.
<margin>5</margin> A canon ought not to be without a prebend.
<margin>6</margin> What is customarily done is seen to be silently included in a disposition or agreement.
<margin>7</margin> A repetitive word repeats the modes and qualities.
<margin>8</margin> A monosyllable repeats modes and qualities.

---

### QUESTION 45.

<margin>1</margin>
**S**econdly, therefore, assuming that the revocation does not take place: it was doubted whether the "poor cleric" <note>A *pauper* in this context is a cleric who has received a papal mandate to be provided with a benefice due to his poverty.</note> ought to be preferred to the Joanninus <note>Likely a person holding a provision from Pope John XXII.</note>? And the majority said yes, because of the clause "to be preferred to all who are waiting by the authority of anyone" <note>original: *anteferri omnibus qui alicuius authoritate expectant*</note>, and thus those who wait for a prebend by the authority of John. But Lord Aegidius held that he should not be preferred, because that clause "to be preferred," with the "notwithstanding" clause joined to it, refers only to those who are waiting in total; but not to those waiting to whom a canonry has been conferred by the Pope. For if the Pope had wished this, he would have made mention of it, as is said in the decree *ad audientiam* under "On Tithes," and "On the Transfer of Bishops" in the chapter *inter corporalia* near the end, and in the Code under "On the Abolishing of Escheats" in the law *ista* in the section *sin autem ad deficientis*. This is also supported by the section *verum* in the chapter *si clericus* on prebends in the Sixth Book <note>The *Liber Sextus*, a collection of Canon Law promulgated by Boniface VIII.</note>. Franciscus de Amely adhered to this via the aforementioned laws, and because the clause "to be preferred" seems to depart from common law; thus it should not be extended beyond its limits, as in "On Rules of Law" in the Sixth Book, chapter *quæ à iure*, and "On the Sons of Priests," chapter *ad hæc*, and in the Digest under "On Rules of Law," the law *quædam contra*, and "On Constitutions," the first law near the end. This is further supported by the notes of the Archdeacon <note>Guido de Baysio, a famous canonist known as "The Archdeacon."</note> on the chapter *cui de non* under the word "to be provided."

---

### SUMMARIES.

A grace granted concerning a canonry with reservation of a prebend.

### CASE 46.

### QUESTION 47.

<margin>a</margin>
**O**n the second Wednesday, the 18th of the same month, such a doubt was proposed by B. de Non. A certain person
<margin>1</margin>
had obtained a grace under this form in effect: for the Pope had spoken thus: "We confer upon you a canonry of such a church; the prebend, however, and the stipends and the stipendiary portions of those resigning or dying, if any are currently vacant, we confer upon you in the same way; otherwise, we reserve them for you to be conferred when they become vacant." Later, it happened that a certain prebend, stipend, and stipendiary portion became vacant through the deprivation of one individual. From these terms, an arduous question resulted: does a prebend becoming vacant in this way fall under the aforementioned grace? And the majority held that it does not, because it seemed provided for only in those specific ways; consequently, the grace is not to be extended to those cases of which no mention was made. Therefore, it does not extend to the case of deprivation, especially since the grace is "ambitious" <note>In legal terms, "ambitious" graces are those sought by the petitioner and are interpreted strictly.</note>, as argued in the chapter *quamuis* and *is cui* and *non potest* on prebends, and chapters 1 and 2 on "The Sons of Priests" in the Sixth Book. This was also argued from the Digest "On the Dissolution of Marriage" in the law *si cum dotem* at the beginning, and "On Verbal Obligations" in the section *insula*. Further supporting this is the Digest "On Children and Posthumous Heirs," the law *commoddissimè*, in the response and similar passages. Likewise, the reason was brought forward that Johannes <note>Johannes Andreae, a preeminent canonist.</note> noted in the Decretals, namely that
<margin>2</margin>
civil death is equated to natural death only in those cases where it is cautioned in the law, as noted in Question 16, Causa 1, chapter *placuit* in the last gloss; and the same is noted by Johannes Andreae on the chapter *susceptum* in the gloss there. Therefore, as it is not found expressed in the law in this case that the case of deprivation is equated to death, we ought not to equate them. The Digest "On the Dissolution of Marriage," the law *si vero*, the section *de uiro*, and "On Public Lands," the law *de pretio*, with similar ones, were cited. Against the aforementioned reasoning and opinion, many laws stand, as is clear in the Digest "On Partnership," the law *actorem* in the section *publicanone*, and "On the Granting of Goods," and "Against the Tablets," the first law at the end, and "On the Property of Freedmen," the sections *si cesse* and *si deportatus*, and in the law *ad Trebellianum*, the first law, in the first and second responses, and "On Donations between Husband and Wife," the law *sed si mors*, in the second response, and in the Digest "On Provisions and Substitutions" under the condition...
